## May the LORD be our Light and our Salvation!

That believers should be especially concerned with the contemplation of Holy Scripture in the latter days <note>The "latter days" or "end times" was a central focus for the Berleburg circle, who believed they were living in the final period of history before Christ’s return.</note> is revealed to us by the prophecy concerning the same, which we find in the Prophet Zechariah, Chapter 14:7: *that at evening time it shall be light.* For it is evident that this "evening time" signifies the final days, because it shall precede the time when the LORD will be King over all the earth; at which time the LORD will be the only one, and His Name the only one: verse 9. Then Christ shall reign over the entire earth, and all shall be rightly united in the unity of faith and true worship; so that then the One, Holy, and Universal Christian Church shall truly appear, where no more divisions or religious disputes shall be found. But if there is to be light before this glorious time, it is clearly understood thereby that God wills to let more light rise in the hearts of believers. From which it will also follow, according to the prophecy of Daniel, that in the latter days many shall go over the writings of the Prophets as well as the whole of Holy Scripture in general, and knowledge shall become great. Chapter 12:4.

To that end, it is the duty of believers to read Holy Scripture diligently and to search within it for the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, and thus to strive most eagerly to attain the knowledge of God’s will and what He has wished to reveal to us in it for His glorification. And this can consist, among other things, of these three parts:

First, because the Holy Scripture was written in the first language, which was first brought forth by Adam at the divine command while he still possessed divine wisdom—namely, the Hebrew language, in which the Old Testament, as the foundation of all mysteries, is written; to which the New Testament was later added, written in the Greek language which was very common at that time. Therefore, it is necessary that those who have attained the gift of these languages, and especially the first one (since it has now become the most difficult for us), should diligently read this original text <term>Grund-Text; literally "ground-text," referring to the Hebrew and Greek source manuscripts rather than later translations</term> according to the measure of their understanding, and then strive, while calling upon the assistance of the Holy Spirit, to translate it into our mother tongue. In doing so, one should provide it in the simplest possible way according to the letter, exactly as it is written—since a particular emphasis and mystery is sometimes hidden within it—while also being concerned with clarity, so that we simultaneously use our own ways of speaking with which we are accustomed to expressing such things, so that everyone may understand it all the better. In this, one must also carefully observe the Hebrew accentuation or punctuation marks which, as some believe (not without reason), were inspired by the Holy Spirit and point toward the true understanding of the Scripture. <note>The Berleburg editors believed that the Hebrew vowel points and accents were not just grammatical aids but divinely inspired guides to the mystical meaning of the text.</note>

This we have endeavored to do here to the best of our ability, and we ask everyone who perceives a better way to remind us of it in love for the edification of their neighbor and for the glory of God; but also to believe that we do not wish, by this work, to set aside the right, true, and best primary text <note>original: "Grund-Text des Geistes." The editors distinguish between the "external" text on the page and the "internal" text written by the Spirit in the heart of the believer.</note> of the Spirit, which everyone can find living in their heart.

Secondly, believers must apply themselves to the gift of prophecy or the interpretation of Holy Scripture, to which God Himself exhorts us: *Strive for spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.* 1 Corinthians 14:1. Therefore, it has always been customary in the Church of Christ to publish the Holy Scripture with explanations and notes. This is necessary so that through such helpful means, the weak may be assisted in further reflection and in attaining an understanding of the Holy Scripture while calling upon the grace of God—which is always required for this—so that He may open our eyes that we might see the wonders in His...

This interpretation, however, is of two kinds. Namely, that one may first of all grasp the literal understanding. In this, there is no better or more certain means to arrive at such than to seek to explain the Scripture through the Scripture: for one finds / that what is said obscurely in one place / is explained more clearly in another. Wherein a special wisdom of the Spirit of **GOD** is to be noted / who wished to reveal Himself in various ways / so that where He has produced a riddle and obscure saying in one place / He has presented it elsewhere in clearer words and at greater length. To this end, the use of concordances is also very useful / as one can arrive at a greater understanding of the Scripture by comparing the passages that must be looked up. That, however, in the first part of this Bible, the Law, both the opinions of the Jews regarding the customs of the Ceremonial Law <note>The "Ceremonial Law" refers to the ritual and sacrificial requirements of the Old Testament, which Christians traditionally view as fulfilled by Christ.</note>, and also those of other teachers, both ancient and modern, have been added here and there; this was done partly according to the usual custom, in order to satisfy the desires of some.

Following this / we seek to apply the Holy Scripture for the general benefit / for which the Holy Spirit intends it to be used / as all Scripture given by inspiration of **GOD** is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness, that a man of **GOD** may be perfect, thoroughly equipped for every good work. 2 Tim. 3:16-17. Therefore it is necessary / that one add the teachings of truth / as one perceives them through the grace of **GOD** / and also the reproof of the corrupt morals of Christendom / in the places where the Holy Spirit gives occasion / in the fear of **GOD** / to see if it might still strike a chord for the improvement and instruction in righteousness in many a soul: but then also / whether the truths / which **GOD's** Spirit has allowed to rise in so many souls who fear the **LORD** and long for His light / might also find entry among others / to perceive the door opened in our Philadelphian congregation <note>The "Philadelphian congregation" refers to a movement of radical Pietists who emphasized brotherly love and an internal, spiritual church over formal denominations.</note> / and thereby to look into many mysteries / which may present the ways of **GOD** ever more clearly to the glorification of His name.

Thirdly, it is to be requested of **GOD** / that we may also perceive and recognize the secret and spiritual sense of Holy Scripture / which is, so to speak, the spirit and the life of the Scripture; of which Christ also speaks: You search the Scriptures; for you think you have eternal life in them: and it is they which testify of me. But you will not come to me, that you may have life. John 5:39-40. This life, then, is also the spirit in the Scripture / and is not found in our spirit / unless it stands in the fellowship of Christ. For he who is joined to the **LORD** is one spirit with Him. 1 Cor. 6:17.

Here, however, among others, two kinds of gifts especially reveal themselves. First, that one begins to see the spiritual meaning of the histories and laws and prophecies / that occur in **GOD's** word / how therein lie hidden either the mysteries of the ways of **GOD** in regard to our salvation. As for example, where the Apostle testifies of the two wives of Abraham / the bondwoman and the free / of whom the former was born first / and the latter afterwards / that these words signify something; for these are the two testaments: one from Mount Sinai / which bears children for bondage / which is Hagar <note>original: "Agar"</note> etc. and the Jerusalem which is above is the free woman / who is the mother of us all. Gal. 4:22 etc. So also where the duties of love lie hidden in the laws: as the Apostle cites the law / that one shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain; which he interprets at length as the provision for the ministers of the Gospel: 1 Cor. 9:9 etc. And likewise the prophecies: where one must see in the light of the Spirit of Christ / what the prophets have spoken not only of the first coming of Christ into the flesh / and therein of His sufferings and resurrection and the establishment of His kingdom among the Heathen; but also what they prophesy of His future appearance for judgment / whereby His glorious kingdom here below on earth shall also be revealed: 2 Tim. 4:1. Which testimony of the Spirit of **JESUS** in His faithful witnesses is the spirit of prophecy. Rev. 19:10.

<meta>This page continues the preface to the Berleburg Bible, specifically defending the mystical commentaries of Madame de Guyon (the "French female person") and explaining the multi-layered nature of Biblical interpretation—literal, spiritual, and prophetic.</meta>

<image-desc>Three decorative floral or fleur-de-lis ornaments arranged in a horizontal row at the top of the page.</image-desc>

The aforementioned French female person <note>original: "Frantzösische Weibs-Person"; referring to the mystic Madame de Guyon mentioned on the previous page.</note> very humbly excuses herself in both prefaces to the Old and New Testaments regarding any errors, should they have been committed. And in this matter, the gentleness of believers toward one another must truly be made known: that what does not immediately reveal itself to our hearts—even if a secret meaning were hidden there—we should rather leave unjudged. Instead, we should recognize our own ignorance, for much remains hidden from us, especially since such inner paths are known to very few, and least of all to the wise and clever of this world. For because they do not wish to come to Christ with genuine humility in their searching of the Scriptures, they also do not attain life or the inner, secret sense of the Spirit. At most, they might grasp something of the spiritual in a **moral sense**, insofar as reason may draw lessons from Scripture aimed at life and conduct; however, as is well known, they prefer to dwell mostly in the **literal sense**. This literal sense is indeed good in itself, but it also easily gives rise to all sorts of differing opinions and interpretations, and thus to all manner of strife, unnecessary questions, and inquisitive knowledge. Poor human beings, who do not possess the spirit of faith, are so fallen that they speak of tangible, physical, and visible bodies as if they were a real and essential matter, while they imagine invisible spiritual things to be merely a figurative concept. Yet, in truth, invisible spiritual things are far more essential to **GOD** than physical, precious things can ever be. So it often goes with the interpretation of Scripture by those who wish to be masters of the Scripture: but they thereby reveal that they speak from their own self.

Furthermore, one well knows how to be modest in acknowledging that the Holy Scripture does not have a double or triple sense, but actually only one sense. This is what these people claim just as strongly—and often with great zeal, though not according to knowledge. However, it is believed that just as Wisdom is one and yet manifold <note>Wisdom of Solomon 7:22</note>, so too does the Holy Scripture—as an outflow from Wisdom and a great prophetic word—speak many things at once and with a single word. These things, in their entire summary, remain one sense, yet in various openings. Everything good that an enlightened person may draw and bring forth from the Scripture is actually intended by the Holy Spirit Himself. For from where else should a person have it, if not from this source? Is not all good from above? And if a person can find more than one thing in one place, why should **GOD** not be able or willing to place more than one thing there? The Jews recognized this well, saying in former times: there was not a single letter in the Scripture upon which entire mountains of knowledge did not hang. **GOD** often speaks something in which the literal, the spiritual, and also the prophetic understanding are all expressed together at once. Because of this, they are not three contradictory meanings, nor a double or triple understanding; rather, one always includes the other, and all together remain only one divine understanding. This is recognized as divine precisely because it knows how to express many things at once. And how should He not be able to do this, since **GOD** is equally near to all times and sees what will happen in each? He then knows how to summarize everything in one utterance in such a way that every age finds its measure of fulfillment therein, until finally everything is fulfilled, and the spoken Word of **God** is recognized in its entire greatness, breadth, height, and depth. And whoever spiritually fulfills and allows the recognized letter to be fulfilled within themselves will also easily and soon be able to look into the prophetic sense, as it shall be fulfilled in the fullness of time in the whole body of the perfect man. If, for example, the letter says one should flee from **Babylon** <note>original: "Babel"</note>: and the person, in obedience, goes out from Babylon and has no fellowship with the works of Babylon, then they will also understand the proclamation of the last times—how **GOD** will one day lead His entire Church out of Babylon and bring them to Zion. Just as in the creeds one represents **GOD** Himself as three persons, who yet in another way and in essence are not three but one: even so, three things are often expressed by **GOD** in one saying, of which He has made one the image of the other, and yet they are not three but one sense; just as a human being, although consisting of body, soul, and spirit, is not three humans, but is and remains only one human.

Finally, in all explanations of the Holy Scripture, by whatever name they may be called, the glorious exhortation of the Apostle must be applied to all believers for their admonition and warning—and it is indeed applied for the sake of fairness: *Do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies: Test all things, and hold fast to that which is good.* 1 Thessalonians 5:19, 20, 21. These very precious truths are especially necessary in this last evening-time, given the rising light and the opened door of mysteries: that one should, on the one hand, surrender oneself to the light that **GOD** wishes to let shine in the hearts of various dear...

<meta>This page continues the preface of the Berleburg Bible. The previous page discussed the tendency of "worldly-wise" scholars to focus only on the literal sense of Scripture, while ignoring the deeper spiritual meanings. It concluded by suggesting that God reveals these deeper truths through specific individuals.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece featuring three symmetrical floral or foliate ornaments arranged horizontally.</image-desc>

...precious souls, through whom God wishes to bring knowledge to other souls, and one should not resist; but afterward, one should also ask God for the testing of the same, that He might work and cause the same to arise in our hearts, so that it might then be said as it was there with the Samaritans: **John 4:42.** "We no longer believe because of this or that witness’s speech, but we are now ourselves convinced, and believe that these are precious truths which God has unlocked in the souls."

One has then surrendered to this spiritual impulse, according to the wonderful providence of the Lord, in this great work, in which one has also noticeably felt His gracious help and assistance up to this point.

Just as was made known at the very beginning—even before setting to work, where others were also invited to contribute—how one intended to proceed and that one gladly wished to let others speak: so too much of this work consists, as it were, of extracts taken from others, without any desire to claim their work for oneself. Just as one might request <term>collectors</term> <note>original: "Collectores"; here meaning those who gather financial contributions or materials.</note> to help cover the publishing costs for an undertaking that is partly harmless in itself and partly aimed at deeper research into Holy Scripture, so too, in gathering materials for the annotations from many writings that not everyone can acquire for themselves, we have acted for the most part as humble <term>collectors</term>. Therefore, one could all the less allow oneself to lust after vain glory in this.

Regarding the arrangement, one has seen to it as much as possible in most places that every verse might receive something; at the very least, a parallel passage that points elsewhere. But where no verse numbers are attached to the annotations across entire columns, it signifies that such notes apply to the text standing above them in general and are mingled with it. And since the topmost annotation right after the text often applies to the entire text, but sometimes also to the nearest or lowest verse in the text—at times even to the topmost alone, or even depends on the annotation of the preceding column—it is for that reason often, indeed mostly, found without a designated verse, and such is left to the judgment of the reader to distinguish.

Just as one has now, as mentioned, brought in the insights of others not sparingly, yet has also not failed to contribute one’s own toward the explanation—according to the gift of prophecy given to each according to the various workings of God's grace: so one believes that such a work will also be useful for all <term>estates</term> <note>A reference to the "Three Estates" or social classes of the time: the clergy, the nobility, and the commoners.</note> to use. Yet one does not present it as anything perfect. Those working on it know well how to be modest, acknowledging that much—and indeed the most part—of divine things is still hidden from them. Likewise, much has had to remain behind, partly for lack of space, and partly because people cannot bear it; what they cannot immediately grasp, they <term>treat</term> <note>original: "tractiren"</note> with hateful opposition and bitter zeal as a stumbling block and offense, even blasphemy. And since one gladly confesses to have taken the most part from other learned and spiritually rich <term>theologians</term> <note>original: "Theologis"</note> of all kinds of names and religions, and has sought only to extract the kernel of everything as far as strength allowed: so too—even if one did not always find it necessary to include the <term>authors</term> <note>original: "Autores"</note>, as has nevertheless often happened, since one did not always stay exactly with their words everywhere—there will be even less room for <term>literary plagiarism</term> <note>original: "Plagium literarium"; the theft of another's writing.</note> or intellectual theft. This is because one seeks no glory for oneself nor to claim anything, but can let it be that the sensible and truth-loving reader views it as nothing but collections from others. By this, at least, the service would have been rendered to many that what is otherwise scattered here and there in many writings—which, moreover, very few can or wish to acquire—is to be found here together. And if the reader can find even some edification from it, that will suffice the workers above all else.

For this very reason, one requests all the more a kind and modest judgment and expects the same from the fairness of all Christian readers, especially regarding certain matters that have flowed in here and there, which cannot be immediately accepted or grasped by everyone. Since one nevertheless felt obligated—as is customary in such large biblical works—to occasionally cite various views, and indeed not only common opinions but also what some enlightened souls (be they man or woman, as they are all one in Christ Jesus, **Galatians 3:28**, whom the Lord has always used in a special way; just as the resurrection of Christ was first made known to Mary, to show men that the Lord is not bound to them in the revelation of His secrets) have brought forth particularly in our days. In doing so, one did not necessarily intend to make oneself a party to those views, but only wished to let many speak of what they have received from God...

...revealed (a) <margin>Philippians 3:15, 16</margin> or unlocked, either through themselves or as witnessed by others. For God in our times has graced several of the female sex with great light and godliness, as well as the gifts to bring such things to light in writings; among whom the English <insert>Jane</insert> Leade, the French maiden <insert>Antoinette</insert> Bourignon, and the late Mrs. Dr. <insert>Johanna Eleonora</insert> Petersen—and from the latter, specifically her learned *Guidance to the Thorough Understanding of the Holy Revelation of Jesus Christ, given to John*—are very famous. One therefore had all the less hesitation in incorporating the explanations of the aforementioned Madame de Guyon—which are as famous as they are spiritual—into this work above others for the most part, since such edifying writings were translated and communicated through the providence of God by a person of high rank <note>likely referring to Count Casimir of Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg or a member of his circle</note>, who is also moved to support this work with their generosity, for which God's rich blessing must inevitably flow back to them. We believe we are doing the public a double service through this: many who do not understand French, yet find a taste for that style of writing, will thus receive Madame de Guyon's Biblical works in translation at the same time. Furthermore, we believe we have used no more liberty in occasionally citing other such persons than such works require and bring with them; for it is nothing unusual among commentators to introduce such things that they might not necessarily want to take full credit for themselves. As for citing where this or that was taken from, it often happened by chance that where the subject matter took up all the space and no time remained at the bottom for citations, they were removed.

The purpose, moreover, is in no way to introduce new doctrines, but rather to everywhere praise the old and new commandment of love <note>A reference to 1 John 2:7–8, emphasizing the continuity of the Gospel</note>, from which we ourselves would like to profit and be treated accordingly. Just as everything that might have been put forward that is not in accordance with the Word, Will, and Honor of God is hereby most solemnly revoked.

And so we now surrender this work to the examination of the faithful, the God-fearing, and those souls longing from the heart for His promised rising light in this evening-time <note>A common Pietist term for the period before the expected return of Christ</note>. Whatever they find within for their edification, let us all praise and glorify God and the Spirit of Jesus Christ for it. But whatever might have flowed in from their prejudices or ours, let us bear with one another in patience until the Day shall make it manifest that it was indeed so, which will also bring the secrets of the heart to light. And if anyone has built upon this foundation of Jesus Christ and His infallible divine Word in the Holy Scripture—whether gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or stubble—each one's work will become manifest; the Day will make it clear, etc. etc. <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 3:11–15 regarding the testing of a believer's work</note>. Until then, those who are set to such work must act in the fear of God to be faithful therein, and keep a close watch on their hearts so that they do not fail knowingly in this, lest they suffer loss, but rather be deemed worthy to receive the <term>reward of grace</term> <note>original: "Gnaden-Lohn"; a theological term for a reward given by God's favor rather than human merit</note> from the Lord. But those who read it must also let love hold the upper hand in their judgment, in which alone one can recognize the good that God's goodness wishes to bestow in such work undertaken for His glory; which the Lord then wishes to bless in all of us for the glorification of His name:

->Amen!<-

Berlenburg, January 19,

# Introductory Report.

Just as Moses—the "Chancellor of God," <note>original: "Canzler GOttes"</note> as Lansius (a) <note>Thomas Lansius (1577–1657) was a prominent German legal scholar and professor.</note> calls him—was an Egyptian by his homeland but a Hebrew by his nation; in his character, he was the greatest theologian, as Eusebius (b) <note>Eusebius of Caesarea was a 4th-century historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> calls him, and at the same time a subtle philosopher who, according to the testimony of Stephen, was "instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians" (Acts 7:22). He was no less an excellent historian, who narrates and presents the first beginnings of all things, and thus also of the Church. He frequently received commands to write down specific portions, as seen in Exodus 17:14, 24:4–7, 33:1–2, 34:27, and Deuteronomy 17:18, 28:58, and 31:9. Thus, there is no doubt that he himself is the writer of all the five books known by his name, which the Hebrews are accustomed to calling **the Law**. This is accepted by nearly everyone without question; even the so-called "Nazarenes"—who are marked as heretics by Epiphanius (c) <note>The Nazarenes were an early Jewish-Christian group; Epiphanius was a 4th-century bishop known for his "Panarion," a catalog of heresies.</note>—conceded that he was the author, even if they otherwise denied the truth of the writing itself and claimed everything was fabricated by him, and that there was no truth to what he narrated about the <term>Patriarchs<note>The "Arch-Fathers," specifically Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note></term>. This is how mockers are accustomed to act; they hold the beginning of all things, the divine wonders, and the godly simplicity of the first Patriarchs in suspicion and contempt, simply so they may indulge their sensual, animalistic lusts unhindered (2 Peter 3:3 and Jude v. 10).

Whether he composed everything in order himself, as the Jewish philosopher Philo (d) maintains, or only recorded things as if in a <term>diary<note>A day-book or journal.</note></term>, or yearbook, while someone else—either Joshua, or one of the priests or prophets—brought everything into order, divided, and completed it, as some believe: we leave that matter in its place. We satisfy ourselves with the glorious truths and mysteries of these scriptures and the testimony of our Savior himself, who in John 5:46 explicitly says that Moses wrote of Him. However, it is quite probable, as others believe, that they were divided into five books by the <term>Seventy Interpreters<note>The Septuagint: the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament, traditionally attributed to 70 (or 72) scholars.</note></term>, just as one seeks to prove from their Greek names.

Thus, it is also most believable that he did not begin writing during his <term>Midianite retreat<note>The 40-year period Moses spent as a shepherd in Midian after fleeing Egypt but before the Exodus.</note></term> as a private person, as the Jews believe and Eusebius also seems to incline—proposing that the First Book of Moses, containing so many promises of Canaan, was composed there to comfort the Israelites. Rather, it is more likely that the very special calling, the liberation of the people, and even the giving of the Law—and thus God's own handwriting—preceded it. Moses, mindful of the special command regarding the recording of the history of the victory against the <term>Amalekites<note>An ancient nomadic tribe that attacked the Israelites in the desert.</note></term> (Exodus 17:14), and having also received a general command, set himself to the task of writing. He recorded what happened from the beginning of the world until the setting up of the <term>Tabernacle<note>The "Hütte" or portable dwelling place for God's presence during the desert wanderings.</note></term> in the wilderness and shortly thereafter, as contained in the first, second, and third books of Moses. Consequently, the place of his writing was the Arabian desert; to which the fourth and fifth books were added at the end of his life in the plains of Moab near the Jordan.

Just as these writings are rightly regarded as the very oldest in the learned world—compared to which all other writers who ever were or remain are much younger, and even the oldest pagans frequently cite this Lawgiver as much more ancient—so too are they not only a wellspring and short summary of all theology (such that neither the Prophets, nor the Apostles, nor Christ himself said or wrote anything not derived from them or belonging to their evangelical explanation and fulfillment), but also of jurisprudence. Indeed, they even bring to light no small knowledge as an introduction to medicine: concerning the primary cause of all illnesses, their types, and the remedies against them, as well as the best Physician (Exodus 15:26). And likewise they are

# Introductory Report.

...also an origin and source of all history and all other scholarship: which can be sufficiently proven, at the very least regarding the first beginnings and traits of the first nations, by the single 10th Chapter of the 1st Book of Moses <note>The 1st Book of Moses is the Book of Genesis; Chapter 10 is often called the "Table of Nations."</note>—as meager as the ignorant are otherwise accustomed to viewing it. Thus, all chronologies must also take their beginning from Moses. And how philosophy—or "world-wisdom"—also has its ground therein, others (a) have demonstrated, concerning both moral and natural philosophy, architecture, and other subjects. Thus, GOD himself, to a certain extent, laid the foundation for all true scholarship with his own writing and then with these Scriptures; just as a Prince lays the first foundation stone for the honor of a building.

The Greeks, from whom all scholarship came to other nations, themselves confess that they received their writing and their letters from elsewhere: which then correspond in their order, as well as in their names and strokes, with none so much as with the Syrian or Hebrew. Among the Seven Sages of Greece, Thales of Miletus <note>Thales (c. 624–545 BCE) is often cited as the first philosopher in the Western tradition.</note> undoubtedly had his doctrine of the origin of the world (b) from Moses. So too did the famous and ancient Homer (c). And the ancient laws of the Athenians, from which the Roman laws later sprang, have their origin in the laws of Moses (d). Numa Pompilius, the second Roman king, who was older than Pythagoras, has—according to the testimony of Clement of Alexandria (e) and Eusebius (f)—drawn the benefit from the writings of Moses that he forbade the Romans to depict GOD in the form of a human or animal. Thus, for a full 170 years, they initially built churches but had neither a painted nor a carved image inside them: whereby Numa secretly instructed them that the highest good was not reached with the tongue (or anything external), but alone with the spirit. And that Pythagoras drew much of his teaching from this well, as did Plato, his student, is fairly well known and settled among the learned (g). Indeed, one even finds this in the remaining fragments of the book of the ancient Phoenician historian Sanchuniathon <note>A legendary Phoenician author whose works are preserved only in fragments cited by others.</note>—who is considered hardly a couple of hundred years younger than Moses—which Philo translated into Greek, but both of which are lost except for some pieces concerning the Creation that Eusebius (h) cites. Likewise, the history of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, just as Moses has it, appears in Berosus, Damascenus, Artapanus, and various other of the oldest historians.

Now, he <note>Moses</note> may indeed have taken much from the tradition and transmission of the ancestors, as there is no doubt that he could have taken it from there, since he lived only in the fourth generation from Jacob and was thus not so very distant from the times that Adam still reached with his lifespan. As some (i) are then also of the opinion that Moses drew the reports of his First Book <note>Genesis</note>—which were nothing other than short chronological and genealogical registers—either from some scattered writings of the patriarchs and forefathers, or from old songs and poems: and still more, that he is not the actual author of the First Book, but already found it left behind piece by piece by the holy patriarchs and only put it into better order; whereas others, and namely Ursinus (k), wish to maintain that Moses was the first who recorded anything in writing: thus this [latter claim] might soon fall away, yet so much would remain beyond doubt: that he was able to draw much from oral reports. Above all, however, it remains equally right and certain that—regardless of how much he may have taken from such sources—divine inspiration and the guidance of the Holy Spirit performed the best part and guided his hand. Just as this must be settled for anyone who is to place faith in such writings, so too is it perhaps the most distinguished main point upon which most depends: but it gives these same writings so much more credit as divine scriptures, that he was not only placed over this people by divine authority according to common and constant legend among the Hebrews, but it is also sufficiently evident from the same that he did not seek his own fame or the interests of his own people at all, for he even reported his own sins and weaknesses, which he could have kept silent, and [shared] the dignity of the priesthood and royal majesty with...

# Introductory Report.

Putting aside his own sons, he dedicated the leadership to others / as they were required to remain among the lowliest of the Levites <note>The author argues that Moses was selfless because he did not establish a dynasty; his sons did not inherit his leadership role, which instead went to Joshua, while his descendants remained ordinary members of the tribe of Levi.</note>.

And indeed, Moses already had many hundreds of thousands of witnesses in his lifetime / that his word was the Word of GOD / whose descendants still unanimously confess and accept it as such. Not a single Jew would have accepted Christ in faith / if this did not remain an immovable foundation / that the books of Moses were correct and divine / and reached their fulfillment in Christ. Not to mention that the Greek translation of the 70 Interpreters <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, traditionally dated to the 3rd century BCE.</note> / which was prepared in Egypt under the authority of King Ptolemy Philadelphus / is also a very credible witness of this even before the birth of Christ. Just as even the Samaritans / who otherwise accepted nothing from the Old Testament / nevertheless recognized these writings to be divine and from Moses.

<margin>(a) Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 33, chapter 6.</margin>
If we now believe / that the books of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and other men / originate from them; why not the same for these? For how does one know / that these very books have their true origin from those authors to whom they are attributed / other than from the successive reports and testimony of our ancestors (a)? The same applies here. But if we wanted to doubt the truth of such history itself / then we must also doubt everything else / that is reported to us from distant lands in travelogues and other historical accounts. Christ himself and his apostles refer to Moses and his writings; they themselves would therefore have to have never existed / if one wanted to cast doubt upon their testimony: which even the enemies of the Christian name and the most malicious Jew himself do not desire to deny / and therefore no one else will easily deny it / who has anything of human reason left. And why does such a person / if indeed such a one should be found / not also deny / that there were ever Jews? whom one can see every day before one's eyes / and who are sufficient witnesses thereof / since their entire history and commonwealth are founded upon the history and books of Moses as a guiding rule.

Finally, if anyone would like to have, as a conclusion, a <term>chronology</term> <note>A calculation of the timeline of events.</note> of these 5 books / which usually gives great light to history / in a brief summary / it is as follows:

The I. Book of Moses <note>Genesis</note> comprises the history until the death of Joseph / spanning 2308 / or / as others prefer / 2369 years.

The II. Book <note>Exodus</note> contains the period from the death of Joseph until the erection of the Tabernacle in the wilderness / which happened exactly at the beginning of the second year of the Israelites' departure from Egypt / chapter 40, verse 17 / a time of 145 to 146 years.

The III. Book <note>Leviticus</note> is not so much historical / as it is an fassung <note>containing/encompassing</note> of the church order or ceremonial laws / which were given in the first month after the erection of the Tabernacle / and thus describes only the history of one month.

The IV. Book <note>Numbers</note> relates what happened within 38 years and 9 months / from the 2nd month of the second year after the departure until the eleventh month of the 40th year after the same.

The V. Book <note>Deuteronomy</note> contains the history of this eleventh month and a few more days of the following final month until the end of Moses. To this are added the 30 days of mourning over his departure / which ended in the 41st year around the 7th day of the first month.

Thus, these five books of Moses contain a history of 2555 years from the creation of the world.

# The First Book of Moses

It presents the greatest mysteries / both of the fall and of redemption ; and for that reason, it is also difficult to understand in certain places / so that it is rightly considered one of the most difficult of the Biblical books. It indicates the origin of all births / creatures, and generations ; and is therefore otherwise called by the Latin / or rather the Greek / word **Genesis** <note>original: "Genesis"</note>, which means birth or generation. In a special way, however, man is led onto the stage <note>original: "Theatrum"</note> within it / showing how he was created by God as beautiful, glorious, and perfect / as well as how he became wretched and miserable through his own doing : and this through the devil's envy and seduction. Thus, we may recognize from it both the origin of good and of evil / the beginning of all things / and also the entrance through which sin and death came into the world / when angels and men abused the glorious freedom of the will with which they were created / and both sides abandoned their origin / their dominion / their dwelling, and their glorious state. On the other hand, however, God's bottomless mercy also presents itself / especially in the acceptance of man / and the word of reconciliation is spoken to him / a new birth / another **Adam** / a holy **Seed** / is promised / who should destroy the works of the devil in man. Who then is also proclaimed as the **Alpha and Omega** <note>original: "A und O"</note> / the beginning and the end / the first and the last / as Jesus Christ yesterday / today / and in eternity / and is presented to the eye of faith through various prefigurations <note>The German "Fürbilder" refers to 'types'—people or events in the Old Testament that foreshadow Jesus.</note>. It is then so rich in figures of our Lord Christ and his kingdom as no other book of Scripture : so that both word and example show nothing other than the one Christ. He / yes even he / is the true **Noah** / who shall comfort the believers in their toil and labor / and preserve this his family in the floods of God’s wrath. He is the right **Melchizedek** / the true King of Peace and High Priest of his people. The actual seed of **Abraham**, **Isaac**, and **Jacob** / in whom all peoples on earth should be blessed. Yes, even **Isaac** himself / the only-begotten and beloved son / whom the Father was willing to give up as a sacrifice for us. **Jacob** actually saw him / and wrestled with him as God and man : **Joseph**, however, experienced the two states / of humiliation and exaltation / quite particularly and vividly in his own person.

The true and false church are also found here in their first beginnings with many significant circumstances. The believers / the lineage of **Shem** / give us an example in their godly, simple way of life / but especially in faith : they must also serve us as prefigurations in their wonderful guidance / for instruction / on how we are brought to salvation in our spiritual state ; namely, that we go out with **Abraham** from Ur in Chaldea <note>A city in Mesopotamia, Abraham's birthplace, representing the world or a state of paganism left behind for God.</note> / be guests and strangers in the world / keep the covenant of circumcision / and like **Isaac** be born of supernatural power / but for the sake of all this, be mocked and persecuted by the **Ishmaels** / the mockers born according to the flesh / and like **Jacob** must endure many tribulations from the earthly-minded **Labans** / and the hateful false brothers / the **Edoms**. And at the same time, the wicked, perverse generation finds not only more of its kind / but also their first ancestor and grandfather / **Cain** / as the firstborn of the devil and the author of false, ungodly religion / in which all works of the flesh can persist. From his lineage came the invention of all kinds of lusts and unnecessary arts / the **Nimrod-like** violent governments / and the contempt of all reminders and warnings of God and his servants / and of all divine patience and long-suffering : whereby also in due time two notable examples of terrible judgments / through the Deluge and the rain of sulfur / were brought upon the first world and **Sodom** / as a reflection and prefiguration for all the ungodly who would come afterward, of the floods of God's wrath and the fire-zeal that will consume the adversaries in the final times.

-># Preface<-

He dedicated his work to others, setting aside his own sons / as they had to remain among the lowliest of the Levites <note>The author suggests that if Moses had been writing a forgery for his own benefit, he would have elevated his sons to high positions. Since they remained ordinary Levites, it serves as proof of his humility and divine commission.</note>.

Indeed, even during his lifetime, Moses had many hundreds of thousands of witnesses / that his word was the Word of God / whose descendants still unanimously confess and accept it as such. Certainly, not a single Jew would have accepted Christ in faith / if it had not remained an unmovable foundation / that the books of Moses were correct and divine / and had reached their fulfillment in Christ. Not to mention that the Greek translation of the "Seventy Interpreters" <term>Septuagint: the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</term> / which was prepared under the authority of King Ptolemy Philadelphus in Egypt / even before the birth of Christ, is a very credible witness to this. Likewise, even the Samaritans / who otherwise accepted nothing from the Old Testament / nevertheless recognized these writings as divine and belonging to Moses.

<margin>(a) Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 33, chapter 6.</margin>
If we now believe / that the books of Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, and other men / originate from them; why not the same for these? For how does one know / that these works have their true origin from the authors to whom they are attributed / except from the successive reports and testimony of our ancestors (a)? The same applies here. But if we wished to doubt the truth of such history itself / then we must also doubt everything else / that is reported to us from distant lands in travelogues and other historical descriptions. Christ himself and his apostles refer to Moses and his writings; they themselves, therefore, must never have existed / if one wished to cast doubt on their testimony: which even the enemies of the Christian name and the most malicious Jew himself do not desire to deny / and therefore no one else will easily deny / who has any human reason remaining. And why would such a person—if indeed one could be found—not also deny / that there have ever been Jews? Whom one can see before one's eyes every day / and who are sufficient witnesses of it / since their entire history and republic are founded upon the history and books of Moses as a guiding rule.

Finally, to conclude, should anyone wish to have a chronology <term>Zeit-Rechnung: a systematic arrangement of events in order of time</term> of these five books / which usually gives great light to history / it is as follows in a brief summary:

**The First Book of Moses** <note>Genesis</note> covers history until the death of Joseph / spanning 2308 / or / as others prefer / 2369 years.

**The Second Book** <note>Exodus</note> contains the period from the death of Joseph until the setting up of the Tabernacle <term>Stiffte-Hütte: the portable earthly dwelling place of God used by the Israelites</term> in the wilderness / which happened exactly at the beginning of the second year of the Israelites' exodus from Egypt / chapter 40, verse 17; a time of 145 to 146 years.

**The Third Book** <note>Leviticus</note> is not so much historical / but rather contains the Church Order or ceremonial laws / which were given in the first month after the setting up of the Tabernacle / and thus describes the history of only one month.

**The Fourth Book** <note>Numbers</note> recounts what happened within 38 years and 9 months / from the 2nd month of the second year after the exodus until the eleventh month of the 40th year after the same.

**The Fifth Book** <note>Deuteronomy</note> contains the history of this eleventh month and a few more days of the following last month until the end of Moses. Added to this are the 30 days of mourning over his departure / which ended in the 41st year around the 7th day of the first month.

Thus, these five books of Moses contain a history of 2555 years from the creation of the world.

# The First Book of Moses

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial "T" embellished with floral patterns.</image-desc>

**T**his book presents the greatest mysteries / both of the Fall and of redemption ; and for that reason, it is also difficult to understand in certain places / so that it is rightly considered one of the most difficult books of the Bible. It indicates the origin of all births / creatures, and lineages ; and is therefore otherwise called by the Latin / or rather the Greek / word *Genesis*, which signifies birth or lineage <note>original: "Genesis". The author is explaining the etymology of the book's title to a lay audience</note>. But especially, man is led onto the stage <note>original: "Theatrum". A common Baroque metaphor viewing human history as a divine drama</note> herein / showing how he was created by God so beautiful / glorious, and perfect / and yet through his own doing became miserable and wretched : and this through the devil's envy and seduction. So that we may recognize from this both the origin of good and of evil / the beginning of all things / and also the entrance / through which sin and death came into the world / when angels and men abused the glorious freedom of their created will / and both sides left their origin / their principality / their dwelling, and their glorious state. In contrast, however, God's bottomless mercy also presents itself / especially in the acceptance of man / and the word of reconciliation is spoken to him / a new birth / another Adam / a holy seed / is promised / who shall destroy the works of the devil in man. Who then is proclaimed as the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "A und O". The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet</note> / the beginning and the end / the First and the Last / as Jesus Christ, the same yesterday / today / and forever / and is presented to the eye of faith through various prefigurations <term>Types: historical figures or events in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow Jesus Christ</term>. For it is as rich in figures of our Lord Christ and His kingdom as no other book of Scripture : so that both word and example show nothing other than the one Christ. He / yes, even He / is the true Noah / who shall comfort the believers in their toil and labor / and preserve this His family in the floods of God's wrath. He is the right Melchizedek / the true King of Peace and High Priest of His people. The actual seed of Abraham / Isaac, and Jacob / in whom all nations on earth were to be blessed. Yes, even Isaac himself / the only-begotten and beloved son / whom the Father willed to give up as a sacrifice for us. Jacob actually saw Him / and wrestled with Him as God and man : while Joseph experienced the two states / of humiliation and exaltation / quite particularly and vividly in his own person.

Also found here are the true and false church in their first beginnings with many significant circumstances. The believers / the lineage of Shem / give us an example in their godly, simple way of life / but especially in faith : they must also serve us as prefigurations in their wonderful guidance / as a report / of how we are brought to salvation in our spiritual state ; namely, that we go out with Abraham from Ur of the Chaldeans / be guests and strangers in the world / keep the covenant of circumcision / and be born like Isaac out of supernatural power ; but for the sake of all this, be mocked and persecuted by the Ishmaels / the mockers born according to the flesh / and like Jacob, must endure many tribulations from the earthly-minded Labans / and the hateful false brothers / the Edoms. And at the same time, the wicked, perverse generation finds not only more of their own kind / but also their first ancestor and grandfather / Cain / as the firstborn of the devil and the author of false, ungodly religion / in which all works of the flesh can persist. From this have come from his lineage the invention of all kinds of lusts and unnecessary arts / the Nimrod-like violent governments / and the contempt for all reminders and warnings of God and His servants / and of all divine patience and longsuffering : whereby also in early times two notable examples of terrible judgments / through the Deluge and the rain of sulfur / were brought upon the first world and Sodom ; as a reflection for all the ungodly who would come hereafter and as a prefiguration of the floods of God's wrath and the fire-zeal that will consume the adversaries in the last times.

The First Book of Moses. Chapter I.

# Chapter I.

<margin>
1. The creation of the world in six days / 2. especially of mankind.
</margin>

**In the beginning GOD created the heavens and the earth.**

---

The holy and blessed Trinity unites itself for the creation of the greater and lesser world <note>The "greater world" refers to the macrocosm or universe; the "lesser world" refers to the microcosm or man.</note>. Therefore the ancients interpret the word

In the beginning as In Wisdom ; according to what David says in Psalm 104:24 and what Wisdom itself speaks in Proverbs 8:22: "The LORD possessed me (at the source and) at the beginning of His way." This Wisdom is the Son of God / who is also the beginning and is so named in Colossians 1:16, Revelation 1:8, 3:14; likewise the Word / through which the Father is said to have created all things in Psalm 33:6. And for this reason, Scripture and the Gospel of John / which primarily deals with this Word / begin with the same word /

In the beginning / in Hebrew *Bereshit* <note>original: בראשית</note>. From which first word of Scripture some have wanted to prove that the world was created on the first of September. For / when one rearranges these letters through the Cabbala <note>Jewish mystical tradition of interpreting text through letter rearrangement or numerical values</note> / there is found within it *Ba Tishri* <note>original: בא בתשרי</note>, "on the first of Tishri," or the first of September / GOD created heaven and earth. Just as among the ancients Ambrose and Augustine, and among more recent scholars Joseph Scaliger, Kepler, Dionysius Petavius, etc., consider it plausible / that it was created by GOD at the beginning of autumn / when all fruits were ripe. Whereas James Ussher <margin>(a) Annals of the Old and New Testament p. 1.</margin> sets the beginning even more specifically in the night before the 23rd of October / 4004 years before Christ’s birth.

Otherwise, the "beginning" is also understood as the start of the seven days and all following times and eternities / and thus also of all creatures / who receive their duration, essence, and life within these eternities : since before this beginning nothing existed but GOD in the blessed communion / which the Father had with the Son / and they with the Holy Spirit. Proverbs 8:22, 30.

To create is to give essence to all things anew through the powerful Word and command / through which they receive their beginning and constant, powerful preservation. For as He speaks / it is done : as He commands / it stands fast. Psalm 33:9. By His will all things have their essence and are created. Revelation 4:11. And so the things / which are seen / were made / not from things which appeared or existed before. Hebrews 11:3. But otherwise, creation is something incomprehensible in itself. For who has known the LORD / and His essence, will, and deeds? Therefore, faith accepts the creation / although it does not know how it happens ; which it leaves to the omnipotence of GOD / who is named here right at the beginning with the name

Elohim / in the plural form <note>The author notes that the Hebrew name for God, *Elohim*, is grammatically plural, which he interprets as a hint toward the Trinity</note> / and reveals Himself in creation immediately as the three that bear witness in heaven / the Father / the Word / and the Holy Spirit / 1 John 5:7. In the single divine essence / which the name Jehovah <note>original: JEhova</note>, Chapter 2:4 / where both names stand together / makes known.

Heaven is, according to the power of the root word, a fiery-watery active masculine quality : Earth the receptive / gentle and passive feminine quality. And thus

Heaven and Earth are the marriage bond / from which all visible bodies of nature originate / and from which parts man is also made : which Moses names Heaven and Earth not without reason / in that *Shamajim* <note>original: שמים</note> signifies as much as "the upper," from *shum*, "to be high" / in Arabic ; but *Aratz* <note>original: ארץ</note> stems from the root *aratz*, no longer common in Hebrew, which in Arabic means "to be low" or "pressed down." This distinction of height and lowness of heaven and earth then aims not only at the location / (especially since both were mixed in the first chaos of the initial creation /) but much more at the inner essence itself : in that heaven has a far higher / subtler and most-active light-nature / while the earth is of a very low / crass / magnetically-attracting and dark quality ; regardless of where they are located in relation to each other. But otherwise and in an exceptional way / through the

Heaven the highest and invisible realm is understood / which is also called the third heaven / 2 Corinthians 12:2; the heaven of heavens / 1 Kings 8:27, Psalm 148:4; and the throne of GOD / Isaiah 66:1; the dwelling of the angels / Jude verse 6; paradise and the dwelling place of the spirits of the perfected righteous. Luke 23:43, Hebrews 12:23. And with such a heaven were simultaneously

The angels created / as the host of heaven / Chapter 2:1. Which heaven was not / like the earth / desolate and empty / but stood there in its most beautiful order and filled with its inhabitants : when these morning stars all together sang joyfully / and shouted as children of GOD / when they saw one work after another come forth. And thus, conversely, through the

Earth is understood the great abyss / which was entirely covered with water / and the thick and viscous parts mixed with water / from which afterwards the dry land arose on the second day / which was specifically called the earth / held as if swallowed within itself. Psalm 104:6.

<column-break/>

### 2. And the earth was desolate and empty / and it was dark upon the abyss / and the Spirit of GOD hovered above the waters.
### 3. And

---

Scripture is very brief and hidden here with its report. Heaven is mentioned only with one word / and it is immediately shown of the earth / that it was desolate and empty / without form and order / without indicating from where / and that it had fallen into confusion through the fall of Lucifer <note>The author suggests the chaotic state of the early earth was a result of the rebellion of the fallen angels</note> / which GOD sought to remedy here through His Spirit. Precisely for this reason the Spirit of GOD hovered over the waters / and thus also over the dark deep / like a bird hatching eggs / or spreading wings over its young / and hovers or flutters over them / with His almighty power and all-powerful fecundation <note>original: fœcundation. The act of making fertile or productive.</note> and infusion of His fiery love-powers : to impress upon the unformed matter the living- and fruit-making power of GOD / and to show / that the goodness and mercy of the Creator would bring everything into a perfect state in its time. And in view of this living-making power and the tender love of GOD toward His new creatures / He takes upon Himself the fervent love and actions of birds / who love their young fiercely. In this way GOD the Father is compared in Deuteronomy 32:11 to an eagle / in Isaiah 31:5 to flying birds / the Son in Matthew 23:37 to a hen. And the Spirit of GOD appeared as a dove. Matthew 3:16. So that the holy Trinity is engaged in the work of the outer and inner creation. And one can therefore also quite fittingly imagine this earth in the shape of an egg / where the white can represent the water / and the yolk the earth hidden in the deep.

And indeed the two spouses / Heaven and Earth, must have a common bond / which united them / so that both could have an entrance into each other for the sake of their effects. And this is the

Water. For the earth consists of earth and water and in water / 2 Peter 3:5. And makes a sphere with water ; and *Shamajim* <note>original: Schamajim</note>, the heavens / from *Esh* and *Maim*, fire and water <note>A mystical etymology suggesting the Hebrew word for heavens is a compound of fire and water</note>. These all three were subsequently ordered little by little through the separation.

It interprets the "hovering" Spirit through the metaphor of a bird hatching an egg, symbolizing the infusion of life into chaos.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 1, moving from the initial act of creation to a spiritualized interpretation of the first few verses. The author draws a parallel between the physical creation of the world and the spiritual "re-creation" or conversion of the individual soul.</meta>

Chapter I. The First Book of Moses. 3

But here, observe a beautiful image of the **rebirth** or the **re-creation of the soul**, which has sunk into the nothingness of sin. Out of this hideous chaos, God draws the sinful human being in order to create them anew. But He does this only through **Jesus Christ**. The first step toward conversion is this new creation: and, just as nothing was made without the Word, so too in the beginning of the Christian and spiritual life—and also in its progress—everything is worked through Jesus Christ, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. Through His Word, God creates the soul anew, which was, as it were, annihilated by sin. But in what manner does God do this? In the first verse of Holy Scripture, the order is expressed: while it shows what occurred at the beginning of time, it simultaneously describes to us the ways of God in the conversion of the sinner; and this is the first step and entrance into the Christian, spiritual, and inner life.

**God created heaven and earth**, it says. This indicates the twofold renewal which must be performed in repentance: namely, the internal and the external. For we must leave sin behind not only in the body, but also with the heart and spirit. And indeed, external conversion must always depend on the internal—that is, on the conversion of the heart and spirit, which is represented by "heaven." This begins in the heart and spirit and afterwards changes the exterior. The first stirring of conversion happens from within. God creates the spirit by drawing it out of the hideous chaos in which it resided. Afterward, He also tears the body away from sin. He gives the heart a secret pull to be in Him who *is*, and without whom it can never truly be: Afterward, He moves the external man to leave all the fetters that held the heart in death and worthlessness, drawing it away from the one supreme Being to place it amidst mere created vanities.

Nevertheless, this "earth" remains void and formless after its creation; that is, it is deprived of all good, whatever it may be: it is only clothed with some shape and appearance, and that is all. There is as yet no plant, but rather a great space and a lack within it. This is the external state of a person during their conversion. **Darkness covers the depths**: that is, such a spirit and heart—which is like a depth that no one but God can fathom—is so surrounded with darkness that the poor soul does not know which way to turn. If it looks inside itself, there is nothing but darkness and terror, which sin has poured into it. Outside of itself, it perceives nothing but emptiness and barrenness: it finds itself completely emptied of all good and surrounded by nothing but evil.

But even though all this is so, the **Spirit of God** nevertheless does not cease to **hover over the waters**. What are these waters other than the **tears of repentance**, upon which grace rests and spreads itself, regardless of the darkness of ignorance (which are the remnants of sin) and the hideous emptiness of all good?

The most-kind Spirit, who hovers over the waters of repentance, seeing the great pains of the ignorant sinner, sends a ray of His light into the midst of the darkness. A certain brilliance strikes the darkened spirit, which proceeds from God Himself and is nothing other than a ray of His Wisdom, which is a powerful word. It is both Word and Light. For created light is an expression of the uncreated Word, just as the uncreated Word is the source of the light that communicates itself to the creature. Therefore, the divine Word is called the **Splendor of the Saints**: because it is a word full of light that spreads over the holy ones. That is why God only speaks when He creates everything from nothing. For His speaking is His Word, and His Word is His Light. Thus God speaks in this newly-becoming creature.

<column-break/>

# 3. And God said: Let there be light! And there was light.
## 4. And

When God, the Creator of the world—says the divine philosopher <note>Likely referring to a title for an enlightened thinker or a specific figure like Plato or a Christian mystic</note>—had brought forth the number of the heavens and the earth (as the matter), He immediately created the light (as the form), through which creatures might be distinguished and clearly recognized. For light is that which makes all things manifest. Although nothing is brighter or clearer than light, yet nothing is more obscure. For no philosopher or worldly-wise man has yet been able to properly say or describe what it is. Thus, it is at once the most well-known good that we enjoy, and yet the most unknown.

In order to bring the earth into order, God first created light, and that in a certain part of the earth: so that through its steady wandering, the change of day and night might arise and continue. And so God, sitting as it were in heaven among all the ornaments of the world, clothed Himself first with light. **Psalm 104:2**. This is not the light in which God dwells, to which no one can approach; **1 Timothy 6:16**, nor is it that which causes the angels to be called Morning Stars, **Job 38:7**, and Angels of Light, **2 Corinthians 11:14**: but rather that which, in its wonderful order and degrees, delights our eyes and shows the works of God. **Psalm 19**. <meta>catchword: And</meta>

As much as the light of God arises and dawns within us, so much is creation rightly recognized and seen, along with the enmity, wrath, and curse that have spread over it and over all of nature; and how lust has decorated and covered everything; and how that which was planted as a vineyard of the Lord has now become entirely a field of Gomorrah and a wilderness and a barren, dry desert.

Mark, therefore, the work and the manner of God’s operation from the beginning! God, who makes the dead live and calls that which is not as though it were, who also knows how to bring something good out of the bad through the exceeding greatness of His power; this same God—just as He first and before all else made light shine out of darkness at the creation of the external world—still works in this way, and always begins with light when He creates the internal world anew. Just as God said: *Let there be light!* to reveal His wisdom, goodness, and omnipotence in the shine, warmth, and movement of light: so He also commanded that light should shine out of darkness in the heart; **2 Corinthians 4:6**. This is the light that enlightens every person coming into this world, as a light of faith that precedes us in our return to God. And it is God’s wonder and great benefit, both in nature and in grace, that He makes sight and light shine out of blackness and darkness. Just as nature reveals this mystery even to the point of wonder in colors, and all bright colors take their origin step-by-step from black;

and—wonderfully—the **red color of suffering** <note>original: rothe Leidens-Farbe; likely a reference to the 'Morning Redness' or the blood of Christ as the first break of light</note> is the first through which the light breaks out of the darkness; as a clear proof of this is seen not only at the break of day in the morning-redness, but also in the breakout and ignition of a still-hidden smoldering fire from a black-dark smoke, and other such experiential signs.

---

But what is His first word that He speaks to the soul? It is: **Let there be light!** This word is no sooner spoken than the light is there; the darkness of ignorance is transformed into a light of truth: which then increases little by little, just as one sees that the sun at its rising gradually drives away the darkness of the night. This light is a **Light of Grace**; namely, the light worked through Jesus Christ: but not yet the light of Jesus Christ <note>A distinction between the initial grace of conversion and the full indwelling presence of Christ</note>. When this arises, then one can say with truth: Those who sat in the darkness of ignorance and sin have seen a great light; and to those who rested in the shadow of the death of sins, the sun has risen. From this it is easy to see that all of this is worked through the grace of the Redeemer and the goodness of the Creator.

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 1, specifically examining verses 4 and 5. The previous page established the spiritual parallel between the physical creation and the "re-creation" of the soul through Christ. This page focuses on the separation of light from darkness, both as a physical event and a psychological process of faith, while also touching upon the origin of evil and the divine nature of the Hebrew language.</meta>

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter I.

4. And **God** saw the light, that it was good: and **God** made a separation between the light and the darkness.

Through this declaration of goodness regarding the creatures of each day, the first glorious state of these things in the original creation is revealed. In that state, nothing but pure blessing was manifested; whereas later, because of sin, a curse was manifested within the creatures, and thus much of their goodness and glory was lost. <margin>Chapter 3, verse 17; Joel 2, verse 10; 4, verse 15, etc.</margin>

The light proceeding from **God**, which is not mixed with the impurity of the creature, is good, and it produces good effects in the <term>new creature<note>In this context, the "new creature" refers to a person who has undergone a spiritual rebirth or conversion.</note></term>. For through this light, the soul begins to recognize its original state once again; because of this, it receives a longing to return to that state. Just as a light shining into a very dark place reveals where it comes from, the same ray that shows the light’s source simultaneously reveals the place where such light is to be found.

As soon as **God** has poured His light of grace into a heart, and the heart accepts it with faithfulness, He immediately begins to perform the separation of light from darkness. He does this because He perceives that the soul is making good use of this light and recognizes it as a "good thing" that this light has been poured into these dark places. Until then, it was a murky day, or darkness mixed with light; but **God** makes the proper separation between His light and our darkness, so that His light is not corrupted by our darkness. This beautiful light is **Faith**; a gift of **God** that entirely takes possession of a soul. Initially, these are pure illuminations that present themselves to the soul, because the soul is stuck in a great night. It is not as if this beautiful light were brighter in those first illuminations than in the ones that follow; rather, it is only the thick darkness of the soul that makes one perceive and notice such illumination more in the beginning, even though they are not as powerful as they will later become.

This is then truly called: **God** separates our darkness from His light. Through this, our light becomes ever purer, spreads further, and becomes more perfect and much higher, even if it seems to the person as if it were becoming darker. For while the individual sees nothing but darkness (because the separation of what is **God’s** from what is human has just occurred), they believe they are stuck in even greater obscurity. Indeed, they may be at the very highest peak of enlightenment: but because they stand before **God** as before an immortal Sun, who unceasingly communicates His rays to them, and they return this light to **God** with great faithfulness, everything on their side appears to be darkness. However, just as one believes the moon to be at its darkest when it stands opposite the sun in its <term>conjunction<note>In astronomy, a conjunction occurs when two celestial bodies appear close to each other; here, it refers to the New Moon phase when the moon is between the Earth and Sun.</note></term>, even though it is then receiving the most rays; and conversely, it appears brightest to our eyes when it is furthest from the sun and thus "full," even though it is then receiving the fewest rays from the sun: so it is with a soul enlightened by the divine light. When **God**, as the holy Sun, pours His bright and burning rays over the soul, it aligns so closely with its **God** that it does not perceive its own luster and bright shine; whereas such a soul, when it receives less light, and its light is therefore smaller, lets it shine more from the outside. And this is precisely the difference between analytical and acquired knowledge—however high it may be—and the universal and unparsed light of faith.

<column-break/>

5. And **God** called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And so evening and morning became the first day.

6. And

**God** made the beginning of the naming of the creatures (see also verse 8, 10, and Chapter 5, verse 2), and afterward He left this to man, who gave names to the creatures according to the wisdom still residing within him. <margin>Chapter 2, verses 19, 20.</margin> From this, the divine origin of the **Hebrew language** is to be inferred, in which many secrets are hidden that will be revealed in their own time.

The preceding darkness, which was the night (including the evening), and the following light, which was the day (including the morning as the day's beginning), together made up the first day. This serves as a testimony that the imperfect—the alternation of light and darkness—must come first, until the perfect comes: the day that has no night <margin>Revelation 22, verse 5</margin>, which will finally swallow up all darkness. And since the "evening" takes its name from the "mixing" <note>The author likely refers to the Hebrew root *ereb*, which can mean evening or to mix/interweave.</note> of light and darkness, one can count the "morning-dawn" as part of the day (since it precedes the morning) and the "evening-dusk" as part of the night (since it precedes the night). Just as in Zechariah 14, verse 7, the morning-dawn is to be understood as the Day of Grace in Christ’s glorious kingdom, when the glimpses of the day will manifest in the hearts of the believers before His appearance.

Furthermore, the fact that it says a single day was made from evening and morning can be understood in a secret and spiritual sense in two ways. First, because light and darkness alternate, this can be called a "day," namely a **Day of Faith**. Second, that the incipient light—which is the light of life—is understood through the "morning" of the inner life (which is full of luster, brightness, and life), and the state of death, extinction, and laying-down is understood through the "night." From these, a "day" arises—namely the Day of Faith and of internal Christianity.

The Hebrew word indicates that the first darkness was something **real** and a **massive substance**, which was not only dark in itself (like our night) but also rejected and pushed back the light. From this, some conclude—not without reason—that just as the suns were created from light, the planets or "earth-watery spheres" were created from this darkness. These properties are tangibly found on the earth we inhabit, which is not only dark in and of itself but also, according to its position relative to the sun, casts a shadow, thereby causing night and darkness.

The question is asked: where did the first darkness actually originate? **Satan**, as a Prince of Darkness, has always covered the true cause from the beginning with the thickest fog of ignorance and darkness, so that his shame and nakedness might not be uncovered. Therefore, he and his accomplices would like to persuade the whole world that the all-good **God** could not have created the world any better. Through others, who claim two equally eternal "Principles" or original beginnings—one Good and one Evil—he wished to make himself equal to **God**, etc. But it is known from Scripture how he was cast out into darkness from the blessed state of heavenly light in which he had his dwelling. After he, as a "Throne-Prince" of this visible expansion, infected it with his poisonous fire, the all-good **God** wished to come to the aid of this "fire-damage" and created the <term>Shamayim<note>Hebrew: שמים (*Shamayim*), usually translated as "Heavens." The author here links it to water, perhaps following the etymological theory that the word is composed of *sham* (there) and *mayim* (water).</note></term>, heavens or waters, through which the fire was extinguished and Lucifer's undertaking was put to shame. This agrees with the tradition of the **Chinese**, which on pages 3 and 4 of the *Chinese Chronology* edited by **Mentzelio** <note>Christian Mentzel (1622–1701), a German physician and botanist who was an early European scholar of Chinese language and history.</note>, reads as follows: "In the most ancient times, there was an exceedingly large, immeasurable, overflowing water, which, mixed with earth, made a thick dark clump; this then separated and divided itself, and from this came forth the <gloss>Railon<note>Likely a transliteration of a Chinese concept such as *Li* (Reason/Principle).</note></gloss> or the Reason and the form of all things."

But what we call darkness or night is the cone-shaped shadow caused by the earth itself: which is now a dwelling for evil spirits and damned souls, who, like bats, flee the light of the sun. This is also the reason why people fear more at night or in the dark than during the day or in the light.
