### 28. And GOD blessed them; and GOD said to them: Be fruitful and multiply / and fill the earth / and subdue it; and have dominion over the fish of the sea / and over the birds of the heavens / and over every animal that creeps upon the earth! <margin>Ps. 8:7.</margin> <margin>29. Furthermore</margin>

---

<margin>Be fruitful etc.)</margin>
Be fruitful etc.) The Jews hold this to be a commandment / which commands one to marry / to which everyone is bound to render obedience as soon as he finds himself capable. Therefore they marry off their children quite early. However, this conclusion is quite weak. Receive the seed of God into the feminine part of your thoughts and desires / and then act according to the received grace as a man; thus you will become fruitful enough / and fill the earth—or the earthly man—with the gifts of the grace of GOD. So that the heart and the flesh will rejoice in the living GOD. Through this, you will make everything within you subject to yourself.

<margin>Dominion)</margin>
Dominion) As a GOD / especially over the lusts and desires. For these are primarily the "animals" over which the Lord commands man to rule. And man is then in the right state when the Word <term>Logos <note>original Greek: Λόγος; meaning the divine Reason or Word of God</note></term>, the mind / the understanding / or the mind of Christ / is the chief ruler in him / and the soul is under him / and under these both are the beastly or craving passions and affects of his heart. <margin>c. 4:7.</margin>

GOD set man as a king over all animals / and also subjected them all to him / so that he conquered everything in this world that was not GOD / and was conversely conquered by nothing / except by GOD. But as soon as he fell / all the animals / over which he previously ruled / brought him under their obedience. Through this, man has overturned not only his own order of creation within himself / but also the entire order of creation in general: whereas previously creatures were found which were subject to man.

GOD also created man in his image because he created him one and simple <note>In this context, "simple" means unified and without internal conflict, like God's own nature.</note> as he himself is. He can therefore not come back into that same state unless he becomes simple again / as GOD is. This happens in no other way than through the abandonment of all the "manifoldness" of the creature and one’s own activity / and the penetration into the unity of GOD / which alone can make man like GOD.

GOD wants man to grow and multiply / that is / that this image of the Word spread through the whole earth / so that there may be no place where he cannot have his pleasure / through the beholding of his image / which he has imprinted into the creatures. Before man's creation, everything was waste and empty; as it is written. How was it then empty / since there was no place that GOD did not fill? Ah, it is considered vacant before GOD when GOD does not yet perceive the noble creatures / which are the living images of his Son / within it. Therefore he wants these creatures to grow and spread over the whole earth. But why that, O my GOD? To this he answers: so that my pleasure may be increased. For since man bears my image / and my Word has expressed itself in him / then all men are my pleasure.

GOD had / as already said / made all things for the sake of man: therefore he also gives him the government over them. But from whence comes such sovereignty of man over all other animals? That comes because of the image of the Godhead which is in him. This image is the imprint of his Word in man. And because / as Christ has said / all power in heaven and on earth is given to him; so man / who is his image and living expression / has all power on the earth. And this power was so much greater / as the influence of the Word was greater in him.

Although we have lost this power through sin / just as the image of the Word lost its form in us through iniquity; nevertheless / when the image of Jesus Christ is perfectly renewed in us again / then he has such a complete and great power over us / that we neither want to nor can resist him any longer. And this not out of a simply understood inability / but out of one which arises from the

<column-break/>

restored order within us: so that / after this has taken away from our will not only the rebellion / but also the contrary sense to doing God's will / we find ourselves so established in the surrender / union / and transformation of our will into the divine / that we can no longer find any will of our own in us / but we want solely and alone what GOD wants / and God's will has become our will.

That this can also happen in this life is indisputable. Because Jesus Christ commanded us to pray in the Our Father: Thy will be done / on earth as it is in heaven! Which he otherwise would not have commanded / if it were not possible to attain this sinking of the will into God's will here in this world / as the blessed possess it in heaven. For should he have commanded us to pray for a chimera? Or should he / when he offered that beautiful prayer: Father, I pray thee / that they may be one / even as we are one! have prayed for such a thing for us? This is certain: this perfect union cannot occur without the total annihilation of our selfhood / which is against GOD. Now, however, Jesus Christ can say of no one in a higher degree, "all power is given to me in heaven and on earth," than of the one who has no will of his own or any opposition against him.

This is also a fruit of the redemption of Jesus Christ / that man / through the appropriation of the blood of Christ / enters again into the former rights of dominion over the other creatures / of which he is the end: because he possesses everything in God / just as he possesses everything in himself. GOD also wanted to reveal this by the fact that some saints even commanded the most ferocious animals and let themselves be served by them: yes / what is more / even in such things which were directly contrary to their element. As: when fire had to serve as a cool bath for some / who preferred to die for the sake of the love of GOD than to live without it / or who could no longer live without the danger of becoming apostate from God / and thus preferred death / rather than wanting to displease GOD.

O what a greatness and power of JESUS Christ in man / and of man in Jesus Christ! But how little are you recognized! We all bear the name of Christians / although we are nothing less than Christians / since we do not even know what it is to be a Christian. Become Christians then / you who bear the most beautiful name / namely to be called a Christian! then you will first recognize your nobility and greatness. You will then fall into a holy pride / to do nothing unbecoming of a Christian. O Christian knights / who shed so much blood for the sake of a false honor / if you knew what it were to be a Christian / how many lives / if you had them / would you not venture to maintain such glorious honor; and how you would take care to do nothing which could rob you of this honor! But one is, alas, not at all instructed by the spirit of truth and godliness! One remains only on the topmost surface / without exploring its depths: and thereby infinite goods are lost! Man is created as a king / and he would also be a very happy king / if he let the image of GOD be renewed in him. Yet he remains a serf! because he lets that be his kingdom: to lead himself: instead of which he should surrender himself entirely to GOD / and submissively subject himself to his commands / yes, also endure all his workings / whether they be workings of grace or of the cross / with reverence. For up to this point we have seen / that nothing but the great goodness of GOD / and not man's knowledge / has brought him to such a high step: who therefore worked in him / because he did not resist God. We can of ourselves do nothing but evil and strive against GOD: And the faithfulness of man toward GOD consists in this / that he lets him be Master in him / whether it be outwardly or inwardly.

### 29. Furthermore, GOD said: Behold, I have given you every herb that bears seed which is upon the face of all the earth / and every tree upon which are tree-fruits that bear seed: that shall be food for you.

---

Thus God intended to ordain for man a physical food and nourishment for his body / the herbs and tree-fruits of the earth: among the former, grain may well be understood / and among the tree-fruits, the grapevine / which were to serve man for bread and drink. See Psalm 104:14–15. Just as the body was originally in a highly elevated nature / so this is also to be understood regarding the first fruits of the earth / which at that time also possessed such a paradisiacal and elevated power and goodness within them / as such will be upon the new, glorified earth: concerning this, see Revelation 22:2 and Matthew 26:29. For the animals, God also intended to ordain their earthly food / the grass / which would have served as their sufficient nourishment / as long as they maintained their essence. They would not, however, have been initially consumed by man: because that would not have been becoming to the nature of the heavenly body. It took on another nature after sin / when they had to serve for the strengthening of the weakened body. See Chapter 9:3–4.

Meanwhile, it is a practice / which / because it is only permitted for the sake of sin / and follows from the Fall / that man now has some need of the irrational animals for both food and clothing / and cannot well preserve life without that which nevertheless causes the poor irrational animals to lose their lives / for that very reason it can very easily become an abuse. Then, if anything is / this is a "service of vanity and corruption" <note>A reference to Romans 8:20–21, describing the suffering of creation under human sin.</note> / under which the poor creature sensitively sighs over the ruthlessness and excess of men. And if wise and conscientious heathens progressed so far in abstinence that they had no need of meat for their diet; what should Christians not be able to do or refrain from in view of such excess and indulgence! The earnest address of Pythagoras to all mortals in Ovid <margin>(a)</margin> <note>original: "L. 15. Metam." referring to Book 15 of Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note> is certainly very emphatic and thought-provoking / when he is introduced speaking thus:

> "Do not defile your bodies / O you men! with reckless
> "foods. There are fruits / there is orchard-fruit / there are
> "grapes / there are enough good herbs / which one can prepare by
> "fire. Nor is milk taken from you. You also have honey from the flowers at your
> "service. The soil gives nourishment in abundance /
> "and meals without blood and execution. The wild and
> "irrational animals eat flesh: and yet not all of them.
> "For the horse and cattle, small and large, have
> "grass for food. But those that are wild / cruel and bloodthirsty;
> "such as the lions and tigers / the wolves and bears: they
> "love flesh and blood for food. Oh, what a hideous
> "and cruel thing it is / to bury entrails and intestines
> "within intestines / to swallow the flesh of animals into the stomach /
> "to fatten one's own flesh or body with their flesh /
> "and to nourish one's life with their death!"

*Herb that bears seed -- Tree-fruits that bear seed*) These herbs / trees and fruits / of whatever kind they may have been / must have been compatible with the <term>angelic man <note>The author's term for the original, spiritualized state of humanity before the Fall.</note></term>: consequently, both the herbs / as well as the trees and fruits / were of an eternal, spiritual, and heavenly nature. *And they were now to be man's food*) The ground and cause of this was in his nature itself. For no created being can exist without its own nourishment and support; not even the angels themselves. These eat / as the Psalm testifies / Angel-bread <margin>(b)</margin> <note>original: "Ps. 78/25."</note>. And so the angelic man was also to be sustained by eating this fruit destined for him here / and his spirit was to become stronger and stronger / his heavenly and divine life was to bloom, grow, and increase within him / and the glorious image of GOD / which was imprinted in his spirit, soul, and body / was to enjoy constant maintenance.

But after our nature once turned its longing and desire from the heavenly toward the earthly / so now / like the

<column-break/>

### 30. But to all the animals of the earth / and to all the birds of the heavens / and to everything that creeps upon the earth / wherein there is a living soul / let every green herb be for food. And it happened so. 31. And

---

*animals of the earth / and everything that creeps upon the earth / every green herb for food*) is good enough / and we seek our diet and nourishment and our pleasure for the most part in something that should be too low and too insignificant for us.

If we do not wish to remain in our irrationality / and eat grass like an ox with Nebuchadnezzar <note>A reference to Daniel 4, where the King of Babylon is humbled by God and lives like a beast.</note>; then we must earnestly ask GOD for a human heart / and not cease to groan and long like a parched and dry, barren land / until He renews the earth within us. But He will certainly renew it / if we allow His speaking Word and His creative hand to work within us. And

Just as the outer earth is the womb <note>original: "Bärmutter," literally "bearing-mother," a term often used in mystical alchemy and theology to describe a source of generation.</note> / from which grass / herbs / plants / trees and fruits / grow out and forth / together with all kinds of fragrant flowers / which are both pleasant for the eye to behold and lovely to eat; indeed, just as from this kingdom of vegetation all kinds of herbs, fruits / seeds and flowers / grow forth for food as well as for medicine and ornament: so too is man's soul or heart the inward ground and earth / in which Wisdom sows her seed; which is such a seed that has life within itself. Thence, from the renewed heart of man, grow forth his herbs and flowers / his lilies / his rosebuds / namely all kinds of gifts of grace and divine virtues / the herbs of meekness / friendliness / gentleness / goodness and pleasantness; peace / love / humility / unity / harmony, patience / purity / innocence / sincerity / steadfastness / faithfulness / hope / faith / courage / constancy / and more such heavenly herbs / which have absolutely no harsh / contrary / fierce / bitter / nor sour / properties or taste in them / but are filled with divine power / with the marrow and fat of the lovely oil / as the sap of fruitfulness / to make them into a pleasant and well-tasting food.

These seeds / herbs / plants and fruits / grow out of man's earth for food and nourishment / so that the soul-spirit shall eat them for its support and live by them / and may also use them for medicine / yes, even for pleasure, ornament, and joy: So that man with his spirit may not only delight himself upon his own ground and soil / but also find his diet and support in his own earth / yes, can even gather and drink the new spiced wine from his own growth of the grapevine within himself. For the fruitful grapevine grows there no less: indeed, also the pomegranate tree / together with all well- and lovely-smelling spice-trees / the myrrh, aloe, cassia, and cinnamon tree. Such a fruitful field / indeed a right richly-manured soil / is the renewed heart: a merry and pleasant land / a land that flows with milk and honey; grain / wine / oil / honey and milk / are therein always entirely superabundant.

And what should man then lack / so that he could not be entirely happy / without having need to take a step away and out from his own ground and soil? But ignorance causes one to seek his nourishment / medicine and pleasure / only outside of himself / and to allow nothing to arise within himself: though by Wisdom's hand all healthy herbs / plants and fruits / could be planted in your own heart / and might grow forth from there freely and of their own accord / even without any toil and labor.

Alas, where has our soul-spirit been and wandered about for so long a time / and will not yet find itself again and betake itself to rest / so that it might regain its own hidden and lost fatherland / of which it is so ignorant / regardless of the fact that it stands hidden within itself in its own heart!

## 31. And GOD saw everything that he had made / and behold, it was very good. Then it became evening / and it became morning / the sixth day.

->That<-

---

Here follows the praising of the goodness of both the creation of man / as well as the whole of creation / and thus all the works of GOD: that each possessed the perfection belonging to it / in which it had to praise and proclaim GOD’S wisdom / goodness, and omnipotence. <margin>Psalm 111:7.</margin> Therefore, we must not compare this state with the current one / which is as different as day and night / after sin entered the world. See <margin>Genesis Ch. 3:17.</margin>

The Jews claim / that on the sixth day between the evenings ten things were created / besides what is reported here. Namely 1) the abyss / which swallowed Dathan and Abiram: 2) the water-well that followed Israel in the desert: 3) Balaam’s donkey: 4) the rainbow: 5) the manna: 6) Moses’ staff: 7) the tablets of the Law: 8) Moses’ grave: 9) the ram slaughtered in Isaac’s place: and 10) the worm <term>Shamir</term> <note>A legendary creature from Jewish folklore used to cut stones for the Temple without iron tools, as iron was associated with war.</note>, which is said to have been shaped like a grain of barley / and possessed the power / as soon as it touched a stone / that the same would split in that place; and nothing was so strong / that it did not have to split from the mere touch of this worm. With this worm, Moses is said to have engraved the names of the children of Israel upon the gemstones in the breastplate of the High Priest / and Solomon had the stones for the Temple split.

One leaves such things to them to believe along with other traditions / and we have enough to contemplate in that / which the invisible God has placed before our eyes in the indicated wonders / as the first scripture / and such letters that are to be read by everyone.

And certainly / the outer visible world is the best book / wherein man may contemplate his inner world: And because he has turned his senses from himself outward into the visible creatures through the Fall of Sin / he may thus lead them back into himself from the outside. Therefore, only consider / what / how, and in what manner the outer world is created; just so is the inner world within you. You find everything in yourself! The <term>Mind</term> <note>original: "Gemüth" — referring to the seat of soul, will, and intellect combined.</note> is your heaven / and your heart is the earth. Just as the visible heaven stands above the earth / and governs the same with its creatures / illuminates and warms it with its sunlight / rules it through the influences of the stars and planets / and makes it fruitful with early rain and late rain: so the mind is set to govern the heart. Understanding, as the sun, should illuminate and warm everything: the will along with its inclinations / affects, and desires / should govern, guide, and rule the heart through its influences: and the heaven of clouds and air / that is / sensuality / along with its powers, should give their early rain and late rain / that is / grasp the divine influences / and let them drip down and flow into the soil of the heart. The uppermost and most invisible of all heavens is the dwelling of GOD / of his angels and spirits. So was the uppermost heaven in us the highest power of understanding: therein dwelt God himself with all powers and the extracted essence of all his hosts; there was the eternal Spirit from GOD / who governed the whole small world <note>The "microcosm," a common mystical idea that man is a miniature version of the entire universe.</note> as the prince of this world. So too the earth / and everything upon and within it is a figure of the inner earth of our heart and all the powers and inclinations / which are therein. There, all the powers of all animals under heaven / all powers of the herbs / trees / roots / minerals / metals / gold / silver / gemstones / were enclosed: yes, there lay Paradise itself / with its noble rivers / the tree of the knowledge of good and evil / and the tree of life. In this garden GOD walked / and stood in such fellowship with our spirit as one friend with another. And

Since all of this has now fallen into confusion and a miserable chaos through the wretched Fall / so that your earth has become desolate and empty again / and nothing but darkness rises from the depth of your ruin; so long incessantly for the promise of the new creature / over which the Holy Spirit wishes to hover for its formation! Then

<column-break/>

the light of grace will rise for you in the midst of darkness from the Gracious and Merciful One / and the sharp living word will separate flesh and spirit within you. The rising from on high will appear in you as the bright morning star and the sun of righteousness / with healing under its wings / and give you new power to soar with wings / to swing yourself upward and to strive for that which is above: and you will then become anew a fruitful soil / which brings forth all kinds of fruits of righteousness. Yes, the earth of your heart will in such renewal not only bring forth all kinds of noble herbs / patience / gentleness / humility / friendliness / etc. but also all kinds of excellent animals: the young eagle / which always soars into the sun of righteousness with its desires; the lion from the tribe of Judah. No less will there be revealed in you the most noble gold from Ophir and the powers of all metals / plants / roots / herbs, and trees; namely the precious and hidden life of God and Christ in the spirit: so that the image of GOD may be rightly renewed in you / and you may thus rule in blessing over yourself and the creatures. Then it will be said again:

**GOD saw what he had made / and behold, it was very good!** For nothing is better for man / than when the image of GOD is seen in him. And likewise, nothing is more glorious to GOD outside of Himself / than that he sees Himself expressed in man. That is precisely the cause of the great love which God has borne for man. For GOD takes His pleasure in / beholding Himself outside of Himself in man / and generating His word during the beholding. And His greatest joy outside of Himself is also / to behold Himself in man as His image / and to form His word in the same. This, St. Paul calls / <margin>(a)</margin> Christ taking a shape within us. <note>original: "Christus solle eine Gestalt in uns gewinnen," referencing Galatians 4:19.</note>

Man must, however, never behold himself outside of God. If he does such / it is the root of all disorders / and he falls into a false self-esteem: in that he exalts himself in his lowliness / and forgets his origin. But if he is faithful / never to have anything else but God before his eyes; then he sees in the same with wonder his nobility / without any pride. For outside of GOD he sees nothing in himself / but the mud from which he was created. But in GOD he sees himself as God through His communication <note>The mystical idea of "participation" in the divine nature.</note>: and indeed in such a way does he see this / that he also at the same time becomes aware / that / when he ceases to look at himself in his origin / and only sees himself in himself / and attributes something to himself / he could not do such without robbing God of something. So that he finds himself to be such a nothingness outside of God / and the desire to behold himself thus will already pass from him. What is moreover most wondrous / is / that the sight of his essence without God does not humble him: but he rather becomes prouder in this his humiliation / and attributes to himself as his own what is not his. Therefore, much depends upon / man not looking at himself / but rather that he always gaze upon God / in whom he sees himself without danger: which is then a perpetual contemplation of man in God. And this contemplation / which is only a beholding or sight of the Spirit of God / draws the contemplation of God after it. For the more man gazes upon God / the more God gazes upon man. In this wonder over this wondrous work, David said in ecstasy: <margin>(b)</margin> O GOD, what is man / that you are mindful of him! <note>original: "Ps. 8/5"</note>

From these recently recounted states or stages, God makes the sixth day or the sixth step of the inner Christian: and herein everything that belongs to man himself is ended. It is the completion of the works of God in man: because the final purpose of God is nothing other / than to press the image of His Son again into man. Afterward, man ceases to wander / and rests in his final purpose: and he goes out from those spiritual mysteries / days / in order to enter into the eternal divine day.

---
(a) Galatians 4:19. (b) Psalm 8:5.

<meta>This page transitions from the physical acts of the six days of creation to the spiritual and mystical interpretation of the seventh day (the Sabbath). It continues the previous page’s theme of seeing the account of Genesis not just as a historical record, but as a blueprint for the history of the Church and the internal transformation of the human soul.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>The First Book of Moses. Ch. II.</header>

# Chapter II.
->The paradisiacal state of man.<-

THus the heavens and the earth were finished / along with all their host.

The translation of the 70 Interpreters <note>original: "70 Dollmetscher"; referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> / which our Savior and his Apostles cited in the New Testament / thereby giving it great authority / renders it thus: God made His works in six days / and rested on the seventh day. To this, Saint Barnabas makes this observation: "What do these 6 days signify? Nothing else than that after 6000 years the world shall have its end." This explanation is likewise held by *Irenaeus (Book 5, Ch. 28), Hippolytus, Photius, Eustachius, Justin, Hilary, Jerome, Isidore, and Cassiodorus.*

The number 6 is the first "perfect number" <note>In mathematics, a perfect number is a positive integer that is equal to the sum of its proper divisors. 1 + 2 + 3 = 6.</note> : because it arises and ascends from the union of its parts / 1 / 2 / 3. Therefore, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, who believed numbers were the key to the universe.</note> called it <term>gamos</term> <note>original: "γάμος"; Greek for "marriage" or "union"</note>, the number of marriage / because the joined parts generate the whole number. When the parts are multiplied by each other / they result in the same. Namely; six times one / three times two / two times three. A number so convenient for the building of the world: which consists of the first proportion; such as / 4 against 2. A number that / as the first perfect number / befits the perfect Architect, Artist, and Master Builder / as well as His work / in which nothing is lacking / and nothing is superfluous or too much. Therefore / when the Creator had finished and brought forth His work of creation / and had divided it into the number 6 / Moses places this remarkable conclusion: *Thus the heavens and the earth were finished / and all their hosts.* And for this reason, Orpheus, who had read these words in the first book of Moses / (just as Socrates, Plato, and many other learned pagans had done / ) makes a complete conclusion of his spiritual hymn of praise in the sixth birth.

If we consider the progress and proceedings of the Master Builder more closely / the number 6 / in which this building was made / is fittingly represented by a triangle / whose base is 3 / the middle is 2 / and the peak is 1. For the entire building of the world is raised and proceeds from the 3 Substances / which are called Persons <note>Referring to the Holy Trinity.</note>. The progress is through two / which is the Matter; and is completed by the union of the Unity / which is the Form. The formless mixture was the Matter / the Light was the Form: the first day’s work. On the 2nd day / according to the formal or essential number / which is three / the shapes of things were declared / and one was distinguished from the other. On the 3rd day / signified by 3 / which is the mark of life / the living souls were created / which fill the air and water. On the 6th day / signified by 1 / which is also the mark of life / the living creatures are created / which fill the earth. And after the house was built and finished / Man / as the lord of the same / was placed into it in the most perfect form.

I. In general, the days of creation signify the times and courses of the Church / which God would build and establish on earth.
1. The matter of the first day was (1) a chaos: the earth was waste and empty and dark / without order. Out of this the Church was to be drawn: therefore the Spirit of God hovered over the waters. (2) Then it was said: Let there be light! Namely, there the promises of the Messiah already occurred in Paradise. This was from Adam until Abraham.
2. On the second day, God divided the waters under the firmament from the waters above the firmament / that is / the children of God from the children of the world / Abraham from the Chaldeans and Canaanites: from Abraham until Moses.
3. On the third day / God let the earth come forth from the waters / so that the dry land might be seen. The sea is the world / and the earth is the Church. The former surrounds the latter. The people of Israel come forth as a church / distinct from all peoples until Christ.
4. On the 4th, God creates Sun / Moon / and Stars: i.e., Christ comes forth: the Church gains a form and light, yet with its spots and waning. The size of the stars is different. The Apostles were the greatest. There are also planets and comets. This lasted from Christ until the 5th century.

<column-break/>

2. And on the seventh day God had finished His work / which He had made: and He ceased on the seventh day from all His work / which He had made.
<meta>Catchword: 3. And</meta>

5. On the 5th day, the water stirred with living creatures / and all kinds of birds came upon the earth. These are various "stinging," evil men: although among the birds some were pure; as Augustine and others say. From the 5th century until the 11th century.
6. On the sixth day, all kinds of creeping things were created, and then man and woman. From the 10th century until the time of Redemption, there are still evil serpents and wolves: but the Christian Church appears in the form of the Woman. God will yet make His Church perfect / and unity between Christ and His bride. The Church appears under 4 symbols: 1) as an earth covered with water; 2) as an earth revealed and separated from the water; 3) as a moon illuminated by the sun; 4) as a woman.
7. On the seventh day, God rested / and sanctified the day. Thus there will be a Sabbath / consisting (1) in rest / (2) in holiness. And we have yet to expect this.

II. In particular, the creation of heaven and earth signifies the New Testament.
1. God has created everything new / heaven and earth / a new heaven and a new earth. Isaiah 66:2, Revelation 21:1. And is not Christ Himself a kingdom of heaven?
2. God finished everything on the evening of Friday / and rested on Saturday. Christ did the same <note>Referring to Christ's burial on Great Sabbath/Holy Saturday after the Crucifixion on Friday.</note>.

III. Even more specifically, it depicts Rebirth.
1. Both happen through God’s powerful Word. And just as the creation of the first world and the first book of Moses is called <term>genesis</term> <note>original: "genesis"; Greek for "birth" or "origin"</note>, the birth; so here is <term>Anagenesis</term> <note>original: "Anagenesis"; Greek for "rebirth" or "regeneration"</note>, the rebirth. Matthew 19:18.
2. On the first day, the light was created / and the Spirit hovered over the water. Thus John 3:5. True enlightenment is the first step.
3. The entire Trinity does its part in man on both sides. 1 John 5.
4. Everything was new. Thus 2 Corinthians 5.
5. Just as creation did not happen all at once / so it also goes from degree to degree in the new creation.

v. 2. Finished) Those translations / which have "finished" in the imperfect <note>original: "im imperfecto"; referring to the grammatical tense suggesting an ongoing action</note> / have not sufficiently guarded themselves against a challenge or objection that can be made against them. For to finish a work is to act. And if God finished His work on the seventh day / then He did not rest the entire seventh day. However / if one allowed a spiritual understanding / then the common translation would have its correctness. For God finished His work in His Son / who is the true Sabbath / in whom God rests and takes pleasure. And
Through His rest after the completion of creation / says Saint Augustine, He reminds us / that we should rest after our labors / and have no hope of rest / until we return to the likeness in which we were created.
It is said: God finished His work. But what was the end and the fulfillment of His works? It was the work of His perfect image of His Word. After that same one, He rested in Himself / and at the same time lets the soul rest in Him: wherein it remains hidden with Jesus Christ / its true Original.
But the Scripture adds something more: and all these expressions are good / and also represent the interior. It does not stand alone as / "His work": because everything good that happens in man is worked by God alone; since no one can say "Jesus is our Lord" without the Holy Spirit: rather it is called / "His work that He made"; to show / that He made it alone. So also does a soul enter the state of innocence through "annihilation" <note>The mystical concept of "annihilation of the self" or "Nothingness," where the ego dies so God can act fully within the person.</note>. God works in the same, as it were, alone / in that He acts limitlessly and without the cooperation of the creature in the soul. And He rested on the seventh day from all the work that He made: which is understood as the glory and the rest which He finds in the sanctified soul. For since the soul can no longer resist Him / and is one with Him; so He can rest in the same / and have His pleasure therein.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the creation account in Genesis Chapter 2. It shifts from the physical completion of the world to the spiritual significance of the Sabbath (the seventh day) and the interior state of the first humans before the Fall. It interprets the physical elements of the garden—such as plants and mist—as metaphors for divine grace and the cultivation of virtues in the human soul.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>Ch. II. The First Book of Moses. 17</header>

3. And **God** blessed the seventh day / and sanctified it : because on that same day he had ceased from all his work / which **God** had created / as he made it.

---

**God** intended to bless the seventh day / and dedicate it entirely to his service / so that man / as many believe / should be occupied during the six days in the work commanded to him for his own benefit / but should rest from it on the seventh day / and spend it in the turning away from worldly things and the dedication of all the powers of his soul to the praise of **God**. For just as **God** wished to bless the place he chose to establish as a memorial to his name (Exodus 20:21) <note>original: "2. Mos. 20 / 21"; the author refers to the book of Exodus</note> ; so must this also be understood of the time which he particularly sanctified for himself / so that the memory of his name might be celebrated by man in songs of praise for the great work of creation. Therefore, one can notice the traces of such a seven-day cycle with Noah (Genesis 8:10, 12) <note>original: "c. 8 / 10, 12"; referring to the intervals Noah waited before sending out the dove</note> where he, without a doubt, served **God** on the seventh day with special prayers for his help and rescue from the impending judgment along with his family. And **God** also reminded them of this before the giving of the Law / that they should not gather food on the seventh day : For that is the Sabbath of the holy rest of the **Lord** (Exodus 16:22, 23). Indeed, he emphasized it with the word of remembrance in the Law: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy (Exodus 20:8) / by which perhaps the negligence of previous times in observing this commandment was indicated and addressed.

But if a legal institution of the seventh day were already indicated at that time / it would follow that the law of the Sabbath would have bound man even in the state of innocence. However, all external worship / bound to time and place / has a view toward the condition of man after the Fall. For what kind of state of innocence would that have been / if man did not serve **God** with his whole heart at all times and in all places? Why would the living image of **God** / which by its nature must constantly be full of the praise and glory of **God** / need a certain day to celebrate? Furthermore, at that time there was no labor that exhausted the body / from which it was necessary to rest and recover / for which purpose the Sabbath was partly instituted. Thus, it also could not have been adopted by the Christian Church of the New Testament / if it had already been instituted here. For whatever is commanded to man from the very creation of the world / that binds all people / and is subject to no change.

Meanwhile, it is nevertheless noteworthy / as Augustine <note>A significant early Christian theologian (354–430 AD) whose writings shaped Western Christianity.</note> also observed / that here no "evening" is mentioned / as was the case with the previous 6 days. And in the fulfillment of the final times it will happen likewise / that on the entire 7th day there will be no more night of darkness and malice / because the ungodly will have been removed beforehand / and the gentle shall possess the earth (Zechariah 14:6, etc.).

**God** blessed and sanctified the seventh day / because on this day he had ceased from all his works / and the soul was entirely swallowed up by him into his holy life / in which there is nothing but rest ; although this work was created so that it should be made. But when one has reached the end of his creation / namely rest in **God** ; then one must remain in this holy rest / namely in **God** himself. There the work is indeed ended / insofar as it was still in the movement bringing it to its end : but not yet in the joyful activity / which continues in the rest itself / and will continue eternally.

<column-break/>

4. These are now the origins of the heavens and the earth / when they were created / at the time when **God** the **Lord** made earth and heaven.
5. And every shrub of the field was not yet on the earth / and every herb of the field had not yet grown forth. For **God** the **Lord** had not let it rain upon the earth / and man did not yet till the land.
6. But a mist rose up from the earth / which moistened the whole land from above.
7. And

---

Through the excessive moisture of rain, the earth would very soon have become a thick, overgrown wilderness of bushes and forests : but in its most blessed state, it would have been like a green meadow and a fertile fruit and vegetable garden in all places / wherever humans might have settled ; who in their first state would have had no need for houses and the like : which followed after sin / when forests were required for this / and for warmth and other necessities. Thus, laborious agriculture would also not have been necessary : because man would have had sufficient first nourishment from the delightful fruit and vegetable plants. This is therefore recounted / to show / that things very soon changed for man / and the other creatures.

The origins of the heavens and the earth / that is / of the two parts of man / are **God** / the Word / and the Spirit. And so his end must also be / as his origin was. He must go back into the same place / from whence he came out. And just as everything in our creation was wrought through the Word / and nothing is made without the same ; so must everything be wrought through **Jesus Christ** / nor can anything be made without him. He takes man to himself right from the beginning of his walk / nor does he let him go for a single moment / if one only submits to his lovely guidance / until he has brought him with himself to **God**.

Therefore, the **Holy Spirit** assures us / who finds joy in instructing us in all truth / that **God** created the plants / without man contributing the least to their production. The preparations of the mind and heart / as plants which our heavenly Father plants / are not from man (Proverbs 16:1). These plantings are the virtues / which sprout in the soul / (as it gives itself over to **God**) / before such a soul even once works at obtaining them. For the desire itself / to obtain virtue / is a virtue / which **God** through his great goodness places in the soul : And one is no sooner enlightened with the true light / (namely a fruit of the gift / which man gives to **God** / is when he gives himself over to the will of **God**) than one recognizes / that **God** alone must place all virtues into the soul.

What then must the soul do? one might say; and in what then does its faithfulness consist / if it is not to consist in the acquisition of virtues? This is the mystery / my dear brothers! The faithfulness of the soul consists uniquely and alone in that it submits itself to the will of **God** without ceasing / 

and as **St. Peter** teaches us / that we humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God / who alone can work all kinds of good in us : and also lay our cares into his hands ; for he himself cares for us : likewise always denying ourselves / so that all objections of nature against grace may be taken away ; and renouncing ourselves / submitting to all the will of **God** / so that **God** in us / when we have thus denied ourselves and died away / may work more freely and unhindered. Herein now consists the work of man with grace. But to be adorned with those virtues / that **God** must do : and he will also do it unfailingly / if we are only faithful / in cooperating with grace in these two parts. And so that one might not think / this grace might fail to appear ; behold, a mist has risen : which represents **God’s** grace / which rises as it were from the earth ; because such grace is near to us / and always ready to flow into our hearts. It also shows / that this happened before **God** had let it rain on earth : so that we may admire the care of **God** over our innermost being / when it is rightly subject to him ; and how he / when by his command we lack some means of help for our perfection / knows how to replace them from elsewhere : Just as he moistened the earth through the mist / as long as it did not rain upon it from heaven.

It contrasts the effortless abundance of the original creation with the toil and wilderness that followed the Fall.</summary>

## 7. And the LORD God formed man / of the dust of the ground / and breathed (a) into his nostrils the breath of life : and so man became a living soul.

Man, therefore, did not remain faithful to the heavenly image / but without doubt, through his desires, longed for and turned too much toward the created things / whereby his love for God was greatly weakened. Yet the fundamentally good God did not wish to count this immediately as a total fall / but first wanted to warn him in every possible way. Therefore, He lowered him into such a lowlier hut / and prepared for him a body from the dust of the earth / into which the spiritual body / which we shall receive again in the resurrection / was placed as if into a housing. Thus, man must already be seen and considered here in a lower degree than before. Yet even this happened in grace. Therefore, this body would have been immortal / and would only have required a transformation / just as the first spiritual body would have required a confirmation in such a state / if man had remained entirely unmoved in his love for God. Furthermore, this body formed from dust / as the outer visible part of man / would have needed such an in-breathing of a divine life / so that it could be a suitable dwelling-place for the soulish spirit or spiritual body / as the invisible inner part or essence / and could stir and move in every way for its service. And because from the very beginning the spiritual body did not last long / but the earthly soon followed ; so now, especially, the spiritual body is not the first / but the natural / which became a living soul. And because we have all been propagated from this earthly child / this state alone is reported / that the first man was earthly and of the earth. 1 Corinthians 15:44-49.

According to some opinions, Adam was formed on the Damascene Field / near the city of Hebron / where the earth is said to be quite red, loose, and loamy even now / which today is called the "Adamic Earth" / and from there he was brought into the earthly Paradise. <note>Traditional medieval geography often placed the creation of Adam's body in the "Field of Damascus" near Hebron because of the red hue of the soil; "Adam" is etymologically linked to the Hebrew word for "red" or "earth."</note> But when the fall occurred / he was brought back to that place with Eve. For this reason, the Turks carry and sell this earth as an amulet / against all kinds of diseases and the bites of poisonous animals. To us, it can matter little whether this be so or not; of which the Scripture makes no mention : and we let ourselves be satisfied with its report therein. That it was no common earth / but an extract and quintessence of the same / a red, fatty, bright-shining loam or clay / or even gold-dust ; in this many agree / who especially hold that the earth before the curse shone like gold / and the name Adam also brings this with it / which / like Edom, signifies blood and redness / and for that reason also designates a ruby, Exodus 39:10. Ezekiel 28:13. A French woman, who became famous in our times through many writings, <note>Likely referring to Antoinette Bourignon (1616–1680), a mystic whose works were widely read in Pietist circles.</note> shared these thoughts regarding the body of the first man; that it was as clear as glass / so that one could have seen through it everywhere. The flesh would have been like the purest crystal / the veins like shining rubies / and the water in him like the most beautiful diamonds. Of which perhaps more elsewhere.

Whether this human body made of earth lay there without any movement before the reception of the human soul ; or whether it was not rather gifted in a way appropriate to it, from the first moment of its formation, with the sensation of a body / after the manner of plants and animals? Is a question whose answer is indeed not contained in express words in Holy Scripture / yet the latter is to be considered most convenient to the nature of things : since / as an Anonymous writer says of it / the earth / from which the first man was made / as its color testifies / was full of spiritual warmth / and therefore was exceedingly fit to lay the foundation of all lovely perfections in man ; so that it is not well possible or believable / that he stood still merely as a carved image after his completion. For all animals received their animal soul immediately through the powerful word of the Creator. Now, however, Adam belonged according to the body to the host of the earth / from which he was taken : and who then would deny him the bodily way of feeling / even before the reception of the human spirit / which had been granted to all living in-

<column-break/>

habitants of the earth regardless of their lack of reason?

But how the soul came into the body / and still comes into it ; regarding such a question, Augustine holds it to be better, more necessary, and more useful / to be diligent / that it may one day come well out of the body / than to worry / how it came into it. And this is certainly so in view of inquisitive reason / which only brings questions and wars of words onto the path / insofar as it stops and holds people back from improvement toward God in faith. But because everything / that was written before / was written for our instruction / and we should search the Scriptures for it ; it would be no less a negligent laziness / to give no attention at all to the modes of speech in Scripture / especially in matters that concern our own household and the knowledge of ourselves and our noblest part / and not to notice the work of the hands and the mouth of God / which is yet so thoughtfully indicated in this narrative. For God did not speak / he did not create / but he

*Breathed* / it says: He gave something forth from His innermost self. And what can that be other than the divine nature? For nothing else is in Him. This is the Spirit from God / which carnal men lack through their own fault / because they neither have nor want to endure Him / and such become those who have no Spirit / who have separated themselves from Him / parted from the wife of their youth / and given Him a bill of divorce / (a) and therefore live only by the power of their natural soul. For 
> "just as God breathed into the nostrils of man from the beginning of
> "creation the heavenly soul / the Spirit from His mouth /
> "so it is still breathed into all men in the mother's womb by God Himself
> "from His mouth / through the means / which it receives and
> "takes up from God / and that is from the angelic world / the mind
> "which is incorporated into the fruit in the mother's womb through the service 
> "of the angels : writes a man of deep insights. <note>This "man of deep insights" is likely the mystic Jacob Böhme, given the specific references to the "angelic world" and the "Spirit from the mouth."</note>

But those who make one thing out of soul and spirit / and only want to know of two parts of man; they must necessarily put themselves into confusion / whenever and wherever the talk of the soul's origin occurs. Just as Jerome judged / that those were rightly to be laughed at / who thought / that the soul was propagated together with the bodies / and thus not communicated by God / but by the bodily parents; and yet he himself doubted this very matter. It went the same way with Augustine, who agreed with Jerome / and who was so earnest about the opinion / that souls were made daily after the example of the first man / that he even cursed and pronounced the anathema <note>A formal ecclesiastical curse involving excommunication.</note> upon those who believed otherwise. But since one or another objection gave him much trouble / he finally confessed his ignorance of the origin of souls.

And how many are there / who rightly understand or recognize / what is said there of the breath or snorting and the soul in the nose of man (b) / which is called the breath of the Almighty (c)! For there is quite a great difference between the snorting of the nostrils from above and the breath of the mouth from below.

Just as the Holy Scripture has now shown us the spiritual origin of man / which is God Himself ; so it also wants to show us his natural origin. Therefore it shows / how he was made : so that he can see / what he is according to his nature. Everything good he has is from God / and belongs to God. Everything he has from himself / is nothing other than ugliness and despicableness. Nevertheless / just as in man two kinds of states / namely his creation according to nature / and his restoration according to the spiritual state / reveal themselves; so it is certain / that / after God has made the inward man of earth / which is the state of his self-denial / in which he has fallen into the despicableness and lowliness of the clay / which is his origin / God creates another new man from this slime : into whom He then breathes His own Spirit / and not a separate one : so that he is then moved and enlivened by no stranger / but by the Spirit of God. But it happens in no other way than through annihilation. <note>The German *Vernichtigung* (annihilation) refers to the mystical process of "naughting" or emptying the self to be filled with God.</note>

### 8. And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden toward the East / and there He put the man / whom He had formed.
### 9. And the LORD God caused to

---

Since man, in this earthly state, required various fruits for his nourishment / the Lord chose a certain well-watered region / and wished to provide it with many fruitful trees / wherein man was now also to till the land for his food and necessary physical exercise, sowing it with all kinds of fruits / and tending to them. Among these trees were two of singular grace and lovely fruit: one of which stood in the middle of this established garden / and was called the Tree of Life; which represented the source of life / Christ / the Son of God / Revelation 2:7. In him alone man should delight / and thus also eat of these pleasant fruits of the physical tree as a confirmation of this. The other, however, was given to him to test his obedience / wherein his highest good would consist; just as in disobedience would lie his greatest evil: from which he was then also forbidden to eat.

And Adam was not created for the purpose / that he should remain in this state or Paradise forever. For if he had endured the temptation of the devil and stood firm against it / he would have been translated from there / to possess the thrones of the fallen angels.

**Eden)** Is either a common name / and means delight and joy: or a proper name / and signifies the joyful and lovely place toward the sunrise / which is called by such a name. This name is mentioned in Ch. 4:16; 2 Kings 19:12; Isaiah 37:12; Ezekiel 27:23. And here it is testified / that it was once a region.

**Toward the East)** And indeed not only in relation to us / but also in relation to Canaan / or Arabia / where Moses stayed / and thus quite literally toward the East / around the region where the Euphrates and Tigris come together. Thus, the Garden of Paradise / as Frederick Spanheim <margin>(a) <note>original: "Introd. ad Geogr. sacr."</note> Introduction to Sacred Geography, p. 4 sq.</margin> along with others holds / is to be seen in a part of southern Mesopotamia or Babylonia / or perhaps even better, according to Hadrian Reland <margin>(b) <note>original: "Dissert. miscell."</note> Miscellaneous Dissertations, Part 1, p. 99.</margin> in Armenia / at that place / which is located in the midst between the sources of the four rivers / Phasis, Araxes, Tigris, and Euphrates.

There is otherwise much dispute / as to exactly where in the world Paradise was located. Some place it in the Valley of Jericho near the Jordan: others in Greater Armenia; from which the four main rivers flow: which Homer and Herodotus also mention; though under different names. Others place it even in the air <note>A reference to the theory that Paradise existed in a higher, spiritual atmosphere above the physical earth.</note>. Some hold that it was in Asia / and indeed in the center of the world / according to the conditions of those times. Others place it on the islands of Sumatra, Ceylon, etc. others on the so-called <term>Terra del Fuego</term> <note>Spanish for "Land of Fire."</note> or Fire-Land.

To some, it was supposed to be the Damascene field around and near Hebron: because an isle is shown there / where Adam is said to have lived. Which opinion Philip Melanchthon may have favored; as William Xylander <margin>(c) in Commentary on Sleidan's *The Four Empires*, book 1.</margin> indicates. This opinion was prompted not only by the fertility of the land / but also by a city located not far from there / which was called Paradise.

Others again say / it stood at the place / where Sodom and Gomorrah were later located: because of the 13th Chapter of the 1st Book of Moses.

Others suspect / the region around the city of Tyre was such: because of Ezekiel 28.

Others even want to make the Garden of Eden out of the Dutch <note>The text uses "Niederländischen," which historically could refer to the Low Countries or specific border regions like Artois.</note> region of Artois around and from the city of Hesdin.

Some want to present as entirely true / that Paradise was at Jerusalem / and that the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil stood at the very spot / where the Lord Christ was afterwards crucified.

The famous Thomas Burnet, in his <term>Sacred Theory of the Earth</term> <note>original Latin: "Telluris Theoria sacra"</note> writes: A large part of the first world was Paradise /

<column-break/>

### grow out of the earth all kinds of trees / pleasant to look at and good to eat ; and a Tree of Life in the middle of the garden / and a Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. <margin>(a) Proverbs 4:23.</margin>

---

which was inhabited by the ancient peoples in the Golden Age. Finally, he says; it was beyond the Equator, in the southern hemisphere <note>original Latin: "hemisphaerio"</note> outside of the Torrid Zone <note>original Latin: "Zona torrida" - the tropics.</note>. Which opinion Ephrem the Syrian and Moses Bar-Cepha, as well as Tatian, introduced long before: whom many others followed thereafter.

Josephus <margin>(d) Book 1, Antiquities of the Jews, ch. 2.</margin>, John of Damascus <margin>(e) Book 2, ch. 9, On the Orthodox Faith.</margin>, likewise Hugh of Saint Victor, Abraham Ortelius, and others / understand the whole circle of the earth by it / and say / that / since such was changed in its quality after the Fall and through the curse / our first parents would have been exiles in their own fatherland; so that the expulsion from Paradise is to be understood not so much by place / as by power: as the learned Syrian Moses Bar-Cepha and others in part believe.

Many more other opinions are passed over in silence. Let them settle it among themselves. We do not need to know. The Paradise of God / mentioned in the last book of Holy Scripture <note>Revelation 2:7.</note> / and where the reader is referred to the remarks occurring there / is in none of these places. And for us / who should not look at the visible / but at the invisible / it is proper to forget what is behind / and to reach for what is ahead.

**v. 9. In the middle of the garden)** Because two trees could not have stood at the same time in the center of the garden / the ancients note / that according to the true spiritual understanding, they must have been a single tree / which could only be touched with the understanding; upon which life hung / and yet death was hidden therein at the transgression / and was found by Adam. In a spiritual manner, this tree still stands in all people along with the seductive serpent; namely, the temptation to sin: that man may attain and find what his will chooses / Good and Evil / love of God or of self / obedience and disobedience / etc.

God places man immediately into the Paradise of delights. This is to be understood as the sweetness of the passive state of light / of love / and of the felt presence of God / which is the greatest pleasure / that one can have in this life.

In this passive state, everything blooms in the soul / and the trees of its faculties are quite full of the fruits of good works or the practice of virtues / without the soul being able to grasp / how such were produced in the earth of its heart. These fruits are pleasant: because then the practice of virtues is very pleasant.

In the middle of the garden is the Tree of Life. This Tree of Life is God Himself / as the source of all life: who through the Spirit of His grace makes the ground of the person alive / who is so fortunate as to be united with Him; so that he can bear nothing but fruits of life. The Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil is Jesus Christ / who / as holy Wisdom / knows very well how to distinguish the evil from the good / to reject the former and keep the latter; as the Prophet says. To most people, this distinction is unknown. They say; evil is good / and good is evil. They call darkness light / and light darkness. Their deception comes from nothing else / but because they rely too much on their own light: whereas they should much more implore Jesus Christ / that He would give them the Spirit of His Wisdom. This Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil necessarily had to be in the garden / in which man was to live: because this knowledge / in order to live well in this world / was highly necessary for him. But he should have been content with what holy Wisdom had revealed to him of it / which was already enough for him to arrange his life accordingly: and not seek to explore such secrets which God had hidden from him; since such would serve for nothing else than to make him prideful.

10. And a river(a) went out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it divided and became four headwaters. <margin>(a) Revelation 22:1.</margin>

11. The name of the first is Pison: that is the one which flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.

12. And the gold of that land is precious. There is also bdellium(b) and the onyx stone. <margin>(b) Numbers 11:7.</margin>

13. And the name of the second river is Gihon: that is the one which flows around the whole land of Cush.

14. And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is the one which flows toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.

15. An <note>The text cuts off here, likely beginning the next verse: "And the Lord God took the man..."</note>

---

<columns>2</columns>

v. 11. **Pison)** Today called the Phasis. The ancient Jewish historian <note>original: *historiographo*</note> Josephus identified the Pison as the river Ganges in India, and the Gihon as the Nile in Africa. With this opinion, he captured and misled not only many ancient writers but also several excellent modern ones, who followed him as a credible historian and ceased further investigation. Even Luther's marginal gloss agrees with this view.

**Pison** is named first because it is the largest and is produced by the other three waters. It is said to take its course from Baghdad to the city of Bessel, and further toward Basra, which lies six days' journey south of Baghdad. From the place where the Euphrates and Tigris meet down to Basra, it is said to run for 75 German miles.

**Havilah)** Named after the son of Joktan; Chapter 10:29, which name also appears in Chapter 25:18. Because people turned the Pison into the Ganges, they necessarily had to turn this land into East India. However, it is much more likely that land which was later called Susiana, after the city of Susa, and is currently called Khuzestan. From this land—and as some believe, from the city of Susa itself—the Magi or Wise Men are said to have come, who attended to the Lord Christ in His childhood at Bethlehem.

v. 12. **Bdellium)** <term>Bedolah: A resinous gum or, as the author suggests, a pearl.</term> Commonly held to be a beautiful, white, round pearl (a). Hadrian Reland (b), who considers Havilah to be the land of Colchis, is of the opinion that the bdellium found there is crystal, and the *Shoham*—otherwise called onyx—is the emerald. He suggests that the fable of the Golden Fleece comes from the gold found in that region.

v. 13. **Gihon)** This is different from the one mentioned in 1 Kings 1:33 and 2 Chronicles 32:30, which had its course near Jerusalem. This one, however, was later called the Araxes, a name which has the same meaning as Gihon. For among the Chaldeans, Gihon meant simply "a river," and the Persians used Araxes in the same way. It is a great stream which separates from the main flow of the Euphrates to the right toward the west, near the city of Naarda (which now lies desolate) at the Babylonian borders. It wins its course southward to the Babylonian marshes, and from there flows toward Asichiam into the Pison or Pasitigris, eventually falling into the Persian Gulf <note>original: *Sinum Persicum*</note>. It should actually be called *Naharsaris* or *Nabarsares*, or *Nehar ragas*, which means a divided or separated river; because it separates itself from the Euphrates, from which it sprang, and spreads out here and there to water and make the land fertile, just as it says here that it "flows around."

**The Land of Cush)** This has hitherto been falsely understood as the land of the Moors <note>referring to Ethiopia or Sub-Saharan Africa</note>, which lies in Africa under the Torrid Zone <note>original: *Zona torrida*, the equatorial region</note> and produces the blackest of nations. Instead, it is much more likely the land which Cush, the son of Ham, occupied with his descendants according to Chapter 10:6-7. It is known from other places in Scripture that they had their seat in Arabia. Thus, Cush in the Scripture signifies that part of Arabia which separates Desert Arabia and Chaldea, beginning from the side toward Egypt at the Arabian Gulf or the Red Sea. It encompasses parts of Stony Arabia and Happy Arabia <note>referring to Arabia Petraea and Arabia Felix</note>, which is currently under the Turks and partly under the rule of the Arabian King. It is inhabited by Arabs and Eubudians who roam about, stealing and robbing; therefore, it is called *Arachcaldar*, which in German means a land of foot-robbers or robbers who go on foot.

<margin>(a) Samuel Bochart, Part 2, *Hierozoicon* <note>A famous 17th-century study of biblical animals</note>, Book 5, page 674 and following. Sulpitius Severus, Book 1, *Sacred History*, Chapter 17. (b) Hadrian Reland, *Miscellaneous Dissertations*, Part 1, Dissertation 1.</margin>

<column-break/>

v. 14. **Hiddekel)** Or the Tigris, which rises in Armenia 150 miles from Jerusalem and flows through a lake so "arrow-swift" that it keeps its water entirely unmixed. It runs around Mesopotamia and enters the Persian Sea beyond Arabia. In its rapid course, it flows so darkly that it is hideous to look upon and is said to cause dizziness.

Since mention is also made of the very famous river Euphrates—upon which Babylon was later built, and of which it is said that it dwelt by great waters and had great treasures (Jeremiah 51:13)—it may be that it was partly built into the Garden of Eden. This shows how man's corruption misuses all the glorious goods of the earth only for sin.

The river which moistened Paradise—which is the innermost land of our souls—signifies the Grace which flows into the heart of the righteous. This grace divides into four parts: both because it has different names according to its different effects (though it is always the same grace in its origin), and also to pour itself out upon all the powers and deeds of men, just as these four rivers came out of Paradise to moisten the whole earth. Furthermore, this shows us that grace is earned for us through Christ Jesus, and that all the graces given to Adam were bestowed upon him for the sake of Jesus Christ and the merit of His redemption.

The first of these rivers signifies the first grace given to us through Baptism. From this comes fine gold, which is the pure mercy communicated to us thereby; indeed, it is "the beginning of the substantial being of the divine nature," as the Apostle calls it (a). This gold of the land of promise is precious, and the Lord of that land or earth seeks to persuade us (b) that we should buy that same gold from Him. If we truly believed that a gold mine was hidden in the Word of God, in the human heart, and in the field of human souls, we would investigate and explore it differently—hacking and digging through it to find this gold. Even if it had to happen with great pain, like a woman in labor, we would still hope to "dig out" the Lord Jesus. The bdellium is Hope, and the onyx stone is Faith. It is therefore certain that with the first grace poured into us with Baptism, the three divine virtues are also infused. The second is a river that curves into the earth of our souls and its powers. This signifies the increase of grace, which grows as if in wanderings, because it increases step by step until it brings us to our goal. The third indicates the voluntary graces given for the sake of others, just as the Tigris pours itself out upon the Assyrians—namely, upon entire nations. The fourth shows us final perseverance, which leads to eternal life; its true effect is to lead us rightly to the place of our origin, serving as a grace not only of sanctification but also of fulfillment.

<margin>(a) Hebrews 3:14. (b) Revelation 3:18.</margin>

<header>Chapter II. The First Book of Moses.</header>

## 15. And the Lord God took the man / and put him into the Garden of Eden / to cultivate it and to keep it.

After God placed man in Paradise / which is the center-point of his soul / and gave him His grace in abundance; namely, a grace which protected him in all places / so that he / without committing a great infidelity / could not depart from the same: so He also wants him to inhabit and cultivate Paradise. In this, then, consists the faithfulness of the soul / to keep and to cultivate that which God has entrusted to the same.

What kind of grace is this / my dear brothers! Let us learn such from Jesus Christ. Watch and pray / He says / so that you do not fall into temptation. For the spirit is willing / but the flesh is weak. Therefore, this earth must be preserved in God through watching / yes, through perpetual watching. For God demands such watching, joined with prayer, from us; as David says: My God, for you I will watch early! and: Unless the Lord keeps the city / the watchman watches in vain. But / many might say / if I do not watch over myself / but merely content myself that I watch in God alone; then my enemies will ambush me. Indeed, rather the opposite. For when we forget ourselves / in order to watch for God; then He will take even more care of us / because He loves us: Because He never lets Himself be outdone in loving / even if He allows Himself to be overcome by love. Are we then not better protected by the Strong and Mighty One / than by ourselves? We may watch as well as we can / yet it is certain / that one stronger than we are / could overcome us / and take from us all that we so carefully guarded. But when we cast all our affairs upon God / can we then not say with an exceedingly great confidence / like another St. Michael: Who is as strong as our God! <note>The name "Michael" in Hebrew means "Who is like God?"</note>

God also wants us to cultivate our Paradise / our innermost being. But what is this "cultivating"? Our holy Master teaches it to us: Deny yourselves / and take up your cross daily! He says. To incessantly deny oneself in everything that nature might desire against God / and according to the measure in which one denies oneself / to constantly surrender in equanimity <note>original: *Gelassenheit*, a key term in German mysticism referring to a state of letting go and yielding to God's will</note> / in order to bear the various crosses / tribulations and adversities / which God allows us to encounter / with an always-equal mind; that is the work of a person who / in the kingdom where the never-failing waters of grace come to his aid / remains in the order of God’s will / and in such a way reaches his purpose.

<column-break/>

## 16. And the Lord God commanded the man / and said: You shall eat freely of every tree in the garden.

## 17. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil / of that you shall not eat! For on the day you eat of it / you shall surely die!

## 18. And

We should not only not allow ourselves to lust after eating what is evil / or to follow our evil lusts; but also not after that which is "seemingly good" / if we wish to return to the right simplicity / to the one thing necessary and to the first blessedness.

What is more "seemingly good" / and at the same time sweeter to man / than to know much? Chapter 3:6.

What shall one say first of the useless curiosity and inquisitiveness / where the flighty man always wants to hear, see, and know everything; where one runs about / seeks all kinds of pastimes / asks for the latest news <note>original: *Zeitungen*, which in the 17th-18th century could mean reports or rumors</note> / and then judges over this and that. That all belongs to the tree of the knowledge of good and evil: from this, man eats in false pleasure / and thereby constantly dies a spiritual death.

Indeed, this tree is rooted even deeper / even within the spiritual being. For when a man seeks to know outside of and without his true and actual improvement / in that he eats more from the tree of temptation / than from the tree of life.

If man were to stand right in the middle of Paradise / and let himself into false / although "seemingly good" / desires / science / and the like; he could still not remain therein / but would lose his good / and fall out of the inward kingdom of God into the mixed kingdom of sins and death.

The forbidden act carries the evil sin within and of itself by virtue of natural consequence / and God forbade it for that very reason / and not from a merely arbitrary decree: almost as one denies knives to children.

You will die / that is / you will begin to be mortal / you will feel such a change in your nature / that it will now be entirely inclined toward frailty / and will have fallen into such a condition / in which it must decrease in strength / become sick, unhealthy, and indeed must even die and perish. A punishment is not so much dictated here / as rather the necessary consequence is indicated and prophesied. No differently than when a father says to his child / or a friend to another: If you do not take care / and eat of that poisonous herb; if you do not stay away from the target range / you will be a dead man! If you do not stay away from the fire / you will fall into it / and burn yourself! And so this law and command proceeds from love / not from wrath. It is indeed a good friend / who warns one against harm and misfortune. Indeed, at the same time a way of reconciliation is pointed out and proclaimed in these words: namely through the daily dying of our sins. Which was doubtlessly one / if not the principal / meaning of what our Lord said here to the man: For truly Adam died his other death <note>Referring to physical death</note> some hundred years later.

---

One must therefore not imagine / as if God acted only as a lawgiver / who gives a merely positive law; or a judge / who imposes a punishment upon the transgression of his will. We do not need to imagine / as if God / who had been rightly angered / had placed an entirely express corruption into the soul and body of man through an extraordinary act / so that He could punish him.

If drunkards <note>original: *Sößlinge*, likely a colloquialism for those prone to excess or "soaking" in drink</note> fathered children / who by a natural consequence of that which happens in the body were inclined to the same vice / then that would be a punishment of those who fathered them; but not of the law. In the consequences of the sin of the first man there is something that resembles this.

God allows man / to taste of all those refreshments / which are represented by the fruits; namely of all virtues. But He forbids him to try the fruit of the knowledge of good and evil: which represents our own ways / which are contrary to the kingdom of Jesus Christ over us. If you eat of it / He says / you shall die the death! because through it one masters that which is God's / appropriates it to oneself / and views it / though it comes purely from the goodness of God / as a fruit which one has brought forth through his own industry. And just as every tree that is not grafted into Jesus Christ can bring forth no good fruit; so all good fruit necessarily comes from Jesus Christ / into whom we are grafted / so that He Himself may bear good fruit in us. The one who now wishes to lead himself / also withdraws himself from the lordship of Jesus Christ / since he ascribes to himself the good that God works in him through Jesus Christ / he has pleasure in himself. Therefore he gives sin an entrance / even if he otherwise stood in a glorious state of grace / so that curiosity and self-seeking in the gifts of God's grace bring him death. Although it is said: on that same day you shall die! the soul nevertheless does not die on the very day that it commits this forbidden reach; otherwise it would still be happy enough; rather it is only condemned to die; and just then the execution of its death penalty begins. Just as Adam did not die immediately / when he had sinned; but from that moment on was (only) destined for death / into whose distresses he also immediately fell.

It stands written: you shall die the death. That signifies / that God is not satisfied with a half-death / not with a thousand deaths or witherings: but a truthful and essential death must follow / without which it is not a right death / but only an image of the same.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter II.
