### # Chap. X. The First Book of Moses.

23. And the sons of Aram are: Uz, and Hul, and Gether, and Mash.
<margin>1 Chronicles 1:17.</margin>

24. And Arphaxad begat Salah; and Salah begat Eber.
<margin>Chapter 11:12–14.</margin>

25. And unto Eber were born two sons: the name of one was Peleg; for in his days was the earth divided; and his brother's name was Joktan.

---

<margin>v. 23. Uz)</margin> He built Damascus. Therefore the valley there—which is counted among the five most beautiful in the world—is still called *Algauta* <note>original: "Algauta," referring to the Ghouta oasis</note> today; for although the spelling has changed, the letters are almost exactly the same, and it is only read and pronounced this way by the Arabs.
<margin>For another Uz, see Chapter 22:21.</margin>

<margin>Hul — Gether — Mash)</margin> The colonies of these three brothers are the most uncertain of all among almost all writers. To the first, some attribute the Aeolians; to the second, the Goths, or the Gerenians, likewise the Bactrians; others also suggest Mysia, a province in Thrace. To the third, some—due to the similarity of the name—assign him as the founder of the Massagetae; others, including Kircher and Montanus, attribute to him Mysia, a province in Thrace.

<margin>v. 24. Salah)</margin> According to the views of Bochart and Hornius, he is said to have gone to the province of Susa and built a city there of his own name.

<margin>v. 25. Peleg)</margin> Hornius cites Epiphanius and Salmasius, who wish to derive the province of Pelasgia in Greece from Peleg; this area is located in what is today called the outermost part of Macedonia toward Achaia, and was previously named Thessaly.

->But<-

Bochart wonders where Epiphanius might have gotten that from, and believes that as a Hebrew, Peleg remained in the vicinity. This Peleg had to maintain and carry forward the family of the faithful; whereas Joktan, with his numerous sons, was passed over.

<margin>In his time)</margin> If the division occurred exactly at his birth, it is to be placed in the year 101 after the Great Flood, as Calvisius and others reckon it: Shem begat [Arphaxad] two years after the flood (Chapter 11:10); Arphaxad at 35 (v. 12); Salah at 30 (v. 14); Eber at 34 (v. 16). The total is 101.

And so it seems probable to many, because the name was given to him at his birth, that at the very least the distribution was decided then, even if the actual separation was delayed for some years and they did not disperse immediately.

<margin>Elias Reusner (a) places the Noahic division in the year of the world 1758, but the Babylonian scattering in 1788; thus he does not interpret the latter here when it says that in Peleg's time</margin>

<margin>the earth was divided)</margin> Friedrich Spanheim (b) also does not want the division of the earth to be confused with the Babylonian confusion and scattering.

And so there are many who posit a twofold division: one which, by divine impulse, was announced to posterity by Noah himself at the time of Peleg's birth; the other, which had to happen against their will during the confusion of languages. Of this, Philipp Cluverius (c) writes most clearly, albeit with a slightly different calculation:
> "Around the year 124 after the Flood, 724 years after Noah's birth, and 1780 from the creation of the world—when the sons and grandsons of Noah increased so greatly that the part of Asia they then inhabited beyond the Tigris River no longer had enough room for them—God reminded Noah that he should divide and distribute the entire earth among his sons and grandsons, so that they might separate from one another and everywhere cultivate and repopulate the land."

<meta>(a) *Introduction to History*. (b) *Introduction to Sacred History*. (c) *On Ancient Germany*, book I, chapter 4.</meta>

<column-break/>

26. And Joktan begat Almodad, and Sheleph, and Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,

27. And Hadoram, and Uzal, and Diklah,

28. And

---

<margin>v. 26. Joktan begat)</margin> Thirteen sons, as the founders of as many nations. And since Moses clearly described their names and dwelling places, it is surprising that almost all interpreters wander so far from the mark here, as Bochart (a) writes.

<margin>Almodad)</margin> According to the accounts of Bochart and Dapper, he likely established his colonies in the middle of Arabia Felix <note>term: "Arabia Felix" was the Latin name for the fertile southern parts of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen</note>, from which the ancient people called the Allumaeotae were said to have later sprouted and been named.

That he was the inventor of geometry, as reported in Jonathan's Chaldean translation or paraphrase <note>referring to the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan</note>, is considered by Bochart to be a fable, which may be based on the name, because *Modad* signifies a "measurer."

<margin>Sheleph)</margin> The father of the Salapeni, who established their quarters not far from the source of the river Berig—which today is called Wadi al-Ula <note>original: "Wadilolif"</note>—which flows between Mecca and Medina and empties its water into the Red Sea.

<margin>Hazarmaveth)</margin> From him, a province is said to have arisen which was later called Hadramaut or Chatramitis.

According to the opinion of the Greek Fathers, he was the inventor of the Arabic language; although the Arabs themselves would attribute its origin to Joktan. Even today, the Hadramaut dialect is rejected by the Arabs as "barbaric."

The province named Hadramaut after him comprises today (as Dapper reports) several cities and many villages. The capital is called Liban, and is also known by the name of the province, Hadramaut, as well as Sartach; it lies seven days' journey eastward from Aden, on a rough and steep mountain of the same name, and is very well fortified.

In German, this name means "the herb of death" <note>original: "Kraut des Todes"; Hazarmaveth literally means "Court of Death" in Hebrew</note>; in reference to Him who said: "Death, I will be your poison." <note>A reference to Hosea 13:14</note>

<margin>Jarah)</margin> From whom the Jerachaeans are said to descend, who are called Alilaeans by Diodorus (b), a people on the Red Sea. Bochart (c) believes they were called Alilaeans because they worshiped the goddess Alilat, which according to Scaliger's indication is nothing other than the Moon, which even today is called *Hilal* during the new moon, and which the Arabs have held in great honor at all times.

<margin>v. 27. Hadoram)</margin> Bochart and Dapper assign him the outermost corner of Arabia toward Persia, where the kingdom and the island of Hormuz are now seen on maps.

<margin>Uzal)</margin> Is said to have built a city of the same name, Uzal or Auzal; which is now called Sanaa or Jinan, Jenan, and Chenna, along with the surrounding province. Yet the Jews, as Dapper reports, have not presumed to destroy the memory of the ancient name, but even today say Uzal instead of Sanaa.

The city of Sanaa lies between mountains and is fortified by nature and art, surrounded by earthen walls that are 10 cubits high and 20 cubits wide. No city in the entire land is said to be older in years, larger in circumference, or more populous in inhabitants. Within its circuit, it is said to comprise about 400 houses, which in beauty are second to none of the European ones, and especially the Italian ones. It extends so far that within its walls many fields, gardens, and meadows are seen. In this region, one enjoys two summers every year.

<margin>Diklah)</margin> Is said to have established his dwelling in the southern part of Arabia Felix, where most date palms are to be found (for in the Syriac and Chaldean languages, the word *Dikla* signifies a date tree or a date forest).

### The First Book of Moses. Chap. XI.

28. And Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba, <margin>Psalm 72:10. Isaiah 43:3.</margin>
29. And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab. These are all the sons of Joktan.
30. And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar, a mount of the east.
31. These are the sons of Shem, after their families, after their tongues, in their lands, after their nations.
32. These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood.

---

**v. 28. Obal)** Is said not to have remained in Arabia, but to have moved from there into Troglodytic Africa <note>An ancient term for the Red Sea coast of Africa, whose inhabitants were said to live in caves (troglodytes).</note>, situated near the Red Sea, in the region where the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb is now seen; that is, by the sound of Babelmandel.
**Abimael)** After whom, it is believed, the land of Mali was named. It would therefore mean something like "father of the Maels" or the Malites. Just as often in genealogies, fathers are named only after their sons.
**Sheba)** A founder of the city and the kingdom or province of Saba, Sabas, or Sabo. The city lay on a low, heavily wooded mountain by the Red Sea and was the most beautiful among all in Arabia. Today it is called Marib.
**v. 29. Ophir)** This was the name in the Hebrew language for a province situated near the Sabaeans in Arabia, and called *Aufar* by the Arabs in their language, which means "the richest" or "abundant in treasure." This was a different place from the Ophir in India, which almost all scholars now unanimously agree is the island of Ceylon <note>modern-day Sri Lanka</note>. 1 Kings 9:28.
The ancient peoples of this gold-rich land are said—because they did not know the proper use of it and lacked silver, copper, and iron—to have traded gold for these metals; such as 3 pounds of gold for 1 pound of copper, 2 for 1 pound of iron, and 10 for 1 pound of silver.
**Havilah)** Whose seat is still called today (as Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart, a 17th-century scholar of biblical geography.</note> states) by the slightly altered name of the land of Chaukan, with its capital Du-Sohaim: 13 days' journey from Mecca, 4 from the port of Hali, almost midway between Mecca and Sana'a. Genesis 25:18. 1 Samuel 15:7.
**Jobab)** Signifies a "wilderness" in Arabic. Indeed, the Sachalitic land where the Jobabites, the descendants of Jobab, lived—as Ptolemy, and after him Bochart and Dapper, testify—is truly of such a nature. For that part of Arabia above the Sachalites Gulf, toward the east, is for the most part desert.
**v. 30. Mesha)** Is, as Bochart suggests, a famous port of that name in *Arabia aromatifera* <note>Spice-bearing Arabia</note>, also called Musa or Muza, on the Red Sea, where Egyptian and Moorish merchants conduct heavy trade; from there they traveled further east to Sephar, the capital, to trade for frankincense, myrrh, and other Arabian incense and spices.
**Sephar the mountain)** If we were to imagine such a place according to our current description of the world, it would be a range of mountains in what is today called *Arabia Felix* <note>Latin: "Happy" or "Fortunate" Arabia</note>, which were called the Sapharitic Mountains after the royal residence city of Saphar located there, but were later called *Climax* by the Greeks.
Dapper has given extensive reports on both, noting that Saphar is called *Daphhar* or *Daffar* by Arabic writers today, and is the name of the capital city of the Arabs. It lies 12 days' journey by sea from Mesha or Muza, at the foot of Mount Climax.
**v. 32. After the flood)** From the Flood until the following building of the Tower, the confusion of tongues, and the scattering of people, 275 years are counted.

# Chapter XI.

And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.
2. And

---

Those saved from the flood in unity spoke essentially only one language, because they were all taught by God and had only one mouth <note>original: "Mund," meaning "speech" or "voice"</note>; because it is one and the same Spirit <note>Matthew 10:20</note> which reveals itself through them.
And so, in the first hundred years after the Flood, all people spoke with one language, namely Hebrew: which also remained pure, and they had only one dialect until it later changed and divided into Chaldean, Syrian, and others. They also remained together in the knowledge of God and His promise in their duties of divine service, as they had been instructed in this by their father and forefather, Noah.
**One language)** The Maronites, as well as Theodoret, <note>A 5th-century bishop and theologian.</note> wish to consider the Syrian or Chaldean language as the very first. However, Bochart, M. Senefus, and Athanasius Kircher have sufficiently proved that Hebrew is the oldest and first. Therefore, one still finds in all languages some words that originate from Hebrew.
According to the opinion of the Hebrews, there are 70 nations, also 70 languages, and just as many angels set over the nations, whose image is represented by the 70 patriarchal ancestors from the three sons of Noah mentioned in the previous chapter. See also Chapter 46:27.
Clemens of Alexandria, Eusebius, and Epiphanius count 72 languages among the Greek Fathers; Augustine among the Latin ones.
In the Scriptures, approximately 20 occur alongside Hebrew. 1) The Chaldean and Syrian: in which much of Daniel from Chapter 2:4 to Chapter 8 was written, and Ezra from Chapter 4:7 to 15 and 7:12 to 26, and Jeremiah a single verse <note>original: "Comma"</note> in Chapter 10:11. In Scripture, it is commonly called Aramaic. 2) Arabic, whose age is evident because the poetic books of Scripture, and especially Job, are filled with its turns of phrase, as Jerome noted long ago. 3) Canaanite or Phoenician. 4) Egyptian. 5) Ashdodite. Nehemiah 13:24. 6) Persian: of which there are many words in the books of Daniel, Ezra, and Esther. Furthermore, in the inscription on the Cross of Christ, Greek and Latin <note>original: "Römische"</note> appear; and in Acts 14:11, the Lycaonian language; the others however appear in Chapter 2:9, 10, 11.

# 2. And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there.

**From the east)** In the *Geographia Sacra* <margin>(a) Book 1, chapters 6, 7.</margin> by Bochartus <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer.</note>, one finds the opinions of various commentators, particularly following the Chaldean translation <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, for whom the word <term>mi-qedem</term> <note>Hebrew: מקדם</note> is said to mean not a region to the east, but rather "from the beginning." Thus, the meaning of Moses' words would be that Noah, with his three sons and their children, set out for the first time and came into the land of Shinar; or that this was the first journey after the Deluge when Noah’s family descended from the mountains into the land of Shinar. However, it is not necessary to force a foreign interpretation. Having come down from the mountains of Ararat in Armenia, they lived in those provinces which were later called Media, Persia, and Bactriana; and from there they turned more toward the west and settled 

**In the land of Shinar)** This is now held <margin>(b) chapter 4, on Noah's Ark; and Book 1, chapter 7, on the Tower of Babel.</margin> by Kircherus <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who wrote on many topics, including the Tower of Babel.</note> and others, quite rightly, to be the Babylonian district. It was also translated as "Babylon" by the Greek interpreters in Isaiah 11:11 and Zechariah 5:11. According to the description by Vapperi <note>Likely referring to Pietro della Valle (1586–1652), an Italian traveler whose name was sometimes Germanized.</note>, it is one of the best lands currently possessed by the Turkish Emperor. One finds there magnificent meadows and fields, and sees a great multitude of livestock grazing; especially horses and buffalo. The female buffalo carry their young until the 12th month and are so rich in milk that some of them give five and a half measures <note>A *Maß* was roughly 1 to 1.5 liters depending on the region.</note> of milk daily. From this, such a vast quantity of butter is made that in some villages built on the banks of the Tigris River, 20 or even 25 ships laden with butter may be seen at once, which is brought to market along the Persian Gulf on both the Persian and Arabian sides. There is no place in the whole world where more beautiful horses are found, nor any more durable and capable of labor than here. Some are found that can continue their run for 30 hours straight without fodder or drink. One also finds here many camels, mules, and common donkeys. — Dates, pistachios, and similar fruits of very good taste, as well as pears and quinces, are found in abundance. — One also finds a type of pomegranate that is not very large but mostly has a thin skin and is sweet-and-sour. Dates and rice are the common food of the ordinary people. This land also yields sugar cane, from which the inhabitants make preserves. Much cotton and silk is also found there, from which they make clothes.

**Dwelt there)** And for a good long time, before they hit upon the following plot and the impious undertaking. No doubt they remained until then under the wise governance of the patriarch Noah. But now things would no longer go well. For as the children of Noah's three sons greatly multiplied during this time, and among the grandsons of Ham the restless Nimrod had already been born—who in his youth likely harbored lofty thoughts and may have heard from his grandfather Ham how things went in the first world <note>The world before the Great Flood.</note>—he went about with thoughts of bringing about a dominion over the others and making a famous name for himself. And this was done "before the Lord," so that all people would be compelled to one kind of speech and worship, and would no longer scatter and separate as had happened before the Flood, when the children of God wanted to imagine themselves superior and separated themselves from the children of men in worship. They wanted to build a high tower there, in which perhaps the worship and the council should be held, so that the people might always be kept in obedience. All of this the pious Noah, in his great age, was likely unable to prevent, and perhaps he did not foresee the danger so clearly.

Just as it was a blessed state in the first days of Christianity that all believers were of one heart and one soul (Acts 4:32), this was soon disturbed by those with the mind of Diotrephes <note>A biblical figure mentioned in 3 John 1:9 as one who "loves to be first" or seeks preeminence.</note>, who sought the highest place (3 John v. 9), and thereby the simple, humble nature in Christ is still being abolished (2 Corinthians 11:3). But in Christ's glorious kingdom, the Lord will again be only one, and his name only one; so that one will use the same pure and clear words concerning divine truths and serve him with a harmonious heart (Zechariah 14:9; Zephaniah 3:9).

# 3. And they said one to another: Come, let us make bricks, and burn them thoroughly! And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for mortar.
<margin>Exodus 2:3.</margin>

# 4. And

Instead of these Babylonians using their shared language in the unity of the Spirit for the harmonious praise of God—to whom they had every reason to show reverence after he had proven himself so majestically against the first sinful world—they wanted to make a great name for themselves in the world. They came upon the idea of building such a great tower that all descendants who saw it might say what great and wise people the nations of that time had been.

Pride was the first fall of the Devil and of man, and is therefore a source of all other sins as well.

It is good, however, when we read such things, that we soon think of ourselves and how we stand in this regard. For it is quite easy to discourse upon and criticize others.

Pride is deeply imprinted in us all by nature and is difficult to overcome. Such thoughts easily arise: "See how far you have brought yourself; this status, this house, this profit, you have achieved for yourself." Just as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> reports of these people, that they attributed their prosperity and well-being not to God, but to their own strength; in which contempt for God Nimrod—who had set himself up as their captain—strengthened them.

All of this, however, is from the Devil and flows from the proud mind of Lucifer; it also leads back to pride as its center. Thereby, man becomes proud, arrogant, haughty: also simultaneously excessive, and further tyrannical and unmerciful. And

That very thing is the true origin of complacency and insolence in men. For what are the

**Bricks)** What are the materials with which the spiritual Babel is built within man, other than his own convictions, his regret, his penance, his faith and trust in Christ, his rebirth, redemption, justification, atonement, sonship, reconciliation, righteousness, etc., from which nothing but complacency and insolence arise?

From such bricks and materials, man and the false church build a system and a state of grace and salvation. But they are, alas, very poorly burned, and certainly not as they are presented. The beginning and the first step of rebirth are already considered sufficient and as the end. Redemption is imagined while one still lies captive under the dominion of sin. The alleged justification finds no place where injustice still finds a place. The bricks are hardly half-burned: and because everything is additionally whitewashed with the loose lime of thin distinctions drawn from reason and human scholarship, how then shall it stand?

**Slime instead of mortar)** Or, mud instead of mortar. The Babylonian builders use mud or carnal affection from flesh and blood instead of the cement of true Christian love. And

This is the image of those souls who strive to become holy through their own works, and who imagine they can achieve it through their own natural strengths, and thus do not recognize their error. These very imaginative people heap one good work upon another so that, they say, "we may become holy." They rely entirely on their own strengths: and without considering that they do wrong, they wish to dictate laws to God. Therefore, the Scripture says they built with brick and slime, thereby indicating that it was all merely human invention.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XI.

4. And they said: "Come, let us build a city for ourselves, and a tower whose top reaches to the hea-

---

**Let us build)** Human reason <note>German: *Vernunfft*. In this pietist or devotional context, "reason" refers to human intellect operating independently of God's revelation.</note> is the true foundation of this confused building of Babel; it drives so many people to presume to teach out of pride, without God's Spirit or impulse. Such people do not build God's kingdom and temple, but rather diminish it under His name, even if they hide behind the Scriptures. Meanwhile, the Tower of Babel is built all the more diligently. Everyone is happy to help patch and piece it together, contributing at least mortar and <term>Tohu</term> <note>Original: *Dohu*. A reference to the Hebrew *Tohu wa-bohu* from Genesis 1:2, meaning "formless and empty." Here it implies chaotic, useless material.</note>.

<margin>(a) Matthew 7:24–27.</margin>
This building of confusion is nothing other than a self-conceived state of grace, salvation, redemption, sanctification, and rebirth, which man establishes within himself and among other men to save himself from the state of sin, eternal death, and future damnation. Christ Himself compared this to a building (a) <note>Referring to the parable of the house built on sand versus the house built on rock.</note>.

Thus, every person's own conscience will tell them whether all their spiritual efforts are directed toward establishing a state of saving grace within themselves that might safely bring them to salvation.

And what is this state of grace, as it is erected by men, other than an empty form of godliness without the power of the Holy Spirit, who does not live, move, or work within it?

Through the Fall, man has lapsed from the love of God into self-love; he has grasped everything in the world with self-interest. By nature, he wants to be God himself, to provide for himself, and to be alone in being honored, cared for, and well-treated. He builds and makes his own things in the world, often under the pretext of God's name and Word—just as these people undertook such a significant work out of their own self-will.

Indeed, we may see from this ancient example—as if in a clear mirror of misery—what a plague and punishment it is when a person, left to himself, continues in his hardened self-will.

For what else arises from this but that they plague themselves with their own passions and emotions, and live in constant confusion, both outwardly and inwardly?

Thus, the departure from God's will is in itself pure confusion and brings nothing else but confusion.

The inherent confusion of unbelieving men is already unspeakably great, let alone when God's punishments and plagues are added to it.

But those who follow their own will and desires, and who seek something other in the world than God and His alone-good will, depart indeed from God's will.

We see in these builders of Babel how their earthly desires drove them to devise all sorts of new things, to seek more convenience for the flesh, splendor, power, majesty, and the like. Through this, they gradually fell into such a disordered state that they undertook the most foolish of things.

For could even a madman undertake anything more foolish than this: that he wanted to build a tower so high that it—

***Reaches unto heaven)*** Had this tower been built only as high as the sphere of the moon, its height would have extended to 44,668—or according to the opinion of others, 48,104—German miles <note>A "German mile" (*Teutsche Meile*) in the 17th century was approximately 7.5 kilometers, making these calculations astronomical.</note>.

If this were so, it must follow, according to some opinions, that:

1) If four million men had worked incessantly on this tower for a period of three thousand four hundred and twenty-six years, and the tower had been built one Italian mile in circumference every week, they still could not have finished it in that time.

2) If all the wood from all the forests on the entire earth were brought to one place and the whole world were turned into clay

<column-break/>

ven; that we make a name for ourselves, so that we are not scattered over the whole earth!"

made for bricks, and the great sea with all the lakes and rivers were prepared into pitch-glue; even then the wood would not have been enough to burn the bricks, nor the earth enough clay, nor the great world-ocean enough pitch-glue to provide for it.

3) If a rider covered 30 Italian miles every day steadily on a journey toward the top of this tower, he would still not have arrived there in 800 years.

4) This tower would have far exceeded the earth itself in weight.

Such fools did these people become while they considered themselves wise!

But what do all the others do, who clash together in great crowds and establish summary principles of Christian doctrine to which everyone confesses? Do they not claim in these things to show the infallible way to heaven and to bring men to the saving knowledge of God and Christ? Are they not presented, written, and printed for that purpose? Does one not think then that the "top reaches to heaven"? Should they not, in the end, lead to God and to Christ in heaven? So that your soul, when you die, might fly up in that very moment through the clouds and above the clouds to God.

Indeed, do not all such textbooks present themselves as guides showing the infallible path to heaven? And does one not see in their thoughts that if one fills the "main work" <note>Referring to the core of their intellect or a specific foundational text.</note> with their knowledge, one cannot go astray on the path to heaven? They hold these instructions to be so sufficient that the Holy Spirit is no longer necessary for enlightenment, beyond how He is already in the scriptures themselves.

What was and is the drive and motivating cause of the mad builders of Babel other than the great confusion into which pride plunged them, that they wanted to

***Make a name for themselves)*** Through this desire, they gradually forgot God entirely and fell from one foolish thing into another.

And so it still goes for all who do not follow the Spirit of Wisdom, but rather their own confused spirit and mind.

In particular, it is too obvious to see in pride how it can set a person into disorder. For, dear reader, where does all disruption, all misunderstanding, envy, and other unrest come from, if not from pride?

Without doubt, as Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> quite rightly holds, they bravely despised the small and low huts of the holy fathers and brothers compared to their magnificent building and looked upon them with scornful eyes.

And what is represented to us by this, other than that the fallen church has always had the greatest splendor before the true Church of God—like an outwardly beautiful white-washed tomb, which however looks all the worse on the inside. Whoever is infatuated only with the outward, pompous nature of the church has envisioned a tower in his heart alongside Nimrod and the Babylonians. When God shall and will show Himself gloriously in the outward realm, then the high towers must fall (a) <margin>(a) Isaiah 30:25.</margin>, and only hearts separated from pride can be there, who do not trample upon the "God in the house of Solomon" <note>Likely referring to the divine presence or the gold/sacred items in the Temple of Solomon.</note> with their feet.

As long as the Babylonian builders still have the upper hand, no temple will be built for God in which His name might dwell. They are only concerned with their own name.

And what kind of name is it that they strive for? Instead of God's name, they want to be called "believers"; they want to be "Christians," "members of Christ," etc., and thereby be distinguished from the heathens and unbelievers. They want to be the "true visible church," have the "right institutions of Christ," the "right worship," the "true and pure doctrine," be called "Evangelical," and whatever other such magnificent names and titles they strive for, assume for themselves, and adorn themselves with.

Mind, will, heart, all powers, thoughts, and senses—all agree that one is in a soul-saving state of grace and will soon enter heaven. And it is still always a very distressing sign when a person sets themselves so firmly in their desires that they cannot be moved from them. v. 7. Let us go down) Bruno of Segni (a) <note>original: "Bruno Astensis". A 12th-century Italian bishop and commentator.</note> understands this as referring to the angels, to whom GOD said: Go down, and bring me and my power with you, and do it in my name.

GOD certainly also meant the divine messengers or powers and workings through which He confused the people. The ancient Jews themselves have confessed that whenever it says in the Scripture, "Let us," it is always indicated that GOD spoke with His <term>Shechinah</term> <note>The dwelling or settled presence of God; often used in Jewish tradition to describe the divine aspect that can be perceived by humans.</note>, or with the Son.

The divine majesty makes Himself known, felt, and perceived in His holy judgments, when godless people will not believe in His presence until they can grasp it with their hands through His judgments.

# 8. So the LORD scattered them from there over the whole earth / so that they had to stop building the city.

He brought their minds into sheer discord / as He has all hearts in His hand and can steer them / so that various people opposed this violent and unjust undertaking / as the truth revealed itself to their hearts. He confused their language / so that they could not understand one another / and thus gradually became tired and weary of the building / and finally went apart from one another / and scattered over the whole earth / and thus withdrew from the [builders'] authority. See Acts 23:7. <note>In Acts 23:7, a similar dissension occurs between the Pharisees and Sadducees, thwarting a common purpose.</note> Since then, with time, in the families and nations living separately, the language also gradually changed / and so different languages arose.

That they had to stop) This follows naturally. The bond of their union was the common language. When this was taken / what else could arise but a heap of disorder / quarreling and strife: since / when one asked for a brick / the other brought water or glue / and so each thought the other was going astray. From the quarrel arose hatred and adversity: and so it was easily done / that they no longer needed to be driven to go apart from one another.

Is this then not a living image of the holy judgments of GOD / which He carries out among men!

But do we not also see a living counter-image in our times? How they teach out of a discordant heart; how each considers his own inventions to be the best / which others, however, do not want to accept; how that / which one establishes / is rejected by the other. One wants to assert this / the other that; each considers his own to be the best: as one sees among the scholars.

What a disruption there is in religions! How almost every man has his own God / whom he serves; also his own worship / which he considers the best! Whoever merely wishes to doubt him / he persecutes. No one wants to truly understand the other in love and wisdom / or at least receive and endure him. Whoever has the power / also presumes the right. Whatever he establishes / that shall count.

# 9. Therefore its name was called Babel / because the LORD had there confused the speech of the whole earth / and

Confused the speech of the whole earth) Each party has its own distinct dogmas: and these are for one "orthodox" or the pure doctrine and the right faith; and every other party is for this one incorrect / erroneous and heretical. What may be said of one / may be said of the other and so of every one. In these different party-matters and divided judgments / opinions / knowledge and self-conceit / each sect strives with great diligence and zeal to build itself up / and to unite in one or another confession of faith: which is their city / which they build. And with just as great vehemence they oppose all others / under the name of the world / of error / apostasy / and heresy. And what one party judges of the other / exactly the same the other judges of it. And in this way / notwithstanding that each party attributes the church to itself alone / they are all / through their mutual adverse judgments / one against the other / of the world. They have all gone astray / and have all together become useless: there is none / who worked good before the other; not even one. In this confusion and muddle, each divided party fawns upon and flatters the worldly authority / and strives to get it on its side: in order to / if possible / make it the proclaimer of its will. And this is their tower / by which they want to suppress / overpower and subdue all / who are of another mind / and do not want to help build.

Meanwhile one should note / wherein the difference consists. Not in who should be the most obedient / the holiest / most sober / most temperate / most just / most patient / most gentle and humble / most loving / etc.: but in a *form of godliness* / which consists in some certain ceremonies / or which each party has either invented itself / or gathered / mutilated from the Word of GOD; and then in a set of doctrines / which one regards / presents / accepts and worships as the pattern of wholesome words. <note>A reference to 2 Timothy 1:13.</note> These one then hedges and protects with all one's might / and each party would like all others to pay homage to it. And because none wants to yield anything to the other / there is no end to the bickering and quarreling. Here is Christ! says one: No! says the other; He is here! And so also the third and fourth. Each one cries: Here is the LORD’s temple!

But when GOD sends such a muddle / and makes people disagree; it does not happen as if He had pleasure in quarreling / but only so that the false peace and unity / or rather conspiracy / <note>original: "Conspiration"</note> of men against GOD might be broken / and His truth might triumph / and the righteous might become manifest.

GOD has many other kinds of scattering and confusion / which one may well perceive in daily life.

How many a Babylonian tower must fall again / or remain unbuilt / when GOD blows into it / and throws one Babel-builder here / another there! How certainly it is often said: Devise a counsel / and nothing shall come of it! <note>Refers to Isaiah 8:10.</note>

Although others believe that the ancient natural language is no longer among men; and that Hebrew, like the others, had its beginning from the confusion.

At the very least, today, due to the expulsion of the Jews from the Promised Land and other scatterings, a good portion of Hebrew itself has been lost. For in the books of the Old Testament, by no means everything that belongs to a language appears. In common civil life and households, and among craftsmen, many things occur that are not mentioned in Holy Scripture. The language is, moreover, concise and consists of few words.

Furthermore, that the Hebrew language is the first and oldest has been confirmed—beyond the usual reasons of scholars—by Helmont and Wagenfeil with two new and previously unknown proofs: by the former <note>Francisus Mercurius van Helmont (1614–1698), a natural philosopher who published "The Alphabet of Nature," arguing Hebrew letters represent the physical positions of the organs of speech.</note> in that our tongue always forms the shape of a Hebrew letter during the movement of speech, which he illustrates with copperplate engravings in his *Natural Hebrew Alphabet*; and by the latter <note>Johann Christoph Wagenseil (1633–1705), a Christian Hebraist.</note> in that one might invent a word however one wishes that means nothing in any language, yet one will always be able to find a meaning for it from the Hebrew language.

This much is beyond all doubt: that the Hebrew language, which flowed from the first pure light of wisdom, may still contain many hidden mysteries within itself, which will likely be better understood in due time.

<margin>v. 27. Fathered) That is, he *began* to father them. For they were not all three fathered at the same time. This is a manner of speaking, as in Chapter 5:32.</margin>

<margin>Abram) Just as the Lord was specifically the God of Shem, He also wished to propagate His church within Shem's lineage, and finally to awaken from it an Abraham, to whom He renewed the promise of the "seed of the woman" and established a special household of His grace among his descendants.</margin>

<margin>However, Abram was not the firstborn of Tharah, just as Shem was not the firstborn of Noah, even though both are named first because of their priority in grace. And since Abram traveled from his father’s house to Canaan immediately after the death of Tharah and was 75 years old at that time, it follows that he was born in the 130th year of his father, and thus may have been the youngest. Since there is a difference of 60 years in the chronology this way, this addition brings us closer to the 4000 years around which time the birth of Christ occurred; and thus the completion of the Temple falls right in the 3000th year from the creation of the world. This is the most remarkable thing: just as Noah was the tenth from Adam, so Abraham was again the tenth from Shem, the first ancestor of the believers after the Great Flood. Thus, an equal division of generations is to be noted: just as there were fourteen generations from Abraham to David, and from there to the Babylonian captivity, to Jeconiah (whose son did not come to the kingdom and whose brother Zedekiah was the last king of Judah), and from there to Christ (Matthew 1:17). Thus, everywhere from Adam to the "Second Adam" <note>A theological title for Jesus Christ, contrasting him with the first man, Adam.</note> in grace, there were 62 generations in those 4000 years. In the first 2000 years, there were 20 generations, and in the other 2000 years, there were 42; as 50 years pass for each birth, it likely hit the youngest through whom the line of birth for Christ was continued, just as Jacob and David were also the youngest.</margin>

## Chapter XII.

->Abraham’s Calling and Temptation in Egypt.<-

<margin>(a) 2 Corinthians 6:14 etc. Revelation 18:4.</margin>
**The** LORD had said to Abram: Go out (a) from your country and from your relatives and from

---

By this, it is made known how Abraham had already received this command to depart while in Ur of the Chaldeans, which was likely repeated later in Haran, where the land was then more specifically pointed out to him. Right at the beginning, Abram was assigned the general lesson of renouncing earthly things and human friends—just as Christ requires of His own in Matthew 10:37 and 19:29—so that love for and trust in earthly things might be extinguished in the partner of the Covenant and turned toward God alone.

To Abram) And also to us, if we are Abraham’s children. For "everything that was written before was written for our learning." Romans 15:4. And thus it touches our hearts much more sensibly than if we only viewed it as an ancient history.

Spoken) The ancients rightly believed that the Father spoke these and all other words to the Patriarchs through His Son, as through His eternal, self-existing Word.

Accordingly, the "speaking" here is actually nothing other than the living, essential Word—the Son Himself—through whom

<column-break/>

the Father made all His counsel known to mankind from the beginning.

It should surely be dear to us if our God and Creator still spoke His will to us today through His beloved Son. Indeed, it gives a person the greatest joy and strength when God deems them worthy to know His will.

But now, this eternal Word has never become silent. Hebrews 1:1–2. The Spirit of Jesus Christ will not cease to proclaim the Father’s will to us from His bosom.

Go) In Hebrew, this can also mean "Go into yourself" <note>original Hebrew: "Lech Lecha," literally "Go for yourself," interpreted here as a call to internal reflection</note>. This is a binding duty—namely, the self-reflection signified by it—which, though disregarded by most people, is always intended by the Holy Spirit through the prototype of the Promised Land. For:

This is an image of the calling of a soul to go out of itself. God speaks into the depths of the heart and shows it a different "earth" than the one in which it currently dwells; and that if the soul would faithfully follow Him in total surrender, He would not only show it that land but also lead the soul into it.

Out — out — out) With this, He cuts off all of the flesh’s attachments.

If God had only said, "Go out of your father’s house," then Abraham’s reason could have thought: "Well, then I may still cling to my other friends." If God had only said: "Go away from your relatives," Abraham might have thought he could remain in his fatherland and home.

But in this way, God wants to have Abraham away from all his fatherly things, from all pieces of his corrupted nature, so that he should keep nothing at all that could be seductive or harmful to his soul.

So God still deals with those He chooses from the world. When He sees a good spark in a person—a willing heart—or when He notices that the person secretly wishes to be free from the snares of the world and the enemy: then He takes hold and drives them to the renunciation of self.

He is not satisfied, however, with a person becoming free of one or two things. He wants the person to be truly free; He gladly tears all bonds so that neither fatherland, nor house, nor friends, nor acquaintances, and such like, shall capture them or draw them away from faith. "The Lord teaches us very clearly through Abraham to despise fatherland, friends, goods, and all wealth if we want to follow God, by making him a stranger," says Clement of Alexandria <margin>(a) Book 3, Paedagogus, chapter 2.</margin>. God wants to have you stripped of everything else. This is why you often feel such an urge within you, so that you can find no rest in any earthly thing. That should compel you to the resolution to gladly let everything go.

One will never let go of the least thing for God’s will, however, unless one first has the right foundation, which gives a person the desire and strength for it.

Therefore, do it also from a right foundation if you want to obey God’s voice in "going out."

Many a wicked person could otherwise appeal to this word and leave their spouse or their parents, whom they are duty-bound to support. There must necessarily be an internal, faithful renunciation and abandonment of the world as the foundation. There must be a spiritual going out and a separation of the heart before one can rightly leave the world with Abraham according to the Lord’s command. But what this consists of, the Lord Jesus has described very precisely, if only we would accept it.

The true "departure from Babel" <note>The author uses Babel as a metaphor for the confused and worldly life</note> consists in the withdrawal of your heart from the confused, disorderly attachment to the created thing.

But in your going out, keep your desire solely upon the eternal good; forget what is behind and reach for the prize. Remember Lot’s wife! Luke 17:32. Looking back is already not a true going out. For the desire still rules. And from what should one go?

Out of your country) Out of your "earth"—your earthly mind, your earthly wisdom.

Out of Ur of the Chaldeans) The "fire" <note>A pun on the Hebrew word 'Ur' (אור), which can mean light or fire</note> of the evil spirits. That land was and is defiled.

From or out of your relatives) Out of your troublesome companions, none of which are worse than your own fleshly senses, inclinations, and lusts—your self-centeredness and ego.

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

...from your father’s house (a); into the land that I will show you. Genesis 12:1.
<margin>(a) Ruth 2:11. Psalm 45:11.</margin>

2. And I will make you into a great nation (a), and I will bless you, and make your name great, so that you shall be a blessing.
<margin>(a) Chapter 13:14–16. 17:4, 5.</margin>

---

<margin>From your father’s house) He was to leave behind the idolatrous places and people (Joshua 24:2), so that he would not be maintained or strengthened in his innate false worship—or, if he had already left it, so he would not remain in danger of being further infected and led astray by it.</margin>

But do not think of this man alone! Or do you believe that you are by nature better than he and his ancestors? Why do you try so long to whitewash yourself and imagine you have an advantage over others, if you had remained stuck in a pagan mind and will until this hour? Galatians 6:15. Has not your conduct since then been mostly or even entirely empty, following the ways of your fathers? 1 Peter 1:18. Do you not still dwell in your father’s house, in the seat of the old, evil Adam? Are you not still stuck deeply enough in the abominations of paganism, even though you call yourself a Christian?

So then, you too must follow the voice of your **God** and go out! It is high time that you leave the old, fragile house of your old, sinful birth, which will otherwise collapse over your head! See, the whole world—and thus also your fleshly relatives, acquaintances, friends, and evil companions—lies in wickedness and burns in the fire of divine wrath. Do you wish to burn with them? Do you truly want to be damned along with the world? Do you not already have enough of your own ruin to carry? Do you also wish to share in the sins of others and maintain fellowship with the evil works of darkness?

It is high time to go out from the confusion of this wicked world, as if from Babel, and to leave all the disorderly desires of the fleshly mind that rules in the world.

And should a person still resist **God’s** counsel if **God** makes their previous life, evil company, or the world’s customs and follies seem worthless to them? In doing so, one leaves nothing behind but a stable full of "bad boys," <note>German: "böse Buben," a phrase implying wicked or unruly characters</note> a burning hell of unrest and God’s wrath, and a slough of all shame and abomination. Who should still hesitate to leave that!

And what more is it, if for the sake of **God** and our conscience we also leave and forget our relatives, acquaintances, and friends? This is intended for nothing else than that we should be taken into the true divine friendship and acquaintance.

If a person had such a pure and detached heart that they could be among all people without damage to their soul, then **God** would not have to make it distasteful to them, and would gladly grant it. But now that everything is poisoned by sin—all interaction, all friendship, and all love—a separation must necessarily occur before a person can become pure.

For once **God** wants to have the heart of man free and lifted up to Him again, so that He can possess it entirely and fill it with Himself.

But now the heart usually clings very strongly to fleshly relatives, to spouses, parents, children, and siblings. And therefore, this has been the general process for all believers: that for **God’s** sake, they have had to leave even their closest and most beloved friends.

Reflect for yourself on how necessary this is for our corrupted nature! How often must **God** tear two people apart by force, even taking one away through death, just so the other heart might finally turn back to **God**.

All of this would not be necessary if one sacrificed their relatives and friends to **God**, withdrew their idolatrous love from them willingly and in good time, and let their heart be cleansed of such idol-worship.

In the land that I will show you) "So that I may exercise your faith, and you may learn to cling to Me amidst all assaults."

It seemed very uncertain for Abraham how things would turn out for him. Hebrews 11:8.

In this way, **God** sometimes lets a person "dangle" <note>German: "zappeln," suggesting the struggling movement of a fish on a hook or a person in suspense</note> for a little while, showing no certain outcome during the time of testing.

Meanwhile, His word remains certain, and He Himself remains faithful. He must show the person’s faith another "place" where it should dwell, even if He does not let human reason know it yet.

Although the Lord did not yet cleverly name a specific place for Abraham, He promised him generally that He would show him one in the future where he should stay, and that He would also give it to him. And what is more, the Lord says further:

<column-break/>

This sounded magnificent, but it cost good Abraham many a difficult struggle before he experienced it. In the meantime, he knew why he was to leave what he currently had: namely, for the sake of a better and spiritual good. For:

We must understand **God’s** speech in a truly spiritual way when He speaks of a blessing and a great name; we must not think that **God** wanted to puff Abraham up or encourage him to strive for great worldly fame.

What kind of honor did Abraham actually have in the world? He was and remained a stranger all his life; he was considered a fool by others because he began a different way of worship and a different way of life than the pagans were used to. No doubt they also mocked him when he was willing to sacrifice his son. That was a "poor name" in the world's eyes.

**God** must then necessarily and primarily be looking at a spiritual name and glory: namely, that his example should shine before many thousands.

And so the blessing and the increase also aim more and primarily at what is spiritual and eternal, as the entire sequence shows.

**God** wanted to reveal His counsel to Abraham: how He intended to make him not only a physical father of many nations—from whom the Ishmaelites, Edomites, Amalekites, and the people of Israel descended—but that he should become a father of a great *spiritual* people. These are the people **God** would cause to be born again through His power, so that they would walk in the footsteps of his faith and thus be blessed with him, the believing Abraham. Galatians 3:9; Romans 4:12, 16. For when the young follow the example of the faithful elders and their teachings, they are, as it were, fathered by them in the spirit. Galatians 4:19; 1 Timothy 1:2. This blessing then indeed went first to the physical seed, even in the earthly, glorious land of Canaan; however, it primarily signified the spiritual blessing in heavenly goods in **Christ**, which was to come upon all the families of the earth, and thus also upon the Gentiles, Romans 4:17–18, and finally upon the full number of the Gentiles. Romans 11:25. And so he received the great name, being called "a Blessed of the **Lord**," a "Friend of **God**," and a "Father of the Faithful." And so he is the blessing in the one who was to be born from him: in **Christ**, who is therefore called a Son of Abraham. Matthew 1:1.

But how are we improved by this in our day? Answer: Very much, if we are only willing to recognize it.

**God** promises the soul that once it has reached the promised land—namely, the rest of **God**—it will have a great people and be glorified. And for all of this, He demands nothing from the soul except that it surrender itself to Him through self-denial and let itself be led by Him with a complete letting-go.

Do you not see how just **God** is in rewarding the good, how He leaves not the slightest obedience unrewarded? For even before Abraham actually departed, **God** already spoke to him of so much blessing. He also subsequently kept His promise so richly that even until now, and until the end of the world, Abraham’s blessing will not cease.

And with this, the mouth of self-serving reason is powerfully stopped—reason which is always worried that **God** will not keep His word, that it is in vain to serve **God**, and what help is it to lead a hard life before the **Lord**?

Oh, one should only dare to do it, and leave all the filth of this vanity with one’s heart! One will see, and also be able to tell others, how faithful **God** is in His promises and how surely He keeps them all.

The best blessing that **God** promised Abraham was and still is the true Messiah, **Jesus Christ**, the blessing of all nations. We should look for this and strive for this most of all. In Him lies everything a soul may wish for.

Learn only to truly trust and build upon your Redeemer, just as Abraham had to believe against all hope and sight; thus you will surely attain the blessing through the **Holy Spirit**. That will be better for you than everything you let go of in the world for the sake of your conscience.

It emphasizes that the ultimate fulfillment of God's promise to Abraham is found in Jesus Christ and the spiritual inheritance of all believers.</summary>

<header>Chapter XII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

### 3. And I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you: and in you shall all the families of the earth be blessed.

**I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you)** **God** takes it upon Himself, as it were, to pay close attention to everyone who has dealings with Abraham: and as they behave toward him, so will He also prove Himself toward them. To those who wished well and did good to Abraham, **God** will also do good: but to his enemies, He will also be an adversary. <note>original: "Wie 2. Mos. 23/22."</note> *As in Exodus 23:22.*

It sounds truly wondrous that **God** the Almighty attaches His blessing and curse, so to speak, to His believers, and thus wills to bless them not only for their own person, or family, or descendants, but even for others and strangers. *Whoever blesses them shall also be blessed.*

Who would not marvel that **God** takes such care of the person who surrenders to Him, that He Himself protects them in this way, and that for their sake He allows mercy to be shown to many others, and marvel at the blessing which such a person draws upon all people devoted to him! This is so essential and true that those who have some experience in this will rejoice to hear it under these images, and will stand in utter amazement when they see the natural order in the Old *Testament* in which all this is expressed.

This wonderful speech of **God's** should necessarily give all people a desire for a true divine walk and life, if they would take it properly to heart.

What else does this show us but the great bliss of fellowship or friendship with **God** and a godly life, and its high importance—how blessing and curse, life and death, for ourselves and others, hang upon it.

**God** looks so sharply upon His chosen friends that He notices exactly what happens to them, and how others behave toward them.

The blessing and wealth of the fullness of **God** in *Christ* is so unspeakably great and high over His believers that it also spreads to others who wish to have a part and fellowship in that very same grace. There is a multiplying power in faith unto many thousand-times-thousand, where it can become mighty in a soul.

On the other hand, the curse or the damning judgment of **God** also certainly enough hits all those who do not want to keep fellowship or unity with **God's** friends, and thus do not want the blessing that was nevertheless intended for them too.

**In you)** As the root of the noble branch and sprout, the *Messiah*, from whom He was to come according to the flesh—namely, from Abraham’s humanity, which was again blessed and sanctified by **God** through faith, and therefore chosen for such a high work. In faith he was made worthy that from his loins the tender, pure humanity of *Jesus Christ* should come forth. It came from the deep ground that **God** could say: In you I will bless the nations. Just as if Abraham were such a Savior or *Jesus* who could bless all people; which he was not in himself: but he was so through faith, as the forefather of the *Messiah* according to the flesh.

In the external person of Abraham, all people could certainly not have or find blessing. He died just like the others, and his descendants were also miserable, oppressed people. Thus **God** primarily meant the internal man: that person should spread out through the power of faith in the life of **God**, and become such a tree whose fruits would be countless and immeasurable.

**All the families of the earth shall be blessed)** The poor creature surely has a most high need of it, since it lies so very deep under the curse and wrath of **God**. This high necessity also drives the Creator to bless us again in love and goodwill.

Oh, may one learn to truly taste, experience, and even grasp with one’s hands, as it were, how friendly the **Lord** is, how full of blessing His blessing mouth and His sharing hand are! It is certain that one will wish to remain in His blessing forever.

May one learn to know **God** rightly, and so one will also learn to know His blessing—how infinite, how exceedingly precious it is.

Blessed is he who rightly grasps it! He will no longer go out, but will remain in the Father’s house, and be blessed forever and ever.

<column-break/>

### 4. So Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken to him: and Lot went with him. And Abram was seventy-five years old when he departed from Haran.

### 5. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their possessions that they had gathered, and the souls they had begotten in Haran <gloss>(a)</gloss>; and they departed to go into the land of Canaan; and they came into the land of Canaan. <gloss>(a) ch. 14:14.</gloss> <note>The "souls they had begotten/acquired" often refers to servants or those Abraham had won over to his faith.</note>

### 6. And

<margin>(a) Book 4, ch. 12.</margin>
Quite rightly, says *Irenaeus* <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>Irenaeus was a 2nd-century bishop and theologian; here the author cites his work "Against Heresies."</note>, he left all earthly kinship and followed the word of **God**. He was a stranger with the Word, so that he might also remain with the Word.

So Lot also wished to participate in this blessing, and went along voluntarily: and he indeed attained it, and **God** delivered the righteous Lot. *2 Peter 2:7.*

If you also wish to inherit the blessing in Abraham, as a father of the faithful; then step here into his footsteps, and thus begin the spiritual pilgrimage.

<margin>(b) Heb. 11:8.</margin>
Through faith he became obedient to **God** when he was called to go out, and he went out, not knowing where he was going <gloss>(b)</gloss>. See, your **God** also demands such simple obedience of Abraham from you, that you provide proofs of obedience to Him. It will soon be revealed whether you have faith or not. If you do not actually follow the pull of the Holy Spirit, then faith is vain. For that is not how Abraham did it. He became obedient to **God** when He called him. Thus you can best recognize your faith by the actual following.

Faith makes a person so faithful in obedience that he sets out and follows blindly with Abraham, whether it be pleasant or painful to the flesh, or whether the world approves or rejects it. He goes straight forward within the bounds of obedience and looks neither to the right nor to the left. He looks only to **God’s** command and calling. If he is certain of this through the Holy Spirit, he has enough *instruction* <note>original: "Instruction"</note> to go where the **Lord** sends him and do what He commands. This is because faith brings his eye to simplicity, so that he speaks and acts only directly according to the trail of the divine Word, and does not think about what people will say, or what harm or benefit it will bring, etc.

Oh, let everyone wrestle for this golden foundation of all spiritual things, that he may learn to preserve and maintain faith and a good conscience! Let everyone seek with unceasing prayer to obtain the Holy Spirit, as the Spirit of faith, from the Father! He must place the heart in a good trust toward **God**, and so hang upon **God** that it learns to venture everything upon Him, and does not consult long with reason or the flesh where nothing but the obedience of faith is necessary.

Abraham is a certain model for you of what must become of you. You also must become truly obedient to the word of the **Lord** in faith, otherwise you will not attain the promise of the blessed seed of Abraham for your person in particular. But if He finds you in such a believing mind, then the blessing can also be spoken into your heart.

Abraham's precise obedience indicates the swiftness and faithfulness with which the soul must go out from itself in order to follow **God**.

Although the promises of **God** are not always fulfilled according to the sense of the one to whom they were given, they are nonetheless infallible. Those who have some assurance and internal words at the beginning and during the inner guidance must neither stand still in them, nor judge them, nor make any interpretation of them. The truth of these words is in **God**, and they do not become true for us until their fulfillment, which is often entirely contrary to our previous imagination of them.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

6. **And Abram passed through the land to the place of Shechem, to the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanites were in the land at that time.**
7. **Then the LORD appeared to Abram and said: To your seed I will give this land. And there he built an altar to the LORD, who had appeared to him.**

This indicates his crossing over the Jordan, just as Jacob also had to cross this river. <note>original: "c. 32 / 23. 24."</note> *See Genesis 32:23-24.* There he had to begin his pilgrimage and wander from one place to another: according to Hebrews 11:8-16. This is where the thoughts of all believers must aim when they are forced to wander from place to place. See 1 Peter 2:11 and Hebrews 13:14.

He had to venture among the crude Canaanites and rely on divine protection and guidance. Wherever he stayed, even for a short time, he made it his first concern to erect an altar to the Lord, in order to perform his sacrifices in faith in the promise of the *Seed of the Woman* <note>The "Seed of the Woman" is a traditional Christian term for the Messiah, based on Genesis 3:15.</note>—which is the source of all blessing—and thereby also to instruct his household in these divine mysteries. See Chapter 4:26 and 18:19. Through this, the Canaanites were undoubtedly enticed to recognize the true God and the service pleasing to Him. For this is God’s ultimate purpose when He leads believers among a crude crowd: that they should be moved and guided to the knowledge and love of the truth by the believers' edifying conduct. See Philippians 2:15 and 1 Peter 2:12.

**v. 6. [In the land]** Nicolaus Damascenus <note>An ancient historian and philosopher who was a friend of Herod the Great.</note> in Book 4 of his *History*—cited by V. Brand, Professor of Mathematics at Marburg, in his 1684 *Geographical Disputation on the Pilgrimage of Abraham* <note>original: "Disputation geographica de Peregrinatione Abrahami"</note>—holds the view that Abraham stayed for a while in Damascus, where the main road and highway from Haran to Shechem usually goes. This is because his oldest servant, Eliezer, was a native of that city. Abraham was allegedly even made a king there, according to the custom of the land at that time, and ruled for a while; although the inhabitants eventually begrudged him such great dignity. He refers in this case to Chapter 14:13-24.

**[To the place of Shechem]** Or rather, the region where Shechem was built later. For, as is held, it was not yet built then, but only later by Shechem, the son of Hamor (Chapter 34). It is also said to have been called Salem and Sychar.

**v. 7. [To your seed — this land]** As the seed is, so is the land. The seed of Abraham according to the flesh received an external land according to the letter; and the seed of Abraham according to the spirit—namely, Christ in His believers—receives possession of the land of Canaan according to the spirit, of which the former was only a figure and prototype. And what kind of land is this? Answer: The inner new earth, of which the Lord made so many promises. 2 Peter 3:13, Isaiah 65:17, 66:22. And what is this new earth? Answer: Renewed humanity, the new body of glory, when the corruptible puts on the incorruptible; the land of holiness, the promised inheritance for which believers wait, and of which the future earth (still to be renewed externally and according to the letter) will be an image.

**[Altar to the LORD who appeared to him]** This altar, which Abraham erected at the place where the Lord appeared to him, teaches us that one must always sacrifice back to God all the graces He gives us. This must be done at the very place where He gives them; for we must not accept them as anything other than to faithfully send them back to their Source. There are few souls who act like Abraham. Each person appropriates God's gifts for themselves and keeps them for their own.

This sadly goes so far that people are often distressed when He takes them back to Himself. They accuse Him as if He had robbed them of something that was theirs. Yet He takes nothing but what belongs to Him. If we did not possess these gifts as if they were our own property, we would pay little mind even if God withdrew His graces. And like some, we would not only let them be taken from us, but on the contrary, we would pass through them all while obtaining them. One finds nothing but people who complain about the withdrawal of comfort and "sensible graces" <note>A term for spiritual feelings or emotional closeness to God.</note>; they present this as a great suffering, and yet it is nothing other than a great self-loving sense of possession.

You will no doubt say that you are not distressed by the withdrawal of these gifts, but that you fear you may have brought this upon yourself through your unthankfulness. Oh, natural craftiness, how well you can hide under all sorts of excuses! If the fear of our unfaithfulness distresses us so, dear brothers, let us instead be all the more humbled by the unfaithfulness which caused God to deal with us in this way; and let us nonetheless be joyful that He strips us of His goods, and does not give them to us for the very reason that we might not misuse them. We must also have a holy joy that He vindicates His own rights. This is the true state of a humble soul. Thus, instead of daily grieving and complaining over these withdrawals, one must rather be humbly cheerful and never desire anything more than what one already has.

<column-break/>

8. **From there he moved on to a mountain east of Bethel and pitched his tent, having Bethel on the west and Ai on the east; and there he built an altar to the LORD and preached of the name of the LORD.**
9. **Then Abram journeyed on, continuing toward the south.**
->Proverbs 4:18<-
10. **H<unclear>ap</unclear>** <note>The text breaks off at the start of verse 10, likely referring to the famine that "happened" in the land.</note>

**v. 8. [A mountain]** Which was later called Ephraim.

**[Bethel and Ai]** Were situated only one mile from each other.

**[Built there — an altar]** To indicate his progress from one sacrifice to another.

**v. 9. [Continuing toward the south]** By which it is made known that he passed through all things in order to reach God alone.

Abraham was first in Shechem: that is a "part" or a "piece." He could not hide or rest in a part or a piece, because he aimed for perfection.

Oh you son, you daughter of Abraham! Do not establish your rest in Shechem—in some partial stage or degree of holiness! The Lord has promised the whole holy land to Abraham and his seed forever. Pull up your tent pegs! Do not dwell in that which is changeable! Follow your father Abraham, just as he followed God, and go forth to perfection!

Suppose one of us had a long journey to take, and yet a short time to complete it; and, if we did not reach the end within that time, not only all our effort but also our life would be lost: Oh, how early we would be up! How we would hurry! How precious every moment would be to us! But do we not have, like Abraham, a long journey—out of the land of the Chaldeans, the fire of the devils, toward the land of Canaan, to the inheritance of the saints in light, into the land of holiness? We are all, like Abraham, called to this by God! But the Lord alone knows how much of our journey is still remaining! Yet our lives testify all too clearly that few have even found the entrance to the narrow and small way. How much less have made any progress in it! And how little of our time may be left! If we do not complete our journey, then all our trouble and work is lost! The gates of the holy city will be closed against us!

<page-num>87</page-num>

### Chapter XII. The First Book of Moses.

<margin>(a) Matthew 2:14.</margin>
10. But a famine came into the land. So Abram went down into Egypt to dwell there as a stranger, for the famine was severe in that land.

11. And it happened, when he was close to entering Egypt, he said to his wife Sarai: "Look, I know that you are a woman beautiful to look upon."

12. "And it will happen, when the Egyptians see you, they will say: 'This is his wife'; and they will kill me, but let you live."

13. "Please say that you are my sister! So that it may go well with me for your sake, and my soul may remain alive because of you."

---

<margin>Psalm 105:14-15; Matthew 10:16; Chapter 26:7, etc.</margin>
Abram's faith had to be tested through various trials, and he had to venture even among the Egyptians. He allowed himself to be moved by a simple kind of prudence <note>The German "einfältige Klugheit" suggests a wisdom that is clever but remains innocent or guileless.</note> to have Sarai pass herself off as his sister. His intent was to escape the initial heat of such fleshly people, thinking they would rather seek her hand in marriage through the brother’s favor; he trusted that God would help him out of the danger at the right time. It then followed that they envied one another, and the high officials judged that such a beautiful person should be brought to the King alone (just as such things often give Kings great occasion for lustful pleasures). But God's providence watched over her protection and kept the King and his household from his intention to marry her by means of all kinds of plagues, such as sickness and the like. This "serpent-wisdom," when joined with "dove-like simplicity" <note>A reference to Matthew 10:16: "Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves."</note> and sought from God through prayer, eventually achieves a good outcome. And even if something of human weakness should slip in, God’s mercy knows how to turn it to the best for His own; as it also happened to his son, Isaac. Therefore, whoever wishes to use serpent-wisdom must guard against the false trickeries of the deceitful heart and walk in the fear of God: thus he will be rescued from danger among evil men through God's mercy.

<margin>v. 10.)</margin>
When God wishes to spread His word and knowledge, everything must serve and help toward that end. Just as later in the stories of Jacob and Joseph, the famine served as a means by which Joseph—and afterward Jacob—was placed "on the lampstand" <note>A metaphor for being put in a position where their faith is visible to all, based on Matthew 5:15.</note> in Egypt, giving them the opportunity to let their light of faith and fear of God shine in the midst of darkness: so too was Abraham driven into Egypt by this same famine. As seen in these twelve successive chapters, Abraham had to change his dwelling fifteen times as a true pilgrim, so that he might sparkle there like a star of the first magnitude. One might well say that all believers and children of Abraham walk this same path; for the sake of the "famine" of God's word and the pure understanding of it, they find themselves in the land of tribulation—which is spiritually called "Egypt"—and must bear their witness there. Even if their light of faith often suffers a period of darkness in the process, it is certainly necessary that they take even deeper root in faith and the knowledge of God, learning to know and grasp Him as the "All-Sufficient One." Thus, they need fear no creature, nor can any famine truly harm them, because they may always have enough in and with God. Even a forsaken soul must remain faithful on this ground, just like Abraham, so that she does not take fright in the dry times, even when she encounters nothing but affliction and suffering on the path where it seemed God would grant her nothing but sweetness. She must follow God tirelessly through bitterness, without ever stopping or losing heart.

<column-break/>

14. And it happened, when Abram came into Egypt, the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful.

15. And the princes of Pharaoh saw her and praised her to Pharaoh. Then the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.

16. And he treated Abram well for her sake: so that he received sheep and cattle and donkeys, and male and female servants, and female donkeys and camels.

17. But the Lord plagued Pharaoh with great plagues, and his house, for the sake of Sarai, Abram's wife.

18. Then Pharaoh called Abram and said: "Why have you done this to me? Why did you not tell me that she is your wife?"

19. "Why did you say: 'She is my sister'? Because of that, I wanted to take her as my wife. And now, look, there is your wife: take her and go!"

20. And Pharaoh commanded some men concerning him, that they should escort him out, with his wife and everything he had.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

---

<margin>v. 15.)</margin>
Once and for all, we must note that the name "Pharaoh" was not a specific surname, but a common title for all kings in Egypt, much like the honorary name and official title "Emperor" in the Roman Empire.

<margin>v. 17.)</margin>
God disciplines Pharaoh for an innocent mistake, which seemingly should have been attributed more to Abraham than to Pharaoh. And He rewards Abraham despite what appeared to be a real sin according to human reason. Who can search out the secret judgments of God? But who can also marvel enough at the security of "yieldedness" <note>The term "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of total surrender to God's will, common in Pietist thought.</note> when things look most dangerous for it? Ah, God rescues both the life of Abraham and the honor of his wife for the sake of the faith of this man, who had entirely surrendered himself and his wife to Him.

---

<margin>v. 11-13.)</margin>
This error apparently committed by Abraham—in that he seems to use a degree of pretense and puts his wife's honor at risk to save his own life—shows us, through the use God makes of it, His care. It shows how God Himself may correct the errors and deviations caused by the fear and weakness of such souls, provided they do not step out of their state of surrender nor leave the path God taught them once they gave themselves to Him. This divine conduct toward Abraham and this permission [of the trial] appears so wondrous to those who stand in the light of truth that infinitely many books would be needed to set it all out at length.
