# Chapter XIII.

->Lot’s Separation from Abraham.<-

**S**o Abram went up from Egypt, he and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, toward the South <note>The German "Mittag" literally means "Midday" or "Noon," but historically refers to the cardinal direction South, where the sun is at its highest.</note>.
2. And Abram was very heavy with livestock, with silver, and with gold.
3. And he went on his journeys from the South even to Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at first, between Bethel and Ai.
4. To the place of the altar which he had made there before: and there Abram preached concerning the name of the **LORD**.
5. And Lot also, who went with Abram, had sheep and cattle and tents.
6. And the land could not support them dwelling together: For their possessions were great, and they could not dwell together.

<margin>
v. 1-4.) There is nothing in the Holy Scripture which does not have an excellent meaning. It is written that Abraham went toward the South. Namely, he always went—as already said—toward God. Nevertheless, it says that he came back by that same way from the South to Bethel. What does this mean now? There seems to be a slight contradiction here, though none is to be found. For all paths lead to God. The one who stops at nothing, and makes use of everything he encounters and meets in order to run quickly to God, will surely find Him.

Furthermore, it says he was very rich: yet he carried that wealth to the place of the altar; that is, he offered it up to God, and drew near to Him through the path of abundance as much as through the path of want. Everything was for him one and the same way to call upon God.

Believers should view wealth as a burden that tends to stir up all kinds of strife, if not within ourselves, then among our people; whereby the mind is also weighed down. But whoever views wealth as a pleasant burden and is greedy for it will easily be sunk into destruction and damnation (1 Timothy 6:9). But if wealth comes from the blessing of the **LORD**, as this physical wealth was promised to Abram (chapter 12:2), then believers seek to resist all its temptations—which in the end bring nothing but pain (Proverbs 10:22)—just as here Abram carefully sought to avoid the strife that had arisen.

Wherever Abram went, he sought above all things to spread the Kingdom of God, and through public preaching of the name of the true God and His promise, to lure and build up others as well (Chapter 4:26, 12:8, and here v. 18).
</margin>

<margin>
v. 5.) Excessive inner wealth <note>The commentator implies that material abundance can overcrowd the "inner room" of the soul.</note> diminishes the peace and unity of the servants, namely, the inclinations of the mind. They hang upon and rely on such things: and by tasting them, they cause imperfect desires.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 6.) Just as believers must not become overly burdensome to one another, so must they not do so to strangers: as Abram may have been wary of the Canaanites, who held the land, so as not to be a burden to them.
</margin>

<column-break/>

7. And there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram’s livestock and the herdsmen of Lot’s livestock. At that time, the Canaanites and Perizzites also dwelt in the land.
8. Then Abram said to Lot, "Dear...

---

All strife regarding earthly things must be carefully avoided by believers, as it withdraws God’s blessing from us: and here they must consider every means to remove it, even by renouncing their own rights. In this, the elders must give way to the younger, and the great to the lesser, behaving more sensibly than the others.

Abraham’s behavior here must be viewed with enlightened eyes and spiritual understanding; how, under the deep governance of divine wisdom, he pursued peace and thus wisely wound his way through this evil world, so that he kept his faith and peace until the end.

Whoever desires may learn here how a Christian in this wicked world, among so many temptations of his soul, must take such careful heed that he can pass through without damage to his soul and reach the goal.

If you wish to know how to manage it, then, to pass through the world with peace and without harm, do exactly as Abraham did. But learn to look right into his heart, to see how his mind stood then; he did not merely act on his outward words or works. Such important matters require a deep foundation of faith.

Abraham knew in the Holy Spirit and was assured that God calls and places people—and him as well—out of the fire of wrath into the kingdom of His love and rest.

What a noble and precious jewel <term>Kleinod<gloss>A "Kleinod" is a precious jewel or treasure, often used metaphorically for a spiritual gift of great value.</gloss></term> true peace of soul is, Abraham knew all too well; and God had given him much to recognize and also to experience of it. At a mere word from his God, he had left everything and gone away from his fatherland and his kindred into a foreign land. God is accustomed to rewarding such obedience with great peace and deep contentment in faith, despite all the outward hardship of life.

Now, however, a hard temptation arose with his friend, which seemed to threaten his peace. He and Lot had many people around them because of their goods. The multitude gradually caused strife among their people, and this threatened to provoke and tempt the minds of the two masters as well.

Abraham knew and saw beforehand what shipwreck he would suffer in his faith and the peace founded upon it should the strife break out. Therefore, he must have often approached and asked God for good counsel, which God faithfully gave him.

And so you too must learn to preserve the jewel of peace, especially during such provocations to strife. Guard yourself against all confusion and all causes of it. Conceive a true horror of all disruption and disorder of your mind. Seek to be well with God and to remain in a quiet conscience and an unshifted, gentle, and still spirit. Do what you do without the heated confusion and haste of nature, so that you may always be bright and cheerful in your mind.

If you first truly come to know and value that deep peace of soul which guards heart and mind in Christ, oh, then you will uphold it and guard yourself in every way against its destruction! Oh, how you will speak with truly careful earnestness and struggle, both with heart and mouth, at any concern of an emerging quarrel: **"Dear, oh..."**

<header>Chapter XIII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

# Please, let there be no strife between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen! For we are brothers.

->(Please, let there be no strife between me and you!)<-

<margin>Ah yes, do not let your soul be woven into the fire of adversity: otherwise you will perish in it.</margin>
Abraham had experienced how blessed one can be in peace; he also knew what a consuming fire of Satan strife is. Therefore, he pursued peace so longingly.

And if you have experienced or seen in others how strife and discord are a living hell for people, you will surely shrink from such fire like a burnt child. But if you do not yet believe it, and have no right loathing for it (as the fiery nature easily thinks it has the right to it), then believe wise people who have described it so horribly! <margin>James 3:6.</margin>

Abraham knew this terrifying enemy well: therefore he armed himself against it with love and yielding. He set his heart entirely upon peace, so that he might not fall into that restless evil.

And this deed of his has been so blessed that it remains a precious model to this day for all who wish to pursue peace.

For true Christian peacefulness consists in this: that one seeks unity with Abraham in every way and manner pleasing to God; and not only for oneself, but also for others. Just as here Abraham also gladly created and maintained peace for Lot and his people.

A very certain sign of true peacefulness is actual love and willingness to serve one's neighbor.

Many are so self-loving that they ask nothing of the other's welfare, as long as they can live quietly for themselves: the neighbor can stay wherever he wants. Abraham could also have thought this way, if he had wanted to follow a wicked nature: "I will see how I can get rid of Lot; he can look out for himself." Instead, he sought with all his heart his brother's well-being as much as his own, and therefore enjoyed not only external peace, but primarily the peace of conscience; he also made his brother and his whole house partakers of the same.

This can be seen in his heroic deed, which he proved in the following chapter, when he rescued this very Lot with the sword from the hand of his enemies who had captured him. How could he have shown greater faithfulness!

The driving motive why we should go through this valley of misery in peace is added by Abraham.

"We are brothers!" Behind this stated reason lies more hidden than one can ever fully grasp. It refers primarily to the "new birth" and thus to God's own work in the soul.

Not that Abraham should not have aimed at physical kinship here—that as such close relatives they should love one another—but this ground of kinship applies and binds even more in a spiritual sense.

It is settled that we humans all come from one ancestor, and that we are therefore all brothers and closely related by nature; consequently, based on this ground, we should apply ourselves to peacefulness.

Those who are truly born again through the Holy Spirit and do true repentance <note>original: "wahre Busse thun"</note> are newly related to one another according to the Spirit or the new life which they have received from God for the divine nature.

Whichever ground one takes, one sees oneself obligated to keep peace with one's fellow man. For he is closely related to us, and is also as near to God his Creator as we are.

It is only right, therefore, that one should recognize and look upon one's neighbor quite differently and more deeply according to his condition than commonly happens. Most judge by appearance and do not respect contemptible, weak, and poor people, easily attacking them, quarreling and striking out at them. But one does not consider that in this, one has to do with God; that the other is so near to God and has the same right as we do, and that he sighs to God, and the Lord hears his cry. He is your brother; consider it well! Whatever you do to him, happens to God, who is his Father. Even if he is not yet fully converted, pious, and good following a rebirth, he is still your brother by nature. You cannot deny that. You will not be able to overturn the foundation of creation with disgusting pride when your poor, miserable neighbor stinks to you. It does no good; you will have to recognize him as your brother before God's judgment when you are judged over your dealings with him!

Oh, where the Spirit of Christ truly unlocks this mystery of spiritual kinship, there true peace and tolerance must necessarily flourish and triumph over all self-love and lust for strife!

<column-break/>

# 9. Is not the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me! If you go to the left, I will turn to the right: or if you go to the right, I will turn to the left.

<margin>Matthew 5:39.</margin>

# 10. Then

Abraham, who had peace both with himself and with God, could not suffer the strife between his relative's and his own herdsmen; and especially concerning that which they both possessed from God alone, since his wealth clung so little to him that he was willing to give it up a thousand and a thousand times over. His self-denial and <term>Gelassenheit: a key pietist concept meaning "yieldedness," "calmness," or "letting go" to God's will</term> were so great that he let his nephew <note>The original German "Vetter" can mean cousin or kinsman; here it refers to his nephew Lot.</note> have the choice, even though it belonged to Abraham by right.

The origin of all anger, strife, and ill-will is "Mine and Thine," or that everyone wants to have, maintain, and defend his own.

Through the devil's envy, man has fallen into such a shameful spirit and self-interest that he wants to miss or let go of nothing of his own. He scrapes and scratches together whatever he gets, sets his mind firmly in it as his own proper good, regardless of the main business in the world consisting of honor, goods, and pleasure.

Now if someone comes and disputes that with him, or wants to take it from him, then desire stirs up anger, anger gives birth to scolding, quarreling, and fighting. There the fountain of great misery is before one's eyes.

And how may one now escape this? Truly, in no other way than through the opposite. If love for temporal things or for yourself has brought you into strife and anger, then self-denial must bring you out again.

This is what Abraham did. When he saw how the herdsmen quarreled over a bit of earth and earthly things, he lifted all this up through true renunciation of it all, so that he gladly yielded to his brother Lot and left everything open to him.

He, as Lot's father's brother <note>Abraham was Lot's uncle.</note>, would have had good reason to point him away and dismiss him immediately. But he did not do that, but sought with the greatest modesty to win Lot’s mind, offered to yield himself, and would rather let something happen to himself than push and annoy the other with impetuosity.

He did not consider it too much for his honor that he should yield to his younger relative. No doubt many an ignorant person laughed at him for subjecting and humbling himself. For it seems quite foolish to many that for the sake of peace one should take something upon oneself, not turn everything into a fight <note>original: "zu Polken drehen," an idiom meaning to descend into chaos or blows</note>, but rather suffer damage, shame, and everything, just so that one might keep peace of mind.

It certainly sounds contrary to flesh and blood, but it is nonetheless our calling, the teaching of Christ and his Gospel, and the most correct way of peace.

If you now want to follow the perfect counsel of your God and Savior, as well as the example of Christ, you must learn with Abraham to cast everything else aside, so that you only rescue what is right.

O we poor blind people! How hard it is until we learn just enough wisdom to prefer the best over the least! Let alone that everyone should learn to wind and press himself so innocently through this evil world that he does not forfeit his highest good and best part!

WHAT will it help us now if we had all the money, all the honor, all the pleasure in one lump together, and yet did not take part in the deepest rest of the soul with God and men!

Blessed is he who no longer claims any of his own in the world, but has it as if he had it not!

10. Then Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole region of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere. Before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, it was like a garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt as you come toward Zoar.
11. Then Lot chose for himself the whole region of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed toward the East. <note>original: "gegen Morgen," literally "toward the morning," an archaic German term for East.</note> Thus they separated, each one from his brother.
12. Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelt in the cities of that region and pitched his tents as far as Sodom.
13. But the people of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the Lord, exceedingly so.

---

<margin>verse 10.)</margin> The highly blessed fertility of the region around Sodom, as well as that of Egypt, is indicated here; these lands watered themselves through blessings from above without any special effort from men. Just as the Nile <note>original: "Nilus"</note> in Egypt is said to overflow at certain times of the year and make the land fruitful. For this reason, some wish to place Paradise there, and others here. However, the more blessed the lands are in earthly things, the more the corruption of men manifests itself; they misuse such blessings in luxury <note>term: "Uppigkeit" - here meaning excessive indulgence or sensory distraction</note> and thus become guilty before the Lord, provoking His heavy wrath against themselves. Lot, and likewise Ishmael and Esau, looked around for the possession of lands and took them for their descendants. Even today, people like to look around for a "fat" place and do not realize how they might be entering a Sodom; for the most fruitful lands are commonly filled with the greatest sinners, as men "kick out their heels" <note>An idiom suggesting rebellion or arrogance</note> when they become fat. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob remained as strangers in Canaan and let themselves be satisfied with the promise. We should also do this, and not strive so much after these earthly goods, so as not to be woven into the sins and debts of men: but rather strive for the promise of the new heaven and the new earth, in which righteousness dwells. <margin>2 Peter 3:13.</margin>

<margin>verse 11. Chose)</margin> Lot, who was distant from the faith, the self-denial, and the unburdening of Abraham, chose for himself the most delightful place. How many people are there who seek only the delight of the spirit in the service of God: whereas they should seek nothing in it but death, self-denial, the cross, and bitterness. The outcome will show that it was more beneficial for Abraham to surrender himself to God than for Lot to choose for himself.

<margin>Separated -- from)</margin> It is indeed praised as fine and lovely when brothers dwell together in harmonious love: but if such harmony cannot be maintained, or if it does not serve to further one’s race toward eternity, then separation is certainly better. For

God does not stop at drawing the soul out of itself: He also separates it from everything that could hold it back, no matter how good it may seem; just as Abraham could have been held back from the way of God by Lot, through the love he bore for him, or at least run the danger of acquiring some self-complacency in his company.

are to Him. Instead of the forsaken children and cousins, [He gives] a pure multitude of spiritual children again; just as it is promised in Isaiah (b): "Sing, O barren woman, you who do not bear! For the desolate one has more children than she who has a husband."

<column-break/>

14. And the Lord said to Abram, after Lot had separated from him: "Lift up your eyes now, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward.
15. For all the land that you see, I will give to you, and to your offspring, forever." <margin>chapter 15:1-5, 21.</margin>
16. "And I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth. If a man can count the dust of the earth, then shall your offspring also be counted." <margin>chapters 12:2; 13:16; 15:5; 22:17.</margin>
17. Arise...

---

God gives the promise to Abram here not only of the land of Canaan, but since he must turn toward the four ends of heaven, the whole earth can also be understood here, which God will give to the spiritual seed of Abram in Christ, as He will give him the ends of the world for a possession. <margin>Psalm 2:8.</margin> And so then the promise is also given here to Abram that he should be an heir of the world: <margin>Romans 4:13.</margin> which will only be fulfilled in Christ's glorious kingdom. Meanwhile, he was to wander through the land in its length and breadth as a stranger during his life, and hold fast in faith to the promise: for which reason God would not let him possess even a foot’s breadth of his own, so that he might walk by faith alone and leave the fulfillment of the promise entirely to God. See <margin>Acts 7:5; Hebrews 11:13.</margin> This should be a lesson to the believers of the New Testament: that even when they do not see the slightest bit of the future glorious promises, they should look through and contemplate them in the spirit, which they will experience hereafter: just as Abraham will have already experienced the possession of the land of Canaan in his spirit.

Oh, what a great goodness of God it is, which immediately repays a soul that denies itself in some thing for His sake! With what friendliness He speaks with Abraham as soon as he has parted from Lot! A good thing often hinders the communication of God and disturbs the course of God's grace when we rely upon it. The promises made to Abraham were only fulfilled (a) four hundred years after the time they were given to him according to the letter, and after many battles between the people of God and their enemies: so that we might learn from this not to attach any [limited] sense, nor time, nor manner, nor anything fixed to the words spoken in the hearts of God's servants internally.

<margin>verse 16.)</margin> God is wonderful in His rewards, even if they are only physical. He measures them, as well as the eternal ones, according to the measure of the self-denials that occur for His sake. Abraham is no sooner removed from his cousin to do the will of God than God promises him, for the sake of the sacrifice of a single person, the greatest lineage that ever was. This great nation was given to him because of this first self-denial, just as the offering of Isaac deserved to have Christ Jesus in his lineage. As soon as we distance ourselves from creatures for God's sake—be it from friends according to the flesh or from imperfect spiritual friends—God gives us a countless multitude of other friends who are our friends in Him; and those whom one has left for the sake of His love, He returns as an innumerable multitude of spiritual children; just as it is promised in Isaiah (b): "Sing, O barren woman, you who do not bear! For the desolate one has more children than she who has a husband."

(a) <margin>Acts 13:20; Galatians 3:17.</margin> (b) <margin>Isaiah 54:1.</margin>

### Chapter XIV.

->Lot’s Rescue from the Enemies.<-

<gloss>The very remarkable stories of Holy Scripture contain a hidden archetype <note>original: "Fürbild," a typological precursor</note> of the end times, so that the believers might have instruction for their comfort from them. Ten kings appear in this chapter, of whom one ruled over most, and one was a righteous and peaceful king, in whose land—as many believe—Abraham stayed with his family. In the end times, there will also be ten kings who will for the most part give their strength and power to the beast: Revelation 17:12, 13. # The First Book of Moses. Chapter XIII.

10. Then Lot lifted up his eyes and beheld the entire region of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere. Before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, it was like a garden of the Lord, even as the land of Egypt, as you come toward Zoar.
11. Then Lot chose for himself the entire region of the Jordan, and Lot journeyed toward the East <note>original: "gegen Morgen," literally "toward the morning." In older German, the directions were named after the position of the sun: Morning for East, Evening for West, Midday for South, and Midnight for North.</note>. Thus they separated, each from his brother.
12. Abram dwelt in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelt in the cities of that region, and pitched his tents as far as Sodom.
13. But the people of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the Lord, beyond measure.

---

<margin>v. 10.)</margin> The highly blessed fertility of the region around Sodom, as well as that of Egypt, is revealed here; these lands watered themselves through blessings from above without extraordinary human effort: just as the Nile in Egypt is said to overflow at certain times of the year and make the land fertile. For this reason, some wish to place Paradise here, and others there. However, the more blessed a land is in earthly matters, the more the corruption of men manifests itself; they misuse such blessings in luxury <term>Uppigkeit: a term implying both physical excess and spiritual arrogance</term> and thus incur guilt before the Lord and provoke His heavy wrath against them. Lot—and likewise Ishmael and Esau—looked around for the possession of lands and took them for their descendants. People also like to look for a "fat" place to settle, not knowing how they might stumble into a "Sodom," for the most fertile lands are commonly filled with the greatest sinners, as men "kick out their heels" <note>an idiom meaning to become rebellious or insolent</note> when they become fat. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob remained as strangers in Canaan and let themselves be satisfied with the promise. We should do the same, and not strive so after these earthly goods, so as not to become entangled in the sins and debts of men; rather, we should strive for the promise of the new heaven and the new earth, in which righteousness dwells. 2 Peter 3:13.

<margin>v. 11. Chose)</margin> Lot, who was far removed from the faith, the self-denial, and the detachment of Abraham, chose for himself the most delightful place. How many people are there who seek only the delight of the spirit in the service of God: whereas in that service they should seek nothing but death, self-denial, the cross, and bitterness. The outcome will show that it was more beneficial for Abraham to surrender himself to God than for Lot to choose for himself.

<margin>Separated -- from)</margin> It is indeed praised as fine and lovely when brothers dwell together in harmonious love: but if such harmony cannot be maintained, or if it does not serve to further one's race toward eternity, then separation is certainly better. For

God does not stop at drawing the soul out of itself: He also separates it from everything that could hold it back, no matter how good it might seem; just as Abraham could have been held back from the way of God by Lot, through the love he bore for him, or at least run the risk of gaining some self-complacency in his company.

God gives the promise to Abram here not only of the land of Canaan; rather, since he must turn toward the four corners of the heavens, the whole earth can also be understood here, which God intends to give to the spiritual seed of Abram in Christ, since He will give him the ends of the world for a possession. Ps. 2:8. And so the promise is given to Abram here that he should be an heir of the world: Rom. 4:13, which will only be fulfilled in Christ's glorious kingdom. Meanwhile, during his life, he was to wander through the land in its length and breadth as a stranger, and hold fast in faith to the promise: for which reason God would not let him possess even a foot's breadth of his own, so that he might walk by faith alone, and leave the fulfillment of the promise entirely to God. See Acts 7:5. Heb. 11:13. This should serve as a lesson to the believers of the New Testament: that even when they do not see the slightest bit of the future glorious promises, they should see through them and contemplate them in the spirit, which they shall experience hereafter: just as Abraham must have already experienced the possession of the land of Canaan in his spirit.

O, what a great goodness of God it is, which immediately rewards a soul that denies itself in any matter for His sake! With what kindness He speaks with Abraham as soon as he has parted from Lot! A "good thing" often hinders the communication of God and disturbs the course of God's grace when we rely upon it. The promises made to Abraham were only fulfilled (a) four hundred years after the time they were given to him according to the letter, and after many battles between the people of God and their enemies: so that we might learn from this not to attach any specific sense, nor time, nor manner, nor anything fixed to the words which are spoken inwardly in the hearts of God's servants.

<margin>v. 16.)</margin> God is wonderful in His rewards, even if they are only physical. He measures them, as well as the eternal ones, according to the measure of the self-denials which occur for His sake. No sooner is Abraham removed from his kinsman in order to do the will of God, than God promises him, for the sacrifice of a single person, the greatest lineage that ever was. This great nation was given to him because of this first self-denial, just as the offering up of Isaac merited having Jesus Christ in his lineage. As soon as we remove ourselves from the creatures for God's sake—be it from friends according to the flesh, or also from imperfect spiritual friends—God gives us a countless number of other friends, who are our friends in Him and
which one has left for the sake of His love, He gives a count-

# Ch. XIII. The First Book of Moses.
<sig>M 2</sig>

17. Arise, and walk through the land, in its length and in its breadth. For I will give it to you.

18. So Abram moved his tents and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is by Hebron, and built there an altar to the **Lord**.

---

The land which **God** promised to Abraham was not only this material earth which he could see; rather, it was also the earth *of his heart*, as the reward for those who are of a meek spirit <note>A reference to Matthew 5:5, "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth."</note>. It was as if **God** had said to him: Now, since your heart is free from everything that could hold you to the earth, it shall possess itself in a complete freedom, which will have as few boundaries as your eyes find in this wide earth which I have reserved for you. And just as you can see nothing here but what belongs to you, so you are the lord over all things through your faithful self-denial.

<column-break/>

The Plain of Mamre by Hebron) This is said to be a valley nearly a quarter-mile before the entrance to the city of Hebron, more than a quarter-hour wide but much longer; very fertile, beautiful, and pleasant, and also planted with vineyards from which very precious wine came. It was otherwise full of terebinth <note>original: "Eich-Terpentin," likely referring to the *Pistacia terebinthus*, often translated as oak or turpentine tree in older bibles.</note> and fir trees. Beyond this, a particularly beautiful tree is said to have stood there, which remained green winter and summer, and whose fragrant sap was healing in all kinds of medicines; no one was permitted to chop it down, and Abraham is said to have lived by that very tree.

In the end times, there will also be the ten kings who will mostly give their power and might to the Beast: *Revelation 17:12–13.* For they will stand under the authority of a powerful one among them; from which some will then withdraw and fight against the Beast with those who remain faithful to it. # The First Book of Moses. Chapter XIV.

10. And the Valley of Siddim was full of bitumen pits <note>original: "Harz-Gruben," referring to the naturally occurring asphalt or tar pits common in the Dead Sea region</note>. But the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah took flight, and fell there: and the rest fled to the mountains.

12. They also took Lot and his goods, Abram’s brother’s son, and went away. For he dwelt in Sodom.
13. Then one who had escaped came and told it to Abram the Hebrew. For he dwelt on the plain of Mamre the Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and the brother of Aner: and these were Abram’s allies.

---

<margin>v. 12. They also took Lot)</margin> Abraham is rewarded because he had separated himself from Lot: but Lot is punished because he had involved himself with the world <note>literally "given himself over to" or "associated with" the people of Sodom</note>. People who leave everything for **God’s** sake receive new glimpses of grace from Him, as well as great peace and rest. But those who withdraw themselves from the godly through self-interest or mistrust receive nothing but war, confusion, and punishment as their reward. Lot represents those who separate themselves from faithful and surrendered people so that they may live in perceived security in the "fortified city" of human reason and worldly institutions, relying on created things. It is as if they were not equally in danger there—both because of the fickleness of created things, which cannot support them, and because **God** justly leaves them to themselves since they think too highly of their own judgment.
Oh, take note of this, O soul, what it is that still often—indeed, for the most part—holds you captive! How is it that you are not truly free and powerful over all that is evil and impure; that your desires and impulses are drawn so strongly into the earthly and the visible? How often does now pleasure, now fear, steal the strength of your will! How strongly reason often takes you captive when you ought to obey **God** more than men! How the false will tears you away toward useless and even harmful things! Oh, what a wretched slavery and captivity this is!
<margin>v. 13. Hebrew)</margin> One who, as Philo explains <note>Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who interpreted the name "Hebrew" as "the one who passes over."</note>, has passed over from the state of sin and corruption into the divine nature; who has gone from Ur of the Chaldeans—which is the "fire" of evil spirits—into the land of holiness.
->Mark your duty, O you children of Abraham, who call yourselves believers!<-
<margin>v. 14-16.)</margin> The help which Abraham gave to Lot shows the care that surrendered souls have for those who distance themselves from them.
<margin>v. 17. Returned from the slaughter of the kings)</margin>
<meta>catchword: And</meta>
The entire course of events that happened here with Abraham presents us with a portrait of a true warrior of Christ.
As children of Abraham who do the works of Abraham, we have kings—that is, ruling lusts—to slay. These are the "many lords" that have ruled over us. <note>References to Isaiah 26:13 and Romans 6:12 regarding the mastery of sin.</note>

<column-break/>

14. Now when Abram heard that his brother was taken captive, he armed his trained servants, born in his own house <gloss>(a) ch. 12:5. (b) Josh. 19:47.</gloss>, three hundred and eighteen, and pursued them as far as Dan <gloss>(b)</gloss>.
15. And he divided himself against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, which lies to the left of Damascus;
16. And he brought back all the goods: and also brought back Lot, his brother, and his goods; as well as the women and the people.

When the believers are under pressure, **God** the Lord will awaken Saviors who will judge the hostile mountain of Esau, which consists of the worldly kingdoms. <note>Obadiah v. 21</note>. These, with the assistance of the Lamb, will overcome these kings and especially the head among them, the spiritual Chedorlaomer—a name which means "a host surrounding the sheaf" (see Job 15:24)—where the "sheaf" is understood as the company of believers bound together in the Spirit, who are persecuted far and wide by this tyrant in the latter days. <note>Revelation 17:14</note>. And so this "Gog" shall fall upon the mountains of Israel. <note>Ezekiel 39:4</note>. And this shall be done through the saints, who shall have sharp swords in their hands to execute vengeance upon the heathen and punishment upon the peoples; to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with fetters of iron; to execute upon them the judgment that is written. Such honor shall all his saints have. Hallelujah. <note>Psalm 149:5-9</note>. This will then be like the wonderful battle Gideon fought with his chosen 300 warriors against the Midianites, when he fell upon them in the night and put them to flight. <note>Judges 7</note>. And here the believers will carry out judgment on their enemies in the true King's Valley, as in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, or the Valley of Judgment: <note>Joel 3:12, 14</note>. So that it will finally become a Valley of Blessing <note>original: "Lobe-Thal," literally "Valley of Praise"</note>, as in the days of Jehoshaphat; <note>2 Chronicles 20</note> where the defeated kings will bow before them. <note>Psalm 72:9-12</note>.
Nephews <note>referring to Lot’s relationship to Abram</note>, show the care that surrendered souls have for those who distance themselves from them, and how they do not fail to assist them in their need.
However, no one should imagine that Abraham, the friend of **God**, conducted war in the same manner as is done nowadays. People vainly excuse and flatter themselves with Abraham's example, but they will not escape **God's** judgment for their unjust bloodshed. Abraham fought neither for honor, nor for land and people, nor for money and goods: but solely and only for the rescue of his brother. He was not concerned with becoming a great and rich lord in the world: for his walk was in heaven, and his honor was in lowliness. He was concerned only with the rescue of his kinsman. And so he did it out of righteous zeal, which **God** demonstrated through his hand against these robbers, punishing them for his servant's sake. When he had performed that, as a holy and righteous will of **God**, Abraham returned again to his place.

# 18. And Melchizedek / the king of Salem / brought forth bread and wine. And he was a priest of the Most High GOD.

->19. And<-

Melchizedek / the priest of the living GOD / must alone bless Abraham : because he alone knows and approves of the pure and high path of self-denial <note>original: "Verläugnung"</note>.

Regarding who he was / there are all sorts of opinions. Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus," a 4th-century Church Father</note> accepted as a truth through a report from the Jews / and others followed him in this / that Shem <note>the son of Noah</note> was Melchizedek. And indeed / what is disputed in the letter <note>referring to the literal historical identification</note> / is resolved in the spiritual sense. The true Shem is the true Melchizedek. Isaiah 32 / 1. 17.

If we were to cite and learn all the opinions of the learned and all their disputes over this matter / as there are entire books available / it would help us little / and would not give a single drop of strength to the soul / indeed it would rather unsettle the mind even more. We would linger on the husk <note>original: "Hülfe," likely a variant of "Hülse" meaning the shell or chaff</note> and miss the kernel.

Rather, let us look with earnestness for the right jewel / which is offered here to our souls; namely the divine priestly office of our Savior / who wants to help us to the right and righteous state before GOD / and who creates peace for us in and with the Father in Spirit / as a King of Righteousness and Peace.

But Abraham was not gifted by this royal priest until the enemies were overcome. And likewise no one among the souls will be crowned / unless they fight properly.

We must first lie well in the field <note>a military metaphor for being on active duty</note> with and for the Lord Jesus / and renounce our friendship with the Devil; if we wish to taste and see how friendly he is. He wants to test us first / and see what we are willing to risk for his sake / or not / and whether we can also endure with him / before we reign with him.

Not / as if he just took pleasure in letting us struggle with the enemy : but there is the highest necessity why it cannot be otherwise. Lot is captured by the barbarian peoples : the poor soul lies buried so deep in unrighteousness / that it cannot be redeemed otherwise than through a great struggle. Not to mention how the enemy lies in wait for you / to rob all faith from your heart / to darken your love for GOD / to weaken the zeal in prayer / the bold hope in his grace / the gentle patience in suffering / etc. / or at least to make them waver. Should it not be a matter of fighting then? And even if you thought you dwelt as securely as Abraham / the enemy can soon come upon your brother and neighbor / and strike him / for whom you are indeed obligated to wrestle.

Abraham had grasped a righteous and great zeal against the robbers / and might have attacked vigorously and exhausted himself with his men. Upon such a righteous struggle Melchizedek met him. And

When we show true earnestness and zeal in wrestling against all evil / the Savior also recognizes us as his true and good warriors / and comes toward us with his love in our innermost being / to refresh us / to support us / and to awaken us anew.

For we must not think / as if a true Christian could have no other spiritual strengthening and refreshment / unless he always seeks it outside himself in this or that external practice.

All means of grace are in themselves precious and good / and not the least is to be despised / in which GOD has placed a blessing. Meanwhile / a true divine faith stands through the Holy Spirit with unmoving eyes upon the beginner and author of all salvation himself / as upon the true High Priest / and learns to take the right life from him himself. Therefore it says : he

**Brought forth**) He has his seat in the innermost and holiest place / into which he does not enter publicly / and after a short time go out again / like Aaron : but he is led in secret behind the curtain / and remains hidden behind the same / until Abraham comes from the battle : then he carries it out / because Abraham with his seed may not step behind this curtain / although Aaron himself is still in his loins <note>a reference to Hebrews 7:10, suggesting the priesthood of Melchizedek is superior to the later Levitical priesthood of Aaron</note>.

Melchizedek has here neither meat-offering / sacrifice of slaughter / nor burnt-offering : but he carries out all those powers and blessings / which Christ [attained] through his bitter

<column-break/>

suffering and death with his blood and death / and so long unceasing intercession / as well as all the members in him distinguished, prayed for, and obtained from GOD through the service of Aaron. Which inexpressible goods of grace have been represented under the images and figures of the most excellent essences of food and drink; namely

<margin>(a) Herberger in the Handbook. Hutter. Book I on the Mass. chapter 6. Walther. Biblical Office. p. 759. <note>original Latin: "Herberger in Manual. Hutter. l. I. de Miss. c. 6. Walther. Offic. Bibl. p. 759." These are references to 17th-century Lutheran theologians</note></margin>
**Bread and Wine**) Some wish to prove the Papal Mass from this text: but others (a) maintain very well / that / although the Church Fathers, such as Augustine and others / interpreted this bread and wine as the Lord's Supper / this is nevertheless only a mere allegory or comparison / but not a true prototype; because it is nowhere expressly confirmed as such in the Scripture.

The narrative shows this much / that this king fed Abraham with his people / that they ate their fill and were refreshed : but not / that he perhaps only offered a little bit of baked flour with certain ceremonies / and let the people go away hungry again / or fed them with mere imaginings / as happens in the so-called Mass.

O you children of the lineage of Abraham! arm yourselves with that very same mind and faith / which the father of the faithful had. If we hold ourselves bravely / then the true Melchizedek / the High Priest of the most high GOD / will also come toward us / present his bread and wine to us / and serve us : Luke 12 / 37. the true bread / which strengthens the heart of man; and the true wine / which gladdens it : the food of eternal life / which <unclear>there</unclear> is on the table for the believers; but only for those / who overcome the world.

Without overcoming we may not count on this friendly welcome and hospitality. But if we shall one day have overcome all our enemies through the faith of Abraham / and now return victoriously from the battle; then this Melchizedek will certainly emerge in our innermost ground / bring the heavenly bread and the wine of the power of GOD into us / and bless us in the highest GOD / who possesses heaven and earth : so that we will be able to speak and testify of it from sufficient experience. For who can say / how sweet bread and wine taste / and what powers they have / who has not yet tasted and tried the same in such a victorious state of faith?

Oh let everyone learn to rightly know him who can satisfy his soul even in all struggle! We know not / when the evil hour comes / when we may well need this Bread of Life. If Christ wants to be our priest / and constantly reach us his bread of immortality; oh how should we then not always hunger and cry : Lord give us always such bread!

Yes he will / when you are chased weary like a deer by enemies / and cry to GOD in your soul for fresh water / and thirst for the living GOD / instill in you not only water of some refreshment / but also the wine of joys. Just endure the struggle honorably / and let all false bread out of your mouth! then you will perceive at the right time the meeting with GOD your Savior.

Just pay attention / whether he does not sometimes powerfully soothe your heated and troubled nature again / turn your sorrow / and pour heavenly power of life into your innermost being. That is certainly nothing other than the reconciling love of GOD / which became man in Christ / and has trodden down the wrath.

Then the soul receives again the power of the divine light / and puts it on for a new joyful life of faith. Then GOD's image is set up again in the same / and the thieves and murderers / who had robbed you of your dearest brother / your spiritual life / must perish / and leave you your salvation as prey.

For Melchizedek was not satisfied / that he only brings Abraham outward strengthening / but he also meets him with overflowing blessing in the spiritual / as a priest of GOD the Most High / and proved his priestly office upon him in that he blessed him.

## 19. And he blessed him / and said: Blessed be Abram to the Most High GOD / who possesses heaven and earth!

**Blessed)** Through a public, solemn blessing and consecration / by which he wished him all good / and at the same time sanctified and surrendered him to the Lord.

These are all uncommonly precious encouragements of faith / for whoever is able to grasp them.

From this blessing, a conclusion is drawn in Hebrews 7:7 <note>The biblical text states: "And without all contradiction the less is blessed of the better."</note> because the lesser must necessarily be blessed by the better and greater / meaning that this Melchizedek must have been no small thing before GOD. And who else could it have been but the Son of God himself? Who is also called Melchizedek / as the true Solomon / whose kingdom is built in peace: wherein the blessing of the same chiefly proves its power.

The blessing was necessary for this reason: because Abraham had pursued the enemies with the sword / and stood in great zeal against them / whose blood he had shed: so that he might not always remain in such zeal out of human weakness / but rather return to love and gentleness / and thus come to rest.

And so also the eternal High Priest <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the fulfillment of the Melchizedek figure.</note> always meets the fiery nature in his believers with his blessing / softening and stilling the same / and making them partakers of love. But especially, he incessantly meets the righteous anger and wrath of the Father on behalf of all people / stilling and holding it back / so that it cannot devour or consume us.

O, what a great wonder and mystery of Christ in us! Our entire well-being or woe depends upon how we truly grasp and experience this in deed / or not. Whoever does not allow this to be fulfilled in themselves / remains locked and buried in death and in the dark, anxious fire of wrath.

We must not think / as if a person need experience nothing of the high-priestly reconciliation and blessing of Jesus Christ in and of themselves: or as if he only sat alone up there in heaven at the right hand of the Father / praying for us; but did not come closer to us / so that we ourselves might notice something of it.

We do not have such a wretched Savior. The right hand of GOD is everywhere / in heaven and on earth. And therefore we must receive / feel / and enjoy the blessing of our High Priest in our own hearts. Indeed, everything depends upon this / that this high-priestly office be gradually fulfilled and accomplished through the Spirit of Jesus Christ in each person specifically through actual application.

All those / who are concerned for their salvation / shall also experience in time / how powerfully they are continually blessed and surrendered to the Father by their Savior / the eternal High Priest.

Jesus Christ meets all repentant, believing sinners in their souls / just as Melchizedek here met Abraham / and pronounces the promise of life over them / that they shall again be in grace and blessed with the Father. That is truly no mere imagination / but they are purely great works / which must occur in such a soul / if it is to be blessed.

There, the High Priest must offer up the desire of faith and the good will of a soul to the Father / so that it becomes a rich blessing for its conversion / and the image of GOD can be restored within it. This is the mystery of this prefiguration.

And thus everything aims at the complete offering up of man to GOD. Then GOD in turn has honor from him / as His renewed creature.

For such a work, the whole heart of our eternal High Priest burns with longing / to see us thus sanctified to the Father / so that he may be praised in and through us for all the victory / which he himself has wrought / since he has given our enemies into our hands / namely sin and death / which shall no longer rule over the one who believes / because he is under grace.

It is good and certainly necessary / that one also be a good steward in temporal matters / so that the miserable and needy are served thereby / and one enjoys or has nothing / of which the poor neighbor does not also receive his portion for his necessity.

But the Holy Spirit aims here at something much deeper. The tithe must be booty captured from the enemies. And what kind of booty do you have / when you have fought in faith against sin? Is it not your soul itself / which you bring away as booty? See, this shall be the tithe / which you shall give to your eternal Priest / with all the qualities and powers of your soul.

One cannot believe / how pleasing such tithes are to GOD / how His desire of love / which He has for us / as it were triumphs and shouts for joy / when it can so empower the soul / that it can grasp and take captive the will.

This is enough to recognize / because the person himself is set in true peace upon the honest surrender to God. That is a sign / that God's righteous claim is silenced and stilled.

May the Spirit of Jesus Christ take possession of many hearts / so that they leave themselves entirely to him and surrender to his possession; so that not only the tithe / but everything that is on / in / and with us / may be appropriated to the Father / be and remain / in the eternal King and High Priest Christ JESUS forever and ever!

**21. Then the King of Sodom said to Abram: Give me the souls / but take the goods for yourself.** <note>The "souls" here refers to the people of Sodom who had been captured and then rescued by Abram.</note>

**22. But Abram said to the King of Sodom: I have lifted up my hand to the Lord, the most high GOD / who possesses heaven and earth;** <note>"Lifting the hand" is a traditional gesture for swearing a solemn oath.</note>

**23. That I [will take] from a thread even to a shoe-latchet / yes, that I [will take] of everything**

<meta>catchword: that</meta>

---

Abraham had recognized and found a much better portion. He had also rightly measured the deception of temporal things / and thus did not wish to weigh down his soul with earthly filth and sand. He had his daily necessities: and so his spirit yearned for God alone.

This offer from the Sodomite king was a temptation from the World-Spirit: he noticed this immediately through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, he resisted these false powers in faith / which sought to stir his natural desires toward greed / and he made a resolution / to let himself be satisfied by his God alone.

He appeals to his wealthy God: who possesses heaven and earth. He will indeed / he means to say / give me enough food and clothing / so that I have no need to turn my desires toward another’s property. Everything is His, after all: and if I have Him / then everything that is His is also mine. He is my Father; so I, as a child, have a claim to His goods. I rely upon that.

To this wealthy Lord I lift my hands / and take Him as a witness against your and my natural greed / that I will not take even a shoe-latchet / which is but a small thing! What use to me is this junk and earthly burden / when I seek an entirely different treasure? Would I be one moment more blessed / if I possessed it?

No, dear King! Keep your gifts for yourself / and give your presents to another / who loves and esteems them. In my eyes, wealth is like filth in the streets. I do not worship such idols. Thank God, I know the living God: He is my all in all.

Thus heroically did Abraham reject the flattery of the world and its goods.

But he also had a righteous reason for doing so.

The people among whom he lived were unbelieving / and thus false and cunning. They would have gladly boasted / as if they had made Abraham rich / rather than God having blessed him. Abraham saw this in full wisdom / and looked into their wicked hearts / how they would gladly rob God of His honor / and make themselves great thereby / as if they were Abraham's God.

Oh, if only one could look rightly into the believing heart of this Father of the Faithful / how it must have burned with love and delight for God; how everything else was like filth and nothing in the world to him; with what joy he trampled these things underfoot and scorned them! Certainly, one would also become eager / to set out upon such a joyful path of faith!

What a precious advantage it is for converted souls / that they do not need to seek their satisfaction in so many countless vain things of this world / and thus do not have to wander far abroad / but can find all good things so near to them / yes, within themselves in God Himself!

If only everyone could recognize it so precisely / and use it so earnestly / just as this all-sufficient Good wishes and offers them! It is a pity / and it grieves God greatly / that so few believe it / let alone ask after it!

But what is the cause of such blindness and carelessness / other than the false pleasure that man places in the creature / where he feeds himself on fantasies? One is so easily satisfied and calls oneself blessed and favored by the possession and enjoyment of visible things / even though one knows / that they will pass away tomorrow. Thus, foolishly, one keeps oneself away from the Truth / only to give honor to the False.

How can a heart be satisfied and filled with the best portion / if it rests in foreign goods? One

must give way to the other. Where love of the world reigns / there love for God is finished.

Afterwards, one must experience how faithlessly all temporal things act / how nothing holds up in a time of need / and how no creature can so fully satisfy and fill the soul / that it does not always long for more. For whoever loves the world is never satisfied with money / and the spirit drives him to seek ever more.

It is no wonder / when true children of God find such sufficiency and fullness in their God / that they gladly do without other things and can be at rest.

O, if one has only first rightly sought the all-sufficient God / then this is not difficult / but becomes possible and easy through the Holy Spirit in faith!

How else could Abraham have rejected with such joy such a considerable booty won from the enemy and the greatest gifts offered to him / if he had not already become full and rich in his God.

But Reason thinks: Oh, that was easy for Abraham / that he took no gift; he was already rich / and had enough.

However / whoever rightly knows true faith / and on the other hand also the nature of greed; he will judge such a work of faith quite differently.

Is it not so / that the more a natural man has and receives / the thirstier he becomes for money and goods? One sees it clearly in experience. This is because / a greedy and world-loving heart is a bottomless abyss / that can never have enough. And furthermore, worldly things are so vain, unstable, and fleeting / that they can never fully calm and satisfy an immortal soul. Therefore, a man who hangs his heart upon them / always floats in the desire to have more / and consequently in unrest.

On the other hand, whoever lets himself be satisfied with what is there / does not look further for more / but allows the ground of his heart and its space to be filled with God's love. Because the heart always wants to have something / on which to satisfy and hold itself; thus a believer stills all thirst with the true fountain / from which everything else flows. And

Even if the mind wishes to wander through temptations / and fall upon this or that in the world; God allows a soul yielded to Him no peace therein. It must tear itself away with its heart / even if it must happen through many crosses. <note>The "cross" here refers to trials, suffering, or divine discipline that breaks worldly attachments.</note>

Let one judge now / whether it should not also have been difficult for a wealthy Abraham according to nature / to scorn temporal things / if he had not had faith.

Certainly, without faith it would have been impossible for him: he would have allowed himself to be taken captive and carried away by temporal goods / so that he would have lost God over them.

However / since he thus in faith esteemed all things as filth / and so magnanimously rejected / what others seek with great desire; he received a far better portion in exchange. For he was deemed worthy / that God Himself in His most high person offered Himself to him / to be his essential reward; as we shall hear in the following chapter.

The magnanimity of resigned <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>Gelassenheit is a key Pietist term meaning a state of total surrender and inner stillness before God.</note> souls / who walk in the way of faith / consists in this: that they despise all wealth and the sustenance of their own powers; so that they may have God alone. They cast everything away: and while they raise themselves into heaven through a holy boldness / they find nothing outside of God that is good enough for them; because God / as their only treasure / makes them rich of Himself.

**A**fter these stories the word of the LORD came to Abram / in a vision / and said: **Fear not / Abram**

After these stories) Abraham received an exceeding encouragement from his eternal Creator.

So very precious and important was the jewel / which GOD offered here to Abraham / that He Himself in His highest person and in a special, friendly manner presented it to him. For it

The word of the LORD came to Abram) To whom this happens in such a way / he must truly be accustomed to GOD and His address / and be well-known and familiar with Him as a friend. Numbers 12:6. <note>The author highlights the intimacy of the "Word of the Lord" coming to a person, comparing Abram's relationship with God to that of Moses.</note>

In a vision) This was a night-vision. For it is then that the stars are seen / and GOD gladly reveals secrets at such times.

And said) How sincere and lovely His love breaks out here toward Abraham! What kindness and unspeakable faithfulness is to be recognized here in Him / by those who can look, as it were, into the heart of dear GOD through the Holy Spirit!

His heart inclines so powerfully toward His believers / that He cannot look upon their misery for long: He soon breaks out into the most blessed and kindest encouragements.

Yet He hardly leaves any person in the world / without sometimes reminding them and seeking to set them right: how much more then should He encourage His friends and lovers / and maintain them in faith. For He has His delight to be with the children of men / and speaks gladly with them / as one friend with another / though in many different ways. <note>This "delight" is a common pietistic reference to Proverbs 8:31, emphasizing God's desire for relationship with humanity.</note>

But if we wish to rightly enjoy His comforting address ; then we must also be / like Abraham / making ourselves well-acquainted with GOD : so that He, as a father, can promise His children all good things / and also keep them.

Since Abraham waited upon GOD with an honest heart / and had turned his desires away from the world and from himself toward the Heavenly ; behold, he was then more worthy to behold GOD and hear His voice.

That GOD’S holy address and fellowship is now so very unknown / yes, even contemptible / among people ; for that, unbelief and ungodly conduct are to blame. People are generally only intent on what is visible / and hardly take the time to spend even fifteen minutes in prayer. Therefore, GOD finds neither heart nor ears / which He could fill and possess with His holy word.

But whoever now wishes to be certain of divine love / and to have a right ground of faith in times of need and death ; let him hand over his heart to the Spirit of GOD / accustom himself to look upon his Savior with a simple eye of faith : then many a comfort and address / many an instruction and good report / will fall to his lot on his pilgrim-way / for which he will praise the LORD.

Abraham undoubtedly received such firmness, strengthening, and delight in GOD through this vision / anew / that in the strength of this food he could go forth and finish his course.

Even if you do not obtain such an extraordinary address from GOD right now / you still have a surer prophetic word / to which you should pay attention / that it may become a light to you / and show you the morning star itself. <note>A reference to 2 Peter 1:19, encouraging readers to trust the Scriptures as a reliable source of revelation even without mystical visions.</note>

If you diligently cling to GOD in your soul / His Spirit will make all the promises of GOD "Yes and Amen" in Christ JESUS / to the praise of GOD. There the Scripture will be opened to you and GOD’S will become so clear / that for such a sealing of the Holy Spirit you would not take all the world’s goods.

And so the word of the LORD still happens daily to His own / who are of the faith of Abraham : as GOD repeats, makes living, and bestows His revealed counsel and will to them always / as they have need / so that they can take certain steps / and not run toward uncertainty / or risk it on mere hearsay.

But what does the dear GOD, the highest good, preach now to a believing soul? Of what does He assure it most? Answer: Of His all-sufficiency <term>Allgenugsamkeit: the theological concept that God is enough to satisfy every need and desire</term> / how the soul already has so much in Him / that it has no need to wish for anything else or better for eternity : how one can have enough of everything in GOD / if one wishes ; protection against evil / and the foundation for all good.

<column-break/>

One might think / Abraham could have become secure based on the victory he had obtained : however, it must be that shortly thereafter a particular concern overcame him again.

The true Father is very careful over His children : He does not let them go on safely for long / but always sends them something again / in which they shall be exercised in faith / and not become proud.

Doubtless something must have occurred in dear Abraham’s soul / that sought to drive him into anxious fear. And indeed, it must have been something internal. For external accidents and changes the Scripture generally relates. But internal sufferings and circumstances it seldom mentions by name / because they are also more indescribable.

There the heavenly Father saw His child stuck in anguish / and His heart broke for him.

Oh, how the Father-heart of GOD lies open there / for whoever wishes to recognize it! How busy He is / to bring man out of his torment! For the dear GOD is not served at all / by a person plaguing himself with fear and doubt. He has no glory from it / when He is not trusted so much / but one always fears the worst.

But many kinds of causes can hunt a Christian into fear / from within / as well as from without. Yes / if one considers it rightly / everything in the world works toward keeping man only under his natural shyness. The heart itself is also by nature more inclined toward darkness / to cares and grief / than to a comforted courage.

So it easily happens / that a person even in his conversion becomes fearful and timid over all sorts of occurrences. For what does not set upon one from without / if one does not always allow oneself to be preserved in faith.

How busy the World-Spirit is in its own / to make all sorts of terrors / so that one should fall into fears / and let go of this or that good resolution.

How quickly some fear of man overtakes one in the obedience of faith / so that one thinks / or rather evil powers speak into the mind : Behold, how will it go for you / if you no longer participate in this and that! How they will laugh at you / persecute you / blaspheme you! What will this one and that one say about it?

Undoubtedly Abraham had many such battles. For he lived among unbelieving people / and had much to do with great lords and kings. To them his conduct likely seemed foolish enough / that he did not want to live along fine and easy with the rest. There his heart might sometimes tremble in the time of temptation / as to how it would finally go with him. Just as such fear still falls upon believing people at this hour / when they live in the midst of a raw and base generation / and see many a danger before them.

And how powerfully the spiritual powers of darkness often work / to hunt a soul out of its rest into anguish and fear! Oh, how many hellish powers of unbelief they seek to set out of grace / and to bring into doubt / uncertainty, and murmuring!

Certainly / if the LORD were not with such a soul / when such enemies set themselves against it ; they would swallow it alive.

But all this comes upon a believer / partly so that he may learn to know ever better his dark and unbelieving ground of corrupted nature / and partly also that he may become all the firmer in faith through battle and patience. Otherwise, one would not believe / that one had such a miserably despondent heart / if this dark essence of unbelief did not thus betray itself.

By this, all timid and wavering hearts may now learn / where they should take right steadiness and joy. Only above all things recognize / what a defiant and despondent thing it is regarding the human heart! Then, according to faith, call out and desire quite earnestly.

For with what did GOD drive away Abraham’s fear? He spoke:

# Ch. XV. The First Book of Moses.

# I am your shield / your very great reward.

**I am your shield)** Which will extinguish all the fiery arrows of the evil one; crawl behind it; let anyone dare to harm you!

With this, He makes—as if through a divine impression—the heart certain and firm in grace, so that it can accept GOD as its own special shield. For

Everything that GOD thus speaks of Himself is pure, present action, power, and essence / and no mere promise for the future. Therefore, Abraham actually felt and enjoyed such powerful protection in reality, as GOD spoke these words to him and he took hold of Him in faith as an invincible shield.

A more lovely and powerful <term>remedy|original: Recept</term> against all fearfulness could not be presented than with this word. It is not a mere metaphor, but pure spirit, power, and life. Blessed are all those who experience and enjoy it!

GOD offers Himself as a shield to a trembling soul: O, what an inexpressible wonder! One might sink to the ground before God’s condescension and deep love, that GOD Himself is not ashamed to become the shield of a poor earth-worm.

So precious are the children of men in GOD’S eyes!

It would have been a great thing for Abraham if GOD had said: I will give you a shield through my grace, or through good angels. But He Himself wishes to be his protection in His very essence.

**Your very-great reward)** A human can give GOD no greater proof of his love than when he despises all other things and surrenders himself to Him alone. Therefore, GOD hastens to testify His gratitude to him through exceedingly lovely words, assuring him that He is his protection and also that He Himself would be his great reward. Incomprehensible bliss! GOD Himself wishes to be the replacement for those lowly things which we leave for His sake. Truly, O Paul <margin>(a) Rom. 8:18.</margin> there is no comparison between the sufferings of this time and the glory that shall be revealed in us! For what could possibly be compared with the possession of GOD?

GOD does not merely want to give a reward / but He Himself wants to be the reward, truly and essentially.

He looked into Abraham’s heart and saw how he now desired nothing as a reward and pleasure but GOD alone; how he also would not be satisfied with mere spiritual gifts, with powers, sweetness, and other outflows of grace: but the abyss of his hungry soul called out to GOD Himself—the immeasurable Good—as one abyss calls to another.

So GOD stilled this longing with Himself: and thus Abraham found what he sought. He would have disdained temporal things and held them as too small for his immortal spirit; he did not wish to rest in other outward things either: therefore, GOD surrendered Himself entirely to his insatiable desire of faith and told him that He would be everything to him.

O, if only we could all learn such an art from this Father of Faith and cast out and clear away all things from our minds! How God’s fullness would fill us with Himself! But if one keeps back even a little of one's love for something outside of and alongside GOD, it certainly hinders the full reward.

All created and uncreated good is the compensation for the obedient person. What more could one want? and yet, O how few there are who, despite this exceedingly great reward or compensation, are inclined toward it!

The human heart is so foolish that it always seeks its reward elsewhere than in GOD. Even when most people do something good, they take their reward right then and there. Matthew 6:2.

But GOD, in His wisdom, turns all reward-seeking cleverness into folly through this pronouncement, saying that He Himself will be the reward and crown of His own. For who can earn GOD Himself, or manage with their own things so that GOD becomes their own property?

GOD gives Himself to His own purely for free and without their merit or worthiness. But He also wants all other things to be forsaken for His sake. One must not be satisfied with any other reward if one wishes to have this one. Otherwise, it is shameful to the glory and all-sufficiency of GOD. Whoever still clings to something else testifies by that action that they do not yet have enough in GOD and have not found everything in Him.

What greater insult can be done to the Divine Majesty than if one says of Him that He is not enough, with all His gifts, treasures, and blessings, to fully satisfy a single soul? O, that we might recognize this in time and become busy through the Holy Spirit in throwing all false rewards out of our hearts! How quickly would GOD Himself then be our reward and crown!

So let us then zealously strive day and night for this immeasurable reward, which GOD Himself wishes to be, and never get enough of GOD, but rather hunger and thirst for Him quite longingly, so that He may fill us entirely with Himself! We certainly lose nothing with Him.

4. And behold, the word of the LORD came to him, saying: This one shall not be your heir; but he who shall come from your own body / he shall be your heir. <margin>Isaiah 9:6.</margin> 5. And

***

<margin>v. 2. Damascene)</margin> One born of the blood and the will of man.

<margin>v. 3. etc.</margin> Abraham / who at that time was like the only one with whom GOD renewed the Covenant of Grace / sought—like Adam—the seed promised by GOD, to see if it should not be born of him; Malachi 2:15. which must have been much dearer to him than many children and entire nations from his body, indeed, than the whole world. He was also not envious of his faithful Damascene, as a sprout from Damascus / where until now GOD had shown His grace among them, the Hebrews, chapter 14:13. and he would have gladly left him the administration of his property, if perhaps he should adopt him as a son who would inherit the promise of GOD. But Abram was promised a seed from his own body, which should be as innumerable as the stars / and should be seen upon the whole earth like the same. Whereby, at the same time, the spiritual seed in Christ is seen, through whom Abraham becomes an heir of the world. And this was the greater promise / while that of the land of Canaan is the lesser, to be noted as a pledge of the greater and of heaven.

<margin>v. 4. Not)</margin> Neither Ishmael / the son of bondage / nor Eliezer / the hired servant / may be Abraham’s heir.

This faithful servant / seeing himself near his end and without having seen the fulfillment of the spiritual promises / and despite this continuing in self-denial / nevertheless seeks some means to provide for the future and thinks of some ways to do so.

But GOD / whose goodness is infinite / quickly comes before him and sifts through all these means which Abraham's weakness had suggested to him, by giving him a new assurance of His providence over him. But because this poor, forsaken man had retreated a little into himself while trying to care for the future; GOD draws him out of there all the more and shows him, through a simple comparison—namely, the stars—the effects of His power, assuring him anew that His promises are infallible / and that He has power enough to fulfill them.
