<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XVII.</header>

## 14. And an uncircumcised male / who has a foreskin / who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin / that same soul shall be cut off from his people : he has broken my covenant.

The one who performs the circumcision first gathers the foreskin together, presses the head <note>original: "Kopff oder die Eschel," referring to the glans</note> back and inward, and rubs the foreskin until it loses all feeling, so that the cut is felt less. He then takes a razor, or a sharp piece of glass, or a sharp flint stone <margin>Josh. 5:2, 3.</margin>, or whatever else sharp he can obtain—though they prefer to use a razor—and speaks clearly and distinctly: Blessed be you, LORD our God, who has sanctified us with your commandments and has given us the covenant of circumcision: with this, he cuts off the foreskin held in his hand so that the head can be seen. Thereupon the circumciser takes a mouthful of wine and sprays the wound with it to staunch the blood and rinse it. If he notices that the little boy is becoming faint, he also sprays some on his face. When the blood has quieted somewhat, he uses the sharp nails of his thumbs to tear the remaining membrane in two and pushes or pulls it back over itself, so that the head of the member is entirely exposed. This final exposure and tearing of the remaining skin causes, as is easy to imagine, far greater pain than the circumcision itself: however, it is said to be so necessary that if it is omitted, even if the foreskin has already been cut away, it is the same as if he were not circumcised at all. Before this tearing occurs, the little boy’s father says: Blessed be you, LORD our God, King of the world! who has sanctified us with your commandments and commanded that we enter into the covenant of our father Abraham! To which all those present say: LORD! As you have received this boy into the covenant of our father Abraham, so help that he also be received to keep the law of Moses, to enter into marriage, and to do good works! And then the tearing of the remaining skin takes place. As soon as this is done, the circumciser draws the blood from the wound with his mouth <note>This practice is known in Hebrew as *metzitzah*.</note> so that no harm comes of it, and places a small cloth, or plaster, or similar dressing upon it. The little boy, while being circumcised, is held by his godfather <note>The *Sandek*, who holds the child during the ceremony.</note> on his lap and in his arms. When the circumcision is complete, the godfather stands up with his circumcised godson; then the circumciser blesses the little boy: LORD our God, you God of our fathers! strengthen this boy and preserve him for his parents, and let his name be among the people of Israel! (Here the little boy is given his name.) Let his father, from whose loins he came, rejoice over him; and his mother delight in the fruit of her womb!

The circumciser could be whoever was desired: either the father himself, or another of the children of Israel, provided it was a male person and not a woman. However, in cases of necessity, circumcision by women was also not invalid. Nowadays they have their appointed and experienced <term>Mohel<gloss>a person specifically trained to perform the ritual of circumcision</gloss></term>.

Whoever despised this sign was to have no part with the believers in eternal life, but after death was to be separated from them and consigned to damnation with the unbelievers. Thus, mention is made of the "soul," from which one can conclude that during his physical life they may have tolerated him in the outward community to give him occasion for repentance and a change of mind.

Through this commandment and the sign of His covenant, God expresses that if one wishes to enter into <term>yieldedness<gloss>original: "Gelassenheit," a mystical state of surrendering one's will to God</gloss></term>, one must labor through circumcision to cut away everything that maintains the Adamic life <note>The "Adamic life" refers to the fallen, sinful nature inherited from Adam.</note> within us. The beginning of the spiritual path is when one continually crucifies oneself and denies everything that sustains the fleshly and animalistic life. By this, the people of God are known. And there is no longer any distinction between the servant and the free, because the state of those who surrender themselves to God is the same.

By the son who is born in the house, one who has led an innocent life is understood: and it seems of such a one as if he needed no self-denial. Nevertheless, he, as well as all others in the beginning, must die to everything that is of the Adamic life, so that the life of **Jesus** Christ can begin within him.

By the servants are understood those who have suffered a long time under the cruelty of sin. These likewise, as soon as they surrender themselves to God, must submit to circumcision. It is true that this circumcision proceeds on their part in a more passive than active manner. This happens to them because, when they are truly yielded, God Himself works with the sword in His hand to circumcise their uncircumcision, without being held back by the pain, the fear, or the weeping of those who must endure this wounding. The more the sensuality has grown old, like the foreskin, the more it resists under the knife. Whereby the circumcision becomes more painful.

But those who have endured neither the knife nor the cutting away of their own life, yet wish to be regarded as yielded; or those who are such in name only, and therefore wish to keep everything and lose nothing: they are excluded both from the number of the truly yielded and the truly circumcised.

<column-break/>

## 15. Furthermore God said to Abraham: You shall not call your wife Sarai by her name Sarai, but Sarah shall be her name.

## 16. For I will bless her, and I will also give you a son from her. For I will bless her, so that she shall become nations; kings over peoples shall come from her.

## 17. Then

God now also wished—through the changing of the name of Sarai (which signifies a princess with emphasis on the singular number) into the word Sarah, with the addition of the final letter H (which is taken from *Hamon*, that is, the multitude, and also from the name of God, Jehovah, in which it is found twice, and which was also given to Abraham)—to transform her, and thus give it to be understood that she should become the princess of a multitude of nations in Christ. He was to be born from her as the blessed seed of the woman through the son coming from her body. From her body also came the great people of Judah and Israel, and the Edomites with their kings. Indeed, the believers also become her children, as children of the free woman. Gal. 4:31; 1 Pet. 3:6. And so this blessing also extends to righteousness and the hope of eternal life, which was promised to her herewith as well as to Abraham.

v. 15. Sarai — Sarah) The former means more "my princess," or princess of my family: but because she was to be a princess over all, she should simply be called Princess or Sovereign; namely, the future Princess of all nations; and that because the Church rules in every nation. Upon which the Lord without doubt had His intention in the final words of the

v. 16. Kings over peoples shall come from her) Thus He wished to expand her dominion.

When God has renewed the ground of the heart, and the highest part through the resurrection of the spirit after its spiritual death—as soon as He has drawn it out of the shadow of death and translated it into the new life, which is represented by the new name—He then also renews the lowest part, in that He changes its name and makes it a partaker in the renewal of the highest part. Therefore, He also changes Sarah’s name after He had changed Abraham's, gives her the same promises as her husband, and adds that she would bear him a son.

<header>Cap. XVII. The First Book of Moses. 109</header>
<sig>D 3</sig>

17. Then **Abraham** fell upon his face and laughed / and spoke in his heart: Shall a child be born to a hundred-year-old man? and shall **Sarah** / a ninety-year-old / give birth?

18. And **Abraham** spoke to **GOD**: Oh that **Ishmael** might live before your face!

19. Then **GOD** said: Yes, **Sarah** your wife shall bear you a son / and you shall call his name **Isaac**; and I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant / for his offspring after him.

---

That **Abraham** laughed did not happen so much out of unbelief as out of wonder and great joy over such an entirely unexpected and incomprehensible blessing. See Psalm 126:2. Out of love also for his own flesh and blood, he wished to see **Ishmael** blessed; which he indeed received in a physical sense: but the extraordinary spiritual goods depend upon the pure and clear free will of **GOD** / to give them to whom He will. See Romans 9:9 etc.

**v. 17.)** The highest part <note>The author uses "highest part" to refer to the spirit or the mind's higher faculties.</note> / which had believed the promises given to him for his own sake / becomes doubtful when he is promised that a son should be born from his union with the lowest part <note>The "lowest part" refers to the physical body or Sarah's aging womb.</note> / upon whom all these promises were centered. Since he considers the weakness of this lower part without **GOD**, he knows it; thus he also doubts himself / and at the same time doubts the divine omnipotence: in that he takes the reasons / which he puts forward / from the experience of his own weakness / impotence, and infertility. These two parts lived contentedly in their misery; and as they hoped for nothing more / they also desired nothing. This is the state of rest in **GOD** / which precedes the Apostolic life.

**v. 18. etc.) Abraham** here represents the believing souls / who find themselves in a state of complete nakedness <note>In mystical theology, "nakedness" refers to a soul stripped of its own desires and ego.</note> / most beautifully. As those / who / when they look upon their wretched and abandoned state / say: Would to **GOD** / that we might be found in spiritual activities / instead of remaining so useless; and that this **Ishmael** / who represents multiplied works <note>Refers to human efforts or "works of the law" rather than grace.</note> / could live before **GOD** alone. But when **God** sees this error / He assures them / that He has blessed this path in all its ways / as much as the soul is worthy of it; and that it would have many advantages. Nevertheless, this path must not be the path of His people: because it is the path of a people / who are not yet free from the flesh; in that they are not yet liberated from sensibility: but His people must be in **JESUS** Christ. Therefore He lets those / who must give birth to this people / who are so dear to Him / reach such an age of despair; so that those / who are to be born of them / as **St. John** says / shall be born not of flesh / nor of blood / nor of the will of a man / but of **GOD** Himself.

**v. 19.)** This **Isaac** / whom one must give birth to / is **JESUS** Christ formed in the souls. But He is not born until there is no more hope in them / upon which they could ground themselves / that they could give birth to Him. This child is not conceived / except in the total despair of all natural help / and in a perfect denial of all supernatural gifts: so that / as **Paul** says / the greatness of the strength may not be attributed to man / but to **GOD**.

<column-break/>

20. I have also heard you concerning **Ishmael**. Behold, I have blessed him / and will make him fruitful / and will multiply him exceedingly. Twelve princes shall he beget / and I will make him into a great nation.

<margin>ch. 18:14.</margin>

22. And he stopped speaking with him / and **GOD** went up from **Abraham**.

24. And **Abraham** was ninety-nine years old / when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.

25. And **Ishmael** / his son / was thirteen years old / when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.

**v. 20. 21.)** Just as in the **Holy Scripture** not a single word is to be found / which does not serve for our instruction; so one must note / that all the promises given to **Ishmael** have their certain boundaries / and are bound to a certain number. But those / given to **Isaac** / who is the image of faith and serenity in **GOD** / are without limits: because he includes nothing less than **GOD** Himself in his lineage. The reward of a believing soul cannot be less than **GOD**. Just as He Himself says to **Abraham**: I am your exceedingly great reward.

The ready obedience of **Abraham** is recorded / in that he put this command into action on the very same day / that he received it: which is the work of true faith.

**v. 23.** From **Ishmael**, his descendants / the Turks and other peoples / have their circumcision: which is also a sign / that **Asshur** <note>Assyria</note> will one day come to conversion as a work of **God's** hands / and obtain this blessing for **Abraham’s** sake. **Isaiah 19:25.** By this, it is not the ancient **Assyrians** and **Persians** / but the descendants of **Abraham** from **Hagar** and **Keturah** / who must be understood / who took over those lands / and multiplied there far and wide according to the blessing spoken over **Abraham**. See Chapter 25:6, 18.

Regarding the circumcision of the Turks, travelogues report / that it does not happen on the 8th day / but in the 4th / 5th or 7th year / or even later. So also **Olearius** <note>Adam Olearius (1603–1671), a famous German scholar and traveler who wrote about Persia.</note> mentions of the **Persians** / that they circumcise their children in the 7th / 8th and 9th year / where they make them drunk with sweet drinks / so that they do not feel the pain.

In **Egypt** and **Ethiopia** <note>original: "Morenland," referring to the land of the Moors or Abyssinians/Ethiopians.</note> many Christians are said even today not only to be baptized / but also to be circumcised.

4. Let a little water be brought to you now, that you may wash your <margin>(a) ch. 19/2. John 13/5.</margin> (a) feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.

<meta>catchword: 13. Then</meta>

---

<columns>2</columns>

Abraham did not have any carnal thoughts about God, as if God truly had need of such physical service and food. But because He wished to appear in the flesh, Abraham did not overthink it, but wished to host the Lord with such physical service, just as Christ, after His transfiguration <note>Original: "Verklärung" — referring to the post-Resurrection appearances</note>, once asked His disciples for something to eat (John 21:5) in order to interact with them more intimately. The Lord also wished to accept this physical hospitality here, and not prevent it (v. 5), to show how He would truly one day appear in our needy flesh and would then be in need of such service: for then the Father would appear in the Son (see John 14:9, 10, 11) and the Spirit of the Father and the Son together; so that these three together revealed themselves in the flesh of the Son of Man, the Son of God: though they appeared as one to physical eyes, here they appeared as three.

v. 4. **Wash feet**) According to Oriental custom, so that no one caused inconvenience to another with an unpleasant odor.

**Under the tree**) Beneath which he had pitched his tent. v. 8.

Such a tree was subsequently held very sacred and honored by later inhabitants. Whether they truly have such stories to tell, such reports seem hard to believe to others who know that already in the year of Christ 310, Constantine the Great <note>Original: "Constantius-M." likely refers to Constantinus Magnus</note>, at the urging of his mother Helena—because the heathens honored this place with false worship and erected idols and altars—had all such things torn down and burned, and a temple erected in their place. (Nicephorus <note>A reference to the church historian Nicephorus Callistus</note>).

v. 8.) Abraham wished to stand by the Lord and thus serve, and not eat with them, in order to show his reverence toward the Lord.

Those who are truly touched by the love of God in the suffering way of contemplation <term>Beſchauung: a state of deep spiritual meditation or mystical prayer</term> find nothing too difficult when it concerns the honor of God. They employ everything they have so that they can give Him some signs of their love. Therefore, they also do everything with speed and ease, without interrupting their inner peace. Their charity is as great as their love. And these virtues are also found in Mary Magdalene in the house of the leper (a).
<margin>(a) Luke 7/37. Matth. 26/6.</margin>

<column-break/>

The Lord wished hereby to repeat the announcement of the birth of Isaac; that now was the time that he should be conceived and born; and that this would happen within a year's time, when this same season and weather usually returns: also to show how this promise of grace should be carried out solely through His governance and omnipotence. Now Sarah, who by the Lord’s providence had to overhear this, could not immediately find her way into it through faith, as Abraham had done—who did not grow weak in faith and therefore did not consider his own already-dead body, since he was almost a hundred years old, nor the deadness of Sarah’s body, etc. (Romans 4:18). Thus she was overtaken by her weakness, so that in unbelief she laughed at this promise that was too wonderful for her, since she was no longer in a state to conceive or bear children. This teaches us how we must view the divine promises of the wonderful glorification of His church on earth not with the weak eye of our reason, but with the eyes of faith: for God's omnipotence only wishes to reveal itself when it appears entirely impossible to men.

Generosity is rewarded by the assurance that the promises would soon be fulfilled. But those who are not established in God doubt; in that they sometimes return to their doubt and mistrust, which are caused by the consideration of their own incapacity and weakness. But those who are well-established in God can neither waver nor doubt. But how rare are these on the earth! And where would one find such?

What Sarah says—"since I am already old, should I still have delight?"—by which she meant to indicate that she no longer intended to make use of the married state: shows that she viewed this not in God, but according to human ways.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XVIII.

**13.** Then the Lord said to Abraham: Why did Sarah laugh at this, saying, "Shall I indeed truly give birth, now that I have become old?"

**14.** Is anything too wonderful for the Lord? At the appointed time I will return to you, when this time of year comes again; then Sarah shall have a son. <term>ch. 17:21</term>

**15.** Then Sarah denied it and said: I did not laugh. For she was afraid. But he said: It is not so; you did laugh.

---

<margin>(a) Rom. 4:18.</margin>
Abraham, who was firmly established in the state of self-denial and faith, is the father of all those who have followed him into that same state. He no longer doubts; therefore, Sarah's sin does not affect him. He believes that even when there is not the slightest hope to be seen, he must still hope. This is also the true (a) praise that Saint Paul attributes to him. The Lord laments the unbelief of his wife by reminding her that nothing is impossible for God. In this way, God is accustomed to exercising faith and serenity <note>The original German "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of surrendered calmness or yielding to God's will.</note> by not making things harmonize again until they are in the most doubtful state possible. But creatures who have not yet been entirely drawn out of themselves doubt, just as Sarah did, because they look at these things according to their own reason; on the contrary, souls standing in pure faith look at them in no other way than from the side of God, for whom nothing is impossible.

<margin>v. 15. Denied)</margin>
The creature who still exists within its own self-will seeks to justify itself when it is corrected; however, it thereby falls inadvertently into lies.

<margin>(b) Rom. 4:16.</margin>
Sarah commits two errors. First, by lying; and second, that while she seeks to excuse herself, she accuses God. For if it were not true that she laughed, she would be casting the lie back upon God, who punished her for it. It is exactly the same with souls who are constantly making excuses. They heap sin upon sin through their contradictions and wavering: and afterward, they cast the blame upon God himself, accusing Him of cruelty or complaining that He has abandoned them and does nothing for them. But the faithful soul remains unmoved and constant under His providences. And through this faithfulness, she draws to herself the good pleasure and the greatest gifts of God’s grace; just as Saint Paul says (b) that Abraham was blessed through faith.

However, Sarah must also have been strengthened in faith through the Lord’s rebuke, even though she sinned through her denial, for she must have later repented of it; because the Apostle gives her this testimony: "Through faith Sarah herself also received strength to conceive, and bore a child past the time of her age, because she judged Him faithful who had promised." <term>Hebr. 11:11.</term>

<column-break/>

**16.** Then the men rose up from there and turned toward Sodom: and Abraham went with them to see them on their way.

**17.** Then the Lord said:

-> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut ornament depicting a winged cherub head.</image-desc> <-

God drew Abraham after Him like a magnet. *To see them on their way*) Because He wanted to reveal the intended judgment in the neighborhood to him—as to His servant and prophet, indeed His friend—also for the sake of his relative, Lot; <term>Amos 3:7.</term> to encourage him to intercede for them. And also as a prototype of how God will one day visit with terrifying judgments of fire those to whom the Kingdom of God has come—in that God sent His own among them, but they did not want to recognize them or heed their correction and testimony, and thus pushed the Kingdom of God away from themselves. Then the Lord will also make this known to His friends, so that they may take up the cause of others, and especially their own kin, through intercession; to see if they might still be saved through fear and snatched out of the fire. <term>Jude v. 23.</term>

The ancients have a clever observation here: why God speaks with Abraham before his obedience as with one who is obligated, but after his obedience as with a friend. The reason is this: because only he is truly God's friend who does what is commanded of him; according to the words of Christ in <term>John 15:15.</term>

We must not find it distasteful or wearisome that we should hear so often and so much about Abraham.

His example should rightly be so much more lovely and sweet to us—so much so that we could not hear enough of it—because we do not easily see such a pure and godly course of life in any other person in the Scriptures as in him.

For this very reason, he is called a father of all believers, so that we should follow him in all his godly conduct, in the very same spirit that he had in his heart. And if we wish to be his true children, as all believers must be according to the Scriptures, then we must also gladly learn to recognize his conduct and behavior.

What is more gracious and sweet to hear of than the friendship of God with His own? How then should we not long to be rightly instructed in the divine connection with mankind!

Since God, moreover, presents us not only with words and precepts of such a lovely thing, but also with living examples of those who have actually experienced and enjoyed all this in reality; how can we be so stony-hearted that such a glorious presentation should not allure and move us to learn and practice the mystery of God’s friendship!

O how blessed those have always considered themselves who have attained such high grace! For they have experienced that therein lies the entire well-being of man, and that everything depends upon it.

But no one can know or believe what it is to have the Lord of Heaven and Earth as a friend, and what gain and advantage are to be found therein, except the one who has experienced both the separation from God in wrath and the union with God in love. To such a person, the comparison will be like Heaven and Hell.

But the question arises here: did God grant such intimacy only to certain Fathers in the Old Testament, and favor them with it as a special privilege and prerogative? Or may a faithful soul in the New Testament also attain to an intimate acquaintance and fellowship with God?

And there, the new teachers <note>Likely referring to contemporary theologians or Pietist writers.</note> also gladly confess that there is a certain familiarity with God, and a friendship in an extraordinary degree: specifically 1. with constant interaction, and 2. with freedom and boldness. To this belong, according to their confession, true inwardness, contemplation, remembrance, speaking to, and clinging to God, for which they praise Albertus Magnus’s little book *On the Paradise of the Soul*. <gloss>(a)</gloss>

Only, we must not claim or seek such grace of divine intimacy before we become pure of heart.

And that is exactly the reason why such secret friendship is so rare and strange on earth: because this is what is lacking—because few people abandon all things from the heart and seek this pearl.

In the meantime, it remains true that in the New Covenant we should have access to all grace. Should we not all be Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise? Now then, we must also have a share in all the grace that happened to him, and take a deep impression from the diligent contemplation of his example.

How far did this grace extend, and what intimacy of God toward Abraham is not to be glimpsed here, when the Lord broke out in these very thoughtful words:

<header>Chapter XVIII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

<margin>Amos 3:7. John 15:15.</margin>
# How can I hide from Abraham what I am doing?

Wherever God finds a heart that is truly and earnestly one with him, he in turn entrusts that heart with his secrets.

This is the greatest part of the bliss of faith that can be found in God.

In Abraham, such a fervent and strong love for his God had arisen that God rewarded and crowned this love with new love, viewing it as his own gift. Therefore, Abraham became so "secret" <note>The German "heimlich" here implies a deep, private intimacy or being "in on a secret."</note> with the Lord, so trusted, and so familiar.

It was already intimacy enough that the Lord revealed himself to him in a certain form. But here is added God’s most loving explanation, as if God could do nothing without Abraham knowing about it. Thus, one degree of friendship emerges after another.

God can hide nothing from his servant who is confirmed in simple faith and rests in him. He cannot refrain from revealing his secrets to him. And just as the servant has the Spirit of God, so he also knows what goes on in the heart of God—yes, even the most hidden things in the conscience—and distinguishes their states immediately through a secret "smell" and divine "taste" <note>The author uses sensory metaphors to describe spiritual discernment.</note>.

Abraham did not desire to know anything out of curiosity; rather, what God discovered to him here was necessary because his relative Lot lived in Sodom, and God intended to destroy that place with fire. Therefore, the Lord communicated first, as it were, with this friend of his, so that he might pray for the place and save his brother Lot.

God loves to find souls who are capable of recognizing his ways and secrets, and of warning themselves and others of harm, and the like. Indeed, his love drives him to present all impending cases, temptations, and events to his own, showing them how they may escape this or that temptation or prepare for it. This is why notable verses from Holy Scripture and other good words sometimes come to their minds, warning them against something evil or guiding them toward something good.

This, then, is a great piece of divine friendship: and it is God's great joy to deal with us humans—if only we are capable and willing—in such a human, condescending, and simple way, like one friend with another, discovering his heart to them and engaging with them intimately.

<margin>Wisdom of Solomon 7:27.</margin>
Reason must not be angered by this: for if God wishes to hide nothing from his own, as he confesses here to Abraham, then he must indeed make it known to them; and if his Wisdom makes prophets, who can or has anything to say against it?

It is more than certain that we should and must follow in Abraham’s footsteps if we wish to come to God and attain fellowship with him.

Now, truly, this kind of promise must also be able to become ours: that God entrusts us with his truth. Indeed:

Our joy in faith consists in this: that the Spirit of God lets his will and good pleasure become living and impressed upon our hearts, from and according to his holy Word, so that we may know what has been given to us by God.

This is the advantage even in a merely natural friendship, when one friend communicates his plans to another. How much more is it our soul’s only life and well-being when God grants us his counsel, when he does not hide what he does—at least as much as is necessary for us. For no Christian desires to know unnecessary things.

O, how must such a bond of love powerfully strengthen the soul when it can so clearly recognize God's unfeigned faithfulness! It certainly sinks and hides itself ever deeper in God; yes, it is surrounded and as if swallowed up by God's love and light!

This powerfully awakens the spirit of prayer in such hearts, just as Abraham was emboldened by God’s intimate speech to plead—though in humility—for the sparing of Sodom. It causes one to venture more for God’s honor against the world and the flesh, and to disregard the enmity of people for the sake of truth and justice, because one is certain that God is a friend.

Therefore, see to it that you may become truly inward, truly "secret," and truly intimate with God in faith and life: then in times of need, you will always have unblocked access to your God, and can rest in him in the midst of unrest, be comforted even without external comfort, and be strong without creaturely strengthening.

<column-break/>

<margin>Gen. 12:2, 3.</margin>
# 18. Since Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him.

# 19. For

Two things are promised here in the briefest and yet most perfect way: namely, the people of Israel according to the flesh, and all nations according to faith. Eucherius <note>Saint Eucherius of Lyon, a 5th-century theologian known for his commentaries.</note>, Book 1 on Genesis, ch. 72.

It all depends on God finding you in such a faithful mind as Abraham’s; then his promise can also benefit you, and the blessing can be spoken into your heart.

You must provide proof to your God whether you are concerned solely with your salvation, or only with temporal things; whether you esteem him and his Word higher than everything in the world.

How many a poor soul feels how greatly such faith is needed, while many feel nothing but the curse and wrath of God within themselves, and pure un-blessing!

In this great corruption in which poor human nature lies, we must not remain and perish if we do not wish to. We need only believe and take what is offered to us, and not let the Gospel stand unfruitful before the door of our heart. For that:

**All the nations of the earth shall be blessed)** This gives us a truly open and wide view or glimpse into God's Father-heart: how impartial, how perfectly pure and expansive God's love is.

Such a ground of universal love of God is absolutely necessary for faith when we grasp it in an enlightened heart, because otherwise the matter looks very dangerous on both sides. For:

On one hand, a crude mind might think: "If all people are to be blessed, then it won't matter whether I change or not; I will probably be saved even without conversion."

On the other side, the enemy can sift a good-hearted soul with timidity, so that when they sometimes feel little or no faith, they may think: "Alas, where is God's blessing for me? I certainly notice no such blessing for my soul, but plenty of God's curse and disfavor!"

But these latter and truly troubled hearts should take well to heart from this general ground of God's love that the blessing nevertheless certainly applies to them, even if they do not always feel it so sensibly or grasp it with their hands. They should hold to simple faith and, with Abraham, learn to hope where there is nothing to hope for: thus they will also inherit Abraham's blessing.

But the secure and wild despisers of grace should know that this general blessing will instead result in their damnation—but by their own fault.

But what kind of blessing is it that God promises here? Answer: Blessing is actually a "good speaking" <note>A literal translation of the German "Segen," related to the Latin "benedictio."</note> and a beneficial communication of a certain good. And thus the blessing of God in a spiritual sense is all the well-being and salvation that God offers or actually gives to man.

Now when the Lord wants to bless all nations, it means nothing but doing pure well-being and good, pure saving, making free, whole, rich, and blessed. There is no good, no peace, no treasure, no life nor grace excluded that God does not actually intend to give when he wants to bless. A great Lord gives something proper; it is a disgrace to him to give something small.

Whoever is now (and indeed, who is not?) among the nations that are to be blessed: let him reach out while it is called "today," for the full blessing of grace! Let no one think that words or imaginations are enough; let no one help themselves with a merely external church blessing. Instead, everything good that is spoken in the name of God by his Spirit, through or without people—grasp that as a blessing from the Lord, and pray for its fulfillment in yourself and your own! In this way, in one's few days of life, one can gather an infinite treasure of benediction in Christ.

### Chapter XVIII. The First Book of Moses. 115

20. And the LORD said: Because the outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah is great (a) / and because their sin is very heavy;
<margin>(a) ch. 19:13.</margin>

This is the state of Sodom / which can very well be applied to our common state.

For what was the iniquity of your sister Sodom? Ezek. 16:48. Not perhaps only the so-called sodomy <note>original: "Sodomiterey"; while specifically referring to certain sexual acts, the author emphasizes it as a broader category of rebellion and vice.</note> / but all other kinds of sins: Lust of the eyes / lust of the flesh / and a malicious nature.

We must not think / as if the people of Sodom were sinners above all others. Christ says / no; but / those who do not repent / they shall all likewise perish / if not in physical fire / then certainly in the fire of God's righteous wrath. And what greed / voluptuousness / and pride / does not reign among most / who yet consider themselves Christians / and better than heathens. Do not many boast of their sins / like those of Sodom? Isa. 3:9.

Ah, this example is nothing other than a clear mirror / of how the natural man / when he is left to himself / appears before GOD.

Therefore, let one look at oneself in the mirror of these wretched people! They were the descendants of the mocking Ham / a shameful-unchaste seed / who sought their life and honor in beastly lusts and abominations.

Such an impure atheistic race is still spread across the earth / of which it may rightly be said: How can you speak and do good / who are evil?

At this, the self-assured heart thinks / that everything it commits in the dark will remain silent in the stillness; no rooster will crow about the wickednesses / if only the authorities and other superiors do not find out. But what does the LORD say about a great

Outcry? This is a strange language to Reason / that sins should cry out. But when GOD opens our eyes / to look into the internal power of sins and into the mystery of wickedness; oh, then we shall surely be astonished by its secret powers and effects!

Every person will be able to believe this / and notice how it happens / if he pays heed to his conscience / what a restlessness arises therein / as soon as he offends his GOD with something wrong. There, as it were, that evil cries out against the spark of divine knowledge in his heart.

Holy Scripture now names various such heaven-crying sins in particular: such as / the insulting of one's neighbor / the withholding of the hard-earned wages of workers / violence and injustice / oppression of the poor / widows and orphans. But almost universal is the heaven-crying abomination / that men do not want to follow all the enticements and admonitions of GOD at all / but let all the labor of the Spirit and the Word of GOD be in vain upon them. Oh, that makes

**Their sin very heavy)** But many a person likely thinks: Oh, I have not committed such cruel sins / as the Sodomites did!

Now, there are indeed certainly certain principal sins / to which / as mentioned above / the crying-out is primarily attributed in Scripture. Meanwhile / however / we must not think / that other sins / which we might regard as minor / are not known to the LORD / nor will be punished by him. GOD speaks here generally of all the sins of the Sodomites. And what kind of sins they were / Ezekiel gives us the key in ch. 16:48.

Over such sins / which are also in full swing among us / the Lord pronounces the judgment / that they are very heavy.

Frivolous nature does not think / that sin is so heavy in GOD's eyes. It judges according to its dissolute concept and delusion / where the devil makes evil so minor and whistles so sweetly to the soul / when he tempts it to it.

But why is sin so heavy? Because it offends an infinite GOD / and thereby inevitably causes the unbearable burden of divine wrath and its punishments.

Therefore, let one beware of further guilt / and no longer burden the conscience with injustice. One should simply believe surely / the more one continues in sins / the deeper one presses one's soul down to the abyss of hell / and will surely become aware with infinite anxiety / how sin is so heavy / when GOD will give the most righteous verdict over everything. For

The effect of the outcry of sins / which inevitably follows upon evil / is the visitation of GOD; of which the LORD now speaks exceedingly thoughtfully:

<column-break/>

21. So I will now go down (a) / and see / whether they have altogether finished / according to the outcry concerning it / which has come before me (b) / or not; so I will know it.
<margin>(a) ch. 11:5, 7. Micah 1:3. (b) Jon. 1:2.</margin>

22. And

Therefore, believe certainly and truly / that the eternal GOD looks into it at the right time / and, as it were, investigates / what has happened. He will and can leave nothing unjudged.

Here he speaks indeed in a human manner / as if he had to go down first) From one place to another / before he could see it. But he did that because / in such a gracious condescension / he appeared to Abraham in human form / and showed a prelude to his holy incarnation <note>The author interprets God's physical appearance to Abraham as a "pre-figuring" or early hint of Christ becoming human (the Incarnation).</note> / and because the sinners dwell on earth and in the abyss of wickedness. So he now means to say / he was so awakened by the outcry / that / to speak simply and humanly / he had to emerge from his inaccessible light and the mystery of his love and eternal rest / and manifest himself in his wrath and justice. Now the righteous judge would indeed have had reason / to break out over these wicked rogues like a lightning bolt / and send them to hell in an instant. For their wickedness really reached unto heaven / and was as clear as day / so that no doubt found room anymore. Nevertheless, GOD will first, as it were, conduct an inquiry / and

**See, whether)** everything had also happened thus. Not from a lack of his absolute omniscience / to which indeed nothing was unknown: but to show us / how cautiously and uprightly our GOD proceeds in his judgments.

GOD says that / as the ancients quite rightly remind us / not out of ignorance / but because he thus <term>dispenses|dispensat: a theological term for God's condescension, where He presents Himself in human terms to make Himself understood</term> or lowers himself / as far as is fitting for him. And he does this as an example for us / that we should refrain from judgment over a matter / until we have been there ourselves.

Let us admire the manner / in which GOD makes use of punishing the sinners! He wants to investigate everything himself: because he seeks to exercise nothing but mercy. He makes this known to his friends / so that they might / if it is possible / soften him. But when he wants to bestow gifts of grace upon his creatures / he precedes them: and when he wants to reward them / he does not investigate everything so very exactly; because his mercy boasts against judgment.

Behold in this the goodness and the severity of GOD. Both are unspeakable mysteries. The goodness / that he acts so long-sufferingly and so very slowly even with the most abominable sins. And in this he is distinct from men / who in their zeal / even if it were ever so righteous / yet tend to over-hasten themselves so quickly.

The severity is no less deep and great / and consists in this / that GOD does not easily sweep away the sinner or a godless place / city and land / in the beginning or progress of sins / but waits / until the measure is full. Therefore GOD says here for great reflection / that he wants to see / whether they have

**Fulfilled or completed it)** It is settled / that there are certain stages of sins / and thus consequently a certain measure and goal / or such a completion and such an extreme degree of evil / where the wickedness has climbed to the highest point.

Where GOD sees beforehand / that a person or a certain place will not stop doing evil earlier / unless he has come to the extreme with it ; so he then awaits such a measure / and does not punish sooner / or over-hasten such a person or place with his judgments.

This is a very important mystery of divine justice / which may give us great light and information in many of the ways of GOD on earth.

GOD always replaces the slowness of vengeance with its severity. The longer the storm holds itself back / the more cruelly it finally breaks out. The holy GOD sees exactly / whether and when someone is ripe for punishment or not.

### The First Book of Moses. Chap. XVIII. 116

22. And the men turned away from there and went toward Sodom: but Abraham still remained standing before the LORD.
23. And Abraham stepped forward and said: Will You then also destroy the righteous with the wicked?
24. There might perhaps be fifty righteous within the city: would You then also destroy it, and not forgive the place for the sake of the fifty righteous who were therein?
25. Far be it from You to do such a thing, and kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be as the wicked! Far be it from You! Should not the Judge of all the earth do right?
<margin>Ps. 7:12.</margin>

---

v. 22. *Abraham still remained standing before the LORD.*) To what end, and what did he want then? There his spirit of faith turned away from all other things and into God's eternal mercy, with all humility and recognition of his own unworthiness.

Just as a child of God becomes a partaker of the divine nature through faith—and therein of the true divine mind—so they become more and more like their heavenly Father, even in their behavior toward the world of the wicked.

And how then is the eternal Father minded toward them? He certainly has no fellowship eternally with the works of darkness: yet, according to His universal love, He has the deepest mercy even toward all the unrepentant, insofar as they are His creatures.

His Son, Christ Jesus, has truly redeemed them all and prayed on the cross for the evildoers; nor does He cease, through His high-priestly Spirit, to represent the sinners against [divine] wrath and to seek their conversion.

This very same mind is now also born in all true children and friends of God when they become partakers of the divine nature and character. They must never seek or have fellowship with a single work of darkness, as dear as the divine friendship and fellowship is to them. Meanwhile, they must not cease to look upon all perverse hearts with mercy and compassion, to work on them with all long-suffering and faithfulness, and to seek their best. But especially the Spirit of Jesus Christ dwelling in them is busy praying for all the wicked and hypocrites.

For this reason, in this mind, and for this purpose, Abraham remained standing before the LORD. And

This example of Abraham is exceedingly remarkable. The cruel sins of Sodom and her neighbors were known to him as well as to Lot. He may also have been as distressed by them as Lot was, and never agreed with them. Nevertheless, he begged and entreated the LORD so very longingly for their rescue and sparing; as the entire rest of the chapter shows in more detail.

One sees sufficiently from this that he had no fellowship at all with the evil ones, and thus did not pray for the removal of their punishment out of love for their sins, but purely in a divine mind, which does not want anyone to be lost, yet loves a just and holy judgment. For

In his intercession, he appeals to divine justice and truth, and touches God's heart with the questions he poses.

Wisdom taught this man to expostulate <note>original: "expostuliren"; to reason earnestly with someone against something they have done or intend to do</note>, as it were, with God in faithful confidence, asking whether He would maintain a fine distinction in punishment, since He is the Judge of all flesh.

<column-break/>

26. And the LORD said: If I find fifty righteous in Sodom within the city, then I will forgive the whole place for their sake.
27. And Abraham answered and said: Oh, behold, I have taken it upon myself to speak to the LORD, although I am dust and ashes!
<margin>Sirach 10:9.</margin>
28. There might perhaps be five lacking from the fifty righteous: would You then destroy the whole city for the sake of the five? And He said: I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there.
29. And he continued further to speak to Him and said: Perhaps forty might be found there. But He said: I will do nothing to them for the sake of the forty.
30. Furthermore he said: Oh, may the LORD not be angry that I still speak! Perhaps thirty might be found there. But He said: I will do nothing to them if I find thirty there.
31. And

---

Here one can see how fervently and powerfully the friends of God entreat Him on behalf of their enemies. They present themselves to Him to be their advocates. They take hold of God at the strongest and most sensitive point by presenting a few holy ones to Him, so that He might forgive His enemies for their sake. But what help are so few righteous among so many unrighteous? Yet if those same ones had been found, they would have saved the whole city. The servants of God also compel Him through His own justice by representing to Him that He never destroys an innocent person for the sake of the guilty.

Yes, from this one can clearly see how a believer can be in great earnest for the sparing and conversion of the unbelievers, even though he must not have the slightest unity or fellowship with their affairs. Indeed, how such a person finds the blessed entrance into God's heart precisely through the true abstaining from all things, so that he dares to pray even for the very worst scoundrels.

->O, if only there were many such souls in the world!<-

Certainly, in whichever souls the Spirit of Jesus Christ, the eternal High Priest, can dwell and rule; there His blood will cry out better to the Father than the blood of Abel, and reconcile people, so that the LORD may visit them with grace and turn from the evil He intended to do to them.

Blessed is he who now places himself in the breach <note>A reference to standing "in the gap" to hold back judgment.</note> in time, and like Abraham takes hold of the LORD in His mercy, so that His wrath does not sweep away the righteous with the wicked, but that He may be gracious to the land for the sake of fifty righteous!

v. 27. *Although I am dust and ashes*) Here humility is to be found along with its ground and cause.

Abraham's faith was, as it were, crushed and purified in the mill through the mortification <note>original: "mortification"; the spiritual practice of "putting to death" the old, sinful nature.</note> and killing of the old man. And there one truly becomes dust and ashes according to the deepest, fundamental sense of these words.

### Chap. XVIII. The First Book of Moses.

**31.** And he said: Oh see, I have ventured to speak to the Lord! Perhaps twenty might be found there. And He said: I will not destroy it for the sake of the twenty.

**32.** And he said: Oh, may the Lord not be angry, that I speak just this—

---

Abraham still persists in asking for this grace, to see if the LORD might forgive these wicked people for the sake of the pious who lived among them, for the sake of their future improvement.

A certain teacher notes five characteristics of Abraham’s prayer in this conversation with the Lord: 1. **Faith**; in that he dares to stop God on His journey and address Him with confidence: 2. **Love**; which caused him to pray even for the welfare of his enemies: 3. **The earnest disposition of the mind**; in that he persisted so long until he realized that nothing more could be done: 4. **Humility**; which turned him into "dust and ashes" <note>Abraham previously referred to himself as "dust and ashes" in verse 27</note>, and continually pleaded against God's anger throughout his persistence: 5. **The foundations** upon which his prayer was based; which were divine justice, mercy, and truth: that God would judge rightly; that He would surely spare the remaining wicked for the sake of some righteous; and that, without a doubt, some pious people might still be found there.

For at that time, he assumed nothing else than that in all places and among all people—even among the most corrupt and godless, such as the Sodomites were—some honest and God-fearing people must and would exist. And

It is the duty of the universal love of believers to present themselves before God with intercession during God’s heavy judgments, to see if God could be moved to spare them in a manner consistent with His holiness and mercy: namely, if even a few well-meaning people might still be present, in whom there might yet be some hope for improvement. God is well-pleased with such intercession and is not angry about it; rather, He demonstrates His long-suffering and goodness, declaring this request to be entirely innocent and practicable, so much so that He would indeed fulfill it if He were to find it so. Therefore, as Abraham descended step by step from fifty down to ten, He always answered him with extraordinary long-suffering, saying that He would grant the request.

By this, God clearly shows that those souls who walk contrary to the world <note>Those who live according to God's values rather than the world's</note> certainly have a great right and claim to God’s love, and may also plead for grace for others.

And the fact that Lot is not mentioned with even a single word sufficiently indicates that his rescue had already been sought and obtained, promised, and granted to him. Just as it is mentioned in the following chapter in verse 29, that Lot was saved in consideration of Abraham, and thus through his prayer and intercession, even though he himself was righteous. For it is no small thing for an ordinarily righteous man <note>original: "ordinar-gerechter Mann"</note> to obtain forgiveness and be spared for himself in a general judgment. <margin>Ezek. 21:3.</margin> Abraham took upon himself something much greater and more significant here, as he pleaded for grace and sparing even for such utterly godless people.

The people of Sodom likely did not think that Abraham had such great love and faithfulness toward them, as to pray for the preservation of their lives. In their blindness and malice, they persecuted everything good; but the righteous man remained constant in love.

The new birth <note>A reference to spiritual regeneration or being "born again"</note> works nothing else in its true children. Their hearts often break over the misery when they see destruction and punishment before their eyes in the spirit. Indeed, the very sins with which unbelief draws

plagues upon its own head are so powerful as to stir the hearts of the members of Christ to faithful intercession.

The godless man, who considers the pious to be his enemies and persecutes them for that reason, does not believe this. But the righteous man persists in compassionate pleading for their best interest, even if he is cast out and rejected by them.

Why Abraham did not proceed further in his intercession after the sixth degree <note>The six steps of his negotiation: 50, 45, 40, 30, 20, 10</note>, it does not befit us to try to guess inquisitively. The greatness and the wealth of divine mercy, in that they could not prevail against the justice of God, only made the guilt and the divine judgment heavier. The Apostle shows in 2 Peter 2:7 that only shameful and vice-ridden people were to be found here, and God knew it well; He could also have given Abraham to understand this.

Had there been only ten God-fearing people in these five cities, Abraham’s request would have saved the lives of all of them together.

Such an overwhelming power and grace is hidden in faith that it could, so to speak, save and preserve many worlds, let alone countries and cities, if their own malice did not hinder it.

Faith is such a divine work when it keeps one unstained by the world. It sets one in sweet harmony with God’s mind and will. It gives the spirit of man the freedom to penetrate into God's heart. It makes prayer so bold and alert that it holds up the Father's own word and will to Him with all daring, yet in humility. And

The humility of the one who prays in a state of total self-nullification, expecting nothing except from the goodness of God, is very strong before God in obtaining what it desires. Therefore, God promises him that if He should find only ten righteous in this city, He would not destroy them. In the meantime, Abraham does not need to continue his prayer further. Yet he hopes that God would nonetheless forgive Lot and his house.

Two things are noteworthy in this. First, because God can refuse nothing to His best friends, and yet there are sinners who stand in great impenitence through their hardness; He does not allow His "bosom friends" <note>original: "Schooß-Freunde," referring to those most intimate with God</note> to ask anything else of Him than what He can and will grant. Therefore, Abraham’s prayer ceased here. And although God refused him nothing, He nonetheless exercised His justice over this sinful city. The second thing to note is that souls who have reached this constant state in God cannot pray otherwise than as He wills, and as He Himself moves them: for they have no other interest than His. This is seen in Abraham, who forgets all personal benefit and everything concerning flesh and blood, so that he may leave everything to God: since he does not even inquire how his nephew Lot would fare in the vengeance that God intended to send upon the city in which he lived; for he has a great assurance of the goodness and justice of God. He does not hold his own benefit higher than that of others, and in God, everything has now become one to him.

After Abraham had ended his prayer, he went again to his place, which is the rest in God, where he had also been before he saw the three angels.

## Chapter XIX.

### Lot's Rescue from the Destruction of Sodom.

**1.** And when the two angels came to Sodom in the evening, Lot was sitting at the gate of Sodom. And when he saw them, he rose up to meet them, and bowed himself with his face to the ground,

**2.** And said: Oh see, my lords, please turn aside into the house of your servant, and stay the night, and let your feet be washed <gloss>(a)</gloss>; then you may rise early in the morning and go your way. But they said: No, but we will stay in the street overnight.
<gloss>(a) ch. 18/3. 4.</gloss>

**3.** Then he urged them greatly <gloss>(a)</gloss>; and they turned in to him, and entered his house. And he prepared a meal for them, and baked unleavened cakes; and they ate.
<gloss>(a) Luke 24:29.</gloss>

Lot's hospitality is praised by the Apostle: *Do not forget to entertain strangers; for by doing so some have entertained angels without knowing it.* Hebrews 13:2. Scripture refers to them by such a name as they appeared; Lot first recognized them as men, but later as true angels, indeed, with emphasis as the Lord, v. 18. This is the name of God, whom he addresses shortly after in the singular, v. 19.

When the Lord initially refuses, He intends to test Lot's sincerity in virtue.

Otherwise, this is particularly understood as Christ, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit, who are sent by the Father. *And now the Lord, the LORD [Jehovah], has sent me and his Spirit.* Isaiah 48:16. There, the two actual names of God, Jehovah and Adonai <note>original: "Jehovali und Adonai"</note>, come from the Father; these names are then also given here to these two messengers, the Son and the Holy Spirit, as the true God; v. 24. Since the former is also the Angel of the Covenant, or the Spirit, who is sent by the Son just as by the Father. John 15:26.

In the midst of such a corrupt city as Sodom was, a person is found who stands in the peace of contemplation, and whom God rescues from the destruction threatened upon the godless.

Lot in his rest (for he sat) represents the contemplative life: and just as he, being related to Abraham, is also among the number of resigned souls <term>resigned souls: those who have surrendered their own will to God</term>; so he does exactly the same as Abraham did the previous day, although it happened in a far lesser degree. For Lot still sat at the gate of the city: which indicates a beginning contemplation, which is not yet far removed from the unrest and tumult of activity. Abraham's sitting at the door of his tent, however, shows rest in God, which is removed from all human society.

To Abraham there also came—which is notable—three men, and indeed at noon, or in the hottest and most fervent state: but to Lot come only two, and that in the evening. Abraham was capable of the full radiance of light. Lot only received those who came to destroy: but Abraham also received the One who wanted to preserve. Lot has no fine flour meal with his cakes, nor does he look to the measure of the Trinity, as Abraham did.

...one should nevertheless not do evil so that good may come. <note>This fragment refers to Lot’s offer of his daughters, warning that even for a "good" end (protecting guests), one should not commit a moral wrong.</note> ...to deliver from temptation. 2 Peter 2:9. Therefore He allowed the preliminary judgment of blindness to fall upon these wicked people, which should have brought them to some degree of reflection.

They were already blind before, as godless people, and here they become even blinder. Lot signifies the hidden Godhead. When people in their impurity attempt to force their way to this and wish to know it, they become even blinder.

Lot was well aware of the conduct of these wicked Sodomites according to the flesh in their impure lust, which he often had to see and hear, as his righteous soul was tormented from day to day with their lawless deeds. 2 Peter 2:7, 8, 10. But since he also had to experience the fear of man—in that he thought to hold back these godless people with friendly words, and was even willing to plunge his own family into danger, and thus sin against them and against God—the LORD nevertheless knew the time to rescue him and his family out of...

### Chapter XIX. The First Book of Moses.

12. And the men said to Lot: Do you have anyone else here? Perhaps a son-in-law, or your sons and your daughters, or whoever belongs to you in the city: lead them out of this place.
13. For we are going to destroy this place, because their cry <margin>(a) Gen. 18:20. James 5:4.</margin> (a) is great before the LORD: and the LORD has sent us to destroy it.

---

The Lord also reveals His counsel to Lot, who receives it in faith, acknowledging that God’s judgment is righteous.

**v. 13. Their cry is great)** What kind of cry does he mean here? Ambrose writes <gloss>(a)</gloss> that it is exactly that which cries out to the One who knows all, and before whom all sins give a sound and resonance. Thus, God is, as it were, called to action by the crying out of our sins, so that He might finally punish them, whereas otherwise He would gladly forgive.

<margin>Gregory the Great (b)</margin>
All injustice has its voice in the secret judgments of God, says Gregory the Great <gloss>(b)</gloss>.

And elsewhere: <gloss>(c)</gloss> A sin with a voice is a debt of actual malice; but a sin that truly "cries out" is a debt of great audacity.

We must understand and interpret all such pronouncements of God in the Scriptures inwardly and spiritually. In this way, sins possess within themselves such a power and quality of wrath and curse, such a contrariety and enmity against God, that they awaken and stir up God in His justice to punish and abolish them.

God rests in His eternal love, as in His quiet Sabbath, and has nothing but thoughts of peace toward mankind. But when men, through malice, tear themselves away from God's will and counsel, and walk directly contrary to divine justice, then justice and zeal—by virtue of which God can leave no evil unavenged—are awakened.

Then God lets His thoughts of peace and purposes of love toward men pass, and must necessarily, as a righteous and holy Being, attack and pursue the evil.

In this way, sin cries out to God and calls to heaven for vengeance: much like when a judge hears of the crimes of his subordinates and is provoked and compelled by the power or hideousness of such crimes to look into the matter.

Thus, sins have such an effect and awakening-power against God’s vengeance that they, as it were, cry into it and stir it up.

This cry reaches the omnipresent, righteous ear of divine holiness and enters the power of judgment, which the Father has handed over to the Son: who therefore, as the eternal Word of the Father, speaks the word here.

The sins of men cry out to this omnipresent and omniscient power of divine judgment as enemies and blasphemers, thereby inciting wrath and sounding an alarm that He must intervene.

Oh, if only all willful sinners would believe and notice how unfailingly all their deeds become known before the LORD! Poor man! You may carry out your affairs as secretly as you wish, yet eventually a cry will arise from them that will terrify you and accuse you before God.

You likely think, when you commit this or that in a corner: "No rooster will crow over it!" <note>The German idiom "kein Hahn drüber krähen" means "no one will ever know or care."</note> Who would find out? God pays no attention! But you should know that not only is the omniscient Judge of all flesh present then, even if you do not believe it; but also your own misdeeds, the work of your hands, will betray you sooner or later and present you as guilty.

You may defend yourself, deny, and lie as you wish; you may forbid others from betraying you: it is all in vain. You yourself have something within you that betrays you: the little dog under the left breast <note>A traditional Pietist metaphor for the conscience.</note> that barks, and can be stilled by nothing but repentance.

Now, if sins themselves cry out before the Lord in this way, how then can God remain silent? Must He not look into it and "destroy those who destroy the earth"?

<column-break/>

14. So Lot went out and spoke with his sons-in-law, who were to marry his daughters, and said: Get up and get out of this place! For the LORD will destroy this city. But he appeared to his sons-in-law as if he were joking. ->15. Then<-

---

Once the heavy judgment of hardening is imposed upon men, one sees how no admonition or threat will help any longer, but rather that wicked men hold all of this in contempt. For these sons-in-law may well have been outside the door and experienced the hand of the LORD earlier. See Isaiah 6:10-11.

Oh, how it is to be feared that many in our own times—and especially in the last days—even among those who side with Lot or the children of God and wish to live in their friendship, kinship, or community, may be seized by this Sodomite leaven of false security! When the time comes that they are exhorted to depart and separate from wicked men so that they are not caught up in the destruction, they may be found unwilling.

The mystery of iniquity is active and has already moved secretly in many who answer the reminders to depart and separate from everything to which God's judgment has a claim with a mocking spirit of scorn. They prefer to remain in the streets of the great city, which is spiritually called Sodom, and where our LORD is daily crucified, rather than enter into self-denial and the dying-off of the outer and inner self, and the dark path of holy faith.

What will happen when the final summons occurs and the voice resounds with the greatest emphasis:

**"Go out!")** How many will then be entangled in the cobweb of their own hypocritical piety and remain stuck in the destructive essence of transitory things, to whom this message will seem like mere fables. For they still have a plausible pretext to which they cling, causing them to remain settled on their dregs, because they see nothing special in many who wish to be regarded by others as having already "gone out." But what is the cause, other than that Sodom and Babylon have gone with them, and therefore have not really been forsaken? For it is in vain, and certainly only

**as if joking)** when one wants to practice "going out" only in an external and sensory way, while remaining far from true and thorough self-denial, contempt for the world and its lusts, honors, goods, and advantages, and far from the proper separation from all defilement of the flesh and spirit. Indeed, the salvation of God will also remain far from them, as they are blemishes upon divine truth. On the day of separation, it will become clear what the difference is, not only between the righteous and the godless, but also between the righteous and the hypocrites.

So let us now fear, lest anyone among us miss the time of visitation, or remain behind in the things that should have long been forgotten and looked upon with our backs turned: so that we do not lose the jewel of the heavenly calling!

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XIX.

<margin>(a) Josh. 6:15. (b) Acts 22:17, 18.</margin>
15. When the morning dawn arose (a) / the angels urged Lot to hurry (b) / and spoke: Arise / take your wife and your two daughters who are present; so that you do not perhaps perish in the iniquity of this city.

---

Thus, a certain sluggishness almost always clings to believers, such that they do not follow God's counsel swiftly enough; so much so that the Lord must almost compel them for their own salvation. This we must observe for our own correction and warning, so that we do not—through such lingering when the command to depart from Babel <note>In this spiritual tradition, "Babel" or Babylon represents the corrupt, worldly system that the soul must leave.</note> is earnestly given—become partakers of her sins, and receive some of her plagues. Revelation 18:4. See also Isaiah 51:14.

But whoever wishes to be saved both from general national punishments and from the particular plagues that the godless have in abundance, must first allow themselves to be truly delivered from sin. For the evil of sin and the evil of punishment hang inseparably together, and the latter necessarily follows the former by virtue of the unchangeable justice of God.

Among such redeemed of the Lord was also Lot, in whose heart the Spirit of Christ had kindled the knowledge of the true Messiah.

Even more was he strengthened in the faith of Jesus—through which he appeared as righteous before God—since the Messiah Himself appeared to him here in the form of an angel and also performed the outward deliverance.

Therefore, all, everyone, must first allow themselves to be redeemed inwardly if they wish to be free and safe outwardly.

It is true, the Savior has earned redemption for all people: But why then do not all people actually remain free from divine judgments? Is it not because they willfully push away the fruit and actual application of such universal redemption?

Necessarily, therefore, we must truly and in fact allow ourselves to be redeemed or torn out from this present evil world, if we wish to be quit of its punishments: according to Galatians 1:4.

This is what all messengers of God and of Christ have testified: that no one can be saved unless he separates himself from the godless and their sins.

He who dies to sin and believes in the name of the Son of God does not come into judgment. And even if common plagues should touch him, it would still be entirely distinct from the judgments upon the world.

Good Lot had not the slightest harmony in his heart with the Sodomites: therefore they tormented his righteous soul. This indicates sufficiently how far he was removed from the world’s abominations, so that he was dead and expired to sin and malice. This is to be understood regarding willful and reigning sins, where the mind and will cling with pleasure to the world and its horrors. Had he shared in these with the Sodomites, surely

the morning dawn of help and rescue would not have risen for him: which appeared to him just at the right time when the need was at its greatest. How anxious Lot must have been when the whole city stormed against him! And at that very moment, the Lord stepped in, stretched out His hand, and snatched him away.

That can still happen at any hour if we have faith. It only depends on our being properly prepared for it.

When things often look darkest inwardly and outwardly, God leads His own out of this spiritual Sodom and Babel, where our Lord Jesus Christ is incessantly crucified anew. Revelation 11:8.

Also, at the first rising of the spiritual dawn of divine truth, He begins straightway to work our redemption in our hearts. Indeed, the faithfulness of the Father’s heart neglects nothing concerning us.

Yes, for this very purpose the Father lets both His prophetic word and His Morning Star <note>A reference to Christ as the "Morning Star" (Rev 22:16), signifying the start of spiritual enlightenment in the soul.</note> itself rise and shine in the heart, so that in such a breaking day of conversion we may learn to perceive our danger and our enemies. And with this, He wishes to drive us, that we should

**Hurry)** Out of sin through true conversion. For in this way, and no other, one also unfailingly comes out from the reward and the fruit of sins.

God’s Fatherly love, which cannot bear to watch His children die, is revealed in that He speaks to His most intimate ones' hearts, indeed, works on them day and night, so that they should depart from Babel or leave the evil world with its examples.

Often He calls in the midst of seductive company and wishes to cut off all superfluous talk and things through inward discipline; He makes the heart anxious because of this and warns faithfully against harm.

Blessed is he who learns to know this voice and follows it!

<column-break/>

16. But as he lingered, the men took him and his wife and his two daughters by the hand, because the LORD spared him, and they led him out and left him outside the city. <margin>Gal. 1:4.</margin>

17. And

---

When words will not help, then heavenly Wisdom, like a loving mother hen, takes action. <note>An allusion to Matthew 23:37, where Jesus compares His care to a hen gathering her chicks.</note>

So deep an earnestness does the Redeemer have, that He does not rest from His work until He sees us in safety.

Ah, He still finds far too much dawdling and postponing in most hearts, as here with Lot! Double-heartedness has so deeply poisoned fallen man that he often, even in the midst of departing or in repentance, still limps, as it were, and holds himself back.

Who knows what good Lot might still have wanted to try with his sons-in-law or acquaintances; and that with good intention. And

how many good-looking things come in our way during our departure, which so easily interrupt our earnest purpose, or at the very least delay it.

Truly the danger is indescribable, much less the countless schemes of the Evil One to make even God's friends lukewarm and sluggish, so that they think like Lot: there is still time enough, the need is not quite so great, etc.

Not to mention how many, besides such subtle and apparent delays, may also be bound and held back with coarser ropes, especially with love of the world and of temporal things.

The Holy Spirit, however, will suffer no "raven’s voice" <note>The raven's cry was traditionally interpreted in Latin as "cras, cras" (tomorrow, tomorrow). Thus, the "raven's voice" represents the sin of procrastination in repentance.</note> or postponement until tomorrow, no rationalizing limitations or hesitation. All that He declares to be "Sodom-like behavior," in which we must perish.

Should it not then be grace when God, during your slow turning away from Sodom, actually seizes you by the hand or by your strength and wants to pull you out of the fire, as Jude gives counsel in his epistle verse 23?

How many times must God take hold and send strong "awakeners" <note>A Pietist term for life events, sermons, or trials that "wake" the soul from spiritual sleep.</note> when a soul is so deeply immersed either in transitory worries or in other considerations of the flesh and reason that it lets inward and outward warnings pass by.

And yet it is still grace when God does not let one go on in ignorance amidst the noise of the world and one's own fantasies: which is a terrible judgment upon those who would not follow so many tugs of grace.

But as certainly as wrath comes upon the children of unbelief—even though they go on safely for a long time to fill up their measure—so certainly the Lord Jesus takes His intimate ones by the hand of their faith and brings them completely out of the internal harmony or understanding with the fallen world.

Whoever feels God’s seizing hand upon them, let them not push it away, as they value their salvation. Had Lot not followed that very moment, not a speck of dust of him would have been saved. Thus, sometimes in a short time, that which is later difficult or impossible to replace is neglected.

God will do nothing without us; we must also put our hand to the work and allow ourselves to be governed by Him, but not lay our hands in our lap, thinking that God is obligated to save us even without or against our consent.

For in this way, and no other, one also unfailingly comes out from the reward and the fruit of sins.
