### Ch. XIX. The I. Book of Moses. 121

**17. And it happened as they had brought them out / that he spoke: Save your soul / and do not look behind you; also do not remain standing in this whole region. Save yourself upon the mountain / so that you do not perish.**

---

The discipline of wisdom demands from us absolutely the total withdrawal from all self-life <note>The "self-life" refers to the ego or the natural, unregenerate will of a person.</note>. For the words

**(Save your soul)** aim at a total separation from Sodom / and completely cut off all fellowship with the wicked.

And it is always the perfect intention of the Savior / that we should save our souls in such a manner. Not / as if we could redeem ourselves: but / because His redemption is in vain / where we do not withdraw ourselves from those things / from which He has acquired and offered us redemption.

If this actual avoidance and separation from evil were not necessary / the Apostles of Christ would not have needed to warn so earnestly after redemption was accomplished / as in 2 Cor. 6:17.

Therefore, may the Spirit of the Lord Jesus constantly repeat and call this out in our hearts! For the false nature is far too inclined / to still keep and make exceptions for this or that / as if one did not exactly have to leave it behind.

One does not like to have someone as an enemy / or to miss some advantage / or to fall into this or that gossip / and the like. The spirit of discipline must cut off all such anxieties / so that we may drive through all objections and protests of reason / and thus save the best thing / namely the soul. And once a resolution is made and the beginning is started / it then further says:

**Do not look behind you!)** What does this mean other than / that our poor soul / once it desires to leave the world / may no longer look back toward Egypt’s fleshpots <note>A biblical idiom for the comforts and pleasures left behind in a life of bondage/sin.</note> or worldly lusts. Luke 17:31.

A converted person is led with Israel into the wilderness / where, in the midst of abstaining from all things, a flattering craving for worldly joy / honor / and the like may inwardly arise. Here it is necessary / that the Angel of God’s Presence / Jesus Christ / often calls out: Do not look behind you!

Much less must our going out / our progress / the course of our calling / be transformed into a

**Standing still)** In the way to heaven, this is nothing other than / when someone has indeed put away coarse vices / but still maintains his own life / his natural rights, and his entire self-will: which can happen in countless ways and ever more subtly.

One who stands in contemplation <note>A reference to the "contemplative life," a spiritual state of focusing entirely on God.</note> / especially when he is just beginning it / still has many things which bind him to the creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created things or worldly attachments as opposed to the Creator.</note> / from which he cannot so quickly become free. This moves the angels to compel him. But words are not powerful enough for this: because the paths of these people / although they are full of apparent fire and zeal / are yet slow and sluggish in practice / in which many difficulties arise to be overcome. God or His angels must take them by the hand / so that they may be saved from the ruin and the fall / which would certainly bring them to shame / if they remained therein.

If God did not go to work in this way / these people would never finish with it. Because they have so little heart / and are so weak and shackled. Since God now wants to withdraw them from everything created / in order to lead them through His providence; so He commands them / not to look back nor to linger. These are also the faults of those people who stand in this state: who either look back / through over-thinking; or remain standing at a lesser thing than God is / through a single reservation. The angels advise leaving all interaction with creatures / and going to the mountain: which is the highest rung of the contemplative life.

The Lord also tends to give other people to the believers / and to do them good for that reason / when they receive the believers. Therefore, the world should indeed not persecute the children of God / or even drive them away with their evil life and the resulting resentment against them / as they soon yielded to Lot: v. 30. which may have then drawn them into the common judgment. v. 25.

<column-break/>

**18. But Lot spoke to them: Oh no, Lord!**

**19. Behold / your servant has found grace in your eyes: thus you would make your kindness great / which you have done to me / that you preserve my soul in life! But I cannot save myself upon the mountain: lest misfortune might overtake me / so that I die.**

**20. Behold / this city is near / to flee there / and it is small: let me save myself there! Is this not a small thing? That my soul may stay alive.**

**21. Then he spoke to him: Behold, I have also regarded you in this matter; that I will not overturn the city / of which you have spoken.**

**22. Hurry**

---

v. 19. Lot was not one of those who should be lost in Sodom / but also not one of the perfect ones like Abraham / who dwell in the heights.

Good Lot was overcome by his natural weakness / so that he did not dare to climb the mountain. He had become trembling before the fiery judgment of God / which was now to break out over the place. For

True children of God sometimes perceive the breaking judgments long beforehand / and sometimes become despondent over them themselves / so that the spirit of faith must strengthen them. This then sustains them especially through the experience of God’s previous goodness and mercy / which Lot also found cause to praise highly here.

Indeed, the exceeding goodness of God is not satisfied / merely to save us from evil / but it also makes itself so far

**Great)** that it grants all the good / which the godless neglect and push away from themselves / through the neglect of the

**Soul)** Truly the covenant of God becomes ever newer and firmer for life to a soul / which holds out through the right trials in self-denial! But

v. 20. Wavering people fear their loss / want to resist it in the beginning / and want to place themselves in safety by means of their reason. They propose a city / which they choose for their safety / that is / a certain way of life / in which they could maintain themselves / to lead themselves / since they cannot yet entirely trust God / nor abandon themselves to His providence. One also takes a plausible pretext / that the city is Small; as if one said: A lower, more certain path is dearer to me / than these great states in which there is more danger. One even wants to draw God into this proposal / by asking Him: Is this not a small thing / which we have chosen for our safety? Will not the way of humility give life to my soul?

v. 21. God hears the prayer of these wavering souls / because of their weakness / and assists them in that which they ask / even through miracles. This gladdens them beyond measure / as they imagine / their request was pleasing to God and profitable to them / because He performs miracles for their sake: whereas it is quite the opposite; as God only granted this to them because of their weakness.

# The I. Book of Moses. Cap. XIX. 122

<margin>
The LORD allows Himself to be so wonderfully held back in His judgments that He does not let them come to pass until His own have either died a blessed death or been rescued. Thus, the righteous are taken away before the misfortune. Is. 57:1, 2. So Methuselah died shortly before the Great Flood; Josiah died before the destruction of Jerusalem and the Babylonian captivity. The Christians were called out of Jerusalem by a divine voice before it was destroyed by the Romans, at which time they had to rescue themselves to Pella across the Jordan.
</margin>
<margin>
It is, however, a certain sign confirmed by a thousand examples that punishments are not far off when GOD commands His own to go out, either through death or through displacement and the like.
</margin>

### 22. Hurry and save yourself there! For I can do nothing until you arrive there. Therefore, the name of the city was called Zoar.

---

<margin>Here Lot called out:</margin>
**Hurry and save yourself!**) O, how necessary at all times is the internal hurrying out of the burning wrath of GOD and out of all the material of the same. For this wrath ignites like a lightning bolt and seizes everything that approaches it in unbelief.

Therefore, the Spirit of faith drives one to such a quick resolution that one must always stand, so to speak, ready to leap, like Israel.

The hurrying of a soul first indicates true earnestness; that it does not consult with flesh and blood <note>A biblical idiom meaning to not seek human advice or give in to natural human hesitation.</note>, but proceeds immediately and becomes voluntarily obedient to GOD.

But we see precisely from Lot’s example what a blessed thing it is to simply follow the living God against all reason. He believed the words of the LORD, and that was credited to him as such righteousness that even the LORD makes this wonderful confession:

**I can do nothing until you arrive there**
In this way, simple faith even binds the power of the invincible GOD, and through the love and mercy it has grasped, it powerfully holds back His justice! This is the greatest miracle in the world.

What cannot faint hearts—who especially become timid at the onset of GOD's judgments—draw in the way of courage from this, when they see how kindly and graciously the dear GOD acts with His friend Lot, like one man with another, so that they may trust this Savior all the more!

He confesses that He can do nothing before Lot's rescue: Is that not an unspeakable goodness and condescension to our weakness! One might well cry out: How great is your goodness <margin>Ps. 31:19, 20.</margin>

As great as the LORD Jesus's love and grace is in this matter, so great also appears His power in the rescue, which one often cannot admire enough under such circumstances. He came to the aid of the pious Lot here in a visible way. And

How many legions or choirs of angels do we think encamp around distressed souls who, in their need, can take comfort in no visible help? The entire kingdom of heaven certainly waits, so to speak, upon the rescue of a single soul: and what would GOD not venture before that soul should perish?

He did not even allow Lot's mortal body to perish in Sodom, let alone his soul. And how many thousand examples have been seen since the beginning of the world, that His love and power have come to the aid of His own in the most wonderful way? How then should we not still be able to trust the love of GOD, that it will protect and save His own even against the general plagues of the land which still lie before the world.

One has such glorious proofs of this at times when everything has gone topsy-turvy and wrath has flooded the land like a tide, that believers have been rescued in a wondrous manner. <margin>Ezekiel saw a glorious vision of this for his comfort, Ch. 9:4.</margin>

**Zoar)** otherwise also called Bela and Segor. <margin>Ch. 14:8.</margin>

<column-break/>

### 23. The sun had risen upon the earth when Lot entered Zoar.
### 24. Then the LORD rained sulfur and fire upon Sodom and upon Gomorrah from the LORD out of heaven; <margin>Num. 11:1.</margin>
### 25. And overthrew those cities and the entire region, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and what grew upon the land. <margin>Isa. 1:9.</margin>
### 26. And

v. 24. **The LORD from the LORD)** This is again a testimony that these two <note>Referring to the two angels/messengers as manifestations of the LORD.</note> were Jehovah, who caused this judgment to proceed from Jehovah the Father; just as the Father has given all judgment to the Son: And thus also from the triune GOD, who willed to reveal Himself thus to the believers and the prophets who wrote this, through such testimonies; <margin>See also Ps. 45:6, 7; 110:1.</margin> so that, when such things would later be entirely hidden from the Jews—indeed, be entirely contrary to them—it should nevertheless not seem strange to the believers in the New Testament, since they find so many clear testimonies of this recorded in the writings of the Old Testament. Thus, one must rightly wonder at the stubbornness of those among the Christians who do not want to recognize this mystery. Which is indeed a judgment upon human reason when one wishes to set it up as a judge in matters of faith and consult it for counsel.

**Sodom and Gomorrah)** God had filled this landscape—Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, and the fifth city Zoar in the same region, which for that reason are together called the <term>Pentapolis</term> <note>original: "Pentapolis"; a Greek term meaning "Five Cities."</note>—with much charm and fertility, so that the Jordan flowed through the middle and made the cities pleasant and fertile, like a paradise: <margin>according to ch. 13:10.</margin> The inhabitants had the example of the wrathful judgment of the Great Flood before them; which had not happened so long ago that it should have fallen from memory. This made their sin, and also the judgment upon them, all the heavier. The punishment by water in the Flood is not as painful to the human being who perishes in it as the fire, when he must be burned alive. Here, amidst the most horrific lightning bolts and flashes of fire, such a rain fell that, as the Hebrew word indicates, might rather be called a "sulfur-stream." Also, salt was mixed in to make the devastation and infertility of the land all the greater; and that thereby at least 4 cities were ruined: is to be seen from <margin>Deut. 29:23.</margin> That the fifth also had to suffer, Theodoretus, Lyra, and others maintain: because on one hand in the Book of Wisdom 10:6 it says that fire fell upon five cities (which stand together above in ch. 14:2); on the other hand, Lot left the same city immediately. Nevertheless, in Isa. 15:5 a Zoar is still mentioned. And travel descriptions also seem to indicate another; according to which this place is said to lie right on the Dead Sea, the location of which Jerome described in his time, at which a Roman garrison was stationed. But the Dead Sea or Salt Sea is said to have arisen afterward on that same spot, and the fire-judgment reached as far as that sea extends: which even to this day is said to have some signs of this curse. Meanwhile, this is a prototype of the final fire-judgment upon the spiritual Sodom, which degenerate Antichristianity has become; just as that Jerusalem is called a Sodom where our LORD is crucified by all the impure lusts—that impure fire of fleshly lusts and all malice and injustice becomes such sulfur, which the breath of the LORD will finally ignite like a sulfur-stream. <margin>See Isa. 1:10; Rev. 11:8; 2 Pet. 2:6, 3:7, 10, 12; Isa. 30:33.</margin>

---

For you must not think that the righteous GOD, who has punished others so severely for their sins, will become unjust toward you and not visit you for similar, or even greater, sins. For they are greater because far greater grace has been bestowed upon you. For if that had happened to Sodom and Gomorrah, says the Savior, which happened only to the Jews—who nevertheless remained stubborn—then how much more for those who actually accepted the Gospel and yet do not walk worthily of it: they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes.

# Chapter XIX. The First Book of Moses.

**26. And his wife looked behind him, and became a pillar of salt.**

She came—as some view the text not without reason—into a state of opposition against Lot during the journey; she lagged behind, kept looking around, and regretted what she had left behind. Because of this, her guilt became so much the heavier.

She had not yet died to herself <note>A pietist term meaning to relinquish worldly desires and ego in favor of divine will.</note>, but rather thought of her good housekeeping and provisions in Sodom, and sighed for them. She had left her heart there with her treasure, appearing as

The image of the flesh, which lusts after Sodom when the spirit has directed its path toward Zion.

<margin>(a) In the *Description of the Holy Land*, Part I, chapter 7, number 24.</margin>
Bochartus <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a famous French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer.</note> (a) writes that on his journey he went to incredible trouble in that region to see such a pillar, but could not reach it. This was because he was informed that one could not easily get to that place—at least not without danger to one’s life—both because of wild animals and poisonous snakes, and because of the evil, inhumane inhabitants of those parts.

The Savior presents this heavy judgment upon Lot’s wife to us as a warning for the last days: *Remember Lot’s wife!* Luke 17:32. For those times shall also be like the days of Lot. verses 28, 29, 30. There, one should also not sin with unbelief in divine judgments or by clinging to earthly things. In this, Lot's wife sinned: she looked back against the prohibition and thought perhaps it would not have turned out so badly, wishing she were back with her people and her possessions. See Luke 21:34, 35, 36. This desire is very dangerous, especially in the last days (James 5:3), because it completely hardens and stubborns the heart against all divine warnings that He will issue regarding impending judgments.

The nature of faith is to leave oneself entirely to GOD, even regarding temporal matters, and for that reason, to gladly renounce such things for the sake of GOD and the truth.

Such faith then experiences great wonders of how GOD cares for His own amidst all abandonment.

It is exceedingly thoughtful and refreshing how GOD restored to Lot, in his descendants, that which he may have left in Sodom and lost in the fire. Genesis 2:9, 19.

One must conclude from his lingering and other circumstances that he must have struggled with all sorts of scruples. Nevertheless, a simple obedience was found in him.

But his wife perished in the middle of the departure: which is terrible, despite the fact that she did not remain in the city. Without doubt, this was because she had only gone out with her body at Lot’s urging, but not with her heart, with which she looked back.

A warning to us: that in all our "going out" or renouncing of the world, we must examine our foundations and with what mindset we do it—whether it happens to please others, for the sake of company, or to avoid gossip as if one were also ungodly, and the like.

Regardless, strong trials often come in the midst of the departure to put us to the test of how we truly mean it.

A soul that has not yet come far now enters into deliberation and looks behind itself, against GOD’s commandment. The most necessary thing on this path is to go forward without overthinking. And GOD gives an example of this by transforming this weak woman into a pillar of salt: to show that the "salt"—one's own wisdom, reason, and caution <note>The author plays on the word "salt" to represent human intellect or "shrewdness" which preserves the old self rather than trusting God.</note>—is useless on the path where <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A difficult-to-translate German term meaning "yieldedness," "calmness," or "letting go" to God’s will.</note> and faith alone must lead; and that all caution which one takes from oneself only hinders the inner way, instead of bringing any advantage to it.

<column-break/>

**27. And Abraham got up early in the morning to the place where he had stood before the LORD.**

**28. And he turned his face toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the region: and he looked, and behold, a smoke went up from the land, like the smoke of a furnace.**

**29. And it came to pass, when GOD destroyed the cities of the region, that GOD remembered Abraham; and led Lot out of the overthrow, when he overthrew the cities in which Lot dwelt.**

**30. And Lot went up from Zoar and stayed on the mountain, and his two daughters with him; for he was afraid to stay in Zoar: and so he stayed in a cave, he and his two daughters.**

**31. Then the firstborn said to the younger: Our father is old, and there is no one in the land who may come in to us, according to the way of all the earth.**

**32. Come, let us give our father wine to drink, and lie with him: that we may preserve offspring from our father.**

**33. So...**

<margin>v. 29.) In consideration of the one standing in the fully contemplative life <note>Referring to Abraham as a spiritual giant of meditation/prayer.</note>, GOD rescues the beginner <note>Referring to Lot.</note> from the destruction of the city which he had chosen for his residence.</margin>

<margin>v. 30.) Through his prayer, or rather because of Abraham, it is instilled in Lot to go onto the mountain, where he dwelt in a cave with his two daughters. This represents the solitude of the person standing in contemplation.</margin>

<margin>v. 31. 32.) This did not happen so much out of fleshly lust as out of unnecessary worry for their lineage, and—as many wise teachers maintain—solely for the purpose and intention that they might become the ancestors of the Messiah (as was also fulfilled in Ruth, who was a Moabitess and brought Obed, the grandfather of David, into the world through Boaz). They supposed that there was no one present in the region whom they could or might marry, because they now preferred to remain by themselves and propagate their own kind; or also, as others (including Josephus and Origen) understand it, because they thought no man was left on earth. Some translations suggest this, as they might have heard something about the world perishing in fire and could have come to the thought that something similar had occurred with fire then as had occurred with water in the time of Noah—that they alone remained with their father. This, however, does not excuse the incest at all; even the weakness of Lot in his drunkenness had to be made manifest for his humiliation. Thus, when one has escaped one danger, one must always be on guard so as not to fall into another temptation. For Satan certainly stalks rescued souls in particular: so much so that some sometimes do not have such great temptation in the middle of Sodom as they do in solitude.</margin>

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XX.

33. So they gave their father <gloss>(a) chapter 19:21.</gloss> wine to drink that same night, and the firstborn went in and lay with her father; and he was not aware of it when she lay down, nor when she rose up.

34. And it happened the next day that the firstborn said to the younger: "Behold, I lay yesterday with my father; let us give him wine to drink this night also, then you go in and lie with him, so that we may keep our lineage alive through our father."

35. So they gave their father wine to drink that same night also, and the younger arose and lay with him; and he was not aware of it when she lay down, nor when she rose up.

36. Thus both the daughters of Lot became pregnant by their father.

37. And the firstborn bore a son, and she named him Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to this day.

38. And the younger, she also bore a son, and she named him Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the children of Ammon to this day.

---

<margin>verse 33.</margin> He believes himself to be out of all danger because he has his two daughters with him: namely, silence and seclusion. But he does not see that, because he trusts himself too much, these very things will be the cause of his fall. God permitted this to show him that he would preserve himself in vain if God Himself did not preserve him, and thereby to move him toward that total surrender to God in which He wishes to lead him.

<margin>verse 36. daughters of Lot pregnant by their father)</margin> Regarding this, the following riddle has been made:
> My father, your father,
> Our children's grandfather;
> My husband, your husband,
> Our both's mother's-husband:
> And yet he is no more than one man.
As Luther judges <note>Referring to Martin Luther's commentary on Genesis.</note>, after Lot became aware of what he had done, he was so troubled by it that he did not live much longer; therefore Moses mentions him no further.

<margin>verse 37. 38. Moab—Ben-Ammi)</margin> From these, two harmful nations arose who were often a plague to the people of God, and thus they carried the mark of their sinful origin at all times in this enmity. For this reason, the Lord commanded that they be punished, stating that no Moabite or Ammonite should enter the assembly of the Lord even unto the tenth generation. This considerable span of time is shortly thereafter expressed by the word "eternity" in Deuteronomy 23:3. Meanwhile, the children of Israel were to inherit nothing of their land, because God had given it to the children of Lot—and thus for Abraham's sake—nor were they to wage war against them, because they had driven out the giants, the Anakim <note>A race of giants mentioned in the Old Testament.</note>, and other idolatrous nations, and had taken their cities. Deuteronomy 2:9, 19. Thus, after the aforementioned "eternity" (restricted to a specific, rather long period) and the tenth generation were fulfilled, the Moabitess Ruth was wedded to Boaz—who was the tenth generation from Abraham, as seen in Matthew 1:5, 17. From this line, through Obed and Jesse, King David and consequently Christ according to the flesh were born, and she was thus received into the community of the Lord.

### The XX. Chapter.

->Sarah’s Protection with Abimelech.<-

But Abraham journeyed from there into the land toward the South, and dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and stayed as a stranger in Gerar.

<margin>2. And</margin> When we look at Abraham’s course of life, this good man certainly had few good days for his flesh in this world. When one trial was over, a new and stronger one usually arrived. The dearer he was to God, the more sharply he had to go to the cross <note>A metaphor for enduring suffering and spiritual testing.</note>.

It was certainly no small thing that the good Abraham had to live not only in places among total strangers and move from one spot to another, but that he also came into such great danger twice because of his wife, and had to expect that the people in the land would act toward him and his own like godless rogues.

This may well be a true mirror showing how little substance and security a cross-bearer of Jesus Christ finds in this evil world; indeed, how he often comes into danger of his life, honor, and all things, only for his exercise and preservation, so that he may live in this world in a fine, lowly, cautious way, and in self-denial.

If God did not give a believer courage and secretly sustain him with His strength, one would never come through the coarse crowd of worldly people with an undamaged soul. One would either fall into the pleasures and delights of the world and sin, or else join in hypocrisy out of fear, and fail to contradict their abominations or oppose them with deeds.

But this is a very healthy state where God brings a person to the point where they must do without all outward counsel, comfort, and protection, and cannot rely on their own strength or cleverness; but must step like a sheep into the midst of wolves and rely solely on God's grace and faithfulness.

Yet this exercise was not enough for Abraham; he also had to fall into danger of losing his wife multiple times. The more he loved her and was united with her in faith, the harder this task may have seemed to his flesh—that he should see such a faithful spouse, bound to him in God, being snatched and taken away by tyrants. But as great as these trials were, the Lord watched over His friends just as faithfully, as can be seen in the following.

<margin>Stranger)</margin> Thus the believers must seek to follow Abraham here with David; so that, even if they were in princely or even royal dignity, they could not behave or speak otherwise on this earth than in truth: *I am both your pilgrim and your guest, like all my fathers.* Psalm 39:12.

<margin>Gerar)</margin> As Heidanus <note>Abraham Heidanus (1597–1678), a Dutch Cartesian theologian.</note> (a) notes, in those places there is a sandy desert that is very dangerous to travelers, both because of the lack of water and because of the high sand dunes—almost mountains—by which travelers are often covered. Because of this, they are forced, like seafarers, to direct their way by the stars. For lack of water, a Jew who had turned to Christianity is said to have been baptized there with sand, as Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> reports.

<gloss>(a) in *Palestine*, chapter 4, section 27.</gloss>

# Chapter XX. The First Book of Moses.

Q 3

<meta>catchword: v. 4.</meta>

**2. And Abraham said of his wife Sarah: She is my sister. <gloss>(a)</gloss> Then Abimelech, the king of Gerar, sent and had Sarah taken.** <margin>(a) chapter 26:7.</margin>

---

<gloss>Abraham said — She is my sister)</gloss> Here, as some observe, Abraham’s weakness was revealed once more; though he had already fallen into danger because of this in Egypt, he now stumbles over the very same stone, even while his wife was pregnant with the promised seed. <note>The author suggests Sarah might already be pregnant with Isaac, though the biblical chronology is often debated here.</note> And although he was certain of her chastity and lived in the good confidence that GOD would take care so that no evil would befall her, and his marriage bed would be preserved undefiled; yet the act in itself was not good. Therefore, GOD’s long-suffering is to be praised, for He forgives such faults of the fear of man in His own and watches over them; nevertheless, they should guard themselves and not tempt GOD.

And so, believers, even if they are in places where there is no fear of GOD and are in great danger, must not seek to escape it through fleshly cleverness: because they only fall into greater danger thereby, and—even if the Lord rescues them—they are rightly put to shame because of their fleshly schemes. However—

Abraham committed no lie in saying that Sarah was his sister; for, as he himself shows further down, she really was his sister, being the daughter of his father, but not of his mother: yet she was not the immediate daughter of Terah, Abraham's father, but of Haran, Abraham's brother. Thus Sarah was Terah’s granddaughter and Abraham’s niece: <note>The German "Baaſe" here refers to a female relative, specifically a niece or cousin.</note> and Abraham could say she was his sister because she was the daughter of his grandfather, and in Holy Scripture the name "son" or "daughter" is often used for "grandson" or "granddaughter."

What might seem to be sin here could be that he knew he risked his life and the honor of his wife. But besides the fact that such a faithful man does nothing without GOD's special command, which drives him to proceed thus; it is also true that GOD allowed these things to happen to show all people the strong faith of Abraham, as well as His great and special protection of those who abandon themselves to Him.

One might further say that if Abraham’s faith was so great, and GOD’s dealings with him so special, then He surely would have revealed to him that Abimelech would not have touched his wife, even if Abraham had immediately indicated she was his wife. To this, it is easy to answer: it is GOD’s way to deal with souls in this manner when He leads them through faith; namely, that He lets them go here and there according to His pleasure, without giving them any certainty of what shall happen. For this reason, He reveals His secrets least of all in this regard, to better test their faith and equanimity. It happened thus so that GOD could more emphatically show His protection over those who surrender to Him without reservation, and could take care of them in such a glorious way that the memory of it would be preserved for all eternity and serve as an example to faithful souls, so that they might be encouraged in their trust.

<gloss>Abimelech)</gloss> This name was a title of honor common to the kings of the Philistines, like the name Pharaoh for the kings of Egypt; though he is otherwise said to have been named Jara or Jerad Kushi. See Psalm 34:1 compared with 1 Samuel 21:12, where the same Abimelech is called by the specific name Achish. <note>original: "Achis"</note> The aforementioned name means as much as "My father the king." This expressed the fatherly office of kings and all rulers, and thus served to remind them, as well as their subjects, of their filial duty.

...seed of the devil, and man rarely or never wishes to rightly recognize such things, so He allows that same corruption to break out now and then for salutary reasons, betraying itself like a thief sitting hidden in the heart.

Abimelech would hardly have recognized his own condition if this occasion had not brought him to it. For GOD showed him that he was on dangerous paths, even if unknowingly, and that he would have to face death if he fulfilled his purpose and kept the woman: whereas it had to serve as a lesson to him after he changed his mind, and it suited him that he—

<column-break/>

**3. But GOD came to Abimelech in a dream by night, and said to him: Behold, you are a dead man because of the woman you have taken! For she is married to a husband.** <gloss>Psalm 105:13-15.</gloss>

### 4. Abi

---

One sees from the whole history that this man truly knew and feared GOD, and a fine faith must have dwelt in him, because he immediately accepted this warning as GOD’s voice and a divine revelation, and did not reject it as devilish or deceptive, as the crude world tosses all GOD’s warnings from within and without to the wind. For what a sign of a heart practiced in faith it was that Abimelech knew immediately that GOD was speaking with him in a dream, and not that an evil spirit was mocking him. Without doubt, he was accustomed to divine fellowship and address, and was taught and assured by the Holy Spirit so that he could distinguish such from all false impressions.

<gloss>You are a dead man)</gloss> It was therefore a dangerous thing, in which Abimelech could easily have suffered great damage to his soul if GOD had not preserved him.

But in what did the temptation and the evil consist on Abimelech's part? Answer: According to the ground of the heart: as soon as this man saw the woman, lust and desire woke up in his heart to long for her. The disorder of such desire consisted in the haste—that he did not first inquire whether this person might be married or not, and whether he could thus take a right to her before GOD. Instead, he lunged forward immediately, used his royal power, and had Sarah brought to his residence. Now, he may have undoubtedly based his actions on GOD’s first ordinance <note>Referring to the general institution of marriage.</note>; and thus his intention was in itself good and permissible. However, the temptation and danger arose from his haste, which came from the intensity of his desires for the person, which he allowed to grow strong within him, and broke out in the taking away of the woman, even if he did not touch her immediately. And to that extent, it was a very dangerous temptation for this otherwise honest man. He was enticed and lured by his own indwelling lust; which then conceived and brought forth the resolution that he wanted to take this woman.

He probably did not think so, and many still do not believe it, that such a secret thief sticks in the human heart, who so gladly grazes and strives after foreign things. But that is really temptation enough when we do not know this evil in ourselves, or do not guard and preserve ourselves against it.

One sees from this act of Abimelech what an evil root of hereditary lust <term>Erb-Luſt: original sin or inherited concupiscence</term> sticks in everyone, not only in the unconverted but also in the converted; and that therefore no one should trust his false heart, but should indeed persist in watching and praying until his end.

How easily one can be attacked and ensnared by such hidden hereditary lust, so that one is moved toward something disorderly; that is also seen clearly and distinctly from this: and especially how quickly this bad trait may overtake the soul, and how the enemy’s advantage or stratagem of war lies precisely in such haste. For—

That is a heavy trial for man, especially for hot and quick natures, when this or that disorderly affect or emotion carries the heart away with power, and does not let it come to testing or investigation, does not let it become still and inward, but makes the man rush forward and break out with something that he afterward regrets and is ashamed of.

And yet GOD has His salutary purpose therein for the godly when He allows such bad traits to break out. He truly has no pleasure or guilt in it: but because He knows that such misery is hidden in the human heart, like a—

4. But Abimelech had not come near her and said: Lord, will you then also slay a righteous people?

5. Did he not say to me: She is my sister? And she herself also said: He is my brother. I have done this in the **sincerity** of my heart and in the **innocence** of my hands.

<margin>Ps. 24:4.</margin>
v. 4. **Had not come near her**) This is not reported in vain, but to show that this man stood under the special supervision and governance of the Spirit of GOD, and thus found grace before GOD, so that He preserved him in the temptation.

If Abimelech had not been diligent in his watchfulness, and had not paid attention to GOD’s influence and speech in his heart, he would have fallen hard. But because he was accustomed to divine correspondence and fellowship, and observed the same as his best treasure, he was happily rescued from the trial and warned against it.

v. 5. So he could also appeal before the LORD to his 

**Sincerity**) <term>Einfalt</term> <note>While literally meaning "simplicity," in this 17th-century context, it refers to a "singleness of heart" or spiritual integrity that is free from hidden agendas.</note> That he had begun this matter without malice or treacherous hidden intentions, and was aware of nothing else than that he wanted to fear the LORD and not offend Him.

For that is actually true sincerity according to the sense of the Spirit: namely, such an uprightness and unadulterated purity of the heart, wherein one is concerned with nothing else in the world but only to follow and please GOD, and to fear and love Him with all one's heart.

Such things are given and worked by the Holy Spirit alone, when He enters the heart of a repentant person and brings him from falsehood to faithfulness and honesty, so that he becomes a partaker of the divine nature; then the works of such a person are done with a sincere heart.

Without such sincerity, no matter is pleasing before GOD. For it is that 

**Innocence**) of the mind and will which Christ grants in the new birth, in which we must be renewed unto the righteousness and holiness of the truth, once we have laid aside all hypocrisy and lies.

There one sees now how the heart of a person must stand if he wants to come out of temptations unscathed. That is rightly said: *The innocent will be delivered.* Job 22:30. <note>The author quotes Job here to emphasize that Abimelech's lack of "guilty knowledge" protected him.</note>

Such upright, innocent, and sincere souls have the privilege and prerogative with GOD that they are preserved in their heavy temptations. Ps. 116:6.

Even if it happens that a good soul is led astray either by its own thoughts or by evil people—as his people presumably brought and pointed out this woman to this king—yet the faithfulness of GOD soon helps him out of such snares again, so that he does not remain lying in them.

This is because in such honest souls there lies a secret spark of grace hidden, which holds them back, so that they do not sink with their whole will and all their strength into abominations and become overwhelmed by them, but soon withdraw their compliance and turn in repentance and faith to GOD.

In this way, the temptation of a righteous person is heaven-wide different from the deceptions of the ungodly. For the innermost ground of the former’s heart never actually consents to evil.

That was also the difference between King Pharaoh and Abimelech. Both took Abraham's wife, but with unequal minds. Therefore, the former was plagued, but this one was not. Thus there is no doubt, as <term>Ambrosius</term> <note>St. Ambrose (c. 340–397 AD), an influential Bishop of Milan known for his biblical commentaries.</note> judges, that the wrath of the LORD was held back by his otherwise pious conduct; because the LORD is truly a judge of the innermost conscience and an interpreter of the mind and spirit.

And what is there yet much to doubt, since the all-knowing GOD Himself gives him testimony therein—

<column-break/>

6. And GOD said to him in a dream: I also know that you have done this in the sincerity of your heart; and I have also kept you from sinning against me: therefore I did not allow you to touch her.

7. So

**I know**) No one can test us better than the eye of the LORD Himself. His Spirit searches through all our mental movements and can place quite precisely into the light before our face our most secret designs and side-intentions, which we would otherwise never know or believe of ourselves.

But if GOD is to look upon the ground of our heart, it must be unstained by such things, and conversely, uprightness must dwell therein. Then the Holy Spirit will give witness to our spirit that GOD knows us and recognizes us as His own. Just as here Abimelech received testimony from GOD Himself regarding his 

**Sincerity**) He had a good intention <note>original: "intention"</note> to marry the woman properly according to GOD’s institution, since he thought and knew no otherwise than that she was single.

Because he had no evil in it nor sought it, and otherwise feared the LORD with right earnestness, and had an abhorrence of offending Him with knowledge and will, GOD could not leave him stuck in this temptation. As He so emphatically expresses His fatherly care for Abimelech in this regard:

**I have also kept you**) See, that is the faithfulness of the Keeper of Israel, who does not like for a soul to offend against Him!

Do you think GOD seeks anything else with all His work on you, through so many knocks, through so many anxieties that you perceive over this or that injustice, than the rescue and preservation of your soul from so many temptations?

Actually, Abimelech would have sinned against Abraham; yet GOD says here that it would have been acted against His Majesty: That you might not

**Sin against me**) So seriously does He take our affairs, and therefore also so gladly prevents our guilt.

**Not allowed**) This speaks clearly of a permission or granting, where GOD, out of great faithfulness, did not leave the man so much time and space to sin, but immediately hindered and warned him.

And indeed, as <term>Lutherus</term> <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> well notes here, GOD not only kept Abimelech from sin from the outside but also kept his heart chaste.

It is certain that many people consider themselves innocent because they did not know a matter; yet they are not so in truth. For to the halting of sin, two things are required: ignorance and sincerity of heart. The latter, however, is the most necessary. Therefore, GOD says to Abimelech that He did not allow him to sin against Him because of the sincerity of his heart. GOD would rather perform a miracle than allow a person who came to Him in the sincerity of his heart to offend Him in his ignorance; not only with a sin of the mind, but also with an actual sin. Just as it is written: *I have not permitted you to touch her.* But how often it happens that those who sin out of ignorance have already defiled the heart through other sins which they commit with knowledge! Therefore, since they have no sincerity of heart, but on the contrary a corrupt heart in all things; they sin in things which they do not recognize as sin because of the corruption of their heart. From which it is to be gathered how beneficial the uprightness and sincerity of the heart is to us. GOD demands this most from us. Sincerity makes the heart pure and straight: and even if it seems as if such a person sins, yet he does not sin because of the sincerity of his heart. Therein they differ from those who seem righteous on the outside but sin because they deal with artifices and complexity, which is the origin of hypocrisy.

<gloss>v. 7. **He is a prophet**)</gloss> That is; he is so well-known and intimate with Me that he maintains a close <term>correspondence</term> <note>original: "Correspondenz"; in this context, a mystical or direct spiritual communication</note> with Me and My Spirit, and therefore possesses great influence.

<gloss>**Let him pray for you; thus you shall remain alive**)</gloss> According to the Hebrew, it can also mean: *He will pray for you, and you shall live.* This means that God says to him: I lift the sentence of death against you, which was issued because of such an intention, and restore you to the possession and enjoyment of life. You shall live and not die.

<gloss>**know that you must surely die**)</gloss> Because the human heart is so heedless of God’s holy reminders and does not always follow good words so earnestly, God finds it necessary to also show severity and to use threats.

God does no differently with every human being, especially when He sees one running toward their own ruin. Then He threatens with words and works. How many does He cast down upon a sick-bed! How many does He strike in their honor, their goods, or their relatives! Are these not certain threats, where God, as it were, says to such a person: Unless you cease this or that, you are a dead man.

As can be seen from the following verses, God had already begun to punish Abimelech here by making the women barren.

v. 8.) Oh, what wholesome news all of this can give us, regarding how we should surrender ourselves to the Lord, so that He may have power over us and make His warnings serve our good! Ah, how soft, how obedient God should rightly find our hearts when He comes to exhort us, just as He found the king here!

One should not take it so poorly, and become so angry and false, when God lets us hear His warnings—when we are outwardly reminded for the sake of conscience! How many are there who cannot bear any outward reminders! When they are rebuked for their sins, they begin to complain about others: saying they were reported, slandered, and the like.

How do you expect to be preserved from evil any longer if you will not follow any voice of God?

If Abimelech had despised this speech from God, perhaps under the pretext that it was from the devil, who was an enemy of marriage, he would have infallibly fallen into God’s judgment. And so it goes for all who rage and strive against God with unbelief.

For this is the greatest harm: that God finds no faith among men, even when He warns them faithfully. Everything is soon frustrated by <term>Reason</term> <note>original: "Vernunfft"; often used by 17th-century spiritual writers to mean human intellect acting in opposition to divine revelation</note>: one looks for whatever can be brought up against it, only so that the false will does not have to obey. This is the greatest misery on earth, that God finds no obedient hearts among the children of men.

Whoever can still be advised should let themselves be warned and reminded by God with great diligence. Let him do as Abimelech did: he immediately sent the wife back to her husband and even scolded him for not making it known. Furthermore, he did not hesitate to call all his servants together and tell them of this divine revelation, and indeed with such power and earnestness that it says:

**The people were very afraid**) See, thus a divine warning often serves many other souls for their improvement and preservation. And:

When kings and superiors first truly dread God’s judgments and take divine warnings to heart—changing what brings such heavy punishments upon them and their realms, and earnestly presenting it to their subjects—that makes a right impression upon them and brings about a fear of God in many.

<gloss>v. 9-11. The rebuke which Abimelech gives to Abraham shows the innocence and simplicity of this king's heart, as well as the fear he had of displeasing God; which also caused God to perform a double miracle: namely, to rescue Sarah and to preserve this prince from sin.</gloss>

He rebukes Abraham for his oversight very modestly, and rightly suspects that he was led into it through the fear of man—just as he, the king, had been too quick to listen to his own desire and had not investigated the matter better. Abraham then revealed to him his opinion of the wretched state of the earth, which he also suspected in this kingdom: that the fear of God was almost nowhere to be found. This is something a traveling pilgrim especially experiences as he wanders through lands one after another; and such a pitiful state now likely prevails in all kingdoms and dominions, according to the complaints the Spirit of God leads concerning the last times.
<margin>Ps. 12:1; 14:1. Ps. 36:2. Rom. 3:18. 2 Tim. 3:1 etc.</margin>

<gloss>v. 12. Abraham’s words can be understood to mean that Sarah was the granddaughter of Terah (Abraham's father) through his son Haran. Haran had two daughters: Milcah, who married Nahor (Abraham's brother), and Iscah, who may also have been Sarai, as the Jews believe. Abraham married her; and thus the two brothers married the two daughters (and thus two sisters) of their deceased brother, Haran: Chapter 11:29. They could also be called "sisters" just as Lot was called a "brother" in Chapter 13:8. In this way, Abraham might not have sinned against the prohibition in Leviticus 18:9, which states that one shall not marry his sister, whether she be the father's daughter or the mother's daughter. This prohibition is grounded in natural decency, which Abraham likely did not overstep.</gloss>

One should not take it so poorly, or become so angry and false, when God lets us hear His warnings or when we are outwardly reminded for the sake of conscience! How many there are who cannot bear any outward reminders! When they are punished for their sins, they begin to complain about others: saying they were reported, slandered, and the like.

How do you expect to be preserved from evil if you refuse to follow the fine voice of God?

Had Abimelech despised this speech from God—perhaps under the pretext that it was from the Devil, who is the enemy of marriage—he would have infallibly fallen into God's judgment. And so it goes for all who persist and stray against God with unbelief.

For the greatest harm is that God finds no faith among men, even when He reminds them faithfully. Everything is soon frustrated by human reason: people look for something they can bring up against the warning, only so that their false will does not have to obey. This is the greatest misery on earth: that God finds no obedient hearts among the children of men.

Whoever can still be advised should let himself be most diligently warned and reminded by God. Let him do as Abimelech did: he immediately sent the wife back to her husband, and even scolded him for not making the truth known. Furthermore, he did not hesitate to call all his servants together and tell them of this divine revelation, and indeed with such power and earnestness that it is said:

**The people were very afraid**) See, thus a divine warning often serves many other souls for their improvement and preservation. And:

When kings and those in authority truly revere God's judgments and take divine warnings to heart—changing what brings such heavy punishments upon them and their kingdoms, and earnestly presenting it to their subjects—that makes a true impression upon the people and brings about a fear of God in many.
</gloss>

<column-break/>

9. And Abimelech called Abraham and said to him: Why have you done this to us? And what have I sinned against you, that you have brought a great sin upon me and upon my kingdom? You have done deeds to me that ought not to be done.

10. And Abimelech spoke further to Abraham: What did you see <note>meaning: what was your intent or observation</note> that you have done such a thing?

11. And Abraham said: Because I thought, there is surely no fear of God in this place; so they will slay me because of my wife.

12. And yet she is truly my sister; she is my father’s daughter, but not my mother’s daughter: and she became my wife.

13. And it happened, when God caused me to wander from my father’s house, I said to her: Let this be the kindness you show me; at every place where we come, say of me: "He is my brother." 14. Then

<gloss>
v. 9-11. The rebuke which Abimelech gives to Abraham shows the innocence and simplicity of this king's heart, as well as the fear he had of displeasing God. This fear also caused God to perform a double miracle: namely, to rescue Sarah and to preserve this prince from sin.

He rebukes Abraham for his error very modestly, and rightly suspects that he was led into it by the fear of man. Likewise, the king himself had acted hastily with his desire without investigating the matter better. Then Abraham revealed to him his opinion of the miserable state of the earth, which he suspected was also the case in this kingdom: that the fear of God is almost nowhere to be found. A traveling pilgrim especially experiences this as he wanders through one land after another; and such a pitiful state now prevails in all kingdoms and domains, according to the complaints the Spirit of God makes regarding the latter times. <note original="Pf. 12/14. 36/2. Röm. 3/18. 2. Tim. 3/1. 2c.">Psalm 12, 14, 36:2; Romans 3:18; 2 Timothy 3:1, etc.</note>

v. 12. Abraham's words can be understood to mean that Sarah was the granddaughter of Terah <note original="Thara">Abraham's father</note>, being the daughter of his son Haran. Haran had two daughters: Milcah, who married Nahor (Abraham's brother), and Iscah <note original="Jisca">Traditionally identified by Jewish scholars as Sarah</note>, who may also be Sarah, whom Abraham married. Thus, the two brothers married the two daughters of their deceased brother, Haran—meaning they married two sisters. <note original="Cap. 11/29.">Genesis 11:29</note>. These could also be called "sisters" in the same way Lot was called a "brother" in <note original="Cap. 13/8.">Genesis 13:8</note>. Thus, Abraham might not have sinned against the prohibition in <note original="3. Mos. 18/9.">Leviticus 18:9</note>, which states that one should not marry his sister, whether she be the father's daughter or the mother's daughter. This law is grounded in natural decency, which Abraham presumably did not transgress.
</gloss>

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XX.

## Left Column

14. Then Abimelech took sheep and cattle / and male and female servants / and gave them to Abraham; and he returned his wife Sarah to him.

15. And Abimelech said: See, my land lies there before you; dwell wherever it pleases you.

16. And to Sarah he said: See, I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver! Behold, he is to you a **covering of the eyes** / among all who are with you; yes, before everyone / so that you may be <term>righted</term><note>The original German "bestattet" here implies being vindicated, settled, or properly covered in a legal and social sense.</note>.

---

This is as much as to say: In the future, do this no more / that you go without a veil / and thereby mislead others. I have given your brother 1,000 <term>shekels</term><note>A weight of silver used as currency; the text equates them to "Silberling" or silverlings.</note>, but to you nothing; so that no one might come to the thought / that I had given you a "whore's wage." Your brother and husband at once is reason enough for you to veil your face / and he shall rightly cover you from the gaze and embrace of others.

God thus directed Abimelech's heart toward generosity / in order to atone for the mistake committed. Since Sarah was also kindly rebuked by him / so that she should honor this her alleged brother as a husband in the future / and should cover herself: which custom was prevalent among the Eastern peoples / that married and betrothed women had to veil their faces; thereby to testify / that they stood under a husband / and thus to keep the desires of such passionate peoples away from the wives of others. See chapter 24:56 and 1 Corinthians 11:10. Now, Sarah had removed this veil here / and carried herself as a maiden: whereby the king was then deceived.

Even a beauty as chaste as can be / can be misused / when she has no **holy shame** / which drives her to hide herself. Such a holy woman / as Sarah / had need of a warning here / since she wished to be regarded as a maiden / and not as a married woman: And a prince gave her such a warning in a very wise manner / even though it was in such a time / in which God had not yet had His law written down / which at that time was only to be engraved in hearts. How much more necessary are such very wholesome admonitions to Christian women! who let themselves be led astray by the vanities of this time. And how strong and immovable must the pastors be / to punish the shameful exposures / which offend the Church of Christ! One must not only have a pure heart / but one must also resist through outward modesty those sins / which others commit / when they look upon a beauty / which shows itself too much / even though the heart of the one who possesses this beauty is far removed from sin.

The veil / which Abimelech recommended to Sarah / can serve as a useful instruction to Christian women / that they should always walk with a veil. This is the counsel of St. Paul. In this point one cannot be too careful. For the outward appearance is often a sign / either of the corruption / or the purity of the heart.

This veil or covering of the eyes also has a quite secret spiritual meaning. Namely, God had a veil recommended to Sarah / who was the only woman of her time / who was most pleasing to God / in order to teach the inner man two things thereby. First / that they must preserve the gifts of God under the veil of **secrecy and inwardness**: second / that God uses pure faith as a veil / to cover the graces and testimonies of love / which He gives to souls; in order to keep them in constancy / when He thinks / that His graces could cause them to fall into the snares of Satan through spiritual pride. Therefore Abimelech says to Sarah / when he told her / that he had given money to her brother; "that you may be righted." From that time on, Sarah had no more danger to endure: just as a soul, when pure faith has been imparted to it, also has no more danger to fear. This is the surest guardian. For because it hides all her gifts and virtues from her / she is kept out of the danger of having any self-pleasure in them / and thus allows her destroyer no entrance into her.

<note>1,000 pieces of silver amounts to approximately 500 Reichsthaler.</note>

<column-break/>

## Right Column

17. And Abraham prayed to God: then God healed Abimelech and his wife / and his maids / so that they bore children.

18. For the Lord had fast closed up every womb of the house of Abimelech / because of Sarah / Abraham’s wife.

---

Abraham is grateful for the benefits / and offers his earnest intercession to God for Abimelech and his people / who were punished in marital matters / in which their lord had intended to sin: since such closing up [of the womb] can have awakened all sorts of burdensome sickness / in which they finally felt the hand of God.

So swift is God / the righteous judge / with His plagues following the deviations of His own / much harder than against the unbelievers.

This is caused by His great earnestness and "jealous love" / which He has for His friends in His heart: since He does not suffer / that they fall away from Him / but steps into the middle with His punishments / and binds them with His power / so that they shall not transgress further.

Such a way of God indeed hurts the flesh / but is excellent for the spirit / healthy and highly necessary.

That this king truly feared God / and is with all right to be counted among the believers; all circumstances of this chapter give enough to recognize. Therefore Luther also very well remarks / that this pious king must have had great understanding in spiritual matters. Which is a clear example of such uncircumcised people / of what light of the Holy Spirit God has also kindled in and among them / and how from all people those were pleasing to Him / who feared Him and did right: which Peter had long to learn / before he experienced it in deed and truth <note>A reference to Acts 10, where Peter realizes God accepts people from every nation.</note>.

That which he himself also refers to shows sufficiently / that he recognized the **grace of God** that has appeared to all men / which disciplines us to deny ungodly life / and to live soberly, righteously, and godly / and he was diligent to act according to the same in simplicity of heart and innocence of hands: for which reason he was also held back by that very same grace from the actual great sin of adultery / as it seems through a secret illness / whereby God interrupted his intention with Sarah: from which illness he was here now healed again upon Abraham's intercession.

<margin>(a) Commentary on Genesis, Vol. IV. Jena edition. p. 114.</margin>

One should therefore / as Luther (a) again judges / not deny / that quite pious Christians have often been among the heathens: as we also read of Nebuchadnezzar / and Naaman of Syria / who were also pious people / and many others more among the heathens. Therefore it is believable / he says further / that this king was also a believer. "For" "let it not be a disgrace / where God does such grace /" "as to this king / that He comes to him / and reveals" "Himself / speaks with him / warns him of harm. He must indeed not" "be a lowly man. And although Augustine may say /" "that God gives no further testimony / than of this single" "work of the king; from which, however, it is not to be concluded / that he" "was a child of God / and stood under grace: yet" "he [Luther] sets his opinion before Augustine with good reason / and" "says; 'But I would stick with the first answer / so'" "'that one lets God's grace also go among the heathens.'"

Cap. XXI. The First Book of Moses.

## Chapter XXI.

->The Birth of Isaac and the Mockery by Ishmael.<-

AND the LORD visited Sarah / as he had said; and the LORD did for Sarah as he had spoken.
2. And Sarah became pregnant / and bore Abraham a son in his old age / at the appointed time / of which GOD had spoken to him.
3. And Abraham called the name of his son / who was born to him / whom Sarah had born to him / Isaac.
4. And Abraham circumcised his son Isaac / when he was eight days old / as GOD had commanded him.
5. And Abraham was a hundred years old / when his son Isaac was born to him.

---

Thus God finally fulfills His promise / for which one must wait in faith from one morning watch to the next / until the glorious redemption of God's people shall finally appear: Ps. 14:7, 130:5-6, Habakkuk 2:3. Then also the joyful laughter over God's help shall be born. Ps. 126:1-2. Then also on this eighth day / or the first day of the resurrection of Christ / which will manifest itself in a special way in His spiritual body, in His Church / the promise will be fulfilled with emphasis: that the Lord will circumcise the heart of the spiritual seed / when Abraham becomes the heir of the world / so that one will love the Lord with all one's heart and all one's soul / and thus the true life of the Spirit will be made manifest. Deuteronomy 30:6, Ezekiel 36:25-27.

<margin>v. 2. In old age)</margin> When the passion of the flesh is gone / the Church will become fruitful.
At the appointed time) The fulfillment of God's promises occurs exactly at the set time / though not always according to our views or insights. The true inner life is born through faith / which is represented by Abraham / and is brought into the world through the proclamation / which is symbolized by Sarah. Abraham is thus the father of all inner persons: because he is the father of all believers / as St. Paul says / and the inner and secret life has its origin in faith.

<margin>v. 3. Son — born — Isaac)</margin> This means as much as / Laughter / Joy.
Without doubt, Abraham and Sarah also looked through faith in Isaac / as a pledge of God's covenant / toward the <term>Messiah</term><note>The original text uses the Latinized "Messiam."</note>, the promised <term>Seed of the Woman</term><note>The "Weibes-Samen" refers to the first prophecy of a savior in Genesis 3:15.</note> / who was to come from their loins / of whom Isaac was a prototype. Christ also aimed at this point: "Your father Abraham rejoiced that he should see my day. And he saw it / and was glad." John 8:56.
As long as we perform our obedience out of a slavish fear or for the sake of reward / Isaac is not yet born. These must be cast out of the house. However, this state also has its time.
The true Isaac is then born in us / when we perform obedience out of a willing and joyful spirit and with happiness and gladness.

<margin>v. 4.)</margin> This inner child is no sooner born / than faith comes immediately to purify it / through cutting away / before trust and serenity sustain it with their milk.

<margin>v. 5. A hundred years)</margin> He had therefore been a stranger for 25 years. Ch. 12:4.

<term>Jerome</term><note>Latin: Hieronymus</note> (a) writes of the noble Roman matron <term>Paula</term><note>A disciple of Jerome known for her pilgrimage to the Holy Land.</note>, in whose honor he composed an epitaph / that after her husband Toxotius died / she traveled to Gerar in her time / and visited the hut of Sarah / in which she gave birth in her old age / the cradle of Isaac / and the remains of Abraham's oak.

When this newborn inner person has been sustained for some time with the milk of sensible trust / he is then weaned from it; namely, insofar as it concerns the tasty outflow / which was his joy in childhood; so that he may have it only according to its essence in the future. It cannot be otherwise / he must suffer pain because of it. But faith rejoices over it / and therefore prepares a feast / because this first tearing-away promotes the growth of the child / and makes it proceed into the maturity of spiritual life.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis Chapter 21, specifically focusing on the spiritual and allegorical conflict between Isaac and Ishmael following Isaac's birth.</meta>

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXI.

9. And Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian / whom she had born to Abraham / that he was mocking /

Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> and others correctly remind us that this mocking is called a "persecution" by Paul <note>See Galatians 4:29</note>; and it consisted especially in this: that Ishmael sought to make Isaac frivolous through such mockery, so that he might not be preferred over him in the inheritance. Therefore, Abraham had to cast him out because of the danger.

But because the Greek word used by Paul indicates an act of violence, and Paul also interpreted it as the persecution of the Jews against the Christians at that time; so some also interpret the word <term>מצחק</term> <note>Hebrew: "mitzachéq," meaning mocking, playing, or laughing</note> to mean that Ishmael sought to kill his brother under the appearance of a joke.

Therefore, the mother Sarah was not to be blamed for what she insisted upon here. For she had to fear a bad outcome, because Ishmael revealed his evil, murderous heart through his mocking words and gestures. This is why Paul called it a persecution: just as Christ in Matthew 5:11 joined together reviling and persecution.

By birth, Ishmael belonged to Abraham's family / yet he plagued the true son. In the same way, some people seem to be pious / and call themselves God’s children: but the spirit of contradiction still stirs within them; it struggles against the simplicity and purity in Christ / casts doubt upon the privileges and freedoms of the true children / and secretly oppresses and stings the "seed of the woman" <note>A reference to the promised savior or the godly line</note> and the mind of Christ in the heels.

This is one of the first fruits of the serpent where it dwells / that it stings its innocent neighbor / and mocks and jeers with Ishmael. and this often happens under the pretext that it is not in earnest / but only to pass the time: while meanwhile the divine truth is being contradicted.

O, how Isaac must sometimes bow or hide himself before Ishmael / just to keep the peace. Jacob must speak kindly to Esau; only so that he might safely proceed to his father’s house.

The patience and faith of Christ are the best weapons here / to endure such arrows of the mockers and to pass them over in silence: because such mocking spirits do not grasp the speech of the Holy Spirit / but only trample all pearls underfoot. Proverbs 9:7.

Meanwhile, such mockery from the ignorant serves as a great blessing / if one allows oneself to be exercised in the truth by it: in order to penetrate ever more from the thorny and agonizing element of reason into faith / and thus to be rid of one's own internal mocker all the sooner. For

It takes much effort / before even a believer fully penetrates into simplicity / so that he recognizes and grasps Christ without any outward form / appearance or image. Mocking reason still seeks to find fault with and miss something in the life of Jesus within His own people. Therefore, one becomes aware of the mocker within oneself daily.

What wonder is it then / if a person / who still stands entirely under the Law / as Ishmael's counterpart / acts as a mocker? especially since legalistic piety mostly remains only appearance and hypocrisy. Therefore

When such people notice a true earnestness and zeal in others / such that one suffers everything for it / regarding no shame or harm / and according to the teaching of Christ would rather give the cloak to the one who takes the coat than resist evil; then it seems ridiculous to them / and they speak in their hearts: Are these not fools! We consider their life to be madness!

The hypocrite and the legalistically pious see their Christianity only in certain outward virtues and exercises: now when others place it in the dying off of the entire self-life / and thus exempt nothing from the obedience and death of Christ; the former think that this is not necessary / and consider the latter / if not as heretics / then at least as those who go too far.

Because the legalistically pious also only manage with one or another literal piece of knowledge / and are afraid of the full light of grace / so that they might not have to become obedient to it; it is again offensive to them / when others insist / that the Holy Spirit with the goodness of His grace should fulfill not only the understanding or some power / but the heart / courage and mind / and they mock it as "revelations" and the like.

But will it now last forever with such unspiritual mockery / and shall it always be allowed to be driven in the house of the Lord / in and against God’s holy generation? Thus the Evil One intends and seeks / who has the opportunity to maintain his kingdom thereby. But what does the Scripture say / and Sarah here in the same?

<column-break/>

10. And spoke to Abraham: <margin>(a) Proverbs 22:10.</margin> (a) Cast out this bondwoman with her son! For

A natural, fleshly man might well conclude from this / that Sarah had spoken this in the disorder of her emotions / and thereby forgot the due respect toward her husband / in that she demanded the expulsion of Hagar so impetuously / and as it were, imposed it upon him.

But when spiritual eyes come upon this text / they recognize Sarah’s heart and mind quite differently / and see in the spirit of wisdom quite well / that Sarah did not speak this so by chance for herself / nor brought it forth from her own will.

Thus spiritual things want to be spiritually judged and assessed.

Sarah was therefore moved by the Spirit to prophesy of one of the greatest mysteries of God / which runs alongside the Covenant of Grace: as shown among others by Luther / from Augustine, as also Jerome, Eucherius, and others. Indeed, some conclude from this / that Sarah had more of the spirit of prophecy than Abraham.

The meaning of the Spirit here concerns the entire inward state of the soul / and the inward condition of every soul / as it stands under the Law or under Grace: not only regarding a certain external time / of the Old and New Testaments.

When the Holy Spirit sets before a person’s eyes their own wicked mockery and falsehood through many trials / so that they are terrified by it / and abandon the horror; then the struggle against it begins. Then the enlightened heart pays attention to all the wild, unbroken words and gestures / that flow from the spirit of mockery; to all the affections and movements / that break out against others. It gives all of that into God’s judgment / and lets it daily be put to death in itself and as it were smothered through the discipline and struggle of the Spirit / so that such a false life cannot spread further.

Accordingly, this casting out or expelling happens through the earnest dying off of all self-will and self-life / with which we may not enter into God’s kingdom.

The false / haughty and self-complacent spirit would like to remain sitting in the father’s house in the heart forever under a pious appearance / and perform its trickery and derision against Christ in the soul / wanting also to be an heir of righteousness. But what does the Spirit say?

Push Ishmael out! Cast him with force out of the heart! Use constant earnestness and diligence for this / so that for your whole life you never again grant him a lodging / favor / or freedom. Your will must stand so abandoned until the end of God’s discipline / that it completely forsakes the mocker and sends him into the wilderness / where he must die in abandonment.

Even the old wicked nature in man must, in the rebirth, completely surrender and renounce every right / which it otherwise had apparently retained during the first legalistic righteousness / yes, even claimed against so many testimonies.

Although this wicked life still reveals itself sometimes through a glance or an outbreak / it only serves to give the believing warrior more zeal / so that he immerses himself ever anew into the death of Jesus Christ / and therein dies to himself and his own.

In such humiliation, one then respects others more than oneself / does not exalt oneself over them / does not criticize or judge them; much less does one mock the gifts or works of others. One finds so much to judge in oneself / that one can easily forget others. And

So finally the Evil One finds no more place in the heaven of our heart / but he is cast out from heaven onto the earth / and still rumbles occasionally in the earthly part for the exercise of faith.

Thus man comes gradually from the state under the Law into the Grace of the Gospel.
