<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 21, moving from the literal event of Ishmael's mocking to a deep allegorical explanation of the two spiritual states: being under the Law versus being under Grace, as discussed by the Apostle Paul.</meta>

# **For the son of this maid shall not inherit with my son / with Isaac.** <margin>John 8:35, 36.</margin>

# **11. But the word greatly displeased Abraham / because of his son. 12. But**

---

<margin>This is a very deep illustration of the legal state <note>The "legal state" refers to living under the strict requirements of the Law rather than the freedom of the Gospel.</note>.</margin>
It would be hard for anyone to believe this or be easily convinced of it if it were not expressly cited and interpreted this way in the New Testament. However, Paul’s explanation of this text in Galatians 4 is so thoroughly clear and profound that it requires no further proof: although many other glorious lessons are hidden in these words which Paul did not find necessary to cite for his purpose.

That these words do not merely point to the external eras of the Old and New Testaments is evident from the fact that Abraham and many other believers lived during the time of the Old Testament and yet were truly under the grace of the Gospel; Paul and other Pharisees, conversely, lived during the time of the New Testament and yet stood under the Law before their conversion.

Every person who accepts God’s Word—and is not stuck in atheism or coarse pagan unbelief, or living like an animal in the world—must stand either under the Law or under Grace, regardless of whether they lived externally during the time of the Old or New Testament. For

Apart from that case, these are the two main states or types of people who wish to be called Christians or pious: namely, those under the Law and those under the Gospel. Ishmael and Isaac / the son of the maid and the son of the free woman / fleshly and spiritual people.

Whoever is still under the Law is a son of the maid, a servant <note>In this context, "servant" implies a slave to the law rather than a free child of God.</note>, and also a mocker.

Ishmael, the archetype of this and a very remarkable person, was just as much Abraham's child as Isaac, and yet the difference was quite tangible.

A person who remains in his mere nature and fleshly mind is a servant for that very reason: because he is born only according to the flesh, as the son of the maid.

In such children of the maid, nothing rules but their own will, which seeks only the visible and the earthly, and thereby becomes its servant, even if they constantly play the hypocrite outwardly and strive to behave respectably. For despite all appearances, nothing but corruption can rule inwardly unless one is born anew and remains in that state.

From such a fleshly mind, when it is not brought under God’s discipline, comes the actual service of sin and vanity; a natural man allows himself to be carried away and driven by his lusts and other emotions—from lust into anger, from anger into pride, and from pride into greed, envy, suspicion, lies, etc.

Thus, a natural man is not only a born slave but an active servant of all evil, and is not master of himself as long as he surrenders his will to evil and does not withdraw it.

In such a state, Ishmael is indeed Abraham's son—meaning, God did indeed create man good from the beginning; but he has forfeited his right of inheritance and has fallen into the slavery of the devil, by whom he is overcome.

From this miserable bondage of sin leading to death arises further the bondage under the Law. This Law is, as it were, the maid who bears the servant and keeps him guarded under the yoke of divine justice.

For example: when some souls see and worry that they might not be saved in their godless life, yet do not wish to fully convert to God and ask for a new heart from Him; they then help themselves with some good works. They begin to abstain from coarse sins and, in contrast, undertake many good exercises: reading and singing a great deal, and leading an honorable life.

But with this, they do not get rid of their inward accusations; instead, the enmity against God in their reason grows ever worse within them, because they do not want to be subject and indebted to God and His justice, but rather to establish their own. So they walk along in confusion, comfortless and dissatisfied, as servants of the Law. For

Secretly they remain in their fleshly mind and pursue their own will as children of the flesh and of reason, and servants of the wrath that rages within them—and which also breaks out externally in hatred, false zeal, suspicion, deceit, lies, and slandering against others, mostly under the pretext of religion and divine service.

All of this is from the son of the maid and belongs to God’s judgment, even if it might shine beautifully on the outside, and misuse Holy Scripture as a crutch, or be defended and asserted as if with the tongues of angels.

And therefore, this servant is at the same time a wicked mocker. For if one does not have the desire to earnestly follow the path of the Gospel toward the new birth, he necessarily rejects and mocks that same path in others.

When Yieldedness <note>The original term "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of total surrender to God's will.</note>—the newborn inner life which has only recently been weaned from the sweetness and milk of the spiritual life—seeks a pastime with the active and manifold life <note>Multiplicity or "manifoldness" refers to a soul distracted by many worldly concerns rather than being focused on the "One" (God).</note>; it says to Faith: Cast out everything that still remains of the self-willed and manifold ways! so that my son may have no fellowship with those who use such things without going further. For as servants of their own inventions, they shall never inherit; they shall never inherit from God alone, who is the reserved inheritance of the son of the free woman—who is my son, whom I wish to lead directly to God through my Yieldedness, so that he may find his eternal inheritance in Him.

<column-break/>

Through this, his own mind and state became more apparent to the good Abraham, since out of fatherly natural love he did not recognize Ishmael’s mocking spirit and therefore wanted to hear nothing of the casting out.

This often happens to a well-meaning person. When he notices some good stirrings and powers of grace, he thinks there is nothing left in him that needs to be cast out, or that could not get along with the true child of the "new creature."

When he then hears God’s sharp judgments—that absolutely everything remaining from the old sinful birth must be cast out—it seems hard to him, as it did to Abraham. He also finds many plausible reasons for it: that the "son" <note>Referring to his current spiritual efforts or natural virtues</note> is, after all, something good and respectable.

Abraham would have liked to keep this "son of multiplicity," because he too is a son of faith. However, he is a son of faith in a comprehensible, persistent way mixed with many idiosyncrasies—and not in a spiritual, incomprehensible way that is lost in God.

There is nothing more common than for such testimonies of nature to be displeasing in their tenderness when the Spirit of Jesus Christ insists on a renunciation of one's own life and of all things, no matter how well-intentioned they may be. This word gives a powerful shock to the self-complacent mind, which cannot find itself in Sarah’s judgment.

One even wants to remain blameless in one's own affairs and does not believe that there is still so much to be cast out. One imagines that they have already passed through the judgment and are just sitting by, watching others be judged; meanwhile, one thinks they have a "privilege" so that no one may touch them or their false favorite child, self-love.

From this arise all the many justifications made secretly and publicly against God’s holy judgments, whereby one pretends to have the approval and praise of others, and does not consider that they are still resting in the arms of the Egyptian maid and nurturing a mocker in their bosom.

Ah, how long it takes, and how many harsh punishments are required before one learns to believe—despite their assumed holiness—that Ishmael’s spirit is still hidden in the heart! This rogue still feeds himself secretly in Abraham’s house, so that he can only be seized and discovered by the full light of the Holy Spirit.

And this is also the only way by which he is cast out, along with the entire legalistic and hypocritical mind.

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter 21.</header>

### 12. But GOD said to Abraham: Let it not displease you because of the boy and because of your maidservant! Everything that Sarah has said to you, obey her voice. For in Isaac shall your seed be named.
### 13. But I will also make the son of the maidservant into a nation, because he is your seed.

<margin>
Jerome (a) notes <note>original: "Hieronymus... mercket an"</note> that Ishmael indeed also received great promises, but they only aimed at external increase and bodily blessing. Isaac, however, became the sole heir through the testament. Gifts are one thing, he says, the substance or the property itself is another. A legacy or bequest is one thing, the inheritance another.
</margin>

How precisely this also applies to the spiritual state! Some have quite glorious gifts and apparent powers in spiritual matters, and yet they are not heirs of the kingdom, but only children of the maidservant: because they have not yet been admitted into the mystery of the inward glory of the children of God, but still cling to many subtle idols.

Thus, the inheritance is much more than mere gifts, knowledge of mysteries, brief sensations, or other passing outpourings and powers of the kingdom of heaven. There must be something constant and innate remaining in the soul, which does not waver nor die, but as an eternal life sustains, nourishes, and strengthens the person among all things.

In a word, it is **JESUS CHRIST**, who takes shape in the soul with his divine image and life: it is the **Kingdom of GOD** that is within us; the precious pearl and the treasure that does not rust; the believers' sole possession and most beautiful, lovely inheritance, in which they have eternal sufficiency, and through which they desire nothing else—not even in heaven, let alone on earth.

Whoever has this Isaac needs no further persuasion as to whether he is under the law or under grace, a son of **Sarah**, or the son of the maidservant. It all depends on this inheritance alone, and by it everyone can recognize their own state. Whoever does not see the seed of divine life rising within himself will surely feel his servitude and must endure his burden.

But he must only cast out the mocker and the antichristian mind, to which Christ appears so mocking, so contemptible and small compared to Pharisaic hypocrisy and the splendor of outward words and works. He must become entirely like a child, and thus encompass the kingdom of heaven and the inheritance in a lowly, small heart: so he enters in, and it enters into him, and bears him again as the heavenly mother to the free child of **Zion** into eternal life.

**GOD** shows to faith that he must leave the son, who is much in nature, and do everything blindly what serenity <term>Gelassenheit: a central term in German mysticism meaning a state of yieldedness or letting go of self-will to God</term> demands of him. He reveals to him that this must be the guiding principle of his house: because from the son of serenity and faith, his lineage should be propagated.

Therefore, Holy Scripture separates **Ishmael** from **Abraham** when it says he should become the father of a great nation. But when it speaks of **Isaac**, it assures that in him Abraham should be the father of an innumerable people: thereby indicating that through this son of blind serenity alone, faith can confirm its offspring.

<margin>(a) Book 2, on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 4, page 145. Volume 9 of the Works. <note>original: "L. 2. in Ep. ad Gal. c. 4. p. 145. Tom. IX. Opp." refers to Jerome's *Commentarius in Epistolam ad Galatas*.</note></margin>

<column-break/>

### 14. Then Abraham rose early in the morning, and took bread and a flask of water, and gave it to Hagar, placing it on her shoulder, and the boy as well, and sent her away. Then she departed and wandered astray in the wilderness of **Beer-sheba**.
### 15. When the water in the flask was gone, she cast the boy under one of the shrubs;
### 16. And went and sat down opposite him, and distanced herself as far as one shoots with a bow. For she said: I cannot watch the boy die. And she sat down opposite him, and lifted up her voice and wept.

**Hagar** had to receive just chastisement because she had held her mistress in low esteem after she had been given to **Abraham** with her [Sarah’s] consent, *Chapter* 16:2, 4. and no doubt also strengthened her son in his malice, so that she was cast out of **Abraham's** house with him and had to experience such distress; from which the **Lord** nonetheless redeemed her in due time for **Abraham's** sake, and also gave her the promise of the multiplication of her seed as comfort: wherein is simultaneously contained the spiritual promise that many of her seed, as **Abraham's** [descendants], will yet come to the knowledge of Christ, and will shine as stars of heaven with the rest in his glorious kingdom among the converted nations. *Chapter* 22:17 and *Chapter* 25:13.

Faith is content to provide a supply for the multiplication. For without it, the multiplied life cannot be sustained. This supply consists of **water** and **bread**—sustenance and nourishment—and in some sensible outpourings of grace, so that it may proceed. But as soon as the water, which is its preservation, is missing—namely, the sweetness of grace—the heart fails him.

**Hagar**, the maidservant, has no well of living water for her boy: but **Isaac** has wells; for the sake of which he must also strive with the Philistines.

The **flask** with **water** is the letter of the Law, from which the fleshly people drink, but quite soon grow faint.

But the **people of faith** drink from the **Evangelical** and **Apostolic** wells, which never dry up, but run through their streets and always overflow in the breadth of spiritual understanding.

*verse 14.)* **Hagar** and her son wandered around in the wilderness: because the multiplied [the fleshly] never have such a certain, steady way as those who walk in simplicity and serenity. They go wandering from one place to another, from one object to another, from one path to another. But as soon as the water of sensible graces is gone, they fall into despondency, stop walking, and finally stand completely still.

*verse 15, 16.)* She leaves her son under a shrub—that is, everything she had hoped for on earth: and, after having gone aside, she weeps that she must see all her labor, produced with such great effort, thus perish. But just as the affliction of such souls drives them back to **GOD**, so they call upon him and sit down. This means as much as saying that they enter a little into rest, since they are quite weary from their unrest and chasing. Then **God** does not fail to send such souls new graces and sweetnesses, so that they may be supported by them to continue their way all the more easily: otherwise, they would leave everything behind.

**17.** Then **GOD** heard the voice of the boy / and the Angel of **GOD** called to Hagar from heaven / and said to her: What ails you, Hagar? Fear not! For **GOD** has heard the voice of the boy / where he lies.

**18.** Arise / take the boy / and hold him with your hand! For I will make him into a great nation.

**19.** And **GOD** opened her eyes / so that she saw a well of water. Then she went and filled the bottle with water / and gave the boy a drink.

**20.** And **GOD** was with the boy / and he grew up; and he lived in the wilderness / and became an archer.

**21.** And he lived in the wilderness of Paran: and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.

**22.** And it happened at that same time / that Abimelech / and Phichol, the commander of his army / spoke to Abraham / saying: **GOD** is with you / in everything that you do.

---

v. 17.) That the Lord hears the child / is the remembrance of the good / which such a manifold soul <note>The author uses "manifold soul" to describe a person who is still distracted by many worldly or legalistic concerns, rather than being single-mindedly focused on God.</note> has striven to do; and the comfort which grows within her through this / is that God is mindful of her weakness.

v. 19. 20.) If this must be understood and interpreted according to the letter and the history / then / as Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar who favored allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> judges / Hagar must have had her eyes closed beforehand. Therefore, he holds to the spiritual meaning / according to which the people of the Law / who are born according to the flesh / should be cast away / and languish for a long time in hunger and thirst; not a hunger for bread / or a thirst for water; but for the word of the Lord: until finally the veil of blindness will be taken away from their eyes at their conversion / through the Gospel of God / to see the well of living water. Now they lie around the well / and He has stepped into their midst: but they do not see or know Him.

Pray to God incessantly with the blind man by the road at Jericho <note>A reference to Bartimaeus in Luke 18.</note> / that He may open your eyes to faith / which does not only get to see a well / but to possess it within itself; according to what the Scripture says: *Out of a believer's belly shall flow streams of living water.* <note>John 7:38.</note> He does not do this for any other / and Hagar does not attain so much.

He only provides that she finds water. For everything happens with these persons through outward activity: therefore they have nothing but earthly water / which they must even fetch themselves / and also carry their own supply. This is done by those who burden and fill themselves with all kinds of exercises of their own supply and many thoughts. Yet God is pleased with their small efforts / and He is also by and with them. But He prepares them for war / and their skill is present in everything they undertake. They live from what they receive either through labor or war. Nothing can better describe the active life than this.

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chap. XXI.</header>

## 33. And he planted a shrub at Beersheba / and preached there of the name of the Lord / the eternal God.

Abraham performed his prophetic office in all places where he stayed for any length of time, primarily to further spread the knowledge of the true God through public preaching of the Name and promises of God.

In the same way, believers should strive in all places where they reside to establish good tree-nurseries / that is / schools of godliness / in which their children may be raised in the knowledge of the eternal true God. For when good schools are first established / then good congregations can also be expected / wherein many trees of righteousness are to be found / among whom the name of the Lord can be proclaimed with power and blessing.

While Abraham planted a shrub for physical necessity / and for shade and protection from the rain during the sacrificial service on the altar built therein; idol-worshippers have since misused such green, shady forests for their idolatry / which were called groves <note>The German text uses "Hayne," referring to the sacred groves frequently condemned in the Old Testament as sites of pagan worship.</note> / from which many places take their names / because such a famous idol-shrub was located there: a heathen custom which is often punished. See Isaiah 57:5; 21:28, etc.

But it happens that in matters of divine service, that which believers do outwardly is gladly imitated by hypocrites. The rest / which comes from the bottom of the heart / from which all plants are to be judged—whether they were planted by the Father of believers, who is the true Father over all that is called "children" in heaven and on earth—this they gladly leave aside.

Therefore, let everyone see to what and how he plants / and whether God can also give the increase to it.

Indeed, those especially should take care / how they wish to stand before the Lord as faithful workers and stewards / who seek to plant and erect nothing but the tree of knowledge in souls instead of the tree of life / from which death arises; who hinder the growth of the tree of life in themselves and in others / choking it in the bud / and taking the strength from the weak beginnings of life in the young plants; resisting the life of God in themselves and in others / and acting upon this noble plant like locusts and caterpillars. This undertaking and beginning is not from Him who has called us to proclaim and magnify the

**Name of the Lord / the eternal God)** For what is this name other than the true *Sem* <note>original: "Sem". This is a reference to the Hebrew word "Shem," which means "Name." The author is likely making a mystical connection between the name of Noah's son Shem and the concept of the Divine Name.</note> / mentioned above / the life of the divine nature / the image / the Son of God / in whom the name of God is found / and in whom alone God has revealed and expressed Himself. This is the true God and eternal life.

And just as a name is strictly that by which one thing is distinguished from another: so Abraham proclaimed the divine virtues and attributes / by which God is distinguished from all creatures / as He had been revealed to him in His eternal power and Godhead / as a shield and very great reward / as the most perfect Being and the highest all-sufficient Good / as the most just Judge / as the God Amen <note>The "God Amen" refers to God's faithfulness and truth, derived from Isaiah 65:16, meaning the God of Truth.</note> / who faithfully keeps His promise. This God and Lord of heaven and earth he sought to praise and recommend everywhere he went / as the most praiseworthy and lovable Being / so that others also might taste and see how friendly the Lord is / and His honor might become great among all people. Thus he was a "good fragrance" of God among the heathens / and through him, the knowledge of the glory of God arose in all places.

Abraham / as the father of believers and the most faithful man who ever was / called upon this name of God in all places. Because he was in a state of constant prayer / he left behind signs of his invocation / his prayer / and his sacrifice everywhere. And

Holy Scripture calls the Lord "an eternal God" here for this very reason / to give us to understand that / because He is God at all times / He must also be worshipped and called upon at all times; and thus our divine service and prayer must last eternally. Therefore Jesus Christ himself said / one must pray without ceasing. And St. Paul wants us to pray at all times. Through the single state of faith alone can prayer last eternally.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<column-break/>

## 34. And Abraham stayed as a stranger in the land of the Philistines / for a long time.

It means something to stay as a stranger <term>stranger: in this context, the German "Fremdling" refers to a "sojourner" or "resident alien"—someone who lives in a land but does not belong to it</term> in a place where one is well-tolerated / and to use this world in such a way that one does not abuse it. Nature very gladly settles down / and would rather be at home than a stranger where things go well for it. But faith knows here of no "abiding city" / but always swings upward / and strives for that which is above. Abraham was not only a stranger / but he also *behaved* as a stranger / and did not dwell upon the things of this life / of this world / of this time / which are transitory: as befits a righteous citizen of eternity.

By this, it can now be recognized who are Abraham’s children and true believers. Truly not those who dwell and stick to the earth as citizens / indeed as dung-beetles <note>A sharp metaphor for those obsessed with worldly, "earthly" matters.</note> / and are like guests and strangers in their true Fatherland: who can speak of nothing better than oxen / dogs and horses / acres / meadows and fields / and their professions; to whom, on the other hand, the eternal things of the invisible world and the mysteries of the kingdom of God are as strange and unknown as if they were coming into a foreign land / so that they even view the truth as heresy / and fear they might fall into error and lose their way in that "foreign" land / though they have already strayed so far into the thick senses and the folly and vanity of their hearts that they no longer even know the way of peace and life / much less the land of their origin.

O the perverse / apostate, and uncircumcised generation in heart and ears! How long will it still last / that people despise the discipline of the Spirit / which calls them back / and give ear to the voice of the stranger rather than the true Shepherd / whom they leave standing and knocking at the door like a stranger! Because of this, many a soul among the fleshly, natural people of the world—as if among spiritual Philistines—must live a long time under much pressure / and is forced to cry out with David: Woe is me / that I am a stranger among Meshech! etc. Ps. 120:5, 6, 7. Just as Abraham, in the long time he had to stay among these uncircumcised Philistines / may often have been moved to sigh over their violence and quarrelsomeness.

God absolutely demands this of believing souls / that they should be as strangers on the earth: so that / while they do not dwell on anything created / be it fleshly or spiritual / they should go straight to God. Therefore Abraham remains a stranger on the earth / as he had no certain permanent dwelling / to be an example to us of the detachment <term>detachment: "Gelassenheit," a key Pietist and mystical term meaning a state of letting go of worldly desires and self-will to be fully open to God</term> in which faith places a soul. God does not demand the same outward [homelessness] from all believing souls / though he demands it from some whom he wishes to make true children of Abraham. But as for the inward [state] / he demands it of all those who are led through faith and self-denial. For without this, their state would not be truthful / but only imagination. Other souls / who are led not by blind faith but by gifts / confirm themselves therein / and are in great peace and very well satisfied in them. But faith-souls have no rest unless they have gone entirely out of themselves: having gone like other Abrahams out of their fatherland / their place and their kinship / to seek another land / which is God; where they leave themselves to lose themselves in their Creator; while they / without resting / wander onward unceasingly / until they have entered again into the place of their origin / according to the promise given to them as soon as faith mastered their hearts. For as soon as faith has taken over a heart / it lets [such hearts] take no more rest either in themselves or in any created thing / and shows them that they must take everything outside of themselves / and that / if they are faithful in the following of faith / though it may be difficult for them / they would certainly also arrive there.

<header>Chap. XXII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

## Chapter XXII.

->The Sacrifice of Isaac.<-

And it came to pass after these stories / that GOD tested Abraham / and said to

Within such testing lies a great and deep mystery. GOD desires earnestness in all the tasks He sets before us. He wishes to exercise and strengthen our faithfulness and the integrity of our faith.

Testing <note>original: "Versuchen"</note> is actually the act of making a real trial or gaining experience of a thing / either in oneself or in another. However, when GOD tests a person / He does not seek to gain experience or new knowledge for Himself / but rather He ensures that the one being tested / recognizes something in and about themselves / which they did not know before.

GOD tests no one for evil / whereas man often tests GOD and his neighbor in an improper way / though he should always act with sincerity; and Satan / who constantly strives to deceive: rather, God tests for good / as He wishes to prove our faith, obedience, and love toward Him: to reveal all this to ourselves and others / for our encouragement and as an example for others to follow / and then to reward such things through grace with the crown of life. <term>James 1:2, 12, 13.</term>

The Lord had previously tested and tried Abraham nine times / as the Jews note / and indeed through great trials. 1. To leave his country. 2. To travel into Egypt. 3. When his wife was taken from him by Pharaoh. 4. When he was separated from Lot. 5. When he overcame the kings / and rescued Lot again. 6. When he was to cast out Hagar / while she was heavy with child. 7. When he had to be circumcised while already old. 8. When his Sarah was taken from him by Abimelech. 9. When Hagar and Ishmael had to be sent away again. Other commentators count as many as ten trials before this one. <note>The author refers to the "Ten Trials of Abraham," a traditional concept in Jewish Midrash, specifically from the Pirkei Avot.</note> Yet Abraham's faith overcame them all.

And now one might have thought / that such frequent and great trials would be enough / and that GOD would henceforth leave Abraham untroubled. For nature is anyway very inclined / to imagine itself secure immediately after the slightest exercise / and thinks / it has already been more than faithful enough. However

The true battle is only just beginning. The previous tasks were great / and had wide-reaching effects: but they had not yet struck Abraham's own life and his entire heart. Therefore, none of them is called a "testing" in the same way as this one. Now he must truly enter the struggle.

After these stories) After so many wondrous ways and leadings of GOD, He undertook this further thing with him / to test his faith one last time / and to bring it to the utmost limit of divine love and to the removal of all supports: Not only human supports / of which He had already stripped him earlier / when He made him go out from his fatherland; but also those supports which he had received from GOD Himself and from His benefits / especially from His promises. He spares nothing: and He does this so that the matter might be all the harder and more magnanimous / to test and purify his love / and to detach him from all self-interest and all foreign love / even if such might seem ever so permissible. And here it was necessary for Abraham to have such a perfect earnestness in faith / that he could have no other purpose / than that he truly wanted to carry out the will of GOD; and indeed without any delay / excuse / condition / or weakening of the divine command.

This testing / proving and trying / is not unique to Abraham alone / but is common to all sons and daughters of Abraham. He requires of every one among us / that we have a loathing and horror for all self-love / for all love and friendship of this world / that we leave them entirely / and depart from everything with contentment / suffering the loss of all things / yes, and even losing our life for His sake. He requires / that we place our whole trust and confidence in Him. He requires all our love with our whole heart / mind, and strength / so that it may be placed and grounded entirely and alone in Him / as its center. And finally, He requires all our obedience

<column-break/>

him: Abraham! And he answered: Here I am.

### 2. And

First, in a person whom GOD wishes to put to the test / faith must exist above all things. For what is not present / cannot be tested and proven. GOD cannot undertake a trial with unbelieving / fainthearted, and false hearts. Therefore, they are even less likely to be worthy of a proof and the promise that follows.

Whosoever, therefore, cannot remember / that he has been tested by GOD in manifold temptations and encouraged to the struggle; he has much to fear / that it might go very miserably with his faith.

But where faith is / there GOD exercises and proves it: so that it does not remain unfruitful or small / but grows and comes to purity.

To whatever person GOD assigns heavy trials / that person may be well assured / that GOD wishes to strengthen his faith thereby. That is His purpose. For everything depends upon faith.

Therefore, whatever is placed before you by the Lord your GOD / from within or without / consider it a good call from GOD. In all your affairs, you will find GOD's Word and commandment as a rule before you / if only you are willing to accept it. Everywhere / wherever you go and stay / your faith can be exercised. Indeed, no station / no labor / no circumstance of our life / is so small / that you should not find opportunity / to follow the call of GOD. How much more, then, can one be certain in the important tasks of a divine calling / no matter how strange they may appear.

That faith was burning brightly and vividly before GOD / like a torch / in Abraham even at that moment when the Lord called him to this fresh trial / is clear from his so-prompt answer:

Here I am!) And what else is faith in the ground of truth but such an agreement and surrender to GOD's will / where the soul despairs of itself / and holds only that to be good and blessed / which GOD places before it / and therefore lives solely by grace / no longer pursuing its own will / but leaving itself to GOD with Abraham / and saying: Here I am / dear GOD! Here you have me: do with me as You will!

So may every person test his faith according to this mark / whether he is always found so lively and awake by the Lord / as often as He calls.

With this resolute answer, Abraham showed his willingness and joy toward all the speeches and commandments of GOD / that he walked faithfully with body and soul in the presence of the LORD.

In this, everyone may see their own reflection / how their heart stands before GOD: whether he also allows such a willingness and faithfulness of faith to be worked in him by the Holy Spirit / so that he can answer with truth and without the contradiction of his conscience: Here I am! namely, as a servant / to do the Lord's will; as a child / to obey the Father.

O, how often the power of the living Word touches your heart / and drives you to obedience! But how do you answer the LORD? Does He find you as willing and eager / as you would wish your manservant or maidservant to answer without delay at your call?

It is very fine / that Abraham answered the LORD's call with the same mind and word / with which his son answered him afterward. From this, we see / how like children and with what faithfulness we should encounter our GOD in faith.

If one keeps a proper watch over their heart / they will sometimes become aware of the invitations of GOD. For as often as something from GOD's Word is placed before you in your heart / wherein you should deny yourself and follow GOD; so often the Lord calls you / just as He called Abraham here.

Even if GOD might have called Abraham through an outward voice / it mostly happened through an internal power of the Holy Spirit / through a divine pull and impulse in the heart; which the believers have felt. And to this, they have also answered in their hearts as intimately and fervently / as Abraham did here: Here I am!

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 22, moving from the general nature of God's testing to the specific, agonizing details of the command given to Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac.</meta>

<header>The First Book of Moses, Chapter XXII.</header>

# 2. And he said: Take now your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah, and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains of which I shall tell you.

Every word here could be a truly painful sting to the natural heart of a father. They must have been so to Abraham, like so many arrows wounding his heart.
It would have been a hard enough demand in itself if the LORD had required even Ishmael to be slaughtered and burned; for the hearts of fathers have a very deep and intimate kinship with their children. But He desires even the
**Only one)** Born of the beloved and rightful wife, Sarah. This is utterly unbearable to human nature.
For was this not the son of promise, whom Abraham had fathered in his old age, and indeed upon the special assurance of God? What could now lie closer to this dear man’s heart? Did not all the great and far-reaching speeches and promises of God rest upon this seed? Was not the blessing of all nations placed upon him? And now God presents such a lowly and foolish-seeming commandment; that this very son should be slaughtered. Will not the entire blessing of all nations then come to nothing? Abraham might have thought. Does the LORD Himself wish to change His purpose with the same mouth that has only just confirmed it? Has He then regretted His covenant?
The one son <note>Ishmael</note> he had to send away; the other he is to sacrifice. Where then does the promise remain? Truly, faith is required here.
But if we wish to become believers in God, we must also learn to grow accustomed to such "contrary-tests" from our wonderful God.
Truly, God still deals so strangely with His own that He soon seems to destroy again what He has barely built: only so that He may put human reason to shame and exercise us in the faith and simplicity of the truth.
**Whom you love)** It was not enough to have named him the "only son." Through these sweet and lovely descriptions, the paternal affection is stirred even more, in order to reach deep into the good man’s heart and awaken the most tender natural love—testing whether it would yield to the divine will or not.
Therefore, the dear God intended with this temptation to strike Abraham in his most beloved and best part; which He finally even calls by his own name:
**Isaac)** So that the memory of all those promises given to Abraham in view of this name might be made fresh again, giving him all the stronger reason to despair.
One can imagine how intimately dear this son must have been to the father. In him, the "seed" had been named, while Ishmael, by contrast, had been set aside. Thus Abraham looked upon this child as his own image, also according to the faith and fatherly walk in which Isaac was to follow him. His obedience also proves that he must have shown a great inclination toward all that is good.
This only, this so highly—even uniquely—beloved son was now to die: and indeed by such a violent death, even by the hand of his own father. To the flesh, that must have been a thunderclap and a deadly sting.
But there is certainly a highly precious prefiguration <note>A "prefiguration" or type is an Old Testament event seen as a symbolic preview of something in the New Testament, here foreshadowing God the Father sacrificing His Son, Jesus.</note> beneath this, that God demands the most beloved thing from Abraham. And what did it signify when He also commanded in the Old Testament that parents must bring their children to the LORD in the temple shortly after birth, and especially that every firstborn should be sanctified to Him? Was the LORD truly served by external ceremonies? Or did He not rather wish to give us to understand how especially that which is our most beloved and closest must be surrendered to the LORD?
If that is to happen, we must first, with Abraham, go out from our house—from the old sinful birth and nature—in true repentance and faith in the name of JESUS Christ; we must constantly practice true self-denial of ourselves and all things, so that we may gradually become strong enough to leave even what is closest and dearest to us.

<column-break/>

3. Then <note>The text continues the verse analysis below.</note>
Whoever still possesses anything in nature that is dear and precious to them, let them reflect whether they have ever sacrificed and surrendered it to the Lord. Let them consider how they would be minded and how they would behave if it were to be taken from them. At some point, one must let it go in spirit and will. For such attachment cannot stand alongside the love of God. Abraham had to give up and surrender either God or his son.
Therefore, one should withdraw one's pleasing, one's seeking and longing, in good time from everything to which nature clings. It must die and burn in the fire of God’s holiness, even if it were the most beloved thing! God does not ask about that: in short, He wants to kill disorderly "creaturely love," <term>creaturely love: loving a created thing (person, object, status) more than the Creator</term> so that He may know His divine love alone to be alive within us.
Nature often takes hold of something pleasant in the world with such tender love and delight as if it were a most beloved child: it nourishes and tends it just as delicately. And before one realizes it, one must let it go again—if not willingly, then out of necessity and compulsion. Then it is as if one's only son were being robbed.
Therefore, one should take warning and learn the wisdom of the righteous: not to hang or cling to anything in the world; or, if one already clings out of blindness, to tear oneself away from it in spirit with haste and learn to die to it, even if one must keep it externally out of necessity.
**Go into the land of Moriah)** See how precisely the LORD determines all the circumstances for His friend which he was to observe in this sorrowful sacrifice. If He had left him his free will in the manner and way of the sacrifice, it might have given nature some relief. But now, even all supports of comfort are ripped away at once, and nature must submit to "dying" even in the smallest circumstances, and thus learn to die to all self-will, even the most seemingly righteous.
But see how the temptation in Abraham keeps rising. God could have first let him go there before telling him what he was to do. But He tells him immediately, so that he would be tormented by the thoughts of it during the long journey, and would experience within himself the conflict between the divine command and the paternal affection.
**Moriah)** That is, "the revealed God," or the "land of seeing," as the Vulgate <note>original: "terra visionis"</note> translates it. Formerly, this name referred to the entire range of mountains from Mount Zion to the place of separation.
But oh, how God still leads His own so joyfully into such a "land of seeing"! Since He Himself has now truly become visible and revealed in the flesh, and also gladly allows Himself to be seen and recognized by converted and believing souls—that is, He gladly reveals His precise care and providence for us. Indeed, He rejoices when we will only believe that He guards and watches for our best; as this is the greatest honor we can give Him.
**Offer him)** Abraham knew very well what this "offering" entailed, for he had often sacrificed to the LORD. This must have been a terrifying message to nature, enough to make the skin crawl. For
It meant nothing less than that Abraham should do to his only and most beloved child what he was otherwise accustomed to doing with a sacrificial animal. Namely: he was to bind his own child’s hands and feet, so that he could not even resist during the pains of death. Then he was to lay the son upon the altar and upon the firewood, take the slaughtering knife, and thrust it into his throat or heart, and thus wretchedly shed his own blood. Afterward, he was to chop this child of his into pieces and roast most of it with fire, burning it to dust and ashes. Such an unheard-of tragedy he was to play out with the fruit of his own body: and he was to do this upon the command of God, who is otherwise a lover of life and the author of natural fatherly love.
This may indeed be an unheard-of temptation and an uncommonly high, unprecedented test of faith, the likes of which are to be found nowhere else in Scripture!

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 22. While the previous page focused on the gravity and apparent cruelty of God's command to sacrifice Isaac, this page explores Abraham’s immediate, faithful response and his internal victory over human reason.</meta>

<header>Chapter XXII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

## 3. And Abraham rose up early in the morning, and saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son, and split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went unto the place of which God had told him.
## 4. On the

---

Although this trial could not have happened without a struggle in his nature—both for his own sake and for the sake of Sarah and the Canaanites (considering what they would judge of such an act)—and likewise in his faith, wondering if this might be a temptation from the Enemy, who has been a murderer from the beginning: yet he overcame all of this in a noble manner. He simultaneously proved his faith in the resurrection because, as the Apostle says <note>Referring to Hebrews 11:19</note>, he thought to himself that God could and would raise him even from the dead. He was therefore immediately obedient and prepared for this sacrifice; and, as the narrative shows, he acted with great haste to comply with this command that seemed so hard and cruel. Abraham did not take even the slightest time for reflection, nor did he excuse himself based on the difficulty of the command; rather, it was <term>dictum factum</term> <note>Latin: "said and done," meaning no sooner said than done</note>; God could not command as quickly as he was ready to obey.

If Abraham had wished to consult his reason, it could have brought many doubts to him: whether it was truly the Lord who had commanded this, or whether instead another spirit was behind it, seeking to rob him of his Isaac. It may well be that melancholy thoughts arose in him which he had to overcome: whether it was right for him to kill his own son against the light of nature and the law of nations? How could these two things agree: on one hand, hearing such great promises that were to be fulfilled in his son in the future; and on the other hand, hearing that he should slaughter this son and thus bring all hope and promises to shame at once? But what reason cannot reconcile, faith unites. Faith thinks that God can call Isaac forth again even from the ashes, give him to him anew, and fulfill the promises in him. For he knew all too well that it was the very voice of his God that had promised the one and commanded the other. Therefore, he did not doubt in the least, nor did he argue much with himself, but turned back the doubtful thoughts and intended simply to do what the Lord had commanded him.

What a terrifying requirement he had to hear from God! And yet Abraham was comforted in it because he was certain of the divine command; he did not ask for long how it would turn out, but became strong in faith and obeyed the voice of the Lord.

How could Abraham prove greater simplicity and, at the same time, wisdom in faith than by holding God’s word as true, holy, and righteous even when his reason saw nothing but the opposite! He was not afraid, nor did he consult long with "flesh and blood" <note>A common biblical idiom for human nature or worldly relations</note> whether his wife would condemn him as the murderer of her child, or whether all people would persecute him for it and hold him in abomination as a child-killer. Rather, in an honest, rigorous struggle against himself, he learned to take reason captive under the obedience of faith. He was divinely certain that the All-Holy One could command nothing unholy. He did not consider as a godless murder that which the Fountain of all Love had commanded him; as Jerome rightly says in his <term>Commentary on Romans 4:11</term> <note>original: "Comment. in Rom. 4, 11."</note>.

Reason cannot get this into its head, and it does not suit flesh and blood at all. Indeed, one's own will is truly vexed when it is not allowed to criticize God's wondrous ways, even when it thinks it has a great right to do so. But

Pure faith transcends all such heights and strongholds with which nature <term>defends</term> <note>original: "defendiret"</note> and delays itself against the mystery of the Cross. Abraham knew that the letter kills, but the Spirit—the living, spiritual will of God—alone makes alive. Whatever law God had written into his heart, he followed in that very hour. For he stood in the power of the New Covenant, and saw in the spirit the day of the Lord Jesus, and rejoiced.

This made him so comforted and courageous that, without any contradiction, grumbling, or delay, he set out immediately. Thus, he hit upon the true purpose the Lord had in this work: namely, that instead of Isaac, he was to put to death his own will, wit, and cleverness, and his entire natural sense.

<column-break/>

What a high wonder of faith shines here! It surely surpasses the wisdom of angels; how then could it be reached with wretched words? Of which the late Luther (a) rightly claimed that this work of Abraham surpasses all the works of the saints of all times.

O you son or daughter of Abraham, step bravely in these footsteps! Rise early! Let it be earnest for you! For those things which concern us closely, one rises early. And what is it that concerns us more closely than the gain of our souls by losing them?

O deep wonder and mystery! How little you are recognized by men! and yet everything lies hidden in you that belongs to faith and a godly walk! You make an end of all disputing, all doubting, hesitating, and grumbling. Whoever seeks you honestly, you secret sacrifice of the Cross of Jesus Christ, he hits the heart of the old Adam and digs at the root of all falsehood: he pleases the Father in Christ through the Spirit of holiness.

Such a person, who seeks to come into Abraham's faith through the hidden dying of himself, becomes incessantly and every moment a holy, well-pleasing, and living sacrifice to the Father, with all that he is and has.

Blessed is he who, through the power of the death of Jesus, lets himself be separated and withdrawn from all things, so that he finds the true freedom of the spirit as a wide space for rest for his soul in the deepest ground of the love of God! He will, with Christ, also inherit and rule all things by overcoming all. Outside of this narrow gate, no true life or salvation is to be found eternally. Christ has shown it; and whoever wants to come to him must submit to it.

If God demands from you your children, goods, or other temporal things, you will never be able to give them to the Lord as a voluntary sacrifice unless you are grounded in faith. Much labor and struggle with self-love is required before one lets something go gladly and without compulsion for God's sake! God knows the hearts—how one truly means it in such trials. Happy is he who prepares himself for it in quiet days!

When things are often meant to look best during sent tribulations, it is still mostly pretense and hypocrisy or forced patience. One sees that one cannot do otherwise, so one finally yields to it according to reason. But such blind and voluntary obedience of faith is rarely found by God, as it was with Abraham.

Instead of such a hard trial holding back the faith of such a patriarch, it rather receives new strengths through it. And although the command so terrifyingly given to him was contrary to the command God had given to all men—namely, not to shed human blood—and therefore should have caused him a loathing according to his reason out of fear of committing a child-murder: yet faith swallows all of this. And by relying on God, who is above reason and even above faith itself, he prepares himself to carry out that which was commanded of him.

Oh, what a speed was that of Abraham—or of faith—to obey! He does not even wait for the day; he departs while it is still dark. The night indicates both his diligence and the darkness in his faith, which is stripped of all light and all testimony. He arranges everything himself: he indeed lets some servants follow, but they do not help him. He prepares the wood necessary for the sacrifice so that no pretext might remain to delay obedience, even though in such a matter reason could view it as something suspicious in various cases. Oh, what a faithfulness and magnanimity of faith! It is not without cause that he is the beginning and origin of a very great people and an innumerable multitude of saints, who are as much more pleasing before God as they are hidden from men.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 22. While the previous page discussed the psychological struggle Abraham faced in the morning as he prepared for the journey, this page examines the three-day journey to Mount Moriah, the spiritual significance of that duration, and the moment Abraham leaves his servants behind to ascend the mountain with Isaac alone.</meta>

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXII.</header>

## 4. On the third day, Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.

<margin>On the third day</margin> These represent the three days of Christ: Yesterday, when He was a servant of the circumcision, placed under the Law; Today, the favorable time of the Gospel and the day of salvation; and the Day of Eternity. These form the threefold <term>Economy</term> <note>original: "Oeconomie"; here referring to the "Divine Economy," the way God manages the world and human salvation through different eras</note> and divine household management, which must be carefully observed in the Scriptures, even though it is generally neglected, haphazardly mixed together, and treated without distinction.

<margin>Saw</margin> Bonfrerius <note>Seraphinus Bonfrerius (1567–1633), a Jesuit biblical commentator</note> cites from Hebrew traditions that God showed him the mountain through a fiery pillar of cloud that stood atop the mountain's peak, which was seen by no one else but Abraham and Isaac.

The sight of the land of Moriah has—as the ancients finely remarked upon this passage—its specific stages and progressions; which Clement of Alexandria <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – c. 215 AD) was a prominent Christian theologian who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine</note> (a) describes as three days: the first day being the sight of beautiful and good things; the second being the longing of the pious soul for them; the third being the insight into spiritual things, when our eyes are opened by the Master who rose on the third day.

One must proceed in faith if we are to reach the true knowledge of God and be able to provide genuine proof of it. Just as Abraham first had to take many a bitter step in the obedience of faith before he could pass the highest test of faith. If he had not been intimately acquainted with God, he could never have possessed certainty and joy during such a terrifying temptation. For he could have doubted a thousand times whether this voice was from the Devil, who might wish to rob him of his son and, with him, all of God's promises. However, a soul can only withstand the most extreme trials when it is accustomed to the divine light and knows through the Spirit that the Spirit is Truth.

<margin>From afar</margin> Why did God point Abraham to such a distant place? Answer: Partly for the sake of the <term>prefiguration</term> <note>a "type" or symbolic foreshadowing of a future event, specifically the sacrifice of Christ</note> and the mysterious purpose of this location in future times; and partly so that Abraham, on this long journey lasting three full days, would be tested within himself all the longer, and might overcome all impulses more deliberately before the actual deed.

This journey must have seemed exceedingly bitter and difficult for the flesh—yes, a thousand times harder than when he had to leave his fatherland. For it was not only contrary to his nature and will, but also beyond all natural strength.

Just consider and place yourself, so to speak, in Abraham's position: what thoughts must have come to him, that he was to plunge the knife through the throat of his only and most beloved child, first binding his limbs, then cutting him to pieces, laying him on the altar, and letting him be gradually burned and roasted by the fire—yes, turned to ashes. Abraham had three full days to think on this during the long journey, and moreover, he saw his child constantly walking before and with him toward such a bloody business; because of this, not only his fatherly heart but his entire flesh could have waged war enough against him. Yet, this is exactly what makes Abraham's faith all the more precious and proven: because it was not some hasty and reckless obedience, but one founded and verified with all deliberation and long-lasting resolve.

Abraham saw with the clear eyes of his faith through the dark veil of this external matter into God's mind, which sought primarily his self-denial and spiritual death. Therefore, he was so comforted and strove only for the main point—the "dying away" from all things—so that he might become dead and foreign to his natural love and attachment to his natural child. As for the external life of his son, God could do with it as He willed.

Self-love does not want to hear of total death, but gladly prolongs its life, even under the appearance of good—yes, under the pretext of God's Word. It is quite agile in defending and helping itself even with God's commandments against God's own command. And in this matter, self-love would have acted quite differently than Abraham, as it could have so plausibly protected and excused itself against this command using the literal words of the 5th and 6th Commandments; wherein love for children is commanded and all murder is forbidden. But...

O wonderful steadfastness of pure faith, which is far from all second-guessing and turning back! It does not become wavering through such a long path, any more than through the presence of his son, by whom Abraham was to become a child-murderer! Could not all these natural and divine reasons have stopped him, caused him to leave the path he had begun, and brought him to turn back? Namely, the fear of being deceived, of being mistaken; or even of committing a sin against God and a cruelty against his son. But how far is pure faith from such reflections! It does not even look at them; it no longer has eyes to look upon itself. The single fact that God commanded it is enough for him; and it is enough that he believes God has commanded it, without investigating whether he believes it or not: he has only ears to hear. O Faith (b), you who move mountains; you allow even more impossible things to happen! But the servant and the donkey must stay behind here.

<column-break/>

## 5. And Abraham said to his servants: "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there, and when we have worshipped, we will come back to you."

## 6. And

How wisely Abraham acts regarding his sacrifice! He does not lead his servants up the mountain, which was to be the place of sacrifice, but let them stay with the donkeys at the foot of the mountain and went up alone. They were too incapable for this and would have been offended by it. One must not reveal the secrets of the inner state to those who still serve God only as mercenary servants <note>original: "Lohn-Knechte"; those who serve God only for a reward rather than out of pure love</note>. However, one can entrust the paths of pure faith to those who already serve Him as His friends without self-interest. But the greatest surrenders are only for the children who, like Isaac, are worthy to learn such sacrifices—sacrifices which have God as their author and in which they themselves must be the sacrificial animals. Perhaps Abraham also left his servants behind so that they might not disturb him through a false compassion or prevent him from fulfilling this magnanimous—though seemingly reckless—undertaking.

So must we also be when we wish to deny ourselves: we must let go of the servant-like and animalistic mind of self-love and our own opinions, and set out purely and freely toward God, without letting either the flesh or the world speak into it. We do not listen to their whispering and act freely and openly before God, according to His dearest pleasure.

A mighty help in this is divine understanding, which the Spirit of Faith wishes to grant us in His light when He is asked for it.

Furthermore, in this matter, Abraham represents a <term>type</term> <note>a symbolic figure</note> of the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave up His only-begotten, most beloved Son as a sacrifice for the life of the world, as the true Isaac. And thus, this staying behind of the servants and donkeys signifies that no creature, but only God and His Son, could perform the work of redemption. Indeed, the sluggish animal—the donkey—and the natural man, who understands nothing of the Spirit of God and His wonders, shall be left behind entirely and kept from beholding the mysteries of God.

<margin>We will come back to you</margin> Hereby he unwittingly gives a prophecy that they would both return to them.

> 6. And Abraham took the wood for the burnt offering / and laid it upon his son Isaac <margin>(a) John 19:17.</margin> ; but he took the fire and the knife in his hand: and they both went together.

> 7. Then Isaac spoke to his father Abraham and said: My father! And he answered: See, here I am, my son. And he said: See, here is the fire and the wood / but where is the lamb for the burnt offering?

> 8. And Abraham answered: God will provide for Himself <margin>(a) John 1:29.</margin> the lamb for the burnt offering / my son! and so they both went together.

**Verse 6.** Abraham had to ascend toward divine victorious strength through struggle / just as he had to physically climb the mountain with Isaac / as a reminder of the inner elevation of the mind from all lowly and earthly desires. Only then can one truly belong to the Lord with body and soul / when the dear Savior calls us into His cross and into His death / and wishes to baptize us therewith.

Which, however, of these two parts is more to be wondered at: the hardness of faith / which is without mercy / in that it burdens this poor sacrificial animal <note>The author refers to Isaac here as the "sacrificial animal" to emphasize his role as a type of the Lamb of God.</note>; or the magnanimity of this soul / which takes upon itself the cross / which was to make its sacrifice perfect / and which is so openly expressed by the wood / which is laid upon him? Faith / the Cross / and Sacrifice / are three companions / which are always joined together / and walk with one another to bring the sacrificial animal to its death.

<margin>(a) Luke 12:49.</margin>
The fire and the knife are united together / to slaughter it and consume it entirely to ashes. O wonderful image of the inner life / which is supported by the word of Jesus Christ: (a) I am come / He says / to bring fire into the world: And how I wish / that it were already burning! And further: <margin>(b) Matthew 10:34.</margin> (b) I am not come to bring peace on earth / but the sword. The knife must kill / and the fire must burn. Bare faith alone causes all this destruction within the soul.

**They both went together)** This teaches us in the <term>antitype</term> <note>A "type" is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows a New Testament reality; the "antitype" is the fulfillment, in this case, Christ.</note> / that / although the Father did not become man / nor was offered for us / but rather the Son / the Lamb of God / He is nevertheless not to be excluded from the work of redemption. <note>original Latin: "Gott war in Christo ꝛc." refers to 2 Corinthians 5:19: "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself."</note>

**Verse 7.** This question posed by Isaac to his father was certainly a very sensitive word of temptation. For how does one think that this must have cut the father to the heart / to give an account to the innocent sacrifice himself upon his question?

This question of Isaac indicates the ignorance / in which faith leads the soul / until it has come to the place of judgment. Abraham's answer expresses a surrender to Providence / which is found in faith: And the docility of Isaac / in which he concerns himself with nothing further / indicates the faithfulness of the soul / in letting itself be led blindly through faith and <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A key term in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness" or "letting go" of one's own will to God.</note>. It would be a small thing for this magnanimous soul / for this innocent sacrifice / to let itself be guided thus in darkness / if it / seeing its approaching death and inevitable execution before its eyes / were to change its conduct.

**Verse 8. God will provide for Himself)** <term>אלהים יראה לו</term> <note>Elohim yireh lo</note> The Jewish <term>Cabbala</term> <note>Kabbalah; Jewish mystical tradition</note> derives from the first three letters of these three words the word <term>איל</term> <note>Ayil</note>, a ram / which Abraham sacrificed in Isaac's stead.

<column-break/>

> 9. And when they came to the place / of which God had told him; Abraham built the altar there / and laid the wood in order upon it: and he bound his son Isaac / and laid him on the altar / on top of the wood.

> 10. And

Who then is prefigured through Abraham but the great High Father?

Who is Isaac but a prefigurement of Jesus Christ / the Son of God / whom the Father did not spare <note>original: "ꝛc. v. 12. 16. Röm. 8/32. 33." referring to Romans 8:32: "He that spared not his own Son..."</note>? And

What was the altar other than a figure of the Cross of Christ?

Accordingly, another very deep mystery was hidden beneath it / which the Holy Spirit thus played out beforehand / which Abraham glimpsed beforehand in the spirit / and had to prefigure through such a wonderful act.

The heavenly Isaac was to go forth in the fullness of time / and offer the sacrifice of His body to the Father / to surrender the same to be burned by the fire of His wrath / and thus erase our sin / and bring back eternal righteousness.

To that end, Isaac had to be bound here by his own father / laid upon the altar and upon the wood for a burnt offering / and be subjected to the slaughtering knife: to show / that the Only-begotten from the bosom of the Father should be bound for the sake of our sin / hung on the cross / slaughtered and pierced; and thus still the fire of wrath / and the demanding justice.

If you now wish to be a son or daughter of Abraham / then prove yourself to be such by doing the works of Abraham. What is Isaac but our joy? What is the altar but the cross? What is the cross but the patience of Jesus Christ? With Christ we must be planted into a similar death / and thus become partakers of His death and suffering in the faith of Jesus. And

Therefore we are not to look upon Abraham's example and prefigurement as idly / as a foreign thing / of which nothing can or must be fulfilled in us / but we should know and believe / that we must necessarily also surrender ourselves into such a prefigurement of dying and suffering: since the LORD Himself let Isaac's prefigurement be fulfilled in Him / and explicitly said / that we should follow Him / and indeed with the cross / with hatred against our own things. <note>Referring to Luke 14:26-27 regarding discipleship and self-denial.</note>

O how blessed is this exercise under the cross of Christ / when one becomes aware of the voice of the LORD in one's heart from His word! How good it is / to bind even one's most beloved own will and the love for oneself with such a will of God / however much it may hurt the flesh.

Where this binding occurs rightly / there follows also an earnest slaughtering and killing of all disordered desires and affections / and the whole life becomes a daily dying according to the flesh / whereby one may first truly live to God according to the spirit.

This pleasing sacrificial animal must let itself be bound to the cross by the ropes of faith. It must bow its neck under the knife / without wavering or complaining. All this takes place under a great stillness and under a deep death / which does not allow nature the slightest relief / indeed not even a sigh / nor any complaint. O certainly / although Isaac's physical death did not occur at that time / yet his spiritual death was accomplished then / since all hope and all will to live longer was cut off from him. The extinguishing of one's own life / in order to live for God alone / was the reward of this great sacrifice / which he had accepted with his whole heart.

**Bound)** means strictly to bind the hands with the feet / not the hands together and the feet also together / but one foot and one hand together. In such a way, Isaac could by no means have knelt on the wood / as the painters and engravers depict him; but he lay / as Luther well notes / on his back upon the woodpile / with his face directed toward heaven / so that Abraham could all the more easily stab him in the throat / as butchers are accustomed to slaughter a lamb.

<header>The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXII.</header>

**10. And Abraham stretched out his hand / and took the knife / to slay his son.**

**11. Then the Angel of the LORD called to him from heaven / and said: Abraham / Abraham! And he answered: See, here I am!**

---

<margin>v. 10.</margin> According to faith, this sacrifice was therefore perfect. For as Abraham lifted his hand / he had a sincere intention to slay his beloved son.

From this it is evident / that fundamentally there was no pretense or mock battle <note>original: "Spiegelgefechten"</note> regarding the matter. <margin>Heb. 11:17.</margin>

He believed that child-murder did not befit divine love. Therefore he knew for certain / that it would only be a sacrifice / which obedience would fulfill. <margin>Alcimus Avitus <note>Avitus of Vienne (c. 450–518), a Latin poet and bishop.</note></margin>

The slaying and dying of the old life is primarily what matters in our spiritual calling / as the purpose of all the words and works of GOD / which He lets us know for our improvement. Just as the purpose of Abraham's entire journey was the actual sacrifice. And

What deep mysteries of self-denial and surrender to GOD were not hidden under the Levitical sacrifices and the entire external Temple service? What does the manifold slaying and blood-shedding / the burning and all the other offerings to the LORD signify / if not precisely such an internal surrender of the whole person to the living and true GOD?

The Cross is the priestly sacrificial knife / with which Christ in us / and we with Him / must slay our Isaac / our dearest little lust / our laughter / our pastime and sinful play.

How is it / however / that painters represent Abraham with a sword / when the text explicitly names a knife? Not to mention that all sacrifices were slaughtered with a knife.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> Here GOD now brings Abraham to a halt / and showed him / that He would be satisfied with the proven obedience / since this had only been His ultimate purpose / and then primarily to further reveal to him the great mystery of the promised Seed of the Woman / how He would be bruised in the heel by the serpent's seed / and thus suffer death: which GOD certainly allowed him to see in the spirit / so that he also saw this day of Christ / how through this the true sacrifice for the forgiveness of his and the whole world's sin / which he was indeed to inherit / would occur / and he rejoiced in his heart because of it.

Just as Abraham here received his son back from death after three days / during which he had been as if dead in his heart / when the knife was already at his throat; <margin>Heb. 11:19.</margin> so also Christ rose again from the dead on the third day.

Then) The manner and the time / which GOD uses / to prevent this extraordinary undertaking / are excellent / thereby showing the manner / which He maintains with those souls standing at this stage <note>original: "Staffel," referring to a level of spiritual growth or a step on a ladder.</note>. First / He waits / until it has come to the very highest point / to come to their aid; when they have no comfort or certainty left / but only the divine moment / which does not let things come or be understood until the moment when they are to happen. Secondly / He lets them walk in a total loss precisely through this. And so that He may tear them away from all that is comprehensible / He does not let them experience these things until they happen.

It also occurs / to test the purity of their love / which does not shy away from losing everything / in order to fulfill the will of GOD / even should sins—according to appearance—be committed through an all-too-great denial and trust in GOD'S wisdom and power.

This haste of GOD / to rescue the yielded <note>original: "gelassenen," referring to the Pietist concept of Gelassenheit or total surrender to God's will.</note> and faithful souls in their utmost danger / increases their yieldedness and their faith. This yieldedness and faith / however / cause Providence to double its care for those who are devoted to it. And these are truly the souls of Providence.

<column-break/>

**12. And he said: Lay not thine hand upon the lad / and do nothing at all to him! For now I know / that thou fearest GOD / and hast not spared thy son / thine only one / before me.** <margin>v. 16. 1 Sam. 15:22. Hos. 6:6.</margin>

**13. Then**

---

(Lay not thine hand upon the lad) Shortly before, it sounded quite different. Abraham was willing in his heart for what GOD demanded of him; and GOD was satisfied with that / and now explicitly forbids him / what He Himself had previously commanded him.

What does that mean other than / that we should above all things see to it / that our inner ground is rightly prepared and divinely minded or becomes one with GOD. Then we may become an acceptable and well-pleasing sacrifice to the LORD with all that is ours through the power of the obedience of JESUS Christ.

GOD demands no greater proof of our faith / than faith itself / that we leave ourselves entirely to GOD above all our own knowledge / thinking / willing / and working / and simply and strictly follow His word and will / let it go with us as it may. This is the highest work of the Holy Spirit / which He can again work and establish in the creature. When He has obtained this purpose / He desires nothing further.

Eternal love / essential holiness / showed clearly through the revocation of the command / that it was not concerned with the miserable body / but with the precious life of the soul. That is what it wanted to possess in Abraham and Isaac: and therefore it also gladly granted the external life.

How finely this governance of the LORD corrects well-meaning souls in all their scruples / when out of good intention they linger more in external exercises / and believe repentance to be in mere physical and external abstinences / yet do not spare the body in the process. To such the LORD also calls out / that they should not lay their hand on the Isaac / on nature itself and its being / wherein the Spirit wishes to have His dwelling; but on the ram / on the contrary qualities and desires / on the disorder in the heart. These one should slay more through spiritual weapons and internal mortification / with prayer / humility / patience / and yieldedness.

(Now I know / that) GOD knew it before as well / but the trials must be gone through.

For Himself, GOD indeed does not need to examine us first in His omniscience. But for the manifestation of the hidden evil in us, it is highly necessary; so that it may become known / what is in our heart / whether we will fear the LORD or not. The dear GOD is only concerned / that evil comes to light / and is judged / and thus also done away with.

And when does it then become truly manifest?

(That thou fearest GOD?) Answer: When the LORD tries us so far / that we leave and surrender everything / that we have / our joy / the delight of our souls; when we suffer even unto blood in the struggle against sin.

(Before me) There you see / what GOD is concerned with in all His tasks. Namely not / that He has pleasure in our harm or loss and distress; but in our obedience / in the pure sacrifice of our heart to Him.

(Not spared) Although Abraham did not actually slay Isaac / but had spared his only son at the outcome; yet GOD accepts the full will for the deed itself. But not the half-will. <margin>Heb. 11:17.</margin> In Abraham's heart it was as good as done / he who with his whole will / and spirit had already given him up. Therefore it is also so recorded and spoken by GOD.

But oh, how few complete the test before GOD even so far / that He can give them the testimony: I know / that thou fearest me; because thou hast not spared thy money and thy honors for my sake / but hast sacrificed and given up everything for my honor / only so that thou mightest win Christ and follow the word of GOD!
