<header>Ch. XXII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

13. Then Abraham lifted up his
eyes and looked/ and behold, there was a **ram** behind him, caught in the thicket <margin>(a) Matt. 27:29.</margin> by his horns. And Abraham went and took the **ram**/ and offered him up for a burnt offering in his son's stead.

<column-break/>

14. And Abraham called the name of that place/ **The Lord will provide**: As it is said to this day; In the mount of the Lord it shall be **provided**.

15. And

---

<column-break/>

<margin>God often presents Himself as if He requires everything to be sacrificed; though in the execution of it, He allows Himself to be satisfied with the smallest part: just as He accepts the ram instead of Isaac.</margin>

This ram had to become lost and caught in a thicket through the providence of God/ as a **prefiguration of Christ** / who came into this world / and had to give His life among the prickly thorns / that is, among mankind: whereas Isaac then became a **prefiguration of the believers** / who are released in this manner.

However, it is also indisputable that Isaac is a prefiguration of Christ. How does this work / or how do both reconcile in Him? Namely, Christ is both God and man / and has two natures. He indeed suffers; but in the flesh: He dies; but according to the flesh: of which the ram is the image. According to the spirit, however, He is Isaac / and does not die / but goes free. Therefore, He is both Priest and Sacrifice at the same time.

->So then is<-

### the ram a prefiguration
### of the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.

->And indeed<-

1. Because it was a ram / it was a male / as most sacrifices were. So also was the gender of the Messiah.
2. It was a ram among the sheep. This signifies the innocence / patience / meekness / and humility of Christ / the Lamb of God. Isaiah 53:7.
3. This ram had its horns / in which its strength lies / and by which one seizes it. The Lamb also has horns. <note>In biblical imagery, horns often represent power or authority.</note>
4. This ram was not chosen by Abraham for this purpose / but / "The Lord," he said to his son, "will provide himself a sheep for a burnt offering": v. 8. It was not chosen from his own stall / but given freely by God. Thus John 3:16, Isaiah 9:6.
5. When God called Abraham / and he lifted up his eyes and looked around; then he beheld the ram. Even so must God reveal Christ.
6. Abraham saw the ram behind him: So he also saw Christ as one coming after him. John 8:56.
7. This ram remained caught by its horns in the hedges and thorns. Our lusts and sins have bound Christ and held Him to the slaughtering block: indeed, for their sake, He is crowned with thorns.
8. Just as this ram came in Isaac's stead / when the knife was already set to his throat: so also is Christ sacrificed in our stead; the punishment lies upon Him / so that we might have peace.

<column-break/>

Accordingly, we can be assured in our highest needs / that God will finally prove a gracious providence upon such a mountain of greatest difficulty / so that we / delivered from all temptation / can afterwards praise and glorify Him with joy. See Psalm 116.

How then should our eye not be constantly directed in faith toward these mountains / from which alone help can come to us! Especially since God is concerned with exactly that; as it is said: Your eyes, Lord, look toward faith. This is the right sacrifice that is pleasing to God / and which He safely guides through the hidden dying-away of the self. This is the right "reasonable" or "rational" service <note>original: "vernünfftige oder verständige... Gottesdienst"</note> well-pleasing to God / which Paul desires. (a) And for such a purpose the Lord also speaks to you (as the Chaldean translator <note>A reference to the Targum, the Aramaic translation and interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> renders it): Go into the land or the earth of the **Service of God** / where God is worshipped / that is / into your heart and spirit. John 4:23.

If we only walk in a constant surrender to Him in His fear / then everything will be provided by the Lord for our best: and that

**Upon the mountain of the Lord** / Upon the Mountain of Calvary / where this matter occurred; where the old Adam is dead and buried. There the true Isaac / the Christ of God / the foundation and the ground of the Temple of God / is certainly laid. There is the altar of divine patience / upon which the daily sacrifice is offered. There is the fear of God and all divine service. There is the mountain of vision / where the Lord is seen and His providence recognized. There is the divine doctrine and the Spirit of God / who leads into all truth. There is **Ornan** / the child of light / the Jebusite / who previously trod righteousness underfoot / but now treads unrighteousness underfoot / and finds the good grain among the husks / the spirit out of the letter. <note>Ornan the Jebusite owned the threshing floor where the Temple was eventually built; the author uses this as an allegory for separating spiritual truth from the literal "husk."</note>

Many things worthy of the greatest note are told to have happened on this mountain. Such as: that Adam first sacrificed there / and was buried there: as Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> relates from the ancient memorials of the Jews. Also, David built an altar there at God's command / and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings upon it: so that the destroying angel was appeased / and the plague was stayed. So also, above all, the Temple of God was built by Solomon on Mount Moriah. 2 Chronicles 3:1.

It is said to have had three distinct peaks: one upon which the City of David was built; 1 Chronicles 11:4, 5, 7. Upon the second, the Temple of Solomon; on the third, Isaac is said to have been offered in prefiguration / and later our Lord was crucified: as many of the ancients affirm. (b)

<margin>(a) Romans 12:1.</margin>
<margin>(b) Augustine, *The City of God*, Book 16, Ch. 32.</margin>

---

That does not, however, cancel out the fact that we should also sacrifice ourselves to God and go into death with our Savior and die to ourselves.

**Isaac** / a figure of spiritual joy / shall live / and all our joy should be precisely in the Lord. But our **ram-like** fleshly joy we should sacrifice / which subsequently pushes us and distresses us in the time of our sorrow. For such joy generally ends in sadness.

Where one is now surrendered / and believes God / that He can bring forth children of righteousness even out of a stony heart / and gives oneself over entirely to the will of God; then the nature of the "butting goats" <note>Referring to the stubborn, aggressive nature of the ram/flesh.</note> is shown in the hawthorn of our hearts / so that we should kill them / shed their blood / and sacrifice them.

That happens then in this way: When one learns to live constantly contrary to one's own will / leaves one's own desires / and does not indulge one's own pleasure / but is as if dead and numb to all things that one must use out of necessity / and places and leaves everything in God's governance.

The Spirit of Christ is certainly helpful in this / if we only will it. He / as the Spirit of discipline / reminds His own constantly of the divine judgment / when the "own-life" wants to rise up again and nourish itself: then He punishes / and points us again into the death of Jesus Christ / so that the ram shall indeed not live / but remain dedicated to dying.

And all this happens for the true preservation of Isaac / or the new divine life in the soul / in whose place the old must perish / and becomes a sacrifice to the Lord in the fire of the righteousness of God; so that the spirit / separated from soul and body / may finally be presented perfectly to the Father for an infinite blessing in Jesus Christ / the blessed Seed of the Woman.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis 22, shifting from the physical act of the sacrifice to the divine response. It explains the spiritual rewards Abraham receives for his obedience and distinguishes between the "earthly" and "heavenly" promises made to his descendants.</meta>

<header>The First Book of Moses, Ch. XXII.</header>

# 15. And the Angel of the Lord called to Abraham a second time from heaven;

**GOD** does not fail to reward this magnanimous sacrifice of His servant. And just as this spiritual death was concluded through an actual death and the annihilation of the sacrificial animal—for the ram, which was an image of it, was reduced to nothing and turned to ashes—so God gives to this, His faithful servant, more and even more noble gifts of grace than those that came before.

It should be noted that ever since the slaughtering and sacrificing were first mentioned, all promises seemed to have ceased, and the Scripture says nothing that might resemble them. On the contrary, these holy Patriarchs walked toward death; and because of this sacrifice, all the promises that had been made to them seemed empty and useless, because they saw that everything was about to be reduced to nothing for them. But faith relies neither on the goods and graces of the past, nor on that which has been promised. When the soul remembers these, such a memory only increases its "death," because the soul can no longer see them within itself nor claim anything for itself. However, as soon as the sacrifice is completed and the soul is annihilated <note>In this context, "annihilated" refers to a mystical state of total surrender where the self-will is "extinguished" to make room for God.</note>, God restores all its goods, and indeed much more than it had before—but in a very different way. For the soul no longer possesses them as its own property, nor views them as belonging to itself, but as being in God and belonging to God.

<margin>Regarding this fruit of Abraham's faith.</margin>
After this trial of faith, Abraham was taken even further into divine intimacy, says Hilary <note>original: "Hilarius"; likely referring to St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a prominent Latin theologian.</note> (a).

The Angel of the LORD is the Son of GOD, whom the Fathers identify as the God-man, sent even then to "play" <note>A reference to Proverbs 8:31, where Divine Wisdom "rejoices" or "plays" in the habitable parts of the earth with the sons of men.</note> with mankind. And when this Son of Man

Appears a second time from heaven to those who wait for Him for salvation, then it will truly become known what was contained in the promise made here. For

This second calling of Abraham from heaven certainly carries more weight than might be apparent. It might seem as if the following promise and blessing are nothing more than a repetition and confirmation of the previous ones already given to him, with nothing further added. It might even seem almost superfluous and not entirely necessary to repeat the same promises so often. But the Wisdom of God is more understanding than men are and knows well what He says and what must be said. If Abraham were only to be regarded according to the flesh, and were only the forefather of a certain people according to the flesh, then a one-time promise would have been sufficient. But now, in order to indicate that he should first be a father of a people that was to be circumcised according to the flesh, this promise is given to him the first time at the institution of the covenant of circumcision, as it was specifically and primarily to concern the people of the circumcision. However, because he was also to be and become a father of all believers who should come to the inheritance through Christ's sacrifice of suffering, this promise is renewed at the figurative sacrifice of Isaac, as it was properly to concern the people of faith and the New Covenant. And although the same things seem to be repeated in the promises, they are nevertheless very distinct. For that which was spoken first, just as it primarily concerns the first people, was also spoken only on the earth, as if to a people most capable of earthly promises. For God <margin>as it says in Ch. 15:5</margin> led him out and said to him: "Look now toward heaven." But here, the promise occurs a second time *from heaven*, and thus aims at a people whose "conversation" or way of life should be in heaven. And what else are these two kinds of people than those also indicated by the Apostle (b): "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven, heavenly." Furthermore, a difference is found in these promises in that, in the former, the promise is simply made, but here the matter is confirmed with an oath.

---
(a) Exposition on Psalm 1, p. 345. (b) 1 Corinthians 15:47.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 12. Rom. 8:32. (a) Jer. 22:5.</margin>
# 16. And he said: By myself have I sworn (a), says the Lord, because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son;
# 17. That in blessing I will surely bless you, and in multiplying I will greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore; and your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies by inheritance.
# 18. And

v. 16. **Because you have done this**) Upon the proven loyalty of faith follows a rich reward. Thus, one loses nothing at all through such obedience of faith and the denial of one's own things; rather, according to Christ’s clear promise, one finds it again a hundredfold. And one sees this clearly in Abraham. After he had renounced and surrendered his son and all the promises hanging upon him, he not only received him back, but also an innumerable and incomparable blessing upon many thousands of thousands of descendants. This was done so that it would be manifest both to Abraham and the whole world what power, granted by God, lies within the faith of man toward every blessing, even in the physical realm.

Yet a thousand times more do spiritual rewards of grace follow upon honest trials of faith. There, above all things, the secret bond between God and the soul is tied faster and more closely, just as between lovers, a love already established becomes incomparably greater and more inward through actual protestations of loyalty and through trials.

This is learned better from experience and cannot be so easily believed without it. But if one becomes faithful to God in small things, one after another, and learns to proceed step-by-step in the granted power of faith, one will see what an increase is hidden therein.

The eternal love of God opens itself to such a faithful soul with very close friendship in an intimate communion; because He sees that His gifts are well-used in such a good vessel, He makes such souls stewards of greater and varied graces.

And therefore, may the finger of the Spirit of God write this great example of faith and reward into everyone’s heart for blessed imitation, so that we do not view it in vain, but may also become partakers of a blessing!

v. 17. **Multiply seed as the stars — as the sand**) Those who sacrifice their pleasure and joy to the Lord shall receive the fullness of joy.

The promise made to Abraham concerned a twofold seed: the one, that it should be like the dust (Ch. 13:16) or sand; the other, that it should be like the stars of heaven (here and Ch. 15:5). The first is fulfilled in Israel according to the flesh; the other is fulfilled in Israel according to the promise. The former were of a hard, unconverted heart, like the sand, and earthly-minded, like the dust. The latter shall be heavenly and purely righteous.

**Your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies by inheritance**) By this it is indicated that the soul, which previously had enemies that greatly opposed it and were cruel toward it, finds itself through "annihilation" in such a state that it is above them, rules them, makes them subject, and holds them captive. For when someone holds the gates or the dwelling where his enemy resides in his power and keeping, it is as much as if he held him captive and were his master. Thus, such souls cannot fear the devil, since God—to whom they have surrendered themselves through a magnanimous love without exception—has made the devil subject to them.

### 18. **And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because you have obeyed my voice.**

### 19. **So Abraham returned again to his servants, and they rose up and went together to Beer-sheba; and Abraham dwelt at Beer-sheba.**

### 20. **And**

---

<margin>v. 18. In your seed shall they bless themselves)</margin> While similar promises have been read twice before, this one is only like them and not exactly the same. In previous instances, the blessing was given to Abraham in his own name, centered in him so that it might go out from him to all nations. Here, however, the promise is made to him *in his seed*, and through his seed to all nations. Likewise, the conjugation of the word has changed. In earlier places, the blessing was given in a passive sense—"shall be blessed"—but here it is promised in a reciprocal or reflexive form: "shall bless themselves." <note>This refers to a grammatical shift in the original Hebrew from the *Niphal* (passive) to the *Hithpael* (reflexive) verb stem, suggesting that people will actively seek or find their blessing in the Messiah.</note> Vatablus <note>François Vatable, a 16th-century French humanist and scholar.</note> alone expressed this in his translation: *All the nations of the world shall call themselves blessed in your seed:* that is, as he explains it himself, they shall consider themselves blessed and happy for the sake of your seed, Christ. Castellio <note>Sebastian Castellio, a 16th-century theologian known for his work on religious tolerance.</note> aims for the same point. All other translations have not nearly expressed the Hebrew, which means much more: namely, that all nations shall know, believe, and confess that they are blessed in the Son of God. Indeed, they shall bless one another again because they are thus blessed. See Psalm 72:17.

What can seem more unbelievable than that God would want to bless all other peoples and humans throughout the whole world in the seed of a single man?

Nevertheless, God says this here, and even more: which no one can rightly understand or experience according to its power unless they have, through the Holy Spirit, a true divine faith in the rightful Savior and Seed of Abraham.

Therefore, we must first follow with the faith of Abraham if we wish to rightly enjoy the Messiah and his salvation.

Abraham is a certain model for you of what must become of you.

You must become truly obedient to the word of the Lord in faith; otherwise, you cannot grasp the promise of the blessed Seed of Abraham for your own person in particular.

But you must also be certain and assured for yourself particularly of the coming and redemption of the Savior, so that you know whether the general promises of God also apply to you specifically and come true one after another. You must be able to remember a time when you truly turned to Him, and when He actually began your purification and rescue.

If that is to happen in and through you, the Lord Jesus must find you standing in true faith.

For, dear reader, how did it stand here with Abraham? Was he not occupied with the very fact that, at the Lord's word, he was willing to put the knife to his son's throat without hesitation, and to strangle and burn him—despite the fact that God had given him this very promise through this very son? In and through this "hero-faith," God now repeats and confirms this promise to him as a new blessing and reward for his faith.

But let one pay close attention to what this signifies: that God did not want the Messiah to be born from an unbelieving or hypocritical seed, but from one who stood in the covenant of God regarding the restoration of the fallen, and who remained in the line or succession of the faithful Abel, Seth, Noah, Shem, and other holy fathers—one who himself stood in the actual power and grace of faith and a walk with God.

Oh, this is a great and deep wonder of the holy incarnation of Jesus Christ: that this promise of his coming in the flesh occurred exactly during such a glorious trial of faith as Abraham demonstrated at the sacrifice of his son!

Christ should and had to come from the fathers, from the seed or essence of human nature, from the root and the stem that was created good and holy in Adam.

Into this root of the holy, blessed humanity of Jesus Christ, the Father wanted to place His blessing again for all people through His eternal Word, which was in the beginning and afterward became flesh.

<column-break/>

The sin and corruption that still remained in Abraham and others, Christ was not to take upon himself with the seed; rather, he took what was still good in nature, the human essence, insofar as it is not sinful in itself but only has sin dwelling within it.

For the essence of fallen humanity is also what God did not want to let perish eternally, but rather to seek out again and bring out of corruption, and to clothe again with His new power for holiness.

To this end, he is and must be and is called a "blessed seed of the woman," because not only may no curse or un-blessing cling to him, but because he should come—and has come—to drive all curses away from the poor creature and transform them back into blessings.

What the main parts of the spiritual blessing contained primarily under the blessing of the Messiah are, Paul has set down a right interpretation of this text in Galatians 3.

O, if only one would ask God for open eyes of understanding, so that one might behold the immeasurable store of treasures and gifts of God which He has intended for us in Christ! If one only perceived it rightly for a moment, how would one not spit out everything else that has until now kept us away from this sea of blessing!

It is rightly said here: what one does not know, one does not desire. The enemy diligently keeps the eyes of people closed so that they shall not recognize the bright light of the Gospel and its blessing, nor become hungry for it.

The blessing of God in His Son is so very overflowing, so very up-welling and spreading, that in all believers it increases and propagates itself unto infinity.

All nations on earth) Not only the Jews, Abraham's descendants; also not only certain other nations and parties: but all, all nations on the entire earth shall enjoy it.

God’s purpose for restoration in Christ Jesus extends as far as the Fall has ever spread. If not all actually reach the blessing, they have themselves to blame because they do not want it in the right and proper order.

For unavoidable reasons, God has stipulated that fallen man should allow the Holy Spirit to work faith within him and follow the draw of grace. Why does one not let that become true in oneself? Who is now to blame for the lack of blessing? Is it not the unbelieving creature?

If you now find no true well-being or blessing in your soul, but rather a curse and unrest in your conscience, then notice where the problem lies. Without any doubt, it lies in faith, and that you do not truly want to take it from God and let your old things go, or deny them for Christ's sake.

Abraham had to yield himself so completely to God that God could do with him whatever He willed: and so he was blessed out of faith, as from the root of all spiritual blessing. Thus, his descendants in faith have also propagated the blessing one to another.

This indicates what unspeakable goods God shares with others for the sake of those who have surrendered themselves entirely to Him. One of the very greatest gifts, however, is that He uses them to form Jesus Christ in the hearts of others. For through Him, all holy nations are blessed.

If you now wish to see the curse of sin dwelling within you transformed into blessing, then turn through repentance with believing desire to the blessed Seed of Abraham, and see above all things that you grasp the true blessing—Jesus Christ himself—in your heart. Then you will also be able to share it with others who seek it. Thus, your tree of faith will grow as a wonder and a testimony to divine grace.

Do not neglect this all-sufficient good! It is there at the door of your heart! Whoever takes it has it for free: no one can earn it, but one can certainly neglect it. In this, the Father has gathered all blessings together; He wants them to be fetched from Him. The entire fullness in Christ Jesus is open: let everyone reach out, for it is called "today"!

### 15. And the Angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven;

God does not fail to reward this noble-hearted sacrifice of His servant. And just as this spiritual death was concluded through an actual death and the annihilation of the sacrificial animal—when the ram, which was an image of this, was reduced to nothing and ashes—so God gives to this, His faithful servant, more and even more abundant gifts of grace than those that came before.

It is to be noted that, from the moment there was talk of slaughtering and sacrificing, all promises ceased, and the Scripture says nothing that might resemble them. On the contrary, these holy patriarchs walked into death; and because of this sacrifice, all the promises which had been made to them seemed empty and useless: because they saw that everything was about to become nothing for them. But faith stands neither upon the goods and graces of the past, nor upon that which has been promised to it. When faith remembers these, such a memory increases its death: because the soul cannot see them within itself, nor claim anything from them. But as soon as the sacrifice is completed and the soul is annihilated <note>In the mystical tradition, "annihilation" refers to the total surrender of the self-will to God, a "death" of the ego.</note>, God gives back to it all its goods, and indeed much more than it had before—but in a very different way. For the soul no longer possesses them as its own property, nor looks at them as belonging to itself, but as being in God and belonging to God.

After this trial of faith, Abraham was received even further into divine familiarity, says Hilary (a) regarding this fruit of Abraham's faith.

The Angel of the LORD is the Son of God, whom the Father has sent from time immemorial as the God-Man to "play" with mankind <note>This "playing" refers to a theological concept from Proverbs 8:31, describing the joyful interaction between Divine Wisdom and humanity.</note>. And when this Son of Man

Appears a second time from heaven to those who wait for Him for salvation, then it will truly become known what was contained in the promise made here. For

This calling of Abraham from heaven for a second time certainly holds more significance than it might at first appear. It may well seem as if the subsequent promise and blessing were nothing more than a repetition and confirmation of the previous ones already given to him, with nothing further added. Thus, it might seem almost superfluous and not entirely necessary to lead into the same promises so many times. But the wisdom of God is more understanding than men are, and knows well what He says and has to say. If Abraham were only to be regarded according to the flesh, and had only been the forefather of a certain people according to the flesh, then a single promise would have been sufficient. But now, in order to indicate that he should first be a father of a people who were to be circumcised according to the flesh, this promise happens to him for the first time at the institution of the covenant of circumcision, as it was especially and primarily to concern the people of circumcision. But because he was also to be and become a father of all believers, who were to come into the inheritance through Christ’s sacrifice of suffering, this promise is renewed at the figurative sacrifice of Isaac, since it was actually to concern the people of faith and the New Covenant. And although the same things seem to be repeated in the promises, they are nonetheless very distinct. For that which was spoken first, just as it mainly concerns the first people, was also spoken only on the earth—as if to a people who were most capable of earthly promises. For God, it says in Chapter 15:5, led him outside and spoke to him: "Look now toward heaven." But here, the promise happens for the second time *from heaven*, and thus aims at a people whose "conversation" or conduct is to be in heaven. And what else are these two kinds of people than those also indicated by the Apostle (b): "The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is from heaven, heavenly." Just as there is also a difference in these promises: there, the assurance is given simply, but here, the matter is confirmed with an oath.

### 17. That I will indeed richly bless you, and will greatly multiply your seed, as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand which is upon the sea shore: and your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies by inheritance.

### 18. And

v. 16. **Because you have done this)** A rich reward follows upon proven faithfulness in faith. Consequently, one loses nothing at all in such obedience of faith and the denial of one's own things; rather, according to Christ’s clear promise, one finds it again a hundredfold. And one sees this clearly in Abraham. After he had withdrawn from and surrendered his son and all the promises hanging thereon, he not only received him back, but also an innumerable and incomparable blessing upon many thousands of thousands of descendants. This was done so that it would be manifest both to Abraham and to the whole world what power, granted by God, lies within the faith of man for every blessing, even in physical matters.

Yet a thousand times more do the spiritual rewards of grace follow upon honest trials of faith. There, above all things, the secret bond between God and the soul is tied faster and more closely—much as the already established love between beloveds becomes incomparably greater and more intimate through actual demonstrations of loyalty and through trials.

This is learned better from experience and cannot be so easily believed without it. But if one becomes faithful to God in small things one after another, and learns to proceed step by step in the gifted strength of faith, then one will see what kind of increase is hidden therein.

The eternal love of God reveals itself to such a faithful soul with very close friendship in an intimate communion; because He sees that His gifts are well-used in such a good vessel, and He makes such souls stewards of more and varied graces.

And therefore, may the finger of the Spirit of God write this great example of faith and reward into the heart of every person for a blessed following, so that we do not look upon it in vain, but may also become partakers of a blessing!

v. 17. **Multiply seed like the stars — like the sand)** Those who sacrifice their desire and joy to the Lord receive the fullness of joys.

The promise made to Abraham concerned a twofold seed: one that should be like the dust (Chapter 13:16) or sand; the other that should be like the stars of heaven (here and Chapter 15:5). The first is fulfilled in Israel according to the flesh; the other is fulfilled in Israel according to the promise. The former were of a hard, unrepentant heart, like the sand, and earthly-minded, like the dust. These [the latter] shall be heavenly and purely righteous.

**Your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies by inheritance)** By this it is indicated that the soul—which previously had enemies who stood greatly against it and were cruel toward it—finds itself through "annihilation" in such a state that it is above them, rules over them, makes them subject to itself, and holds them captive. The eternal love of GOD opens itself to such a faithful soul with very close friendship in an intimate communion; because He sees that His gifts are well applied in such a good vessel, and He makes such souls stewards of more and varied graces.

And therefore, may the finger of the Spirit of GOD write this great example of faith and reward into everyone’s heart for a blessed following, so that we may not look upon it in vain, but may also become partakers of a blessing!

v. 17. **Multiply seed like the stars — like the sand**) Those who sacrifice their delight and joy to the Lord shall receive the fullness of joys.

The promise made to Abraham concerned a twofold seed: the one, that he should be like the dust, Chapter 13:16, or sand; the other, that he should be like the stars of heaven: here and in Chapter 15:5. The first is fulfilled in Israel according to the flesh; the other is fulfilled in Israel according to the promise. The former were of a hard, unrepentant heart, like sand, and earthly-minded, like dust; the latter shall be heavenly and purely righteous.

**Your seed shall possess the gate of his enemies**) This indicates that the soul, which previously had enemies who opposed it and were cruel toward it, finds itself through its "annihilation" <note>Self-denial or the mystical death of the ego.</note> in such a state that it is above them, rules over them, makes them subject to it, and holds them captive. For when someone holds the gates or the dwelling where his enemy stays in his power and keeping, it is as much as if he held him captive and were his master. Thus, such souls cannot fear the devil, since GOD—to whom they have surrendered themselves through a magnanimous love without exception—has made him subject to them.

# Chapter XXII. The First Book of Moses.

**18. And in your seed shall all the nations of the earth bless themselves. Because you have obeyed my voice.**

**19. So Abraham returned to his servants, and they arose and went together to Beersheba; for Abraham dwelt at Beersheba.**

**20. And**

---

<margin>verse 18.</margin> *In your seed shall they bless themselves*) Although a similar promise is read twice before, it is only similar to this one, and not exactly the same. In the previous instances, the blessing was given to Abraham in his own name, centered, as it were, in himself, from whom it was to go out to all nations. Here, however, the promise is made to him in his seed, and through his seed to all nations. So also the <term>conjugation</term> <note>The author is referring to the Hebrew grammar; previously the verb was in the passive form ("shall be blessed"), but here it is in the reflexive form ("shall bless themselves").</note> is changed. In the previous places, the blessing is given **passively**; they "shall be blessed." But here it is composed in a **reciprocal** <note>reflexive</note> form; they "shall bless themselves." Vatablus <note>François Vatable (d. 1547), a French humanist and Hebraist.</note> alone expressed this in his translation: "In your seed all the nations of the world shall call themselves blessed." That is, as he himself explains: they will consider themselves blessed and happy for the sake of your seed, Christ. Castellio <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563), a theologian and Bible translator.</note> aims at the same point. All other translations have by no means fully expressed the Hebrew, which signifies much more: namely, that all nations shall know, believe, and confess that they are blessed in the Son of God. Indeed, they shall again bless one another among themselves, declaring that they are so blessed. <margin>Psalm 72:17.</margin>

But what can seem more incredible than that God would wish to bless all other peoples and people in the whole world in the seed of a single man?

Nevertheless, God says this here, and even much more: which no one can rightly understand or experience according to its power unless he has, through the Holy Spirit, a true divine faith in the right Savior and seed of Abraham.

Therefore, we must first follow the faith of Abraham if we wish to rightly enjoy the Messiah and His salvation.

Abraham is a certain model for you of what must become of you.

You must become sincerely obedient to the word of the Lord in faith; otherwise, you cannot grasp the promise of the blessed seed of Abraham for your own person in particular.

But you must also be certain and assured for yourself in particular of the future and redemption of the Savior; so that you may know whether the general promises of God also occur in your case specifically and come true one after another. You must be able to remember a time when you truly turned to Him, and when He actually began your purification and rescue.

If that is to happen by and in you, then the Lord Jesus must find you standing in true faith.

For, dear one, how did it stand here with Abraham? Was he not occupied with the very fact that, at the Lord's word, he was willing without hesitation to put the knife to his son's throat, and to strangle and burn him; regardless of the fact that God had given him this very promise concerning this son? In and through this heroic faith, God now repeats and confirms this promise to him as a new blessing and reward for his faith.

But let one take good heed of what this signifies: that God did not want the Messiah to be born from an unbelieving or hypocritical seed, but from such a one who stood in the covenant of God for the restoration of the fallen, and who remained in that line or <term>succession</term> from the faithful Abel, Seth, Noah, Shem, and other holy fathers—one who himself stood in the actual power and grace of faith and in walking with God.

Oh, this is a great and deep wonder of the holy incarnation of Jesus Christ, that this promise of His coming into the flesh happened precisely during such a glorious trial of faith, which Abraham demonstrated at the slaughtering of his son!

Christ was to and had to come from the fathers, from the seed or essence of human nature, from the root and the stem that was created good and holy in Adam.

Into this root of the holy, blessed humanity of Jesus Christ, the Father wanted to place His blessing again for all people through His eternal Word, which was in the beginning and afterward became flesh.

<column-break/>

The sin and corruption that still remained in Abraham and others, Christ was not to take upon Himself with the seed, but rather that which was still good in nature: the human essence, insofar as it is not sinful in itself, but only has sin dwelling within it.

For it is the essence of fallen humanity that God also did not want to let perish eternally, but to seek out again and bring out of corruption, and to clothe again with His new power for sanctification.

To this end, He is and must be and is called for this reason a "blessed seed of the woman," because not only may no curse or un-blessing cling to Him, but also because He was to come, and has come, to drive all curses away from the poor creature and to transform them back into blessing.

But as to which main parts of spiritual blessing are primarily contained under the blessing of the Messiah, Paul has set down a correct interpretation of this text in <margin>Galatians 3.</margin>

Oh, if only one would pray to God for open eyes of understanding, so that one might behold the immeasurable store of treasures and gifts of God which He has intended for us in Christ! How would one not—if one truly realized it for only a moment—spit out everything else that has kept us until now from this sea of blessing!

It is truly said here: "What one does not know, one does not desire." The enemy diligently keeps the eyes of people closed so that they shall not recognize the bright light of the Gospel and its blessing, nor become hungry for it.

The blessing of God in His Son is so very exuberant, so very overflowing and spreading, that in all believers it increases and propagates into infinity.

*All nations on earth*) Not only the Jews, Abraham's descendants; also not only certain other nations and parties: but all, all nations on the entire earth shall enjoy it.

God’s purpose for restoration in Jesus Christ extends as far as the Fall has ever spread. If not all actually reach the blessing, they have themselves to blame because they do not want it in the right and proper order.

For unavoidable reasons, God has stipulated that fallen man should let the Holy Spirit work faith within him and follow the pull of grace. Why does one not let that become true in oneself? Who is now to blame for the lack of blessing? Is it not the unbelieving creature?

If you now find no true well-being or blessing in your soul, but rather a curse and unrest in your conscience, then take note of where the fault lies. Without any doubt, it lies in faith, and that you do not truly want to take it from God and let your old things go, or deny them for Christ's sake.

Abraham had to leave himself so completely to God that He could do with him what He wanted: and so he was blessed out of faith, as from the root of all spiritual blessing. In this way, his descendants in faith have also propagated the blessing to one another.

This indicates what unspeakable goods God communicates to others for the sake of those who have completely surrendered themselves to Him. One of the greatest gifts, however, is that He makes use of them to form Jesus Christ in hearts. For through Him all holy nations are blessed.

If you now wish to see the indwelling curse of sins transformed into blessing, turn through repentance with faithful desire into the blessed seed of Abraham, and see above all things that you grasp the true blessing, Jesus Christ Himself, in your heart: then you will also be able to share it with others who seek it. Thus, your tree of faith will grow as a wonder and a testimony of divine grace.

Do not neglect this all-sufficient good! It is there at the door of your heart! Whoever takes it has it for free: no one can earn it, but one can certainly neglect it. In this, the Father has summarized all blessing: He wants it to be fetched from Him. The entire fullness in Jesus Christ is open: Let everyone reach in, while it is called "today"!

### The XXIII. Chapter.

->Sarah’s Death and Burial.<-

**And the life of Sarah was one hundred twenty-seven years: these are the years of the life of Sarah.**

It is worth considering that among all the women in the Holy Scripture, the years of no one's life are calculated except for Sarah. This is the first woman whose age, death, and burial are mentioned in the Scripture; and the only one whose entire age is indicated according to a yearly reckoning. This is primarily for the sake of her faith, by virtue of which she stands in the place of honor as a mother of believing daughters and is held up as a model in 1 Peter 3:6. This can then also remind the believers how all their days were written in God’s book before any of them came to be (Psalm 139:16); not only the days of their lives but also of their trials—how they all reach a good end. Finally, they die in Hebron, which means a "union" or "association," and thus in union with their dear Savior, who then wishes to take them to Himself (Luke 23:43, Philippians 1:23).

However, the idea that Sarah died from shock over the distressing message of the sacrifice of her son, as the Jews believe, can be recognized as false because she...

<column-break/>

**2. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Then Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.**

<meta>catchword: 3. Then-</meta>

<margin>Died at Kiriath-arba)</margin> Abraham must therefore have moved there from Beersheba—where he had returned with Isaac from Mount Moriah according to Chapter 22:19—and changed his dwelling.

Abraham goes into her tent—as women were accustomed to having their own separate tents (Chapter 24:67)—to mourn and weep for his beloved Sarah, thereby showing his high esteem for her godliness and faithfulness toward him. He had also obtained through her the promised seed, who was to be the rightful heir of the spiritual blessing. This then must also be the true reason for us to mourn our dead: when they have feared God, and one could perceive in them that the divine promise had been born in them; because through them, we could be comforted, gladdened, and built up and encouraged toward the good in our lives. And so one has reason to mourn and weep over the death of pious people; this is done by believers who knew them well, especially because they feel the loss most tenderly as they are deprived of a loving fellowship and also of a support. On the other hand, the careless people of the world are rebuked by the Prophet for precisely this: that they do not heed such deaths. Another cause for the lamentable death of the righteous is that such events are commonly an indication of impending judgments. All other mourning, however, is merely natural and carnal, and mostly even hypocritical.

After faith and <term>resignation</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a mystical term for the soul's total surrender to God's will.</note> have brought about spiritual death, one must also lose this resignation. One must die, not so much according to that which is real within him—which is all the more perfect as it is hidden in God—but rather according to that which he possesses from enlightenment, according to the ease of producing certain effects. For as this is still an obstacle to annihilation <note>In the mystical sense, the "annihilation" of the self-will to be replaced by God's will.</note>, it must also be taken away. In such a way, resignation (represented by Sarah) then dies. This means that the more this soul has surrendered itself, the more it loses all power to surrender itself further: because it enters into God, in whom it remains in total surrender, and where the resignation which had helped it to enter thus far now leaves it. It costs the soul some tears when one sees that one can no longer rely on oneself. For one takes that as a certain sign of one's loss. But when one is established in surrender and in being lost in God, the sorrow ceases; and the resignation, which no longer perceives itself, is much purer than it was before.

### Chapter XXIII. The First Book of Moses.

3. Then Abraham stood up from before his dead, and spoke to the children of Heth <note>also known as the Hittites</note>, saying:

<margin>Matthew 27:7. (a) Hebrews 11:9, 13.</margin>
4. I am a stranger <gloss>(a)</gloss> and a sojourner among you: give me a hereditary burial place among you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.

5. And the children of Heth answered Abraham, saying to him:

6. Hear us, my lord! You are a prince of God <note>original: "Fürst Gottes," translating the Hebrew "Nasi Elohim," implying one chosen or elevated by God</note> among us; bury your dead in the best of our sepulchers! None of us shall withhold his grave from you, so that you may bury your dead.

---

Here we read of the first burial, and how Abraham was especially careful to obtain a specific, owned place for this purpose, where he himself might later be buried, and where the bones of the dead might not be disturbed.

Because the human body was the dwelling of an immortal spirit, and because GOD Himself dwelt within the believers, the body must not be cast away like that of an animal. Instead, according to God’s ordinance—since it is dust and shall return to dust, Chapter 3:19—it must be honorably committed to the earth. Furthermore, it should be placed properly in a casket and lowered therein: Chapter 50:26. This is especially true since we also expect the blessed resurrection in our bodies, in order to see and praise GOD in them.

Therefore, burial should not be denied to any single body; for with physical death, all physical punishments are rightly paid.

The burning of bodies <note>cremation</note>, although it may not result in their total annihilation, is nonetheless an invention of the heathens and is contrary to God’s ordinance.

Now, while Abraham otherwise desired no property, but chose to stay as a stranger and a resident among the Canaanites until GOD would grant his seed the entire promised land in His time; yet he still wished to have a hereditary burial place for himself and his kin within it. This was to awaken in his descendants a love for this land and faith in the promise of the same, so that they should wait for it with patience. See Chapter 25:9, 49:30-31, 50:13.

<margin>v. 4-6.</margin> There are princes of GOD and princes of this world. The princes of this world have nothing but to command in their territories; and commonly they are also the servants of those whom they have to command, because without them they can neither live, nor defend themselves, nor undertake anything. But the princes of GOD, who as His children have entered into His freedom, are powerful and independent even in their wilderness. They rule over the whole world and are ruled by no one. They are among men as strangers; yet they do not depend on them, and they possess a certain prestige and earnestness which terrifies and compels those who see them—and who do not grasp this mystery—to look upon them with awe. For they carry the image of divinity upon them, just as princes carry the signs of their human power.

Abraham—whom the greatness of his faith allows to be a wanderer and a stranger in the world, so that he might have no other portion than heaven; and who also left his inheritance in his fatherland so that GOD Himself might be his inheritance—Abraham, I say, is the highest prince in every place where he dwells. His independence can be seen in all places. He makes all people rich, although he receives nothing from them: just as it was said to the King of Sodom, it shall not be said that anyone made Abraham rich. Oh, how rich is he whose inheritance is GOD Himself! Faith is accustomed to making one poor, so that it can afterward make one rich; and to take everything away, so that GOD alone may be our wealth. David had experienced this blessed state of unburdened faith when he says: The LORD is my inheritance; and afterward adds: The lot has fallen for me in the most pleasant places, and my inheritance is very pleasing to me <note>Psalm 16:5-6</note>.

<column-break/>

7. Then Abraham stood up and bowed himself before the people of the land, before the children of Heth.

8. And he spoke with them, saying: If it is your will that I bury my dead out of my sight, then hear me, and intercede for me with Ephron the son of Zohar:

9. That he may give me the cave of Machpelah which he has, which is at the end of his field; for the full price <note>original: "völlige Gelt," meaning the complete monetary value</note> he shall give it to me among you for a hereditary burial place.

10. Now Ephron dwelt among the children of Heth. And Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the children of Heth, before all who went in at the gate of his city, saying:

11. No, my lord, hear me! I give you the field, and the cave that is in it, I give it to you; in the presence of the children of my people I give it to you: bury your dead.

12. Then <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page</note>

---

Abraham wanted the hereditary burial place for money, and not as a gift: so that he or his kin—since human minds are quite changeable—could not be driven out of this possession, and also that through this they might be maintained in their desire for this hereditary burial. Also, because GOD had already promised him the entire region of the land as an inheritance, he did not want to accept it as a gift from another, but hoped in faith for what was promised to him by GOD: as the ancient Irenaeus <note>St. Irenaeus of Lyons, a 2nd-century Church Father</note> has noted.

The cave of Machpelah may represent the "Bosom of Abraham" <note>a traditional term for the place of comfort for the righteous dead</note>, in which all believers rest.

But because in the New Testament the inheritance of the world is promised to the believers, it must be all the same to them where they are called by the providence of GOD, and where they will find their resting place.

The fear of God and outward blessing brought Abraham into great prestige among the Hittites: therefore they were happy to grant his wishes and would likely have granted him even more had he requested it. However, he chose to be content as a stranger among them, and thus wisely kept their jealousy and envy away from him. He also met them with all honor and justice; which in turn awakens mutual love and friendship: just as Christians are especially bound to this, to outdo one another in showing honor. Romans 12:10.

## Chapter XXIV.
-> Isaac’s Marriage. <-

1. Abraham was now old and well along in years, and the Lord had blessed Abraham in all things.

This passage shows the constancy of faith: just as faith has placed the soul in God, so it draws all kinds of blessings to it. For the soul that is essentially united with God is showered with all kinds of graces in God. And since faith alone can lead the soul into God, the soul is also blessed in all matters through the same. This great blessing, however, is not granted to it until it is truly "old"—by which I mean, in its spiritual completion.
Nature and hypocrisy are quite quick to presume—so wicked and frivolous—and know how to pretend outwardly as if all their affairs came from God, and as if they took counsel and help from God therein.
But alas, the natural man only deceives himself in his hypocrisy. He thinks that with a single thought or sigh all is well and done with God, even if otherwise he consistently seeks and intends his own will, his advantages, lusts, and honors in all things; or even lives directly against the will of God with coarse sins.
Oh, something else entirely is required if our affairs are to stem from God. For if a person remains left to himself, he allows himself to be governed by nothing less than God, nor does he begin his own affairs with Him. He can do or have nothing good without God, but only do wrong and harm according to his nature.
But how all our ways of life should be rightly begun with God, and what that means—to "begin with God"—we may clearly recognize from the present example.

<column-break/>

2. Then Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his house, who ruled over all that he had:

<meta>catchword: Dear</meta>

In the case of important changes, a good beginning is the primary and most important thing. But no beginning can be good unless it comes from the eternal, unique Good itself, which is God. Also, no beginning can have a truly good progress unless this same highest Good is present with counsel and deed. And thus all things that are to be salutary for us must also stem from God, without whom not the slightest thing in the whole world can be truly good.
...that she begins her affairs with God. Indeed, there is no person...

Among the most important matters of human life is marriage, in which one should rightly strive above all else that it happens "in the Lord" <note>This refers to marrying within the faith and with God's blessing</note>: so that one may also experience blessing and contentment in their wedded state.

The marriage of Isaac is a very magnificent model in all its parts. Therefore, it was also a very blessed marriage, which was neither defiled by polygamy during life nor disturbed in any way after death. Likewise, Isaac did not experience any extraordinary tribulations, except in the matter with Esau and Jacob, whom he had to do without for a long time during their wanderings, but was finally gladdened by their presence once more.

First, we see here the paternal care of Abraham, who sought out a wife for his son when he had reached his proper years of manhood—forty years of age. Isaac, for his part, showed himself entirely composed and obedient in this matter. From this, we can understand the authority of parents and the duty of children: that children are not authorized to marry without the will of their parents, but should rather let their parents be concerned with providing for them in this regard.

Abraham, as a faithful friend and acquaintance of God, had received the great promise regarding Isaac: that through him, the blessing would come upon all people. Therefore, as one can easily imagine, he lay before the Lord day and night with his prayer, persisting for certainty and a revelation of the divine will as to how and whom he should give to his son as a wife.

Thereupon, the Lord put it into his heart that he should not take any of the pagan daughters, nor mingle his seed with their impurity. Instead, he was to send his servant to his fatherland to seek a wife from among his own kindred. There, a greater knowledge of the true God, as well as decency and virtue, must have still been found, compared to the pagan Canaanites, whose lives had already become very wild.

Thus, he entrusted this business to his steward, or oldest and very faithful servant <note>traditionally identified as Eliezer of Damascus</note>, to whom he had committed the entire management of his rich estate, so that he might strive to put this into effect. He also had him swear a solemn oath over this. All of this contained great mysteries.

It must certainly have been a matter of great importance, as Abraham demanded an oath regarding it. Indeed, it was precisely because the children of God had previously intermingled with the daughters of the ungodly and unbelieving *Nephilim* <note>original: "Nephilim," a Hebrew term often translated as giants or "fallen ones," referring here to the ungodly lines before the Great Flood</note> before the Flood—taking them as wives according to their own pleasure and fleshly lust—that the Flood came. In this also consisted the cunning and harmful plot of Balaam, when he advised Balak to see to it that he married the daughters of his land to the Israelites, which would lead to their downfall.

Believers have therefore always looked to this, and are bound for conscience’s sake to ensure that they do not unite themselves with unbelievers through such a close bond as marriage. This union alone may rightly bear the name of "marrying out of one's station" when a child of God and a person highly born of God gives themselves to a member of the world. All other inequalities of social rank, and the resulting contrary imaginations, are pride and vanity before God in this matter. But such unequal marriages are truly an abomination before God, because the true purpose of marriage must necessarily be hindered and brought to nothing by them. For the part that stands under the dominion of sin will always be a hindrance and a source of harm to the other.

It least of all befits a true Christian to join themselves with an unbelieving party; rather, they should view and treat the mystery of marriage with holy reverence.

<column-break/>

It is deceit, guile, and treacherous intention when one thinks or claims: "Who knows if I might not yet win over such an unbelieving person." For who knows whether such an unbelieving person might not ensnare and pervert you—just as the Moabite and Ammonite women ensnared and perverted even the wise Solomon.

The land of Canaan is an image of the corrupt world. Faith never unites itself with it. Faith gladly joins with those who fear God, even if they still walk in the ways of "the many" <note>referring to those not yet fully enlightened but seeking God</note>; for Faith hopes that, because they are already free from gross sins, it can all the sooner bring them into unity. To that end, Faith calls all its oldest servants it has ever had. The very oldest servant of Faith is Prudence <note>original: "Vorsichtigkeit"</note>, who is the oldest faithful servant serving Faith in its path. However, Prudence would become very troublesome over time if Faith did not know how to change it, as shall be taught further below. This servant is the oldest and most necessary to Faith in the beginning, because he instructs the soul to give itself over to God through a holy prudence. This causes the soul—seeing that its affairs are in a bad state in its own hands—to throw such affairs into the hands of God through a total surrender. This prudence is, according to the saying of the Wise Man (a) <note>Proverbs 9:10</note>, the wisdom of the saints. This must be the proper office of prudence. But when Faith sees that Prudence—which was so useful in this point—becomes very harmful if it tries to mingle with human caution after one has completely surrendered to God, then Faith calls to it in the person of Eliezer. Faith makes it swear that it will never unite the inner life (which has already been brought quite far) with the world. This cannot happen without making the most loathsome mixture. Instead, Prudence must go into the land of the children of God—even if it is still concealed—from where Faith itself takes its origin. There, it is to settle his son, which is the inner and already spiritual life born of surrender and faith.

Thus, the image and this history are very charming, but the "counter-image" <note>The "counter-image" or antitype is the spiritual fulfillment of the historical event</note> is even more pleasant and of greater value. And so the Bible is opened to us rightly and, as it were, anew. We see perspectively from the image into the counter-image: from the shadow into the body, from the physical into the spiritual, from the perishable into the lasting, from the lower into the upper, and from the kingdom of nature into the kingdom of grace and glory. For as the lower is in shadow, so the upper is in proportion; only it is much higher, both in its nature and in its richer understanding.

The Heavenly Father, who prepares the wedding for His Son, sends out the true servants and Apostles as "matchmakers," that they may lead a pure bride to Christ. She must not be from a crooked, wild generation, nor of foreign blood; rather, she must be of His own race—yea, flesh of His flesh and bone of His bones—to be led and married to Him as a wife. Bridegroom and Bride come from One, according to their new humanity: the Bridegroom who sanctifies, and the Bride who is sanctified. (b) <note>Hebrews 2:11</note>

The soul that wishes to be chosen as such a bride must therefore earnestly strive for the qualities that the Lord, the Bridegroom, requires of her in the Song of Solomon (Chapter 6, verses 8-9): that she be united in spirit with Christ and all true believers, and thus be "One"; that she be simple as a dove; sincere and perfect; dead to herself and the world; a true daughter of the first Christians, and born again through the Holy Spirit.

<note>(a) Proverbs 9:10. (b) Hebrews 2:11.</note>

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXIV.

5. And the servant said to him: Perhaps the woman will not be willing to follow me into this land. Should I then certainly bring your son back to the land from which you came?

6. And Abraham said to him: See to it that you do not bring my son back there! <margin>Deuteronomy 17:16.</margin>

7. The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house and from the land of my kindred, and

While the servant raises all sorts of scruples and worries, Abraham is so divinely certain of the matter that he can confidently give assurance that it will go and turn out according to God's will. He comforts himself especially with the fact that the Angel of the Covenant <note>A term often used in older theology to refer to the pre-incarnate Christ</note>—as Christ was known to him—would govern all of this and would surely let it succeed.

Just as God's governance in the marriages of the godly is quite remarkable and blessed, having the holy angels as "bride-leaders" <note>The German "Brautführer" refers to those who escort the bride; here, it suggests divine guidance in matchmaking</note> within them (as can also be seen with Tobit, Chapters 5 and 7), one cannot entirely withdraw the marriages of natural men—even the godless—from God's governance. This is true even though the evil within them, such as false intentions and other perverse ways in which they are established, must be attributed to humans and the deception of Satan. Because there are almost always godly people to be found among the generations who have their origin in these marriages, the evil in those unions cannot be imputed to them; they also intercede for their own. The human race was created for something so great that it will only truly reveal itself in eternity; thus, the majority were not born by chance or solely through Satan’s rule.

Foreseeing prudence takes all kinds of means in hand from afar; it would even like to—if perhaps no souls could be found who would enter into the inward ways (which is precisely the covenant that faith wishes to make)—lead the inward man, represented by Isaac, back into the manifold ways <note>original: "vermanichfaltigte Wege." In this mystical tradition, "multiplicity" or "manifoldness" refers to the scattered state of the soul in the world, contrasted with "unity" in God.</note> rather than leave him alone in the simple and level ways: even though God had drawn him out of them in his father, even before his birth. For faith takes the soul out of multiplicity and places it into unity: and by communicating to it the growth of its own life, it places the soul in a state where it can never return to its own origin, unless it transgresses God’s command or walks without His will. Therefore, faith—which does not leave the soul until it finds itself in God, where, after having lost everything before, it finds it again in perfect unity—says,

<margin>v. 6, 7. very powerful:</margin> Watch yourself well, O you Prudence! that you do not lead my son back into the land of multiplicity, from which God through His immeasurable goodness has led us. I have confidence that the Lord of Heaven and Earth, who drew me from my father’s house, out of this way and interaction with the creatures among whom I was born, and who swore to give me this earth of rest in God; and that not just to me alone, but also to all my children who will follow these ways in which I have placed Isaac: (he is the image of souls sacrificed and surrendered to God:) the Lord, I say, will send His angel before you, who will prepare everything; so that the faithful bride, whom He intends for my son, may enter into these His ways and likewise possess the land of peace and rest in God, which she must leave to her descendants.

<column-break/>

who spoke to me and who swore to me, saying: To your offspring I will give this land; He will send His angel before you, so that you may take a wife for my son from there.

8. But if the woman will not be willing to follow you, then you shall be free from this oath of mine. Only do not bring my son back there.

10. Thus

<margin>v. 7. Who spoke and swore to me)</margin> This essential truth had promised Abraham that in his offspring all nations should be blessed. If this were now to be fulfilled, then that same Faithful and True One had to be present in and with that very marriage matter upon which this promise rested.

<margin>He will)</margin> Truly, nothing can make all our ways of life—but especially marriage—honorable and holy, except for a composed faith. In this, one should marry; in this, one should enter other states, callings, offices, and ways of life: then one becomes certain that the Lord will sanctify everything.

This faith then says to prudence that if the maiden whom it sends out to be chosen will not come, it shall be free from all oaths: only it shall not bring his son back there, but leave him in peace and unity; because he is chosen for spiritual rest, he should not return to multiplicity under any pretext. This agrees with what is written elsewhere: "If you keep my covenant, then you shall be the one people which I will possess in particular. You shall be the priestly people and the holy generation which shall be sanctified to me."

<margin>v. 9.)</margin> Since the oath with the placing of the hand under the thigh could very fittingly have happened during their kneeling, so that he placed his hand on the thick part of his leg under the hip; he may well have looked thereby to the faith in the "Seed" <note>The offspring, referring ultimately to the Messiah</note> who would come forth from the hip/thigh of Abraham: as this manner of speaking is used in Chapter 46:26 and Exodus 1:5. Of this promise, as the sole ground of all blessing, the members of Abraham’s household were doubtless instructed by him. Chapters 21:33 and 18:19.

Thus the thigh is made into a token of life and truth, and such respectful regard is attributed to it because Christ according to the flesh—who is eternal life (1 John 5:20) and the essential truth (John 14:6)—was to come from it.

---

The angel, however, spoken of here, is Providence: there the spiritual covenant begins.

According to the prophetic sense, it is indicated here quite clearly that in the last times, some of the true friendship of the spiritual Abrahamites would still remain in spiritual Babylon, but would be led out in Rebecca, and the spiritual Isaac should not dwell therein. The members of the Bride who remain in Babylon must come to Christ and go out from Babylon, because He shall not and will not dwell there.

### Chapter XXIV. The First Book of Moses.

<margin>
Abraham's faith was so powerful that it brought the servant to the very same simplicity of trust, so that he ventured forth in the name of God. He also does not fail to provide for himself in earthly matters, since his master was richly endowed with them: also to incline hearts toward love through these things; because one should prove oneself generous on such occasions, so that hearts might not be turned away by the withholding of the same. But where worldly means are lacking, believers must not look to that, but rather pray for heartfelt affection toward one another as a grace from God.

When the great mission of the servants and apostles of Jesus Christ goes forth, He does not send them empty, but adorns them with many noble gifts, signified by the 10 camels with their various goods, which the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ sends along. He allows the rich goods of His house to be offered to the future bride of the Son of God, powerfully attracting and luring her through the presentation of heavenly treasures of grace and riches in Christ, and the actual bestowal of certain spiritual gifts through the Gospel, so that she may be pleased to move toward Him who sends such great goods; from which she may conclude how great He Himself and His Son must be, whom the believing soul is to choose as her husband and bridegroom.

He loads ten camels, which represent the Ten Commandments that were to be given to Moses, which are kept inwardly by those who are spiritually learned; and indeed in a much more perfect way than occurs outwardly. He places all his master's goods upon them, that is, a great addition of grace which this path had brought to him: so that love, faith, trust, and all virtues were pure riches that covered and sweetened the hardness of the Law. One sends to her (to this daughter who is being sought out) from all the goods of the house which is offered to her: so that, when nothing of the wealth and sweetness of this path is hidden from her, she may surrender herself all the more willingly into the same and enter into it with joy.

Mesopotamia is the place where God is indeed feared, though it still happens in a state of dispersion: but from that very place, teachable people are drawn out so that they may be led into the land of rest and unity.

In the final times, many children of God may still travel there outwardly and find their stay there during God's judgments over the "spiritual Sodom." However, these children of peace shall not remain there, but be led toward Canaan to meet the heavenly Isaac, and upon the proposal of marriage, resolve in a willing spirit to follow the eldest servant of Abraham to Isaac their bridegroom, the Son of God.

The city of Nahor) The brother of Abraham and grandfather of Rebekah; it is the same place called Haran above in chapter 11, verse 32, and was located 116 miles from Hebron.
</margin>

10. So the servant took ten camels from his master's camels and departed. But he also had all kinds of goods from his master in his hand. And he arose and went to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.

<column-break/>

11. And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by a well of water at evening time, at the time when women go out to draw water;

12. And he said: Lord, You God of my master Abraham, grant me success today, and show mercy to my master Abraham!

13. Behold, I stand here by the well of water, and the daughters of the people of this city are coming out to draw water.

14. So—

---

-> As a faithful messenger and suitor, he takes refuge in prayer to God, asking that He might govern everything in this important work, and even point out, show, and demonstrate the person whom He has provided for His God-fearing servant, Abraham, for his son—who also walks in his father's footsteps and is His servant. By this he wishes to show that blessed marriages depend in a special way upon God and, as the saying goes, are "made in heaven." <-

-> Faith seeks the face of the Lord in every undertaking above all else, and does not let a person go anywhere unless God goes with them—indeed, ahead of them—becoming, so to speak, the *primary actor* <note>original Latin: "fac totum"</note> in the work. <-

-> See how this man of God seeks encounters with God and His powerful presence, governance, and grace! How solely and simply he submits himself to God's providence! How he does not torture himself long with human reason and deliberate whether he might be deceived: who knows who might then fall to Isaac's lot? In faith, he regards God as faithful, believing He would not lead him wrongly nor permit anything evil. And how the good old Abraham must have lain on his knees before God, praying with his faith for God's full direction in the matter! See Proverbs 19:14 and chapter 18:22. <-

-> No less should we also seek the Lord as a gracious and merciful one, who is full of love and desire to do us good and to further our cause that is pleasing to Him: just as this believing servant appealed to and relied upon this. <-

-> If we lay the foundation firmly in our undertakings in this way, we afterward have the advantage of ascribing all blessing and a good outcome to the undeserved mercy of God and thanking Him humbly, rather than attributing it to ourselves and our own cleverness, strength, or worthiness, and thus remaining in humility before God. For <-

-> therein lies a great mystery of wickedness: that nature so gladly begins its own work without God, and places everything upon its own cunning, power, running, and striving. This is so that it may later secretly rob the Lord of the glory, so as not to be obligated to ascribe all thanks or praise to Him. <-

-> On the contrary, the Lord is always moved by such lowly submission to continue and complete His work in and upon us, and to crown it with a thousandfold grace. <-

-> The arrival of him who is sent to lead this maiden (an image of the soul) out of her scattered state occurs in the evening. This indicates that she already stands in a half-begun rest, or is very near to it, being at the end of her day of activity. For in this way, when the time is right, God sends such people who show the inner way. <-

-> He seeks her at the well: that is to say, in the very practice of prayer, in which she sought with all her might—as all young souls do—to draw the water of grace. <-

-> He lets the camels rest outside the city: to show that the graces which come from a suffering faith are not imparted in the turmoil, but in stillness. <-

-> Afterward, he turns to God and offers his prayer: in which this servant, although he was very devoted to God, nevertheless mentions nothing of himself: he asks only for the sake of his master, Abraham: because he well knows that faith can obtain everything. <-

-> He prays to God that He would grant him to recognize, among so many people who all walk the same paths, which one He has ordained for rest. <-
