# The First Book of Moses, Chapter XXIV.

### 14. Let it come to pass / that the maiden / to whom I shall say; "Please tip your pitcher / so that I may drink"; and she shall say; "Drink / and I will also give your camels water to drink": let this be the one / whom you have appointed for your servant / Isaac / and by this I shall know / that you have shown mercy to my master. <margin>1 Samuel 14:10.</margin>

---

The condition in his prayer is altogether wonderful and full of mystery. He sees / that the only thing that can bring the soul out of the land of multiplicity / in order to lead it into spiritual unity / is Love alone: that this love must be united with the tranquil soul; and that the soul receives this through a purified love / albeit in the darkness of faith. Therefore, Eliezer seeks nothing other than <term>charity</term> <note>original: "Mildthätigkeit" — in this context, it refers to an active, overflowing benevolence and kindness rooted in love.</note> for Isaac: yet not a mediocre charity / but an exuberant charity / which is fit to water the flock of Jesus Christ / who is enclosed within Abraham. This is a mystery / which would require an entire book / to explain. And since the generosity of love does more / than is requested of it; so this charity finds more water than is necessary / to give everyone their due. This passage of Holy Scripture brings one joy / when one sees / how everything fits so well into the inner life. Isaac's wife also had to become a mother and nurse for the people of faith. Therefore, she must be charity itself. Namely, she must give us such things in her person / and be an excellent image in her conduct.

What the servant undertook here and discussed with God was, strictly speaking, an innocent kind of "lot" or sign / by which he wished to perceive God's ways. In doing so, he gave God His due honor / and let the entire matter depend on His outcome. Such boldness is not audacity / but rather a faithful confidence in God / that He would not refuse it / but rather come to the aid of our weakness through it / and show His fatherly will and the certainty of the same.

Accordingly, it was not truly a "tempting of God" / which the Lord otherwise so earnestly forbade: *You shall not tempt the Lord your God!* <note>original: "Du sollt GOtt deinen HErrn nicht versuchen!" — a reference to Deuteronomy 6:16 and Matthew 4:7.</note> And when unbelieving and superstitious people undertake all kinds of forbidden signs and other sorceries / such things are heaven-wide apart from the faithful and innocent pure inquiry into the divine will. This inquiry happens with complete tranquility of faith / without one's own choice / superstition / or trust in signs and creatures. Indeed, it is fundamentally nothing other than a begging and pleading for the opening of divine pleasure / that one asks of God in humility / as it were / that He might show by this or that sign or circumstance / how one should behave: of which the entire Scripture testifies with examples and words.

Even if one might not desire extraordinary signs or miracles / as those are otherwise only given to unbelievers: yet a believer must not entirely despise or reject other kinds of divine assurance / but accepts them with thanks. And

So one experiences / how every creature of God is holy and good / when it is sanctified through the Word and prayer. Prayer, however, must happen in pure submission to God's will: then it is a work of pure faith in the Holy Spirit.

Like a well: the more it empties itself of its water / the more [it flows]. Hence it comes / that these both here under this [heading] are unavoidably necessary for souls dedicated to unity in God. [True charity] consists of being full for others / and seeking to keep nothing for herself: [giving] the waters of grace / which have been shared with her / and she has received from Him.

The Scripture says / that Rebekah "stepped up": [this is] to indicate / that although charity is benevolent toward all / she nevertheless allows nothing to stop her; and [she shows] what she is by doing good whenever something is requested of her.

<column-break/>

### 15. And it happened / before he had finished speaking / behold, there came out Rebekah / who had been born to Bethuel / the son of Milcah / the wife of Nahor / Abraham’s brother: and she had her pitcher on her shoulder.
### 16. And the maiden was very beautiful to look upon / a virgin / and no man had known her. And she went down to the well / and filled her pitcher / and stepped up.
### 17. There [the servant ran to meet her...]

---

The singular providence of God knew how to govern everything so wonderfully in this marriage / that everything had to occur / exactly as the servant had prayed. Not only did Rebekah come from Abraham's own kindred / but he also had to perceive / besides the beautiful form of her body / which is also a gift of God / the most noble thing about her / her virtuous mind: namely her industriousness / as she diligently took up the lowliest of household tasks / fetching water / and was not ashamed of it / even though they were people of good means. See Exodus 2:16 / where Moses had a similar providence / and found his bride while drawing water.

Are these merely fables? Or does one think / that the Holy Spirit is concerned with the telling of mere histories? Certainly not! His teaching is spiritual / and aimed at the instruction of the soul. It wants to teach you / that you should come daily to the Well / which is inexhaustible / that you should daily draw from the waters of the Holy Spirit / and daily carry a full vessel home / like Rebekah. The Son of God wants such a one for His spouse / who is altogether beautiful / and has no wrinkle nor spot / nor anything of the kind about her. He adorns her at the first approach of the courtship with His gifts / with a golden headband / with which she is sealed / and with two bracelets / by which she is bound to the Bridegroom. Christ wants to be betrothed to you. And therefore He sends His servant to you beforehand. This servant of His is the prophetic Word. If you do not first receive that / you cannot be betrothed to Christ. But no one receives the prophetic Word / except the one who knows how to draw water from the depths / and who draws so much / that he also has enough for the irrational and perverse / the humped and crooked generation / represented by the camels.

v. 15. *Before he had finished speaking*) For the complete conviction / that God hears His faithful petitioners even in the smallest circumstances / and does what those who fear God desire. Yes,

O, how God is so ready / to hear the righteous prayers offered in faith! As soon as Eliezer had finished his prayer / the maiden came.

*She was very beautiful*: for there is nothing more beautiful than charity / which makes itself pleasing to all.

*She was a virgin*: because charity must always be pure. And since she receives her growth from God Himself / she remains always chaste among the creatures / without defiling herself through her interaction with them.

*She went down to the well / and filled her pitcher*: Charity is always united with humility / which / while it empties itself / is filled; and its source / which is God Himself / shares new water with it. [These represent the] virtues of a soul dedicated to self-denial and unity. Since the faithfulness of charity [consists] in always [giving] / and the perfection of humility [consists] in always emptying oneself / to give back to God in such purity / as she received from Him.

[Rebekah stepped up] thereby to show / that although charity is benevolent / and though she hurries away with speed / she nevertheless shows [her true nature] / and gives even more than what is requested.

### Chapter XXIV. The First Book of Moses.

17. Then the servant ran to meet her / and spoke: "Please let me drink a little water from your pitcher!"

18. And she spoke: "Drink, my lord!" And she hurried to let her pitcher down upon her hand / and gave him to drink.

19. And when she had finished giving him a drink / she spoke: "I will also draw water for your camels / until they have all drunk."

20. And she hurried and emptied her pitcher into the trough / and ran again to the well to draw / and drew for all his camels.

21. But the man was altogether astonished by her / and remained silent / in order to learn / whether the LORD had made his journey successful / or not.

Who would not admire the swiftness and the great propriety with which Rebekah does everything? She desires to give the camels drink herself / because <term>charity</term> <note>original: "Mildthätigkeit" — active benevolence rooted in divine love.</note> provides water and makes things alive. She leaves not a single one / without filling it from her waters. As soon as she has emptied her pitcher / she fills it again at its source / where she draws many goods. Charity is not satisfied with words; it comes immediately to actions / in that she actually gives water to the camels / just as she promised.

But now / you may say / if the servant is an image of the prophetic Word / why does he then desire to drink from Rebekah / when she should rather be given drink by him? Answer: Even the LORD JESUS / who is already the Bread of Life / and feeds hungry souls, nevertheless says; "I was hungry / and you fed me": and although he is the well and the water of life / he nevertheless speaks to the Samaritan woman; "Give me to drink."

But if you do not come to the well daily / and do not draw daily; then not only can you not give others to drink / but you yourself will suffer thirst.

But you must, of course, first be thirsty / before you will come and draw. For why do most people remain so empty and dry / if not because they lack this thirst?

**v. 21. Astonished** Her uncommon friendliness / kindness / and readiness to serve / toward him as a foreign man / to whom she also offered her parents' house for lodging / and finally her great humility / in also watering all the camels / put him into a state of great wonder / and allowed him to sufficiently recognize the wonderful governance of GOD / and a blessed beginning thereof.

He gazes upon her / as the Scripture rightly says; because he is from the house of faith / in which all servants are <term>contemplatives</term> <note>original: "Beschauende" — those who practice the quiet observation of God's work.</note>. He gazed upon her in silence: which indicates the rest and stillness of contemplation. And so he meditated in the silence / to learn / whether GOD had blessed his journey or not. He asks this maiden no questions; he does not use the meddling of language / to escape his doubt: He makes use only of this stillness / through which he is instructed more than through all other care that might be applied. Therefore, he now had no hesitation in speaking with her.

<column-break/>

22. And it happened / when the camels had all drunk / that the man took a golden headband / which was half a shekel in weight / and two bracelets for her hands / whose weight was ten shekels of gold /

23. And spoke: "Whose daughter are you? Please tell me. Is there also room in your father’s house for us to stay overnight?"

24. And she spoke to him: "I am the daughter of Bethuel / the son of Milcah / whom she bore to Nahor."

25. And said further to him: "There is also much straw and fodder with us / and also room to stay overnight."

v. 22. He reveals his riches to her / so that through his actions more than through his word / she may learn to recognize the ways and the land / into which he wishes to lead her.

But what are the gifts / that he brings her? Ear-pendants or a headband. So that she may know / that she must do nothing / but hear and remain silent; and that these are the customs of that same land / into which he wished to bring her. He also gives her bracelets: to give her to understand / that faith / stillness / and good works / are inseparable from charity. From all this she had to learn to hear / to work / and to remain silent. She / who is to be the bride of the true Isaac / must have both the word of faith in the hearing ear / or the obedience of faith / as the true earring / and the work of faith / the right bracelet / upon her hands.

She accepts this pledge / as a sign / that she is ready to take this path / whenever obedience permits her. The ear-pendants are golden: to indicate the purity / with which one must obey GOD. Together they weigh only one <term>shekel</term> <note>original: "Seckel" — an ancient unit of weight and currency.</note>: which suggests / that one must obey only GOD alone and His holy will. But the bracelets weigh several shekels of gold; because virtues and good works must be multiplied. Attention must be directed toward GOD alone / but exercises must be directed toward many.

v. 23-25. Prudence / which never rushes / causes the servant to ask the maiden who she is: which she then reveals to him. Thereupon he asked her / whether he also had room to lodge in her father’s house? Charity / which is never empty / assures him that with her father (who represents the image of GOD) there is enough provision for everyone / and room enough / to lodge and receive all those who take their refuge in her.

Moreover, one must wonder at the sincere simplicity of the ancients / how they so faithfully offered their property down to the smallest straw and fodder for the animals.

O, blessed are those / who always show mercy / love and compassion / gladly harbor divine thoughts / and receive the messengers of GOD! By this they will prove / that they are of Abraham’s lineage; they shall also not remain in their father’s house / at the well where they must only carry water and load it upon their shoulders: but they shall journey to Isaac / their true Bridegroom / who has dug and found the living well. There their mouth shall be full of laughter / and their soul shall be satisfied!

---

Then their Bridegroom will go to meet them / and when they have left their father's house / the King will take pleasure in their beauty / receive them as a wife / and remain dwelling with them by the well of life and vision (where all things shall be clearly seen).

<summary>This page interprets Rebekah’s hospitality as a model of spiritual charity and the servant’s gifts as symbols of the "obedience of faith" (hearing) and "good works" (acting). It concludes that the soul, like Rebekah, must leave its old life to find fulfillment with the true Bridegroom, Isaac, who represents Christ.</summary>

30. And it happened / when he saw the headband and the bracelets on his sister’s hands / and when he heard the words of Rebecca / his sister / as she spoke: "Thus the man spoke to me"; then he came to the man; and behold, he stood by the camels at the well.

v. 26. 27. <term>Prudence</term> <note>original: "Klugheit" — here personified as a spiritual faculty that recognizes God's hand in timing and events.</note> worships God / and marvels / that faith is never without truth / and that God allows everything to succeed so well for him; since indeed there is nothing that can lead so straight as this faith.

This servant is completely astonished / that / having followed [faith] blindly / he was led by a straight path to the desired place / and that he found much more / than he could have previously dared to wish for. Whereby he is compelled / to give testimony to the truth of the way of faith / and to proclaim / how straight and certain such a way is. He does not know / which he must admire more: either divine providence / which knows how to accomplish everything at the appointed time; or the magnanimity of faith / to undertake everything in darkness and without assurance. He sees nonetheless / that God blesses such a faith with so many graces / that he cannot possibly do otherwise / than to surrender himself to the same / and to worship God in all His ways.

v. 28. The believing soul cannot remain silent for joy regarding the goodness of the LORD / which has been so abundantly shown to her. And the house of the mother—the <term>Jerusalem above</term> <note>A reference to Galatians 4:26, often used in mystical literature to represent the spiritual source of the soul.</note>—also rejoices / when a new soul has been won for the Son of God and chosen as a bride.

v. 30. As Laban sees the pledges / which had been given to his sister; which are testimonies of the way of faith: so he goes out / to seek the one / who teaches it; so that he might allow him to enter into his home. This likewise happens to well-intentioned souls / when they have knowledge of these ways. They desire to have such things / and to possess them within themselves. They receive them with joy / and assure them / that they have prepared the house of the heart in the best way / to receive them into it.

<column-break/>

31. And he said: Come in, you blessed of the LORD! Why do you stand outside? For I have cleared the house / and [prepared] a place for the camels.
32. Then the man went into the house / and they unsaddled the camels: and they gave the camels straw and fodder / and water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him.
33. And food was set before him; but he said: I will not eat / until I have spoken my words. And he said: Speak on.
34. And he said: I am Abraham's servant.
35. And the LORD has blessed my lord abundantly / and he has become great / and has given him sheep and oxen / and silver and gold / and menservants and maidservants / and camels and donkeys.
36. Moreover, Sarah / my lord’s wife / bore a son to my lord / after she had become old: and he has given him all that he has.
37. And

---

Eliezer shows here a singular faithfulness and his zeal in the business commanded of him / in that he himself did not wish to eat / until he had performed his commanded business / and had promoted it to a good end according to his ability. This he does in a wise / sincere / short / and yet very emphatic / presentation: where he praises the blessing of God in truth without any vainglory / with which God had abundantly showered his lord / Abraham; just as they could also sufficiently notice this from his journey and behavior toward Rebecca.

In this way / a faithful servant of God and Jesus Christ also tends to present the matter of his recruitment in the best way / and offers purely moving causes / which can move the future bride / to give her "Yes" / and to depart with him to the heavenly Isaac. Thus he praises the exceeding riches of God in Christ Jesus / and what treasures are there / which we are to expect in His Son. Everything that the Father has belongs to the Son. This Son would inherit everything / and consequently the bride through the Son / who would be introduced into all the goods of the Son. The Father, furthermore, had a special eye on a daughter from his own kindred / and wished to know of no other bride ordained for his Son / than the one who was of his family.

v. 33. They wish to feed him immediately; but he / being instructed in these ways / says: I shall not eat / until I have performed my business. For such is the LORD’s will. O faithful servant / who forgets yourself / only to carry out the will of God!

v. 35. 36. When he speaks so extensively of his lord’s riches / and boasts of the graces / that God has shown him: he thereby exalts the greatness of this way / and how God blesses it; in that he shows it to be exalted above all other ways. For although Prudence has a poor taste for the ways of faith / she must nevertheless afterward admire it in its outcomes. He reveals its origin to her / and shows / that he has nothing to withhold from her: because / since faith appropriates all that it possesses to her / it has given her its truth to understand. He also adds / that <term>yieldedness</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit" — a key term in German spirituality meaning a state of letting go of one's own will to be filled by God.</note> is the mother and the nourishment of this way.

He reveals to them all the mysteries of faith / in order to move them thereby / to surrender themselves to the same; as he recounts everything / that Abraham had told him / and what had afterward happened with him at the well.

The commentary interprets this allegorically as the Gospel's "recruitment" of the soul (the bride) for Christ (the heavenly Isaac).</summary>

### Chapter XXIV. The First Book of Moses.

37. And my lord made me swear an oath / and said: You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites / in whose land I dwell.
38. But you shall go to my father’s house / and to my kindred / and take a wife for my son.
39. But I said to my lord: Perhaps the woman will not follow me?
40. Then he said to me: The **LORD** / before whose face I have always walked / will send His angel with you / and let your way succeed / so that you may take a wife for my son from my kindred and from my father’s house.
41. Then you shall be free from my oath / when you have come to my kindred; and if they do not give her to you / then you shall be free from my oath.
42. So I came today to the well / and said: **LORD** / You **GOD** of my lord Abraham! If You would now let my way succeed / upon which I have traveled!

---

Thus he presents the work commanded of him in all sincerity and simplicity / and emphasizes especially the wonderful providence of **GOD** / how it may be sensed in this work / and how he has praised **GOD** for the gracious guidance received thus far. It now depends on them / whether they, along with him, will recognize this providence of **GOD** / and be minded to show a similar inclination toward their kinsman / Abraham: Or / if this should not move them / that they say so outright / and not delay him. In all of this he may well be a model of an envoy / when they strive to accomplish something for their masters' best interest through blessing: whereas all the worldly-prudence and the pomp common today brings about nothing but loss of time and great expense / and in the main work often brings about little / or even nothing at all.

v. 40. His angel) What is this angel or messenger other than the power of the divine will / which **GOD** places into the hearts of His own / to make known His counsel to them through His holy spirits and messengers / as through the <term>mighty heroes</term> <note>A poetic reference to angels often found in German Baroque theology, based on Psalm 103:20.</note> / so that one hears the voice of His word. For before all important dispensations of **GOD**, such divine messengers will announce themselves to believers / such internal stirrings and impulses / through which hearts are prompted to faith and obedience according to His word / and are compelled and bound by a special, friendly power.

<column-break/>

43. Behold, so I stand by the water-well: If it happens / that a maiden comes out to draw water / and I speak to her; Give me, I pray, a little water to drink from your jar!
44. And she will say to me; Drink both you / and I will also draw for your camels: let that be the wife / whom the **LORD** has assigned to my lord’s son.
45. Before I had finished speaking this in my heart / behold, Rebekah came out with her jar on her shoulder / and went down to the well / and drew water. Then I spoke to her: Give me, I pray, something to drink!
46. And she quickly took her jar down from her / and said: Drink / and I will also water your camels. So I drank / and she also watered the camels.
->47. And<-

---

v. 43. By the water-well) Do you think / writes <term>Origen</term> <note>original: "Origenes" — a prominent early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> regarding this place / that it happens by mere chance / that the patriarchs come to wells / and reach their marriages by the waters? Whoever thinks that is only a <term>natural man</term> <note>original: "natürlicher Mensch" — a person lacking spiritual insight or "rebirth" in Pietist terminology.</note> / and does not perceive what belongs to the Spirit of **GOD**. Yet / whoever wishes / may believe it / and may remain in nature. But I follow the Apostle Paul / and say: These words signify something / and indicate among the heights of the saints the union of souls with the Word of **GOD**. This union, however, cannot happen otherwise / than through the instruction of the divine Scriptures / which are specifically called wells: to which when someone comes / and draws water from them / that is / contemplates and weighs their meaning; then he receives a higher understanding / and finds the way to a marriage worthy of **GOD**.

v. 44. The **LORD** — assigned) Chosen / disciplined / prepared.

The entire transaction is carried out without Isaac's intervention: The spiritual Isaac does not trouble himself with his wife. She is first made a disciple in the <term>school of discipline</term> <note>original: "Zucht-Schule" — a term for the trials or training God uses to prepare a person's character.</note> / adapted / instructed / and in every way prepared by the Father; and then revealed and assigned to him. Therefore it was not without a great mystery / that Adam had to be cast into a death-sleep / when his wife was taken from him. For it happens with holy marriage and the betrothal between Christ and His bride in the same way: as the mystical Abraham / **GOD** the Father / leads a bride to His Son / just as He also led Eve to Adam. The Father is the first / who draws us to His Son / without whose drawing and movement we could not come to the Son. Therefore He is the one / who makes the wedding for His Son.

It is easy to imagine, however, that **GOD** the Father does not ordain for His Son an unmerciful / unfriendly / proud / impatient bride / no quarrelsome wife / no body subjected to sin: but rather one who is clothed with heartfelt mercy / a bride who is adorned / chosen with all virtues and gifts of grace of the Spirit. The Father shapes and forms the disciples of the Law through discipline and instruction / and ordains them then to the Son. Therefore one reads in the Epistles of the church or community in **GOD** the Father and in the **LORD** **JESUS** Christ.

# The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXIV.

47. And I asked her and said: Whose daughter are you? And she answered: I am Bethuel’s daughter / the son of Nahor / whom Milcah bore to him. Then I put the headband on her forehead / and the bracelets on her hands.

49. And now / if you are those who wish to show love and faithfulness to my lord; then tell me! But if not / then tell me; that I may turn to the right or to the left.

---

v. 47. Bethuel’s daughter) Bethuel means / as Joh. Leiden explains in his *Biblical Name-Book* / God's daughter / God's virgin. For **God** seeks a virginal spirit / a "God-virgin" as a wife for His son.

<column-break/>

50. Then Laban and Bethuel answered and said: This matter has come from the **Lord**;

---

->Thus the friends of Rebekah are also divinely convinced that this work began in and with **God**. They recognize that this marriage does not come from nature or reason / but has a higher Author; namely the spirit of wisdom. This made such a work very venerable and precious to them: just as the blessing of the world rested upon it.<-

->They have either taken the sign / which the servant recounted / as a decree of **God** / or also the words of Abraham as prophetic; because they knew / that Abraham was a prophet. <note>original: "Eucherius L. II. in Gen. p. 906."</note> Eucherius, Book II on Genesis, p. 906.<-

->And it might well be rightly said / that *This matter has come from the **Lord***) Because everything was undertaken in and with **God’s** most holy presence / power and arrangement. Thus it certainly did not come merely from men / not from Abraham’s flesh and blood / not from reason’s schemes and intentions / for money / honor or pleasure / as the world draws its things from such an evil fountain: but from and out of the living **God’s** heart and will. And<-

---

...drinking / and other heathen abominations / which prevail at weddings; thus it is impossible to say with truth of the current marriage / that it comes from the **Lord**.

According to the first general order and institution it certainly comes from the **Lord** / and stands under His patience; **God** also knows how to bring good out of evil / and in this respect does not entirely withdraw from ungodly marriages / as was indicated above. But the special governance and sanctification of **God** is also required / if it is to come from the **Lord**. And so with all other stations and ways of life.

Blessed is he / who in his spiritual walk thus dies to himself / and perishes in his own seeking / so that nothing of himself is done / willed or spoken any longer / but that all his doing and speaking comes from the **Lord**!

How however could these ancient believers be certain / that their affairs came from **God**? Answer: Only in faith: namely / because they let themselves be governed and driven in everything by the Spirit of faith by **God** and His grace / but did not forestall or infringe upon the divine will with their own choice / as unbelief is accustomed to do. They looked primarily and solely at the internal guidance and movement of the minds / how **God’s** will and counsel stirred and opened itself therein. They waited in all circumstances for the divine assurance and instruction / as their heart gradually became firm or not regarding this or that matter.

To this end they fought with mighty earnestness against the rule of their flesh and reason / which always likes to rise up and speak into grace. They kept themselves mostly passive under divine guidance / and stood before the **Lord** in *Gelassenheit* <note>The term "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of surrendered stillness, serenity, or "yieldedness" to God's will, a central concept in German mystical and pietist thought.</note> for all His pleasure / like wax / or like the clay in the hand of the potter.

That this is true / that the ancient believers thus let themselves be governed and driven internally here by **God** and His Spirit alone in faith / and arranged their affairs accordingly; that is clear from this story. For

Was that not the serenity of faith in Abraham / that he sent his servant at a venture into a distant land / when he did not know the person / whom **God** had determined? The servant himself / when he came to the place / also did not know / how he should begin according to reason. For himself he wanted to choose or venture nothing. How then did he tackle it? In a purely faithful and serene way. He turned to the living **God** / began to take his confidential agreement with Him / and proposed a sign himself for his assurance.

Thus the affairs of the ancient believers came from **God** / so that even others could be powerfully convinced by them. As here Laban and Bethuel / (where the son is mentioned first / because he perhaps directed the household / and had to lead the speaking /) when they heard this event / how the man’s agreement with **God** had been granted and succeeded / broke out in the unanimous confession: *That comes from the **Lord**!*

And so with believers everything depends solely on the inward power of faith / and consequently on the pure grace of **God** / who has all men’s hearts in His power / and directs them like streams of water. Thereby **God** is given His honor / that it may rightly be said of our doing and letting: *That comes from the **Lord**.*

Whether such assurances are now with us in our heart over our life and walk / that one may learn to test and recognize without falsehood. If it has not been so until now / then it has been such a person's own harm and a delay to the joy of the spirit.

If one does not wish to suffer shipwreck here / and perish in the multitude of one’s own ways; then let one not run so into the uncertain. One should seek to ground all his affairs firmly in **God’s** will / and find no rest anywhere without it. One should persevere diligently in prayer day and night for certainty. He will certainly give it / if we only do not want to mix our choice and will into it / but rest in serenity <note>original: "Gelassenheit"</note> from our willing and working. Let one then struggle rightly for this / so that one becomes thus still. And when **God** draws one even into a station or such a calling / which does not suit the flesh; then let one think / if it is not all the more from the **Lord** for that very reason.

Once one is then certain and rightly convinced of a matter / then one can also accept it as from **God**; according to the example of these persons / who / as soon as they were convinced of the matter / uprightly confessed:

### Chapter XXIV. The First Book of Moses.

we are unable to speak anything against you / neither evil nor good.

51. Behold, there is Rebecca before your face; take her and go: and she shall be your lord’s son’s wife / as the **Lord** has spoken.

---

**we are unable to speak anything against you)** It is a good sign that faith and trust dwell in a heart / when it, at the very least, restrains itself from saying or interjecting anything against **God’s** providences. This shows / that such a mind nevertheless carries a sense of awe and hesitation to strive against **God**.

This is caused by that deep respect / which faith immediately awakens in the soul / when it is worked therein by the Holy Spirit. For in the conversion to **God** we are placed into such submission and humiliation under His holiness and justice / that we must retain a constant impression of it / and no longer dare to remain bold / proud and rebellious.

When, then, something divine comes to the hand of such a soul / or is merely shown in the mind from **God’s** Word; the mind immediately sinks down, as it were, under **God’s** almighty hand / and melts like wax in the fire / so that **God** can form from it whatever He wills. And

There, indeed, the thorny reason <note>original: "stachelichte Vernunfft"; a metaphor for human intellect that "pricks" or questions divine mysteries</note> with its foolish objections must be overcome: and even if it resists for a time / even with a considerable appearance of truth; it is nevertheless rebuked by the light / and taken captive under the obedience of faith.

The working of grace is so strong in the mouth of a person who has turned inward <note>referring to "Einkehr," the practice of internal spiritual focus</note> / that one can neither answer such a person nor deny them anything: in that one must confess / that everything comes from **God** / whom one can hardly resist.

Thus the relatives here are compelled by a sweet necessity to give their "Yes" to it / after which love is then entirely united with self-denial. After which the fully spiritual wedding between bride and bridegroom is completed / who are united for this reason / so that they may complete their course in the inner ways / and may happily assure themselves in **God**.

It is quite fitting / that these people here speak with such deliberation. They do not say; We *will* not speak against it: but only; we *cannot*. Thereby giving to understand / that indeed their reason still thought to mention much / but the power of the testimony of **God** was so strong in their hearts / that with a quiet conscience they dared not nor could not bring anything up /

**neither evil nor good)** What else does this speech indicate / but such an equanimity <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central Pietist concept of letting go of one's own will to be receptive to God's will</note> and indifference of the mind and will / where one yields oneself in a passive manner into everything /

whatever may come / be it this or another.

<column-break/>

52. And it happened / when Abraham’s servant had heard their words / that he bowed down to the earth before the **Lord**.

53. And the servant drew forth silver and gold jewelry and clothes / and gave them to Rebecca: but to her brother and her mother he gave other treasures.

54. And they ate and drank / he together with the men who were with him / and stayed there overnight. But in the morning they stood up / and he said: Release me to my lord.

55. But her brother and her mother said: Let the maiden stay with us for some days (or ten); after that you shall go.

56. Then

---

**v. 52. That he bowed down to the earth before the Lord)** This indicates his deep reverence and eagerness to give thanks / with which he worshipped **God’s** holy providence. For us to follow / so that we may learn to deeply humble and bend ourselves in spirit under His holy hands / and to offer up honest thanks for all His providences and leadings in the faith of truth.

**v. 53. Gave them to Rebecca)** It does not appear / that the father gave his daughter anything to take with her. The bride of Christ is not brought to Him in her own clothes and righteousness / but in the clothes that He has sent / in the adornment of His righteousness.

**To her brother and her mother he gave)** In that the relatives of Rebecca had received many gifts because of her / these represent to us / how beneficial it is / to be united with love; in that one becomes a partaker of their happiness: and that all those / who are linked with those highly esteemed by **God** / receive special graces from the same.

<column-break/>

They wanted thereby to indicate / that **God’s** revealed counsel was so powerful / that they were bound and taken captive in their hearts / to leave the matter to the **Lord** / as He would show the outcome: They wanted in an impartial mind to follow the footsteps of **God** / as He would lead them and carry out His work.

All this may serve as a fine pattern / of how good and advisable it is / in such cases and scruples / in which one must not trust oneself / or does not yet know any way out / to indeed leave it resignedly to the eternal wisdom alone / and to find no fault with nor change anything in the ways.

This is certainly the very safest and straightest way / both to come out of all doubt / as well as afterwards to prevent all future unrest and displeasure. If one remains quite still with one's will / and tames one's desires and choices / then **God** has a free hand / to allot the best to us.

No one believes / except he who has experienced it / how true equanimity and the denial of one's own will rewards itself so gloriously! One gets to enjoy it for a lifetime / where in all one’s denials one has fought only for the sake of denial <note>meaning the intentional letting go of self-will</note>! And even if ever so many storms should come afterward / such a mind nevertheless remains in its fortress and rest / which is **God’s** will. There one can stand in faith before **God** and say: See **Lord** / you have sent this or that to me / led me into this and that; it has come from you; I have said neither evil nor good regarding it! Well then, you will also carry it out! I am yours / and my way and calling is yours: it remains yours alone!

Even if it does not go according to the courage of the flesh / one nevertheless remains standing under **God’s** will / and speaks nothing against it in impatience and murmuring. Therein is the best comfort in all suffering: The **Lord** has done it; it comes from the **Lord**: therefore we can speak nothing against it.

So also in the inward state / when the **Lord** Jesus woos the soul and wants to move in with it / the most proper answer and declaration should be: This comes from the **Lord**; therefore I can speak nothing against it.

If one has previously flirted with Christ’s enemies / and turned one's will away from Him; one must now with double earnestness subject the same to the right **Lord** / and say: He is the **Lord** / let Him do what pleases Him!

Thus the will of man bows before the **Lord** in the most inward way / as it is written here outwardly of the servant:

**The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXIV.**

**56. Then he said to them: Do not hold me back! for the LORD has made my way successful. Let me go / that I may travel to my master.**

**57. Then they said: Let us call the girl / and ask her mouth.** <note>The phrase "ask her mouth" is a literal translation of the Hebrew idiom meaning to ask her personally or seek her own word on the matter.</note>

**58. And they called Rebecca / and said to her: Will you go with this man? And she answered: I will go.**

v. 56. **Do not hold me back)** Since Laban and Bethuel recognize **God’s** providence / and have submitted themselves to it; the servant hastens his return journey / and now desires to soon gladden his masters / Abraham and Isaac / with this blessed outcome / and will not be deterred by any suggestion of delay. Then Rebecca also shows her consent in all sincere simplicity / and submits herself to her parents' approval / and also resolves to follow quickly: as the Lord has also steered her heart toward a longing mutual love for her bridegroom.

**The Lord has made my way successful)** Whoever, therefore, wishes to have a blessed progress and outcome in their actions / should concern themselves above all things with the **LORD** and His assistance. For He is indeed called **LORD** and Ruler for this reason / that He wishes to be **LORD** over all our affairs / through His eternal Word **Jesus Christ**. One must give Him a free hand in all things.

If we let Him rule alone in this way / and follow His good pleasure with pure sincerity; then we may unfailingly expect His help / even if it does not appear so at the beginning. For He wishes to be sought, recognized, and found in everything. He also takes delight / when He can prove Himself powerful and glorious / even in the smallest actions of men / and much more so in weightier matters.

O, what a golden foundation and beginning for all ways of life / estates / businesses and actions / especially that of marriage / when everything therein flows purely from the clear source of the divine pure will / and afterwards returns again with praise and glory to this very same origin!

By right, it should go no differently with all our doing and leaving / and it should look no different before **God’s** holy eyes / if it is to succeed.

False reason and proud self-will are busy / offering us other suggestions every moment / as to how we should begin our affairs / changes / and ways of life / following the fashion of the world and the mind of the flesh.

Whatever is begun in such a way / people generally praise / and the blind masses flock to it. Whoever can push through his affairs with intrigues and cunning / and other worldly practices; is called wise and fortunate by the world. It often goes not badly for such people for a time according to the flesh.

But finally all such apostates must experience / that they began it without **GOD**! When the slightest distress comes / (as **GOD** does not fail / to discipline and seek even the worst rascals /) then pure despair / murmuring and impatience are there! One has no joyful access to **GOD**: for one did not begin with Him. Thus, an ungodly beginning is followed by a wretched ending.

v. 57. 58. Even though **GOD** is almighty / He nevertheless desires to have the bride's own determination / before He allows her to renounce her first ways / which are represented by her father's house / and permits her to accept those / which lead her into the simplicity and depth of the inner life.

But she agrees willingly / and answers without pretense in a way that expresses a soul / which is beginning to be instructed in the ways that faith maintains. These ways of faith, however, are entirely simple.

O, if only men recognized the highness and riches and glory / that a Bride of the Lamb <note>A mystical term for the Church or the individual soul united with Christ.</note> has to expect from her Bridegroom / how quickly would they leave their old father Adam’s house and friendship / cut themselves out of the wild trunk / and let themselves be grafted into the fruitful olive tree of the Son of **GOD**!

**63. And**

v. 60. They give her their heartfelt blessing / which they indeed / according to custom / directed toward great physical increase and prosperity / (see Chapter 1:28) but with it they must also assign to her the blessing of increase promised by **GOD**: just as this custom may also be the origin of the public blessing of marriages.

The holy power of the divine life increases infinitely in all / who surrender themselves to the **Lord** as a bride to her bridegroom. For

In **God’s** own works and ways, nothing is to be found but the fruit of righteousness and a steady growth toward perfection. Yes, this is indeed the true way / upon which the Messiah, the Anointed One, perfectly satisfies His bride with His love unto eternal life.

**May your seed possess the gate of those who hate them)** Which they possess against right and in godliness and tyranny.

When evil is driven out of the good / and sin and corruption out of the creature; then the good / which remains / takes the place / and rules with righteousness.

To this it will truly come at last / when grace rules in nature / and nature and grace kiss each other in the great union.

v. 62. Isaac was walking by the Well of the Living and Seeing One / that is / by the source which is **GOD** / who alone lives and stands. He was walking in **God**; where the expanse of his soul was not retracted. He had "gone out of himself" <note>A technical term in mystical theology referring to *ecstasis* or detachment from the ego to be present with God.</note> / so that he could all the better dwell with **God**. In this excellent communion, pure Love was brought to him / to be bound with him with indissoluble bonds. He goes toward her / as soon as he catches sight of her. Pure love is given to no one except to him who has gone out of himself / and dwells with nothing but **GOD**: which, however, only happens toward evening / in the last moment of life and after great storms.

**Toward the South)** <note>original: "gegen Mittag"; literally "toward noon," a common German idiom for the direction of the midday sun (South).</note> At the outermost borders of the promised land / toward Egypt.

The single phrase, **I will go**, is enough / to express everything / that the soul desires / when it is touched by the love of **God**.

Isaac had the praiseworthy habit / of practicing godly contemplations in quiet solitude in the field and in common communion with GOD in prayer; (see Ps. 102:1. where the word used here also appears / and signifies both:) <note>The Hebrew word *suach* can mean both to meditate and to pray.</note> and without doubt also to call upon GOD for a blessed outcome in the intended marriage. She climbs down from her camel / to go toward him even more quickly. But she covers herself with her veil / which signifies faithfulness: and in this attire she unites with him.

But what does Isaac do? He does not stop to admire Rebecca's beauty: for he has already come far in the way of faith / which possesses nothing perceptible to the senses: rather, he leads her immediately into the tent of his mother; that is / he leads her immediately into total abandonment <note>German: *Verlassung*; a spiritual state of letting go of worldly attachments to rely solely on God.</note> / which is prefigured by Sarah. This self-denial, however, is the state that follows immediately after the union and enjoyment of the Bridegroom. Therefore, he leads her through it. But after he had recognized the value of love / which alone makes the soul one with GOD; he loved her so strongly / that he entirely forgot the pain / which he had felt through Sarah's death: namely, the loss of self-denial / which then becomes unnecessary to him / as he is confirmed in GOD himself through love in true serenity <note>German: *Gelassenheit*; the mystical concept of yielding one's will to God.</note>.

**5. And Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac.** <margin>Psalm 17:14. Revelation 21:7.</margin>

**6. But to the children whom Abraham had from the concubines, Abraham gave gifts / and sent them away (a) from his son Isaac, while he yet lived, toward the sunrise, into the East.** <margin>(a) John 8:35.</margin>

Abraham indeed had more children / but they received no part of the inheritance. Faith also has many children / to whom it does good: but Isaac alone / as the true son of faith and self-denial / is to expect the inheritance. The children of the other paths are distributed as servants. They also do not share the same dwelling with Isaac: Isaac is set apart as the only son / and has no lesser inheritance than God Himself; because God was the possession of that faith and self-denial / from which Isaac was born. No soul will come to the enjoyment of God / unless it is first stripped of all [external] pieces and self-interest. <note>The author uses Isaac as an allegory for the advanced spiritual state where the soul seeks nothing but God.</note>

To the children of the promise, God gives the true, essential good: Proverbs 2:7, 8:21. But the children of the world He dismisses with gifts of the perishable goods of this world.

The best gift / which / according to the prophetic sense / these descendants of Abraham will receive in their posterity in the latter days / will be / that they shall be converted to Christ and incorporated into the Church: as Isaiah (a) points toward.

There is no human to be found on earth / who / according to the inner, hidden being / does not have a gift from God / and who could not participate in Christ for a real breakthrough / if he lets the hidden seed lying within him sprout and emerge through the grace he receives. The Word that was from the beginning illuminates all people / who come into this world / and shines into their conscience. Such a hidden seed will break forth in the latter time / as in others / so also in these children of Abraham by Keturah / and bring forth fruit of Christ according to its measure. The light / that rises over Zion / will shine upon them as well / and they too shall receive their presents and gifts / and be blessed in Christ. At the time / when the fullness of the Gentiles shall come in / it will explain itself / what is so manifoldly indicated and promised in the Prophets (b): when the kings among the nations shall be gathered as one people to the God of Abraham / and God shall be greatly exalted among the shields upon the earth. Psalm 47:10. (a) Chapter 60:6. (b) Isaiah 2:2, 3; 49:18, 20-22. Zechariah 8:20-23.

...and night / and thus 6 / lamps burn / also each grave has its own particular inscription: such as Abraham’s grave; <note>original Hebrew: "וזה קבר אברהם אבינו" (And this is the grave of Abraham our father)</note> This is the grave of Abraham / our father of blessed memory. <note>This text appears to be a continuation of a description of the patriarchal tombs, likely citing Benjamin of Tudela, a famous Jewish traveler.</note>

Abraham / who is the image of Faith / after he united his son with Love or Charity / having previously led him into God alone through serenity and bare faith / falls into a weakness / and faith itself dies. Now that this patriarch has passed according to his essence into his son / and through him into all his descendants; so all insights of faith / and the use of this light / remain as if dead and buried in a soul which has come to God alone: because all / even the most necessary and holy / means come to an end / when one has reached the ultimate end. Then this soul need only enjoy pure love; but in God Himself / with a wonderful purity and simplicity. And this precedes the Apostolic life / which is both one and manifold. For / just as God acts in everything without departing from Himself and His unity: so also these souls work from without / without stepping out of their unity in God. Self-denial and faith are left in one and the same place / when one arrives in God alone.

v. 11. Isaac was blessed by God after his father's death as the heir of the covenant / as all the grace-promises of God / which were given to the father / were confirmed anew to him. Chapter 26:3, 4. And so the blessing of godly parents often reveals itself only after death in their children / especially in those who walk in their faithful footsteps / like Isaac; while the others, like an Ishmael, remain stuck in the world. And these godly children then come upon the true tracks of truth / which reveal themselves in them with ever greater power: so that the parents themselves still feel the blessing in these children in eternity. See Chapter 18:19.

That he settled by the well designated by the providence of the Lord / and chose it for his dwelling; shows / how he leaned toward this fountain of salvation / which will not leave us in any need / but will constantly guide, refresh, and strengthen us. Chapter 16:14.

Isaac remains with his wife after the death of his father in the same place: because no other residence exists for a soul / such as this / even if it were to run through the whole earth; for it could go through the whole world / without moving from its place.

<margin>Here the promised physical blessing of the twelve princes was fulfilled, as in Chapter 17:20, who also became famous and well-known nations. Of these, the first, Nebajoth and Kedar, also have the promise that their descendants will be gathered to Christ in His kingdom; among whom the others may well be included. Isaiah 60:7. Otherwise, his tribe came to external prominence in the world sooner—as did Esau—than Isaac and Jacob, who only attained such external dignity and increase long afterward; for such external things are not the true, lasting good, and are also given to worldly people who strive most for them.</margin>

<margin>v. 17. **To his people**) This can also refer to those who are outside the covenant of God: because carnal birth cannot bring us into the fellowship of our pious fathers; rather, each person goes to his own place and to those like himself. See Acts 1:25. Romans 9:7, 8.</margin>

<margin>v. 18. **Havilah**) This is said to be different from the one in Chapter 2:11, being located in Stony Arabia. See 1 Samuel 15:7.</margin>

<margin>**Over against his brothers**) According to the prophecy in Chapter 16:12 <note>The original text cites 17:12, but the prophecy regarding Ishmael living "over against his brothers" is found in 16:12.</note>. And so the believers must live among worldly people for the testing of their patience, and as a testimony over them. See Philippians 2:15.</margin>

<margin>v. 20. **Rebecca**) Who, as some show from chronological calculations, is said to have been 14 years old.</margin>

<margin>v. 21. Thus Isaac was also tested by the barrenness of his wife, even though the blessing of his father had already been announced to him by God. His faith, like his father's, had to be tested, though he might have found it easier to accept since he himself was conceived so late in his parents' lives. Meanwhile, he turns to prayer, together with his wife, as is the duty of godly married couples: to unite themselves in prayer before God with one mind, both at all times and especially in times of extraordinary need and concern.</margin>

<margin>The love that is united in God alone finds itself in such rest that it would no longer think of bringing forth external fruit, were it not awakened from its sweet sleep by the opportunity which Providence places in its hand; for in Him, it possesses all goods.</margin>

<margin>v. 22. Since Rebecca was very troubled by her peculiar condition, in which she may not have felt at ease, she inquired of the Lord. It is probable she did this through her father-in-law, Abraham, who was a prophet and who conducted himself like a priest of God in his family, to whom one was directed to inquire after the will of God. See Judges 20:18, 27, 28. Malachi 2:7. 1 Kings 14:1, etc.</margin>

<margin>The soul that is not yet established in the experience of God's ways is distressed to see persecutions grow: and its distress causes it to seek counsel with God. This is the godly practice of the saints, that they take refuge in God in their needs and doubts, for their entire trust rests upon Him. The example of the Patriarchs in this matter shames all Christians who, for the most part, consult nothing but the world and their own natural inclinations.</margin>

<margin>**Struggled**) There are opposing births within us that wrestle, fight, and strive for the upper hand. Examine yourselves! Does not each of you find this conflict in your soul? Does not the flesh lust against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh? Is there not an enmity there between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent? If one notes and feels no such enmity in his heart—alas for your poor soul, if you know nothing of this and are unfeeling!</margin>

<margin>**She went**) Where? asks Origen. From the place where the Lord was not, to the place where He was. But is God not in all places? Precisely for that reason, he says, we must not think she went from one physical place to another, but from life to life, from good to better, from holy to holier, through a progression in the growth of grace. She left time and place behind and went toward Him who is above all time and place; to Him she drew near in her elevated spirit. For it would be absurd to think that Rebecca—who had sufficient instruction in the house of the wise Abraham and under a most highly understanding man like Isaac—was so foolish as to believe the Lord was enclosed in a certain physical location.</margin>

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.</header>

## 23. And the LORD said to her: Two nations are in your body, and two kinds of people shall be separated from your innermost parts; and one people shall be stronger than the other, and the greater shall serve the lesser.

->24. Then<-

Because this is a divine prophecy, it must certainly have had its fulfillment, either during the lifetime of Jacob and Esau, or after their death, or it is yet to be fulfilled.

Those who interpret this as referring to the individuals or the two tribal patriarchs of the two nations are obligated to show that this prophecy was fulfilled in both of their lives. Indeed, they must show it as clearly as the sun at midday before they can build such a doctrine upon it, as they still do daily with this text.

<margin>Numbers 20:14-17.</margin>
But how? Was not Esau a mighty prince compared to Jacob, from whom Jacob had to flee, whom he feared, to whom he bowed, to whom he brought gifts, whom he called his "Lord," and himself his "servant"? <note>See Genesis 32:5-13 and 33:3.</note> All of which was a poor sign of Jacob’s dominion over his brother Esau; which Esau (or Edom) moreover remained a great prince while Jacob and all his children stood under the domain of Pharaoh in Egypt; whose descendants remained so for several hundred years after the deaths of Jacob and Esau.

Therefore, this was not fulfilled in the persons of Esau and Jacob, but rather the opposite, as Jacob humbled himself before Esau in almost all things.

It is also not without reason that it does not say **the elder; but rather:**

The greater shall serve the lesser) Not the oldest son, who first came from the mother's womb, serving the youngest: but the oldest, greatest, and most prominent nation serving the youngest and least.

<margin>Numbers 24:17-19. 2 Samuel 8:13-14. 1 Chronicles 18:12. 1 Kings 11:15-16.</margin>
However, this prophecy—which is confirmed in Numbers 24:17-19—was fulfilled according to the literal sense in the times of David; as can be read in 2 Samuel 8:13-14, 1 Chronicles 18:12, and 1 Kings 11:15-16.

And the dominion of Jacob over Esau, or the servitude of Edom under Israel, lasted not only the entire time of David's reign, but also under Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, and Jehoshaphat, until the time of Joram. <note>2 Kings 8:20.</note> It may also have been fully fulfilled at the time when John Hyrcanus <note>Son of Simon Maccabeus, a leader of the Jewish Hasmonean dynasty.</note> so overcame the Edomites that he forced them to be circumcised and to adopt Jewish ceremonies, so that they no longer remained a distinct people; until they inhabited their own land again after the destruction of Jerusalem.

According to the prophetic and spiritual sense, it is still fulfilled daily. There, the two persons represent the first and the last world, and then the earthly and the heavenly man.

Luther notes very well in this sense that everything was written for the sake of Christ, who came from the line of the smaller people. And

thus it is also a glorious archetype of the state of the Church: namely, how Esau’s mind and spirit rule over Jacob’s humility long enough, until finally Christ the Lord brings the same under Himself and makes an end of it through the appearance of His coming.

In the same way, the two dispositions of Isaac’s children can be very beautifully interpreted, without force, as the two states of the human race, or as the natural and the reborn man. Both come from one origin, just as Jacob and Esau come from one father. The first Adam shall serve the second. The second and new man indeed has his roots in the nature of Adam, but he follows God and rules over nature.

The old sinful nature in the believer must become subject to the new and divine nature. And although the former may persecute and oppress the latter for a time, eventually that pride must submit to humility and break its own will, if it wishes to be saved and become an heir of the glory of God.

Esau’s rough spirit and mind shall, in its time, be cast down from all its power and dominion; whereas the gentle and humble Jacob shall be exalted to rule over him. That is: Whatever has resisted Christ and His cause here with unbelief, disputing, and persecution, shall come to nothing, and instead, the mind and spirit of the Lord Christ

<column-break/>

in His own people—as followers of the Lamb—shall be recognized, revealed, and glorious over all enemies. And that

When Jacob’s time awakens, then the spiritual Edomites, who until then had the upper hand and persecuted the children of the covenant, will finally be overcome by them; and the children of Jerusalem, after the downfall of the beast-like and antichristian Edomites, will receive the victory and the kingdom in the "time of refreshing." <note>A reference to Acts 3:19.</note>

Currently, the external church-party is still the strongest, which overwhelms and floods the "little flock" of the pious within and outside of it. But when, in the last times, Esau’s reign in the Antichrist has reached its peak, then the beginning of the future age appears with the victorious Subduer: when the majority of the antichristian people, along with their allies Gog and Magog, are defeated; yet a small number of them shall remain and must be witnesses to the triumphant Jacob and his blossoming Church.

So, let Esau and Jacob clash for as long as they will; it may even take on the appearance as if Esau would swallow up little Jacob: yet it shall turn out well for the "good party" in the end, and the greater shall serve the lesser.

If we truly believed this—that good is stronger than evil—oh, we would certainly not let ourselves be recruited by the evil generation nor fall in with it, but would hold with the greatest party, which is greater before God.

But the dear God judges and acts quite differently with His creatures than reason thinks. He chooses only the despised, miserable, weak, and small, which can rely on nothing, which leaves itself and yields purely to Him, which does not act with defiance and haughtiness. And the world does exactly the opposite.

Accordingly, this divine answer contains a great mystery, which did not only include the birth of these two sons and their occurrences: nor even the two great nations that would come from them, namely the Jews and the Edomites, who would mostly live in enmity against each other, and finally the people coming from the younger brother would be superior to the people of the older, so that the latter would have to serve the former; as happened in the times of David. Rather, it pertains to the two great nations of the wicked and the pious who all come from one stem; and since the evil is by nature the first, which also has the upper hand in most men; who then also hate the good and strive to lord it over them: yet eventually they must succumb when first our heavenly David, Christ, arrives at His full dominion in His glorious kingdom. See Psalm 125:3, Daniel 7:26-27. Indeed, these two opposing forces are in every human being: the evil, which is in us first by nature, the flesh; and then the good, the universal grace of God which has appeared to all men, and Christ as the Light that enlightens all men coming into the world, the Spirit. These two are against each other.

Just as everything redounds to the glorification of God and the best for His elect; so also to the extent that a holy people is conceived in the innermost parts of love, she also conceives a perverse people to exercise and cause the former to suffer. To conceive and give birth to the generation of the elect is to conceive and give birth to crosses and persecutions. This holy people was already persecuted before it had seen the light of day: it also endured hard trials before its birth. For the elect, there is not a single place safe from persecution. God lets them find the Cross everywhere: it grows with them; it grows under their steps: indeed, they must lose their lives upon it.

But God comforts them and gives them to understand that it is necessary for this to happen so; and that after He had allowed the wicked to test the elect, the former should afterwards be subject to the latter; and that the elect, who seemed to be the least because of their humility, would become masters over their enemies.

24. When her days were fulfilled for her to give birth; behold, there were twins in her womb.

25. And the first came out; he was reddish; he was all over like a hairy garment: and they called him Esau.

There were thus two children in one body—the persecutor and the persecuted; and in contrast, the master and the servant. The one who persecutes is a slave to his own passions and inclinations, while the persecuted, meanwhile, enjoys a wondrous peace and freedom. Both the good and the evil come from the womb of God <note>The author suggests that all life originates in God’s creative power, though moral character diverges later.</note>, and yet the godless are constantly against God and the devout! Sin alone stirs up this discord.

Esau and Jacob were born under the same constellation: and yet one was good, and the other bad: so says *Gregory* (a) <note>original: "Gregorius". Likely referring to Gregory the Great.</note>.

Therefore, we truly have twins within us: we have two nations inside ourselves; we have two kinds of people within us. For there are not a few on either side. From the heart come forth evil thoughts, etc. And the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, etc.

Thus, the letter of the text and the history present a mystery to us: and if we wish to understand it, we must turn our eye inward and read the secret figure there which is offered to us in the written word.

Two is a mystical number, and the mystery of duality is within one womb and one person. Who these two or twins are, Paul (b) indicates in these words: Although our outward man perishes, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.

This is a wonderful union: two opposing natures in every human being! For through Rebecca, every one of us is prefigured.

As soon as the outward man has life, according to the testimony of those experienced in these mysteries, the inward man is supernaturally poured into the nature of the outward: so that our natural parents only produce the outward and natural man, who is, as it were, the husk or shell of the inward and spiritual man. This spiritual man finds himself in this outward visible world and nature as a stranger and a pilgrim, like one born in a foreign land, outside his true fatherland. Therefore, Christ enlightens every man who comes into the world. *John 1:4, 9.* But we are also by nature darkness. And here, then, the light also shines in the darkness of every man. For the entire creation or creature consists of light and shadow, and is comprised of day and night. Therefore, these two men, peoples, and nations are also distinct in their birth, natures, customs, and all their properties. The outward man is called Esau, and is generated and born through natural birth, in the line of nature, from natural parents, into this visible world for the sake of earthly life, in which he may reach out to explore the wonders of the world.

<margin>(a) homily on Matthew. (b) 2 Cor. 4:16.</margin>

1. Just as God let His sentence and decree be passed upon Esau and Jacob before the boys were born: so the election of grace <term>Gnaden-Wahl: the theological concept of predestination or God's sovereign choice</term> happens in His measure before men do evil or good with an actual outbreak in this time. *Rom. 9:11.*

2. But just as Esau justified and deserved the decree passed upon him by the sins he committed afterward, while Jacob did not deserve God's love toward him: so the godless will one day be unable to excuse themselves, and the devout will not be able to justify themselves.

3. As the two children pushed against each other in the mother's womb, so the enmity remains between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent.

4. But as Jacob did not only hold his brother's heel at birth, and thus wished to be the firstborn by force, but also—even though God's decree was known to him, how the elder should serve the younger and thus the latter become the firstborn—did not defiantly rely on this, but sought the birthright and blessing with diligence and zeal: So the devout work out their salvation with fear and trembling, even if they are already certain of their election, *2 Pet. 1:10,* and take the kingdom of heaven by force. They do not say: "What use is the birthright to me! I shall die anyway," etc.

26. And after this (a) his brother came out; and his hand held Esau's heel: and they called him Jacob. Isaac was sixty years old when they were born. <margin>(a) 1 Cor. 15:46. 4 Esdras 6:8, 9.</margin>

27. And

Jacob is a figure of the heavenly man, but Esau of the earthly. So great is the goodness of the heavenly man that he lets the earthly man break out first, and lets him have his full freedom to do what he desires, or to take his full swing: but he wrestles and struggles with him, and even though the earthly man breaks out, the heavenly man seizes and holds him, and hinders him in his heated race.

In these two persons, we have a special
->Prefigurement<-

### I. Of the Old and New Testaments;
->or of the Jews and Christians, or of Christ:<-
->and a counterpart of Cain and Abel, Ishmael and Isaac.<-

1. Esau was a fleshly man, a man of the field and the world: Jacob was a simple man <note>German "Schäter" refers to a quiet, upright, or simple person</note>, dwelling in tents. So the Jews were fleshly Edomites, as they are called by the prophets. Herod the Edomite was their king, and they were very active in the world at that time. Christ, on the other hand, was the Good Shepherd.

2. Esau was hated by God, even though he had more temporal blessing than his brother Jacob, who was loved by GOD. *Malachi 1.* The Jews had a fat land before the Christians, but were not more loved because of it.

3. Esau was the firstborn according to the flesh, Jacob the younger. Thus the Old Testament is before the New.

4. But Esau sold and despised his birthright to the youngest for a dish of lentils and bread, and thus Jacob became the firstborn. Because of their land and bread, the Jews disregarded the Rock of Salvation, the Firstborn, and even sold their privilege, so that the last have become the first.

5. Just as Esau hated and persecuted Jacob because of the birthright, so that the latter had to flee to Mesopotamia: So not only did Herod the Edomite hate and persecute Christ, because He was to be over him, but the Jews also persecuted the Christians.

6. Jacob was blessed in the lovely-smelling garments of his firstborn brother: So the lovely fragrance of the sacrifice of Christ is credited to us; He also has garments that smell of amber <note>Amber: likely referring to ambergris or precious incense-like scents</note>.

7. As Esau sought the blessing he had lost with tears; *Hebr. 12:17* but without faith, without love for holiness, out of pure desire for an earthly blessing: so that which Christ says is fulfilled in the Jews: You will seek me, but not find me. *John 7:34.*

8. As Esau finally kissed Jacob, so we hope for the conversion of the Jews.

These two persons are also a prefigurement

### II. Of the Elect and the Lost.

5. But as Esau also sought the blessing with tears, so the godless also seek a physical blessing.

Let us therefore not be as Esau was: (1) a crude and rough man of the world, hard and stubborn; for a gentle and quiet spirit is precious before God: *1 Pet. 3:4.* (2) too much devoted to the earth and earthly blessing; (3) despising the birthright and the signs of heavenly blessing: but rather live holily like Jacob, and be careful regarding God's counsel, not becoming overconfident, but struggling to enter in.
