# The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXV.

27. And when the boys grew up, Esau became a man who was skilled in hunting and a man of the field; but Jacob was a simple <term>simple: The German 'einfältig' here translates the Hebrew 'tam', implying integrity, guilelessness, or being 'whole' in God's eyes.</term> man and remained in the tents. <margin>Ps. 15:1.</margin>

28. And Isaac loved Esau, for he enjoyed eating venison. But Rebekah loved Jacob.

29. And Jacob had cooked a pottage; then Esau came from the field, and he was weary.

30. And Esau said to Jacob: "Let me taste of that exceedingly red [stuff]! For I am weary." Therefore he was called Edom <note>original: "Edom". The name means 'red', referencing both the pottage and Esau's own ruddy complexion.</note>.

***

Esau thus followed after the likeness of Cain and Nimrod <note>Cain (the first murderer) and Nimrod (the 'mighty hunter') are presented here as archetypes of the worldly, violent man.</note>: Ch. 4:2, 10:8–9. Just as Jacob followed Abel and his father Isaac; who indeed loved that sensory-driven nature out of weakness for the sake of his bodily appetite, yet did not take to heart the prophecy regarding these his two sons as Rebekah did. She, therefore, urged Jacob to strive to obtain the birthright, so that his brother might willingly yield it to him. At that time, perhaps only the priestly office depended upon it, and thus the dominion—or rather the governance—in the service of God; from which a blessing also flowed, which the mother wished to bestow upon Jacob.

v. 27. **A simple man)** The word in Hebrew has a twofold meaning: 1) to be consumed, corrupted, or destroyed; 2) to be finished, or made complete and perfect. Both may be captured here: to be consumed and perfected. Because the nature of perfection consists in the consumption and destruction of everything that is opposed to us, and in the fulfillment or completion of the holiness and righteousness which God requires.

**Remained in the tents)** As one who recognized that nothing is accomplished by hunting or running and toiling. This indicates his perfect state, that he had completely gone out from himself. The full harvest had come to him, as when one holds the Festival of Tabernacles <note>The 'tents' or 'huts' (Hütten) are linked here to the Jewish Sukkot, symbolizing spiritual rest and dependence on God.</note> with great joy.

Esau exercises his cruelty upon the animals he catches in the hunt; Jacob, however, who is gentle and simple, meanwhile enjoys the peace of solitude. And since he imitates Jesus Christ in advance, he practices inward reflection and prayer before engaging in external affairs. Grace leads to reflection and rest, until the holy calling compels the soul to show itself.

v. 28. Isaac loved Esau with some self-interest. It is something very rare to be able to act through pure grace, without having a view toward oneself. The holiest of people often err in the choice of their friendships. This choice is never perfect as soon as self-interest is mixed in. But Love [itself] loves Jacob because he was after God's own heart; and since he had no self-love, his love was joined with justice and supported by equity.

<column-break/>

31. But Jacob said: "Sell me today your birthright."

32. And Esau answered: "Behold, I am going toward death; what use is the birthright to me now!"

33. And Jacob said: "Then swear to me today." And he swore to him; and so sold his birthright to Jacob. <margin>ch. 48:18. 49:3, 4.</margin>

34. Then Jacob gave Esau bread and the pottage of lentils, and he ate and drank, and stood up and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright.

<meta>catchword: That</meta>

***

That was a shameful rejection of divine benefits, as the Holy Spirit himself notes with great gravity in Hebrews 12:16, especially with such contemptuous and frivolous speech. On that account, and because he esteemed the spiritual blessing so lightly and trifled it away, he is called a profane person <note>original: "Ruchloser". Translated here from the context of Hebrews 12:16, referring to one who lacks a sense of the sacred.</note> who regards the spiritual and heavenly treasures of grace—presented under such physical symbols—as little or nothing at all. Therefore he is a symbol, indeed a father and mother of all fleshly and earthly-minded people; who for the sake of the lusts of the flesh do not respect the excellence of heavenly things, and thereby also entirely lose their birthright of grace, which has been regained for us by Christ.

But whoever has no eyes to recognize the things of the Spirit of God and the mysteries of the Kingdom of Heaven sees the birthright just as Esau did, and thinks: "I must die anyway; what does the birthright help me then, whether I have it or not! And why should I care much whether I know the mysteries in the Word of God!" In such low esteem are spiritual and heavenly things held by the earthly man. And who or where is that very man? Please, look for him within yourself, and examine impartially your own false estimation, your own lusts and desires, whether you would not rather be something great on earth than a member of the "church of the firstborn." Heb. 12:23.

Conversely, whoever recognizes from God's Word what privilege lies in the birthright, which lasts for all eternity, and at the same time notices that the present world-dish and "lentil-pottage" of vain honor, pleasure, and the like can rob us of this birthright: he applies all diligence so that his crown is not taken from him.

It is, however, an excellent stewardship of God that causes His creatures, even the most rebellious ones, to serve His will. Everything happens as if it were not foreseen, and in the most natural way. God permits Esau to relinquish the right he had over his younger brother himself; and therefore he was allowed to sell it for a trifle, for a dish of lentils. All of this, which seems so improper and absurd, nonetheless serves to carry out the will of God, who does no violence to our freedom, but who leads everything slowly to its end.

***

Our nature is all the swifter, and we may recognize from this event the violence of human desires, which are so much more forceful and impetuous in the presence of their objects. They lead man through all misfortunes, dangers, and the loss of goods and good name.

As soon as Esau sees the lentil pottage, he cries out: "Please give me of this red, of this red [stuff] to eat!" His appetite was so fierce that he did not have the patience even to wait until it was named. And after he had bought it, he flew at it immediately with an impetuous lust. But

An extremely fierce lust, set upon something, when it is not held back by reason and is without the fear of God, turns a rational human being into a truly irrational beast.

How foolish you are, O Esau! That the lentil dish tasted so good to you! O how you will weep when Jacob has taken the blessing! When he attains the crown of the birthright with all its glory! You will yet weep and howl bitterly over it! You will weep loudly when you cannot regain it!

O how great is the loss of such a privilege! How may he come back to the kingdom who has once lost such a thing! Whoever sells his house from this royal city once and has not redeemed it again by the appointed time; he will never come back to such a right of his. He may indeed finally behold the city, and go in and out there: but he has no dwelling within it, because only kings dwell therein.

## Chapter XXVI.
### Isaac’s Experiences Among the Philistines.

But there arose a famine in the land, besides the previous famine that had been in the days of Abraham: and Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, to Gerar.
2. Then the Lord appeared to him, and

When God punishes lands with famine and hunger, He knows how to preserve His own, and often points them to another place where they can be abundantly fed. See Judges 1:1; Psalms 33:19; 34:10, 11; 37:19.

No matter how high a soul may have risen in grace, it must nevertheless frequently experience the withdrawal of that grace, which is a kind of spiritual famine. Yet there are times when this is no longer so burdensome: for although the famine is on the earth—namely, in the <term>sensitive part: the part of the soul related to physical feelings and emotions</term>—one still has something to quiet it. This happens when the soul no longer has a will of its own. Then it suffers no more, because it satisfies God perfectly with His own will.

There is yet another famine: namely, the total cutting off of those very things which seem necessary. This is not spoken of here regarding Isaac; unless we wish to understand the famine as that state which comes when God wants to drive a soul out of itself and completely <term>annihilate: a mystical term referring to the dying-away of the ego or self-will</term> it within Himself. In this case, it was this final lack that brought Isaac, at God’s command, to leave the place where he was.

But where does he go? Into a foreign land: because for a time he finds himself as a stranger even to himself. He remains there as a pilgrim, for he is not there in his true state, which he will find in the place he is meant to possess.

<margin>v. 2. Appeared)</margin> Concerning this appearance, Luther teaches <note>Volume 11, Wittenberg edition, folio 49a.</note> that it is twofold in Holy Scripture: in a dream, and in an external shape or visible form and manner. This appearance did not happen in a dream, but in a visible form, perhaps an angel appearing in the shape of a man. This was a great honor for Isaac, because here God came with a new kind of promise. It also reminds us what a great thing it is for God to appear to a man and direct His promise so specifically to an individual. And after he proves that the Lord also proves Himself through His means and words, he concludes: everything is full of divine appearances and conversations that He holds with you; namely, through His <term>means of grace: traditionally the Word and Sacraments</term>.

It is to be presumed, however, that Isaac, along with the other patriarchs, may have been accustomed to the inward approach and appearance of God in their hearts, which might also be the best and safest way, without fantasy or deception of the senses. There, the Lord made His gracious presence known in a way unspeakable to <term>reason: 'Vernunfft' here often implies worldly or carnal logic as opposed to divine wisdom</term>, and impressed His will and Word upon them so that they became certain of divine communication. Of which the Lord Jesus speaks in John 14:21.

In such a revelation of the divine presence, the Lord dealt so lovingly with His old friends and always showed them His will, so that they could walk forward in divine certainty and knew what they should do or leave undone.

<note>(a) Vol. XI. Witt. fol. 49. a.</note>

He will give this not only to Isaac, but to all those who, like him, sacrifice themselves without exception to His will. And He even promises that there shall be a great number of his descendants who will walk in the way that he has walked.

<margin>v. 3. 4. Thy seed)</margin> Thus the benefit of a godly walk extends even to child and grandchild, and the blessing spreads to so many descendants, especially if they also follow God.

<column-break/>

spoke: You shall not go down into Egypt! Dwell in the land that I shall tell you.

3. Be a stranger in this land, and I will be with you and bless you. For to you and your seed I will give all these lands, and I will confirm the oath that I swore to your father Abraham.

4. And I will multiply your seed like the stars (a) of heaven, and will give your seed all these lands, and in your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed. <margin>ch. 22:18. (a) Dan. 12:3.</margin>

5. Because—

God shows him thereby how he must, above all things, be dead and deceased to earthly things by the power of faith, through which he should choose a better portion. And

Herein lies the beginning of true godliness still before us: that we first turn ourselves away from friendship with the world and from the love of temporal things through true conversion. We must also guard ourselves so that we do not enter into the idolatrous spiritual Egypt and Sodom with our will, where our Lord was crucified and is still daily crucified; namely, into the mind of the flesh and of reason. For in all such abominations, we cannot please or follow God for a single moment. Indeed,

God also forbids His own to seek their nourishment in Egypt—namely, among natural, worldly men—as the sense goes in 1 Thessalonians 4:12: that the believers may walk honestly toward those who are outside, so that they may have need of nothing.

But God wanted to renew for Isaac, in this physical temptation, the great blessing He had given to Abraham, his father, at the sacrifice of Isaac, where he himself had been present and had heard it. Ch. 22:16, 17, 18. At the same time, He sets before him the glorious obedience of his father for him to follow, so as to bring the paternal blessing upon himself. And here the commands of pilgrimage, the statute of circumcision, and the law of love for God and neighbor are distinguished.

This place, and the prohibition that Isaac should not go into Egypt, is very instructive for us. Namely, in the time of withdrawal, even in extreme spiritual famine, one must not support oneself, nor withdraw from the suffering one feels through distraction and one's own strengths. Instead, one must persist with much patience in the place where God has set us, until He Himself delivers us from it. Yet God assures us that He will be with the soul that abandons itself entirely to Him, in whatever place and state it may find itself. For a troubled soul, is not this assurance which God gives it more than enough? He also assures it further that He will give it the promised land: which is the unchanging state called the "transformation into another form."

The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXVI.

# 5. Because Abraham obeyed my voice / and kept my charge / my commandments / my statutes / and my laws. 6. So

---

**Obeyed my voice)** Here we have the clear path for the restoration of that which was lost.

We humans have been torn away from the Creator and our Origin through sin and disobedience. Just as Adam no longer followed the voice of God, he became deaf in his heart, so that he no longer perceived or understood it. If a fallen sinner is to be set right again, he must learn to hear God’s voice once more and follow it.

For this very reason, the Creator now makes His voice audible again and allows it to reach the hearts and consciences of men, so that He may entice them, just as a father entices and draws back his abandoned child through the sound of his fatherly voice.

This voice of the Lord is God’s effective, living Word, which manifests and announces itself in the heart of man. This must be grasped and received into the heart with equal longing; just as God and His Spirit long for us, we must also desire Him in return. For

It is nothing other than the expression and pronouncement of the hidden will or counsel of God regarding how He wishes to make us blessed again: which good intention and purpose of His heart God also discovered and made audible to Abraham.

<margin>(a) <note>original: "Homil. II. in Hexaëm. p. 25."</note> Basil the Great, Homily II on the Hexaemeron <note>The "Hexaemeron" refers to Basil's famous series of homilies on the six days of creation.</note>, p. 25.</margin>
And it is perhaps not even necessary to remind ourselves that this voice of the Lord was nothing external or sensory; rather, as Basil the Great (a) describes it most thoroughly, it is a glance and an inclination of the Will, which is formed into the shape of a commandment so that those who are taught by it may grasp it well.

<margin>(b) <note>original: "L. XI. Confess. c. 9."</note> Augustine, Confessions, Book 11, ch. 9.</margin>
Regarding this voice, Augustine (b) asked there: what is it that begins to shine upon me and strikes my heart? And he concludes from experience: Whoever can hear You (O Voice) speaking inwardly, let him surely make use of it. But he means the divine truth from God's Word, as he further writes: I will also confidently cry out from His word; How great are Your words, O Lord! in Your wisdom.

The unbelieving have never heard this voice of God. John 5:37. Therefore, they do not know what it is, but instead reject everything that has been testified about it through experience in all ages. This is because:

The evil flesh is not at all inclined to follow the voice of the Lord as Abraham did. Therefore, it casts doubt on the discipline of the Holy Spirit, under the pretense that it might be a deception. Yet God presents nothing else to His own than what stands in the Scriptures: as those who give ear to the truth will well realize.

Truly, herein lies the entire communication of the Godhead toward fallen humanity, to whom the Father, through the Son, allows His voice—His word of truth—to reach. This is also nothing other than what stands revealed in the written Word, and which the Lord Jesus, as the Father’s only Word, wishes to constantly open to us, apply to us, and make powerful within us. For the Father lets His voice be heard in His Son. He has not only proclaimed all the counsel of God to us in His Word, but He Himself knocks at the hearts so that they can hear His voice if they are willing. Revelation 3:20.

In short: Everything that God reveals to us for our improvement is God's voice, speech, or explanation. Whoever now submits himself to it, is and is called:

**Obedient)** We must not think of any other obedience than that which happens in true faith. For you will [submit] your will with all confidence into God's will and grace, and give yourself to Him as His own. Therefore, John also points us alone to this great commandment of the Lord in 1 John 3:22-24.

<column-break/>

**Commandments — Statutes — Laws)** These are not empty and useless words that mean only one and the same thing: rather, in each one, a mystery of the will of God is hidden.

Because the Creator has condescended according to the understanding and condition of His corrupted creature, He has made His will known in various ways.

Thus, from the beginning, God gave certain **commandments** which He not only wrote into the heart but also repeated, emphasized, and explained specifically to His friends; and therein all His holy will, as Moses later expressed it specifically in the 10 Commandments.

Yet one may also simultaneously understand by this the special obligations and specific commands or requirements of God, which God presents to a soul according to the circumstances of its inner state or external calling, and demands this or that in particular, which He does not require of others at that time.

This is clearly seen in Abraham’s example. He had the Lord's law in his heart, as it was later recorded externally: and yet God specifically demanded obedience from him in many unusual circumstances.

O how precious this report is for us all, how we also should keep our hearts open to follow all the commandments of the Lord!

It often happens that a believer notices certain requirements and impulses from God’s Spirit in his heart, that he should do this or that according to God's will, which may serve for God's glory and the good of other people. If one then sees this purpose—that it will truly be good—then one should not reject it so carelessly or consult with flesh and blood for long.

For we see that God also wants His special commandments kept: which He praises in Abraham and has richly rewarded him for. This is for our encouragement, so that we may stand ready at every hint and pull of the Lord and His Spirit, like a servant waiting for his master, and saying with Samuel: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears!

So it is also with the **statutes**, which God mentions after the commandments; as He desires His children to be well-disciplined and orderly, and thus prescribes to them the right way in which they should act and walk worthily before Him.

Luther explains this "way" very well as the service of God, which God prescribes to someone, indicating how He wishes to be served. And

So God presented to Abraham exactly the manner in which He wanted to be served by him. There was not only circumcision as a special statute for him and his descendants, but He also taught him His will regarding sacrifices and other matters, and how he should especially interpret everything in light of the coming blessing and the Messiah.

These seemed from the outside to be very minor, even often quite ridiculous things: as one might think of circumcision. Nevertheless, Abraham was so obedient in everything without exception that God here gives him the very best testimony of it.

Similar special ways and prescriptions of how we should serve God are also found in the New Testament, which points us primarily to inner, spiritual worship.

Through the **laws**, the Lord undoubtedly wishes to indicate the entire, perfect will of how He intends to bring the creature out of the Fall and back to the original innocence.

A faithful Christian then does well when he accepts all the counsel of God regarding his salvation—as it spreads through the Old and New Testaments in Law and Gospel—as such a perfect Law of Love, according to which he should direct himself in everything. Thus he will accept all God’s prescriptions as necessary <term>lessons: specifically, spiritual teachings or exercises</term>, and never stumble upon thoughts such as that he were free to choose whether he wanted to follow or not. One will also not look upon this law or the whole word of God with dread, as a commandment in which there is no life; but will gain a delight for it, because all salvation and life lie hidden within it.

Look now at Abraham here, all you who give yourselves out to be his children—namely, as believers and Christians! Has he not received the testimony from God here that he kept God's commandments? And how then do you say that one cannot keep God's commandments? Was he not by nature as weak a human being as we are? What was possible for him, God must and will give to all who only wish to follow Him.

But if we deny that it is possible for us to keep God's commandments, then we cut ourselves off from all of God's blessing.

### Chapter XXVI. The First Book of Moses.

->X 3<-
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

6. So Isaac lived in Gerar.
7. And when the men of that place asked about his wife / he said: (a) She is my sister. For he was afraid to say; She is my wife: lest the men of the place should kill me on account of Rebecca; for she was beautiful to look upon. <margin>(a) chapter 20:2.</margin>
8. And it happened / when he had been there for a long time / that Abimelech / the king of the Philistines / looked through the window: and he saw / and behold / Isaac was sporting <note>original: "scherzte"; implying intimate or playful affection</note> with his wife Rebecca.
9. Then Abimelech called Isaac / and said: Behold / she is surely your wife! How then did you say; she is my sister? And Isaac said to him: Because I thought / I might perhaps have to die because of her.
10. And Abimelech said: Why have you done this to us? It could easily have happened / that someone from the people might have lain with your wife / and you would have brought a guilt upon us.
11. Then Abimelech commanded all the people / and said: Whoever touches this man or his wife / shall surely be put to death.

---

Here Isaac falls into the same temptation and weakness / in which his father failed twice and was placed in danger: Chapters 12 and 20. This shows how children are prone to easily commit the faults of their otherwise godly parents. Yet God did not withdraw His goodness because of such fear of man / but rather rescued him from the danger / and guided the king’s heart toward his protection. Although the king named "the people," he himself might have already been taken with desire for her; yet he also shows some fear of God / in that he forbids his own people from harm. See Psalm 105:14, 15.

v. 7. In a similar occurrence, Isaac gives the very same answer / which his father had also given; when he says / that Rebecca was his sister. Even if this seemed to be untruthful / there was no actual lie to be found here: because "brother" in Hebrew means a relative / and it was customary at that time / to call the closest relatives brothers and sisters; this is also to be understood regarding Rebecca in relation to Isaac / who was her first cousin <note>original: "Geschwister-Kind"</note>: Just as in the Gospel the friends of our Lord JESUS Christ are called his brothers. This manner of speaking / though appearing human / holds great mysteries within it. The inward-turned souls <note>original: "Eingekehrten"; referring to those focused on a mystical or contemplative inner life</note> can sometimes understand such things. And it is so far from darkening the majesty of the divine Word / that it rather makes us honor the same through a greater faith.

v. 8. 9. This charity of Abimelech / in not forming evil thoughts about Isaac / condemns the audacity of those / who immediately criticize everything / and take offense at the most innocent things / which one does in holy freedom.

v. 10. 11. Who would not admire the divine protection of those / who abandon themselves entirely to Him? He takes an interest in all their needs: He causes / that the strongest precautions are taken on their behalf / so that they are not harmed: indeed, He even draws from their faults what may be good and advantageous for them. Was Isaac’s wife not much safer after the king's command / than she had been before?

<column-break/>

12. And Isaac sowed in that land / and received in that same year a hundredfold (a): For the LORD blessed him. <margin>(a) Matthew 13:23.</margin>

13. Thus

---

Isaac was once his father’s faithful follower in faith and his entire conduct. Just as Abraham had experienced in his godly walk / that the blessing of GOD was given to him even physically in the realm of nature / and as it were sprouted and bloomed through the visible: so Isaac experienced it in a similar measure.

There are many more examples of holy people in the Scriptures / and in all histories / to whom GOD also threw in the goods of this world as an addition / because He knew / that they would be good stewards of them. As He also extensively promises in Leviticus 26 <note>original: "3. Mos. 26"</note> / how He wishes to bless the righteous.

But that this does not happen to everyone / we must attribute solely to the providential love of GOD. This love sees in its wisdom / for whom such a temporal thing will be useful or not; who can withstand the temptations that come with it; and who will hang their heart upon it or not.

Meanwhile / wherever He blesses someone in temporal things / He always lays a rod <note>original: "Ruthe"; a tool of discipline or correction</note> beside it / and salts all the peace / that one seeks in the creatures / sensibly enough: so that one might indeed not forget GOD and suffer shipwreck of the faith.

Thus Isaac / despite all his external abundance / nevertheless fell into various adversities: first with Abimelech regarding his wife / then with the shepherds over the wells. This shows us very clearly / that we should not expect or claim such undisturbed and unclouded happiness for our flesh in this world from GOD: but rather / we should learn to dig and search for the true well and fountain of life / JESUS Christ / in whom alone is contentment.

The progress of the Apostolic life is also indicated here. After the soul has long enjoyed rest in GOD / she scatters her seed: of which the fruits are not yet to be seen; but which in the future bears hundredfold fruit.

That Isaac obtained a hundredfold blessing from the seed / and it is said to have yielded even two-hundredfold in Babylonia; shows us / what the blessing of GOD will be capable of on the blessed new earth in Christ’s glorious kingdom: Where then all people will surely be able to be abundantly nourished / even if they all remain alive until the very end of this earth.

But since wealth is also subject to the envy of men through divine blessing / what will that wealth be / which is brought about through all kinds of unrighteous means / which descendants commonly misuse in a curse / whereas a godly Jacob and his children did not misuse their parents' goods / but led a modest, simple life with them. Therefore / it is no human / or quick-witted Christian / wisdom / to strive after the goods of this world / and thereby draw the envy of others upon oneself. See Matthew 6:19, 20; 19:21, 23, 24; 1 Timothy 6:9, 10, 17, 18, 19.

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.

**13. Thus the man became great; and he grew greater and greater / until he became very great:**

**14. So that he had many possessions of small and large livestock / and a great household. Therefore the Philistines envied him.**

**15. And all the wells / which his father's servants had dug / in the time of Abraham his father / the Philistines stopped up / and filled them with earth.**

**16. And Abimelech said to Isaac: Depart from us! for you have become much too powerful for us.**

**17. Then Isaac departed from there / and encamped in the Valley of Gerar / and dwelt there.**

The Philistines seek to hunt a poor pilgrim <note>The author uses "pilgrim" to describe the patriarchs as temporary residents on earth, reflecting the Christian idea of being "in the world but not of it."</note> in the world from one place to another / and thus keep him in unrest / just as Isaac here had to move away from Gerar / because envy could not tolerate him.

What is there to do in this misery / but to hold fast to the covenant of God / just as a ship floating in wild waves is kept steady by the anchor.

The Patriarchs held this as their only refuge / and encamped themselves, as it were, constantly by the Well of the Living and of Joy / waiting for the salvation of God: from which their souls also found enjoyment and great peace.

How faithfully, however, God preserved these dear forefathers from greed and love of the world / that in their whole lives He did not let them possess even a foot-breadth of the land / which He nevertheless promised to them as their own! So much so / that even Abraham had to buy a place for Sarah's burial plot. And Isaac had to wander like a beggar from one place to another.

By this He showed them clearly / that they should not turn or set the slightest desire or pleasure for themselves toward temporal things / but should be and remain pilgrims / both in body and in heart: although they knew for certain / that their descendants would inherit all those same lands.

And so God still deals with those whom He has purchased and chosen from the earth. According to the Word of God, they would have a right and claim to all the good things in the world / and the blessing actually belonged to them by right. But God, through His sharp discipline, does not allow them in their minds to retain the slightest lust for visible goods / or to become infatuated with them / let alone to possess anything as a property. They must only be stewards and administrators for others over such things / if indeed they have anything.

<margin>v. 14. 15. The blessing of spiritual souls draws after it the envy of common souls; because they cannot see that same blessing from their own labor. This happens, however: because they work for themselves / or at least mix much of their self-interest into their spiritual duties; thus they receive no such blessing from their work / as those who have no self-interest. God works alongside where one works only for Him. But if He works / why then should He not also lay His blessing upon His work?</margin>

These self-interested people, however, persecute the Apostolic souls / by stopping up the wells / which faith / represented by their father / had dug. They strive to take the source of the water / which flows from them / and which was dug through the purest faith / while they accuse the same of an evil doctrine. For since they cannot reject their conduct / they nevertheless reject their faith / which they wish to cover with earth; that is / with evil fabrications / which they add to their godly and profound speeches.

<column-break/>

**18. And Isaac had the water-wells dug up again / which they had dug in the days of Abraham / his father / and which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death; and he called them by the same names / that his father had called them.**

**19. Also Isaac’s servants dug in the valley / and found there a well of living water.**

**20. But**

<margin>v. 18. Our Isaac or Savior <note>The author uses "Isaac" here as a "type" or symbol for Jesus Christ.</note> digs up the wells again / which were dug in the Father's time; namely the Law and the Prophets: and shows / that everything / that stands written therein / points to Him and speaks of Him / as the only most perfect well of all salvation and life: which the Philistines / that is / the evil spirits / whether they be visible or invisible / always seek to cover with filth and vanity / so that our poor soul shall not drink its fill and be refreshed.</margin>

Who, however, are actually these Philistines / who stop them up with earth, but those uncircumcised in heart and ears / who / because they are earthly-minded / and possess no other than earthly wisdom of the flesh / are also therefore neither able nor desiring to dig deep into the understanding of the Spirit / but rather stop it up / and also their ears against it.

In this way / and no other / the source-springs of Holy Scripture are stopped up through incorrect interpretation and translation / as well as false glosses <note>A "gloss" is a brief marginal or interlinear explanation of a difficult word or passage.</note> and dark interpretations: so that the people / as they might otherwise well do / cannot draw water with joy from the spring-wells of salvation. And

The servants of God must often leave their work standing / and dig other wells / which always hold within them the waters that faith has found / and are at all times ready to water those with them / who have the good fortune / to be the spiritual children of those / who know how to distribute the same.

One can also observe Isaac's faithfulness / that he makes nothing new / nor changes anything / that has been confirmed through faith: he does not even change the names.

<margin>v. 19. Who are Isaac's servants and shepherds other than the Evangelists and Apostles / with their successors / who dig the wells of the New Testament.</margin>

But the shepherds who prophesy out of their own spirit do not like to let something new / new wells / arise / and also do not like to scour out, clean, and reform the old.

Therefore, the discovery of the precious sources of truth is always made difficult for the faithful shepherds by the earthly-minded shepherds and other worldly-wise people / who immediately stir up pure strife over it / so that they are feuded against and suppressed for that reason. But the Lord will also one day in His time make room for them / so that one can teach confidently / and the truth can be fruitfully proclaimed. See Amos 5:10, 13; Isaiah 57:19; where the Lord will create fruit of the lips / when the right wells of salvation shall be opened: Isaiah 12:3; where the Evangelists go out again into all the world / and their Gospel / more than ever / shall spread into all lands and into the whole breadth of the earth.

In those works / which are done for God's sake / far too many people are found / who credit such things to themselves / and want to have the honor from them: as those shepherds did / who did not know / that there was living water there / until Isaac had revealed it to them. He had no sooner found it / although with great effort; then they quarrel with him / as they want to keep it for themselves. Isaac, however / as the true pattern of all virtues / does not quarrel with them. For he went back / leaving the well to them: whereby he thus fulfilled the Gospel / before it was even there. True love is recognized by the relinquishing of everything otherwise pleasant and necessary to us. Whoever does not prefer peace to property / will lose love for the sake of the property.

# Chapter XXVI. The First Book of Moses.

20. But the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s herdsmen / and said: The water is ours! Therefore he called the well **Esek** <note>original: "Esek" — meaning "Contention" or "Quarrel."</note> / because they had quarreled with him.
21. Then they dug another well: and they quarreled over that one too: therefore he called it **Sitna** <note>original: "Sitna" — meaning "Enmity" or "Opposition."</note>.
22. Then he moved from there / and dug another well: over which they did not quarrel. Therefore he called it **Rehoboth** <margin>(a)</margin> <note>original: "Rehoboth" — meaning "Broad Places" or "Room."</note> / and said: Now the LORD <margin>(b)</margin> has made room for us / so that we may be fruitful in the land. <margin>(a) ch. 26/37. <note>This likely refers to verse 33 or a related cross-reference, as Chapter 26 contains only 35 verses.</note> (b) Ps. 31/8. 66/12.</margin>

Isaac retreats twice / and keeps only the water for himself / which no one wants to dispute with him; because he required still and peaceful waters: and since his soul was set in the vastness of the interior <note>This refers to a state of inner spiritual freedom or "broadness" of the soul, a common theme in mystical Christianity.</note> / it did not need to find anything on the outside that would have restricted it.

The Evangelical preacher must be exactly like this; and especially one who preaches the inward Gospel. He must dig his wells in peaceful places / and not leave such places until GOD Himself provides the opportunity. Since his soul is in that vastness / without being restricted by anything; so he also must not restrict himself in his office. Since the purity of faith and of the Gospel is drawn from GOD Himself / who is all peace; so one must dig his wells / as in those places / in which the water is received quite clearly / and where one can possess it quietly.

v. 20-22. <term>Esek</term> <note>Contention</note> — <term>Sitna</term> <note>Enmity</note> — <term>Rehoboth</term> <note>Broad Space</note>) These three wells also represent the three spiritual states and ages of a Christian: the **Beginners** / the **Advancing** / and the **Perfect**; those of a child / a youth / and a man or father.

1. There is a great struggle between the flesh and the spirit / for the first water of life.

2. Satan opposes the youth in his race / and he encounters hatred, envy, and enmity: which resistance is a name shared with the Devil <note>The Hebrew name "Satan" literally means "adversary" or "accuser," which shares a root with "Sitna."</note>.

3. Through such things we come to expansion and wide space.

Our LORD requires of us / that we should go through narrow ways / before we can come to the vastness. Matt. 7 / 13. 14.

The wellsprings represent the hardships and accidents of our journey. The beginning is occupied with many difficulties; at the end is freedom and expansion.

### 28. And

In all adversities, the LORD always lifts up His own with His promises of grace / so that they feel a very living comfort in their inner being: they then also set up an altar of thanks to the LORD in their heart / and offer up to Him the calves of their lips <note>original: "Farren ihrer Lippen" — a biblical idiom from Hosea 14:2, meaning the sacrifice of praise or spoken prayer instead of animal sacrifice.</note> / which praise His name / and proclaim how much good the LORD has shown them. Hebr. 13 / 15.

Isaac steps here into the godly footsteps of his father Abraham / in that he is immediately mindful of his priestly office / as soon as he has pitched his dwelling anywhere: in order to entice and lead others to the knowledge of the true God with such public proclamation of the name of GOD. See Ch. 12/8. 13/18. 21/33. and 18/19.

v. 24. The LORD appeared to him the night after / when he had received these still waters. In order to better fortify him against all adversity / He says to him: **Fear not! I am the God of your father / and am with you.** He favored him once more with His appearance / to show him / how well it pleased Him that he had practiced in advance that which His Son taught us later: <margin>(a)</margin> **But I say to you; you should not resist / when one does you wrong.** One cannot deny the slightest thing for God's sake / which He would not reward with Himself. And the more we deny ourselves / the more He approaches us.

---

**I am with you / and will bless you**) This is no small advantage of godliness / that GOD is especially present with and stands by such friends of His / so that they can rely entirely on Him. Yes, certainly this is an invaluable jewel / that can make the soul completely satisfied / that GOD wants to be so near / so inward / so familiar and so helpful to her in everything. What distress could be so great / that one could not find comfort / when GOD is so near?

It goes without saying / that GOD'S loving presence is not empty / but creates and brings with it the greatest blessing: just as a great lord never enters anywhere without gifts and grace.

The blessing now is in itself partly physical / partly and primarily spiritual. Yes

This alone satisfies the soul so deeply / that she has no reason or desire to seek anything further.

The Father's love expresses it most dearly in v. 4 through the blessing / in which all nations of the earth should bless themselves or be saved. This blessing is the eternal Savior / the most perfect love of the Father / which cancels every curse / creates nothing but life and peace / and holds all grace and blessing enclosed within itself.

v. 25. The divine assurance moves the Apostolic men / in this place of peace / which they have found / to bring sacrifices to the LORD; to pitch their dwellings there / to remain there / and to carry out everything that GOD shall command there.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.

13. **Thus** the man became great; and he became greater and greater, until he became very great:
14. So that he had many possessions in small and large cattle, and a great household. Therefore the Philistines envied him.
15. And all the wells, which his father's servants had dug in the time of Abraham his father, the Philistines stopped up and filled with earth.
16. **And** Abimelech said to Isaac: Depart from us! for you have become much too powerful for us.
17. **Then** Isaac departed from there, and encamped in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.

The Philistines seek to hunt a poor pilgrim of the world from one place to another, and thus keep him in unrest, just as Isaac here had to move away from Gerar because envy could not tolerate him.

What is now to be done in this misery, other than to hold fast to the covenant of God, just as a ship floating in wild waves is maintained by an anchor.

The Patriarchs considered this their only refuge, and encamped, as it were, constantly by the Well of the Living One Who Sees <note>original: "Brunn des Lebendigen und Schauenden" — a reference to Beer-lahai-roi, meaning "Well of the Living One who sees me."</note>, waiting for the salvation of God: from which their souls also found enjoyment and great peace.

How truly, however, did God preserve these dear ancestors from greed and love of the world, in that throughout their entire lives He did not let them possess a foot-breadth of the land that He nevertheless promised to them as their own! So much so, that even Abraham had to buy a place for Sarah's burial site. And Isaac had to wander from one place to another like a beggar.

By this He showed them clearly that they should not turn or set the slightest desire or pleasure toward temporal things for themselves, but should be and remain pilgrims, both in body and in heart: although they already knew for certain that their descendants would inherit all those same lands.

And so God still deals with those whom He has ransomed and chosen from the earth. According to the Word of God, they would have a right and claim to all good things in the world, and by right the blessing actually belongs to them. But God, through His sharp discipline, does not allow them to keep the slightest pleasure in visible goods in their minds, or to become infatuated with them, let alone to possess anything as a personal property. They must only be householders and stewards for others over such things, if indeed they have anything.

<margin>v. 14. 15.</margin> The blessing of spiritual souls brings the envy of common souls after it; because they cannot see that same blessing resulting from their own labor. This comes about, however, because they work for themselves, or at least mix much of their own self-interest into their spiritual duties; thus they receive no such blessing from their work as those who have no self-interest. God works along with those who work only for Him. But if He works, why then should He not also place His blessing upon His work?

These self-interested people, however, persecute Apostolic souls by stopping up the wells which Faith—represented by their father—had dug. They strive to take the source of the waters that flow from them, and which were dug through the purest faith, by accusing them of false doctrine. For since they cannot condemn their conduct, they condemn their faith, which they wish to cover with earth; that is, with evil fabrications that they add to their godly and profound speeches.

<column-break/>

18. **And** Isaac had the water-wells dug up again, which they had dug in the times of Abraham his father, and which the Philistines had stopped up after Abraham's death; and he called them by the same names his father had called them.
19. **Also** Isaac’s servants dug in the valley, and found there a well of living water.
20. **But**

<margin>v. 18.</margin> Our Isaac or Savior <note>The author interprets Isaac as a "type" or symbolic figure of Christ.</note> digs up the wells again which were dug in the Father's time; namely the Law and the Prophets: and shows that everything written therein points to Him and speaks of Him as the only most perfect well of all salvation and life; which the Philistines—that is, the evil spirits, whether visible or invisible—always seek to cover with filth and vanity, so that our poor soul shall not drink its fill and be refreshed.

But who are these Philistines exactly, who stop them up with earth, other than those uncircumcised in heart and ears? Because they are earthly-minded and possess no wisdom other than the earthly wisdom of the flesh, they are neither able nor do they desire to dig deep into the understanding of the Spirit, but rather stop it up, and their ears as well.

In this way, and no other, the spring-wells of Holy Scripture are stopped up through incorrect interpretation and translation, as well as false glosses and dark explanations: so that the people cannot, as they otherwise might, draw water with joy from the spring-wells of salvation. And

The servants of God must often leave their work and dig other wells, which always hold within them the waters that faith has found, and are ready at all times to water those who have the good fortune to be the spiritual children of those who know how to distribute them.

One can also take note of Isaac's faithfulness, in that he makes nothing new, nor changes anything that has been confirmed through faith: he does not even change the names.

<margin>v. 19.</margin> Who are Isaac's servants and shepherds other than the Evangelists and Apostles, with their successors, who dig the wells of the New Testament.

But the shepherds who prophesy out of their own spirit do not like to see anything new—new wells—arise, and also do not like to scour, clean, and reform the old.

See Amos 5:10, 13; Isaiah 12:3, when the Evangelists shall go out again into all the world, and their Gospel shall spread more than ever into all lands and across the whole breadth of the earth.

In those works that are done for God's sake, all too many people are found who wish to credit themselves for them and have the honor of them: as did these shepherds, who did not know that there was living water there until Isaac had revealed it to them. He had no sooner found it, though with great effort, than they quarreled with him, wishing to keep it for themselves. But Isaac, as the true model of all virtues, does not quarrel with them. For he went back, leaving the well to them: whereby he fulfilled the Gospel even before it was there. True love is recognized by the relinquishing of everything otherwise pleasant and necessary to us. He who does not prefer peace over goods will lose love for the sake of the goods.

->### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.<-

28. And they said: "We see clearly that the **LORD** is with you; therefore we said: 'Let there now be an oath between us, between us and you; and let us make a covenant with you,'
29. That you will do us no harm, just as we have not touched you, and as we have done nothing but good to you and let you go in peace. You are now the blessed of the **LORD**."
30. Then he made them a feast, and they ate and drank.
31. And they rose early in the morning and swore an oath to one another; and Isaac let them go, and they departed from him in peace.

<margin>Here Isaac had to experience what is written in **Proverbs 16:7** <note>original: "Sprüchw. 16/7"; the verse says, "When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him."</note>. Though the adversaries were first filled with nothing but envy and suspicion, after they experienced his upright conduct, they must eventually confess that the believers they drove away were indeed the blessed of the **Lord**. See **Revelation 3:9**, which is taken from **Isaiah 60:14-15**.</margin>
<margin>Even if it might seem as if the spirit of this world wants to gain mastery over a God-fearing person and destroy him, it must often turn around in a wonderful way, so that the adversaries work only toward a more steadfast peace and help to promote the very prosperity of those they once persecuted. Just as Abimelech confirmed a firmer covenant with Isaac after he had ordered him to depart.</margin>

<margin>v. 32. 33. **God** blesses the work of these, His "apostolic workers" <note>The author views Isaac’s servants as symbols of those who spread the Gospel</note>, by promising them that He will increase their children of grace into eternity because of their faith. Therefore, this well dug in peace provides so much water that it deserved to bear this name. Everyone who works in the name of **GOD** will certainly find within themselves the source of living water.</margin>
32. And it happened on that same day that Isaac's servants came and told him about the well they had dug, and said to him: "We have found water."
33. And he called it **Siebeah** <note>original: "Siebeah," meaning "oath" or "seven"</note>: therefore the name of the city is **Beersheba** <note>original: "Ber-Saba," meaning "Well of the Oath"</note> unto this day.

<margin>v. 34. 35. This is the second example of the profanity of Esau <note>original: "Unheiligkeit," referring to his lack of reverence for sacred things</note>, by which he excluded himself more and more from the covenant of God: for these wives of his were strangers to the true worship of God and the teaching of godliness. From this, nothing else could arise but stubbornness and dislike toward their pious parents-in-law, and great distress of spirit for the latter. This stands here as a warning to all such headstrong and profane children, which believers must guard against. See **2 Corinthians 6:14** and also **1 Corinthians 6:16**. Whoever clings to an idolatrous, earthly-minded, and vain woman becomes one body with her.</margin>
34. When Esau was forty years old, he took as wives **Judith**, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and **Basemath**, the daughter of Elon the Hittite.
35. And they were a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebecca.

<column-break/>

<margin>Parents' love for their children is often blind, so that they do not rightly perceive the ways of the **Lord**, what the **Lord** intends for them, or how He judges them. For Isaac certainly knew of the blessing promised by **GOD** to his younger son, Jacob. And yet here he wishes to set the elder as lord over the younger and wants to bestow upon him the blessing of Abraham—which was the blessing of the covenant, as seen in **Chapter 12:3** compared with **verse 29** here—even though it was intended for Jacob over Esau, just as it was intended for Isaac over his older brother Ishmael. Likewise, he did not pay attention to the light-mindedness of Esau, who had despised his birthright and sold it to Jacob, which had undoubtedly become known to him. But the providence of the **Lord** knew how to direct all this marvelously, so that the purpose of the **Lord** according to His righteous and holy election—where He preferred the quiet Jacob over the wild Esau—had to be carried out. This was so even though many weaknesses on the part of Rebecca, Jacob, and also Isaac (who had to be diverted from his intention in this way) were mixed in. Yet **God’s** holiness was not stained by this; He also knew how to discipline these weaknesses with a "domestic cross" <note>original: "Haus-Creuz," a common term for family suffering or trials</note>, so that the parents were deprived of their pious son, and Jacob of his pious parents, for such a long time.</margin>
<margin>And so **GOD** is always accustomed to carry out His counsel through our weakness, as our faults cannot harm **God’s** holiness: so that it may be attributed to **God** alone, who then graciously forgives His own their faults, but also disciplines them as a father because of them.</margin>

## Isaac’s Blessing over Jacob.

---

Rebecca’s conduct is holy, so that one can easily conclude from her example that a soul placed in **God** alone and established in love acts through the inspirations of the Spirit, even if it seems as if she is erring. **God** makes use of the mother's love and the son's faithfulness to remain in solitude to fulfill His will and promises. According to the laws which **God** had given these Patriarchs, everything depended on the father's blessing. **God**, however, allows this to fall upon Jacob in a natural way. In all these things there was no lie (a). The truth of this is found both according to nature and according to the order of grace. Specifically, since Jacob had won the right of the firstborn from his brother: and since he already had it in view of his preference in the inner ways; because he was in a constant union with **God**, and was to be a father of the inner and spiritual men: indeed, since **God** Himself was to be born from him: he could in truth say to his father Isaac, that he was his firstborn son.

<column-break/>

---

If Rebecca undertook this business from divine inspiration, then and to that extent one must put one's hand over one's mouth <note>A common idiom meaning to remain silent or refrain from judgment</note>. Just as human nature and the flesh like to mix themselves in, so besides this, all this cunning, disguise, and false claims were nothing other than lies and deceit; and thus in themselves evil and sin, even though it did not happen for the sake of earthly things, but out of desire for the spiritual and for the sake of something good, as Rebecca sought to obtain by all means the blessing promised to Jacob by **God**. Therefore the rule remains firm, that one shall not do evil so that good may come of it; and the so-called <term>pia fraus</term> <note>original: "pia fraus"; Latin for "pious fraud," a deception intended for a good end</note> or "pious fraud" is sin before **God**, and **God** indeed forgives it for His own for the sake of the good intention, but He also chastises them because of the impermissible means.
Indeed, just as Jacob here deceived his father, so was he later deceived by his children because of Joseph. Chapter 37, 31.

v. 9. **Young goats**) Goat meat was in ancient times held very high and considered a dainty meal among the Hebrews (b). See Leviticus 4:23 <note>original: "3. Mos. 4/23"</note>.
v. 11, 12. Jacob's fear came from his sincerity. Inner souls fear the slightest detour more than death itself. Nevertheless, they are reassured again through obedience. Moreover, an inner and truly-resigned soul, such as Jacob was, lets the matter rest once it has carried out its motives; thereafter surrendering itself without reflection or fear. All faithful and resigned souls follow this same path. Therefore, Providence lets everything succeed for them, even down to their very mistakes. But in these circumstances in which Jacob stood, nothing but pure mysteries were hidden.

**v. 22, 23.** **God** hides the indwelling souls <note>German: *eingekehrte Seelen*, referring to those focused on the inner spiritual life</note> beneath an Esau-skin—namely, under the appearance of ordinary life. There is nothing external about them, nor in their clothing, by which one can distinguish them; language alone makes them known. Worldly creatures speak as creatures, but the sanctified souls have only the Word of **GOD** in their mouths and all speak (a) the same language. All souls may indeed possess Esau’s clothes and skin, but the sanctified souls alone possess Jacob’s voice. It is impossible to instill another language into such souls than the one **God** has taught them. They are helpful to all people and accommodate themselves very willingly to everything that is not against **GOD**; however, one cannot make them change their language. O holy Patriarch Isaac! How could you hope to know Jacob by hearing, when he is always the same? Did you not know that his voice alone could make him known to you? But perhaps you let this matter proceed—even though you recognized the voice of Jacob—because you recognized the will of **GOD** and acted as the order of Providence required. Yet one must adhere to the Holy Scripture here, which says you did not recognize him, as **GOD** allowed it to be so in order to fulfill His will.

And finally, the spiritual blessing is promised to him, from which the source of blessing would spring for all people, of which he would then be the first to partake. This occurred in Christ, who was to be born of his descendants, and thus from his loins. With this, the priesthood was also transferred to him, which is the great privilege and dignity of the faithful even into eternity.

**v. 27-29.** In this blessing, Isaac proceeds step-by-step: first, he promises the physical blessing, with which **God** is accustomed to entice mankind <note>referring to the Prophet Hosea 14:17 in the original text, likely an error for verse 7 or 8</note>, and which also belonged to the goods of the land in the Old Testament, where they were promised a land flowing with milk and honey. Afterward, dominion is promised to him: not only over other nations, such as the Philistines, Syrians, Moabites

---

Just as Jacob was blessed under the name and clothes of his firstborn brother, so we are blessed by the heavenly Father in Christ's name and the robe of righteousness granted by Him. Isaiah 61:10.

**v. 29. You)** Namely, in the lineage of his descendants.

He sets him over his brothers and over his mother’s children. Precisely in this, the contemplative life <note>the quiet, prayerful life</note> is far higher than the active life, and is rightly preferred over it; according to the testimony of **JESUS** Christ himself, which he gave to Mary Magdalene: "Mary," he says, "has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her."

This passage also truly shows how sensitive **God** is when the self-loving <note>those motivated by ego</note> cry out against these inner ways and persecute those who stand in the contemplative life. He threatens his curse upon those who mistreat them; those, however, who honor such people and follow them, he will shower with blessings. For there are no other souls whose love is more purified. None are more pleasing to Him—indeed, so pleasing that He calls them men after His own heart and looks upon them as the apple of His eye; because they, by surrendering themselves without exception to His entire will, give Him the opportunity to rule over everything within them.

### Chapter XXVII. The First Book of Moses. ###

33. Then Isaac trembled (a) with a very great trembling beyond measure and said: "Who was it then that hunted venison and brought it to me? And I have eaten of everything before you came and have blessed him. He shall also remain blessed." (a) Dan. 10:11.

---

Isaac’s conscience awakens, leading him to recognize the wonderful governance of **GOD**. He realizes that the blessing was intended by **GOD** for Jacob, as he could have sufficiently gathered from the clear revelation regarding the state of these two sons. Therefore, he submits himself to the counsel of **GOD** and denies his natural affection. This was the "Fear of Isaac" before **GOD** <note>The "Fear of Isaac" is a specific biblical title for God used in Genesis 31:42</note>, upon which Jacob later relied and used as an oath, so that this **GOD** would also be his fear and his confidence, Chap. 31:42, 53.

... The Prophets do not always possess the spirit of prophecy, and their natural actions often serve in the hands of **GOD** to carry out His mysteries. It is nonetheless believable that he recognized at that time the wonderful mystery hidden beneath it. This worked in him a constancy, so that he did not change anything of what he had done and stood by it: always to subject Esau—who represents the active life—to Jacob, who signifies contemplation <note>The author is using an old spiritual distinction: the "active life" (outward works and labor) must be servant to the "contemplative life" (inner prayer and focus on God).</note>.

**He shall also remain blessed.)** According to the choice of the Most High **GOD**, who takes more pleasure in being still and remaining at home within oneself than in much hunting.

Because Isaac now saw and perceived from all circumstances that this choice—even against his own mind and opinion—had prevailed so far that he himself had to seal it through the blessing; so he would not now revoke, change, or overturn what he had once spoken according to **GOD’s** mind and impulse. This regret—or rather the penance that Isaac might have felt—Esau indeed sought with tears; of which also the Epistle to the Hebrews 12:17 speaks. But with all his begging and shedding of tears, he could not soften his father or bring him to other thoughts, to make him regret it; rather, he remained firm that Jacob should keep the glory and the privilege of the birthright and be the blessed of the **Lord**.

This blessing among the holy Patriarchs was something quite extraordinary, prophetic, and, as it were, their testament. It was granted only to those who, as heirs, were to be partakers of those promises given to Abraham and his seed, and who were to be counted among **GOD’s** people. Therefore, Ishmael was not permitted to inherit with Isaac. Such a blessing, which the wonderfully-governing hand of **GOD** had turned toward Jacob, Isaac then confirms with these words rather than wishing to revoke them: because Jacob had chosen and seized the best lot of a sweet savor before **GOD** and the "best part" with Mary <note>A reference to Luke 10:42, where Mary chooses the "better part" by sitting at Jesus' feet while Martha works.</note>, it should not be taken from him again.

Isaac does not even regret this error, just as Rebecca bears no sorrow over this committed "apparent sin"; because souls standing in **GOD** can see nothing outside of Him. Therefore, they can attribute nothing to the creature; rather, they climb higher and make use of all this in a divine manner. One of the surest signs of whether a soul is truly in **GOD** is this strange immovability of the spirit even in those things that cause the most shame.

<column-break/>

34. When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried out loud with a great and exceedingly bitter cry and said to his father: "Bless me, yes even me, my father!"

35. But he said: "Your brother came with guile and has taken away your blessing."

36. Then he said: "Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has now tripped me up twice. He took my birthright, and see, now he also takes my blessing!" And he said: "Have you then kept no blessing for me?"

37. Then Isaac answered and said to Esau: "Behold, I have set him as lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants! I have also provided him with corn and wine: what shall I now do for you, my son?"

38. And...

---

Thus Esau learns that he has accomplished nothing with all his hunting.

**v. 34.** When Esau, armed with his hunting, sought to move his father to change his mind and give him the blessing of the birthright, these were not tears of true repentance or remorse for having valued his birthright so little, or for having truly taken to heart his wickedness and wild disposition, and that **GOD** had justly deprived him of this privilege. For it stands in His free power to give His special grace to whom He wills; about which man cannot argue with **GOD**, because **GOD** owes him nothing: as these righteous ways of **GOD** are demonstrated by the Apostle in Romans 9:10-21 and Hebrews 12:16-17. *Lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. For you know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place for repentance* (or regret—namely, in his father, that he would have changed his will; from which the fear of **GOD** held him back) *though he sought it carefully with tears.*

**Yes even me)** *Sam ani* <note>Original: "Sam ani". This is likely a transcription of the Hebrew *Gam ani*, meaning "Also I".</note> is the Nominative: I, I am he! I am also your son, my father! His words are interrupted by his passion.

**v. 36.** The name Jacob, which means a "supplanter" <note>German: *Untertreter*, literally "one who steps under" or trips another up</note>, had been given to this patriarch because at birth he held the heel of his brother. Here Esau makes use of this to complain that his brother has deceived him with guile. It is true that Jacob gains the upper hand. However, this happens rightly: because it is due to him for the sake of so many privileges.

**v. 37.** Notwithstanding Esau’s complaint, Isaac nevertheless confirms that which he has done, and says once more that he subordinates the active life to the contemplative life. For although the active life is necessary and also has its use, it nevertheless regards the contemplative life as its perfection and end-goal: since all good works have their aim in the enjoyment of **GOD**, which is precisely the inheritance of contemplation. Therefore, it is said that the elder shall be subject to the younger: because the active life is the first to be led. But it is so subordinate to that contemplative life which follows it, just as the means are lesser than that for which they are dedicated.

Therefore, he submits himself to the counsel of God and denies his natural affection. This was the "Fear of Isaac" before God, upon which Jacob later relied, and which he even used for an oath: that this God might also be his fear and confidence. Chapter 31:42, 53.
... The prophets do not always possess the spirit of prophecy, and their natural actions often serve in the hands of God to carry out His mysteries. It is nevertheless believable that he then recognized the wonderful mystery hidden beneath it. This worked in him a steadfastness, so that he changed nothing of what he had done and stood by it: to always subject Esau, who represents the **active life**, to Jacob, who signifies **contemplation**. <note>The author uses "active" and "contemplative" as technical terms in mystical theology; the active life involves outward works, while the contemplative life involves inward focus on God.</note>
**He shall remain blessed.** According to the choice of the Most High God, who finds more pleasure in being still and remaining at home within oneself than in much hunting.
Because Isaac now saw and perceived from all circumstances that this choice—even against his own mind and opinion—had prevailed so far that he himself had to seal it through the blessing, he would not revoke, change, or overturn what he had once spoken according to God’s mind and impulse. Esau sought this regret (or rather a change of mind <note>The text distinguishes between mere regret and true "penance" or *Busse*</note> which might make Isaac sorry) with tears, of which the Epistle to the Hebrews 12:17 also speaks. But with all his begging and shedding of tears, he could not soften his father or bring him to other thoughts so that he might regret it; rather, Isaac now remained firm that Jacob should keep the glory and the privilege of the birthright and be the blessed of the Lord.
Among the holy patriarchs, this blessing was something quite special and prophetic, serving as their testament. It was granted only to those who were to be participants and heirs of the promises given to Abraham and his seed, and who were to be counted among God’s people. Therefore, Ishmael was not permitted to inherit with Isaac. Such a blessing, which the wonderfully-ruling hand of God turned toward Jacob, Isaac confirms with these words rather than revoking them: because Jacob had chosen and seized the best lot of a "good scent" <note>An allusion to the smell of Jacob's clothes in verse 27</note> before God and the "better part" with Mary, so also should it not be taken from him.

<column-break/>

34. When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried aloud with an exceedingly great and bitter cry, and said to his father: "Bless me, even me also, my father!"
35. But he said: "Your brother came with guile <note>original: *List*</note> and has taken away your blessing."
36. Then he said: "Is it not because his name is called Jacob? For he has now tripped me up <note>original: *untertreten*</note> twice. He took my birthright, and behold, now he also takes my blessing!" And he said: "Have you then reserved no blessing for me?"
37. Then Isaac answered and said to Esau: "Behold, I have set him as lord over you, and all his brothers I have given to him as servants! I have also provided him with corn and wine: what shall I do for you now, my son?"
38. And

---

Thus Esau learns that with all his hunting, he has accomplished nothing.
**v. 34.** When Esau armed himself and sought to move his father to change his mind and give him the blessing of the birthright, these were not tears of true repentance or remorse—not that he had esteemed his birthright so lightly, or truly taken to heart his wickedness and wild spirit, or realized that God had justly deprived him of this privilege. For it stands in God's free power to give His special grace to whom He will; man cannot dispute with God over this, for God owes him nothing. These righteous ways of God are demonstrated by the Apostle in Romans 9:10–21 and Hebrews 12:16–17: *that there be no fornicator or profane person like Esau, who for one morsel of food gave up his birthright. For you know that afterward, when he wanted to inherit the blessing, he was rejected. For he found no place for repentance* (or regret, namely on his father's part, to change his will; from which the fear of God held him back) *though he sought it with tears.*
Isaac, however, does not regret this error even once, just as Rebecca bears no sorrow over this "apparent sin" committed; for souls standing in God can see nothing outside of Him. Therefore, they can attribute nothing to the creature, but they climb higher and make use of all this in a divine manner. One of the surest signs of whether a soul is truly in God is this singular immovability of spirit even in those very things that cause the most shame.
**Even me also)** *Gam ani* <note>original Hebrew: *gam ani* (also I / me too)</note> is the nominative: "I, it is I! I am also your son, my father!" His words are interrupted by his passion.
**v. 36.** The name Jacob, which means a "supplanter" <note>original: *Untertreter*</note>, had been given to this patriarch because at birth he held onto his brother’s heel. Here Esau makes use of it to complain that his brother has deceived him with guile. It is true that Jacob gains the upper hand. But this happens by right, because it is due to him on account of so many privileges.
**v. 37.** Notwithstanding Esau's complaint, Isaac nonetheless confirms that which he has done, and says once more that he places the "active life" after the "contemplative life." For although the active life is necessary and has its uses, it nevertheless looks to the contemplative life as its perfection and end goal: since all good works have their aim in the enjoyment of God, which is precisely the inheritance of contemplation. Therefore it is said that the elder shall be subject to the younger: because the active life is the first to be led. But it is so subordinate to the contemplative life that follows it, just as means are lesser than the purpose for which they are dedicated.
