# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXVIII.
<page-num>180</page-num>

### 17. And he was afraid / and said:
### How dreadful is this place! This is

Jacob received such a deep impression in his soul from this majestic appearance of **God** and His holy angels / that he was afraid / and, as it were, trembled in his weak nature before this heavenly opening.

This is a wonderful effect of the divine presence and revelation / that it commonly impresses a shudder or horror upon man. This happens, however, not so much on **God’s** part / who gladly approaches in love and refreshment; but rather through the guilt of the human heart / which through the Fall has become so estranged and unaccustomed to divine communion / that it immediately falls into terror at the slightest outburst of divine majesty. This is because the uncleanness within a person is then awakened and stirred / so that the person sees himself in **God’s** light as unclean and base and is terrified by it.

Yet it could also simply mean here that a holy awe and reverence arose within Jacob before the majestic **God** / who had appeared to him / wherein there might have been no actual terror.

This much is certain / that Jacob fell into a deep sensation of the divine majesty and His presence / which worked a powerful *alteration* <note>original: "alteration"; meaning a profound inner change or transformation.</note> or change in him / so that he broke out into these wondering words:

<margin>Gen. 28, 17.</margin>
How dreadful is this place! That is: how venerable / or what reverence is this place worthy of! How cautiously and reverently one must behave in such a place / where the **Lord** works so powerfully!

This may serve as excellent news for us / that we should by no means become impudent and proud / or despise others / when the **Lord** shows us His holy presence in grace / or gives other marks of His special friendship-love. For it happens all too easily / that one secretly imagines something of oneself because of it / and clings more to the gift than to the Giver. **God** must commonly give His glimpses of grace so sparingly for this reason / or else take them away again quickly.

If one senses something good from **God** / let it serve for humble awe and veneration of **God** / so that one bows ever more before Him in one's misery and unworthiness / like Jacob / who was not proud / but was afraid or felt a childlike shyness.

His exclamation then also occurred as a consequence of the knowledge given to him of the dreadful sufferings / through which all those chosen souls / who wish to reach the door of heaven / must pass. For what else was dreadful at this door? And should he not rather / since he beheld the victory of glory / have been placed in joy and admiration over it? Yet on the contrary he cries out: how dreadful is this place! This expresses nothing less than the House of **God** and the Gate of Heaven. Should he not rather have said in the common way: Oh, what a desirable place this is! How lovely and pleasant it is / since it is the House of **God** and the Gate of Heaven! But because he felt more of it in that moment than he was permitted to speak / he let it rest with this speech. He knew all that was to be suffered / and all the strange ways through which **God** leads souls in order to bring them to the door of heaven. But he says nothing further of it / because they are mysteries of which (a) man may not speak.

If anyone wishes to be Jacob's true successor in faith / let him learn poverty and lowliness of spirit even amidst the greatest gifts.

A place is all the more dreadful / (writes *Bernard* (b) <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153).</note>) the more certain and clear the **Lord** is there: namely, where not just two or three / but so many are gathered in His name; yes, where the holy angels and the **Lord** Himself are present: but only / where we serve Him in spirit and truth. And

This is nothing other than God's House!) He could not have understood this as an external house / as the idolatrous nature interprets it only as external church-buildings / contrary to the clear sense of the Spirit. For

There was no house built there at that time. Necessarily, he must therefore speak of a spiritual house. Especially since he had also had the vision internally in his heart.

<meta>(a) 2 Corinthians 12:4. (b) *Sermon VI on the Dedication of a Church, page 350.*</meta>

<column-break/>

### nothing other than God's House / and
### this is the gate of heaven!
-> 18. And <-

He calls it a house / a permanent dwelling / to indicate / that **God** wishes to dwell and walk among His own for eternity / because they are eternal spirits / and not fragile huts like external houses.

In that very place **God** opens His heaven / where He Himself has His spiritual house in the heart. Within us, heaven shall be opened to us / and internally the **Lord** wants to make Himself known to us / there where His kingdom is within us.

Where such souls then also come together / or are simply united in spirit; there He is in their midst as if in His temple. Ephesians 2:22.

But we should / writes *Luther* (a) thoughtfully / not place the true dignity of the Church in such shameful, foolish things that are worth nothing; as those do who dream that the Church should be a physical assembly.

**God’s** house is such a place where **God** dwells. (These are again Luther’s beautiful words.) But where does **God** dwell? Is it not true that He dwells in heaven? Therefore, He sets the earth to heaven and heaven to the earth / and thus binds the two together. He sets the heavenly dwelling and the kingdom of **God** there where the way to heaven goes. Yes / what is even more / Jacob senses / that he is already now in the kingdom of heaven and lives within it.

If this were not so / Jacob could not have said here / that **God’s** house was on earth. For **God’s** house is indeed heaven. Where **God** is / there is heaven: and where heaven is / there is blessedness. But now **God** is certainly with His believers / even here on earth. Necessarily, then, **God’s** house must also be there / where **God** Himself is and dwells with His loving presence. Necessarily, then, heaven must already stand open here to the believers.

Oh, how necessary it is to note this against the delusion of dull irrationality / which seeks heaven only up there above the stars / and wants to enter it from the outside / but does not desire heaven within itself / nor believes that it is so near; yes, which thinks / only after death / and certainly not before / might one come into **God’s** heaven!

Alas, heaven is truly on earth in the believers / but it is not grasped or recognized by the earth or the earthly mind. Whoever learns to despise the earthly / and to take heaven by force; he breaks in: otherwise no one. For

This is the gate of heaven) of which Jacob says here / which the **Lord JESUS** describes as one that few find: namely, the narrow gate.

What does it then depend upon on our part / other than a courageous approaching in faith to grace / an earnest knocking at the door of the Kingdom of **God** or at the heart of the Father?

He who knocks loudly / to him it will be opened all the sooner. He who uses force / and even tears the door open; he finds the path clear.

This gate is not perhaps bound here or there only to certain places or circumstances / but everywhere and at all times all blessedness is prepared for us and at the door of the heart / so that we do not first need to travel up into heaven / but can have everything near at hand.

Jacob truly meant such an inner door. For he found heaven open before him everywhere / wherever he only dealt with his **God**. And

How gladly **God** would open His whole kingdom of heaven to all people / if they were only capable of it! But for the most part, they bind their heaven to mere external things / and seek to hit the gate with habitual ceremonies: there / they think / is the entrance into heaven.

Oh, that we would notice the true advantages / how this heavenly gate could remain constantly open to us!

The best thing may be / to be watchful and sober in the mind / and learn to lead one’s conduct in that heaven which reveals itself in the heart / where Father, Son, and Spirit / have their temple / and give their glory / wisdom / truth / holiness, and love / to be enjoyed.

Oh, well for those / who thus let the gates of righteousness be opened to them / so that they enter therein as the righteous / who preserve the faith / and thus surely hit the gate!

<meta>(a) *Commentary on this passage, folio 143. a.* Catchword: This</meta>

It emphasizes that heaven is accessible on earth through faith and inner devotion, rather than through external rituals or post-mortem travel.</summary>

<header>Chapter XXVIII. The First Book of Moses.</header>

## 18. And Jacob rose early in the morning / and took the stone he had placed at his head / and set it up as a pillar / and poured oil on top of it. <note>1 Peter 2:4; Acts 10:38.</note>

<margin>
**Beth-El.**
**Lus.**
Judges 1:23.
</margin>
## 19. And he called that place **Beth-El**: but before that, the city was named **Lus**.

This may sufficiently refute those who maintain that Jacob had this dream on Mount Moriah. For **Beth-El** lay far from Jerusalem, in the tribe of Ephraim.

<margin>v. 18. As a pillar)</margin>
Nothing was done by him here out of idolatry or a superstitious infatuation with the stone or the place: rather, he was concerned with the matter itself, which he signaled with such circumstances according to the custom of the time, also secretly pointing to the future Messiah or Anointed One.

Doubtless, he anointed the stone with oil out of a secret purpose, so that he might signify **Christ**, the stone anointed for us: says Gregory of Nazianzus <note>original: "Gregorius Nazianzenus"</note> (a).

This was no idolatry, says Eucherius (b). For he did not frequently return there afterward to worship the stone or to offer sacrifices to it. Instead, it was a sign of prophecy concerning the anointing of the Messiah.

Furthermore, this monument was to serve as a memorial for his descendants, of what happened to Jacob there and what he recognized there. Just as he himself would have often thought of the grace enjoyed here. And

It is a great advantage when a believer carefully notes those circumstances in which **God** has allowed him to experience a particular grace.

For example: **God** might give someone a strengthening of their faith on a specific occasion, or He might powerfully turn their mind away from the world at a certain time, in this or 그 place, through this or that instrument of **God**, etc. One should not simply cast this to the wind or immediately forget it: rather, because we tend to be very frivolous in spiritual matters anyway, we do well to set up certain landmarks in our minds, as it were, so as not to forget the good the Lord has done.

Indeed, even if we had nothing else by which we could rightly notice **God’s** presence, our heart is witness enough for us. Certainly, so many wonders of **God** occur within it—if we pay attention—that we would have enough to learn from them. For

Let everyone believe this for certain: all the divine stirrings toward good that one notices within oneself—spiritual devotion, comfort, rest, joy, and other divine encouragements, communications, and powers—are pledges of the presence and nearness of **God** and His kingdom or heaven.

One should carefully learn to collect and polish all these things like pearls and treasures, so that from the first enlightenment one might grow further into greater firmness, and from one clarity to another, being transformed into His image by the Spirit of the **Lord**, and thus dwelling and remaining in the true heaven.

The oil which he poured upon it he may have had with him for nourishment on the journey: which he now gladly gave up, since he had been so gloriously strengthened by **God**.

This was, however, an image of anointing, which may have been common at altars; according to which Christ would be the true anointed Altar, Sacrifice, and Priest.

<margin>v. 19. Lus)</margin>
Named for the many almond trees that stood there. **Ulam Lus** <note>A combination of Hebrew words often interpreted in older commentaries to contrast "the porch" with "perversity."</note> actually means: the hall of perversity. The hall is the entrance into the true temple of **God**, and is the fear of **God**, which is the beginning of wisdom: which fear is neglected and despised. From this then proceeds adultery, murder, (chap. 20:11), indeed all perversity.

But when the fear of **God** drives out sin, then Jacob calls the name **Beth-El** <note>Hebrew: "House of God"</note>. And in this, the first disciples of Christ dealt with one another. Acts 2:43, 5:11, 12.

If we therefore find ourselves in **Lus**, in perversity and sin; we must enter into **Ulam**, into the hall, and pray to the **Lord** that He might plant us in His fear: then we shall become **Beth-El**, the House of **God**.

<column-break/>

## 20. And Jacob made a vow / and spoke: If **God** will be with me / and

<margin>If **God** will)</margin>
To many, these words of Jacob seem, according to human reason, like a distrustful speech against **God**, as if the good man doubted **God’s** providence and had decided within himself not to serve **God** unless He gave him such temporal things.

But we must not judge Jacob’s honest heart so poorly, but rather reflect on how faithfully and blamelessly **God** dealt with him, and how, in turn, Jacob proved himself toward Him.

Jacob’s meaning must therefore only have been this: that he wished and longed in his heart to actually experience all the goodness of God for himself, which he had heard his parents and ancestors praise, and thereby to strengthen and assure himself all the more in **God’s** service and love.

**God** had given him such great and precious promises here, and had even deemed him worthy of such a glorious vision: how then could the dear Jacob still be so distrustful toward the love of **God** revealed to him so highly and certainly, that he would not want to cling to **God** until he had returned home rich and healthy? Is it not enough witness to his honest faithfulness toward **God** that he did not want to seek his future maintenance according to the way of the world and mere reason, but that he wanted to have everything from **God** alone?

All circumstances therefore show that this speech of Jacob flowed from a childlike trust in **God’s** love, and must also be accepted and used by us as such.

One need only look into dear Jacob’s believing heart to see how his whole mind was directed toward and thirsty for **God** alone, as the eternal, only sufficient good and life of his soul! How simply, how directly and purely he turns his all toward **God** in His hidden kingdom, which was opened up within his soul! How sincere was his conclusion for his whole life!

Consider the trust he placed in his heavenly Father after he had been forced to leave father and mother out of necessity and now saw nothing before him. There the enemy might well have shot many dangerous suggestions like arrows into his heart—that he should seek his fortune in the world, as the world says, with cunning or force, with a life and actions pleasing to the world. But

His eyes look so directly at the **God** revealed to him, that he gathers his heart into this one thing: that he will fear His name. And for this he asks **God** for grace, and wishes for nothing more than **God’s** communion and friendship.

**(If **God** will be with me)** he says: If only the **Lord** will be with me / then I have enough / then I also want to be with Him.

How beautiful it would be to learn from Jacob here, that in all one’s circumstances one should make a similar conclusion in one’s heart: Now I will also seek and love **God** alone, as the only eternal life! Especially where **God** has allowed someone to know and taste in a gracious way how friendly He is. There the conclusion should rightly always emerge: So shall the **Lord** now be my **God**!

Thus, when Jacob desired here that **God** would be with him; he threw himself with great trust into the sea of **God’s** love: he wanted to be surrounded, enclosed, and captured by **God**, so that he might remain eternally in Him, and **God** in his soul.

Thus he also sought all necessary strength, wisdom, delight, and refuge in **God**. All this he wanted to have with and in **God** near him, yes, within himself, as a perfect treasure of all good, of all necessity of body and soul.

There was no other meaning among the dear ancients when they so earnestly relied upon and called upon **God** to be with them.

---

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Jacob’s vow at Bethel from Genesis 28. While the header incorrectly identifies the chapter as XXIX (29), the text concludes the reflection on verses 20 and 21 of chapter 28, focusing on Jacob’s request for God's protection and basic sustenance.</meta>

<page-num>182</page-num>
<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXIX.</header>

### ...and keep me in this way that I go, and give me bread to eat and clothes to put on;

---

<margin>
Bread to eat / and clothes to put on) Jacob does not seek his nourishment from reason, nor from his own strength, but alone from God's hand. And
</margin>

This was by no means a distrustful speech, as if he did not trust the eternal God for a piece of bread and only wanted to test whether God would be able to nourish him. It is rather to be viewed as a most contented prayer, wherein Jacob declared before God how he would be gladly satisfied with the humblest treatment. For

It is well to note that Jacob does not beg God for delicate foods or fine clothes, but only for bare daily bread and a covering for this old <term>bag of worms</term> <note>original: "Madensack." A common Baroque-era German term used to emphasize human mortality and humility before God.</note>.

Take good note, says <note>original: "Bernhardus"</note> Bernard of Clairvaux (a), he asks only for clothes as a covering. Thus should we also be content with clothes that merely cover us, not so that we may strut in pride or indulge in luxury, or even to make ourselves equal to and pleasing to women.

That was the great wisdom of the ancients: they lived so contentedly and simply, seeking neither splendor nor superfluity. Therefore, they were not only healthy, strong, and active in the body, but also calm, sober, and wise in the spirit.

Furthermore, this is a precious example: that we should not seek our nourishment according to the course and mind of the evil world, thereby gaining a bad conscience and an ungracious God; but rather, with Jacob, fetch everything from the rightful Father. Just as a pious child does not steal from others, but goes straight to his father and seeks there what he needs.

This reveals God’s great faithfulness: when we notice his providence even in the smallest things. Oh, how that may mightily strengthen our faith, so that we can trust Him for everything even in greater matters!

Thus, both the poor and the rich may let this serve as a great awakening, so that they may learn to know God better from his internal and external governance.

A poor person has to consider whether he has not at least received his morsel of bread and clothes for necessity, however meager it might seem. For God owes us no more than necessity, even though he always provides much more from his good treasury.

If God has given everyone until now—even the poorest—bread to eat and clothes to put on, so that no one has had to die of hunger or go naked; why, then the conclusion must rightfully follow: that one recognizes the Lord as his God.

Certainly, the poorest and most miserable should learn to seek and grasp their God all the more fervently, because they have so many pledges of his providence—so many morsels of bread that God, as it were, puts into their mouths. For it must necessarily follow: If God gives me bread, then I will give him my heart. But if he gives me everything and himself, then I must also be entirely his own.

How much more, however, should the rich—or those who at least have enough left over—make this resolution: "God has given me bread and clothes; so he shall also be my God." For the Lord seeks this: that he be thus recognized by his creatures.

If many fathers or mothers of households were to calculate and say where they got so much to spend, and were to hold their income against it, they would have to confess it would have been impossible without God's special blessing. God alone did it. So he alone should now be the God of all people, and not the belly, nor the spirit of the world.

This foundation is just as true in spiritual matters: that God should be our God because he so powerfully provides for, feeds, and clothes our souls. And so the resolution should be in our hearts generally: Because God does so much good for my soul, he shall be my God, and no stranger, no idol.

---

<margin>(a) Letter 2 to Fulk, p. 1419.</margin>

<insert>
...preserved on such a dangerous and slippery road; but if I immediately give myself blindly to his providence, even for a long time, I can still have no true assurance and experience of my Father’s house—namely, in the rest of my origin—knowing that I would receive instability.
</insert>

<column-break/>

### 21. and I) come again to my father’s house in peace; and

---

With this, Jacob also asks for the governance and guidance of God, which he, as it were, makes a condition: he does not want to govern himself, or arrange his affairs according to his own will; as human nature often presumes to do, considering it a great pleasure to govern and provide for itself.

Jacob had already learned this much through the Holy Spirit and diligent instruction: that a person is in a bad way if he wants to provide for and lead himself. Therefore, he left it to God and wished for himself—in recognition of his impotence and ignorance—the pure governance of God over body and soul.

And it will also be to our advantage if we allow ourselves to be increasingly captured and convinced by the truth of how unfit we are to lead ourselves.

If one learns early to bow under God's discipline with Jacob, before one is made wise by suffering; then one also calls upon the dear God for his guidance quite earnestly and humbly, and requests that He himself might bring one home again with peace to the true fatherland, through the difficult wilderness of this world.

Whoever has sometimes gone astray and run into trouble will not begrudge praying with David more diligently than before: "Send your light and truth, that they may lead me and bring me to your holy dwelling, where my true home is, from which my soul departed!"

And this applies not only to inner guidance—where many a person may finally confess that one had to be led by God—but also externally, nothing fruitful can happen, much less can the entire course of life be uprightly completed, without the sole governance of God and his Spirit.

But whoever wants to submit to this must be prepared for very contrary and strange paths that God will walk with him. We must not imagine such governance of God, which Jacob wished for here, to be sweet and comfortable for the flesh!

Just reflect a little on the guidance of Jacob. How strange things often looked for him! God indeed did honestly what he requested here and brought him home again, not only in peace but also with blessing and wealth. But my! How wonderfully was poor Jacob tossed about before he came home thus! What did he not have to endure with Laban, and with Esau! Yet God kept and delivered to him what he had asked for.

O, what blessed news for us all, that we should not imagine any paradise for our flesh under God's governance, thinking: "Whoever God governs has nothing but good days." No, the cross is right in the middle of it, yet it does not hinder or cancel God's providence.

The more "colorful" <note>The author uses "bunt" (colorful/variegated) to mean chaotic, complex, or unpredictable.</note> God sometimes allows things to go for a person, the more certain is God's governance there. He seeks to make his honor great in this: that his counsel is wonderful, and yet he brings it out gloriously. We must not be frightened by this. Where he is most present, he often does not wish to reveal it, but rather exercises the faith that has entrusted itself to him.

Therefore, the nature of the knowledge with which one is occupied regarding these so dark paths is prone to make one fearful and to doubt. In the way of faith and <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A key Pietist/mystical term meaning "yieldedness" or "letting go" to God's will.</note>, one can linger neither upon visions, nor words, nor tendernesses, nor whatever else might want to make one secure. For this security would delay the course. Therefore, Jacob said—because he had been taught for himself as well as for us—without lingering over what he had seen, nor over what God had spoken with him, he then went through everything with courage, only to dwell upon the holy moment of providence, which is the only assurance without assurance for yielded souls within themselves: "If God will be with me, and if he will lead me through his providence, so that he preserves me from sin..."

...then I shall recognize that he is my God; I shall then be at rest, while the darkness of this way keeps me always in a cer[tain]...

...and so the LORD shall be my God:
22. Then this stone, which I have set up for a pillar,

<column-break/>

shall become a house of God; and of all that you give me, I will constantly give the tenth to you!

---

<columns>2</columns>

v. 21. **So the LORD shall be my God)** Jacob means to say: I know and am convinced through the Spirit that the great Jehovah is the only eternal God, who dwells in an unapproachable light. <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 6:16.</note> But what does it help me that He is God in His glory for Himself alone? What does it help me that He is also Abraham’s and Isaac’s God, if He is not also my God in particular, and remains so?

Jacob thus expresses here the childlike affection of his heart toward God, that he no longer wished to look upon the recognized Lord as a mere Creator, Ruler, and the like, but as a loving Father who would provide for him in body and soul: Not only as a common God, who communicates His fellowship to all who seek Him; but as his own God, whom he grasps in faith and carries in his heart.

In this way, all believers have endeavored to grasp and know the Lord their God with divine faith: and especially in distress and sorrow, it has been their only consolation that the true God is also their own God.

Whoever has not truly turned to God <note>referring to the process of "conversion" or "repentance"</note> will not be able to believe this, but will instead consider it a fantasy—that one merely creates such sweet thoughts of God and Christ, believing He is also our God and Christ.

But truly, it reaches deeper than mere thoughts! It brings nothing but real treasures of grace into the heart when God becomes the soul's God in particular. It is experienced and tasted then better than it could ever be told, how it transpires in the deepest ground of the heart when God is our God.

Oh, who can express how an immortal spirit feels when God thus unites and pairs with it, when God becomes the Bride’s God, and the Bride in turn becomes God’s Bride; when she knows no one anymore—not even Christ according to the flesh <note>original: "nach dem Fleisch." A reference to 2 Corinthians 5:16, suggesting a spiritual rather than physical understanding.</note>—but everything in the Spirit, just as she is known and loved by God!

Blessed, and blessed again, are those who have found this Good as their own!

v. 22. **Then shall)** Here we find the first vow, which Jacob made not as a hireling <note>original: "Mietling." Someone who works only for pay rather than out of loyalty or love.</note> who wanted to serve God for a reward, but who wanted to bind himself all the more firmly to the service of God, to maintain such service as a priest in his family all the more carefully; and therefore to always give the tenth of his cattle for sacrifice

<column-break/>

and also from his remaining wealth, so that through this, what was necessary for the service of God—the instruction in the ways of the Lord—might be observed by others, and they might be supported for that reason. For this purpose, he undoubtedly dedicated the tenth out of divine impulse even then, just as Abraham had done (Chapter 14, v. 20), which was later commanded in the Law. He then also fulfilled this vow afterward (Chapter 35, v. 1, 3, 7).

**Become a house of God)** Jacob’s whole mind clearly shows us that he was not intending to restrict the majesty of his God to a certain house, or to set goals and limits for Him as to where he should seek or worship his God.

For that would not have been good for him when he came into distress with Laban, with Esau, and elsewhere. If he had believed then that his God dwelt only at Bethel, or—as the idolatrous mouth-Christians <note>original: "Maul-Christen." A disparaging term for those who are Christian in name or speech only, lacking true internal faith.</note> think—in the church alone; he would have been in a bad way and remained without help.

Thus, this was his pure meaning with this vow: he wanted to establish a memorial to the Lord at that same place, where one should serve Him according to the custom of the time with sacrifices, worship, and thanks: and he thus dedicated the place to set up an altar there, and thereby, according to the manner of his father and grandfather Abraham, to publicly proclaim the name of the Lord, and so also to bring others to the knowledge of the true God.

To this end, he wanted to dedicate and hallow so much of his own that those who served the Lord there should be given their sustenance.

**Give the tenth)** This custom was afterward confirmed among his descendants through certain ordinances of God (Numbers 30, Deuteronomy 12 and 23).

Certainly, we will also be driven to all outward good deeds and gentleness if we have rightly grasped God as our God. For where this Good dwells, it also works communication toward the needy.

The love of God will drive us to flow out in love toward our neighbor. Just as God has become ours in faith, so we will gladly want to be our neighbor's through love.
<meta>Catchword: and</meta>

Upon this, all vows, gifts, and legacies which are dedicated to spiritual things should rightly be founded.

->15. Then<-

<margin>
v. 11. He kisses her as a sign of the union he makes with her, as he joins her to the path of the life of faith through this kiss. He sheds tears because it is evident that although she was very beautiful and virtuous, she would not have the fortune of bringing forth the Lord Jesus Christ in those souls. This came about because the love he had for her was mixed with nature: whereby he then hindered the bringing forth of Jesus Christ in those souls. This shows, then, that an Apostolic life requires a much purer love and self-denial than any other life, no matter how holy it may be or how full of virtue it might seem.
</margin>

---

If one holds to the true source of wisdom, the Word of the Lord, and the Savior revealed therein—who offered himself to the Samaritan woman as the source of living water at a well, John 4:10, 14—and also remembers how one should not remain with the outward Word, but should also come to Him, John 5:39, 40; then one receives heavenly Wisdom as a bride. Wisdom 8:2 <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom, found in the Apocrypha.</note>. She then becomes our true helper who is around us; our companion who will be a good counselor and a comforter in cares and sadness.

Otherwise, one can also perceive here again the simple way of life of the patriarchs and forefathers, among whom God wished to show His governance particularly, in how they kept their children to simple livestock farming: Ch. 47:3. There, eternal Wisdom had her pleasure among these lowly persons; (see Proverbs 8:31) whereas He abandoned the descendants of Ishmael and Esau, who set themselves to becoming princes and lords on this earth through all kinds of violence. See Ch. 25:16, 36:15 etc. and Ch. 16:12, 25:27 compared with Ch. 10:8, 9, 32:6.

Just as Jacob’s heart was immediately captured here with chaste love for Rachel, which brought forth his tears; so a soul eager for wisdom must turn heartily to its eternal origin and Creator, by whom it was created according to His image, and is thus of His lineage—yes, He who, in taking on our flesh and blood, wished to become our <term>Goel: A Hebrew term for a "kinsman-redeemer," a relative who has the right or duty to assist a family member or reclaim property.</term> and blood relative. Thus He will complete the spiritual marriage with the soul; then the soul will become a member of His body, of His flesh and of His bones, Ephesians 5:30 and here v. 14; indeed, His bride. He will kiss her with the kiss of His mouth <note>An allusion to the Song of Solomon 1:2.</note>, and she will have much to boast of regarding His love. Yes, He will so embrace her that she will become intoxicated by it. Through such a kiss He will breathe His Spirit into her; He will thereby communicate Himself and His breath to her. This will surpass all words of love; His embrace will be above the glance of His eyes. For a kiss from Him is better than all knowledge; His tasted love surpasses all science. Oh, how high it is to be loved by the Son of Man! Whoever loves much, let him come to the Son of Love, who came for this purpose, that He might betroth Himself to you for eternity!

v. 10. Jacob gives water here in service of Rachel; and Rebekah likewise gave such in service of Isaac’s servants and camels. This difference shows us a great mystery. At that time, when the water was poured out, neither Jacob nor Rachel was sufficiently prepared for the spiritual marriage. Rachel at that time still had no appearance of spiritual life: therefore Jacob himself must let the waters flow, because the promise had been given to him in regard to his fathers. Moreover, Rachel also had to be barren; and although she, with Jacob, contributed her part to the bringing forth of two populous tribes, nevertheless the source of living water, Jesus Christ, was not to come from her, but from Jacob, who for this reason gives the water as the image of grace and perfections which are shared with the world through the Savior. But Rebekah, who was a source from which the pure life-giving water was to come, which is Jesus Christ, was able to water the nations in Eliezer and for Isaac’s sake. Jacob performs the office of a shepherd for Rachel because he was in Jesus Christ, or rather Christ was the true Shepherd in him, so that (a) his flock should be watered from the water of the Rock.

### Chapter XXIX. The First Book of Moses.

15. Afterward, Laban said to Jacob: "Even though you are my relative, should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me, what shall your wages be?"
16. Now Laban had two daughters: the eldest was named Leah, and the youngest was named Rachel.
17. And Leah had weak eyes <note>original: "blöde Augen." In this context, it suggests eyes that lack luster or are dim-sighted, often contrasted with Rachel's physical beauty.</note>, but Rachel was beautiful in form and beautiful of countenance.
18. And Jacob loved Rachel and said: "I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your youngest daughter."
19. And Laban answered: "It is better that I give her to you than that I should give her to another man; stay with me."
20. <margin>(a) Matthew 20:28.</margin> So Jacob served (a) seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but single days because he loved her so much.

---

Jacob immediately presented his situation to Laban, explaining why his parents had sent him: to marry someone from among his own kin. Then Laban undoubtedly remembered what had occurred with his sister, Rebekah, and how that matter had also come from the Lord. Chapter 24:50. However, for the bride-price <note>original: "Brautſchatz." In ancient customs, the groom provided a gift or service to the bride's family.</note> which the bridegrooms were required to give, Laban chose to accept Jacob's service with his flock. This was because Jacob did not arrive with great wealth, as Eliezer had when he brought plenty for his sister’s marriage; thus, Jacob wished to pay this bride-price through his bitter labor as a shepherd.

In the same way, Christ did not seek to acquire us from his heavenly Father with gold or silver, but rather presented himself as a servant, so that through his bitter service—which cost him his own blood—he might acquire us as his Bride. See Isaiah 43:24, Philippians 2:7, Titus 2:14.

v. 17. The industrious, active life, which busies itself with external duties, is hindered in contemplation and vision, and therefore does not have such clear sight. Conversely, that which makes its work the contemplation of eternal beauty must necessarily become beautiful itself and be transformed into that very image.

v. 18, 20. The natural love that Jacob had for Rachel was a weakness which God permitted in this holy patriarch. For this reason, the seven years he served for her—without yet marrying her—were not counted, and they seemed to him only as single days. Yet these weaknesses in such strong souls serve God's own purposes, as they lead to the soul's self-abnegation <term>Vernichtigung: the mystical process of setting aside one's ego or will</term>, making the soul more fit for the Cross and preparing it for the Apostolic life. This life is granted through the Cross, which is represented here by Leah. The sweetness of contemplation alone (typified by Rachel) can never, on its own, bring forth a life that is holily fruitful for the soul's best interest. The Cross must provide this. Prayer must be united with the Cross so that it may bring forth much fruit of grace. The Cross pours the blood of Jesus Christ into the lap of prayer so that it may become fruitful; prayer, in turn, pours the Spirit of God upon our Cross—a Spirit which it draws down from heaven to sanctify the Cross.

<column-break/>

21. And Jacob said to Laban: "Give me now my wife; for my days are fulfilled, that I may go in to her."
22. Then Laban gathered all the men of the place and made a feast.
23. And it happened in the evening that he took his daughter Leah and brought her to him, and he went in to her.
24. And Laban gave her Zilpah, his maidservant, to be a maid to his daughter Leah.
25. And it happened in the morning, behold, it was Leah. And he said to Laban: "Why have you done this to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?"
26. And...

---

God, who is full of goodness, deceives us in a most wonderful way. He first makes internal sweetnesses pleasant to us; and afterward, when we intend to cling to them and live peacefully with them, He gives us the Cross in their place. Internal consolations (typified by Rachel), which are always pleasant, cause the soul—through unfaithfulness and weakness—to cling to them immoderately. Yet God allows the soul to love these for a time and even gives them in abundance. But this happens only so that the soul may be able to endure the Cross He is preparing for it.

v. 24. **Zilpah**) She had a flaw in her, in that she liked to drink and became intoxicated. <note>This specific detail about Zilpah is not found in the biblical text itself but reflects extra-biblical traditions or the commentator's specific interpretive lens.</note>

v. 25. By day one loves Rachel; namely, as long as the state of enlightenment lasts. But by night one possesses Leah; for the darkness of faith has come. Faith loves Leah for her fruitfulness; but nature loves Rachel for the sake of her beauty. Though Leah has weak eyes, she is just as pleasant in the stillness of the night as Rachel—indeed, she is even mistaken for her. The Cross is ugly when viewed with specific intentions; but the soul that possesses it in the stillness of unity and without selfish intent finds as much pleasure in it as in the greatest sweetnesses. Now Self-love, which served God for the sake of its own sweetness and thought to possess such forever, finds nothing but annoyance and the Cross. It complains to God Himself, saying: "What? Is this the reward you promised me for my long service? I thought you would overwhelm me with spiritual joys afterward, and yet you send me nothing but sorrow and bitterness! From whence comes such an unexpected change?"

This is certainly a very profound representation of Jacob, showing how it goes for a converted person in this world. First, he must learn to go out from the house and domain of his father—the Old Adam—and become a stranger, even a servant, in the world.

Thus, and not otherwise, does Eternal Wisdom find the soul—as a true Bride—sitting by the way, at the well of Grace, in thirst and weariness of longing for God. Here, such a person not only learns to enjoy the comfort of divine love as a foretaste, but is also received into an ancient friendship.

Yes, the true heavenly wedding of the Lamb is promised to him in spirit, and in return, he pledges himself to divine service. But while he seeks to satisfy himself in this new love, he finds Leah with him instead of Rachel—that is, the unpleasant Cross. He must spend his time with this companion amidst much suffering and labor of the spirit, even though the covenant of love with Christ remains firm and will finally be fulfilled. For...

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXIX.

26. And Laban answered: It is not the custom in our place to give the younger before the firstborn.
27. Finish this [wedding] week, and then this one shall be given to you as well, for the service you shall serve with me for another seven years.
28. And Jacob did so, and finished the week; then he gave him Rachel, his daughter, to be his wife.
29. And Laban gave his daughter Rachel Bilhah, his maidservant, to be her maidservant.

v. 26. 27. **God**, who is full of mercy for such a soul, comforts it and says: Suffer these sorrows I have assigned to you for only a few days; afterward, I will give you these sweetnesses as a true possession—which you now possess only outwardly and for a few brief moments. However, pain must precede delight. For the Cross <note>original: "Creutz." Here referring to the burdens and sufferings of the Christian life.</note> has the right of the firstborn with me: and such must go before secret and lasting delights. For the entire enjoyment of this life is to be held in low esteem, and I allow you this only for the sake of your weakness. But when you have tasted of the heavenly sweetness that I promise you, you must serve me for another seven years, so that this priceless treasure may be paid for with some labor. Just as

The active life must precede the contemplative or meditative life. And a person does not belong to Christ's family if they do not practice both the active life with Martha and the contemplative life with Mary. Indeed, through the industrious works of penance and repentance toward **God**, a person must be purified and made capable of elevation and ascending to the contemplation of divine things.

v. 27. Another seven years) Seven is the number of purification. Whoever wishes to devote themselves to **God** and contemplation must pass through the number seven twice; they must be changed and transformed twice, from glory to glory, so that they may fix the eye of the mind without offense upon the eternal spectacles.

v. 29. Bilhah) She had the failing <note>original: "Gebrechen." A character flaw or physical infirmity.</note> that she enjoyed speaking many words.

<column-break/>

30. So he went in to Rachel also, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served with him yet another seven years.
31. When

---

It is worth considering how Jacob was already at a considerable age when he began his marriage: namely, in the 84th year of his life. This can be concluded as follows: Jacob was 130 years old when he stood before Pharaoh: Chapter 47:9. And Joseph was then 39 years old: Chapter 41:46, etc.; 45:6, etc. Thus, Joseph was born in the 91st year of Jacob's life, and that was the 14th year of his service: Chapter 30:25. Therefore, he came to Laban in his 77th year and did not wish to take Rachel in marriage until he had earned her with his seven years of promised service. Thus, he was 84 years old when he actually entered into marriage. This reveals his chaste mind, which held the gift of abstinence for so long a time, and thus in his marriage he aimed primarily for the promised seed and blessing from **God**. See Tobit 8:9. Just as Isaac did not rush with an early marriage to obtain the promised seed but left all this to **God**, who would gloriously carry out everything He promised in His own time.

Even though Jacob's polygamy <note>original: "Mehrweiberey."</note> was against **God's** institution, and he was not without "crosses" <note>meaning trials or burdens</note> regarding the children from these different marriages, **God** nonetheless looked upon his simplicity in the matter. He overlooked this widespread evil custom, which was to be completely abolished by Christ in His kingdom. Indeed, He also permitted this marriage with the two sisters, which He later expressly forbade in Leviticus 18:18. Like the marriage of Abraham with Sarah and Hagar, He made it an image of the two kinds of people in the Old and New Testaments. The first is to be compared to Leah, who was fruitful first, from whom the Messiah according to the flesh (namely, from Judah) was to be born. She had a dim vision of the mysteries of salvation and was not as pleasant as the people of the New Testament. In contrast, Rachel is an image of the Church of the New Testament, which was at first barren but later became fruitful, whom the **Lord** accepted with very great and tender love, as the entire 54th chapter of Isaiah testifies at length. The name Rachel means a "Sheep" <note>original Hebrew: *Rahel*</note>. For the **Lord** has truly made these the sheep of His pasture, Psalm 100:3, who must possess the nature of their Savior, who is also called a Lamb, John 1:29, etc., and Matthew 11:29. Among them, He presented Himself as the Good Shepherd and took this office upon Himself. John 10:11, 14, etc. See Ezekiel 34:11, etc.

Souls that have not yet come far in the ways of truth prefer the love of sweetness to the love of the Cross: which then greatly hinders their progress. **God** allowed all of this to Jacob in order to instruct us. Since nothing is contained in Scripture, as the great Apostle says, that was not written for our instruction. Thus also are

## Leah and Rachel,
### the two wives of Jacob,
### counterparts of Hagar and Sarah,
### and prefigurations of the Old and New Testaments,
### or of the Jews and Christians.

1. Jacob had two wives who were two sisters: And **God** has betrothed Himself to two congregations; one at Mount Sinai, the other is called the Daughter of Zion. Because they nevertheless have one faith and one Father, they are also two sisters.
2. The eldest was named Leah, which means the "Weary One"; the other Rachel, which means "Sheep." Those in the Old Testament are the weary; those in the New Testament are the dear sheep, who eat and drink from Christ's morsels and sleep in His bosom. 2 Samuel 12:3.
3. Leah was fruitful sooner than Rachel, who was barren for a long time: And even now, the Church of **Jesus Christ** is called the barren one, as in Isaiah 54:1.
4. However, Rachel was promised earlier than Leah, though Leah was married first. Thus, the first and best promises were made to the New Testament.
5. Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was pretty and beautiful. Those in the Old Testament could not endure the radiance of Moses. Exodus 34. The New Testament is the "fairest among women." Song of Solomon 4.
6. Therefore, Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah: And Christ shows more grace to the Church of the New Testament than to the people of the Law.
7. Jacob served seven years for Rachel as a servant: And Christ came, not to be served, but to serve, and for that end took upon Himself the form of a servant.
8. These seven years seemed to Jacob as if they were single days. So, a thousand years are to the **Lord**, until the wedding of the Lamb, like a day. 2 Peter 3:8.
9. During this time, Jacob worked hard for his Rachel. So also did Christ, as the Arch-Shepherd of our souls. Isaiah 43. Since we are to be the children of the beautiful Rachel, for whom Christ worked so hard, let us also be like Joseph and Benjamin, and act beautifully!

### Chapter XXIX. The First Book of Moses.

31. But when the **Lord** saw that **Leah** was unloved <note>original: "verhaßt," literally "hated," reflecting the Hebrew term for being set aside or less favored.</note>, he opened her womb; but **Rachel** was barren.

<margin>
Leah may have been more easily persuaded by her father to enter this marriage with Jacob because she knew how much her sister Rachel was cherished, and because she herself loved Jacob’s pious spirit. However, because of this act, she had to experience her husband's dislike—or rather, his disinclination—to her great sorrow. Yet the Lord softened this for her because of her sincerity by granting her children. He also allowed her to enjoy the right later established in law: that although she was the unloved one, her children still retained the right of the firstborn regarding the most noble part, the sovereignty. This was fulfilled in Judah, since the first three sons were passed over due to their sins. But God also allowed Rachel a portion of the birthright, in that the sons of Joseph, as her firstborn, received two parts in the inheritance of the promised land. See Deuteronomy 21:15, etc., and here in Chapters 49:3 and 48:5.
</margin>

<margin>
Behold, however, what God especially looks upon or reflects when distributing His gifts. Not on beauty, not on status, appearance, splendor, power, or such fleshly things; but on that which is unloved, despised, and rejected. He who is unworthy before men is worthy before God. What a strange, reversed way of dealing! How foolish it appears to proud, hypocritical reason that the highest and most glorious Being stoops down to that which seems like nothing!
</margin>

<margin>
Although nothing particularly coarse or wicked may have been done by Rachel, the fact remained that Leah was held in contempt; indeed, she was "hated," as the Hebrew text actually phrases it. That was reason enough for the Lord to make her worthy.
</margin>

<margin>
For what poor humans deem unworthy, what they blaspheme, strike down, belittle, and cast out—that is what God exalts, honors, counsels, and accepts. He does this specifically to defy human reason and pride, and as a testimony that His thoughts are not their thoughts, and that men err and do not understand the true foundation of God.
</margin>

<margin>
Jacob was obligated to love and value these two sisters in equal measure. But his desire outweighed him, so that he preferred one over the other. Because of this, the Lord punished him tangibly for such partiality or "sectarianism" <note>The author uses the word "Sectirerey" to compare personal favoritism to religious factionalism.</note> by making Leah fertile.
</margin>

<margin>
It happens a thousand times more crudely in the world! Oh, this example is an incomparable archetype of how the world, in its splendor, status, and superficial existence, can so highly despise everything that is plain, miserable, and weak. The world does not know that through its mockery and scorn, it actually promotes the breakthrough to the Kingdom of God and the birth of God's love in such lowly souls! For
</margin>

<column-break/>

32. And **Leah** became pregnant and bore a son, and she named him **Reuben**. For she said: "The **Lord** has surely looked upon my misery! For now my husband will love me."
33. And she became pregnant again and bore a son and said: "Because the **Lord** has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this one also." And she named him **Simeon**.
34. And she became pregnant again and bore a son and said: "Now this time my husband will be joined to me! For I have borne him three sons." Therefore she named him **Levi**.
35. And she became pregnant again and bore a son and said: "This time I will praise the **Lord**!" Therefore she named him **Judah**. And she stopped bearing.

->This<-

---

One sees here the fear of God in Leah, as she turned to God in her misery and pleaded for His hearing. She also sought her husband's company in a proper manner and praised God for His benefits. It was from this Judah that the Messiah was to be born, as Jacob later saw in the Spirit of God and prophesied in Chapter 49:8-10, recognizing the Lord's providence with Leah.

Divine fear and awe are the first fruit and the beginning of wisdom. This son and this fruit are born when a person recognizes their failings and God's righteousness.

Above all things, "sight" must first be born in a person if they are to come to the knowledge of truth. Christ calls this fruit the "single eye," which is the holy <term>Intention</term> <note>The inner focus or spiritual aim of the soul.</note> that directs everything straight toward God, looking neither to the right nor to the left, nor having designs on other things.

Thereupon follows "attentiveness" or "obedience," so that one opens the ears of the heart and hears what God speaks within us.

Thereupon follows the "joining" and "union" with God.

> Furthermore, the praise and glory of God, because of His grace and great goodness.

v. 32. The Cross <note>Throughout this section, the author uses Leah as an allegory for "The Cross," meaning the life of spiritual struggle and suffering.</note>, represented by Leah, expresses the joy it has in being a mother, in the hope that its "husband"—which signifies the soul with which it is united—seeing its fruitfulness, will have all the high esteem for it that it deserves. Yet it does not exalt itself; it recognizes that everything comes from God, who gave it this preference to pull it out of the lowliness in which it naturally existed: it gives the honor to Him alone. One must judge the Cross by its fruits. The senses cannot taste them, but the spirit discovers them through faith.

v. 33, 34. It is something incomprehensible that the Cross, which has so many advantages, has so much trouble making itself beloved. Here it brings forth the priestly tribe (Levi) and with him the very greatest things. Nonetheless, it can hardly make itself lovely. The first time it gives birth (Reuben/Sight), it desires nothing else but to be less despised. The second time (Simeon/Hearing), it hopes it might be loved. The third time, however, after it has born Levi (Union), which is the royal priesthood, it believes it will now be desired, and that the soul to whom it was given, having become more understanding, would long to be united with it.

v. 35. The fourth time, she now praises the **Lord**: which means proclaiming Jesus Christ in Judah—namely, the one from whom He was to come. And just as the fulfillment and the end of all desire is found in Jesus Christ, so also, after getting Judah, she stops bearing.

The Cross, which rejoices in its own great fruitfulness, remains so far above all created things that it no longer speaks of Jacob; it shows no more desire to possess him as it did before. Instead, it cries out as it reaches the contemplation of such a wonderful production with a courageous flight: "O, this time I will praise the **Lord**!" For now there is nothing more on earth that could hold back my desire! The Cross could bring forth nothing greater than the redemption of the whole world, which it actually bore when peace was made between that which is on earth and in heaven through the blood of Jesus Christ shed on the Cross.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the marriages of Jacob. Having established Leah as a symbol of the "active life" (associated with the Cross and toil) and Rachel as a symbol of the "contemplative life" (associated with spiritual delight), the text now moves into Chapter 30 to discuss the birth of the sons of the handmaids, interpreting these events as stages of spiritual development and the soul's struggle for fruitfulness.</meta>

The First Book of Moses. Chap. XXX.

### Chapter XXX.
->Jacob’s Children and Wages.<-

1. When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, she envied her sister and said to Jacob: "Give me children; or else I die!"
2. Then Jacob’s anger was kindled <margin>(a)</margin> against Rachel, and he said: "Am I not under God <note>original: "unter GOtt," meaning 'in the place of God' or 'subject to God's will'</note>, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?"
<margin>(a) Gen. 31:36. Num. 16:15. Job 32:2, 3, 5.</margin>
3. But she said: "See, there is my maid Bilhah; go in to her, that she may bear upon my knees, and I also may be built up <note>or 'receive a family'</note> through her."
4. And she gave him Bilhah, her maid, as a wife: and Jacob went in to her.
5. So Bilhah became pregnant and bore Jacob a son.
6. Then Rachel said: "God has judged my cause, and has also heard my voice, and given me a son!" Therefore she called his name **Dan** <note>Dan means 'Judge'</note>.

---

This is a symbolic representation of true faith, which is always eager for spiritual fruits; otherwise, it wishes to die: which it then can obtain in no other way than through the power of God by means of the spiritual struggle in prayer alone.
**v. 1. 2.** Thus, among the believers, all kinds of perverse impulses and jealousy—and from that, strife—can arise; and then the chastisements of God will not be absent.
Spiritual delights, even if they are godly, would gladly take precedence over the Cross <note>the 'Cross' here refers to suffering and spiritual discipline</note>. However, after they become vexed because of their unfruitfulness, they say to the souls possessing them: "Produce some effects from us; otherwise we die! Why should the Cross have all the precedence alone?" They either do not wish to exist, or they wish to share in the fruitfulness of the Cross. But the soul, seeing the lack of stability in these ways of delight, becomes angry and shows them that God alone can grant them fruitfulness. Both the Cross and consolation can exercise a person as trials, just as these two women, who were images of them, did to their husband, Jacob. In order to be faithful in these trials, one must accept them directly from the hand of God and look upon them only in Him.
**v. 3-8.** When Rachel saw that she could bring forth nothing because of her unfruitfulness, she took refuge in her maid. Thus, a soul that stands in the delights of contemplation often has its confidence in a "maid" when it sees itself without effectiveness, in order to obtain some results from her: namely, when the soul makes use of certain outward works of love, which it adopts to comfort itself regarding its unfruitfulness, making of them a natural support.
When the contemplative life is not yet so perfect that it can bring forth proper fruits—because the eye is not yet purified enough to stand directed straight and firm upon God—it falls into a holy envy, zeal, and resentment upon perceiving the fruitfulness of the active life. It then seeks to build itself up through the help of the "maid," and to elevate itself to the invisible God through the contemplation of created things. From this, a double fruit arises: 1) The judging of the greatness of divine things from created ones; or also the subtle, secret judgment with which one judges oneself over one's own incapacity. 2) The expansion of the heart follows upon contemplation and purification.

<column-break/>

7. Bilhah, Rachel’s maid, became pregnant again and bore Jacob a second son.
8. Then Rachel said: "I have had a very great struggle with my sister, and I have also gained the upper hand"; and she called him **Naphtali** <note>Naphtali means 'my wrestling' or 'my struggle'</note>.
9. When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing, she took her maid Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
10. So Zilpah, Leah’s maid, bore Jacob a son.
11. Then Leah said: "A troop has come!" and she called him **Gad** <note>Gad means 'troop' or 'good fortune'</note>.
12. Afterward, Zilpah, Leah’s maid, bore Jacob a second son.
13. Then Leah said: "This is for my happiness! For the daughters will call me blessed!" <margin>(a)</margin> and she called him **Asher** <note>Asher means 'happy' or 'blessed'</note>. <margin>(a) Luke 1:48.</margin>
14. And

---

There was a great longing among them for children because of the promise given to Abraham regarding the great multiplication of his seed. And so, Rachel followed the example of Sarah and wished to produce her family through her maid, Bilhah, and thus build her house through her. See Chapter 16:2. This poor custom, which was against God’s original order, was then followed by Leah; she was not satisfied with her four sons but also desired to have such adopted children from her maid, Zilpah.
Meanwhile, the polygamy of the holy fathers was nevertheless built and founded upon an entirely different ground than the animal lust of today’s "stallions and whoremongers" <note>original: "Hengste und Huren-Jäger," a harsh Baroque polemic against contemporary immorality</note>; it by no means came from the root of lewdness. Rather, a play of the Wisdom of God was hidden beneath it, which placed His deep mysteries before our eyes under such images, as if in a shadow-play.
Jacob has two principal main-powers: the Will and the Understanding. Through the former, he unites himself with the active life; through the latter, with the contemplative life. Each of these lives also has its "maid." Jacob unites himself with such when his understanding rises to the contemplation of the invisible God through the consideration of creatures and lower visible things; or when his will takes pleasure in the exercise of good works of love. This pleasure is the maid of Rachel. But when Jacob acts directly for God’s sake, he unites himself with Leah; and when he contemplates and beholds God, the original Light, directly in His light, he has to do with the beautiful Rachel.
In this, however, he commits no adultery with the maids. For a person may indeed contemplate and handle created and visible things and take pleasure therein, and does not sin thereby, if only everything is directed toward God as the final end.

14. And Reuben went out in the time of the wheat harvest / and found mandrakes <note>original: "Violen" (violets); these are the biblical *dudaim*</note> in the field / and brought them to his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah: "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes!"

15. And she answered her: "Is it too little / that you have taken my husband; and would you also take my son’s mandrakes?" And Rachel said: "Therefore he shall lie with you tonight / in exchange for your son’s mandrakes."

16. Now when Jacob came from the field in the evening / Leah went out to meet him / and said: "You must come in to me; for I have surely hired you for wages / for my son’s mandrakes." And he lay with her that same night.

---

**Mandrakes)** Ludolf (a) <note>Hiob Ludolf (1624–1704) was a famous German orientalist and scholar of Ethiopian history</note> suspects / they were figs / of the kind the Arabs call **Mus, Muz** and **Mauz** / which are as large as cucumbers / of which 150 to 200 grow on a tree / called **Musa** <note>the banana tree</note> / growing close together / like the grains on a cluster without seeds / sweet and pleasant-tasting like buttered pastries.

Many understand them to be the **Mandragora** or the **Mandrake**: others, however, a kind of fragrant flower / which some Hebrews call Violets / others Jasmines. Many suppose / that they were winter cherries <note>Physalis</note>. Still others hold it as most probable / that they were lilies: which were frequently encountered among the crops during the wheat harvest of that time / as Rauwolff reports in his travel description (b) <note>Leonhard Rauwolf (1535–1596) was a German physician and botanist who traveled the Levant</note>.

The entire "illuminated" life <note>a state of spiritual insight</note> is, compared to the life of faith / which must follow it / only a childlike and weak life. Rachel is so childlike / that she prefers to seek and smell the delight of the Mandrakes <note>original Hebrew: *Dudaim*</note>—which is a fruit of excellent appearance and scent—over the essential possession of her husband. Effeminate souls, full of sensitive taste and zeal, resemble her in this. They prefer the pleasant to the essential; which is the possession of God in Himself above all gifts.

v. 16. The soul surrendered to God runs with joy / to show / that she is worthy to possess Him / in that she has acquired Him through the abandonment of all gifts.

The strong and magnanimous souls / and those who have become such through the Cross <note>symbolizing suffering and trials</note> / gladly give up all sweetness / and what is external / to attain the essential possession of their husband; as Leah also did here. Therefore God also blesses this choice with a new fruitfulness / and gives her two more sons and a daughter.

Thus the connected Cross brings the spiritual pilgrim much more fruit of the Spirit / than if he were fed with nothing but inner sweetness and beauty / and thereby gradually became sleepy and complacent. And

So also the active life brings forth fruit sooner and more abundantly than the contemplative; the latter, however, brings forth sweeter and more lovely fruit.

(b) *Part 1, Chapter 9.*

<column-break/>

17. And God listened to Leah / and she became pregnant / and bore Jacob a fifth son.

18. And Leah said: "God has given me my reward / because I gave my maid to my husband:" and she called his name **Issachar** <note>meaning 'Man of Reward' or 'Wages'</note>.

19. Leah became pregnant again / and bore Jacob a sixth son.

20. And Leah said: "God has endowed me with a good gift! This time my husband will dwell with me; for I have borne him six sons!" and she called his name **Zebulun** <note>meaning 'Dwelling'</note>.

21. Afterward she bore a daughter / and called her name **Dinah** <note>meaning 'Judgment' or 'Vindicated'</note>.

---

Since God bestowed upon both wives and sisters another pair of sons / the secret number of the twelve tribes of the physical and spiritual Israel has thus become full: showing how God knows how to direct the weaknesses of men / and especially of believers / toward a good end.

Just as the mystery of the Number Twelve may offer opportunity for discussion elsewhere / so it is also beyond all doubt / that in the order of these 12 sons / and the tribes and generations that sprang from them and were prefigured by them / which are presented now in this order and now in another / as seen in the Blessing of Jacob, Chapter 49 / in the Military Order, Numbers 2 / in the Blessing of Moses, Deuteronomy 33 / where finally the spiritual Israel is presented with these same names in yet another order in Revelation Chapter 7 / none of this happens by chance / but has its holy and wise secret causes / which can be researched in the light of the Spirit through the mysterious names / which were given through the inspiration of the Spirit of God.

Thus one can also note from the different mothers the different ways of guidance and spiritual "offspring" of the believers: since some are led and brought forth through love / others through fear; while the former has something noble and free about it / the latter has something servile. In these various ways God knows how to rule His own according to His wisdom: since the noble-minded and kind-natured are, as it were, from the free woman / and yet again different; so that some must go through hard trials / in which they become most like the Savior / as a Job and David experienced many sufferings: and these are the most beloved to God / just as Rachel was the most beloved to Jacob: from whom also Joseph came / who experienced the most suffering / but for that very reason attained the greatest glory here in the image of spiritual and heavenly things. Others, however, are led along common paths / where God also tends to share many physical and spiritual benefits. Others are led more by a servile spirit of fear: which may well happen because of a great innate corruption / and whatever further holy reasons Divine Wisdom and Justice may have / that such souls do not so soon break through into the childlike and bold nature of love / or may not attain to it / being, as it were, from the maidservants.

---

So also in the names, different ways can be noted: since some must later go through special "judgments of love" / which **Dan** signifies: others are placed in many struggles from within and without; which is represented in **Naphtali**. So also there are those / who despite their corruption / and the resulting spirit of fear / yet experience physical happiness / which the word **Asher** signifies / and live among the common crowd / as suggested by the word **Gad**; whom God / even if it should happen at the end / will know how to prepare / and otherwise deal with each according to His wisdom in time and eternity. In short, these various tribes are of a great mystery / which we may research in the fear of the Lord / and each can present his own interpretation of the divine riddle.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXX.

22. And GOD remembered Rachel / and GOD heard her / and opened her womb.
23. Then she became pregnant / and bore a son / and said: GOD has taken away my reproach!
24. And she named him Joseph / and said: May the LORD add another son to me.
25. And it happened / when Rachel had borne Joseph / that Jacob said to Laban: Let me go that I may journey / to my own place and to my country.
26. Give me my wives and my children / for whom I have served you / that I may go. For you know my service / with which I have served you.

**v. 22. 23.** God / whose goodness is infinite / and who leaves nothing unrewarded / deals with these people according to their weakness. He took pity on Rachel / and made her fruitful. This teaches us / that / when those souls who have been graced with sensible gifts <note>Spiritual experiences or "feelings" of grace that can be perceived by the senses.</note> have finally become ripe / they also bring forth some fruit. However, this fruit does not approach / in either goodness or quantity / that which is brought by those who have been led through such a hard path / by which they have been crucified. She therefore has an indescribable joy over her outcomes / and says / God has lifted her out of her lowliness.

**v. 24. Joseph)** It is noteworthy / if one does not count the children of the maidservants / that he is the seventh in order among the sons of the two true wives: and it is thereby secretly indicated / that / when the six **Church-Ages** <term>Church-Ages (Kirchen-Zeiten)</term> <note>A mystical chronological framework popular in the 18th century, dividing history into seven eras based on the Book of Revelation.</note> have run their course in their births / the seventh Church-Age of the greatly-multiplied Joseph shall follow / the seventh age of the Church / in which there is rest / and with which at the same time a new era begins. For Joseph was the first / whom Rachel bore. With him also the reproach / which has lain so long upon the poor Jewish Rachel / or upon the Jewish people / and has been inflicted upon them by all nations / is taken away / and she is crowned instead with honor and adornment.

**The other son)** She received him as well / but not until her death. *Chapter 35, 16-18.*

**v. 25.** After the birth of Joseph / the dear Jacob feels a strong stirring within himself / to move away from the Chaldean and Babylonian land: as a true prototype / that / when the time comes / that the true Joseph of Israel is born in the spirit / the Jews will then become longing in their hearts / to travel to the promised land of Canaan.

As soon as the path of light and its pleasantness has become fruitful / and brings forth some signs of its beauty; it is the earnest will of the soul—which is entirely delighted to see such beautiful fruits / because they still have something of their mother's beauty about them—to depart from this first path / and to turn with her fruits toward the path of self-denial. Therefore Jacob strongly urges Laban / to let him go: as if he feared / his children might take on something foreign in this land / if they remained therein longer; which would cause an evil mixture.

Thus the clever children of this world often behave toward the simple children of light / and act as if they were also from a spiritual father with them / and wished to have fellowship with them. How they hug and kiss as it were with Judas and Laban / or coax and flatter with such enchanting gestures / speeches, and works / that they may gain an entrance into the heart.

In particular, the spirit of this world juggles powerfully with religious matters / with the name of piety / truth / wisdom and sincerity / yes, with the most holy name of GOD himself / which must serve as a cover for all malice. There, no evil is wrought / no deceit / no persecution carried out against GOD and His own / without the name of GOD being spread over it.

34. Since...

Since Laban, out of self-interest, kept Jacob from his desire to travel home to his dear parents in the land of promise according to the will of GOD / and finally left it free to him to name his own wages; so here too Jacob bows beneath his father-in-law / and awaits the time / when GOD would redeem him from this burdensome service / and bring him back to his fatherland. And since he was very modest and sufficient in his demand / therefore asking for that which would be granted to him through the providence of GOD; and since he chose the livestock of different colors / which would be born from those of a single color; which is rare among sheep / as they are commonly of one color and wool: yet GOD wished to bestow the most of them upon him through an extraordinary blessing.

Laban here disguised himself for the sake of profit / because Jacob made him so rich. Therefore he acts

**v. 27.** as if he also feared the GOD of Abraham / Isaac, and Jacob; only so that Jacob might trust him / and thus remain with him.

# Chapter XXXI.

-> Jacob’s Departure from Laban. <-

1. And he heard the talk of Laban’s sons, saying: "Jacob has taken away everything that belonged to our father, and from what belonged to our father, he has brought about all this glory."
2. And Jacob looked at Laban’s face, and behold, it was not toward him as it was yesterday and the day before.

Natural men <note>Worldly people who lack spiritual insight.</note> cannot well tolerate the blessing of the children of God; instead, they are accustomed to looking at them with envious eyes and always think that whatever the believers have is something they themselves are lacking. Therefore, believers must also fear being violently robbed if GOD did not take them into His fatherly protection.

22. And **GOD** remembered Rachel, and **GOD** listened to her and opened her womb.

26. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, that I may go. For you know my service with which I have served you.

---

v. 22. 23. **GOD**, whose goodness is infinite and who leaves nothing unrewarded, deals with these people according to their weakness. He took pity on Rachel and made her fruitful. This teaches us that when souls, graced with perceptible spiritual gifts, have finally matured, they also bring forth some fruit. However, this fruit matches neither the quality nor the quantity of that produced by those led through a harsh path, by which they have been crucified <note>The author uses "crucified" here in a mystical sense, referring to the "death of the self" or the "daily cross" of spiritual trials.</note>. She therefore has an indescribable joy over her results and says that **GOD** has lifted her out of her lowliness.

v. 24. Joseph) It is noteworthy that if one does not count the children of the handmaids, he is the seventh in order among the sons of the two true wives <note>Leah bore six sons (Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun); Joseph is the firstborn of Rachel, making him the seventh son of the primary wives.</note>. This secretly indicates that when the six "Church Ages" <term>Church Ages (Kirchen-Zeiten): A concept in mystical theology where history is divided into seven periods, corresponding to the seven churches in Revelation.</term> have run their course in their births, the seventh Church Age of the greatly increased Joseph shall follow—the seventh age of the Church, in which there is rest, and with which a new era begins. For Joseph was the first whom Rachel bore. With him, the reproach that has long lain upon the poor Jewish Rachel, or upon the Jewish people, and has been inflicted upon them by all nations, is taken away, and she is instead crowned with honor and adornment.

The other son) She did receive him as well, but not until her death. (Chapter 35, 16-18).

v. 25. After the birth of Joseph, the dear Jacob feels a strong urge to depart from the Chaldean and Babylonian land. This is a true prototype: when the time comes that the true Joseph of Israel is born in the spirit, the Jews will then feel a longing in their hearts to travel to the promised land of Canaan.

As soon as the path of light and its pleasantries become fruitful and bring forth signs of beauty, the soul—rejoicing to see such beautiful fruits because they still retain something of their mother's beauty—earnestly desires to leave this distant path and turn toward the way of self-denial with its fruits. Therefore, Jacob strongly urges Laban to let him go, as if he feared his children might take on something foreign in this land if they remained longer, which would cause an evil mixing.

Thus, the "clever children of this world" <note>A reference to those who are worldly-wise but spiritually blind.</note> often present themselves to the simple "children of light" and act as if they were from the same spiritual father and wished to have fellowship with them. How they hug and kiss, as if with the spirit of Judas or Laban, or flatter with such enchanting gestures, speeches, and deeds, that they might gain entry into the heart!

In particular, the spirit of this world powerfully conjures with religious matters—using the names of piety, truth, wisdom, and sincerity—indeed, even with the most holy name of **GOD** itself, which must serve as a "cloak for malice" <note>original: "Schanddeckel"; literally a "cover for shame."</note> over all wickedness. No evil is wrought, no deceit, no persecution carried out against **GOD** and His own, without the name of **GOD** being spread over it.
