Since Laban, out of self-interest, kept Jacob from his desire to travel home to his dear parents in the land of promise according to the will of **GOD**, and finally allowed him to name his own wages, Jacob here bows before his father-in-law and awaits the time when **GOD** would deliver him from this burdensome service and bring him back to his fatherland. And since he was very modest and content in his demand, asking for that which would be granted to him through the providence of **GOD**; and since he chose the livestock of various colors that would be born from those of a single color—which is rare among sheep, as they are commonly of one color and wool—**GOD** nevertheless willed to bestow the majority of them upon him through an extraordinary blessing.

Laban behaved hypocritically here for the sake of profit, because Jacob made him so rich. Therefore, he acts:

v. 27. As if he also feared the **GOD** of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, only so that Jacob might trust him and thus remain with him.

Thus people are accustomed to making all kinds of cunning plots to take advantage of the righteous. Proverbs 1:11 etc. Then he who departs from evil must become everyone's prey. Isaiah 59:15. And even natural blood relatives do this, for they are not always the best friends, but rather often the enemies of the faithful; as Christ foretold regarding those of one's own household in Matthew 10:36. Just so here, Laban showed such poor friendship to his kinsman and faithful son-in-law, Jacob—who had two of his daughters—that he begrudged him the blessing of **GOD** and changed his wages so many times. But **GOD** knows how to deliver His own from the hand of their adversaries at the right time. And since Jacob did not have enough courage on his own to break free from this weary servitude and from his envious father-in-law and brothers-in-law, **GOD** had to encourage him with His gracious command and promise. This then had a blessed reception with his wives, so that they joyfully left their unjust parents' house; for the injustice that one shows to one's own kin usually takes away all natural love. They were then of good cheer, confident that since **GOD** had seen the injustice and was willing to free them from it, He would also protect them and bring their husband to his own people in peace.

**v. 13.** Jacob had to be reminded of his vow by **GOD**, as man very quickly forgets his duty and allows himself to be hindered by all kinds of occurring events, which he should overcome and always be mindful to fulfill his promise; then **GOD** would also grant him more blessing in his undertaking. See Chapter 28:20 and 35:1.
"Remember," says the **LORD**, "the stone where you made your vow and I promised to lead you! I will bring you back to that very place. For that is the place of your origin, to which I want to bring you back, so that you may lose yourself in Me and flow back into the source from which you sprang."

**v. 5. Your father's face not as yesterday)** See how the envious spirit reveals itself tangibly in the eyes! Oh, this is a truly hellish poison that can inwardly gnaw and destroy poor hearts that do not fight against it! Everyone, great and small, <note>original: "Roß und Mann" — literally "Horse and man," an idiom for everyone.</note> should rightly guard against this, and seek to kill even the slightest resentful, squinting thoughts against one's neighbor at the first outbreak through watching and prayer!
People live among and beside one another; one sees and notices the other's spiritual or physical gifts. If he does not watch over the ground of his heart, it happens all too easily that he is thrown into an envious fire of hell and provoked to all kinds of secret or public hostilities.
This plague also creeps into spiritual matters and hides behind a veneer of zeal. One often wants to warn others that they should not be conceited about their gifts; which is indeed good and necessary in itself. But one should also leave such gifts to the Giver and not seek to defile them with one's venom or secretly diminish them, and think that **GOD** already humbles His own amidst every blessing.

### Chapter XXXI. The First Book of Moses.

17. Then Jacob arose and set his children and his wives upon camels;
18. And he led away all his livestock and all his goods which he had acquired; his own livestock, which he had acquired in Padan-Aram <note>original: "Padan in Syrien"</note>, so that he might come to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.
19. Now Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole the images <note>original: "Bilder" — referring to the Teraphim or household idols</note> that her father possessed.

21. So he fled and all that was his; and he arose and passed over the river <note>The Euphrates</note>, and set his face toward the mountain of Gilead.
22. And on the third day it was told to Laban that Jacob had fled.
23. And he took his brothers with him and pursued him for seven days' journey, and reached him on the mountain of Gilead.
24. But

---

<margin>v. 34. 35. Judges 17:5. 2 Kings 23:24.</margin>
20. And Jacob stole the heart <note>A Hebrew idiom meaning to deceive or act without one's knowledge; original: "stahl Jacob das Hertz"</note> of Laban the Syrian, because he had not told him that he was fleeing.

Thus Jacob followed the command of **GOD**, making his escape secretly with all his people and his own goods—which he had earned honestly—without the prior knowledge of his parents-in-law. In this he did not sin, for Laban's unjust disposition was well known to him; Laban would have prevented his departure by any means and with force, and would have tormented him in other unlawful ways. Jacob also took advantage of a good opportunity while Laban had gone to shear his sheep; which they were accustomed to do with special solemnities and joys at the end of spring: 2 Samuel 13:23, so that it might not be noticed immediately.

During the difficult journey of a pilgrim toward the original fatherland and the Father's house, things happen strangely for such a person. He must always "steal away" secretly from Laban's house with Jacob: that is, in divine wisdom, he must constantly withdraw his mind and will from transitory earthly things and tear himself away in earnest, if he does not wish to remain an eternal slave to Laban <note>In this commentary, Laban represents the world or the "old man" who enslaves the soul</note>.

However, one does not go out empty-handed; rather, in the midst of the struggle against sin and corruption, **GOD** bestows upon the soul one treasure of grace after another as an inheritance. No tyrant can take these goods from us; rather, we carry such goods in and with us, along with all the divine fruits of the spiritual marriage, and finally bring everything unharmed into the next world for eternal security and enjoyment.

<margin>At the furthest borders of the promised land toward the East.</margin>
<margin>v. 23. Pursued him) He had nothing but war against Jacob in his mind. And indeed, he drove for 7 full days in a row until he reached him.</margin>
<margin>Such 7 days remind us well that the persecution of the wicked against the godly lasts throughout the entire lifetime or "week of life." The serpent stings the heels as long as a single honest Christian remains in the world: just as **JESUS** Christ is with His own through all 7 days or ages of life.</margin>
v. 18. 19. Jacob took everything that belonged to him and left nothing behind. However, through Rachel's theft, the difference between enlightened souls and those led through the cross is easily recognized—how far the former are from total nakedness <note>In a spiritual sense, "nakedness" refers to being stripped of all earthly attachments</note> compared to the latter. The former always have some idols or attachments that they take with them, which the latter do not have. Leah takes nothing but her children; there, **GOD** is all-sufficient.

The causes of such hostilities against the godly generally arise from the godlessness of the mind, in which the godly walk directly opposite to the wicked. For it vexes the old serpent most of all when fallen man begins to leave him, the beast, and the false prophet, and no longer worships their image. Over this, the serpent rages and storms within its members and instruments.

Another strong cause of persecution against the godly is miserable envy, a poisonous brood of the old serpent and a true basilisk's egg, whether it rules in spiritual or physical matters. v. 2. 5.

When the spirit of this world sees that faithful Christians even use temporal goods to further their salvation, and that everything in the world serves them for the best; and especially that they withdraw their best part—namely, the spirit—from the servitude of worldly lusts and slaveries: then fierce envy becomes active within it, and the wicked and hypocrites arise, pursuing the escaped soul with strict earnestness and wrath; and sometimes they even reach it.

Here it is time for **GOD** to make an objection and intervene, showing the enemies His "privilege" <note>A legal or divine right of ownership</note> which He has granted to such a soul from eternity. And that is what follows.

v. 19. 20. Images) Teraphim: These were small images or figures formed of metal, wax, or other materials, which had human or angelic forms. They were prepared under a certain constellation of a planet with special ceremonies. The ancient Magi and star-wise Egyptians—as Kircherus (a) among others notes—are said to have used them to investigate future things. Michal is also said to have placed such a thing in David's bed. 1 Samuel 19:13. What these looked like has been described by Kircherus along with others (b). Some, like those of Laban, are said to have looked like a swaddled child sticking its tongue out of its mouth.

Now, as for Rachel stealing these idol-images of her father: perhaps because of their costliness, as they may have been of gold and silver, and she thought that since they had received no dowry from their father, they would recover it this way; or to turn him away from idolatry all the sooner; or so her father might not learn of their path through these images, as they may have used these household gods for that purpose: in this she certainly does not do right. But one also sees how quickly idolatry with such images took root among men, whereby men fell away from the true living **GOD**, whom they should have feared and honored in their hearts and called upon for protection and counsel at all times. Instead, they want something visible that strikes the eyes of the body, through which they believe they can be more powerfully moved to devotion. Satan misused this and misled them into carving and casting all sorts of wonderful images, which they eventually took for gods, or believed that **GOD** was present in them with His power. Therefore, it is highly astonishing that such an error could even creep in among Christians, to whom service in spirit and in truth was so clearly and earnestly commanded, that they should keep themselves from idols, and thus also from all idolatrous images. 1 John 5:21.

By this, Laban's "heart was stolen"; because his heart hung dearly upon these mute idols: and he was also robbed of the pleasure of being able to say goodbye to them; or rather, that he could have used their service for his earthly profit, in which the heart of natural men consists. Matthew 6:21.

However, beneath such a theft, this archetype is hidden: that when it happens again with the Jews—the house of Jacob—that they move toward the land of Canaan again, one will soon thereafter see idolatry taken away from the Oriental peoples. Psalm 87:4.

# 24. But **GOD** came to Laban the Syrian in a dream at night / and spoke to him: Take heed / that you do not speak with Jacob / either good or bad!

### 25. Thus

Since *Laban* was full of wrath against *Jacob* / **GOD** restrained him through His appearance and a serious threat / so that he should deal with *Jacob* peacefully.

Who would not wonder at **GOD’s** care / which He has for the souls devoted to Him! He anticipates all kinds of impending troubles on their behalf. He does not even spare revelations nor miracles / to preserve them against the persecutions and the hardship of their persecutors: as is sufficiently recognizable in the wonderful rescue of *Jacob* and his entire house / from *Laban’s* wrath.

At first glance, **GOD’s** speech seems to contain nothing more than an external deliverance from the scolding of external enemies / so that they should not treat a godly man poorly / or do too much against him.

But divine faith looks much deeper into the foundation / and perceives therein a general privilege <note>original: "Privilegium"</note> against all conceivable hostilities / damages, and obstacles / in both physical and spiritual matters / and an invincible assertion of the divine counsel and way with His own.

Yet the persons must be well recognized / who can be privileged <note>original: "privilegiret"</note> by **GOD** in such a manner. For a great deal of deception mixes in: because all those who suffer something want to be regarded as pious.

Nothing is more common / than for people to want to be seen as pious simply because they complain about persecutions. They then claim for themselves, without distinction, that same privilege / and want to be coddled, justified, and comforted by **GOD** and His messengers.

But there is a mighty difference among the persecuted. Who was it here / for whom **GOD** made such a letter of protection? It was *Jacob* / an honest, pious man; no hypocrite / no pretender. He proved this from his youth with deeds / and not with mere words.

Who must not give him witness / what an upright will toward **GOD** and his neighbor dwelt in him? For twenty whole years he served the stubborn, greedy *Laban*; and did so / in such a way that he not only made him rich / but also patiently endured and overcame all of *Laban’s* injustice, deceit, and lies. *v.* 6. 38-42.

Now, by this righteous mind and behavior, he was deemed worthy / to enjoy **GOD’s** special defense. And indeed, the most diligent preservation by **GOD** Himself is a mark of this. For truly **GOD** would not have taken his side so / if he had not been of one will with Him.

Let one see here a living mirror / of what a noble treasure an honest conscience is / how it helps through death and danger / and is in everything the only ground of all safety, joyfulness, and blessedness! Understand here a conscience purified in faith and governed by the Holy Spirit / not a mere pagan appearance of virtue or freedom from external vices.

Let one always learn to highly esteem true godliness! Think / how useful it is for all things! Who would want to exchange his free, upright conscience toward **GOD** for all the world's goods? After all, all rest / all protection and preservation / lie in the fear of **GOD**!

Not that pious people should suffer nothing at all: but that they shall not suffer harm in their best part / or perish entirely.

Thus it remains settled and certain: Those enjoy **GOD’s** protection / who suffer injustice for the sake of conscience; but not those who suffer blows for the sake of misdeeds.

Therefore, let one test oneself well / and search / whether one has the Lord’s will and command before them in the matter / in which one must suffer. Otherwise, it is very hard to suffer / when something else is witnessed inwardly / and one is condemned in the heart by **GOD** for one’s disobedience. Even enemies soon notice / when things are not right with a person / and when they catch them on the wrong paths.

*Jacob* had here the specific command of **GOD** before him: therefore **GOD** could not deny him His privilege. For whomever a great Lord uses in his service / he must also provide with protection and passports <note>original: "Päspforten"</note>.

<column-break/>

*Jacob* became simply obedient to the word of the **LORD** / which He / according to *v.* 3, 13 / had spoken in his heart / regardless of the fact that he well foresaw *Laban’s* resistance. Nevertheless, he ventured it at his greatest peril: and therein lay the very power of his protection; namely, in the simple obedience of faith.

Therefore, let everyone now begin to fear **GOD** sincerely: then he will also be united with Him / and find everything therein. Such people alone are those / who can assure themselves of the great freedoms of **GOD**: from which all those greedy for blood, money, and honor are excluded / along with all false people or hypocrites and "mouth-Christians."

But what kind of enemies are they / against whom one shall have protection? How do they look and what is their nature / outwardly and inwardly? *Answer:* Outwardly they mostly shine beautifully / and often deceive very powerfully with appearance. According to the body, they present themselves as friends and relatives / according to the mind, as the pious and fellow believers. All of this is vividly presented here in

*Laban*) According to the flesh he was related to *Jacob* / and called him his brother; whom he embraced and kissed in the first greeting / and led into his house. *c.* 29/13. 15.

According to the mind, he wanted to have the reputation / as if he knew and feared the **GOD** of *Jacob*. *c.* 30/27. and below *v.* 49. 53.

And that is a precise image of worldly people / of all hypocrites and secret enemies of **GOD** and His members / what a deceptive appearance they can put on / to catch the simple / and draw them into their net.

Thus **GOD’s** children dwell with *Jacob* right among snakes and scorpions / and rarely get away unstung.

In all such dangers, protection and preservation may well be necessary. But they are not only necessary / but also possible and certain / as this example teaches us.

**GOD’s** letter of protection or safe-conduct / which He gave to dear *Jacob* / reads thus:

> Take heed!) As dear as your life is to you / refrain / so that you / as it sounds very thoughtfully in the Hebrew / do not speak with *Jacob* from good to bad / that is / according to the Hebrew meaning of the little word <term>unto <note>original Hebrew: "עד" ('ad)</note></term>,

Neither good nor bad) Accordingly, the full sense of **GOD** in this speech is not only that *Laban* should not speak evil against *Jacob* / as the 70 interpreters <note>Referring to the Septuagint</note> give it: but he should also speak no "good" / that is / he should not offer him such plausible persuasions / by which he might hold him back and withdraw him from the intended journey; namely because **GOD** had once decided and commanded otherwise. *v.* 3.

This understanding of the words provides so much for reflection / how **GOD** holds so strictly to His arrangements and commands / that He faithfully maintains those who follow them / and holds back the adversaries with power / and does not permit / that they may turn a faithful heart away from following Him with cunning.

**GOD** wanted His once-issued command to be fulfilled. Since *Laban*, out of greed / so that he could enjoy *Jacob* longer / wanted to hinder him; see, so **GOD** strictly commanded him on the contrary / to proceed briskly on the journey.

*Luther* <note>Martin Luther</note> derived a very fine meaning from this / that according to the Hebrew it could mean: You shall not begin to speak friendly with *Jacob* / and afterwards conclude the speech with scolding words! That is; *Laban* should not bring the accusations against *Jacob* and the reproach onto the track at all / because they were lies and errors.

Oh, how precious is **GOD’s** goodness / that we poor children of men are allowed to dwell under the shadow of His wings! How highly is this privilege to be held / that **GOD** wants to carry out and assert His cause in and through us!

**GOD** keeps His words: one can rely on that. Whoever follows them / will be powerfully protected. For he is in the service, protection, and conduct of a great Lord. One only needs to show his letter of freedom / and trust in **GOD’s** promise: Who is he that can harm us?

Oh, what a great multitude of such privileges are found in the Scripture! What an assurance is the 91st Psalm! One should venture everything on a single word / when it becomes alive in the heart!

### 25. Thus Laban overtook Jacob. Now Jacob had pitched his tent on the mountain / and Laban pitched his with his kinsmen / on Mount Gilead.

### 26. Then Laban said to Jacob: What have you done / that you have stolen my heart <note>The idiom "stolen my heart" in this biblical context means to deceive or trick someone, acting behind their back.</note> / and have carried away my daughters / as if they were captives taken by the sword?

### 27. Why did you flee secretly / and steal away from me ; and did not tell me / so that I might have sent you away with joy and with songs / with drums and with harps?

<margin>v. 25. Mount Gilead)</margin> Which in its length comprised approximately 25 German miles. <note>A historical "German mile" was roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers.</note>

<margin>v. 26. etc. etc.</margin> In this way, natural men <note>The "natural man" refers to someone acting on worldly impulse rather than spiritual guidance.</note> / when they are hindered by **GOD** in various wonderful ways from exercising their malice / know how to craftily disguise themselves / as if they had meant well / and were inclined toward what is good; which they do not truly mean: For Laban would never have allowed it to reach the point / where he would have released his family with joy. And thus the blame must always lie with the godly / that they must have acted dishonestly / simply because they will not conduct themselves in everything according to the perverse mind and will of worldly people.

In all persecutions of the godly, the enemy seeks to bring forth plausible excuses / and wants to appear to have the law on his side. Indeed, he seeks in every way to blacken and slander them as if they were evil people.

How plausible it sounded here in Laban's accusations against Jacob / that he had led away his daughters secretly / against his knowledge and will / as if they were captives of the sword? When these were, after all, his own children / and he was his son-in-law / who had him to thank for everything.

That had a fine appearance of justice and truth; but at the very foundation, it was all lies and deception.

Jacob had not begun the slightest thing out of his own will / but purely followed **GOD**. Likewise, Laban's daughters were no longer under their father’s power / but had to cling to and follow their husband. What then did Laban want / and what right did he have / to pursue Jacob?

But thus acts the wicked spirit of the world. It flees to where it can catch those who have become unfaithful to it / even under the smallest pretense.

<margin>v. 27.</margin> On the other hand, hypocrites do not know how to justify themselves enough / and to boast of their good works / claiming they wanted to do good to such "hateful" people. As Laban says here; he would have wanted to have

**Guided them with joy and songs / drums and harps)** He would have wanted to give a feast / so that it appeared respectable / and not so wretched.

But that is precisely Lucifer / who also drives the worst rogues / to want to conduct themselves as saints / and meanwhile strike down the true believers. Yet the value of their holiness is easily recognized by its tone and sound / and one soon hears / that there is nothing behind it but a sounding brass and a clanging cymbal. <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 13:1.</note>

...to do harm / even if they are already dead in the body according to the flesh / and the more of his followers were killed / the more new witnesses of his truth arose / who grew / as it were / out of the seed of the shed blood of martyrs. <note>The author is drawing a parallel between Jacob's protection and the historical growth of the Church through persecution.</note>

Then Laban dared not utter a word more / than what **GOD** permitted him. The impression / which he received in the dream / held him back; because self-love feared its own harm and **GOD’s** punishments.

Many a smoking oath is pregnant with nothing but swords / spears / murders / lies, and blasphemies: therein he thinks to accomplish his task. But it takes only a single little word to fell him / and grip his conscience; then he is condemned as an evildoer / and feels **GOD’s** heavy hand / even if he will not confess it out of pride.

<column-break/>

### 28. And you did not allow me / to kiss my sons and my daughters? Now you have done foolishly!

### 29. It would be in the power of my hands / to deal poorly with you! But your father’s **GOD** spoke to me yesterday and said: Take heed / that you do not speak with Jacob either good or bad!

### 30. And

<margin>v. 28. You have done foolishly)</margin> In the whole world, there is no sinner / except those alone who have **GOD’s** Word / and believe in Jesus Christ. But those who persecute the Way / they are righteous and pious / and think / they are doing **GOD** a service. This is Luther’s (a) observation on this point: who also well reminds us / that Laban did not keep **GOD’s** command well / in that he nevertheless addressed and accused good Jacob so harshly: that he had stolen his heart / his daughters, and everything; had acted foolishly / deserved this and that / etc.

Certainly, the wicked mind does not let go. If it cannot speak good things for appearance and deception / then the indwelling hell overflows with sulfur and burning pitch of blasphemy and false accusation. **GOD** permits this a little / but He also sets a goal and measure to all such adversities / so that they can be endured.

It is true / fierce nature can spit out much venom against **GOD** and His friends / and even present such things to the world in writings: but it all does not reach into the true foundation; they are blows to the air / which are not felt: as is experienced.

<margin>v. 29. But **GOD** has spoken to me)</margin> **GOD’s** Word and voice are so mighty / that they reach even into the hearts of the worst people / and excite great terror and awe therein.

O how **GOD** can inwardly place a bit into the lying mouth or heart of many a boaster and braggart / and hunt him back with terror along the way / by which he came!

This is still the only refuge against all coarse atheistic mockers / that they cannot deny / that something stirs in their conscience / which they cannot entirely extinguish or dampen.

Laban knew it exactly / that Jacob's and Isaac's **GOD** had spoken with him in a dream / and forbidden him what he had in mind.

Even the worst and most perverse hearts still feel **GOD’s** power and voice against their will / and notice well / that it is not fantasy.

So it also goes with **GOD’s** instruments and friends. **GOD** attaches such a hidden power of the Spirit to them / that their enemies / blasphemers / liars, and enviers / are immediately secretly shaken / if they only become aware of them / or hear them from afar. Indeed, they often gladly crawl away from a believer out of the impulse of a guilty conscience. And

Even if entire parties often band together against a believer / and forge the most cunning, hypocritical plots against him: **GOD** blows into them with His breath / and scatters all their designs / so that such hostile birds must be ashamed of their malice all their lives. And

Certainly / where **GOD** did not often set boundaries to the persecution of ungodly and perverse men / neither body nor soul would endure it for long. But this is also the greatest treasure of our **GOD’s** faithfulness / that He already knows how to create the outcome along with the temptation / and also to moderate the malice of the creature.

How gladly would the enemy have completely rooted out Christ and His apostles! How he hated the priests and scribes against the little flock! But **GOD** did not permit it until they were killed. The Lord Himself soon rose again from the dead / and the more of His followers were killed / the more new witnesses of His truth arose / who grew / as it were / out of the seed of the shed blood of martyrs.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXI.

30. And now, since you certainly wanted to depart, because you longed so much for your father’s house; why have you stolen my gods?

31. And Jacob answered and spoke to Laban: Because I was afraid, for I thought that you might take your daughters from me by force.

32. With whomever you find your gods, let him not remain alive! Investigate what is with me in the presence of our brothers, and take it! But Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.

**v. 30.** Finally, natural men <note>The "natural man" is a term used in Pietist theology to describe someone living according to worldly impulses rather than spiritual rebirth.</note> cannot hide their malice and show what grieves them most: namely, when someone has touched their idols. This happens whether they feel they have suffered a physical loss, or when someone rejects the religious matters upon which they misplace their trust; this is where one can offend them most deeply, and they are prone to great zeal in defending such things.

Satan is afraid his kingdom might perish if some were to dare to take the gods away from the idolatrous. Therefore, this was one of Laban’s chief complaints:

Why have you stolen my gods from me?) The natural man, instead of the living **GOD**, grasps with all his desires so many false gods upon which he builds: be it his own intellect, or pleasure, or self-love, and the like. For:

All love that is not directed purely toward **GOD** makes an idol in the heart out of the beloved thing, becoming an abomination and annoyance to the true Master of the Temple.

Now, if an enlightened person comes and wants to take the gods from such a servant of idols—that is, to expose his sins and make them loathsome, or to hinder him in his follies—oh, how Laban lashes out at Jacob! How he defends his false worship, through which he thinks he will escape hell and reach heaven!

One should take care to remember whether one also feels anger toward those who wanted to dispute or take away this or that idol. It is one of the most common enmities experienced in the world when the false god sitting in the heart is touched.

Do not many think that one blasphemes **GOD** Himself when one casts doubt on their reliance on their outward religious service—going to church and the Lord’s Supper—without repentance and improvement? They think that because they inherited such ways from their fathers, as Laban did from Nahor, then living, true conversion and the new birth is a "new doctrine" that was not valued in the old days.

**v. 31. 32.** Believers must take care not to provoke natural men without a lawful cause; rather, they must always demonstrate a heart that loves even outward justice.

The fruit of the divine privilege, once it is written and imprinted upon our hearts, is joy and boldness.

Just consider: Laban had many armed men with him, and yet poor, weak Jacob dares to face him thus and scold him, or give him sharp rebukes, and uncover his malice one point after another.

Where would Jacob have dared this if he had not carried **GOD’S** protection and a good conscience within him? Oh, how joyful this makes one! Yes, many thousand times more courageous than when a civil servant carries a great letter from his sovereign in his pocket.

Thus, a weak instrument may sometimes venture to tell the truth to the face of the cleverest person. Yes, a boy will put his hand into the holes of adders and basilisks <note>A basilisk is a mythical reptile mentioned in older Bible translations, often used as a metaphor for deadly sin or danger.</note> without harm. For such unjust spirits are like chained dogs that reach no further than they are permitted. They are locked and barred in their own hell by **GOD’S** judgment.

<column-break/>

33. Then Laban went into Jacob’s tent and into Leah’s tent, and into the tent of the two maidservants, and found nothing: and he went out of Leah’s tent and went into Rachel’s tent.

34. Then Rachel took the images and laid them under the camel’s saddle and sat upon them. But Laban searched the whole tent and found nothing.

35. Then she said to her father: Let no anger burn in my lord’s eyes that I cannot rise before your face! For the way of women is upon me. And he searched, and found the images not.

36. And Jacob became angry and quarreled with Laban; and Jacob began and spoke to Laban: What is my transgression, or what is my sin, that you have so hotly pursued me?

37. For you have searched all my household goods: what have you found of all your household goods? Lay it out here before my brothers and your brothers, that they may judge between us both!

**v. 34. 35.** The **LORD** has patience with the weaknesses of the faithful and knows how to help them so that their harmless cunning sometimes succeeds. They must not, however, misuse this gracious protection or turn it into wantonness.

<margin>(a) ch. 36. p. 91. ed. Vorst.</margin>
**Images)** <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Household idols or oracles.</note> The Jews claim these were human heads. Rabbi Eliezer in the *Pirke* <note>original: "Pirke" - referring to the *Pirke De-Rabbi Eliezer*, a midrashic work on the Torah.</note> (a) says that a firstborn human was slaughtered, his head split, preserved with salt and oil, and the name of an unclean spirit was written on a golden plate and placed under his tongue. Then the head was placed on the wall, a light lit before it, and it was worshipped: it would then answer the questions asked.

**v. 36.** Thus, in their own time, the faithful can also confront earthly people—to whom they have often shown so much faithful service—with their own diligence and care, and in contrast, with those people’s treacherous minds, ingratitude, and great injustice. However, they must take care not to break out into this from ill-temper or a desire for revenge, but rather seize the opportunity when they are too grossly offended; they must also keep themselves within the bounds of modesty and the fear of **GOD**, so that they may also appeal to His protection and continue to find comfort in it.

38. These twenty years I have been with you: your sheep and your goats have not been barren, and I have not eaten the rams of your flock!

40. It happened to me that the heat consumed me by day and the frost by night, and my sleep fled from my eyes.
41. I have now been in your house these twenty years; fourteen years I served you for your two daughters, and six years for your flock: and you have changed my wages ten times!
42. If the **GOD** of my father, the **GOD** of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac <note>A unique title for God used only in this passage, referring to the profound reverence or "dread" Isaac felt for the Almighty.</note>, had not been with me; you would surely have let me go empty-handed now! **GOD** has looked upon my misery and the labor of my hands, and he rebuked you yesterday!

***

**v. 38-40.** These are the marks of a good shepherd, who brings no harm to the flock and allows nothing to be stolen by the enemy: who stands before the sheep and lays down his life for them: who looks after their benefit and takes upon himself all the damage that could be inflicted upon them. In all of Holy Scripture, one will hardly find an image more filled with **JESUS**, the true Shepherd, than that which we find in Jacob: nor are all the virtues that the true shepherds of souls must have better presented than here. But let no one flatter himself that he is equal to these great duties unless he is like Jacob: namely, strong in **GOD** through a deep inwardness.

**v. 42.** If **GOD** did not preserve the physical blessings of the believers, they would soon have to leave such things as prey for the ungodly.

While Isaac was still living, Jacob lets it rest there, referring only to his great fear and terror before **GOD**, as he did not wish to resist His will and left the blessing to him. Chapter 27:33, 28:1, etc. But because Abraham had already overcome <note>A Pietist term meaning "to pass away" or "to triumph over the trials of life through death."</note>, he calls Him the **GOD** of Abraham, just as **GOD** later calls Himself the **GOD** of Isaac and the **GOD** of Jacob after their death and blessed overcoming. Exodus 3:6.

**v. 44, 45.** Believers must show themselves very ready for reconciliation, even when they have done nothing wrong.

**v. 46-51.** In the setting up of such stone markers and the naming of them, they were accustomed to remember the things they had discussed and promised to one another: because at that time writing had not yet been invented, and this is also always a living testimony, the reason for which one person tells to another. See Joshua 23:26, 27, 28, and chapter 24:26, 27, where the already-invented art of writing was added to it.

# The XXXII. Chapter.
->Jacob’s Fear, Prayer, and Struggle.<-

<image-desc>large ornamental initial J</image-desc>
Jacob, however, went on his way, and the angels of God met him.
2. And—

***

v. 52. Thus the Almighty gradually delivers and distances us from those who must test us according to His will.

It was a special providence of God toward Laban that he declared himself with such kindness toward Jacob after this dispute.

Could anything be more beautiful for our naturally faint hearts than this holy governance of God: that the adverse powers and spirits, which for a while seemed almost unbearable to us, must finally resolve and reveal that they no longer wish to harm us, but will stay far enough away from us? This is so that we may learn to see how the Lord creates peace around us from our enemies, if only we rely on Him in a truly godly manner.

Often, one should not even pray to God out of one's own will to have adversity taken away entirely. For one does not know if it is necessary and good for the soul’s self-denial. Therefore, it is like a tree of life afterward when God Himself governs it so.

Fear now, all you who carry a false Laban or a raging Esau against the God-fearing within your own bosom! See what God has promised to those who love Him! See the dividing wall that God has set between you and His own, so that there can be no union of light with darkness!

v. 53. In the swearing of this covenant, Laban indeed appeals to the God of Abraham, acknowledging Him as the true God; however, he also wishes to honor Him in the manner of his father Nahor; where, without doubt, much superstition remained from their common father, Terah <note>Joshua 24:2 mentions that Terah, the father of Abraham and Nahor, served other gods.</note>, as can be seen from his idols. Ancestral ways, especially in religious matters, make such a strong impression that people do not easily abandon them.

v. 54. 55. God wished to grant this pleasure of reconciliation to Jacob as well as to Laban and his kin; otherwise, Providence could have prevented them from ever meeting: because God takes great delight in friendship and love among men, provided it is truly sincere.

The true deep meaning and purpose of God in this meeting was that God wanted to strengthen Jacob's faith; he was certainly in the fellowship of God and His angels: therefore he should venture everything upon Him and continue the journey in His name.

No other ground is yet open to all true believers than the inner spiritual fellowship, friendship, and kinship of the holy angels with them. They now meet those who are worthy in pure heavenly powers, pure love, wisdom, justice, power, and strength.

<column-break/>

In the previous chapter, we find the excellent privilege which the eternal God gives into the hand—or rather, into the heart—of His own against their enemies: here, the actual protection is presented, which one truly enjoys through faith in Him.

A great lord is not satisfied with merely giving an honest subject, or even his son, a blank piece of paper; rather, he also provides him with an actual safeguard <note>original: "Salvo-Garde" — a military term for a guard or protection-order given to a person or place.</note> or bodyguard, and fulfills and confirms his granted privilege.

Now, however, every hypocrite and wicked fellow wants to comfort and tickle themselves with the protection of the holy angels. Thus, the promise from Scripture is often applied carelessly and without condition to all listeners without the necessary distinction. For this reason, it is good and necessary to pay close attention to the person we encounter in the text, and to see for everyone's conviction who may truly comfort themselves with the protection of God.

Jacob was an honest, God-fearing, and believing man: but Laban was a hypocrite, a miser, and a deceiver. These two could not possibly stay together. Jacob escaped and withdrew himself and his family from Laban and his seduction, and turned instead to the path of reconciling with his brothers.

The Spirit of God makes this understood with the words: *Jacob went his way.* Why would it otherwise matter to us whether we knew anything of Jacob's journey? It should serve as an example to us, so that we might see how we must necessarily withdraw from the evil world and follow God, if we wish to have Him and His angels with us.

It is impossible to find the Kingdom of God and His heavenly hosts open where one has not first closed his heart to the world and its wicked things, seductions, and examples. Two kingdoms cannot reveal themselves in one place at the same time.

This is exactly what the 91st Psalm stipulates, and what the devil omitted in Matthew 4: that the angels of God protect us *in all our ways.*

The heavenly guard and power of the spiritual kingdom cannot well open and communicate itself until the earthly kingdom is closed to the will—for the earthly kingdom keeps the spiritual eyes shut and enchanted, so that they cannot see or perceive God's angels in the spirit.

All those who leave the evil world with its foolish customs, fashions, and godless rules out of an honest heart and desire for God should take note of this. The world cannot harm them; rather, it must return with Laban. Even if its adherents send a heap of blasphemies after them, they shall do them no harm: For here is Immanuel and his heavenly host!

But for him whom God does not find in His ways of truth, righteousness, and love, His privilege is worth nothing. He gives it only to obedient subjects. Or does one think that the holy spirits will have the desire or will to serve those who do not fear and serve the Lord? That would eternally never rhyme with their holy and divine mind.

*The angels of God met him*) This expression may give us great cause for reflection as to what God intended with such a meeting.

Good Jacob was caught in a tight spot. <note>original: "stack zwischen Thür und Angel in der Klemme" — literally "stuck between the door and the hinge."</note> He had hardly gotten rid of Laban when he had to go like a sheep into the jaws of Esau. There, protection and assistance were surely necessary. And the faithful God showed him this through such a heavenly representation of the hosts or armies consisting entirely of angels.

<margin>Jacob saw the angels of God upon his departure from Laban. For</margin>
Only those souls can truly perceive and value the gift and benefit of the holy angels who are enlightened and sanctified through the breakthrough of true repentance, so that they may judge spiritual things spiritually.

Hypocrites and the disobedient may indeed have seen angels at times, but this happened only through God’s special permission, and God first had to open their eyes.

It is therefore a established truth that whoever wishes to recognize and enjoy the divine benefit of angels must necessarily be enlightened by God for that purpose.

Even if you heard every verse recited that deals with the holy angels, if your will were trapped and occupied by worldly lust, anger, envy, pride, or similar devilish powers, you would not be able to rightly grasp the least bit of it or be able to rejoice in it.

Dear Jacob’s eyes of faith had already been opened in the previous vision at Bethel, where he saw the angels of God ascending and descending. Thus, he recognized them here all the more easily from experience.

So must we also learn to obtain not only knowledge but also experience in life, in all circumstances, regarding such holy angels.

God’s holy providence expresses itself most powerfully in all things for a believer—so much so that He even lets them know how faithfully He preserves them through the presence and powerful fellowship of the holy angels. And

Certainly, believers have a spiritual eye of faith and an enlightened vision of understanding, through which they see their Savior in the spirit of faith! Why then should they not also perceive or become aware of the holy spirits and angels in a spiritual way?

There is no doubt that many in the Scriptures have seen angels in this way, and that Jacob himself perhaps recognized these hosts primarily in the spirit of his mind and found them present.

There are powers and authorities among the angels who are subject to Christ. Thus, they must be able to be noticed and felt where they are present. For a power is called such because it is found to be powerful.

One can indeed notice evil and unclean spirits so precisely, as is often experienced with ghosts; where one sees nothing, and yet one's hair often stands on end, and one notices a supernatural shudder and dread in one's nature.

If the inner senses of the soul can feel evil spirits, how much more the good ones? Especially when a person has senses trained in the faith of the truth and learns to distinguish the presence of good angels from the evil ones.

Thus, in this teaching, one is not led toward a mere delusion or human opinions, but toward the idea that one should strive for trained senses and enlightened eyes to experience the wonders of the Kingdom of God even in this: that one may often realize how near and powerful these holy powers and spirits are.

There are certain angelic influences and spiritual communications from such heavenly spirits that grant a believer much good in times of need through grace from above. For just as it is no insult to the dear God—or even a king—that he administers his rule through earthly authorities and ambassadors, so too is it no dishonor to God (indeed, it is a greater praise) when He spreads and shares His gifts through holy spirits.

A camp of God; God’s armies; such great and mighty multitudes or choirs that bring with them an unspeakable power: just as one or more armies can either protect and maintain a whole kingdom, or shake and ruin it.

"How can I be so terrified," Jacob wishes to say here, "that I should fear for even a moment! For God sends entire armies to meet me, which could easily chase away a thousand Esaus and ten thousand Labans, along with all the evil spirits, however many there are!"

<column-break/>

<meta>3. Yes</meta>
This makes God's glory tremendously great: that He can assign such a large and powerful multitude of princes and authorities to His own, of which even a single one could strike down an innumerable multitude of enemies.

At the same time, it is an excellent strengthening of faith to know that such great and mighty lords are appointed as assistants—those whom the Spirit rightly calls "mighty heroes" <note>original: "starcke Helden" — refers to Psalm 103:20, describing the strength of angels.</note>, Ps. 103:21.

These are not idle or useless among those who fear God, but they are busy pitching a camp all around them and helping them. Psalm 34:8. Just as Jacob here names "two armies" in the Hebrew <note>Mahanaim is the dual form of the word for camp/army, meaning 'Two Camps'.</note>; as if a single angel or one host were not enough, God sends two whole armies to meet him.

Some Hebrew interpreters have believed that these armies—which in Hebrew signify two—should be understood such that one host or choir had come with Jacob from his previous dwelling place, and the other had come to meet him from the land of Canaan.

Sometimes a person must struggle with literal princes and powers, with the lords of the world and evil spirits; often also with such wicked and malicious people who are actually possessed by more than one evil spirit in a spiritual way and according to their vices, as a "legion" was in one man.

If sufficient angelic powers were not also given for protection there, a poor sheep would often perish; they would swallow one up like bread.

Therefore, this makes God's glory and majesty very venerable and high: that this LORD of Hosts <term>Zebaoth: Hebrew for 'Hosts' or 'Armies', emphasizing God's command over the celestial forces</term> has so many armies of the mightiest spirits under His command, and sends and uses them wherever He wills—just as if a monarch could field an army consisting of innumerable princes or kings.

This is what the Scripture aims at when it so often calls the Creator the LORD Zebaoth, the LORD of Hosts, a commander and ruler of such innumerable armies and choirs of angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, and principalities. Oh, that we were more diligent in getting to know, honor, and love this infinite majesty better!

We should rightly use every opportunity for this knowledge and, whenever God gives us special proofs of His holy protection and help, we should make and keep certain memorials of them, just as Jacob here named the place of the miracle Mahanaim.

These are nothing other than certain NB <note>Latin: "nota bene," meaning "note well."</note> and signs that a believer makes to remember the wonders of God, much like a reader makes a mark or an "NB" next to the things that seem most remarkable to him.

Such an "NB" is also this comfort which the angels give, and which has the ultimate goal of preparing the soul for the great struggles it must endure before it enters into God. It no longer has to fear the persecutions of creatures, but God Himself. But before that, it must experience the assault of earthly enemies, which are only the precursors of another struggle—for which one does not fear, because one knows nothing of it. One fears a visible skirmish, which has only the appearance of a conflict; and one does not fear a true struggle, which is unknown.

To the tempted, the sorrowful, and the forsaken, God is nearest with His good spirits. They gladly take part in our misery; they rejoice in our redemption, just as they rejoiced over Christ’s birth.

Should a troubled heart see how compassionately and carefully such holy spirits act toward them, it could never be sorrowful again. For

It is nothing but help, counsel, protection, comfort, and joy, prepared for those who seek eternal life with patience in good works.

So now, conceive truly great and blessed thoughts of your God, all you who bear grief or suffer under afflictions! Do not hold Him to be so small and powerless, as if neither He nor His messengers and angels could help! The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our protection!

v. 52. Thus the Almighty gradually frees and removes us from those who must test us in His will.

**The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXII.**

**3. And Jacob sent messengers before him to his brother Esau, into the land of Seir, the territory of the Edomites.**

**4. And he commanded them, saying: Thus shall you speak to my lord Esau: "Thus says your servant Jacob; I have stayed with Laban and have tarried until now.**

**5. And I have cattle and donkeys, sheep and menservants and maidservants; and I have sent word to tell my lord, so that I might find grace in your eyes."**

**6. And the messengers returned to Jacob, saying: "We came to your brother Esau; and he is also coming to meet you, and has four hundred men with him."**

**7. Then Jacob was very afraid and distressed; and he divided the people who were with him, and the sheep and the cattle and the camels, into two armies.**

**8. And he said: "If Esau comes to the one army and strikes it, then the remaining army will escape."**

As Jacob, on his journey to his father in the land of Canaan, was forced to pass through the land and territory of his brother Esau (who was also called Edom), he greeted his brother to request a peaceful passage, while simultaneously wishing to test his disposition toward him. In a similar way, Moses later asked the Edomites, the descendants of Esau, for such a free passage (Numbers 20:14, etc.). However, both had to experience a hostile disposition; for the hatred between brothers is very difficult to overcome (Proverbs 18:19). Yet, believers must always demonstrate a heart fully inclined toward peace and reconciliation on every occasion. Just as Laban pursued his pious son-in-law in anger, so too was the wrath of Esau immediately stirred when he received the message from his humble and gentle brother, who had been blessed by their father and now so dutifully announced himself. Thus, believers often have to deal now with natural men, now with hateful brothers and relatives, who do not fail to show their ill-will whenever the opportunity arises.

One often falls into internal unrest over an imagined evil, even while remaining immovable and steadfast in actual battles. Thus, Jacob is very afraid of Esau’s approach; yet he does not yet shudder at the entirely different struggles that God has prepared for him, although he shall happily escape them through His special assistance.

Otherwise, this entire encounter between Jacob and Esau very accurately depicts the pilgrim’s journey of true believers toward their Father’s house.

v. 6. The spirit of this world is enraged at the followers of Christ because of their good mind toward Christ, which does not agree with the world. Therefore, the world and its prince approach with so many hundreds of men—indeed, with many armies—and wish to prevent their return home to the heavenly Fatherland and Canaan.

v. 7. Here the Holy Spirit teaches His own that they should wisely divide what belongs to them.

(In two armies) Namely, they leave the body and all transitory things to the enemies; but the soul and that which is spiritual and eternal they keep for themselves with great diligence, so that they may carry it away as a prize.

<column-break/>

**9. Jacob said further: "O you God of my father Abraham, and you God of my father Isaac! O LORD, who said to me: 'Return to your land and to your relatives; and I will do good to you!'" 10. I...**

---

A faithful Israelite always turns to God Himself in prayer, holds His word before Him, remembers the faithful guidance received thus far in the middle of the dangerous path through the wilderness of this evil world, and seeks further protection and grace.

There one first learns the true foundation of prayer in faith, which this faithful patriarch sets forth here so precious.

Every person generally thinks that they pray, but the prayer is only as good as its foundation.

Whoever wishes to pray rightly must be a child of God, or at least truly wish to become one. Those, however, are children in whom the Spirit of the Son dwells and prays.

One should look at Jacob's childlike prayer, how he appeals to God’s Fatherhood and to his right as a child, as to a true rebirth.

(O you LORD of my father Abraham — Isaac) With this, he refers to the holy and spiritual lineage or genealogy, as it were—to the propagation of faith from his ancestors, through which he had also become a partaker of the childhood of God in the Messiah <note>The author uses "Messiah" here to connect the Old Testament patriarchs to the Christian concept of salvation through Christ.</note>, just as in 2 Timothy 1:5.

But who can grasp or apply this foundation in us except Him who must lay it Himself? Namely, the Spirit of adoption <note>original: "Geist der Kindschafft," referring to the biblical concept of adoption as sons of God.</note>, when we allow ourselves to be truly renewed and reborn in the spirit of our mind. For His testimony alone in the heart counts before the Father: that we, as children in the greatest simplicity and intimacy, may cry out to Him—or rather, the Holy Spirit must cry out within us.

This is the Spirit of adoption, who alone can pray rightly and unite the mind with the Father.

So let one consider from what basis one calls God "Father" in prayer. One must truly be Abraham’s spiritual seed in unfeigned faith (Galatians 3:29).

This is best proven in the actual obedience of faith toward God’s commandment. Jacob relies here solely on God’s command that he had heard in his heart; he refers to the expressed command and will of God, who had explicitly ordered it and said it to him.

(Said) This gives us a beautiful pattern for what our longing before God should be directed toward and why we should pray: namely, solely for the sake of God’s will.

Jacob wanted to say: "My Father, did You not impose this journey upon me? It is precisely because of this obedience that I fall into such danger. If You now wish to uphold Your word, You must surely rescue me."

A faithful pilgrim in his distress may hold the same before his heavenly Father: "You have indeed imposed this difficult journey to Paradise upon me! The enemies are enraged precisely because I am leaving their ways; otherwise, they would leave me in peace. If You now wish to have me back in my heavenly Fatherland, You must also help me along the way."

With this, the Father’s heart is powerfully moved—when we are not occupied with our self-chosen or self-pleasing paths, no matter how shining and clever they might seem, but when we are sincerely concerned only that God’s will be done.

If one wants to see it rightly, this true foundation is nothing other than Jesus Christ Himself, who alone does the Father’s will in His own, and through His Spirit alone prays for the Father’s will and for nothing else.

(Return to your land — do good) When the LORD gives Jacob this command and promise, it says: "Return; and I will be with you" (Chapter 31:3). The LORD’s "being-with-us" is thus the same as "doing good." In the return, when we seek our Fatherland again, God is with us and wishes to do us good.

**Chapter XXXII. The First Book of Moses.**

<margin>(a) 2 Samuel 7:18.</margin>
# 10. I am ⁽ᵃ⁾ too insignificant for all the
# mercies and all the faithfulness
# which You have shown to Your servant!
# For with only my staff I crossed
# over this Jordan / and now I have
# become two armies.

In true Christianity, it is impossible to proceed without experience. A believer always experiences something good on the narrow road of the Cross. And that is also a precious ground for prayer / which Jacob presents here to the Lord: namely, the actual grace of God.

Jacob had experienced it firsthand / how God had been with him from his childhood in both spirit and body. From this, faith drew a firm conclusion: If You have helped me thus far / then You must complete and crown Your work.

And he did this in the deepest humility of his heart / with these words:

> I have been small against all your acts of kindness and faithfulness! ) as it actually reads in the original text <note>original: "Grund-Text", referring to the Hebrew "qatonti".</note>.

Which beautifully expresses / how Jacob, in the depths of his heart, thought nothing of himself / or considered himself worthy of the slightest grace / but rather held the most humble view or judgment of and concerning himself.

Note this well, all you who wish to be called Christians; how you must truly feel God's government of grace upon and within yourselves!

Oh, how many thousands of people grow old and grey / and go to the grave / before they have vividly perceived even the slightest of the power and effect of faith within them! In such cases, prayer is thereafter no better than the babbling of the heathens.

This man of faith here remembered with great certainty what God had already done for him. And that was a great help and encouragement for the future.

Would that we also often set aside a time / in which we remembered the holy guidance of God! Perhaps His Spirit would sometimes show us more within it / than we had noticed before.

Yet, in this, one must guard against natural pride as if against Satan himself / so that one does not transform God’s gifts and benefits into one’s own exaltation / and fly up with Lucifer / only for the fall to be all the heavier.

Jacob had learned a great wisdom in the school of the Holy Spirit / and therefore used even the greatest graces for his deeper humiliation. He made himself so small against the greatness of the merciful and faithful God / so that only the Source might receive His due honor.

And that is an indispensable ground in prayer / that God gives grace to the humble.

One should weigh the immeasurable mercy, patience, and constant faithfulness of God in Christ / against one's own hardness, ungratefulness, and unfaithfulness! Indeed, if one sees through the light of the Spirit even a single benefit of God thoroughly / and alongside it one’s own ungodly behavior: then one will surely fall down in the dust before Him / and acquire Jacob’s mind. If this realization is divinely grounded in the soul / the confession will surely follow.

This ground of prayer is once again invaluable / if, in all our asking and begging, we always mix in God's praise / even amidst the deepest suffering; so that we repeat before God from experience / the good He has done for us.

Not only does God receive the greatest honor from this / but we ourselves receive a powerful strengthening and encouragement toward all joyfulness of faith / so that we will also unfailingly trust ourselves entirely to God for the future.

All the saints have done so / and one will notice especially in the Psalms / that David also ends in the midst of the most anxious lamentations with lauding, praising, and thanking; just as Jacob here praises God in the midst of his fear.

For God's praise consists primarily in this confession. For this reason, in the Old Testament, one finds this expression almost throughout the original text / that the saints above in heaven and below on earth told of and freely confessed the Lord’s goodness and wonders.

<column-break/>

# 11. Deliver me, I pray, from the hand
# of my brother / from the hand of Esau.
# For

To human reason, this prayer of Jacob seems to come across as very silly and childish. For it has no artistic form / and is composed without any rational order / much less in a learned and methodical way / and least of all expanded into Pharisaic or heathen babbling.

He acts naturally like a simple child / who tells his dear father his concern and desire so straightforwardly / and mentions therein / what the father has promised him; then lets the father worry / how he will handle it with him. So very short, simple, and fragmented / yet pure and sincere / does this prayer appear.

This example will also be able to show us more / than all human instructions or affected and reduced prayer formulas / which the Holy Spirit does not Himself work in the mouth and heart.

May the light of the Spirit incessantly and faithfully present to us our inward and outward danger and distress / so that we may learn to cry out in faith with Jacob:

> Deliver me! ) He did indeed also ask for physical help; but he was primarily concerned with the rescue of divine honor / because God had promised him such great things concerning the Messiah. And

We should learn to look primarily and most of all at our inward and hidden enemies / who can cause us the most distress. Truly, external persecutions / blasphemies / and the like / are mere child's play compared to the spiritual powers of darkness / which can destroy body and soul together in hell / if they gain the upper hand.

Poor men must surely leave one in peace at last / if God terrifies them or turns them away. But the indwelling evil and the invisible powers of the Wicked One are the closest and most secret enemies / and consequently the most dangerous.

The good Jacob had to deal with the predatory and fierce Esau / and we find in our hard and stubborn self-will an even more powerful enemy / who, in the midst of the course of obedience, marches against us with more than 400 armed men / that is / with a thousandfold contrary thoughts and fancies / and has nothing but destruction in mind.

By right, there should be a whimpering and lamenting within us before God: Oh Lord, deliver me from the hand or power and dominant strength of my evil brother / the **Old Man** <term>Old Man: A biblical term referring to the unregenerate human nature or sinful self before spiritual transformation.</term> / who begrudges me my heavenly inheritance / and will not let me into my fatherland!

That is the chief petition / which the Spirit shall constantly demand from God: namely, the redemption from the **body of death** <note>A reference to Romans 7:24, representing the struggle against one's own sinful nature.</note> or from the old sinful birth. It is the entire work of Jesus Christ / which He must carry out in the soul / and truly desires to do; for which He also made perfect provision through His death.

Whoever now begins to rightly feel the burden of sin in the flesh / also learns with Jacob to pray the seventh petition for deliverance from this chief evil according to the mind of Christ. And if one must perhaps also experience evil from the outside in all kinds of adversity / so that the floods roar within and without; then one prays all the more vehemently with the suffering Jesus.

Conflicts without / and fears within: 2 Corinthians 7:5. These are fiery coals of temptation / which bring a sweet-smelling incense-offering to the Lord for His pleasure / even though we ourselves have no joy or pleasure in it at the time.

This is the true primary work of all prayers / to seek redemption again / which happened through Jesus Christ out of the evil of the Fall / and is now to be revealed and completed in every individual. Whoever understands this / will also in the future be well instructed and governed by the Holy Spirit in the **School of Prayer**.

The state of all true worshipers is for the most part distressed and dangerous.

Jacob had hardly escaped from the hands of a treacherous Laban / when he was informed by his people / that Esau was coming to meet him with 400 men. This now awakened in him a considerable fear / which he also honestly confesses to his God and says:

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXII.</header>

**For I am afraid of him / lest he come and strike me / the mother with the children.**

---

**I am afraid of him.)** Thus this soul was truly stuck in great danger from without, and in deep anxiety from within. And —

This is a very precise illustration of how a believing person is mostly pressed from within and without, so that he shall be awakened to right, earnest prayer.

A true man of prayer is not for one moment without suffering. The following of Christ and the taking up of His cross brings this along with it. And even if everything seemed quiet on the outside, there is never a time without distress and struggle on the inside against evil / against the earthly man / who is always on the march against us with an army of earthly thoughts and lusts.

Jacob certainly prayed in this external necessity / but there is no doubt that he must have prayed just as earnestly before because of his internal misery. For an enlightened person has his spiritual concerns constantly before his eyes.

If one looks at the prayers of all the godly in the Scriptures / one will always see them standing, at the very least, in inner bowedness and self-denial. For what does he want to ask for / who feels well in his flesh and knows of no need? No prayer can happen without an inwardly broken heart / that has become aware of its need and danger / and thus complains to God.

This might well be considered by all voluptuous / bold, and secure hearts / who wish to pray so presumptuously with an unbroken mind / and only mock God.

The manner in which Jacob returns to God in his affliction shows how useful anxiety and affliction are. They make one mindful of God's benefits; not only to comfort oneself with them / but also to double one's confidence in God thereby. Jacob holds all His promises before God: he does not complain; rather, he only presents to Him all the benefits He has shown him / so that they might not be made useless. He begs Him for help in such a strong and heart-breaking way / that the words recorded in Scripture express it even better than one could otherwise say. The terror and affliction in which he finds himself / very well represent a soul which / on the path of faith and serenity in God / is returning to its origin. For at that time, it is in nothing but doubt and anxiety. The anguish of death surrounds it / and appears to the soul to be inevitable. But what death does it fear? The death caused by sin. It knows / that it has often overcome this enemy / that it has tamed it / and trodden it underfoot. But since it now sees that it might easily fall into its hands; it does not doubt that the enemy should take revenge on it: and since it expects nothing else than that the enemy will then not spare it in the least; it seems to the soul that it must now be lost. Then such a soul, distressed from all corners, reminds God / that He has placed it in this way; that it has given itself into the same to serve Him blindly; that it has surrendered itself entirely to Him: and afterwards begs Him that He would protect it. It further presents to Him / that its fathers walked the same path / and that He declared Himself to be their God through that very path. It humbles itself before Him / and reminds Him of His truth.

It is a beautiful expression to say / strike the mother with the children. Sin strikes the mother; which is the righteousness acquired through grace: and also the children; which are the virtues and good works. This soul, pressed by anxiety, is about to lose almost both. It forgets all other good / and thinks only of its own righteousness / which it almost expects to lose. It gives up its other goods voluntarily: namely, it consents to the loss of all heavenly taste and sweetness. It is fitting / that all this should be taken from it by sin / which seems inevitable to it. But the individual righteousness / and the fruits / which are the holy virtues / oh, to lose these it cannot consent. No, O you poor afflicted soul! You shall receive more terror than evil from it. Do not fear! Since God intends to prevent these falls / which are threatened against you.

<column-break/>

**12. But You have said: I will surely do good to you / and make your descendants as the sand of the sea / which cannot be numbered for the multitude.**

---

->13. And<-

---

Yet another ground for true prayer is **God's** promise / which is grasped into the heart through the spirit of faith.

Thus Jacob here holds before the heavenly Father His gracious assurance:

> You have said: I will — your descendants &c.) Therein he primarily recognized the promise of that salvation in the Messiah <note>original: "Messia"</note> / for which he was still waiting even on his deathbed.

By holding such a highly important assurance before the Lord / he seizes Him, as it were, in the right place / so that He could not do otherwise than be heard. For now it came down to / whether God wanted to keep His promise, or not; to save His honor, or let it be shamed.

Just as one cannot urge an honest man <note>original: "Bidermann", an upright citizen of integrity.</note> more closely to the fulfillment of his word / than when one holds his own written bond <note>original: "Handschrifft", referring to a signed legal document or promissory note.</note> before him / and asks / whether he will fulfill his word, or not; his honor depends on it, and the like.

But what does that concern us? Answer: A great deal indeed. For as many letters as there are in the Scripture concerning the promised restoration of fallen mankind / so many written bonds of God's truth are there likewise. And moreover, the Holy Spirit confirms and repeats the same to all who will believe in them as certainly and truly / as He made this promise to Jacob.

We must not let this firm foundation of God be stolen from us in prayer or be drawn into doubt / for that is what the enemy works upon most of all.

In this, the whole ground of faith is hidden / which is based solely on **God's** truth / and on nothing else in the whole world. It is also no greater joy to **God** the **LORD** / than when a soul, against its own false heart and against all evil spirits, holds fast to **God's** truth / that He alone is faithful / and all men are false.

Thus one experiences only after a long struggle / that / as many as are the promises of **God** / they are all Yes and Amen in Christ / to the glory of **God** / who gives us the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts. 2 Corinthians 1:20.

When now this gifted Spirit repeats / appropriates / and makes the divine promises tasty or powerful in our hearts; then it is time / to humbly hold such words before the dear Father / like Jacob: **Lord** / did You not say this and that? Has this not become especially alive in my heart? Did You not give me this and that assurance in response to my prayer before? &c.

David had learned this piece of craftsmanship excellently in his manifold needs. **My heart holds Your word to You! it held with him.** <note>A paraphrased reference to Psalm 27:8.</note>

And although God for Himself does not need / to be first reminded of His promises; yet it powerfully breaks His heart / and it wakes us up with strength in the struggle of faith / so that we do not let our confidence be frustrated.

Oh, if one always held fast to this immovable ground in praying and pleading before God / one would certainly experience great wonders!

**God** cannot deny Himself: how then would it be possible / that by refusing our petition He should either strengthen His and our enemies in unbelief / or make us falter in faith?

And although He does not always let us grasp the thing prayed for immediately with our hands / He nevertheless lays it up for us as a treasure for the future / and we nonetheless have the petition / that we have prayed / if we otherwise learn to dwell with our mind outside of time, in eternity.

The Lord inclined Jacob’s heart toward generosity toward his angry brother in order to win him over with good deeds; just as Christ commands His own: Love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who insult and persecute you. And in this case, gifts are permitted when one wishes to appease and soften the hearts of those who are adversely minded—but not when one intends to provoke or mislead them into impropriety. For then the proverb is a truth: Gifts can reconcile God and men. God says: My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes take pleasure in my ways. <margin>Proverbs 23:26.</margin> Proverbs 23:26. This is the single most pleasing gift that we can give to God: our whole heart. And then it is said: Honor the Lord with your wealth, and with the firstfruits of all your income. <margin>Proverbs 3:9.</margin> Proverbs 3:9. This occurs in those things that serve the honor of God and the expansion of His kingdom; and also when one does good to the poor. Just as Daniel gave counsel to Nebuchadnezzar: Break off your sins by righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the poor; <margin>Daniel 4:27.</margin> so He will have patience with your sins. Daniel 4:27. But how men can be reconciled through gifts is taught by experience: just as the wise Abigail reconciled the angry David. <margin>1 Samuel 25:18, 27. See also Chapter 43:26.</margin> 1 Samuel 25:18, 27. See also Chapter 43:26.

Thus, Jacob was concerned with the thorough reconciliation and improvement of his brother, so that the latter should be delivered from his deeply-held anger, and thus from unrepentance. That was the reason why he humbled himself so faithfully. Why else would he have spent such a multitude of gifts if he were concerned with something temporal? Could he not have passed by in silence, or even taken a detour? But he sought neither deceit nor his own advantage. Therefore, he did not dismiss his brother with mere words, after the fashion of hypocrites and flatterers; instead, he presented him with such abundance that even Esau was convinced that he must necessarily mean it with a sincere heart.

For Jacob, however—according to the mind of God, which Wisdom had granted him—it was not actually about the outward spending, which even a pagan could have done; rather, it was about Esau's heart, that it might be delivered from the hell of wrath.

Such prudence <note>German: *Klugheit*, referring to a spiritual discernment or practical wisdom.</note> is not craftiness; rather, it comes from God, when His children seek to meet the hostile grimness of the

The poor pagans and many atheistic minds at courts and elsewhere make much boast of their magnanimity toward their enemies. But it is all deception, falsehood, and self-seeking if it does not flow from the pure fountain of the love of God.

All other outward signs, customs, and practices can be imitated by hypocrites. Only true divine love for enemies, and the overcoming of evil with good, is the unique hallmark of the true disciples of Christ and the Israel of God—as is the love for one another, according to Christ’s watchwords. <margin>John 13:35.</margin> John 13:35. Jacob’s gift flowed from his gentleness, and this from his love, so that he met the one who had truly sworn him to death with such sweetness and mildness. And his example and his loving encounter with Esau show that this way of love has been prescribed and known to all believers since the beginning of the world, and did not perhaps arise as a new doctrine from Christ in the New Covenant. Oh, how gladly a Christian would share all good things inwardly with his adversaries, if he could come to them with spiritual gifts and reach their hearts. But they usually close their wills against all grace and make themselves unworthy and incapable of true divine fellowship.

Just as Jacob sent certain herds of livestock toward the angry Esau, in which Esau might find pleasure and thus spare Jacob himself: so a spiritual traveler very willingly gives up all his animal passions and desires <note>German: *thieriſche Affecten*, referring to the lower, unredeemed nature of man.</note> to the enemies to be judged and slaughtered. Let them always descend upon the remaining evil dwelling in the flesh, and let them judge and condemn it, if only he brings his soul through blamelessly and can lead it undamaged into Canaan.
