### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXII.

21. So the gift went on ahead of him, while he himself stayed that night in the camp.
22. And he rose that same night and took his two wives and his two maids, and his eleven

<column-break/>

children, and crossed over the ford of Jabbok.
23. And he took them and led them across the stream; afterward he led across everything he had.
24. And Jacob remained behind alone; and

<column-break/>

Jacob risks—as has been said—all his goods and remains alone. O you poor human! You think you have only one enemy to contest, who might yet be appeased with gifts. You have indeed already endured the persecution of your father-in-law <note>Laban</note> (this signifies the creaturely world <note>In this context, "the creature" refers to earthly, created things that can distract or persecute the soul</note>), and you intend, according to your reason, to escape your other enemies in the same manner. But you do not know that you must struggle with GOD Himself, and that it is He who will set upon you. This struggle, however, is the last and most violent of all. To endure a struggle with GOD—indeed, to endure the power of GOD—is something that nothing but experience can teach. In such a struggle, one must always leave something behind, just as Jacob became lame from it.

The first law which a spiritual fighter must observe according to the Scripture is the abstaining from all things.

The pious patriarch carefully observed this when he left everything behind before the struggle and remained entirely alone before the Lord. He brought his wife, children, property, and goods—everything—first across the water so that he might stand alone and unencumbered before GOD.

Yet it was not merely external abstinence or solitude that he sought, but primarily the internal liberation, unburdening, and purity of his heart, which cannot be dispensed with in the struggle, as we see in our Savior Himself. <note>Luke 22:41. This refers to Jesus withdrawing from his disciples to pray in Gethsemane.</note>

This is a highly necessary law or condition for spiritual fighters: that they must, before all things, earnestly withdraw themselves from all earthly and worldly matters. <note>1 Corinthians 9:25. The apostle compares the spiritual life to an athlete's strict training.</note>

The Lord Jesus demands strictly from all who wish to enter the struggle that they should, like Jacob, leave or deny wife, children, and even their own life in heart and will, even if they might use everything according to external necessity within the divine will. <note>Luke 14:26.</note>

For Jacob did not cast away his wife and children externally for that reason, but returned to them after enduring the trial. Thus, a God-taught fighter remains obediently in his bound duty toward all that is his, yet in the internal denial and abandonment of the same, he finds this precious advantage: that he can struggle onward unhindered.

A soldier is quickest to fight when he has no pack or burden upon him. And this is precisely what Wisdom teaches her pupil in the way and work of self-denial, if he aspires to be a good soldier of Jesus Christ and wishes to please Him who has accepted or recruited him for war.

While there is still time, one does well to use it carefully and perform this work honestly. For when the final night comes, no one can work.

If one wishes to rightly heed the great advantage of this first law, one should especially cast off the external things of this world at the time when the Holy Spirit wishes to set the heart into earnest prayer and wrestling, and one finds a divine pull within for it. Everything should rightly give way to this call of our Commander; and whoever esteems and desires this will not let vain things stop him from following Him.

**v. 22. Two wives -- two maids)** A person also has two "wives" within: Desire and Reason (or Understanding). Sensuality is the follower or handmaid of Desire or cravings, and can never drink enough of perceptible things. Imagination is the handmaid of Reason, and has this defect: that she carries all sorts of images to her mistress.

<column-break/>

<insert>
It is good to also externally take Christ’s counsel and seek a hidden and closed-off little chamber for prayer and struggle. It is good to avoid all the bustle and noise of the world as much as possible and to remain alone with Jacob at times.
</insert>

But it is even better and more necessary to become solitary in the heart, and to close it against worldly cares, thoughts, and imaginings, especially in the time of struggle. If these impudent guests nevertheless wish to break in and disturb one's devotion, one should simply think of GOD again and again and rouse oneself in faith, which can command all unclean spirits and powers.

But whoever chooses to stay alone and seeks solitude only for the purpose of living more quietly and being spared from struggle and strife deceives himself and misses the true purpose. Rather, solitude must be sought for the very reason that one may apply oneself more earnestly to the true struggle against sin and wait upon it more unhindered. Otherwise,

solitude can easily become a snare instead of an advantage, and result in greater danger for the soul; because then, in the absence of opportunity for an outburst, many vices remain hidden, but for that very reason are less recognized and attacked, and much less rooted out.

Whoever says, for example (as it is written in Nilus <note>original: "beym Nilo." This refers to St. Nilus the Elder, a 5th-century ascetic author.</note>): "I will live alone so that I have no one around me who provokes me to anger," is no better than an irrational beast. For even the beasts are quiet and do not become fierce as long as no one provokes them. Thus one hides the passion within oneself and often falls back into old passions over trivial matters. There, one has abandoned great opportunities only to be confused by small ones. We should learn better what true self-denial is. Like Jacob, one should go with Christ out of the confusion of this world into the wilderness—not to be idle, but to be tested with Him.

So, let us never forget this instruction following Jacob’s prudence: that we should send all transitory things away from us, as it were, and let ourselves be torn loose more and more from false attachment to the creatures through the sharp discipline of Wisdom, who wishes to clearly show us all the stains of the world in her mirror.

Jacob did not wrestle, Paulinus <note>Paulinus of Nola, an early Christian bishop and poet.</note> notes, until he had brought the things he had to care for across the river. From this example, we understand the Gospel commandment and in what manner we are unfit to struggle with GOD. But we struggle when we seek to fulfill His Word and desire to prevail over divine virtues through following Him. Therefore, we cannot be capable of grasping the way of life and seizing GOD’s Word, or doing violence to the kingdom of heaven—which since the days of John the Baptist suffers violence <note>A reference to Matthew 11:12.</note>—if we do not, before the evening of our death, send on ahead everything that clings to us, hinders us, or holds us back on the journey of this world, whether through love or care. Thereupon, through the whole night, we should grasp and hold Christ, and also through earnest diligence in spiritual struggle, not let ourselves be separated from the love of Christ until we wring the blessing from Him. Therefore, because we have to struggle on the stage of this world before the eyes of GOD and His angels, let us lay aside all contrary burdens so that we may finish the works of salvation!

**v. 22. Ford Jabbok)** Which, as many believe, was only named so later because of this struggle and wrestling <note>The name Jabbok (Yabboq) sounds like the Hebrew word for wrestling (yē'ābēq).</note>. It carries its water into the Jordan and is mentioned in Numbers 21:24, Deuteronomy 2:37, 3:16, Joshua 12:2, and Judges 11:13.

The author uses Jacob's actions as an allegory for the internal battle between reason, desire, and divine will.</summary>

# Chapter XXXII. The First Book of Moses.

### and a man wrestled with him / until the dawn broke.

**25. And**

When GOD places a person into various trials, there is no other means of escape than through a most earnest struggle.

This spiritual battle takes place in the darkness.

<margin>Jacob was in the night when he began the battle: whether it was friend or foe.</margin>
*Jacob* was enveloped in the pitch-black night when he began the struggle: and indeed, not only outwardly, but also inwardly. In fact, the inner night or darkness was most terrifying, partly due to the fear of *Esau’s* murderous intent, and partly due to the harsh resistance of his counterpart, of whom he did not know whether he was friend or enemy.

In the same way, struggling souls are often placed into a pitch-black night of temptation, of inner anguish and the deprivation of all divine light, where all previous enlightenment, clarity, and certainty seem to vanish. In their place, very wicked powers of unbelief, doubt, grumbling, and even blasphemous thoughts arise.

No one can believe what a sorrowful darkness this is unless they have been stuck within it. It is truly that "hell" about which so many saints in the Scriptures have lamented.

The spark of faith, through a secret assurance of the Holy Spirit, willingly enters the darkness with the Lord *Jesus* at the Mount of Olives <note>The author compares Jacob’s struggle to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane</note>, knowing that we shall suffer no harm anywhere, and that finally, the darkness must become to us as the light, and the night shine as the day.

Accordingly, the process of God with souls proceeds in this order: First, one is driven in repentance to a true disdain for the world and a renunciation of all things. When false pleasure and rest in all visible things are gradually brought to nothing in the heart, so that one desires no comfort except God; then the "first love" of God comforts and gladdens such an empty heart.

The soul would gladly remain standing here forever because it feels well therein. But the true suffering and dying with Christ is still to come.

Thus, for holy reasons, God allows the deep corruption of our nature to truly awaken, and Christ begins to withdraw His previous grace, appearing as it were in a completely different form—just as He met *Jacob* here as an enemy who wanted to kill him.

For who else could be meant here but the Son of God, the Angel of the Covenant? For He is so explicitly called "GOD" and "the Angel" in Hosea 12:4–5. Here He is called a "man," and He calls Himself both God and man—using the plural—because He was the second person of the Holy Trinity, and also the root and image of all humanity. According to the mystery as many believers see it, He assumed a "heavenly humanity" before the foundation of the world. In this state, as the firstborn of all creatures (Colossians 1:15), He was already a true Human and Man, according to whose image *Adam* was created. He then appeared here and elsewhere to the faithful as a true heavenly man. See Joshua 5:13, etc.; Judges 13:1, 13:8, etc.; 1 Chronicles 17:17. Likewise, He is emphatically called "the Heavenly One" in 1 Corinthians 15:48–49; although according to this first essence—as with the glorified essence of His body—the Heavenly One also chose to take on our earthly and weak flesh and blood, in order to suffer in this needy humanity, and thus, after living in transfiguration, to wear the full heavenly essence once again.

However, He wished to wrestle with *Jacob* to show all believers how they, in their great misery of sin, must wrestle with Christ in faithful prayer to obtain spiritual blessing from Him. By this, He also intended to assure them of a gracious hearing, as He is willing to allow Himself to be overcome.

Should someone nevertheless wish to hold with *Augustine* <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD)</note> that this man was a created angel and a prefiguration of Christ, there is no reason to quarrel over it; however, such a person would deprive themselves of that healing comfort which is felt through faith in the frequent appearances of Christ in the Old Testament.

Rather, the question is: why did this wrestling happen? For very few believe that the Lord *Jesus* can encounter His believers in such an adverse way. And yet it cannot be denied that even during His walk on the

<column-break/>

earth, He occasionally encountered well-meaning hearts in a quite adverse manner—as is known regarding the Canaanite woman, the royal official, and others. If one goes to the true foundation, one will easily grasp it. To practiced senses, the great mystery and prototype of Christ becomes clear and audible here: how the Son of God first meets *Jacob* as a righteous judge, and afterward as a man of blessing or a helper.

Certainly, He is that man in whom the Father has decreed first to judge all people with righteousness, and afterward to rescue them with mercy: not only publicly on the Last Day, but also in secret within each person's conscience during their conversion.

This righteous judge stands in His holiness and truth against the fallen sinner and demands from him, by every right, that power of righteousness and sanctification which was lost in *Adam*. But in the midst of such a struggle of repentance, He grants and awakens the tiny spark of faith, so that faith begins to wrestle with God’s righteousness, which presses hard upon the conscience and demands its due.

Some also hold that it displeased GOD that *Jacob* sent so much of his goods to *Esau*, since he had promised the Lord a tithe of them. For this reason, He supposedly encountered him so harshly here.

While that perspective remains valid in its place, we notice even more the two forms in which the Lord encounters *Jacob* and all his followers: that of righteousness as well as that of love and reconciliation. For both are Christ’s work, which the Father gave Him to do; both to judge and to release, to bind and to loose. The former serves for humbling and dying to self, the latter for awakening and translation into new life. And in both, Christ is called a "man" in the Scriptures.

That it is nothing blasphemous or wicked to struggle with GOD, as human reason might think, can already be seen from the ground of divine righteousness; by virtue of which GOD must necessarily set Himself against our corrupt nature and contest it.

But how a heart that is driven into a corner by God's wrath can emerge from it is clearly shown by *Jacob’s* example. He possessed a power of living faith and trust in the promised Seed. In this pressured power, he struggled against Righteousness and held fast to the pure love of GOD.

It is well known that the word in Hebrew indicates such a wrestling and striving where the "dust of the battle" almost rises into the air, after the manner of ancient combatants. This indicates what sort of earnestness must have been present in this battle, which the text presents with such a singular expression. *Luther* therefore provides in his gloss <note>original: "Glosse"</note>: "A man dusted with him." <note>Luther’s translation uses "rang" (wrestled), but his notes reference the Hebrew root 'abaq' meaning 'dust'</note>

From this, one may judge that a true struggle does not proceed gently or sweetly; indeed, it cannot be expressed in words what a wrestling and laboring becomes manifest before GOD in secret.

It truly costs suffering and death when, through Christ in us, wrath is broken, hell is destroyed, and the devil is to be driven out of his entire dwelling.

One need only try it in a single matter where satisfaction must be given to the righteousness of GOD: see if faith does not then have to soar upward with all its might against the Law and its accusations, holding God’s clear promises before Him, as if GOD had forgotten them.

No one has the power to engage in a struggle with GOD Himself out of their own strength; the Spirit of the Gospel alone does it. He awakens the tiny spark of faith in the midst of the opposition, as a wind blows upon a fire; and faith gives birth to the new divine mind, the "new creature," which alone counts before GOD.

With this, the Father’s wrath is stilled; because Christ dwells in the soul, in whom the Father must be well pleased.

Accordingly, the spiritual struggle spreads through the whole of Christianity and does not consist merely in empty imaginations, as hypocrites think. Rather, power and action and a total conversion of the whole person occur within it; so that one must see by the fruits who has wrestled with GOD and who has not.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXII.

### 25. And when he saw / that he did not prevail against him; he touched the socket of his hip: and the socket of Jacob’s hip was out of joint / as he wrestled with him.

Through the dislocation of Jacob’s hip, from which he was forced to limp, Christ intended to teach that one must sometimes patiently endure and take upon oneself sufferings in the flesh, as part of His fatherly discipline and submission to God, even when one is given over into the power of enemies; as David confesses of himself: *For I am ready to halt <note>original: "zum Hincken bereitet" — an archaic expression for being ready to fall or fail, often used in older Bibles to describe limping</note> / and my sorrow is continually before me.* Psalm 38:17. However, they may comfort themselves with Jacob, that the Lord in His own time will let His face shine upon them, so that they may recover. Psalm 80:3, 7, 19.

**Did not prevail)** The God-man <note>A theological term for Christ, emphasizing His dual nature as both fully God and fully human</note> did not take upon Himself more strength than that which Jacob—through the strength gifted to him by Christ for this purpose—was able to overcome: a strength which he then applied with the full power of his soul. It is no different than how a father, wanting to test how strong his little son is at holding on, does not use more strength, and does not hold this or that more firmly than his son’s strength allows, and gladly gives him the victory.

But so that Jacob might notice that a Greater One had struggled with him, and that He had willingly allowed Himself to be overcome by him; He left a reminder and a mark upon his body, and

<margin>1 Sam. 15:29. [He gives strength] to us / who have no power or ability, Isaiah 40:29. increases our strength / and calls us the Israel of God. Gal. 6:16.</margin>
**The socket of his hip was out of joint)** The entire house of the human body rests upon the two hip bones, as if upon the most noble pillars. And we must recognize that our own hip bone—our own ability, the power of natural strength in which our greatest vigor lies—must be weakened, made powerless, and as it were, dislocated. We must become aware of a spiritual hip-pain, a weakness, within ourselves. At that point, God, who is the strength of Israel, will increase our power.

Regarding this socket of the hip, it is noted in the medical arts <term>Arzney-Kunst: the historical practice of medicine</term> that its dislocation causes indescribable pain: because the many nerves that come together at such a joint are displaced and contracted; from which great agony usually arises.

This shows us once again Jacob’s great earnestness, that he disregarded all such pains, but steadily continued in his persistence; and indeed out of a living hope for the blessing, which supported him and made him joyful.

Just as the lameness disfigured Jacob and undoubtedly made him a subject of ridicule among the heathens; so it also certainly happens that those souls appear absurd, lame, and miserable to the world—those who, with Jacob, withdraw themselves from all false Laban-like and harsh Esau-like temperaments, and wrestle with God in faith.

<margin>(a) Gregory the Great, Book II on Ezekiel, Homily 14; and Book IV on Job, Chapter 30.</margin>
The Christian teachers (a) interpret this lameness quite elegantly as the weakening of carnal lusts and love for the world.

In truth, it is certain enough that the more we hunger for divine grace and struggle for it in faith, the more we forget temporal things and learn to plant our feet solely upon the deepest foundation of God’s love, whereas before we still secretly leaned on something worldly.

As Jacob’s power of movement was inhibited, so the "joint" of the evil natural will is, as it were, lamed and broken in such a struggle, so that it may no longer skip upon the earth so unbroken and free and retain no worldly pleasure, but becomes lame and powerless in its old habits. For this we must then thank the power of the Holy Spirit of Christ, who has powerfully touched us and vigorously attacked us in the contrition and crushing of the heart, when we felt God’s judgment.

<column-break/>

### 26. And he said: Let me (a) go! for the dawn has broken. But he answered: I will not let you go / unless you have blessed me! <margin>Song of Solomon 3:4. (a) Exodus 32:10.</margin>

### 27. And he said to him: What is your name? And he answered: Jacob.

### 28. And

Here, may the Holy Spirit Himself open up to everyone the wonderful and, to human reason, completely unknown nature of the struggle of faith, which is heaven-wide different from all self-wrought and legalistic <note>Refers to trying to earn God's favor through following the Law rather than through faith</note> struggles.

Jacob overcomes here more through suffering than through doing: whereby even his power to walk correctly was taken from him.

During the strong attacks of Divine Justice, faith turns its weapons completely around; and instead of defending itself for a long time, it willingly throws itself into the holy and blameless "Nothing" of God and says: "Yes, yes, my nature is this and that bad; but You are this and that exceedingly good and loving according to Your mercy!" Before this, my natural wickedness and falsehood sink down, and shall now surrender entirely into Your death, and no longer seek any self-righteousness through hypocrisy, but confess all Your judgments and decrees to be right.

Then faith, by virtue of the promise given to it, demands of Justice that it surrender itself to the love of God which faith has seized, and let the wrath be extinguished therein, so that the dawn of grace may rise.

This is a completely inverted conflict, which does not suit our pride, which would always like to still the wrath with its own righteousness but is unable; and therefore must learn to trust out of the invisible.

So a repentant heart throws itself with great struggle into the promised love, as into a sea, in which all the fire of wrath must be felt and extinguished; and the whole nature of man surrenders to the fellowship of the death and suffering of JESUS, so that God may carry out His judgment over the old man, and the new man can break through all judgments into the true light of the Gospel and the New Covenant.

For it is a great mystery in such a struggle of faith that God’s demands only take claim upon the old, corrupted part of the believer. When this is willingly abandoned, then the new life of the spirit stands there unharmed, as one who has been brought over from the struggle of death into life, and comes into no judgment—precisely because through repentance it has pressed through from the death of sins to the life of grace and rebirth. This is what it means to hope against all hope, and to hold fast to the One who is invisible.

It cannot be said how pleasing such an unadulterated and unshifted mind is to the dear Savior. For His own Spirit alone grants and works it. He Himself sustains Himself in such souls and binds Himself, so to speak, with His own bond of love. And

He does this not only in high temptations, but also in all asking, pleading, and persisting before the Father. For strictly speaking, all prayer must have this sense:

**I will not let you go without a blessing!)** Let everyone pay attention to their heart, whether the Spirit of prayer does not unceasingly sigh and work this in the depths of the heart. It is not too much, nor is it contrary to God, if it is repeated in the depths of the heart a thousand—indeed, countless—times. Yes, it is the proper occupation of faith and the love of JESUS that they constantly declare themselves in this way: not to let Him go.

Then the blessing is certain enough. For just as the struggle is not placed in mere words, but in actual deed: so also does the blessing consist, which Jacob’s followers carry away. This is the reward, the prize, the jewel, the gain, the victory, which one carries away in this struggle.

***

In particular, this prize of victory will become manifest in the end times, when the night is over, in which no one can work, but certainly can suffer. For when the dawn arrives, the conflict has an end: the night-owls and all other nocturnal animals crawl into their holes and caves; on the other hand, the nightingales and other lovely birds let themselves be heard, and announce with their joyful song a beautiful, pleasant day following the beautiful rising dawn—the day of great peace, the holy Sabbath, when one rests sweetly from all labor.

In memory of such a faithful victory, the Lord changed Jacob’s name—

30. And *Jacob* called the place *Pniel* <note>original: "Pniel" or "Peniel," meaning "Face of God"</note>: For I have seen God face to face (a) / and my soul has been delivered.
<margin>

31. It

<column-break/>

v. 28. Your name shall henceforth — be called — *Israel*] that is / a prince / a sovereign and overcomer of God.

Here one can imagine what joy arises in heaven and in God Himself when faith has brought a person through the judgment of God and placed them into perfect grace. For

When a person is converted, their name is also changed, so that before God they no longer have to bear the old name of *Adam* to their shame; instead, they are then called a true Christian / who has wrestled with God and men / and has prevailed through faith in JESUS.

God and men) Here *Christ* gives Himself this very remarkable name / to show / that this is a mysterious union / which will be recognized partly in time / and even more and more perfectly in eternity. Of which *Christ* already made a beginning here / to reveal such to *Philip*. *He who sees me / sees the Father.* etc. John 14:9, 11.

So we should not quarrel over how *Christ* calls himself a man in the plural <note>The author refers to the theological idea of the Trinity or the "plurality" of God's personhood appearing in human form</note> / just as the one God is cited as three men or persons in Chapter 18:2. When we are up in heaven / then the true *Pniel* will appear / where we shall be deemed worthy to look more clearly into this great mystery / of which we may only stammer here in the fear of the Lord.

You — have prevailed] O the unutterable glory / that the invincible God confesses with His own mouth to be overcome! This is exactly what He seeks / that He be so overpowered. For it is no pleasure to Him / that we remain stuck and succumb in distress and death. His entire will is / that the mercy seized by faith should boast against judgment; and that thus the judgment in God should confess and declare / how it is conquered by love.

Now since this struggle is the last of all / the soul must take on another name after its conclusion: which is then also shared / as happened also to *Abraham* and *Sarah*. But here the soul loses its own righteousness and strength / so that it may be clothed with the strength of God: Just as the name *Israel* / which was bestowed upon him / signifies strong against God; as if it meant / strong as God / and equal to the strength of God. Therefore all children of *Jacob* and his people / who are to be God's spiritual people / must be called the people *Israel* / who are clothed with the power of God Himself. Just as it is said to this people in the 2nd Book of Moses: *The Lord will fight for you / and you shall remain at rest.* Which indicates / that / if they only remain still / then He will fight in them. And in the Book of Kings: *You come to me with sword / shield and spear; but I come to you in the name of the God of hosts.* The soul now / which is clothed with the strength of God / fears neither man nor devil. For what does he need to fear / who has endured a struggle with God Himself?

v. 29. When *Jacob* asks the Lord in turn what his name is; He shows clearly / that he should not make for himself any external or figurative image of God / or merely grasp God in his fantasy and senses; but should keep Him in his heart / as the eternal essential Good and source of all good / who gives and offers Himself to His own to enjoy in deed and power secretly / without a sensory or rational concept: Which then God most highly glorifies in us.

Otherwise, however, it is nevertheless very necessary / that in all trials we truly learn to look *Christ* in the eyes / and recognize Him more precisely; as *Jacob* here confidently asked: Who are you? For

It is a great advantage / when one knows whom one is dealing with. Many thousand souls would have come out of their temptations sooner and better / if they had first learned to know God and *Christ* better.

What is more common / than people / and even preachers themselves / crying out that all temptations are merely the work of the devil / indeed, attributing the most tender discipline of the Holy Spirit / when He wants to withdraw a person from worldly lust and vanity / to the evil spirit?

So also such a tempted heart easily imagines for itself / that it has nothing to do with God in its distress; that there are only evil spirits in and around body and soul. Thereby the Lord Jesus does not achieve His healing purpose at all / and all labor and tribulation brings no desired fruit.

Therefore it is highly necessary / that we learn to know *Christ* rightly / and indeed be His before we fall into the battle ourselves. For that may provide us with excellent help in the time of need.

Much asking belongs to this. Not a forward and curious brooding / but a humble pleading and seeking for the divine light and for the transfiguring Spirit of Jesus Christ / an earnest searching in God's Word / a faithful testing of what goes on in our heart.

Even if *Jacob* did not immediately receive an explicit answer to his question / he nevertheless learned to know the Lord in the midst of the battle from deed and power more than well enough: therefore he also / having once recognized Him as the Savior / did not want to let Him go.

<column-break/>

<insert>
Thus *Jacob* made a "Note Well" <note>original: "NB" for the Latin "Nota Bene"</note> at the place of battle / which should serve us for teaching and instruction even to this day.
</insert>

The Lord Jesus becomes known to one no better than in battle. For how can we know Him better than by His redemption? But this must not only be imagined / but also actually experienced / so that we can praise Him for it in deed and from experience / *that our soul has been delivered*) Such deliverance presupposes / that *Jacob* must have stood in great and extreme danger / and would not have been equal to it without the special help of God. But now *Jacob* confesses therewith / that he is made completely free and secure from all hostility / and especially from *Esau's* wrath.

O how gladly the Savior brings all to such deliverance / who do not shy away from the battle! How powerfully He proves to faithful souls / that they shall inherit everything / because they overcome!

But then most people think: Yes / who can do the same as *Jacob*? He was a great hero of faith. But look at what stands in James 5:17. <note>Refers to Elijah being a man of like nature to us, yet praying effectively</note> Why then do we still want to excuse ourselves or delay? Did they not also receive their strength of faith from God with weeping and begging? As it explicitly stands in Hosea 12:4.

May one only learn to become faithful in the smallest things first / until faith grows through smaller trials! There will not be a single struggle without victory; indeed the war itself first brings forth peace / and without a preceding war there is no peace. The love of God will arrange everything for our deliverance. She dare not discover much of her glory / because we are still too self-loving / and would not use the victory in humility. Meanwhile, the crown is nevertheless held up or laid aside and the peace / which passes all understanding / preserves Christ's warriors like armor and a fortress: behind which they can fight well.

What now is the conclusion of all this? This / that eternally in *Christ* nothing counts but the new creation: and whoever walks daily according to this rule of battle in lowliness of heart and true labor of [new] birth / over him is peace / as over a newly named *Israel* or overcomer of God. Gal. 6:16.

Just as the lameness disfigured Jacob and undoubtedly made him a target of mockery among the heathens; so it also certainly happens that those souls appear absurd, lame, and miserable to the world, who with Jacob withdraw themselves from all false "Laban-like" and harsh "Esau-like" dispositions, and wrestle with God in faith.

<margin>(a) Gregory the Great, Book 2 on Ezekiel, Homily 14, and Book 4 on Job, chapter 30.</margin>
The Christian teachers (a) interpret this lameness quite finely as the weakening of fleshly lusts and love for the world.

In truth, it is certain enough that the more we hunger for divine grace and fight for it in faith, the more we forget temporal things and learn to stand solely upon the uninjured ground of God's love, whereas before we still secretly leaned on something worldly.

Just as Jacob’s power of movement was inhibited, so too the "socket" of the evil natural will is, as it were, lamed and broken in such a struggle, so that it may no longer skip and hop so freely and unbroken upon the earth to keep its pleasure, but becomes lame and powerless in its old habits. For this we must then thank the power of the Holy Spirit of Christ, who has powerfully touched us and bravely attacked us in the contrition and crushing of the heart, when we felt God’s judgment.

seeking, in the complete and perfect redemption and salvation. The victory that one carries away in this struggle.

Specifically, this victory prize will become manifest in the end times, when the night is over, in which no one can work, but can certainly suffer. For when the dawn arrives, the struggle has an end: the night-owls and all other nocturnal animals crawl away into their holes and caves; on the other hand, the nightingales and other lovely birds let themselves be heard, and with their joyful singing, announce upon the beautiful rising dawn a lovely, pleasant day—the day of great peace, the holy Sabbath, when one rests sweetly from all labor.

To commemorate such a faithful victory, the Lord changed Jacob’s name

<column-break/>

### 26. And he said: Let me go! For the dawn has risen. But he answered: I will not let you go, unless you have blessed me!
<margin>Song of Sol. 3:4. (a) Exod. 32:10.</margin>

### 27. And he said to him: What is your name? And he answered: Jacob.

28. And

---

Here may the Holy Spirit Himself open up to everyone the wonderful nature of the struggle of faith, which is entirely unknown to reason and is heaven-wide different from all self-working and legalistic <note>Refers to "legalism," or trying to reach God through strict adherence to laws rather than through faith.</note> struggles.

Jacob overcomes here more through suffering than through doing: whereby the ability to rightly credit his own strength was taken from him.

Against the strong attacks of Justice, faith turns its weapons completely around; and instead of defending itself for long, it willingly throws itself into the holy and blameless Right of God and says: "Yes, yes, my nature is this bad and that bad; but You are so exceedingly good and lovely according to Your mercy!" Before this mercy, my natural wickedness and falsehood sink down, and shall now surrender entirely into Your death, and no longer seek any self-righteousness through hypocrisy, but confess all Your judgments and decrees to be right.

Then faith, by virtue of the promise given to it, demands of Justice that it surrender to the love of God which it has grasped, and let the wrath be extinguished therein, so that the dawn of grace may rise.

This is a completely "inverted" struggle, which does not suit our pride, which always wants to still the wrath with its own righteousness, but cannot, and therefore must learn to trust in the Invisible.

Thus a repentant heart throws itself with great struggle into the promised love, as if into a sea, in which all the fire of wrath must cool and be extinguished; and the entire nature of man surrenders to the fellowship of the death and suffering of JESUS, so that God may execute His judgment over the "old man" <note>A Pauline concept (Romans 6:6) referring to the unregenerate human nature.</note> and the "new man" may pass through all judgments into the true light of the Gospel and the New Covenant.

For it is a great mystery in such a struggle of faith that God’s demands only take claim upon the old, corrupt part of the believer. When this is willingly abandoned, then the new life of the Spirit stands there uninjured, as one who has been brought over from the death-struggle into life, and comes into no judgment, precisely because through repentance he has pressed through from the death of sin to the life of grace and rebirth. This is then called hoping against all hope, and clinging to the Invisible One.

It cannot be said how pleasing such an unadulterated and unwavering mind is to the dear Savior. For His own Spirit alone grants and works it. He Himself holds Himself in such souls, and binds Himself, so to speak, with His own bond of love. And

He does this not only in high temptations, but also in all praying, pleading, and persisting before the Father. For actually, all prayer must have this sense:

**I will not let you go without a blessing!)** Let everyone pay attention to their heart, whether the Spirit of prayer does not unceasingly sigh and work this in the depths of the heart. It is not too much, nor is it against God, if it is repeated a thousand—even countless—times in the depth of the heart. Yes, it is the proper business of faith and the love of JESUS that they thus constantly declare they will not let Him go.

Then the blessing is certainly sure enough. For just as the struggle is not placed in mere words, but in actual deed: so also consists the blessing which Jacob’s follower carries away. That is the reward, the prize, the jewel, the gain,

God and men) Here Christ gives himself this

Even if Jacob did not immediately receive an explicit answer to his question / he nevertheless learned to recognize the Lord 
in the midst of the struggle through deed and power more than well enough: therefore he also would not let go of Him 
as the once-recognized Savior.

**31.** And the sun rose upon him / as he passed by Penuel / and he limped upon his hip.
**32.** Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the tension-nerve <note>original: "Spann-Ader"; this refers to the sciatic nerve</note> / which is upon the joint of the hip / unto this day: because he had touched the joint of Jacob's hip at the tension-nerve.

---

v. 31. After this terrifying wrestling, the sun finally rose. Now that the creaturely self had been further dissolved and annihilated / melted away and made into nothing even more than it had been before; it perceives in a true way / what God / the true Sun of all beings is / even if the soul can understand it even less: because its exceedingly great immersion in Him makes Him even more incomprehensible / even though the soul knows Him better than it ever has before.

These so happy souls / who have faithfully endured the spiritual struggle / may indeed seem even weaker in the eyes of other creatures than they were judged to be before: but in truth they have never been stronger; since they have now entered into the power of God through the loss of their own strength: Just as Jacob / although he became lame / nevertheless bears the name Israel / and fulfills its meaning; namely, strong against God.

Blessed is he who holds fast to the Lord / and desires to be blessed by Him! He will be touched upon his hip / and then no longer limp on both sides <note>A reference to 1 Kings 18:21, meaning to waver between two opinions</note> / but will always lean toward one side; namely, inclining toward God.

v. 32. Just as the children of Israel do not wish to eat from the hip of animals in memory of this struggle / so should we constantly think of the denial of our own physical and soulful powers / in order to present ourselves to the Lord in outward weakness / in which we are saved from all our enemies through His power alone. See Psalm 147:10, 11.

It is indeed the common opinion / that the Hebrews were distinguished from all other peoples by circumcision. However, one finds in the Scriptures / that other peoples / who were not Jews / and yet were from Abraham’s descendants / from Hagar and Keturah / also retained circumcision; namely the Ishmaelites / Midianites / Amalekites / and others in Arabia and elsewhere.

But the true distinction between the Israelites and other peoples is found in this / that the former ate no tension-nerve upon the joint of the hip / in glorious memory of Jacob’s struggle with Christ <note>The author interprets the divine messenger as a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ</note> / when his hip was dislocated / and yet he was victorious; as Lightfoot <margin>(a) Observations on Genesis, page 158.</margin> notes.

This shows a thoughtful prefiguration / of how the Savior wishes those children / whom He wants to bring to glory through suffering / to be distinguished from others not through outward ceremonies and shadow-works / but through the true sign of victory over all enemies / namely His love and His entire mind toward them.

Even if the flesh receives its pressure during such a struggle / and is lamed in its desires and powers; it is nonetheless a mighty help and glorious victory for the spirit / from which the spiritual Israel of God obtains its new name / and a complete separation and distinction from all unbelievers.

# The XXXIII. Chapter.
->Jacob’s Rescue from Esau.<-

AND Jacob lifted up his eyes / and looked / and behold, Esau came / and with him four hundred men: and he divided the children unto Leah and unto Rachel / and unto the two maids.
**2.** And he put the maids with their children in the front / and Leah with her children behind them / and Rachel with Joseph last of all.
**3.** And he went before them / and bowed himself to the ground seven times / until he came near to his brother.
**4.** And Esau ran to meet him / and embraced him / and fell on his neck / and kissed him fervently / and they wept.

---

v. 3. That Jacob bowed seven times before his brother / can remind us / how in the seven secret periods of the New Testament Church <note>A reference to a historical-prophetic interpretation of church history divided into seven eras</note> the believers will always have to bow before the people of the world / who generally possess the honor and prestige / as well as the goods and the power and authority / on this earth / because of these outward privileges.

As long as the years of the Church's humiliation flow in its seven periods / the godly must bow seven times according to the will of God / until the rams of Nebaioth and Kedar <note>referencing Isaiah 60:7; symbolic of worldly powers eventually submitting to God's kingdom</note> come to the church of the reigning Jacob.

But just as Jacob / who had previously conducted himself so princely and manly toward God / did not hereby subject himself in a slavish manner / nor weaken or surrender his right of the birthright / but left this honor in the Lord’s hand / until it would be fully granted to him at the right time: so too is the heavenly honor and birthright of believers not harmed by their humiliation / for they shall be exalted in their time; and those who have exalted themselves here / shall then be humbled in their time. Matthew 23:12. Then these must come and fall down before the feet of the believers / and recognize / that God has loved them. Revelation 3:9. Isaiah 60:14.

v. 4. Kissed him fervently -- they wept) This is a powerful testimony / of what true love can do. As hard as Esau otherwise was / he became so soft / even though men otherwise do not consider it an honor to weep.

It has been noted here with special diligence / that the otherwise hard and rough Esau wept at Jacob / fell upon his neck / and kissed him many times. For by this it is indicated / that the power of love and humility in Jacob broke the wrath and hard mind of Esau / and powerfully extinguished his wild fire.

Esau initially thought he had every right to be angry / because Jacob had taken his birthright along with the blessing. And now / when he saw Jacob coming to him so bowed and so sincere / he forgot all his demands / and surrendered himself to Jacob's seeking / to Jacob's great joy and strengthening.

Who does not see / that what Jacob did here / he did not only for himself / but also carried and presented a prefiguration of the Savior / who also as a lamb in the deepest gentleness / patience, and silence / went to meet wrath / and thereby interrupted and stilled the power of the same / so that it might not devour us; just as Esau here had to spare and let live the entire host of Jacob.

In particular, it shows us / how even the entire curse of the law together with the wrath and vengeance of God’s justice is overturned and turned into blessing / when a sinner bows before God’s judgment / and seeks grace / just as Jacob did here before Esau. For then the Father’s heart breaks / so that He must have mercy / and meets him in love and sparing: after the example of the prodigal son / which the Savior Himself presents to us.

### Chapter XXXIII. The First Book of Moses.

**5.** And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women with the children, and said: Who are these with you? And he answered: These are the children which GOD has bestowed upon your servant.
**6.** And the maidservants approached, they with their children, and bowed down.
**7.** And Leah also approached with her children, and they bowed down. Afterward, Joseph and Rachel approached, and they bowed down.

---

How many enemies the good Jacob had to overcome, one after another! One struggle always offered its hand to the next. Scarcely had he escaped the murderous intent of Esau than he fell into the hands of the deceitful Laban. No sooner had this one departed from him than GOD Himself stood against him as an enemy. And when he had emerged victorious here as well, Esau came toward him with 400 men.

With what, then, did his soul finally find rest through so many wars? With nothing but love, which pure faith worked within him.

Yes, truly, this is the single and true victory over all wrath, through which GOD, in those who are His, has overcome the villain <note>meaning the devil or the spirit of malice</note> in Christ. For wrath has been in the world since the fall of Lucifer; thus, it is necessary that the victory of all believers must be obtained through love.

This divine meekness—which helps promote God’s own cause even in His fallen creatures—ventures everything for this reason: just so that wrath may be stilled. This is precisely that love which is stronger than hell and its fire, which is wrath, without which there would be no hell. And what is love other than God Himself? 1 John 4. Yes, it is truly God’s image, wherein God’s children show their Father’s mind in themselves and continually increase it. Matthew 5:45.

Oh, if only one could learn to practice this divine mindset on every occasion, even if it should cost much effort to overcome oneself! It is certainly the only true way to attain peace for ourselves and others. No other weapons will strike down the hostility in man but these.

Whoever wishes to overcome another must have stronger weapons. If one intends to repay insult with insult, lies with lies, or wrath with wrath, then he fights only with the enemy’s sword and will never prevail.

But whoever puts on the mind of Christ—namely patience, love, meekness, and humility—must necessarily experience victory in the end. Why? Because he uses such weapons as the other does not have, and whose secret strength the other does not know. With these, Jacob also made his way through, so that he departed from Esau in peace. And because we also have to deal with so many contrary spirits in this wicked world, the gentle and humble heart of Christ shall be our only refuge, in which we are rescued from the hand of our enemies.

**8.** And he said: What do you mean by all this company <note>original: "Heer," meaning a host or army</note> that I met? And he answered: That I might find grace in the eyes of my lord.
**9.** And Esau said: I have enough; my brother, keep what you have.

<margin>
v. 8. This love of the Holy Spirit brought Jacob first to true humility, with which he stole the heart of the hardened Esau right from the beginning. For he called him his lord, and himself his servant. He said that he sought grace in his eyes.
</margin>

All of this he did not do out of a false or flattering heart, as corrupt nature is quite quick to do; but rather from the ground of true lowliness of heart.

Oh, how difficult and hard—yes, how impossible—this is for corrupted nature! According to its own impulse and mind, people only want to be the master and, as it were, to float on top. The proud heart loves it when others must live by its grace. On the other hand, it is the greatest pain for the heart when it must subject itself to others, appearing small and insignificant before them, and recognizing its own nothingness or confessing it to others.

<column-break/>

Therefore, it is pure grace and a pure work of the Holy Spirit when we can meet our adversaries or slanderers with true humility from the heart. We must truly be entirely changed in our hearts and tuned according to Jesus Christ if we wish to act humbly toward enemies as He did.

One comes to this especially through the knowledge of the great love of God and Jesus Christ toward us while we were still enemies. *Romans 5:6, 8, 10.* When a repentant person experiences and enjoys the Father’s inexpressible grace, patience, and long-suffering—as well as the Son’s deep humiliation and inexpressible love—his heart cannot help but become soft, even toward those he must view as sinners and enemies. For there the spirit of faith pours the blood of Jesus Christ into a contrite heart as the poured-out, gentle love of God. This sweet medicine makes everything bitter in man sweet, everything hard soft, and every wild and untamable mind supple, gentle, and mild.

Particularly, God’s shared love has a mighty power to lay our natural pride in the dust before Him, so that we demand no satisfaction or revenge from anyone, after we have experienced how well it pleased us that God did not treat us according to our merits, but lowered Himself to our misery and humbled Himself to the deepest degree in Christ Jesus.

Next to this, it can also powerfully bend us and bring us to humility toward others when we recognize in the light of the Spirit that we are by nature no better than they. Jacob humbled himself so much before Esau for this reason: because he considered him his brother, and the firstborn at that, who had been given real cause for wrath through the robbery of the blessing.

If we take to heart how the very same root of evil lies within us which incites the other to hostility—even if it may not rule in us—it must certainly move us to very deep mercy and a feeling of common misery, provided we truly understand the Fall of Man <note>original: "Sündenfall"</note>.

If anyone takes this evangelical ground to heart, they will learn with Jacob to consider it a grace when an adversary becomes compliant. For they are convinced that they have not deserved it of themselves.

A Christian who continues in repentance <note>original: "Busse"</note> humbles himself toward others out of the deepest recognition of his own nothingness, and thus out of unfeigned loyalty and truth. Through enlightenment, he knows with David that he is worthy of all shame and contempt, and that God will not allow too much to happen to him.

If someone were to suspect the good Jacob of merely flattering Esau, they will easily be able to see the opposite in this entire chapter, with what earnestness he sought Esau’s love.

What is then the conclusion of this? He who is born according to the flesh persecutes him who is born according to the Spirit, until the time when the Spirit becomes strong and rich. Then the Spirit goes out to meet Esau with a multitude of gifts and overcomes him with goodness by making himself small.

v. 9. Enough) Usually indicates satisfaction: But a learned Rabbi <note>original: "R."</note> notes that Esau spoke these words out of pride and the puffing up of his heart.

It is noteworthy that in his [Esau's] entire history, one finds nowhere that he named God or attributed anything good to Him; whereas Jacob everywhere recognizes and confesses God as the Giver of all the good that has happened to him. Just as Isaac, in his blessing over these two sons, includes the Lord and God in the blessing for Jacob, but in the blessing of Esau uses neither one name nor the other. *Chapter 27:27-29, 40.*

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIII.

**10.** And Jacob answered: Oh no; if I have now found grace in your eyes, then take my gift from my hand! For I have seen your face as if I had seen the face of GOD, because you have taken pleasure in me.

**11.** Please accept the blessing <note>original: "Segen," here meaning a gift that carries a blessing</note> that has been brought to you! For GOD has bestowed it upon me, and because I have enough of everything. Thus he urged him until he took it.

**v. 10. Oh — take)** This may directly remind us how the children of GOD must often obtain most things in the world only through pleading and begging.

It is good, then, to simply resolve to seek nothing more through force or other fleshly weapons, but to remain a beggar with Christ, who also had nowhere to lay His head, yet continually pressed His benefits upon mankind and urged them to come in.

<margin>Seen your face as GOD’s face</margin>
In Jacob, the image of divine love shone forth most gloriously, with all its blessed qualities. Therefore, it held such power over Esau’s wrath that, at the first sight, the latter could show nothing but friendliness. Because of this, Jacob became so joyful that he gave this testimony: "You have received me so lovingly that your face appears to me as the face of GOD."

This is an art above all arts: that love can transform a hellish disposition into a heavenly image.

Jacob had cast a little spark of his love into his brother’s heart, so that he now glimpsed GOD’s face in him. Now, he had often seen GOD’s face before—how full of love, patient, gentle, and sweetening it is. He now noticed something of this in Esau; namely, that his nature was softened. At this, he praised GOD and was strengthened in faith.

When the new name <note>Israel</note> has been given and the soul has already progressed far, it sees everything in GOD and GOD in everything. Sin, which previously (a) caused it so much terror, no longer (b) does so. Indeed, all of hell cannot frighten it: because it can no longer view anything as separate from GOD, in whom there is no guilt, but rather perfect holiness. This simple and open-hearted way of expressing one's mind is so characteristic of a soul at this level that even if it wished to, it could not depart from it. Let no one who does not understand this hold it to be impossible. It must be so: for a soul that has been taken up into GOD cannot view these things otherwise than GOD views them; namely, without fear, without inward unrest, without agitation, without malice or defect; because it becomes a partaker of His divine attributes according to the measure in which it has been taken up into GOD’s unity.

**v. 11.** Jacob thereby opened his heart, which was full of blessing and grace, and offered everything to his brother as a witness of his gentle love. He showed his brother that it was a matter of GOD’s

<margin>Blessing</margin>
shared good, which increases a thousandfold precisely by being shared with others. In this sense, the ancients were accustomed to calling their temporal goods "the blessing of GOD." <note>See 1 Samuel 25:27 and 30:26, where gifts are called "blessings."</note>

This reminds us of the earnest blessing which, according to Christ’s command, we also owe to the wicked. Poor souls need such things most of all, because they draw the curse into themselves daily.

<margin>GOD has bestowed it upon me</margin>
Jacob also shows his brother Esau that everything he gave him was from GOD: since the same One gave him everything. This is what all those who stand in divine truth are accustomed to do: namely, they attribute nothing to themselves, but everything to GOD.

<margin>I have enough of everything</margin>
He has enough of everything who has GOD in and with him, who is the All-Sufficient.

<note>(a) When the soul feared being overcome by sin.</note>
<note>(b) When the soul sees itself occupied by the power of GOD.</note>

<column-break/>

**12.** And he <note>Esau</note> said: Let us depart and travel, and I will travel alongside you.

**13.** But he <note>Jacob</note> said to him: My lord knows that I have tender children with me, as well as nursing sheep and cows; if one were to overdrive them for even one day, the entire flock would die.

**14.** Let my lord pass on before his servant, and I will drive on very slowly behind, according to the pace of the livestock before me and according to the pace of the children, until I come to my lord at Seir.

**15.** And Esau said: Then let me leave with you some of the people who are with me. And he answered: Why should that be? Let me only find grace in the eyes of my lord!

**16.** So Esau returned that same day on his way toward Seir.

**17.** And Jacob traveled toward Sukkot and built himself a house and made booths for his livestock; therefore the place was named Sukkot <note>Sukkot means "Booths" or "Huts"</note>.

---

One must deal prudently with overcome and reconciled enemies, lest the power of the former or the old hatred of the latter recover itself. Therefore, just as one should—according to the proverb—build a "golden bridge" for a retreating enemy, so should one cautiously avoid long association with them; as Jacob here sought to detach himself from his brother. Though he may have sincerely promised to visit him in Seir, it seems that Providence later turned this aside so that it did not happen; because for believers, an overly close association with natural and worldly people is dangerous. <note>Psalm 1:1: "Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly..."</note>

**v. 12. Let us etc.)** The Hebrew indicates a great intensity, and Jacob understood him in this way.

**v. 14. Very slowly — according to the pace)** Every servant of the Church can drive the flock of Christ like Jehu <note>a biblical king known for driving his chariot furiously</note> or Esau: but only the modest Jacob drives them as they are able to go. Just as a careful nurse goes only step by step and knows how to adapt so that she makes the way easier for the child until it can walk alone.

**v. 17.** One can see here the simple way of life of Jacob, who was content to seek his nourishment from cattle-rearing and only concerned himself with a comfortable dwelling and pasture for the livestock. And when he seemed to have used up the pasture in one place, he moved to another: although he also purchased a piece of land here as a permanent possession for his dwelling, just as Abraham previously purchased only a hereditary burial place. <note>Genesis 23</note>

**Sukkot)** This is not to be confused with the place in Numbers 33:5, which lay at the furthest borders of Egypt toward the Red Sea, where the children of Israel had their first night-camp during their Exodus.

# Chapter XXXIII. The First Book of Moses.

18. **T**hereafter Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem, which lies in the land of Canaan, after he had come from Padan-aram in Syria; and he pitched his tent before the city:
19. And he bought the piece of land where he had pitched his tent from the hand of the children of Hamor, Shechem's father, for a hundred pieces of money.

<margin>v. 18. Safely.) Or with peace: namely, that Esau had been unable to do anything against him. For this must properly be rendered here, and not as a city called "Salem," as some translations do; the Samaritans themselves testify that no place of that name ever existed in their land. <note>original: "(a)" referring to a source or variant reading</note></margin>

After such hard struggles in the spirit, Jacob attained true peace, even though through faith he was but a stranger in the promised land and lived in tents. Hebrews 11:9.

**GOD** proved in him all too clearly what Solomon says in Proverbs 16:7: When a man’s ways please the **Lord**, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.

There is an unspeakable blessing in true love, which rewards its lovers most richly, even though it extends over one's enemies! For when that "fire-heart" is won and the anger is stilled, then **GOD** the **Lord** also creates rest all around us.

But even if the fire of anger in an evil person will not be stilled immediately, one must only have patience. For when fire is to be extinguished by water, it usually rages most violently at first, but must finally go out.

Therefore, let it not seem strange if love is not recognized and accepted right away, but is instead attacked with anger. A time will come when **GOD** justifies His work and stirs the conscience, so that the anger subsides and is extinguished.

Thus **GOD**’s most holy order remains unbroken: that love alone extinguishes anger, and that the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.

May such peace of restoration and such love of the redeeming **Immanuel** be with us in every way, especially in times of temptation, when the help of love is needed for our loveless nature!

Pitched his tent before the city) He also dug a well a quarter-hour before the city, toward the north, near the great road to Jerusalem, which was later called Jacob’s Well, and is still called *Bir-Jacoub* by the current Arabian inhabitants. The mouth of this well, according to the testimony of Quaresmius <note>original: "Quafremii" - likely Franciscus Quaresmius, a 17th-century traveler and author of "Elucidatio Terrae Sanctae"</note> (b), is said to be very narrow, so that a thin person can barely get through (as he himself climbed down into it). In May, June, and July, it is usually without water, exceedingly cold and fresh, and very deep; and inside it is neatly lined with stones, but covered with stones at the top so that grazing cattle might not fall in; thus it is level with the ground. It is thought that here the conversation took place between the **Lord JESUS** and the Samaritan woman.

<margin>v. 19. Piece of land)</margin> Which was situated between two large and high mountains, about half an hour long but not quite so wide; it was subsequently called not only Jacob’s but also Joseph’s field, because he received it as an inheritance from his father. It is said to be very fertile because of the abundant water and is moistened by dew in the summer; also, a plant called *Sesame* <note>original: "Semsem"</note> is planted there, from which precious oil is pressed.

A hundred pieces of money) These may have been solid pieces of currency, according to which one had to calculate the sum of value in buying and selling, just as one is accustomed to using Reichsthalers and guilders. And since the Chaldean and Greek translations use the word "lambs," a lamb may have been stamped upon the coin, just as we have "Lion-thalers" and stamp horses and similar animals upon them.

<margin>v. 20.</margin> Since Jacob had been rescued from great danger, he erected an altar of thanks to **GOD**, as it seems, in the same place where Abraham had previously built the first altar when he was called by **GOD** to go out from his fatherland. Chapter 12:7. This altar Jacob then named with this motto: that the strong **GOD** is the **GOD** of Israel; who truly knows how to powerfully rescue him and all believers from their enemies and from all distress. We should always be mindful of this whenever we are rescued from any danger: thus our heart is the altar of thanks, upon which fervent praise must ascend to **GOD**. Psalm 50:15.

Thus believers go from one cross <note>meaning a trial or burden</note> into another, and must be tested thereby: as here Jacob is again very heartily grieved and falls into great terror. Here, one sin followed another, and sins were punished with sins. It was the negligence of Jacob and Leah that they permitted their daughter’s curiosity <note>original: "Fürwitz" - can mean curiosity, nosiness, or a lack of proper caution</note>, so that she went out to see the foreign heathen daughters in their customs and clothing at what was presumably a public gathering of people at a fair or festival—times which always provide occasion for many sins. There she was seized by a spoiled, lustful son of the prince of the land and was defiled in a violent manner. And so the proverb became true: "Curiosity makes maidens dear" <note>meaning curiosity leads to a high price or great loss</note>. And this teaches maidens primarily that they, like young wives, should be keepers at home (Titus 2:5); namely, that they stay at home, be obedient to their parents, and attend to household work.

When princes persuade their servants and subjects to change their religion under the promise of all kinds of physical advantages—and when the subjects also comply and obey out of a desire to please men or for fleshly intentions and profit—such a thing can bring nothing but heavy punishments and judgments upon both. And these judgments will be even heavier upon all those perverse zealots among the scribes who lure people to join their party with promises of earthly honors and goods, insisting they only adopt certain external ceremonies while caring little for the inner state of the heart, which should be truly directed toward God. Therefore, Christ announces a woe: *Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves.* <note>Original: "Matth. 23/15." The author is comparing the forced or bribed conversions in the story to the religious hypocrisy condemned in the New Testament.</note>

What else brought the Church of the New Testament away from its first purity than when heathen minds forced their way into the Church in crowds, sufficing themselves with taking the name of Christian along with the sacraments and signs of the covenant, yet filling everything with sheer hypocrisy?

Indeed, this very matter presents a living image of false religious zeal: when one begins a bloodbath because of a defiled

Because wounds tend to be at their worst on the third day—as they commonly become inflamed then and begin to hurt greatly—they could most conveniently carry out this evil deed against all these weakened people; likely, they also took some servants to help them. ## Chapter XXXV.

-> The Establishment of Bethel, the Deaths of Rachel and Isaac. <-

1. AND God said to Jacob: Arise and go up to Bethel and dwell there; and make there an altar to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.

If you wish to serve God, you must first learn to know Him in a truly living way.

This living knowledge consists both in true acquaintance with God and in actual experience. Both are found here in Jacob.

He recognized not only the Lord Himself but also His will and the manner of His service: both in a living and powerful way.

One can easily imagine how certain and undeceived this soul must have known God, since at such an appearance and address from God, he was so certain in his heart that it was God, and no false spirit disguised as an angel of light <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 11:14, warning that even the devil can appear as an "Engel des Lichts."</note>, who had commanded this thing of him.

To such a certainty of heart, a believer must truly come in the light of God through earnest practice and through grace, so that he knows how to test and distinguish the spirits—that is, to distinguish the deceptive thoughts of nature and the serpent from the voice of his Shepherd and true Prophet, through whom the Father has revealed His will to Jacob and all believers.

The Spirit gave witness to Jacob that this pronounced will of God was spiritual truth; and thereby his heart became firm, knowing that God willed to be served in this way and no other.

So must we also learn to perceive the living GOD and His will: to which end His Spirit most gladly wishes to open all Scripture to us, so that we may know how to serve Him, and that we should worship Him as a Spirit in a spiritual and internal manner.

that these Hivites and Canaanites were so thirstily murdered because their outward agreement to the religion and their undertaken circumcision happened more out of Shechem’s natural love for Dinah and the Shechemites' desire for the Israelites' goods than out of love for God and His will—and because He had already decided to clear them out through the Israelites. What appearance, however, does fleshly zeal have among Christians, who want to be and should be a people of the New Covenant of love, when they—for the sake of their church customs and religious practices, which they imagine to have been offended by others in some way—stir up such a noise and war, and thirstily go forth to defend religion with the sword and take revenge against others?

2. Then Jacob said to his household and to all who were with him: Put

Before Jacob puts into effect the work undertaken for the honor of God—the establishment of an altar and the public proclamation of God’s name there—he first wants to reform his family from all idolatrous ways and worldliness that is displeasing to God. He does the former by taking away all the foreign gods <term>fremde Götzen</term> which they still had with them from Laban’s house (Chapter 31:30) and may have plundered from the Shechemites; and the latter when they also had to give up their ornaments and earrings, whether they had worn these in service to idols or according to the usual worldly pomp. This teaches us that true reformation should not stop at the abolition of all idolatrous teachings and ceremonies in worship, but that worldliness in sinful, ostentatious clothing and other fleshly lusts should also be abolished; otherwise, one cannot establish an edifying assembly in which the pure service of God can be held in spirit and in truth, and thus a true Bethel <note>Bethel literally means "House of God."</note> and spiritual house of God be established. See Romans 12:1-2, 1 Peter 3:3, and 2:5.

God commands a soul, after so many endured hardships and struggles on its path, to return again to the place of its origin, where He accompanied it through His wonderful providence with so much goodness, and there to set up an altar. But the highest part of the soul, before it can be occupied by God, must first have reached the purity of its creation: indeed, at this time all self-centeredness must be taken from the lower part of the soul, and all stains and sins cut away from it, as was prefigured by Jacob’s family.

As He also always urges in the heart, [we] should.

---

Whoever takes good heed of their soul will constantly notice such instruction in the ground of their heart: that they should wait steadily upon God and always revere Him as present.

This is actually the perfect will of God, which we have to recognize daily and hourly: so much so, that one does not forget it even when one is drawn into external circumstances with Jacob.

Away, then, with all self-chosen worship <note>original: "selbst-erwählten Gottesdienst"</note>, which happens according to one's own choice, even if it shines ever so beautifully! It is all an abomination before God that God Himself has not commanded and ordained! Just as Luther often testifies against the papacy <note>original: "Papstthum"</note>—born of nature—which so gladly falls upon the external and forgets spirit and power.

According to such true Lutheran teaching, everyone who otherwise professes it should examine their previous worship: thus they would soon notice that they have known their God little or not at all up to this hour, much less actually experienced how they should serve Him.

It is only right, however, that one should now learn better from this; so that one might finally realize how good and blessed it is to serve such a Lord.
