<meta>This page continues the commentary on Genesis Chapter 35, where God commands Jacob to return to Bethel. Having previously discussed the violent actions of his sons, the text now turns to the spiritual preparation required for Jacob’s household to encounter God again.</meta>

Chapter XXXV. The First Book of Moses.

# Put away the foreign gods that are among you / and purify yourselves / and change your clothes!
<margin>(a) 2 Cor. 7:1.</margin>

Now, all you who belong to the house of Jacob, you who wish to be with Christ and hold fast to Him, yes, you who truly desire to serve God:

Put away the foreign gods! Oh, how necessary is this call to all of us! Are they not all "foreign gods"—those things outside of and alongside God that we love and esteem in an extraction of order? How quickly the heart is captured by a creature! One that is "foreign," that is, one that cannot be our portion or our highest good, and which by right should have no claim upon our hearts.

Mammon <note>A term used in the New Testament to personify wealth or profit, often as a false god.</note> is a foreign god, and greed is idolatry. The belly is made into a god by those who strive after earthly things. Lust is a false god, and those are idol-worshippers who love it more than God.

In fact, according to the original text, it reads: "Put away the gods of the strangers," meaning foreign nations or people.

This reminds us quite healthily how quick our nature is to adopt all sorts of ungodly things—unclean and evil habits, customs, and ways—from other people, to conform ourselves to the world, and thus imperceptibly fall into coarse or subtle idolatry.

All such foreign gods do not belong in our poor hearts: they are thieves and murderers who cut off our access to the true, living God; indeed, they are such abominations and horrors that the Lord of Hosts will never tolerate them beside Himself.

If even the external, coarse idol Dagon could not stand before the Ark of God, how much less can the "doctrines of demons" and their false services stand before the Lord of Glory Himself!

*Among*—actually *within*, or *in the midst*. The Hebrew word <term>thochu</term> <note>original: "thochu," likely referring to 'toch' or 'betoch,' meaning 'in the midst of' or 'inside.'</note> signifies the middlemost or innermost part, as the heart is the unlawfully occupied seat of idols. Ezekiel 14:3. For what union does Bethel—the house, the temple of God—have with idols?

So let each of us go into his heart and look around at what resides and lodges there! Just pay attention to what goes in and out all day long, what one thinks, seeks, and means: then one will catch so many wicked idols, and so many false intentions will rise up from the abyss of corruption like frogs, toads, and snakes.

Oh, let no one imagine he is free from foreign gods just because he does not live under the Papacy! Most people truly worship as many images, as many false saints, as the self-love and self-deception they harbor within themselves, and as much as they make idols of themselves through hypocrisy.

Of the truly coarse idols—greed, love of the world and its pleasures, self-exaltation, and other manifest sins—we need not even speak. One must only learn to know the evil roots and the ground upon which the vexing image of the "old man" <note>A biblical concept referring to the unregenerate, sinful nature of a person before spiritual renewal.</note> rests to the annoyance of the Master of the house: then the temple of our heart will gradually be purified. But

It requires tireless care to notice all one's own idols, and a sober and watchful life in God's presence.

To each and every foreign god that has crept into the heart through a thousand opportunities, one must say with all earnestness, as it stands in Isaiah 30:22: "Away, away with you!"

The putting away of foreign gods is therefore nothing other than the cleansing and clearing of the heart from the clutter of sin, or true repentance. For without doubt, Jacob meant by the outward removal also the inward separation of the heart from false worship. And

So the Spirit even today commands us to repent of "dead works," not only regarding outward, coarse outbreaks but also regarding secret impurity and idolatry.

Oh, let everyone learn to submit to the sharp but healing discipline of the Spirit, and trust nothing good in himself; let him not excuse or cloak his idolatrous heart, but pray to God day and night that He might increasingly convert him from idols—however subtle they may be—to Himself, the living and true God! For

<column-break/>

### 3. And

The perfect will of GOD cuts off all idolatry at once, even if the world proclaims it as holy or at least does not punish it.

Would we dare to stand before the most holy Majesty of GOD with soiled clothes, or retain something of the old nature? Why then would the Holy Spirit urge such precise purification, as it says further:

**Purify yourselves.** What constant earnestness is required for this, may the Spirit of Truth Himself reveal to everyone! For it must be practiced more than spoken of. It is true daily repentance, in which the "old man" is to be entirely submerged and drowned.

We must truly be concerned with the eradication of the "body of sin," even if we do not achieve it immediately. Whoever willfully and complacently retains even the smallest thing that he knows does not belong to the Kingdom of God brings no true service to God. No matter how long he resists, he must also cast out this idol and put it away from himself. And

If eager hearts ask how one comes to such purification of the heart, this purification performed by Jacob leads us, as a prototype, to the actual washing through the blood of the eternal covenant.

If someone looks into the depth of the defilement of his own nature and anxiously seeks true purification, the Spirit of Christ offers it in this red flood of His blood, which intends to leave no spot or wrinkle upon His bride. Yes

It is precisely through the purification of Christ that we must first be prepared for the service of GOD. Hebrews 9:14.

We should, therefore, let ourselves be driven by our great need and impurity to seek this purification from the bottom of our hearts. Where else will we get rid of all the abominations if we do not seek it in the right fountain? We would only torment ourselves forever with them. But the Father has opened a free, open fountain for us in Christ's heart against impurity and sin. Let us immerse and sprinkle ourselves therein at every moment with faith; especially when we wish to worship the Father: just as Jacob's family and the Levitical priests had to purify themselves before the sacrifice.

Everything must be exceedingly pure, and one must put on other clothes, and everything must be entirely changed through renewal. Jacob does nothing by himself to prepare himself for such a great good. For this was God's work alone, who had guided him on this path and now brought him back to his origin. But he commands the "lowest part" <note>Refers to the household servants or perhaps the more carnal aspects of the community.</note> to let go of everything foreign they possessed as their own, so that nothing might hinder this blessed falling-in-love with God.

But let us take note that even in a household as holy as Jacob’s, idols were nonetheless found. And perhaps some of his servants might have been idolatrous. Where is there a place so holy, where is there a soul so holy, in which some impurity does not mingle?

Jacob does not say to his people without reason:

**Change your clothes)** The Spirit reminds us thereby how hideous the clothes of the "old man" and the defiled garment of the flesh appear before God's face, and how we must necessarily strive for the white garments of the true righteousness of Jesus Christ, so that we may be clothed in His innocence and His holy life.

If we apply all diligence to putting off the old man and putting on the new, the Lord Himself takes hold, and His Spirit washes and makes our clothes bright in the blood of the Lamb: whereby we gain a joyfulness to approach the holy God and to seek mercy and help.

Oh, how sweet the promises become in such earnestness, that He Himself will purify us!

God and we are then served by this. For faith has its dominion therein, giving God the glory and us our salvation. And

That is precisely the true essence and the core or centerpiece of true worship, in which we become nothing and God becomes everything. That is what it means to serve God: to give oneself entirely to Him and to sacrifice oneself.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> **I am the Almighty GOD)** The Hebrew word <term>Shaddai</term> <note>original: "Schadai"</note> actually means "sufficient," and consequently "perfect." This name thus indicates an all-powerful, overflowing sufficiency, full of all good—the most perfect all-sufficiency of the eternal Good: both in itself, as it is, so to speak, satisfied within itself; as well as toward the creatures, as it can and will satisfy, calm, and please all things.
&emsp;For the Hebrews also derive the origin of the word from the idea that GOD fills the creature with His treasure until they say, as it were, "it is enough," and thus recognize and praise His all-sufficiency. From this perfect wellspring Isaac also drew his blessing for Jacob in Chapter 28 / 3.
&emsp;Augustine says: That man is far too greedy who cannot be satisfied with GOD. For you can desire nothing which you do not find in Him. Consider any happiness you wish, you will find it a thousandfold in Him. If you desire love, faithfulness, truth, comfort, or constant company; all this is to be obtained in Him, beyond all measure and manner. If you desire beauty; He is the most beautiful of all. If you desire power; He is the most powerful of all. If you desire wealth; He is the wealthiest of all. Thus you find everything that your heart may desire in the most perfect way in the simplest, highest Good, which is GOD.
&emsp;What a precious advantage it is for truly converted souls that they do not need to seek their satisfaction in so many countless vain things of this world, and thus do not have to wander far and wide, but can find all good so near to them—indeed, within themselves in GOD Himself!
&emsp;Oh, that everyone recognized it so precisely and might use it so earnestly, just as this all-sufficient Good wishes and offers to them! What a pity it is, and how GOD laments, that so few souls believe that, let alone ask for it! That is caused by the false pleasure that man places in the creature, feeding himself on imaginations. One is so easily satisfied with the possession and enjoyment of visible things, even though one knows they will pass away tomorrow. Thus, one foolishly keeps oneself from the Truth, only to give honor to the False.
&emsp;But where can a heart be satisfied and filled with the "best part" if it rests in foreign goods? One must surely give way to the other. Where love of the world reigns, the love of GOD is, alas, finished.
&emsp;Consider it and take it to heart, all you who have not been satisfied with GOD until now! Have you then found a complete and better satisfaction in the creature? When has your heart ever been truly satisfied and completely quiet in temporal things, or so sated that it neither could nor would desire anything more?
&emsp;But does that truly and in truth come to pass, which is so often boasted of by many and spoken without power, and even chosen as a funeral text from Psalm 73 / 25? <note>Psalm 73:25: "Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you."</note>

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXV.

16. And they journeyed from Bethel; and when there was still a little way to go before coming to Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had a hard labor.
17. And it happened, when she was in hard labor, that the midwife said to her: "Fear not! For you shall have this son also."
18. And it happened, as her soul <gloss>(a) was departing</gloss>—for she died—that she named him Benoni <note>original: "Benoni," meaning "son of my sorrow"</note>: but his father named him Benjamin <note>original: "Benjamin," meaning "son of the right hand"</note>.
<margin>(a) Luke 2:35.</margin>

---

Rachel had sinned by murmuring because of the infertility sent to her by GOD (Chapter 29:31, 30:1); thus, she had to lose her life here in a difficult birth. and as she called the child a "son of my sorrow," Jacob called him a "son of the right hand," who should gladden and strengthen him in his old age. Youngest children tend to be the most pleasant for this reason, as they still possess a pliable mind; whereas adults commonly grieve pious parents with their own self-will and worldly mind, as Jacob had experienced with Simeon, Levi, and Dinah.

**v. 18. Died)** How elegantly does Rachel prefigure the old Jewish Church! At the time of Christ, she was to pass away and close her eyes—along with the customs and ceremonies of the Old Testament and the decrees of the elders—and go into the grave just as JESUS Christ was born and this "Son of the Right Hand of GOD," the true Benjamin, came forth!

But the Jewish Church did not recognize Him in His majesty, nor that He was the one of whom the prophets testified throughout; they had even named the place and other circumstances by which this JESUS should have been known as the true Messiah. They saw nothing special in Him, such as they wished to see, and His lowly form did not please them, for they had painted an entirely different portrait of the coming Messiah. Therefore, He was all too lowly in their eyes, and there was no form that would have pleased them; instead, He was the most despised and unworthy, and like a true

**Benoni)** a man of sorrows. <note>original: Isaiah 53:3-4</note>. Even His first, tenderest childhood in the stable and the manger had to receive the firstfruits of this sorrow, and He had to flee from the rage of Herod. At the same time, the sorrowful condition of the Jewish children began, who were killed and sacrificed as the firstfruits of the martyrs of the New Testament; of which it is explicitly said: "Rachel weeps for her children."

**But)** Those who were still true believers, who saw further than the common, then-unenlightened Jewish Church, saw and recognized Him—with Peter—as the Son of the living GOD, and—with Nathanael—as the King in Israel; though they themselves became weak and went astray at the time of Christ's suffering, until He proved Himself as a LORD when He rose from the dead.

Though the "Jewish Rachel" calls Him Benoni, yet

**His Father — Benjamin)** by saying to Him: "Sit at my right hand!" <note>original: Psalm 110</note>. Indeed, He is Himself the right hand of His Father, through which He accomplishes all things, and to whom, for that reason, all power in heaven and on earth is given. <note>original: Psalm 118:15-16</note>.

How sufficiently did the Scriptures of the Old Testament testify beforehand in many places that Christ would become both a Benoni and a Benjamin, and would make both names true in Himself, if only the Jewish Church had wanted to pay attention! Among many examples, one need only look at the two places, Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53. Oh, how the Savior is presented and depicted there as a Son of Sorrows! But is He not also immediately thereafter introduced as an exalted King? <note>original: Philippians 2:5-11</note>.

These two things—namely, the state of humiliation and exaltation in Christ—the poor Jews cannot grasp to this very day. Likewise, many Christians still do not grasp His state of exaltation in all its circumstances; they partly fail to recognize, and partly even reject, His kingdom and the great power He is to assume at the seventh trumpet. These Christians do not see His glory in the future expanded power of His Church; and the "Jewish Rachel" saw nothing but what was unseemly in this, her son. But whoever looks deeply into both the great measure and length of this mystery recognizes how wonderfully it is foreshadowed in this naming: Christ was truly called Benoni by the mother, Rachel, but Benjamin by the father, Jacob.

When, however, in the final time, the "Benjamin-state" of Christ truly reaches its fulfillment, the Jews will no longer be offended by His humiliation. For just as He entered into His glory through suffering, He has also ordained that all His believers must enter into glory through much suffering—and so, finally, the Jews, who will also believe in the last time, shall enter into their promise.

19. Thus Rachel died, and was buried on the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. <margin>Matthew 2:1.</margin>
20. And Jacob set up a pillar over her grave: that is the pillar of Rachel's grave unto this day.
21. And

---

**v. 19. Bethlehem)** It is indeed very remarkable that in the very same place where Rachel gave birth to her son Benjamin, Christ was also born of Mary: of which the prophecy of Micah is well known. <note>original: Micah 5:1</note>.

**v. 20. A Pillar)** Made of twelve stones, according to the number of the twelve sons of Jacob, with a vault. All Jews who pass by write their names on these stones; as is testified by Rabbi Benjamin and D. Geier <gloss>(a)</gloss>.

This erected grave-monument was intended only to remind the descendants of the promise of the land of Canaan, so that they might make themselves partakers of the same through faith and a godly life before GOD. However, when the great and the rich erect such costly mausoleums or grave-monuments, it would be better instead to ordain godly foundations or donations, through which poor children could be raised and led to the knowledge of GOD, and other works aiming at the honor of GOD could be promoted. From these, they could expect a certain blessing in eternity; whereas the former only increase the vanity of the world and the wrath of GOD toward their certain destruction. For the fact that the ancients practiced such excess in this—<note>original: 1 Maccabees 13:27, etc.</note>—is not written for us to emulate.

And so, the soul that is established in GOD is now entirely detached from natural and spiritual feelings; and if any should still remain, GOD rescues them, as He did for Rachel. The Scripture does not say that Jacob wept for her. Since he was likely standing firmly in the will of GOD at that time, he could not grieve over this loss, which, by contemplating it in GOD, he judged to be more useful to him. And this is precisely a light of this spiritual state: it shows that GOD does everything for our best, and that everything must serve our highest good. Here the soul stands, robbed of its most beloved possession in nature. It now has nothing further but GOD and the Cross. It has known the worthiness of the Cross all too well and is too strong in GOD to be grieved by having to carry it. Yet, a secret love for the "fruits of Rachel" remains; because these are sweet and lovely, while the fruits of the Cross are somewhat wilder. Moreover, the fruits of sweetness and unity have their beauty within themselves and show what they possess even outwardly. But the fruits of the Cross are bitter at first sight; they are not pleasant until their later consequences; for they do not end until they have brought forth Jesus Christ.

->The<-

---

<margin>v. 21. Tower of Eder) This stood a quarter-mile from Bethlehem and took its name from the flock <note>original: "Heerde"</note>, because year-round, summer and winter, flocks of cattle lay there and grazed. Jacob took notice of this opportunity, not only for the sake of his cattle, but as a prophetic prelude to the wonders that were one day to happen there. For, as Jerome <note>original: "(a) de loc. Hebr." — "On Hebrew Places"</note> credibly maintains, this was the place where the angels announced the birth of the LORD Christ to the shepherds at Bethlehem; and there, after Christ was born, a church was built, which was called *Angelus ad Pastores* <note>original: "Angelus ad Pastores" — "The Angel to the Shepherds"</note>.</margin>

<margin>v. 22. Jacob had sinned by his thoughtless consent to Rachel’s demand to lie with her maid Bilhah and take her as a concubine: and so he is now visited through her with a new cross <note>a burden or trial</note> of incest, which his firstborn committed with her, with whom she may have maintained an all-too-common intimacy. Jacob took vengeance for this shameful deed on his deathbed, punishing him and depriving him of his birthright; namely, the leadership, the priesthood, and the double portion of the inheritance. See Chapter 49:4 and 1 Chronicles 5:1.</margin>

<margin>To express the great indignation of Jacob when he heard this evil report, there is an unusual punctuation here: because the previous verse does not seem to be brought to an end, as if to indicate the shamefulness of this deed in the holy family; and then this also seems to be the beginning of another verse that is also not finished: (as an *Atnach* <note>a Hebrew musical/punctuation mark indicating a major pause</note> stands on both sides;) to show how he swallowed this sorrow within himself and wanted to endure it with silence, until he gave voice to his loathing on his deathbed. See Psalm 38:14.</margin>

<margin>Reuben was not yet 24 years old at that time. For this happened before the selling of Joseph, who was 16 years old at the time. Chapter 37:1. Reuben, however, was only 7 years older than Joseph.</margin>

<margin>(a) On Hebrew Places.</margin>

The twelve patriarchs are presented here again in a different order than they were born. (See Chapters 29 and 30). First, all the sons of Leah are mentioned as the lawful wife whom the father-in-law gave to Jacob; then those of Rachel, whom Jacob intended as his true wife; and then the sons of the two maids as concubines. This is done to show how Jacob presented this fruitful blessing of children to his father, Isaac. GOD wished to grant this great pleasure to both father and son, so that the former could still take comfort for a considerable time in this pious son, to whom he had handed the divine blessing of Abraham. Although we do not know the exact length of time, twenty-three years passed from Jacob's departure from Laban until Isaac’s death.

v. 23. Twelve sons) Moses mentions very little of any of them except Judah and Joseph; nor does he record the death of any, except for Levi, of whom it is said in Exodus 6:16 that he lived 137 years. However, according to the testimony of Stephen in Acts 7:16, their bodies were brought to Shechem into the ancestral tomb purchased by Abraham and Jacob.

Furthermore, it is significant that the Savior chose for Himself twelve disciples—as twelve children whom He begot through His Spirit—according to the number of these twelve sons or patriarchs. Also, the woman clothed with the sun and with the moon under her feet, who appeared to John (Revelation 12:1), had a crown of twelve stars on her head, which signifies nothing other than the twelve tribes of Israel, who will shine in the teaching of the twelve apostles in the end times. And we may certainly believe that twelve seals lie before the twelve sons of Jacob; and since GOD has set other events with the patriarchs as a model for future things, the generation of the twelve sons of Jacob also represents something great and future in the Church.

v. 26. These are — born to him in Syria) Except for Benjamin. This historical description focuses on the majority of them.

v. 27.) Rebekah is not mentioned: therefore she must have already died and might not have seen her son again; she was somewhat to blame for his flight and servitude. Thus Providence knows how to measure out all pleasure and sorrow in a just manner.

v. 29. Isaac — died) At which time Jacob was 120 and Joseph, as one calculates, was already 29 years old, and had thus already been sold by his brothers 13 years prior. For this <note>the selling of Joseph</note> happened in the year that Rachel died and Benjamin was born, at which time Joseph was 16 and Jacob was 107 years old.

Undoubtedly, Moses wanted to tell the history of Joseph together in its complete order, and therefore saved the account of his selling until then, even though it otherwise occurred before the death of Isaac.

Esau and Jacob buried him) Following the example of Isaac and Ishmael, who also buried Abraham together. With this, Esau proved both his repentance for his former ill-will and his filial respect toward his father alongside Jacob.

Esau, like the other heathens, immediately strove to attain great power and prestige on earth, as he was able to march against his defenseless brother with 400 men; thus he followed in the footsteps of Nimrod, who descended from Ham (who was under the curse). In this, believers should follow, and at the very least should not strive for the glory of this world. Those to whom such glory is inherited should possess these things with great self-denial. For believers, their honor is reserved in the glorious kingdom of Christ, whom He will set as princes in all the world: Psalm 45:17. 32. And Bela, a son of Beor, reigned in Edom; and the name of his city was Dinhabah.

---

It may be, according to the opinion of some Jewish scholars, that these kings were not descendants of Edom or Esau, but rather reigned in the land earlier, before it was called the land of Edom after Esau. However, because mention is made here of the kings in Israel through a prophetic spirit <note>The author suggests Moses wrote this through divine foresight, as Israel had no kings in his time</note>, and since these kings in Edom reigned before them, it is quite possible that the later ones were primarily descendants of Esau. This is because, immediately after these kings, the chiefs from Esau’s tribe are mentioned in 1 Chronicles 1:51, who are to be distinguished from the first chiefs of this same tribe mentioned in verse 15, who were Esau’s sons and grandsons. Thus, this royal dignity could have been transformed into a "chiefly" or princely status through its abuse—much as happened among the Romans, when the kings were driven out and magistrates <note>original: "Bürgermeister" (mayors), referring here to the Roman Consuls</note> were elected who held a princely rank.

Thus God exalts, and thus He also humbles (1 Samuel 2:7). And all this according to His justice, which He exercises even among the heathens (Psalm 9:10). However, that Esau’s descendants attained such princely and even royal honors so quickly, while at that same time Jacob’s descendants had to spend time in heavy servitude in Egypt and later in the land of Canaan in a lowly state and under much pressure, shows that the godless are fortunate in the world and become rich; meanwhile, the people of God have a "multitude of waters" or many tears pressed out of them, as it is phrased in Psalm 73:10, 12. The former are set on slippery ground and cast down to the bottom with violence; just as the Edomite kingdom was soon destroyed, and all worldly kingdoms will have a similar fall. But the kingdom of the believers will emerge at the end and then endure for all eternity (Daniel 7:27).

v. 33. **Jobab**) According to some opinions, this is thought to be the pious Job, who is so famous for his patience. And although the name in this place is written with a *Yod*, but in the Book of Job with an *Aleph*, it is known to scholars that these letters are often exchanged, especially in the Hebrew and Syriac languages. For example, Jesse, the father of David, is written both as *Jesse* and *Isai*.

The primary reasons are as follows: 1) The royal glory, which is also testified to in Job 1:3 and 29:9, 12, 14. 2) The land of Uz, where he was born, raised, and lived, was incorporated into the land of the Edomites, as Jeremiah clearly testifies in Lamentations 4:21. And Philo, Origen, Athanasius, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, the Hebrews, the Muslims <note>original: "Mahemedaner"</note>, and other oriental peoples agree that Job was of Esau's descendants (a). 3) Among Job's friends was Eliphaz of Teman, etc. (v. 39. **Me-Zahab**) Because this name is written as two separate words <term>מי זהב</term> (*Me-Zahab*), it means "Water of Gold." For this reason, some wish to prove from it the existence of *aurum potabile* <note>original Latin: "drinkable gold," an alchemical elixir thought to grant long life</note>, which others who understand gold-working consider a fabulous myth and something not to be found in the world. The ancient Jews made Me-Zahab out to be a gold-smelter and alchemist, because the Hebrew names in Holy Scripture were not given by chance, but in view of some remarkable event. Therefore, the Chaldean Jerusalem Targum <note>A translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible into Aramaic</note> says: Because he could transform other metals into gold, he thought little of gold and asked: "What is gold?"

Cap. XXXVII. The 1st Book of Moses.

# Chapter XXXVII.
## Joseph’s Persecution.

Jacob, however, dwelt in the land of his father’s pilgrimages, in the land of Canaan.
2. These are the histories of Jacob: Joseph was seventeen years old when he was tending the sheep with his brothers; and he was a servant with the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives: and Joseph brought an evil report of them to their father.

Here begins the wonderful history of Joseph, first in his great humiliation and then in his exaltation: the former first among his brothers and later in Egypt; the latter first in Egypt and later also among his brothers. In this, he was a glorious <term>type of Christ</term> <note>A "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ.</note>, just as Christ was first rejected by the Jews—who were his brothers according to the flesh—and later is greatly oppressed in the "spiritual Egypt" within his true believers. He was also ultimately exalted by the Gentiles and will at last be recognized and greatly glorified by the Jews, as more will be noted in the following text.

Jacob then raised this dear son of his—whom he undoubtedly loved especially for his piety—not in a delicate manner in his house, but he also had to tend the sheep, and moreover serve the sons of the secondary wives as a young boy.

In this, as in many parts, we have in him a clear model of Christ, who also behaved as a servant among his disciples and also the Jews, since he came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. Matthew 20:28, Luke 22:27. He also rebuked them for all their evil deeds. Matthew 23.

v. 2. *Brought an evil report of them to their father*) When it is of great importance to our neighbor that his sin be made known to those who may punish and improve him in time, it is good and necessary to open the "abscess" with a lancet so that the infection does not become dangerous.

Among Joseph's brothers, the abomination of their sin was great, and is said to have been one of those sins that should not be named. The Hebrew words used here suggest a strong suspicion that it was a great misdeed, and that they became dishonorable because of it.

Thus Joseph also feared that their evil example might infect his brothers. Hatred toward sin and love for his brothers moved him to reveal it to the one who had the power and right to punish them.

The Jews, Christ's brothers according to the flesh, also showed such hatred toward Christ, who was the Beloved of the Lord, his heavenly Father, and appeared, as it were, in the "many-colored coat" of various miraculous gifts and holiness. In this, the Jews envied him and finally became his mortal enemies, so that they—especially the Pharisees and scribes—could never speak with him peacefully or in sincerity, and always had something to say against him. Now here, now there, things did not seem right to them, and he was intolerable for them to look upon. In this, his believers also tend to become like him according to their measure; the "natural man" envies the gifts with which they are graced by GOD. The many-colored coat stings their eyes, and the children of the bondwoman hate the children of the free and become their enemies. <meta>catchword: Indeed</meta>
he had the preference in love, and for the sake of that
love was so shortened. Joseph himself was an obedient child, and

<column-break/>

3. Israel, however, loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he had fathered him in his old age; and he made him a many-colored coat.
4. Now when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.
5. And <meta>catchword: And</meta>

---

Jacob acted somewhat imprudently here by having this special many-colored coat made for his dear son (of such fabric as one used to ask concerning the daughters of kings; 2 Samuel 13:18) and thereby only awakened the brothers' envy against him, while also bringing great heartache upon himself.

Certainly, parents must take great care that, even if they feel a well-founded love for one of their children, they should rather keep it hidden in the heart and instead call upon GOD for the increase of good in such a child, but not let it be noticed outwardly that they wish to prefer one child over another. For equality maintains peace, love, and unity. And GOD will know how to prefer the pious children, so that the others cannot harm them.

v. 3. *Israel*) When GOD—as <note>original: "Origenes"</note> Origen notes regarding the words "Jacob" and "Israel"—uses the word *Jacob*, He presents the Jews as Jews; but when He uses the word *Israel* in this history, He means the "Israel of God" who has seen the Lord and clings to Him.

*Loved, because—fathered in old age*) This carries a mystery with it. The Jews of the latter time, who are yet to be "begotten" by GOD through conversion, will be much more pleasing to the Lord than the former ever were. For one could have no more hope for so long a time that the "Jewish Rachel" would ever give birth. But when the time finally comes that she gives birth, oh, what joy will arise from that for the old Israel!

*Many-colored coat*) Thus the Father also adorned Christ with great heavenly gifts, as with a many-colored coat full of divine wisdom.

When a person—as the <term>German Philosopher</term> <note>Likely referring to the mystic Jacob Böhme (1575–1624).</note> writes not incorrectly of this—places his hope in GOD and lives in the simplicity and humility of his heart before Him, then a "Joseph" is already born within him; then GOD the Father clothes his soul with the many-colored coat, as with divine power, and begins to play with his soul as if with Joseph.

v. 4. *His brothers—hated him etc.*) According to the judgment of their evil hearts, the envious brothers had a "semblance of right" against the seemingly unjust love of the father in which he preferred Joseph, because they were nonetheless the eldest and first-born of Leah, and were also more in number. But according to the true judgment of love, Jacob had reason for such preference: because Rachel was the mother for whom
he had served so many years, and the time for her great
distinguished himself thereby.

---

The history of Joseph is a living expression of a chosen soul, and the various occurrences recorded in Holy Scripture show exceedingly beautifully the different "states" through which one of these chosen souls must pass to reach the intended perfection. GOD first lets them wander through a spiritual, childlike state in which they experience nothing but sweetness and caresses. It then seems as if GOD wants to do nothing more than to adorn and decorate them, while giving others up. This even draws the envy of other people, seeing that everything happens only for this soul. But she will have to pay dearly enough for all of it!

### 15. And a man found him / and behold, he was wandering in the field / and the man asked him, saying: What are you seeking?
### 16. And he answered: I am seeking my brothers; please tell me / where they are pasturing.
### 17. And the man said: They have departed from here. For I heard them say: Let us go to Dothan. Then Joseph followed after his brothers / and found them at Dothan.
### 18. Now when they saw him from afar / before he came near to them / they took counsel against him / to kill him;

Once the hearts of men are possessed by envy and hatred / especially against the witnesses of truth; they do not rest / until they have done harm: they cling to one another / and devise evil tricks. *Psalm 10:2.* And so worldly people always intend to destroy the counsel of **GOD** / which such witnesses hold out to them / with their fleshly plots / by which they seek to stifle such a testimony: how their defiant and angry thoughts hasten against the innocent / and how they cast aside all fear of **GOD** in this / is presented more fully in the 10th Psalm. Thus Christ presents this same murderous plot of the Jewish leaders / as the husbandmen / how **GOD** the Father finally sent His Son to them / who was to promote the peace and welfare of the Jews in every way: but when the husbandmen saw the Son / they said among themselves: This is the heir; come, let us kill him / and take his inheritance for ourselves. And they took him and cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. *Matthew 21:38-39.*

Here, just as Reuben does now, Nicodemus once / and then during the blood-sentence Joseph of Arimathea / sought to rescue the Savior from the hands of the Jews / as one who had not consented to their counsel and deed. *John 7:51. Luke 23:50-51.*

<margin>v. 17. Dothan)</margin> Is today a small village / inhabited by Moors. <note>original: "Moren." In early modern German, this term broadly referred to North Africans or Muslims.</note> *2 Kings 6:13.*

<margin>v. 18. Among the envious brothers</margin> are found those / who / because they have distanced themselves from the path of truth / interpret everything in the worst possible way; and by pretending / as if they wanted to punish a vice / which is a vice only in their imagination / they seek by that very means to kill an innocent person. Of this kind are the perverse zealots / who accuse those who teach and defend the inward ways <note>A reference to "Pietism" or "Mysticism," focusing on the internal spiritual life rather than external rituals.</note> of crimes / with the intent of taking their lives / if not in body / then in spirit and reputation / in order to suffocate these inward ways.

Just so it happened to Christ with His brothers according to the flesh / the Pharisees / who also / because He rebuked them with words and deeds for their evil conduct / daily took counsel with themselves / how they might kill Him. *Luke 19:47.* This very same Christ is still envied and persecuted today in His children by false brothers. Indeed, it is He / as **JESUS** Christ yesterday and today / who already in the time of Joseph endured in Joseph himself everything that Joseph had to suffer from his wicked brothers.

So also reason and an evil will commonly take counsel together against Christ / how they might suppress His holy discipline within themselves and stifle His Spirit / indeed, bring Him into the deep pit of oblivion / so that the unbelieving man may carry on his abominations unhindered.

<margin>v. 19. <margin>v. 21. 22. Reuben spoke)</margin> The Jewish historian Josephus (a) explains Reuben's speeches and reasons somewhat more extensively / how he sought to turn them from their purpose: It is a great sin before **GOD** and men / to strike a man dead / even if he is not related to us: Much more gruesome it is / to murder a brother / whereby they would not only lay hands on their brother's blood / but also grievously offend the father / and cause the mother great heartache. Therefore they should spare the parents / and consider for themselves / what grief and cross the murder of their pious and youngest son would bring them / and refrain from this inhuman deed. So also they should stand in awe of **GOD** / who knows all things / and from whom nothing remains hidden. If they were to lay hands on him / then **GOD** would surely avenge this fratricide in all places and ends: because it is to be believed without doubt / that wherever a man is / **GOD** is also there. Furthermore, they would gain a restless conscience / which would accuse them at all times in all their doing. Moreover, it would not be proper / that one should strike his brother dead / even if he had been offended by him; rather, one should much more hold something to the benefit of such close friends. Joseph, however, had done them no harm. Therefore they were much more obligated / for the sake of his tender youth, to have compassion for him / and to shield him against all his enemies, etc.

Such and more Reuben brought forward / but could obtain nothing by it. Therefore he finally advised / they should at least think of a lesser and milder death / than to murder him with their own hand. To which they finally agreed / and lowered the boy into a deep pit.

To bring him back to his father) And to restore himself to his favor / which he had lost through the incest committed against Bilhah.

Hardly have the sweetnesses of spiritual childhood passed / when the very heaviest sufferings are prepared. One sees oneself presented to the most extreme persecutions. Joseph is like the lamb among the wolves. But **GOD** / who always watches over the souls / who surrender themselves to Him without exception / always finds a defender / to rescue them from the hands of their enemies.

Luke 19:47. That very same Christ is still to this day envied and persecuted in his children by false brothers. Indeed, it is He / as **JESUS** Christ yesterday and today / who already in the times of Joseph endured everything in Joseph himself / which Joseph had to suffer from his evil brothers.

So also do Reason and an evil will commonly take counsel with one another over Christ / how they want to suppress his holy discipline within themselves and stifle his Spirit / indeed, bring him into the deep pit of oblivion / so that the unbelieving man might carry on his abominations unhindered.

The brothers later recount the great anguish Joseph felt / in which he found himself during this stripping of his coat / and he undoubtedly pleaded with them for his life / though they would not hear him / and therefore they later had to fall into similar anguish before Joseph / Gen. 42:21. He was, however, thrown into an empty pit / in which he had to spend some time languishing and starving in great fear: just as the faithful are also represented as prisoners in a pit where there is no water / at the time of their soul’s anguish / Zech. 9:11. He was then sold to the Ishmaelites and Midianites / who both descended from Abraham / Gen. 25:2, 12 / and had devoted themselves greatly to commerce / Isa. 60:6 / for twenty pieces of silver. In this, Christ once again appears to us / whom they also robbed of his clothes in his great anguish / and plunged him into the pit of destruction on the Cross: after they had also first delivered him to the Gentiles / because they were not permitted to lay hands on him themselves / and bought him for thirty pieces of silver from the treacherous Judas <note>original: "vaderathischen Juda"; the author plays on the name Judah/Judas</note>; whereas here, Judah, out of some mercy, promoted this sale of Joseph for his deliverance. <gloss>Reuben was distressed that Joseph might have perished; and his dear father even more so: so that throughout the long time in which he could learn nothing of Joseph's life—as can be gathered from verse 2 here and Chapters 41:46, 47, and 45:6—he was constantly grieved and mourned for his son. Neither all his sons nor his daughters—such as Dinah and Serah, Asher’s daughter, Chapter 46:17—nor his sons' wives and daughters, were able to talk him out of it. On the other hand, Joseph's brothers did not take his miserable state in such servitude to heart at all, but rather deceived their old father with lies and increased his sorrow by leading him to believe that he had been so piteously torn apart by a wild beast. The Prophet uses them as a symbol of those who live in their pleasures and care little for the "affliction of Joseph," <note>original: "Schaden Josephs"</note> Amos 6:6, when their brothers in faith live under the pressure of persecution or otherwise in heavy tribulations.</gloss>

<gloss>v. 29. Came to the pit) By night, as Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> reports, in order to secretly set Joseph free behind his brothers' backs, after he had called out to him several times in vain.</gloss>

<gloss>There is always an all-too-natural friend who wants to pull us out of the guidance of Providence. It seems people would gladly pull us out of the pit through pity—that is, out of the Cross, the self-denial, and the temptation through which God leads us. But God, through His Providence, can play His hand so well that no one can rescue us from His hands.</gloss>

<gloss>v. 31. Dipped the coat in blood) Josephus adds, quite probably, that they also tore it: so that the father might the more readily believe that a wild beast had torn Joseph apart.</gloss>

<gloss>Those who, by the command of divine Providence, rob us of gifts and felt graces, dip such things in blood. For all these sweetnesses and benefits of God change into a seeming cruelty. But it is only a seeming cruelty, which has nothing substantial but the image. Everything becomes blood and murder to such a soul; everything is its Cross: but only externally. For inwardly, it is at peace through resignation <term>Gelassenheit: a state of surrendered equanimity or letting go of the self to God.</term>.</gloss>

<gloss>...but he would have come slowly in and through the grave: regarding which, more elsewhere.</gloss>

<gloss>Wept for him) The saints are distressed, weep, and take penance upon themselves for the sake of those who have surrendered themselves, in order to soften the mercy of God. Jacob had not wept for Rachel, who was so dear to him: but because of Joseph, he is so greatly distressed. Namely, because he viewed everything in God, the death of Rachel was useful and necessary, and he saw nothing in it but the death of a body that was indeed dear, but which he wished to possess only in the will of God. Whereas here, he perceived the misfortune of a spiritual soul, which was thought to be lost under the dominion of the Devil; even though such a soul was in fact holier than it had ever been. Jacob saw in this only the external bloodiness and sorrow; but he did not know that his son was full of life and peace.</gloss>

<gloss>v. 36. Sold him) Joseph is sold for the second time. Does it not seem as if he were born only for sale and servitude? But just as a noble soul finds its freedom even in chains, so a soul surrendered to God is never in greater freedom than when it seems to be the greatest servant.</gloss>

<gloss>In Egypt) Into anguish and tribulation.</gloss>

->Thus the pious *Jacob* had to experience one household trial <note>original: "Hauẞ-Creutz," a metaphor for a heavy domestic burden or cross to bear</note> after another in his family as a test of his faith. According to the common proverb: Great children, great worries!<-

Although many sinful abominations arose from such a heathen marriage; nevertheless, the unfathomable providence of God knew how to punish them in such a way that He also brought something good out of it, so that *Perez* / one of the ancestors of Christ / had to be born from this Canaanite woman through *Tamar* / who was undoubtedly from this place and her kindred. To which God, among other things, points through the prophet: <margin>Ezekiel 16:3.</margin> *Your origin and your birth is from the land of the Canaanites, etc.* This was to convince the Jews and all of us of humility and the recognition of our sinful nature and perversity from the womb: especially since the Jews boast greatly of the holiness of their ancestors and the patriarchs, and therefore seek all sorts of vain excuses to twist such an act or otherwise excuse it.
In the meantime, we must pay attention to this wonderful history in all its circumstances with all the greater diligence, because Jesus CHRIST / the Lion of the tribe of *Judah* / chose to take His origin according to the flesh from there. To us, this is a testimony of His incomprehensible loving-kindness; since He was not ashamed to come from such as these / and to incorporate them into His lineage / who were not of such pure origin / so that all people might be sanctified in Him and through Him. Therefore, He also wished to spring from the Gentiles to a certain extent through the maternal line / as the one who intended to gather Jews and Gentiles in Him according to the Spirit / and unite them through faith.

### Chapter XXXVIII. The First Book of Moses.

11. Then Judah said to his daughter-in-law <note>original: "Schnur," an archaic German term for a daughter-in-law</note> Tamar: Remain a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up. For he thought: Perhaps he might also die, like his brothers. So Tamar went away and remained in her father's house.
12. Now after many days had passed, the daughter of Shua <note>OCR reads "Suha," likely a transcription error for "Schua"</note>, Judah's wife, died: and when Judah had finished mourning, he went up to his sheep-shearers at Timnath, he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
<margin>Joshua 15:57. Judges 14:5.</margin>
13. Then it was told to Tamar, saying: Behold, your father-in-law is going up to Timnath to shear his sheep.
14. Then she took off her widow’s garments, covered herself with a veil, wrapped herself up, and sat at the entrance of Enaim <note>German: "vornen an den Scheidweg," literally "at the fork in the road"</note>, which is on the way to Timnath. 15. When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute; for she had covered her face.
16. And he turned aside to her by the way, and said: Please, let me come in to you! For he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. And she answered: What will you give me, that you may come in to me?

---

The ancients were accustomed to holding great feasts at their sheep-shearing, and to show themselves joyful during this good harvest. 1 Samuel 25:2, 8, 36. Here Judah also seeks to refresh his spirit from his mourning; which never ends well when one seeks to drive away sorrow with earthly lust. This light-minded deed of Judah—who was chosen from the twelve tribes to be the ancestor of Christ—the Holy Spirit by no means wished to conceal; just as the sins of David and other saints were recorded, to show hereby how before GOD no flesh has anything to boast of, and that one must strive for the second birth from GOD (John 1:12-13), which alone can make us capable and worthy of GOD's grace. Thus the Jews are also put to shame hereby, who boasted that they were not born of fornication (John 8:41), since they nearly all descended from this Judah and this very incest <term>Blutschande: literally "blood-shame," the historical term for incest</term> with Tamar, through Perez and Zerah. 1 Chronicles 2, 3, 4. They see clearly though, that they had one Father, GOD: a claim which only the pious among them could truly make, and not the whole multitude.

<column-break/>

17. And he said: I will send you a young goat from the flock. And she answered: If you will give me a pledge until you send it.
18. And he said: What pledge shall I give you? And she answered: Your signet ring and your cord <note>German: "Schnur." Note the wordplay: in verse 11 "Schnur" meant daughter-in-law; here it refers to the cord or ribbon used to carry the signet ring</note>, and your staff that is in your hand. So he gave them to her and went in to her, and she became pregnant by him.
19. And she arose and went away, and laid aside her veil, and put on her widow’s garments again.
20. And Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend the Adullamite, to receive the pledge back from the woman’s hand: but he did not find her.
21. Then he asked the people of that place, saying: Where is the prostitute who was by the road at the crossroads? And they answered: No prostitute has been here.
22. And he returned to Judah and said: I have not found her; and also the people of the place say: No prostitute has been here.
23. Then Judah said: Let her keep the things for herself, lest we be put to shame! Behold, I sent this goat, and you have not found her.
24. And

---

However, Tamar’s deed is also not to be excused, though it is more easily forgiven, because Judah’s promise to her was not kept, and she thus wished to maintain herself within Judah’s family and inheritance. As a gentile <note>original: "Heydin"</note>, she did not understand the shamefulness of this union, as Judah later recognized, and he did not touch her again afterward (v. 26). Otherwise, he sought to avoid shame before men, but did not think of the shame before GOD, for whose sake we should most be ashamed of sin. Romans 6:21.
It is nevertheless notable that his father Jacob—who in his final blessing gave each son a special prophecy and sharply rebuked them for where they had done wrong—did not confront Judah with this deed: rather, he passed over it all in silence and promised him very great things.
And who must not pause here <note>original: "ein Selah halten," a reference to the musical/liturgical pause in the Psalms</note> and in silence wonder at and worship the ways of the Lord! The rightful wife of Judah is passed over, and from Tamar, his daughter-in-law, whom he used as a prostitute—and from this very incest itself—the lineage of Christ was to be carried forward.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of Genesis 38. After Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute and conceived by her father-in-law Judah (who did not recognize her), three months have passed. ### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXVIII.

24. And it came to pass after three months, that it was told to Judah, saying: Tamar your daughter-in-law <note>original: "Schnur"</note> has played the harlot; and behold, she is also pregnant from her harlotry! Then Judah said: Lead her out, that she may be burned!

25. When she was led out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying: By the man to whom these things belong, I am pregnant. And she said: Please examine whose things these are! The signet ring, and the cords, and the staff.

26. And Judah examined them, and said: She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah! Yet he did not know her <note>A biblical idiom for sexual intimacy</note> any further from that time on.

---

When a person should have mercy on their neighbor's sinful guilt, they are sometimes all the more zealous against them, even though they themselves are stuck in the very same guilt.

Judah wanted to have his daughter-in-law burned on account of harlotry, yet he had defiled himself with the very same act. See 2 Samuel 12:5, 7 <note>This refers to King David judging the man in Nathan's parable, only to realize he was judging himself</note>. Among some nations, adultery was greatly detested and punished by death: just as God commanded, even if someone slept with only a betrothed bride; Deuteronomy 22:23-24. Indeed, if a priest's daughter played the harlot, she had to be burned with fire. Leviticus 21:9. Thus, Judah wanted to show his zeal, demonstrating that as a people of the true God, they wished to see such sins punished most severely. It may also be that after the incest of Reuben, and after Simeon and Levi defiled themselves with the murder of the Shechemites, Judah may have administered the priesthood as the firstborn in Jacob's family: just as a portion of the birthright in dominion was granted to him.

<margin>v. 24. Then Judah said</margin> From this, it may be concluded that they had no sovereign authority over them at that time, except that each man exercised the right of a patriarch <note>literally "house-father"</note> within his own lineage or family.

<margin>Lead her out, that &c.</margin> How cruel, how hasty, how unmerciful we are toward others, whom we wish to see disposed of immediately in their sins, regardless of the great experience we have of the Lord’s patience and longsuffering toward us! Consider how godlessly one robs even the longsuffering God of His gracious purpose! The servant who owed his master ten thousand pounds, and with whom his master had patience, would have no patience with his fellow servant, but threw him into prison. And was he not in the same, indeed much greater, condemnation? The counsel of our longsuffering Lord is found in John 8:7, Luke 9:55-56, Galatians 6:1, 2 Timothy 2:24-25.

<margin>Burn</margin> Perhaps also only branded <note>original: "gebrannt," suggesting a mark of shame rather than execution</note>; so that here a funeral pyre is not necessarily to be understood, but rather that she should only be branded as a harlot. For women of this profession at that time had to have a certain mark on their foreheads so that they could be recognized.

<margin>v. 26. She is more righteous than I</margin> Thus we should always say with Judah. When we accuse someone of a spiritual fault, we should think whether we have done nothing out of greed. And if it has happened (for greed is the root of all evil, and creeps secretly through our bodies like something under the earth), then we should all say: He is more righteous than I. When we are angry with someone, they may well have less guilt, and we may well consider within ourselves: Perhaps this person whom I accuse is more righteous than I. For when we say this, we preserve ourselves, so that the Lord Jesus may not one day say to us: "You see the speck in your brother's eye." Therefore, we should not be ashamed to speak out, saying that our guilt is greater than that of the one we wish to punish. <margin>Ambrose (a)</margin>

(a) <note>original: "L. II. de poenit. c. 8."</note> Book II of *On Repentance*, chapter 8.

<column-break/>

27. And it happened at the time when she was to give birth, behold, there were twins in her womb.

28. And it happened as she was giving birth, a hand reached out. Then the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread, and said: This one came out first.

29. And it happened as he drew his hand back again, behold, his brother came out! And she said: How you have broken through! Because of you, the breach has happened! And they named him Perez <note>The name Perez means "Breach" or "Bursting forth"</note>.

30. Afterward, his brother came out, who had the scarlet thread around his hand: and they named him Zerah <note>The name Zerah implies "Brightness" or "Rising light"</note>.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

Since Christ chose to be born from Judah through this Perez, and that from this otherwise sinful cohabitation in the field; and since his birth proceeded so wonderfully, and one was born with him who seemed destined to be the firstborn, yet was born only afterward: the ancients also sought a special mystery in this. Specifically, regarding the Jews and the Gentiles: for the light of grace first rose for the former; to which the word Zerah points, which signifies a rising of light. The latter, however, truly "broke through" to the grace of God that appeared in Christ, which the word Perez means, and thus became the firstfruits, while the Jews drew back, though they shall also be fully brought forth later.

However, this also points to the different types of believers. Indeed, they are all brought forth through the Lord, who finds us lying in the field in our unclean birth, Ezekiel 16:5-6; He also enters into the covenant of spiritual marriage with us, verse 8. He also gives the Holy Spirit as a pledge, like the true wedding ring, with which He seals us: which is also the cord of our inheritance; Psalm 16:6. Here, "cord" can be understood as the cord around the neck or otherwise; and since it may have been double or manifold, it is called "cords" in the plural; which the ancients may have worn as an ornament. Yes, the Holy Spirit is the royal crown and ornament of believers; Isaiah 62:3. Just as such things are usually surrounded by a precious cord of pearls: and He is also our staff and rod.

So also the light first rises for some, and they even lay their hand to the work; but afterward, they draw back because of the difficulty, Luke 9:62, and thus do not truly break through. Yet Christ will look upon their sincerity and, because of their good intentions and works, grant them the scarlet thread of His bloody merit, and have mercy on them, so that afterward, after undergoing purification, they will be brought forth to grace. Others, however, truly break through in the power of Christ, in complete denial of the world and taking up the cross of Christ, and in total following and conformity to the Head. Romans 8:29. These are true "Perezes" and breakers-through: just as Christ is also called such, and in Him these believers break through. Micah 2:13. And from this comes the well-grounded distinction in God's Word between the firstborn and the later-born. See also Matthew 19:30, 20:19.

Whoever considers this event in this way will find this otherwise very offensive history to be much more joyful, and it will awaken in them a quiet praise of wonder over the mystery of love toward the poor Gentiles.

# Chapter XXXIX. The First Book of Moses.

### Chapter XXXIX.
->Joseph’s Temptations.<-

1. AND Joseph was led down into Egypt / and Potiphar / an officer of Pharaoh / the captain of the guard / an Egyptian man / bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites / who had brought him down there.
2. And the Lord was with Joseph / so that he was a man who succeeded in all things: and he was in the house of his master / the Egyptian.
3. And his master saw / that the Lord was with him. For everything that he did / the Lord made to prosper through his hand.
4. Thus Joseph found grace in his eyes / and served him: and he appointed him over his house / and everything that he had he committed into his hand.

Those whom God wishes to exalt / He usually first humbles / so that they may learn humility / in which alone one may please God. And so Joseph first had to become a servant and a slave / and later even be thrown into prison / yet God always raised him up again / and allowed him a glimpse of his future exaltation / which He had announced to him in a dream.

<margin>v. 2.</margin> Is it not a guidance well-becoming of the right hand of God / to maintain such great souls under such a lowly and despised form? God was always with Joseph : for He never removes Himself from those most dear to Him who are surrendered <note>original: "Gelassenen," a Pietist term referring to those who have yielded their will entirely to God</note> ; and it is never better for them / than when the whole world accounts them as lost : because then God has a special watch over them ; which they also truly feel / so that in the midst of their bitterness they cry out with David (a): The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?

<margin>v. 3.</margin> God kills and makes alive / and sustains with the very same hand with which He strikes. He deals deadly wounds; but He also immediately applies the healing balm to the tips of His arrows : so that one cannot say / which of the two is more felt / the pain / or the joy. It is a joy full of pain / and a pain full of joy. O God / why do You not always kill in this manner!

<margin>v. 4.</margin> Served him) He was previously also his servant / but still in lowly tasks. But here he is permitted a greater closeness / to wait upon him / in a freer manner / so that he was now his favorite.
<margin>(a) Ps. 27:1.</margin>

<column-break/>

5. And it happened from that time / when he had appointed him over his house / and over all that he had / that the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake / and the blessing of the Lord was in all that he had / in the house and in the field.
6. Therefore he left all that he had in Joseph’s hand / and he concerned himself with nothing except the food / which he ate. And Joseph was beautiful of form and beautiful of countenance.
7. And

<margin>v. 5. The blessing of the Lord was in all things)</margin> This is produced by the fear of the Lord / which reigned in Joseph’s heart. For otherwise the Lord could not have been with him. Ps. 103:13.

This was then also proven outwardly in the gracious governance of God in all his doing and leaving. For it is a certain sign / that a person allows himself to be driven and led inwardly by a holy awe and reverence before the Spirit of God / when his affairs are also well-ordered and graced by God outwardly / in words / deeds / and sufferings. One sees from such behavior in a person / that he notices and waits for the light of the Holy Spirit with the eye of his heart / recognizes his own unworthiness and blindness / and therefore merely abandons and gives himself over to grace in all things. Then it cannot be otherwise / wisdom precedes such a person in all things ; because he is willing to honestly pursue and follow it. One does not easily rush through one’s duties ; one does not follow one’s own passions <note>original: "Affecten"</note> or one’s own blind impulse / much less the detours of the enemy / or the godless rules of the world and its customs : but one learns with Joseph to trace the path of wisdom.

Then nothing can come but blessing / salvation / and everything good : at the very least a well-ordered / unconfused / peaceful way of life / which in itself is already enough contentment and advantage. For what does all abundance help without true peace of mind?

The Spirit reports such a happiness here of Joseph and his master / that through God’s blessed governance everything went well for him / that he arranged and carried out all things wisely / and thus nothing but growth was to be perceived.

But Reason might here object ; that this is certainly no right sign of the fear of God / if it goes well for someone outwardly : since it commonly goes well for the godless outwardly. And it is indeed so / that the prosperity of the flesh is certainly no sign of the fear of God. But

It is quite another thing to have such an orderly / sensible and blessed / or God-contented life / in which God’s wisdom / love and goodness / can reveal themselves. This is indeed a true fruit of godliness / which also has the promise of this life. 1 Timothy 4:8.

Whoever now finds himself in a shattered / disorderly and perverse state ; he has to examine himself / whether he has lost sight of the true fear of the Lord / and remains stuck merely in his dark and self-willed nature / so that God cannot master him / to lead him rightly to all that is good.

Whoever, on the other hand, lives with Joseph in some prosperity / let him believe / that he has only divine governance and undeserved grace to thank for it : let him also remain therein in the right awe of God / and recognize his danger / how easily he could become secure, careless, and thus lose his prosperity at the slightest rest. For truly

The fear of God not only drives its children to all astonishing good / but it also most powerfully keeps them from evil : as Joseph’s example further demonstrates.

<margin>v. 6. Beautiful)</margin> When outward beauty is accompanied by the inward beauty of a virtuous soul / that is something excellent : as was also the case with Moses / Acts 7:20 / and with David. 1 Samuel 16:12. Otherwise, a sinful soul often dwells in a well-formed body ; as can be seen with Saul / 1 Samuel 9:2 / and Absalom : 2 Samuel 14:25 / because man commonly misuses natural gifts.

In contrast, true Christians commonly receive a friendly expression in their faces from Christ / so that / even if they are not otherwise of such beautiful features in their outward form / yet something so lovely and truthful looks out from their eyes / that one can well see in them / that a good spirit dwells in them / and a mystical Joseph resides within them.

# Chapter XXXIX. The First Book of Moses.

## The XXXIX. Chapter.
->Joseph's Temptations.<-

2. And the LORD was with Joseph / so that he was a man who prospered: and he was in the house of his lord / the Egyptian.

v. 5. **The blessing of the LORD was in everything**) That is caused by the fear of the LORD / which reigned in Joseph's heart. For otherwise the LORD could not have been with him. Ps. 103:13.

This then also proved itself outwardly in the gracious governance of God in all his doing and leaving. For that is a certain sign / that a person allows himself to be driven and led inwardly through a holy awe and reverence by the Spirit of God / when his things are also well-ordered and graced by God outwardly / in words / deeds / and suffering. One sees from such conduct of a person / that he marks and waits upon the light of the Holy Spirit with the eye of his heart / recognizes his own unfitness and blindness / and therefore merely abandons and gives himself over to grace in everything. Then it cannot be otherwise; wisdom commands such a one in all things; because he is willing to follow and pursue it honestly. One does not easily over-hasten in his duties; one does not follow his affects or his own blind drive / much less the detours of the enemy / or the godless rules of the world and its customs: but one learns with Joseph to track the pull of wisdom.

There nothing else can come but blessing / salvation / and all good: at the very least a well-ordered / unconfused / peaceful way of life / which in itself is already satisfaction and advantage enough. For what does all abundance help without true peace of mind? <term>Gemüths-Ruhe (Peace of Mind): A state of spiritual tranquility and contentment derived from faith.</term>

Such a happiness the Spirit reports here of Joseph and his master / that through God’s blessed governance everything went well for him / that he arranged and carried out all things wisely / and thus nothing but growth was to be sensed.

But reason might object here; this is surely no right sign of the fear of God / if it goes well for one outwardly: since it commonly goes well for the godless outwardly. And it is also so / that the prosperity of the flesh is certainly no sign of the fear of God. But

It is something quite different / such an orderly / sensible and blessed / or in-God-contented life / in which God's wisdom / love and goodness / can reveal themselves. This is certainly a true fruit of godliness / which also has the promise of this life. 1 Timothy 4:8.

# The First Book of Moses. Ch. XXXVIII.

24. And it came to pass about three months later / that it was told to Judah / saying: Your daughter-in-law Tamar has played the harlot / and behold / she is also pregnant from her harlotry! Then Judah said: Lead her out / that she may be burned!

25. As she was being led out / she sent word to her father-in-law / and said; By the man to whom these things belong / I am pregnant: and she said; Please / see whose things these are! the signet ring and the cords and the staff.

26. And Judah examined them / and said: She is more righteous than I / because I did not give her to my son Shelah! But he did not know her <note>In the biblical sense of intimate relations.</note> any more from then on.

---

Though a human being should have mercy for the sinful guilt of his neighbor / he is sometimes all the more zealous against him / even though he himself is stuck in the very same guilt.

Judah wanted to have his daughter-in-law burned on account of harlotry / yet he had defiled himself with the same. See 2 Samuel 12:5, 7. Adultery was greatly abhorred among some peoples and punished with death: just as God also commanded / even if someone only lay with a betrothed bride; Deuteronomy 22:23, 24. Indeed / that a priest's daughter / if she played the harlot / must be burned with fire. Leviticus 21:9. Thus Judah wanted to show his zeal / so that they / as a people of the true God / would know such sins to be most vehemently punished. He may also / after the incest of Reuben / and after Simeon and Levi defiled themselves with the murder of the Shechemites / have administered the priesthood as the firstborn in Jacob's family: just as a portion of the firstborn's right to rule was granted to him.

v. 24. **Then Judah said**) From this it can be concluded / that they at that time had no sovereign authority over them / except that each man in his tribe or family exercised the right of a patriarch.

**Lead her out, that etc.**) How cruel / how hasty / how unmerciful we are toward others / whom we want to see done away with immediately in their sins / despite having such great experience of the patience and longsuffering of the Lord toward us! One should consider / how godlessly one robs even the longsuffering God of His gracious purpose! The servant who owed his master ten thousand pounds / and with whom his master had patience / would have no patience with his fellow servant / but threw him into prison. And was he not in the very same / indeed much greater / condemnation? The counsel of our longsuffering Lord is John 8:7; Luke 9:55, 56; Galatians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:24, 25.

**Burned**) Perhaps only branded; so that a funeral pyre is not necessarily to be understood here / but that she should only be branded as a harlot. For women of this profession in those days had to have a certain mark on their forehead / so that they could be recognized.

v. 26. **She is more righteous than I**) So we should always say with Judah. When we accuse someone of greed / we should think / whether we have done nothing at all out of greed ourselves. And if it has happened / (as indeed greed is the root of all evil / and secretly creeps through our body as if underground) / then we should all say: He is more righteous than I. When we are angry with someone / he perhaps has less guilt / and we may well consider within ourselves: Perhaps this one whom I accuse is more righteous than I. For when we say this / we protect ourselves / so that the Lord Jesus may not one day say to us: You see the splinter in your brother's eye. Therefore we should not be ashamed to speak out / saying that our guilt is greater than that of the one we wish to punish. — Ambrose. (a)

<margin>(a) Ambrose, *On Repentance*, Book II, chapter 8.</margin>

30. Afterward / his brother came out / who had the red thread around his hand: and he was named Serah <note>Serah means "rising" or "brightness," like the dawn.</note>.

Since Christ wished to be born of Judah through this Perez / and that from this otherwise sinful cohabitation in the field; and since it happened so miraculously with his birth / that one was born with him who seemed destined to be the firstborn / yet was born only afterward: the ancients <note>The "ancients" usually refers to early Church Fathers.</note> have also sought a special mystery in this. Specifically / in the Jews and the Gentiles: for to the former the light of grace first rose / which the word Serah refers to / signifying a rising of the light: but the latter [the Gentiles] truly broke through at the actual appearance of God's grace in Christ / which is what the word Perez means / and thus they became the firstlings / while the Jews withdrew / though they shall also be fully brought forth afterward.

This also refers to the different kinds of believers. Indeed / they are all brought forth by the Lord / who finds us lying in our unclean birth in the field / Ezekiel 16:5 / where He also enters into the covenant of spiritual marriage with us. v. 8. He also gives the Holy Spirit as a pledge / as the true wedding ring / with which He seals us: which is also the cord of our inheritance; Psalm 16:6. In this context / the "cord" <note>Judah's cord from v. 25.</note> can be understood as the cord around the hat or neck or otherwise: and as it may have been double or manifold / it is called "cords" in the plural; which the ancients may have worn as an ornament. Indeed / the Holy Spirit is the royal hat and ornament of the believers; Isaiah 62:3. just as such things are accustomed to be surrounded by a precious string of pearls: and He is also our staff and rod.

So also / to some the light first rises / and they set their hand to the work; but they afterward withdraw it because of the difficulty / Luke 9:62 / and thus do not truly break through. Yet Christ will look upon their sincerity / and because of their good intention and works / will grant them the red thread of His bloody merit / and have mercy on them / so that they may yet afterward / after undergoing purification / be brought forth into grace. The others / however / truly break through in the power of Christ / in complete denial of the world and taking up the cross of Christ / and in total following and conformity to the Head. Romans 8:29. These are true "Perezes" and breakthrough-makers: just as Christ is also so named / and these believers break through in Him. Micah 2:13. And from this also comes the well-founded distinction in God's Word between the firstborn and the later-born. See also Matthew 19:30, 20:19.

Whoever views this event in this way / to him this otherwise very offensive history will instead become joyful / and awaken in him a quiet praise of wonder at the mystery of love toward the poor Gentiles.
