# Chapter XXXIX. The First Book of Moses.

## The XXXIX Chapter.
->Joseph's Temptations.<-

**A**nd Joseph was led down into Egypt; and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s chamberlain <note>A high-ranking official or eunuch in the royal court.</note>, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian man, bought him from the hand of the Ishmaelites who had brought him down there.
2. And the **LORD** was with Joseph, so that he was a prosperous man: and he was in the house of his master, the Egyptian.
3. And his master saw that the **LORD** was with him. For everything he did, the **LORD** caused it to succeed through his hand.
4. Thus Joseph found grace in his eyes and served him: and he appointed him over his house, and everything he had he entrusted into his hand.

Those whom **God** wishes to exalt, He is accustomed first to humble, so that they may learn humility, in which one may please **God** alone. And so Joseph first had to become a servant and a slave, and afterward even be thrown into prison; yet **God** always raised him up again and allowed him a glimpse of his future exaltation, which He had announced to him in a dream.
<margin>v. 2.</margin> Is it not a guidance well-becoming the right hand of **God** to maintain such great souls under such a lowly and despised form? **God** was always with Joseph: for He never removes Himself from those who have surrendered themselves to Him; and it is never better for them than when the whole world considers them lost: because then **God** takes special notice of them; which they also truly feel, so that in the midst of their bitterness they cry out with David (a):
> The **LORD** is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?
<margin>v. 3.</margin> **God** kills and makes alive, and sustains with the very same hand with which He strikes. He strikes deadly wounds; but He also immediately applies the healing balm to the tips of His arrows: so that one cannot say which of the two is more keenly felt, the pain or the joy. It is a joy full of pain, and a pain full of joy. O **God**, why do You not always kill in this manner!
<margin>v. 4.</margin> **He served him)** He was his servant before this as well, but still in lowly duties. Here, however, he is granted a greater closeness, to wait upon him in a freer manner, so that he was now his favorite.
(a) Psalm 27:1.
Wisdom, love, and goodness. This is certainly
the promise of life. 1 Timothy 4:8.
Anyone who finds themselves in a shattered, disorderly, and perverse state should examine themselves to see whether they have lost sight of the true fear of the Lord, and remain merely in their dark and self-willed nature, so that **God** cannot take hold of them to lead them rightly into all that is good.
Whoever, on the other hand, lives in some prosperity like Joseph, let him believe that he has only the divine government and unmerited grace to thank for it: let him also remain in the right awe of **God**, and recognize his danger—how easily he could become secure, careless, and thus lose his prosperity at the slightest bit of rest. For truly, the fear of **God** not only drives His children to all astonishing good, but it also most powerfully restrains them from evil: as Joseph’s example further demonstrates.

Then it cannot be otherwise: Wisdom goes before such a person in all things; because he is willing to honestly pursue and follow her. One does not easily rush through one's duties; one does not follow one's passions or own blind impulses, much less the wrong paths of the enemy, or the ungodly rules of the world and its customs: but instead, one learns with Joseph to trace the path of Wisdom.
Then nothing other than blessing, salvation, and all good things can come: at the very least a well-ordered, unconfused, peaceful way of life, which in itself is already contentment and advantage enough. For what use is all abundance without true peace of mind?
The Spirit reports such a happiness here of Joseph and his master, that through **God’s** blessed rule everything went well for him, that he arranged and carried out all things wisely, and thus nothing but growth was to be perceived.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIX.

## 7. And it came to pass after these events, that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: Lie with me!
## 8. But he refused and said to his master’s wife: Behold, my master does not concern himself with anything that is in the house, and everything he has, he has put into my hand!
## 9. There is no one greater in this house than I, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife.

Since Joseph was held in high regard and well-treated in his master’s house, the Tempter <note>The author uses "the Tempter" to refer to Satan or the personification of evil.</note> set upon him through the unchaste wife of Potiphar, seeking to plunge Joseph into temporal and eternal ruin: just as the enemy always seeks to entrap the godly, so as to destroy the counsel of God as much as is known to him and as much as lies within his power. Thus his virtue was tested here, but the fear of God protected him, so that he did not fall for another man’s wife: Proverbs 2:5, 11, 16, 17. Without this fear, a person cannot stand against the strong allurements of sin.

This attraction is so extremely dangerous and at the same time hidden and secret, that without special warning and enlightenment from God, it cannot well be recognized in its depth and deceitfulness. It is like this adulterous woman who wished to seduce Joseph.

So let whoever wishes to do so now learn to recognize the allurements of sin; but believe at the same time that they cannot become sin for him if he withdraws his will from them and does not consent. For sin itself is something entirely different from the allurements toward it. Joseph was also enticed, but he did not sin.

v. 8. *He refused*) See here a brave and strong youth! 1 John 2:14. Such a highly alluring and seductive opportunity, which offered itself spontaneously, would surely be bought by many a frivolous lover even at the risk of their own life's blood. But Joseph

Spoke) He brought to the woman’s mind how ungrateful and abominable it would be for him to act this way against his master; and inwardly he must have earnestly considered how much good his master had done for him: whereby he withdrew himself from this evil. On this ground, Gregory the Great <note>original: "Gregorius M." referring to Pope Gregory I, a central figure in medieval theology.</note> teaches quite elegantly <sup>a</sup>: when lust tempts someone during prosperous days, one should set this very "good" against the temptation, so that we are ashamed to do evil after enjoying such undeserved good. For because lust seeks to arise out of prosperous days, one must strike it down with these very weapons, so that our enemy may die.

One should therefore confidently reject the harlot-like world! For this Delilah <note>A biblical reference to the woman who robbed Samson of his strength; used here as a metaphor for temptation.</note> must not rob any of the Lord’s betrothed of their strength.

<margin>(a) Book 30, *Moral Expositions on Job*, Chapter 9, page 991, Volume II of his Works.</margin>

Whoever still has the slightest feeling must surely acknowledge the evil. But whoever does not take it to heart may well be in the—

<column-break/>

## How then could I do this great evil, and sin against God? 10. And

v. 9. *How could I — sin against God?*) Many are accustomed to pray in the morning, according to Luther’s so-called Morning Blessing <note>original: "Morgen-Segen," a specific daily prayer written by Martin Luther.</note>, that God would protect them from sin, shame, and all evil.

It is easily said; but very few know what they actually want. Many do not even allow themselves to be preserved from sin by God, even though God is quite willing to preserve them. For there is no fear of God before their eyes, and they thus only mock God in their morning prayer. For

Through the fear of God alone is one preserved from sin; and this is the basis of the fear of God—by which one is preserved from it—namely, when one learns as a child to so heartily dread offending the most holy face of his dear heavenly Father with any intent.

But above all things, we must learn to know our enemy intimately, from whom we are to be preserved. That enemy is sin, that

*Great evil*) An abomination that corrupts the whole world, and especially destroys the body and soul of man; indeed, nothing so bad can be said of it that it would not be a thousand times more true.

Sin, however, is here the abominable outbreak of evil itself, and the actual obedience that a person knowingly and willingly renders to the devil, while conversely refusing obedience to his Creator. This can be clearly recognized here in the adultery sought by the woman.

We must not think, however, that only outward, gross adultery is such a great sin, from which we must not let ourselves be seduced.

This adulterous woman did not succeed in her purpose, and yet it was fundamentally just as wicked: because God judges not according to the appearance or outward show and work, but according to the heart. And thus every deviation from God's will is more than certainly sin, and therefore

*Against God*) Thus wickedness primarily and actually provokes God Himself; in that it offends His—as the Lawgiver—supreme respect and glory, His truth, justice, holiness, and love. For

First, God has every right to claim us as His creatures: and His Son has further bought us doubly and most dearly. Thus, all deviation attacks the Divine Majesty itself in the most shameful way and robs God of what is His; namely, the powers of the body and the soul.

To all appearances, an unchaste person sins only against himself and his own body. But Joseph, through the Spirit, saw much deeper into the mystery of wickedness: how even the most secret sins offended the Creator's holiness and grieved His purest love.

Accordingly, Joseph did not do too much when he called sin "the great evil" and described it as a gruesome fruit. Some may think that one only makes sin so great to cause terror. But truly, no person has yet been born who could make this evil great and terrible enough!

A fool, of course, does not believe it: but whoever has tasted the bitterness of sin in repentance even a little will not need to be persuaded of it by words. Indeed, they will certainly believe the honest Joseph, that sin is a truly great evil. But whoever does not take it to heart may well stand in the judgment of hardening.

Is it not evil enough to be cut off from the life of God, and to fall prey to the fiery judgment in the conscience, which is the immediate damnation that follows as the wages of sin? Does this evil not gnaw at the sinner wherever he goes and stands, as a foretaste of future damnation? Do not crude people seek to soothe such a devouring fire of wrath through new sins, and yet in vain? And

Who can calculate all the other countless evils that flood the whole world because of sin? Oh, for God's sake, let no one joke with sin anymore, as unfortunately the more-than-heathen people are accustomed to make a joke out of harlotry, adultery, and similar shameful acts! It is certainly the devil’s game, which all godly hearts should oppose with word and deed and reveal its infinite evil.

Let no one, therefore, excuse, deny, or belittle their sins any further. For whoever still cloaks evil already betrays his secret desire to sin more. But whoever admits the evil as it is evil, he will also allow himself to be preserved from it.

If you love and fear God, and your eye, hand, foot, etc., seek to entice you to some pleasure; stand firm, and it must also be said by you: How could I do this godlessness and sin against God! Should I take the members of Christ and make them members of a harlot? From this, may God preserve me!

<margin>v. 10. Day by day)</margin> Oh, how evil desire, which has forced its way into the flesh through sin, drives such words daily against the poor soul! How the serpent in the flesh constantly seeks to mingle with the poor spirit and to defile it! It always pursues the will in every way, as a masculine power which sin would gladly master, thereby strengthening and fixing itself in wickedness! *James 1:13.* <note>James 1:13: "Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man."</note> But it can do nothing more than try to see if it might succeed, and thus it actually has no right to the spirit and its will; rather, like a harlot, it must offer its shame from afar.

<margin>(a) <note>original: "Lightfoot. observ. in Gen. c. 12. p. 156. T. I."</note> John Lightfoot, *Observations on Genesis*, chapter 12, page 156, Volume I.</margin>
The learned prove regarding Potiphar’s wife that she, as an Egyptian, was black. (a) It was no wonder then that she was so much more lustful for the beautiful Joseph. And truly, the serpent-seed of sin also hungers and longs just as much for the noble spirit of man! Because, as an ugly brood of the devil, it cannot exist alone. Therefore, sin seeks so vehemently to occupy the immortal eternal mind and spirit of God’s glorious creature and to mix with it, and thus to give birth to children of wickedness and hellish fruits.

<margin>The wanton woman fell upon Joseph when he was alone, v. 11. When none of the people of the house were in the house)</margin> And the Wicked One also lurks especially at such a time when the soul, as it were, walks alone in secret security, such that its love is not turned toward the Lord Jesus. Then the false spirit rushes in and seizes the stained coat of the flesh, by which he storms the spirit. Therefore, it is necessary to be on guard without ceasing, from within and without. We shall not lack the power and support for this. God wants to become everything in all to us in close preservation, so that we may not help ourselves with our natural weakness. The dear Immanuel <note>Hebrew for "God with us," a title for Christ.</note> has already acquired so much power for us that we can keep our garments, washed in his blood, clean, after we have once glimpsed or tasted his sweet love: and the power of his suffering will also sustain us in daily mortification <note>The spiritual practice of "dying" to worldly desires.</note> with humility, so that the enemy does not find us alone and surprise us.

If anyone desires to sit in worldly offices of honor with Joseph, he may do so with all the more great vigilance under constant prayer, and must earnestly resist the flattering Potiphar’s wife, so that she does not pull him to herself with her rope and bind his strength: otherwise, let him stay away and leave the offices of honor untrodden; or he will certainly perish in such offices and be captured by the will of the adulterous world.

But if anyone wishes to escape the evil of sin, let him prepare himself with Joseph so that he can confidently let go of his garment, property, goods, honor, and everything he has. One should surrender oneself to the Lord in good time, so that He may become everything to us instead of all things. For sin and the world try everything to the utmost on a person, so that they may get hold of him. If they can achieve nothing with words, they proceed to action; as the shameless disgrace did here to the chaste Joseph, who finally, when he would not give her request a hearing, reached for—

<margin>v. 12. Seized by his garment).</margin> Satan is not lazy in laying snares and nets from the outside as well, and attacking a struggling soul with power through the darting arrows of wickedness, whereby he often makes the indwelling evil in the flesh strongly active, and thus catches the wrestling spirit as if by its garment.
Hidden herein is a glorious message for struggling souls: that they should not be terrified by such attacks, let alone despair. For when sin only rumbles in the outer man, it is a blessed sign that it has no power over the will and the inner man. Just as one does not have power over another person when he merely catches him by his garment. Indeed—
For an eternal memorial and example, it is told of Joseph here:
**He left his garment in her hand, and fled)** These are truly the surest weapons against sin: namely, to flee and avoid, and to withdraw oneself from the opportunity. No one can practice this rightly unless he allows himself to be taught by Wisdom. For natural folly likes to remain lying in sin, as if in a soft bed, in which it thinks how well it is.
But one is now wiser, and does not let the sleeve be torn. One now has the clothes made better to fit the body, so that they fit tightly, so that one can be sure of oneself within them.

<margin>v. 16-18.</margin> Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian, whose "Antiquities of the Jews" often added dramatic dialogue to biblical accounts.</note> recounts her words thus:
> O dear husband, you are not worthy to live if you do not inflict well-deserved punishment upon your shameful servant, who has dared to attempt to defile your marriage bed. He has already forgotten how he came into our house and what great kindnesses you have shown him. Although he should have shown himself thankful in every way, he has instead violated your marriage bed and sought to commit such shame with me on the **holy feast day** and in your absence. From this, it is easy to see that he is not chaste by nature, but has hitherto only assumed a feigned honorability because he had to fear you as his master. That he has become so bold is entirely your fault, for you have given him too long a rein.

<margin>v. 19.</margin> **According to these words has your servant done to me)** Here, things do not stop with Joseph; even those to whom he performed the greatest service must believe the slander. He must spend several years in prison; there he is forsaken by all and regarded as a evildoer. But you, O Joseph, you are imprisoned and innocent! You have lost nothing of your own righteousness! You are much happier, you innocent prisoner, than <margin>(a) 2 Kings 11.</margin> (a) David, the guilty king! <note>The author cites 2 Kings 11, which in older German Bibles refers to the book we now call 2 Samuel 11, containing the account of David’s sin with Bathsheba.</note> Ah!

What a beautiful comparison one could make between these two persons to show God’s way with **yielded souls**! <note>The original German "gelassenen Seelen" refers to "Gelassenheit," a state of mystical detachment and surrender to God's will.</note> In His own time, He will give what is pleasing to Him. Some remain innocent and yet must experience the pains of an evildoer; whereas others, along with the punishment, possess the sin itself. The more innocent Joseph is, the greater a bondservant he becomes. David, however, remains in power, even though he is punished more severely and must carry the sorrow alongside his guilt.

Meanwhile, GOD still preserved Joseph, so that his master did not fall into a greater rage upon the false accusation of the woman and kill him outright as a servant and slave. Nevertheless, he had to endure a heavy imprisonment for a time: They forced his feet into **stocks**; his body had to lie in irons. <margin>Ps. 105:18.</margin> Through such anguish, his heart had to be prepared for true humility in his future high station.

We should not fear the harsh treatment of which we read here regarding Joseph. For in this godless world, we can expect nothing else in the following of Christ. This harlot <note>Likely an allegorical reference to the world or the "false church" that persecutes the righteous.</note> can tolerate no purity beside her, by which she is shamed and convicted.

Thus the LORD knows how to protect the simple and the innocent. As long as our Lord does not forsake a soul, and it is assured of His help and presence, nothing is so bitter that it does not become sweet. ## The XL. Chapter.

->The Incident of the Two Court Officials.<-

And it came to pass after these things, that the **cupbearer** of the King of Egypt and the **baker** offended their lord, the King of Egypt.

---

v. 1-3. Here one may observe the **fickleness of courtly favor**, which often results from a just judgment upon certain court servants who greatly abuse their masters' favor and are then accustomed to oppressing others; whereby others must then often suffer innocently, for nothing is more changeable than human favor. Therefore it is well said: *Do not put your trust in princes, in a son of man, in whom there is no help.* <note>Psalm 146:3.</note>

v. 5. It was a wonderful act of **Divine Providence** that two dreams had caused Joseph's misery at the hands of his brothers; and two dreams, which he interpreted here in prison, gave occasion for his deliverance; and two dreams, which he interpreted for Pharaoh two whole years later, raised him to his high standing and honor. Thus, just as Joseph was brought low through dreams, he was also raised up again through dreams.

v. 6-7. Divine dreams leave a deep impression on the soul, because God typically chooses to reveal Himself to mankind in this way during special occurrences, so that they may also be brought to the recognition of His Providence. Through this Providence alone, all good and evil flows to us according to His justice; thus, one should expect the former in recognition of one's unworthiness, and seek to turn away the latter with repentant sighs whenever one has troubling visions in dreams.

---

v. 8. *We have dreamed a dream*) That these dreams could not have been natural, but were sent and presented by God, is clear for two reasons: because the forthcoming fate of both was announced at the same time, and because the dreams left an effect of anxiety upon the soul, or a deep impression. Likewise, they indicated that which was still hidden in the King's mind—and thus were a ray of God's infinite discernment—and could be interpreted by no one except Joseph through divine enlightenment, which interpretation was later proven by the accurate result.

The interpretation of dreams certainly cannot happen through **human understanding**, which gives nothing other than frivolous and groundless conjectures; rather, such interpretation comes solely from divine revelation, which is also the source of such visions during sleep. And there, God is occasionally pleased to grant a prompt explanation and provide the interpretation; or, the outcome later makes it clear, so that one should admire His Providence therein to the praise of God.

God often shares an extraordinary light with sinners for the sake of those who are surrendered to the guidance of Divine Providence, so that they might be moved to share it with others. This is so they may learn the ways God keeps with such souls, and that these poor straying ones might be delivered from the imprisonment of sin. Joseph's answer certainly indicates a faithful, surrendered man who, ascribing nothing to himself, casts everything back upon God. And this is exactly what gives a **holy courage** and causes one to undertake all things: by being able to rely on the divine strength from which one takes one's origin, just as Joseph had taken his from Jacob. But this is often mistaken for pride and audacity by souls who have not yet come very far.

v. 10. *Three branches*) which, like the parable in Mark 4:28, represent the **three degrees of growth** in spiritual age (1 John 2:12-13). A sprouting branch represents the little children in Christ; a flowering one represents the youths in the best bloom of their spiritual age. The third, with the ripe berries, signifies the elderly, who are of a mature and perfect age in Christ.

Was not Christ also in the company of two prisoners? And did He not also promise and vow good things to one, but let the other die in his sins? Did He not also preach to the spirits in prison, who had not believed in the time of Noah, and announce grace to many of them? 1 Peter 3:19.

v. 13, 19, 20. Through the "lifting up of the heads," the muster and orderly counting of servants is made known, as such a figure of speech is used for the census of a people, where one takes them head by head and perhaps writes them down or reads them from a roll: (see Exodus 30:12, Numbers 1:2, 26:2). This may have been customary at such feasts, where the <term>great ones</term> <note>Meaning royalty or high officials.</note> also used to grant many positions of honor, which is called an elevation of status. This meaning can also apply here: that one’s head was raised while the other was lowered; which is also the aim of the <term>reduction of status</term> <note>original: "Capitis diminutio," a Roman legal term referring to the loss of civil rights or liberty.</note> used among the ancients. The greatest reduction was when one lost his freedom, property, and goods because he had forfeited something great.

In a spiritual sense, the different fates of believers and hypocrites may also be noted. The former have Christ, the true vine, before them, upon which they—as spiritual branches—press out the grapes of repentance and the powerful grace of the Spirit in their hearts, offering it from this cup of the heart to their King in gratitude; whereby they come out of the prison of sin and back to the table of grace. The latter, however, while haughtily carrying only the spiritual food of the Word upon the "head" of their reason, have it taken away by the hellish birds of prey before it enters the heart to be presented to the Lord (Matthew 13:4), and they themselves must finally fall to these birds.

The same Word of God is often a word of life and death at once. It gives life to one by tearing him out of the bondage of sin; but to the other, it causes death—though innocently—because he misuses it. It was not the words of Joseph that caused the baker’s death, because the cause of it lay within the one who had committed the misdeed. They only warn him so that his death might not be far off. But he undertakes nothing by which he might perhaps escape it. We can avoid sin through our diligence when we are supported by the grace of God and repentance, but life comes from God alone. Therefore, Joseph also exhorts the cupbearer that he should, when he is back in favor, remember him and the words of God which he had announced to him, and which personal interest often causes one to forget.

It is a seed (a); which, however, lies buried in the earth and will bring forth its fruit in its time.

v. 20. On the day that -- he made a feast) One finds in God's Word two evil kings who celebrated their birthdays with such joyful festivals: namely, Pharaoh here, and Herod there in Matthew 14:6. These expressions of joy, however, were disturbed in both places by tragedies and sad events; in the latter case, it cost John his head. So one also finds two godly men who cursed their birthdays: namely Job (Chapter 3:1) and Jeremiah (Chapter 20:14). Although the day of death is indeed better than the day of birth (Ecclesiastes 7:1) because one is then released from misery, this was nevertheless a trial of faith. And indeed, one certainly has reason to remember the day of his birth with heartfelt thanksgiving for all God's benefits, and to sigh that one day the day of complete rebirth might be celebrated with joy in the spirit. But when such birthdays of our sinful birth are celebrated with all kinds of vanity and immoderation, as is an old evil habit, then it is sinful. Therefore, some of the early Church Fathers held the celebration of such days to be impermissible. Indeed, because of the many abuses in which Christians followed the pagans, as <term>Tertullian</term> <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note> testifies, the Council of <term>Nicaea</term> <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church in 325 AD.</note> abolished them. Just as then, at times, special judgments of God have been accustomed to disturb such joyful feasts.

->Joseph’s Exaltation.<-

v. 1. After two years) The two years that Joseph remained in prison, being exalted in the third year (which he also partly spent there), can represent the two nights Christ spent in the grave, being exalted on the third day through the Resurrection. For whatever parallels we find in the occurrences of Joseph and Christ, faith can note them as a mystery-filled prototype of Christ.
The ancients also investigate the reason why Joseph had to spend so long, even into the third year, in prison. And it may well be asked of one of them (a) <note>original: "Augustin. Serm. 82. de tempore."</note>, having truly experienced that GOD gave him favor in the eyes of his master and the jailer. But after he grew weary of the long duration of his imprisonment, he devised ways to free himself <note>Refers to Joseph asking the cupbearer to mention him to Pharaoh.</note>. But the LORD opposed him in this and caused him to remain there for two more years.
It is vexing to a friend when his friend distrusts him and holds his loyalty in suspicion. The LORD cannot tolerate such a thing. Even the slightest mistrust in GOD is usually severely punished. Now, seeking the favor of a man is a kind of mistrust in GOD, when the friends of GOD grow weary of submitting to Him and wish to create their own relief.

Did not think—forgot him) By this, the cupbearer committed a shameful act of ingratitude; for it is customary to thank and give gifts even to those who merely bring good news. But it often happens that nothing is sooner forgotten than benefits received, and nothing stays longer in the memory than wrongs endured.
But GOD here allows His faithfulness to shine, supporting the word He placed in the mouth of His servant. Even if it is delayed, it always remains true. > GOD is accustomed to reveal remarkable events in kingdoms and in His Church to the great, and also to others among His friends, through dreams and visions: as also happened to Nebuchadnezzar, Dan. 2, where GOD revealed the succession of the four great world empires, and how finally the glorious kingdom of His Son would bring an end to all the kingdoms of the world, but would itself never be destroyed. Just as the Reformation of the Church was revealed to princes and others through various dreams and visions. From this, one should learn how all events in the world and the Church stand under the wise providence of GOD and are ordered and governed by Him for His holy purpose. Nothing was more fitting to indicate such plenty and famine than such cattle and grain. <header>The First Book of Moses. Ch. XLI.</header>

**9. Then the chief cupbearer spoke to Pharaoh, saying: I do remember my sins this day.**

I do remember my sins this day) To our **self-loving nature**, it is a very bitter medicine when it must remember its sins and corruption, and through this, allow itself to be humbled.

One gladly wishes to appear good and holy enough before GOD and men, and even enjoys being worshiped as such by the ignorant, becoming an enemy to those who will not flatter or agree.

However, just as this is a sorrowful sign of a false conversion, a truly repentant heart is recognized by the opposite: when a person does not withdraw from the memory of their sins, but rather accepts it with gratitude when given the occasion.

Without doubt, such a soul—one that willingly and with humility remembers its sins—stands in new obedience and trust toward GOD.

That the chief cupbearer of Pharaoh, here in the midst of his prosperity, though his sin had long since been forgiven by his lord, thought of it again; he did this so that he might remind himself of the royal favor and be stirred to double his loyalty thereby.

And so it may also do no harm to a soul, but rather serve for greater humiliation and the awakening of faith, if, even after reconciliation, it thinks of its old sins when the opportunity arises.

Not as if someone, in whose heart the **Holy Spirit** of the High Priest **JESUS** has sealed their reconciliation, should nevertheless doubt the same and spend their time in doubt when they should instead love and praise GOD. Rather, insofar as the memory of one's previous transgressions may drive one partly to constant humiliation under GOD, and partly to greater confidence, mutual love, and a desire to praise—to that extent it is quite healthy to say with this court official: *Today I remember my sin.*

One ought to rightfully use all opportunities for this exercise which are placed before us by divine governance from within or without: just as this cupbearer wisely used the King’s dream for this purpose, and thereby established himself much more firmly in the King’s favor.

Thus, all circumstances sometimes give us occasion for this, if one remembers this or that person, time, place, and the like, where this or that occurred. And

It is impossible to describe how powerfully such internal memories can humble and shame a person before GOD, and how necessary such an exercise is for a proud and daring nature.

Also, the Spirit of discipline works joyfully in converted people to this end: because He not only likes to begin repentance in us but also to continue it. But the continuation happens most powerfully through a repentant memory of one's former misery, out of which GOD has snatched us through conversion.

This is so entirely in accordance with the Gospel that Paul not only faithfully reminded converted Christians of their former misery and constantly held before them what kind of people they had been: <margin>1 Cor. 6:11, Eph. 4:22</margin>. But he also considered it indispensable for himself, so much so that he did not hide it from his students, nor did he consider it shameful to say what kind of man he had formerly been. <margin>1 Tim. 1:13, Tit. 3:3</margin>.

If such a truly converted and sanctified man, despite his high state of grace, nevertheless remembered his former sins and drew no harm but great blessing from it; how then could others consider such a holy exercise superfluous or even harmful?

How much more necessary would this very thing be for all those who have either never, or at best hardly, converted from their sins! Indeed, no one can repent and come to GOD without such a crushed memory of their sins.

Whoever wants to come to GOD must believe. Whoever is to believe must have a longing for grace and improvement.

If we do not want to think of our sins ourselves in good time, while it is still called "today"; then GOD must necessarily place them in the light before His countenance tomorrow. But it is terrible to fall into His hands and forced conviction; and conversely easier and more tolerable to bow voluntarily under His holy and gracious convictions, and thus judge oneself, so that one is not judged.

<column-break/>

**10. Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and put me in custody in the house of the captain of the guard, both me and the chief baker.**

**11. And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he; we dreamed each according to the interpretation of his dream.**

**12. And there was with us there a Hebrew youth, a servant of the captain of the guard; and we told him, and he interpreted our dreams to us; to each he interpreted according to his dream.**

**13. And it happened, just as he interpreted to us, so it turned out. I was restored to my position, and the other was hanged.**

**14. Then Pharaoh sent and called for Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon; and he shaved himself and changed his clothes, and came in to Pharaoh.**

**15. And**

---

The awakening and the thinking upon GOD are wonderful means to rescue the soul from prison, even from the captivity and the shadow of death. After the soul had some hope of coming out of its miserable and forsaken state, it must nevertheless spend several years in a total abandonment and complete oblivion. No more hope remains for it, and it thinks of nothing else but to remain thus <margin>(a) Ps. 38:6</margin> a) / like the eternally dead, who are no longer remembered. It only seeks with composure to bear this state and to be content with the same, as it sees itself in the will of GOD: It never thinks to come out from there.

When this soul is thus sunk into the forgetfulness of death, it is astonished to see the prison open, that someone approaches it, that it is robbed of this state of death, that the signs of its servitude are taken away one by one, and that it is covered with the robe of life and freedom. For a time, such a soul is as if half-asleep: It knows not whether it sleeps or wakes, whether it be a dream or something substantial, until all at once it sees itself drawn out of this dark and gloomy place and placed into the day of true light. Then it knows the truth of its transformation; and all the sooner, in that it is led to appear before the King. From this moment on, it is thus placed into the resurrected life: yet it is not yet confirmed in the same; which likely has greater advantages. GOD makes use of this word itself, which was hidden in the earth of forgetfulness, to draw this soul out of death and eternal oblivion: Just as the Son of GOD through His word drew Lazarus out of the grave.

...have hunger. Whoever is to have this, their misery and corruption must truly be known to them and be a cause of sorrow. But to whom can their sins become known, who does not even wish to rightly remember their sins?

### Chapter XLI. The First Book of Moses.
<meta>catchword: v. 25. GOD</meta>

15. Then Pharaoh said to Joseph: I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. But I have heard it said of you that when you hear a dream, you can interpret it.
16. And Joseph answered Pharaoh and said: It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer. <margin>Chapter 40, verse 8.</margin>
17. Then Pharaoh spoke to Joseph: In my dream, behold, I stood on the bank of the river.
18. And behold, out of the river there came up seven cows, fat in flesh and beautiful in form, and they grazed in the reed grass.

---

The inspiration of this dream, the desire stirred within him for its interpretation, and the fact that no one but Joseph could provide it, all occurred to the end that the knowledge of Christ, the Savior of the world, might be spread throughout all the land of Egypt, a flourishing kingdom. For through this, Joseph received the opportunity to make the Messiah known in Egypt and to plant the true religion there; as Psalm 105:22 testifies, and as can be perceived from verse 38 of this chapter, showing that the King himself was not without knowledge of the mystery of the Holy Trinity. <note>The author interprets this Old Testament event through a "Christological" lens, suggesting that Joseph's promotion was a divine strategy to introduce Christian-like concepts, such as the Trinity, to the Egyptian court long before the New Testament era.</note>

<margin>verse 15. (No one)</margin> **THERE** was not a single person in all the land of Egypt who could interpret Pharaoh’s dream: because that which is (a) purposed in the heart of God can be recognized by no one except the Spirit of God.

<margin>verse 16.</margin> Joseph’s answer shows that nothing but the emptying of oneself, and the loss of all desire to be something, brings such a soul to the point of attributing nothing to itself. On the contrary, because the soul is assured that it is only a weak instrument and that God can do everything without it, it reveals itself with such boldness as is fitting for such a truth. God can work all that He does with the soul even without it. However, when He makes use of it, all honor must still be given to Him. Therefore, the soul leads the creature in advance to give God alone the honor for it, and to regard no single good thing as having been worked without Him.

->God will — give a favorable answer<- Joseph here points the King to divine providence, which always intends well for mankind: and even when judgments are presented, it happens as a warning, so that through repentance, man may either turn them away or make them bearable.

<margin>verse 17. etc.</margin> Here the dream lay quite clearly in Pharaoh’s mind, whereas for Nebuchadnezzar it had entirely left his mind. <note>original: "Daniel 2:5"</note> Here, everything was to take place in the King’s own time; and he therefore gained all the more confidence that Joseph would arrange everything for the best and with blessing. In the other case, however, it concerned future things, and God showed how the changing of empires would happen entirely according to His arrangement and not according to human calculation. Just as no "Fifth Monarchy" <note>The "Fifth Monarchy" refers to a 17th-century theological belief in a final earthly kingdom of God that would succeed the four great empires of antiquity.</note> will be able to arise, even if one or another person might have strived for it from time to time.

->On the bank of the river<- Of the Nile River. This bank of the river represents either the waters of Baptism or of Repentance, out of which a soul emerges very beautiful and in a "fat" <note>meaning: healthy and spiritually robust</note> condition.

<margin>verse 18.</margin> The seven cows, or the seven years which they prefigure, are the ordinary time in which souls remain in the attainment of virtues. They seem then to be quite beautiful, and one perceives no lack in them: because God gives them so many graces that they walk there as if on a good pasture, where they become strong, fat, beautiful, and very pleasant.

<margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 2:11.</margin>

<column-break/>

19. And behold, seven other cows came up after them, they were meager and of very ugly form and thin of flesh: I have not seen the like of such ugliness in all the land of Egypt.
20. And the thin and ugly cows ate up the first seven fat cows.
21. And when they had entered their bellies, one could not notice that they had entered their bellies, and their appearance was ugly just as in the beginning: and I awoke.
22. And I saw in my dream, and behold, seven ears of corn grew on one stalk, full and beautiful.
23. And behold, seven ears, withered, thin, and scorched by the east wind, grew up after these.
24. And the thin ears swallowed the seven beautiful ears: and I have told it to the soothsayers; but no one can explain it to me.
25. Then

---

<margin>verse 19. 20.</margin> But after these lovely, sweet years—watered so much by those calm and still waters—have passed, the soul becomes very dismayed when, thinking of nothing less, it sees those same years swallowed up by the following years: and that in such a hunger and drought that, if it had not made a provision for itself, it would have to die of hunger.

It is to be noted that it does not say in the Scripture that the lean cows killed the fat ones; rather, they swallowed them. This indicates that in this very dry time, all the graces and virtues of the other years are enclosed within, even if one can see nothing of them from the outside: just as the fat cows were swallowed by the lean ones, and yet one could not recognize it in them.

<margin>verse 21.</margin> These lean cows still look just as hideous after they had swallowed the fat ones as they did before. This is the great mystery which is hidden from those who are not yet divinely enlightened, but revealed to the lowly. From the outside, one notices nothing but ugliness and deformity, and (a) the beauty of the King’s daughter is hidden within her during these seven years. One sees nothing but pure defects on all sides: everything appears to one as if it were void of all grace, just as the cows had no flesh on them. Yet it is certain that never were more graces found there than at that time. But they remain hidden in the hideous belly of drought until the day of appearance.

However, it is also true that where the blessing of God is withdrawn, all abundance is wasted: and no matter how much one takes in, it is never sufficient, and there is always a lack. See Isaiah 9:2 and Haggai 1:6.

<margin>(a) Psalm 45:14.</margin>

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLI.

25. Then Joseph said to Pharaoh: / Pharaoh’s dream is one and the same. That which **God** will do / he has revealed to Pharaoh.
26. The seven beautiful cows are seven years / and the seven beautiful ears of grain are seven years: it is one and the same dream.
27. And the seven thin and ugly cows / that came up after them / those are seven years: and the seven empty ears of grain, scorched by the east wind, those shall be seven years of hunger.
28. This is the matter / of which I have spoken to Pharaoh: What **God** will do / he has shown to Pharaoh.
29. Behold, seven years will come / when there shall be a great abundance in all the land of Egypt.
30. And after them, seven years of hunger shall arise / so that all such abundance in the land of Egypt shall be forgotten / and the hunger shall consume the land.
31. And the abundance will not be noticed in the land / because of that hunger that follows. For it will be very severe.

<column-break/>

32. But that the dream was repeated to Pharaoh a second time / is because the matter is firmly decreed by **God** / and **God** will do it in haste.
33. And now let Pharaoh look for a discerning and wise man / whom he may set over the land of Egypt.
34. Let Pharaoh do this / that he appoint officers over the land / and take a fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven years of abundance:
35. That they may gather all the food of these good years / that are coming / that they may heap up grain under Pharaoh’s hand for food in the cities / and keep it:
36. And that same food shall be as a reserve for the land for the seven years of hunger / which shall be in the land of Egypt; so that the land be not destroyed by the hunger.
37. And

---

<margin>verse 25.</margin> **God has — revealed**) Souls filled with grace judge very quickly what comes from **God** / based on the experience they have of it: just as Joseph immediately assures Pharaoh / that his dream is divine.
<margin>verse 26-31.</margin> Just as in physical matters, expensive times <note>original: "theure Zeiten," meaning periods of inflation or famine</note> usually follow blessed years; because people commonly misuse physical blessings: so it also happens in spiritual matters / where we, especially in our times, should take to heart the great measure of knowledge / since **God** reveals many mysteries through the "open door" given to the congregation of Philadelphia. <note>Philadelphia is one of the seven churches in the Book of Revelation (3:7-13), often interpreted by Pietist writers as the true, spiritual church of the last days.</note> Revelation 3:8. But because most do not wish to accept the love of the truth / that they might be saved; therefore **God** will also send them strong delusions / so that they believe lies: so that all those who do not believe the truth / but have pleasure in unrighteousness, might be judged. 2 Thessalonians 2:10, 11, 12. And that is exactly the hunger / which the **Lord** will send into the land: not a hunger for bread / or a thirst for water; but for hearing the word of the **Lord**: Amos 8:11. Namely, the living word that promotes and strengthens the soul for the spiritual life.

<column-break/>

<insert>
verse 33-36. The enlightened leader / who sees beforehand that which will happen / moves the soul / to acquire as much provision as is possible for it. For the more it makes use of the first graces given to it / the better it will be for it. Its loss will indeed be that much greater. But even if it loses everything / as if it were its own; it still finds everything again in **God** / as if gathered in his storehouse. Therefore, it is necessary to select a skillful and experienced leader / to whom one may entrust the guidance of all things. <note>This "leader" refers to a spiritual director or "confessor" who guides the soul through its internal development.</note>
</insert>

---

Abundance is always accustomed to drive away all thoughts of lack and infertility. But it is also common to those who stand in the "trial" <note>original: "Prüfung," a period of spiritual testing or "darkness"</note> that they soon forget all the good they had received. Nothing remains for them; because **God** so purely erases every trace from the outside / that it appears to them only as if it had been pure deception / and as if they had never been in **God**. And yet they were never more in **God** than then. The **confessors** themselves <note>original: "Beichtväter," spiritual advisors who hear confession</note> doubt them. No one can discover the mystery / except an experience and light similar to Joseph's: because this hunger must consume the entire earth / so that nothing remains / so that the great lack swallows up the great abundance. For if something were to remain / then it would be no true loss / and this mystery would not be fulfilled. Therefore, O soul, you have nothing else to wait for / but that you must lose everything / what you possess / without exception / and measure your loss according to the greatness of that which you possessed. The more beautiful and excellent you have been / and the more you have been admired by the nations; the more you must become ugly / hideous / loathed and despised. Oh, what a guidance of my **God** is that! The soul must / in order to come into You / its origin / lose all your gifts. You give them to the soul / to tear it out of sin and bring it back into its heart: but you also take them away from it / so that it can go out from that same heart / and may fall in love with You. Your gifts drive out sin / and fill the soul with your graces: but you yourself chase your gifts out again / to fill the soul with Your very self once more! O all-too-unknown truth!

### Chapter XLI. The First Book of Moses. 241
<header>Ch. XLI. The First Book of Moses. 241</header>

37. And the word seemed good in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of all his servants.

38. And Pharaoh said to his servants: "Could we find another such as this, a man in whom the Spirit of God dwells?"

39. And Pharaoh said to Joseph: "Since God has made all this known to you, there is none so discerning and wise as you.

40. You shall be over my house, and according to your command shall all my people kiss the hand <note>an expression of obedience and homage</note>: only in the throne will I be greater than you."

41. And Pharaoh further said to Joseph: "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt!"

<margin>(a) Exod. 28:8.</margin>
42. And Pharaoh took his ring from his hand and placed it on Joseph’s hand, and clothed him in garments of white silk, and placed a golden chain around his neck:

43. And he had him ride in the second chariot which he possessed; and they cried out before him: <term>Kneel down!</term> <note>original: "Abrech"</note> and so he was set over all the land of Egypt.

---

v. 37-39. In the choice of a leader, one must always prefer the one who possesses the most of the Spirit of God. Pharaoh provides us with a beautiful example here; he does not mock, as others often do to those who offer advice for their own good without personal gain.

He accepts the very person who gave him this advice in this important matter as a leader, and he commanded that Joseph be obeyed in all things.

Thus was Pharaoh inwardly convinced that this must be a revelation from the true God, who so benevolently warned him and his land from destruction: just as such divine wisdom was also noted in Daniel. Dan. 5:11. For even natural men can, to some extent, notice the difference between divine and earthly wisdom, if only they would diligently observe what effect both have upon their souls.

v. 38. the Spirit of God) From this it appears that Pharaoh was instructed in the mystery of the Holy Trinity. For in the words "the Spirit of Elohim," all three are expressed: because Elohim, being in the plural, indicates the Father and the Son, from whom he believed the Holy Spirit proceeded. Augustine says that the third testimony of the Holy Spirit is found here in the First Book of Moses. The first is in Ch. 1:2, the second in Ch. 6:4.

v. 40. kiss the hand) Through such kissing of hands, the testimony of a submissive reverence was made known. Therefore, the word "to adore" <note>original Latin: "adorare"</note> comes from the custom where worshippers "brought the right hand to the mouth" <note>original Latin: "dextram ad os retulerunt"</note> and thus kissed it. See 1 Sam. 10:1, 1 Kings 9:18, Hos. 13:12, Ps. 2:12.

v. 41. 42. The power which the King gives him over all of Egypt indicates the authority that leaders must possess. Now Joseph is placed and confirmed in the "state of resurrection." Not only is his freedom restored, but he receives it back with far greater advantages than he had possessed with his father before his captivity. God gives to a risen and renewed soul all the graces it possessed before its misfortune, not only back again, but He adds infinitely more to them—things the soul would never have dared to ask for.

v. 43. Who would have told Joseph two years ago, when he thought of nothing but ending his life in a dark dungeon, that he should become the commander in Egypt? Who would have told this abandoned soul, forsaken, covered with darkness, and sitting in the shadow of death, that so much evil should produce such a great good? The soul would not have been able to believe it. But it has all indeed happened.

Kneel down!) The word <term>Abrech</term> <note>Hebrew: אברך</note>, regarding which Hugo Grotius and Heidegger (a) are so upright and modest as to confess they do not understand it, can signify the command to bow the knee as a sign of the deepest reverence, being the imperative in the Chaldean form *Aphel*: and the reason is immediately added; that he is set over all Egypt. See Ps. 105:19-22, Acts 7:10.

This great exaltation properly belongs to Christ, in whose name every knee shall bow, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth. Phil. 2:10-11, Ps. 22:31.

<margin>(a) Hist. Patriarch. Vol. II. p. 629.</margin>

<column-break/>

44. And Pharaoh said to Joseph: "I am Pharaoh, yet without you no one shall lift up his hand or his foot in all the land of Egypt."

<margin>(a) Prov. 8:12.</margin>
45. And Pharaoh called Joseph "one who reveals the hidden" <note>Zaphenath-Paneah</note>; and he gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, the commander at On, as a wife. Thus Joseph went out into the land of Egypt.

46. And

---

v. 44. Pharaoh) Münsterus in his *Cosmography* (a) translated the word "Pharaoh" as "Savior."

v. 45. Called) This then is the risen soul. Here she stands confirmed in her resurrection and showered with graces. Only then does she attain the purity of her origin: yes, then she likewise receives a new name, as did the holy fathers. You shall no longer be called Joseph, but the Savior of Egypt. The soul is always given a new name after its resurrection and when it has reached its origin; namely, a complete renewal takes place: and then the marriage of the Lamb is held.

The one who reveals the hidden) An interpreter of hidden things; in the Egyptian language, "Guardian" or "Savior of the world," as Jerome also rendered it. The Jewish historian Josephus (b) contracted it into one word (*Poutomphanechus*). Christ is also the true "Secret Counselor" <note>Wonderful Counselor</note> who has revealed to us the hidden counsel of the Father regarding our redemption through His blood, and who also opens the seven seals of the hidden apocalyptic book. Therefore He is also called the "Wonderful Counselor," Isa. 9:5, in whom lie hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge: Col. 2:3. And in Him, the Spirit of God was without measure. John 3:34.

The Commander) For this is what the word signifies, which is otherwise rendered "priest"; here it means as much as a commander or governor: such as the sons of David were, whom he had set over the provinces, and thus they were the closest to the King, having free access to him; which is the meaning of the word <term>Kohen</term> <note>Hebrew: כהן</note>. See 2 Sam. 8:18, 20:26, 1 Chron. 18:17, Exod. 1:11.

On) Now called Damiata; previously called Heliopolis, or "City of the Sun." Isa. 19:18, Exod. 1:11.

46. And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before the face of Pharaoh, the king in Egypt; and Joseph went out from Pharaoh's presence and traveled through the entire land of Egypt.
47. And in the seven years of abundance, the land bore fruit by the handfuls.

49. Thus Joseph heaped up grain like the sand of the sea, exceedingly much, until he stopped counting; for it was beyond numbering.

54. And the seven years of hunger began to come, just as Joseph had said: and there was a hunger in all lands, but in the entire land of Egypt there was bread.
55. Now when the entire land of Egypt also suffered hunger, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread. But Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians: "Go to Joseph; whatever he tells you, do that." <margin>John 2:5.</margin> <note>This mirrors Mary's words at the wedding at Cana, pointing the people toward the one who provides.</note>
56. When the hunger was now in the entire land, Joseph opened everything in which there was anything and sold to the Egyptians. For the hunger became overwhelming in the land of Egypt.
57. And all lands came into Egypt to buy from Joseph. For the hunger became overwhelming in all lands.

---

<insert>
One can understand all the lands lying around Egypt here, which were plagued by this hunger: since the king then directed everyone to Joseph; who also behaved mildly and refreshed everyone in their need. In this, we are to look upon Christ, to whom the Father directs everyone and says: "You shall hear Him!" whom the Father has also sealed for this purpose, that He should be the Bread of God, which comes from heaven and gives life to the world. Therefore, all are also kindly invited by Christ: "I am the bread of life! Whoever comes to me shall not hunger; and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." John 6:27, 33, 35. He is a good householder, says Bernard <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>original: "Bernardus," referring to St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note>, who provides for his household, that he might nourish them in the time of scarcity; in that he feeds them with the bread of life and of understanding. And in truth, all lands shall still gather to Him to still their hunger, which will come upon them at the time of the open door, which Christ will open everywhere through the Spirit of the Lord.
<margin>(a) Sermon 71 on the Song of Songs, page 781.</margin>
</insert>

---

v. 46. **Thirty years old**) Just as Joseph did here, Christ also entered His ministry in His thirtieth year: Luke 3:23. Since He also strove for the food, to provide it for men, which should remain into eternal life. John 6:27. Thus, in all these pieces, he was a glorious prefiguration of Christ.
**Traveled through the entire land of Egypt**) Thus the Apostolic life begins, namely when one does not appoint oneself, but only enters such a path according to the command of God. It is very beautifully depicted here, that Joseph, after his renewal, travels through all the lands of Egypt. Before one wishes to work, one must first be renewed. Jesus Christ, our holy pattern, had to spend 30 years in His hidden life before He appeared publicly. He also did not do so any sooner than until He had endured the forty-day temptation in the wilderness.
This agreement of the old images with their holy truth will greatly delight those who look into them.
v. 48. 49. Blessed is he who has a good Joseph in the court of his heart, who knows how to provide a storehouse when the hunger for the divine Word is present!
v. 50. **Two sons**) These two sons are an image of the community of Christ in His glorious kingdom, which shall then be born out of the Spirit of Christ, and which, as His exalted Church, will forget all previous misery that she suffered in the six great days and times of labor and persecution: and she will also be very fruitful, for only then will the promise given to Abraham reach its fulfillment, that God would bless and multiply his seed like the stars in the sky and like the sand on the shore of the sea. Gen 22:17. See also Psalm 8:2, 10; 72:8, 19; Isaiah 54.
After renewal, one begins to beget children for Jesus Christ.
v. 51. Joseph here forgets all the work and trouble he endured, just as he, when he was in poverty, had also forgotten all the graces he had received.
v. 52. Because Joseph was well-instructed in the inner ways, he recognizes that all his goods have come to him because of his poverty: in that, as long as the seed remains in the earth, it <gloss>(a)</gloss> decays, sprouts, and brings much fruit.
<margin>(a) John 12:24, 25.</margin>

# Chapter XLII. The First Book of Moses. #

## Chapter XLII. ##

->The Testing of Joseph's Brothers.<-

When Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, Jacob said to his sons: "Why do you look at one another?"
2. Furthermore, he said: "Behold, I have heard that there is grain in Egypt; go down there and buy for us from there, so that we may live and not die."
3. Thus ten of Joseph’s brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
4. But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with his brothers, for he said: "Lest a mishap befall him."
5. Thus the children of Israel came to buy among those who also came, for the hunger was in the land of Canaan.
6. Now Joseph was the regent over the land; it was he who sold to all the people of the land. When Joseph’s brothers came, they bowed down before him with their faces to the earth.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLI. #

46. And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before the face of Pharaoh, the king in Egypt; and Joseph went out from Pharaoh’s presence and traveled through the entire land of Egypt.
47. And during the seven years of abundance, the land brought forth grain by the handful.
48. And he gathered all the food of the seven years that were in the land of Egypt and stored the food in the cities: the food from the fields surrounding each city, he placed within it.
49. Thus Joseph heaped up grain like the sand of the sea, in such vast quantities that he stopped counting; for it was beyond numbering.
50. And to Joseph were born two sons before the year of hunger came, whom Asenath bore to him, the daughter of Potipherah, the commander <note>The German "Befehlshaber" is used here, though traditionally Potipherah is identified as a priest of On.</note> at On.
<margin>(a) Job 11:16.</margin>
51. And Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh: "For God has made me forget (a) all my hardship and all my father's house." <note>The name Manasseh sounds like the Hebrew word for "causing to forget."</note>
52. And the second he named Ephraim: "For God has made me fruitful in the land of my misery." <note>The name Ephraim is related to the Hebrew word for "fruitful."</note>

<column-break/>

53. And the seven years of abundance that had been in the land of Egypt came to an end.
54. And the seven years of hunger began to come, just as Joseph had said: and a famine arose in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
<margin>John 2:5.</margin>
55. When all the land of Egypt also began to suffer hunger, the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. But Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians: "Go to Joseph; whatever he tells you, do that." <note>This phrase mirrors the words of Mary at the wedding in Cana (John 2:5), pointing toward the spiritual authority of Christ.</note>
56. Since the hunger was now throughout the entire land, Joseph opened everything in which there was grain and sold it to the Egyptians. For the hunger grew severe in the land of Egypt.
57. And all lands came to Egypt to buy from Joseph. For the hunger grew severe in all lands.

<insert>
All the lands surrounding Egypt can be understood here as having been plagued by this hunger; the King then directed everyone to Joseph, who conducted himself with mercy and refreshed everyone in their need. In this, we are meant to look upon Christ, to whom the Father directs everyone, saying: "Him shall you hear." The Father has also sealed Him to be the Bread of God that comes from heaven and gives life to the world. Therefore, all are kindly invited by Christ: "I am the bread of life! Whoever comes to me shall not hunger; and whoever believes in me shall never thirst." (John 6:27, 33, 35). He is a good master of the house, says Bernard <note>original: "Bernardus (a)" referring to Bernard of Clairvaux</note> in his 71st Sermon on the Song of Songs, page 781, who cares for his household by nourishing them in times of scarcity, feeding them with the bread of life and understanding. And in truth, all lands shall yet gather to Him to still the hunger that will come upon them at the time of the "open door," which Christ will open everywhere through the Spirit of the Lord.
</insert>

v. 46. **Thirty years old**) Just as Joseph did here, Christ entered His ministry in His thirtieth year: Luke 3:23. He also sought to provide the food that should remain for eternal life. John 6:27. Thus, in all these details, Joseph was a magnificent prototype of Christ.
**Traveled through the entire land of Egypt**) Thus the Apostolic life begins; namely, when one does not appoint oneself, but enters into such work only by the command of God. It is beautifully illustrated here that Joseph, after his renewal, travels through all the lands of Egypt. One must first be renewed before one desires to act. Jesus Christ, our holy pattern, had to spend 30 years in His hidden life before He appeared publicly. He did not do so until He had endured the forty-day temptation in the wilderness. This correspondence between the old "images" <note>or types</note> and their holy truth will greatly delight those who look into them.
v. 48. 49. Blessed is he who has a "good Joseph" in the court of his heart, who knows how to provide supplies when the hunger for the Divine Word is present!
v. 50. **Two sons**) These two sons are an image of the Community of Christ in His glorious kingdom, which shall then be born out of the Spirit of Christ. As His exalted Church, she will forget all the previous misery she suffered in those six great days and times of labor and persecution. She will also be very fruitful, for only then will the promise made to Abraham reach its fulfillment: that God would bless and multiply his seed like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore (Gen. 22:17). See also Psalm 8:2, 10; 72:8, 19; Isaiah 54. After renewal, one begins to bear children for Jesus Christ.
v. 51. Joseph here forgets all the labor and toil he endured, just as he—when he was in poverty—had forgotten all the graces he had received.
<margin>(a) John 12:24, 25.</margin>
v. 52. Because Joseph was well-instructed in the "inner ways" <note>the mystical path of the soul</note>, he recognizes that all his goods came to him because of his poverty: for as long as the seed remains in the earth, it (a) decays, sprouts, and brings forth much fruit.

# The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLII. #

<margin>
v. 15-18. Since Joseph swears by the life of Pharaoh, he follows the custom of courtiers: just as the Romans later used to swear by the *guardian spirit of the Emperor* <note>original: "Genio Imperatoris" — the protective spirit or "genius" of the ruler</note>; and this custom was also used among the people of God, as when Uriah swore by the life of David. 2 Samuel 11:11. However, this was sinful, as God commanded that one should swear only by His name, Deuteronomy 6:13, and punished His people for swearing by those who are not God. Jeremiah 5:7.

One can so easily be enticed to sin in the courts and among other worldly affairs by conforming to them and thus becoming guilty before God. Although Joseph also makes his fear of the true God known in verse 18—which must always shine forth and prevail among the pious—to guard himself against all sinful habits. See Nehemiah 5:15. With this, he also wanted to give his brothers heart again: for one can expect all good things from those who fear God.

Let everyone learn from this example today to regard every sin as truly great; thus can one overcome it in repentance and avoid it. God does not let even the offending of a child go unpunished. No injury to one's neighbor is so small that it does not simultaneously wound God and His truth and holiness. No matter how small a wrong might seem from the outside, it is nonetheless disobedience against God’s clear will in the eyes of divine justice. By committing something against a visible creature, you simultaneously strike at the invisible truth and the inviolable will of God—indeed, the highest majesty of God Himself, who has forbidden such things to you.

First, you become guilty toward your neighbor, who is your brother by nature.
If you think the sin is not so great when the person or matter seems contemptible against whom you do wrong or violence; then learn, O vain man, from this example, how unbearably the evil later grows over the head of one who, like Joseph's brothers, previously regarded the sin as so insignificant!

Yet much greater are the sins committed against God’s instruments and friends. Joseph was not only these people's brother but also a witness of truth among them. For he brought all their evil things before the father. Therefore, in Joseph, they mocked and persecuted the most holy truth of God Himself.

Just as sin against our brother committed outwardly is rightly recognized and judged—whether committed with words and deeds or inwardly with thoughts and schemes—so too is that transgression even more cruel which happens in secret against the Lord Jesus and His Spirit.

This most precious heavenly Joseph [Jesus] has, as we know, desired out of infinite love to become flesh and our brother; and specifically so that He might deal with us as our equal—brotherly, kindly, and confidentially—regarding that which serves our salvation. In such a brotherly and most faithful spirit, He constantly warns people to keep them from sins. But

Oh, what a guilt occurs here that we must constantly judge and overcome in ourselves! Namely, the disobedience and the hardness of heart: which Joseph's brothers here mournfully confess;

### Chapter XLII. The First Book of Moses. ###

...saw the anguish <margin>(a) Chapter 37:24. Psalm 25:17.</margin> of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we would not listen! Therefore this distress has come upon us!

**22. And Reuben answered them and said: Did I not tell you?**

v. 21. *We saw the anguish of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we would not listen!*) Oh, how necessary it is to recognize and judge such hardness within oneself!

Our true brother, Jesus Christ, truly pleads with every soul and always works toward the anxious birth, awakening, and preservation of the divine life within us, both outwardly and inwardly.

Can anyone truly deny that this Word is far from their mouth and heart? Where do so many good reminders and warnings against evil come from? No one often tells a person these things from the outside, and the person himself never likes to hear such things within: yet the eternal light pleads, asks, and begs the poor soul day and night, as it were, to follow Him.

But how do people commonly treat Him? Unfortunately, not much differently than Jacob's sons treated Joseph—indeed, just as it went for this eternal Word of the Father in the days of His flesh. Fleshly reason mocks the Lord Jesus; others make the Word of Life seem suspicious. Indeed, if one considers it rightly, every sin suppresses the innocent life of Jesus, which by right should rise up and bear fruit in every human being.

*Therefore this distress has come upon us*) Joseph's brothers would never have believed that he would come to light again and cause them such distress. But they were repaid in kind. Because they had so distressed Joseph, God allowed them to fall into such distress and danger for their own lives, thereby drawing out their confession of sins. Elihu testifies gloriously to this in Job 36:8, 9, 10. See also Hosea 5:14. For this reason, a person does well to confess his sin to God immediately, which brings him mercy, Proverbs 28:13, and not wait until he is stretched upon such a rack. Oh, God knows how to wake the conscience regarding old sins! Though it sleeps in times of prosperity, it is awakened in adversity; and then the sins we previously cast behind us come and place themselves before our eyes. Psalm 50:21, 90:8.

And so, in the end times, a particular anguish and torment will come upon the Jews when they are to be converted and Christ is to be born within them. Revelation 12:2. Then they will also recognize their guilt, how they sinned so grievously against their brother—who wished to be born from them according to the flesh—and brought him into such anguish of soul that his blood is now rightfully demanded from them, just as they themselves demanded that the innocent blood of Christ be upon them and their children for vengeance. Matthew 27:25.

v. 22. Just as Christ and His Spirit are treated, so it happens to His members, who for His sake must warn such disobedient children, whether they are ordained preachers or others.

God uses so many faithful reminders from the outside to preserve people from sin. Indeed, there is not a single sinner in the world who is not occasionally warned outwardly against sin through all sorts of means that God finds necessary for him.

But what does it help with most people? They cast it to the wind and do not believe that God is so angry. Indeed, they are still resentful toward those who rebuke them in the gate <note>A biblical idiom for public correction or legal judgment</note> and demand a false peace from those who tell them the truth, so that their rotten wound might not be uncovered and the innocent blood of Joseph might not come to light.

And oh, how flippantly people often deal with lowly, powerless, and defenseless persons—with widows, orphans, strangers, and the poor! They do not believe that God asks after such blood because these people seem contemptible in the eyes of the proud.

But oh, how comforting it is for all the oppressed that their sighing and tears cry out to the Most High, and that their need reaches into His very heart!

<column-break/>

**when I said; Do not sin against the boy? And you would not listen. Behold, now his blood is required!**

---
<margin>23. They</margin>
->O how holy, how just, how truthful are all, even the smallest, ways of the Lord! How richly He repays everyone as they have deserved!<-
---

Truly, we have here a clear mirror of how God proceeds so very accurately and precisely in His retributive justice. Joseph’s brothers had first caused him anguish, so he, in turn, had to cause them anguish and fear. They had thrown him into a pit, so they had to spend three days in prison for it. He had pleaded with them in vain; they, in turn, were not heard despite all their begging and protests.

Oh, how the unfaithful brothers learn there to strike their own breasts and gladly admit their abominations!

Let one truly learn to believe this precious foundation of divine justice before such hard-learned wisdom <note>original: "Witzigung" — a term for learning a lesson through punishment or experience</note> falls into someone's hands.

Oh, the retributive holy justice of God does the sinner an inexpressible grace when it chastens him for his improvement and thereby makes sin bitter and disgusting, even if his lack of understanding does not yet recognize it as a blessing!

That is the richness of His goodness, patience, and longsuffering: And everything that seems hard to the delicate flesh leads only to this: that we should be moved out of the fire of wrath and translated into the gentle kingdom of love of His Son. He does not seek our ruin or despair with this, but rather He wants us, in the remembrance of our evil, to humble ourselves before Him and judge ourselves, so that He does not have to judge us in His wrath.

Such a depth of wisdom, justice, and mercy of God shines forth from all such wonderful dealings, which can only be seen in the spirit of wisdom! The ancients also noted this most wise mixture of love and wrath.

<margin>(a) Book 2 on Ezekiel, Homily 12, page 1184. Volume II of the Works.</margin>
God must, writes Gregory the Great (a), show outward severity to the wicked, even if He has love within. Just as Joseph thought of the guilt but nevertheless remitted the wrong: He did not repay the brothers with evil, and yet He did not release them without purging and cleansing. He spoke harshly to them, imprisoned them, and remained in his former sharpness even on the third day. There they learned to go into their hearts, and the memory of their guilt knocked so that they said among themselves: "We have well deserved it!" Thus he released their souls from guilt after he had well distressed them over it. Oh, a merciful pain! He tormented them, and yet He also loved them.

The Holy Spirit wanted to remind everyone of such a wonderful process should they enter into their repentance. But if someone already stands under the earnestness of God’s convicting punishment, let him believe that it is not at all the intent of the firstborn brother, Christ, to destroy him—just as Joseph did not seek the destruction of his (albeit wicked) brothers. He chastens, instructs, and causes distress from within and without only so that we may attain His holiness and, for the rest of our lives, shrink back from such a plague upon our souls.

Thus, it is aimed at nothing but rescue and salvation when we specifically anticipate divine judgment and judge ourselves without hypocrisy.

But the best thing is to walk prudently from now on, so that one no longer needs such hard chastening and punishment, but rather remains in the offered and received grace through daily repentance, finding the friendly face of the heavenly Joseph always unchanged—especially at the time when we are in need of help.

In such a state of faith, one can thereafter suffer with confidence. For faith teaches a Christian how closely God watches over His own and how He leaves nothing unpaid to their enemies. If only one can wait out the time with Joseph and let things play out as God allows and governs. The time is already coming when the innocence that the enemy wanted to suppress or smudge will suddenly come to light with the long-forgotten Joseph, and shine like a lightning bolt before the eyes of the false brothers.
