### A Type of Christ. <note>The author uses Benjamin as a "type"—a historical person whose life foreshadows the life of Jesus Christ.</note>

1. **Benjamin** was not born to Leah, but to **Rachel**, the most beloved wife. The Jews do not consider Christ to be the Son who was to be born to them. Isaiah 9.
2. He was named by his mother **Benoni**, which means "a son of sorrow" <note>original: "Benoni / ein Sohn des Schmerzens"</note>. Christ was likewise full of sorrows and sickness, and a sword pierced through his mother’s soul.
3. He was his father’s most beloved son on both sides.
4. He had to go to Egypt to his brothers and redeem them through his presence.
5. He was named **Benjamin** by his father out of love, which means "a son of the right hand" <note>original: "Benjamin / ein Sohn der Rechten"</note>.
6. He was born during the journey.
7. Not far from **Ephrath** or **Bethlehem**; not far from the Tower of **Eder** or the sheep and herds. Micah 5.
8. Just as the midwife wanted to comfort **Rachel** in her pains with the birth of a son: so this is our comfort. Isaiah 9:6.
9. Just as **Joseph** said, "you shall not see my face unless **Benjamin** is with you": so it is in John 14.

<note>
It is asked here: why did neither Joseph during those 22 years, nor God through a special revelation (which had otherwise often happened to Jacob), give this mourning father any news of his son's condition?

Augustine <note>A famous early Christian theologian (354–430 AD).</note> attributes it to God's special counsel and will, who desired that Jacob should feel the painful loss for so long so that he might be purified more and more from his daily sins, shortcomings, and failings, from which even the lives of the saints are not yet free.

Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential commentator on the Bible.</note> says: the prophecy of the stranger-status of the Israelite seed in Egypt had to be fulfilled thereby. If Jacob had learned of his son's imprisonment, he would undoubtedly have ransomed him, even if it had cost a great deal.

He also had to remain hidden and unknown so that his dream would be fulfilled all the more clearly and tangibly, to great wonderment.

v. 23. *Your God and your father’s God*) One can see from this house-steward’s speech that he feared God in his own way, and allowed himself to be led by Joseph to the knowledge of the true God whom Joseph and his fathers honored—namely, that this was the God of the Hebrews, as Joseph identified himself in Chapter 40:15, and as these brothers were regarded by him. v. 32.

Thus, godly masters must also strive to have God-fearing servants around them; indeed, they should lead others to the knowledge of the true God: then their business will be faithfully discharged, and they will also have a blessing in the administration and provision of the lands entrusted to them by God.

v. 26. 28. This friendly behavior from Joseph could give them courage again, and so their fear vanished, though they remained in dutiful reverence, and here had to fulfill the dream once again, as all eleven bowed before Joseph. And since they simultaneously called their father a "servant" of Joseph, their father’s humiliation was also fulfilled (as mentioned in Chapter 37:10), which Jacob would not have suffered from his father, as he embraced him as a child (Chapter 46:29); but here Joseph’s brothers demonstrated such in their father’s name.
</note>

<gloss>v. 32. By himself) The saints, being full of the Spirit of God, possess wonderful reservations in order not to offend people in indifferent matters <note>Indifferent matters or "adiaphora" are actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God.</note>. Joseph finds a way to avoid being offensive to the Egyptians, yet he can still host his brothers in his company and presence: by having them all served separately and at separate tables, even if in the same room. Thus he had the pleasure of honoring both parties and—what was even more—entering into the will of God through this. All of this, however, was not without a hidden meaning. Joseph's brothers were not yet in as great an internal elevation as Joseph, so they could not have sat at one table with him. He sent them only the dishes that were prepared for him, so that they too might partake of the fullness of his grace and the anointing of his spirit. The best portion, however, fell to Benjamin, who was most united with him both by blood and by spirit.</gloss>

<gloss>Abomination to the Egyptians) Because the Hebrews slaughtered and sacrificed those animals which the Egyptians revered and worshipped, they had a loathing for them and for shared social interaction. Gen 46:34, Exod 8:22. Furthermore, as the believing Hebrews, who pass over from the world to Christ, must kill their "animal man" <note>Referring to the carnal or base nature of humanity.</note>—which natural men, standing as spiritual Egyptians in the service of sin, revere and keep alive—they are also an abomination to them, and they flee from their company. Gal 6:14.</gloss>

<column-break/>

33. And they had to sit before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth. And the men marveled at this, looking at one another.

34. And portions were carried to them from before him; but Benjamin's portion was five times more than all of their portions: and they drank and were merry with him.

<gloss>v. 34. Benjamin's portion five times more) This was both as a sign of special affection and to investigate how his brothers felt toward Benjamin—whether they would look askance at him and if envy still pricked them as it had formerly against Joseph. Furthermore, the Lord will, in the end times, also gather His "Benjamins" or "Sons of the Right Hand" from among the Jews and the Gentiles. Before His final glorious revelation, He will reveal Himself to them with a singular look of grace and great mercy: He will prepare for them a "feast of fat things" (Isaiah 25:6) where a great light will rise for both Gentiles and Jews (v. 7), just as here both Joseph's brothers and the Egyptians were hosted by him separately. But it will not yet be the revelation of Christ Himself, in which Jews and Gentiles shall be one; just as Joseph here did not yet make himself known. Rather, a great trial and anguish must first precede it, as followed here. 4. But when they had gone out of the city and had not gone far, *Joseph* said to the one who was over his house: "Get up and pursue the men! And when you reach them, say to them: 'Why have you repaid evil for good?

5. Is it not the one from which my lord drinks, and by which he can easily perceive <note>The original German "spüren" implies sensing or discerning things that are hidden.</note> things? You have done evil in what you have done!'"

8. See, the money that we found in the top of our sacks, we brought back to you from the land of *Canaan*; so how then should we have stolen silver or gold from your lord’s house?

9. With whomever among your servants it is found, let him die! Moreover, we also will be my lord’s servants."

10. And he said: "Let it now be according to your words! He with whom it is found shall be my servant; but you shall be blameless."

11. And they hurried and each one let down his sack to the earth, and each one opened his sack.

---

v. 5. *Joseph* did not actually divine with the cup, as such a pagan abomination would not have been customary for him. Thus, the word can be taken in a good sense, where one can guess or perceive and notice something based on probable grounds. It is in this sense that it also appears regarding soothsayers, who guess things partly through conjecture and partly through the inspiration of Satan.

v. 9. This was a very rash commitment to such a harsh punishment of death, since they should have thought that it might have happened with the cup just as it had previously happened with the money. It was the same with *Jacob* in *Genesis* 31:32. One should therefore not proceed so harshly regarding punishments: it might affect someone in a way that would cause great sorrow if it were actually carried out; as can also be seen with *Saul* in 1 *Samuel* 14:24 etc.

<column-break/>

12. And he searched; he began at the eldest and finished at the youngest: then the cup was found in *Benjamin’s* sack.

13. Then they tore their clothes, and each one loaded his donkey, and they returned to the city.

14. And *Judah* went with his brothers into *Joseph’s* house; for he was still there: and they fell down before him to the ground.

15. *Joseph* said to them: "What is this deed that you have done? Do you not know that such a man as I am can easily perceive such things?"

16. And *Judah* said: "What shall we say to my lord? What shall we speak, and how can we justify ourselves? **God** has found the iniquity of your servants. See, we are my lord’s servants; both we and he in whose hand the cup was found."

17. But he said: "Far be it from me to do such a thing! The man in whose hand the cup was found shall be my servant: but as for you, go up in peace to your father."

18. Then...

---

Oh, how these brothers were pressed by their own deceits, since *Joseph* placed them in sorrow and anxiety for so long and so often! As three whole chapters here deal with this in succession. This great anxiety brought them to a humble confession of their sins: yet it is difficult to hit upon the right thing or to confess outwardly what actually makes us guilty before **God**; which here was the unmerciful mistreatment of *Joseph*, which only later truly dawned on them to their final shame when he made himself known.

Whenever we are harshly attacked by **God** for this reason, even if we cannot immediately find the cause of our tribulation, we must nonetheless look to the secret and holy counsel of **God**, who punishes us in a righteous way for the sake of our sins.

This trial is an image of the hour of the great temptation that will come over the whole world before the revelation of the glorious kingdom of *Christ*; *Revelation* 3:10. This is intended so that they too may rightly recognize their faults and iniquities and humbly confess them: 1 *Peter* 4:17. And then this will also particularly strike the Jews, so that—though some light will have dawned on them before, during which they still did not want to rightly think of their chief sin, namely the rejection of the Rock of Salvation, *Jesus Christ*—their minds will be made truly tender <note>The term "mürbe" describes someone being softened or worn down by trial until they are ready to yield.</note> through this, so that when *Christ* then makes himself more fully known, they may be all the more inwardly contrite and prepared for the willing recognition of the truth.

And that will be the heavier toil and anxiety, which will surpass those of the previous earlier times, when—upon the disdain of the great light that rose among them at the coming of *Christ*—the great judgment of the *Romans* came upon them, in which judgment they were devastated. Through this latter judgment of love, however, heavy though it will be, they will conversely be wholesomely prepared for the recognition of *Christ* in his glorious future. See *Isaiah* 9:1-2.

<gloss>Joseph wanted to explore the hearts and inclinations of his brothers toward his youngest and full brother <note>Joseph and Benjamin shared the same mother, Rachel.</note> through such a staged test. Because he could then perceive no secret hatred which the brothers might have harbored against little Benjamin, he concluded all the more that his fate was to be attributed not so much to the brothers' betrayal, but to the wise, forward-looking providence of GOD.</gloss>

<margin>v. 1. Could not restrain himself)</margin> When our Savior has truly humbled the pious, and the uprightness of their hearts toward him and their neighbor has been clearly revealed, and when the anguish and the trial by fire is at its greatest, then he can no longer restrain himself; rather, his heart breaks within him so that he must have mercy on them. Jeremiah 31:20.

<margin>No one stood by him)</margin> No one gets to know when and how Christ reveals himself to the Jews in the last time; he will discover himself to them immediately in their hearts, just as Paul was likewise enlightened and converted immediately by Christ JESUS and by his brilliance as a prototype. And even where such does not happen, the veil would still remain hanging for a long time before the hearts of the Jews.

<margin>Made himself known to his brothers)</margin> If these brothers could play their parts in secret, God could also maintain Joseph in secret until the proper time. If the world can hide its malice so that the righteous person is betrayed and sold innocently and unnoticed, oh, then God can also nourish his own in the wilderness and keep them under a foreign habit <note>historical: "Habit" refers to clothing or an outward appearance/disguise.</note>, under which they are not recognized, until the time of the revelation of his glory.

<margin>v. 3. 4. I am Joseph your brother etc.)</margin> So it will be when Christ, in his own time, makes himself known to his brothers according to the flesh <note>The author is using a typological interpretation, seeing Joseph as a "type" or foreshadowing of Christ and the brothers as the Jewish people.</note>, and he will call out to them—as he once did to Saul—"I am JESUS your brother, whom you delivered to the heathens and have hated so much until now!"

<margin>They were terrified before his face)</margin> Thus will the Jews also, just like Paul, be converted with trembling and hesitation, and recognize how God has found their iniquity in the rejection of the Rock of Salvation; they will seek the Lord their God and their King David, and will come trembling to the Lord and to his grace in the last time. Hosea 3:5, 2:21-22. Then they will also understand the meaning of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament better than now, when they only stick to the outward history of Joseph, in which they could have so beautifully found and seen the fates of their church and their future condition, which will then be opened to them therein.

If ever a history was full of wonders of divine wisdom and providence, it is certainly this history of Joseph. How craftily and hiddenly did his brothers begin their murderous plots! Who watched them? Who could be a witness when they threw the good Joseph into the pit? How great was the anguish of soul for Joseph when he pleaded with them, and how faith must have struggled and wavered within him!

You dear Joseph! Why do you fear so in evil days, when the iniquity of your oppressors surrounded you? Could your false brothers play so subtly and so maliciously with you that your innocence did not finally break through? What did it help that they told the old Jacob a heap of lies? That they acted sadly and comforted their father? And what does it help still that countless slanders and accusations are scattered by the enemy through his tools, which also deceive well-meaning souls? Does not the time of revelation finally come, when Joseph comes to light and becomes known—to the terror of his brothers—he whom they thought their cunning and lies had long ago cleared out of the way?

Yes, let only a few days or years pass, and the innocent Joseph will come to light again from imprisonment. Oh, how his enemies and envious brothers will then be terrified before his face! Yet Joseph, and those minded like him, do not seek their own elevation in this when God pulls them out of the dust of contempt or persecution: but rather the glory of the Lord alone, and then the winning over of the adversaries, so that these too may come to knowledge, repentance, and salvation.

Over this Joseph then rejoices with his brothers; he loves and cherishes them as his greatest benefactors, who have benefited him a thousand times more than all the kings of the earth could have done. From this, Jacob afterward has joy, and Israel will be glad.

Therefore it specifically concerns the eyes when it is said: <term>The face is the indicator of the mind <note>original: "Facies indicium animi"</note></term>, the face is an indication of the soul.

### Chapter XLV.

->Joseph reveals himself to his brothers.<-

Then Joseph could not restrain himself before all those who stood by him, and he cried: "Let everyone go out from me!" And no one stood with him while Joseph made himself known to his brothers.

2. And he raised his voice with weeping, so that the Egyptians heard it; even the house of Pharaoh heard it.

3. And Joseph said to his brothers: "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" And his brothers could not answer him, for they were terrified before his face.

Since Joseph’s heart was deeply moved by the sincere and humble confession of Judah, he now revealed himself to them in a most loving and heartfelt manner, however harshly he had first behaved toward them. He thus combined the wisdom of the serpent and the sincerity of the dove, as in Matthew 10:16. He acted as it is said of Wisdom in <note>original: "Sirach 4 / 18"</note> Ecclesiasticus 4:17–18: "At first she will walk with him by crooked ways, and bring fear and dread upon him, and torment him with her discipline, until she may trust his soul, and try him by her laws. Then will she return the straight way unto him, and comfort him, and show him her secrets."

v. 1. **Restrain himself**) When our Savior has truly humbled the godly, and the sincerity of their hearts toward Him and their neighbor has become manifest—and when the anguish and the trial by fire is at its greatest—then He can no longer restrain Himself; rather, His heart breaks within Him so that He must have mercy on them. Jeremiah 31:20.

**No one stood with him**) No one gets to know when and how Christ reveals Himself to the Jews in the last times, for He will discover Himself to them immediately in their hearts, just as Paul was enlightened and converted directly by Christ Jesus and His radiance as a prototype. And even if such a thing did not happen, the veil would still hang over the hearts of the Jews for a long time.

**Made himself known to his brothers**) If these brothers could play their parts secretly, then God could also keep Joseph hidden until the proper time. If the world can hide its malice so that the righteous man is betrayed and sold innocently and unnoticed, then God can also nourish His own in the wilderness and keep them under a foreign <term>habit <note>a distinctive set of clothes, often religious or formal</note></term>, under which they are not recognized, until the time of the revelation of His glory.

v. 3. 4. **I am Joseph your brother, etc.**) So it will also be when Christ, in His own time, reveals Himself to His brothers according to the flesh <note>meaning the Jewish people</note>, and calls out to them as He once did to Saul: "I am Jesus your brother, whom you delivered to the Gentiles and have hated so much until now!"

**They were terrified before his face**) Thus the Jews, just like Paul, will convert with trembling and quaking, and recognize how God found their iniquity in their rejection of the Rock of Salvation. They shall seek the Lord their God and their King David, and shall come trembling to the Lord and to His goodness in the last days. Hosea 3:5; 2:21-22. Then they will also understand the meaning of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament better than they do now, while they stay only with the outward history of Joseph; in which history they could otherwise so beautifully find and see the <note>original: "fata"</note> destinies of their church and their future state, which shall then be opened to them therein.

<column-break/>

4. Joseph further said to his brothers: "Please <gloss>(a)</gloss> step closer to me!" And they stepped closer. And he said: "I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt."

<margin>(a) See Acts 4:12-14.</margin>

5. "And now, do not be grieved, and let no anger kindle in your eyes because you sold me here! For God sent me before you for the sake of preserving life."

### 6. For

---

If ever a history was full of the wonders of divine wisdom and providence, it is certainly this history of Joseph. How craftily and secretly his brothers began their murderous plots! Who watched them? Who could be a witness when they threw the good Joseph into the pit? How great was the anguish of soul in Joseph when he pleaded with them, and when his faith might have quite trembled and wavered within him!

You dear Joseph! Why do you fear so in evil days, when the iniquity of your suppressors surrounded you? Could God let your false brothers play so subtly and maliciously with you that your innocence did not finally break through? What did it help that they made the old Jacob believe a heap of lies? That they acted sadly and comforted their father? And what does it still help that countless slanders and accusations are scattered by the enemy through his tools, which even deceive well-meaning souls? Does not the time of revelation finally come, when Joseph comes to light and becomes known—to the terror of his brothers—whom they thought their craftiness and lies had long since removed from the way?

Oh, what a thunderclap that was in the hearts of the brothers when they heard from the one who stood before them, and in whose power they were: "I am Joseph your brother!"

Yes, let only a few days or years pass, and the innocent Joseph will again come to light out of imprisonment. Oh, how his enemies and envious brothers will then be terrified before his face! For behold, he is no longer in the wretched and powerless form as before: but the Lord of Hosts clothes him with power, with light, and grace, so that you will have to bow before him and worship at his feet, and recognize that the Lord has loved him!

Yet Joseph, and those of the same mind as him, do not seek their own elevation in this when God pulls them out of the dust of contempt or persecution: but rather the glory of the Lord alone, and then the winning over of their adversaries, so that these too may come to knowledge, repentance, and salvation.

So it went sometimes with the Jews, that in good days they persecuted the prophets as erring, blind, and harmful people. But when a misfortune came, oh, how they would ask after them or consider their prophecies!
v. 8. Not you — God) Joseph confesses that this was not exactly the intention of his brothers when they persecuted him; rather, it was the will of God, who knows how to guide all things according to His eternal counsel.
He also reveals to them something of God’s will concerning him, and His unsearchable ways with His chosen ones, whom He humbles only to exalt them; and also regarding the truth of the dreams, of which they now see the fulfillment.
A soul that has reached such a stage as Joseph does not attribute the persecutions inflicted upon it to its persecutors. Instead, because it views everything in God as a wonderful order of Providence, it turns everything back to God. Joseph was very faithful in carrying this out. This also enables one to love one's enemies as much as one's friends, because one never dwells on the evil they do, but only eyes the good that can come from it. In this sense, for those who are permeated by a living faith and have tasted His love, the commandment given to us by Jesus Christ—to love our enemies—is so easy that one could not hate them even if this commandment had not been given.
Father to Pharaoh) Great lords should honor wise counselors and faithful servants of Christ as fathers, as God has appointed them for that purpose. See also Judges 17:10 <note>In this Bible passage, a young man is asked to be "a father and a priest" to a household, indicating "father" as a title of respect and guidance.</note>.
</note>

v. 9. God has made me lord) Indeed, everyone who has anything to say or command in the world wants to say this and attribute their status to God. But where is Joseph’s heart and mind? Where are the proofs of his faithfulness and fear of God? Where is the guiding wisdom? Therefore, it is the spirit of the world that favors most people in this regard, because they worship it.
v. 12. My mouth speaking to you) Since he had previously spoken to them through an interpreter, he now does so orally; and with this, he proved three magnificent virtues in his behavior: tender brotherly love, as it arose from the fear of God, and then especially toward his dear old father; a reconcilable, kind heart that knows how to forgive every insult and interpret everything for the best (See Matthew 5:25 <note>The verse advising to settle matters quickly with an adversary</note>); and his humility, in that in his princely status to which he had been raised, he was not ashamed of his lowly brothers, and even though they were such hated shepherds.
v. 13. All my glory) Joseph says this not to exalt himself, but because he knows that the mysteries of the spiritual life are known to his father. He also gives him, through the gifts he distributes to all, right evidence of the truth of his status.
</note>

Thus, the long imprisonment in which Christ has been dead to the Jews will not allow them to believe that it is so. ### 256 The First Book of Moses. Chap. XLVI.

**27.** And they told him all the words of Joseph, which he had spoken to them. And when he saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him, the spirit of Jacob their father became alive.
**28.** And Israel said: It is enough; Joseph my son is still alive; I will go and see him before I die!

v. 27. The great joy that made the pious, elderly Jacob entirely alive again is a remarkable example of God’s wonderful providence, which turned this tragedy into such a wondrous comedy <note>In historical literature, a "comedy" refers to a story that begins in distress but ends in joy and restoration.</note>. Just as the most remarkable and truly heart-rending story in this First Book of Moses is the offering of Isaac in Chapter 22, through which Christ’s death was prefigured; so too is this revelation of Joseph to his brothers and his father a similarly heart-stirring and tear-inducing mysterious history. For in the end times, the heavenly Joseph <note>A "typological" comparison where Joseph represents Jesus Christ.</note> will also reveal and manifest himself to his poor brothers according to the flesh, after they have been thoroughly refined; and they will then recognize their true heavenly Joseph. This would not have happened for a long time if Jesus Christ had not first made himself known to them, for all salvation must come upon his brothers from him, as the author and perfecter of their faith. Then the kissing of one another will begin; they will kiss the Son, and the Son will kiss them in return, and they will hurry to tell their father—the Jewish Church—how great Jesus Christ is, how he is the Prince and Lord of the entire world, and that the kingdoms of the world have become those of our God and his Christ. Then the Gentiles, among whom Israel dwells, will be moved to bring the Jews on horses and in wagons, on litters and mules, to Canaan. Isaiah 66:18–20. Then they will become alive again and be satisfied that Jesus Christ—whom their ancestors sold and killed—lives and that his kingdom will begin. Then the dry bones of the entire house of Israel will flourish again. Ezekiel 37:9–16. Then the re-acceptance of the children of Israel will be like life from the dead. Romans 11:15. Then the mouths of those who previously were like dreamers, unable to believe such great things, will be full of laughter and their mouths full of praise. Then it will be said among the Gentiles: The Lord has done great things for them. And they, the Jews, will say: The Lord has done great things for us; of this we are glad! Psalm 126.
It does indeed happen that the Savior sometimes withholds or delays his comfort: but in doing so, he does not miss the right time, and the glory and joy are afterwards all the more overflowing, the greater the sadness seemed to be.
This mystery is vividly depicted in the elderly Jacob. In his weak old age, he had to sit in sorrow for so long over his lost son Joseph. But as great as his previous suffering was, so overflowing was the joy when the news of Joseph’s life was confirmed to him by the sent wagons. Of which the Holy Spirit says beautifully: it
**Became the spirit of Jacob alive)** That is: as much as Jacob’s joy and peace had previously been killed and dampened, so much did it live within him again.
Is it any different for God-seeking souls who feel their spiritual life suppressed and as if dead within them due to natural corruption? As deep as they sit in the struggle of repentance in darkness and sorrow, mourning the lost divine life as if it were an only child; so highly does the dampened and almost smothered life of God rise and rejoice in them again when the heavenly Joseph sends the spirit of faith into their heart as a swift wagon, upon which they can soar to their Savior.

understand the "bringing up" as referring to the withered corpse of Jacob. For God is not a God of the dead, but of the living. Rather, God wanted to lead Jacob down and lead Israel up again. And he has done this time and again since the beginning of the world. When the first man had to wander out of the Canaan of Paradise, He brought him into the Egypt of this world, amid various sorrows, labor, and hardship. And the other man, His Son, He both sent and brought down into this world, and also led him up again above all heavens.

## Chapter XLVI.

-> Israel’s Journey into Egypt. <-

**1. AND** Israel journeyed with all that he had and came to Beersheba: and he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
**2.** And God spoke to Israel in visions of the night: and he said; Jacob, Jacob! And he said: Here I am!
**3.** And he said: I am God, the God of your father; do not fear to go down into Egypt! For there I will make you into a great nation.
**4.** I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will also surely bring you up again, and Joseph shall lay his hand upon your eyes.

v. 1. **Beersheba)** Since Abraham and Isaac had their dwelling here for a long time, and therefore, besides the preaching of the Lord’s name, also built altars for sacrifice (Chapter 21:33; 26:23, 25); so too does Jacob wish to perform his calling upon God for a blessing on his journey to Egypt here, where his fathers sent many fervent prayers to God.
v. 2-4. Since Jacob was undoubtedly troubled about leaving the promised land of Canaan and going into Egypt, where the heavy bondage that God had foretold to Abraham (Chapter 15:13) might await him; God encourages him so that he should not fear, but rather rely on His mighty protection, and thereby on His faithfulness and truth, according to which He would gloriously fulfill His precious promises of the land of Canaan and the great multiplication of his seed in his descendants in due time. Also, his dear son Joseph was to show him the final service of love at his blessed death and close his eyes <note>To "close one's eyes" is a traditional term for being present at the moment of death to perform the final rites.</note>.
Thus must believers begin and carry out all their undertakings in the fear of the Lord; then God will reveal His gracious will to them as they proceed and let them experience a blessed end, so that they may depart from here in peace and satisfaction.
v. 3. God assures Jacob that the journey to Egypt is a work of His hand.
**There)** In distress and tribulation, the Lord will multiply the seed of righteousness.
v. 4. **I will go down with you — I will also bring you up)** After God has allowed the souls who surrender to Him to enter the Egypt of trials and temptations, He does not fail to lead them back into their land of rest.
This promise was not only for Jacob but also for all those who, like him, are willing to deny themselves and go into "Egypt" for God’s sake; that is, to leave the land of peace and, through the will of God, to wander into the land of confusion and corruption as necessity requires and as God wills. It is nothing clearer than that God spoke in the person of Jacob to all surrendered souls, as to the true children of Israel, and not to Jacob alone: since He promises him at the same time that He would lead him out of Egypt again; yet also says he would die there, by promising him that Joseph would close his eyes.

v. 5. **The sons of Israel**) Most translators miss the mark intended by the Holy Spirit by commonly putting "the children of Israel" instead of "the sons of Israel." For it is not at all the same thing according to the intent of the Holy Spirit, who uses the words *Ben* <note>original: "Ben", Hebrew for "son"</note> and *Sachar* <note>original: "Sachar", Hebrew for "male" or "man-child"</note> as words that indicate dignity and strength. This is also to be noted in the New Testament; for example, Matthew 5:44-45, Luke 20:36, Romans 8:14-17, Galatians 3:7, 26; 4:1-7, Revelation 21:7. Male children are the pillars of their houses: just as, on the contrary, women in Hebrew have their name derived from "forgetting" <note>The author likely refers to a traditional etymology connecting the Hebrew word for women, *nashim*, to the root *nashah*, meaning "to forget," suggesting that a woman "forgets" her father's house to join her husband's.</note>, because their birth-name and the memory of their father's house is swallowed up in their husband's name. However, this does not mean they lack anything in spiritual matters, nor does it grant the male gender a spiritual superiority.

Moreover, through their common oversight, translators fall into right absurdities, which they could have avoided if they had rendered the word as *Bene* <note>Hebrew: "sons of"</note> "sons." For instance, what distinction do they make in Exodus 12:37 between children and children, when it says: "The children of Israel went out in such and such strength without the children"? And even more clearly here in our own text:

v. 7. **His children and — his daughters**) Were his daughters then not also his children? So too with his grandchildren and his granddaughters. Under "grandchildren" <note>literally: "child-children"</note> his granddaughters would already be included.

In Holy Scripture, the word "child" actually indicates the smallest age of childhood—those who cannot yet, or can barely, speak; those who are still in their minority <note>legal infancy or lack of maturity</note>. 1 Corinthians 3:1, 13:11, Galatians 4:1, 3, 19, Ephesians 4:14.

From this arises the confused translation—which in the French Bible even chooses the very first age, *enfans* <note>French for "children" or "infants"</note>, the little children of Israel—as if God intended to lead out children "a span long" (Lamentations 2:20). This leads to misunderstanding and misuse, whereby people deceive themselves into having such weak and purely "frailty-centered" thoughts about the state of a believer. They always view a believer's increase and growth as an immature, childish age and confine it within these boundaries: whereas we should no longer be children, but grow up into our head, Christ, in all things. Ephesians 4:14-15.

### The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLVI.

24. And the sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel and Guni, and Jezer and Shillem.
25. These are the sons of Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel; and she bore these to Jacob: all the souls were seven.
26. All the souls who came with Jacob into Egypt, who had come from his own loins, excluding the wives of Jacob's sons, all the souls were sixty-six.
27. And the sons of Joseph, who were born to him in Egypt, were two souls. All the souls of the house of Jacob, who came into Egypt, were seventy.
28. And he sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph, to point the way before him toward Goshen; and they came into the land of Goshen.

---

<margin>v. 27. 70)</margin> This count is reached when Jacob and Joseph are included. The seventy souls, writes <term>R. Menachem<note>Likely referring to Menachem Recanati, a 13th-century Italian rabbi and kabbalist.</note></term>, signify the seventy angels who stand around the Throne of Glory and are set over the nations. This opinion is based on Genesis 10, where seventy sons or grandsons are also counted from the three sons of Noah.

<margin>v. 27.</margin> This number of seventy is so specifically noted and also repeated in Exodus 1:5 and Deuteronomy 10:22 for the purpose of indicating the miraculous multiplication of the seed of promise; how from these seventy souls, in the following 215 years until the departure from Egypt, over 600,000 men fit for war alone—and thus without women and children—emerged; so that the Lord made them there like the stars in the heaven in multitude.

According to this number of seventy, the seventy elders were also later chosen (Numbers 11), and Christ also chose and sent out the seventy disciples according to this (Luke 10); just as the twelve Apostles were chosen according to the number of the twelve tribes, as spiritual patriarchs of the Israel of God in the New Testament.

<margin>v. 28. He sent Judah ahead of him to Joseph)</margin> Whose meeting he wished to await at the entrance of the land of Egypt, in order to receive instruction from him at the same time on how he should behave toward the King and the Egyptians. For

-> The Land of Goshen <-

Lay there near the source of the Nile River, toward Arabia and the land of Canaan, and was thus the first province for those coming from Canaan.

It was, however, Joseph’s wise arrangement, brought about through God’s governance, that he obtained from the King—who was very well-disposed toward him because he had served Egypt so well—a very fertile region, Goshen, for his family. This was so they might live there together and thus live separated from the idolatry of the Egyptians; although their descendants also defiled themselves with it (Ezekiel 20:7–8).

<margin>v. 32-34.</margin> There may have been various reasons why Joseph preferred that they identify themselves as livestock shepherds. Namely: so that his brothers would be less separated from each other and from their father; or, so that they might not be drawn into public offices by Pharaoh and thereby bring the envy of the Egyptians upon their necks; likewise, that they might avoid association particularly with the prominent Egyptians and courtiers, and not be infected by their customs and superstitions; and finally, so that they might obtain the land of Goshen all the sooner.

<column-break/>

29. Then Joseph prepared his chariot and went up to meet his father Israel in Goshen: and when he appeared before him, he fell on his neck and wept a long time on his neck.
30. Then Israel said to Joseph: "Now let me die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive!"
31. And Joseph said to his brothers and to his father's house: "I will go up and tell Pharaoh, and will say to him; My brothers and my father's house, who were in the land of Canaan, have come to me.
32. And the men are shepherds: for they are men who deal with livestock. So they have brought their sheep and their cattle, and everything they have.
33. And it shall happen, when Pharaoh calls you and says: 'What is your occupation?'
34. Then you shall say: 'Your servants are people who deal with livestock, from our youth until now, both we and our fathers': so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen: for every shepherd is an abomination to the Egyptians."

---

<margin>v. 29.</margin> As soon as he caught sight of him, Jacob fell on the neck of his so beloved son Joseph, for whose sake he had shed so many tears of mourning, and now shed very gentle tears of joy; and it actually stands in the original text, "he wept *still* on his neck": which may be understood to mean that as often as he beheld Joseph again during his life, he repeated such tender embraces with tears of joy; because Joseph, as a man burdened with many public duties, could not be around his father at all times.

Just as Joseph came to meet his father, even so at the end of time will Jesus Christ appear and come to meet the Jewish Church and its members. This, however, will not pass without heartfelt emotion, since He has not been able to speak with them for so long. The Jewish Church will weep for joy, kiss the Son, and melt in love over their <term>Goel<note>original: "Goel", a Hebrew term for a "Kinsman-Redeemer" who restores family rights and property.</note></term>.

<column-break/>

But the primary reason why the Egyptians held the livestock and sheep-herders as such an abomination may be this among others: because they considered that way of life to be lowly and contemptible, and perhaps they even regarded the shepherds as wicked people; as happened with the tax collectors, whom the Jews placed among the sinners. Which contempt should also remind the believers of their calling: that God has not called many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble (on which the proud Egyptians were accustomed to boast): but that He has chosen the ignoble of the world and the despised, and that which is nothing; that He might bring to nothing that which is something (1 Corinthians 1:26, 28). Just as then also all kinds of evil are commonly spoken of them (Matthew 5:11). In contrast, the Lord gives them a particularly rich inheritance in the spiritual realm, the green pastures of His precious mysteries, upon which He grazes them, and where He leads them to the gentle waters of His glorious refreshments of the spirit (Psalm 23:1–3).

->Israel’s dwelling in Egypt / and the great hunger therein.<-

THEN Joseph came and announced it to Pharaoh and spoke: My father and my brothers / along with their flocks and their cattle / and all that they have / are come from the land of Canaan; and behold, they are in the land of Goshen.
2. And he took from among his youngest brothers five men / and presented them before Pharaoh.
3. Then Pharaoh spoke to his brothers: What is your business? And they spoke to Pharaoh: Your servants are shepherds / both we and our fathers.
4. Furthermore they spoke to Pharaoh: We are come to reside in the land; - because there was no pasture for the sheep / which your servants have. For the hunger is heavy in the land of Canaan. So let your servants now dwell in the land of Goshen!

<gloss>
v. 1. Joseph observed here his duty / to announce his father and his brothers to the King; and at the same time demonstrated his humility / in that he, in his high station, was not ashamed of his family / who were occupied with livestock breeding, which was despised among the Egyptians / and that he let his brothers freely confess this.

As a type <note>In biblical interpretation, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament seen as a foreshadowing of Jesus Christ.</note> of the Savior / who is also not ashamed / to call us his brothers. Hebrews 2:11.

v. 2. Joseph wanted to present Jacob because of his venerable age / and only half of his brothers / whether it be from the oldest or youngest / because both can be understood / although it is more probable / that it was the youngest / or at least from the oldest and youngest / so that from their appearance the rest could be judged / and among them his true brother / Benjamin / was present / so that Pharaoh might show them his great favor for him / which should also move them to greater reverence for Joseph.

v. 3. Pharaoh asks them first about their business / with which they are accustomed to nourish themselves: which should also be the foremost concern of the authorities / that they receive industrious people into their lands / and no useless or lazy people / who are only a burden to others.

v. 4. 6. Dwell in the land of Goshen) It was very important to Joseph / that they might obtain their dwelling there. For the best pasture was there; they remained thereby removed from the royal court and the most prominent Egyptian cities / and that much closer to the land of Canaan. And for that reason there was at the same time a special Divine Providence <note>original: "Vorsehung GOttes"</note> therein / to the great advantage of the Hebrews / with a view toward their future return to Canaan. For if they had lived on the other side at the outermost borders of the land of Egypt / or even deep within the land / toward the south / they would have had to press through the middle of the Egyptians during their departure from Egypt: which they would likely never have dared so easily; since they were by nature fearful / and had already experienced the hardness of the Egyptians long enough.

One must not, however, think / that / because the land of Goshen had been assigned to them as a dwelling / they lived in it alone. For the land was already inhabited before them / and now they and the Egyptians lived among one another. Why else would they have needed / according to Exodus 12 / to mark the posts of their doors with the blood of the Passover lamb / so that the destroying angel might pass by? And how could they have, at the end of their hurried departure / when the Egyptians drove them out / borrowed silver and gold vessels and clothes from their Egyptian neighbors?
</gloss>

<column-break/>

5. And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph and said: Your father and your brothers are come to you;
6. The land of Egypt is before your face: Settle your father and your brothers in the best place of the land; let them dwell in the land of Goshen. And if you know / that there are capable men among them / then set them as overseers over the livestock / over those which I have.

<gloss>
v. 6. Set them as overseers) This will truly happen in the latter times / that the Jews who have become believers in Christ will be set as princes over the cities of the heathens and in Egypt: just as Daniel and his fellow confessors / Shadrach / Meshach and Abednego / were set in a foreshadowing over the offices in Babylon.

v. 9. Living / and yet short / Jacob presents his life’s course here / as he describes it under the image of a pilgrimage <note>original: "Pilgrimschafft"</note>.

It certainly has something significant behind it / and is not just an empty play on words of a boasting funeral orator / when Jacob here in such great earnestness at the audience of such a powerful King calls his entire life’s course nothing other than a pilgrimage.

Just as the words of the wise in their power are spears and nails / which press and penetrate: so also does this word point to a very deep mystery of the truth.

Insofar as man had stood firm in the divine trial / and had not deviated from God’s love; he could have eaten from the tree of life on the blessed earth in Paradise and lived eternally. But after his mind became ungodly, false, and earthly in the Fall; this is a sensible kind of punishment for him / that he must live in a mortal hut <note>The "mortal hut" or "tabernacle" is a common metaphor for the human body in pietistic literature.</note> on the earth cursed by God outside of Paradise.

Now if God had not shortened the life of fallen man / but had let him live miserably forever; this would be the most terrible vengeance and pain for us poor humans.

There, burning love moved the Creator / to remove the fallen Adam immediately after the Fall from the tree of life / so that he would not eat of it and live eternally / Chapter 3:22. but that there would finally be an end to this temporal misery.

Thus we are to look upon our short pilgrim-life as a mystery of divine love and a highly precious order / whereby both the punishment of the Fall is softened and shortened / and also the drive and pull toward the true fatherland is powerfully sharpened. In a word: There is unspeakable wisdom / faithfulness and truth of God / hidden beneath it / when even believers must look upon their life as a pilgrim’s path.
</gloss>

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLVII.</header>

# The days of the years of my pilgrimage / are one hundred and thirty years / few

With this word about "pilgrimage," what else is Jacob saying but this: recognize God’s holy ordinance and arrangement / which He made with him and all people after the Fall / that they should be as pilgrims / foreign to this entirely earthly kingdom and withdrawn from it in spirit / looking instead toward a completely different homeland? It is God’s good counsel / that this outer life should pass quickly as something secondary / so that no one might seek or find anything true / eternal / or satisfying within it. Consequently / on the contrary / an entirely different and eternal foundation for a heavenly life must be laid in the midst of this present life. This is the pure intention of God / which He taught and confirmed to Jacob and all believers through His Spirit throughout.

Whoever is earnest with Jacob / in seeking to find a true building from God and a house not made with hands in heaven; he will always let this be his first and last priority / that he becomes a stranger to the creaturely world in the depths of his heart / and the creaturely world becomes a stranger to him / and that he learns to live on the earth as one / who possesses nothing of it as his own through his love.

But this requires much watching and casting away / so that through faith with Abraham / Isaac / and Jacob / one clings solely to the eternal good / and constantly turns away earthly thoughts / senses / and desires / drowning them in the death of Christ. One must continually be baptized with His baptism / and learn to overcome the earthly mind in His pure Spirit. Then one walks with Him on the lonely pilgrim’s road toward home.

This "pilgrim-mindset" must be practiced and renewed every hour and every moment: otherwise, the end usually becomes worse than the beginning / and one soon settles firmly again into what one had scarcely left behind with the will. Therefore, we must always flee out of this Sodom with our desires.

And to this end, it will be very beneficial / if we especially take to heart more often / how short our pilgrimage is / and how

**Few** — (the days of the years) One might think / such a reminder would not be necessary; because everyone surely knows / that he cannot live forever. But Jacob also sought to give his heart to wisdom in this / that he might know the number of his days; for which prudence David so longingly prayed in <note>original: "Ps. 39 / 4"</note> Psalm 39:4.

It is very remarkable / that Jacob here names such a great age of 130 years / such as is no longer common today / and yet calls the same only "few days." Wisdom had taught him / to count all his time as nothing compared to eternity / and consequently to seek eternity rightly even within time / as the greatest thing within the smallest.

If even before God a thousand years are like a day that has passed / and if one day in the Lord's courts is better than a thousand days spent elsewhere without God; then a true pilgrim must necessarily hold onto eternity in the midst of transitory time / and learn to find his time again within it.

Even if someone lived for many long days / time is to him nothing more than time / and no blessed eternity / unless it has been spent in God. Just as Jacob had to recognize the "fewness" of his days / even though he had lived twice as long / as is common nowadays; they remained in his eyes "few days." He made nothing of length or quantity / but had learned in the school of wisdom / how a life of many years is not venerable / nor to be measured by the number of years / but rather that understanding is the grey hair of men / and an undefiled life is the true stature of old age. <note>original: "Weish. 4 / 8. 9"</note> Wisdom of Solomon 4:8-9. Yet, he did not despise God’s blessing / when He adds many years to a person: rather, he only knew / that all thinking / speaking / and doing at all times / would be as much as nothing / if it were not built upon eternity and found again therein.

Abraham lived to 175 / and Isaac to 180 years old. One could cite many reasons for this: but the most probable is the

<margin>
Hebrews 11:13.
(a) Job 9:25.
</margin>

# and evil (a) have been the days of the years of my life / and have not reached the days of the years of the lives of my fathers / in the days of their pilgrimages.

10.

In the same sense, he also called his lifetime "Evil Days." Not as if God or he himself had made them evil through an evil life. For he had indeed walked in the world with all good conscience. Rather, he wanted to remind himself and the King / how one must not make a paradise or a kingdom of heaven or an eternal thing out of this earthly life / insofar as it stands in nature and in the Fall / even if one could live in it regally and according to all one's own will. For it remains by the first judgment of the Creator after the Fall / that man must eat his bread in the sweat of his face: and this is again from a most loving counsel and purpose of God / so that our eternal spirit might grow weary of this miserable life / and become hungry for a better one.

For such a blessed purpose / even for a faithful Jacob, the days must be "evil," so that we might learn to seek the blessed eternity all the more eagerly.

But the days of Jacob and his followers are "evil" both inwardly and outwardly.

They are evil enough from the outside / because of the manifold misery / which tends to fall daily upon the flesh. Therefore /

Even if a man lived many years / his soul is not satisfied by it / and the most apparent things are often the most vain / and an evil plague on top of it; as Solomon’s Ecclesiastes powerfully expresses throughout.

Nevertheless, the outward misery is to be counted as little compared to the inward / which Jacob may have felt painfully enough through so many various temptations: namely, the innate corruption <note>A reference to original sin or the fallen nature of humanity.</note>.

Meanwhile, Jacob speaks very deliberately / when he says / the days of his life were "evil," but not his life itself / or the walk he led before God. He thereby assured the King / that he did not regret his faith and obedience: because the same belongs not to time / but to eternity.

This is also the essential foundation for all believers in the midst of the greatest tribulations; namely, that all their evil days give birth to nothing but good for them / though under much struggle and suffering.

Innate corruption and the resulting evil days cannot and should not hinder us / from enjoying good days or a blessed eternity in God in the middle of time / if only we learn to live in the faith of the Son of God.

<margin>Hebrews 11:9, 16.</margin>
From this, faith is grounded in the spirit / as often as evil days are felt: in that it knows / that its labor in the Lord will not be in vain. Just as Jacob remained comforted in all his evil days / as a co-heir of the promise / who desired a better fatherland / namely, a heavenly one.

O how a God-seeking mind / in such hope / can give itself so gently to contentment through all evil days / since such eternal glory hangs upon a short suffering!

Ah, let no one consider that time or day as "good" / in which one can live according to one's own will / in pleasure / honor / and abundance!

Ah, let everyone endure as a good soldier of Christ / and be content even with his evil days / wrap himself in patience / and believe that it is highly necessary for his flesh / thus to be exercised and proven with Jacob.

Let one not lose oneself in apparent vanities / but rather keep / as a called pilgrim of the earth and citizen of heaven / the spirit lifted up to God his origin: thus one brings a joyful conscience even into old age / and the blessed eternity finally swallows up the short time of suffering with infinite jubilation and triumph / as it will be an eternal day without darkness or change in the infinite light of divine glory.

**Not reached the years of my fathers)** Abraham lived to 175 / and Isaac to 180 years.

Jacob's continuous and manifold sufferings / from his childhood until late old age.

<note>v. 10. Jacob blessed Pharaoh at both his entrance and his exit; this was the most important reward Pharaoh could receive for his kindness. Kings and princes should also strive to obtain such healing wishes from the godly, which might assist them in their great responsibility before God and in the very important office of wisely governing land and people. See Daniel 6:21. 1 Timothy 2:2,3.
There is also a basis in Jacob’s blessing—as a prophetic image—that Egypt will be blessed in the same way through the Jews who are accepted back as God’s people in the spiritual fulfillment. And when that happens, it will be said: "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance!" <note>original: "Gesegnet bist du Egypten mein Volck / und du Assur meiner Hände Werck / und du Israel mein Erbe!"</note> and the altar of the Lord shall be in the midst of the land of Egypt. Isaiah 19.</note>

<note>v. 11. Land of Rameses) This was the best part of the land of Goshen, which received this name from the city of Rameses, built by the Hebrews during the time of their hard servitude (Exodus 1:11), and referring to the surrounding area of that city. It does not mean the land was already called that when Jacob arrived in Egypt; rather, it was called so later when Moses wrote this book, which many believe happened after the Exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt. Thus, the meaning of the words would be: Joseph gave them an inheritance in the land which is now called Rameses.</note>

<note>v. 12. Provided for his father) Joseph had been raised and nourished by his father for 17 years, and here he in turn nourished his old father for 17 years: in this, Providence sometimes reveals such a wonderful and equal repayment (Chapter 37:2; here v. 9 and 28), which is recorded for all faithful children to follow, so they may repay their elderly parents in kind, which carries a great blessing. 1 Timothy 5:4.</note>

<note>v. 13. Became quite senseless) This is the most terrifying aspect of heavy national plagues: the judgment of hardening and despair, where people do not yield to the rod of God with composure and humble confession of their sins, nor do they plead for mercy from His righteous judgment through true repentance. Such "senselessness" is thoughtfully presented in Isaiah 8:21, 22 and Revelation 9:20, 21. Yet it was still a grace of God that they were kept from public rebellion and the violent breaking open of storehouses by such a wise ruler as Joseph, and were maintained within the proper bounds of obedience. Therefore, such wise counselors and rulers are to be regarded as a great blessing from God.</note>

<header>The First Book of Moses. Chapter XLVII.</header>

21. And as for the people, he removed them to the cities from one end of the borders of Egypt even to the other end thereof.
22. Only the land of the priests he did not buy; for the priests had a fixed portion assigned to them by Pharaoh, and they ate their fixed portion which Pharaoh had given them: therefore they did not sell their land.

---

"That the priests did not sell their land to Pharaoh," writes Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian known for his allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> thoughtfully, "indicates that they were worse than the rest of the Egyptians; because of the favorable standing they held with Pharaoh, they suffered no change. Indeed, just as the Lord speaks to those who have increased in faith and holiness, saying: *I call you not servants, but friends*; so Pharaoh speaks to those who stand in the priesthood of perdition: *I do not say that you should be servants or serfs, but friends.* Do you wish to know the difference between the priests of God and the priests of Pharaoh? Pharaoh gives his priests land; but the Lord gives His priests no portion on earth, but says to them: *I am your portion.* Take heed of this, all you priests, and see what a difference there is among priests! Let it not appear to those who have their portion on earth and are devoted to earthly things as though they were priests of Pharaoh rather than priests of the Lord. For it is Pharaoh who desires his priests to possess something of the earth, to cultivate the field and not the soul, and to attend to the land and not the Word of God. But what Christ our Lord commanded His priests, let us hear. *Whosoever does not renounce all that he possesses,* He says, *cannot be my disciple.* I tremble as I speak these words! For in this way, I am before all—I say, I am my own accuser: I pronounce my own condemnation! Christ will not recognize as His disciple anyone whom He sees possessing something and who does not renounce all that he has. And what do we do? How can we constantly either read this ourselves or explain it to the people? We, who not only do not renounce what we possess, but also gladly wish to have that which we never had before we came to Christ. Or should we, because our conscience convicts us, hide and not declare what is written? For my part, I do not wish to be guilty of a double crime. I confess it openly before all the people; I confess that this is so written! Though I am well aware that I have not yet fulfilled it. But let it at least serve as a reminder to us, that we may hasten to fulfill it! Let us hasten to pass from those priests of Pharaoh, who possess something on earth, to the priests of the Lord, who have no portion on earth, but whose portion is the Lord! For such a one was he who said: *As being poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.* <note>The author is quoting the Apostle Paul from 2 Corinthians 6:10.</note> Paul is the one who glories in this. Do you wish to hear what Peter also says of himself? Rather, hear what he confesses together with John: *Silver and gold have I none; but what I have, I give to you: In the name of Jesus Christ, rise up and walk.* See what treasures the priests of Christ have! See what great gifts those who have nothing can bestow! Earthly possession cannot share such treasures. We have compared priests with priests: let us now also compare the Egyptian people with the Israelite people, by 
<meta>catchword: occasion of the words</meta>

<column-break/>

23. Then Joseph said to the people: "Behold, I have bought you and your land today for Pharaoh; lo, here is seed for you, and you shall sow the land."
24. "And it shall come to pass that of the harvest you shall give the fifth part to Pharaoh, and four parts shall be your own, for seed of the field and for your food, and for those in your houses, and for food for your little ones."
25. And they said: "You have saved our lives; let us find grace in the sight of my lord, and we will be Pharaoh's servants."
26. Thus [it became a law].

---

<margin>v. 24. Fifth part</margin> "The Egyptian people give Pharaoh the fifth part, while the Israelite people give the tenth part to the priests. See how the Holy Scripture rests upon such a deep foundation even in this matter! See how the people of the Egyptians deliver their tax in the number five! By this are indicated the five senses, which the fleshly people serve. The Egyptians hold to visible and bodily things. The Israelite people, however, honor the number ten, the number of perfection. They received the ten words of the Law, and thereby accepted such mysteries as are unknown to this world. But in the New Testament as well, the number ten is equally venerable: just as the fruit of the Spirit is declared to be expressed in ten virtues."

"Recognize from this the difference between the Egyptians and the people of Israel, and examine yourself, to which people you belong. If you still serve the senses of the flesh, you pay your tribute in the number five, and you look upon what is visible and temporal, and not upon what is invisible and eternal; so mark by this that you belong among the Egyptian people. But if you have the Ten Commandments and the aforementioned number ten of the New Testament constantly before your eyes as your aim, and yield the tenth therein; then you are a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit."

While Joseph had previously set the fifth part to be given to Pharaoh in the good years (Chapter 41:34), he here ordains the fifth as a permanent right; he then divides the remaining four parts (v. 24) in such a way that the burden finally seems to have been bearable. Indeed, he even accepted them, the subjects, as servants and serfs according to their own will, which was quite common among the heathens under violent regimes. In this, he proceeded according to the custom and worldly wisdom prevailing in earthly kingdoms, whereby he nevertheless still observed equity to some extent.

However, if we were to consider ourselves in our times as the Kingdom of Christ—who indeed still tolerates worldly authorities for the sake of great imperfection, maintaining them for the punishment of the wicked and the protection of the godly—then these authorities, who also confess Christ as their Lord, should lead a gentle regime over their fellow brothers as Christian authorities. And since such a thing cannot be established without taxes and tolls, these should be bearable. By no means, however, would they be authorized to keep their fellow Christians (whom Christ has made free) as servants and serfs, which was already forbidden to the Jews in the Old Testament (Leviticus 25:39, 43) and which the Holy Spirit expressly forbids to believers in the New Testament: *You are bought with a price; do not become the servants of men.* (1 Corinthians 7:23; see also Joshua 8:36). Thus, for this same reason, it is forbidden to those lords who wish to be Christians to make their fellow Christians into serfs or servants. And if they were to claim that most subjects are not Christians, they are nonetheless recognized as such, at least outwardly, through general Baptism and the Lord’s Supper; therefore, godly authorities should apply themselves to advancing them toward becoming true Christians. Those who act to the contrary must fear that what can be concluded from Revelation 13:10 will come upon them. Just as he who unlawfully leads into captivity shall go into captivity; and if anyone kills with the sword, he must be killed with the sword: so also he who leads into serfdom shall be led back into serfdom.

<margin>Exodus 1:7.</margin>
<margin>28.</margin> And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years: so the whole age of Jacob was an hundred forty and seven years.
<margin>29.</margin> And the time drew nigh that Israel must die: and he called his son Joseph, and said unto him, If now I have found grace in thy sight, put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh <note>original: "Hüffte". This ancient gesture was a solemn form of oath-taking, often associated with the covenant of circumcision and the promise of future offspring.</note>, and deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt:
<margin>(a) Gen 24:3.</margin>
<margin>30.</margin> But I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt, and bury me in their burying-place. And he said, I will do as thou hast said.
<margin>31.</margin> And he said, Swear unto me. And he swore unto him. And Israel bowed himself upon the bed's head.
<margin>1 Kings 1:47.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 28.</margin> Thus, the twenty-two years that Jacob had to spend in great sorrow over the loss of his dear, pious son Joseph were richly compensated by the goodness of God through these seventeen years in Egypt, during which he was able to delight in him once more.
<margin>v. 29.</margin> Jacob wished to bind his son, who stood in such high esteem, to a matter very close to his heart with such a friendly and humble address; and further with an oath, in order to show his earnestness all the more, and also to remove any envy from the Egyptians, as if Joseph did not deem them worthy enough to bury his father in their land.
<margin>v. 30.</margin> The reason for his desire—and later for Joseph’s own desire—to be buried in Canaan was, on one hand, the foundation of their faith regarding the future exodus of their descendants from Egypt and the taking of the Promised Land; on the other hand, it was a sign of the expected Messiah, who was to be born in that same land. Not to mention that after Christ passed away on the cross, many bodies of the saints arose and appeared (Matthew 27:52–53). There is no doubt that the holy patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph—were among them. Thus, perhaps by a secret divine impulse (whether or not he fully knew why), Jacob may have yearned for this burial place.
<margin>v. 31.</margin> Now that Joseph had bound himself by oath according to his will, Jacob raised his head upon the bed and bowed, undoubtedly out of grateful recognition of God’s gracious providence. Though he had to move to a foreign land for important reasons, he would in death return to the bones of his dear, faithful fathers to rest with them, to share in the blessed resurrection there, and to attain the true and eternal heavenly inheritance, of which the earthly one was only a pledge.
However, since in the New Testament the earth is the Lord’s everywhere, and all that matters is the union of hearts in life, it is not strictly necessary to yearn for the physical grave of one’s parents or other dear friends. Rather, it is enough if we have been rightly united in heart here; then we shall be together with Christ in spirit after our departure.

<column-break/>

# Chapter XLVIII.
->Israel’s Blessing of the Sons of Joseph.<-

And it came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick: and he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.
<margin>2.</margin> And one told Jacob, and said, Behold, thy son Joseph cometh unto thee: and Israel strengthened himself, and sat upon the bed.

<margin>3. And</margin>

---

<margin>v. 2. Israel strengthened himself)</margin> That is: through faith, he drew a special power to himself, as he wished to bless his children and grandchildren by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; so that he might be strong in body and soul to pronounce such a blessing over them. He gathered all the powers of his soul into the evangelical promise of the "Seed of the Woman" <note>This refers to the first prophecy of the Messiah in Genesis 3:15.</note> and prepared himself rightly for the task—as Luther speaks of this—and thus powerfully pronounced the intended blessing in faith (Hebrews 11:21).
The greatest distress arises, as is known, in untrained souls when they feel no, or very little, power of faith in the Lord Jesus within themselves. They do not think, however, that they are so near to the Fountain of Blessing, which requires nothing more than the diligence of drawing from it. And the Lord wishes to impart even this drawing to them most powerfully through the Holy Spirit.
In no other way can God Himself, the eternal Fountain, pronounce a single blessing—let alone bring it forth and let it flow into and upon mankind—except through this same eternal Spirit. How then could Jacob, or any human, do otherwise than through the spirit of faith?
From this it is evident that all spiritual blessing is given solely through the Holy Spirit on God’s side and taken on our side.
Practiced senses also perceive, when reading such words of blessing, by what a mild and loving Spirit of Blessing they were spoken. Jacob became, as it were, intoxicated in spirit by the joy of faith regarding the future, in Luther’s words. And if a person is to pronounce a blessing over others according to God’s mind, he must certainly be filled with the Holy Spirit, who blesses through him, lest it result in a miserable sham.
But we have a most precious promise from the Savior Himself: that we shall not believe in Him in vain, but shall be so powerfully filled with His Spirit that the blessing may flow over to others and multiply (John 7:38–39).
Let everyone then look for the right strength, the spirit of faith, and place the mouth of their longing in their heart at the Fountain of the Living One, to taste the streams rich in blessing, so that their soul may be strengthened and refreshed.

3. And Jacob said unto Joseph: | God Almighty appeared unto me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and blessed me;
4. And he said unto me: Behold, I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a multitude of people; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession.
5. And now thy two sons, who were born unto thee in the land of Egypt before I came unto thee into Egypt, are mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, even as Reuben and Simeon.

---

Thus did the providence of God rule, as the end of Jacob drew near, that he should bear witness to his faith and his hope in the promise before his death to his children, and thereby encourage them also to have faith in this promise. Whereupon, in a prophetic spirit, he had to announce beforehand the spiritual state of his physical and spiritual seed—the Israel of God—who were to be accepted as children of Abraham from among the Gentiles, until the coming of Christ, who was to be born of Judah; indeed, even into His glorious kingdom. And so he first reported the blessing which God had bestowed upon him for the very first time when he had departed from his father, and on the journey had received the vision of the heavenly ladder, and with it the glorious promise of God regarding the land of Canaan and the spreading of his seed, and then also of the Seed who was to be the source of all blessing: Christ. (Chap. 28). This blessing he could now share again with his sons, according to the wonderful governance of God, which was to take place among them according to their various tribes and thus also in various occurrences in the meantime.

<margin>v. 3. Blessed me)</margin> If we wish to truly enjoy the blessing, it truly requires more than a fleeting devotion or mere imagination. Some indeed bring their vessels to the well of blessing at times—when they confess, read, and the like at certain seasons. But they soon run away from the well again and delight themselves in other things: therefore the blessing of Christ does not take root in them.

But what is lacking now other than the **new birth**? <note>original: "neuen Gebuhr". A Pietist theological term referring to spiritual regeneration or being "born again."</note> for which one does not constantly let the Holy Spirit work within themselves with all persistence, asking, pleading, and watching, so that one may, like Jacob, attain the right of the firstborn and thus not only taste something of the blessing but actually inherit it.

<margin>v. 5. If Jacob's grandsons were to have his blessing,</margin> they had to actually be made into his children, as Jacob demands here beforehand: to show that we must come right near to God and become partakers of His divine nature if we wish to be heirs. Since children are the rightful heirs, and heirs are counted as children.

In a mysterious way, this adoption into childhood may remind us of the high grace of the New Covenant, where God, out of pure mercy, so certainly receives back into His covenant those who truly believe in His Son, and grafts them into His divine nature as if they were His natural and not fallen children: just as Jacob makes the two children of Joseph equal to his first and own sons and grafts them into the main root of his tribe.

By this, he gave Joseph the right of the firstborn in view of a double inheritance, as his two sons were to be counted not as his grandsons, but as two of his sons—specifically as the two oldest, which were Reuben and Simeon. See 1 Chron. 5:1 and Num. 1:32, 34. And so the secret number of the 12 tribes was restored, as no earthly inheritance was to be given to the tribe of Levi. <note>The tribe of Levi was dedicated to the priesthood and received no land allotment, so the "double portion" given to Joseph's two sons maintained the number of landed tribes at twelve.</note>

Therefore, when godly parents have been deemed worthy of a blessing from GOD in their guidance, they can also share the same again with their children; and that according to divine governance, which they must request in spirit from GOD, so as to also announce to them their various future events.

<column-break/>

6. And thy issue, which thou begettest after them, shall be thine, and shall be called after the name of their brethren in their inheritance.
7. And as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died by me in the land of Canaan in the way, when yet there was but a little way to come unto Ephrath: and I buried her there in the way of Ephrath; (the same is Bethlehem.)
8. And Israel beheld Joseph's sons, and said: Who are these?
9. And Joseph said unto his father: They are my sons, whom God hath given me in this place. And he said: Bring them, I pray thee, unto me, and I will bless them.
10. Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not see. And he brought them near unto him; and he kissed them, and embraced them.
11. And Israel said unto Joseph: I had not thought to see thy face: and, lo, God hath shewed me also thy seed.
12. And Joseph brought them out from between his knees, and he bowed himself with his face to the earth.

<meta>catchword: 13. Then</meta>

---

<margin>v. 9, 11.</margin> Believers recognize their children as a gift from GOD; which they then also strive to bring up for the honor of GOD and to give them back to Him, so that they may arrive at His knowledge. Ps. 128:3, 4. Since they find, among other things, that they should praise to their children all the benefits of GOD, which they also generally received so unexpectedly, and thus they make it their concern to request a blessing from GOD for them. They must, however, let God take charge in this, how He wishes to order it with their children, and not look therein according to their own favor or some privilege in nature, but leave it to God's wise and just governance, how He often tends to prefer the younger and weaker in spiritual goods over the others.
