# Chapter I. The Second Book of Moses (Exodus)

### Page 285

15. And the King of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, of whom one was named **Shiphrah**, and the other **Puah**;
16. And he said: When you assist the Hebrew women in the pains of childbirth, and see them upon the birth stool; if it is a son, then kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live.

<margin>v. 15. Spoke)</margin> This occurred at the prompting and instigation of an Egyptian priest, who had prophesied: One will be born among the children of Israel who, when he is grown, will cause the Egyptians much sorrow and make the Israelites great! (a)

<margin>(a) Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 2, Chapter 5.</margin> The Jews recount it thus: in the 130th year after the Israelites' arrival in Egypt and the 60th after Joseph’s death, this Pharaoh dreamed that a man stood before him with a scale in his hand. In one bowl lay all of Egypt—men, women, and children—and in the other bowl was a single boy, yet he outweighed all of Egypt. The wise men called to counsel were terrified by this, and finally one of his great lords gave the interpretation: that a great misfortune was announced for their kingdom. The single boy would be a Jew who would distress Egypt with much misfortune and many plagues. To prevent this, the best course would be to kill all the infant sons of the Israelites. <note>Josephus was a first-century Romano-Jewish historian whose works were often used by later Bible commentators to provide historical and legendary context.</note>

**Shiphrah — Puah**) These seem to have been the most prominent among them, placed in charge of the others, as there must have been many midwives for such a large nation.

However, this can also beautifully symbolize the *Old* and *New Testaments*, the *Law* and the *Gospel*, which perform the service of midwives in the spiritual rebirth of a person. Pharaoh, however, seeks to instill a perverted sense and understanding in those who handle and work with these Testaments, in order to hinder and weaken the life of the spirit.

<margin>v. 16.</margin> It is a strange thing that hatred against these newly arrived people does not only ignite against the people themselves. One also wants to prevent that which they bring forth, and extinguish it immediately at birth. How many people are there—even among those who are "enlightened"—who strive to turn such beginning souls away from these paths! Though they are like kings of the earth and established in God to be the fathers of these souls, they nonetheless do not cease to oppose them; for they think (b) they are doing a good work. But if they will not agree with this most holy and certain way of *Gelassenheit* <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism and Pietism, meaning a state of surrender, composure, and letting go of one's own will to God</term>, they must at least be careful not to condemn it; they must also allow those who are beginning to happily taste this path to enter into it, so that they do not bring the warning of Jesus Christ upon their own necks (c): that they themselves will not enter the kingdom, and they forbid those who desire to enter from coming in.

<margin>(b) John 16:2.</margin>
<margin>(c) Luke 11:52.</margin>

The male children represent the strong souls who are capable of God's unsearchable guidance; the girls are the image of weak and fearful people, who are too full of themselves and self-interest to surrender themselves to God in a way that is full of the Cross. These people are allowed to live, because one enjoys living with them. But the others are condemned to death, because self-love and selfish love cannot endure the magnanimity of pure love.

But also, the "flesh" and the carnal mind are indicated by the female; while the spirit and understanding—the heavenly mind that seeks what is above—are indicated by the male. The prince of this world, the King of Egypt, cannot tolerate this, but wants it killed. But he gladly lets the *flesh* live. For it is his will that people should be carnally minded.

Therefore, when you see people spending their lives in pleasures, seeking and loving earthly things, and occupied with the works of the flesh, think then: there the King of Egypt is killing the boys and letting the girls live.

But when one out of thousands turns to the Lord, seeks the eternal, looks upon the invisible, hates the lusts of the world and the flesh, loves moderation and abstinence, and practices the virtues of the spirit; he is persecuted by Pharaoh as a son, as a male heir, and his life is suppressed in every way. For he hates such "manly" figures and loves only the "womanly" ones.

<column-break/>

17. But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the King of Egypt had said to them, but let the infant sons live.
18. Then the King of Egypt called the midwives and said to them: Why do you do this, that you let the infant sons live?
19. And the midwives answered Pharaoh: that the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; for they are vigorous women: before the midwife comes to them, they have already given birth.
20. And...

<margin>v. 17. It is not possible to use the Law and Gospel for a bad purpose when they teach the fear of God and remain steadfast in it.</margin>

If we also fear God, we will not do what the prince of this world wants. He wants you to fulfill the will of the flesh, to love the world, and to strive for that which is on earth. But you, if you fear God and wish to be a midwife for your soul—if you wish to be helpful in its recovery—you will let the little boy live who is within you, namely the inward man; indeed, you will even cherish him and wait upon him.

Oftentimes, even those who are used as tools to turn grace-filled souls away from their paths are won over when they have the fear and love of God. They then not only preserve this heavenly life for others but also accept it themselves, considering their simple hearts and as a fruit of their teachability. Instead of taking the lives of such innocent sheep, they begin to walk with them in those same days: and God rewards them with His grace in such a way that they grow more and more in Him every day.

<margin>v. 19. Answered)</margin> They may well have spoken some truth, that various women had already given birth before their arrival; but they nonetheless concealed the true circumstances. Therefore, one must not use this to defend "service-lies" <note>original: "Dienst-Lügen" - white lies or lies told to perform a service or duty</note>, or suggest that one could represent a matter differently than it actually is, just because some part of it might be true or because one wants to achieve something good; let alone when one cunningly deceives another to their harm, which is all sin. For this reason, God did not do them good because of the lie, but because they feared Him. Similar unequal reports are read regarding Rahab in Joshua 2:5-6, David in 1 Samuel 21:2, and Elisha in 2 Kings 6:19.

Yet who knows whether the midwives did not reveal Pharaoh’s bloodthirsty counsel to the Jewish women, and thereby intentionally caused them to help each other in their need. In which case they would have spoken the full truth, that the Hebrew women had already given birth before the midwife came to them.

Vigorous women) *vivaces* <note>original Latin: "vivaces" - lively or long-lived</note>, lively. The Jews translate this as "midwives"; that they did not wait for the midwives because they themselves were as experienced and skilled as midwives: as the Chaldean Onkelos <note>The Targum Onkelos, an ancient Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah</note> rendered it; for they are wise and experienced in the art of midwifery, as Paulus Fagius <note>A 16th-century German Renaissance scholar of Hebrew</note> explains it. The Septuagint <note>original: "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> omitted it entirely. The Vulgate <note>The 4th-century Latin translation of the Bible</note> renders it: "For they have the knowledge of midwives." The Rabbis, such as Rashi, Ibn Ezra, etc., follow Luther’s interpretation.

### 15. And the king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives / of whom one was named Shiphrah / and the other Puah /

### 16. And said: When you help the Hebrew women in their labor / and see them upon the birth-stool; if it is a son / then kill him: but if it is a daughter / let her live.

<margin>v. 15. Spoke)</margin> This was done at the prompting and instigation of an Egyptian priest / who had prophesied: One will be born from the children of Israel / who / when he is grown / will cause the Egyptians much sorrow / and will make the Israelites great! (a)

The Jews tell it this way: they say that in the 130th year after the Israelites' arrival in Egypt and the 60th after Joseph's death, this Pharaoh dreamed / that a man stood before him with a scale in his hand / in one pan was all of Egypt / men / women and children / but in the other pan was a single boy / who yet outweighed all of Egypt. At this, the wise men called to counsel were terrified / and finally one of his great lords gave the interpretation; that by this a great misfortune was announced to their kingdom: the single boy would be a Jew / who would distress Egypt with much misfortune and many plagues. To prevent such a thing, it would be best / to kill all the little boys of the Israelites.

Shiphrah -- Puah) These seem to have been the most prominent / who were placed over the others. For there must have been many for such a great people.

But through this may also be symbolized the Old and New Testaments / the Law and the Gospel / which perform the service of midwives in spiritual rebirth. Pharaoh, however, seeks to instill in those / who handle and work in these matters / a perverse sense and understanding of them / in order to hinder and weaken the life of the spirit.

<margin>v. 16. It is a strange thing /</margin> that hatred against people who have come to stay does not end with the people themselves. One also wants to prevent that which they bring forth / and extinguish it right at its birth. How many people are there not / even among the enlightened / who strive to turn such beginning souls away from these paths! Although they are as kings of the earth / and established in GOD / to be the fathers of those souls; yet they do not cease to stand against them: thinking then (b) / that they are doing a good work. But if they will not agree with this most holy and certain way of Gelassenheit <note>A technical term in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness" or "letting go" to God's will.</note> / they must also take care / that they do not condemn it: they must also let those / who begin / to happily taste such a thing / enter into it; so that they do not bring the warning of Jesus Christ upon their own necks (c) / that they themselves will not enter the kingdom / and also forbid those / who desire to enter / from coming in.

The male children represent the strong souls who are fit for the unfathomable guidance of God: the girls are the image of weak and fearful people / who are too full of themselves and of self-interest / to surrender themselves to God in such a way / which is full of the Cross. These people are happy to let live; because they enjoy living with them. But the others are condemned to death; because self-love and selfish love cannot tolerate the magnanimity of pure love.

But also, by the female, the flesh and the carnal mind are indicated: by the male, however, the spirit and understanding / the heavenly mind / which / seeks what is above. The prince of this world / the king in Egypt / cannot tolerate this / but wants it killed. But the flesh he gladly lets live. For it is his will / that one

When you thus see people spending their lives in lusts / seeking and loving earthly things / and having their business in the works of the flesh; then think / that there the king in Egypt is killing the little boys / and letting the girls live.

But if one out of thousands turns to the Lord / seeks the eternal / looks upon the invisible / hates the lusts of the world and the flesh / loves moderation and detachment / and practices the virtues of the spirit; he will be persecuted by Pharaoh as a son / as a male heir / and his life suppressed in every way: because he hates such manly figures / and only loves the feminine ones.

### 17. But the midwives feared GOD / and did not do as the king of Egypt had told them / but let the little boys live.

### 18. Then the king of Egypt called the midwives / and spoke to them: Why do you do this / that you let the little boys live?

### 19. And the midwives answered Pharaoh: because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women; for they are strong women: before the midwife comes to them / they have given birth.

### 20. And

<margin>v. 17. It will not work /</margin> for what purpose one wishes to misuse the Law and the Gospel. For they teach the fear of GOD / and remain unchangeable in that.

If we also fear God / we will not do / what the prince of this world wants. He wants / that you should fulfill the will of the flesh / love the world / and strive after that which is on earth. But you / if you fear God / and want to serve as a midwife to your soul / if you want to be helpful to its recovery / then you will let the little boy live / who is in you / namely the inward man; yes, you will even suckle him and tend to him.

Often even those very ones are won over / when they have the fear and love of GOD / who are used / to turn graced souls away from their paths: so that they then not only preserve such heavenly life for these / but also accept it themselves in consideration of their simple heart / and as a fruit of their teachability. Instead of taking the life of such innocent sheep / they begin to walk in those same paths with them: and GOD rewards them with His graces in such a way / that they grow daily more and more in Him.

<margin>v. 19. Answered)</margin> They may well have spoken some truth / that various women had already given birth before their arrival: but they nevertheless concealed the true circumstances. And therefore one must not defend "service-lies" <note>White lies or lies told to perform a service or duty.</note> from this / or that one could present a matter differently / than it actually is / if only some part of it might be true / even if one wants to bring about something good with it; let alone when one craftily deceives another to his harm: all of which is sin; therefore GOD also did not do good to them [because of the lie] / but because they feared Him. Similar uneven reports are also read of Rahab in Joshua 2:5, 6; David in 1 Samuel 21:2; and Elisha in 2 Kings 6:19.

Yet who knows / whether the midwives did not reveal the bloodthirsty counsel of Pharaoh to the Jewish women / and thereby intentionally caused / them to help one another in their need. In which case they would have spoken the full truth therein / that the Hebrew women had already given birth / before the midwife came to them.

Strong women) <term>חיות</term> <note>Hebrew: Chayot</note> lively, vigorous. The Jews translate it as "midwives"; they say they had not waited for the midwives / because they themselves were as experienced and skillful as midwives: as the Chaldean Onkelos <note>The author of a famous Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah.</note> rendered it; for they are wise / experienced in the midwife's art / as Paulus Fagius <note>A 16th-century Hebraist.</note> explains it. 20. And God did well to the midwives / and the people multiplied and became very mighty.
21. And it happened / because the midwives feared God / that He provided houses for them.
22. Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying: Every son that is born / you shall cast into the river; but every daughter you shall let live.

---

<margin>v. 20. 21.</margin> The midwives here obeyed God more than men; as is our bounden duty: and therefore God also showed them goodness / in that He protected them from the King's wrath / and otherwise showered them with blessings. For those little boys / whom they permitted to live / God built houses / as He preserved them in life / and bestowed upon them numerous families. See 1 Sam. 2:35, 2 Sam. 7:11. This benefit refers to the boys / since the Hebrew text uses the masculine / and not the feminine / gender / <term>להם</term> <note>original: "lahem" - a masculine plural pronoun</note> / and thus must not be applied to the midwives / as is commonly done; since they / as is usual <note>implying their age or station</note> / were no longer accustomed to having children.

This beautiful saying / that God built them houses / shows / that He Himself works on their spiritual building: by placing them in the way of suffering; which is the reward of the good / which one has done in the active way / which is granted to all those / who have enough humility / to let themselves be led into the same / when the Spirit of God calls them to it.

<margin>v. 22. Pharaoh commanded)</margin> This cruel command corresponds with that of Herod / when he had the innocent children killed. Matt. 2:16. Therefore the terrible judgment of God also fell upon both: of which all bloodthirsty and hard tyrants make themselves guilty / according to Ps. 55:23, Wisdom 6:6-7.

Persecution would be too sweet / if it did not go further than some suffering. Pharaoh / the prince of this world / must use all his inventions / to root out this people beloved by God. Therefore he commands his own / who are the wicked and the devils / to kill all the little boys / that would be born / to stifle the inner way right at its birth in the souls / who set out upon it: by making them die / either to grace / through all too hard temptations; or in regard to their way / when he drives them so far / that they / out of mistrust and fear of perishing upon it / abandon it; or even to make them suspicious through the loss of their good name. And this happens, alas, all too often. One throws such souls either into the river; which is a place of inevitable death: or one puts them in extreme danger. But the little girls / who are the people standing in their active blessings <note>referring to those focused on outward religious works rather than inner spiritual growth</note> / oh, those are not offended at all! They are safe in their ways; they are subject to no persecution / no temptation nor evil gossip: but on the contrary, one seeks to build them up upon the remains and ruined or torn-down wall-pieces of the others. "Be very careful," it is said, "about attacking these people who are very strong in themselves" / (who, however, are in truth very weak / ) "and let them stand before us!"

This was a foreboding of the martyrdom of so many little saints / which would follow the birth of Jesus Christ.

But when this mother sees / that one must yield to force; she chooses rather, as a well-instructed woman, to rely on—

# The II. Chapter.
->The Birth and Preservation of Moses.<-

AND there went a man from the house of Levi / and took a daughter of Levi.
2. And the woman became pregnant / and bore a son: and when she saw him / that he was beautiful; she hid him for three months.
3. And when she could hide him no longer / she took for him a little chest of bulrushes / and smeared it with slime and pitch / and put the little boy in it / and laid him in the reeds by the bank of the river.
4. But his sister stood afar off / that she might learn / what would happen to him.
5. And—

---

<margin>v. 1. A man from the house of Levi)</margin> It was Levi's grandson / Amram / who had taken his father's sister / Jochebed / as his wife / Ch. 6:20, Num. 26:59. From which marriage Miriam and Aaron had been born previously / and then after this, Moses: whose beauty of body as well as of mind—

<margin>v. 2.</margin> —is indicated by the emphatic word "Good" / which properly belongs to God / and makes His virtues known. Therefore Stephen calls him "a fine child before God" / Acts 7:20. Which some also translate as "divine beauty" / and thus look to the mind / when something very lovely and friendly shines forth from the face: which beauty Paul also praises in Heb. 11:23. And indeed, in both places stands the word <term>ἀστεῖος</term> <note>original: "asteios" - meaning urbane, refined, or handsome</note>, with which the Athenians / to whom the word is attributed / wanted to make known / how they surpassed others in fine manners and / as one is accustomed to say / were polite and mannerly.

Since the persecution was already in full swing from Moses' birth / and the exodus only followed in his 80th year; one see from this / how long such heavy tribulations were hung over the children of Israel / whereas otherwise the heavy Diocletian persecution of the Christians lasted only ten years: through which God intended to make them truly "mellow" / so that they would yearn all the more earnestly for their redemption.

<margin>v. 4.</margin> It was indeed only right / that he / who was to be the leader and guide of the people of Providence / should himself be a child of Providence. This child, surrendered to the wild waves, had to become the shepherd of Israel. God / who governs everything through His wisdom and goodness / also gives this child much loveliness and grace / which took away from his mother all power to give him over to death. She preserves him as long as she can / in such a time when the death of many innocents accompanied the birth of Moses / who had to be the most perfect image of Jesus Christ:

This poor innocent is then thus given up: but his sister remains there to watch over Providence. What could she imagine / other than that the waves would soon take him away? Indeed, what else could one hope for this innocent, abandoned one / than death and the water as his grave? His death seemed so certain / that they even laid him alive in the coffin / from which God alone could deliver him.

—begin from the cradle / which was at the same time his coffin. One cannot say / whether his cradle was his coffin / or his coffin was his cradle. But God / who does not show the wonders of His providence until the moment of extreme need / lets him find life in the danger of death.

### 5. And the daughter of Pharaoh went down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along the riverside. And when she saw the little basket in the midst of the reeds, she sent her maidservant to fetch it.

### 6. And when she opened it, she saw the little boy; and behold, the boy wept. Then she had compassion for him, and said: This is one of the Hebrew children.

### 7. Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter: Shall I go and call a wet nurse for you from the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the little boy for you?

### 8. And Pharaoh’s daughter said to her: Go. And the young girl went and called the mother of the little boy.

### 9. Then Pharaoh’s daughter said to her: Take this little boy with you, and nurse him for me; and I will give you your wages. And the woman took the little boy and nursed him.

Wonderful Providence so arranged it that the King’s daughter herself had to carry out this preservation, and out of special affection adopt him as a son, so that he could be educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians: whereby he then became mighty in words and in deeds. Acts 7:22. This eloquence and bravery later served him well, as Grace knows how to sanctify all things.

v. 5. The daughter of Pharaoh) Who, according to the claim of Josephus (a), was named Thermuthis; according to the opinion of Artapanus found in Eusebius (b), she was called Meris.

The daughter of the very man who so unjustly condemned the Hebrew children to death had to become the mother of this child; and thus, in him, she gives life and birth to the entire people that others sought to root out.

This King’s daughter is an image of the Church gathered from among the heathens, which goes down to the water-bath of rebirth into the death of the old man, and there receives Moses or the Law of the Lord, which lay in the reed-basket, smeared over with Jewish pitch—that is, covered with the spirit of the Jews and their fleshly interpretations.

v. 7. His sister) Miriam, who may have been 10 or 12 years old: therefore she is called a "maiden" or young girl in the following verse.

v. 8. 9. Since the help provided by Providence lacks nothing—guiding everything to the right end and every person to the calling for which it ordains them—it gave to this child of Providence, through an unexpected occurrence, his own mother as his wet nurse. For it would be a small thing that a child of Providence were born and began his life in serenity, if he did not also live according to his calling.

<note>(a) Josephus, Antiquities Book 2, ch. 5. (b) Eusebius, Book 9, ch. 4. of the Preparation for the Gospel.</note>

Who else is this but Moses? He is the "drawer" <note>Moses’s name is linked to the Hebrew verb meaning 'to draw out.'</note> sent by the Father, and God’s faithful messenger to you. Thus, when you look upon a woman and the opportunity makes you lust after her, the Father’s faithful servant Moses draws your heart back, so that you should not gaze upon a woman. Job 31:1. When you are angry and would gladly strike and kill one who has done you harm, what is it that holds back your hand? Answer: You have a faithful and gentle Moses within you, who says: Do not sin! Be angry with yourself, that you may not sin!

People therefore do very poorly when they pay no more attention to the work of Moses within themselves: because it is precisely for this reason that one allows oneself to be drawn away from the right path by earthly lusts and desires. For the father of lies also has his "drawer," just as God the Father does. We have a pull to the right hand and to the left hand. Moses at the right hand draws us from vanity toward Christ and His kingdom; the other draws us from Christ toward vanity. Let one therefore be faithful to the inner Moses, just as Moses is faithful in the whole house of God: so it will be our wisdom to follow his pull; and the benefit and advantage that will grow for us thereby will be inestimable.

<column-break/>

### 10. And when the child grew up, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son; and she called his name Moses: and she said; because I have drawn him out of the water.
<margin>Ps. 18:17, 11 and 16</margin>

---

This mother did not give him back until he was grown: because he had to be so strongly established in his way that neither the high status of the court nor the danger to his life could turn him away again.

Outwardly he resembles the Egyptians, and is even regarded as a son of Pharaoh's daughter: but in deed and in heart he is a Hebrew. How many people does one not see who seem to live according to the common way, and yet possess within themselves the greatest treasures of grace! Ah, one must not judge by appearances! God’s judgments are very far removed from ours: and it is not the true Jew, according to St. Paul’s declaration, who is one only outwardly; but he is a true Jew who is one inwardly.

In this, Moses was also the image of Jesus Christ; who, though He appeared outwardly to be a child of man, yet was the true God inwardly; and who under the form of a sinner was the Most Holy. These wonderful images are full of comforting mysteries. For example: Who does not see, under the shadow of the history of Moses’s childhood—who was saved from the cruel persecution of Pharaoh by great Providence—the light of the Gospel of the child Jesus, who was saved by so many wonderous works from the poisoned rage and grim fury of Herod?

(He became her son) Whom she had instructed in chemistry and all the arts of the Egyptians. (a)

(She called his name Moses) He must therefore have had a name before this. It is said, however, that his parents named him Joachim at his circumcision (b): which name fits the circumstances of that time excellently well, and means as much as "God arise!" or "the Resurrection of the Lord": with which they, as it were, prophesied that the Lord would, through this Joachim, wake His people Israel again as if from the dead and arise to their help.

However, the name Moses was not given to him, as many believe, because—as Josephus would have it—he was taken up and saved from the water. For if it were given to him for that reason, then, to speak properly and fundamentally, his name would not be "Moseh," but "Moschui." "Mosche" is of an active—not passive—meaning, and signifies one who *draws* toward something, not one who *is drawn*. Pharaoh’s daughter herself correctly gives the origin of the name:

— Because I have drawn him out of the water) Not because he *was* drawn. And herewith she unwittingly prophesied what Moses should do, and the Lord through him: namely, to bring the people out from the waters. Isa. 63:11–13. It was also, however, through this prefigured and foreshadowed what the spiritual Moses should do. 2 Sam. 22:17. Moses withdrew the people from Pharaoh, just as Moses according to the Spirit withdraws men from the obedience and subjection of sin. Through Moses, the "pull" of God the Father in our souls is prefigured, of which the Son speaks in John 6:44. And this work of the Father is performed faithfully by Moses in men, whether they observe it or not. Can you really deny it, whoever you are, if you will only pay attention to it? For example: if you have some opportunity to overreach your brother in buying and selling, the opportunity will pull you to do such a thing. For opportunity is the great temptation to sin. But you will also become aware of something in you that pulls you back, so that you should not do it. And what is

### 11. And it came to pass in those days, when Moses had grown great, that he went out to his brothers and looked upon their burdens; and he saw an Egyptian man who struck a Hebrew man from among his brothers.

When Moses recognized that he was of the Hebrews, such was his faith—which the Spirit of God worked within him—that he was not ashamed of his despised and persecuted brothers according to the flesh, nor did he wish to prefer his own honor and days of ease. Rather, he was mindful of the God of his fathers and turned himself toward such a people. God, in turn, wished to wonderfully prepare him as a great instrument for the redemption of his brothers, so that he (presumably) struck down such a cruel <term>taskmaster</term> <note>German: *Frohnvogt*, an overseer of forced labor.</note> for his harsh conduct. From this, the children of Israel should have understood that God intended to provide them salvation through such an esteemed man from their own people in Pharaoh’s court. But because of their lack of love for one another, when they were rebuked by him with only friendly words, they rejected him, as it were, and sought to put him in mortal danger. See Acts 7:23–28. In this, Moses—as also regarding the danger to his life in infancy—became a special <term>type</term> <note>A "type" is a historical person or event believed to foreshadow a later one, specifically Christ.</note> of Christ, who was persecuted by Herod in infancy and rejected by His brothers to whom He was sent for salvation, because they did not wish to be rebuked by Him. See John 1:11, 8:37, 45.

**When Moses had grown great)** Saint Stephen says in Acts 7:22–23 that at the time it came into his heart to visit his brothers, he was fully 40 years old and mighty in words and deeds. This makes probable what Josephus <margin>(a) Book 2, ch. 5, Antiquities</margin> and Clement of Alexandria <margin>(b) Book 1, Stromata</margin> as well as Artapanus in Eusebius <margin>(c) On the Preparation for the Gospel, Book 9, ch. 4</margin> relate of Moses: namely, that in the distressed state of the kingdom, when the neighboring <term>Ethiopians</term> <note>original: *Mohren*. In historical texts, this refers to the people of Kush or Ethiopia.</note> invaded the land and devastated it, even seeking to bring it under their control, Moses commanded the royal army as General Field Marshal at the king’s request, and thereby especially proved his bravery and experience in military matters. For it is said, for example, that when he wished to surprise the enemy before they could become aware of his arrival, he did not lead his march across the water as was otherwise usual, but took the march by land. Because this path was difficult to pass due to the multitude of snakes commonly found in that region—of a species found nowhere else, which were altogether poisonous and terrifying to behold, some even having wings and harming people not only on the ground but also in the air and in flight—Moses devised this wonderful invention so that he might bring the people through safely and unharmed. He had a heap of baskets made of reeds, like little crates; into these he put storks and took them along. When they came to the region where the vermin of snakes was found, they let the storks out to fly at them. Thus they proceeded successfully on their march, surprised the Ethiopians when they least expected it, and utterly defeated them.

But why do we look so much at these external things, when they actually happen, or may happen, daily within us? We also have a spiritual Moses in and with us; namely, the one of whom the Lord said He would raise up one who should be like Him. Deuteronomy 18:15–19; Acts 3:22. It is to be wished that He had already grown to manly stature within us (Ephesians 4:13), so that He might work the same deeds in us as Moses did among the Hebrews according to the flesh after he had grown great.

---

This is a great point of fidelity: to keep oneself hidden as long as one is not compelled to reveal oneself for the sake of the truth. But when the truth is attacked, one must venture everything to defend it.

Moses had barely left his mother and been set out when he immediately served the office of a shepherd; for since God wished to make him a leader of others, He promoted him in the cradle, and while with his nurse, made him fit to become an apostle. Thus, here he tears a sheep away from the oppression of its enemy and performs a true work of justice through a seeming manslaughter. He performed this deed in the will of God, namely by destroying the enemy of God, which corrupt race he was one day to annihilate entirely. One should therefore not ask by whom he was appointed as a shepherd. He is so by God Himself, so that he might be both the image and the successor of Jesus Christ, the true Shepherd and Shepherd of all shepherds. His brothers should also have learned to grasp through this that God would redeem them by his hand; but they did not grasp it, as Saint Stephen noted.

<column-break/>

### 12. And he turned this way and that, and when he saw that no man was there, he struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

### 13. And he went out on the second day, and behold, two Hebrew men were quarreling. And he said to the unjust one: Why do you strike your neighbor?

### 14. But he said: Who has set you as a prince or judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian? Then Moses was afraid and said: Surely the matter has become known!

**v. 12.** Moses came forth the first day and struck the Egyptian as a symbol of sin and unrighteousness; and even so, the spiritual Moses, at His first coming, destroys the "black Egyptian," which is sin.

**v. 13.** The second day, Moses appeared again and sought to settle a dispute between two Hebrews, rebuking the unjust one. And so the spiritual Moses, at His second coming, rebukes false righteousness. John 16:8.

Moses killed and buried the Egyptian, but not the Hebrew; that is, the natural man who does wrong to his brother, the spiritual heavenly man. It is not the killing or burying of yourself, but of your sin, that the Lord demands of you.

**v. 14.** Just as the redemption of the Hebrews from Egypt was interrupted and delayed because they did not believe Moses (Acts 7:25), so also the spiritual Moses cannot do and work His great deeds in us because of our unbelief. Matthew 13:58. People have too low thoughts of Him and of His redemption.

**Who has set you as a judge over us?)** Such is the actual state of all those who hate punishment and are averse to discipline. When one presents to them their ungodly mind and the inclinations of their evil-perverted heart, along with the crooked ways of their cursed nature, and they find themselves thus exposed, they fly up in anger and indignation and say: "Who has set you as judges over us?" Indeed, there are many who confess and say to those in whom God has planted His judgment: "We must certainly recognize what you say as good, and cannot reject your teaching and words; if only you would leave off your judging and passing of sentences!" But these are precisely the ones who hate judgment and love darkness more than light. For their deeds are evil, and they do not wish them to be brought to light and judged by the same. But—

<page-num>289</page-num>
<header>Chapter II. The Second Book of Moses.</header>

15. Now when Pharaoh heard of this matter, he sought to slay Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and settled in the land of Midian, and sat down by a well.

<margin>v. 15. After the hatred and envy of the Egyptians had long pursued Moses, they finally found this apparent opportunity to accuse him before the King because of the murder he had committed. And because the King already held him in suspicion and lived in fear that he might start something in Egypt—while the <term>priests</term> <note>German: *Pfaffen*, often a derogatory term for clergy in this era.</note> and the priestly folk were incessantly whispering in his ears—it was decided that he should be seized by the head; had he not caught wind of it just in time and, because he heard that they were lying in wait for him on the roads, saved himself by fleeing through the desert regions. And although he had nothing to eat or break his fast, he endured hunger with patience. In this state, he finally caught sight of the city of Midian, located by the Red Sea, and there, quite weary from the difficult journey, sat down by a well at the noon hour.</margin>

The persecutions stirred up by the overt enemies of the truth always follow the defense of that truth: this could not be absent in the case of Moses. Therefore, he had to give way and share the fate of those <term>yielded</term> <note>German: *eingefehrten* (likely *eingekehrten*) *und treuen Seelen*. Referring to the "inward" or "quiet" souls of the Pietist tradition.</note> and faithful souls, which is to be persecuted to the utmost—even unto flight—for the sake of righteousness. But why does he flee according to the counsel of God? It is so that he may practice the office of a shepherd.

16. Now the <term>ruler</term> <note>German: *Befehlshaber*, meaning a commander or official.</note> in Midian had seven daughters; they came to draw water and filled the troughs to water their father's sheep.

<margin>v. 16. The Ruler) This was a commander and official appointed by the sovereign of the land, just as Joseph’s father-in-law was: Chapter 41, 45. God surely preserved both of these holy men from marrying the daughters of idolatrous priests (though the word can mean that), taking them instead as daughters of worldly officials, as David’s sons were in 2 Samuel 8:18. He is also called Jethro and Jether: Chapter 3:1; 4:18; and also Hobab in Numbers 10:29 and Judges 4:11; such various names for one person occur frequently in Scripture. Midian) Located on the Red Sea, named after one of the sons of Abraham and Keturah: Chapter 25:2.</margin>

17. Then the shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their sheep.

<margin>v. 17. Because there was a lack of water in this place, Josephus writes, the shepherds always sought to occupy the wells first so that others would not draw the water before them and their livestock would suffer thirst. Because the young women had preceded them here, the shepherds sought to drive them away with unjust force. Moses, on the other hand, proved himself helpful and was therefore received again with friendship. He found his bride at a well, just as Isaac and Jacob did: Chapter 24:11, etc.; 29:2, etc. This is a sign that if one holds to the right source of all knowledge—to the <term>inner light</term> <note>A central concept in mystical Christianity, identifying Christ as a presence within the soul.</note> which Christ wishes to be in the soul—then one also receives Heavenly Wisdom as the true bride, with whom one can refresh oneself in the truth during this pilgrimage on earth. See Wisdom 8:2, etc.</margin>

We have previously read how all those whom God has chosen to lead the holy office of a shepherd began by watering their flocks. But Moses, who was no ordinary shepherd but the chief shepherd of this great flock, does not only water this flock but also begins to defend them himself. Thus must the true shepherds of Christ’s sheep be. One must not only give them water but also preserve it for them by protecting it against those who, through their ill-will, wish to prevent them from drinking.

<column-break/>

18. And when they came to their father Reuel, he said: How is it that you have come so soon today?

19. And they said: An Egyptian man delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds; and he also drew enough for us and watered the sheep.

20. And he said to his daughters: Where is he then? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread!

21. And Moses agreed to dwell with the man; and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah.

22. And she bore a son, and he called his name Gershom. For he said: I have become a stranger in a foreign land.

23. And

---

v. 18. 19. God often sends such "Moses-figures" to those <term>yielded souls</term> <note>German: *gelassenen Seelen*, souls who have surrendered their will to God.</note> who give them water and deliver them from the oppression in which unworthy and ignorant shepherds keep them, preventing them from drinking spring water. Such people called to yieldedness may be wherever they are, and they may groan under as great a power as is possible; so long as they are faithful, God does not fail to send them a capable guide to lead them in the ways of God. And this happens through a wonderful as well as infallible Providence.
The daughters of Jethro return in time to their father; this signifies returning to their Origin, because they found a good shepherd who, by giving them fresh water, enabled them to move forward.

v. 21. If Providence was great over Reuel by the sending of a Moses who watered and pastured his flock, it was no less great over Moses, letting him find a faithful company in this house. This company, by recognizing the inward ways and standing in those same ways, was to contribute its part to the <term>spiritual offspring</term> <note>German: *geistlichen Ausgebuhrt*, referring to the internal birth of Christ or spiritual progress.</note>. Furthermore, it provided him there with safe keeping and sustenance as long as he would be separated from his people.

v. 22. The sign of a soul enlightened by living faith is to ascribe everything—our children and all our "offspring"—to God and His Providence, as well as to give Him the due thanks for His assistance.
**I have become a stranger in a foreign land)** Though Moses received a bride pleasing to him and kind, loving in-laws, he was still mindful of his people as the people of the true God. Even at the birth of a son, he wished to remember his status as a stranger there—as the name signifies—in order to make known his longing for his people. Even if things go very well for a person among natural men, and one enjoys all friendship from them, one should still always be mindful that one is a stranger there (**Ger-shom**) <note>original: "Ger-scham". A wordplay on the Hebrew *Ger* (stranger) and *Sham* (there).</note>, which can soon change. Therefore, one should long for communion with God's people—with true believers—whom one will only truly encounter above in the right Fatherland, due to the great corruption and weakness here.

23. And it happened within those many days that the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned and cried out because of their servitude. And their cry went up to God because of the servitude.

24. And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.

25. And God looked upon the children of Israel, and God took notice of them.

Thus God allows distress to reach its peak so that one truly learns to groan and cry out to God from the depths, and so that prayer becomes truly earnest; then the hearing of that prayer is also near; Psalm 120:1, James 5:16. Then God will indeed think of his promises, that he will lay all the enemies of Christ as a footstool for his feet; Psalm 110:1. This is so that the scepter of the godless does not always remain over the lot of the righteous, lest the righteous stretch out their hand to iniquity; Psalm 125:3. It is so they do not fall to the party of the godless, just as the children of Israel did not want to join with the Egyptians and become one people with them. See Chapter 34:21-22. Thus God also permits the increase of physical burdens and heavy forced labor so that many might yet learn to turn rightly to God: who will also soon make an end of the hard masters with terror.

While God led the leader of Israel in this manner, the people were stuck more and more in a harder servitude. Pharaoh died, indeed, but the work of this poor people was not diminished. They cried to God, and he had mercy on them. He remembers the covenant which he had made with those <term>inwardly turned souls</term> <note>German: *eingekehrte Seelen*. Refers to the Pietist ideal of the "still" or "quiet" believer who focuses on the inner spiritual life.</note>, of pure sacrifice, and of <term>total surrender</term> <note>German: *Gelassenheit*. A central mystical concept meaning the casting off of self-will to be filled by God.</note>. Abraham was the father of faith; Isaac represents the pure sacrifice, and Jacob represents total surrender. All inwardly turned souls must pass through bare faith, through pure sacrifice, and through total surrender if they wish to attain again the purity of their creation.

**Bare faith** is a faith without witness or support, whether of the understanding or of the spirit.

**Pure sacrifice** is a whole sacrifice: not only of all that is ours and in us, but also of all that we ourselves are, both in the order of nature and of grace.

**Total surrender** is the complete giving over of ourselves into the hands of God, so that he may fulfill his entire will in, on, and through us, both outwardly and inwardly, without the slightest exception of time or eternity.

God remembers these ways of guidance, which are the purest and most necessary so that the soul can be taken up into him: and he wishes to redeem this people, pleasing to him, from the captivity which presses them down and prevents them from being able to serve God in freedom and purity.

### The III. Chapter.

->The Calling of Moses.<-

<margin>(a) ch. 4:27. (2) ch. 2:16. ch. 18:1.</margin>
1. Now Moses kept the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, the commander in Midian (a), and led the sheep behind the desert, and came to the mountain of God, Horeb.

<margin>(a) Matt. 17:2. Luke 2:7, 8.</margin>
2. And the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire (a) out of the midst of a thorn-bush; and he looked, and behold, the thorn-bush burned with fire, and the thorn-bush was not consumed.

3. Then

v. 1. Moses had to leave the vain life of the court and take up the laborious and simple life of a shepherd according to divine providence: by which he was to be shown how he would one day take upon himself the laborious governance of the people of God, and lead them as a flock of sheep; Psalm 77:21. Just as God himself in Christ calls himself the Shepherd of Israel, who tends Joseph like sheep; Psalm 80:2. Therefore he also took David from behind the sheep and appointed him as a king of his people. Which should teach all rulers to lead the Lord's people like sheep, and not like Nimrod to hunt them like wild animals and to rule and govern over them in a slavish manner.

Since Moses thought of nothing else but to pasture the flock which God had given him in his father-in-law’s house as an insignificant shepherd, he was raised to a higher union with God, as he drew even closer to the mountain through a higher deepening within himself.

<margin>(a) <note>original: *vid. Adrichom. theat. terr. sanct. in Pharan n. 67. & 92.*</note> See Adrichomius, *Theater of the Holy Land*, regarding Paran, numbers 67 & 92.</margin>
Mount Horeb is called the Mountain of God here in advance because God revealed himself on it to the entire people of Israel, spoke to them with words, and gave them the law of the ten commandments: Chapter 19:11. There it is also called Mount Sinai, from the many thorn-bushes that were there, as the word signifies. It lay by the Red Sea toward the east and bordered the deserts there and Mount Sinai, of which it was a part (a).

v. 2. Here Christ appears as the Angel and Messenger of his Father with emphasis to Moses for the first time, and reveals himself to him as the Lord Jehovah, the only true God and gracious Covenant-God of his faithful fathers, who now also wished to appoint him as a messenger to his people. But he also appears to him in the human form which he had truly taken upon himself, and in the same could have been seen, if Moses had not been terrified because of the fearsome form of the fire in which he revealed himself; in which fire Christ will also come to judge the world; Psalm 50:3.

2 Thess. 1:8. He wanted to appear in a thorn-bush to show that he would soon set fire in his wrath to the Egyptians, who had set themselves like thorns and hedges against him in his people; Isaiah 27:4. Whereas his people should not be consumed in this fire, but rather preserved.

**The Angel of the Lord**) How Christ is called an Angel, see also Chapter 14:19, 13:21, 23:20, 21; Genesis 48:16; Judges 6:12; Job 33:23; Isaiah 63:9; Malachi 3:1.

**In a flame of fire out of a thorn-bush**) God was in the flame, and the flame in the bush. This flame indicates the love which God has toward inwardly turned men, even though they are still weak. He wanted to leave a good portion of it to this shepherd because he had chosen him to lead a very great people: as the first virtue of a shepherd must be the love which moves him to give his life for the sheep.

This flame is surrounded with thorns; because those who lead souls must suffer much. One cannot imagine the sufferings prepared for them, nor the thorns and persecutions to which they are subject.

<margin>(b) 2 Exodus 32:32.</margin>
This bush burns and yet is not consumed. This is the likeness of the love of those shepherds which must always remain in one state without becoming tired or weary. One later read how much this holy leader was kindled and filled by it when, seeing his people not far from God's punishment for their sins, he stilled his righteous wrath with this prayer prompted by a pure and burning love: (b) Either forgive them, Lord, this iniquity, or, if that is not pleasing to you, then blot me out of your book which you have written, etc.

3. Then Moses said: "I will now go over there and see this great sight, why the thorn-bush is not burnt."
4. But when the LORD saw that he went over to see, God called to him from the midst of the thorn-bush and said: "Moses, Moses!" And he answered: "Here I am."
5. And He said: "Do not come any closer; take your shoes off your feet! For the place on which you stand is a holy land." Joshua 5:15. (a) Ruth 4:7.
6. And He said further: "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God.

<margin>v. 3. 4. This burning bush is a <term>type</term><note>A "type" is a person, object, or event in the Old Testament seen as a symbolic foreshadowing of something in the New Testament.</note> of the Incarnation of Christ.</margin>

1. This vision appeared to Moses while he was tending sheep: likewise, the birth of Christ, or the appearance of the angels for that reason, occurred while the shepherds in the field were tending their flock. Luke 2.
2. Moses called this a "great sight." It is a great mystery of godliness, God revealed in the flesh. Isaiah 60:17.
3. Here was fire, which burned, shone, and gave light; and the Angel of the Covenant spoke out of the fire. Christ is the Light (John 1), the Deity, the Fire.
4. Here was a bush grown up from the earth, wood that was green. Christ called himself "green wood," Luke 23:31. He is the branch of the Lord, a fruit of the earth. Isaiah 4:2, 11:1.
5. This fire was in the bush and united with it, yet did not consume the bush, nor was it mixed with it: wood remained wood. So it is with God and man in Christ.
6. This vision appeared to Moses when God wanted to redeem His people from the house of bondage through the Angel of the Covenant.
7. As Moses wanted to step closer, he was commanded to take off his shoes. The mystery of the Lord is among those who fear Him. Psalm 25:14.

We must now become like this bush. God's Spirit must dwell in us to warm and enlighten us, but not to consume us—indeed, to make us joyful. But when the spirit of darkness is in us, it awakens nothing but blindness, hatred, lovelessness, and finally eternal sadness.
Thus, this bush also represents a person's soul as it is under the Fall. Micah 7:4. The flame within it indicates the divine fire that is ignited there for our purification (Isaiah 4:4), which then does not come to consume, but to refine and make perfect. This internal divine fire will soon make itself better known to those who desire to overcome themselves and detach the soul from the animalistic life. Then one will recognize through living experience the ways of Him who still dwells in the bush, and perceive in oneself this heavenly burning which proceeds from the holy and righteous God: and so one will also understand how everyone must be salted with fire. Mark 9:49.

v. 5. Where God wishes to appear, there one should strive with fear and trembling to renounce all of one's impure and earthly lusts: in order to be deemed worthy of God's gracious revelation for one's sanctification in such a holy place. See Ecclesiastes 4:17, Joshua 5:15.
Those who now take off their shoes of the <term>old nature</term><note>The "old nature" refers to the sinful, unregenerate state of humanity before spiritual transformation.</note>, which is entirely defiled, and who listen to God in His word while renouncing all their own wisdom—to them God makes Himself and His name, His counsel and will, His wonders and ways, more closely known.
**Do not come near etc.)** It is as if the Lord said to him: Do not draw near to such a pure and disinterested love, to such an expanded love that is equal toward all, unless you find yourself stripped of all self-love. This extreme stripping is what I still require of you: namely, that your sensuality, which is represented by your feet, be entirely naked; so that you may maintain a true equality among all this people, to judge them in righteousness and holiness; for the earth of love is entirely holy.

<column-break/>

7. Furthermore, the Lord said: "I have surely seen the oppression of my people who are in Egypt; and have heard their cry (a) because of their <term>taskmasters</term><note>German: *Treiber*. Literally "drivers," referring to those who forced the Israelites to work.</note>; yes, I have known their sorrows."
<note>(a) c. 22:23. 27. James 5:4.</note>
8. "And I have come down to rescue them from the hand of the Egyptians, and to lead them up out of that land into a good and a wide land, into a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites."
9. "And now behold, the cry of the children of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them."
10. "So go now, and I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may lead my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt!"
11. And

v. 7. **Their taskmasters)** Rulers should be drivers toward righteousness, who urge their subordinates toward everything good and be helpful to them in it, as is promised in the glorious kingdom. Isaiah 60:17. But when, instead, they only grind out gold and silver through heavy <term>executions</term><note>In this context, "executions" refers to the enforcement of taxes or legal seizures of property.</note> (2 Kings 23:35) and apply such things to lusts and all sorts of follies; then the threat of the prophet is fulfilled: "Children are the taskmasters of my people, and women rule over them." Isaiah 3:12. Such taskmasters, however, will entirely cease in Christ’s glorious kingdom. Ezekiel 45:8-9. And

When oppressions have gained the upper hand everywhere, God will surely send the believers their Moses, who will pull them out of the waters of tribulation and make them partakers of the glorious redemption.

v. 8. **Good Land)** Natural good things are types of spiritual ones. And thus the natural wealth and prosperity of this land—such as grain, wine, oil, honey, figs, mountains, springs, forests, temperate air, lovely vistas, and the like—were images and living representations of the spiritual blessing and supernatural comfort intended for those who love God and follow Him: and the land itself represented peace and rest in God.

**Wide Land)** Although the land of Canaan is said to have been only up to 160 miles in length, from Dan to Beersheba, and 60 miles in breadth, from Joppa to the Jordan; yet it was wide and broad enough in view of Goshen, and also because of the special goodness of the land, which had everything in abundance for the nourishment and refreshment of life, which is to be understood by the figure of speech regarding the abundance of milk and honey. And that was also enough for such a people, who were especially to guard themselves against mixing with other nations, and therefore had no need to invite foreigners into their land.

v. 9. **The oppression)** of the spirit is also frequently felt by the "Israel according to the spirit" from external business and the distracting variety of burdensome Egyptian labor.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between God and Moses at the burning bush. Following God’s command to lead Israel out of Egypt, Moses expresses deep humility and hesitation, leading to the revelation of the divine name.</meta>

<page-num>292</page-num>
<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter III.</header>

### 11. And Moses said to GOD: Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh, and that I should lead the children of Israel out of Egypt?

### 12. And He said: I will certainly be with you; and this shall be the sign to you that I have sent you: when you have led the people out of Egypt, you shall serve GOD upon this mountain.
<margin>ch. 19, 20.</margin>

### 13. Then Moses said to GOD: Behold, when I come to the children of Israel and say to them: "The GOD of your fathers has sent me to you," and they say to me: "What is His name?" what shall I say to them?

v. 11. **who am I?**) According to Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note>, his speech is expressed in this way: "O Lord, I am not so foolish as to doubt Your power, which I hold in high esteem and which was revealed to my ancestors. However, I cannot understand how I, as a simple, ordinary man (a shepherd for forty years), could persuade my people to leave the land where they now dwell and follow me into another land; or, even if they were persuaded, how I should compel King Pharaoh to grant a free departure to a people whose help and labor bring great benefit to the entire land of Egypt."

v. 12. **I will be with you**) As the *Immanuel* <note>original: "Immanu-El"; Hebrew for "God with us."</note>. For the name Immanuel and "I will be with you" are one and the same. The Chaldean text <note>Likely referring to the Aramaic Targum.</note> explains this in reference to Christ: *My Word will help you.*

Moses recognizes his unworthiness and incapacity for such a difficult work; therefore, GOD raises him up with His powerful assistance and assures him that he will carry out the work gloriously; for they would serve Him on this mountain. This was intended to encourage him, showing that the Majestic GOD who appeared to him would not leave him stranded.

Moses, in consideration of his lowliness, excuses himself by recognizing he is unfit to lead such a great people on such a difficult path as the path of *yieldedness* <term>yieldedness</term><note>German: "Gelassenheit." A central concept in German mysticism and Pietism, referring to a state of total surrender to God's will and detachment from worldly desires.</note>. But the most unruly task for him is to bring such a people out from the driving of the taskmasters and from the jurisdiction of Pharaoh. That is: it is very difficult to lead these souls out of their old habits and customs in order to introduce them into the wildernesses of faith. Therefore, GOD assures him that He would be with him, and would Himself perform this great work: the visible protection which would accompany the words of Moses would be the invisible sign that GOD had sent him.

v. 13. For his authority, Moses desires the actual knowledge of the true GOD, so that he might present Him to them, so they might obey this true GOD.

Moses thinks it is not enough to announce to the children of Israel that the GOD of faith, of sacrifice, and of yieldedness has sent him: he therefore wants to know the name of this GOD who is so powerful that He can lead such an unnumerable, great people through such a singular way. But GOD, who wishes to instruct this faithful shepherd in all things, is not resentful of this answer, even though it might have seemed provocative. What does He then answer him?

<column-break/>

### 14. And GOD said to Moses: I will be who I am <note>(a)</note>. Furthermore He said: Thus shall you say to the children of Israel <note>(b)</note>; "I will be" has sent me to you.
-> (a) John 8:25. (b) Matthew 21:3. <-

### 15. And

GOD calls Himself the *I will be*; namely, that He is bound to prove Himself to their fathers, that He will redeem them from bondage (as He had already foretold to Abraham, Gen. 15:13, 14), and that He would lead them up into the good land He promised their fathers. And indeed, He will be who He is: namely, He who by nature is the kind, loving, gracious, truthful, and faithful GOD, who will prove all these attributes to His people; but also the just and almighty GOD over their enemies, who will punish and judge them according to their merit. And His glorious name *Jehovah* specifically aims at such promises of grace; it shall be His name and memorial forever, from generation to generation, which first became revealed in full power in Christ—in whom all the promises of God are "Yes" and "Amen" in Him to the glory of God through us: 2 Cor. 1:20. Thus we can always remind ourselves that Christ will one day *Be* what He promised to become through His prophets: so that His glorious promises of the blessed state in His glorious kingdom will all one day be perfectly fulfilled.

The nature of the Essence in GOD is also expressed herewith: that He is who He is, and remains the same consistently for all eternity, He who does not change (Malachi 3:6). What He is at present, He also was in the past, and will ever be in the future: just as these three attributes of time (according to our weak human concept of time) lie within the secret name *Jehovah*. Therefore Christ calls Himself the Lord *who is, and who was, and who is to come* (Revelation 1:4, 8; see also Hebrews 13:8 and 11:6).

Jerome, or the *Vulgate* <note>The late-4th-century Latin translation of the Bible.</note>, and others following them, render it as: *I am who I am* <note>Latin: "Ego sum qui sum."</note>. But if men are free to swap tenses as they please, where then is the distinction? Especially when good reason and cause can be given why one should stay with the actual expression of the text. The great name *Jehovah* is composed by divine art in such a way that it encompasses the past, present, and future time within itself. Since the Lord directs and draws this "to be" toward the future time, He gives a clear indication that He intends to reveal His divinity in humanity more clearly in the latter part of time.

The entire revolution of time from beginning to end is generally divided into two parts or ages: one of the type, prophecy, and promise; the other of truth and fulfillment. The latter began in an excellent way when Christ appeared in the flesh. Just as the Lord and His prophets foretell what shall happen, so in the first age or part of time they point us toward the fulfillment of the same in the latter part of time, when the Lord intended to reveal Himself and His ways and works more clearly in the Messiah, as the Lord of the future time. Thus, He who at the beginning of this work called Himself *I will be*, then calls Himself *I am* (John 8:58), intending to carry out in the Spirit the very works that happened here in Moses' time as a shadow/type.

So far-reaching and, as it were, "perspectival" is the Lord in His speeches: as one who did not communicate Himself all at once, but gradually made His name known in many ways. But in these last days He speaks to us through Him who fulfills all types, where the *I will be* becomes *I am*.

**I am**) the Essence of all essences, the Being from which everything that bears the name of a "being" originates. I am He who alone is something: for everything in Me is nothing. Whoever still calls, believes, or recognizes themselves as being "something" is not yet fit to be My people. I must have a people of truth who are so "annihilated" <note>A mystical term for the total stripping away of the self-ego.</note> that they find themselves in the truth of "nothingness," just as I am the "All" in truth. Therefore, you must say nothing else to the people of Israel: so that by reminding them of their nothingness and My "All-ness," they may surrender themselves to My leadership with less effort, detach themselves from their own inventions, and depart from the smoke of human arts to follow the path of yieldedness, which will lead them safely to Me.

<meta>catchword: You</meta>

### 15. And GOD spoke further to Moses: Thus shall you say to the children of Israel; The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you. This is my name forever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.

You shall tell them that the God who led their fathers—who walked at all times through the way of <term>serenity and surrender<note>original: "Gelassenheit." A key term in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of one's own will to be filled by God.</note></term>—sends you now to be their visible leader: but that I alone shall do all things; for I will be He who I am, and without whom nothing exists. This name shall remain mine eternally, and I wish to be known by it at all times. Is it not as if He said: He who is, and is all Being, has no need to give Himself a name to distinguish Himself from other beings; for outside of Him there is no being. His name is His essence, and His essence is His name: and just as His essence encompasses all, so also does His name express all. Creatures, which at their core are nothing but true nothingness—covered only by a small, dependent existence lent to them by God—require names for their distinction. But He, who loses all within Himself, needs no other name than that which is "Being": because that which is still "something" is either He Himself, or so closely united with Him through the root of its origin that nothing is to be found outside of Him. This beautiful name then serves God to make Himself known to His people: it also serves Him to distinguish this same people—that is, His dear children, who know to attribute everything to Him and nothing to themselves—from those who deal differently with Him. Those who attribute something to themselves rob Him of His name.

**The LORD!** This great, glorious, proper name of God awakens in and of itself the understanding to the highest and most essential supernatural knowledge, beyond which thought cannot reach nor soar, and it encompasses all circumstances of time within itself. *Hayah* <note>Hebrew: היה</note>, He was: *Jehovah* <note>Hebrew: יהוה</note>, He will be: *Havah* <note>Hebrew: הוה</note>, Being/He is. Primarily, however, it points to these present and final days, in which the fullness of the Godhead shall be poured out; as was mentioned somewhat in the preceding verse. And thus it is a name that may signify His nature to some extent. In contrast to the creatures, this name signifies the Author of all created beings: past, present, and future.

The Jews held an indescribably high regard for this name above all names of GOD, holding it in the greatest honor, and were accustomed to expressing it through all manner of idioms; they called it the Name of 4 Letters <note>The Tetragrammaton.</note>, the Name, the Great Name, the Glorious Name: and therefore, so that it might not be profaned by use, they spoke in its place **Adonai** <note>Hebrew for "My Lord."</note>. Also, this name was heard no more than once in an entire year, spoken by the High Priest: and that only on the Day of Atonement; and indeed only in the Most Holy Place.

This great name arises from the יהוה in v. 14, which has a **י** [Yod] as the mark of the Father: so that, just as the Son proceeds from the Father, so also the Son's name begins with **יהוה** the **ו** [Vav], as the letter and the sign of Life, which He gives to all things. He who in the **א** [Aleph]—that is, in the Father—was according to number only One, here enters through the **ו** [Vav] into the Number Six, and imparts life to all things through the 6 days of creation. Furthermore, the letter **ה** [He] is formed from a **ו** [Vav] and two **י** [Yod]s, which added together make the number 26, exactly as much as the name **יהוה** <note>This refers to Gematria: Y(10)+H(5)+W(6)+H(5)=26.</note>. Thus it is understood to some extent what the Son himself says: *I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.*

**God of your fathers**) By this He wishes to remind them of the promises given to the fathers, to hold them before the children of Israel so that they might long in faith for their fulfillment.

**The God of Abraham**) To whom I have given the high name.

**The God of Isaac**) Whom I have gladdened and made joyful.

**The God of Jacob**) For whom I have trodden all malice underfoot.

It is very remarkable here that the LORD God attributes His own name to the three Patriarchs as prototypes of the Trinity. **Abraham** represents the Father, as the wise man gives the origin of his name in Sirach 44:20. **Isaac** is famously a prototype of the Son. **Jacob** is a prototype of the Spirit. This may have its purpose regarding the 3 parts or degrees of the Kingdom of GOD. Ps. 97:1. *The LORD has reigned.* Ps. 10:16. *The LORD is King.* Ps. 146:10. *The LORD shall reign forever and ever.*

<column-break/>

### 16. Go and gather the elders in Israel(a), and say to them: The LORD, the God of your fathers, has appeared to me, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and has said; I have indeed looked upon you, and upon what has happened to you in Egypt: <margin>(a) Ch. 4:29.</margin>

### 17. And I have said; I will lead you up out of the oppression of Egypt, into the land of the Canaanites and the Hittites, and the Amorites and the Perizzites, and the Hivites and the Jebusites, into a land that flows with milk and honey.

### 18. And they will hear your voice: thereafter you and the elders in Israel shall go in to the king in Egypt, and shall say to him; The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now let us go three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God!

### 19. But

<margin>(a) it is thought there</margin>
v. 16. **The elders in Israel**) it is thought there were 72 elders over the people of Israel in Egypt.

**I have looked upon you**) Truly this is one of the dearest works of GOD, which He does most joyfully: namely, His gracious looking upon the wretched. Oh, in that He has His joy—in saving, helping, comforting, and awakening: yes, it is His nature and His own work.

How heartily He always testifies in Scripture that He looks so faithfully upon the wretched and the oppressed! One cannot read without wonder how often and in what detail He presents such looking of His. And

This is precisely the most all-penetrating comfort of all the forsaken, the fearful, and the wretched: that the Guardian of Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers, but that His eye is so awake, so alert, and at the same time so compassionate toward all who seek Him.

v. 18. **They shall ask that they might go into the wilderness to sacrifice to their GOD:** because one must go through the wilderness of pure faith before one can arrive at a pure sacrifice. The way is long: one desires this sacrifice immediately; but one arrives there late: and very many do not arrive there at all.

**Three days' journey**) The first day's journey with **Faith**, to come out of all distress: the second in **Hope**, that the way of tribulations will come to an end: the third day in **Love**, where one shall remain and rest, and offer up the burning, fiery, loving heart.

**That we may sacrifice**) The LORD allows only the first part to be reported—the sacrifice—but He keeps silent regarding the total abandonment of Egypt, as Pharaoh would have been most hardened by that, since he already opposed the first request.

Thus we are obliged to tell the truth at all times, but not the *whole* truth, where the other is unworthy of it and would only use it to harm us.

Our corrupt nature is filled with nothing but mistrust / especially in divine things / whether it be to believe the mysteries of God with a simple heart / or to recognize the divine will and obey the same. In both pieces, <term>Reason<note>original: "Vernunfft." In this mystical context, Reason is often contrasted with Faith, seen as a human faculty that tries to over-analyze and resist God's simple commands.</note></term> will always run ahead / and make all sorts of objections; either to reject the mysteries entirely / or to grasp them perversely / and to become disobedient to the will of God. That which should therefore be our walking stick and staff in this pilgrimage / in the valley of death / here on earth; that becomes a serpent to us / through the cunning of the old serpent / which proves itself active in our reason / and thus leads to destruction. But if we went to work simply in all things / and only confidently grasped that / which seemed terrifying to our nature / and did not deliberate upon it with Reason; then such would become a staff to us / upon which we could lean in all tribulations / and thus comfort ourselves. Psalm 23. And so must all tribulations and all difficulties / especially in the calling to the service of the Word / be viewed in the end / and therefore not be shunned / but only confidently engaged.

The mistrust and resistance of Moses shows us sufficiently / that one can still possess unfaithfulness and resistance against God even in the highest states of grace. v. 1. They will not obey my voice) In the Hebrew, it actually says "in my voice" word for word / just as in Psalm 95:8. Therein lies a special emphasis and a mark of divine wisdom. For the Word is one thing / and the voice is another; says St. Anselm. First sounds the voice / so that the Word may be heard; says St. Gregory. But there is an inward and an outward Word; and between these two is the voice of the one to whom the Lord has appeared; that voice is, as it were, the carriage of the Word / which conveys it to the heart of the listener. This inward, essential Word must first be in those / and appear in those / who are carriages or means of conducting the same to men / before they can be the voice of God and Christ / crying out within them / to the people.

Behold herein yourself / you who call yourself a minister of the Word! whether the Lord and His living Word has appeared in you / and has spoken in you or not; and whether the Word is conveyed through your voice into men / so that of those / who hear you / it may be said with truth / that they hear Christ speaking in you and through you. Romans 15:18.

v. 10. **Oh my Lord!)** Not only does our flesh and blood resist the extraordinary ways of God; though it is a great grace / when one can proceed immediately like Paul in such revelations / and not consult or take counsel with flesh and blood for long: but also in the ordinary ways / where one could know the will of God. Here one then indeed has need to pray with <term>Augustine<note>original: "Augustino." Refers to St. Augustine’s famous prayer: "Give what You command, and command what You will."</note></term>: that God would first work in us / what His will was; and then command / what He willed.
The <term>Rabbis<note>original: "Rabbinen." Specifically referring to a Midrashic legend found in Jewish tradition.</note></term> relate of Moses / that in his childhood he once reached for the King's golden crown / and tore it from his head. Now when the King wanted to test / whether he had done such a thing out of childish simplicity or malice; he had brought, alongside a vessel full of gold, also one with coals / to see / which he would reach for.
