**Lord / I cannot speak!)** since my voice is a voice of silence: and moreover / because You have spoken with me / I now have even less freedom to speak. For the Word of God is accustomed to devouring our own / and / according to the Prophet (b) / as soon as the Lord approaches His sanctuary / all flesh must be silent before His presence. As soon as God speaks to a soul / everything in it must be silent / in order to hear the same. But if everything must be silent before God / when He wishes to speak; then on the other hand everything must speak before Him / when He commands it.

**I have a heavy speech and tongue)** As long as Moses was in Egypt / and while he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; he had no heavy speech or tongue / but was of great eloquence. After he began, however, to hear the voice of God / and to perceive the divine utterances; he becomes aware / that his speech and tongue are heavy: and he confesses himself to be mute / as he began to recognize the true Word / which was with God in the beginning. If a rational man / even if he is not learned or eloquent / is compared with irrational animals; he will seem eloquent in comparison to them. But if he is compared with skilled / learned and eloquent men / who are proven in all wisdom; he will seem as if mute and ineloquent. Thus if someone beholds the divine Word / and fixes his eye upon heavenly wisdom; he may be as learned and as wise as he ever wishes / yet he must confess / that he is a mute beast before God. David recognized this well; and therefore / when he weighed himself against divine wisdom / he said: I am like a beast before thee.

v. 11. **Is it not God / who binds the tongue / and looses it again?** The more ignorant a person is / and the less ability they have to express themselves; the more suitable they are in the hand of God / to make from them / whatever He wishes. Therefore / after He has sufficiently shown to Moses / that it does not lie in the power of nature / to express oneself in spiritual things / but stands in divine power; He promises him / He will speak through him.

v. 12. **All apostolic men / who are sent by God / have the advantage / that God speaks through their mouth / and that He teaches them / what they should say.** For in that they have surrendered themselves to Him for everything / He never fails them in their need. St. Paul expressed it very clearly before all (c): do you wish / he says / to finally become aware of the truth of Jesus Christ / who speaks through my mouth?

### Chapter IV. The Second Book of Moses.

6. And the Lord spoke further to him: Now put your hand into your bosom. And he put his hand into his bosom / and pulled it out; behold / then his hand was leprous, as white as snow.
<margin>Numbers 12:10. 2 Kings 5:27.</margin>

7. And he said: Put your hand back into your bosom. And he put his hand back into his bosom / and pulled it out of his bosom; behold / then it had become again like his flesh.

8. And it shall happen / if they will not believe you / nor obey the voice of the first sign / then they will surely believe the voice of the second sign.

9. Furthermore it shall happen / if they will also not believe these two signs / nor obey your voice / then take some water from the river / and pour it upon the dry land; then that same water / which you took from the river / shall become blood upon the dry land.

<column-break/>

10. But Moses spoke to the Lord: Oh my Lord / I am not a man of words / neither from yesterday nor the day before / nor since the time you have spoken to your servant! For I have a heavy speech and a heavy tongue.

11. Then the Lord spoke to him: Who made man's mouth? or who made the mute / or deaf / or seeing / or blind / made? Was it not I / the Lord?

12. So go now / and I will be with your mouth / and teach you what you shall say.

13. He

<columns>1</columns>

---

The second sign was intended to represent / that / where Moses and the people of Israel, when offered redemption, would merely "put their hand in their bosom" <note>This is an idiomatic expression for idleness or hesitation.</note> and not wish to take up the work / then their whole life would be subjected to a constant, unhappy drudgery. Conversely / if in the recognition of their misery they would only let God take control / so that He might carry out the work / then they would be redeemed from that misery / and restored to a blessed state. And the third sign indicated / that persistent resistance would finally be punished with extermination; just as it happened to the Egyptians. And thus, in the two or three testimonies of divine omnipotence / as so many witnesses / the truth of his calling should also stand.

v. 6. **Then his hand was leprous, as white as snow**) There he discovered / what he was like within himself.

O how necessary it is for us / to reach into our bosoms / to search our hearts / to learn to rightly know our leprosy <note>The author uses leprosy as a metaphor for internal sin or corruption.</note> / to place it before our eyes / and to be terrified by it! Nevermore will we otherwise be helped! If we remain hidden and unknown to ourselves / then we must die in our sins: because nothing unclean will enter into God’s Kingdom.

v. 10. **Oh my Lord!**) In this way our flesh and blood resists not only the extraordinary ways of God; though it is a great grace / when one can proceed like Paul in such revelations / and not confer or take counsel long with flesh and blood: Galatians 1:16. But also in the ordinary ways / where one could know the will of God. Here one truly has need, with Augustine, to pray: that God would first work in us / what His will was; and then command / what He will. <note>original: "daß GOtt zuvor in uns wircken wolle / was sein Wille wäre; und dann befehlen / was er wolle." This refers to Augustine’s famous prayer: "Give what You command, and command what You will."</note>

The Rabbis tell of Moses / that in his childhood he once reached for the King’s golden crown / and tore it from his head. When the King then wanted to test / whether he had done such a thing out of childish simplicity or malice; he had a vessel full of gold brought, along with one full of coals / to see / which he would reach for. He reached for the coals / and at the same time put them to his mouth / and burned his tongue so / that he kept a deformed speech his whole life. (a) <note>This is a famous Midrashic legend explaining Moses's "slow speech."</note>

**Lord / I cannot speak!**) because my voice is a "voice of silence": and furthermore / because You have spoken with me / I now have even less freedom to speak. For the Word of God is accustomed to swallowing up our own / and / according to the Prophet (b) / as soon as the Lord approaches His sanctuary / all flesh must be silent before His presence. As soon as God speaks to a soul / everything in it must be silent / in order to listen to Him. But if everything must be silent before God / when He wishes to speak; then on the other hand everything must speak before Him / when He commands it.

**I have a heavy speech and tongue**) As long as Moses was in Egypt / and while he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians / he had no heavy speech and tongue / but was of great eloquence. But after he began to hear the voice of God / and to perceive the divine pronouncements; he became aware / that his speech and tongue were heavy: and he confessed himself to be mute / as he began to recognize the truthful Word / which was in the beginning with God. If a rational man / even if he is not learned or eloquent / is compared with irrational animals; he will seem eloquent in comparison to them. But if he is compared with skilled / learned, and eloquent men / who are proven in all wisdom; he will seem as if mute and inarticulate. But if anyone beholds the Divine Word / and fixes his eye upon heavenly wisdom; he may be as learned and as wise as he ever wishes / yet he must confess / that he is a mute beast before God. David recognized this well; and therefore / when he weighed himself against divine wisdom / he said: *I am like a beast before you.* <note>original: "Ich bin wie ein Thier vor dir." Referring to Psalm 73:22.</note>

v. 11. Is it not God / who binds the tongue / and loosens it again? The more ignorant a person is / and the less ability to express himself he has; the more fit he is in the hand of God / for Him to make of him / whatever He wishes. Therefore / after He has sufficiently shown Moses / that it does not lie in the power of nature / to express oneself in spiritual things / but stands in divine power; He promises him / He will speak through him.

v. 12. All apostolic men / who are sent by God / have the advantage / that God speaks through their mouth / and that He teaches them / what they shall say. For because they have surrendered themselves to Him in all things / He never fails them in their need. St. Paul expressed this very clearly above all (c): Do you wish / he says / to finally perceive the truth of Jesus Christ / who speaks through my mouth?

->(b) Zechariah 2:13.<-
->(c) 2 Corinthians 13:3.<-

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter IV.

13. But he said: Oh my Lord, send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send!

**Send, I pray thee, by the hand of him whom thou wilt send)** Because Moses knew through divine revelation beforehand that the Lord intended to send His Son, the great Redeemer and Savior of the world, to lead His people out of Egypt; and that He would be *Shiloh* <note>original: "Schiloh." A Messianic title from Genesis 49:10, often interpreted as "he to whom it belongs" or "the one sent."</note>, that is, the one who was to be sent: even though he did not yet know whether he himself was to go before Him as a prefiguring redeemer; because at his first entrance or call to the work, he stood and saw clearly that he would find great opposition on all sides: therefore he prayed that the Lord would excuse him and send the great Redeemer in his place.

He also judged himself, out of deep humility, unworthy of such a high performance of office—to be used in an embassy from the only-true Potentate, the King of all kings, to the king in Egypt. For

->Wise men neither hope for nor promise as much from themselves as they are actually able to do; whereas ignorant and presumptuous people blindly force themselves into the greatest undertakings.<-

Consider this, you who are so rich in your own imagination because you are instructed in some of the wisdom of the Egyptians: you who presume to be an ambassador of *Jesus Christ* because He says to His apostles: *as the Father has sent me, so I send you also: John 20:21.* and because the apostle speaks of himself and his fellow-apostles: *We are ambassadors in Christ's stead. 2 Cor. 5:20.* Has the Lord therefore also sent you? Are you for that reason exactly His ambassador? Moses, a divine man learned in all divine and human wisdom, feared to take such a heavy burden upon himself and would have gladly withdrawn his shoulders: and you, out of pride in your bit of imagined science, with a mere unarmed head, dare to take the burden upon yourself so lightheadedly and presumptuously! Ah,

->How true it is that much inward, upright, divine, and human wisdom makes men humble and lowly! But very little and outward wisdom makes men proud and puffed up.<-

Oh, dear ones, let us wait upon the Lord until He provides us with sufficient and necessary ability and strength, and opens a door for us, and opens a way, and speaks to us: *whom shall I send?* Then let us be well prepared, yet not so bold as to speak of things that Christ has not worked in and through us. *Rom. 15:18.*

Moses's desire was for the Messiah, whom he regarded as the true Redeemer not only of this people, but also of the whole world. Nevertheless, all desires, even the most righteous, must be banished from a yielded <note>original: "gelaſſenen." A key term in German mysticism referring to "Gelassenheit," or the state of total surrender and letting go of self-will.</note> and annihilated soul: because they must desire nothing except in the will of God, who does everything at the right time. Also, the sign of his yieldedness is this impossibility of wanting or desiring anything; and one cannot depart from this complete death of all desire without greatly displeasing God.

<margin>(see Chapter 7:1.)</margin> <note>This margin note likely refers to the later passage where God explicitly tells Moses he will be "as God to Pharaoh" and Aaron will be his prophet.</note> who should be the mouth of God to the people, and also again the mouth of the people to God in prayer, especially in all public needs and concerns.

<column-break/>

14. Then the anger of the Lord was kindled against Moses, and He said: Is not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. And look, he is also coming out to meet you: and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.

15. And you shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth: and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you what you shall do.

16. And he shall speak for you to the people, and it shall happen that he shall be to you instead of a mouth, and you shall be to him instead of God.

17. And you shall take this staff in your hand, with which you shall do the signs.

18. And

---

v. 14–16. Since God had not been angered by all of Moses's questions, even though they seemed unjust, He nonetheless becomes angry at this desire: because those questions were asked in simplicity and in a very common way; but he could not wish for anything without stepping out of his station. Therefore God now ceases to be his speech and gives him a human mouth because of his lack of faith. Ah, how necessary it is never to depart from blind yieldedness and the hands of God under the pretext of good desires! However, that does not prevent God from giving everything necessary for the best of His sheep, without dwelling on this lack of faith in the shepherd.

After Moses's sin, God nonetheless promises He would be in his brother’s and his own mouth; and that Moses should always be Aaron's shepherd. Aaron is placed between the people and Moses: but Moses between God and Aaron.

God intended here to divide the two greatest and most necessary gifts upon Moses's excuse: the gift of governing, which He assigned to the authorities—hence He also attaches His name to them here, which specifically points to judicial power, as seen in *Chapter 22:8, Psalm 82:6*; and the gift of teaching and presenting the will of God to men, which is the office of prophets and shepherds: and also again to be the mouth of the people to God in prayer.

Whoever has received these gifts from God must use them in the fear of God, and may not withdraw from them without fearing God’s wrath. For this also stood against Moses, so that he did not have the honor of leading the people into the promised land of Canaan.

v. 16. Instead of God) <term>Elohim</term> <note>Hebrew: אֱלֹהִים. While usually meaning "God," the author notes it can also signify a judge or ruler acting with divine authority.</note> means God and also a judge or prince and regent. *Chapter 22:28. Psalm 82:6, 7.* And so the ancient interpreters of Scripture, the Chaldean and Arabic translations, have rendered the word. The <term>Jerusalem Targum</term> <note>original: "Targum Hierosolym." An Aramaic translation and commentary on the Torah.</note> also renders it not incorrectly as "God's interpreter," through whom Aaron should understand what the will of God was. For this reason, Justin Martyr <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD), an early Christian apologist.</note> says that Moses was called *Mercury* <note>original: "Mercurius." The Roman messenger god, associated with the Greek Hermes; both were patrons of eloquence and interpretation (hermeneutics).</note> by the Egyptians because of his deep understanding and explanation of the will of God: just as the people at Lystra called Paul *Mercury* for the very same reason. *Acts 14:12.*

It behooves us to work toward obtaining the precious promises of God, so that we may become partakers of the divine nature: which happens when we flee the corruption that is in the world through lust. *2 Peter 1:4.* And because God's characteristic is to preserve from evil and do good, let every man strive to be the "God" of the other in this regard.

v. 17. This staff) This staff was the power of God by which Moses was supported, because he could not and should not trust his own power.

### Chapter IV. The Second Book of Moses.

18. And Moses went and returned to Jeter, his father-in-law, and said to him: Please let me go, that I may return to my brothers who are in Egypt, and see if they still live! And Jethro said to Moses: Go in peace.
19. Also the Lord said to Moses in Midian: Go and return to Egypt! For all the men are dead who sought your life. <margin>Matthew 2:20.</margin>
20. So Moses took his wife and his sons, and set them on donkeys, and returned to the land of Egypt; and Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
21. And the Lord said to Moses: When you depart to return to Egypt, see that you perform all the wonders, which I have put into your hand, before the face of Pharaoh! But I will harden his heart <margin>(a) chap. 7:3, 9:12.</margin> so that he will not let the people go.

---

**v. 18. 19.** Out of humility and prudence, Moses did not wish to reveal the whole matter to Jeter (who is also called Jethro), his father-in-law, so that he might not seem to exalt himself over this great honor, nor give occasion for all kinds of rational hesitations, which would only have caused resistance to such a great undertaking. Moses also had to be encouraged again by God in Midian to fulfill the command laid upon him, so that he would not fear for his life from his former enemies, whom God knows how to remove from the way at the right time. For he may well have delayed out of fear of man.
**v. 20.** Moses, 80 years old.
**The staff of God)** It is called this because God placed a special miraculous power into it; otherwise, it was a common stick like any other. It is not necessary to invent stories, as if it were from the Tree of Life in Paradise; such wretched fables are the inventions of the blind Jews <note>The author reflects the common anti-Judaic polemics of the 17th and 18th centuries, dismissing extra-biblical Rabbinic traditions (Midrash) as "fables."</note>, with which their interpretations are entirely filled, and which one should not deem worthy of repeating. Sadly, Christians have also fallen into such fables through the blinding of Satan when they have attributed such wonders to images and other similar things, to which God never intended to attach miraculous power as He did to this staff of Moses—as we no longer need such signs and wonders in the New Testament.
**v. 21.** God hardens the heart when He withdraws from it the means of grace (to which it has no inherent right) and leaves it to its own inclinations, which are subject to the temptations of Satan. Therefore, nothing else can arise but blindness upon the withdrawal of divine light, disobedience, contempt for divine ways, malice, and hardness of mind.
Because it is sometimes said that God does it; sometimes that Pharaoh himself does it; and sometimes that his heart was hardened, without attributing it to God or Pharaoh: it is to be seen from this that these different expressions of a matter, in one case, must also have the same meaning.

<column-break/>

22. And you shall say to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord; Israel is my firstborn son:
23. And I say to you, let my son go, that he may serve me! But you have refused to let him go. Behold, I will slay your son, even your firstborn!
24. And it happened on the way at the lodging place, that the Lord met him and sought to kill him.
25. Then Zipporah took a sharp knife <margin>(a) Joshua 5:2.</margin> and circumcised the foreskin of her son, and laid it at his feet, and said: You are surely a bridegroom of blood to me!
26. Then he let him go. At that time she said, "bridegroom of blood," on account of the circumcision.

---

**v. 22.** The honor of the firstborn status was granted to Israel above all nations in the Old Testament, because God had never before chosen an entire people to whom He made Himself so common; Psalm 147:19, 20; 148:14. And because He especially had His holy and glorious ones among this people, in whom He has all His delight, Psalm 16:13, the likes of which were rarely, if ever, found among other nations. Afterward, this honor came to all believers among the Gentiles. See Exodus 19:5, 6; 1 Peter 2:9.
According to the secret sense <note>term: "secret sense" (German: *geheimer Sinn*). This refers to a mystical or allegorical interpretation popular in Pietist circles, looking for deeper spiritual truths beneath the literal text.</note>, Israel is called the firstborn son of God to indicate that souls led into the inner life should have the preference in the heavenly inheritance. This, however, does not exclude the others: since many paths lead to the heavenly fatherland; but this one to God is the most glorious and the most advantageous to those souls.
**v. 24-26.** The Lord allowed Moses to fall into a deadly sickness, as can be concluded from all circumstances, because he had given in to the softness of his wife and had not wanted to circumcise his son against her will: whereby he not only broke the covenant of God himself, but would also have given a great offense to his people in this. Zipporah then saw herself forced—namely, so that she would not lose her husband—to circumcise her son according to his instruction, since he himself could not perform it due to weakness. She then laid the foreskin at the feet of the weak man on his bed, and perhaps out of indignation called him a bridegroom of blood, whom she had to preserve with the blood of her son. Following this, it seems—perhaps due to the weakness of the child—that her release to return home followed: Chapter 18:2. Thus, in his extraordinary calling, he was not to be burdened by domestic care, and also the foreign Midianite woman might have been offensive to the people of Israel.
Zipporah well knows that the unions which God makes between souls occur only through the Cross: therefore she calls Moses, according to the secret sense in this regard as well, a bridegroom of blood; because she recognized that it was impossible for such a holy man to be united with her without her sharing in his sufferings. Therefore she removes herself from him on account of the circumcision, which was the first of his sufferings and only the beginning of those to follow, and she feared it—namely, the cutting off and the killing. There are few faithful souls who keep each other company in the way of blood and the Cross.
**v. 26.** Some testify that the Jews in their circumcision ceremonies are also said to use the words: "You are a bridegroom of blood to me!" And then the words could also be rendered: "At that time it was customary to say, 'bridegroom of blood,' on account of the circumcisions or during the circumcisions." However, this also points primarily to Christ, who had to acquire His bride with His blood, and thus also became a true bridegroom of blood to us, to whom we are bound even unto blood, since He could not obtain us without His blood. See 1 Peter 1:19; Hebrews 12:4; Revelation 2:10.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter V.

27. Now the Lord had spoken to Aaron: Go out to meet Moses in the wilderness: and he had gone, and met him at the mountain 
<margin>(a) chap. 3:1.</margin> 
(a) of God, and kissed him.

28. And Moses showed to Aaron all the words of the Lord, who had sent him, and all the signs which he had commanded him.

29. And Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the children of Israel. <margin>chap. 3:16, 5:14.</margin>

30. And Aaron spoke all the words which the Lord had spoken to Moses, and performed the signs before the eyes of the people.

31. And the people (a) believed: and when they heard that the Lord had looked upon the children of Israel, and that he had seen their oppression; then they bowed themselves and worshipped. <margin>(a) chap. 14:31.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 27.</margin>
The Lord had to reveal himself to Aaron in an extraordinary way, so that he would set out on the journey and meet his brother, who would have been entirely unrecognizable to him during the 40 years of his absence, in order to also equip him as a co-helper in this great work.

Met him at the mountain) And will you not also come to meet Moses at the mountain? That is, to reach the high understanding of the Law and its spiritual meaning; or will you remain at the lowly letter and look primarily only at the Jewish history? If so, God will not be with your mouth, nor teach you what you should speak. Aaron would not have been used for this high calling had he not done so.

<margin>v. 31.</margin>
The people believed) And in the faith of this Name they came out of Egypt: and they could not go out of Egypt until they believed Moses. In the same way, we also cannot be redeemed from our spiritual Egypt unless we believe in the one who is the Prophet like Moses, who comes in his Father’s name, "I am": <note>original: "Ich bin"</note> John 8:24.

But no one believes as quickly as the inwardly gathered <note>The German "eingekehrte" refers to people focused on their internal spiritual life.</note> people: for their entire guidance is founded upon faith. For this reason, Moses and Aaron find no resistance in bringing the knowledge of God’s counsels to the people of Israel and introducing them into the same. Those people who deal only with their reason and want nothing but evidence do not act this way: they do not yield immediately, but everything must be maintained with them by force.

Three days' journey) Contained in the saying:

We perform these 3 days' journeys out of Egypt when we cleanse ourselves from all defilement, and our entire (1) Spirit, and (2) Soul, and (3) Body are preserved blameless for the day of Jesus Christ. <note>A reference to 1 Thessalonians 5:23.</note>

<column-break/>

### Chapter V.

->The heavier tribulations of the people.<-

And afterward Moses and Aaron went in, and spoke to Pharaoh: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel; Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness!

2. And Pharaoh answered: Who is the Lord (a), whose voice I should obey to let Israel go? I do not know the Lord: nor will I let Israel go. <margin>(a) Proverbs 30:9. Job 35:10.</margin>

3. But they said: The God of the Hebrews has met us; so let us now go three days' journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to the Lord our God; lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword. 4. Then

---

<margin>v. 1. Moses and Aaron)</margin>
Aaron seems to have appeared in the name of the elders of Israel, as God had first commanded Moses in Chapter 3:18.

<margin>Hold a feast)</margin>
This was one and the same: that they wanted to hold a feast and sacrifice; for sacrificing was the most prominent part of the feast.

<margin>v. 2.</margin>
Just as Pharaoh haughtily refused to obey God, so is this the mindset of all the godless who let go of the fear of God: by following their evil mind in everything, they then fall into great hardness against their neighbor. As Job thoughtfully notes: to him whose mercy vanishes for his neighbor, he abandons the fear of the Almighty. Chapter 6:14. See further Chapter 21:14-15. Psalm 10:3-4. 36:1–5. And this is the heavy judgment of obduracy <note>original: "Verstockung"</note> upon rulers when they lose all love and mercy toward their subjects and think of nothing but burdens and grievances with which they oppress their subjects: which then finally brings the heavy judgments of God upon such rulers and their lands, as is seen here with Pharaoh and Egypt.

Pharaoh indeed had reason to say he did not know the Lord. The proud do not know him, but only the humble, who serve him in the simplicity of their hearts. This way of speaking—"Who is the Lord? I do not know him!"—indicates a pride worthy of a thousand hells. The brazen and proud spirits of the world speak thus when one talks to them about something concerning their soul's best interest. They do not want to obey God, who speaks to them through the mouths of his servants, because they do not know him.

I do not know the Lord) I do not recognize him as my Lord.

Here it is now revealed that Pharaoh first hardened his own heart against God’s commandment.

<margin>v. 3. Met)</margin>
or also, "is or will be called upon in and over us": which might perhaps fit better as an answer to Pharaoh’s question than "met," and in the Scripture the Chaldean translator <note>The "Chaldean translator" refers to the Targum, an Aramaic translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible.</note> also has it: "The God of the Jews is called upon over us."

This should awaken a reflection in us, that we consider well who and whose name is called upon over us, and who it is that recognizes us as his people. Thus we, as many of us as name the name of the Lord in truth, shall depart from iniquity. 2 Timothy 2:19.

I am (1) the way, (2) the truth, and (3) the life.

---

Into the wilderness) Do not think that it was only then that Moses wanted to lead the people out of Egypt: we also have a Moses with us, namely the Law, the will of God, which wants to lead you out of Egypt. If we give ear to this, he wants to bring us far away from Pharaoh, and lead us out of the work of mud and stubble <note>A reference to the slave labor of making bricks.</note>. But an obedient ear is required, and that we understand the Law spiritually. The same now desires that we should not stay, or let ourselves be kept, in the works of the flesh and of darkness, but go out into the wilderness and enter into a state that is free from the turmoil and bustle of the world, namely into the rest of silence. For the words of wisdom are learned in stillness and rest. When you now come to this place of rest, then you can sacrifice to the Lord; there you can recognize the Law of God and the power of the divine voice. Therefore Moses wants to tear you out from the midst of the noise of those unfruitful works and worldly affairs, and lead you out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of ignorance, so that you may perceive the Law of God and receive the light of wisdom.

### Chapter V. The Second Book of Moses. 299

4. Then the King of Egypt said to them: You, Moses and Aaron, why do you turn the people away from their labors? Go back to your burdens!

5. Pharaoh spoke further: Behold, the people of the land are already too many, and yet you want them to stop their labors!

6. Therefore, on that same day, Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters among the people and their officers, saying:

7. From now on, you shall no longer give the people straw to burn bricks as you did yesterday and the day before! Let them go themselves and gather straw for themselves!

<note>v. 4. Why do you turn the people away?) So it goes even today when "Moses and Aaron"—that is, the prophetic word—lure and invite the soul to serve God uprightly, to go out from the world, to renounce all that one possesses, to seek one's delight in the Law of the Lord, and to follow the Word of God. Then one soon hears Pharaoh’s companions saying: "See how they lead the people astray so that they will not work!" Under the pretext of godliness, they claim one only seeks to pursue laziness and idleness.</note>

<note>v. 5. Pharaoh) Was, as noted elsewhere, a general great title for a king in this land, much like the name Emperor is used today in the Roman Empire, Sultan in Turkey, and Sophi <note>A term for the Safavid rulers of Persia</note> in Persia. It signifies a "completely free man and lord." From this word, the Spanish Jesuit Pineda <margin>(a) Book 4, On the Affairs of Solomon, chapter 2.</margin> argues that the title "Baron" is also derived. According to the report of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, the kings in Egypt were so named from the time of Menes, who ruled before Abraham, through the times of Solomon, for over 1300 years. There are likely twelve such kings who appear in Holy Scripture and had dealings with the children of Israel. 1. The first in Genesis 12:15; 2. The second is mentioned in Chapter 41 and following; 3. The third in Chapters 46 and 47; 4. The fourth in Exodus 1; 5. The fifth in Chapter 2:15; 6. The sixth in Chapter 14; 7. The seventh in 1 Kings 3:1 and 9:16, who is said to have been Solomon's father-in-law; 8. The eighth in Chapter 11:18; 9. The ninth in 2 Kings 17:4; 10. The tenth in Isaiah 37:9; 11. The eleventh in 2 Kings 23:29; 12. The twelfth in Jeremiah 44:30.</note>

<note>v. 6. 7. It is a sign of perverse human cleverness—which is merely earthly, sensual, and even devilish—to think that by increasing burdens one can steer the people away from perceived "frivolity." Such measures mostly strike the poor and the pious who groan under these loads. Instead, one should guide the people through healthy laws and close observation of the same; then all could enjoy God's blessing in moderation and apply physical prosperity to the salvation of the soul through the planting and love of truth. See Jeremiah 7 and Psalm 81:9-17.</note>

<note>Let us recognize and revere, O children of Adam, the gentle governance of God! It bears no comparison to human—or rather, inhuman—severity and hardness. Let us watch what we do and guard ourselves from forming a wrong concept or thought of God, imagining Him to be irrational or unjust, or making Him equal to Pharaoh or his taskmasters, who wanted bricks made but gave no straw. That would be to think He demands obedience from us but refuses to give us the strength for it.</note>

<note>Our God is not like that. He who commands and bids us also gives us the strength and courage to do what He commands. He requires no more from us than what He has given and still gives. His service is so fair that He either gives us strength to do what He bids, or He is satisfied with what we are able to do.</note>

<column-break/>

8. And the number of bricks which they made yesterday and the day before, you shall lay upon them; you shall diminish nothing thereof! For they are idle; therefore they cry out, saying: "We want to go and sacrifice to our God."

9. Let the men be burdened with service so that they must work at it and not look around for false words!

10. Then the taskmasters of the people and their officers went out and spoke to the people, saying: Thus says Pharaoh: "I will give you no straw!"

11. Go yourselves and get straw wherever you find it. But not the slightest bit of your service shall be diminished!

12. Then...

<note>v. 8. They are idle) In the same way today, people who have turned inward are accused of idleness. Inexperienced leaders, and those who do not know what "mystical rest" <note>A state of silent, contemplative prayer</note> is, see a soul devoted to contemplation and quiet prayer—desiring nothing but to offer itself up in the simplicity of its heart—and say to one another: "We want to burden them with 'good works,' for all their service to God is just idleness." But God well knows how to snatch these souls, whom He has chosen for His rest, out of their hands, to hide them in the secret of His presence against all the confusion of men.</note>

<note>v. 9. Let us just burden them with the outward works we wish to impose, so that they do not dwell on their "deceptions" or their "inner word," which are nothing but lying words and fraud. Ah, you bold people who, like Pharaoh, mock the servants and handmaids of God as frauds and fantasists! Do you not think that God will punish you just as He punished him?</note>

<note>Let the men be burdened with service: There is a time of "willing service to sin" when it does not feel heavy, but rather the work and service of sin come easily to people; this state is spoken of in Numbers 11:18.</note>

<note>But when the Lord comes to visit and redeem, then the spiritual Pharaoh and his taskmasters—the dominant lusts—lay on a burden through the service of sin that becomes very heavy for the soul. Paul speaks of this state in Romans 7:15, etc. The servant then cries out for deliverance (v. 24).</note>

<note>When the number of bricks is doubled, then Moses comes: and then the people are most willing and ready to receive him. When people groan under the Egyptian burdens of their sins, then a Prophet like Moses is very welcome. Likewise, such people—those who are weary and heavy-laden—are in turn very welcome and invited by him. And these are the only ones who shall find rest for their souls and partake in redemption.</note>

<note>v. 10. 11. It is indeed a heartless hardness when one imposes heavy financial burdens and yet provides no means of livelihood by which subjects might earn the money to pay them. But a merciless judgment will fall upon him who has shown no mercy, and mercy triumphs over judgment (James 2:13). The "great ones" of the world especially need this because of their many worldly pleasures and other sins; they would do well to take to heart the wise counsel Daniel gave to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4:27).</note>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter V.

**12.** So the people scattered throughout the whole land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

**13.** And the taskmasters pressed them, saying: "Complete your work, what is appointed for each day, just as when you had straw!"

**14.** And the officers of the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them, were beaten; and it was said: "Why have you not completed your set work of burning bricks as yesterday and the day before, both yesterday and today?"

**15.** Then the officers of the children of Israel went in and cried out to Pharaoh, saying: "Why do you deal thus with your servants?"

**16.** No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us: "Make bricks!" and behold, your servants are beaten, and your people must have sinned! <note>The German phrase "dein Volck muß sich versündiget haben" suggests that the people are being treated as if they are at fault, or that the fault lies with Pharaoh's own people for their cruelty.</note>

---

<margin>v. 13. 14.</margin> These taskmasters or forced-labor overseers were Egyptians, who in turn took officers and supervisors from the children of Israel and set them over their brothers to keep them at the work assigned by them; they were held responsible for delivering the full count of bricks.

Severity is combined here with threats, and even blows, so that these poor souls might be oppressed—souls who, even under the hardships imposed upon them, place their entire trust in God. They are burdened with impossible tasks; and when they do not perform them all, they are accused of disobedience. Comfort yourselves, you inward friends of God! The more you must endure the contradiction of men, the more you will share in His holy life.

<margin>v. 15. 16.</margin> The poor oppressed ones, under the labor imposed on them by their unenlightened leaders, cry out that their exercises are unbearable, at least in such great quantity. They also complain that while they can be overloaded with rituals/customs, they cannot be given the ease to fulfill them, which has even been taken from them—undoubtedly by the very one who gave it to them: that they are given no rest, and that more severity is used against them than against others.

See Isaiah 45:11: "Ask me of things to come concerning my sons, and concerning the work of my hands command ye me." <note>This verse is used here to suggest that God eventually takes command of the "work" His people are forced to do.</note>

...me and the spirit of the world. We shall one day be idle to the world so that we can be occupied with Him.

<column-break/>

**17.** Then he said: "You are lazy, lazy are you! That is why you say: 'Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.'"

**18.** "So go now and work! No straw shall be given to you, but you shall deliver the full count of bricks."

**19.** Then the officers of the children of Israel saw that things stood poorly for them, because it was said: "You shall not diminish anything from your bricks, from what is appointed for each day."

**20.** And they met Moses and Aaron, who stood opposite them as they came out from Pharaoh.

**21.** And they said to them: "May the Lord look upon you and judge, for you have made our scent stink in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants, and you have put a sword into their hand to slay us!"

**22.** Mo-

---

<margin>v. 17. 18.</margin> To this, it is answered: because their inner self is idle <note>The commentator interprets "laziness" as an inward stillness or "quietism" that the worldly-minded Pharaoh perceives as sloth.</note>, and they find pleasure in remaining thus in rest in God in the spirit of sacrifice, they are further burdened with all kinds of exercises of penance and with unbearable works of the "active life."

<margin>v. 20. 21.</margin> They then go to those who have brought them through grace into the ways of sacrifice, and say to them in their astonishment: "You have led us into a way of death!" For those who previously led us with some kindness now use only hardness against us; and your knowledge has been to us as a sword of death.

These officers, who may also have been partly from the elders of Israel, were thus indignant at the free witnesses of God. This is usually the price when God's grace does not appear according to the timing and logic that people imagine. But God usually wants to test faith and its sincerity through trials, whereby the world shall be made truly distasteful to a person, so that they turn all the more eagerly to God and long for His help; so that then God, who always appears with His help at the right time and knows how to fulfill His precious promises to His own glory, might be praised all the more heartily for it. And such temptations then also come upon the witnesses themselves, whose faith and patience God also wants to test, in order to leave the execution of what God lets them witness entirely to Him, as God always reserves the time and manner in His own doing.

...of my hands! Namely, how God wants to rescue His people.

God wants to have such "idlers": let Pharaoh scold and say what he will.

<column-break/>

It is true that under the name of Christianity, curiosity and laziness have been practiced time and again, just as such disorderly conduct was already punished by the Apostles in those who wanted to be idle under the appearance of godliness: 2 Thessalonians 3:11. And examples of such hypocritical idlers have never been lacking. However, one also sees and experiences how many act as true Egyptian taskmasters; in the worldly spirit of Pharaoh, they do nothing but drive and drive toward physical work, whereby neither they nor others can breathe <term>respiriren</term> <note>From the Latin *respirare*, meaning to take a breath or recover spiritually</note> and recover for spiritual work. Such people, however well they may mean it and however useful the work may otherwise be, truly make themselves similar to the Egyptian taskmasters insofar as they hold back or turn away a single member of the "Israel of God" from the way to true soul-rest, which is the entrance into Canaan. They have nothing else to expect than that such oppressed spirits, amidst all their gathering of stubble, will cry all the more vehemently to the Lord. He will afterwards lead them out with a strong hand, to the wonder of the oppressors, and drown the taskmasters and tyrants—even those who did not yet want to hear the Lord's voice—through penance. Then such taskmasters must realize how precious-bought and yet willing souls are not to be tied so sclavishly to external services, but how in Christian modesty and freedom a thousand times more is accomplished and with greater blessing.

**22.** Moses however turned back to the LORD and said: "LORD, why have You dealt so poorly with this people? Why have You sent me here?"

These few words, which Moses sends to God, are the prayer of a tender heart and a faithful shepherd, who complains to God Himself about himself—that He did not immediately deliver this poor people from cruelty as soon as He had created them. O holy promise, how far is your fulfillment generally removed from what one thinks! The moment of Providence, which reveals you, shows in its outcome quite different things than those which one presumed through the hope one had for it. You promised in few words to rescue this people: and it seemed even to the Saints, who are the ministers of such a great work, that You would do this immediately. But with what wonders and special Providence must this rescue occur! And of all those who were delivered from Egypt with so many miracles, only two persons will enter into the promised land! Who shall fathom the deep counsels of God! Oh, how beautiful and good it is that they remain hidden from the creature, until that which He has appointed comes to pass!

### The VI. Chapter.
->The Explanation of the Name JEHOVAH, and the Lineage of Moses.<-

**1.** And the LORD said to Moses: "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh! For by a strong hand he must let them go; yes, by a strong hand he will drive them out of his land."

**2.** Furthermore, God spoke to Moses and said to him: "I am the LORD!"

<margin>v. 1.</margin> God answers Moses with a very great kindness, accommodating Himself to the weakness of His creature when it acts in simplicity. Does it not seem as if God were excusing Himself to Moses? He says: "Now you shall see how I will go to work!" O Simplicity, you are truly the language that pleases God! Since she seeks nothing else, nor desires many inventions, which do not please God.

...have well recognized my omnipotence in all those leadings; but my name I have not revealed to them, which indicates that I am who I am. Since I have now chosen you as the lawgiver, not only of the people of Israel but also of the inner people, it is necessary that you have more knowledge of my entire being and of the "nothingness" of the creature: so that from this, both through your experience and through my inspiration, you may instruct those souls chosen for <term>annihilation</term> <note>German: *Vernichtigung*. A mystical term referring to the soul's process of stripping away the self to become nothing so that God can be everything.</note>. This deep knowledge, my dear Moses, is reserved for you as a great prince of the mystical people and my dear "annihilated ones," and as the most essential and perfect image of my only Son—the head and firstborn of all those who honor my terrible name through their secret annihilation: who also, through the knowledge and confession of their nothingness, rightly worship the sovereignty of my Being. You shall also see even more effects of my omnipotence than your fathers did: because through you, even through unheard-of miracles, I will fulfill what I had only promised to them.

(*Name JEHOVAH*) Is called by the Hebrews *Shem ha-Mephorash* <note>original: "Schem hamphorasch"</note>, the separated name, or the explained name, and according to their report was to be kept exceedingly secret, and spoken only by the priests and the High Priest, and indeed in the Temple alone, and that very softly. Outside the Temple, it was absolutely forbidden to be spoken. Whoever spoke it outside the Temple, they said, would have no part in the world to come, and should also be burned: as happened to *R. Chanina* <note>Rabbi Hanina ben Teradyon, a martyr during the Roman persecutions.</note>, who for that very reason was wisely condemned to the fire; his wife was likewise condemned to death, and his daughter thrust into a brothel. It is also known that because this name was held so secret and holy, today it is not known how it should rightly be pronounced, since even the *Points* <note>Vowel markings (nikkud) in Hebrew manuscripts.</note> that stand under it do not belong to the name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton: YHWH</note>, but to the name אדוני <note>Adonai, meaning "Lord."</note>.

<column-break/>

**23.** "For since I went in to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has done evil to this people, and You have not delivered Your people at all!"

(Since -- to speak in Your name) In the very same way, the spiritual Pharaoh deals with us when the Lawgiver sends His law to us. Sin becomes more powerful and violent when the law comes than it was before.

Before the Word of God is heard, before the divine preaching resounds, all is quiet and still; the "strong armed man" <note>A reference to Luke 11:21, often interpreted as the devil or the ego holding onto its possessions.</note> keeps his own in peace, and there is little temptation and tribulation. As long as the trumpet does not blow, the battle does not begin. But when the trumpet of the Word gives a signal, then the fight starts! Then follows the pressure of persecution. Since Moses and Aaron began to speak with Pharaoh, the people of God were treated badly: and since the Word of God will have pressed into your soul, a conflict will also arise within you.

---

**3.** "And I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, under an All-Sufficient God: but by my name JEHOVAH I was not known to them."

**4.** "So I have also established my covenant with them, that I will give them the land of Canaan, the land of their pilgrimages, wherein they stayed as strangers."

<margin>see Jeru.</margin>
<margin>v. 3.</margin> I indeed appeared to Abraham in bare faith, to *Isaac* in pure sacrifice, and to *Israel* in true <term>resignation</term> <note>German: *Gelassenheit*. A central concept in German mysticism meaning yieldedness or letting go of self-will.</note>, as the Almighty God; they into whom I have guided them: but my very greatest name I have not revealed to them, which indicates that I am who I am.

(*Not known*) Namely, as one who fulfills his promises and gives essence to his word. Names, according to their initial conception, were certain external designations and characteristics of things. Therefore, God also assumed different names according to His various revelations. Now He wished to become known to the Israelites in the name *Jehovah*, and to reveal to Pharaoh His highest and unrestricted sovereignty and royal preference in the defense and protection of the Israelites and the punishment of the haughty Egyptians—that they had despised the message of the Lord of Lords. Thus, this name agreed with the manner in which He wished to reveal Himself to them.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter VI.

**5.** Furthermore, I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, how the Egyptians compel them to serve; and I have remembered my covenant.

**6.** Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rescue you from their service, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments.

**7.** And I will take you to me for a people, and I will be your God<gloss>(a)</gloss>; so that you shall experience that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians;
<margin>(a) 2 Cor. 6:16-17.</margin>

**8.** And I have brought you into the land concerning which I lifted up my hand, that I would give it to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob; and I will give it to you for an inheritance;
->I am the LORD!<-

---

Thus He gives them to know the reason for His will: that He wishes hereby to fulfill His promises to their faithful fathers and the covenant He made with them. In that covenant, He offered Himself to them as the all-sufficient God <note>original: "allgenugsamen GOtt," referring to El Shaddai</note>, Genesis 17:1-2; 35:11, who wished to be their gracious God, from whom they were therefore to expect every good thing: See 1 Timothy 6:15. But as far as the mystery-rich name JEHOVAH is concerned, which was indeed known to them according to the word—as may be seen in Genesis 2:4, 22:14, 24:7, 26:24-25, 27:20, 28:13, etc.—it was now also to become gloriously known according to its essence. This would happen as God would now indeed prove to them what He is in the present: namely, the kind and merciful God, which He has also been from all eternity; as Love itself, which cannot flow out in any way other than in love. And He would now soon actually prove this to them in deed, when He would give them the promised glorious land entirely as an inheritance, in which their pious, faithful fathers had to stay only as strangers. First, however, He would powerfully lead them out from under the burden of servitude, along with the evidence of His righteous punishments upon their unmerciful masters; in contrast, He would again show them goodness in the promised land and would gloriously bless and protect them therein as His own special people. Chapter 19:5-6.

Furthermore, God also indicates herewith how He wishes one day to prove all His glorious promises to all believers from all peoples, tongues, and languages in His dear Son. And He will once more become truly known in the appearance of His glorious kingdom. 2 Timothy 4:1. Then everything will be presented that God has spoken through the mouth of His holy prophets since the world began.

Finally, however, everyone must see to it that this glorious name also becomes known to them according to its essence; that Christ also becomes our essential wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, who redeems us from all ignorance, godlessness, unholiness, and finally from sin, death, the devil, and hell. See 1 Corinthians 1:30, Titus 2:14, Luke 1:74.

**v. 5.** Nothing affects the heart of God more than seeing His dear surrendered ones <note>original: "Gelassenen," referring to those who have yielded their will to God</note> captive and complaining under the yoke of servitude.

**v. 6. With an outstretched arm)** This word "arm" indicates that He intends to stretch it out with an extraordinary power.

**v. 7.** The LORD also assures that He wants to make this surrendered people a people of His own possession, and that He wants to be their God in a special way, further adding that they would experience that He is their LORD. That is: because no people approaches God more than those who know how to surrender themselves and leave themselves to Him without the slightest exception; so God gives Himself to these, His true friends, more than He does to any other people. For He does not allow Himself to be surpassed in this lovely gift, and gives Himself most gloriously to the one—even in this life—who also gives themselves perfectly to Him.

**v. 6-7. I will (1) bring you out / -- and I will (2) rescue you / and I will (3) redeem you / and I will (4) take you)**
<gloss>(+)</gloss> Because God uses 4 words here, every father of a household among the Jews drinks 4 cups of red wine at Easter <note>the Passover Seder</note>.

**v. 9.** When the powers of darkness manifest themselves greatly in the children of unbelief and in the powerful, the courage of the believers very quickly fails, so that they almost forget all of God's promises because of it, and very easily sin with unbelief when they feel the scepter of the godless heavy upon them, such that they are unable to break through. Then they must hold onto the words which also contain the promise of the Savior, where He says: "In me you have peace, but in the world you have anxiety; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." John 16:33.

There are many who obey the way of God as long as it is full of sweetness and accompanied by nothing but miracles; but they hardly obey Him when He brings only the Cross (and labor). This is the unfaithfulness that beginners often commit.

**v. 12.** Moses’s excuse seems just enough, as he suggests that if the children—who are in their father's presence—will not obey because of the Cross, then the wicked and the enemies will be much less likely to follow that which is contrary to their own benefit.

**Uncircumcised of lips)** By nature we are uncircumcised of lips, that is, incapable of glorifying God with our mouths to others, until natural ineptitude and ignorance are taken away. Christ alone, however, can give us a mouth and wisdom which all adversaries may not contradict nor resist. Luke 21:15. See also Chapter 4:10-11.

### Chapter VI. The Second Book of Moses.

**14.** These are the heads of each of their fathers' houses. The sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel, were Hanoch and Pallu, Hezron and Carmi. These are the families of Reuben.
**15.** And the sons of Simeon: Jemuel, and Jamin, and Ohad, and Jachin, and Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the families of Simeon.
**16.** And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their births: Gershon and Kohath and Merari. The years of Levi’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven years.
**17.** The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, according to their families.
**18.** And the sons of Kohath were: Amram, and Izhar, and Hebron, and Uzziel. And the years of Kohath’s life were one hundred and thirty-three years.
**19.** And the sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These are the families of Levi according to their births.
**20.** And Amram took his aunt <note>original: "Baase," referring to his father's sister</note> Jochebed as his wife, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. And the years of Amram’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven years.
**21.** And the sons of Izhar were: Korah and Nepheg and Zichri.
**22.** And the sons of Uzziel were: Mishael and Elzaphan and Sithri.

---

It is evident from this that the children of Israel maintained the form of government customary among their fathers within their families; that the elders in each family were also the head of the same, whom the others had to obey. This is the natural order that God wished to be observed among His people. However, just as Pharaoh may have interrupted this order and appointed officials over them according to his whim, so the people themselves later desired such a heathen style of government by kings over them; kings who were then appointed over them according to their own pleasure, where instead of a loving fatherly government, a harsh and domineering one commonly followed. See 1 Samuel 8:5, etc.

Only the families of Reuben, Simeon, and Levi are recounted here to show that, despite the harsh rebuke and pronouncement made by Jacob over them in Genesis 49, they nevertheless retained their rights among the twelve tribes: for the children shall not bear the iniquity of their fathers. The tribe of Levi, and then that of Aaron, is detailed more extensively to show how the priestly generation of the faithful—and especially the firstborn, whom God wishes to make into priests and kings—will be very precisely observed by God, so that they shall always stand and serve before the Lord. See Judges 20:28, Psalm 134, Revelation 1:6.

<column-break/>

**23.** And Aaron took Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab <margin>(a) Matthew 1:4.</margin> and sister of Nahshon, as his wife; and she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.
**24.** And the sons of Korah were: Assir and Elkanah and Abiasaph. These are the families of the Korahites.
**25.** And Eleazar, Aaron's son, took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife; and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers of the Levites according to their families.
**26.** This is the Aaron and Moses to whom the Lord said: Lead the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt according to their hosts.
**27.** These are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh the king in Egypt, that they might lead the children of Israel out of Egypt. This is that Moses and Aaron.
**28.** And it happened on the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
**29.** That the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I am the Lord; speak to Pharaoh the king in Egypt everything that I say to you.
**30.** And Moses said before the face of the Lord: Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips <note>A Hebrew idiom meaning Moses felt he lacked the eloquence or "purity" of speech to be persuasive</note>, how then will Pharaoh listen to me?

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

---

Thus the name of godly rulers and teachers will remain a blessing with God and the faithful, through whom the Lord wishes to protect His people and lead them out of the bondage of natural corruption and sin. They must confidently oppose the powers of darkness in the strength of the Lord, while denying their own strength and ability. See Psalm 77:21, Daniel 12:3.

It is remarkable that in verse 26, Aaron is named first and then Moses; and in verse 27, Moses is named first and then Aaron. This shows that the Lord observes no preference or so-called "rank" among His faithful servants, but rather each should attend to his commanded business with all faithfulness of heart. See also Matthew 10:2, etc., Mark 3:16, etc.

**v. 20. His Aunt)** Since the number of the children of Israel was still small, God overlooked this marriage with the father's sister—as can be seen in Chapter 2:1—so that they might remain among themselves and marry one another. This type of marriage God later forbade, and it is henceforth counted as an act of incest <note>original: "Blut-Schande," literally blood-shame</note>. Leviticus 18:12, 20:19.

# Chapter VII.

->Pharaoh’s hardening through his wise men / and the first plague of the land.<-

AND the Lord spoke to Moses: Behold, I have made you as a (a) God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet! <margin>(a) Ps. 82:6.</margin>
2. You shall speak all that I command you: but Aaron your brother shall speak it to Pharaoh, that he let the children of Israel go out of his land.
3. But I (a) will harden Pharaoh's heart, that I may multiply my signs and my wonders in the land of Egypt. <margin>(a) ch. 4:21. ch. 8:15. ch. 10:27. Rom. 9:17.</margin>
4. And Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may lay my hand against Egypt, and lead out my hosts, my people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt through great judgments.
5. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord, when I stretch forth my hand over Egypt, that I may lead the children of Israel out from their midst.
6. Then Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded them; so they did.
7. And Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
8. And the Lord spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:
9. When Pharaoh speaks to you and says: Perform a miracle for yourselves! then you shall say to Aaron: Take your staff and cast it before Pharaoh, so that it becomes a dragon <note>original: "Drachen," here likely referring to a large serpent or crocodile.</note>.

<margin>Since kings wish to recognize no one as their superior except God and the sword, they must accept how God, either directly or through others, chooses to exercise this supreme authority over them.</margin>
Moses was to act here as an emissary from God, both to present God’s command to Pharaoh and, if he should be disobedient, to threaten him with God’s judgments and actually execute them. All powerful rulers should take this to heart and bow under the mighty hand of God when He lets His command be presented to them through His servants; they could test the spirit of these servants if they were willing to be humble and recognize the justice of the matter that God demands of them.

v. 1. **I have made you as a God to Pharaoh)** That is: You, good man, are afraid of him now, but he shall be as afraid of you as if you were his God! I will impress such a secret awe into him. Therefore, Moses afterwards often spoke the harsh truth to his face.

The annihilated souls <note>A term from mystical theology referring to a soul that has completely emptied itself of self-will and "creaturely" identity to be filled entirely by God's presence.</note> are like the gods set over princes. For when everything belonging to the creature has first disappeared within them, then necessarily nothing but God must remain in them. The interpreters of such annihilated people are their prophets: because they preach nothing but the words of God, when they bring forth for the benefit of others that which these souls—who have become "god" through the complete annihilation of themselves—speak out.

**Prophet)** Prophets here are those who present the word revealed by God to others to whom God wishes His will to be made known. To the former, God gives the spirit of revelation, and to the latter, the gift of eloquence, and the requirement that they must recognize the finger of God in the former and thus receive it on God’s behalf. See Ch. 4:15, 16. See also an example of this in Ananias and Saul, Acts 9:10, 20.

v. 3. **I will harden Pharaoh's heart)** That is: I will achieve nothing with Pharaoh through all the wonder-works except the hardening of his heart; so that his heart will not be made soft thereby, but rather more hardened.

God has a great wealth of goodness and longsuffering: But when a person has gradually gathered a great treasure of evil through the deceit of sins and has grown strong in malice, then first the judgment of hardening comes upon him, such that God withdraws from him and takes away His grace. After this withdrawal, the person falls from one sin into another, from one evil into another. And God can certainly do this out of righteous judgment. Thus Pharaoh hardens himself, and is hardened, or his own hardening is, as it were, sealed by the Lord.

Paul likely understood best how it is said of God that He hardens the heart, when he cried out: Do you despise the riches of the goodness, patience, and longsuffering of God? Do you not know that God’s patience is intended to lead and move you to repentance? But you, according to your hardness <note>original "Zärtigkeit" here used ironically or as an archaic term for a self-indulgent, unyielding heart</note> and your unrepentant heart, are storing up wrath for yourself for the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God! Rom. 2:4, 5.

Because the Lord does not punish Pharaoh in his own person nor his close relatives initially, it is said by the Lord that He hardens his heart because of this goodness and leniency; whereas otherwise, strictly speaking, Pharaoh hardened his heart more and more through the opportunity that God spared him; until the death of his firstborn son woke him up. For then he began to yield, and his hard heart became more flexible, because he feared he would have to be the next one.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 7. There is a noteworthy division in the lifespan of Moses. 40 years he spent in his courtly life, where he was raised in the manner of the great and wise of the world; 40 years he had to stay in a foreign land in the land of Midian in a simple way of life, and therein, as it were, forget again the vanities of the world and its sciences; and 40 years he led the people in the wilderness and administered the heavy office of ruler among them.</margin>
Thus souls must first be weaned from all earthly things and let themselves be emptied in a stillness, until they can then be deemed worthy of a greater grace and divine revelation.

v. 9. Unbelievers demand signs and wonders, and God also gives them the same: but experience teaches how little these take effect with perverse souls. On the contrary, such people believe more in lying powers, signs, and wonders, whereby they only allow themselves to persist and be hardened in their error and unrighteousness, as also happened here. See 1 Cor. 14:22, 2 Thess. 2:9, 10.

This miracle, however, should teach all rulers that if they turn the staff and scepter of governance entrusted to them by God into a rod of the wicked and a scepter of tyrants—namely, through harshness—then God will break it in due time. With such a rod they strike the nations in wrath without ceasing and rule over the heathens with fury, Isa. 14:5, 6; yes, with which they also become too burdensome a burden to the lot of the righteous, Ps. 125:3. But this staff will also become a dragon to them, and, as they have taken on the power of the dragon (the old serpent) and exercised its cruelty, they will also share in its fate, Rev. 13:4, 12. They should therefore rather learn to wield the scepter of love of the Kingdom of the Lamb in mercy, goodness, justice, and wisdom, as a blessing over themselves, their descendants, and their subjects and lands.

10. Then Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD had commanded; and Aaron threw his staff down before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a dragon. <note>original: "Drachen." In early modern German Bibles, this term often refers to a large serpent or sea-monster.</note>
11. Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and the sorcerers, and the Egyptian magicians also did the same with their enchantments.

<note>Commentary on Verses 10-11</note>
GOD permits Satan to blind the eyes of the unbelieving with lying powers; and it is of no concern to us how it may have happened—whether their staffs truly transformed into such cruel dragons, or whether such creatures were brought in from elsewhere through the incantations of these sorcerers, or if their eyes were merely deceived. It is enough that GOD, by a righteous judgment, allows such power to the enemy; yet He already knows how to put that power to shame and to show how His omnipotence is greater, or to expose the fraud of those lying wonders.

Furthermore, the Apostle—drawing from ancient testimony in the scriptures—held that among these sorcerers, the most prominent were Jannes and Jambres, who resisted Moses (2 Timothy 3:8). Thus, they are noted as an image of all those who resist the truth; they keep people in error with their lying wonders, or even with "true" miracles that the LORD permits through evil powers as a judgment, now that the truth of the Gospel no longer requires miracles. They also represent those who, with their <term>sophistry</term> <note>clever but false reasoning</note> and perverted eloquence and reason, always resist the testimony of the truth and seek in every way and with every effort to make it suspicious. See 1 Timothy 6:3, 4, 5.

->Note, on the other hand, in the<-
### Staff of Moses
->a beautiful prefiguration of Christ.<-

1. The Staff of Moses was a growth of the earth. Christ is called a Rod, a Branch, or a Stem (Zechariah 3:8, 6:12; Isaiah 11:1, 10).
2. It was a staff to lean upon, to rest upon, and with which to rule and count the sheep. Christ counts and rules His sheep (Psalm 23:1, 4), and upon Him we lay ourselves and lean.
3. This staff was a scepter and a rod of government, held high in the hand of Moses. So was Christ exalted in the hand of GOD as eternal King in heaven.
4. It was thrown from Moses down to the earth. So Christ came from the bosom of His Father to us on earth.
5. The staff became a serpent. Christ came in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), where He presents Himself as a worm (Psalm 22).
6. The staff, which previously stood upright in the hands of Moses, was cast down. So Christ was laid in the grave in a state of humiliation.
7. But Moses took it back into his hand, exalted it again, and the serpent became a staff. Thus Christ has become our King through the resurrection, the one on whom we rest; He no longer appears as a sinner or unclean, and will appear a second time without sin.
8. If the Egyptians would not believe the first two signs with the staff, then GOD would send the third: namely, the turning of water into blood. Thus, if the Jews would not and did not believe in Christ and the sign of Jonah, then their waters would be colored with the shedding of blood.
9. Just as the staff later swallowed all the other staffs, so Christ has put to shame all those who resisted Him as the seed of the serpent and the brood of vipers.

<column-break/>

12. And they each threw down their staff, and they became dragons: but Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.
13. And so Pharaoh's heart was <margin>(a) ch. 14:4.</margin> hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken.
14. And the LORD said to Moses: Pharaoh's heart is heavy; he refuses to let the people go.
15. Go to Pharaoh in the morning; see, he will go out to the water: so stand across from him on the bank of the river, and take the staff in your hand that was turned into a serpent;
16. And say to him: The LORD, the GOD of the Hebrews, has sent me to you, saying: Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness: but behold, until now you have not wanted to listen.
17. Thus says the LORD: By this you shall know that I am the LORD; behold, I will strike the water that is in the river with the staff that I have in my hand, and it shall be turned into blood. <margin>Revelation 11:6.</margin>
18. And the fish that are in the river shall die, so that the river will stink: and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the river. <meta>19. And</meta>

<note>Commentary on Verse 12 and the Cross</note>
v. 12. Some who are devoted to evil and erroneous teachings want to imitate spiritual people and do what they do: but the Spirit of GOD swallows everything and distinguishes the evil from the good; and the truth very quickly swallows the lies.

But should not the staff—through which so many miracles happened, by which Egypt was subdued and Pharaoh overcome—also be the Cross of Christ, through which we conquer the world and overcome the prince of this world with his principalities and powers? Has not this Cross—after being thrown to the earth, that is, after its "foolishness" was made known on earth through the "foolish" preaching—transformed into wisdom and swallowed all the wisdom of the Egyptians or of this world?

---

O how good it is when we have this staff with us on our journey, even if we have nothing else (Mark 6:12 <note>The author likely intends Mark 6:8, where the staff is the only thing permitted for the journey.</note>), and steer our way by it through true faith. This is the rod and staff that comforts us in our labor and weakness, and upon which we may cast our burden (Psalm 23:4).

Let one choose no other staff, such as a "reed-staff of Egypt"—neither one’s own righteousness, nor the merits of others, nor <term>indulgences</term> <note>original: "indulgentien," referring to the Catholic practice of granting remission for temporal punishment of sins</note>. For the true staff of comfort has swallowed all these serpents: otherwise, it might become an iron rod to us that would dash us to pieces (Psalm 2). But if we hold to Him alone, we will, with good progress and through His help, be able to climb the mountain and reach Zion.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter VIII.

19. And the LORD said to Moses: Say to Aaron, take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters in Egypt, over their rivers, over their streams, and over their lakes, and over all their pools of water, that they may become blood; and let there be blood in all the land of Egypt, both in wooden and in stone vessels.

20. And Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded; and he lifted up the staff and struck the water that was in the river before the eyes of Pharaoh and before the eyes of his servants: and all the water that was in the river was transformed into blood.

21. And the fish that were in the river died, and the river became stinking, so that the Egyptians could not drink the water from the river; and the blood was throughout all the land of Egypt.

22. And the Egyptian magicians did the same with their incantations. Then Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken.

23. And Pharaoh turned and went to his house, and he did not take even this to heart.

24. But all the Egyptians dug for water around the river to drink: for they could not drink of the water of the river.

25. Thus seven days were fulfilled after the LORD had struck the river.

> This was then the first of the ten plagues with which God punished the physical Egypt; which was a just retribution for their bloodthirsty disposition <note>The commentator suggests the punishment fits the crime: because the Egyptians shed the blood of Hebrew children, their water is turned to blood.</note> that they showed toward the children, especially of the people of Israel: as they thirsted for blood to utterly destroy this people, so God also gave them blood to drink. See Psalm 78:44 and 105:29. And this is also among the most common plagues of the spiritual Egypt <note>original: "geistlichen Egyptens." In pietist and mystical theology, "Egypt" often represents the state of the world or the unregenerate soul.</note>, where our Lord is crucified with blood-red sins (Revelation 11:8); so that in the seven secret periods of the Church, it has been visited at all times with such bloody wars, which is also the aim of the second and third bowls of wrath, which threaten these very blood-judgments. (Revelation 16:3-4).
>
> v. 22. The sorcerers may have also transformed the water they had newly dug up into blood, or they may have merely blinded the eyes <note>An "optical illusion" or deception of the senses.</note>; God permitted this for the hardening of the heart. It may also be an image of how false teachers are often such unhappy instruments of the enemy, through whom such bloodthirsty religious wars are primarily stirred up. See Revelation 16:13-14 regarding this.

# Chapter VIII.

->The second, third, and fourth plagues: of frogs, lice, and vermin.<-

And the LORD said to Moses: Go in to Pharaoh and say to him: Thus says the LORD; Let my people go, that they may serve me.

2. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague your entire border with frogs!

3. So that the river shall swarm with frogs: and they shall crawl up and come into your house, and into your bedchamber and upon your bed, also into the houses of your servants and among your people, and into your ovens and into your kneading troughs.

4. And the frogs shall crawl upon you and upon your people and upon all your servants.

> Since the dug-up earth gave water back to the Egyptians, and the stubborn Pharaoh viewed the act of God more as a magical illusion than as a divine miracle, it could not remain at that state; rather:
>
> v. 1. The LORD spoke to Moses) And how has this happened so often? Necessarily, a divine inspiration and secret speaking <note>original: "geheime Einsprache." Refers to internal revelation or the "still small voice."</note> must take place: for which reason one holds this speaking of God to Moses as such until it may be proven otherwise with established reasons.
>
> Let my people go) When the days of patience finally reach an end—wherein the LORD has tolerated the wicked and allowed them to remain for the purification of the children of God—and the days of the oppression of the Church are over; then the LORD will also demand His own with authority, tear them out of their bonds with power and an outstretched hand, and out of the power of their enemies. He will also make it known to His children through His messengers sent in the latter days that the time of their redemption is here, and they should no longer delay in departing from Babylon. <note>The commentator links the Exodus from Egypt to the command to leave "Babylon," a common metaphor for a corrupt world or church system.</note>
