At the very least, no distinction is explicitly mentioned here between them and the Egyptians, as in other plagues. Thus, the godly also tend to experience the punishment in common national plagues as often as the godless.
>
> One might ask; how does that happen? Answer: Because they so easily make themselves partakers of others' sins, they also become partakers of their plagues. They make themselves partakers of others' sins most often by remaining silent so frequently in the face of evil, and not showing enough zeal for GOD, so as not to bring trouble, hatred, and enmity upon their own necks.

No one could draw or drink water for frog spawn and revulsion. — They also befoul the daily nourishment, so that they were found in the food and in the drink, etc.

> Note how the plagues escalate! This one was already heavier than the previous one, during which the King and the noblemen could at least quench their thirst with wine and other juices. But here, nothing is safe from the frogs. Therefore, the King's plea for mercy follows here in v. 8, although without true repentance.

# Chapter VIII. The Second Book of Moses.

5. And the **LORD** said to Moses: Say to Aaron; Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the streams, and over the lakes, and cause the frogs to come up over the land of Egypt.
6. And Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters in Egypt: then frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
7. Then the magicians did the same with their incantations, and caused the frogs to come up over the land of Egypt.
8. Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron, and said: Pray to the **LORD** that he may take away the frogs from me and from my people; then I will let the people go, that they may offer sacrifices to the **LORD**.

The omnipotence of **God** thus very suddenly brought forth a great multitude of frogs from all the waters of Egypt, so that they crept after the people—even up to the King—at their very feet; and therefore, because of their great number, the people could not defend themselves against them; indeed, they crawled into every crack, onto beds, and into vessels, to defile everything and to become an unbearable nuisance with their croaking. Psalm 78:45, 105:30.

Since the Holy Spirit, among the plagues of the spiritual Egypt, also mentions the three unclean spirits like frogs that go out from the mouth of the dragon, the mouth of the beast, and the mouth of the false prophet; so these can represent all bloodthirsty, warlike spirits, all clever, political "Ahitophel-spirits," <note>A reference to Ahithophel, King David’s counselor who betrayed him; his name became synonymous with a cunning but treacherous advisor.</note> and all false teachers who stand in the spirit of Balaam and Cain, and who oppose the testimony of truth in its witnesses. Especially in the end times, they will go out to the kings of the earth and the whole world to gather them for battle on that great day of the Almighty **God**, which will be the final persecution. Revelation 16:13, 14. And since these latter ones especially cry out against the testimony of truth as "quackery"—which the croaking of the frogs signifies—so it may be imagined that the falsely-famed art of rhetoric and the school-wrangling of such people deserve this name with even more justice in the judgment of **God**: (see 1 Timothy 6:5, 20) which are also called the "words of the puffed up." 1 Corinthians 4:19.

**v. 7. Did the same.)** This and other circumstances lead some to believe that these were not false miracles, but true miracles that **God** Himself allowed to happen through the magicians: and that they were unable to produce lice in the following plague merely because **God** withdrew His power from them; otherwise, it would have been just as easy for them. For this reason, Moses discovered no sorcerous fraud among them. By this explanation, scholars seek to resolve the difficulties that arise when one elevates or magnifies magical powers and arts too highly—as if they could not be detected and put to shame by the use of human senses—and thereby denies the human senses the ability to distinguish true miraculous workings from sorcerous illusions; thus making the power of the devil greater than it truly is. (a)

Now, it is certainly established that **God** may perform extraordinary things even through wicked rascals, and has occasionally done so; as the example of Balaam is well known. However, it still appears that these fellows—and Pharaoh through them—were fooled into presenting special things to the eye through their incantations. Just as they, as workers of darkness, could turn water into blood, but could not turn the blood back into water.

<margin>
(*) Compare William Fleetwood’s *A Thorough Examination of Miracles*. <note>William Fleetwood (1656–1723) was an English bishop who wrote extensively on the nature of miracles, arguing they were performed only by God or by His permission.</note>
</margin>

<column-break/>

9. And Moses said to Pharaoh: Have the honor before me <note>A respectful idiom meaning "Command me" or "I leave to you the honor of setting the time."</note>, as to when I should pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, to root out the frogs from you and from your houses: so that they remain only in the river.
10. And he said: By tomorrow. Then he said: Let it be according to your word; so that you may know that there is no one like the **LORD** our **God**:
11. So the frogs shall depart from you and from your houses and from your servants and from your people; they shall remain only in the river.
12. Then Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the **LORD** because of the frogs that he had brought upon Pharaoh.
13. And the **LORD** did according to the word of Moses, and the frogs died away out of the houses, out of the courtyards, and out of the fields.
14. And they gathered them together in heaps here and there, and the land stank.
15. But when Pharaoh saw (a) that he had gotten relief; he hardened (b) his heart and did not listen to them: as the **LORD** had spoken.

<margin>
(a) Chapter 9:34. (b) Chapter 7:3.
</margin>

16. And

**v. 9.** Moses seeks to prevent the false concept that Pharaoh might form—namely, that Moses might be bound to certain constellations or laws of time in his miraculous workings.

**v. 10. By tomorrow)** The conversation may have taken place toward evening, and the unbelieving man [Pharaoh] might also have wanted to wait and see if the plague would subside on its own, so that he would be less bound to his promise.

**v. 15. Hardened his heart)** Note: it is said ten times in this history of Pharaoh that he hardened himself. Ch. 7:13, 14, 22; Ch. 8:11, 15, 32; Ch. 9:7, 34, 35; Ch. 13:15. Thus, it is no wonder that he fell into this hardening after such a long-practiced cruelty. For what other fruit could such malice, which despised both **God** and men, produce? Therefore, **God** Himself pronounces him free [of excuse] and he confesses his own willful and voluntary guilt, Ch. 9:27; Ch. 10:16, 17.
When it is simultaneously said that **God** hardened him and his heart—which also happens ten times—it can be understood as nothing other than a righteous divine allowance and the gradual withdrawal of His grace, which Pharaoh had willfully despised and voluntarily cast away.

**Did not listen to them)** It is likely that the King postponed the audience for several days, neither wanting to fulfill his promise nor explicitly revoke it, and thereby brought a new disaster upon his own neck. They [the magicians] can do something, but only that which is harmful. They can turn water into blood, but not blood back into water. They can indeed bring forth frogs, but not take them away—

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter VIII.

16. And the **LORD** said to Moses: Say to Aaron; Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, that it may become lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
17. And they did so; and Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the lice came upon the people and upon the livestock: all the dust of the land became lice throughout all the land of Egypt.
18. And the magicians also did so with their incantations, that they might bring forth lice: but they could not. And the lice were upon the people and upon the livestock.
19. Then the magicians said to Pharaoh: This is **God's** finger. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them: just as the **LORD** had spoken.

---

All the wonders which **God** performs before people who have turned inward only serve to harden the hearts of their enemies more and more. Often the most godless are forced to confess that it is the finger of **God** <note>The "finger of God" is a biblical idiom for a display of divine power that is small yet undeniable, distinguishing it from mere human trickery.</note> which performs these wonderful works; while meanwhile the hearts of the rest always remain in their stubbornness.

Concerning this and the following plague, it is also written in Psalm 105:31. And it was extraordinary that the lice came out of the dry dust, whereas they usually grow out of sweat and other decay. In this work, which seems so small, **God** put an end to the sorcery of Satan, so that they could not be brought forth by the magicians, who were thus forced to recognize the power of **God**. See Luke 11:20 and how the enemies of the testimony of truth shall finally be forced to give glory to **God** after the glorification of the witnesses, and must recognize the witnesses of truth whom **God** has loved. Revelation 11:12-13 and 3:9.

This plague can also represent, in the spiritual Egypt, the beggar-folk <note>The author is likely influenced by 18th-century Pietist social reforms, such as those by August Hermann Francke in Halle, who sought to address poverty through education and work-houses.</note> who increase greatly out of laziness and other stinking vices—among the elderly and especially children, who then grow up in all manner of vice. To check this plague, it would be most salutary if many poor-houses and orphanages were established, wherein such children might be raised in knowledge and kept to honest labor.

<column-break/>

20. And the **LORD** said to Moses: Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh; behold, he will go out to the water, and say to him: Thus says the **LORD**; Let my people go, that they may serve me!
21. But if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send vermin <note>The German *Ungeziefer* is often translated as "swarms of flies" or "biting insects" in English bibles.</note> upon you and upon your servants and upon your people and into your houses, and the houses of the Egyptians shall be full of vermin: and also the ground whereon they are.
22. And on that day I will do something special <note>The original German phrase *besonders thun* implies making a distinction or acting in an exceptional way.</note> with the land of Goshen, where my people dwell; so that no vermin shall be there: so that you may know that I the **LORD** am in the midst of this land.
23. And I will set a redemption <note>original: "Erlösung" — here implying a separation or a ransom that spares one group while the other suffers.</note> between my people and your people: tomorrow this sign shall happen.
24. And

---

v. 22. The **LORD** wishes here to make a distinction between the Egyptians and His people, who may well have felt the first three plagues along with them—to feel the righteous hand of **God** on account of their unbelief—but were henceforth to be spared from them. Chapter 9:4, 26; 10:23; 11:7.

**God** separates His people from those who will not surrender to Him. And while meanwhile those who persecute them must feel the painful stings of the flies of their own vanity and wickedness—which leave them neither rest nor peace—these happy souls enjoy with delight the dwelling-place of peace.

**Do something special**) This "something special" was a powerful means that might have persuaded the heart of Pharaoh to recognize and wonder at the great power of **God**, had he not been hardened, but had instead reflected on the exact separation which **God** made between the oppressed and their oppressors.

The **LORD** also did such a "special thing" when He distinguished Noah and his household from the world of the ungodly, and Lot and his household from the Sodomites. Through this precise separation of the good from the evil, in which He preserves His own and noticeably punishes the wicked, He makes Himself known. Just so, the **LORD** also made a

<margin>(a) Eusebius, Book 3, Chapter 5.</margin>
separation between His Church and the rebellious Jews when Jerusalem was to be destroyed: by warning His people that they should withdraw from Jerusalem to Pella, <note>Pella was a city in modern-day Jordan where, according to the church historian Eusebius, early Christians fled to escape the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 AD.</note> as into a Goshen (a). This is **God’s** constant providence in the world, even if it shines more gloriously in some examples than in others.

---

Therefore, whoever does not pay attention to this—as all atheists and Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus; in this context, the term is used to describe those who believe God does not intervene in human affairs.</note> do—sins against the clear light of his conscience. For the Creator, who has given us our soul, knows His work very well, and knows how humans are otherwise able to conclude rationally from the observation of human deeds and actions: why not then also, when **God** does something so special, and they can perceive such an apparent distinction? Should there not arise from this a conclusion within them that there is a wisdom-working Goodness that acts and governs in the world?

Certainly, this is **God’s** ultimate purpose in such ways: that ungodly people in the world may be moved and brought to believe in **God** the Father, that they may recognize and observe His eternal power and deity (Romans 1:20) and believe that He is, and that He is a rewarder of those who seek Him (Hebrews 11:6). If this truth is suppressed in unrighteousness, then one ensures for oneself—just like Pharaoh—that one has no excuse.

But you, O Israel—and whoever you are who wish to be counted among the Israel of **God**—must yourself also do something special, and keep yourself special in Goshen; that is, in proximity to **God**, if evil and the plague are not to approach you!

v. 23. **A redemption**) Beneath the external redemption, the meaning of the Holy Spirit aims at an eternal redemption through the **Lord JESUS Christ**; as also in Psalm 111:9 and 130:7. This spiritual Redeemer is, without doubt, the "outstretched arm of the Lord" so often mentioned in this history of the exodus from Egypt; just as he is often explicitly called the Arm of the Lord in the prophets.

### Chapter VIII. The Second Book of Moses.

24. And the **LORD** did so: and there came a great swarm of vermin into Pharaoh's house and into his servants' houses; so that in all the land of Egypt the land was corrupted because of the vermin.

25. Then Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said: Go and sacrifice to your **God** within the land.

26. And Moses said: It is not fitting to do so. For we would be sacrificing the abomination of the Egyptians to the **LORD** our **God**. Behold, if we sacrificed the abomination of the Egyptians before their eyes, would they not stone us?

<note>The following sections in smaller type are commentary on the preceding verses.</note>

v. 24. This fourth plague consisted of all kinds of harmful small animals that tend to emerge in great numbers; such as mice, rats, and all kinds of flies: such as blow-flies, horse-flies, and dog-flies, which greatly harm food and livestock; and also venomous wasps, which harm people with their stings so that they fall into deadly illnesses. Therefore, Psalm 78:45 states that such creatures devoured and consumed the people, as their strength was sucked out or their blood was poisoned.

Thus the proud king had to learn how **God** can severely plague mankind through such lowly, despised little creatures. How much more so if He had sent lions and other ravenous beasts among them.

In a spiritual sense, this plague in "spiritual Egypt" <note>A common Pietist metaphor for a worldly or unrepentant state of society.</note> can represent the rampant spread of vices, where lands become so full of murderers, thieves, rogues, whoremongers, adulterers, cursers, drunkards, gluttons, brawlers, fighters, and similar vice-filled people. To stem this mischief in all places—at least where there are rulers—houses of correction should be established. There, people who no longer heed sermons or magisterial laws and ordinances must be kept to repentance through punishment and hard labor, in hopes that they might wake up and tear themselves loose from the snares of Satan.

Just as a good beginning has been made through various orphanages and houses of correction, it is to be wished that thought be given to how the second plague might be checked through the establishment of many godly <term>collegia</term> <note>Small study groups or schools focused on practical piety rather than just academic theory.</note>, wherein the youth could be better supervised in smaller numbers, so that true wisdom and exercises of godliness might be pursued more than merely "puffed-up knowledge."

v. 25. **Within the land**) The devil and the spirit of the world are satisfied for one to serve **God**, provided it happens within "Egypt" and under their jurisdiction. However—

v. 26. Moses insists that to serve **God**, it is necessarily required to go out of Egypt: because otherwise one cannot recognize the **LORD's** will (Chapter 10:26). Furthermore, he presents here:

**The abomination of the Egyptians**) Namely, the Egyptians would not eat sheep. But what they considered an abomination, the Israelites sacrificed to **God**. In the same way, the unrighteous despise simplicity of conscience as the most insignificant and worst thing in the world; but the righteous offer such to **God** as a virtue. Like sincere people, they offer **God** a pure and gentle heart: this is an abomination to the godless, and they consider it foolishness and fantasy. <note>original: "Gregor." This refers to Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential theologian.</note>

The **LORD** knows His time, when He can also powerfully attack hardened and stubborn hearts, so that they must feel the heavy wrath of **God** and the foretaste of hellish fire. Then the plagues strike the heart, which previously remained entirely unfeeling during all kinds of external plagues. This then awakened even here some outward humiliation before **God** and recognition of his sins during this plague of hail (v. 27) and in the following one of the locusts (Chapter 10:16-17), until the rage of such sensitivity in the heart resisted again in the ninth plague of darkness (Chapter 10:28), and thereupon the actual destruction followed when a person resists all of **God's** external and internal punishments.
</insert>

<insert>
v. 14. **All my plagues**) **God** does not like to plague mankind and does a "foreign work" when He must indeed punish. He would so gladly have people come to Him through the obedience of faith without any judgments, and enjoy His noble love and its fruits. But because such does not happen, He is yet so kind that He takes up all punishments for our improvement. And if He does not succeed with us the first or second time, He has more kinds of plagues and lights a greater fire over us, until the sufficient fire and punishment comes that brings a person to the recognition of sin. For **God** has time enough; He can certainly wait for His creature until it humbles itself; He therefore does not force it to conversion with violence; but He lays it so close to the person, through sweet and hard means, that they have no excuse, as if they had not been enticed and provoked enough. For this He also has power enough to attack them in the place where it hurts them most.
</insert>

<margin>(a) Question 1 on Exodus.</margin>
<insert>
**None like me on the whole earth**) **God** also showed, as Theodoretus <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential theologian</note> (a) well notes, through this plague that He is the Master of all elements. For since the Egyptians (and the Greeks likewise) believed that the gods had divided the governance of the world among themselves—and that some were set over the heavens, others over the earth, others over the sea and subterranean places; some proved their power and dominion on the mountains, others in the fields—so **God** had to show them that He is **Lord** in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all depths, and therefore He chastises them not only through the rivers and earth, but also through the air and the sea, as well as with dispatched fire and lightning from heaven. Wisdom 16:22.
</insert>

<insert>
v. 6. The pestilential disease that moved among the livestock of all species and swept away a large part of them, as if it wanted to consume everything—although some always remained, which was also struck afterwards by the hail (v. 25)—this same disease **God** has also sent in our days, now into this land, now into that. These Egyptian plagues are then signs of "spiritual Egypt," wherein Christ is indeed confessed with the mouth, but is crucified with the great slavery of sins, with heavy pressures upon the people, and also with the oppression of His own (Revelation 11:8); and which are also harbingers of the remaining plagues, indeed of the final destruction of the entire godless heap with its evil rulers.
</insert>

<insert>
Because the Egyptians worshipped almost all animals as gods, it was fitting that **God** also attacked their wretched idols and thereby put their deities and follies to shame. He still does it, if only one will take note. Beauty, wealth, honor, health, parents, children, etc., are such idols that **God** shames for you, so that you should seek, fear, love, and honor Him alone. But the people of these last times would rather perish themselves in what they naturally comprehend than the unreasoning animals!
</insert>

<insert>
v. 10. 11. Thus **God** also sometimes attacks people, both old and young children, with such evil boils, and shows us thereby the "blood-boils" of our very corrupted nature and the blood-guilt hovering over us. See Psalm 38:6, 51:14. This plague, which also manifests in the first vial of wrath, gives us to recognize in a spiritual sense the great bitterness in all kinds of religious and worldly affairs, which ignite people in anger and enmity against one another: from which nothing but heavy bloody wars tend to arise; just as Isaiah predicted such for "spiritual Egypt" (Chapter 19:1-2), that the **Lord** will set the Egyptians against one another, so that a brother will fight against another, a friend against another, a city against another, and a kingdom against another. All of which arises from the much injustice with which one offends the other: whereby love grows cold, and which then creates such bad blood that breaks out in its time like those blood-boils and causes such plagues.

<meta>catchword: 27. Then</meta>

---

In the final seventh bowl of wrath, **GOD** also threatens to send hail weighing a hundredweight from heaven upon mankind, to justly punish the "hundredweight-heavy" sins with which the godless—both the great and the lowly—have oppressed their subjects and their neighbors. See Revelation 16:21. These judgments of fire and hail are also threatened by Isaiah against "spiritual Egypt," which relies only on its fleshly power of chariots, horses, and riders (see Isaiah 30:30; 31:1-2; 32:19). The **LORD** will shatter these with his hail, just as the army of the Marcomanni <note>A Germanic tribal confederation that fought the Roman Empire</note> is said to have been scattered and shattered by hail through the prayer of the Christian legion under the Romans; because of this, they received the name *Legio fulminatrix* <note>original: "Legio fulminatrix", meaning the "Thundering Legion"</note>. See Joshua 10:11.

<margin>v. 16.</margin> **GOD** shows Pharaoh that He could easily have snatched him away through pestilence. However, He had let him "remain"—as the Hebrew word actually says and as the seventy translators <note>A reference to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> well translated as *dieterēthēs* <note>original Greek: "dieterēthēs", meaning "you were preserved" or "kept alive"</note>. This was intended to be a sign of **GOD'S** long-suffering, should he still wish to obey; but also a sign of **GOD'S** heavier judgment, for which **GOD** would have reserved him should his stubbornness continue. And so the outcome would show that he was, so to speak, "raised up" for such a terrible hardening and heavy judgment, as the Apostle also expresses through the Holy Spirit in Romans 9:17: that, since he had resisted **GOD** so often, he was destined to be a sign of His wrath. This was a righteous decree over him *at that time*, and must not be derived from eternity or from his birth. This is how **GOD** deals with all very hardened sinners out of righteous judgment: He determines such a heavy judgment for them in time and then truly allows it to pass upon them.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 26.</margin> **In the land of Goshen)** In the drawing near to **GOD**, in the transition where one has crossed over from the flesh into the spirit; the "cooling of love" <note>A reference to Matthew 24:12, suggesting spiritual safety from the "hail" of divine judgment</note> does not reach there.

<column-break/>

**Let you remain for this reason)** He deliberately let him stay alive for this purpose; after He had tested him in so many extraordinary ways and employed so many uncommon means to bring him to reason and to the recognition of His sovereignty over him, or to bend him under His made-known will.

If **GOD** had cut him off at the first instance of his disobedience—as He certainly could have done—and taken away his power to remain standing, then the power of **GOD** and His name would not have become so widely known.

<margin>v. 20. 21.</margin> Thus, when divine judgments are threatened, there are always two kinds of people: those who fear the name of the **LORD**, and those who do not care in the slightest for such threats. The **LORD** will spare the former as His own property and His sons; but these reckless and godless ones will be like straw, which the coming day will set ablaze, leaving them neither root nor branch. See Malachi 3:16-19, Isaiah 66:5-6.

27. Then Pharaoh sent and called for Moses and Aaron and said to them: I have sinned this time; the **Lord** is the <margin>(a) Ps. 11:7. <note>original: "Ps. 11/8." <margin>v. 27. etc. We can note here how far a hypocritical repentance can go, which is usually squeezed out by the heavy judgments of God; the person is forced to recognize how God is the righteous judge against whom they have grievously sinned, and that they, as a wicked person, have well deserved such heavy punishment. But because the deceitful heart does not truly want to abandon its own self-love, and does not call upon God fervently enough for a true fear—from which alone sincere obedience toward God follows—it remains without that tender fear of God. Therefore, as soon as it receives some relief from the punishments, it falls back into its old, perverse mind. Believers often have a sense of this from other people when their hard nature continues to oppress even in the midst of such outward testimonies.</margin>

<margin>v. 28. *For it is enough*) This can also be applied to what preceded: Pray to the **Lord**, and indeed much, earnestly, and fervently. For without doubt Pharaoh soon had enough of the thunder and hail.</margin>

to pray to the **Lord**, and also to incline the **Lord** to hear their prayer, and thus does some violence to the clear text; it is not necessary to seek in Moses' words a motivating reason to pray for them, but rather it is a proof that their fear of God was mere hypocrisy. And just as it says in the Prophet: *You turn, but not rightly*; so it might also be said here: *You fear, but not rightly before God the **Lord**.* For they feared only as long as the judgment was upon them. But Moses well recognized the false and corrupted nature of men, who very soon cease to fear and return to follow their previous mind. Our nature is so evil and slavish that it is much better when kept in subjection than when it is in freedom. The Church of Christ was purer, holier, more righteous, more loving, more patient, etc., in the time of the Apostles and thereafter, than it has ever been since. Because the **Lord**’s hand is upon many through illness or other chastisements, they are flexible and exceedingly mild with promises of improvement and good intentions, full of confession of sin, like Pharaoh. It is, however, nobler and more to be built upon when one allows oneself to be turned away from one’s corrupt inclinations by the secret whispering of God’s voice—which convinces and persuades us in private—rather than by His terrible thunders, which tend to threaten us. It is better to be led by the goodness of God, which guides us gently, than by His strict judgments, which compel us to repentance like a bit and bridle. But may God hallow for us all divine service that may win us for Him, whether it be His rod or His Spirit of gentleness.

**v. 5. That they cover the land)** Literally, it says "that they cover the eye of the land": namely, as far as their eyes reach, or as far as they could see; as when one, for example, sees everything flooded with water as far as the eye can see.
**The remainder that was rescued — left from the hail)** Specifically the wheat and the spelt <note>A hardy type of grain common in the ancient world.</note>, Chapter 9, v. 32, and whatever grass and herbs were left.
**v. 6. He turned and went out)** Without waiting for an answer, as a witness of his indignation, being weary of the many warnings given to the wind for such a stubborn head.
**v. 7. Then they spoke)** Not out of repentance, but moved by love for their worldly well-being.
**A snare)** The godless always complain that believers are a snare and a ruin to them, specifically when they must threaten them with the righteous judgments of God. Just as Ahab blamed Elijah, as if it were he who troubled Israel and brought it into such distress. 1 Kings 18:17, 18.
**Do you wish — that Egypt perish)** So powerful is often the hardness of the great that they do not cease from their stubbornness and do not wish to be turned from their undertaking, even if the land and the people should perish.

11. "Not so: you men go now and serve the **Lord**! For this is what you sought." And they were driven out from the presence of Pharaoh.

v. 5. **That they cover the land**) Properly it says, that they cover the *eye of the land*: namely, as far as their eyes reach, or as far as they could see; as when, for example, one sees everything flooded with water in such a way, as far as one can possibly see.
**The residue which has escaped, —left from the hail**) Namely, the wheat and the spelt <note>Spelt is a type of hulled wheat common in the ancient world.</note>, Chapter 9:32, and whatever grass and herbs were still remaining.
v. 6. **He turned and went out**) Without waiting for an answer, to testify to his indignation, as one weary of warnings given to the wind so many times to such a stubborn head.
v. 7. **Then they spoke**) Moved not by repentance, but by a love for their temporal well-being.
**A snare**) Thus the godless always complain that the believers are a snare <note>original: "Strick," literally a rope or trap used for catching animals.</note> and a ruin to them: namely, when such people must threaten them with the righteous judgments of God. Just as Ahab blamed Elijah, as if it were he who troubled Israel and brought them into such distress. 1 Kings 18:17, 18.
**Do you want — that Egypt has perished**) So powerful is often the hardness of the great, that they will not yield from their stubbornness, and do not wish to be dissuaded from their undertaking, even if land and people should perish.

<column-break/>

v. 8. **But who are the ones**) He seeks an opportunity to pull back with one hand what he gave with the other. That is how serious he was.
v. 10. Sometimes hypocrites are willing to recognize the will of God to some extent and to follow it slightly: but it must still be arranged according to their own mind. Otherwise, they accuse the witnesses of truth of stubbornness and a malicious heart: even though those witnesses cannot deviate a hair's breadth from the truth but must proclaim the whole counsel of God. See Acts 20:27 <note>original: "Apost. Gesch. 20/27"</note>.
v. 11. **You men**) He wants to keep the women and children as hostages, to ensure their return through them.
**This you have sought**) Or rather, Pharaoh simply does not want to understand it any other way. For when did they ever think of such a thing?
**They were driven out**) Let yourselves be cast out, O you servants of the Lord! Shake the dust from your feet!
Whoever can flatter the world, the world flatters them in return: and whoever lays down these cushions sleeps softly in its lap.
But God’s servants are not like that, whom He sends in the spirit of Moses and Elijah: they rebuke the stubborn and go straight through.
Darkness rages when it is rebuked by the light. Whoever is evil cannot endure chastisement.
But they must still hear it, so that their ears tingle! The messengers of the Lord do not allow their mouths to be stopped.
How gladly they would speak softly, if they only had to do with sheep and lambs! But with goats, the staff must be hard in the hand.
The Law must be sharpened for those who are without law. The staff of Moses must be lifted up, to see if they might fear the God of Sinai!
If they cannot suffer that, then they will surely have to hear harder voices when the Lord lets His thunders be heard: but God will deliver His servants from their sighing.
Just go away from them, you witnesses of truth, when your testimony is finished! It is a sign that they are ripe for their judgments when they reject God in His servants.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the ten plagues in Egypt, specifically focusing on the eighth plague: the locusts. The commentary bridges the biblical text with historical events (like a 16th-century locust swarm in Poland) and spiritual interpretations regarding destructive armies and false teachers.</meta>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter X.

12. Then the **Lord** said to Moses: "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, that they may come up over the land of Egypt and eat every herb of the land; everything, namely, that the hail has left behind."
13. And Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the **Lord** brought an east wind into the land all that day and all that night. When morning came, the east wind brought the locusts.
14. And the locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled in all the borders of Egypt, in such great numbers that there had never been locusts like them before, nor would there ever be again.
15. For they covered the whole land as far as one could see, so that the land was darkened; and they ate every herb of the land and all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left; and nothing green remained on the trees or the herbs of the field in all the land of Egypt.

With this plague of locusts, God also sometimes punishes lands because of "Egyptian sins." <note>This refers to sins of pride and stubbornness similar to Pharaoh's.</note> For instance, it is remarkably recounted that in the year 1575, in Poland and Silesia, such a swarm of locusts is said to have darkened the light of the sun for a distance of one and a half miles. To this also belongs the uncommon multitude of caterpillars and other pests when they consume the crops far and wide. See Joel 1.

In a spiritual sense, however, these locusts signify highly destructive armies when they consume everything far and wide: as seen in the unchristian devastations of crops and the burning of places currently in fashion, so that the enemy shall find no sustenance. <note>This likely refers to the "scorched earth" military tactics common during the 17th-century wars in Europe.</note>

It also applies here when, even in times of peace, such a multitude of soldiers must be maintained, who greatly consume the wealth of the lands—wealth that could be more usefully applied to the neighbor’s best interest and the glory of God.

By these locusts are also understood—according to Revelation 9:3—the multitude of false teachers who are very dangerous to the seed of truth and destroy it wherever they can, so that it shall not sprout in the hearts of men.

v. 13. **An east wind**) Which in those lands tends to be very violent and harmful because it takes its path from the Arabian deserts. For this is precisely the wind that the Scripture describes as coming up from the wilderness. Hosea 13:15. Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymus"</note> calls it everywhere the burning or cutting wind. Just as it does not always bring benefit in Germany and is particularly harmful to the grapevine in springtime. But one must judge the nature of the winds according to the location and region of each country: for this very reason, this wind brings the most pleasant air to those living in France and the Netherlands; whereas the west wind is the most delightful to the Italians, but the Netherlanders fear it most as their most harmful and stormy wind because it comes from the sea.

The Septuagint <note>original: "LXX," the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> and the Jew Philo <note>A Hellenistic Jewish philosopher</note> turn the east wind here into a south wind: How this may be reconciled, see hereafter.

<column-break/>

16. Then Pharaoh hurriedly called for Moses and Aaron and said: "I have sinned against the **Lord** your God and against you.
17. And now, please forgive my sin only this once, and pray to the **Lord** your God that he may take away only this death from me!"
18. And he went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the **Lord**.
19. Then the **Lord** turned a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and thrust them into the Reed Sea. <note>The Hebrew "Yam Suph" is traditionally translated as "Red Sea," though it literally means "Sea of Reeds."</note> Not one locust remained in all the borders of Egypt.
20. But the **Lord** let Pharaoh’s heart be hardened <gloss>(a)</gloss>, so that he did not let the children of Israel go. <margin>(a) ch. 9/12.</margin>
21. And

---

Here it seemed that Pharaoh was in earnest: in that he admitted himself guilty not only before God but also before men, saying that he had also sinned against them—Moses and the people of Israel. This is something proud nature finds very difficult—to sincerely confess the iniquity committed against one's neighbor—as it always wants to attribute some blame to the neighbor. And here, hypocrites are also accustomed to demand the intercession of the godly in great distress, whom they previously would not have looked upon. To this, the godly must also show themselves quite willing, even though they might find reason to doubt the sincerity of such people who only show a humbled spirit in times of need. But once the distress has vanished, the hypocrites cannot hide themselves, for they have never seriously sought the true fear of God and sincere obedience.

v. 16. **Hurriedly called**) As long as one has peace, one despises God's voice and asks who the **Lord** might be whose voice must be heard. But when the knife is set to the throat, even the worst person cries out in repentance: "Rise up and help us!" First, one seeks help from all idols and creatures; but when nothing will work or help, then God shall be good enough for them.

Accordingly, all those must examine their prayers who do not use real earnestness until they are in distress.

Oh, what a forced work is this false prayer and crying, which does not happen until the greatest need! Truly, such has nothing other for its foundation than loathsome self-love, where man only wants to preserve himself and be rid of the distress. But he does not ask after God, whether it be His will or honor, if only the anxiety were gone. Therefore, such can be nothing other than a loathing and abomination to God, who looks into the hidden depths of the heart. Meanwhile, God is so kind and righteous that He allows even such a forced prayer to achieve something and not be entirely in vain, as seen here in v. 19.

**Against the Lord**) Through contempt for His command.

**And against you**) Through the harsh treatment of having you cast out and keeping your people in such heavy servitude until now.

v. 17. **This death**) This deadly evil. From this, it is recognizable how heavily this plague fell upon them.

v. 19. **West wind**) Or rather also a northwest wind; for the "wind of the sea," as it is actually called in the Hebrew, is indeed a west wind in view of the land of Canaan, because it points to the Mediterranean Sea; which, however, is toward the north in view of the land of Egypt; just as, conversely, the Reed or Red Sea is half toward the south and half toward the east. Thus, a southeast wind brought the locusts from the Red Sea, and its opposite drove them back there again.

21. And the **LORD** said to Moses: "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that a darkness may come over the land of Egypt, so that one may even feel the darkness."

22. And Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven: then there came a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days.

23. They did not see one another: nor did anyone rise from his place for three days. But among all the children of Israel, there was light in their dwellings.

24. Then Pharaoh had Moses called and said: "Go forth and serve the **LORD**; only let your sheep and your cattle remain here. Your little ones may also go with you."

<note>This thick darkness—which may have been accompanied by evil, misty vapors so that they could be felt and even grasped—represents the great darkness that will strike the spiritual Egypt in the last times: of which Isaiah prophesies in Ch. 60, 2. Even in the bright light of truth and so many precious testimonies, most people, along with their leaders, willfully remain stuck in the darkness of their fleshly prejudices and earthly-minded worldly wisdom; which cannot withstand the light, but rather extinguishes it. 2 Corinthians 6, 14. To this belongs the thoughtful lament in Isaiah: We grope for the wall like the blind, and we grope as if we had no eyes! We stumble at noon as in the twilight; we are in the gloom like the dead. Ch. 59, 10. Also belonging here is the pouring out of the fifth vial of wrath upon the throne of the beast, whereby his kingdom is darkened. Revelation 16, 10.</note>

<note>The day of the wicked is turned into cruel darkness when God stretches out His hand of judgment to place them into the truth: which teaches them through a holy experience that all (a) light they imagine they possess is nothing but darkness; and that the more enlightened they consider themselves before men, the more ignorant they are before God (b). But the righteous, who unite themselves with God through faith alone, are always in a righteous light: which, instead of diminishing or passing away, (c) rather grows until the full day. Who would dare to describe the deep truths that God reveals to faithful souls? And how very much they are holily enlightened, even if it seems as though they have lost all their light? Those who have some experience of this must be the judges. Everything drawn from God is always truth: because God is truth itself. But what is drawn from the creature, the senses, and reason is generally error: because man of himself is nothing (d) but vanity and lies. Thus, the infallible means to enter into the truth, to remain in it, to grow in it, to die in it, and to live in it eternally, is to abandon oneself to God alone above all things, and to see them exactly as He sees them.</note>

<note>v. 29. **I will see your face no more** ) The question arises: how can this be consistent with what is read in Ch. 11, 1–8 and Ch. 12, 31? Answer: A good translation can easily help out of this labyrinth: for the <note>original Hebrew: "wayyōmer"</note> in Ch. 11, 1 must not be rendered "spoke," but "had spoken." Moses certainly did not go to court again from then on, nor appear before Pharaoh; and thus he did not change his resolve, which was taken by divine impulse. He well noticed the imminent destruction of Pharaoh, and therefore in Ch. 12, 31, he deemed him no longer worthy of an answer when Pharaoh had him called—that is, when he had his <term>resolution</term> <note>decision or decree</note> made known to him through his servants. What is found in the following 11th chapter, which Moses still had to say to Pharaoh, happened during this last audience: and the words in verse 8 there, "he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger"—specifically out of divine zeal, because all hope for his improvement was gone—explain these words here; namely, that Moses had <term>declared</term> <note>officially stated</note> to him in such anger that he would certainly no longer deign to come before his face; because the time would soon come when they would have to run after them and <term>supplicate</term> <note>beg or petition</note> for their departure.</note>

## Chapter XI.

->The announced destruction of the firstborn.<-

The **LORD** had said to Moses: "I will bring one more plague upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt; afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will surely drive you out of here completely.
2. So speak now in the hearing of the people, that every man ask of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor for silver vessels and gold vessels."
3. For the **LORD** will give the people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the eyes of Pharaoh’s servants and in the eyes of the people.
4. Furthermore, Moses said: "Thus says the **LORD**: 'About midnight I will go out through the midst of Egypt;
5. And all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the mill, and all the firstborn of the livestock.'" <margin>ch. 13:2</margin>

<column-break/>

6. "And there shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever shall be again.
7. But against none of the children of Israel shall a dog move its tongue, from man to beast: so that you may know how the **LORD** makes a distinction between the Egyptians and Israel.
8. Then all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying: "Go out, you and all the people who follow you!" And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
9. But the **LORD** said to Moses: "Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."
10. And Moses and Aaron performed all these wonders before Pharaoh: but the **LORD** let Pharaoh’s heart be hardened, so that he would not let the children of Israel go out of his land. <margin>ch. 10:27</margin>

---

<columns>2</columns>

v. 1. At the time of the threat made by Pharaoh, it was spoken into Moses' heart by God that only the last plague remained, after which the final destruction in the sea would follow. This would overtake Pharaoh unawares, because he had continually hardened his heart against all previous warnings. This plague would seem so sensible <note>Meaning "perceptible" or "painful" in 18th-century usage</note> to Pharaoh and all the Egyptians that, out of fear of death, they themselves would drive everyone out of the land without exception—indeed, at the Israelites' request, they would even give them their silver and gold.

v. 3. **The man Moses was very great**) When God imparts divine wisdom and power to someone, it can bring a man true prestige; but it is not the outward splendor with which the foolish seek to earn honor and reputation. See Proverbs 3:16, 35.

v. 5. This slaughter of all the firstborn in the last plague also represents, in the <term>spiritual Egypt</term> <note>A common theological concept referring to the world in a state of sin or bondage to the flesh</note>, the great and final judgment which will eventually come upon the great and powerful and strike them directly. In the previous plagues of the land, they could always find ways to help themselves, while the common subjects were pressed the most. But here the great supper <note>A reference to the "Marriage Supper of the Lamb" or the "Great Supper of God" in Revelation</note> will be held, where the barbarian nations will be awakened and called by God to eat the flesh of the mighty and drink the blood of the princes of the earth—the rams, the lambs, the goats, and the bulls, all of whom are fat and well-fed. Ezekiel 39:17-20; Revelation 19:17-21. There it is explained how such people constitute the beast and the false prophet, with all their members and tools: these are the powerful and prominent in both the so-called spiritual and worldly estates who have resisted the truth and misused their power to persecute the witnesses of the truth. Therefore, they must perish in the fiery pool, just as Pharaoh did in the Red Sea, and thus they must feel the righteous judgment of their hardening and stubbornness.

v. 5. The firstborn of Egypt are the image of sinners, who generally bear nothing but sins; and the firstborn of the children of God are the inner souls. Sinners want to destroy the inner self: but God humbles the sinners and kills the sin for the sake of the soul.

<column-break/>

v. 8. **In hot anger**) Although Moses was of a very meek spirit, more than all men on earth (Numbers 12:3), he was nevertheless ignited into such a hot anger against Pharaoh by the king's terrible malice. Though Pharaoh had previously humbled himself, he now, at the threat of the heaviest judgment—of such a bloodbath—broke out into a murderous rage and remained stubborn. This was similar to what happened during the grave sin of idolatry (Exodus 32:19) and the violent rebellion of Datan and Abiram (Numbers 16:15). Thus, one may indeed be zealous in anger for the honor of God against the terrible malice of men (Psalm 4:5); just as the meek Savior also broke out in anger over the hardness of hearts, though it was at the same time accompanied by sorrow (Mark 3:5).

v. 10. **The LORD let Pharaoh’s heart be hardened**) Satan, says Augustine (a), hardens through persuasion; man through consent; God through abandonment <note>God "hardens" by withdrawing His grace and leaving the sinner to their own choices</note>.
(a) Chapter 33, *Against Faustus* <note>original Latin: "c. 33. cont. Faust."</note>

---

<columns>1</columns>

>*The angels, as servants of God's vengeance, kill by His power all the firstborn of the world, whom men value so highly and in whom they place a vain trust. His inner friends, however, are in safety under His protection: and although He allows them to be treated poorly by fleshly men in order to purify their love and increase their crowns, they are not struck by His wrath, but only visited by His mercy. For it is actually they, and not the children of the world, who trust under the shadow of His wings.*

**Maidservant behind the mill**) Hand-mills were more commonly used among the ancients; and since this was very laborious work, it had to be performed by maidservants, and also by prisoners in the dungeons where they had such things. See Judges 16:21, Isaiah 47:2, Lamentations 5:13, Matthew 24:41.

Ch. XII. The Second Book of Moses.

### Chapter XII.
#### Institution of the Passover Lamb / Killing of the Firstborn and Departure.

But the **LORD** spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt and said:
**2.** This month shall be the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first for you among the months of the year.
**3.** Speak to the entire congregation of Israel and say: On the tenth day of this month, every man shall take for himself a lamb according to the houses of their fathers / one <margin>(a) 1 Peter 1:19.</margin> lamb for each house.
**4.** But if the household is too small to consume the lamb / then he and his nearest neighbor at his house shall take it / according to the number of souls. You shall count every man toward the lamb according to what he can eat.

<column-break/>

**5.** You shall have a perfect lamb / a male that is one year old: you shall take it from the sheep-lambs or from the <margin>(a) 2 Chronicles 35:7.</margin> goats.
**6.** And you shall keep it in custody until the fourteenth day of this month: then they shall slaughter it / every assembly of the congregation of Israel / between the two evenings.
**7.** And

---

<margin>The glorious redemption in this month of Abib / Ch. 13:4, which begins in the middle of our March / was to make for them the beginning of their year in ecclesiastical matters / such as the festivals; because they were then born as it were into a people of God in freedom: whereas in civil matters the year began in mid-September / the time when it is very probable the world was created; according to which not only all contracts and agreements / etc. were directed / but also the years of the world / likewise the years of release and Jubilee years were counted.</margin>
Since the most glorious prototype of Christ is presented here / who is explicitly named as such; for "our Pascha <note>original: 'Pascha', the Greek/Latin term for Passover</note> or Passover Lamb is sacrificed for us, Christ: 1 Cor. 5:7," we can immediately note the glorious correspondence of all these ceremonies / which were ordained for the Passover Lamb / with Christ and the communion of the faithful with him / and in what manner such can be maintained.

Four days before its slaughtering, this lamb had to be selected from the flock / and kept for this purpose alone: and / as the Jews say / they were to have tied it to their bedposts / in order to have it constantly before their eyes. So was Christ separated from sinners / Hebrews 7:26. and had to walk in his public teaching office for the eyes of the Jews during the last four years of his life; so as to suffer and be slain at the end of this time: whereas previously he had been as if hidden among the common mass of people.

**v. 2.** For this very reason, the month of Nisan / formerly Abib / is set as the first month / as an image of the renewal of the world / occurring in the resurrection of Christ / which also took place in this month. Just as some have been led to believe / that our redemption from all bondage will also happen at this time.

**v. 3. On the 10th day of this month)** Namely, on the new moon of April / which often falls in March.

So too Christ / the Passover Lamb of the whole world / when he was now to die / and intended to fulfill the figure in deed / came to Jerusalem on the 9th day / namely on Palm Sunday; but went out of the city again that same day / and came back / as Mark 11:15, 27 reports / the following day.

This very lamb must be taken into our houses on the 10th day after the new moon. In the figure, the moon signifies our life: and Christ Jesus is the Sun / which illuminates our life and renews it in virtues. If we now arrange our lives according to the 10 commandments of God / we have the lamb in our houses.

**v. 4. According to the number -- count)** The society or company / as they called it / had to be no fewer than ten / and no more than twenty / strong (a). For one could then conclude the size of the population from the number of Passover lambs.
<margin>(a) Maimonides, treatise 1. on the paschal sacrifice. ch. 7. §. 6.</margin>

**v. 5. A perfect lamb)** Because in Jesus Christ no sin was ever found / and so that his righteousness might cover our unrighteousness. For Christ was perfect / holy / innocent and undefiled / (Hebrews 7:26) in his first manly bloom of thirty years / when he was to be sacrificed.

**One year old)** Which has experienced one complete revolution of the months and the heavens.

**v. 6. Until the 14th day)** The cause of this 4-day separation / say the Hebrews / was (1) so they would not forget it during the departure itself / as they would have much to do / and be overloaded with business; (2) so they could notice more closely / if there were any defect in the lamb; (3) so that from looking at the lamb they might have the opportunity / to speak among themselves and with their children of their impending redemption from Egypt; (4) so they could prepare themselves in time for the coming festival (a).

These 4 days also have their spiritual sense. The first day of these is the displeasure with ourselves and all our works: the second, the desire to love God and all virtues: the third, a general loyalty / love and goodness / toward all people: And on the 4th day / on which the moon becomes full / so that it turns its back toward evening / we must forget all things in the world / and turn our faces toward the morning to the eternal Sun. Just as on the 4th day of the creation of the world God created the sun and the moon / and placed the former in the east / and the latter in the west / so that the whole world would be illuminated.

In the full moon, therefore, the lamb had to be slaughtered and eaten. This full moon signifies the completion of the shadow-work of the law <note>The 'shadows' refer to the Old Testament rituals being a mere reflection of the reality of Christ.</note> on one side / and the fullness of the goods of grace on the other / since Christ wanted to unite our first Passover lamb with the last of the Jews / and let himself be slaughtered and roasted as the true Passover Lamb of the Old and New Testaments at that very time.

The time / when it had to be slaughtered / was
**Between the two evenings)** Since the Jews used to reckon time such that the first six hours of the morning made up two parts / and thus as it were two mornings / the middle of which was the third hour <note>9:00 AM in modern time</note>: and so the afternoon / when the sun again inclines toward setting / had two evenings / the middle of which was the ninth hour / which corresponds to our three o'clock in the afternoon / at which hour Christ also died; Matthew 27:45, 46. since he was crucified at the third hour / at nine o'clock according to our time / and thus between the two mornings. Mark 15:25. See regarding this way of counting the hours John 11:9, Matthew 20:3, 5, 6.

Some of the Hebrews therefore also make a great and small evening. The great they begin from half-past twelve <note>Original: 'halb-sieben', calculated by the Jewish system.</note> (half-past twelve for us) until half-past three (or half-past three in the afternoon) / from which the small begins until the setting of the sun.
<margin>(a) Bochart. part. 1. hieroz. book 2. ch. 50. p. 583. Heiberg. magnal. on this passage, num. 24. Goodwin. Moses & Aaron, book 3. ch. 4.</margin>

**v. 7. And**
<margin>(b) Blood)</margin>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

**7. And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two doorposts and on the upper lintel, in the houses where they shall eat it.**

**8. And they shall eat the flesh in that same night, roasted by fire,**

<column-break/>

**and unleavened bread: with bitter things they shall eat it.** <margin>Numbers 9:11.</margin> **9.**

---

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 7. Blood)</margin> Those who have entered in <note>that is, those seeking refuge in God</note> cannot distinguish themselves in any other way than through the mark of God: and this mark of God is the blood of the Lamb, with which they are signed. For since they possess no worthiness of their own, they have everything in Jesus Christ; and in his blood and through his blood they are preserved. Therefore they hope even against hope (a): because despairing of themselves happily brings them into a true confidence in God.

**Strike it on the two doorposts and the upper lintel)** Thus must our spirit and the powers of our soul and body be sprinkled with the blood of Christ in true faith in him, so that the evil destroying angel—the devil—may have no power over us. See Hebrews 9:13, 14; 10:22; 12:24; 1 Peter 1:2. <margin>Yes</margin>

What else does this image wish to teach us, other than that we should always keep Jesus Christ the Crucified in our memory, deeply impress his love and faithfulness upon our understanding, and follow his death with our very will through the mortification of ourselves? In this way, we will strike the posts and lintel of our house with the blood of the Lamb, and then no enemy shall dare to approach our door.

<margin>v. 8. But we must not only be washed and marked with the blood of the Lamb; his people must also</margin>

**Eat the flesh)** For the same makes one grow and bring forth fruit, and strengthens one to wander through the terrible long wilderness of naked faith; which, although it is full of freedom and accompanied by a thousand heavenly sweetnesses that sustain the soul in such a difficult pilgrimage, is nonetheless harder to endure than the first servitude: because of self-love, which would rather be burdened with the heavy labor of baking bricks (which signifies trivial work) than be free and used only to attain heaven (which signifies the promised land, namely God himself), without yet seeing the fruit of the labor.

Christ must be eaten, and like food, he must penetrate with his Spirit into our spirit, and thus out of himself give life, power, comfort, and refreshment to our spirit. See John 6:48-58.

The flesh of Christ, the Lamb, is the Word that became flesh, John 1:14, through the receiving of which we keep the spiritual Passover—the exit and transition from sin to righteousness.

**Roasted by fire)** Because it represented the perfection of the love of Jesus Christ, which was entirely fiery.

The Jews used no iron or other metal roasting spits: because, when these became warm, they would have helped roast the meat from the inside; which was not supposed to happen. If they wished to roast in a metal or stone vessel, it could eventually be done: but the vessel had to be entirely perforated so that the fire could reach the lamb and roast it. Yet it was mostly roasted on a wooden spit, specifically of pomegranate wood, which, because it is full of moisture, did not easily become warm from the fire nor burn. (b)

The spit was thrust through the lamb's mouth and neck, and so through the entire body, coming out again at the hind part; and the two front feet were fastened upon a cross-wood (c). This served as a foreshadowing of the manner of Christ’s death and his cross. For they had to roast a whole lamb, together with the head and feet; not the torso alone: nor cut it into two or several pieces, but roast the entrails together with the heart, lungs, and liver inside the lamb. Although the entrails were also sometimes roasted separately.

When one looked at it thus, with its head hanging and its front feet fixed to the roasting spit, it looked no different than a crucifix, even as it lay before them in the dish: so that the form of the Crucified might be imprinted deeply and early upon the people of God.

Christ had to be stuck, as it were, upon the spit of the cross, and there feel the consuming fire of God against sin, and thus be roasted as it were in this fire, so that body and soul were quite exhausted. See Hebrews 12:29; Matthew 27:46, 48; Hebrews 2:9; Psalm 69:10.

And this fire is also the most pure love, by which we must be entirely ignited if we wish to eat of this spotless Lamb.

<note>Citations for left column:</note>
(a) Romans 4:18. (b) Maimonides, *Treatise 1 on the Passover Sacrifice*, chapter 8, section 9 and following. Buxtorf, *Talmudic Lexicon* under the word <term>דכר</term> <note>original Hebrew: "dekar," meaning a ram or to pierce</note>. Bochart, *Hieroz.* part 1, book 2, chapter 50, page 597. (c) Bochart, as above, page 613, from Justin Martyr's *Dialogue with Trypho*.

<column-break/>

**Roasted, and unleavened bread)** Both required less time, because they had to hurry. Boiling and seething, as well as leavening bread, requires time. But God uses these reasons of necessity and turns the matter into pure mysteries: from which the depth of divine wisdom is to be noted.

**Unleavened bread)** These unleavened cakes were quite tasteless: because they were neither salted, nor prepared or spread with oil or butter, but were baked from mere flour and water. Therefore it is called the bread of misery, Deuteronomy 16:3. They had to eat this in memory of their hurried flight, as they did not have time to leaven their dough, but had to take it with them unleavened. v. 39.

When we wish to keep the Passover, that is, to eat and enjoy Christ in faith, it must happen not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. 1 Corinthians 5:8.

This unleavened bread, which is made without long preparation, indicates the nourishment suited to a simple state: since such is without the slightest preparation, but also without the slightest corruption of self-love; in which the creature <note>the human being</note> has not the smallest part.

**With bitter things)** What these actually were is not known for certain today. Buxtorf (a) considers them to be endives. Drusius (b) and Bochart understand them as wild lettuce, or like chicory. Feustel (c) considers them not to be salad herbs, but the gall of the Passover lamb, which had to be eaten with it.

These bitter things were afterwards dipped in vinegar. Therefore a vessel of vinegar was also kept ready. In Canaan they also made a special paste, which they call <term>Charoiseth</term> <note>Haroset</note>, from figs, nuts, lemons, almonds, and similar fruits, which they boiled with wine or vinegar; and, to make it quite thick, they put in much spice: which thick paste they then formed like a brick. They also took cinnamon, ginger, and other spices, and threw them coarsely crushed onto this paste, so that it would be like stubble and straw; in order to remind themselves how their ancestors in Egypt worked in stubble and straw and made bricks. (d)

Christ must be enjoyed in the fellowship of suffering, which feels bitter and harsh to flesh and blood, which must be surrendered and crucified even unto the death of lusts and desires. Galatians 5:24; 1 Peter 4:1; Romans 8:13, 17.

The bitter things thus represent the mortification in which the soul of faith must be exercised. For it does not enter the wilderness of faith until it has first gone through all the mortifications possible according to its strength and calling.

Ah, the bitter things are so very healthy, and they create a good appetite, so that one becomes eager for the pure milk of the word, to grow thereby! For affliction teaches one to heed the Word. One need only ask the best doctors if it is not so? Indeed, one need only ask the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is a master at helping: he will tell us what a good thing it is regarding persecution, scorn and mockery of the world, poverty, sickness, and all kinds of affliction. For these all create an appetite and desire for memory, for repentance, and that one becomes weary of this world; they awaken a hunger for Christ and an imperishable inheritance; whereas otherwise the "old man" <note>the sinful nature</note> will not move forward, and little desire for Christ is found.

<note>Citations for right column:</note>
(a) *Talmudic Lexicon* under the word <term>עולשי</term> <note>original Hebrew: "ulshin," referring to endives or chicory</note>. (b) *On Difficult Passages*, Numbers, chapter 37. (c) In *Sacred Miscellany*, page 227. (d) Buxtorf, *Dissertation on the Lord's Supper*, thesis 14, page 291.

### Chapter XII. The Second Book of Moses <note>Exodus</note>.

9. You shall eat nothing of it raw, nor anything boiled, such as is boiled in water; but roasted at the fire: its **head** along with its **legs** and along with its **innards**.

---

<margin>Nothing raw)</margin> Half-cooked or medium-rare. The question arises: Why not that? Answer: The Law forbids eating with blood, and explains why at the same time. GOD wants us to have no fellowship with the animal life. For the life of the animal is in the animal’s blood. He does not want us to eat of his Word in the raw letter, nor to accept it so crudely.

Christ must be enjoyed in fervent, fiery love, and not be accepted and believed so crudely and superficially, which is merely a literal faith that imparts no essential feeling to the soul.

Thus, those who only enjoy him in a sacramental way without true love also eat him raw.

<margin>Nor boiled in water)</margin> Seething and boiling, as well as steaming, requires water or some other liquid in which to make the food fit for eating, by working out the scum and drawing out the rawness.

The water here represents human doctrine; the Passover Lamb should not be cooked in it: because it is from below, muddy and turbid, and tastes of the earth from which it comes—that is, according to the wisdom of the earthly man. The weak water of human doctrine cannot prepare the Passover Lamb—which is strong meat—nor make it tender or fit for the nourishment of our souls. Christ cannot be prepared as food for the soul by the powers of our reason; because the corrupt moisture of one's own thoughts, desires, and imaginings are always found therein. How long have the scholars of Christendom merely seethed and boiled the mystery of the Lord’s Supper; but alas, accomplished little with it! The Lamb remains raw and is not roasted in love.

Therefore, let those watch what they are doing who light their own fire and cook the Word in the water of their own teaching: and also those who eat with pleasure the Word that is cooked in the water of human doctrine, heated by the fire of their own spirit, which does not draw out the rawness and the scum of a sinful life.

<margin>Roasted at the fire)</margin> The question arises: how then should the Passover Lamb be roasted? When something is roasted, the superfluous moisture and rawness are dried up and drawn out. But is there any superfluity in the true Passover Lamb? By no means: rather, everything that has been seethed and cooked by interpreters and explainers, and every false gloss that anyone has added according to their own innate manner, nature, and character, must be consumed by the fire of the Spirit of GOD.

Another fire consists of internal and external temptations. Oh, how good the Word tastes when we enjoy it during internal trials and tribulations! At other times, it is like food to people who have no appetite. Indeed, Christ must also be enjoyed with and in his trials. The Lamb must be eaten roasted.

<margin>Head)</margin> We must accept Christ as our Head, Ruler, and Sovereign. Many find him sufficient as a Prophet, or a Priest and Sacrifice for them. But that he should rule over them, they do not want. Luke 19:14. They do not want to be ruled by the gentle Lamb, but would rather have their own hard will as their head and king.

But the sum total of the Law and faith—namely, love from a pure heart (1 Timothy 1:5)—is what we should allow to be our food in and with Christ.

<margin>Legs)</margin> These are the instruments of movement and action, like the arms and legs of a person. Therefore, eating them is the same as having fellowship with Christ in movement and action, walking and doing just as he walked and did: 1 John 2:6. Likewise, it means fellowship in power and strength.

<margin>Innards)</margin> Especially the heart. And by the heart, the will, love, and mercy are understood. Thus, eating this is the participation in the will of Christ, so that it may be our "food" to do his will. John 4:34. All commands, prohibitions, promises, and threats must be accepted, eaten through faith, and inwardly digested and transformed into life.

It is not enough to eat the head and leave the legs and innards lying there: as the "mouth- and imagination-Christians" do, who only desire to know the Word but not to be doers of it.

It is not enough to eat the legs and perform external works, but never reach the internal parts.

It is not enough to eat the innards; for the envious man devours his own heart: rather, Christ’s inner being must pass into us.

In short: We must have a vast desire within us, and draw Christ into ourselves not only according to the flesh, but also according to the spirit; not only according to the external, but also according to the internal; not only according to his humanity, but also according to his divinity.

Similarly, Christ must also be enjoyed with all his benefits, which cannot be separated—one accepted and the other neglected. Whoever wishes to become wise or righteous through Christ must also become holy and redeemed from sin; and whoever wishes to become righteous and holy must also become wise, and hold in high esteem the knowledge of the manifold wisdom in Christ.

So let us strive for a complete communion and fellowship with Christ, as he is made for us by GOD as wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. 1 Corinthians 1:30. That is what true communion shall first be called.

<meta>catchword: When</meta>

<column-break/>

10. And you shall leave nothing of it until the morning: but what remains of it until the morning, you shall burn with fire.

---

->11.<-

<margin>Leave nothing)</margin> Christ must be accepted wholly and sincerely, and our heartfelt repentance must not be postponed to another time, where a person still waits for another "morning of grace" and persists until then in their mere imagination of Christ. See Hebrews 3:7-15; Acts 24:25.

Just as the Jews' enjoyment of the Passover Lamb was the image of the sacrifice of JESUS Christ, so too was it the representation of the pure sacrifice through which the soul must be perfected in GOD in the wilderness of pure faith.

This sacrifice wants nothing left over: it must be whole. And for that reason, it must be a burnt offering <note>original: "Brand-Opfer"</note>, which leaves nothing in the world behind, be it ever so small. Everything must be consumed and swallowed up: not only the flesh and everything external to the creature; not only the powers, represented by the head, and the inclinations, represented by the feet: but also all the innermost parts of the soul, yes, its very center-point and the highest peak of its spirit. Everything must be brought to nothing, so that nothing remains, either internally or externally. And this innermost part is indicated by the innards.

Since this so-necessary sacrifice is recognized by all as the most perfect of all, how is it nevertheless despised in practice! Oh, how much it costs a soul before it can surrender itself to it! And where might one find someone who keeps absolutely nothing for themselves? Yet these "half-sacrifices" cannot possibly be the right burnt offering, which is that which GOD has especially reserved for himself, so that it may be dedicated solely and alone to his honor: therefore it is also called the pure sacrifice. It is a sorrowful thing that so many great souls, who have allowed themselves to be sacrificed in so many things, keep almost all the innards—or at least some parts—for themselves. Oh, if they only knew how much honor GOD would receive from such a pure sacrifice, and the advantage they themselves would gain from it; how they would be so generous in surrendering themselves to GOD without exception! But they do not want to understand it, even though GOD highly commends it to their hearts: because that which is "gain" is commonly regarded as "loss," and that which is "loss" is held as "gain." To lose everything for God's sake is to gain everything. To lose GOD himself, as far as it lies within us—namely, in so far as he can be "ours"—so that he may gain the supreme power in us without us mixing the slightest bit of our own benefit into it; oh, that is the greatest happiness and the highest testimony of the purest love!

<summary>This page provides a mystical interpretation of the Passover lamb's preparation, arguing that Christ must be "consumed" entirely—intellect, action, and will—and "roasted" in the fire of divine love rather than "boiled" in human reason. It emphasizes the necessity of total surrender and immediate repentance, likening the spiritual life to a burnt offering where nothing of the self remains.</summary>
