<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XII.</header>

# 11. And thus you shall eat it: Your loins shall be girded /

---

When we wish to enjoy Christ in the spirit, the loins of our mind must also be girded, and that in the sobriety and alertness of the mind; because Christ’s Spirit cannot dwell in an earthly-minded, carnal, and sluggish mind. 1 Peter 1:13. Ephesians 6:14. Furthermore, verse 15 states: That we should put on our feet the readiness of the Gospel of peace; so that we should be ready and willing to proclaim Christ in all places and ends, wherever Providence gives us the opportunity.

It was to be eaten with the staff in haste; namely, that believers here below should conduct themselves as pilgrims and strangers <note>The author emphasizes the "alien" status of Christians in the physical world</note>, who have no lasting city here, but should be risen with Christ and seek what is above, where Christ is, and not what is here below on earth. 1 Peter 2:11. Hebrews 11:13, 13:14. Colossians 3:1–2.

Painters, to be sure, invent further that they ate it standing up; however, nothing of this is found in the text.

It is, however, called the Lord’s Passover or "Passing Over," because it should call to mind the protection and redemption that the Lord granted them in Egypt, when the destroying angel had to pass over the houses where the blood was to be seen. And just as Christ also calls the bread his body, which is broken for us; so he also intends to make known that this bread should represent his body broken for us, and that all those whose hearts were sprinkled with his blood and who have his Spirit dwelling within them, should be freed from all claims of the devil, and thus from all his power and authority, in time and eternity. Hebrews 2:14–15. Indeed, Christ also intends herewith to give himself to be enjoyed in the spirit by all his true believers, so as to eat his flesh and drink his blood. Matthew 26:26, 28. John 6:53, 56.

**And thus you shall eat it)** At God's call for departure and obedience, the spirit of faith presses for a swift resolution. There is no room for much looking back or hesitating. One must, like Israel, always be ready to jump, and remain prepared for constant flight and avoidance, even while one is continually enjoying the Passover Lamb of God’s love.

<margin>(a) Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 40, p. 667. <note>original: "Gregor. Nazianz. orat. 40. p. 667." — Referring to a 4th-century Church Father.</note></margin>
**Your loins shall be girded)** Constrained through abstinence. For no one departs from Egypt pure and perfect, and escapes the destroying angel, unless he has conquered and dampened his lusts. Therefore, the kidneys must undergo a laudable transformation, so that they lead all power of desire, or everything desirable, into God, so that one can say: Lord, before you is all my desire. For we must be men of spiritual desires. Thus we shall first overcome the dragon, whose powers consist mostly in the belly and loins: namely, when that power which sticks in these members is destroyed and cast out. (a)

The girded loins thus indicate the purity of obedience to the will of God, which is the belt that fortunately binds us. Without it, all purity is sheer impurity; and physical purity is only an image of inner purity, namely of the spirit. Inner purity consists in equality with the will of God: and the greater this equality is, the purer the spirit is also. First, the will of the creature is made equal to the will of the Creator; then it becomes harmonious; and afterward, it is transformed into that same will of God: and then all self-will is so annihilated <note>German: "vernichtiget" — a key term in mystical theology meaning the total surrender of the individual ego</note> and merged into God's will, that it even changes its name, and is called only the Will of GOD.

<column-break/>

# your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and you shall eat it in haste. It is the Lord’s Passover.
->12. For<-

---

The shoes on the feet are taken here as a sign of pilgrimage, and not for inclinations. For since Moses, as he wished to approach the burning bush, had to take off his shoes; how much more necessary is it in the spiritual sense to do so, since one must purify one's sins in order to eat the Lamb? But they shall be on the feet here, just as the staff is in the hand, to facilitate the departure.

The lamb is eaten in haste as a sign of the imminent transition.

It is now certain, however, that the perfection of the pure sacrifice is the annihilation <note>German: "Vernichtigung"</note>, which is the preparation for the approaching transition of the soul into GOD: and as soon as the soul reaches this level of annihilation according to the will of God, it transitions into Him instantly, and He Himself becomes the fullness of this very great emptiness.

All other emptinesses, which are only emptinesses of the powers <note>Refers to the faculties of the soul like memory or intellect</note>, are filled with such graces that match the object and the concept of their emptiness: but annihilation cannot be filled by anything other than GOD.

God first empties the soul of its sins: and the more He empties it of its sins, the more He fills it with His gifts and graces.

Afterward, He empties this soul of His gifts and graces, at least in terms of its perception. For the soul no longer possesses them except in an incomprehensible way, and as if it actually no longer had them; so that He may fill it with Himself. And this emptiness of graces serves the soul by taking away a certain restricted nature and natural self-containment, which made it unfit to be made more expanded and larger. For one must know that all God’s graces, let them be as extraordinary as they will, are always according to the capacity of the creature, and in their own way are always received under a hard and restricted form, opposing the breakthrough of the divine life.

In this restricted and narrow creature, sin once dwelt. When God then comes into it through His grace, He drives out the sin in a sweet and quiet way. The more this vessel is later cleansed of its filth, the more God fills it with His anointing of grace. This causes a living joy, even in the most severe penance. But when the soul is to be cleansed of its deepest rust, and a residue that remained in its depths through sin is to be taken away—which rust and residue can indeed exist alongside grace, but not alongside GOD in the soul—then such a soul must go into the fire, into a more subtle, consuming fire, which lets it feel a very painful effect. This fire burns fiercely, and it seems as if it stains the soul rather than purifies it. Therefore, one is often deceived in this: because one cannot see the beauty of this work until it is finished; just as one cannot recognize what a master craftsman intends to make from metal as long as it is in the furnace and completely permeated by the fire, and covered with earth and rust. So this fire must remove all ingrained rust from the soul, either in this world or the next, so that nothing impure remains in it.

In this crucible <note>German: "Schmältz-Tiegel"</note>, God takes from her everything that filled her, no matter how choice it may have been. Therefore she feels nothing but pain, without relief. The more this fire takes away the rust of this soul, the more it also takes away from her a certain dense, restricted, and limited manner: which is nothing other than selfhood <note>German: "Eigenheit"</note>, which, by flowing together and making itself firm within itself, prevents it from pouring itself out into GOD. And this very thing causes her such great pain: because she is attacked in the most sensitive and living part of herself; namely, in the ground of her own will. The more subtle and thin this selfhood becomes, the harder it is to tear it out. But as soon as it is entirely consumed, and the soul is delivered from its narrowness, and possesses nothing of itself within itself; then it falls into annihilation. Then it is so soft and pliable that, instead of its former hard and forced manner—which was caused by selfhood, or was rather selfhood itself—it afterwards finds itself capable of expanding infinitely in a completely easy manner. And then it has reached the purity of its origin. For GOD created it thus soft and pliable, and fit to be expanded, by Him and in Him. But since sin had made it self-willed, it also made it simultaneously hard and obstinate, and unfit to be able to expand, until GOD the Restorer has brought it back again into the purity of its creation.

When such a faithful soul has come to the total loss of its selfhood and self-containment, it becomes fit for the closest union and for being lost in GOD. But just as GOD can communicate Himself infinitely, so He can also expand such a soul daily more and more, and communicate Himself to it more and more.

<page-num>321</page-num>
<header>Chapter XII. The Second Book of Moses.</header>

### 12. For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of the Egyptians I will execute judgment: I am the LORD!
### 13. And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where you are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt.

---

What is the firstborn of Egypt other than the old sinful birth—the first Adam, the man of sin—who was in a state of dignity but, because he did not know how to prize it, became like a beast or cattle? Psalm 49:20. If this nature is now willingly surrendered into the judgment of death and sacrificed to the Lord, then the Lord is moved by this blood of "mortification" <note>original: "Abdödtung"; the spiritual practice of "dying to the self"</note>—as the mark of the Lord Jesus—not only to take such a soul into His shelter and <term>protection <note>The original uses the Latin "protection."</note></term>, so that no plague may come near their dwellings, but He also cannot pass by any creature without rather passing entirely into them. For where the "I" of the creature disappears, there "I the Lord" is revealed: and where the soul honestly enters into her "nothingness," then God must necessarily become "All" in her.

Certainly, when all self-interest is banished from the soul and she is thereby annihilated, she is in that moment full of God. For He leaves nothing void within her: and just as He fills the void of the faculties with His gifts, so He also fills this void of the essence with Himself. A vacuum can indeed be filled by some created gifts; but that which is completely emptied can only be filled with the uncreated All.

Since this capacity daily increases through the working of God Himself—who expands it as He fills it, and fills it as much as He expands it—there is not a moment in such a soul that is empty. And thus it is also true that she can always proceed in her annihilation (namely, in her emptiness) and increase her fullness: not from her own side, for she can do nothing for herself, but on God’s side, who works unceasingly toward that end.

It is indeed very remarkable that faithfulness in this state does not consist in maintaining and preserving the graces of God, but rather in allowing oneself to be deprived of them according to the will of God without resistance. A faithfulness at this stage is a "passive faithfulness," through which one surrenders oneself entirely to the working of God. When it was time to clothe oneself with virtues and to fill oneself with heavenly gifts, an "active faithfulness" was required to work at it with all one's strength. But after the signal of "divestment" <note>original: "Entblößung"; the mystical process of stripping away the ego and spiritual attachments</note> has been given, one must suffer such things with submission to the divine operation.

However, it is very difficult for the creature to submit to this, so that nothing remains of what is left to it that does not resist as much as possible. and although one is convinced of this truth, one still fails greatly in its practice—even more than one might imagine. Meanwhile, the soul prolongs her pain the more she resists Him. Thus, many, for lack of faithfulness, never arrive at annihilation in this life.

Therefore, souls who were otherwise of an extraordinary holiness have had to go through the fire of purification <note>likely a reference to Purgatory or a similar state of post-mortem refining</note> in order to endure in the next life an operation to which they would not submit in this one. Others, on the contrary, spend their lives building up and tearing down, and can suffer no void within them; for that reason, they immediately fill the void that God wanted to make in them with their own artifice. One never becomes perfect because one always wants to attain perfection but never wants to lose anything in the process. Even the philosophers recognize that the downfall of one is the rise of another: and eternal life is never given to a soul unless she has lost her own life. But no one wants to give themselves into that. Those who are experienced well understand what is meant here.

<margin>v. 12.</margin> *Against all the gods of the Egyptians*) Whether it be that they were cast down like Dagon, the idol of the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:3), or that they were put to shame along with their idol-worshippers and soothsayers, and their impotence publicly demonstrated: just as their earthly gods—Pharaoh with his mighty men—were also destroyed.

<column-break/>

### 14. And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations; ye shall keep it a feast by an ordinance for ever.
### 15. Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses: for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. 16. And...

---

<margin>v. 14.</margin> They were to observe this day annually with joy, to remember such a glorious redemption from heavy servitude and the fulfillment of the promise through the entry into the land of Canaan, with thankful praise of God, and that forever; until, after a long and unknown time, the true Passover, Christ, should appear. Through His blood, we Gentiles were to be redeemed from the spiritual servitude of Satan, when God's judgments were also executed upon all pagan idols by the destruction of their idolatry (Isaiah 19:1, 46:1). Then this "shadow," involving the slaughter of a physical sacrificial lamb, was to give way and be abolished. Colossians 2:16; 1 Corinthians 5:7, 8.

<margin>v. 15.</margin> The seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread also pointed toward this, which they were to keep for greater reflection on the precious benefit of God. No leaven was to be seen in their houses, much less was anything leavened to be consumed; they were to remember how they had been driven out of Egypt in great haste with their raw, unleavened dough (v. 39). This also suggests the seven mysterious periods <note>original: "Zeit-Läuffe"; often referring to the "Seven Ages of the Church" in pietistic theology</note> of the New Testament, which should be a constant sacrifice or Passover feast for believers, to be spent in the enjoyment of righteousness and peace earned through Christ’s blood, and thus in the joy of the Holy Spirit (Romans 14:17, 18). Consequently, this entire time is to be spent not in the "leaven of malice and wickedness," but in the "unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" and the upright essence that is in Christ, where one must put off the old man with his lusts and desires and put on the new man, walking in true righteousness and holiness. Ephesians 4:21–24.

And just as a willful transgressor there was subject to the judgment of "cutting off" by a sudden death, or by a violent one from the authorities (see Chapter 31:14), so also must such a depraved person, who willfully persists in the old nature of the flesh, be delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. 1 Corinthians 5:5. Immediately following this, mention is made of the purging of the old leaven of sin during the Easter of the New Testament.

The seven days also signify seven years, or a considerable length of time, which the soul spends gradually losing her own "inventions" <note>original: "Erfindungen"; here meaning human-made religious practices or self-willed efforts</note> before she enters the wilderness of pure faith.

Those who, during this time of "divestment," willfully retain their own habits are generally banished from Israel: namely, they never succeed in becoming part of this inward, highly purified people.

16. And on the first (a) day there shall be a holy convocation / and on the seventh day there shall be a holy convocation among you. No work shall be done in them: only what is eaten by every soul, that alone shall be done among you. <margin>(a) Leviticus 23:7.</margin>

17. And observe the feast of unleavened bread. For on this very day I led your hosts out of Egypt. Therefore you shall keep this day among your descendants as an everlasting statute.

18. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread / until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.

---

<margin>v. 16. On the first—and on the seventh day)</margin> On the intermediate days, it was permitted to perform some tasks. For example, court was held / and certain wrongdoers were put to death / namely those who were seducers of the people / and those who defiantly resisted the laws of the High Court. Indeed, such persons were expressly held until one of the high festivals / whichever was nearest. However, everyone otherwise abstained from work on these days / as much as possible / and no one was allowed to bring home his bride on these days. (a) <note>These "intermediate days" are known in Hebrew as Chol HaMoed.</note>

The first day is / when we leave our sins / and overcome the world. Then we should work at nothing else / except what belongs to this food or Passover celebration. Thus we come into the seventh day of rest / which is praised in Canaan.

<margin>v. 17. As an everlasting statute)</margin> The word "everlasting" <note>German: "ewig"</note> is / as is known / understood to mean a long period of time / which nevertheless has a certain cycle.

<margin>v. 18. At evening)</margin> The evening before / namely the 13th / which together with the following day was called the Passover Eve / as well as the searching for the leaven (b) <note>original: "חמץ" (chametz)</note> / before the stars appeared in the sky / the master of the house brought water home for the unleavened cakes / which were to be baked the following morning / and said: *This is the water for the unleavened bread!* But he brought it into his house covered. The following night he took a bowl with a feather duster / lit a wax candle / so that it would not drip much / and said: *Blessed be thou Lord our God / thou Lord of the whole world / who hast sanctified us with thy commandments / and hast commanded us to put away the leaven.* If the house was large / and the chambers many; he sometimes took several boys or other men with him / who then said *Amen* to his prayer. Each one had a burning wax candle in his hand / and with it they searched all chambers / chests / cupboards / and all corners / yes, even all mouse holes / to see if they could find even a crumb of leavened bread. What they found / they picked up / and kept carefully until the following day / and the master of the house said: *All leaven that is with me / and which I have neither seen nor removed / let it be scattered and esteemed as the dust of the earth!* The following morning the sweet cakes were made / and then they ate early at noon / an hour or so before midday / and not long nor much / so that they would have a better appetite for the evening. Immediately after the meal they made a fire under the open sky / and threw into it / what they had kept of the leavened bread. While burning it, the master of the house said: *All leaven / which I have either seen or not seen / which I have either brought out or not brought out / let it be scattered or destroyed / and be esteemed no more than the dust on earth!* If the preparation day fell on a Sabbath / they did this a day and night beforehand / and kept only as much leavened bread in their houses as they could eat during the Sabbath meals. (c)

<column-break/>

19. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses. For whoever eats what is leavened / that soul shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel / whether he be a stranger or a native of the land.

20. You shall eat nothing that is leavened: in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread.

21. And

---

<margin>v. 19. Whoever only—shall &c.)</margin> If someone eats the slightest leavened bread / as long as the Passover festival lasted / even as much as the size of an olive / and did so knowingly; he was / when it came out / whipped. If it happened out of ignorance / he had to bring his standing sacrifice for it.

*Cut off)* Because this way of speaking occurs very often in the books of Moses / it should be well noted. For there are many different opinions regarding its meaning. One understands it one way / another another way. Meanwhile, the Hebrews have the custom of whipping such people / whom God threatens to cut off because of their sin / but to whom no capital punishment by the authorities is indicated in God's word / if their sin is manifest / they were also warned beforehand / and nevertheless committed the sin / and they held that such a person could escape being "cut off" after the whipping.

<margin>v. 20.</margin> If there is anything in the world / that the Jews still handle today with great caution and care / it is the bread / which they prepare and eat at Passover / so that they may avoid even the slightest leavening. Concerning the corrupt leaven of the heart / these slaves to the letter care little.

With the sweet breads or Matzah-cakes / as they call them / which are round and very thin / they take the greatest care / that not the slightest thing / which could provoke a leavening / is added.

The water for the Matzah-cakes must be drawn at least 12 hours before / before one uses it: and indeed one draws it in the evening after sunset / or in the night; for the water during the day might be warmed by the sun / and cause some <term>fermentation <note>original: "Fermentacion"</note></term> in the flour. Therefore the water must be quite cold / and everything kneaded with great diligence and effort / so that not the slightest bubble is in the dough or bread. For where that is / may God cut off and shorten the life of one / who eats such Matzah-bread / in which there is the slightest bubble. Because the Jews now take the words of verse 18 "at evening" to mean that they are only obligated to eat Matzahs on that same evening / while for the rest of the Passover time it is only forbidden to eat leavened bread; and since it is so dangerous with the Matzah-cakes that there is danger to life involved / the most religious Jews gladly abstain as much as possible from the Matzah-cakes during the Passover days (except for the first evening) / and eat either very little / or no bread at all / and instead / whoever can / eats nothing but almonds.

Furthermore, it cannot be said / how everyone works with zeal at the preparation of the Matzah-cakes. In Frankfurt in the large Jewish Bleaching Garden / where the 5 large baking ovens stand / a very long hut of boards / in which from one end to the other are long tables / is erected: there it teems and swarms with people; old men and women / boys and girls / and whoever can / helps with a great bustle / and everyone gladly wants to have a part in it / because it is such a great <term>Mizvah <note>original: "Mizvah"; a Hebrew term for a commandment or a meritorious deed.</note></term> and meritorious work.

<margin>v. 21. Isaiah 26:20, 21. Revelation 18:4.</margin>

And so no righteous person will serve as a plague and destruction to another; but certainly the wicked will; they are accustomed to plague the righteous according to God’s just and wise ordinance.

**According to the Spirit)** When your children shall say to you: What kind of way is this to glorify God? by which one loses all worthiness and personal benefit / only to be clothed with that of Jesus Christ; in whom all our hope must stand: then you shall answer them; It is the pure sacrifice of the LORD / which he has reserved for himself / and the sign of the transition of the soul into him / through the loss of all self-interest. Thus the true inward people will bow down / namely subject themselves to him / and listen to this most just commandment / which takes everything from the creature / to give it back to God.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

29. And it came to pass at midnight / that the LORD struck <gloss>(a) chapter 11:22; Revelation 16:6.</gloss> all the firstborn in the land of Egypt / from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne / to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon / and all the firstborn of the livestock.

32. Also take with you your flocks and your herds / as you have said / and go / and bless me also!

34. And the people carried their dough / before it was leavened / namely their kneading bowls / bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders.

---

**Verse 29.** Finally, the judgment of the LORD is carried out upon Babylon / or / which according to the sense of the Spirit is the same thing / upon Egypt. <note>The author uses "Babylon" and "Egypt" interchangeably as symbols of worldly power and spiritual captivity.</note>
**At midnight)** When it has become truly dark in the spiritual Egypt / and no child of light / nor the lamp of the Lamb / is to be found in it any longer.
**The LORD struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt)** Come, you birds under the heaven / and gather yourselves to the supper of the great God! Revelation 19:17.

**Verse 30. Then)** Thus the LORD knows how to strike the hardened and obstinate sinners most sensibly in His own time; and when they will not let themselves be warned and humbled by the lesser punishments / then finally comes the extermination; then such wretched souls in the prisons of hell, in the long night of death, will be brought to painful reflection upon their hard and stubborn self-will / which they would not allow to be broken here on earth. Then they will call out to Lazarus and the godly / whom they left helpless here / just as the rich man did; to see if they might ask a refreshment and blessing from them: but it will then be too late; for Moses no longer intercedes before Pharaoh here / as he did before. And this will then also be the final plague upon the spiritual Egypt / when God will strike and kill the great and powerful / as the firstborn of the earth / who were always able to save themselves during the other land-plagues / and deliver them to the following sword and the eternal prisons: regarding which the following passages should be consulted / and should be weighed in the fear of God by the great ones during this time of grace. Psalm 2:10, 12; 149:8; Isaiah 2:12, 21; 24:21, 22; Ezekiel 39:18; Revelation 19:18.

**Verse 34. Before it was leavened)** In the departure from the sinful life, it is necessary / that we be without deceit and sincere. <note>Leaven often represents sin or corruption in biblical commentary; "unleavened" thus signifies spiritual purity.</note>

<column-break/>

35. And the children of Israel had done according to the word of Moses / and had requested from the Egyptians vessels of silver and vessels of gold and clothing.

36. Moreover, the LORD had given the people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians / so that they granted them their request; and they plundered the Egyptians.

37. So the sons of Israel journeyed from Raemses <gloss>chapter 3:22.</gloss> toward Succoth / about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the little children. <gloss>(a) Numbers 33:3, 5.</gloss>

38. And a large mixed crowd also went up with them / and sheep and cattle and a great deal of livestock.

39. And they baked unleavened cakes from the dough / which they brought out of Egypt: For it was not leavened; because they were driven out of Egypt / and could not tarry: nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves.

40. The <meta>catchword</meta>

---

**Verse 35. Had requested)** They had not requested anything belonging to others / but their own property / which God had gifted and bestowed upon them.

**Verse 36. Plundered)** Not as a theft. For everything belongs to God / that men possess. And since both silver and gold are the LORD’s, Haggai 2:9, He can turn it toward whomsoever He wills; for God always has His hidden, righteous reasons. God had the power / to bestow upon the children of Israel from that which was His own / and not the Egyptians' own property.
<note>The commentator is defending the Israelites against the historical charge of "stealing" from the Egyptians.</note>
*That which happens at the command of God, the supreme Lord of all things, is no vice or theft.* Hugo Grotius. <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>original Latin: "de Jure Belli ac Pacis" (On the Law of War and Peace).</note>
According to the root text, it can also be rendered: they robbed and plundered the Egyptians / as victors do to their defeated enemies.

**Verse 37. The sons of Israel)** One should note here the absurdity of many translations / which arises because the Hebrew word *kol* <note>The commentator likely means "kol" as "all" or is discussing the specific term for "children/people" vs "infants."</note> is translated everywhere as "children" without exception. These translations then have it here: "The children of Israel went out without the children."
**From Raemses)** To which place the Israelite people had gathered at Moses' command / so that they might there, according to divine ordinance, keep the Passover feast all together for the first time / and thereafter begin their journey out of Egypt from there at once.
**About 600,000 men)** So that at that time / as is proven by some, <gloss>(b)</gloss> there were at least three million people counting women and children.

**Verse 38. Large mixed crowd)** Partly Egyptians / who were moved to join the Jewish religion through association with the Israelites / or through the miracles that happened in Egypt; partly servants and other strangers.

## Chapter XII. The Second Book of Moses.

40. Now the sojourning of the children of Israel / which they dwelt in Egypt / was four hundred and thirty years.
41. And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years / even on that very same day it came to pass / that all the hosts of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.

**Verse 40. The sojourning of the children of Israel in Egypt 430 years)** How can this be? The entire age of <term>Kohath</term> <note>original: "Kabaths"</note> / as the grandfather of <term>Moses</term> / was 133 years; <term>Amram’s</term> was 137: chapter 6 / 18-20. <term>Moses</term> was 80 years old / when he departed from Egypt: chapter 7 / 7. Then the years he lived after the birth of <term>Amram</term>; thirdly also those <term>Amram</term> reached after the birth of <term>Moses</term>: all of which <term>Moses</term> did not record. Answer: The wandering of <term>Abraham</term> / <term>Isaac</term> and <term>Jacob</term> must be counted here: which the 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> also explicitly mention here in their translation. Likewise, the Jewish historian <term>Josephus</term> (a) calculated these years from the time when <term>Abraham</term> came into <term>Canaan</term>. Indeed, in some Greek Bibles these words are also found: *where they and their fathers have dwelt*. In reality, Israel spent only half that time, namely 215 years, in Egypt. Therefore, in the following verse 41, only the end / but not the beginning / of their dwelling in Egypt is mentioned.

**At the end of the 430 years it came to pass / that all the hosts of the Lord went out)** And here the blessing of the great multiplication / which was promised to <term>Abraham</term> / was fulfilled at the beginning, since despite the heavy persecution in the killing of the male children, the people nevertheless grew into such a great multitude that they went out in entire hosts: which happened within the mentioned 215 years / being half of the 430 years; whereas in the other half of those years they had come into Egypt as only about 70 souls. And thus these 430 years begin from the proclamation of the Egyptian servitude, Genesis 15 / 13. Acts 7 / 6. where 400 years are written; yes, from the first departure of <term>Abraham</term> out of <term>Chaldea</term>: Genesis 12 / 4. at which time <term>Abraham</term> was 75 years old; and in his 100th year <term>Isaac</term> was born: Genesis 21 / 5. that is 25 years. Afterwards <term>Jacob</term> was born in the 60th year of <term>Isaac</term>: Genesis 25 / 26. And <term>Jacob</term> was 130 years old when he came into Egypt. Genesis 47 / 9. Since 25 and 60 and 130 together make 215 years / before <term>Jacob</term> came into Egypt. Accordingly, the 430 years must necessarily be counted from the first promise / which was given to <term>Abraham</term> in <term>Chaldea</term>; as is clear from the words of God to <term>Abraham</term> Genesis 15 / 16. and even more from the testimony of <term>Paul</term> in Galatians 3 / 17.

And so God is accustomed to fulfill his promises at the exact point of time / which are never postponed / or even canceled because of the sins of men; just as the time of the threat of his judgments is often postponed / or even changed because of repentance. See Jonah 3 / 4, 10.

**On that very same day**) As soon as the time of captivity was completed / on that same day one had to depart from this land / to begin the way of the wilderness.

**Verse 42.** It is also noteworthy / that this feast had to begin and be kept in the night: since the promise of it was also given to <term>Abraham</term> at night. Just as it also reminds us of the blessed night in which Christ / our Passover Lamb / was born. Luke 2 / 8. etc. When the eternal light was to rise in our darkness of sin and death. John 1 / 5. Which shall be recognized with deep gratitude / so that this light may also truly rise in us.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

45. A sojourner (a) and a hired servant shall not eat thereof. <margin>(a) Leviticus 25:6.</margin>

**Verse 45. A sojourner)** This type of person was neither circumcised nor baptized / but merely renounced idolatry / and took upon themselves the 7 Laws of the Children of Noah. They were otherwise also called "countrymen" / or "strangers within the gate." These were free to dwell in the land of Canaan among the Israelites / if they wished / and wherever they wished / except in the city of Jerusalem / where no one was allowed to dwell because of the city's holiness. However, they were not required to dwell in the land of Canaan if they did not wish to. As for example, Naaman remained living in Syria. But if they did not accept the 7 Laws of the Children of Noah / and did not make a confession of them in the presence of 3 witnesses; the children of Israel would not let them dwell in their land / but instead forced them either to accept the commandments / or put them to death where they absolutely refused: so that they would not be led into idolatry by them. This they did as long as they were not subject to foreign kings / and while the Jewish years were still faithful. After the Babylonian captivity, they could no longer force anyone to do so: yet they diligently exhorted them to it. But if a heathen lived well among them / as the laws of Noah required; he was ultimately tolerated among them / even if he had not been publicly accepted as a "stranger within the gate": as in Acts 10:1, 2 and 17:4. (a) <note>original: "vid. Selden. de J. N. & G." (See John Selden, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations according to the Hebrews*.)</note>

Regarding the 7 Laws of Noah, the Jews say that God gave Adam 6 commandments: (1) that he should avoid all idolatry / and recognize Him as the only true God; (2) that he should not misuse the name of God / but call upon and honor it; (3) that he should shed no blood / but guard himself against all murder; (4) that he should abstain from all incest and wanton unchastity; (5) that he should steal or rob nothing; (6) that he should hold court and see / that law and justice were in force. To Noah, however, God added one more commandment; he was not to eat a limb from a living animal. Genesis 9:4. These 7 commandments bound humanity until Abraham / when circumcision / and thereafter more and more commandments / emerged / until everything reached perfection on Mount Sinai. (c)

**Hired servant)** By this, many understand—not incorrectly—foreign traveling craftsmen / who tend to travel abroad to experience something / or to learn their art more skillfully. (b)

**Shall not eat thereof)** Yet they were allowed to share in the unleavened bread and the bitter things. (d)

**Verse 46. See 1 Corinthians 10:16, 17 and 11:17 etc. Ephesians 4:3, 4. Hebrews 3:6.

**Carry nothing out of the house)** This is exactly what the Savior intends: You shall not cast that which is holy before the dogs. For outside are the dogs.

**You shall not break a bone of it)** This had to be fulfilled in the body of Christ itself / so that they were not permitted to break a bone of Him / as they did to the other two evildoers. John 19:33, 36. Which should also give believers the comforting assurance / that the Lord will preserve all their bones / that not one of them shall be broken. Psalm 34:20.

Figuratively, this commandment and prohibition teaches us / that we should will what Christ wills / and should practice such a will at all times and everywhere without weakening, breaking, or tearing. For just as the strength of a man consists in his bones / so all the strength of Christ consists in His will.

### Chapter XIII. The Second Book of Moses.

51. And it came to pass on that very same day, that the Lord led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, by their hosts.

<margin>v. 51. The Lord leads out of the land of Egypt)</margin> And in just the same way, the Lord will lead His people—those who in the latter days hope in His name—out of the spiritual Sodom, Babylon, and Egypt. He will lead them out even in a physical sense, just as they previously went out with their hosts, and for that very reason, they have been hated, oppressed, and persecuted by the spiritual "Egypt" of the New Testament. <note>The author is comparing the literal Exodus to a future spiritual deliverance of true believers from a corrupt world system.</note>

We have, therefore, in this
->**Egypt**<-
a clear and distinct prototype
of the spiritual Egypt,
the kingdom of the Antichrist;
and at the same time, a counterpart to Sodom, Babylon, and Tyre.

I. In regard to the land and what is within it.

1. Just as after the passing and death of Joseph and his 11 brothers the children of Israel multiplied, so too did the believers multiply after the death of Christ and the 11 Apostles.

2. But just as shortly thereafter a king arose who knew nothing of Joseph’s good deeds: so the "mystery of iniquity" was already stirring in the time of Paul. 2 Thessalonians 2:7.

3. This king is called Pharaoh, which means "Crocodile": <note>original: "Crocodil". In biblical imagery, specifically in Ezekiel, Pharaoh is often likened to a great dragon or crocodile lurking in the Nile.</note> thus he is the king of the spiritual Egypt, who is opposed to the true Joseph, or takes no heed of His people. Ezekiel 29, likewise 32, and Isaiah 27, Psalm 62, where he is called a sea-dragon.

4. This crocodile stayed especially in the Nile River. Revelation 17:15.

5. The Nile had seven streams: likewise Revelation 17:9-10; Isaiah 11:15-16.

6. The crocodile is a symbol of a cunning predator: and so is the king of the spiritual Egypt. Daniel 11.

7. In Egypt was the most terrifying idolatry: everything was deified; all sorts of ceremonies, feast days, images, etc. So it is and will be in the spiritual Egypt. Revelation 9:20-21.

8. Egypt was full of soothsayers and sorcerers: and there is no lack of these in the kingdom of the Antichrist. Revelation 16:14.

II. In regard to Pharaoh,
what he did and what happened to him.

1. Pharaoh feared three things regarding the children of Israel, who had a different religion than he and his Egyptians: (1) that they might join his enemies; (2) or stir up an internal war; (3) or depart from the land, and thus weaken his rule.

2. Therefore, Pharaoh sought to suppress them with cunning through heavy burdens, so that they would "crawl under the cross," <note>An idiom meaning to submit to suffering or forced labor.</note> become one people with the Egyptians, and remain with them.

3. But when he could achieve nothing with the elders, he commanded the small sons to be killed and the children to be taken from their parents: so that after the death of the elders, everyone might become one people. The reasons of state <note>original: "Staats-railons", from the French "raisons d'état".</note> of the spiritual Egypt are handled in the same way.

4. He did not want to let the children of Israel go, nor grant them the freedom to serve GOD in the wilderness according to their conscience. And it is against the nature of the spiritual Egypt to allow this.

<column-break/>

5. Although Moses and Aaron protested against Pharaoh. Revelation 11:3-7.

6. His heart was hardened by the sorcerers in Egypt, who performed false wonders. 2 Thessalonians 2:9-11; 2 Timothy 3:1-8.

7. Because of Pharaoh's malice, Moses and Aaron brought 10 plagues upon Egypt; one finds almost all of these repeated in Revelation 9, 11, 16, and 18.

8. During such plagues—at least most of them—the Israelites went free. The same benefit happens in the kingdom of the Antichrist to those who are marked with the seal of GOD and distinguished from the crowd of the godless.

III. In regard to the departure from Egypt.

1. Finally, GOD led His people out of Egypt. And we also say in the 10 Commandments: "I the LORD am your GOD, who led you out of the land of Egypt."

2. Indeed, they were driven out by the Egyptians, who would otherwise have gladly held them back.

3. They departed with much wealth, with which they were later able to adorn the Tabernacle.

4. Many went out with them whose hearts still longed for Egypt because of the abundance of bread.

5. They went out in the night and carried their unleavened dough with them out of Egypt. Mark 8:15.

6. Pharaoh pursued those who had departed, even though he had let them go.

7. But just as the children of Israel as a whole never returned, even though one or two might have gone back; and indeed, just as Pharaoh perished in the Red Sea: so will a "Red Sea" of bloody wars—yet without the hand of Israel, who will only be spectators—overwhelm the spiritual Pharaoh. Therefore:

->One must never despair, even when the leaders—Joseph and the 11 patriarchs—die. GOD still takes heed of His people, sends them a Moses and an Aaron, and leads them out of misery when there is the least appearance of hope, yes, even when they are stuck in the deepest distress.<-

One should gladly suffer affliction with God's people; which is the hallmark of Israel—that they are held harshly by the Egyptians—and bear the reproach of Christ. One must by no means look back like Lot’s wife. Luke 17:32.

But what would all this profit us if we belonged to the church outwardly, had rejected Egyptian idolatry, and had endured much for the sake of Christ's name, if we were meanwhile a disobedient people, grumbling against GOD and unwilling to walk in His ways? Truly, all that would not profit us! Not everyone who says to me: LORD, LORD, etc. We would not enter into the land of Canaan, into His rest.

**By their hosts)** Out of the spiritual Egypt, the believers must always go forth in spiritual armor, and that with united hearts; so that they must close their ranks properly in a spiritual battle-order: and thus they could be a match for their enemies. See Ephesians 6:10-11, etc.

The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

## 45. A sojourner ʘ and a hired servant shall not eat of it. <note>The symbol ʘ appears in the text, likely marking a cross-reference or a specific legal category.</note> (a) Leviticus 25:6.

## 46. In one house shall it be eaten. You shall carry none of the flesh outside of the house; and you shall not break a bone of it.

v. 45. A sojourner) This class of people allowed themselves neither to be circumcised nor baptized, but merely renounced idolatry and took upon themselves the seven commandments of the children of Noah. <note>These are known as the Noahide Laws, which according to Jewish tradition are binding on all humanity.</note> They were otherwise also called "compatriots" or "strangers at the gate." These were free to live in the land of Canaan among the Israelites if they wished, and wherever they wished, except in the city of Jerusalem, where no one was permitted to live because of the city's holiness. However, they were not required to live in the land of Canaan if they did not wish to; for example, Naaman remained living in Syria. But if they did not accept the seven commandments of the children of Noah and did not make a confession of them in the presence of three witnesses, the children of Israel did not allow them to live in their land. Instead, they forced them either to accept the commandments or, if they absolutely refused, put them to death, so that they would not be led into idolatry by them. They did this as long as they were not subject to foreign kings and still observed the Jubilee years. After the Babylonian captivity, they could no longer force anyone to do this, yet they diligently exhorted people toward it. However, if a Gentile lived among them well, as the laws of Noah required, he was eventually tolerated among them even if he had not been publicly accepted as a "stranger at the gate," as seen in Acts 10:1–2 and 17:4. (a)

Regarding the seven commandments of Noah, the Jews say that God gave Adam six commandments: (1) that he should avoid all idolatry and recognize Him as the only true God; (2) that he should not misuse the name of God, but call upon and honor it; (3) that he should shed no blood, but guard himself against all murder; (4) that he should abstain from all incest and reckless unchastity; (5) that he should steal or rob nothing; (6) that he should hold court and see that law and justice prevailed. To Noah, however, God gave one additional commandment: he should not eat a limb from a living animal. Genesis 9:4. These seven commandments were said to have bound mankind until Abraham, when circumcision—and thereafter more and more commandments—arose, until everything reached perfection on Mount Sinai. (a)

Hired servant) By this term, many—not incorrectly—understand foreign journeymen craftsmen who travel abroad to experience things or to learn their art more skillfully. (a)

Shall not eat of it) They did, however, share the unleavened bread and the bitter herbs with them. (d)

v. 46. In one house. The believers shall enjoy the spiritual food of Christ together in community, and there should be no division among them; rather, they should be united in spirit and thus be as if in one house. See 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 11:17 etc.; Ephesians 4:3–4; Hebrews 3:6.

Carry nothing out of the house) This is precisely what the Savior wants: "You shall not throw what is holy to the dogs." <note>Matthew 7:6</note> For "outside are the dogs." <note>Revelation 22:15</note>

You shall not break a bone of it) This had to be fulfilled in the body of Christ himself, so that they were not permitted to break any of his bones as they did to the other two evildoers. John 19:33, 36. This is also intended to give believers the comforting assurance that the Lord will preserve all their bones, so that not one of them shall be broken. Psalm 34:21.

Figuratively, this commandment and prohibition teach us that we should want what Christ wants, and should exercise such a will at all times and everywhere without weakening, breaking, or tearing it. For just as the strength of a man consists in his bones, so all the strength of Christ consists in His will.

(a) See Selden, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations*, book 1, ch. 10; book 2, ch. 3, 5. Buxtorf, *Talmudic Lexicon*, under the word "Ger" <note>original: גֵּר, meaning stranger or proselyte</note>. Leusden, *Hebrew Philology Mixed*, dissertation 21, etc.
(b) *The Kuzari*, part 1, section 83; and Buxtorf's notes; and part 3, section 73. Cunaeus, *On the Republic of the Hebrews*, book 2, ch. 19. <insert>Selden, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations*, book 1, ch. 10; and book 7, ch. 12, etc.</insert>
(c) Osiander, cited in Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 1, ch. 1, thesis 16, observation 2. Leusden, *Hebrew Philology Mixed*, dissertation 21, etc.
(d) Hottinger, *On Hebrew Laws*, no. 21.

## 47. All the congregation of Israel shall do this.

v. 47. All the congregation of Israel) The entire multitude of the surrendered children <note>The term "surrendered" likely refers to the Pietist concept of *Gelassenheit*, or total submission to God's will.</note> shall observe this sacrifice.

v. 48. But if a stranger wishes to join himself to them—that is, wishes to enter into that same state—he must first cut off everything he had retained of his old corners and practices; and afterward he shall be joined to them. His children will then also enter into the state of their fellowship through this "cutting off" <note>circumcision</note> and shall eat with them of the same food of the Lord’s "passing over."

v. 49. There will then be only one law for the one born in this way—that is, one who by a rare fortune fell into it in his childhood—and for the one who, although he had walked in another way for some years, nevertheless willingly enters into it. Secret surrender <note>term: *Gelassenheit* (resignation or yielding to God)</note> is the passage which neither one nor the other can escape.

Strangers) This name, or "Jews from among the strangers," was given to the Jewish proselytes along with their children and descendants, as long as no marriage with the children of Israel took place. But if a proselyte took an Israelite wife, or an Israelite took a female proselyte, they themselves were not, but their children produced with Israelites were simply called Jews and were considered proper Jews.

Thus, such strangers could also hold no offices, neither in war nor in times of peace; nor could they be in the High Court, nor in any way command or preside over the native-born Israelites. But if they married Israelites, their children could attain to these things. Yet no one of foreign descent was admitted to this who did not have at least an Israelite mother. (a)

These strangers were the lowest among the people, excluding the freedmen; even below the *Mamzerim* <note>original: *Manzeres*, children of forbidden or illegitimate unions</note> who were fathered from forbidden marriages among the Jews; also equal to the Gibeonites and the freedmen.

v. 50. Did) The Passover must be celebrated in obedience. For through this, all the firstborn in Egypt die; namely, whatever the world holds dear and beautiful—honor, goods, lust, and worldly comfort—which have until then held the people of God captive in the hard bondage of sin and under their dominion. When these now die in us, we become free, and then the departure follows, and

---

<gloss>
**verse 4. Abib)** After the Chaldean <note>Babylonian</note> captivity, this was called Nisan. The former name signifies fresh, ripening ears of grain / which one could obtain from the barley at that time / as it was the first to ripen in the land of Canaan. For they generally sowed it toward the end of our October; and because the winter was mild / it could well be ripe by Easter in a land / where at the time of the equinox / it is just as warm as it is with us during the Dog Days <note>The hottest weeks of summer, usually July and August</note>. If the barley was not yet ripe at that time / they would insert an extra month into the year / though for other reasons as well / and created a double February or Adar. <note>Original: "Nifan," likely an OCR error for "Nisan." The "double Adar" refers to the Jewish leap year (Adar II).</note>

**verse 5. when the LORD shall bring you into the land / -- so)** They were only to keep the Passover in the land of Canaan / and not in the wilderness: partly because they could not maintain such large herds there / and for that reason only kept it once in the wilderness in the first following year, Numbers 9:5 / and then 38 years later in the land of Canaan, Joshua 5:10. In this, one should imagine / that one cannot truly partake of Christ / until one first has a share in the promised goods in Christ; such as His wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption: otherwise the soul is still in the barren wilderness of its natural corruption. See Ephesians 4:17-21.

**verse 6. On the seventh day is the LORD’S feast)** The seventh day was particularly the joy-filled feast / just as the first day was celebrated with a holy assembly: which indicates / how especially the first / but primarily the seventh and final church-age of the New Testament will be very glorious and full of joy in Christ’s glorious kingdom / when the believers will heartily rejoice over the complete redemption from the spiritual Egypt and Sodom / where Christ is crucified anew in the spirit. See John 7:37. Psalm 18:1. where David sang in a prototype of this glorious victory and praised God for it.

**verse 7. Seven days)** The Hebrews say / they were only bound to eat the bread of affliction on the first day / but not on the following days; rather / although they were not allowed to eat leavened bread / it was permitted for them / instead of the miserable bread baked from nothing but water and flour, to eat something else; such as / millet, rice, or dried fruits. (a)

See Romans 6:3-11.

### Chapter XIII. The Second Book of Moses.

11. And it shall come to pass, when the LORD has brought you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and to your fathers, and has given it to you;

12. Then you shall set apart <note>literally "pass over"</note> to the LORD all that opens the womb, and every firstborn that comes from your livestock; the males shall be the LORD’S.

13. But every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb. If you will not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. And all the firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.

14. And it shall be, when your son asks you in time to come, saying, "What is this?" that you shall say to him: By a mighty hand the LORD led us out from Egypt, out of the house of bondage.

---

->The LORD wanted all the firstborn to be handed over to him, or, as it actually says, "to pass over" to him. Specifically, he wanted the males and not the females: by which he wanted to indicate that he demands the most noble part of us—the spirit and the heart—which we should give to God. Proverbs 23:26. However, the weak part, which is the corruption within us—also understood under the image of unclean animals (Numbers 18:15), of which the donkey is cited here (animals they dealt with much in the Orient and made use of, among which horses are also understood)—those they were to kill by breaking their necks. Likewise, we should especially kill the sluggish and unruly nature within us. See Psalm 32:9. Yet the firstborn of the sons were to be redeemed: which made it known that the true firstborn and only-begotten Son of God had to redeem us with his blood, so that we can now be an acceptable offering in Christ, when we present our bodies as a sacrifice that is living, holy, and well-pleasing to God. Romans 12:2.<-

<margin>
v. 13. **But every firstborn of a donkey)** Whether it be male or female, defective or without blemish.
**You shall redeem)** Our animalistic man had to be redeemed through the Lamb of God.
**With a lamb)** Or a goat. Whoever did not have one gave as much as a lamb or goat was worth. A generous person gave a shekel <note>original: "Seckel"</note> or half a Reichsthaler; a stingy miser gave half a shekel or a quarter-thaler <note>original: "Ortsthaler"</note>; an average person gave 2/3 of a shekel, or nearly 9 Batzen <note>a small silver coin</note>. But whoever did not want to redeem it was not allowed to raise it for his own use, but had to chop off its neck with an axe and afterwards scrape it into the earth. (a)
</margin>

(a) Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue*, chapter 38. <note>original: "Buxtorff. synag. jud. c. 38."</note>

And this shall, as Schudt (c) indicates, concern all firstborn today, not only of the father but also of the mothers: so that if a man has already fathered a firstborn son with his first wife, and after her death takes another wife who also bears a son first, such a one is also a firstborn of the mother, with whom it is handled in exactly the same way; because he first "opened" the mother: so that in such a way a man may well have 3 or 4 firstborn sons.

v. 16. **With a mighty hand)** The mighty hand of God is praised here several times, by which they were led out of Egyptian bondage: As a prototype <term>Vorbild|A historical event serving as a symbol for a spiritual truth</term> of how the Lord, in his hour, will also lead his people out of the spiritual Egypt and Babylon with his strong arm, and will slay the enemies of his people with the hard, great, and strong sword. See Isaiah 30:30, 27:1.

<column-break/>

15. And it came to pass, when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, that the LORD slew all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man even to the firstborn of livestock. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.

16. And it shall be as a sign on your hand, and as frontlets <note>ornaments or phylacteries</note> between your eyes, that the LORD led us out of Egypt with a mighty hand. 17.

---

v. 15. **Therefore)** To this day, all firstborn also fast on the day before Easter <note>Passover</note> from morning until night, because on that same evening the firstborn in Egypt were struck down by the destroying angel. If the firstborn is still a small child, the father fasts for him. But if the father himself were also a firstborn, so that he had to fast this day for himself, then the mother fasts for her firstborn little son.

**Sacrifice)** Because they can no longer sacrifice today and have no Temple, such a firstborn [animal] must be raised and fed by the Jews until it dies, or until their Messiah comes; it is called the "Calf of Moses." This is something very burdensome for them, as they are not allowed to slaughter such an ox, nor use it for plowing or in any other way.

**All the firstborn of my sons I redeem)** The Jews keep this redemption <term>Lösung|Specifically the 'Pidyon HaBen' ceremony</term> strictly to this day, except that the child can no longer be presented to the Lord in the Temple. The redemption happens thus: The father invites one who boasts of being from the tribe of Levi and a priest, lays the child before him on a table next to two and a half Reichsthalers, and addresses the priest with these words: **My wife has borne me a firstborn son, whom the law assigns to you.** The priest says: **So you surrender him to me?** **Yes,** says the father. Thereupon the Cohen <note>Priest</note> asks the mother whether this is her firstborn son, or if anything "opened" the mother before? If she says it is he, he asks the father what is dearer to him: his firstborn son or the money? The father says, **the son**, and asks the priest to take the money, and thanks God for the permitted redemption. Then the priest places the money at the child’s head and says: **This is a firstborn son, whom God commanded to be redeemed. While you were yet in the womb, your heavenly Father and your parents had power over you; but now you belong to me, as the Lord’s priest. But your parents have resolved to redeem you and have given for you and your redemption this money, which is due to us priests. Grow up in the fear of God, get married, and be diligent in good works! Amen.** After this, they hold a feast. (b)

This redemption takes place on the 31st day after birth. If it falls on a Sabbath, the redemption is postponed until the following day. If the son dies before the 30th day, the father is not obligated to redeem him; and if he has already given the redemption money to the priest, the priest must return it. But if the father dies before the time of redemption or the 31st day, the mother is not obligated to redeem the child; rather, a parchment slip, or sometimes a square silver plate, is hung around his neck with these or similar words inscribed or engraved: **A firstborn not yet redeemed**, or **A priest’s son**. He wears this around his neck until he enters his age of manhood, when he is 13 years and a day old, at which time he must redeem himself from the priest.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XIII.

17. And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not by the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was nearer. For God said: Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt.
18. But God led the people about, by the way of the wilderness of the Red Sea <note>original: "Schilff-Meer," literally "Sea of Reeds"</note>: and the children of Israel went up ordered by fives <note>historically translated as "harnessed" or "in battle array"</note> out of the land of Egypt.

---

<margin>v. 17. God yielded here to the weakness of the people: otherwise He could indeed have endowed them with power and struck the enemies with terror. See Deuteronomy 20:8.</margin>
Thus God does not tempt us beyond our ability, and does not lay more upon anyone than they can bear. 1 Corinthians 10:13.

Those who walk through the deserts of pure faith do not endure such violent temptations from the devil: both because they have quite different things to suffer, and because, as they are to be led through such a great loss, they might be moved to choose their former ways again and go back if the temptations attacked them right at the beginning of this path. For since they have only recently departed from those ways, they would not yet be sufficiently established in the new path of abandonment <note>the spiritual practice of "Gelassenheit" or surrendering one's will to God</note>.

<margin>v. 18. The way toward the wilderness)</margin> God wanted to lead them into the wilderness to make the return journey entirely difficult, indeed impossible, for them: just as God already intends to send pure difficulty to the believers and witnesses of the truth, so that they might not fall back into the service of the world.

Once they have traveled further into the wilderness, war no longer terrifies them: because they no longer fight, but the Lord fights in them. In the wars of the "illuminated way" <note>an early stage of the spiritual life characterized by divine light and consolation</note> (even though it is also enlightened), one resists with strength and power because of the illuminating grace that supports there. But in pure faith, it does not happen this way: for the soul, in this beginning nakedness in which it is still weak, could easily turn back again to the exercises of the illuminated way in light and in love, which is sensory and tasteful; wherein it could perhaps easily allow itself to be overcome by an impulse that would bring about sin. Therefore, the wise Guide leads His people through the wilderness of faith, by the Red Sea: which is indeed another kind of trial than war, but nonetheless also safer, even if it is much slower and more arduous.

When a person has lived in the world, and then converts from it and begins to come into themselves; they then find nothing but a mournful, wild wilderness, a heart full of weeds, full of worms and unclean animals, full of evil habits, beastly images and customs, and much time is spent before they emerge from this wilderness; whereas otherwise, they came out of Egypt and the world in a single day. Oh, what a person must experience in this wilderness! How often they must lie still! They may even go back, and then forward again, before they can get through.

<margin>Ordered by fives)</margin> They went in their orderly members and rows, each by fives: whereby they could be counted all the more conveniently by 10s, 100s, and 1000s, and so on.

The number five points to fifty, as the hallowed number of the Jubilee or Year of Release.

They had to depart in an orderly fashion, and not as a wild mob: and that without weapons, which they may perhaps have taken afterward from the dead Egyptians. See Chapter 14:30, 17:9.

The word may also be rendered as "girded" according to its proper meaning, which is based on the fact that the belt used to be girded under the fifth rib, which in Hebrew is called <term>chamelsch <note>transliterated from Hebrew "homesh," referring to the abdomen or the area of the fifth rib; the author connects this to the word "hamushim" translated as "ordered by fives"</note></term>, that is, the fifth, the flanks under the ribs, under which are the liver, the gallbladder, and the spleen.

But the Lord prefigures in the journey of the Israelites out of Egypt our journey out of the spiritual Egypt, the oppressions of sin.

Truth, purity, and faithfulness is the belt of the Israel of God, which is required foremost of a Christian when he comes out of the spiritual Egypt. Ephesians 6:14. Thus the belt also signifies power, strength, and steadfastness. Psalm 18:39. Moreover, it also requires chastity. On this belt or sword-belt hang the remaining weapons of the spiritual knighthood.

And these would also be the weapons with which Israel should be armed as they went out of Egypt. For where should they have obtained other weapons? Is it at all likely that an openly known tyrant, such as Pharaoh was, who held a people in slavery and sought to suppress them, would have permitted them weapons? And

So also will the people of God be led out of the spiritual Egypt, indeed in good order, but without earthly weapons. See regarding this the glorious promise in Isaiah 52:11, 12; 55:12.

<column-break/>

19. And Moses took the bones of Joseph with him. For he had strictly sworn the children of Israel, saying: God will surely visit you! Then you shall carry up my bones from hence with you.
20. So they took their journey from Succoth, and encamped in Etham, at the edge of the wilderness.
21. And

---

<margin>v. 19. Moses took with him)</margin> Also as a public testimony of the fulfilled promise and Joseph's prophecy.

<margin>The bones of Joseph)</margin> Whether the bones and relics of the saints may be brought from one place to another is therefore not the question when speaking of this matter and drawing proof from this passage: but whether one should carry them around, put them on display, honor them with lights, or dedicate them to a liturgical use, or also seek help and refuge in them. (a) However, these bones were buried again in Canaan. Joshua 24:34 <note>In most modern Bibles, this is Joshua 24:32</note>.

The children of Israel here fulfilled the precious promise which their fathers—namely, the remaining rest of the Patriarchs—had taken upon themselves. Acts 7:16. As it is then a matter of the highest fairness to fulfill the last will of one's ancestors and thereby give them satisfaction. Otherwise, this ingratitude will be seriously punished by God as a violation of the required love of neighbor, especially when it concerns us so closely, as our parents and nearest relatives do.

<margin>You shall carry my bones up with you)</margin> Joseph did not want to be buried and lie with his fathers and his people in the land of Canaan after his death solely or even primarily out of love for them: but most of all for the sake of the Messiah, who was to be born in that land, preach, do miracles, suffer, die, be buried, and rise again; for which reason it is also called in a special way Immanuel's Land: in hope of the first resurrection with Christ along with the other patriarchs, when Christ would have accomplished the great work of redemption; as then happened to many, and without doubt to him also, after the resurrection of Christ. Matthew 27:53.

<margin>v. 20. Etham)</margin> Extends far and wide also to the other side across the Red Sea <note>Schilffmeer</note>: which is rather to be concluded from Numbers 33:7, 8, than those who believe that the children of Israel did not go across the Red Sea, but stayed on one side and took their path in a circle, might find grounds there.

# Chapter XIII. The Second Book of Moses (Exodus). 331

21. And the Lord <margin>(a)</margin> went before them: by day in a pillar of cloud, to lead them on the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light; to travel by day and night. <margin>Numbers 9:21. Deuteronomy 1:33. (a) ch. 14:19. ch. 23:40.</margin>
22. The pillar of cloud did not depart by day, nor the pillar of fire by night, from before the people.

---

Since Christ, as the **Angel of the Covenant**, went before them; He wished to prove His presence to them in this image of the pillars of cloud and fire, to be their refreshment from the heat in this parched wilderness by day, and their light by night: just as He has graciously promised these benefits to His people at all times—and especially at the last—in the heat of temptation and in the night of manifold troubles, errors, and deceptions. Isaiah 4:5-6. Psalm 121.

The cloud can also represent the human nature, and the fire the divine nature, which has enveloped itself within humanity as if with a cloud.

The Son of God assumed such a pillar of cloud for the benefit of poor Israel, so that their eyes could truly see His holy humanity in it day and night. For if He had not assumed something external alongside His heavenly God-humanity <note>original: "Gott-Menschheit"</note>, they could not have endured Him because of His majesty and clarity, in which His heavenly humanity shines. Therefore, He **condescends** <term>condescendiret: to stoop down or adapt oneself to a lower level</term> and takes on something so that they can see Him constantly with their eyes and perceive the way by which He wished to lead them; He who loves mankind so much and so gladly desires to be around them.

Since the soul has entered into the wilderness of bare faith and allows itself to be brought to God through a total **serenity** <term>Gelassenheit: a state of surrendered detachment or letting go of one's own will</term>; He Himself takes upon Himself the care of leading such souls, and that with such caution that He does not leave them for a moment until He has brought them into the promised land; unless they depart from this serenity through unfaithfulness. By day He is to the soul as a cloud; so that the excessive light does not burden it or even hold it back. For the soul gladly lingers amidst these perceivable enlightenments. Therefore, God hides them from the soul so that nothing may hinder its progress. This same cloud also serves as a refreshment for it, so that the heat of the sun does not hinder the secret soul: as sensible love <note>The author refers to "sensible love" as feelings or emotions that can make a person lazy or sluggish in their spiritual journey, just as physical heat weakens the body.</note> makes its course more difficult and sluggish to complete, just as heat weakens the body. God takes all this away and encloses it in the **sanctified darkness of faith**; as **Saint Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an early Christian mystic who wrote about the "divine darkness" where God dwells.</note> says: under which covering, as under a cloud, one can then travel much better through the wilderness. But just as night is as common in this wilderness as day, and is also much more hideous; so God, who softens the heat of the day, also scatters this darkness of the night a little. And this is also why souls can endure in this terrible wilderness. This way of God never fails those who are truly surrendered.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XIV.
->Pharaoh’s Pursuit and Downfall, and Israel’s Passage.<-

1. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel, that they turn back and camp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, before Baal-zephon; you shall camp opposite it, by the sea.
3. For Pharaoh will say of the children of Israel: They are lost in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.
4. And I will allow Pharaoh's heart to be hardened, that he may pursue them: so I will be glorified through Pharaoh and all his power, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord. And they did so. 5.

---

The Lord did not want to let the people take the straight highway to the land of Canaan, but they had to turn back and turn toward the wilderness and the sea: so that their faith might be tested and finally strengthened by the wonderful hand of God; and on the other hand, Pharaoh would be provoked to pursue them in the wilderness, seeking to catch them there as if in a net and bring them back under his power.

v. 3. **Pharaoh will say -- They are lost**) Without doubt he had gathered intelligence that they had taken such a strange path and concluded from it that they must have lost their way.

v. 4. God hardens people when He gives them over to their perverse, wicked minds, where they allow themselves to be blinded by self-interest, so that they forget all their assurances and promises they have made, and only seek their own benefit to their neighbor's harm.

One cannot emphasize or present for observation enough in this matter that it is said of God that He does this or that, when He only gives the occasion and opportunity for it to be done: as in Psalm 105:25.

**I will -- harden**) That is; I will provide the occasion for him to harden his own heart. Otherwise, God does nothing toward it. And indeed:

1) The primary occasion was God’s gentleness, goodness, and long-suffering toward Pharaoh. For from this, Pharaoh took the occasion to harden himself against all God’s commands given to him through Moses and Aaron: just as he also misused the grace and mercy that the Lord showed to Pharaoh. And in this way, a father hardens his disobedient child. As is clearly seen in Chapter 8:15 and Chapter 9:34.

2) Pharaoh considered and esteemed the punishments with which God had afflicted him much less than the loss that would result from losing the labor of so many thousands of people, which he enjoyed for free.

3) The punishments did not affect him as much as his subjects.

4) His pride stood in his way. He considered it a disgrace that he, as such a great king, should obey the commands or orders of another God—a God he did not know—and that, too, to his own great harm and loss. Chapter 5:2.

If one were to understand God’s hardening as an explicit and actual or essential influence, impression, or communication of hardness, then God Himself would have to be the true cause and author of Pharaoh's disobedience and sin. To say such a thing would be blasphemous. Indeed, how can the hardening of a single person in sin—which is the completion of sin—be truly and properly attributed to Him, when He does not even do so much as to tempt a single person to sin? James 1:13. Furthermore, if the Lord had truly and properly impressed a hardness into Pharaoh's heart, it could not be said of Pharaoh with truth and propriety that he hardened his own heart; but rather, that he necessarily had to yield and obey God’s superior power over him: and thus he would have been innocent of all sin and disobedience, of which Scripture clearly accuses him here and there.

Certainly, those who attribute Pharaoh's hardening to God, and not to Pharaoh himself, have a worse opinion of God than the priests of the Philistines had of Him. 1 Samuel 6:6.

# The Second Book of Moses (Exodus). Chapter XIV.

5. And it was told to the king of Egypt that the people had fled; and the heart of Pharaoh and of his servants was turned against the people, and they said: "Why have we done this, that we have let Israel go from serving us?"
6. And he made ready his chariot, and took his people with him;
7. And he took six hundred chosen chariots, and all the other chariots of Egypt, and the captains over all of them.
8. For the Lord allowed the heart of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, to be hardened, so that he pursued the children of Israel. But the children of Israel had gone out with a high hand. <note>original: "hohe Hand"; this idiom suggests they left with confidence and divine protection.</note>
9. And the Egyptians pursued after them, and all the horses and chariots of Pharaoh, along with his horsemen and his army, overtook them where they were camped by the sea, near Pi-Hahiroth, before Baal-Zephon.
