11. And they said unto Moses: "Is it because there were no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? Why have you dealt thus with us, to carry us forth out of Egypt?
12. Is not this the word that we spoke to you in Egypt, saying: 'Let us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than that we should die in the wilderness."
13. And

---

Good counsel is expensive <note>A German idiom meaning one is at a complete loss for what to do</note> when one is driven into such a corner, and the heart stands in a vice or a press; there appears to be no help from within or without, but rather the wild floods of one’s own thoughts rise up against oneself, the wilderness of abandonment lies ahead, and the Egyptians with horses and riders press from behind.
Tertullian <margin>(a) Book 2, against Marcion, chapter 20.</margin> relates from an old tradition that the Egyptians first sent their envoys into the wilderness to Moses to demand back the property that had been taken; the children of Israel, however, demanded in return their wages for their heavy service and the many years of hard labor they had performed. When they met and calculated both sides against each other, it was found that the value of the treasures taken away did not nearly reach what was owed to Israel as wages for their work, but that the latter amounted to much more. Therefore, the Israelites still had just claims against the Egyptians.

<margin>v. 7. chariots)</margin> These were special war-chariots upon which they placed soldiers and drove them among the enemies to shoot arrows at them.
The captains) are called <term>Schalischim: a Hebrew term derived from the number three</term> in Hebrew, which comes from the number three; they may have this name because they were the third estate in the kingdom, as they may have divided the realm into the peasant estate, the citizen estate, and the knightly estate, because such men are usually placed over soldiers for the defense of the lands and are endowed with special privileges.

<margin>(a) Book 2, against Marcion, chapter 20.</margin>

<insert>
Thus the Lord is accustomed to put His own into the greatest distress, so that they may then learn to take their refuge in God; (see Psalm 46:2, 3, 4.) just as Israel here had the sea before them, great mountains on both sides, a terrible wilderness, and behind them the enraged and armed enemies, the Egyptians. Then also their unbelief became manifest, for they cried to the Lord not out of heartfelt confidence, but out of a faint and anxious heart, and they complained against the faithful servant of God, Moses; though they had sufficiently experienced the mighty hand of God through him, and should have trusted him further, that Moses, according to the wise counsel of God, would be powerful enough to bring them out of all distress. So too must the faithful servants of the Lord always understand it in their leadership when adversities rise up against the testimony of truth, and it is always said: "one should have left things in the old state, then everything would have remained at peace." This is because people would rather remain in the slavery of sin and human ordinances than desire to wait for and experience the precious salvation and the grace-promises of God in faith. But if one learned to be quiet and still, and thus to cease from all one's own activity, and to wait in best confidence for the help of the Lord; then one would surely experience the high hand of the Lord and His wonderful deliverance in His time. Thus the name of the Lord may then be rightly glorified, and man might not attribute something to his own strength and understanding, whereby he would—as much as in him lies—diminish and curtail the honor of the Lord. See Psalm 46:9-12. Isaiah 30:15, 16. Psalm 115.

<column-break/>

v. 10, 11. The evil spirit often brings a person so far with his temptations that he regrets ever having left the world.
The first trials of the soul in the wilderness of faith, however, consist more in fear than in reality. It is true that before they go into the Red Sea, they are very violently pursued by their enemies: and indeed with such great violence and in such extreme distress that few souls are found who are composed enough not to regret their former ways. On the one hand, they see themselves about to fall into the hands of their enemies; and on the other hand, they become aware of the danger of being drowned in the Red Sea. How then should they not seem to face certain death in this distress? "Ah," they say, "was our first captivity not still sweeter than death? And since we have only come into this wilderness to die, was death not just as good in the former way as in this one?"
v. 12. Better to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness) O no, my friends! Do not believe it. On the contrary: it is better, yes, far better, to die in the wilderness than to serve the Egyptians. For he who dies in the wilderness, and has thus separated himself from the Egyptians and escaped the powers of darkness and the power of Satan, has indeed made some progress through that very act, even if he could not reach perfection. It is better to die on the journey while striving for a perfect life than not to set out on the journey at all for the sake of such a goal. Therefore, those also err greatly in their judgment who, imagining the journey to be difficult, do not want to begin it at all. "Ah," says Origen <margin>(a) on Exodus chapter 14, homily 5.</margin>, "I would much rather die on this journey, if it must be so, than remain among the Egyptians and die and perish with them!"

# Ch. XIV. The Second Book of Moses.

<columns>
13. And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the **Lord**, which he will show you today! For these Egyptians, whom you see today, you shall see no more forever.
14. The **Lord** shall fight for you, and you shall hold your peace."
15. Then the **Lord** said to Moses, "Why do you cry out to me? Tell the children of Israel to move forward."

<margin>v. 13. Fear not)</margin> No, no, dear souls; fear not! It is true that death seems unavoidable to the outward appearance; you cannot rescue yourselves, as your own strengths have been taken away, and you will find no help in any created thing. But **God** alone will prepare a way for you through this cruel sea. Only take care that you do not abandon your calm composure <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a key spiritual term meaning a state of surrender or internal stillness before God.</note>. The extreme anguish of a soul pursued from all sides does not allow it to remember the wonderous works that **God** has done on its behalf. All is darkness within it. It sees nothing but imminent death. And in such a moment, a "Moses" is certainly necessary to lead the souls through this passage. The fear exceeds anything one might say about it; everything is filled with the image of the shadow of death.
> Oh faithful soul, how necessary you are in such a hard transition! Take heart, dear souls! These enemies you see now, as you stand before the Red Sea—as soon as you have passed through it, you will see them no more.

<margin>v. 14. But follow,</margin> I beg you, the counsel of Moses in this great distress, for he is the true leader on this path. His counsel is that you remain as immovable as the rocks, as if the matter did not even concern you. Take great care not to move in the slightest, no matter how good the pretext may seem.
The **Lord** must fight for you, and you must remain at rest. Here many people perish, and it is also the reason they go no further. Because they do not have the heart to go through the Red Sea, nor to continually present themselves for what **God** wants of them, they stop right there and advance no further. Ah, what great patience and compassion a leader must have with such souls, to endure all the complaints that the fear of their own loss forces from their mouths.

<margin>v. 15. God never lets</margin> his power and goodness be more revealed than in the most extreme distress. In this daunting passage, nothing is required but courage and surrender. This deep sea, which is meant to swallow all others, will be found completely dry for those truly surrendered souls who find life where others receive their death. One must simply walk on without standing still, and pass courageously through all dangers.

<margin>Why do you cry to me?)</margin> And yet he had not said a word. Can one then cry out without a voice? Answer: To the secret ears of **God**, it is not our words but our desire that makes a voice. <note>original Latin: "Gregorius M. (a) L. 27. in Job. c. 18." refers to Gregory the Great, Book 27 of his commentary on Job, chapter 18.</note>
<margin>(a) Gregory the Great, Book 27 on Job, ch. 18.</margin>

<column-break/>

16. But lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the children of Israel may go into the midst of the sea on dry ground.
17. And I, behold, I will let the hearts of the Egyptians be hardened, so that they shall follow them. Thus I will be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his host, in his chariots, and in his horsemen.
18. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the **Lord**, when I have been glorified in Pharaoh, in his chariots, and in his horsemen.
19. Then the Angel <note>original: "Engel"; Malachi 3:1 is cited here to link this angel to the messenger of the covenant.</note> of **God**, who went before the camp of Israel, moved and went behind them; and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them. (a) *Malachi 3:1.*
20. And it came between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. The cloud was both darkness and it also enlightened the night, so that the one could not come near the other all night long. 21.

<margin>v. 16. The separation</margin> must first take place before one can walk through with dry feet. The spirit must necessarily be separated from the senses. Thereupon the soul goes in a blind surrender and walks happily through the sea, which is a stumbling block to all others, but is a safe harbor for the soul.

<margin>v. 19. The Angel of God)</margin> The **Lord** himself. v. 24. *Moved from before them)* One cannot sufficiently admire the greatness of faith through which **God** wants such souls to go as they enter this sea, and how much such faith must be stripped of all support. What support did these poor, abandoned souls wandering in the wilderness have left, other than the guidance of **God**, who walked before them day and night? Yet, it must be that even this is taken away from before their eyes, and they lose all perceptible divine assistance at the same time. This is the very preparation for entering the Red Sea: namely, having no other assurance or support than the "downfall" itself. But even if they seem to have nothing of **God** that is known to them, it is certain that he never protects them more powerfully.

<margin>v. 20. He sets himself</margin> between them and their enemies, so that he might be their most secure protection. This signifies that **God** then takes all power over these souls away from Satan; and that all the trials that happen to them thereafter no longer come from these enemies, but from their own nature or from **God** himself.

---

See what divine help is prepared for you when you depart from the Egyptians and leave the service of the world! See what mighty helpers establish a chasm between you and them! It only behooves you to show yourself brave in faith, that you do not fear the horsemen and chariots of Egypt, and that you do not speak harsh words against Moses or the law of **God**.

<margin>Both darkness, and also enlightened)</margin> On Israel's side, **God** let the fire in the pillar remain as a light; but toward the Egyptians, he let the cloud become black, thick, and dark—just as one has certain lanterns <note>This refers to a dark lantern or a "bullseye" lantern, which can direct light in one direction while remaining dark in others.</note>.

This represents the different effects that the testimony of the Gospel and its truth have, which is also perceived through the "cloud of witnesses." *Hebrews 12:1.* To the people of the world, it becomes darkness; the **god** of this world blinds the minds of such unbelievers so that the bright light of the Gospel does not shine for them. On the contrary, through the bright glow that Christ has given in the hearts of the faithful witnesses, the enlightenment of the knowledge of the glory of **God** arises in the hearts of the other well-meaning souls, as the Israel of **God**. *2 Corinthians 4:3-6.* See also *Isaiah 8:14.*

The **Lord** will also use such a skill in the last times against the Anti-Christ, when he will take up the cause of his own and destroy the enemies, being at the same time both heat and shadow; so that the heat destroys the vines of the tyrants, and the cloud gives shadow to the believers.

# The Second Book of Moses. Ch. XIV.

<columns>
**21.** Then **Moses** stretched out his hand over the sea; and the **Lord** caused the sea to go back by a strong east wind all that night, and made the sea dry land, after the waters were divided.

**22.** And the children of **Israel** went into the midst of the sea upon the dry ground, and the waters were a **wall** unto them on their right hand, and on their left. <margin>v. 29.</margin>

**23.** And the **Egyptians** pursued, and went in after them to the midst of the sea, even all **Pharaoh’s** horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.

---

<margin>v. 21. By a strong east wind)</margin> Which at the same time dispersed the thick vapors that usually rise from such a large body of water, especially at night, and tempered the excessive moisture of the air, so that it might not be burdensome to the children of **Israel**, nor harmful to their little children.

<margin>Waters divided)</margin> Which, at the place where it happened, is said to have been 9000 paces wide; as **João de Barros** reports in his histories, which he called **Asia**, <gloss>(a) <note>original: "Decad. 2. l. 8. c. 1." – referring to Decade 2, Book 8, Chapter 1 of Barros's history of Portuguese exploration.</note></gloss> based on the Oriental voyages of the Portuguese; he further adds that such a division occurred opposite a small town on the Arabian side, which he calls **Tor** or **Tauris**, but which is commonly called **Eltor** on land maps, directly opposite which lies the town of **Grondol** on the Egyptian side: as may be seen in **Abraham Ortelius**, and even better in the map of the Turkish Empire.

<margin>v. 22. Went into)</margin> And—as **Torniellus** maintains and calculates—<gloss>(b) <note>original: "apud Quaresm. in Elucid. Terr. S." – referring to Francisco Quaresmio's "Elucidatio Terrae Sanctae" (Elucidation of the Holy Land).</note></gloss> they were finished and safely through this Arabian Gulf within 10 hours. Others, however, calculate the sea at the place of the division, according to **Ptolemy**, to be about 15 miles wide.

<margin>Upon the dry ground)</margin> Upon the ground dried by the east wind; so that they would not be hindered by mud on their journey.

<margin>The waters were a wall unto them)</margin> Note here the goodness of the Creator, who, when you obey His will and follow **Moses**—that is, His Law—makes it so that the elements must serve you, even against their ordinary course of nature.

<margin>On the right and left)</margin> All those who wish to flee the world have the "Sea of Bitterness" on both sides.

<margin>v. 21. 22.</margin> After the Holy Spirit, through His help, has made the separation of the two parties—the spiritual and the animal <note>The author uses "animal" in the archaic sense of "sensual" or "soulish" (Latin: *animalis*), referring to the unregenerate human nature.</note>; then those waters which drown the whole world serve His chosen people as a rampart and a ring-wall: and through those very waters, which naturally cause death, the people are covered from all corners against every assault. But take note of one thing here! Namely, that **Moses** can indeed stretch out his hand to give the sign for the impending division: but this division is brought about by no human means, but by **Ashem** <note>Hebrew: "The Name," a traditional way of referring to God (Hashem) without pronouncing the Tetragrammaton.</note> in the waters of the darkest night. Through the severity of this consuming wind, He dries up the sea: because the separation of the spirit and the senses—yea, even of the spirit and the soul—cannot happen until the soul first reaches a state of utter exhaustion and dryness through the loss of its internal perceived workings, and the loss of all that still flows with flavor, where everything is hidden in the center of the secret abyss.

<margin>v. 23. It could well happen that souls who still live for themselves might believe they could also go through this sea with a dry foot. They will, however, be caught in that very sea and covered with waves. The sign to pass through it is recognized by the stretching out of the arm, which the leader stretches out to give the command or to assure the spiritual calling; and when the **Lord** has so dried out the soul that He has brought everything in it to nothing: or when He lets it pass through by His own power, without guidance; after the soul has accordingly consented to what He wishes to undertake with it, whether it be known to it or not.</margin>

<gloss>(a) Decade 2. book 8. ch. 1. (b) in Quaresmius in Elucidation of the Holy Land.</gloss>

<column-break/>

**24.** And it came to pass in the morning watch <gloss>(a)</gloss>, that the **Lord** looked unto the host of the **Egyptians** through the pillar of fire and of the cloud, and troubled the host of the **Egyptians**. <margin>(a) Matthew 14:25.</margin>

**25.** And took off their chariot wheels, that they drove them heavily. <gloss>(b)</gloss> So that the **Egyptians** said: Let us flee from **Israel**! For the **Lord** fighteth for them against the **Egyptians**.

**26.** And the **Lord** said unto **Moses**: Stretch out thine hand over the sea, that the water may come again upon the **Egyptians**, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen.

**27.** And **Moses** stretched forth his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its strength when the morning appeared; and the **Egyptians** fled against it. And the **Lord** overthrew the **Egyptians** in the midst of the sea. **28.**

---

<margin>v. 24. In the morning watch)</margin> As is known, the Jews used to divide their nights into 4 parts or watches, each of which comprised 3 hours: and they are said to have entered the Red Sea at God’s command around the third night-watch.

<margin>Looked—and troubled)</margin> This terror arose from the violent storm, which was now to bring the sea back into its ordinary course; from which the horses became shy, the chariots collided with one another, and the wheels were thereby broken, so that they could not move them forward except with great difficulty.
->And so **God** looks toward that place where He wishes to prove the signs of His omnipotence.<-

<margin>The Lord)</margin> From this it is sufficiently clear that the Angel of God in verse 19 and the **Lord**, as He is also called in Chapter 13:21, are one and the same. And so **Asaph** also speaks of it when he says of **God**: "Thy way was in the sea, and thy path in the great waters; and thy footsteps were not known. Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of **Moses** and **Aaron**." Psalm 77:19-20. All of which is a very clear proof that the Angel of God, the Angel of the Covenant whom the believers expected, is none other than **Jehovah** the **Lord**, **God** Himself; who is nevertheless, as the Angel or Messenger, distinguished from Him who sent Him, namely from **God** the Father.

<margin>v. 26. 27. The sea returned/Egyptians fled against it)</margin> What some Egyptians from **Memphis**—as **Artapanus** wrote, according to **Eusebius's** report <gloss>(a)</gloss>—have alleged: that **Moses** well understood the ebb and flow of the sea, and passed through with his people at the ebb—while the Egyptians perished at the following flow; this is without foundation. How could the so-wise Egyptians not have understood the nature and condition of the Red Sea, which lay so near?
<margin>(a) Book 9 of the Preparation for the Gospel, ch. 4.</margin>

### Chapter XIV. The Second Book of Moses.

**28.** Then the waters came back / and covered the chariots and the horsemen of the entire army of Pharaoh / who had followed them into the sea. Not a single one of them remained.

**29.** But the children of Israel went on dry land through the midst of the sea / and the water was a wall to them on their right and on their left.

<margin>The *Egyptians* / as *Josephus* writes quite handsomely / did not understand / that this path was made for the Hebrews alone / and not for everyone / and stood open only to those / who had to flee to save their lives / and not for those who desired to destroy the lives and bodies of others.</margin>

v. 28. **Entire army of Pharaoh)** 50,000 on horseback / and 200,000 on foot / if the ancient historian *Josephus* (a) is to be believed. <note>original: "L. 2. Antiq. Jud. c. 6." refers to Josephus’s *Antiquities of the Jews*.</note>

**Not a single one)** Not even one who could have brought the news back.

After all the most noble men had perished in this manner / and no one was left to govern; the widowed noblewomen gathered together / and—according to the testimony of the Arabian writers *Ben Lehiaja* and *Abdalla Ben Geled* contained in *Athanasius Kircher* (b) <note>original: "in Oedip. Ægypt. syntagme 1. c. 9." refers to Kircher’s 17th-century work on Egyptian mysteries.</note> —they elected the drowned Pharaoh’s surviving daughter, *Dalukam*, who was already 160 years old at the time / to be their Queen. Thereupon / in order to be safe from enemy attacks / she secured the land with fortifications / and provided the cities well with provisions / also establishing a sconce <note>A "sconce" is a small protective fortification or earthwork.</note> every 3 miles / and between these, a smaller sconce every mile / well-manned with soldiers / and at the same time ordered / that / whenever the enemy appeared / a signal should be given from one sconce to another / so that within an hour the whole land would know / that the enemy was present. Thus / she spoke to her women / the enemies will leave us in peace / and lose their desire for the land of Egypt.

v. 29. **Through the midst of the sea)** There are indeed many writers (c) / among whom are almost all the Hebrews / *Abulensis, Paulus Burgensis, Thomas Aquinas*, and also *Quaresmius* (d) who hold the opinion / that the sea was not divided from one side directly to the other ; as they could hardly have completed such a journey in one night : but rather that they entered on one side from Egypt / and came out again on the same side in a half-circle ; because the camp / where they stayed on this side of the sea before the crossing, Chapter 13:20 / was the very same Etham / where they arrived after the crossing / and where they spent three days in the wilderness of Etham. Numbers 33:8. Such a journey could well have been completed in 3 hours / as in the 12th night-watch. However, this opinion is contradicted by *Josephus* (e), *Philo* (f), *Gregory of Nyssa* (g), *Lyranus*, and others.

<margin>*Origen* (h) on the other hand reports another curiosity. 
> "I have / he says / heard / that according to the 
> "interpretation of the ancestors / at this crossing of the sea 
> "a separate dividing of the water 
> "occurred for every tribe of the 
> "children of Israel ; and thus a separate path was 
> "opened in the sea for each tribe ; and that this 
> "is proven from what is written in the 
> "Psalms (i). And having noted this from our 
> "forefathers and from Holy Scripture / 
> "I felt a concern of conscience / 
> "to keep it silent."</margin>

(a) *Antiquities of the Jews, Book 2, Chapter 6.*
(b) *In Oedipus Aegyptiacus, treatise 1, chapter 9.*
(c) *See Bonfrère's commentary on verse 22.*
(d) *Elucidation of the Holy Land, Volume 2, Chapter 7.*
(e) *Antiquities, Book 2, Chapter 7.*
(f) *On the Life of Moses, Book 3.*
(g) *Book on the Life of Moses.*
(h) *Commentary on Exodus, Chapter 14, Homily 5.*
(i) *Psalm 136:13.* <note>The Psalm mentions God dividing the Red Sea "into parts," which led to the tradition of twelve separate paths.</note>

<column-break/>

**30.** Thus the Lord saved Israel that day out of the hand of the Egyptians / and Israel saw the Egyptians dead upon the sea shore.

**31.** And so Israel saw the great hand / which the Lord had shown upon the Egyptians : and the people feared the Lord (a) / and believed in the Lord and in his servant Moses.
<gloss>Chapter 4:31. (a) 1 Kings 8:42.</gloss> **The**

This truly astonishing deliverance of the people of Israel through the midst of the sea / and the subsequent destruction of their enemies by that same sea / stands as a glorious image for the Church of Christ / as the Israel of God. It shows how the Lord—at the end of this, His Kingdom of the Cross / when Satan will yet stir up the sea of the nations / and bring a persecution upon the true Church of believers / with the intention of completely swallowing these believers of the last days / since he also wants to bring his own into the wilderness / and nourish them there—will arise to lead His people through the sea of anguish / which on the contrary shall utterly swallow his enemies : just as the earth opened its mouth / and swallowed the river / that wanted to drown the woman. Revelation 12:13–16. And then not a single enemy will remain / but they will all be worn down and destroyed by the bowls of wrath. And this is the glorious deliverance / when in the great distress of the believers the world shall pass away / and the mountains of the world-kingdoms shall sink into the sea. Then the City of God and the holy dwellings of the Most High will appear ; whereas all the equipment of war will be burned with fire. Psalm 46. And after such a glorious revelation of the great hand of the Lord / the believers of the last times sigh / and hold up to the Lord this great wonder-work of the deliverance of the former Israel in the sea and the rooting out of the enemies therein. Isaiah 51:9, 10, 11; 63:11, 12, 13.

This great work also brought about a faith in Moses among the people / so that they could be assured / that God had sent him for their rescue / and that the laws / which he gave them / were imposed upon them by God’s command. See Chapter 19:9. And this is what the Apostle calls a "baptism into Moses" in the cloud and in the sea, 1 Corinthians 10:2. Because this deliverance through the water occurred through the service of Moses : just as the deliverance in Noah’s ark through the water of the flood is cited as a type <note>A "type" or "antitype" is a biblical event or person that foreshadows a future reality.</note> of baptism, 1 Peter 3:20, 21. And both aim at the great deliverance from the waters of tribulations in the last times.

v. 30. **Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore)** And they obtained a great spoil / including weapons / from them.

That was thus a useful spectacle for them. For it is well believable / that the Egyptians marched out magnificently and expensively / so that they might all the more quickly strike terror into the Hebrews as their masters / but according to God's intention / they had to make rich those whom they intended to terrify.

v. 31. **Feared the Lord / and believed in the Lord)** One must believe God just as much when He commands / forbids / and threatens ; as when He promises. Otherwise, it is no faith. For true faith is bound with the fear of the Lord.

Therefore, those are not believers according to the mind of God and the Holy Spirit / who believe only the word of promise ; as ignorant people imagine. For faith is an assent to divine truth : which, however, encompasses not only the truth of the promise / but just as much the truth of the commandments, prohibitions, and threats.

**And in Moses)** Those people misuse this passage / who refer to it when it is pointed out to them / on the one hand (a) that Christ must be true God / because one should believe in him : on the other hand / that one should call upon no one / except the one in whom one is also to believe ; and consequently not the saints. <note>original: "Ostorod. Instit: relig. Christ. c. 15." refers to Christoph Ostorodt, a Socinian theologian who argued against the divinity of Christ.</note>

This aims at what Moses objected in Chapter 4; *They will not believe me* : and it is further explained in Psalm 106:12, 24 / that it is to be understood as faith in the Word / of which Moses was merely a servant and messenger.

(a) *Ostorodt, Institutes of the Christian Religion, Chapter 15.*

# Chapter XV.
->The Song of Moses/ and the Journey to Marah and Elim.<-

THEN sang Moses and the children of Israel this song to the LORD / and spoke thus, saying: I will sing to the LORD / for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea!

Here occurs the first mention of a song / with which Moses and the children of Israel praised and glorified God for the miraculous deliverance from their enemies.

God has created within man a power / both to speak and also to sing: so that in the first way he might make his thoughts common with other men / and one might be suited to serve the other; indeed, that he might also present his thoughts and desires before God: not so much for God's sake / who already understands the innermost stirrings of the heart / before a word even comes to the tongue: <margin>Psalm 139:4.</margin> but for the sake of man himself; that he might surrender himself to the working of the Spirit / and then might be assured / when he has presented it to God / that God would also hear it. See Psalm 90:1. In the second way, he should be able to express his movements of joy: which, however, should be sought in God / and thus be directed to God in a song of praise for all benefits. As James distinguishes: <margin>James 5:13.</margin> Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms. See also Ephesians 5:19, according to which place singing and making melody can also happen in the heart.

Just as God is praised here in this song for the mighty deliverance of his people and the destruction of his enemies / so shall it also happen / when God shall deliver his people of the New Testament from the power of the spiritual Egypt and the spiritual Assyrians / the Anti-Christ and the Turk / <note>In the 17th century, the Ottoman Empire (the "Turk") was often interpreted through a biblical lens as a major adversary of Christendom.</note> Isaiah 11:15, 16 and Chapter 12, where the song of thanksgiving is written. See also Isaiah Chapters 25, 26, and 27. And this is the Song of Moses / which will then be linked together with this Song of the Lamb / which has been started here by the prophet Isaiah / and will be sung to the praise of the LORD throughout the whole earth. Revelation 15.

From which it is to be seen / that the Spirit of the LORD in such words of Moses and in his songs / of which another is found in Deuteronomy 32 / looked further / and reflected upon the last times; because the final conquerors of the Beast / who would not worship it with its mark / but rather have overcome it through their martyr’s death / will make use of this very song: and therefore the same spirit / which was in Pharaoh / will also be found in the Antichristian Beast / and will be included with its malice in the same.

<column-break/>

## 2. The LORD is my strength and song / and he has become my salvation! This is my strong God; therefore I will prepare him a lovely dwelling! He is my father’s God; so I will exalt him!

<margin>Verse 2.</margin> The soul which has been faithful enough / to surrender itself to God without limits or exception / recognizes / when it is delivered from this blessed shipwreck / that all its strength stands in God / and not in created steps / indeed, not even in itself. It finds everything in God / which it previously considered lost: and while it finds itself full of wonder / it cries out: I have indeed lost all my own strength; but through that very thing I have found / that God has been my strength. I have indeed lost all power to love him; but he himself has become my praise. I have indeed put my salvation at risk / so far as it was founded on any possible good in me / considered according to nature / yes, even lost it: but for that very reason he himself has become my salvation. Now I can rightly say / that he is my God / and that I worship him as my God. Now I recognize / that he is thus the God of my father: therefore I will glorify him through himself / and in him himself I will exalt his greatness!

A lovely dwelling) This word aims at the dwelling mentioned in verse 13 / of which Moses had to prophesy in a prophetic spirit / that they were now traveling toward the land / in which God dwelt among their fathers with his Spirit in their hearts / and was there publicly proclaimed and worshipped and honored with sacrifices: which he also promised to them / as the descendants / that he would likewise dwell among and in them and desired to be honored by them. Indeed, he also prophesies of the mountain of the inheritance / verse 17, which God would especially choose for the revelation of his glory.

My father’s God) Also of the eternal Father of Christ / whom he himself called his God and our God. John 20:17.

---

Then) The 7th day after the departure from Egypt. For on the first day / or on the 15th of the month Abib / they went out from Raemses before daybreak / and kept their night-camp in Succoth. On the second (the 16th) they moved from Succoth toward Etham: on the third (17th) toward Pi-hahiroth. On the 4th (18th) it was told to Pharaoh / that they had gone astray in the wilderness: on the 5th and 6th (or 19th and 20th) Pharaoh pursued them. In the following night before the 7th (or 21st) the Israelites went through the Red Sea / whom the Egyptians followed / and drowned toward the breaking morning of the 7th day. (a)

The soul is then first truly in the state to sing a song of thanksgiving to the LORD / when it has climbed out of the Red Sea. But it must be a new and pure song / which is sung in the presence of the Lamb (b) / where it cries with a loud voice: To our God / who sits upon his throne / and to the Lamb / belongs the honor of our salvation! Then the faithful, surrendered ones recognize the happiness of their salvation. For until now / although they had seen extraordinary wonder-works / they did not yet have eyes pure enough to see these wonders in God himself / nor were they in the state to sing this new song; and it had not yet been given to them. But then they can attribute everything to God / and faithfully give back all praise to him for that which he has done on their behalf.

Sang Moses) lead /
And the children of Israel) follow; and thus answered one another in the manner of a choir.

The horse and his rider) According to the figure, the horses are nothing other than the animalistic, fleshly people / who let the qualities of beasts be seen more in themselves / than those of rational men. These now also have their riders. Just as God also has his horses / upon which he rides / Habakkuk 3:8, 15. So the riders of those horses are the devil with his angels. Thus Judas Iscariot was a horse; and indeed the LORD’s / as long as he stood in his service. But when he let the devil mount and possess him / after the morsel; then he let himself be spurred by him against the LORD. And so, in particular, the persecutors of the children of God are such devil-horses / who let themselves be ridden and driven by evil angels.

The horse / says Rupertus / <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129) was a Benedictine theologian and mystic.</note> is the world / and the devil the rider. This one was cast down / when it was said: <note>John 12:31.</note> Now is the judgment of the world; now will the prince of this world be cast out. From then on, the LORD does not cease to throw this rider into the sea: which to us is indeed like glass / and mixed with the fire of the Holy Spirit / but to him mixed with pitch and sulfur. Formerly, indeed, this rider / when he spoke haughtily: I will set my throne above the stars of God! was thrown down and cast into this dark air. But now this rider / who rides upon the horse of human folly / of those who let themselves be seduced by him and led by a fool’s rope / will also be cast into the abyss of the pool. This we see in part / and will see it more fully on the Day of Judgment / and then sing to the LORD.

3. The LORD is a (a) **man of war**: <note>original: "Kriegesmann"</note> LORD is his name! (b)
<margin>(a) Psalm 144:1. (b) Isaiah 42:8. Jeremiah 32:18.</margin>

4. Pharaoh's chariots and his host has he cast into the sea: and his chosen captains are drowned in the Red Sea! <note>original: "Schilfmeer" — literally "Sea of Reeds."</note>

5. The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone!

6. Thy right hand, O LORD, has shown itself glorious in power! Thy right hand, O LORD, has dashed the enemy in pieces!

7. And in the greatness of thy majesty thou hast overthrown those who rose up against thee: Thou sentest forth thy wrath, which consumed them like stubble!

<margin>In those parts of the Scripture which are judged to be written as verses for singing, such as in the Psalms and similar books, it is a common thing that the latter part of a verse is an explanation of the former. This song is also of such a nature.</margin>

<margin>v. 4. **Captains**) These were actually the *Grandes* or the most prominent men of the kingdom of the second rank, and in the government, the third. The first in order was the King; thereafter the second. Such a one was Joseph under Pharaoh. Genesis 41. Daniel was one of the third. Daniel 5:29.</margin>

<margin>v. 5. **Have covered them/they sank**) In this way, it refers to the past and, at that time, most recent event. However, because the words may also be given—and indeed according to their closest and most proper meaning—regarding the future: *they shall or will cover them, they shall or will sink down*: so there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit here had his aim more upon the spiritual understanding of this history. And therefore, although the leading of the children of Israel out of Egypt and the drowning of the Egyptians is a true and certainly famous history, of which both the 1st and 4th verses speak in the past tense; yet we are hereby given the secret teaching that we should not rest therein, but look around for a more general mercy of God. Therefore, a long time afterward, a promise is given to lead the people of God out of Egypt. Zechariah 10:10.</margin>

Accordingly, the history speaks not only of that people and those past times, but also concerns us and our present times, and explains the everlasting ways of God and the spiritual states of men in all ages. For what the Lord did then for his people according to the flesh happened as a figure, and represented what he did then and also does now—yea, at all times—for and in his people according to the Spirit, especially what he wishes to do in these last days. The spiritually-minded reader need only compare with this spiritual explanation what the prophet Micah speaks through the entire 7th chapter. The Lord wished to sink our mighty sins, <term>Amos 5:12</term> <note>The author equates "mighty sins" with the "mighty waters" of the Red Sea.</note> and all our ruling lusts into the depths of the sea; so that we may have a part in the triumph and song of praise of Moses!

<column-break/>

8. And with the blast of thy nostrils the waters were heaped up: the floods stood upright as a heap; the depths were congealed in the heart of the sea.

9. The enemy thought: I will pursue them and overtake them; I will divide the spoil; my soul shall be satisfied upon them; I will draw my sword, and my hand shall destroy them!

10. Thou didst blow with thy wind, then the sea covered them: they sank like lead in the great waters!

11. LORD, who is like unto thee among the gods? who is like unto thee, who has shown thyself glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders? 12. There...

<margin>Because the entire history is to be explained not only literally, but rather in a mysterious manner, as has just been attested and demonstrated regarding the verses above: so we must also on all occasions strive to interpret the history toward a secret and spiritual sense, which the words offer. And in this way, by the **wind** we are to understand the Spirit of God, and by the **sea** or water, **Baptism**: just as such is confirmed by Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:1–2. The Spirit of God hovers over the waters, just as in the first creation, so also in the second, and makes the new creatures after the Egyptians are drowned, Micah 7:19; that is, after the body of sin is destroyed. Romans 6:6.</margin>

This should be considered and taken to heart by all those who say—and want to make others believe—that they are baptized in the name of Christ, yet still live in their sins. In no way can such things stand together: It is against the pure apostolic teaching, <term>Romans 6:3</term> <note>Referencing the idea that baptism into Christ's death necessitates a death to sin.</note> even though it is the common practice. Let us rather plead to the Lord that he might send out his Spirit into us, through which we may kill our sins and thus live! <term>Romans 8:13</term>. Then the truth of that which the Psalmist (a) speaks shall be confirmed and fulfilled in and upon us: *The waters covered their enemies (the Egyptians/the sins), so that not one of them was left. And then they believed his words, and sang his praise.*

<margin>v. 11. **LORD, who is like unto thee**) The worshippers of the beast are not ashamed to cry out: *Who is like unto the beast?* Revelation 13:4. But they shall surely be ashamed and come to naught when God receives honor on earth and brings all false gods to nothing.</margin>

However, as Origen (b) <note>original: "Origenes"</note> maintains, the "gods" here are not understood as the idols of the heathens under which they worshipped devils—for that would be a far too unworthy comparison—but rather those who, through the grace and participation in God and his divine nature, may be so called, as well as those of whom <term>Psalm 82:6</term> <note>Referring to the verse "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."</note> is commonly explained. But although they may become partakers of this name by grace for the sake of [his] nature,

---

yet no one is found equal to God, neither in power nor in nature. And although John (c) says that when he shall appear, what the children of God shall be, they shall be like him; yet this is not to be understood otherwise than how a painting or image is like its original.

After that lover of whom verse 2 spoke—namely, the loving soul—has been better instructed, she now no longer loves the strength and holiness of other strong and holy souls, because they are not strong nor holy [except] in God. Therefore she says: one should look among the strong and wise to see if in them any such strength and wisdom is to be found as in God himself. What holiness is to be found that can be compared to the excellence of that which is entirely united with God? Does anything deserve praise except that which God does?

<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XV.</header>

12. When thou stretchedst out thy right
hand / then the earth swallowed them.
13. Thou hast led in thy goodness
the people whom thou hast redeemed: Thou
hast guided them by thy strength to
thy holy habitation!
14. When the nations heard this / they
trembled: anguish took hold of the inhabitants
of Palestine.
15. Then the princes of Edom were
amazed; trembling took hold of the mighty men
of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan
became faint-hearted.
16. Terror and dread fell upon
them; by the greatness of thine arm
they became as still as a
stone: until thy people, **LORD**,
passed over / until the people
passed over which thou hast purchased.

v. 12. **The earth swallowed them**) Tell me / has the earth not
sufficiently swallowed him who constantly thinks of
the earth / constantly has to do with the earth / talks of the earth /
squabbles over the earth / desires the things of the earth /
stretches all his cravings toward the earth / and sets all his
hope upon it? He who does not look to heaven / does not
think of what is to come / does not fear the judgment of **God** /
does not seize His blessed promises with longing;
but instead constantly directs his thoughts to the present /
and highly values the earthly: or even wallows in the mire
of the pleasures of the flesh / and is sunken in the mud of
fleshly lusts? Instead of allowing themselves to be beckoned,
helped, and drawn by the right hand of **God** / which He stretches out
all day long / and which He especially stretched out on the Cross
toward sinners / and through which our Savior Himself is exalted.

Meanwhile, one must not cast away all hope even for
those who are swallowed. For it is possible / that /
when they do penance / they can be vomited out again / like
Jonah. Were we not all swallowed by the earth / yes, even by hell
itself; and for that very reason the **LORD** came / not
only to the earth / but also descended into the lowest parts of the
earth / to lead us out from the depths.

v. 13. When the soul sees / that it has been redeemed from those
distressing dangers / into which it had placed its composure;
then it is assured / that it has happened only through the goodness
of **God** / and that He leads His inner people through His mercy.
What sometimes appears to be a strict justice of **God** /
exercised upon His servants / is found at another time to be
a great mercy of **God**. This people seemed to be sold
to sin: but Thou / O **LORD** / hast bought them! Thou
hast brought them through Thy strength into Thyself / which
is Thy holy habitation.

**Led / guided**) These words are figurative / and borrowed
either from a shepherd regarding his flock / or from a father
regarding his child / or from a ruler regarding his subjects: all of
which relationships are foundational and require both love
and mercy as well as power and strength / in the shepherd /
father and ruler / each according to his distinct office.
The **LORD** takes all these and other loving names upon Himself
for the sake of our weakness / according to which He
so gladly accommodates Himself and wondrously condescends: just
as for example in Psalm 80:1; Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 43:15.

Recognize then your Shepherd / your Father / and your
King / O Israel! and do not abuse His love and patience;
lest He grow weary of you on the way / and you fail or
neglect to enter into His holy habitation.

<column-break/>

17. Thou shalt bring them in and
plant them on the mountain of Thine inheritance /
which Thou, **LORD**, hast prepared for
Thine own dwelling; to a sanctuary,
**LORD**, which Thy hands have
established.
18. The **LORD** shall be King for
ever and ever.
19. For the horses of Pharaoh went in
into the sea with his chariots and with
his horsemen / and the **LORD** brought back
the waters of the sea upon them:
But the children of Israel went on dry
land through the middle of the sea.
20. And

v. 17. **On the mountain of Thine inheritance**) Mount
Zion / on which the Temple of **God** was to be built / and
the royal residence established / and around which mountain the
holy city of Jerusalem was to be built. See Psalm 48:2, 3;
76:2; 135:21.

This verse indicates / that the subject is the state of
confirmation in **God** / or of immovability / which is represented
by the mountain of the inheritance. For the inheritance
itself is one thing / and the mountain of the inheritance is another.
To reach the inheritance is to reach into **God**: But to be on the
mountain is to be established in **God**. Therefore it says; Thou
shalt bring them in: which signifies the entrance into this state.
Afterward, however, it stands; Thou shalt plant <note>original: "befestigen" — to fix or strengthen</note> them:
which indicates the confirmation in this state. Therefore
the Scripture calls this mountain a firm dwelling; because
it then becomes a firm and abiding place for such a soul / which
has arrived there. It is, however, a dwelling that **God**
Himself has made: a sanctuary which His hands have established /
without the slightest addition of any creature.

v. 18. It is the **LORD**, the Angel of the Covenant, whose
kingdom he praises here / that it will not only last in
the eternity of this world / but also forevermore in all the
following eternities / where it will rise ever higher / until
all His enemies shall be laid as a footstool for His feet.
This holds the meaning of both words עדי <note>adei - "further/still"</note> and עולם <note>olam - "age/eternity"</note>
and is thus to be distinguished. See also Psalm 146:10.

Whenever "an eternity" is mentioned / says Origen /
a long time is indeed indicated / but at the same time one that has
an end: and when it is said "from eternity to eternity" /
the term is without doubt set further out; yet a limit is still
set: and when "eternities of eternities" are named /
a certain term / although unknown to us / yet set by **God**,
may well be indicated. But what is set here / "in eternities
and still" <note>original: "in Ewigkeiten und noch" — translating the Hebrew "forever and ever" literally to show the additive nature</note>: (as it may also be rendered:) that leaves absolutely
nothing of such an understanding that might point to an end
or goal. For there you may think what you will / wherein you
suppose the end might consist; the prophetic word speaks
against you: *and still*: and you may take and interpret
the matter of the boundaries of His kingdom as you will / the Prophet
always answers you; "*and still*."

According to the sense of the Spirit, it also has the meaning
that / although His kingdom / which He has over the
souls devoted to Him / be eternal and unchangeable / it can
nevertheless be increased at all times; just as their composure and
expansion can always grow through the greatest expansion
that is possible.

v. 19. The very same means / which **God** uses to save His
people / He also uses to destroy the wicked world: and so
conversely.

How blessed, however, is the man / who sees the sea of this
world not before him / but behind him / and can triumph
over his conquered enemies!

# Chapter XV. The Second Book of Moses. 339

20. And Miriam the prophetess / Aaron’s sister / took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her / with tambourines and in dances.

21. And Miriam answered them: Sing to the **LORD**! For he has exalted himself greatly: both horse and rider he has thrown into the sea.

<margin>
v. 20. This Miriam (from whose name the Roman Church quite wrongly derives the name Mary / although both names may be derived from <note>original Hebrew: מרר (merar)</note> bitterness /) was Aaron’s sister / because she spent most of her life with him / rather than with Moses / since Moses stayed at the Egyptian court and then in a foreign land for a full 80 years. She was a prophetess / whom **God** had graced with the gift of prophecy / and he also spoke through her: Numbers 12:1-2. as there have been several such women: Judges 4:4, 2 Kings 22:14, Luke 2:36, Acts 21:9. for grace makes no distinction between man or woman. Galatians 3:28.
</margin>

With tambourines) Which / as some hold / they brought with them from Egypt / because they could well have expected the great wonders of **God**: unless it was also part of the spoil from the dead Egyptians.
</margin>

Our "old man" <note>A theological term for the sinful human nature before spiritual rebirth.</note> makes a good tambourine / when he is stretched out upon the Cross: and if we wish to bring music to the **Lord** / then this tambourine must be present; otherwise our singing and playing will not be pleasing to him.

<margin>
In dances) Junius, Tremellius, and others render the word <note>original Hebrew: במחלות (bemicholot)</note> "with pipes." At the very least, those who seek to use this as a shield for modern dancing are overshooting the mark.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 21. Answered) Namely, Moses began to strike up the song / and the men followed him by repeating it after him / and then the women answered / and repeated those same first words / it seems / at all the following verses of praise: as can also be seen in the 136th Psalm / where the final words / "for his mercy endureth forever" / are always repeated. And this is then a pattern for the various choirs that perhaps arose later: where one part begins / and starts to recount a certain praise or something else; the other then answers / and makes its opinion known accordingly: just as in eternity the two choirs of angels / the Cherubim and Seraphim / and then again the angels and men / may thus strike up the praise of **God** / and answer one another / and thus exercise themselves together in searching out the great wonders of **God** for all time.
</margin>

<column-break/>

22. And Moses let Israel journey from the Reed Sea / and they went out into the Wilderness of Shur / and wandered three days in the wilderness / and found no water.

23. There <meta>catchword: There</meta>

Not without cause does Moses pray to **God** / v. 17. that he would please establish his people / in such a state / in which they have need of the greatest possible steadfastness / to pass through that which still remains on the inner path / which is far more terrifying than everything that has happened until now. But alas! the end of this state is still very far off: and perhaps they will never even arrive there. As soon as one has passed through the Red Sea / one thinks for a long time / that one is beyond all misery: because it seems / as if everything were now done / that one has received a new life / and possesses an inexpressible happiness. This happens / however / because one does not consider / that one has not found **God** so that one may immediately possess and enjoy him; but rather to let oneself be possessed by him. This state requires a very pure love. And it is an astonishing thing / that of so many people / who have the heart to go through the Red Sea / so few are found / who have enough heart to go through what follows / as will be seen further: because one must be free from all active and passive self-interest / and take back nothing of that which one has once abandoned.

---

To understand this better / one must know / that in all states of the inner life there are sacrifice / surrender / and abandonment <term>Gelassenheit: a core mystical concept of letting go of the self-will to be filled by God</term> / which are common to every state.

In the passion of enlightenment and of "tasty" love <note>A term for the initial period of spiritual joy and emotional sweetness in prayer.</note> the soul enters through the sacrifice / which she herself brings to **God**. Afterward she surrenders herself to him. Further she abandons herself to him / yet no further in this state / than according to her own understanding and according to the sight which was given to her (at that time).

Now after this passive abandonment has come to its perfection / she goes out from that same state / to enter into the state of contemplation or of bare faith. At the very entrance of this way she finds herself so different from the other state / that she finds herself compelled to bring a new sacrifice. Now after she has thus sacrificed herself anew / she surrenders herself to **God** / as far as this sacrifice reaches: afterward she abandons herself entirely / until she has arrived at the end of this state.

In the state of being lost in **God** / or of the spiritual life / there must again be a new sacrifice / and indeed one much greater and more extensive / than the previous ones were. However, as the soul finds herself too powerless to do this / because / since she is entirely melted into **God** / not the slightest movement remains of her own / nor is anything to be found in her that is her own: she now looks on / so that she may be sacrificed / and that the High Priest / to whom she so often slaughtered herself / [may do so]; and thus she is found surrendered to the sacrifice; and remains also entirely abandoned in the same.

When this abandonment is completed / then the soul is placed in the childlike state. For when the soul entered into **God** / she was indeed placed in the state of innocence / but not yet in the state of pure and recognized childhood. As a person grows / more and more he goes out of childhood: but on the contrary / the more he approaches his inner perfection / the more he returns to his childhood / even to the very smallest infancy / until the new birth (a).

And in all these states there are indeed people / who practice sacrifice and surrender: but few / and fewer than can be said / abandon themselves entirely. Some are indeed abandoned in one degree / but not in the other. And this is also why / of so many people / who give themselves over to the inner life / very few arrive at their origin: because most take themselves back / after they had previously given themselves / or even still keep themselves in some things.

This being presupposed / one should note / that after the Red Sea there is a wilderness / which is even harder to wander through / than everything that has ever been seen: because one went through the Red Sea through sacrifice and surrender; which are swift effects and powers of courage / in which the soul has a great part. But the length of abandonment will afterward be so tedious / that most will become weary of it. Yet even here the soul has no possession before her anymore / although she is full of **God**. Therefore nothing satisfies her / and she finds herself in a great wilderness without water: She believes / she must die of thirst. For since the separation of the two parts has occurred / nothing more of the water of the upper part falls upon the lower: this is / however / very difficult for nature.

<margin>
Wilderness of Shur) Is the very one / which is otherwise also called the Wilderness of Etham.
</margin>

<margin>
3 Days in the wilderness -- no water) When a person with the 3 powers of his soul / Intellect / Will and Memory / has left the Egypt of this world / and entered into the wilderness of himself / and wandered for a while; then indeed / whereas he previously sang happily and from the heart by the sea / the waters of holy devotion are withdrawn from him / so that he becomes dry / lukewarm and cold / and it wearies him to fast and to wake / and it also becomes too much for him to spend time in virtuous exercises.
</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chap. XV. <page-num>340</page-num>

## 23. Then they came to Marah: but they could not drink the water of Marah; for it was bitter: therefore they called its name Marah. <margin>Ruth 1:20.</margin>
## 24. Then the people murmured against Moses / and said: What shall we drink?

After **God** had shown His help against Pharaoh / He allowed a new temptation to come upon the people / so that at first they found no water / and afterward they did encounter some / but could not drink it because of its bitterness. With this, **God** intended to test the people / to see if they would be satisfied with everything **God** sent them / and always hope in His gracious help / which they had already so gloriously experienced against their enemies / and also wait for the same in all tribulations with patience. But because they sinned against His faithful servant / Moses / who led them according to the divine nod and command / they thereby revealed their unbelieving and disobedient heart. **God**, however, helped them nonetheless upon the prayer of Moses / who had to take a piece of wood / and lay it in the water / whereby it became sweet: which wood, however, is not identified / as to what kind of tree it was; so that one might not attribute the effect to its natural properties / which would have been a natural impossibility / to sweeten such a vast quantity of water. It was meant, however, to be an image of the wood of the Cross ordained by **God** / upon which His dear Son was to be hanged / and which the believers should take as their own through faith: thus all the bitterness of tribulations / which **God** sends for our purification / would be sweetened and driven away. See 1 Peter 2:24.

**v. 23. Bitter)** When a person in the wilderness of spiritual drought even comes to water; e.g., to the contemplation of the example of Christ and His saints: or when he forces himself to prayer and the exercise of virtues / in which he otherwise felt devotion and sweetness; yet it is unpleasant and contrary to him / because he finds in it neither delight nor taste. And then it goes with him as it did with the Jews.

**v. 24. Murmured)** against all those who advised him to leave the world / and he regrets that he has left the world. Yes, indeed.

All these things are clear types of how we / who have gone out of the Egypt of the New Testament / still see it among us to this very day. What murmuring against **God** does not immediately arise / as soon as things do not go as we want them to! If it does not break out outwardly / it nonetheless seethes in the heart; until at last it goes so far with some / that they resign from **God's** service altogether.

**v. 23. 24.** If indeed some water flows from the Most High to the soul / yet it is so bitter / that the sensory part cannot drink of it / and dies of sorrow. The nature, thus left to itself, then falls into such wrath and extreme despair / that it even breaks out in murmuring: which it did not do in the beginning. Therefore the will has no part in it; and it is certain / that many in these surges do not sin: both because such things occur in the animal nature / and not in the spirit / which is hidden and protected in **God**; and also because **God** Himself / after their surrender, gives them over to such weaknesses.

Yet it is to be feared / that nature might finally draw the spirit after it / and also make the will speak. Which, however, cannot happen / unless one steps out of surrender: but in yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit: a central Pietist concept of letting go of self-will to be fully available to God</term> it will never happen. The cause of this is / that / as long as this will remains united with the will of **God** / and conversely is separated from all that happens here in the lowest part of nature / it can take no part in it / and thus also cannot sin. Through yieldedness, however, the will of the creature remains always united with the will of **God** / from which it cannot go out / unless it takes itself back / or goes out of surrender.

---
the command concerning sacrifices / but concerning obedience to the voice of the **Lord** / and that they should walk in all the ways He would show them. So Psalm 81:9, 12, 14. Isaiah 55:2, 3.

<column-break/>

## 25. And he cried to the Lord / and the Lord showed him a tree / which he put into the water: then the water became sweet. (a) There he set for them a statute and an ordinance / and there he tested them; <margin>(a) Wisdom of Solomon 14:7.</margin>
## 26. And

**Tree -- sweet)** But does one really think / that **God** could not have made the water sweet without the tree? If He had not wanted to make something secret understood by it. Origen <note>original: "Origenes (a)" referring to Homily 7 on Exodus 15</note> understands the bitter water to be the Law according to the letter. For what is more bitter / he says / than that every little boy on the 8th day had to have the wound of circumcision made? That is a truly bitter cup of the Law / so much so / that even the people who are baptized in water and Spirit cannot drink of the water. But when **God** shows the tree / which makes the bitter waters sweet; then they can drink of it. What kind of tree that is / Solomon teaches us <note>original: "Salomon (b)" referring to Proverbs 3:18</note> / where he speaks of Wisdom: She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her. If Christ is brought into the Law / and it is shown to us / how the law of circumcision is to be understood / how the Sabbaths / how the law of leprosy / how the distinction between the clean and the unclean is to be kept; then the bitterness of the letter is transformed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding: and then God’s people can drink of it. But whoever / without the tree of life / that is / without the mystery of the Cross / without the faith of Christ / without spiritual understanding / wishes to drink of the letter of the Law / he will die of all-too-great bitterness. This is exactly what Paul says in 2 Corinthians 3:6. The letter kills / namely as long as it remains the letter / and is not transformed into the Spirit.

If also some suffering or bitterness encounters a person / he should take the noble bitter wood of the Cross and the bitter suffering of **Jesus Christ** before him / and think / out of what great love He suffered the unspeakable pains on the wood of the Cross / and weigh his suffering against the suffering of Christ: then he would see / that his suffering is nothing compared to the innocent suffering of our **Lord Jesus Christ**; and that would make his suffering sweet to him.

**The wood of the Cross** / viewed in bitterness or cast into it / thus has the power to make such things sweet; because the Cross is sanctified and softened in **Jesus Christ**: And **God** gives to those souls / in order to comfort them in this cruel wilderness / a little of the sweetness of this Cross. It will, however, be difficult to understand for one / who has no experience of this.

Thus one must know / that the state of Nothingness in the wilderness of faith / where the soul has neither sorrow nor joy / is something so heavy to bear / that the soul must be deemed worthy of some suffering / in order to relieve it. For self-love is so proud / that it would rather have suffering than nothing / and would rather feel a painful evil / than neither good nor evil. Those who have come this far will enjoy / that the truth is spoken here. Even those know it through their experience who have not yet come so far. There is nothing so terrifying as Nothingness: and if one can only possess something / even if it were the very greatest pains / then one is nonetheless satisfied. This is the only sweetness / which **God** allows to come to those souls / who stand at this level; where He Himself / through the sufferings / denches them with some comfort.

**Statute and ordinance)** It is not mentioned / what statutes and ordinances specifically they were / which **God** was supposed to have given them as a measure: so that in general the commandment of obedience can be understood here / that the people should yield themselves to **God's** leading in everything / He who would lead them according to His wise counsel / and would lead all temptations to a glorious end for their benefit. See Jeremiah 7:22, 23. where **God** testifies / that He did not at the beginning give the commandment...

---
**Tested)** to prove their faithfulness / and to let the lack of it become apparent to themselves.

# Chap. XV. The Second Book of Moses. <page-num>341</page-num>

26. And said: If thou wilt diligently hearken to the voice of the **LORD** thy **God** / and do that which is right in His eyes / and give ear to His commandments / and keep all His statutes; then I will put none of the diseases upon thee / which I have brought upon Egypt. For I am the **LORD** thy Physician.

27. And they came to Elim / where there were twelve wells of water and seventy palm trees / and they encamped there by the water.

---

<margin>
v. 26. **Then I will**) The precious promise consists in this / that the Angel of the Covenant <note>A term often used in older theology to refer to the pre-incarnate Christ.</note> wished to be their Physician / who would preserve them from all the bodily plagues they had experienced in Egypt / and primarily would release their souls from the infirmities of sin. Just as He afterwards appeared as the Physician of Israel / who healed all bodily sicknesses / as a sign of the more grievous spiritual sicknesses / which would be healed by Him alone. See Deut. 7:15. Isa. 53:4. Ps. 103:3. 1 Pet. 2:24. etc.
</margin>

**None of the disease — that upon Egypt)** Which were the plagues of sinners: although He still wished to exercise them with much labor and hardship; these, however, are common to the godly: from which the **LORD** nevertheless heals them / as He transforms these trials into pure love and crowns for eternity.

<margin>
v. 27. **12 wells of water and 70 palm trees**) The **LORD's** providence brought forth this image in this place / which was to remind the physical Israel of the Old Testament of their twelve tribes and the heads thereof / that they should strive for the spring of the Holy Spirit / in order to obtain therein the blessing for governing the tribes: and then of the 70 elders who were afterwards appointed by **God's** command / so that they should help Moses bear the burden of government; Num. 11:16, 17. so that they too should constantly strive for the Holy Spirit / that their governing cares might bring forth sweet fruits / (such as the palm tree bears / ) of rest / of peace / and of righteousness; but not bitter fruits / of burdens / hardships / and all kinds of unrest and injustice. The spiritual Israel in the New Testament, however, can here be reminded of the springs of the Spirit in the twelve Apostles and the seventy disciples / whom the Lord **JEsus** chose for the spreading of the Gospel. See Luke 6:13, 10:1. Yea
</margin>

As long as the people remain by the letter of the law / they are thereby nothing but a people of the Old Testament and know nothing of the pleasant Elim. But when the law is led into spiritual understanding / then you pass over from the Old to the New Testament / and come to the 12 apostolic wells / from the legal burdens to the evangelical place of refreshment.

Just as **God** is also accustomed to give some relief after a cross has been endured / so a soul not yet rightly practiced in His ways immediately believes / that she has already carried away the victory / and reached the palm branches. But she does not see / that the **LORD** has only tested her: to show her / that in this state the devils have nothing more to do; since they have all been swallowed up by the Red Sea.

There are 12 wells there / so that every tribe may have its own spring of refreshment. But just as these 12 tribes only make up one inner people / so also these 12 wells are only one spring in **JEsus Christ**.

According to outward appearances, these 12 wells are said to lie about half an hour from the Red Sea / and now only a few are to be seen as small puddles / yet quite deep / and the water is found to be black / muddy and foul.

<note>This paragraph seems to be a fragment or a continuation of a thought on the soul's struggle.</note> hinders these souls from remaining in yieldedness! <note>The term "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of surrendered calmness or submission to God's will.</note> They can [regret] this / in that they greatly lamented the good days / which they had hoped for in the state of suffering light and in the sweetness of the soul's emotions / where they had been nourished under the appearance of zeal in a still very sensory manner.

## The XVI. Chapter.
->The Feeding with Manna.<-

And they journeyed from Elim / and all the congregation of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin / which lies between Elim and Sinai / on the fifteenth day of the second month / after they had departed out of the land of Egypt.

2. And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness.

3. And

---

<margin>
Since the children of Israel had spent a month in the wilderness / and in that time their bread had run out / which they had taken with them from Egypt as raw dough / and therefore a lack of bread and meat manifested itself / because they could also perceive / that the cattle would not suffice in the long run / if they were to sacrifice them and also slaughter them for their necessity: So they began to doubt the omnipotence and gracious providence of **God** / and wished rather to have remained in their former slavery with its regular nourishment / than to spend their life in this freedom that seemed dangerous to the flesh. And so we humans also commonly do / that we would rather persist in the Egyptian bondage of body and soul / and thus under human statutes / whereby we have our regular livelihood; than that we should long for the freedom of the spirit / especially when we are called to it / and thereby should be tried through outward lack / though **God** would already provide for our necessity in an extraordinary way. When **God** then tries those who enter upon such extraordinary ways following the guidance of other witnesses; they are accustomed to turn against the same / and to make their testimony suspicious to themselves and others: thus they murmur against the witnesses of truth / and will not recognize / that such happens against the Spirit of **God**.
</margin>
