# The Second Book of Moses. Chap. XV. <page-num>340</page-num>

23. Then they came to Marah: but they could not drink the water of Marah; for it was bitter: therefore the name of it was called Marah. <margin>Ruth 1:20.</margin> <note>The name "Marah" means "bitterness." The margin refers to the book of Ruth where Naomi asks to be called Mara because of her afflictions.</note>

24. Then the people murmured against Moses / and spoke: What shall we drink?

---

After God had shown His help against Pharaoh / He allowed a new temptation to come upon the people / in that they first found no water / but afterward did come upon some, yet could not drink it because of its bitterness. By this, God wished to test the people / whether they would be satisfied with everything God sent them / and whether they would always hope for His gracious help / just as they had already experienced it so gloriously against their enemies / and whether they would wait for the same in patience during all tribulations. But since they sinned against His faithful servant / Moses / who led them according to the divine nod and command; they thereby revealed their unbelieving and disobedient hearts. Yet God helped them nonetheless upon the prayer of Moses / who had to take a piece of wood / and place it in the water / whereby it became sweet: which wood, however, is not named / as to what kind of tree it was; so that one might not attribute the effect to its natural properties / which would have been a natural impossibility / to sweeten such a vast amount of water with it. But this was intended to be an image of the wood of the Cross determined by God / upon which His dear Son was to be hanged / and which the believers were to claim for themselves in faith: thus all the bitterness of the tribulations / which God sends for our purification / would be sweetened and driven away. See 1 Peter 2:24.

**v. 23. Bitter)** When a person in the desert of spiritual dryness finally comes to water; for example, to the contemplation of the example of Christ and His saints: or when one forces oneself to prayer and the practice of virtues / in which one previously found devotion and sweetness; yet the same is unpleasant and contrary to him / because he finds no delight or taste in it. And then it happens to him as it did to the Jews <unclear>...</unclear>

**v. 24. Murmured)** <margin>against all those who advised him against the world / and he regrets that he left the world. Yes, certainly.</margin> All these things are clear types of what we see among ourselves / we who have gone out of the Egypt of the New Testament / even to this very day. What murmuring against God does not immediately arise / as soon as things do not go as we wish! If it does not break out outwardly / it nonetheless bubbles in the heart; until at last it comes so far with many / that they resign their service to God altogether.

**v. 23. 24.** If indeed some water flows from the Most High to the soul / it is nonetheless so bitter / that the sensitive part cannot drink of it / and dies from sorrow. Nature, thus left to itself, falls into such wrath and extreme despair / that it even breaks out in murmuring: which it did not do in the beginning. Therefore, the will has no part in it; and it is certain / that many do not sin in these agitations: both because such things occur in the animal nature <note>The "animal nature" refers to the physical or lower instincts as opposed to the higher spiritual will.</note> / and not in the spirit / which is hidden and protected in God; and also because God Himself gives them over to such weaknesses after their surrender.

Yet it is to be feared / that nature might finally draw the spirit after it / and also make the will speak. Which, however, cannot happen / unless one steps out of surrender: but in equanimity <term>Gelassenheit: a state of surrendered calmness and letting go</term> it will never happen. The reason for this is / that as long as this will remains united with the will of God / and, conversely, is separated from everything that occurs here in the lowest part of nature / it can take no part in it / and thus also cannot sin. But through equanimity the will of the creature remains always united with the will of God; from which it cannot depart / unless it takes itself back / or goes out of its surrender.

<column-break/>

25. And he cried unto the Lord / and the Lord showed him a tree / which he cast into the water: then the water became sweet. <sup>(a)</sup> There He made for them a statute and an ordinance / and there He tested them; <margin>(a) Wisdom of Solomon 14:7.</margin>

26. And

---

**Tree—sweet)** Does one truly think / that God could not have made the water sweet without the tree? If He had not wanted to signify something secret by it. Origen (a) <note>original: "Origenes"; refers to the early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note> understands by the bitter water the Law according to the letter. For what is more bitter / he says / than that every little boy on the 8th day must have the wound of circumcision made? That is a truly bitter cup of the Law / so much so / that even the people who are baptized in water and spirit cannot drink of the water. But when God shows the tree / which makes the bitter waters sweet; then they can drink of it. But what that tree is / Solomon teaches us (b) / where he speaks of Wisdom: She is a tree of life to all who lay hold of her. If Christ is brought into the Law / and it is shown to us / how the law of circumcision is to be understood / how the Sabbaths / how the law of leprosy / how the distinction between the clean and the unclean is to be kept; then the bitterness of the letter is transformed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding: and then God's people can drink of it. But whoever wishes to drink from the letter of the Law without the tree of life / that is / without the mystery of the Cross / without the faith of Christ / without spiritual understanding / will die of too great a bitterness. That is exactly what Paul says in 2 Cor. 3:6. The letter kills / as long as it remains merely the letter / and is not transformed into the spirit.

When some suffering or bitterness encounters a person / he should take for himself the noble bitter wood of the Cross and the bitter suffering of Jesus Christ / and think / out of how great a love He suffered the unspeakable pains on the wood of the Cross / and weigh his suffering against the suffering of Christ: then he would see / that his suffering is nothing compared to the innocent suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that would make his suffering sweet to him.

**The Wood** of the Cross / viewed in bitterness or thrown into it / thus has the power to make it sweet; because the Cross has been sanctified and soothed in Jesus Christ: And God gives those souls / in order to comfort them in this cruel wilderness / a little of the sweetness of this Cross. But this will be difficult to understand for those / who have no experience of it.

Thus one must know / that the state of "Nothingness" in the wilderness of faith / where the soul has neither sorrow nor joy / is something so difficult to endure / that the soul must be deemed worthy of some suffering / in order to find relief. For self-love is so proud / that it would rather have suffering than nothing / and would rather feel a painful evil / than neither good nor evil. Those who have come this far will confess / that the truth is spoken here. Even those who have not yet come so far know it themselves through their experience. There is nothing so terrifying as Nothingness: and if one can only exist in something / even if it were the greatest of pains / one is yet satisfied. This is the only sweetness / which God allows to come to the souls / who stand on this level; where He Himself, through suffering, gives them some comfort to drink.

**Statute and ordinance)** It is not recorded / what specific statutes and ordinances these were / which God was supposed to have given them as a measure: so that generally the commandment of obedience can be understood here / that God's people should yield to His leadings in everything / as He would lead them according to His wise counsel / and would gloriously bring all temptations to an end for their best. See Jer. 7:22, 23. <margin>not commanded concerning sacrifices / but concerning obedience to the voice of the Lord; and that they should walk in all the ways / that He would show them. Thus Ps. 81:9, 12, 14. Isa. 55:2, 3.</margin>

**Tested)** In order to prove their faithfulness / and to let the lack thereof become manifest to themselves.

<margin>(a) Origen's 7th Homily on Exodus 15. (b) Proverbs 3:18.</margin>

### Cap. XV. The II. Book of Moses.

**26. And said: If you will diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God / and do what is right in His eyes / and incline your ears to His commandments / and keep all His statutes; then I will put none of the diseases upon you / which I put upon Egypt. For I am the LORD your physician.**

**27. And they came to Elim / and there were twelve wells of water and seventy palm trees / and they encamped there by the water.**

<margin>v. 26. So will)</margin> The precious promise consists in this / that the Angel of the Covenant <note>original: "Engel des Bundes"; a theological term referring to a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ acting as God's messenger</note> wished to be their physician / who would preserve them from all the physical plagues that they had experienced in Egypt / and primarily would redeem their souls from the infirmities of sin. Just as He also afterward appeared as the Physician of Israel / who healed all physical sicknesses / as a sign of the more grievous spiritual sicknesses / which could only be healed by Him. See Deut. 7:15. Isa. 53:4. Ps. 103:3. 1 Pet. 2:24. etc.

<margin>None of the disease -- which upon Egypt)</margin> Which were plagues upon the sinners: even though He still wished to exercise them with much labor and hardship; these, however, are common to the godly: from which the LORD nevertheless heals them / as He transforms these into pure love and crowns for eternity.

<margin>v. 27. 12 wells of water and 70 palm trees)</margin> The Lord's providence brought forth this image in this place / which was to remind the physical Israel of the Old Testament of their twelve tribes and the heads of the same / that they should strive after the source of the Holy Spirit / in order to attain in the same the blessing for the government of the tribes: and then of the 70 elders who were afterward appointed by the command of God / that they should help Moses bear the burden of government; Num. 11:16-17. that these too should constantly strive after the Holy Spirit / so that their governing cares might bring forth sweet fruits / (such as the palm tree bears /) of rest / of peace and of righteousness; but not bitter fruits / of burdens / hardships / and all kinds of unrest and injustice. But the spiritual Israel in the New Testament can remind itself here of the sources of the Spirit in the twelve Apostles and the seventy disciples / whom the Lord Jesus wished to choose for the spreading of the Gospel. See Luke 6:13, 10:1. Indeed,

As long as the people remain with the letter of the law / they are thereby nothing but a people of the Old Testament and know nothing of the pleasant Elim. But when the Law is led into the spiritual understanding / then you pass from the Old to the New Testament / and come to the 12 apostolic wells / from the legal burdens to the evangelical place of refreshment.

Just as God is also accustomed to give some relief after a cross has been endured / so a soul not yet rightly practiced in His ways immediately believes / she has already carried away the victory / and reached the palm branches. But she does not see / that the Lord has only tested her: to show her / that in this state the devils have nothing more to do; since they have all been swallowed up by the Red Sea.

There are 12 wells there / so that every tribe may have its source of refreshment. But just as these 12 tribes only make up one inner people / so also these 12 wells are only one source in Jesus Christ.

According to outward appearance, these 12 wells are said to lie about half an hour from the Red Sea / and now are only to be seen as wretched, small puddles / yet quite deep / and the water is found to be black / slimy and foul.

...hinders these souls from remaining in serenity! They cannot endure the extreme nakedness <note>meaning a state of spiritual emptiness or lack of comfort</note>: They turn against their leaders / as they greatly lamented the good days / which they had enjoyed in the state of suffering light and in the sweetness of the emotions of the mind / where they had been nourished in a still very sensory way under the appearance of zeal.

**And they journeyed from Elim / and the whole congregation of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin / which lies between Elim and Sinai / on the fifteenth day of the second month / after they had departed out of the land of Egypt.**

<insert>
When the children of Israel had spent a month in the wilderness / and in that time their bread had run out / which they had taken with them as raw dough from Egypt / and therefore a lack of bread and meat manifested itself / because they could also perceive / that the cattle would not last in the long run / if they were to sacrifice them and also slaughter them for their necessity: So they began to doubt the omnipotence and gracious providence of God / and wished rather to have remained in their former slavery with their regular nourishment / than to spend their lives in this freedom that seemed dangerous to the flesh. And so we humans also commonly do / that we would rather persist in Egyptian servitude of body and soul / and thus under human statutes / whereby we have our regular livelihood; than that we should long for the freedom of the spirit / especially when we are called to it / and thereby should be tried through outward lack / since God would already provide for our necessity in an extraordinary way. When God then tries those through such extraordinary paths / who enter into such according to the guidance of other witnesses; they are accustomed to go against the same / and to make their testimony suspicious to themselves and others: thus they murmur against the witnesses of truth / and will not recognize / that such happens against the Spirit of God.

# The II. Book of Moses. Chap. XVI.
<meta>catchwords: preserves; v. 5. A</meta>

**3. And the children of Israel said to them: Would to GOD we had died in Egypt by the hand of the LORD, when we sat by the fleshpots <note>original: "Fleischtöpffe"; refers to the pots of meat the Israelites remembered eating in Egypt</note>, when we ate our fill of bread! For you have led us out into this wilderness, so that you might kill this entire assembly through hunger!**
**4. Then the LORD said to Moses: Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall**

<margin>v. 3. Fleshly people!</margin> How difficult it is for you to become a spirit, and for you to be satisfied with bare faith! Often such souls depart from their state of surrender <note>original: "Uebergabe"; a Pietist term for the total yielding of the self to God's will</note> for a time; and often their will has no part in these excesses, but rather nature alone, which—having been stripped of its spirit—laments like an irrational animal. An enlightened leader, however, easily distinguishes this state.
Many of those who enter into this path—indeed, almost all—are so blind that they regret not having died during the time of their surrender; believing that at such a time their salvation would have been more certain.
<margin>Would to GOD we had died in Egypt by the fleshpots</margin> Oh ungrateful people, who long for Egypt and yet have seen the Egyptians perish! Who long for Egyptian meat, and yet have seen the flesh of the Egyptians become the portion of the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven!
<margin>Sat</margin> This word "sitting" signifies the rest which they enjoyed in their enlightenments and sweetness.
<margin>When -- fill of bread</margin> The first temptation of Israel, and of Christ, and of all those who go out from Egypt into the wilderness, is the lack of bread. Commonly, the disciples and followers of the LORD Jesus first suffer physical lack and poverty: into which they come either through the malice, deceit, violence, robbery, rejection, and persecution of the world; or through lingering illnesses and other accidents; or at their conversion through the restitution of stolen or withheld goods.
<margin>v. 4. Bread from heaven</margin> Such bread of heaven is also called the "bread of the mighty" in Psalm 78:25 <note>The German text cites Psalm 78:26-27, which in many English bibles corresponds to verse 25, "man did eat angels' food."</note>, because in its own way above, it may be the food of angels: but when it falls down through the air, it may well take on another form and nature.
The LORD wished to feed His people with bread from heaven in order to accustom them to expecting their nourishment from above, from GOD—even when it is reached to them in an ordinary way, and much more so when it must happen extraordinarily—and that they should not dig so much in the earth and the earthly to obtain it through their own labor and cleverness. But He also wished to give the believers a glorious prototype of His Son, who would one day come from heaven as the Bread of GOD and give life to the world: as Christ later instructed more fully regarding this mystery. Matthew 4:4. John 6:31–58.
And that the Spirit or "Finger of GOD" <note>A biblical metaphor for the power or direct action of God</note> points here to a secret understanding of the bread from heaven is not only healthy and clear from the circumstances of this entire narrative, but also from the whole of Holy Scripture. For what is more common in the same than that the Word of GOD be compared to bread? It is according to this figurative way of speaking that the LORD also threatens a hunger for this bread. Amos 8:11. And thus through

<column-break/>

**go out and gather the portion of each day on its day; so that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.**
**5. And**

---

<margin>The portion</margin> Which, moreover, according to the Hebrew, the word may also be given as our daily modest part of the heavenly food and drink. This word "of each day" is our daily bread, for which we are taught to pray. Luke 11:3.
Oh, the goodness of my GOD! You reward the grumbling of this people with purely heavenly manna. This reward itself, or this nourishment which God gives them (regardless of their grumbling), sufficiently indicates that the will had no part in it. You leaders <note>The author addresses pastors or spiritual directors</note> who have such people under your supervision, have compassion for them! For they are well worthy of it. Deal with them as God deals with them: and above all things, do not take the Holy Supper <note>Communion/The Eucharist</note> away from them! The weaker you find them, the more you must communicate it to them for their nourishment and strengthening. For this spiritual strength is highly necessary for them. Do you not see how GOD wills that they should enjoy it every day as long as they have need of it? "So that," He said, "I may learn whether they will walk in my ways or not." GOD requires no other test from these souls in the time of their extreme abandonment <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a state of peaceful detachment or letting go</note> than the receiving of such a great good. GOD wants to test them and see if they will be faithful in receiving it daily.
But how is it possible to receive it daily? Answer: As often as you eat, as often as you drink, do it in remembrance of the Lord, and enjoy therein the communion and participation with His holy body. All people who eat and drink more than necessity requires and according to their lusts, do not do it in remembrance of the LORD, nor for the proclamation of His praise and honor. Now, to guard against this, there is no better nor more powerful means among all things than to eat and drink at all times, or as often as we hold a meal, in the remembrance and presence of Jesus Christ. And because this Table of the LORD has been neglected—that is, one has not at all times taken all food and drink in the pure fear or presence and remembrance of the LORD—one is so burdened and occupied by gluttony and excess, as well as by the cares of nourishment and other unchristian things, and so corrupted into error through the vile lusts of the flesh, that in such a state, and as long as one persists in it and does not become sober, one is found entirely ruined for faith and unfit in the eyes of the LORD. But to prevent this, the Lord Jesus instituted His Supper and commanded His disciples to keep His remembrance in all their eating and drinking.
One should therefore by no means think that the matter is settled in the way the greatest multitude is accustomed to doing it nowadays: namely, that one chooses a day to seek out and enjoy the heavenly manna in self-willed and self-chosen holiness, once or three, four, or even seven times a year, or every month, as one’s own opinion suggests. And even if it happens with a hanging head and assumed hypocritical gestures, or with more seclusion on that day; the Lord’s Supper is still not rightly held, received, and enjoyed thereby. The manna wants to be gathered daily, and offers itself as the supernatural bread and drink of life—certainly in, with, and under the creature <note>A theological reference to Christ being present within physical elements</note>, and primarily the natural bread and wine—to be enjoyed powerfully every day by the essence of faith, and

it also thus powerfully preserves against excess, gluttony, and all those things that arise from lust, and from which lust in turn arises, or everything that is contrary to GOD and essential goodness.
But know rather, you who indeed go for a few hours and days of the year to the Lord's remembrance and Supper, but for the remaining time live according to your lusts as much as your means allow and feed yourselves without fear—not having the remembrance of the Lord and His presence before your eyes in all your meals or as often as you eat and drink—but sit down with the apostate Israelites to eat and drink, and rise up to dance and play; know that you are those whose self-willed worship will be recognized on the Day of Judgment as nothing less than an ordinance and institution of Christ: because you have kept the test so poorly in that which the Lord tried you, whether you would walk in His law or institution or not, and have cast the obedience of His fear and love out of your sight.

# Chapter XVI. The Second Book of Moses. 343

5. And it shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare what they have brought in, so that it may be double what they gather daily.

6. Moses and Aaron spoke to all the children of Israel: At evening you shall know that the LORD has led you out of the land of Egypt.

7. And in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD; for he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. And what are we, that you grumble against us?

<margin>
v. 5. There come certain days of rest in which the soul is held back by God Himself from gathering this Manna; after it has already acquired a store of it for itself. But this state must end, like everything else: and that very Providence which placed the soul in this state for a few hours also lifts it; so that labor and the usual refreshment may follow once again. Meanwhile, this soul nevertheless lives from its hidden Manna, and receives double grace through it; for its rest gives it more than its labor.
</margin>

The sixth day is the present life. For in six days the LORD made this world. On this day, therefore, we should gather, set aside, and preserve so much that we may have enough and survive for the following or future day. Now, whatever good happens here, and however much fruit of righteousness, mercy, and godliness you gather, you shall also have that much to enjoy in the future world. Therefore the Savior says (a): Work for food that is not perishable, but which remains into eternal life <note>original: "Wircket Speise die nicht vergänglich ist..."; quoting John 6:27</note>. Every man shall eat the fruit of his works. He who received ten talents and traded with them shall be set over ten cities. How is it then that we prefer to gather and preserve such things which cannot remain with us, and from which we have no benefit on the Day of Eternity!

That it be double) They were to cook on the sixth day for two days, so that they would have enough for that day and the following one; and so they were to gather twice as much on the sixth day as usual, for the seventh day at the same time.

<margin>v. 6. The LORD) And not we by our own authority.</margin>

<margin>v. 7. What are we) We are indeed far too insignificant to perform such wonders through which you were led out of Egypt. Therefore your grumbling is against the LORD.</margin>

However, the great and admirable patience of God toward these souls certainly gives the leaders to understand how great their patience must be toward such people. It is a certain sign of a person’s progress when one is not surprised or angered by such great weaknesses, but judges them according to the truth. Whereas the unenlightened cover them with insults and burden them with penitential exercises; and while they cause such souls to leave everything behind, they simultaneously place insurmountable obstacles in the path of their perfection.

<margin>v. 6. 7. It is a thoughtful and far-reaching speech, that the LORD as a leader out of Egypt shall be recognized through experience in the evening, and on the morning following, the glory of the LORD shall be made manifest. What might that mean? Those who know the prophetic word will understand it.</margin>

<margin>(a) John 6:27.</margin>

<column-break/>

8. Further Moses spoke: When the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning to satisfy you; for the LORD has heard your grumbling with which you have grumbled against him: what are we then, since your grumbling is not against us, but against the LORD? <margin>(a) 1 Cor. 3:5.</margin>

9. And Moses spoke to Aaron: Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: Come forward before the face of the LORD; for he has heard your grumbling!

10. And it happened, as Aaron spoke thus to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they turned toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud. 11.

***

Moses summoned them before the LORD because he could appeal to no one else but the LORD; for it was He, and not Moses, who had led them into this wilderness. And so he could also assure them of extraordinary provision in the name of the LORD: but as a sign of this, and that they had sinned against the LORD, they would see the glory of the LORD in the pillar of cloud that usually led them; whether it be through a powerful fire-glance or unusual darkness, both of which could have been signs of God's righteous wrath.

<margin>v. 8. The LORD) Who lets it rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, and seeks thereby to put the unworthy creature to shame.</margin>

Meat in the evening, -- and bread in the morning) Is there also something special of divine generosity to be expressed in this, that in the evening they should have meat without bread, and in the morning bread without anything else? Is there to be recognized in this such a wise stewardship and distribution of heavenly grace? The natural man does not understand the things of the Spirit of God <note>original: "Der natürliche Mensch verstehet nicht die Dinge des Geistes GOttes"; a reference to 1 Cor 2:14</note>. He sticks with the meat of the letter, and lives indeed only by bread alone, and does not know the Word of God. But we know that in the evening of this world the Word became flesh <note>original: "das Wort ist Fleisch worden"; John 1:14</note>, in order to be known as a leader out of the land of Egypt. For the coming of the LORD in the flesh occurred in the evening, and he has brought a new day and morning to those who believe in him through such a coming, because he is the Sun of Righteousness. And on this morning, which the true Light of the World has brought forth out of darkness, his people, who receive his commandments, receive bread in abundance in him and in the opening of his Word. Furthermore, in every person who is enlightened, there is found a morning or beginning of the day: which is the time when the light first rises for him. At such a time, we as beginners and newborn infants cannot yet eat meat—that is, we are not yet capable of the strong food from the word of righteousness. But after long practice and after sufficient growth has occurred, when we have come closer to the evening and the goal of perfection, the time comes when we may also enjoy strong food. Hebrews 5:12-14. Meanwhile, one can manage quite well with the Manna alone, because it is not like other bread, but contains within itself the power and taste of all good things. However—

That which is born of the flesh is and remains flesh without this bread, until the spirit is suppressed. And therefore, there must certainly also be enough meat to eat in the evening at the Great Supper, when it shall be said: Gather yourselves and come here, all you birds, from wherever you fly! But not to serve as food for others, but to devour the flesh of the strong, of the princes, of the captains and the mighty, of the free and the slaves, of the small and the great <note>An allusion to the apocalyptic imagery in Revelation 19 regarding the "Supper of the Great God."</note>.

<margin>v. 9. Moses spoke to Aaron: Say to -- Israel) Why then did he not say it himself? He had meanwhile, as it seems, received a secret call from God to come to a conversation; which he followed by going to one side or up the mountain.</margin>

<margin>v. 10. In the wilderness) They were indeed in the wilderness. But because they had the sea behind them and the Amalekites to their side, it seems to be indicated here that they turned their faces forward, toward Mount Sinai, where their march was directed, and toward the pillar of cloud.</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XVI. 344

11. And the Lord spoke to Moses, and said:
12. I have heard the grumbling of the children of Israel; speak to them and say: Between the two evenings you shall have meat to eat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.
13. And it happened in the evening that quails <margin>(a) Num. 11:31.</margin> came up and covered the camp; and in the morning the dew lay around the camp.
14. And when the dew that had lain there had risen, behold, there lay in the wilderness something thin and round, as thin as the frost on the ground.
15. And when the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: What is that? For they did not know what it was. But Moses said to them: It is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.

---

The almighty providence of God knew how to provide meat and bread for such a mighty people very quickly: just as these two wonders are described more fully in Psalm 78:23-29 and 105:40. There, such a vast multitude of healthy and tasty birds had to fly to them from all ends and let themselves be caught quite easily; on such light fare, their bodies could remain healthy and their spirits cheerful. For God, for holy reasons, wished to cut off all excess and choice of food.

v. 12. I have heard... grumbling) Here we hear that God hears our grumbling, which we so often direct against Him: sometimes about the weather, that it rains too little or too much; sometimes about our circumstances, or that others fare so well compared to us, that we do not have this or 그, that we were not created such and such, etc.

Between the two evenings) See the note at Chapter 12:6. <note>This refers to the twilight period between sunset and total darkness.</note>

v. 13. Quails) Which birds, Josephus says, have their nesting grounds by the Arabian Sea.

In a letter from the Dutch Consul of Aleppo written to Mr. Ludolf (found in Tenzel’s *Monthly Conversations* (a)), these words are cited: As for the *Salair* <note>original: "Salair", likely referring to a specific bird species or local name</note>, which is generally given as quails, the Jews here in this land say they were fieldfares <note>original: "Kramets-Vögel", a type of thrush</note>; which are found in incredible numbers in Palestine. Jean Le Clerc, along with the aforementioned Ludolf, holds them to be locusts.

v. 15. What is that?) This is how Onkelos, Jonathan, and the Syrian translator, together with the Seventy <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interpreters, render it. And so Josephus (b) and Suidas in his Lexicon also explain it, whom Piscator follows. The French translation, however, and the States Bible <note>The *Statenvertaling*, the standard Dutch Bible translation.</note> give the word a meaning as Luther does. Luther in his marginal gloss explains it through

Buxtorf (d); Walther, the Weimar Bible, Osiander, and others. Plenty of opinions can be found in Pfeiffer’s *Dubia Vexata* (e) <note>original: "Pfeiferi Lublisvetis", likely a corruption of "Dubia Vexata", a famous work by August Pfeiffer on difficult Bible passages.</note>.

Since they were startled by it, they likely asked with a somewhat half-broken word in their wonder: מן הוא <note>Hebrew: *Man hu*</note> *Ma na* What is it then? and said *Man*. From this, the word *Manna* arose: which is what it is called in Hebrew, and which has been kept as such in the expression of all languages; just like Passover, Amen, Selah, Hallelujah.

Bread) By this, a nourishing power is attributed to it, which common manna <note>Natural resins or saps often called "manna" in the Middle East.</note> does not possess.

<column-break/>

16. This is the word which the Lord has commanded: Gather of it, every man according to what he may eat; a gomer for each head, according to the number of your souls; you shall take it, every man for those who are in his tent.
17. And the children of Israel did so, and gathered, some much and some little.
18. But when they measured it with the gomer, he who gathered much had nothing over; and he who gathered little had no lack. Every man had gathered according to what he could eat.
19. And

---

God also wanted to prescribe a certain measure for them; namely a gomer: which is said to be nearly the third or fourth part of a *Maß* <note>An old German unit of volume, roughly a liter.</note>, weighing about 3 pounds; and for one person, even one with a good appetite, it was enough for their proper filling; as they were able to prepare it, partly baked, partly boiled, according to each person's taste. In this, God also wanted to command moderation: according to Numbers 11:13-14. Especially since he who wanted to gather more out of greed nonetheless found no larger measure at home; and he who gathered with contentment nonetheless received his modest portion. See 2 Cor. 8:13, 14, 15.

v. 17, 18. They all gathered as much as each one could or would: one much, the other little. Now, what was gathered by those belonging to a family was put together in a pile, from which the father of the house then distributed to each his portion according to the prescribed measure, and did not look at whether one had gathered much or little.

O wonderful image of the Lord’s Supper! If one wanted to explain you better, one would in a certain way only obscure you more. Who does not see here the unspeakable miracle by which he who receives only a very small portion of it nevertheless receives no less of the essence of the Sacrament than he who takes it in a larger amount? And he who receives a large part of it nevertheless has no more of it than he who communicates under a smaller form; for no one can receive more or less of it than he can enjoy: namely the whole Jesus Christ; everything under the smaller as well as the larger form: since You, O Lord, give Yourself entirely to all in this adorable Sacrament!

It is also the image of the divine state, in which all have fullness, yet each only according to his capacity: and a small one is as full as a large one; although the fullness of the larger is more expanded than that of the small: he has more of God; but it is the same God, who is all in all and everything in every one among them, and who alone can cause their fullness and satisfaction.

The question remains, however, what the word means as a gift: and many Hebrews are of this opinion (c); as also

Some among them hold the word *Man* to be an old Egyptian word, which means exactly the same as: "what": which Rashbam had already noted long before in his glosses on the Pentateuch, according to Jablonski. Or else,

### Chapter XVI. The Second Book of Moses. 345
->X<-

19. And Moses said to them: Let no one leave any of it over until morning.
20. But they did not listen to Moses, and some left part of it until morning: then worms grew in it and it became foul-smelling. And Moses became angry with them.
21. And they gathered it every morning, each according to how much he could eat. But when the sun shone hot, it melted.
22. And it happened on the sixth day that they gathered twice as much bread, two gomers <note>A gomer (or omer) was a dry measure, roughly equivalent to 2 liters or 2 quarts.</note> for each person. And all the leaders of the community came and reported it to Moses.
23. And he said to them: This is what the LORD has spoken: Tomorrow is the rest of the holy Sabbath of the Lord; bake what you wish to bake, and boil what you wish to boil: but all the rest leave for yourselves to be kept until the morning.

---

In this way, God intended to forbid them from worrying about the next day; instead, they were to depend daily on His providence and receive their bread each day from His generous hand. Christ also wished to bring this to our minds in the petition: *Give us today our daily bread*; namely, that which is necessary for our daily preservation here on earth. Matthew 6:11, 34.

**v. 19 Let no one leave any of it over until morning)** God desired this for the daily exercise of obedience, of trust in Him, of contentment, and of industrious diligence: however, this is not to be understood as if everyone had to eat it all in one day even beyond their capacity; rather, it was enough if one left nothing remaining for use on the following day. Whoever then could not finish his measure could burn the remainder with fire at night, or bury it in the earth, or give it to the livestock.

**v. 20. Then worms grew in it)** This can teach us that from excessive worrying, nothing else will arise before God but a gnawing worm and a bad conscience. 
Earthly goods gathered for the coming day are subject to rust and worms. But the treasures gathered for the great Sabbath and eternal day of rest will be found again in eternity. v. 24. Matthew 6:19, 20. 
Reflect therefore on what you do and where your gathering is directed. If you seek only to gather for this present life because the love of the world lets you think of nothing else, you will soon become aware of the worms. And 
What kind of worms are those? Remember the words of the prophet when he cries out concerning those who love the world: *Their worm shall not die!* <note>original: "Ihr Wurm wird nicht sterben!" — referencing Isaiah 66:24 and Mark 9:48.</note> These are the worms produced by greed and anxiety over sustenance. These are the worms that grow from the accumulated savings-box of temporal things when one has the goods of this world and sees his brother in need, yet shuts his heart against him. 
But someone might say: If the manna is God's Word, how then can worms grow in it? Answer: And from where else do worms arise in us but from the Word of God? This is what the Word of Truth itself says: *If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin.* <note>John 15:22</note> Thus, if someone sins against the Word of God that he has heard, the Word itself becomes to him a worm of conscience, which constantly gnaws and distresses him inwardly.

**v. 21. They gathered each according to what he could eat)** Because one gomer was enough even for the strongest appetite, when it was collected, it was measured exactly according to that measure. If someone had gathered more, it was added to the one who had not gathered a full gomer; so that everyone received his modest portion.

<column-break/>

24. And they let it lie until the morning, as Moses had commanded: then it did not become foul-smelling, and there was no worm in it.
25. Then Moses said: Eat that today; for today is a Sabbath to the LORD: today you will not find it in the field.
26. Six days you shall gather it; but on the seventh day is the Sabbath <margin>(a) ch. 31:13.</margin> / there shall be none in it.
27. But it happened on the seventh day that some of the people went out to gather, and they found nothing.
28. Then the LORD said to Moses: How long do you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?
29. See, because the LORD has given you the Sabbath, therefore he gives you bread for two days on the sixth day. So let everyone stay where he is, and let no one go out from his place on the seventh day.
30. So the people rested on the seventh day.
31. And the house of Israel called it Manna <note>In the text "Man," meaning "What is it?"</note>, and it was like coriander seed, white, and its taste was like honey-cakes.
<meta>catchword: 32. And</meta>

---

**v. 24. Then it did not become foul-smelling)** So much depends on whether one does something out of one’s own self-will or whether one does it by the command of the LORD.

**v. 25-30. Sabbath)** Thus God also wished to bring back to their memory the Sabbath established at the very beginning of Creation, which had also been maintained to some extent by the faithful ancestors—Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—who especially preached of the LORD’s name in assemblies on that day; but afterwards among the Israelites in Egypt, it had fallen entirely into disuse, as they had greatly adopted the customs of the Egyptians, including their idolatry. Ezekiel 20:7, 8, 9, 18, 20, 21. Therefore, God also wished to forbid them here from physical labor and concern for earthly things, in order to confirm among them the holy and mysterious commandment of the Sabbath. For after that, it was no longer seen on the seventh day; because on the previous day, a food was prepared for the entire time of the New Testament, which is a constant Sabbath. See also concerning this miraculous feeding in Numbers 11.

<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XVI.</header>

**32. And Moses said: This is the word which the LORD has commanded: Fill a gomer of it to be kept for your descendants, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I led you out of the land of Egypt.**

**33. And Moses said to Aaron: Take a small jar, and put a gomer full of manna in it, and leave it before the face of the LORD, to be kept for your descendants.**

**34. As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron left it before the Testimony to be kept.** <margin>Exodus 27:21; Numbers 17:10.</margin>

<margin>v. 32. So that they may see the bread)</margin> As a miracle.
Indeed, even to this day, manna is found and collected in various lands. Among these, the manna of Briançon is well known to us, being counted among the seven wonders of the Dauphiné in France; throughout the entire month of August, at daybreak, it is found in great quantities on the so-called larch trees. It is initially a dew, which immediately becomes thick like a gum and has the taste of unrefined sugar. Even better, however, is that which is brought in boxes from Sicily and Calabria and found in apothecaries; of these, the Calabrian is considered the best.
But that this did not approach—much less was identical to—the manna that fell here in the wilderness, as some (a) <note>original: "Franc. Vallesius c. 57. de sacr. Philos. Vossius l. 3. de idololatr. c. 11." — Refers to Francisco Vallés, *On Sacred Philosophy*, and Gerardus Vossius, *On Idolatry*.</note> maintain, thereby diminishing the miracle, is sufficiently understood from this word of the LORD, since He wished something of it to be preserved as a miracle and a memorial of something extraordinary.

<margin>v. 33. Small jar)</margin> As Buxtorf (b) <note>original: "Hist. arc. foed. c. 5. & c. 8. Hist. Mannæ." — Refers to Johannes Buxtorf’s *History of the Ark of the Covenant* and *History of Manna*.</note> reports, the Hebrews generally hold that it was an earthenware jar. However, the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators call it a golden jar, as does Philo (c) <note>original: "Lib. de congress. quærend. erudit. grat. p. 343." — Philo of Alexandria, *On the Preliminary Studies*.</note>: which Paul confirms in Hebrews 9:4.

<margin>v. 34. Before the Testimony)</margin> But how could this be "before the face of the LORD," or how should one understand this? At that time, there was neither the Tabernacle <note>literally: "Hütte des Stifts" (Tent of Meeting)</note> nor the Ark of the Covenant. Answer: Because Moses tells the entire history of the manna here, this command is included (as is considered most probable), though it was likely only given after the Tabernacle was completed.
That which is related here in advance—that this manna had to be kept in the Tabernacle before the Ark of the Covenant—was meant to be a prefiguration of how Christ, our Bread of Life, is always present before the face of His heavenly Father to intercede for us, and thus to pray for the spiritual strengthening of our souls in their weakness. Hebrews 9:4; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1.

It was only to be sought during the six days, even before the seventh: to be sought during the six days of this time, when He gives Himself as food to His own through all the great "work-days" of a thousand years (which are like a day before God), and will be found of its own accord before the seventh period of eternal rest.

<column-break/>

**35. And the children of Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to a settled land: they ate manna until they came to the border of the land of Canaan.**

**36. A gomer, however, is the tenth part of an ephah.**
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<margin>v. 35.</margin> We may well pause here a little and consider the mystery of this beautiful image more closely, as we perceive in the manna such a distinct and clear

->**Prefiguration of Christ.**<-

1) The manna was heavenly bread, and it was precisely regarding the elevation of this miracle that our Savior said to the Jews: I am the true bread of life that has come from heaven. John 6.
2) The manna had fallen from heaven to earth: and Christ proceeded from the Father and came into the world; He came to earth poor, and lies in Mary's lap, whom the whole circle of the world could never enclose.
3) It was not made by human hands but came with the morning dew, so that no one knew how the dew fell, nor saw it until it lay there: And the conception of the heavenly manna is not from a man, but from the Holy Spirit, through the overshadowing of the Most High, occurring beyond all human understanding. Luke 1.
4) God gave the manna to the children of Israel out of His own impulse and unmerited grace, when they deserved something quite different with their grumbling and rebellious behavior: And God commends His love toward us, etc. Romans 5:8, 10; John 3:16.
5) The manna fell during the night: and our Savior was also born in the night. Luke 2:8, etc.
6) It was found in the wilderness for nourishment: and Christ is the true food with which we are preserved for eternal life in the wilderness of this world.
7) The guests who were treated to it there were the Israelites according to the flesh, who were moved from physical servitude into physical freedom and had directed their journey toward the earthly Canaan to occupy it as God's own people: Here it is the Israel according to the spirit (Galatians 3:29), who, rescued from spiritual servitude, has directed his face toward the heavenly Canaan, the seat of peace and eternal freedom.
8) It was a food for everyone in common, none excluded: and Christ is a universal good from which no one is excluded except him who excludes himself through unbelief.
9) The manna was snow-white and shining like bdellium, and also had a perfectly round and thus most perfect shape. The innocence of Jesus Christ is entirely white, and His holiness perfect.
10) Yet it lay there very small, like coriander, as a despised little seed: and Christ became the most despised and unworthy. Isaiah 53.
11) Just as the manna was often crushed in mortars, rubbed and ground in mills, and baked in the fire without melting: so the heavenly manna had to let Himself be rubbed and crushed in all kinds of "mortars of the cross," without allowing Himself to be overcome by suffering or to perish under the pain.
12) The manna kept the day of rest on the seventh day, and Christ also kept His Sabbath in the grave.
13) It had to be sought early, in the early hours: likewise, Christ and the kingdom of God must be sought first before all things. Matthew 6:33.
14) The manna was measured out to the children of Israel by measure. God deals to everyone the measure of faith. Romans 12:3.
15) The manna did not leave the children of Israel on their entire journey until they entered Canaan. I am with you always, says the Savior, even to the end of the world. Matthew 28:20.
16) The manna was exceedingly sweet and a delicate food that everyone could prepare according to his pleasure and taste: but he who has tasted Jesus will not admit that anything surpasses Him; in Him everyone may have all that he can desire: a teacher in ignorance, a light in darkness, a physician in sickness, strength and power in weakness, a treasure in poverty, protection in persecution, life in death, etc.
17) But just as the Israelites soon grew weary of this good and pleasant food and despised it: so it is to be lamented, and cannot be lamented enough, that most of His people find a poor taste in Christ and disdainfully despise this hidden manna, etc. etc.

<margin>v. 36. A gomer is the 10th part of an ephah)</margin> An ephah is as much as would hold 432 eggs: And thus a gomer is as much as 43 eggs and a fifth.
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<header>Ch. XVII. The Second Book of Moses. 347</header>

### Chapter XVII.

->The Watering from the Rock and the Battle with Amalek.<-

AND the whole congregation of the children of Israel journeyed from the wilderness of Sin by their stages according to the command of the LORD, and camped in Rephidim: and there was no water for the people to drink.

2. And the people quarreled with Moses and spoke: Give us water, that we may drink! And Moses spoke to them: Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you tempt the LORD? <margin>v. 7. 1 Cor. 10:9.</margin>

3. But the people thirsted there for water, so the people murmured against Moses, and spoke: Why have you led us up out of Egypt, to let me and my children and my livestock die of thirst?

4. Then Moses cried out to the LORD and spoke: What shall I do with this people? In a little while, they will stone me!

---

<note>Commentary begins here</note>

The LORD has His holy reasons for persisting with His trials of faith; through which only our great perversity and unbelief are revealed, so that we may take our refuge all the more in the knowledge of such corruption to the merciful love of God and His almighty providence, which always rules over us and which would come to our aid in all our deficiencies at the proper time.

<margin>v. 1. No water)</margin> The people of God may for a time lack many things that are necessary for natural life.

<margin>v. 2. the people quarreled -- tempt the LORD)</margin> This represents such a soul that has to struggle with impatience and is provoked, because of the total withdrawal of sensible comfort <note>Sensible comfort: A term used in historical theology to describe the feeling of God's presence or emotional spiritual satisfaction.</note>, whereby it is greatly cast down and weakened, turning away from the light of life.

<margin>v. 3. Thirsted for water)</margin> Man generally likes to have much water of eager devotion in his prayers and works toward God. But he should do as Moses did when he lacked the water of devotion and inwardness: take the staff of the holy Cross and strike his hard, stony heart with it.

<margin>v. 4. Will stone me)</margin> It is so dangerous to govern a large multitude: because one may not please them at all when one must govern and lead them according to the will of God. But one must then rely only on God, who can still the raging of the nations in His own time, so that they may not harm us. Ps. 65:7. See also 1 Sam. 30:6.

...stoops down, and provides refreshment out of the same, whereby hands may be strengthened anew, hearts awakened, and faith renewed.

When we find ourselves in the utmost aridity of soul and abandonment, so that one might almost ask whether God is still gracious to us; even then Christ, the Rock of our salvation, at His own hour, opens a stream of comfort and a small river of divine refreshment within us: to convince us thereby that God is faithful, and does not want us to be tempted beyond our ability, but wants to provide a way out at the right time along with the temptation. 1 Cor. 10:13.

<column-break/>

5. And the LORD spoke to Moses: Go on before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel; and take in your hand your staff, with which you struck the river, and go.

6. Behold, I will stand there before you on the rock in Horeb, and you shall strike the rock; then water <margin>(a)</margin> will come out of it, so that the people may drink. And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel. <margin>(a) John 19:34.</margin>

7. Then...

---

<margin>v. 6. Just as Christ wished to reveal Himself in the Manna as the Bread of Life, so He also wished here to testify to His people as the Rock of Salvation: upon whom one should rely and to whom one should take refuge in all adversities, for from Him alone would one expect all refreshment and quenching in such aridity and thirst of the soul; as Christ Himself promises this, John 4:10, 13, 14; 7:37, 38, 39; and the Apostle explains it, that they all drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, which Rock was Christ. 1 Cor. 10:4. From which one can also conclude that this water flowed constantly as a river, and they always moved along it and drank from it, just as the heavenly bread was given to them for the entire 40 years. See Ps. 78:15, 16; 105:41. And so Christ is also called the Rock of Salvation in Deut. 32:15; Ps. 95:1, who was also present as the Angel of the Covenant upon this physical rock beneath Him.</margin>

Christoff Führer in his travel description (a) <note>original: "p. 119. sq." — page 119 and following.</note> says that this rock is still shown today on the right side below Mount Horeb: he also describes it as a fairly large rock, which has 12 small cracks over each other in the front, and just as many in the back, though not as clear; and it has such an appearance as if water had run out of it only a short time ago. Horeb, however, is a part of Sinai. For Mount Sinai is said to be exceedingly large and high, and has 2 high peaks, one of which toward the sunset is called Horeb, the other toward the sunrise, Sinai. Self-love reveals itself here through the complaint about the thirst which the people of Israel must endure on this path. This so chosen and so beloved people murmurs against God: but God, according to His infinite goodness, does not grow weary of performing wonders for its sake. The rock gives the waters of grace to refresh them: and God was found above this rock because He is the source of these graces. It takes great effort to completely surrender oneself in a pure sacrifice: And where does one find those who do not, now and then, withdraw themselves again? # The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XVII.

7. Then the place was named **Massah** <note>Meaning 'Testing'</note> and **Meribah** <note>Meaning 'Quarreling'</note> because of the quarreling of the children of Israel, and because they had tempted the LORD and said: <margin>Phil. 4:5.</margin> Is the LORD in our midst, or not?
8. Then came Amalek and fought against Israel in Rephidim. <margin>Deut. 25:18.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 7. Tempted the LORD)</margin> Moses gives the people's error its rightful name by calling it a "temptation." This is because they said: we want to see whether the LORD is with us or not. One cannot restrain oneself from demanding signs, especially when one has been led in these ways. This causes one to generally do nothing but fuss and undo everything, because one cannot allow oneself to be completely stripped of self-will. This is what makes the wilderness journey so long; it is also the reason why almost all die in the wilderness before they reach the promised land.
<margin>Said)</margin> Regarding how they may have concluded this, see Psalm <margin>95:9.</margin>
<margin>Is the LORD in our midst, or not?)</margin> The LORD knew their lack well and, instead of their murmuring, He expected their prayer for the fulfillment of that need. Ps. 107:5, 6. He knew that the Manna was present with them and sufficient to meet their natural necessity.
We should not prescribe to God how He should deal with us.
The LORD may well be among His people even if they do not have an abundance of outward things, even if they are in the wilderness where there is a lack of all things. Thus we read of many holy men who stood in great need, with whom God was nevertheless present: such as Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, David, etc.
Therefore, let no one tempt God in times of anguish and need, but rather wait upon Him, call out, and pray to Him.
These people doubt God's presence without cause; others, for example, the modern congregations of today, boast of God's presence without cause, and pride themselves that He is in and among them. Yet the lives of those in whom He is supposed to dwell in this or that congregation clearly and obviously testify that He is not with them. Indeed, God is far from their desires and their inner heart! <note>original: "Nieren" - literally 'kidneys,' used biblically to refer to the seat of emotions and conscience.</note>
<margin>v. 8.</margin> The first enemy that rose up against Israel and sought to hinder them from the land of promise was Amalek, a grandson of Esau and also a prince among his people: Gen. 36:12, 16. He thus continued the old enmity of his grandfather in his descendants against the descendants of Jacob, envying them because of the blessing they had received and were now in the process of possessing. Therefore, God also threatened him with total destruction. Deut. 25:17 etc., 1 Sam. 15:2, 3.
Amalek means "a striking people," "a locust-people," or "the hidden locusts," and represents earthly spirits that cling to fleeting things, as well as the desires and temptations that fall upon us on our spiritual pilgrimage. When we then wish to crucify our flesh along with its lusts and desires, and begin to kill the members that are on earth; then the fleshly spirits, lusts, and desires are soon ready, like so many locusts, to fall upon the fruits of the Spirit and—if no resistance is present—to devour them. But there one finds
as soon as the will gives in to looking at itself. Doubt and hesitation, in anxiety and restlessness, set everything into disorder and cause Amalek (who signifies nature and self-love as the only enemies remaining at this level) to immediately triumph. To avoid this disorder, one must only remain sitting upon the stone, hold oneself unswervingly in surrender, and persist in the rest of serenity <term>Gelassenheit: a key spiritual term meaning a state of calm, detached surrender to God's will</term>; while meanwhile faith and trust, like hands stretched out toward God, support the soul in its surrender.

11. And it happened, whenever Moses lifted up his hand,<sup>(a)</sup> Israel prevailed; but whenever he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. <margin>(a) Josh. 8:26. Jas. 5:16.</margin>
12. But Moses' hands were heavy; therefore they took a stone and put it under him, so that he sat on it. And Aaron and Hur supported<sup>(a)</sup> his hands, one on this side and the other on that side. Thus his hands were steady until the sun went down. <margin>(a) Rom. 8:26.</margin>
13. And

---

<margin>v. 9. 10. Joshua)</margin> That is, Jesus <note>The names Joshua and Jesus are the same in Hebrew (Yeshua); the commentator links the Old Testament leader to the New Testament Savior</note>, through whose guidance we are to subdue them. For He has come to save us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us. Luke 1:71.
<margin>v. 11.</margin> Only the believers must constantly persist in prayer and not grow weary; then they will surely keep the upper hand. Otherwise, their spiritual enemies gain the upper hand and weaken the strength of their faith. But our faith is the victory-banner by which we overcome the world. 1 John 5:4.
The lifting up of your hands or prayer to God must be added to an active and working faith. When these are united with one another, they make a warrior of Jesus Christ exceedingly strong in the Lord and in the power of His might. Otherwise, Amalek—the flesh—easily gains the upper hand.
Persecutions are unavoidable in all states of life. Created things wage war against this people and want to bring them to nothing. But when Moses lifts his hands—that is, as long as one is faithful in remaining raised to God through serenity and faith, and as long as one is immovable in looking only to God—then one carries away the victory, no matter how powerful the enemies one has. And when Moses lets his hands sink—that is, as soon as one falls back into oneself through self-reflection—one is immediately overcome. For the creature, finding itself deeply immersed in its own weakness, becomes entangled in vain retreats. That is the unfaithfulness of this state. One immediately falls into disorder and causes Amalek (which signifies nature and self-love as the only enemies remaining at this level) to immediately triumph.
<margin>v. 12. Hur)</margin> It is believed that Hur might have been a son of Caleb from the tribe of Judah (1 Chron. 2:19) and Moses' brother-in-law, the husband of Miriam, who was therefore also drawn into the governance of the people (Ch. 24:14). Meanwhile, there is also a beautiful image here of how rulers, with their secret councilors and preachers, should lie before God in prayer in times of war and other necessities; since they could then conduct wars through their generals, just as Moses here appointed Joshua for that purpose. And these two should then also be the supports of the rulers, to assist them before God in all difficult cases, when they themselves first humble themselves before God and lift their ruler’s staff to the Lord with faithful hands, that He might help them bear this burden in grace and grant wisdom and strength to all their deeds. See Ps. 141:2, Isa. 1:15.

->Jethro’s Arrival and Wise Counsel.<-

<margin>It is believed that Jethro—since he lived in Midian, that is, among the Midianites, and may have been a leader or tribal elder among them—must have descended from Midian, the son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2). <margin>Indeed, some even hold that this Jethro was the famous **Mercurius Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom, writing, and priesthood</note>, who is otherwise called Hermes. Because he was a great philosopher, a great ruler, and a great priest, he was called the "Thrice-Greatest."</margin>

15. And Moses built an altar and called its name, "**The LORD is my Banner.**"
16. And he said: "Because the power is raised against the throne of the LORD, the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."

ended? Oh no! The LORD has sworn that He will wage war against Amalek from generation to generation, both under the Law and under the Gospel. And where are we to find this war continued now? Nowhere else than in each person's own heart! Therein lies an Amalek: there is a kingdom and a "brood" of the devil, a seed of the serpent that turns the people away from obedience to God and strives to rule over them, thereby devouring, ruining, and killing them. For that is also what the name "Amalek" signifies <note>A folk etymology suggesting "people who lick up" or "dwellers in the valley"</note>. With this destroyer in the soul, the LORD will war from generation to generation. An eternal enmity is set between the seed of Christ and the seed of the serpent. And these are the enemies of whom the LORD foretold us in Matthew 10:36. This Amalek, these enemies, the LORD will destroy by a hidden hand. This is how the Greek translators <note>Referring to the Septuagint</note> give the words: "The LORD has sworn that He will war with Amalek through the hand of Christ, the Power of God" (Habakkuk 3:4).

> Without doubt, Jethro was eager to inquire about his son-in-law's condition after the return of his daughter with her two children—or at least the one who was still a minor—to him. Now that Providence had allowed him to hear what had occurred in Egypt, he wished to bring Moses' family back to him. There, they heartily renewed their friendship, and Jethro revealed his God-fearing heart through his joy and his praise of the true God. He rejoiced that God had made Himself known so powerfully among this people and knew how to punish all proud enemies and violent oppressors according to His justice—and that through a "like-for-like" retribution: as they had thrown the children into the water, so they themselves had to drown in the water.

When Jethro also mentions other gods, he may well be indicating that he might not have been free from all idolatry: because the knowledge of the true GOD is very easily stained through interaction with other natural <note>Meaning "unregenerate" or worldly</note> men.

But here he has now been powerfully strengthened in the knowledge of the true GOD, as he has also confessed Him with his sincere declaration, and was therefore also invited to the holy sacrificial meal before the presence of the LORD—namely, in the Pillar of Cloud: to converse there about all the works of the LORD, and to praise and glorify GOD for them. And so the holy meal, where the unique atoning sacrifice of the death of Christ is proclaimed, should have been continued with such holy conversations during moderate physical refreshment, as happened during the first love-feasts of the Christians.

Jethro must have given Moses the wise counsel of a well-organized and subordinate government here out of a divine impulse: from which it can be further concluded that he may also have been a ruler among his own people, who, from precise knowledge and his own experience of the matter, judged reasonably that such a heavy burden is unbearable for one person; and therefore, several must be appointed and also subordinated to one another, so that everything could be maintained in a proper order, and the subordinates could be assisted in all cases.

### Chapter XVIII. The Second Book of Moses.

25. And Moses chose capable men out of all Israel and appointed them as heads over the people; namely, leaders over thousands, leaders over hundreds, leaders over fifties, and leaders over tens:

26. So that they judged the people at all times. They brought the difficult matters to Moses, and all small matters they judged themselves.

27. Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away into his own land.

One sees how this order is observed in great worldly kingdoms according to their kind: that there are villages, cities, districts, lordships, and principalities; where the smaller associations settle minor matters among themselves; but those who are appointed to the government of larger ones, such as lordships and principalities, judge and settle the more important matters everywhere. And so also entire armies are divided into squads, corporalships, companies, and regiments: hence the name of the captains, <note>original: "Centurionum," from the Latin for a hundred</note> and the colonels, <note>original: "Chiliarcharum," from the Greek for thousands</note>.

And it is the same with the Church of the New Testament, which should be noted as spiritual scouts and as the Kingdom of Christ; where the subjects still require much oversight and external government. There, ten houses should have their elder and schoolmaster. Fifty families already require a teacher and shepherd. Just as there can also be overseers and head-overseers over these in large countries, so believers know—if it happens under the oversight and guidance of the Holy Spirit—to regard such as a good human order, and for the sake of the Lord, who is a God of order, they must not resist it. However, these leaders must also constantly observe the Lord's will: that believers should be brothers, and the greatest among them should be the servant of the others. Matthew 23:9, 11. Thus there are also minor matters which the elders should take care to settle: and then there are greater matters which must be brought before those to whom God has entrusted more gifts and upon whom a greater administration rests.

In every human being, the senses are also appointed, as it were, as sub-judges of earthly things: over these, the soul should conduct rational government: but the spirit in man should be the supreme ruler in the light of God, leading the government over the whole being of the man, and must pray for grace from above to judge the mysteries of faith spiritually. 1 Corinthians 2:15, 16; Hebrews 5:14.

Spiritual leaders have two important rules for their conduct to learn from this: one from Jethro, and the other from Moses. From Jethro: that it is not their business to concern themselves with the temporal affairs of the souls they lead; but only to care for that within them which concerns the honor of God and pertains to their perfection. Because they are to excuse themselves from temporal matters regarding others, should such things be entrusted to them: both so that they may not be too burdened by this weight, which would take away the time they should use for more important and eternal things; and also because God does not demand this of them: so they must not seek after it. From Moses, however: they should learn from his humble acceptance of the wise counsel of his father-in-law—even though Moses was so full of the Spirit of God and Jethro was not even of his own people—that one must accept truth and good counsel, no matter where it comes from. For it often pleases God to let it be given to us through people who stand far below us in highness and grace: in order thereby to humble the greatest leaders; so that they may recognize that He alone is the author of all true light.

# The XIX. Chapter.

->The Preparation for the Giving of the Law.<-
->Luke 22:39.<-

In the third new moon after the departure of the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, on this very day, they came into the wilderness of Sinai.

2. For when they had departed from Rephidim, they came into the wilderness of Sinai and camped in the wilderness. And Israel camped there in front of the mountain.

3. And Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain and spoke: "Thus shall you say to the house of Jacob and proclaim to the children of Israel:

<margin>(a) Revelation 12:14.</margin>
4. 'You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you on eagle's wings (a) and brought you to myself.'"

5. And

---

v. 1. **In the 3rd new moon — on this very day**) This was the month of Sivan, Esther 8:9, which falls in our June: and indeed, this first day of the month was the 46th day from the departure from Egypt. For one day was spent on this discourse, and three days were appointed for their sanctification and preparation for hearing the Law, and so the Law was given on the fiftieth day: hence the name Pentecost <note>original: "Pentecostes"</note> originated, for which a festival was later appointed in its memory.

**They came**) Even today, one is said to find many large stones on the road with ancient Hebrew—though almost faded and unreadable—writing.

<column-break/>

**Wilderness of Sinai**) Or Shur.

v. 2. **In front of the mountain**) God's Horeb, Chapter 3:1, which had two peaks, v. 11, 20, etc.

v. 3. **Thus shall you say to**) The providence of God always gives a leader to those souls whom He leads in faith, so that the leader may reveal the will of the Lord to them. Therefore, they must also have a blind obedience to let themselves be led. Since they cannot stop at anything given to them except for the leadership and providence, they must necessarily carry out blindly whatever the enlightened leader commands them.

**House of Jacob — Children of Israel**) God called the people the "House of Jacob" here because they were born of this patriarch Jacob according to nature. But since he was named "Israel" by God according to the promise, his descendants are mostly called "Children of Israel" according to this promise, which is hereby also attributed to them; just as the believers of the New Testament are called "the Israel of God," Galatians 6:16; because God regards and names His own not according to physical birth, but according to His gracious promise. Otherwise, both names appear together in various places. Psalm 114:1, 147:19, etc.

v. 4. **Carried you on eagle's wings**) He describes His special protection under the image of eagles, who take their young upon their wings and soar high with them, in order to accustom them to such a high flight. With this, God wanted to lead them to heavenly-mindedness, to raise their minds above earthly things, just as Christ also compares His own to eagles, Matthew 24:28, who [rise] with him in his resurrection, Colossians 3:1, 2. See also Deuteronomy 32:11.
