<meta>This page continues the exposition of the Ten Commandments from Exodus 20. The previous page concluded the commandments regarding murder, adultery, and theft. This page moves to the Tenth Commandment concerning covetousness and describes the Israelites' terrified reaction to the divine revelation at Mount Sinai.</meta>

->## The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XX.<-

**17. You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that is your neighbor's.**

<margin>That is: Let yourself be content with what you currently have, in whatever station or rank God has placed you, whether outwardly or inwardly.</margin>

God finally wanted to uncover the root of all evil as it lies in the heart, and to forbid all evil desires to man. By this, He indicated the great corruption of the heart, so that man, in the recognition of this great misery, might turn to God and call upon Him for the healing of his deadly malady of sin.

But with this very commandment, God also wanted to show the good seeds of virtues that stand against these evil inclinations of the mind: such as friendliness, kindness, chastity, justice, truth, contentment, and the like; which man should make it his business to request from God, as the giver of all good and perfect gifts.

And so Christ and the Apostles have explained the meaning of these commandments to us in greater detail; as can be seen in Matthew 5, Ephesians chapters 4, 5, and 6, Colossians chapters 3 and 4, etc., where all these vices are rebuked and the virtues opposing them are commended to the believers.

Desire <note>original: "Lust." In this period, "Lust" referred to any strong desire or inclination, not exclusively sexual.</note> can thus become either a virtue or a vice, depending on what it lights upon and pursues, or according to its source, means, and purpose.

There is a desire that is neither good nor evil, which is not sinful and yet is not a virtue. Thus, the desire to eat, to drink, and to sleep is according to nature and is not forbidden.

The desire to see and hear Christ, and to recognize the mystery of godliness more clearly—which many kings and prophets and the angels themselves have so greatly desired—is so far from being forbidden that, rather, the opposite and the lack of it is to be scolded.

But to wish for, do, or desire something that is either evil in itself, or even something that is not evil but is either natural or even good in itself, yet stems from a sinful intention and purpose, in a sinful way, through sinful means; and thus not out of love for God and His honor, but for the sake of one's own honor or pleasure: that is the desire <note>original: "Lust"</note> meant here. <meta>And</meta>

In such a way, everything can become carnal desire. Even natural and spiritual desire can become sinful when it is not directed toward the glory of God; and "neutral things" <note>The author refers to *adiaphora*, or things that are morally indifferent in themselves.</note> no longer remain neutral through the use of the regenerate and the unregenerate. Thus, even most of the virtues of the heathens are considered nothing other than "glittering sins," or disguised and beautifully painted vices, because they were stained with this desire.

This desire is otherwise called in the Scripture: the lusts of the flesh, carnal mind and thoughts, human ways, the opinions and plots of the flesh, carnal wisdom, the will of the flesh and of reason, the thoughts and strivings of the human heart. And

Who can count the desires of the human heart in this case! As many inclinations as there are in man, into so many branches does desire divide itself. God would have enough to do if He were to fulfill everyone’s manifold and often conflicting wishes.

Against such addiction and disease, however, there is no better medicine or prescription than that which God the Lord has twice prescribed here:

**Do not covet! Do not covet!** Do not let your eyes dart wherever they please! Rather, tear them out if they want to offend you; or make a covenant with them!

And so, what is required of us here is what the Gospel law also wants, and what it drives and presses toward everywhere, explaining it even more precisely: namely, true self-denial and renunciation of the world; hatred, anger, and zeal against original sin as the mother of all actual lusts and sins; as well as against all actual sins that lead us away from the true good and purpose: pure love of God from the whole heart: total satisfaction in and with God, as the sole Good that can still our desire and longing. <meta>And</meta>

Accordingly, this commandment is the "lock" of the two tables <note>The "two tables" of the Law: Commandments 1-3/4 (God) and 4/5-10 (Neighbor).</note>, where God expressly and clearly forbids once more the desire that was already forbidden in all the other commandments—just as the opposite of desire, namely pure love of God and neighbor, as well as simplicity and sincerity, was commanded in all of them. Thus, it belongs as little to the second table alone as the introduction belongs only to the first table. But the fact that specifically

The neighbor’s house, wife, etc., and thus the second table, are mentioned happens because sinful desires are first recognized in the longings against the second table, just as the love of God is seen in the love of the neighbor.

<column-break/>

18. **And all the people saw the thundering <gloss>(a)</gloss> and the torch-like flames, and the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain. But when the people saw such things, they recoiled and stood from afar,**

<margin>(a) chapter 19:16. Matthew 17:5, 6.</margin>

19. **And said to Moses: You speak with us, and we will obey; but do not let God speak with us <gloss>(b)</gloss>, lest we die!** <margin>1 Samuel 12:19.</margin>

<margin>(b) Psalm 2:5. 20. And</margin>

God wanted to show Himself with such terror so that the great perversity of the heart would become manifest—a heart that should cling to God in childlike love and would then, in return, feel the great fatherly love of God. But because man will not willingly allow himself to be brought to such childlike love, simplicity, and humility before God, God must allow all kinds of terror to precede, which are meant to break us from our self-centeredness and teach us to approach God in prayer.

*v. 18. Saw the thundering and the sound]* As Augustine already noted <margin>(a) Question 72.</margin>, <term>sight</term> <note>original: "Gesicht"</note> is used by the Hebrews to stand for the use of any and all senses. Thus, in Scripture, "seeing the good" means as much as experiencing and enjoying the good.

*v. 19. You speak; not God]* It must have been a wondrously powerful voice with which God spoke here. A human voice, let him shout as loudly and strongly as he will, extends no further than perhaps ten to twelve thousand people might hear it. Here, over six hundred thousand people stood at the base of Mount Horeb, and they all heard it. It is no wonder that human nature in its current state is seized by a horror at it.

To man as a sinner, God is a "consuming fire": therefore, man cannot endure the voice of God Himself, let alone His presence. And for this reason, God deals with us through our fellow creatures, who must have patience with us because they are also weak humans; and even when they stand upright, they must remain on guard lest they fall, and therefore must carry their weak neighbor in patience and gentleness (Romans 15:1, 2; Galatians 6:1, 2).

When the soul sees God approaching, it fears death greatly, knowing well that if one wishes to see Him, one must die. As soon as the state of death begins—which then lasts a long time—the soul enters into great fears and would like to say: "Ah, how I wish I did not have to go further than to walk through such terrible plagues!" It remains far removed and seeks to defend itself against death, even imagining that it is approaching God, while it actually takes pleasure in remaining at a distance from Him. And being now deceived by self-love, it would rather preserve its own life than allow itself to be taken away by a holy death, which would nonetheless happily awaken it again in God. This causes the soul to say to its leader (more through its actual resistance than through words): "Speak you yourself with me: for as long as you alone speak with me, and I hold to human words and human means—which can at least be grasped by reason—I shall not die." But to walk upon the Word of God alone, and under His special guidance, in the darkness of pure faith—to that I cannot accommodate myself, out of fear of death and loss.

<meta>v. 20. Moses</meta>

<summary>This page concludes the Ten Commandments by explaining the inward nature of the prohibition against coveting and describes the Israelites' profound fear of God's direct voice at Mount Sinai. The author argues that God uses human mediators because fallen humanity cannot endure the unshielded presence and voice of the Divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Exodus 20. Having concluded the Ten Commandments on the previous page, the text now addresses the Israelites' reaction to the divine presence and God's specific instructions regarding worship and the construction of altars.</meta>

->### Chapter XX. The Second Book of Moses.###<-

20. And **Moses** said to the people: **“Do not fear! For God has come to test you, and that His fear may be before your faces, so that you do not sin.”**

21. **So the people stood afar off** (a); **but Moses drew near into the darkness where God was.** (a) Chapter 24:1 etc.

---

<margin>v. 20. Moses spoke)</margin> This excellent leader assures his people that it is not yet time to be afraid, because this is not yet the place of death, but only a trial through which God wishes to test His friends, to learn whether they are courageous enough to enter into the paths of death.

<margin>God has come)</margin> Or, He has shown Himself near.

<margin>That His fear may be before your faces, so that you do not sin)</margin> God is so gracious that He wishes to preserve you from falling away precisely through the revelation of His holy presence.

Whoever does not keep his unruly heart strictly and precisely in the fear of God and live before God will do whatever he lusts after, and afterwards only act hypocritically before people so that he is not punished.

On the other hand, the presence of God immediately impresses such a holy awe and reverence upon the soul that it learns to walk before such bright and holy eyes with all humility and caution, and does not easily go astray. Just as a child is kept from evil when it remains under the eyes of parents or teachers, and thus does what is its duty in an orderly, modest, and honest manner.

Thus, God’s holy presence, when we let it become powerful within us through constant remembrance, makes us truly upright toward Him and toward men; for we are then captured and convinced that nothing is hidden from Him. What use would it be then to hide and play the hypocrite for long? Rather, we learn to love Him and our neighbor honestly.

<margin>v. 21. The people etc.)</margin> These people, although they had already come far in the ways of the inner life, nevertheless remain standing far behind: namely, out of the fear of death. But Moses, who had passed through death and was resurrected in God, could no longer die; therefore, he no longer feared. God was no longer a stranger to him; so that what killed others gave him life, because of his secret state of resurrection in God. Yet he enters here only into the darkness in which God was: to show us that all revelations which God gives of Himself in this life are always a darkness to the creature, which has only a limited and bounded knowledge of Him, indeed, one veiled with the shroud of faith.

<margin>Moses drew near into the darkness)</margin> God dwells in darkness, 1 Kings 8:12, because He does not want us to see everything before our eyes regarding how He intends to deal with us; rather, He wants to test our faith, humility, and serenity <note>original: "Gelaſſenheit" — a key mystical term meaning yieldedness or letting-go</note>, and then help us in His own time. He who otherwise dwells in a light, but in such a light that no one can reach with their reason; 1 Timothy 6:16; but rather in the dark faith, when we see nothing before our eyes.

We should certainly not ascend to God in our own wayward and as yet unpurified spirit, nor seek to contemplate who He is and what His unfathomable divinity might be, lest we be consumed by the infinite brilliance of His glory. It is a freedom and access that is not granted to everyone. Neither Aaron nor Hur were permitted to step as near as Moses was allowed to go up and in, to see and hear such things that had never entered into any man's heart before his time: just as none of the others, neither Abraham nor Noah, nor Enoch, nor Adam, attained to such high dignity.

If the word **Enthusiast** <note>In the 18th century, "Enthusiast" was often a slur for religious fanatics. The author is reclaiming it here to mean someone literally "filled with God."</note> had not been turned into a word of abuse and a name of shame by the enemies of truth and godliness, then Moses could be called such a person here in a pure and holy sense.

God and His essence, and the things that are in Him, are so exceedingly high that we cannot reach them with all our understanding, and may only recognize something of them—and especially this: that they are so high that they cannot be known. And that is precisely the divine darkness, which far, far exceeds all light of knowledge.

O divine darkness! How bright you are to those who know and love you! But how dark and black also to those who find no taste in you! And how terrifying and frightening to all the fainthearted and delicate ones, who do not want to risk their lives and enter into the death of self-will!

<column-break/>

22. **And the Lord said to Moses: Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken with you from heaven.**

23. **You shall make nothing beside me. You shall not make for yourselves gods of silver or gods of gold.**

24. **An altar of earth you shall make for me, and shall sacrifice upon it your burnt offerings and your thank offerings, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where I establish a memorial of my name, there I will come to you and bless you.**

25. **And if you will make an altar of stone for me, you shall not build it of hewn stones. For where you have used your iron tool upon it, you have profaned it.**

26. **Neither shall you go up by steps** (a) **to my altar, so that your nakedness is not uncovered before it.** Chapter 19:22.

<margin>(a) 2 Chronicles 4:1.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 22, 23. The Lord herewith proceeds to the explanation and further expansion of His commandments: and so the second one especially is interpreted more extensively here, namely that God had not shown His form, but only let His majestic voice be heard, and for that reason nothing should be made that was intended to represent Him.</margin>

Men should then not cling to external visible things in their worship, but seek to honor the true God in the heart, where He would witness His presence with His working, and there He wishes to be sought and honored. Proverbs 23:26.

<margin>v. 24, 25. Following this, the most prominent part of worship is ordained, the altar, such as the holy fathers—Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob—had made, upon which they performed their sacrifices and thereby preached of the Lord's name and His ways.</margin>

It was to be made of earth in all simplicity; by which Christ was aimed at, who is also called our altar in Hebrews 13:10, 12, who wished to take on our poor human nature, which is dust and earth, in order to suffer in the same. But if they did indeed want to make an altar of stones so that it might be permanent, they should not work it artistically with a chisel: to show that our sharp-witted reason should not meddle with the great mystery of Christ's incarnation.

We should also the less search into this mystery with our corrupted, impure thoughts, because thereby only our nakedness makes itself known—how the natural man can grasp nothing at all of the things that are of the Spirit of God. 1 Corinthians 2:14.

<margin>v. 26. Not by steps)</margin> The ascent went from below gradually into the heights, like one climbs a mountain.

<margin>So that your nakedness is not uncovered before it)</margin> But how could that have been, considering the undergarments and long robes? Answer: One must lift up a long robe in front for the sake of convenience when climbing a staircase, which gives the appearance of exposure.

<margin>(a) Josephus, Book 4, Antiquities, Chapter 8.</margin>

<summary>This page discusses Moses' unique role as a mediator who enters the "divine darkness" of God's presence, contrasting his courage with the people's fear. It also outlines laws for simple altars of earth or unhewn stone, emphasizing that human artifice and pride have no place in approaching the divine.</summary>
<keywords>Moses, divine darkness, fear of God, altar of earth, unhewn stone, humility, worship, incarnation, Enthusiast, Exodus 20</keywords>

The Second Book of Moses. Ch. XXI.

# Chapter XXI.
->Laws concerning Servitude and Injuries.<-

And these are the laws which you shall set before them.
2. If you buy a **Hebrew** <margin>(a) Deut. 15:12. (b) Ch. 22:3.</margin> servant (b), he shall serve six years, and in the seventh year he shall go out free for nothing.
3. If he came in by himself, he shall go out by himself. If he has a wife, then his wife shall go out with him.
4. If his master gives him a wife, and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master’s, but he shall go out by himself.

---

<margin>v. 1.</margin> In these two chapters, and partly in the 23rd, several judicial ordinances regarding civil actions are established. This category of laws is specifically called "Rights" or "Judgments," by which God intended to arrange a peaceful government among them and to punish vices and damages.

<margin>v. 2.</margin> **Hebrew servant)** God wished to tolerate the practice of servitude among His people, which had spread among the heathens, but He restricted it significantly. This was because the freedom of believers under Christ had not yet been revealed; today, it is unchristian to hold one's brother—who is baptized with us into one body—as a permanently bound servant in one's power.
**In the 7th year)** A person could become a servant either through debt <note>original: "Verschuldung"</note> (see Ch. 22:3) or by selling himself due to poverty (Lev. 25:39). However, he had to go free in the seventh year, which is generally understood as the seventh Sabbath-year. This pointed toward the spiritual freedom found under the New Testament.
**If the Year of Jubilee** was so near that it fell within those six years, or if his master died and left no male heir, the servant could be freed even before the six years expired.

<margin>v. 3. 4.</margin> His wife enjoyed this freedom with him, unless she had been given to him by his master. In that case, she and her children had to finish their years of service. However, this seems to refer only to women who were purchased from the heathens (Lev. 25:44), because the situation for Israelite women was different. As seen in Deut. 15:12, a Hebrew woman who sold herself as a maidservant also went free in the seventh year.
A master could give a servant a heathen wife and raise "house-born" <note>original: "leibeigene"</note> servants from her (a practice from which people in the Orient still profit greatly today). This was permitted if the servant already had a wife and children and had contributed to the lineage of Israel; otherwise, it was not appropriate.

<column-break/>

5. But if the servant shall plainly say: "I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free":
6. Then his master shall bring him to the judges <note>original: "Göttern" (gods), a term used here for the divinely appointed authorities</note> (a); then he shall bring him to the door or to the doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl; and he shall serve him forever. <margin>(a) Deut. 15:17.</margin>
7. And if a man sells his daughter to be a maidservant, she shall not go out as the menservants do.
8. If she does not please her master, so that he does not take her in marriage, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no power to sell her to a foreign people, because he would be acting faithlessly toward her.
9. But if he gives her to his son in marriage, he shall deal with her according to the rights of daughters.
10. If he takes another for himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her dwelling.
11. And if he does not do these three things for her, then she shall go out free without money.
12. Whoever...

---

<margin>v. 5. 6.</margin> It was a remarkable thing for a servant, out of love for his master and his wife, to prefer to remain in servitude. The authorities had to investigate whether he did this voluntarily and was not perhaps talked into it or forced by his master. His ear was then fastened to the door with an awl.
By this, the Holy Spirit points to the great mystery of Christ, who took upon Himself the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7) and bound Himself forever to the service of His heavenly Father and His Bride out of love. This is the meaning of the phrase in Psalm 40:7, <note>original: "Ps. 40/7. welches der Apostel Erklärungs-weise ausdrückt Hebr. 10/5. Du hast mir den Leib zubereitet"</note> which the Apostle explains in Heb. 10:5 as: *“You have prepared a body for me.”* That is, He had to fulfill this service and obedience even unto death on the Cross; He was likewise pierced and nailed to the wood of the Cross with such awls and nails, and there He was bound to the eternal service of His Church.

<margin>v. 6.</margin> **Serve forever)** This means until the Year of Jubilee, or until the master died, even if he left a son behind.
With a Hebrew daughter, the situation was different: after seven years of service, her master either had to marry her, give her to his son, or keep her provided with food, clothing, and a home—or, as one says, "shelter." This is indicated by the word <term>עֹנָתָהּ</term> <term>Gnona</term> <note>This Hebrew term refers to "marital rights" or "habitation"</note>, which can mean the same as <term>מְעוֹנָה</term> <term>Megnona</term>, a "dwelling" (Deut. 33:27). For if it meant "marital duty," then polygamy would be expressly commanded here, which God never approved. Furthermore, they were directed to show all fairness and equality toward their own people, so that the wealthy would not exalt themselves over the poor or hold them in too low a regard. See Lev. 25:35, 39.

<margin>v. 8–10.</margin> Our own servants and maids are in a different situation, as they always remain in their freedom. Even if they serve us faithfully for a long time, they do not thereby earn a right to marriage; however, they should be generously assisted when they do marry, or be treated well in their old age.

### Chap. XXI. The Second Book of Moses.
## Chapter 21.

12. He who strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death.
13. But if a man did not lie in wait, but **God** let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.
14. But if a man acts presumptuously against his neighbor, to kill him with cunning, you shall take him from my altar, so that he may die.
15. And he who strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.
16. And he who steals a person and sells him, or if he is found in his power, he shall surely be put to death.
17. And he who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.

---

<margin>v. 12. Here the Sixth Commandment is provided with specific penalties, so that people might guard themselves against such crude outbursts of hatred and quarreling.</margin>

<margin>v. 13. Even an accidental killing—which reveals a sorrowful destiny from **God** over such a perpetrator, since God's righteous ways are hidden in this—was punished by such an expulsion from one's homeland, so that he would not appear before the eyes of others and constantly stir up a sorrowful memory.</margin>

<margin>v. 14. But a bold murder, committed out of malice, had to be avenged by death; as was commanded immediately after the Great Flood <note>original: "Sündflut"</note> in Genesis 9:6, whereas previously it was left to divine vengeance alone, as in Genesis 4:15. In such cases, the holiness of no place should be respected such that he could not be taken from there and killed. See 1 Kings 2:28-31. Therefore, it is quite unjust that churches and monasteries give even the slightest refuge to such murderers. See Numbers 19:11, 12, 13.</margin>

<margin>v. 15. 17. **God** wished to maintain the reverence toward parents so holily that if anyone should sin against them with blows or cursing, or similar highly punishable harsh words of abuse, it should be unfailingly punished by death. This was to serve as a terror to naughty children and also as instruction for judges; where such unseemly behavior of children toward parents became public, even if the parents did not report it out of fear that it would reflect poorly on themselves, the judges should punish and rebuke it themselves as highly criminal, so that evil might be put away and others might see it as a warning. See Deuteronomy 19:19, 20.</margin>

<margin>v. 16. The theft of a human being and delivery into servitude is reckoned equal to physical death, because he is thereby robbed of noble freedom, which is to be valued as highly as life itself.</margin>

<margin>v. 17. **Shall surely be put to death**) Through this phrasing, where the Scripture names no specific type of punishment, the Hebrews understand it to mean suffocation or strangulation, which was regarded by them as the mildest form of capital punishment.</margin>

<margin>...use immoderate punishment; otherwise, he is to be regarded as a murderer.</margin>

<margin>v. 22–25. The right of equal retribution <term>Lex Talionis: the principle of "an eye for an eye"</term> was committed to the investigation and judgment of the judges, and not to the self-authorized revenge for such a harm. And it also does not seem to be commanded here that an equal harm should literally be inflicted upon the body; rather, it should be appraised how the inflicted harm could be compensated and replaced by the other. Christ, however, commanded his own people to have patience and tolerance of evil and injustice: Matthew 5:38, etc. In doing so, he did not wish to forbid judges from punishing such acts of mischief, which must be rebuked according to justice, so that the offended may be protected.</margin>

<column-break/>

18. And when men strive together, and one strikes the other with a stone or with a fist, so that he does not die but lies in bed:
19. If he rises again so that he may walk back and forth outside on his staff, then he who struck him shall be innocent; except that he shall pay for his loss of time and shall cause him to be thoroughly healed.
20. And if anyone strikes his servant or his maid with a rod so that they die under his hand, he shall surely be punished <note>original: "gerochen," literally "avenged"</note>.
21. However, if he survives for a day or two, he shall not be punished, for he is his money.
22. And when men quarrel and strike a pregnant woman so that her fruit departs from her, but no further harm happens, he shall be punished with a fine, as the woman's husband shall lay upon him; and he shall pay it through the judges.
23. But if any harm happens, then you shall give life for life,
24. Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,
25. Burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
26. And when someone strikes his servant or his maid in the eye and destroys it, he shall let them go free for the sake of the eye.
27. And if he knocks out a tooth of his servant or his maid, he shall let them go free for the sake of the tooth.
28. And

<margin>v. 20. 21. If someone struck his servant dead in a fit of cruelty, he was punished with death as a murderer, for he had killed a human being. But if he had done too much in his discipline such that the servant died only a day later, it was reckoned as his money or property that he had lost. This also served to indict the servitude of sin, by which we have, as it were, lost the noble essence of human nature. This has a different status today, where no one has such power over his servant or subject that he can...</margin>

<meta>This page continues the civil laws from the previous section. It concludes Chapter 21, which deals with injuries caused by animals and negligence, and begins Chapter 22, focusing on property crimes, specifically theft and the required restitution.</meta>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chap. XXI.

28. If an ox gores a man or a woman so that they die, then the ox shall surely be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be held blameless.
29. But if the ox was prone to goring in the past, and it has been testified to its owner, and he has not kept it confined, and it kills a man or a woman; the ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death.
30. If a ransom <note>original: "Löse-Gelt"</note> is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed upon him.
31. Whether it has gored a son or gored a daughter, according to this same judgment it shall be done to him.

> God wanted the crime of killing to be avenged even when caused by animals, so that the offense <note>original: "Aergerniß," meaning a public scandal or stumbling block</note> might be removed from sight (see also Leviticus 20:15), and thus these acts might be all the more abhorred. Indeed, God wanted the damage caused by our livestock—and likewise by other things—to be compensated. And if it happens through negligence that someone is killed, such a person was also to be put to death. This is also to be understood regarding other animals, such as biting dogs, or wild animals kept for pleasure, and the like; for God will demand the guilt from those who kept them, or perhaps even trained them so, and did not get rid of them or have them put down.

### Chapter XXII.

->Laws concerning theft, damage, entrusted property, fornication, sorcery, idolatry, behavior toward strangers, widows, and orphans, etc.<-

If someone steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters it or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep.
2. If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no blood-guilt for him.
3. But if the sun has risen upon him, there is blood-guilt.

> Here God wanted to confirm the observation of the Eighth Commandment with penalties, so that everyone could possess their property undiminished by others. Therefore, He wanted to punish theft with a restitution of fivefold, fourfold, or double (if the stolen item was found immediately); and if the thief did not have the means, he was then required to work it off in servitude. By this, God intended to deter them from this vice, but did not wish to avenge it with the death penalty, because there is no comparison between earthly goods and life. Therefore, regarding the harsh death penalties often established elsewhere because the vice spreads so widely, one should proceed cautiously whenever the stolen goods can be somewhat replaced by condemnation to public labor and the like.

<column-break/>

32. If the ox gores a male or female servant, he shall give to their master thirty silver shekels, and the ox shall be stoned.
33. And if someone opens a pit, or if someone digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it:
34. The owner of the pit shall make restitution; he shall give the money back to its owner, but the carcass shall be his.
35. And if one person’s ox gores another’s ox so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and divide the money from it, and also divide the carcass.
36. Or if it was known that the ox was prone to goring in the past, and its owner did not keep it confined: he shall surely restore an ox for an ox, and the carcass shall be his.

> v. 32. **Thirty silver shekels**) The valuation of a servant at 30 pieces of silver also happened to our Savior through God's wonderful providence at the hands of the high priests: Matthew 26:15. By this, their disparaging contempt was made known (Isaiah 53:3), as He also willed to take the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and become a servant of God and of men (Isaiah 52:13, Luke 22:27, John 13:5).
> v. 33. **Ox or donkey**) From this ox or donkey, the Savior took His parable against the "tender" saints and legalistic zealots, the Pharisees, who wanted to take offense at Him and made a scandal of the fact that He performed works of love on the Sabbath, despising the law as a Sabbath-breaker. Yet they themselves were nothing but blind leaders who, despite all their apparent zeal, led poor people away from the true Sabbath of soul-rest and into the pit of destruction.

He shall make full restitution. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.
4. If the stolen animal is found alive in his hand, whether it be ox, donkey, or sheep, he shall restore double.
5. If

<margin>v. 3. **He shall be sold**) The court compelled him to be the servant of the one from whom he stole.</margin>
> Such a person had to serve for six years and work off the principal sum of the stolen goods. He could not gain anything for himself with his six-year service but served the master merely for what he had stolen. The master had to wait for the double, fourfold, or fivefold payment until the thief perhaps came into better means after gaining his freedom. If the one from whom he stole did not wish to keep the poor thief as a servant, he could sell him to someone else. This was done privately, however, so that the thief would not be utterly shamed. If such a man had a wife and children, the master who took him as a servant had to provide them with food, clothing, and free housing, though they did not serve him; and the master must not rule over such a servant with rigor and could also release him earlier if he wished.

<meta>This page continues the civil laws found in Exodus 22, specifically focusing on restitution for property damage, theft, and the handling of entrusted goods. It also provides a theological and linguistic commentary on the use of God's name in legal proceedings and the role of judges.</meta>

**Chapter XXII. The Second Book of Moses.**

**5.** When someone allows a field or vineyard to be grazed over, by letting his livestock into it so that it grazes another’s field; he shall make restitution from the best of his own field and from the best of his own vineyard.
**6.** When a fire breaks out and catches in the thorns, so that a stack of grain, or the standing grain, or the field is consumed; then he who lit the fire shall make full restitution.
**7.** When someone gives money or goods to his neighbor for safekeeping, and it is stolen from that man’s house; if the thief is found, he shall restore it twofold.
**8.** If the thief is not found, then the master of the house shall be brought before the gods <note>The German text uses "Götter" (gods) to translate the Hebrew "Elohim," which in this legal context refers to the judges acting as God's representatives.</note>, to see whether he has laid his hand upon his neighbor's goods.

<margin>
Regarding how one might proceed more leniently in cases of theft—such as when a person steals out of great need simply to satisfy hunger—or how one might deal more harshly when a person already has plenty yet becomes unfaithful with a neighbor's goods entrusted to them: in such a case, to avoid shame, they must restore it sevenfold (meaning much more than the original). One may read of this in Proverbs 6:30, 31.
It then requires a Christian wisdom on the part of the judges to determine how such injustice, which is so common to the natural man, might be hindered in every way, so that everyone remains free from harm.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 8. **Whether**) To whom the word "whether" <note>original: "ob"</note> does not properly express the matter or is too obscure; they may substitute "if." The Hebrew word also has this meaning when it stands with a negative, as seen in 1 Kings 1:51 and Psalm 95:11, compared with Hebrews 3:18. Then it will become much more evident that a sign of an oath is contained here. It is common for an oath to be understood where one or more words are missing and omitted. If one deemed it necessary to insert an addition for completion, it could consist of the words "to swear," just as Jerome <note>The Latin translator of the Vulgate.</note> and the Greek translators expressed it according to the similarity in the 11th verse.
</margin>

<margin>
This gives us cause to note with what fear and reverence one should take or use an oath. Scripture prescribes here an incomplete form of speech in the expression of an oath; just as those who speak out of fear are accustomed to leave out one word or another while speaking. And it primarily omits such words that proclaim evil, such as those indicating curses, which are commonly understood within oaths. Should this not rightly teach us to avoid all curses and evil wishes against ourselves and others, and to suppress them under a good name, or rather to sweeten them with some other words, instead of pronouncing them roundly and clearly? For God Himself, when He swears, uses broken and imperfect speech, under which the rest must be understood, Psalm 95:11.
</margin>

<column-break/>

**9.** In every case of trespass, whether it concerns an ox, a donkey, a sheep, clothing, or anything lost, of which someone says, "This is mine," the case of both parties shall come before the gods. Whomever the gods condemn shall restore twofold to his neighbor.
**10.** When someone gives his neighbor a donkey, or an ox, or a sheep, or any livestock for safekeeping, and it dies, or is injured, or is driven away so that no one sees it:
**11.** Then an oath to the LORD shall stand between them both, as to whether he has not laid his hand on his neighbor's goods; and the owner shall accept it, so that he does not have to make restitution.
**12.** But if it was indeed stolen from him, then he shall make restitution to its owner.
**13.** But if it was indeed torn to pieces, then he shall bring testimony of it; he shall not restore that which was torn.
**14.** But when someone borrows something from his neighbor, and it is injured or dies while its owner is not with it; then he shall surely make restitution.
**15.** But if its owner is with it, then he shall not make restitution. If it was hired for a wage, then it is covered by the wage.
**16.** And

<margin>
v. 9. **Gods**) God has attributed His name "God" (Elohim) also to the authorities, because they are to exercise the office of judge (which otherwise belongs to Him alone) over their neighbor according to His will. Thus, the name "Lord" (Adon) is also applied to men (Genesis 45:8, 9; 1 Kings 22:17), because God wishes to entrust authority to men for the governing of their neighbor. However, the name "LORD" (Jehovah) is nowhere given to any creature, because God alone is and remains the origin and sustainer of all created beings.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 10. 11. Since the oath to the LORD required by a judge is intended to make an end of strife (Hebrews 6:16), the judge must weigh this well in the fear of God. He must strive to ensure that while injustice is detected and punished in every way, perjury—and thus the dishonoring of God's name—is prevented among ignorant men.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 12-15. When someone neglects the goods entrusted to them by their neighbor, it is right that they should compensate for the damage. But if it perishes through no fault of their own, then one must not be an unjust, greedy Laban, who nevertheless demanded such from his pious son-in-law <note>Refers to the biblical story of Jacob and Laban in Genesis 31:39.</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
In general, authorities should also guard themselves against over-taxing the poor too harshly, and others should be inclined to help them in their need, so that they do not provoke the poor to steal (Proverbs 30:9). The hoarding of treasures also gives occasion for this (Matthew 6:19). See also Ephesians 4:28; 1 Thessalonians 4:6.
</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXII.

16. And if someone seduces a virgin who is not betrothed, and lies with her; he shall surely marry her and provide her with a bride-price <note>original: "Morgengabe" – a gift traditionally given by a husband to his bride on the morning after the wedding, here serving as a marriage settlement.</note>.
17. But if her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall weigh out money according to the bride-price for virgins.
18. You shall not allow a sorceress to live.
19. Whoever lies with an animal shall surely be put to death.
20. Whoever sacrifices to any gods, except to the LORD alone; he shall be devoted to destruction <note>original: "verbannt" – this refers to the Hebrew concept of 'herem,' where something is set apart for destruction as an offering to God.</note>.

---

v. 16. Here, GOD intended to explain the seventh commandment and to forbid all fornication. Therefore, whoever seduced a virgin to fulfill his lust was required to marry her with the customary bride-price, which had to be given to her father, and thus take her as his wife: so that unrestrained fornication would not become common, and children would not have to bear the shame of their parents. See 1 Samuel 18:25; 5 Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> 22:28, 29. The New Testament also loathes such fornication even more. 1 Corinthians 6:13-18; Colossians 3:5, 6.
v. 17. **Weigh out money**) According to the custom of that time, which was also practiced with minted money, to ensure that the given coins were valid and had their full weight. Just as is still done today in Turkey; though they also have minted money, it is not counted out to the soldiers but weighed out to them, so that no one may complain that he received money that was too light or clipped. (a)
v. 18. This abominable sin, where a person through the delusion of Satan gives himself over to him and renounces GOD, is mentioned here in the female gender because Satan pursues them more due to weakness of understanding and a tendency toward superstition; though it otherwise also occurs among men. 3 Moses <note>Leviticus</note> 19:26, 20:27; 5 Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> 18:10, 11.
This terrifying sin is best prevented by uprooting ignorance and superstition and carefully planting the knowledge of GOD.
v. 19. This unnatural sin is also brought about through the seduction of the unclean spirit, who can incite depraved people to such disgraceful acts when they are mired in gross stupidity and lust. See 3 Moses <note>Leviticus</note> 18:23, 20:15, 16.
v. 20. **He shall be devoted to destruction**) This "banishment" likely meant nothing less than extermination by death, since even a false prophet who spoke in the name of other gods—and thus wanted to persuade people to serve false gods—had to be killed. 5 Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> 18:20.
Whoever does not confess Christ as the true GOD and the only cause of our salvation through His merit cannot be tolerated within a Christian congregation. However, to kill such a person would be against the mind of Christ, who desires faith in Him to come from free will and not from compulsion. See John 6:65, 67.
But if all those who sacrifice to their belly, to Mammon, to the world and its high status, to themselves and their own benefit, were to be cast out of today's congregations; who would remain standing? And how many would be left? Meanwhile, it is and remains a certain and settled matter that they do not belong to the congregation of Christ, nor do they have any part in Christ Himself.
(a) Busbequ. <note>Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq, a 16th-century writer known for his letters about the Ottoman Empire</note> in the 3rd Letter, page 294.

21. And you shall not wrong a stranger, nor oppress him: for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.
22. You shall not afflict any widows or orphans.
23. If you afflict them in any way, and they then cry out to me in any way; I will surely hear their cry.
<margin>Exodus 3:7; James 5:4.</margin>
24. And my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall be widows, and your children orphans.
25. If you lend money to my people, to the poor among you, you shall not behave like a usurer toward him; you shall not charge him interest.
26. If you take your neighbor's garment as a pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down.
27. For that is his only covering: it is his garment for his skin; in what else shall he lie down? Therefore, it shall happen that when he cries to me, I will hear; for I am gracious.

<meta>Catchword: 28. The</meta>

---

v. 21, 22. GOD specifically calls Himself a Father to the orphans and a Judge for the widows (Psalm 68:5), who will take them in when others forsake them. The believers can also apply this to themselves, as they sometimes fall into such abandonment, internally and externally, that no one wants to take them in, and they are pressed by everyone as strangers. See John 14:18, 16:33.
v. 23, 24. Truly, all injustice, violence, and cunning practiced against weak, lowly, and defenseless persons—among whom widows and orphans are specifically included—is a sin that cries to heaven, which can bring nothing but wrath and a curse upon its authors.
For in such sins, the extreme malice and audacity of nature rule so openly that it displays and expresses itself most clearly through them.
v. 25-27. GOD wants mercy to be shown to the poor, who are to be our members in the spiritual body of His people, and that one should not burden them with usury when they borrow something for their necessity. See 3 Moses <note>Leviticus</note> 25:37; 5 Moses <note>Deuteronomy</note> 23:19; Psalm 15:5; which is also the will of Christ in Matthew 5:42 and Luke 6:35.
But when a neighbor uses our money to create trade and profit, then a rate of interest moderated by the authorities is indeed permitted: because it is a type of purchase, and one is entitled to a fair annual payment for its use...

28. You shall not revile the gods <note>The German "Göttern" refers to the Hebrew *elohim*, which can mean God, gods, or sometimes human judges acting with divine authority.</note>, and you shall not curse a ruler of your people.
29. You shall not delay the offering of your dry and your wet fruits. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.

v. 28. We should not become hostile toward the authorities, even if they perhaps rule against us in legal disputes in a way we did not expect—as everyone is prone to favor their own cause. Likewise, we should not resist them during times of hardship: for in such things there is often a hidden judgment of God, which one can better turn away through sighs to God than by grumbling against superiors, or which one must simply bear. See 1 Samuel 8:11–18; Ecclesiastes 10:20; Acts 23:5.
v. 29. **Your dry and your wet fruits**) According to the letter <note>literally "according to the literal Hebrew sense"</note>, it says "your fullness and your tears": by which nothing can be more fittingly understood than the dry fruits, which are either in their full ripeness or which fill the sack—as one is accustomed to call such things "sack-fruits" because they are packed into sacks and brought in them—while the other signifies the wet fruits, such as must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> and oil.
**Not delay**) Here one should also honor the Lord in His servants; not withholding the designated maintenance of firstfruits and tithes from them, or forcing them to have to beg for it, thereby delaying it. See Proverbs 3:9, 10, where both types of fruit from the barn and the winepress are mentioned.
**The firstborn**) The firstborn of humans and livestock was already dealt with above in Chapter 13:2, 12; except that here...

## The XXIII. Chapter.

->Laws concerning judges, feasts, and other matters:<-
->The commanded destruction of the Canaanites.<-

---

1. You shall not accept a false report: You shall not join your hand with a wicked man to be a malicious witness.
2. You shall not follow the crowd to do evil, and you shall not speak in a dispute so that you turn aside after the crowd to pervert justice.
3. You shall not favor a poor man in his legal dispute.

v. 1. Here the Lord explains the ninth commandment: that not only should every person not immediately believe everything said about their neighbor—since natural corruption is quite inclined toward suspicion and slander—but especially that judges should be wary of such accusers, so they do not immediately proceed with severity based on a one-sided claim, thereby often distressing the innocent. See Psalm 15:2, 3 and 101:4, 5.
v. 2. They shall also not let themselves be swayed by the great multitude to carry out their evil intentions, for the crowd is almost always opposed to the truth and its witnesses: just as Pilate, against his better knowledge, allowed himself to be swayed by the multitude toward the condemnation of the Savior. Matthew 27:24 etc. For it is a perverse political wisdom to think one must give in to the great crowd to maintain public peace. Better it is said: *Let justice be done, though the world perish!* <note>original: "Fiat justitia, & pereat mundus!"</note> Justice must be upheld, even if the world were to go under! Here one should learn to rely on God, who will stand by the right.
v. 3. In times of need, one should take care of the poor to help them: but in matters concerning outward justice, one shall respect no person, whether rich or poor, but judge only according to the law, and thus also help the rich against the poor if the law requires it: Leviticus 19:15. Otherwise, however, one must also not let the poor be oppressed by the rich.

<column-break/>

30. So you shall also do with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother, on the eighth day you shall give it to me.
31. And you shall be holy people to me: therefore you shall eat no meat that is torn in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.

v. 30. ...it is added that this should not be brought before the eighth day, so that it might first have some strength. For this is the meaning of the words:
**On the 8th day**) Not that it must be brought exactly on the 8th day, but certainly later; just not earlier.
v. 31. They should also observe their purity in food, so that they were not allowed to eat a torn animal, or one that had died on its own; because rot could very quickly set in; and also, the cruelty by which it perished should be an abomination to them. See Leviticus 22:8; Ezekiel 44:31.

4. If you meet your enemy’s ox or his donkey going astray, you shall surely lead it back to him.
5. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying under its burden, would you refrain from helping him? You shall certainly stop to assist him.
<margin>Philippians 2:4.</margin>
6. You...

One should show oneself helpful toward one's neighbor's livestock in its distress, even if that person were our enemy, and even if he is not of our people or faith, so as to suppress all malice of the heart and to show mercy even to the animal. Deuteronomy 22:4; Proverbs 12:10.
This practice and demonstration of actual love, which must be in the heart, toward the enemy, was thus already imposed by God on His people in the Old Testament, and He required it with such seemingly minor circumstances in such outward signs.
This instruction, as small as it might seem, clearly shows us how even the smallest service of love, shown to enemies from a sincere heart, truly has a secret blessing and entry into their heart, and will prove in time that one has not followed God in vain.
It is something uncommonly noble and a particularly great wisdom when one is diligent in encountering those of an opposing mind with such services of love, even unremarked, and neglects no opportunity to soften their hard spirit thereby, and so in time to heap burning coals upon their head, through which love may also be kindled in them. Romans 12:20, 21.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII.

6. You shall not subvert the rights of your poor in their legal disputes.
7. Stay far away from false matters; and do not put to death the innocent and the righteous: for I will not hold a wicked man to be righteous. <margin>1 Kings 8:32. Proverbs 17:15.</margin>
8. Furthermore, you shall take no bribe. For a bribe blinds those who have sight and subverts the words of the righteous.
9. And you shall not oppress a stranger: for you have experienced how a stranger feels, since you were strangers in the land of Egypt. <margin>Deuteronomy 10:18.</margin>
10. And for six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield.
11. But in the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, so that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave behind, the wild animals in the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard and your olive grove.
12. Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest: so that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your maidservant and the stranger may be refreshed.

---

<margin>v. 6, 7. Judges should be diligent to ensure that no innocent person is oppressed by others—and even less so by the judges themselves. Therefore, they should also guard their hearts and hands against bribes, which cloud the intellect and subtly steer the mind; natural men, who do not trust the merit of their own cause, believe they can win over the judge with such things. The godly, however, should trust in GOD, who will stand by them and bring justice to light in His own time. Psalm 37:5, 6; Deuteronomy 16:19; Proverbs 17:8, 23.</margin>
<margin>v. 8. **Blinds**) That is, it brings such disorder that they deviate from what is right and wander into crooked, tangled paths.</margin>
He who is blinded can neither recognize a distinction nor a sound judgment in any matter.
<margin>v. 9. The LORD remembers the strangers so often (as in Chapter 22:21, etc.) so that no malice should be shown toward them, especially when they have been forced to leave their fatherland for the sake of conscience <note>This likely refers to religious refugees, a significant group in the 17th and 18th centuries</note>: these people should also not be burdened with common taxes, since they must support themselves by the work of their hands or consume what little they have, and they possess no house or property of their own, which is why common taxes are properly carried.</margin>
<margin>v. 10–12. This seventh year of rest is dealt with at greater length in Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15, where the mystery <note>German: *Geheimniß*—often used in this period to refer to a deeper spiritual or prophetic meaning</note> of it can be further investigated.</margin>
Thus, the fourth commandment regarding the Sabbath is very often reinforced, because GOD wanted this observed as a special sign of the mystery of the great coming rest: primarily for the soul under the New Testament, and then for both body and soul in Christ's glorious kingdom. The LORD wishes to sanctify and prepare us for this, as the true refreshment of the soul is to be found there for those groaning under the burdens and yoke of spiritual Egypt. See Ezekiel 20:12; Matthew 11:29; Hebrews 4:9, 10, 11.

<column-break/>

13. And in all things that I have said to you, you shall be watchful: and you shall make no mention of the names of other gods; they shall not be heard in your mouth.
14. Three times a year you shall hold a festival for me.
15. The Feast of Unleavened Bread you shall keep: seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time in the month of Abib. For in that month you marched out of Egypt. Also, no one shall appear before my face empty-handed.
16. And the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, which you have sown in the field: and the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you have gathered in your labor from the field. <margin>Chapter 34:22.</margin>

<meta>catchword: 17. Three</meta>

---

<margin>v. 13. This command—that Israel should utterly root out the memory of idols and their service among them, to the point that they should not even take their names into their mouths—reproves modern Christianity. Today, scholars and others not only diligently investigate pagan matters, but the names of pagan gods constantly appear in poems and plays; this betrays the pagan mindset of such people. However, the time will come when all human prestige in the church, which diminishes Christ, will be rooted out: this is the aim of the prophecies in Psalm 16:4 and Hosea 2:17 or 19.</margin>
<margin>v. 14. **Three times - Festival**) One can well judge that these three high festivals were established for the honor of the Triune GOD; for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which was linked with the Passover Lamb, represented the benefits of Christ; the Feast of Harvest represented the outpouring of the Holy Spirit; and the Feast of Ingathering—which they held at the end of the spiritual year but at the start of the civil year (which began at the creation of the world)—represented GOD the Father, the origin and conclusion of all benefits for body and soul.</margin>
<margin>v. 15. **No one shall appear before my face empty-handed**) They were to come with their gifts, because GOD wished to maintain His figurative worship <note>referring to the ceremonial laws of the Old Testament as "figures" or "shadows" of spiritual truths</note> through these: since they were giving to GOD from His own blessing, they should take comfort in this when they showed their duty in it. Proverbs 3:9, 10. And so they appeared before GOD’s face (v. 17 and Ch. 34:23, 24; Isaiah 1:12) and looked again upon GOD’s face in His holy service (Psalm 63:3), until we shall one day look upon Him in righteousness in eternity. Psalm 17:15.</margin>
v. 16. **The Feast of Harvest of the firstfruits**) Pentecost.
**The Feast of Ingathering**) Tabernacles.
**At the end of the year**) GOD acts as an honorable father of the house, whose children must pray before and after the meal. (a)

### Chapter XXIII. The Second Book of Moses.

17. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the face of the Ruler, the Lord.
18. (o) You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened / and the fat of my feast-offering shall not remain overnight until morning. <margin>(a) chapter 34:25.</margin>
19. The firstfruits of the first produce of your land you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat while it is still in its mother's milk.
20. Behold, I send an angel before you / that he may guard you on the way / and bring you to the place I have prepared.

---

v. 17. **Shall appear)** on foot.
**All your males)** Exempted from this were the lame / the deaf / the mute / the blind / and those who had only one eye / the sick / the elderly / the simple-minded / as well as those who were too delicate to walk so far; as well as servants not yet set free. However, this did not exclude those who were far from Jerusalem; as <note>Nicolaus of Lyra (c. 1270–1349), a prominent Franciscan biblical exegete.</note> Lyra argues.
v. 19. The commandment not to boil the young goat while it is still in its mother's milk corresponds with Chapter 22:30. Just as it could not be brought as an offering before the eighth day / so they should not consume it for their own benefit before that time: especially since it is a form of cruelty to take young animals away from their mothers so quickly, for whom they have a very tender love.
v. 20. Here, Christ is emphatically described as the **Angel of the Covenant**, who was previously called the Angel of the LORD, but shortly thereafter called God the LORD himself; he who appeared in the burning bush / and went before the people in the pillar of cloud and fire. Chapter 3:2, etc. Chapter 13:21 and 14:19. He was to bring them into the promised land of Canaan / and they were to be obedient to him in everything / and stand in awe of him. For God’s Name was within his innermost being / he who knew God most intimately / in his most inward communion with Him / and in whom God’s attributes were entirely essential / and would also be seen outwardly when he appeared in the flesh. John 14:9, etc. This Angel is to be distinguished from the created angel whom God intended to send later / after the sin of idolatry with the golden calf had been committed. Chapter 33:2. For
All circumstances make it clear enough that no created angel is meant here / though many are of that opinion.
If <note>The Socinians were a rationalist Christian sect that denied the pre-existence and full divinity of Christ.</note> Enjedinus and other Socinians wish to object here and say that he who is sent by another must surely be lower and lesser than the one who sent him; one can certainly grant them this in a certain sense, if only they knew how to distinguish between the divinity of Christ and his **heavenly humanity**, which he possessed even before the foundation of the world; according to which the Father is indeed greater / and indeed appears all the more glorious in His greatness alongside the majesty of this magnificent Being / who is no creature. This glory would not shine forth so magnificently if one merely said that the immeasurable, infinite Father of our Lord Jesus Christ was greater than the man Christ Jesus, insofar as he was viewed merely according to his <gloss>frail humanity assumed from Mary in time</gloss>. This explanation resolves many difficulties. Through this heavenly God-Man, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ has accomplished everything forever / and still accomplishes it / and will also accomplish all future great works through him / as through his Angel and Messenger / who is God and Man.
God gives us this Angel at all times, as long as we have need of him. He is the leader who guards us in our ways. However, he can only bring us into the place prepared for us: after that, God Himself is our leader.

<column-break/>

21. Therefore, take heed before his face, and obey his voice, and do not provoke him. For he will not forgive your transgression: because my name is in his innermost being.
22. But if you shall fully obey his voice, and do all that I say; then I will be an enemy to your enemies, and distress those who distress you. <margin>Genesis 12:3.</margin>
23. When my angel goes before your face, and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites; and I will destroy them:
24. So you shall not bow down before their gods, nor serve them, and not do according to their works; instead you shall utterly tear them down, and utterly break their pillars.
25. But you shall serve the LORD your God: then he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from your midst.
26. It

---

Here, the first and second commandments are more fully impressed upon them as the occasion arises / that they should neither revere the idols of the Canaanites / nor tolerate their images and pillars in the land / but rather tear them down and utterly destroy them: then they would also expect every blessing and the turning away of all evil from the true GOD; who would gradually drive out their enemies through all kinds of judgments / and thus put them in possession of the land according to its boundaries / as he promised to Abraham, Genesis 15:18, where the great river Euphrates is mentioned by name / of which boundaries more is discussed in Numbers 34.
v. 21. The LORD commands us to honor this leader / and to obey him / and not to provoke him; for His Name is in him: which means as much as: he represents His person / he carries His word / and works through His power. Yes,
**In his innermost being)** is as much as "in his essence." But God’s Name is God Himself / as <note>David Kimchi (1160–1235), a medieval Jewish rabbi and grammarian.</note> R. D. Kimchi says regarding the 89th Psalm: <note>original Hebrew: "הוא שמו ושמו הוא"</note> **God is His Name, and His Name is God.**
v. 23. **My Angel)** Through the transposition of the letters in <note>original: "מלאכי" (Malachi - my angel/messenger)</note> it is quite elegantly found who this angel shall be; namely <note>original: "מיכאל" (Michael)</note> **Michael**: as <note>Johann Reuchlin (1455–1522), a German humanist and scholar of Greek and Hebrew.</note> Reuchlinus (a) shows.
**Goes -- before)** This is repeated once more to better show that guidance is necessary as long as one has not yet reached the promised land / which signifies the state of rest in God alone.

370 The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII.

26. There shall be nothing that miscarries or is barren <gloss>(a)</gloss> in your land: I will fulfill the number of your days.

27. I will send my terror before you / and make all the people terrified / to whom you shall come / and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.

28. And I will send hornets before you / which shall drive out the Hivites and the Canaanites and the Hittites before you.

29. I will not drive them out before you in one year: lest the land become desolate / and the wild animals multiply against you.

30. Little by little I will drive them out before you; until you become fruitful / and possess the land.

According to the letter <note>literal interpretation</note>, this refers specifically to the people of Israel under the Old Covenant / both in its promises and reminders: but according to the spirit <note>mystical or allegorical interpretation</note>, there lies within it a foundation / which binds the people of GOD and His Israel for all time / also promising much good to them under the guidance of the Holy Spirit / especially at the end of days / when an end shall be made of the miscarriages of darkness / and the lowly and small Zion shall become a fruitful mother of children; the Lord will also give long life to His obedient children. Then their enemies will have to crawl away / and not dare to show themselves. And who are these? Canaanites and Hittites are not as bad as the spirit of the Antichrist / who sets himself in the middle of the church of God. But even this is not only to be sought outside of us and near to us. There are yet other wild animals / which are closer to us. The abomination of desolation is in our very midst / from which we must cleanse ourselves. Who will deliver us from such misery / if God does not help us? If He does not make our wilderness into a fruitful field; if He does not drive out the ancient inhabitants of the land / the ungodly thoughts and the heathen senses and lusts / which unlawfully possess the earth of our heart / the land of His own property.

<column-break/>

<margin>(a) Deuteronomy 11:24.</margin>

So this is now what the LORD wants from you, O Israel! even unto this day: Make no friendship with those heathen lusts! There shall be an eternal enmity between Israel and Amalek! The body of sin must depart: land and body must be sanctified to the LORD. So the LORD Himself will dwell within your borders / and establish His peace in you for your eternal security!

v. 31. **Philistine-Sea)** The geographers <note>original: "Geographi"</note> call it the Syrian and Phoenician Sea. This was to be the border from the west.

**Desert)** This refers to the desert of Arabia / as well as Mount Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, which are so named / because both were full of forests, wild animals, and wildernesses.

v. 32. But how Christians should carry themselves in their various parties and ceremonies / there the fear of GOD is required / to call upon Him for divine wisdom / so that one might behave according to His divine will / neither to do damage to the service in spirit and in truth / nor to act against Christian tolerance / where such would be necessary.

# The XXIV. Chapter.
-> The Establishment of the Covenant and the Drawing Near of the Elders to GOD. <-

1. And He said to Moses: Come up to the LORD / you and Aaron / Nadab and Abihu / and seventy of the elders in Israel / and worship from afar.

v. 1. **Seventy of the elders)** It seems all the overseers / over 10 and 50 and 100 and 1000 / had the name of the elders: from whom Moses again chose 70 / from the most gifted men / who administered the government of the people particularly with him / and who may have been taken according to the number of the 70 souls / who moved into Egypt / or whatever other mystery may be hidden in this number seven. At once they were to be regarded as the firstfruits of the people / and be deemed worthy of a special glory in the beholding of God / for the strengthening of their faith in the GOD of Israel. But they presumably had to remain standing in the middle of the mountain / and Moses alone approached / as the prefiguring mediator / to God / and received all the laws of which mention was made in the three previous chapters / and what is mentioned hereafter concerning the Tabernacle.

v. 2. **Moses alone)** Aaron had indeed also been on the mountain; which is a great progression in view of the rest of the people: but to reach the summit belonged only to Moses; because no other had reached such a high state / nor such a great pure love. He was the well / from which the spring unburdened itself for the benefit of the others.

### Chapter XXIV. The Second Book of Moses.

<margin>verse 3. After Moses had revealed the laws of GOD to the people / he now demanded covenant-obedience from the people / and received from them a unanimous promise and vow of the same.</margin>
The spirit of the people was quickly willing to promise obedience to the commandments of GOD / and did not consider the weakness of the flesh / in view of which they should have called upon GOD for His Spirit to grant them obedience in His ways.

<margin>verse 4. Moses wrote the laws / which he had received up to this point / and which are contained in Chapters 20, 21, 22, and 23 / in which the sum of the entire civil, spiritual, and moral law is comprised / into a book / which in verse 7 is called the Book of the Covenant / and then made preparations for the very solemn sacrifice / for which GOD had promised to bring them out of Egypt to this place, Chapter 3:12, 18. There He intended to renew the covenant of their faithful fathers with them / as a now great nation / and to accept them as His Covenant-People.</margin>
He writes down the words of GOD; because he had to leave them behind for posterity. GOD lets His servants write down what He reveals to them of His holy and hidden truths; so that they may remain / and be useful to many.

<margin>Built an altar)</margin> As a symbol of the LORD / who is one party of the future covenant-partners.

<margin>12 pillars)</margin> Which were to represent the people / as the other party. These 12 pillars may have represented those souls especially grounded in the spirit of faith / and thus also the elders from all the 12 tribes / who were to shine before others with a good example in such constancy of faith. See Galatians 2:9.

<margin>verse 5. The young men are considered to be the firstborn / who assisted the fathers with the sacrifices / in place of whom the priests from the tribe of Aaron were later accepted; and for the lesser services, the rest from the tribe of Levi / while all Israel was entirely excluded from the sacrificial service because of the sin of idolatry. Ezekiel 20:26.</margin>
Moses sends these young men from Israel to offer burnt offerings and peace offerings to GOD.

For this is what those souls must do. The offering of the youngest <note>referring to those new to the spiritual path</note> is nothing but peace and sweetness. But it is not so with those souls who have already progressed: they must offer burnt offerings. Just as there are two kinds of children of grace: some who are newcomers in the spirit and the way; and others who, through their rigorous journeying in that same way, have become like children again: thus Moses distinguishes two kinds of sacrifice: one of peace / belonging to the first children: and the other of the burnt offering / which belongs to the latter.

<column-break/>

6. And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins / and the other half of the blood he sprinkled on the altar.

7. And he took the Book of the Covenant / and read it in the hearing of the people; and they said: All that the LORD has spoken, we will do and be obedient.

8. Then Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people / and said: Behold, this is the blood of the covenant / which the LORD has made with you concerning all these words.

9. Then— <note>catchword for the next page</note>

<margin>verses 6-8. Hereupon the covenant was made with Israel over these sacrifices; and indeed through their blood; with half of which the altar / and at the same time also the Book of the Law / which perhaps lay upon the altar / according to Hebrews 9:19, was sprinkled; and with the other half the people / as some believe / upon the 12 pillars / which represented the people: but it may also have happened toward the people themselves. Whereby / as Paul again reports more regarding these circumstances / the blood was mixed with water / and the sprinkling itself was performed with a sprinkling-brush of wool and hyssop.</margin>
This showed / however / that no forgiveness of sins was to be expected without the shedding of blood / and that this was the blood of the only true propitiatory sacrifice <term>atonement</term> of JESUS Christ / with which He Himself was sprinkled; but the power of it has come upon the believers / who are sprinkled with it in the spirit. See 1 Peter 1:2. Hebrews 9:12-22. Therefore Christ called His blood, which was now to be shed, the blood of the New Testament / which was shed for many for the forgiveness of sins. Matthew 26:28. And these are only the truly holy ones / who make the covenant with GOD over this sacrifice, Psalm 50:5 / as it is so appropriately called; who thus let their hearts be cleansed by this blood from all their sins. 1 John 1:7.

<margin>verses 7, 8. When Moses read the Law / he perceived / that the people promised to keep it with great haste and boldness of heart. But as an experienced leader, he knew well / that some self-conceit was hidden herein: namely, that they relied on their own strength / and did not carry sufficient mistrust toward themselves / to expect all their faithfulness from GOD alone. Therefore he sprinkled them with the blood that was in the basins; because this was the image of the blood of Christ: to instruct them / that all necessary strength / to fulfill the faith / depended on this blood; and that they must be washed and clothed with the same: further assuring them / that every covenant between GOD and man would be confirmed through this blood / without which no covenant could exist.</margin>
One sees therefore / how the nature of the covenant / which the LORD made here with the people of Israel / was entirely and completely figurative / and represented and promised the essence of the future goods of the Covenant of Grace under many kinds of dark shadows and images. Therefore it was also imperfect / and had to grow old or be abolished / when the time was fulfilled / and the essence of the New Covenant presented itself; which is not made with the Jewish people alone / but now invites all nations to a feast of fat things and marrow / and presents to them the true mediator JESUS Christ for reconciliation through faith in His blood: through whom not only words of the covenant are read to be kept / but also grace and truth are abundantly communicated for obedience.

In the meantime, the power of this covenant and blood is nevertheless not yet so manifest / as it shall one day be and is to be expected in the renewal of all things / for which the believers long day and night in secret. For the time comes / says the LORD <gloss>(a)</gloss> / when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah. But now we do not yet see / that all of this is truly manifest and fulfilled / in its fullness: but it has only been fulfilled in its dawn and as a prototype of the still further fulfillment / just as everything else was / at the dawn of the New Testament / and is cited in this view in Hebrews 8:8, etc. But it will first be rightly fulfilled / when the fullness of the Gentiles shall come in / and also all Israel shall be saved. Romans 11:25, 26.
