# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXIV.

9. After this, Moses went up, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel.
10. And they saw the God of Israel: and under His feet it was like a work of square sapphire stones, and like the appearance of the heavens when it is clear. <margin>Ezekiel 1:26. Revelation 4:3.</margin>
11. And He did not lay His hand upon the nobles <note>original: *Ausgesonderte*, meaning those set apart or chosen</note> of the children of Israel. And when they had beheld God, they ate and drank.

<note>
Following this, these 75 persons—chosen from all of Israel—go up the mountain again and are deemed worthy of beholding the God of Israel. They did not merely see Him, but were able to gaze upon and contemplate Him from nearby, as indicated by the two Hebrew words used here: *ra’u* <note>original: ראו - they saw</note> and *chazu* <note>original: חזו - they beheld/gazed</note>. Exactly what form they saw is not explicitly stated, yet it is likely that He took the form of a man (a), just as the prophets saw Him. Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne (Chapter 6). Ezekiel saw the glory of the God of Israel above the wondrous image of the four faces, which was undoubtedly a visible manifestation of God (Chapters 1, 10:19-20). Daniel saw Him even more clearly as the Ancient of Days, whose garment was white as snow and the hair of His head like pure wool, sitting upon a throne to which one like a Son of Man came, to whom all dominion under heaven was given (Daniel 7:9, 13-14). Through these accounts, the Father and the Son are clearly understood. Therefore, the pious and learned Coccejus <note>Johannes Coccejus, a 17th-century Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology"</note> says of this passage: They saw Him like a man, standing on a floor of precious stones, or like a bright carbuncle. This is how Isaiah saw the Lord (Chapter 6) and Ezekiel (Chapters 1 and 10), as the Jews also acknowledge. This was a foretaste of the Incarnation (John 1:14). Thus He is expressly called "the man who is God the Lord on high" (1 Chronicles 17:17, 2 Samuel 7:19). In this way, we shall behold His face in righteousness and be satisfied, when we awake, with His likeness (Psalm 17:15), for we shall see Him as He is (1 John 3:2) and know even as we are known (1 Corinthians 13:12).
When some believers suspect something essential in this, they nevertheless recognize that this is not an earthly form like ours, but something heavenly and spiritual. Since God is a Spirit, He cannot be seen with earthly eyes, nor can glorified bodies be seen, unless God and they choose to reveal themselves—as happened here and as Christ did after His resurrection. One should not take offense at this as if it diminished God, for Christ retains the human form for all eternity, and His divine majesty loses nothing by it.
v. 10. *Like a work of sapphire stones*) By this, some understand the pavement upon which the Son of God revealed Himself, appearing like sapphire tiles or stones shaped like bricks.
v. 11. That the elders ate and drank here seems to have been a heavenly meal prepared for them by angels, just as the believers in heaven will sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8:11).
(a) So also Osiander in this place <note>Latin: *h. l.* [hoc loco]</note>. Herberger, *Magnalia*, no. 28. Compare Momma, *On the state of the Church under the Patriarchs* <note>Latin: *de statu Ecclesiae sub Patriarchis*</note>, Vol. 1, Book 2, Chapter 8, Section 37.
</note>

<column-break/>

12. And the Lord said to Moses: Come up to me on the mountain and remain there, that I may give you the stone tablets (a), and the law and the commandment which I have written, to teach them. <margin>2 Corinthians 3:3. (a) ch. 31:18 ff.</margin>

15. When Moses came up the mountain, the cloud covered the mountain.
16. And the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it for six days; and He called to Moses on the seventh day from the midst of the cloud.
17. And the appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a consuming fire on the peak of the mountain, in the eyes of the children of Israel. <margin>Leviticus 9:23-24.</margin>
18. And

<note>
v. 13-15. Moses was in God, but the rest of the mountain was covered in pure darkness for the others. This state is terrifying and dark to those who do not stand within it; they can hardly grasp the little that is told to them about it, regardless of how many testimonies they have, until they experience it themselves.
v. 16. The glory of the Lord dwelt on the mountain and showed itself frequently with a singular fiery glow and a burning flame, as seen in the following verse.
*The cloud covered it*) Or "them," referring to the glory which was not seen.
*6 days*) During these, Moses had to be completely still before he was allowed to hear anything from God on the 7th day.
Even though Moses had already been with God for so long and had interacted with Him in such a high manner—and God had graced him with such intimacy that one might almost doubt whether he had not already seen the divine essence for a short time in this life—he still had to remain for 6 days in hope, and as if in a purgatory <note>original: *Feg-Feuer*, literally "cleansing fire"</note>, before he could penetrate further into God and interact with Him so intimately. Oh, how very pure God is!
*On the 7th day*) In the great six "world-days" <note>A common historical-theological concept that the world's history spans six 1,000-year periods</note>, it is still dark; this darkness will be removed on the 7th greatest day by those people who reach that 7th day.
O, let holy silence be better and most highly recommended! In it, the spirit of man must be still and rest from all his own works, actions, and speculations, so that in such silence—in a spirit stripped of all things and of itself—one can hear on the 7th day, as on the Sabbath, the pure words that the Lord wishes to speak with him and His Spirit wishes to tell him.
v. 17. God can make Himself known as He pleases: and since He wishes here to instill a fear of Him in the people, He appears as a consuming fire, just as He is to the sinner who will not be able to approach such eternal heat (Hebrews 12:29, Isaiah 33:14).
</note>

# Chapter XXIV. The Second Book of Moses.

18. And Moses went into the midst of the cloud, after he had climbed the mountain:

<margin>
**He went into the midst of the clouds, after he — had climbed)** In this way, God brings the spirit of man—whom He leads to His high contemplation—ever higher and higher, and places him into a holy darkness (as in chapter 20:21), where he leaves behind all things, including himself and his own speculations, and sinks into God for union with Him. Thus, he recognizes God in His greatness, who cannot be known as He is by any man or angel. So man is brought to the realization that God is not that which he can yet recognize and grasp; rather, God far transcends all things, even all concepts, no matter how spiritual they may be. Moses and David were led to this point, and it was granted to them to look so deeply into the Tabernacle not made with hands <note>A reference to the heavenly archetype of the sanctuary mentioned in Hebrews 9:11.</note> that they were able to provide the pattern for the external Tabernacle and the Temple in Jerusalem as an image of it.
</margin>

God proceeds here in stages, both in the communication of Himself and of His graces; for He expands the capacity of the creature gradually, and not all at once, because the creature would not be able to withstand such an effect.

See how Moses does not take a single step of his own accord,
and performs everything only as God allows him to perform it;
the faithfulness that is necessary in the entire state of suffering; but especially in the state of annihilation <note>In mystical theology, "annihilation" refers to the emptying of the self to be filled with God.</note>, where one
must [follow], without getting ahead of Him, nor resisting Him.

As you descend, you ascend. O wonderful hiddenness of the divine ways! In the depths of the abyss of your nothingness, in your self-loss and sinking away, you find the mountain and the height where the glory of God dwells and is enthroned! If you practice this diligently, a great stillness will open up in your spirit of its own accord, and in that stillness, you will worship your God with silence—in the darkness of silence, as Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian famous for his writings on "Divine Darkness."</note> calls it; and He will then through the secret...

# Chapter XXV.

->The Heave-Offering, Ark, Table, and Lampstand.<-

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

2. Speak to the children of Israel, that they take for Me a heave-offering <term>Heave-offering: a type of sacrifice or gift that was ritually "heaved" or lifted up toward heaven</term>: from every man whose heart moves him willingly, you shall take My heave-offering.

3. And this is the heave-offering <margin>(a) c. 30/13.</margin> which you shall take from them: gold, and silver, and bronze,

<margin>
Here begins the very precise description of a physical sanctuary, which is indeed interrupted by the committed sin of idolatry and its consequences in Chapters 32 and 33, but thereafter its construction and erection are described at greater length until the end of the book. In this, God intended to represent His indwelling among the people of Israel—indeed, in the hearts of true Israelites—through the Angel of the Covenant, the Mediator Jesus Christ, who was to be painted before their eyes in all these images according to all His gifts and offices. These images were to represent the reality in Christ, so that the hearts of believers, both of the Old Testament and now primarily of the New Testament, might be awakened to it. Now that the reality has appeared, such images must give way as shadows; indeed, they even had to be destroyed in a violent manner since the Jews did not want to let them go, but rather willfully despised and refused to accept the true sanctuary when it appeared among them, revealing itself to be full of grace and truth (John 1:10-14). We must now strive to be such living sanctuaries, in which Christ, indeed the Triune God, may dwell with all His gifts of grace. See 2 Corinthians 6:16, Hebrews 3:6, John 14:23.

v. 2. They were to bring a voluntary heave-offering for this, both from what they had requested from the Egyptians by divine command and what they may have possessed themselves. See 2 Corinthians 8:11, 12; 9:5, 6, 7.

v. 3. It was called a "Heave-offering" because it was lifted up on high to the honor of the Lord.
</margin>

<column-break/>

and Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.

<margin>
**40 days and 40 nights)** during which He lets you experience and discover so much of His will on the mountain that you will also be able to teach others what belongs to life and a godly walk, or to true divine service. Just as Moses received so many laws, teachings, customs, and rights from God on the mountain—indeed, the entire arrangement and establishment of divine service in the Old Testament—in order to make all that known to the people and not keep it to himself alone.

So too must Christ fast 40 days and nights in the wilderness to become fit for His teaching office; there the image of the inner Tabernacle and of divine service in spirit and in truth was shown to Him, in order to instruct His own in this. Therefore, His teachings have nothing but godly virtues as their subject. And...
</margin>

and how he does not move forward through his own motion; but
very precisely according to what has been commanded him. And this is
the soul, which has died to itself, applies itself with all diligence to that which God requires of her.

Doubtless, there is something secret hidden in those 40 days and 40 nights, as Elias <note>Elijah</note> also fasted for as many days; and thus exactly the three who were together at the Transfiguration of Christ before His disciples on the mountain had a similar practice in this.

4. And blue wool, and purple wool, and scarlet wool, and fine linen yarn, and goats' hair,

5. And ram skins dyed red, and badger skins, and shittim wood <term>Shittim wood: wood from the acacia tree, known for its durability</term>;

<margin>
v. 4. The colors shall be dealt with in the following, as space does not permit it here; therefore, let us touch only briefly on the two last-translated items themselves, the
**Wool and fine linen yarn)** Which were spun from fine Egyptian flax.

It is probable that God requested such wool and linen rather than silk, because silk may not have been available in such abundance, and God also intended to look toward the anti-type, Christ, who was represented as the innocent Lamb of God in this entire sacrificial service, and as the fruit of the earth (Isaiah 4:1), with whose wool and pure linen we are to be clothed. The **sky-blue** represents heavenly wisdom; the **purple** represents the assurance of the gracious forgiveness of sins in the blood of Jesus Christ, which commonly manifests upon repentance, and thus as it were the initial righteousness; and then the **crimson** or **scarlet-high** color represents the confirmation in perfect justification attained in complete rebirth and the sealing of the Holy Spirit, from which grace a soul completely cleansed with the blood of Christ may not fall away again; for then the accusing worm of conscience is also completely decayed (see Romans 8:1); and finally, the **pure linen** can represent to us the holiness of Christ and daily renewal through His Spirit. See Isaiah 61:10, Revelation 19:8.

v. 5. The skins shall also be dealt with in the following, and so we consider here briefly the
**Shittim wood)** Jerome is said to claim <note>original: (a) Ap. Buxtorff. hist. arc. foed. c. 4. q. 1. Ursin. arboret. bibl. c. 22.</note> that this wood still grew in the Sinai desert in his time, and that it resembles the hawthorn in color and leaves; it is also such a thick, strong tree that very wide boards can be sawn from it. It is an exceedingly firm and durable wood, of unbelievable lightness and beauty; it is also found nowhere else but in this Arabian desert. This place then seems to have received its name from these trees, which is mentioned several times in Scripture.
</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.

6. **Oil for the light / spices for the anointing oil / and for the incense of sweet spices;**

<note>v. 6. 7. Regarding the spiritual meaning of these remaining materials and precious stones / this can be examined in greater detail with each piece of this sanctuary.</note>
<note>v. 8. A Sanctuary) What does this mean? Answer: Holiness. 1 Corinthians 3:17. If we remain in God / then He remains in us. Although most translators prefer to use the word "among" rather than "in."</note>
<note>Amidst/Among) This translation certainly has its place here / and can be granted based on the circumstances of the text. However, since almost all places / where the Hebrew says "in" / have been translated by many as "among"; except where they could not avoid it / and were forced to translate it as "in" : it is almost to be feared / concluded / and taken as a testimony / that people do not at all like to see or have God be as near to us / as He has promised to be / if we would build Him a sanctuary or a holy dwelling within us. Or perhaps one fears / that through such an indwelling of God one might be guilty of an inherent or indwelling holiness and righteousness : and before one will admit that / one prefers to always put it "among them."</note>
<note>The same thing happens / when it is said of Christ / that He is in His people. Galatians 3:1. Colossians 1:27. John 1:14.</note>
<note>v. 9. Pattern of the tabernacle) The dwelling was made according to a certain pattern or model and original / and was also itself a pattern. For</note>
<note>This sanctuary represents the ground and the center of the soul : which is the place of God's dwelling / in which the supersubstantial and inexpressible union takes place / and where the adorable Trinity dwells and reveals itself. One must preserve such a place for the Lord / and for that reason keep oneself free from all other things / so that He may dwell therein and reveal Himself. This holy place is for Him alone.</note>
<note>v. 10. The Ark of the Covenant was in the sanctuary; because from it the oracle of the Word of God was to come. Up until this point, God had spoken with His people as if from afar / without staying in a specific place : but in the future He intends to speak and dwell among them / and let Himself be known and heard in the sanctuary of the center-point of their souls.</note>
<note>This Ark / as the Most Holy of all the furnishings of the sanctuary / specifically represented Christ / as the Mediator of reconciliation / who is the ground of all blessings / as in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge : Colossians 2:3. Here the Shittim wood / as a species of the noblest and most durable cedars (a) / represents Christ's immovable human nature / according to which He is also a fruit of the earth. Isaiah 4:1. ### Chapter XXV. The Second Book of Moses.
<center>Verse 23. The</center>

17. **You shall also make an atonement cover <note>original: "Versöhn-Deckel"; traditionally known in English as the Mercy Seat</note> of pure gold: two and a half cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> shall be its length / and a cubit and a half its width.**

18. **And you shall make two cherubim of gold: of hammered work shall you make them / at the two ends of the atonement cover.**

19. **And make one cherub at one end on this side / and the other cherub at the other end on that side: onto the atonement cover shall you make the cherubim on its two ends.**

<margin>
v. 17. Atonement Cover) Which was meant to cover and blot out the accusation and the curse of the law; Romans 3:25, 8:3. This atonement was made powerful and pleasing especially through the divinity of the Mediator: therefore this cover had to be of pure gold. See Ephesians 1:6-7.
</margin>

This is that which is otherwise called the Mercy Seat <note>original: "Gnaden-Stuhl," literally "Grace-Chair"</note> / because the name comes from the fact that God showed and wished to show Himself merciful to the people above this cover; also, on the Day of Atonement, He was reconciled with the people by the sprinkling of blood against this cover.

The word "Mercy Seat," however, is not very suitable / because the word "Seat" / when one hears it / immediately gives a person the impression that something one sits upon is meant; this cover, however, was much more like God's footstool / and thus could rather be called the "Mercy Footstool" <note>original: "Gnaden-Schemel"</note>.

<margin>
Of Gold) As the Hebrews claim (a) it was about as thick as the palm of a hand.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 18. The two cherubim represented the angels / and also, according to some opinions, the believers. And what should hinder one from wanting to understand both / since the believers will become like the angels? Both have also desired to look into this great mystery: both the angels / 1 Peter 1:12 / to whom it was previously dark / and to whom it also had to be revealed; 1 Timothy 3:16 / as well as the believers / who previously hoped in Christ; Ephesians 1:12 / and especially the prophets among them / who sought and searched for such salvation / and also prophesied of this future grace. 1 Peter 1:10.
</margin>

<margin>
Regarding the origin of the word [Cherubim], opinions are very different / and partly very forced (b). Most among the Hebrews derive it from *Ke* [as] and *Rubia* [youths] / because they were supposedly shaped like young men. To derive this from the meaning that the angels are called God's chariot is also not subject to as many difficulties as others. <note>The commentator is referencing a Hebrew wordplay where "Cherub" sounds like "as a youth."</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Of one piece) By solid work that remains entirely together.
</margin>

23.

---

<margin>
v. 20. They were thus made so that they held their wings high toward each other / as if they wanted to fly / and spread them out / one toward the other / so that the right wing of one cherub touched the left of the other / and his left touched the other's right. Between the wings, they had their faces turned toward each other in such a way / that one did not look at the other / but both turned their faces somewhat downward.
</margin>

Pure faith and total serenity <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central term in German mysticism meaning yieldedness or resignation to God's will</note> are the two cherubim which cover the Ark of the Covenant: namely / they are the atonement cover of which God speaks. Faith covers the soul / and prevents it from examining itself / nor can it see anything of what is presented to it. Serenity likewise hides it on the other side / in that it prevents the soul from observing itself / so that it may see neither its harm nor its advantage: whereby it is then compelled to surrender itself blindly. This faith and serenity, however, face each other / just as the cherubim did there: because neither can exist without the other in a well-ordered soul; and faith agrees just as well with serenity as serenity is subject to faith.

<margin>
v. 21. On top of the ark) As a lid. Not high above the ark on the wings or hands of the cherubim: as many claim / that the ark otherwise had its own lid / and this was a golden tablet / which was held aloft above the ark by the cherubim / and was God's throne: but He rather sat upon the wings of the cherubim / and had the atonement cover as a footstool.
</margin>

And for that very reason, this was also of the same length and width as the ark / so that it might completely and exactly cover the opening at the top.

<margin>
v. 22. I will unite with you and speak with you) From this, some (a) wish to conclude / that Moses was allowed to go into the Most Holy Place as often as he wished.
</margin>

That he occasionally went in / is beyond all doubt / and can be seen in Numbers 17:4, 10 and 20:8-9.

The Lord means to say / that in the future He would make Himself heard from this center and ground of the soul / as from His oracle <note>original: "oraculo"</note> / and no longer from the [natural] faculties. The experienced will already grasp the distinction of these communions: which one will find explained further elsewhere / as much as it is possible / to give some light to such incomprehensible matters.

Through Christ, God wishes to unite with us again / so that through Him we have access to the Father. Ephesians 2:18. And through Him He also spoke with us personally in the days of His appearance in the flesh / Hebrews 1:1 / and still wishes to reveal Himself in believers as the powerful inner Word / if we would only hold ourselves rightly to Him in faith / and strive to be worthy of His indwelling by keeping His words; there Christ would certainly prove Himself effective in us / and through His Spirit lead us into all truth. John 14:23, 16:13-14.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.

23. **You shall also make a table of Shittim wood <note>Acacia wood</note>: two cubits shall be its length / and one cubit its width / and a cubit and a half its height.**

24. **And you shall overlay it with pure gold / and make a golden molding <note>original: "Krantz," meaning a wreath or crown-like border</note> around it.**

25. **And you shall make a frame for it / a handbreadth high all around / and you shall make a golden molding on its frame all around.**

26. **And you shall make four golden rings for it / and you shall put the rings on the four corners that are on its four feet.**

27. **Opposite the frame shall the rings be / as places for the poles / so that the table may be carried.**

28. **And you shall make the poles of Shittim wood / and overlay them with gold / so that the table may be carried with them.**

v. 23. The Table represented Christ once again / and now specifically as the prepared nourishment / food and refreshment / and thus as the Bread and the Vine of Life / both in His human and especially His divine nature / which imparts divine power for this purpose : just as here it was an external table / entirely overlaid with gold / and also provided with bread and wine / as the mystery of this is explained by David to all believers in Psalm 23:5-6 / to long for this table prepared for us by the LORD / in order to be strengthened in the struggle against enemies / and to be always anointed with the goodness and mercy of the Lord.

v. 24. 25. There was a molding at the top around the table / and on the frame / which consisted of four joined slats / at the four corners of which were the four feet / upon which the table rested / on which the molding served both as an ornament / but also signifies the provision of this King in His kingdom / which He bestows upon His subjects at all times. See Psalm 111:5, 132:15.

<margin>
Josephus (a) makes the molding four fingers wide above and four fingers wide below the table / so that the slat with the upper and lower molding was three handbreadths high.
</margin>

v. 26. On its four feet) Which / as Josephus reports / were square on the upper half / and round on the lower half.

On these four feet, just below the slat / along the length of the table / were the four golden rings / one golden ring on each foot.

<margin>
Josephus (b) writes / that there were also handles here / made of wood / and overlaid with gold leaf / which were fitted into the table above and the ring of the foot below / for which purpose the surface of the table was somewhat hollowed out there. And even if this had not been the case / the feet would have had no stability / and could not have been moved along with the table.
</margin>

v. 27. 28. So that it may be carried -- so that it may be carried) The Bread of Life is carried forth through the preaching of the Gospel to all four corners of the earth.

<margin>
(a) (b) Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3, Chapter 7.
</margin>

Of the faces or of the countenance / which was nevertheless also before the face of God.

Always) This also had to happen in the wilderness.

The face of the believers should be constantly directed in faith toward this Bread / and thus toward Christ / who is always before the face of His Father at His right hand / and is there always sought by believers in faith for the nourishment of the spirit. See Psalm 27:8, 13; 84:10, 12; Ephesians 1:3.

29. **<sup>(a)</sup> You shall also make its dishes and its bowls / and its pitchers / and its jars / with which they may be covered <sup>(b)</sup> : out of pure gold shall you make them.**

30. **And on the table you shall set showbread <note>original: "Schaubrode," literally "bread of display" or "bread of the presence"</note> before my face always.**

31. **You**

<margin>
v. 29. Dishes) Which / according to the report of the Hebrews / were for the purpose of carrying the showbread into the dwelling and serving it (a).
</margin>

Bowls) Others (b) translate this as censers. These are understood to be the two incense bowls / which stood on the table next to the showbread. Leviticus 24:7.

They were / as Munsterus cites from the Hebrews / formed like a hollow hand; as the Hebrew word also implies.

The LORD has richly provided His holy table in the Sanctuary with dishes for the Bread of Life and with bowls for wine / so that we may drink to His Spirit; also with censers; to show how this spiritual food must be requested with prayer.

Pitchers and their jars) Into the pitchers / as some believe / the wine of the drink offering was poured: see Numbers 4:7. where it is actually called / the pitchers of the drink offering; to which also Psalm 23:5 points: *My cup overflows.* And the jars were to be placed on the pitchers / so that the wine underneath remained pure: which is also the meaning of the word קְשָׂוֺת <note>Hebrew: *Kessavot*, generally referring to jars or flagons</note>. And thus the following word has the meaning of covering / that with these the wine in the pitchers was covered / and / which is also possible / the bread in the dishes and the incense in the bowls.

But the Hebrews have an entirely different opinion regarding these two words / and understand by the first one golden branches or tubes / and by the other golden forks / each with three golden teeth or prongs / four of which were at this table / and were like the shelves / upon which the bread lay / so that the air could pass between each loaf / so that they did not become moldy. According to this, the sense of the following words /

With which they may be covered) refers to the table itself / that it should be covered with them (the forks and tubes): which sense Junius and Tremellius, likewise Pagninus, also maintain.

Those translations / which instead put something here about pouring out or serving / have followed the Seventy Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX)</note> / not the Hebrew.

v. 30. Table) The way to this table went through the courtyard past the washbasin and altar.

The guests at this table were priests alone.

We must go through the courtyard through the fear of God / as the beginning of wisdom / through which we turn away from evil / if we wish to have access to God’s holy table.

Then we come to the bath of rebirth. Titus 3:6.

From this, one goes to the altar / upon which we offer ourselves to God in Christ / Romans 12:1. burning and consuming our fleshly lusts and desires / and proclaiming the Lord's death.

If we remain standing in the courtyard / we will never enter the Sanctuary.

We must first come to the water-vessel / and wash our hands in innocence / and thus step to the altar of our God / the patience of Jesus Christ / and offer ourselves as living sacrifices to God. Such guests the Lord welcomes at His table: *Eat, my friends,* etc.

Showbread) According to the Hebrew, actually Bread

### Chapter XXV. The Second Book of Moses. 377

31. **You shall also make a lampstand of pure gold: the lampstand / its shaft and its branches shall be made of one piece; its bowls / its knobs <note>Original: "Knöpffe," referring to the bud-like capitals or calyxes</note> and its flowers / shall be of the same.**

32. **And six branches shall come out of its sides: three branches of the lampstand out of one side / and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side.**

33. **Three bowls shaped like almonds shall be on one branch / along with a knob and a flower: and three bowls shaped like almonds shall be on the other branch / along with a knob and a flower. So it shall be for the six branches / that come out of the lampstand.**

34. **But on the lampstand itself shall be four bowls / shaped like almonds / with their knobs and flowers.**

35. **And there shall be a knob under two branches of the same / and again a knob under two branches of the same / and another knob under two branches of the same: namely, for the six branches / that come out of the lampstand.**

---

v. 31. The lampstand also represented Christ / as the Light that has come into the world to enlighten all people / but especially His congregation / which He first accepted from among the whole people of Israel; but afterwards He wished to accept from among the Gentiles / and to enlighten through the preaching of the Gospel / as if by a light.

This lampstand had to be made of pure gold / and of one piece / to show how this Light is entirely divine / and also how everything hangs together in the most magnificent order / so that one truth always flows from another.

The shaft / as the foundation of all branches and bowls / is Christ / the head-truth and foundational truth.

v. 32. The six branches / upon which the six lamps were placed / along with the shaft / upon which the seventh lamp was placed / represent the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit / considered as seven spirits, Revelation 1:4, which are to be found in the seven congregations of the entire New Testament Church / just as that same Church is considered in seven secret periods of time. Revelation 1:20.

v. 33. The bowls shaped like almonds / or as others translate / cups of hammered work / which caught the oil / and the lamps / in which the wick was placed / which was lit and shone / represent the believers / in whose hearts the oil of the Spirit must be gathered: see Matthew 25:1, 4; 2 Peter 1:19; 2 Corinthians 4:6. For they then give off a bright glow in their confession / and in their virtuous life. Matthew 5:14-16; Philippians 2:15, 16.

v. 34. The knobs and flowers indicate the light that sometimes lies hidden in the heart / and then blossoms in its own time / where it must give off a good fragrance through public confession / among those who allow the rising light to serve them as a fragrance of life unto life.

v. 35. A knob under two branches / as if these branches came out of the knob on both sides.

<column-break/>

36. **Their knobs and their branches shall be of the same: it shall all be one single piece of pure gold.**

37. **And you shall make seven (a) lamps for it / and one shall light its lamps / so that they give light over against it. <margin>Numbers 8:2. (a) Zechariah 4:2.</margin>**

38. **And its tongs <note>Original: "Lichtschneuzen," tools for trimming wicks</note> and its snuff dishes <note>Original: "Löschnäpffe," small trays for the burnt wicks</note> shall be of pure gold.**

39. **It shall be made from one talent <note>Original: "Centner," a hundredweight unit</note> of pure gold, with all these utensils.**

40. **And see that you make them according to their pattern / which was shown to you on the mountain. <margin>v. 9.</margin>** ->The<-

---

v. 36. Entirely of one single piece / through solid and completely joined hammered work / not cast hollow / as Josephus claims.

v. 37. The light had to be directed inward toward the lampstand / and since the almond-shaped bowls had a point in front and were wide in the back / the point must have been turned inward toward the lampstand: to show that the divine light first has its glow inwardly / and then also gives its glow outwardly in other hearts / through the rays that travel back from the shining gold of the lampstand / from Christ / and create light around them in those hearts eager for the light. See 2 Corinthians 4:6 and especially v. 7 / where it is mentioned / how the light in our earthly vessels must give its luster through the overflowing power of God / and that in the face of Jesus Christ / who must shine into the hearts with the rays of His Spirit.

v. 38. Snuff dishes / some believe / that these were vessels full of water / into which the trimmings were put / so that they would not smoke: which is also what Luther may have intended with the word "Löschnäpffe." But the Jews describe these vessels much differently (a): namely, as something shaped like a small spoon / with which one removed the ash and filth from the wick / which had collected in the lamps throughout the night; or the oil / that was left over in the extinguished lamps.

v. 39. A talent of gold / according to Rabbi Judah Leo’s (b) calculation, one talent equals 6,000 Rose Nobels <note>A 15th-century English gold coin</note>: according to Bunting (c) 12,000 Hungarian gold guilders of the best gold. Ruysbroeck (d) identifies three kinds of talents among the Jews: a merchant's talent / of 50 pounds; a citizen's talent / of 70 pounds; and a talent of the sanctuary / which is meant here / holding 120 pounds / and therefore was as heavy as the other two combined. By this heavy weight, he understands the eternal weight of love / which we should have for God / and which should outweigh ourselves and all things; as much as the merchant's and citizen's weight. We must not only be merchants / who exchange everything for the precious pearl: but we must also be citizens of the Jerusalem above. The weight of our love must be so heavy / that we ourselves are outweighed by love / and are incessantly immersed in God.

v. 40. Everything / and so especially the lampstand / had to be arranged very precisely according to the given pattern in heaven: to testify / how in divine things / and so also in divine truths / nothing of one's own should be added / but rather hearts should stand very carefully on their guard / so that everything might be worked in them through God's Spirit. See 2 Corinthians 2:17; Acts 7:44; Hebrews 8:5.

This pattern is God Himself / in whom are the eternal concepts of all things: and Jesus Christ His Word / who interprets the same. Everything that is to serve for the sanctification of the soul must be formed according to this model.

## Chapter XXVI.

->The Dwelling and its Distinction.<-

And you shall make the dwelling <note>Referring to the Tabernacle or Sanctuary</note> of ten curtains: of twisted fine-linen yarn / and sky-blue wool / and purple wool / and crimson wool. You shall make Cherubim of skillful work upon them.

2. The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits / and the width four cubits for each curtain. All curtains shall have one measure.

---

Since these holy things had to be enclosed with curtains / in order to represent a hut or tent; this was also intended to depict / how Christ would take on our weak flesh and blood / and dwell therein among men / and be seen by them for a certain time as a bodily temple / as he himself calls his body / in which all these holy vessels would be found in their true essence. See John 1:14, 2:19.

However, these curtains also represent the hearts of the believers / who are to be prepared by the Spirit as a hut / house, and temple of God / so that all these holy things / namely Christ with his atonement / comfort, and light / can dwell in them. There, the hearts are to be interwoven with holiness / heavenly wisdom / righteousness, and perfect rebirth / in order to become like the angels of God in their purity and obedience once again. They shall be united together by the bond of love / and by the golden clasps in the unity of faith: so that they may constitute the One / Holy / Universal Christian Church / according to verse 6. To this, the Apostle also so heartily exhorts: that they should be diligent to keep the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace: and that they should grow in Christ the Head / from whom the whole body is joined together / and one member hangs upon another / through every joint / whereby one provides assistance to the other / according to the working of every member in its measure / and causes the body to grow for its own edification in love. Ephesians 4:3, 15, 16. Likewise Colossians 3:14.

Whoever has properly recognized / indeed experienced and practiced / the departure from Egypt and the passage through the Red Sea / as well as the entire way through the wilderness; and has thereafter received the Law of God / written not with ink / but with the Spirit of the living God / upon the heart: he has come so far in his progress and growth / that he now also gets to see the Tabernacle of God / the holy dwellings of the Most High. And where else is this / than in the heavens within ourselves? Hebrews 10:34.

v. 1. Cherubim) <term>Cherub</term> <note>original: "כרוב"</note> is a work or painting and image of every distinct form / and signifies according to another interpretation manifold knowledge / or the various orders and sciences; from <note>original: כרוב (kerub) and כבוש (kabush)</note>. Just as the earth is adorned with flowers / the heavens with stars / so the "cherubic mind" is adorned with many forms of knowledge from the highest wisdom / with which the angelic spirits of the Cherubim are also filled / in order to order the lower things and to flow into them based on what they receive immediately from God.

Of skillful work) According to the description of the Hebrews / this means that the coverings were the same on both sides / having the same appearance: which required extraordinary art and knowledge.

v. 2. This beautiful tapestry was the lowest part of the roof of the hut / and served instead of a ceiling above the dwelling / which one saw lying above like a ceiling when looking up from the inside.

Joined together, the whole tapestry was 28 cubits long / and 40 cubits wide.

<column-break/>

3. Five curtains shall be joined together / one to another; and five curtains shall be joined together / one to another.

4. And you shall make loops of sky-blue wool on the edge of the first curtain at the end / in the joining: and likewise shall you do on the edge of the outermost curtain / in the other joining.

5. Fifty loops you shall make on the first curtain / and fifty loops you shall make at the end of the curtain / which is in the other joining. The loops shall take hold of one another.

6. And you shall make fifty golden clasps / and shall join the curtains / one to another / with the clasps / so that the dwelling may be one.

7. You

---

v. 3. The entire tapestry consisted of 2 large coverings / and each of those again of 5 pieces / which 5 pieces / each of which is called a "curtain" in these verses / were joined and sewn next to and to one another: so that each such large covering was 20 cubits wide.

One covering, with its width of 20 cubits, covered the length of the Holy Place from the top of the dwelling / which was 20 cubits long. The other covering was placed over the Most Holy Place. These two coverings were then clasped together exactly over the veil / which was inside the dwelling between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. v. 33.

Now, as the first covering with its width covered the Holy Place in length / so only 10 cubits of the length of these coverings came inside across the ceiling / as wide as the dwelling was: the remaining 18 cubits of the 28 cubits of length hung down the walls for decoration. The other covering covered the Most Holy Place at the ceiling 10 cubits long and wide / the remaining 18 cubits of the length of this covering / and the remaining 10 cubits of the width / likewise hung down the walls for decoration.

v. 4. These 2 coverings / each consisting of 5 pieces / were clasped together by beautiful sky-blue loops.

v. 5. The loops were at the ends of the length of the two coverings / where they were to be clasped together / 50 at each end in a straight line / namely a little over half a cubit / apart from one another.

v. 6. And when one loop from both sides was to be joined with the other / it was done through a golden clasp / which had, as it were, 2 barbs / and with one hook it grasped the loop of one side / and with the other the loop of the other side / and thus held both loops together.

So that the dwelling may be one) From the union and linking together of all divine commandments / which / like the curtains here / are contained in the number ten / there arises only one spiritual state.

# Chapter XXVI. The Second Book of Moses.

7. You shall also make curtains of goat hair / for a tent over the dwelling: you shall make eleven such curtains.
8. The length of one curtain shall be thirty cubits <note>An "Ehle" or cubit is an ancient unit of measure, roughly the length of a forearm from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note> / and the width four cubits for each curtain: the eleven curtains shall all have one measure.
9. And you shall join five curtains together by themselves / and six curtains by themselves; and you shall double the sixth curtain / at the front of the tent.
10. And you shall make fifty loops on the edge of the one outermost curtain in the coupling / and fifty loops on the edge of the curtain of the other coupling.
11. And you shall make fifty bronze clasps / and put the clasps into the loops / and thus join the tent together / so that it becomes one.

---

<margin>
v. 7. **Of goat hair**] Josephus (a) writes / that they were so skillfully woven / as if they had been made of fine wool. For much cloth is made from goat hair in the Orient / and some of it is so neat and subtle / that it is little inferior to silk: because the goats there have long, beautiful hair / not unlike human hair / as Bochartus (b) reports. And as Busbequius reports (c) / this is the fabric / which is called camlet <note>original: "Schamlor"; a costly fabric traditionally made from goat or camel hair</note>. The goats are said to have a very delicate, bright-shining hair / hanging down to the ground: which the shepherds do not shear / but rather comb out.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 8. **The length**] and number of the curtains thus exceeded the inner curtains by one curtain / so that they might adequately cover them.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 9. Of those 11 pieces, 5 were joined and sewn together / making a covering 30 cubits long and 20 cubits wide. The other 6 pieces were also sewn together / making the other half of the covering / 30 cubits long and 24 cubits wide. Thus, both together were 30 cubits long and 44 cubits wide.
</margin>

<margin>
**The 6th curtain you shall double**] This hanging was stretched in such a way / that the covering of 6 pieces lay at the front and the one of 5 pieces at the back. But at the front, by the entrance to the dwelling / this hanging was pulled out 2 cubits further than the dwelling was / and folded back / so that the first piece of the frontmost covering lay doubled / folded over 2 cubits upon 2 cubits.
</margin>

<margin>
Doubtless for this purpose / so that / if rain should come from the sides / these 2 cubits could be turned out / and thus the rain at the front and sides would do no harm. As Josephus says / this hanging at the front by the entrance formed something like a chamber / or a screen / and during rain, it stood out and protruded 2 cubits on all sides at the front.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 10. 11. That these curtains were joined by loops and bronze clasps / so that the tent became one; can indicate, among other things / how one / besides the inner union in the Church through faith / can also live externally connected with others in a common life of honorable conduct through civil laws and ordinances. Therefore, Christ himself did not withdraw from external order / and allowed the tax to be paid for himself.
</margin>

<margin>
(a) Book 3, Antiquities, ch. 5. (b) *Hierozoïcon* part 1, book 2, ch. 51, p. 626.
(c) Book 1, *Turkish Letters*.
</margin>

<column-break/>

12. And the overlapping part / that remains of the curtains of the tent / the half of the remaining curtain shall hang over the back of the dwelling:
13. And there shall be a cubit on this side / and a cubit on that side / of what remains in the length of the curtains of the tent / hanging over the sides of the dwelling / on this side and on that side / to cover it.
14. You shall also make a covering for the tent of ram skins dyed red / and a covering of badger skins <insert>(a) on top of it. (a) Ezekiel 16:10.</insert>

---

<margin>
v. 12. The half-curtain / that remains at the back / you shall let hang over the back of the dwelling.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 13. And on each side a cubit / that is extra in the length of the curtains of the tent / shall hang over the two sides of the tent / to cover it.
</margin>

<margin>
On the walls, this hanging hung from the outside on the south and north sides one cubit above the ground / and at the back toward the west, it hung down 2 cubits further than the colorful tapestry / and had a long tail / which either lay one cubit long on the ground / or perhaps / just like at the front / was folded over double.
</margin>

<margin>
LUTHER'S translation is somewhat obscure here. But with this explanation / it can be understood quite well according to the Hebrew. For
</margin>

<margin>
The length of the dwelling took up 30 cubits at the top / one cubit for the thickness of the boards on the western wall / and 10 cubits for the height of the western wall. These together make 41 cubits. Now this hanging was 44 cubits wide / and thus 3 are left over. 2 cubits are for the front covering which is doubled: the single remaining cubit / on the other covering toward the west / was / as said / either folded back / or perhaps lay on the ground / so that the western side / from where most rain came / was well protected.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 14. **A covering for the tent**) The roof on top of the dwelling was not pointed / but flat / and consisted of beautiful hangings.
</margin>

<margin>
**Of red ram skins**) Whether the skins were used with the wool / or the wool was removed; Moses does not report. It is certain / that smooth skins are not nearly as durable in the rain / as rough skins / where the wool is still present.
</margin>

<margin>
**Of badger skins**) This word has been retained / because 16 translations (which are at hand) agree on this and give it so: but this is not intended to oppose others / who view it as something else. Bochartus (a) considers the Hebrew word <note>Hebrew: *tachash*</note> to be the name of a color: as do the 70 Translators <note>The Septuagint</note> / whom the common Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note> followed. Junius (b) also subscribes to this opinion / and considers it a color / because Josephus also writes (c) / that / whoever saw these coverings from a distance / had to marvel at them / because the color gave off such a brilliance / as if it were the sky. He thus believes that / just as the former was reddish / so these were bluish ram skins.
</margin>

<margin>
This is no matter for quarreling / but for investigating what is hidden under these coverings. Otherwise, one would act like the fools / who, when biting open a nut, quarrel over the shells / and let the kernel slip away. Indeed:
</margin>

<margin>
The covering of red ram skins can signify / in Christ as in the believers / external tribulations and sufferings / even unto the shedding of blood. And the covering of badger skins / since such animals stay in the caves of the earth / how also our perishable body / of which the tent was also an image / must be buried in the earth / just as Christ also had to experience burial.
</margin>

<margin>
(a) part 1, *Hierozoïcon* book 3, ch. 26 & 30.
(b) *Jewish Sanctuaries* Book 1, Ch. 5, no. 34. (c) Book 3, Antiquities, ch. 5.
</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.

15. You shall also make the boards for the dwelling of Shittim-wood <note>Acacia wood; known for its durability</note>, which shall stand upright.
16. Ten cubits <note>German: *Ehlen*; a unit of measure roughly the length of a forearm</note> shall be the length of one board, and one and a half cubits the width of one board.
17. One board shall have two tenons <note>German: *Zapffen*; wooden pegs or projections used to join pieces of wood together</note>, so that they are joined one to another, one over the other. Thus shall you make for all the boards of the dwelling.
18. And you shall make the boards for the dwelling thus: twenty boards shall be for the south side, toward the south <note>original: *Mittags-Seite*, literally "midday side"</note>.
19. And you shall make forty silver bases <note>German: *Füſſe*; literally "feet"</note> under the twenty boards, two bases under one board for its two tenons, and two bases under the other board for its two tenons.
20. Likewise on the other side of the dwelling, on the side toward the north <note>original: *Mitternacht*, literally "midnight"</note>, twenty boards;
21. And their forty silver bases, two bases under one board, and two bases under the other board.

---

v. 15. These boards made of Shittim-wood and overlaid with gold can represent souls established in faith / such as teachers, elders, and other believers standing in a fair growth of grace / who stand rooted and grounded upon faith and love / as if upon two such silver bases; Ephesians 3:17-18. These must also receive and bear others who are weak in faith: Romans 14:1, 15:1. Therefore, such are also noted as pillars and columns, Galatians 2:9, 1 Timothy 3:15, Revelation 3:12. And whenever such individual, specially-gifted men are raised up by God / they are, as it were, the corner-boards / who hold the joints of the remaining teachers together / so that the congregations are especially built up through them.

v. 16. **Ten cubits**] The Hebrews identify three kinds of cubits: the small, of 4 palms; the medium, of 6 palms; and the largest, which had more. But here / according to the testimony and agreement of almost all Hebrews / a cubit of 6 palms is to be understood / which is also called a "Cubit of Moses" for this reason / because Moses measured the Tabernacle <note>German: *Stiffts-Hütte*</note> according to it. (a) Now, 6 palms is as much as 24 inches or finger-breadths; which is to be noted once and for all.

**One and a half cubits**] Thus the length of the dwelling was 30 cubits. For 20 boards of one and a half cubits in width make 30 cubits. It was, however / as is held according to the remaining calculation / three times as long as it was wide / just like the Temple.

v. 17. **One board shall have two tenons**] Which were at an equal distance from one another.

v. 18, 20. **Toward the south -- toward the north 20**] These two sides made up the length of the Tabernacle.

v. 19. **Two bases -- for its two tenons**] For each tenon a silver base was made / which was as hollow as needed for the tenon to enter / so that each board with its two tenons could be sunk into the two silver bases / and thus could stand upright.

v. 21. **Two bases under one board**] Each base must have been quite wide, large, and strong / so that two of them could carry a board: concerning which see chapter 38:27.

(a) Buxtorf, *History of the Ark of the Covenant* <note>original: *hist. arc. foed.*</note>, chapters 5 & 7.

<column-break/>

22. And for the sides of the dwelling toward the west <note>original: *Abend*, literally "evening"</note> you shall make six boards.
23. And two boards you shall make for corner boards for the dwelling on both sides.
24. And they shall be paired from beneath, and together they shall be paired at the top in one ring. Thus shall it be for both of them; they shall be two corner boards.
25. So that there are eight boards with their silver bases; namely sixteen bases: two bases under one board, and two bases under the other board.
26. And...

---

v. 22. **Six boards**] This then made 9 cubits in the width or breadth of the dwelling. Now because Philo (a) sets the width at 10 cubits; and Josephus also points to this when he says the dwelling was equally wide and high / and it was 10 cubits high: one sees from this / that from those

v. 23. **mentioned end- or corner-boards** no more than the 7th part or half a cubit on each side was taken into the width / so that it became 10 cubits wide on the inside.

From this, the thickness of all the boards is to be concluded / about which Moses mentions nothing explicitly. Josephus (b) to be sure makes them only 4 fingers thick: others, however, think that they may well have been one cubit thick. With this the translation of the 70 Interpreters <note>The Septuagint</note> agrees best / who rendered it *stulos* <note>Greek: στύλος</note> or pillars: because they were, as it were, large beams / which because of their thickness or strength could pass for pillars. And because the wood was exceedingly light / it could have been that much thicker / and indeed probably had to be. This is further confirmed by the

v. 24. **corner- or end-boards described further**. For since from each of them a whole cubit remained over and fell away / which was not added to the width of the dwelling; this same cubit in the corners of the dwelling / where the south and north sides meet the west side / was placed against the thickness of those same side-boards / so that the last boards on the south and north sides were joined together with these two end-boards on the west side. From which it is to be concluded / that the boards were about one cubit in thickness. For had they been only 4 fingers thick / the end-boards would have stood out by nearly a cubit / and the west side would have been nearly 2 cubits wider on the outside: which would not have looked well at all.

However the rear boards of the tent were to be joined to the side-boards by the two corner-boards / so that they might all be fastened to one another: in just this way must our spirit / as long as it wanders in this mortal body / be entirely surrendered to all virtues on both sides with its physical nature / so that it practices them and brings them into action / but resists vices; which two parts are equally important. For as much as we love the virtues / so much do we despise the things that are contrary to them. And to this end the physical nature must be united with the spirit / and the spirit with the body.

v. 25. **Bases**] A clean conscience is the foundation or the support and the base of every board / with or in which all good works are begun.

(a) Philo, *On the Life of Moses* <note>original: *de vit. Moſ.*</note>, book 3, page 516. (b) Josephus, *Antiquities* <note>original: *Antiq.*</note>, book 3, chapter 5.

<meta>This page continues the detailed architectural instructions for the Tabernacle (the "Dwelling"), specifically focusing on the bars that stabilize the wooden walls and the ornate veil that separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. ->### Chapter XXVI. The Second Book of Moses.<-

### Chapter 26. The Second Book of Moses.

26. And you shall make bars of Shittim-wood <note>Acacia wood</note>: five for the boards on one side of the dwelling;
27. And five bars for the boards on the other side of the dwelling, and five bars for the boards of the side of the dwelling for the two sides facing the west <note>original: *gegen Abend*, literally "toward evening," the direction where the sun sets</note>.
28. And the middle bar in the center of the boards you shall allow to pass through from one end to the other.
29. And you shall overlay the boards with gold <gloss>(a) 1 Kings 6:21.</gloss> and make their rings of gold as places for the bars; and you shall overlay the bars with gold.
30. Thus shall you set up the dwelling according to its manner, which was shown to you on the mountain.

---

<margin>v. 26. 27. Bars)</margin> So that the three walls would stand more firmly and the boards could not easily be separated from one another, various rings of gold were made on the outside of each board on all sides, through which rods or bars were thrust on each side to hold the boards together.

The five gold-overlaid bars, which were slid into the golden rings fastened to the boards to hold the boards together in their joints and keep them more upright, may represent the true fundamental truths of knowledge. Through these, teachers should also be held together in the unity of the Spirit. There should be few of these truths, so that all can be maintained more harmoniously within them: just as the five main articles of the Christian religion are known. These can also be noted as the doctrine of the Triune God, the incarnation of the Son of God, his death as the sole cause of our righteousness before God, faith as the only means to partake in such merit, and finally the rebirth of the Spirit, through which alone faith can be worked in us. In these fundamental truths, we must stand firm and also be bound to one another.

<margin>v. 28. Middle Bar)</margin> There was namely another special middle rod, which was neither on the outside nor the inside held by rings on the boards, but went through the drilled thickness of the boards themselves. It was inside the boards, so that it could be seen neither from the outside nor the inside of the dwelling. Thus, the meaning is understood:

"In the middle of the boards you shall allow to pass through") which, according to some translations, is not easily guessed. The middle rod shall go into the middle of the boards—that is, through the thickness of the board—as all Hebrew scholars agree. This held the boards so firmly together on all sides that it was impossible for them to give way.

Strictly speaking, that which is translated here as "pass through" actually means "to flee" <note>original: *fliehen*</note>, as noted by many. This cannot be said of an external middle rod; but the rod that went inside "fled," as it were, out of sight when it was inserted, so that one did not see where it remained.

Just as the long external rods were joined together from various smaller ones, it is to be presumed the same was true here.

<margin>v. 29. overlay with gold)</margin> Not as one gilds today, where there is nothing more than a thin film of gold; rather, they were covered and plated on all sides with golden sheets or golden plates.

<column-break/>

31. You shall also make a veil of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine linen yarn. One shall make Cherubim <note>Angelic figures</note> on it of artistic work.
32. And you shall hang it on four pillars <gloss>(a)</gloss> of Shittim-wood, which are overlaid with gold, whose hooks shall be of gold, standing on four silver bases. <gloss>(a) ch. 36:36.</gloss>
33. And you shall hang the veil under the clasps, and shall bring in the Ark of the Testimony there inside the veil, so that the veil makes a distinction for you between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place. <gloss>Hebrews 9:2, 3.</gloss> 34.

---

<margin>v. 31. Veil)</margin> It was square, 10 cubits high—as high as the pillars—and 10 cubits wide, from one wall to the other, from south to north.

<margin>Cherubim)</margin> All kinds of floral work were also woven into it, as Josephus <gloss>(a) <note>original: "L. 3. Antiq. c. 5." referring to Antiquities of the Jews, Book 3, Chapter 5</note></gloss> reports.

<margin>Of artistic work)</margin> With identical figures on both sides.

<margin>v. 32. Hooks)</margin> The letter Vav <note>ו</note> means as much as a "hook," not a "knob"; and the letter Vav also has the shape of a hook, from which it received its name. The magnificent veil was hung upon these very hooks.

<margin>v. 33. This Veil,</margin> which covered the Most Holy Place so that no one but the High Priest alone could see it once a year on the great Day of Atonement, represents—according to the Apostle’s interpretation—the flesh of Christ. That is, his weak human nature, which had to be put to death, and thus this veil torn, and heavenly things opened up. Hebrews 10:20 and 9:7-8, where the mystery of these things is explained at length: namely, how our true reconciliation became manifest through it; and what the blood of atonement is, through which God could make the covenant with us humans: so that here the true treasure chest of all divine gifts and his infinite goodness had to be revealed in Christ. Therefore, as a witness to this, this veil in the Temple tore into two pieces from top to bottom at the death of Christ. Matthew 27:51.

<margin>Distinction)</margin> God wants the Sanctuary to be separated from the Most Holy Place. The Sanctuary is the center-point of the soul: but the Most Holy is God himself. They are united and yet distinct. United, in that the center is in God, and God is in the center. Distinct, through the difference of their states. For to possess God in the center is indeed something very great: but that God remains in himself and for himself, this is a much higher level. It was explained above in Chapter 20:8 what it means: God in us, we in God, and God in himself.

This veil of separation between the Holy and the Most Holy also represents the essential distinction which remains eternally between God and the creature, alongside the incomprehensible unity of love and transformation which occurs through the annihilation of the soul in itself and its flowing into God. God remains God, truly distinct from the transformed soul, although the soul sanctified by this excellent union <gloss>(b) <note>John 17:21, 1 Corinthians 6:17</note></gloss> becomes one thing with God. The lamp of love must burn at all times and shine unceasingly in the presence of God.

<gloss>(a) Book 3, Antiquities ch. 5. (b) John 17:21. 1 Cor. 6:17.</gloss>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXVII.

34. And you shall put the Atonement Cover <note>original: *Versöhn-Deckel*, often called the Mercy Seat</note> upon the Ark of the Testimony in the Most Holy Place. <margin>1 Kings 6:19.</margin>

35. But the table you shall set outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table on the side of the dwelling toward the south <note>original: *Mittag*, literally "midday"</note>; and the table you shall place on the side toward the north <note>original: *Mitternacht*, literally "midnight"</note>.

36. And you shall make a screen for the door of the tent, of blue wool, and of purple wool, and of scarlet wool, and of fine twisted linen yarn, of embroidered work. <margin>ch. 36:37.</margin>

37. And you shall make five pillars of Shittim-wood <note>Acacia wood</note> for this screen, and overlay them with gold; their hooks shall be of gold: and you shall cast five bronze bases for them.

---

v. 34. The Most Holy Place specifically represented Heaven. Hebrews 9:12.

v. 35. Toward the South) As if at God's right hand; but to the one entering the Holy Place, it would be on the left.

v. 36. The other cover, or another curtain, which served as the door to the dwelling—since the eastern side had no wall of boards—also covered the Holy Place. Within this stood the lampstand and the table, as well as the Altar of Incense (according to Chapter 30:6) along with the other vessels. These were not permitted to be seen uncovered even by the Levites, let alone the common people. Only the priests were allowed to enter to perform the daily service, Hebrews 8:6. Thus, believers in general were still kept back from this, to show them that the Holy Spirit, in His full power and light, was not yet there because Christ had not yet appeared, much less been glorified through His suffering and resurrection. John 7:39.

Therefore, the Holy Place represents the Church here on earth, and especially that of the New Testament.

Now, since in the New Testament all believers together are made kings and priests before God the Father, Revelation 1:6, and are thus a royal priesthood, 1 Peter 2:9, they can now receive the Holy Spirit with His light and comfort when they ask the Father for it in the name of Jesus Christ. To this end, He shall be poured out upon them as the Spirit of grace and prayer. Zechariah 12:10. The precious promises of Christ regarding the Holy Spirit in John 14, 15, and 16 also point to this, showing that He wanted to make His believers into such a living sanctuary where He would dwell perpetually with the gifts of His Spirit.

The fact that after the trumpet of the seventh angel, the Temple of God in heaven was opened, and the Ark of His Testament was seen in His temple, Revelation 11:19, indicates that Christ will reveal Himself even more clearly and gloriously among believers in His magnificent kingdom. Thus, the Most Holy Place will, as it were, manifest itself on earth in the glorious peace and great holiness of the believers. See Revelation 21:3.

<column-break/>

# Chapter XXVII.
->The Altar, Court, and Oil for the Lamps.<-

1. **A**nd you shall make an altar of Shittim-wood; five cubits <note>An "Ehle" or cubit is roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> shall be the length, and five cubits the breadth: it shall be four-square, the altar, and three cubits its height. <margin>(a) Joshua 22:28.</margin>

2. And you shall make its horns on its four corners: its horns shall be of one piece with it, and you shall overlay it with bronze <note>original: *Ertz*, meaning ore or bronze</note>.

3. You shall also make its pots to clean it of the ashes; and its shovels, and its sprinkling-basins, and its meat-hooks <note>original: *Feuerzangen*, literally fire-tongs, used here for handling meat</note>, and its firepans. All its utensils you shall make of bronze.

---

v. 1. An altar) This was the regular altar in front of the Tabernacle of Meeting, upon which the daily and festival sacrifices, as well as the voluntary and other ordained sacrifices of the people, had to be prepared and burned. Exceptional altars, such as those that might first appear to the people, were permitted to be made of earth or raw stones. Chapter 20:24, 25. For since these altars were established through the priesthood, and only those from the tribe of Aaron were permitted to offer sacrifice, all other such altars seem to have been forbidden. If anyone erected such a thing, they were called "High Places," 1 Samuel 9:14, 19; 1 Kings 11:7, which were made by one's own will, whereas God had thereafter bound all sacrifices to this altar alone.

This altar represented Christ, just as He, under the open sky in the sight of all people, offered Himself on the wood of the Cross to His heavenly Father as a valid sacrifice of atonement for the sins of the whole world. See 1 John 2:2; 1 Timothy 2:6; Romans 8:3. Therefore, it is also said of Him regarding former times that He offered Himself to God through the eternal Spirit. Hebrews 9:14. And thus, in Him, we have the altar in whose fellowship we stand when we believe in Him. Hebrews 13:10.

v. 2. Horns) Pillars or posts, four-sided in shape, sharpened and hollowed out.

That these horns on the altar served for binding the sacrificial animals is indeed concluded by some from Psalm 118:27 (a); but others will not accept or believe this, because not only do the Hebrews know nothing of it, but also the altar would have suffered no small damage from it. Furthermore, the priests would have been hindered in their official duties from walking around the ledge of the altar, and it was also not necessary. However, it prefigured the divine strength in Christ, through which He could perform His sacrifice and endure the wrath of God. See 1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 89:25.

Its horns shall be of one piece with it) Not only of the same material from which the altar was made, but also one piece with it. This was omitted in Luther's translation.

v. 3. Shovels) According to the report of the Hebrews, these were made of fine, thin cast copper, like the lids on the pots, with long handles so that one could reach across the altar and conveniently gather the ashes with them.

Sprinkling-basins) These were for the priests to catch the blood of the sacrificial animals, so that they could afterwards sprinkle some of it on the altar.

Meat-hooks) These were forks with three teeth, used to turn the sacrificial meat on the fire of the altar so that it would be consumed more quickly. They were also used in the kitchen to take the boiled sacrificial meat out of the pots. 1 Samuel 2:13.

Firepans) This is the same word that was translated as "snuff dishes" in chapter 25:38; however, it cannot mean the same thing here. That they were vessels in which coals were placed for incense is quite probable.

<note>(a) Targov. biblical exercises, p. 379 and following.</note>

### Chapter XXVII. The Second Book of Moses.

4. You shall also make a grating for it of bronze network; and on the network you shall make four bronze rings at its four corners.

5. And you shall place it under the ledge <note>original: *Umgang*, a rim or walkway</note> of the altar from below, so that the network reaches to the middle of the altar.

6. You shall also make poles for the altar, namely poles of Shittim-wood <note>Acacia wood</note>, and you shall overlay them with bronze.

7. And its poles shall be put into the rings, so that the poles are on both sides of the altar, that it may be carried.

8. You shall make it hollow, out of boards: as it was shown to you on the mountain, so shall they make it.

<margin>v. 4. Most scholars hold that this grating was inside the altar between the four walls, and that the altar fire lay upon it, with the sacrifices burned there; the ashes would then fall through the holes onto the ground. Josephus describes it as a grate. However, this is not at all believable, as with other things mentioned here, because the hollow of the altar was to be filled with earth according to chapter 20:24.</margin>

According to the opinion of the Hebrews, it was meant to show the distinction in the sprinkling of blood: some was sprinkled above the grating, while some was poured out beneath it. Junius (a) <note>original: Franciscus Junius, a Reformed theologian</note> however, maintains that it had a prominent network, and that the fire was carried on the hoops in the lower latticed part of the altar, which was perforated specifically so that the fire would have air.

<margin>v. 5. Under the ledge)</margin> That is, the ledge which went around the outside of the altar.

To better understand the shape of this altar, one should know that this altar of Moses first had its foundation or base, which was square and slightly elevated from the earth. On this base stood a square chest that was narrowed at the top, so that the base protruded all around. This chest was perforated here. Upon this square chest was another section, which was again narrower than the section or chest it stood upon, so that the lower part protruded around the upper part, allowing one to walk around the top edge of the lower part. This space was called the ledge <note>original: *Umgang*</note>.

<margin>v. 6. 7. Poles — that it may be carried)</margin> The carrying of the altar represents the proclamation of the crucified Christ to the four parts of the world. This sacrifice was also entirely carried out on earth according to the wise counsel of God in heaven and His providence. Acts 4:28.

<margin>v. 8. Hollow)</margin> Not entirely, but the uppermost part, then a floor, and then hollow again below. The top part was filled with earth when it was to be used.

(a) J. H. <note>original: likely a reference to a specific theological work</note> book 5, chapter 33, numbers 31, 32.

9. You shall also make a courtyard for the Tabernacle. On the south side <note>original: *Mittags-Seite*, literally "midday side"</note> toward the south, there shall be hangings for the courtyard of fine twisted linen yarn. The length shall be one hundred cubits <note>original: *Ehlen*</note> on one side.

10. And its pillars shall be twenty, with their twenty bases of bronze. The hooks of the pillars and their bands shall be of silver. <margin>ch. 38:10, 28.</margin>

11. Likewise for the north side <note>original: *Mitternacht*, literally "midnight side"</note> in length there shall be hangings of one hundred cubits long, and their twenty pillars and twenty bases of bronze. The hooks of the pillars and their bands shall be of silver.

12. And the width of the courtyard on the west side <note>original: *Abend-Seite*, literally "evening side"</note> shall have hangings of fifty cubits, their ten pillars and ten bases.

13. And the width of the courtyard on the east side <note>original: *Morgen-Seite*, literally "morning side"</note> toward the sunrise shall be fifty cubits.

14. And there shall be fifteen cubits of hangings on one side, with their three pillars and three bases.

15. And on the other side fifteen cubits of hangings, with their three pillars and three bases.

16. And

<margin>v. 9.</margin> The courtyard was given over to the people; in it, those who were obligated to bring their prescribed sacrifices could appear, as well as those who wished to be present for the usual daily and other festival sacrifices. Here also the public instruction of the people would have occurred, according to the arrangements made by the priests. See Psalms 84:3, 11; 116:17, 18, 19; Malachi 2:6, 7.

It was without a roof, under the open sky. The hangings were quite simple, white and transparent.
<margin>v. 10. Bases)</margin> In which the pillars stood with their pegs.
<margin>v. 11. Twenty pillars)</margin> Which stood at equal distances of about 5 cubits from one another.

<margin>v. 12. Ten pillars)</margin> Whether these are to be counted such that the two outermost pillars from the south and north sides are included, or whether there were fully 10 separate pillars: Moses does not say. If one counts only 8, the pillars toward the west stand at nearly the same distance from each other as the south and north pillars; also, in this way, the wall was much better covered when the hangings for the west and east were attached to the outermost pillars of the south and north sides, rather than if 2 pillars had stood next to each other in both corners, which would have allowed one to see through the gap—which is not at all elegant. Philo also seems to incline toward this view, writing (a): There were 60 pillars in total, 40 on the two long sides, and 8 on each side of the width. Since 40 and twice 8 only make 56, and he nevertheless sets the number at 60, he must have counted the corner pillars twice, so that in the 4 corners each corner pillar is counted for both the length and the width; in reality, however, there were only 56 distinct pillars.

<margin>v. 13-15.</margin> At the entrance toward the east, the hangings were divided thus: At the morning corner that faced south, there was a hanging 15 cubits long, hanging on 3 pillars; at the other corner that faced north, it was the same;

(a) book 3 of *The Life of Moses* <note>original: *de vit. Mos.*</note>, pages 516 and following.
