# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXVII.

16. And for the gate of the courtyard shall be a screen of twenty cubits, of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine linen yarn, of embroidered work; with their four pillars and their four bases.

17. All the pillars of the courtyard round about shall be provided with silver bands; their hooks shall be of silver, and their bases of bronze.

18. The length of the courtyard shall be one hundred cubits, and the width fifty cubits throughout, and the height five cubits, of twisted fine linen yarn; and their bases shall be bronze.

19. All the utensils of the Tabernacle for all its service, and all its pegs, and all the pegs of the courtyard, shall be bronze. <margin>(c) 38/31.</margin>

---

v. 16. Between the two hangings, a space of 20 cubits wide remained in the middle of the East side: and there hung a beautiful curtain 20 cubits long, made of twisted precious white linen and blue, purple, and scarlet wool yarn, nicely decorated with floral patterns <note>original: *verblümt*</note>, yet without Cherubim, sewn with a needle, of embroidered work. This was, as it were, the door that blocked the entrance to the courtyard. But whenever someone was to enter, or the people watched the divine service, this curtain was lifted or pushed back so that one could see inside across the 20-cubit width. This curtain hung on 4 pillars.

However, the pillars on the East side did not stand at equal distances from one another like the others; rather, the 3 pillars on each corner stood far enough apart that the 15-cubit hanging could hang between them; and the other 4 pillars in the middle stood in such a way that the two outermost ones stood directly next to the pillars where the hanging ended, and the remaining 2 were in the middle at equal intervals. Regarding this, <term>Josephus</term> <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note> gives this report: The 4th side was 50 cubits, and the door was 20 cubits wide, and it had double pillars on both sides, like posts, and on each side (toward the corners) there were 3 pillars.

v. 17. Moses does not mention what the pillars themselves around the courtyard were made of. <term>Josephus</term> sets them as bronze: <term>Philo</term> <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher</note> on the other hand writes that their material was cedar. It is more likely that the pillars were made of wood, not copper <note>or bronze</note>: because in the calculation of the total sum of copper used for the entire Tabernacle, not much remains for the pillars. Now, however, for 56 pillars, each 5 cubits high, much copper would have been required.

All pillars around this courtyard were decorated with silver rings or foliage-work that went all the way around the pillars.

**Hooks**) These were between the foliage-work, intended so that one could hang the sacrificial animals upon them, as <term>Munster</term> (a) <note>Sebastian Münster, a 16th-century Hebraist</note> cites from the Hebrews.

v. 18. **Length** -- **Width**) This enclosed courtyard represented the Church of the Old Testament, then contained within the narrow borders of the land of <term>Canaan</term>, which was also to be distinguished from the other peoples of the earth by holiness and honorable virtuous conduct, of which the hangings made of pure linen could be a symbol. Psalm 93:5. This is then contrasted with the Church of the New Testament among the Gentiles, which was to make the space of its tents wide and spread out the curtains of its dwelling. For it would break out to the right and to the left, and its seed would inherit the Gentiles and inhabit the desolate cities. Isaiah 54:2-3.

**The height 5 cubits**) Thus 5 cubits lower than the Tabernacle building, so that the Tabernacle stood out 5 cubits above it and could be seen from the outside down to its midpoint.

<meta>(a) ad Exod. 38. not. b.</meta>

<column-break/>

20. And you shall also command the children of Israel that they bring to you olive oil <note>original: *Baumöl*, literally "tree oil"</note> that is pure and beaten, for the light, so that the lamps may be lit at all times. <margin>(a) Leviticus 24:2-4.</margin>

21. In the Tabernacle of Meeting, outside the veil which is before the Testimony <gloss>(*)</gloss>, Aaron and his sons shall tend it from evening until morning <gloss>(b)</gloss> before the face of the LORD: this shall be an eternal statute among their descendants from the children of Israel. <margin>(a) chapter 16:34. (b) chapter 30:8.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 20. Olive oil that is pure) Not made by artifice, but natural.</margin>

After they came into the Promised Land, they obtained the oil for the lamps from <term>Tekoa</term>, a small town in the tribe of <term>Judah</term> that was exceedingly rich in oil (a).

The pure and clear oil, which had to be crushed only by a pestle <note>original: *Stempel*</note> and not forcefully squeezed out with a press (which could have allowed many dregs and impurities to run in), represents the pure light of divine truths. These flow more freely from a humble and contrite spirit without compulsion, and are unlocked by the grace of God in such humble hearts, rather than when one tries to squeeze them out, as it were, with reason and intellectual gifts, or tries to force conclusions and press them upon others in every way.

v. 21. **From evening until morning**) <term>Josephus</term> (b) says that every day 3 lamps burned, but at night all 7, of which 4 were extinguished in the morning and lit again in the evening. And that lamps burned during the day is very believable: because the Tabernacle had no windows, and at the front entrance to the Holy Place the curtain hung all the way down to the ground, so it must have been pitch black inside. But the seven lamps were kept burning through the night to be a prototype of the future light of the New Testament; for now it would no longer be necessary to light lamps in churches during the bright day, which could rather be a sad indication that the true light of knowledge must have been extinguished in many hearts. See 2 Peter 1:19, Isaiah 60:1-2. There, following the darkness and gloom that has spread among the peoples, a great light is again promised in the glorious kingdom of Christ.

If we are now in the New Testament, as we boast, then we must also testify to its essence, and that the dark shadows and symbolic things have passed away for us, as they were only meant to last

**From evening until morning**) That is, quite literally, from the Old to the New Testament. The night should now be passed, and the day should have arrived. Yet the lamp of love must burn at all times and shine without ceasing in the presence of God.

This is the purest and beaten oil. When we display heartfelt love and compassion toward one another in each person's need, then our lamp will burn rightly and our light will shine before and among men; we will thus have the lampstand that the Law described within us, and stand before the LORD as is fitting.

(a) <term>Schindler</term>, Pentaglott Lexicon on the word <note>original: כתית (katit) meaning "beaten" or "crushed"</note>.
(b) book 3, Antiquities, chapter 9.

Cap. XXVIII. The Second Book of Moses.

# The XXVIII. Chapter.
->The High Priestly Garments.<-

1. But you shall let Aaron, your brother, draw near to you, and his sons with him, from among the children of Israel, that he may minister in the priest’s office to me: Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's sons.
2. And you shall make holy garments for Aaron, your brother, for glory and for ornament.
3. And you shall speak to all who are of a wise heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they make Aaron’s garments to sanctify him, that he may minister in the priest’s office to me.

---

Here once again Christ is presented as the true High Priest, according to his two natures <note>The divine and human natures of Christ</note> and gifts, prefigured in the high priest Aaron and his mysterious holy clothing; and hereafter the believers are represented under the image of the priests and their holy garments.

v. 1. After GOD had mostly arranged the Sanctuary according to its most prominent pieces, now the servants are also described who should serve therein, and especially perform the priestly office.

This involves a "drawing near" to GOD, specifically according to His instruction, to pray for and achieve reconciliation before GOD. By this it was shown that the sinner cannot approach GOD except through a mediator and his true reconciliation. As long as that same person <note>Christ</note> would not yet appear in person, such prefiguring persons were to be chosen, who were to bring only an image of reconciliation in the blood of animal sacrifices. And this person was to be a High Priest: Aaron, and after him, whoever was chosen from his descendants as the eldest or otherwise to take his place: and then his other sons and descendants, who as priests were also to have their administration in the priestly office to reconcile GOD.

v. 2. 3. So that they, and especially the High Priest, might be rightly sanctified for this great office and set apart from the rest of the people, GOD wanted to provide them with certain holy garments, which they had to put on only at the time of performing their office. In this they were to represent Christ with his natures and gifts, who was to possess the essence of these garments himself. Therefore, when he appeared, he did not walk about in any special clothing distinct from the people, but had the essence and the true brilliance and glory within himself, which he did not need to borrow from any earthly precious stones. Therefore it is written of him: *The Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we beheld his glory, a glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.* John 1:14. In this, his servants should follow him, and distinguish themselves from other believers not with clothes, but with gifts of the Spirit above all.

These 4 colors, says Philo (d), resemble the 4 elements. The precious linen came from the earth; the purple from the water; the deep blue color resembles the air, and the scarlet resembles the burning fire.

<column-break/>

4. These are the garments that they shall make: The breastpiece, and the ephod <note>original: *Leibrock*</note>, and the robe <note>original: *Ober-Rock*</note>, and the tunic <note>original: *Unter-Rock*</note> embroidered with many eyes, the turban <note>original: *Hut*</note> and the sash. Thus they shall make holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, that he may minister in the priest's office to me.
5. And for this they shall take the gold, and the sky-blue wool, and the purple wool, and the crimson wool, and the fine linen yarn.
6. And

---

v. 4. Here the garments are recounted according to the order of their dignity, of which there were eight pieces in number. 1. The ephod <term>ephod: a waistcoat-like garment worn by the High Priest</term>. 2. The artistic sash upon it. 3. The official breastpiece. 4. The robe. 5. The golden forehead-plate. 6. The tunic. 7. The turban: and 8. the sash. In the 3rd Book of Moses <note>Leviticus</note> 8:7-8, they are recounted as he put them on: 1. the tunic; 2. the sash, and so forth. However, the calculation of the Hebrews is somewhat different in this: they also count 8 pieces, but do not include the sash of the ephod, because it was woven from one piece with it, but instead they count the under-breeches as the 8th piece; so that half of these 8 pieces belonged to the High Priest alone, and exactly the other half he had in common with the other priests.

The priests did not wear shirts during their service, but the under-breeches were against the bare body (a): they also wore no shoes, but served barefoot; which custom is said to have come from the example of Moses and Joshua (chapter 3:5).

v. 5. Sky-blue) The Hebrews generally consider it to be a very deep blue color, shaped like the sky during clear weather (b) (chapter 24:10).

Purple wool) This color also came from a sea-snail, namely the purple-snail <note>the Murex</note>, which had the juice or blood, with which the dyers used to dye, in its mouth or in the middle of its throat, and had to be caught alive. For as soon as it died, it gave up the juice (c).

Crimson wool) Or rather, wool-grain or scarlet: because Philo (d) compares this color to fire, which best suits the burning fiery scarlet color: although one can otherwise dye this color differently, so that the material goes in once or twice. Here it was undoubtedly twice, because the Hebrew word *shani* refers to "twice." Indeed, the Hebrew signifies the cochineal color, as Paul explicitly gives the word in Hebrews 9:19.

However, the color is made from the scarlet-berry, which grows not on one—but on various trees and shrubs, especially on certain holm oaks, and bears grains as large as a lentil. When these grains begin to ripen, a little worm grows inside, which, when it becomes ripe, gets wings, tears apart the little skin in which it is hidden, and flies away. Therefore, the grains must be taken off before the little worm gets wings: then the blood is squeezed out of these worms, and from this, the color is prepared (e).

<sig>Lcc</sig>

---

(a) Rabbi Judah Leo, book 1, *Concerning the Temple*, chapter 19.

(b) See Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, part 2, book 5, chapters 9, 10, 11. Philo, book 3, *The Life of Moses*, page 516. Wagenfeil, note 9, to the *Gemara* [commentary] on *Sotah*, chapter 2, section 2, who also cites from the Talmud how this color was prepared. The material to be dyed was first soaked in lime and then washed well, then boiled in lye or with soap. When that was done, they took a special sea-snail, which outwardly resembles the sea in color, but has black blood, and is found in the Mediterranean Sea. Its blood was warmed with other things in a kettle, and then they put the wool in until it got a color like the clear sky.

(c) Pliny, book 9, chapters 36 ff., where it is also described how the dyeing proceeded. (d) In the place cited.

(e) See Dioscorides, book 4, chapter 34. Pliny, book 9, chapter 41; book 16, chapter 8; book 24, chapter 4. Ursinus, *Analecta*, part 1, book 3, chapter 28, section 2. Lonicer, *Herbal*, part 1, chapter 97. Dietericus, *Biblical Antiquities*, on Isaiah 1:18.

<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXVIII.</header>

6. And they shall make the ephod <note>original German: *Leibrock*, literally "body-coat." In biblical tradition, this is the Ephod.</note> of gold, of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, of crimson wool, and of twisted fine linen yarn, of artistic work.
7. It shall have two shoulder-pieces joined together, so that it may be joined at its two ends.
8. And its artistic belt, which is upon it, shall be of the same workmanship and of the same materials: of gold, of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine linen yarn.

<note>The ephod—also called by its Hebrew name *Ephod*, which comes from the word for "girding" because it hung outwardly over the other garments—was tied with an artistic belt woven directly into it. This garment represents the Divinity of our Mediator and only High Priest, Christ, who entirely encompasses humanity and is intimately joined to it in a secret, eternal bond of Personhood. This Divinity possesses a pure and simple essence, for which gold serves as a symbol. Furthermore, within Him is essential wisdom, righteousness, and holiness; for He is the Lamb of God who bears the sin of the world, remaining entirely untainted in His union with humanity. Therefore, the belt had to be made of these same materials: thus are recounted the glorious attributes of our Mediator along with His Divinity, as He was "higher than the heavens" (Hebrews 7:26, 1 Peter 1:19, John 1:29, 36).</note>

v. 7. This ephod had to be joined at the shoulders and rest upon them. From this comes the name of the *Scapular* commonly used in the Roman Church <note>From the Latin *scapula*, meaning shoulder-blade</note>.

v. 8. **Twisted)** The priest's garments were six-threaded, and undoubtedly so were the other items made from this yarn. Because of its great and subtle fineness, it could hardly have been less than six-threaded. Indeed, the Hebrew name for the yarn itself indicates this, being the same as the number 6. For it is called <term>Schesch</term> <note>Shesh</note> (fine linen yarn) <term>שֵׁשׁ</term> in Hebrew. Since Pliny <margin>(a) Natural History, book 19, chapter 1.</margin> (a) also reckons cotton among the linens, writing that linen brought great trade to Egypt because of its excellence; and that specifically in a part of Egypt bordering Arabia, a shrub grows that is quite small and bears a fruit like a bearded nut, from whose inner silk this "wool" is spun—a cotton-linen to which no other linen can compare in whiteness and softness; for which reason the Egyptian priests had their garments made from it (b): some judge this to be the more common material. Others, more likely, understand it to be the most subtle and precious linen that came from Egypt, which was snow-white in color. This is also mentioned in Genesis 41:42, Ezekiel 27:7, and Luke 16:19. <margin>(b) Compare Polydore Vergil, *On Discovery*, book 5, chapter 5.</margin>

[the governance] is said to be upon his shoulder: and also because he represents them at all times before the Father, and is mindful of them in his high-priestly prayer. Romans 8:27.

->Prefiguration <note>A "Type" or historical person/object that foreshadows Christ</note><-

1. Aaron carried the names before GOD as a memorial.
2. He carried them on his shoulders.
3. They were precious stones, which one does not easily neglect.
4. The names were engraved upon them, not merely written.
5. There were 2 stones, which Aaron wore on both shoulders.
6. Upon them stood the names of the 12 tribes.

v. 13. **Settings)** <note>original: *Aeuglein*, literally "little eyes"</note> Also perhaps clasps, by which the front and back pieces of the ephod had to be joined together at the top of the shoulders.

v. 14. **Chains to the settings)** At each clasp on the shoulder, there was a ring for this purpose.

<column-break/>

9. And you shall take two onyx stones, and engrave upon them the names of the sons of Israel.
10. Six of their names on the one stone, and the six remaining names on the other stone, according to their births.
11. With the work of a stone-cutter, as one engraves a seal, you shall have the two stones engraved with the names of the sons of Israel. You shall make them so that they are surrounded by golden settings.
12. And you shall set the two stones upon the shoulder-pieces of the ephod, that they may be stones of memorial for the children of Israel, that Aaron may bear their names upon his two shoulders before the face of the LORD as a memorial.
13. And you shall make settings of gold,
14. And two chains of pure gold: you shall make them of two equal ends, of braided work, and you shall fasten the braided chains to the settings.
15. You...

<note>At the junction of the ephod on both shoulders, a large precious stone was set in a golden casing, which had the shape of an eye: because the precious stones rested within it like an eyeball, yet sparkled all around with their brilliance like eyes; also, the prongs holding the stones are like the hairs of the eyebrows. These casings were made fast with two golden braided chains.</note>

v. 10. **Six and six)** In the Gemara Sotah <margin>(a) - chapter 7, section 19. Compare Wagenfeil's notes.</margin> (a) it is reported that the 6 oldest stood on one, and the 6 youngest on the other, but in such a way that they stood on the left shoulder as they were born: namely, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, Benjamin. On the right shoulder, however, Judah had precedence over Reuben: Judah, Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Dan, Naphtali. On each stone were 25 letters, so that there were 50 letters in total.

Just as Christ, as the almighty GOD and the powerful Word, "upholds all things" (Hebrews 1:3), so He especially bears His people with His gracious providence, protection, and governance; see Isaiah 19:4 and Isaiah 9:6, where His Lordship is also [carried] with His patience, long-suffering, and great mercy.

So Christ bears us in His intercession before GOD.
This indicates His love and union.
So the believers are a precious jewel in GOD’s eyes.
The names shall never be blotted out, which are drawn into Christ’s hands and inscribed in the Book of Life.
Namely, Christ is a Savior for the believers in both the Old and New Testaments.
There is a certain number of the believers whom Christ represents. Revelation 7.

<meta>This page continues the description of the High Priest's sacred garments, moving from the Ephod (the outer bodice) to the "Brustschildlein" or Breastplate of Judgment. It details the craftsmanship, the specific gemstones representing the twelve tribes, and the symbolic spiritual meanings attributed to these physical objects.</meta>

### Chapter XXVIII. The Second Book of Moses.

**15.** You shall also make the breastplate <note>original: *Brustschildlein*, literally "little breast-shield." In biblical tradition, this is the Breastplate of Judgment or *Choshen*.</note> of judgment with artistic work: you shall make it according to the workmanship of the ephod <note>original: *Leibrock*, referring to the bodice-like garment described on the previous page.</note>. Of gold, of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine linen yarn, you shall make it.

**16.** It shall be square and doubled. A span <note>A span is an ancient unit of measure, roughly the distance between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the pinky finger when the hand is spread out.</note> shall be its length, and a span its width.

**17.** And you shall fill it with set stones, with four rows of stones. One row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and a carbuncle. This is the first row.

**18.** And the second row an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond.

**19.** And the third row a jacinth, an agate, and an amethyst.

**20.** And the fourth row a turquoise, and an onyx, and a jasper. They shall be set in golden enclosures in their mountings.

**21.** And these stones shall be for the twelve names of the sons of Israel, according to their names, like the engraving of a seal, each with its name: they shall be for the twelve tribes.

---

v. 15. Upon the artistic belt of the ephod was fitted the mysterious breastplate of judgment: it was made of the same materials as the ephod and its belt, and thus it also pointed toward the Divinity, in which essential light and love reside; as this shone forth especially in Christ in both respects—that in Him the light and life of humanity, and the perfect love of God and Christ toward us humans, has been revealed.

v. 16. **Doubled)** Folded together; so that when laid out it was 2 spans long, but otherwise only
**One span)** which is as much as half a sacred cubit, or 3 flat hands, or 12 fingers wide.

v. 17-21. Upon this artistically-woven woolen cloth, twelve precious stones were set into their little cases in four rows, upon which the twelve names of the sons of Israel were engraved, which Aaron had to carry upon his heart; namely, that he should appear before GOD in the sanctuary not in his own name, but in the name of all the children of Israel.

What specific gemstones these were is a matter of differing opinions, and their powers and virtues are also mostly unknown; these will become more common and better known in Christ’s glorious kingdom. Therefore, all these are seen as the inner virtues worked in the hearts of believers through the radiance of the Spirit of Christ: just as one can observe the fruits of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22, and the Christian virtues in 2 Peter 1:5, 6, 7, as being such "precious stones."

<column-break/>

**22.** And you shall make for the breastplate chains of equal ends of twisted work, of pure gold.

**23.** And you shall also make two golden rings for the breastplate, and set the two rings at the two ends of the breastplate.

**24.** And put the two twisted golden chains into the two rings at the ends of the breastplate.

**25.** But the other two ends of the two twisted chains you shall fasten to the two enclosures <note>These are the settings or "eyes" holding the shoulder stones.</note> and attach them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod on its front side.

**26.** And you shall make two more golden rings and set them at the two ends of the breastplate, on its edge that is on the inside facing the ephod.

**27.** Furthermore, you shall make two golden rings which you shall set on the two shoulder pieces of the ephod from below, on its front part, opposite its seam, from above the artistic belt of the ephod.

**28.** And they shall bind the breastplate by its rings to the rings of the ephod above with a sky-blue cord, so that it sits upon the artistic belt of the ephod, and the breastplate does not become detached from the ephod.

---

v. 22-25. The golden chains were to be fastened at one end to the rings at the top corners of the breastplate, and at the other end into the clasps where the sardonyx stones were set, high on the shoulders.

v. 26. Also at the bottom, at the two lowest corners, but from the inside on the interior part of the breastplate, which, as mentioned, was doubled.

v. 27. On each clasp on the shoulder there was also a ring, as well as at the bottom of the ephod, above the belt—one under the right arm and one under the left.

v. 28. At the top, from each corner of the breastplate, a golden chain—fastened in the ring of that same corner—went up to the ring on the shoulder clasps and was secured there. At the bottom, however, from the ring at each lowest corner (which was on the inside), a blue ribbon went on each side to the ring at the bottom of the ephod, above the belt, and was tied there.

---

Otherwise, the six primary colors are to be noted in them: as in the black agate and dark carbuncle; in the bright and white diamond; in the red sardius or ruby; in the blue sapphire; in the yellow jacinth; and in the green emerald—and how these colors are found enhanced, diminished, or mixed in the remaining stones. With these, the virtues can be compared: such as **faith** which goes into the darkness; **love** which is entirely bright, pure, and sincere; **mercy, friendliness, and goodness** which surge in the blood; **wisdom** which must go into heavenly things; **divine love, devotion, and fear of GOD**, which must burn in the heart like a yellow fire; and **hope** which flourishes green.

<meta>This page continues the detailed description of the High Priest's vestments, specifically focusing on the Breastplate of Judgment and the blue Robe worn beneath the Ephod. ### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXVIII.

**29.** Thus shall Aaron carry the names of the sons of Israel in the breastplate <note>original: *Brustschildlein*, literally "little breast-shield."</note> of judgment upon his heart, whenever he enters into the Holy Place, as a constant memorial before the face of the **LORD**.

**30.** And you shall put the Urim and the Thummim <note>The *Urim* and *Thummim* were mysterious objects, possibly stones or lots, kept in the breastplate and used to determine God's will. The names translate roughly to "Lights" and "Perfections."</note> into the breastplate of judgment; and they shall be upon Aaron’s heart whenever he enters before the face of the **LORD**. Thus shall Aaron carry the judgment <note>original: *das Recht*, meaning the legal cause or divine decision.</note> of the children of Israel upon his heart before the face of the **LORD** at all times.

---

v. 29. This was intended to prefigure the great love of Christ, with which he now constantly appears in heaven before the face of **God** for the saints, *Hebrews 9:24.* as he always pleads the cause of his believers, and carries out his acquired right for them—and likewise their right against the world—gloriously, as their intercessor and *Advocate*. Therefore, all judgment is committed to him. *John 5:27.* See also *Ezekiel 21:32*, where he is called the one "who has the right." So also *Psalm 72:1-2.* The Bride also speaks of this love when she says she wishes to set Christ like a seal upon her heart and upon her arm; this refers to these high-priestly stones on the shoulders and on the heart with the engraved names of the children of Israel: *Song of Solomon 8:6-7.*

v. 30. Regarding the Urim and Thummim, which could be translated as Light and Perfection: it is difficult to know whether something especially hidden was delivered by **God** to Moses to be placed in such a breastplate; or whether a promise was thereby given to reveal the truth and righteousness—what to believe and what to do or leave undone—through a clear internal or external answer when the High Priest, in this finery of holy garments, would inquire of **God**. See *Numbers 27:21, 1 Samuel 23:9, 30:7-8.*

In Christ’s Spirit, the true Urim and Thummim have now been revealed, who, as the Spirit of Truth, leads believers into all truth, so that they may know what to believe and what to do or leave undone, if only we would earnestly strive for the pledge of our inheritance. *John 16:13-15.*

Because this item is called a "breastplate of judgment" in addition to the two pieces that were to be put inside it, these components can be distinguished as: Judgment, Doctrine, and Truth. Judgment is something that is not as certain as Doctrine; because it depends on the one who pronounces it, and is also an application of the Doctrine to the matter that must be judged. Doctrine, however, is more certain than Judgment; in that it is the application of knowledge and the experience by which one must judge. But Truth is above all these. Since Truth is the final end of all, upon which Judgment and Doctrine are founded—indeed, even the source from which they flow—one must pass through these steps to reach the Truth. This was engraved upon the breastplate to show that our reason exercises itself through Judgment; that it allows itself to be taught and submits through Doctrine; but yet receives its entire light from the Truth. Judgment is found within us. Doctrine communicates itself to others to obtain their obedience and submissiveness. But Truth remains in **God**, and one must be in **God** if one wishes to abide in the Truth. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is also called a Spirit of Truth.

It is remarkable that these two words <note>Urim and Thummim</note> begin with the first and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet <note>Aleph and Tav</note>, which the **Lord** himself adopts as his name in Greek, calling himself A and Ω <note>Alpha and Omega</note>. *Revelation 1:8.*

(a) *John 14:17.*

<column-break/>

**31.** You shall also make the robe <note>original: *Oberrock*, the blue robe of the Ephod.</note> to be worn under the ephod <note>original: *Leibrock*</note>: it shall be entirely of sky-blue wool.

**32.** And its opening for the head shall be in the middle of it: there shall be a woven border around the opening; it shall be like the opening of a coat of mail <note>original: *Panzer*</note>, so that it does not tear.

**33.** And upon its hems you shall make pomegranates of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, all around its hems; and golden bells between them all around.

**34.** A golden bell and a pomegranate, then another golden bell and a pomegranate, all around the hems of the robe.

**35.** And Aaron shall have it on to serve, so that its sound may be heard when he enters into the Holy Place before the face of the **LORD**, and when he comes out, so that he does not die.

---

The robe, which was entirely of sky-blue wool, signified the humanity of **Jesus Christ**, which was entirely filled with heavenly wisdom and grace before **God** and men. *Luke 2:52.* In this humanity, especially through the shedding of his blood, he had to acquire the righteousness that counts before **God**: therefore it is also called a "robe of righteousness," which believers receive in this imputed righteousness of Christ; *Isaiah 61:10.* and we must also put on this righteousness as armor, *Ephesians 6:14.* which cannot be torn by any power of temptation or assault from the enemy. This righteousness must ring out through the preaching of the Gospel in the whole world, and it is also filled with the pleasant fruits of righteousness, which are through **Jesus Christ** to the honor and praise of **God**. *Philippians 1:11.*

v. 32. Opening) This was not across toward the shoulders, but, as *Josephus* (a) writes, a long slit from the back to the middle of the chest, which was covered with a wide border woven into it: it is also said to have had a slit where the arms are put through. For this robe did not have sleeves.

v. 33. On) this silk-like robe (as called by *Luther*), over which the belt was put and the *Ephod* or bodice was cast, and which was a long robe consisting of one piece, as *Josephus* testifies; it signified both the robe of righteousness of **Jesus Christ**, and also his seamless robe of *John 19:23.* There were:

Pomegranates) which smell lovely, are good food, and protect clothes from moths. This teaches that Christ would become a sweet fragrance, a food, and through the strong scent of his sacrifice, protect us from danger.

v. 34. Between every pomegranate was a bell. Thus, every benefit of Christ must be proclaimed in the Gospel, as each deserves a special praise.

(a) *Book 3 of Antiquities, chapter 8.*

### Chapter XXVIII. The Second Book of Moses.

**36.** You shall also make a forehead-plate of pure gold, and engrave upon it, just as one engraves a seal: **The Holiness of the LORD.**

**37.** And you shall put it upon a cord of sky-blue wool, so that it is on the turban; it shall be on the front of the turban.

**38.** Thus it shall be on Aaron's forehead, so that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their gifts of hallowed things; and it shall be constantly on his forehead, to make them acceptable before the face of the **LORD**.

<note>v. 36. The name of **God** had to be engraved on the forehead; for this name is the All of **God**; and he who is the Spirit, or all holiness, belongs to Him who is. 
The golden plate, upon which was engraved "the Holiness of the Lord," through which **God** wished to be reconciled over all the perversity of the children of Israel in all their hallowed sacrificial gifts—so that he would not reckon it to them, and thus reject the gifts (see Leviticus 10:17, Numbers 18:1)—represented Christ as the Holiness of the Lord, as he is so expressly named in Malachi 2:11, and "the Holy One" with emphasis, namely of the Lord, in Luke 1:35. He alone can sanctify us in all our imperfection and make us acceptable before **God**, since he first bore our sickness and took our pains upon himself, etc., bore our iniquities, and then also, as the righteous servant of the Lord, has made many righteous and holy through knowledge of him. Isaiah 53:4, 11.</note>

<note>v. 37. *At the front of the turban.* Not, as it is commonly painted, like a half-moon; rather, it went around toward the ears and was two fingers wide, according to the report of the Hebrews. <margin>(a) Wagenseil, *Mishna, Tractate Sotah*, chapter 7, section 6, note 5. — Buxtorf, *Talmudic Lexicon* under the word *Tsits* <note>ציץ - the golden plate</note> & *Hebrew Lexicon* under *Kadosh* <note>קדוש - holy</note> p. 162.</margin></note>

<note>The turban <note>original: *Hut*, "hat," referring to the priestly mitre.</note> is noted by many as a sign of bondage and servitude, indicating that the High Priest was not permitted to go about with an uncovered head, which is a sign of freedom (2 Corinthians 3:18), but had to carry on himself a sign of the power of sin in the covered head. See 1 Corinthians 11:7, 10. Therefore, Christ also was placed under the power of the law (Galatians 4:4), and in this bearing of transgressions is called the "servant of the **LORD**" in Isaiah 53:11, but also in that very same place "the Righteous One" because of the essential holiness dwelling within him.</note>

<note>v. 38. *On the forehead.* The soul carries this name on its uppermost part, depicted by the forehead: because she cannot, without having come into a very high state, recognize the "All" of **God** and the "Nothingness" of the creature as it truly is. Many think they possess this knowledge entirely, yet they only possess it superficially. Only the conviction of experience can provide the true correction for this. Why, however, does the Scripture add: 
*To make them acceptable?* Because **God** cannot be opposed to a soul that is established in the truth of the All of **God** and her own nothingness. Inasmuch as she hereby declares her Creator to be righteous, she draws his most loving gaze upon herself. And it is this very truth which she carries in the image upon the little breast-shield, and in essence upon the forehead. For the truth of **God** as **God** cannot fall under human reason, except according to appearance and image. It is, however, essentially engraved in the uppermost part of the soul, in which it was placed at the very moment of creation; from there it was as if scratched out by sin, but now stands imprinted with abundance through **Jesus Christ** into the annihilated souls.</note>

<column-break/>

**39.** And you shall weave the inner tunic of fine linen yarn with a checkered pattern <note>original: *voll Aeuglein*, literally "full of little eyes," referring to a patterned weave.</note>; also make a turban of fine linen yarn, and you shall make a sash of embroidered work.

**40.** And for Aaron’s sons, you shall make tunics, and make sashes for them, and you shall make caps for them for glory and for beauty.

**41.** And you shall put them on your brother Aaron and his sons with him; and you shall anoint them, and fill their hands <note>A Hebrew idiom for "ordain."</note>, and sanctify them, so that they may serve me in the priest’s office.

<margin>(a) Leviticus 16:4.</margin>
**42.** And have linen under-garments <insert>(a)</insert> made for them to cover the flesh of their nakedness; they shall reach from the loins to the thighs.

<margin>(2) Ezekiel 42:14.</margin>
**43.** And Aaron and his sons shall wear them <insert>(2)</insert> whenever they go into the Tabernacle of the Congregation, or whenever they approach the altar to serve in the sanctuary, so that they do not bear an iniquity and must die. This shall be an everlasting statute for him and for his offspring after him.

<meta>Catchword: The</meta>

---

<note>v. 39. This inner tunic, which went down to the feet, represented the holiness of Christ in his entire walk; therefore he could rightly say of himself: "Who can accuse and convict me of a sin?" (John 8:46). Thus he arranged his whole way of life quite exactly and carefully, so that no one could have rightly blamed him. This is what these "little eyes" <note>the checkered pattern</note> embroidered on the entire tunic can indicate: therefore it is translated better this way than if it were given as mere boxes or cubes, because this can more emphatically indicate such holy circumspection in conduct to the priests as well. See Ephesians 5:15. 
The sash is explained in Isaiah 11:5: "Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and truth the belt of his waist"; meaning that he will, as it were, gird himself up and keep himself ready in everything to carry out his promises, but also his threats, gloriously. See Revelation 1:13.</note>

<note>v. 40 etc. The priestly garments consisted only of linen tunics with sashes over them, and that instead of the [High Priest's] turbans they had such caps or head-bands that were wound around the head and so tied (Chapter 29:9), just as turbans are still in use among the Asian peoples. And along with this, they had to wear linen undergarments or trousers, so that in the climbing up and down the altar their nakedness might not be exposed toward the altar (Chapter 20:26). 
These trousers, however, had no slit in the front <margin>(a) Selden, *On the succession in the high priesthood*, book 2, chapter 7. Leusden, *On mixed Hebrew philology*, dissertation 27.</margin> and are said to have been tied shut at the top around the navel with linen bands like a pouch.</note>

<header>The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXIX.</header>

# Chapter XXIX.

->The Sacrifices of the High Priest and the Daily Sacrifice.<-

AND this is the thing that you shall do to them, to sanctify them, that they may minister to me in the priest's office. Take a young bull and two perfect rams;
2. And unleavened bread, and unleavened cakes mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers spread with oil. You shall make them of wheat flour;
3. And you shall put them in a basket, and bring them in the basket, together with the bull and the two rams.
4. And you shall have Aaron and his sons come to the door of the Tabernacle of Meeting, and you shall wash them with water.
5. Afterward you shall take the garments, and put the tunic on Aaron, and the robe of the ephod, and the ephod, and the breastplate, and you shall gird him with the skillfully woven band of the ephod.
6. And you shall set the turban upon his head, and put the holy crown upon the turban.
7. And you shall take the anointing oil, and pour it upon his head. Thus you shall anoint him. <margin>Leviticus 8:12.</margin>

v. 1. Because Aaron and his descendants were sinners just like the rest of the people, and thus had no inherent advantage over them; yet because God had chosen them to perform the prefiguring priestly office and the sacrifices: they first had to be reconciled through three sacrifices—namely the Sin, Burnt, and Installation Offerings—and thus be sanctified and publicly ordained for this holy office.
v. 2. They also had to bring three kinds of food: bread, which was the common eating-bread; then cakes; and then wafers, which are very thin cakes; both of which were made of fine or wheat flour: and all of them were unleavened.
**Spread with oil.** Or anointed, according to the Hebrew <term>Mashach</term> <note>original: משח</note>, where oil was smeared on with the finger. (a)
v. 4. Then first occurred the washing; namely of their bodies: by which their sinful impurity was brought to their minds.
v. 5. Secondly, the putting on of the holy garments: by which their sanctification for this holy office was prefigured to them. See Psalm 132:9. There they all (1) put on the tunics; v. 9. afterward the High Priest (2) was girded with the belts, and then (3) the robe, and (4) the ephod over it, then (5) the breastplate was put on, and (6) with the skillfully woven band it was girded, so that everything lay firmly.
v. 6. Thereupon they (7) set the turban on him, with (8) the golden plate on it, which is here called a holy crown, and in Hebrew is called <term>Tzitz</term> <note>original: ציץ</note>, which surrounds the whole head and is proper to kings. This, however, was as it were a crest and sign of his great dignity, wherein he was set apart from all the people; which is the origin of the word <term>Nezer</term> <note>original: נזר</note>. And these were the eight pieces of the holy garments.
v. 7. Thirdly occurred the anointing of his head with the holy anointing oil, which happened only to the High Priest; by which the sharing of wisdom and blessing for this high office was signified. See Psalm 133:2.

(a) Rabbi Solomon <note>Rashi</note> as cited by Lyra on Exodus 29.

<column-break/>

8. Afterward you shall have his sons come near, and put the tunics on them:
9. And you shall gird them with the sash, Aaron and his sons, and bind the caps on them; so that they shall have the priesthood for an eternal statute; and you shall fill the hand of Aaron and the hand of his sons. <note>This "filling of the hand" is the literal Hebrew idiom for ordination.</note>
10. And you shall have the bull brought before the Tabernacle (*) of Meeting, and Aaron and his sons shall lean their hands upon the bull's head.
<margin>(*) Leviticus 8:14 etc.</margin>

12. Afterward you shall take some of the blood of the bull, and put it on the horns of the altar with your finger; and all the blood you shall pour out at the base of the altar.

v. 8. 9. After the sons were also dressed in their garments, then followed fourthly the filling of Aaron and his sons, by which they were consecrated to their offices, after the Sin Offering and Burnt Offering had first been performed for them.
By the "filling of hands" is understood a certain ceremony where the priests were given certain pieces of the sacrifice into their hands, and they were thereby publicly installed into the priestly office.
v. 10. That sacrifice consisted of a young bull of the male sex, which was still suckling its mother: there they had to lay their hands on it, in order to confess their sins and their unworthiness for this office.
v. 11. 12. Thereupon the bull was slaughtered, and its blood was smeared on the horns of the altar with a finger, and the rest was poured at the base of the altar: to show that a blood would be shed for them, through which they and the whole people would be reconciled, and also their entire service, which was to happen on the altar, would be acceptable to the LORD in the true blood of the right Atonement Sacrifice.
It is to be noted, however, that the horns of the Incense Altar are meant whenever the Scripture mentions Sin Offerings. Conversely, what was poured at the base is to be understood as the Altar of Burnt Offering.

---

The second ram was prepared as an offering of fullness or "filling of the hands" <note>original: *Einweihung* - the Hebrew term for ordination literally means "filling the hand."</note> for their office. Its blood was smeared on their right earlobe, thumb, and the big toe of their right hand and foot to remind them of their obedience to God’s commandments and statutes. Furthermore, it signified that this office was the work of their hands and their proper calling, in which they were bound to walk and dedicate themselves solely and exclusively for all the days of their lives.

v. 13. For all the fat had to be set on fire to show that they must sacrifice all the strengths of their body and soul to the Lord in fervent love, as well as toward their neighbor.

v. 14. And finally, its flesh, hide, and offal were burned outside the camp to show that all corruption of the sinful nature must be put to death, and consumed by the fire of divine love here on earth, if we wish to have a share in the heavens above.

The Apostle <note>Referring to the author of the Book of Hebrews.</note> interprets this sacrifice burned outside the camp specifically as pointing to Christ, who also had to suffer outside the gate of Jerusalem so that he might sanctify the people, along with the priests, through his own blood. **Hebrews 13:11, 12.** He was holy in himself, but through his blood we had to be cleansed and washed. **1 John 1:7.** He possessed essential righteousness and holiness in himself, but he desired to clothe us with the robe of righteousness and the garments of salvation. **Isaiah 61:10.** He possessed the Spirit without measure and did not need to be anointed with any physical oil; however, he wished to bring about the anointing of his Spirit for us, for all wisdom and sanctification. **1 John 2:20.** And finally, he wished to "fill" and ordain us as priests, **Revelation 1:6, 5:10**, provided we first accept his sacrifice in true faith and allow ourselves to be sprinkled with his blood. **1 Peter 1:2.**

v. 15–18. The first ram, which is a male from the sheep, was prepared as a burnt offering: it was entirely cut into pieces, and along with its entrails—after everything had first been washed—everything had to be burned. Aaron and his sons first had to lay their hands upon it.

This was a burnt offering and, like the sin offering, it represented Christ, who took our sins upon himself—**Isaiah 53:4–5, 6, 11; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 8:3**—and entirely sacrificed himself to his heavenly Father in fervent love. By this, he reconciled the Father's wrath against sin, as God, so to speak, smelled the sweet aroma of Christ’s obedience unto death. And here we must seize this sacrifice in faith, and thus, as it were, lean, support, and rely entirely upon it. For taking refuge in this sacrifice and trusting in it are the two essential parts of faith. **Psalm 2:12; Romans 3:25, 26.** And so we must also sacrifice our bodies, along with soul and spirit, entirely to God as a sacrifice that is living, holy, and pleasing to God, in order to test and fulfill his holy will in everything. **Romans 12:1, 2; 1 Thessalonians 5:23.**

v. 19. **The other ram)** Which was the actual heave offering or thank offering, and was called the ram of consecration, by which the priests were, so to speak, completed and made capable for their office.

**Lay on with their hands)** To indicate that it was no longer to be considered common livestock, but was set apart by God so that, with its blood and death, it should point toward the bloody death of the Messiah.

v. 20. **Upon the earlobe)** Not on the upper part, but on the lowest soft part; to serve as a reminder of ready obedience.

**Upon—upon—upon)** The whole human being, from the crown of the head to the feet, is entirely corrupted and there is nothing good in him; even his "right" <note>Meaning his best or most capable side.</note> and best parts are unclean. Through the blood of Jesus, however, not only the soul but also the body and all its members are sanctified and made pure again. **1 Corinthians 6:26.**

v. 21. Therefore, they and their garments were also sprinkled here with the blood and anointing oil, as a sign that they should be sprinkled with the blood of the true sacrifice for their reconciliation and sanctification, and should be gifted with the Holy Spirit to instruct others as well.

The oil of dedication was the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which He Himself pours out upon Apostolic people, as priests of the Lord, for their installation through His holy infusion.

The blood with which they are sprinkled teaches us that they can have no power over souls except through Jesus Christ: and that even then, everything already happened through His blood, in that all holiness and all priesthood has been sanctified through the shedding of this blood.

Through these two things—the blood and the Spirit of Christ—our salvation is brought about. One without the other does not achieve its proper effect in us. v. 22.

22. Afterward you shall take from the ram the fat and the tail, and the fat that covers the entrails, and the fatty lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, and the right shoulder; for it is a ram of **ordination** <note>German: *Füll-Opffer*, literally "filling-offering," referring to the "filling of the hands" of the priests to authorize them for service.</note>:
23. And one loaf of bread, and one cake of bread made with oil, and one wafer out of the basket of unleavened bread that stands before the face of the LORD:
24. And you shall lay all of this upon the hands of Aaron and upon the hands of his sons, and you shall move them back and forth as a **wave offering** before the face of the LORD.
25. Afterward you shall take these things from their hands and let them be burned upon the altar over the burnt offering, for a sweet <note>The text uses an asterisk (*) to point to the cross-reference below.</note> aroma before the face of the LORD: This is an offering made by fire to the LORD.
->(a) Leviticus 1:9.<-
26. And you shall take the breast from the ram of ordination that is before Aaron, and shall wave it as a wave offering before the face of the LORD, and it shall be your portion.

---

v. 22–25. Afterward they were required to take all the fat, the right shoulder, and a loaf, cake, and wafer upon their hands, and move such things back and forth—as the Jews believe—toward the East and toward the West, toward the South and toward the North; and afterward all of it had to be burned upon the burnt offering of the first ram. By this it was indicated how they were hereby obligated to apply all their bodily and spiritual powers, their actions, and their sustenance to the service of God and their neighbor.

All other offerings are mixed with self-interest. They are performed either to obtain the forgiveness of some sins, or to be released from a burden, or to still the wrath of God, or even to pray for some graces from His goodness. They all reserve something for themselves and are thus still imperfect. In the burnt offering alone, everything is consumed. This is the perfect sacrifice, which represents the **annihilation** <note>German: *Vernichtigung*; in this context, it refers to the mystical concept of the total surrender or "naughting" of the self before God.</note> through which everything belongs to God alone. Therefore, it is also called the offering of the LORD, which creates a pleasant aroma for Him.

v. 26. Just as the breast became the portion of Moses, who administered the first priestly office and thereby consecrated Aaron and his sons—thus representing the place of Christ, who entrusted him with this prefiguring office—so also did this remind them to dedicate their hearts entirely to God in perfect love and obedience.

<column-break/>

27. And you shall thus sanctify the breast <note>Asterisk (*) refers to Leviticus 7:34.</note> of the wave offering and the shoulder of the **heave offering**, which was waved and which was lifted up from the ram of ordination, from that which is for Aaron and from that which is for his sons.
->(*) Leviticus 7:34.<-
28. And it shall belong to Aaron and his sons as an eternal statute from the children of Israel; for it is a heave offering: and the heave offering from the children of Israel shall be from their thank offerings; their heave offering shall be before the LORD.
29. And the holy garments that Aaron had shall his sons have after him, to be anointed in them and to have their hands filled <note>To be "filled" refers again to the process of ordination and being equipped for the office.</note> in them.
30. Seven days shall he among his sons who becomes priest in his stead put them on, he who shall go into the Tabernacle of the Congregation to serve in the sanctuary.
31. You <note>The text breaks here to continue on the next page.</note>

---

v. 27. **Waved and lifted up**) This was done through four movements: right, left, forward, and backward; and then through two more: upward and downward.
v. 28. From all the thank offerings of the children of Israel, the shoulder and the breast were henceforth to belong to the priests, to remind them of their duty of labor in love. Even so, Christ, out of pure love, took upon Himself the great labor of our redemption through a perfect obedience to the law and also through the suffering of death. See Isaiah 43:24. Whereby Christ has also been, as it were, ground and baked into our Bread of Life, and thus prepared for our nourishment and delightful refreshment, like such a cake and wafer. See John 6 and Psalm 81:16. Who also is and shall be proclaimed in the four quarters of the world, and in the lifting up of the heart to God, must be prayed for from God.
v. 29. Hereby the high-priestly office was transferred to the sons of Aaron, and so further to his male descendants—presumably always to the eldest—who, as a sign of this office having come upon them, had to be dressed in these same holy garments by another priest: just as Moses first consecrated Eleazar, the son of Aaron, with his garments as High Priest in his stead. Numbers 20:28.
v. 30. They had to spend seven days, and thus a full week including the Sabbath, with their anointing and the filling of their hands: and that before the door of the Tabernacle, before they were permitted to go into the Holy Place to perform their office. Leviticus 8:35.
The office of teaching should be entrusted to those in the succession who stand in the anointing and have dedicated themselves to labor in love: who are thus faithful and capable of teaching others also (2 Timothy 2:2), being blameless (Titus 1:6, etc.) and clothed with righteousness (Psalm 132:9).
However, not only these, but all who wish to be found among the number of the faithful, must strive for the garments of salvation (Isaiah 61:10), that they may be washed and purified in the blood of Christ, the loins of their minds girded, and they thus be alert to perform each their commanded business in all faithfulness of heart (1 Peter 1:13). To offer spiritual sacrifices to God as priests of the New Testament, and to strive to serve Him constantly with reverence and fear (Hebrews 12:28). For this pure and bright, precious linen the faithful should strive, which are the righteous deeds of the saints (Revelation 19:8) and the beautiful garments (Isaiah 52:1) that Christ acquired for His faithful in the sanctification of the Spirit and wishes to give to them: for then they must also hate the garment spotted by the flesh. Jude verse 23. See Ezekiel 44:17–18.

394 The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXIX.

43. <margin>(a) John 4:24.</margin> Indeed, there (a) I will meet with the children of Israel, so that they may be sanctified through my glory.
44. Thus I will sanctify the Tabernacle of the Congregation and the altar; and Aaron and his sons I will sanctify, that they may serve as priests unto me.

<column-break/>

<columns>1</columns>

> This comforting union of God with His people now occurs in Christ Jesus, through whom God has glorified Himself, and in whom one can attain fellowship with God and be sanctified in Him, to become a tabernacle and a priest of God the Most High. He also dwells in us through faith, and not merely beside us—where one might only hear preaching about Christ from the outside, and thus Christ's benefits would only be proclaimed among us. Such a state would serve more for our greater judgment and accountability. Instead, we must strive for such an actual indwelling of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that we may become a true sanctuary of the Triune God, in which He is praised in time and eternity. See John 14:23 and v. 17; 1 Cor. 6:19, 20.

### Chapter XXX.

->The Altar of Incense, half-shekels of atonement, the washbasin, anointing oil, and incense.<-

<columns>2</columns>

1. <margin>ch. 37:25.</margin> YOU shall also make an altar to burn incense; of Shittim wood <note>An incorruptible wood from the acacia tree, symbolizing endurance.</note> you shall make it.
2. A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its width; it shall be four-square: and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be part of it.
3. And you shall overlay it with pure gold—its top, its walls all around, and its horns; and you shall make for it a golden crown <note>A decorative molding or rim.</note> all around.

<column-break/>

4. And you shall make two golden rings for it under its crown: at its two corners you shall make them on its two sides, to be places for the poles to carry it with.
5. And you shall make the poles of Shittim wood and overlay them with gold.
6. <margin>(a) ch. 40:5. Lev. 16:18.</margin> And you shall set it (a) before the veil that is before the Ark of the Testimony, before the Mercy Seat that is over the Testimony, where I will meet with you.
7. And Aaron shall burn thereon incense of sweet spices. Every morning, when he tends the lamps, he shall burn it.
8. And

<columns>1</columns>

> Just as the Altar of Burnt Offering represented Christ’s high-priestly office in the sacrifice and shedding of His blood for atonement—done quite publicly in the eyes of the people—so here the other part of His high-priestly office is presented: His intercession. While He performed this here on earth (John 17), He now does so especially in the true Sanctuary in heaven at the right hand of His heavenly Father, where He represents us: Rom. 8:34, Heb. 7:25, 1 John 2:1. There He can no longer be seen with human eyes, just as the priest could not be seen in the Holy Place when he offered incense morning and evening. This points to the constant intercession of Christ, which He performs early and late for His believers.

<columns>2</columns>

v. 2. **Four-square**) This enclosure is made for all believers in all four corners of the earth, and is thus powerfully applied to them.
**two cubits shall be its height**) The humanity of Christ is exalted both by the power of the Father and through His own merit.
**Its horns**) These were not curved goat horns, as Scacchus (a) <note>Fortunato Scacchi (1573–1643), an Augustinian scholar who wrote on biblical antiquities.</note> depicts them; but rather small pillars or columns made of Shittim wood, which were also worked as one piece with and out of the altar.
v. 3. The **Shittim wood**, entirely overlaid with gold, once again indicated the humanity of our High Priest, completely surrounded by the Divinity.
The **horns** signify His strength; the **crown** His royal dignity. Note how Zechariah thoughtfully joins these two together: *He shall rule on His throne, and He shall also be a priest on His throne.* Ch. 6:13.
**Top**) <note>German: *Dach*, literally "roof."</note> Bonfrerius <note>Seraphinus Bonfrerius (1567–1633), a Jesuit commentator.</note> is rather awkward regarding the word "roof," believing the altar was flat and solid on top. He instead praises his Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible.</note> which gave it as "a grate" <note>original: *craticulam*</note>, and cites the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Josephus (b) who call it "a hearth" <note>original: *ἐσχάραν* (eschara)</note> to support him. See ch. 37:26.
<margin>(a) Sacred Oils and Ointments, book 2, ch. 47. (b) Antiquities of the Jews, Book 3, ch. 7.</margin>

<column-break/>

v. 6. **Before the veil**) Not behind the veil, as Augustine (a) is very much in error. It stood before the curtain that hung in front of the Most Holy Place, directly opposite the Ark of the Covenant where the entrance to the Most Holy Place was, so that when it was opened, the altar seemed almost to be within it. Therefore the Apostle says that the Most Holy Place had this incense altar, even though it was actually in the Holy Place. Heb. 9:3, 4. And thus Christ now appears before the face of God for us. Heb. 9:24.
v. 7. **Every morning**) The altar was also always cleaned beforehand and the ashes swept up, for which there were special vessels kept in a golden bowl.
**When he tends the lamps**) Before the pieces of the sacrifice were placed upon the fire.
<margin>(a) as cited by Gerhard on Heb. 9:4.</margin>

<margin>
v. 8. **Between the two evenings)** After the pieces of the sacrifice were laid upon the fire. Thus the daily sacrifice was both begun and concluded with this ritual.
</margin>

<margin>
**He shall light it)** Each time, half a pound of incense was used and lit at once; it must therefore have produced a large, strong, and thick cloud of smoke.
</margin>

<margin>
When the lamps were lit, the incense was also ignited. Through the **sharing of the light**, the spirit of prayer is given to the believers, so that their hearts may be prepared as such altars of incense in burning devotion. See Psalm 141:1–2. And so Christ also sanctifies their prayers and brings them before the heavenly Father, just as he is presented as the Angel of the Covenant with the golden censer. Rev. 8:3.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 9. **No strange incense)** It was also forbidden to use any strange fire; rather, the fire had to be taken from a specific place on the Altar of Burnt Offering. Num. 16:46.
</margin>

<margin>
No **strange fire** of false light or self-will must come upon the hearts of the believers, but only the pure fire of the Holy Spirit.
</margin>

<margin>
**Neither... nor... no)** The Hebrews write (a) <note>original: "ap. Hottinger. de jur. Ebr. n. 10." Referring to Johann Heinrich Hottinger's work on Jewish Law.</note> that if a priest offered anything other than incense on this altar, he deserved a flogging.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 10. The sprinkling of the horns of this altar occurred on the Great Day of Atonement once a year with the blood of the sin offering (see Lev. 16:34) to show how, through the sacrifice made once for all, the sins of the believers are taken away. Likewise, an **everlasting validity** was thereby brought to their prayers, so that in the name of Christ they may continually approach the throne of God's grace. See Heb. 9:28, 10:14, 19, etc.
</margin>

<margin>(a) in Hottinger's *Jewish Law*, no. 10.</margin>

<column-break/>

11. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

12. When you take the census of the children of Israel according to those numbered among them, then every man shall give a ransom for his soul to the LORD when you number them; so that there may be no plague among them when you number them.

13. This they shall give, everyone who passes among those who are numbered: half a shekel, according to the shekel of the sanctuary. The shekel is twenty <term>Gerahs</term> <note>A Gerah was the smallest unit of Hebrew currency, roughly equivalent to the weight of a bean.</note>: the half-shekel shall be the heave offering to the LORD. <margin>ch. 25:2, 3.</margin>

14. Everyone who passes among those who are numbered, from twenty years old and above, shall give the heave offering of the LORD.

15. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, when they give the heave offering of the LORD to atone for your souls.

16. And you shall take the atonement money from the children of Israel and shall give it for the service of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, that it may be a memorial for the children of Israel before the face of the LORD, to atone for your souls.

17. And

---

The fact that, alongside the sacrifices, a certain **ransom money** for the atonement of souls was required—and a modest one at that, which both the poor and the rich could pay as an equal value (namely, approximately a quarter-thaler in our currency)—indicated that we must not only be reconciled with the heavenly Father but also be redeemed from the power of the enemy as his prisoners, Luke 1:74, through the ransom that Christ gave for our souls, 1 Tim. 2:6. This ransom was not paid to the enemy, but rather had to be rendered to the justice of God, so that we might be snatched from the power of the enemy, and that power also had to be destroyed through the death of Christ, Heb. 2:14–15; in which this ransom likewise consisted, and not in silver and gold. 1 Pet. 1:18–19.

v. 12. **Every man a ransom)** This was therefore a poll tax. No one was free from it, even if they were so poor that they lived on alms and had to beg for it or sell the coat off their back. Only women, children, and servants were exempt. However, it was accepted if they wished to give it voluntarily; but not from a Gentile. Those who lived in other countries sent it to Jerusalem through authorized representatives.

v. 13. **Shekel)** This is otherwise the same as a "piece of silver," and a coin among the Hebrews equal to four Athenian drachmas, as Josephus writes (a); that is, in our currency, half an ounce of silver or half a Reichsthaler; this refers to the **Holy Shekel**. The common shekel, however, was only half as much and was otherwise called the Country Shekel or the King’s Shekel.

v. 14. **Give the heave offering)** For this purpose, Joash had a special chest constructed. 2 Kings 12:9.

v. 15. **Half the shekel)** At the beginning of the second temple, they gave only a third of a shekel. Neh. 10:32.

v. 16. **For the service of the Tabernacle)** This money had to be given at that time for the service of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, whether for its construction or its maintenance; later, it was requested only in times of special necessity for the temple to repair it. 2 Chron. 24:6, 9; Neh. 10:32.

Just as believers should also contribute their physical means toward the maintenance of the ministry under the Gospel in the spirit of the New Testament, as the Apostle demonstrated at length in 1 Cor. 9. This should not necessarily happen through "confession pennies" <note>Small coins traditionally given to a pastor during the rite of private confession or before Holy Communion.</note> and the like, as if one intended to bind oneself to such charitable acts at the Lord's Supper where the atonement of souls is to be powerfully presented; for a great abuse has crept in there. Rather, a loving heart will find opportunity to sow physical things so that they may reap spiritual things in blessing.

## The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXX.

17. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
18. You shall also make a bronze washbasin, with its bronze stand, for washing; and you shall place it between the Tent of Meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it:
19. So that Aaron and his sons may wash their hands and their feet from it.
20. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, so that they do not die; or when they approach the altar to minister, to burn a fire offering to the LORD.
21. Thus they shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they do not die; and this shall be a perpetual statute for them, for him and for his offspring throughout their generations.

-> This washbasin represents Christ, how he has become the cleansing of our souls. <-

**v. 18. Bronze)** Copper.
**Between the Tent and the altar)** Not directly in line, but somewhat to the side toward the right, or toward the south.

**v. 19. 20.** Just as the Altar of Burnt Offering points to righteousness in Christ <note>Justification</note>, so the washbasin placed after it points to sanctification <note>Heiligung</note>; for we must first be purified in our conduct and way of life before we, as spiritual priests, may enter into the Holy Place and offer up our prayers to GOD. See Hebrews 10:22, 23; Psalm 26:6. To this end, blood and water flowed out of Christ’s opened side on the Cross, John 19:34, to represent precisely these two benefits. And so Christ has become the free, open fountain against sin and uncleanness. Zechariah 13:1.

It is therefore not fitting, concludes Ruysbroeck <margin>(a) Explanation of the Tabernacle, ch. 35, p. 72.</margin> <note>Ruobrochius: Jan van Ruysbroeck, a 14th-century Flemish mystic</note>, that anyone should trust in their own holiness, but rather place all their hope primarily in the mercy of God; in which we, with humility and repentance, must lament and confess before the divine goodness and mercy that we fail very often daily through inattention, both in disordered works and desires: and thus we shall wash our hands and feet.

**v. 21. All priests of the New Covenant,** and whoever is of Christ’s seed, is bound to this: to wash themselves in the water of grace as often as necessity requires, especially when they wish to enter the Sanctuary, and to practice in life the truth of that which was prefigured by the imagery of the Old Testament.

**Colors.** In this land, the root is not particularly special and has no scent; but the best violet-roots <note>Orris root</note> come from Illyria and Florence. (d) That these are meant here is quite believable.

**Shekel of the Sanctuary)** Is said to be the same as an ounce.

**v. 25. By the art of the apothecary)** Everything was macerated in water and boiled in oil. (f)

<column-break/>

22. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
23. Take also for yourself the most excellent balsamic spices: five hundred of the finest myrrh; and half as much of fragrant cinnamon, two hundred and fifty; and two hundred and fifty of fragrant cane; <margin>(a) Isaiah 43:24.</margin>
24. And five hundred of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary; and a hin of olive oil:
25. And you shall make from these a holy anointing oil, an ointment blended according to the art of the apothecary. It shall be a holy anointing oil. <margin>Psalm 133:1, 2.</margin>
26. And...

-> The holy anointing oil represents the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Christ received for mankind when he ascended on high; when he entered into the Most Holy Place and triumphed over the enemies through his sacrifice (Psalm 68:19). There he made the believers into priests and anointed them with the spiritual oil of the gifts of the Spirit. <-

**v. 23.** Regarding what these balsamic spices—which one may infer from the word <note>original Hebrew: *besem* בשם</note>, which has a similarity to the word "balsam"—are actually called, and what species they are; one cannot know precisely, as they grow in distant Asian, African, and Indian lands.

**The finest myrrh)** According to the Hebrew, "free myrrh." Some understand this to mean the best, others the unadulterated. However, it actually refers to the sweat that emerges by itself, and indicates "stacte," which is not forced out by external violence or slashing the bark, but oozes out freely on its own: which is said to happen when the tree is strongly moved by the north wind. See Song of Solomon 4:14.

**Cinnamon)** As many believe (a), this was a very precious and rare cinnamon, which the Emperors used to keep in their most secret treasury. Lonicerus (b) writes that in our times, no one has yet seen true cinnamon. We today have nothing other than Cassia; the very best piece of which can hardly be compared to the smallest and worst piece of true cinnamon.

However, it may well be that the finest Ceylonese cinnamon is meant, and that it is one and the same as the true cinnamon.

**Fragrant cane)** <note>original: *Kalmes* (Calamus)</note>. It is said to be a thin tree, full of knots, and shaped like a reed: therefore it is called *Calamus*, from which the German word <note>Kalmus</note> originates.

**v. 24. Cassia)** The LXX <note>Septuagint</note> give this as *kidda* <note>original Hebrew: קִידָה</note>, and Josephus (c) does as well: which is a known flower, called Sword-lily or blue Iris, whose root is very fragrant and very potent in medicine, and is called "violet-root" because of the similar scent; the flower, however, is called *Iris* because of the various colors somewhat resembling a rainbow.

**Hin)** They also obtained that much anointing oil from it; namely 12 *Log*. (e)

---

Just as it can be enough for us to know that these are aromatic, pleasant, powerful, and warming plants that also make food pleasant and healthy; so too they represent the lovely fruits of the Spirit: such as love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, chastity (Galatians 5:22). These make the soul pleasant before GOD and before men, as they are enjoyed, so to speak, in fellowship with others, and the same are strengthened and refreshed thereby. They are also mixed and linked together like such a balsamic oil, so that no single one may be of the right kind without the others.

# Chapter XXX. The Second Book of Moses.

26. And you shall anoint with it the Tent of Meeting and the Ark of the Testimony,
