## 7. And Moses took the tent and pitched it for himself outside the camp, far away from the camp, and called it the Tent of Meeting. And so it happened that whoever wished to consult the **LORD** had to go out to the Tent of Meeting, which was outside the camp.

## 8. And it happened that whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people rose up, and every man stood at his tent door and watched Moses until he had entered the tent.

## 9. Furthermore, it happened that whenever Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the door of the tent, and the Lord spoke with Moses.

## 10. And when all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the door of the tent, all the people rose up and worshipped, every man at the door of his tent.

<margin>v. 7. Moses pitched the tent—in which he was accustomed to consult **GOD** and to pronounce judgment for the people—outside the camp, so that they had to go out whenever they wished to seek counsel.</margin>
But what kind of tent was this? **Answer:** Most understand this, based on the direction of the Scripture, to be a special small tent that Moses used before the actual large Tabernacle was built; it could not have been the official Tabernacle yet because Moses had only just come down from the mountain where he received the instructions for it.

<margin>v. 8. Whenever Moses went out)</margin> He who otherwise stayed among the people and had his dwelling-tent there: it cannot be meant by the aforementioned text that he took his dwelling away from the people and no longer wished to live among them, as Momma <note>original: "(a) de stat. Eccles. lib tripl. oeconom. tom. 1. l. 2. c. 10." — This refers to Wilhelm Momma's "The State of the Church under Threefold Economy," a 17th-century theological work.</note> suggests.

<margin>v. 9. Descended) from Mount Sinai.</margin>

<margin>v. 10. In the tent)</margin> There, the poor transgressors found their refuge, where they prayed to **GOD** for everything they needed.

As soon as they perceived by the pillar of cloud that **GOD** was with them, they began to pray to Him from their tents, or

**Every man -- at his tent)** as it says; that is, in the place of their rest. For a truly suffering soul can do this in all things without losing its inner peace. And this way of worshipping is more perfect than any other kind.

They worshipped standing from afar: because perfect worship—which happens in spirit and in truth, through faith and love—reaches through all distances and surpasses every physical condition, in that it soars up to **GOD** above all outward means.

But although this worship by a spiritual people, who were repentant according to their station, was a very advanced form of worship, it still did not come close to the worship of **Moses**.

<margin>(a) On the State of the Church, threefold economy, vol. 1, book 2, ch. 10.</margin>

<column-break/>

## 11. But the **LORD** spoke to Moses <margin>(a) ch. 24 / 12.</margin> face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. Afterward, he returned to the camp; but his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, the young man, did not depart from within the tent.

It is the habit of those young souls who are beginning to enter into the inner life to remain constantly in prayer. They enjoy it so much that they cannot bring themselves to leave it. The sweet, penetrating love that takes hold of them causes them to remain enclosed within themselves; and a strong and living presence of **GOD**, which is poured into them, concentrates them as gently within themselves—as if in a tent—that they cannot leave it. A wise guide must leave them in that state, just as **Moses** did; for then is not the time to pull them out of it.

But this friend of **GOD**, who was exalted above all, chosen, and unique, speaks with **GOD** face to face, in the most intimate union of all unions—in that precise, essential union that is raised above all human powers. For after **GOD** had somewhat exalted the understanding of the creature and humbled Himself, so that some harmony of love might be found there, He spoke with him face to face, and dealt with him in such a familiar way that it deserves to be compared with the intimacy a friend has with his most secret friend: in that He hid nothing from him and, in a certain way, made him His equal. For the most intimate friendship makes friends equal to one another.

But such secret friendship is something quite rare on earth, because few people abandon all things from the heart to seek this pearl. The ungodly and earthly nature is all too dear to the human heart for it to easily tear itself away and cling to the invisible alone.

To be sure, this interaction with **Moses** was a special kind of intimacy, which happens to very few in such a sensory and outward manner. Meanwhile, in the New Covenant, we have such precious promises that we shall come near to the Father through **JESUS Christ**, the Mediator, and shall have access in faith to all grace, and can become **GOD’S** friends once again. **John 15:15.**

Oh, what blessedness there is in knowing **GOD** in **Christ**, hearing His voice, finding the way to the Father through Him, learning the truth from Him, and being governed and corrected by Him! No physical friend does for another what He does: communicating so directly, so intimately, and so constantly with the other. But

This friend never departs: His light is an eternal light, full of divine power, full of comfort and strengthening. A single word of comfort from His Spirit is more powerful than a thousand words from worldly friends. Where no human word suffices, this friend reaches in with His work.

So let enemies and false friends rage, plot, and persecute: If you have the Head as your friend and are loved by **GOD**, what can the crowd of enemies and adversaries do to you?

Only see to it that **GOD’S** friendship is right within the heart. Value it above all else and set everything else aside in comparison. See to it that you become truly intimate, truly secret, and familiar with **GOD** in faith and life: then in times of need, you will always have unhindered access to your **GOD**, and can rest in Him in the midst of unrest, be comforted even without any outward comfort, and be strong without any creaturely strength.

->O how happy is the one whom you, **LORD**, thus admit into your holy friendship!<-

---

There is, however, something else very remarkable here: that **GOD** spoke face to face with **Moses**, as one friend interacts with another. This again gives cause for the thought that there must be something essential of this in **GOD**, and not something merely assumed; which we must by no means compare to our earthly bodies, but must be something heavenly and spiritual, which we shall one day be dignified to behold in glory. It is therefore reported in the famous English Annotations <note>likely referring to the "English Annotations" or "Assembly's Annotations," a 17th-century Bible commentary</note> on the whole Bible at this passage, that **GOD** interacted with **Moses** in human form, as He did with **Abraham**. **Genesis 18**, also **ch. 32:30**, and so **v. 23** there. See also **Numbers 12:8**, **Deuteronomy 34:10**, and the notes here on **ch. 24**.

**Joshua -- did not depart from the tent)** **Lundius** <note>original: "(a) Jüd. Heil. 1, B. 1, Cap. n. 6." — Johann Lundius, "Die alten jüdischen Heiligthümer" (The Ancient Jewish Sanctuaries).</note> thinks it actually means this: When **Moses** returned with his servant **Joshua**, He (**the LORD**) did not depart from the tent. Yet the words give a better sense if one understands the latter part to refer to **Joshua**: that he had to remain as a watchman and doorkeeper in this Tent of Meeting, so that no one might approach out of audacity. See **Psalm 84:11**.

<margin>(a) Jewish Sanctuaries, Book 1, Chapter no. 6.</margin>

12. And **Moses** spoke to the **LORD**: See, you say to me: Lead this people up; but you do not let me know whom you will send with me; and you have said: I know you by name, and you have also found grace in my eyes.
13. And now, if I have indeed found grace in your eyes, then let me know your way, that I may know you, so that I may find grace in your eyes. Indeed, consider that this nation is your people.

18. But he said: Then let me see your **Glory**!

**v. 12. 13. Moses** continues to plead with **GOD**, desiring so greatly to be assured of a complete reconciliation with **GOD**. He could not be satisfied if **GOD** only wished to send one or more created angels with them; rather, he desired that **GOD** Himself might again be pleased to journey with them, as He had done in the Angel in whose innermost being His name was. <note>original: "Cap. 23/21." This refers to the "Angel of the Lord" mentioned in Exodus 23:21.</note> For in this alone would His grace, which He had promised him, be truly revealed toward him and toward this people, who were, after all, His people.
If this prayer of **Moses** were not entirely full of mystery, it would seem to be presumptuous, detrimental to **GOD**, and useless. It would be presumptuous: for what man dwelling in a mortal body could ever strive to see **GOD** clearly? It would also be detrimental to **GOD** to demand that He unveil His face, when He had nonetheless assured him that it could not happen in this life. It would likewise be useless, because the Scripture says that He spoke with him face to face. However, such is not the case here. In this circumstance, the prayer of **Moses** was right, as it concerned not himself, but such a great inner people. **Moses** thus wants to know—and desires that his people might likewise know—whether **GOD** Himself, or His angel, would lead them: and that they might be convinced that **GOD** alone could lead them through the terrible way which they still had to traverse; a way which is all the more terrible the closer it comes to its end.
Just as **Moses** desired to know whether **GOD** Himself would lead this people—to recognize from this their restoration to grace and the certainty of their path—so it also signifies that it is not enough for a leader to speak with **GOD** in such great intimacy, as this is indeed a grace for himself alone. Rather, he must also, beyond this, see the face of **GOD**; that is, he must have the pure knowledge and the clear vision in the words spoken to him, in order to be able to teach them to others without wandering into error.
It is a strange thing that many a person has the enjoyment and knowledge of a matter for themselves, and yet does not possess the power of expression and the light to impart it to others. For this reason, **St. Paul** (a) distinguished these two gifts: namely, the gift of speaking in tongues and the gift of interpreting them. And among the gifts of the **Holy Spirit**, there is also a great distinction: namely (b) between wisdom, understanding, and counsel. Wisdom is the discernment of divine truths through the "taste" of experience, which is given alongside it. Understanding makes it possible to perceive them more vividly and to penetrate them with greater concept and discernment. But counsel is precisely the ease of expressing such things for the instruction of others. For this reason, the great Apostle and chosen leader of **GOD** also said that the face of **GOD** had been unveiled to him. (c) But we, he says, in whom the unveiled face of **GOD** imprints His **glory** as in a mirror.
(a) 1 Cor. 12:10. (b) Isa. 11:2. (c) 2 Cor. 3:18.

So **Moses** is comforted, and desired to partake of an even greater grace as assurance; namely, to see **GOD's** **Glory**. For although **GOD** had appeared to him face to face, He was nevertheless surrounded by much darkness and kept the brilliance of His **glory** hidden, just as **Moses** later had to cover his own shining face.
Such a soul is not satisfied with a temporal reward or with a limited good. **Moses** begs insistently, though in different words:
->Then let me see your **Glory**!)<- As if he would say: I shall never be satisfied until I have seen your **Glory**, and what You are in Yourself.

<column-break/>

14. Then he said: Should my face have to go, so that I might bring you to rest?
15. And he said to him: If your face does not go, then do not lead us up from here.
16. And by what should it now be known that I have found grace in your eyes, I and your people? Is it not if you will go with us? Thus we shall be set apart, I and your people, from all the people who are upon the face of the earth.
17. Then the **LORD** said to **Moses**: This word also, which you have spoken, I will do (a). For you have found grace in my eyes, and I know you by name.
(a) Jer. 44:16.

19. And

**v. 14. GOD** wishes to test **Moses** to see if he would continue to insist on this, even when He presented to him the people's unworthiness and the danger involved if He were once again provoked to anger by their disobedience—as indeed happened later (Num. 14). Therefore, the words can be given more as a question than as a promise:
->Should my face have to go, just to satisfy you? Would you consider that to be fitting for my holiness, and also advisable according to my justice, which could very soon be provoked again?<-
**v. 15. Moses**, however, remains steadfast; if **GOD’s** face <note>term: "Face" (Angeſicht). In this context, it refers to the Divine Presence or the "Angel of the Presence."</note> did not go with them—which must happen through the Angel of the Face (Isa. 63:9, Deut. 4:37)—then it would be better to remain in the wilderness than to travel to the promised land without this presence, and there, like any other people, merely enjoy the earthly goods of this world. They would much rather wish to be distinguished from all other peoples of the earth by the indwelling of **GOD** among and in His people.
The magnanimous heart of **Moses**, which forgets itself only to look to the benefit of his people, does not accept this <note>the idea of going without God</note>, but continues to hold fast to his **GOD**, such that if he did not see Him Himself going before his people, he could not allow Him to let them depart from this place.
**v. 16.** How can we hope for forgiveness? How can we defeat our enemies? How can we walk in safety if You Yourself do not go with us? Oh, such a soul would rather lose everything than its **GOD**! O, how safely one walks when one journeys under the leadership of **GOD**! All other walking is subject to many dangers.
**v. 17. You have found grace — and I know you)** No sweeter words could the Most Loving One give.
**GOD** grants this loving shepherd his request because He knows him by name, full of love, as the true and rightful shepherd; and because He can refuse him nothing on account of his pure and fervent love. And this is precisely what it means to find grace before Him. However, He only grants him here the victory over his enemies alone. Not that He does not also wish to give him the rest; but it pleases Him to let him consume himself in the seeking of such a great good, which well deserves that some pains should precede its attainment, and that it be sought with a burning desire.
**v. 18.** Since **GOD** promises to hear him completely, because He loved him specifically; as the **LORD** knows the righteous: Ps. 1:6.

<meta>This page continues the intimate dialogue between Moses and God. Moses has asked to see God's glory, and God responds with both a promise of revelation and a warning about the limits of human nature.</meta>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIII.

19. And he spoke: I will cause all my goodness to pass before your face / and will preach the name of the **LORD** before your face. For I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious / and will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.

20. Furthermore he spoke: You are not able to see my face. For no man shall see me <margin>(a) 1 Timothy 6:16.</margin> and remain alive.

---

**v. 19.** **God** finally promises **Moses** that he will show him everything good when he reveals himself and shows himself; for **God** is the highest good and the center-point of all that is good. With this, He testifies to him how He would clearly make known His nature—which is nothing but love—to him. In this also lies the explanation of His mystery-rich name **Jehovah**: that He graciously accepts and has mercy upon those whom He has determined according to His holy purpose, who would embrace with all their heart the grace shining upon them and offering itself to them. And this could and must be enough for him, because no human could endure the brilliance of His face in this life (see Revelation 1:17), and we shall only be capable of this after death in our glorified bodies.

And so **God** indeed promises him what he seeks, but in such a wise way that it seems as if He takes it poorly that **Moses** approaches Him so vehemently. But ah, **Moses**, do not let this apparent harshness drive you back! It will bring about a much greater good for you than all the previous endearments. This is precisely a sign that the **LORD**, out of special love for you, wants to give you everything you desire. When **God** promises His very greatest graces to His servants, He does so with a thousand assurances of His love; but when it concerns the highest good, He gives it as if He were pushing such souls away. Yet even as He drives one away, He draws them to Himself; and when He pushes one out, He wants to lead them in: just as **Jesus Christ** (a) <margin>(a) Matthew 15:24.</margin> refused the **Canaanite woman** her request so that He could hear her with all the greater mercy. The creature must first be annihilated within itself before it is taken up into **God**; and it must also know that it receives this indescribable grace solely out of the pure grace of **God**; as **St. Paul** (b) <margin>(b) Romans 9:15-16.</margin> says while explaining this passage of **Moses**, that it depends not on anyone's willing or running, but on **God's** mercy alone.

**v. 20. You are not able to see my face)** **God’s** ultimate purpose in this refusal is to instruct **Moses** on the necessary state one must be in to fully enjoy **God**.

No one can see Him, nor enjoy Him fully, unless he has completely escaped and died to all his own "self-life"—both of nature and of grace—and to everything that is not **God**. Therefore He does not say, "no one can see me without dying," but rather, "no one who *lives* shall see me," to show that neither one death, nor even many deaths, are sufficient to reach this highest bliss; rather, not the slightest bit of self-life, however small it may be, may remain.

There are different spiritual deaths, all of which are necessary for the purification of the soul: the death of the senses, of their powers, and of the soul's center. And all these deaths happen in no other way than through the loss of many "lives," because there are an infinite number of attachments and supports in created things to which a person clings in selfishness. But to see **God**, to be united with Him in the very closest union, one must necessarily be robbed of all these "lives." And if the flame of pure love does not annihilate them all in this life, then the purifying fire must consume them all in the world to come.

<column-break/>

21. Furthermore the **LORD** spoke: See, there is a place by me / where you shall stand upon the rock <margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 10:4.</margin>.

22. And it shall happen, when my glory passes by, I will set you in the cleft of the rock, and will cover you with my hand, until I have passed by.

23. And when I have taken my hand away, you shall see my back. For my face cannot be seen.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

---

**v. 21. A place by me)** The place dedicated to the enjoyment of **God** is *by* Him, because He is in Himself, and He Himself is this place.

This place is **Christ** himself. For <term>Makom</term> <note>Hebrew for "place," often used as a name for God in Jewish tradition to signify His omnipresence.</note> is one of the names of **God**, which signifies the foundation and ground upon which all things consist and have their being. That is the divine nature (Psalm 24:3). Therefore that same place was truly not only *by* but also *in* Him, as the Father is in the Son. Therefore, the rock is pointed out immediately.

To receive the priceless good, one must be placed upon the rock of holy immutability: and then, says the **LORD**:

**v. 22.** My glory shall pass by, and I will cover you with my hand of protection; so that you may be able to withstand a grace such as this: otherwise it would consume you.

Yet you shall see me only as if through a narrow opening, or the outermost part of the rock, which is the most subtle pinnacle of the spirit.

**v. 23.** And when this majestic state of my glory—which in this life can be seen only as a flash of lightning—has passed by; then I will withdraw my hand again, which covered my glory so that you could not see it, so that your soul would not depart from the body, since nature is far too weak to bear the weight of such a great grace: then you shall see me, and understand in a certain measure, with a special vision of my divinity, with which I will grace you, that I am who I am, and that everything is in me. But you shall only look after me from behind: namely, only in that which can fall into the comprehension of a human raised to such levels; which is as much as looking from behind and perceiving the essence of **God** superficially. **God** Himself, however, is always incomprehensible in Himself; as **St. Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian famous for "apophatic" theology, which argues that God is best described by what He is not.</note> has so profoundly said: "If anyone who has seen **God** has understood that which he saw, <margin>(a) Letter 1 to Gaius.</margin> then he has not seen **God**, but only some things of Him which can fall under human knowledge."

Thus, the manner of speaking—*seeing my back*—carries a great mystery within it, which we may understand least of all in this state of weakness. For it is all expressed in a human way, and yet it is spoken by no human. Thus it must necessarily mean such a lower degree of divine vision. For:

Just as one cannot recognize a person exactly or by their face if they are only seen from behind, but only gains a weak and insufficient concept of them; so it is with all spiritual visions of **God**, however glorious and clear they might occur in this life. It is still only piece-work and imperfection compared to that which is perfect.

Therefore, wretched "Reason" should not complain so much about the superstitious and "friends of God," as if they were boasting or presuming such a high revelation of **God** and the like. For all such souls who know the **LORD** will very gladly confess in humility that their knowledge and seeing is only piece-work; and it thus serves to humble them more than it could puff them up, <note>Original: "blähen könne" - part of the fragmented line from the previous column.</note> provided they use it rightly according to **God's** purpose. Since all gifts, even the greatest, should only remind us how unworthy we were of them, and how freely **God** gives them to us. <note>These concluding sentences were reconstructed from the fragmented lines at the bottom of the source page.</note>

Cap. XXXIV. The Second Book of Moses.

# Chapter XXXIV.

->The Revelation of the Lord to Moses / /<-

**A**nd the Lord spoke to Moses: Cut two stone tablets like the first ones were; then I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke. <margin>(a) chap. 31:18.</margin>
2. And be ready by the morning, that you may go up Mount Sinai in the morning, and present yourself there before me on the top of the mountain.

<margin>God looks upon Moses with a particularly gracious face, or, He lets Himself be seen by him: but with the condition that His law should be engraved into stone tablets, which would not need to be broken again; thereby indicating that He wished He could engrave such things upon hearts which, through their deep-seated steadfastness, were free from all unfaithfulness. For</margin>

Thus the ancient heathens also used to engrave and write in a durable manner that which they did not want to be forgotten through the passage of time, so that it might have more permanence: just as Pliny <margin>(a)</margin> <note>original Latin: "l. 7. c. 56." refers to Pliny the Elder's Natural History, Book 7, Chapter 56.</note> reports that the Babylonians and Phoenicians wrote their laws on baked clay bricks.

To assure His grace, the Lord wanted to renew the covenant with His people, as it were, and therefore had the tablets of the testimony made anew, which Moses now had to make himself, and therefore they might not have been as precious <note>The author suggests the second tablets, made by human hands, were humbler than the first, which were entirely of divine workmanship.</note>, even if they had to have the form of the first ones, into which God Himself wanted to write the words again, as a sign that the Spirit must always work together with the outward ministry of the Word, and rightly unlock the mysteries in the spirit and write them into the heart. See 2 Cor. 3:3. Just as after the great sin of rejecting the Rock of Salvation in the crucifixion of Christ—for which reason God scattered them among the heathens—God nevertheless wants to renew His covenant of grace with them again, and through His Spirit sanctify them again as His people. Ezek. 36:22-27.

v. 1. 4. Stone tablets like the first ones) Of the same kind of stone, of the same form and shape and of the same size, which, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, was one <term>cubit<note>An ancient measure of length, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note></term>, both in length and breadth; thus they made them square. The thickness, however, they set at only half a cubit. <margin>(b)</margin>

We wish to direct our contemplation toward something more important, and notice how

->the two stone tablets<-
->are a representation of our heart.<-

1. They were stone tablets. Whether they were made of sapphire, as the Jews claim, and a cubit long and half a cubit thick, we do not know. It is enough that they were of stone. <margin>(1)</margin> Such, unfortunately, is our heart. Ezek. 36:26, Zech. 7:11. It does not easily accept God's Word and Law. <margin>(2)</margin> But nevertheless, if the believers accept it, it is not written in dust, but they keep it in a fine, good heart.

Thus the commandment of the love of God and neighbor is written by nature in our heart; but especially, after we have broken the covenant with God, it is written out of grace. And therefore these second tablets specifically represent the renewal of the divine image.

3. By the finger of God, that is, through the Holy Spirit, who says: I will put my law in their hearts, and write it in their minds. Jer. 31:33.

3. And let no one go up with you, that also no one be seen on the entire mountain: also let no sheep or cattle graze opposite this mountain.

5. There were two tablets. Thus we must keep and fulfill the law with body and soul. Glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God's. 1 Cor. 6:20, 1 Thess. 5:23. Likewise, the law requires a love for God and for one's neighbor.

6. They were written on the outside and inside; not as our sculptors and painters represent them: but on both sides, so that nothing more could be added to them. So shall our heart be full of God's Law and His Word, that no other word finds space there: unlike some who place God's Word on one side and the word of men on the other.

Indeed, should one not be allowed to say of most people, as in Zechariah 7:11: They make their hearts like a diamond, so that they do not hear the law and words which the Lord of Hosts sends in His Spirit through the prophets. Where is faith, loyalty, love? Where is prayer?

But because we cannot form ourselves, we do best when we ask the Spirit of God that He would take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh, Ezek. 36:26, and write His law deep into our heart, that it remains firm therein, as if in marble, on all sides, so that we may praise God in our body and spirit, and conversely, not accept human traditions.

The first tablets thus also depicted, in likeness, the first Adam, who was created in the image of God as a work of God, and had the law written in his heart: which therefore, as an eternal, unchangeable, and inviolable order, corresponds not only with the holiness of God but also with the consciences of all men, so that they know it by nature and can do it; Rom. 2:14. For that reason, it cannot be softened or diminished in the slightest, nor increased, much less abolished. But after the Fall occurred, this beautiful work nevertheless came to shame, and the law was weakened through fleshly and natural inability, as man went out from unity or simplicity into duality or division, and his frailty became manifest; just as, according to the image, the tablets were broken into pieces. Therefore, the second Adam, Christ the image of God, had to appear, in whose body and soul, as a double tablet, God Himself engraved the whole law and all His will: which tablets we should now diligently read and contemplate, so that we also may be renewed in the image of Him who created us. For thus we likewise become God's workmanship through the rebirth and renewal of the Holy Spirit, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand for us to walk in; Eph. 2:10. and to which faith, which is also God's work, John 6:29, as the law of the Spirit of life, constantly drives us.

And because now this renewal of the image of God in man happens through faith by means of the divine office of preaching in the service of the Spirit, which is administered by men; so here Moses himself had to hew and prepare these tablets, into which God afterwards inscribed the writing.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Exodus 33, focusing on Moses’ request to see God’s glory. # The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIII.

### 19. And he said: I will let all my goodness pass before your face / and will preach of the name of the Lord / before your face. For I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious / and will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.

### 20. Furthermore he said: You are not able to see my face. For no man shall see me <margin>(a) 1 Tim. 6:16.</margin> (a) and remain alive.

**v. 19.** God finally promises Moses that He will show him all good when He reveals and shows Himself to him; for He is the highest Good and the center-point of all that is good. With this, He testifies how He wishes to give him a clear understanding of His nature—which is nothing but love—which also contains the explanation of His mystery-rich name, Jehovah. He would graciously accept and have mercy on those whom He had designated according to His holy purpose, those who would grasp with their whole heart the grace that offers itself and cuts into them. And this should and must be enough for him, because no human being could endure the radiance of His face in this life (see Revelation 1:17), and we shall only be capable of this after death in our glorified bodies. 1 Cor. 13:12; 15:49-50.

And so God indeed promises him what he seeks, but in such a wise way that it seems as if He takes it poorly that Moses petitions Him so vehemently. But ah, Moses, do not let this apparent hardness drive you back! It will bring about a much greater good for you than all the previous endearments. This is precisely a sign that the Lord, out of special love for you, wishes to give you everything that you desire. When God promises His greatest graces to His servants, He does so with a thousand assurances of His love; but when He is about to grant the highest Good, He gives it as if He were pushing such souls away. Yet even as He drives one away, He draws them to Himself; and when He thrusts one out, He intends to lead them in: just as Jesus Christ <margin>(a)</margin> refused the request of the Canaanite woman so that He could hear her with all the greater mercy. The creature must first be annihilated within itself before it is taken up into God; and it must also know that it receives this indescribable grace solely out of the pure grace of God; since, as St. Paul <margin>(b)</margin> says when interpreting this passage of Moses, it depends not on someone's willing or running, but on God's mercy alone.

**v. 20.** (You are not able to see my face) God's purpose in this refusal is to instruct Moses on the necessary state one must be in to fully enjoy God.

No one can see Him, nor fully enjoy Him, unless he has entirely escaped and died to all his "own life," both of nature and of grace, and to everything that is not God. Therefore He does not say; no one *can* see me without dying: but rather; no one who *lives* shall see me: to show that neither one death, nor even many deaths, are sufficient to attain this highest bliss; rather, not the slightest bit of "own life," however small it may be, may remain. 

There are different spiritual deaths, all of which are necessary for the purification of the soul: the death of the senses, of the powers, and of the center-point. And all these deaths occur in no other way than through the loss of many "lives," because there are an infinite number of attachments and supports in created things to which man remains stuck in his selfhood. But to see God, to be united with Him in the most exact union, one must necessarily be robbed of all these lives. And if the flame of pure love does not annihilate them in this life, then the purifying fire must consume them all in the other world.

<note>The following notes refer to the annotations (a) and (b) in the commentary above.</note>
(a) Matt. 15:24. (b) Rom. 9:14.

...might be able to reveal where they use it rightly according to God's purpose; how unworthy we were of it, and how God gives it to us for nothing.

<column-break/>

### 21. Furthermore the Lord spoke: See, there is a place by me / there you shall stand upon the rock <margin>(a) 1 Cor. 10:4.</margin> (a).

### 22. And it shall happen / when my glory passes by / I will place you in the cleft of the rock / and will cover you with my hand until I have passed by.

### 23. And when I have taken my hand away / then you shall see my back. For my face cannot be seen.

**v. 21.** (A place by me) The place dedicated to the enjoyment of God is "by Him," because He is within Himself, and is Himself this place.

This place is Christ himself. For <term>Makom</term> <note>original: "Makom" is a Hebrew name for God, meaning "The Place," emphasizing God's role as the space in which the universe exists.</note> is one of the names of God, which signifies, as it were, the foundation and ground upon which all things exist and have their being. That is the divine nature, Ps. 24:3. Therefore, that same place was truly not only *by*, but also *with*—yes, *in* Him, as the Father is in the Son. For this reason, the rock is immediately pointed out.

To receive the inestimable Good, one must be placed upon the rock of holy immovability: and then the Lord says:

**v. 22.** My glory shall pass by, and I will cover you with my hand of protection; so that you may be able to endure a grace such as this: otherwise it would consume you.

Yet you shall only see me as if through a narrow opening, or the outermost part of the rock, which is the most subtle point of the spirit.

**v. 23.** And when this majestic state of my glory—which in this life can be seen only as a flash of lightning—has passed by; then I will pull back my hand, which covered my glory so that you could not see it, lest your soul depart from your body, as nature is much too weak to bear the weight of such a great grace. Then you shall see me, and in a certain measure comprehend, with a special vision of my divinity with which I will favor you, that I am who I am, and that everything is in me. But you will only look after me from behind: namely, only in that which can fall within the understanding of a human being elevated to such a stage; which is as much as looking from behind and becoming aware of the essence of God only superficially. God Himself, however, remains always incomprehensible in Himself; as St. Dionysius <note>original: Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian mystic often cited for his "apophatic" theology (knowing God by what He is not).</note> has profoundly said: “If anyone who has seen God has understood what he saw; <margin>(a)</margin> (a) he has not seen God, but only some things of Him which can fall under human knowledge.”

Therefore, the manner of speaking, *seeing my back*, contains a great mystery within it, which we probably understand the least in this state of weakness. For everything is expressed in a human way, and yet is spoken by no human being. Thus it must necessarily signify such a low degree of divine vision. For

Just as one cannot recognize a person exactly by their face if they have only been seen from behind, but only gains a weak and inadequate concept of them: so it goes with all the spiritual vision of God, however glorious and clear it might happen in this life. It is still only piecework and imperfection compared to the Perfect.

Therefore, wretched reason would have no cause to complain so much against believers and friends of God, as if they were boasting or assuming for themselves such a high revelation of God, or the like. For all such souls who know the Lord will very gladly confess in humility that their knowing and seeing is only piecework; and it thus humbles them more than it elevates them. Since all gifts, even the greatest, should only remind us,

6. For as the Lord passed before his face (a), he preached: **The Lord, the Lord is a merciful and gracious God, long-suffering and of great goodness and faithfulness!**

Here the Lord now descends and Himself explains His great name *Jehovah*, revealing what glorious virtues lie hidden within it. Namely, that He is: 1. An Almighty God, who can powerfully put all His virtues into action; 2. A merciful Being, who does not wish to leave the miserable sinner in his misery, but gladly helps him toward salvation if only he will allow himself to be helped; 3. A gracious Being, who offers redemption from guilt and punishment entirely for free to the unworthy sinner lying under the shadow of death, along with eternal life, if the sinner will grasp this grace in its origin in Christ through faith; 4. Long-suffering, who does not immediately reject and root out on account of sin, but always holds back His anger and grants time and space for repentance; 5. Of great goodness and faithfulness, whose nature is to do good and show love, and who therefore promises the same and keeps it faithfully; 6. Who also gladly shows love to the descendants of the faithful and lets them grow into thousands, doing good to them and letting them enjoy the benefit of their ancestors' piety; 7. Who, according to this His essential love, is also magnanimous in forgiving innate perversity, actual transgressions, and those public and secret deviations of the heart from Him, when a person acknowledges such things with heartfelt regret. See Micah 7:18, etc. But He is also a God who is just, and who will punish the sins of men even upon their naughty children who walk in the iniquity of their fathers, even unto the fourth generation, since persistent wickedness is usually followed by extermination. See Psalm 49:14, 20. Regarding all these attributes, see also Chapter 20:5, 6; Num. 14:17, 18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:5, 15; 103:8, etc.; 145:8, 9. The Spirit of God so often urges these attributes upon us so that we might gain confidence in God, yet also hold it in holy fear.

v. 5. The Lord) By this, many understand God the Father, who there
Preached) of His Son, whom He revealed to Moses.
v. 6. For as the Lord) the Son of God
Before) Moses and God the Father, who covered Moses, passed by;
There He preached) God the Father praised His Son as the source of all good and all grace, but also as a righteous judge.
The Lord, the Lord is a merciful and gracious God) Twice "Lord" and once "God." There are three that bear witness in heaven. 1 John 5:7.

The word "Merciful" is expressed in Hebrew by that same word of love <note>original: "rachum," related to "rechem," meaning womb or motherly compassion</note> from which the Pelican <note>The author likely refers to the "racham," often translated as a stork or scavenger bird, but in medieval bestiaries, the pelican was a symbol of Christ's self-sacrificing love.</note> also takes its name in Hebrew, because of its great love and mercy toward its young, whom it is said to sprinkle with its own blood and bring back to life when they have been killed by the serpent. Thus God loved the world. John 3. Indeed, mercy can be applied specifically to Israel, and grace specifically to Moses.

What can be lovelier to Israel than this name of grace and mercy, as long as it is still in its infancy and subject to many infirmities and faults? But after the Church has grown to more mature years, He presents to her the kindness and loveliness of His essence and nature in other attributes: such as wisdom, knowledge, righteousness, holiness, truth, patience, gentleness, goodness, philanthropy, etc.

However, the Lord puts "merciful and gracious" first to show that His mercy lasts forever in Christ. For there it is written, *notzer chesed* <note>original: "נֹצֵר חֶסֶד" (notzer chesed) meaning "keeping mercy" or "preserving kindness."</note>,

<column-break/>

7. Who preserves goodness for many thousands; who forgives iniquity and transgression and sin; who will by no means leave unpunished, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and upon children's children, unto the third and fourth generation.
8. Then

<gloss>Who preserves goodness or mercy) A word targeting *Netzer*, the tender branch <note>A pun on the Hebrew "Notzer" (the keeper) and "Netzer" (the branch), a common Messianic title for Christ.</note>, as Christ is often called in Isaiah 11:1 and elsewhere.</gloss>

For this reason, the word *Notzer* has an unusually large first letter <note>The Hebrew letter 'Nun' in the word 'Notzer' is written larger in the Masoretic text of the Torah to draw attention to its significance.</note> in the Hebrew text: also to indicate in whom the Lord shows mercy: namely, in the Little Shoot that sprouts from righteousness.
Forgives) The Hebrew word *nasah* <note>original: "נָשָׂא" (nasa)</note> otherwise actually means (1) to carry, and (2) to take away.
In the first meaning, Isaiah uses it in ch. 53:4. Truly He bears our sins with great long-suffering and patience!
The other meaning and translation, if one wished to use it here, has a deep foundation. For it is a greater honor to God to take away sin than merely to forgive it. To cleanse is a greater work than alone to pardon. 1 John 1:9. Also, it is God alone who can take away sin: whereas a human can also forgive a sin committed against him, and is bound to do so. Matt. 6:14, 15; 18:32, 33; Mark 11:25, 26. Thus, the forgiveness of sins does not make us enter into eternal life; but the removal of them, and the cleansing from them, does. Rev. 14:2; Rev. 21:27.

These causes are worth considering: for they are of great importance, and it is very beneficial to our immortal souls that they be cleansed from all defilement.

Consider also who bears your sins in you, and would gladly take them from you, if you did not actually hold them fast and refuse to part with them. Isa. 8:5. Beware that you do not misuse the name of God, which is so full of grace, goodness, and long-suffering! Remember that offended patience turns to wrath. If you misuse the patience and gentleness of the Lamb, you will—when it is too late to apply them—be forced to feel the wrath of the Lamb against your will. Rev. 6:15-17. For the Lord

Will by no means leave unpunished) or by cleansing (from one degree to another) will not cleanse those who willfully persist in sins.

Thus, after the Lord has promised all names of mercy and grace, He immediately adds this—so that no one might misuse His mercy and grace, or think that all unrighteousness, transgression, and sin would simply be overlooked and not punished—as a warning to all frivolous transgressors.

Otherwise, this speech is generally attributed to Moses as a prayer or praise of God, that he had spoken and cried it out. Although the words explain themselves somewhat, showing that the sense refers to the Lord's preaching—since the Lord can best explain His own name—the other interpretation contains nothing contrary or opposed to the foundation of truth.

Certainly, Moses also knew nothing higher to praise in all the trials of the Lord, nor any attribute of God to hold onto so powerfully, as God's love and patience.

And thus, the expressions of Moses on the mountain, where he is so happy and sees God, would indicate the pleasant edifications that a soul experiences upon receiving such great grace. Just as those who are visited by God in their innermost depths, and feel these pleasant touches, cannot refrain from letting the fire of God's love (by which they feel themselves ignited) flare up through a thousandfold praise which they give to their God. It also helps us learn that in these precious moments, the Bride receives a purer knowledge of God through the revelation of Himself which He gives to her; and while she contemplates His holy attributes and cannot praise them enough, she loves them all equally—His justice as much as His mercy, and His power as much as His truth. For because she seeks no self-interest therein, she is glad that the perfections of her God manifest themselves both in Himself and in His creatures.

The commentary emphasizes the balance between God's infinite mercy in Christ and His necessary justice against persistent sin.</summary>

### Chapter XXXIV. The Second Book of Moses.

8. Then Moses made haste and bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped.
9. And he said: If I have now found grace in your sight, O Lord, let the Lord, I pray, go in our midst! For although it is a stiff-necked people, yet may you forgive our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance.
10. And he said: Behold, I make a covenant! Before all your people I will do wonders such as have not been done in all the earth, nor among any nations: and all the people in whose midst you are shall see the work of the Lord, for it is an awesome thing that I will do with you.

***

v. 8. Moses seizes the opportunity of these divine favors to obtain everything he desires from God. First, he worships Him, thereby fulfilling the obligation of religion <note>Refers to the formal duty of acknowledging God's sovereignty</note>.

v. 9. Afterward, he begs Him to be the leader of this people Himself, to forgive them, and to possess them. For the most certain sign of the forgiveness of sins is that one is possessed by God and possesses Him within oneself. For God cannot dwell where there is sin. The more God forgives sin, the more He must come into possession of the heart, restoring it to how it was before the death of sin.
**Let the Lord, I pray)** be and remain our Protector <note>original: "Protector"</note>.
**For although)** indeed, for this very reason—because it is such a people—it has a great need for such a leader who often forgives its sin and brings it into the promised land with much patience and long-suffering. For where there is much sinning, much forgiveness is necessary.
**Our iniquity and our sin)** Moses includes himself, because the faithful must always be mindful of their corruption for their own humiliation; this is also what Christ aimed at in the fifth petition <note>The Lord's Prayer: "Forgive us our debts"</note>, Matthew 6:12.

v. 10. God now further promises them the great work that He will create among them: which does not so much refer to the passage through the Jordan and the overcoming of all their enemies in the land of Canaan, but primarily aims at the great wonderful work of love in the incarnation, suffering, death, and resurrection of His dear Son. Of this Jeremiah speaks explicitly in Chapter 31:22: "The Lord will create a new thing in the land: The woman shall encompass the man." <note>A traditional Christological interpretation of this verse, often seen as a prophecy of the Virgin Birth</note> See also Amos 8:9, Joel 2:30–31.

God promises Moses what he wishes and assures him that He will allow even more graces to come to him than he has already received. When God wishes to enter a soul, it must be stripped of all its graces through a secret annihilation <note>A mystical term referring to the emptying of self-will to be filled by God</note>. But when He has come, since He is the author of all graces, He brings such graces with Him as the creature has never experienced before, and which, as the adornment of His inner court, can never be without Him.

<column-break/>

11. Observe for yourself what I command you today! Behold, I will drive out before your face the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites. <margin>ch. 23:23, 28.</margin>
12. Take heed to yourself, lest you perhaps make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land where you are going, lest they become a snare in your midst.
13. But you shall tear down their altars, and break their pillars, and cut down their groves.
14. For you shall bow down to no other god. For the Lord’s name is **Jealous**, He is a jealous God.
15. Lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land; and when they go whoring after their gods and sacrifice to their gods, they invite you and you eat of their sacrifice; <margin>1 Cor. 10:20–21.</margin>
16. And you take of their daughters for your sons; and when their daughters go whoring after their gods, they also make your sons go whoring after their gods.
17. You shall make for yourself no molten gods.

-> 18. The <-

***

> Here various commandments are repeated: such as regarding idolatry, which was prevalent in the land of Canaan; that they should not defile themselves with it through all too common association with the inhabitants; for such is a **spiritual harlotry** before God, who has entered into a marriage-betrothal with them; Hosea 2:21–22. Therefore His service could not coexist with the senseless and impure worship of idols; thus they were also not to intermarry. See Chapter 23:23 etc., Deuteronomy 7:1 etc. God often complained of this spiritual harlotry through the prophets, seeing how it had spread among this people. Jeremiah 2:3, Ezekiel 16, Hosea 2, etc. In the New Testament, the love of the world is accused as such spiritual harlotry and adultery; therefore the faithful must also conduct themselves cautiously in their marriages in the fear of the Lord. See James 4:4, 1 John 2:15.

v. 12, 13. This advice is also given to spiritual souls; namely, that they should make no communion with those souls who still belong to themselves, nor with those who walk in self-willed ways: so that such people might not bring them out of their state of guidance in God and, through their reasonings, make them turn back to themselves, and thereby promote their ruin.

v. 14. Moses also urges them that they should worship no foreign gods, as they had already done: for His name is the **Jealous God**. O goodness of God, you have a holy jealousy over the hearts and spirits of your creatures! You want them to be yours alone, and that they take good care not to fall back into any idolatry, just as they had already allowed themselves to be led astray.

v. 16. Rightly He forbids these connections and marks this idolatry as harlotry. For when the soul belongs to God, it must belong to no other but Him alone: and as soon as it withdraws itself from Him to place itself in something else, it commits adultery, just as the Spirit expresses through James (a).

<margin>(a) James 4:4.</margin>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIV.

**18. The Feast of Unleavened Bread you shall keep. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the appointed time of the month of Abib. For in the month of Abib you came out from Egypt.**
<margin>Exodus 12:14, 23:15.</margin>

**19. Everything that opens the womb is mine: and all your livestock that is male, which opens the womb, among oxen and sheep.**

**20. But that which opens the womb of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb. If you do not redeem it, then you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And my face shall not be beheld empty-handed.**

<margin>v. 18. The Feast of Unleavened or sweet bread, which was extensively established above in Chapter 12:14-20, was a</margin>
->**Type of the New Testament.**<-

<margin>*1 Corinthians 5:6-8.*</margin>
1. Leaven is generally a symbol <note>Sinnbild</note> of (1) hypocrisy; *Luke 12:1.* (2) false teaching; *Matthew 16:6.* (3) evil morals and company; *1 Corinthians 5:6.* (4) puffing up and pride; (5) that which is obsolete and aged; (6) also of the "old man" <note>Refers to the sinful nature before spiritual rebirth</note>. We must sweep out this leaven.
2. This had to happen at the Passover Lamb, that is, with Christ.
3. Whoever ate leavened bread during this feast, that soul was to be cut off. Mark well the earnestness of God!
4. This feast lasted 7 days. The New Testament, in which we are to live in sweetness, consists of 7 periods.
5. The first day was to be holy and a Sabbath. So in the beginning of the New Testament there was a feast of holy assembly.
6. This day began when the Passover Lamb was eaten and was no longer present: and the New Testament began after Christ went to the Father and was no longer visibly present on earth.
7. The 7th day was also holy like the first: and the 7th period will lack nothing of the beginning of the New Testament in the fervency of zeal and the workings of the Holy Spirit.

v. 19. The commandment regarding the firstborn of the livestock has already appeared in almost the same words in *Chapter 13:12, 13.*
**Is mine)** Everything is His—heaven and earth, and what is in and upon them. But it pleased Him to choose something special that He wanted to be sanctified to Himself above all else. And these are those who first "break the womb" and "take the kingdom of heaven by force" <note>A reference to Matthew 11:12, suggesting spiritual vigor</note>.
Christ is the firstborn of all firstborns and of all creatures, the firstborn among many brothers, whom He specifically sanctifies so that they shall be the closest to Him in His kingdom.
Or the great glory and preference of such over all other brothers who come to light after them, and are sired and born of God in another order! These are the "excellent ones" who are on earth, in whom He has all His delight; *Psalm 16:3.* as they are distinguished from the holy ones. This firstbirth is so particularly dear to the Lord that He wanted the firstborn of all kinds of livestock set apart for Him because of it.
Blessed and holy is he who has a part in this! To him, the Jerusalem above will surpass everything, as the true Mother over all that are called children in heaven and on earth.

v. 20. **You shall redeem the donkey)** No one was free from this redemption of the donkey except the priests and Levites.

**21. Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest (*): in the time of plowing and in the harvest you shall rest.**
<margin>(*) Exodus 20:9, 23:12.</margin>

**22. You shall also keep the Feast of Weeks; namely, of the firstfruits of the wheat harvest: and the Feast of Ingathering at the turn of the year.**

---

v. 22. The Feast of Weeks and of Ingathering are the feasts of Pentecost and Tabernacles, which were also mentioned above in *Chapter 23:14-17.*
v. 23. **Three times)** The two just mentioned, and then the Feast of Unleavened Bread, v. 18.
There is a threefold harvest, each of which has its festival of joy.
The first is in the month of Abib, which signifies an "ear of grain" and takes its name from *Abih*, the Father <note>The author is making a linguistic connection between Abib and the Hebrew word for Father, 'Ab'</note>. Under whose service those stand who have a sincere good will to seek God, His righteousness, and His kingdom, whom the Father prevents with His gracious discipline and instruction; *Hebrews 12:5.* where usually a rich and joyful harvest follows in such souls.
After the Father's harvest follows the second harvest of the Son: and then also the third of the Holy Spirit.

v. 24. Beyond what was commanded in *Chapter 23:14-17* concerning the three feasts and repeated in previous verses, it is here specially promised that when all the men would have to appear before the Lord, the Lord would hold back their enemies so they would not use the opportunity to lust after their land. Thus, God is the best protection, who can keep the enemies away so that their evil plots must be turned from us. See *Genesis 35:5.*

v. 25. 26. This commandment appears in almost the same words in *Chapter 23:18, 19.* God, in His wisdom, must have found this repeated sharpening of the law necessary for the nature and circumstances of the people.

### Chapter XXXIV. The Second Book of Moses.

27. And the **Lord** spoke to Moses: Write these words for yourself. For according to the pronouncement of these words, I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.
28. And he was there with the **Lord** forty days and forty nights; he ate no bread and drank no water: and he wrote upon the tablets the words of the covenant, the ten words <note>The "ten words" refers to the Decalogue or Ten Commandments.</note>. <gloss>Deuteronomy 10:4.</gloss>
29. And it happened, when Moses went down from Mount Sinai, and the two tablets <gloss>(a) ch. 32:15.</gloss> of the testimony were in Moses' hand as he went down from the mountain, that Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had talked with Him.

---

<margin>v. 27. The Lord commands Moses to record these words or stories now that He has reconciled anew with the people and has provided them again with the words of the ten commandments in His own writing as a sign of the renewal of the covenant.</margin>
<margin>v. 28. Forty Days) These were another forty days, to be distinguished from the previous ones mentioned in Chapter 24:18.</margin>
<margin>He wrote) These words must be understood as referring to GOD and not to Moses; Moses was simultaneously commanded to record the remaining, mostly ceremonial laws in writing. Afterward, he undoubtedly made various copies of the ten words themselves, and perhaps had others copy them for general edification, while the tablets inscribed by GOD were preserved in the Ark of the Covenant.</margin>
<margin>v. 29. So that the people might be certainly assured that Moses had spoken with GOD (see Chapter 32:1), he brought a sign with him: his face gave off such a radiance that it could not be looked upon, so that he had to hang a veil over it when he wished to speak with Aaron and the rest of the people. In this, he received a foretaste of the glorification of our bodies, and at the same time, it impressed upon the children of Israel a greater awe of GOD and an honor for him.</margin>
<margin>If the people had previously harbored ill thoughts of Moses because he stayed away so long, they now had to look at him with entirely different eyes and recognize how highly the Lord loved him. But—</margin>
<margin>Moses did not know) This is the mindset of the truly humble children of God: that despite all the high gifts they receive from GOD, they think modestly of themselves and possess them as if they did not have them, as if they knew nothing of them. In such detachment, they are most fit to perform the office of their GOD, and need not fear that such gifts will be taken from them again, because they do not possess them in pride or attachment, but always offer them back to Him from whom they received them.</margin>
<margin>That the skin of his face shone) The <term>Vulgate version</term> <note>The standard Latin Bible used for centuries</note> rendered this as: *quòd cornuta esset facies ejus* <note>original Latin: "that his face was horned"</note>; and an old German translation printed in Nuremberg says: "that his face was horned from the company of God's speech." From this, the error of painters and engravers arose, who falsely depict Moses with horns. Yet the Hebrew word, according to the interpretation of Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to the medieval commentator Rashi</note>, signifies "to emit light like a horn," <note>original Latin: *lucem emittere instar cornu*</note>, that is, to give off radiance in the shape of a horn. Therefore, Luther hit the mark much better. Painters cannot defend themselves by pointing out that Moses is found with horns on some old coins, for these coins do not come from the ancient Jews, but from Christians who allowed themselves to be led into this error by the Vulgate.</margin>

30. And Aaron and all the children of Israel looked at Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone: and they were afraid to come near him.
31. And Moses called to them: Then they turned back to him, Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation; and Moses spoke to them.
32. And afterward, all the children of Israel came near: and he commanded them everything that the **Lord** had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.
33. And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face.
34. And

---

<margin>v. 30. The rays of Moses’ face were a visible sign of his indwelling and transformation in GOD, the fullness of which overflowed even onto his exterior.</margin>
<margin>So too does our face shine with joy and increased holiness from frequent conversation with GOD and the comfort and sweet refreshment arising from it. Therefore, persist in prayer! If you walk much with GOD, you will be glorified like Moses.</margin>
<margin>To be sure, Moses in the Law had no other radiance than in his face, whereas the Gospel presents the glorification of the whole person; just as Christ was seen with Moses on the mountain. Matthew 17:3. Thus, a much greater radiance is open to us in the Gospel.</margin>
<margin>They were afraid) GOD can easily clothe His servants with power and wonders so that they must be feared by the people, despite all the humility and lowliness of their hearts. Indeed, He will do it in His own time. He will glorify His servants among the wild crowd, so that the darkness will be terrified by their brilliance. What fear and horror will then seize the world when the righteous, at the time of their visitation, shine brightly and run like sparks through the stubble! Wisdom of Solomon 3:7.</margin>
<margin>v. 31, 32. Moses could have always stepped into the congregation with his shining face and appeared formidable among them, just as the congregation of GOD will one day appear terrible to her enemies (Song of Solomon 6:9), but he prefers to condescend and become weak to the weak, so that he might win them and bring them to GOD.</margin>
<margin>v. 33. He put a veil over his face) The Apostle explains the mystery of this, which GOD intended to foreshadow: when Christ—the true essence of all these shadows, the true High Priest, Sanctuary, Ark of the Covenant, Table, Lampstand, Altar of Incense, Altar of Burnt Offering, and Basin—would appear in the flesh, this stubborn people, because of their great departure from GOD, would not be able to behold this radiance. Instead, a veil would hang before their eyes and hearts, so that in reading these things in the Old Testament, they would not be able to perceive that these things were to cease in Christ, as the body. 2 Corinthians 3:14–16. But the believers, who would get to see His glory (John 1:14), would be translated into the freedom of the children of GOD by the Spirit of the Lord, and behold the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, and be transformed into that very image from one glory to another, as by the Spirit of the Lord. 2 Corinthians 3:17–18. The Apostle also reports that the radiance of the Gospel (the glory of which he speaks extensively in verses 7–11, comparing it to this radiance of Moses and the ministry of the Old Testament, but also preferring it) remains covered even among unbelieving and natural men, because they allow their senses to be blinded by the god of this world. 2 Corinthians 4:3–4.</margin>

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXV. 

34. And when Moses went in before the face of the Lord to speak with Him, he took the veil off, until he came out. And when he came out, he spoke to the children of Israel that which he was commanded.
35. And when the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone; then Moses put the veil back on his face until he went in to speak with Him.

---

One might think that Moses had much more reason to place the veil before his face when he spoke with the great God; and, on the contrary, should have removed the veil much sooner when he spoke with the people. But this did not happen without great cause.
Moses is an image of all people enlightened in God, who, in a "manly stature" <note>In the mystical tradition of this text's era, "manly stature" refers to spiritual maturity or a soul that has reached a state of firm strength in God.</note>, may pray before the Lord without a veil and uncovered; whereas others, who are still delicate and, like the female gender, are weak instruments, must have a veil. <gloss>1 Corinthians 11:4, 5.</gloss>
He is also simultaneously an image of the Jews in the latter days. When he went to the Lord, he took the veil away: and when they shall turn to the Lord, then the veil shall be taken away. <gloss>2 Corinthians 3:16.</gloss>
The wise conduct of Moses also teaches us that people of this spiritual standing must not reveal the mysteries they find, nor that which they experience therein, to those who are not yet capable; because such things might frighten them and drive them back. These things must be known only to God alone and to the leaders, or to those who are on the same spiritual level. To the rest, everything is covered with a veil which is impenetrable to their spirit, let it be as sharp and pointed as it will: and if indeed this veil were to be uncovered, they would not be able to endure the radiance that goes out from such sanctified people.

## Chapter XXXV.

->The Sabbath, the Contribution <note>original: "Hebopffer," referring to the 'heave offering' or voluntary gifts for the sanctuary</note>, and the Master-Craftsmen.<-

1. And Moses gathered the whole congregation of the children of Israel and spoke to them: These are the words which the Lord has commanded, that you should do them.
2. Six days shall work be performed: but on the seventh day it shall be holy among you, the Sabbath of rest to the Lord. Whoever does any work therein shall be killed.

---

v. 1. Moses thereupon gathers the whole congregation and proclaims to them what he achieved with God (see Chapter 32:30) and what God had commanded him.
v. 2. Among which he first makes mention of the Sabbath, and is also mindful once again of the death penalty against those who would profane it with any kind of manual labor. <gloss>Chapter 31:14, 15.</gloss>
According to the letter, this commandment expresses the rest of those souls whom God has allowed to enter into His holy Sabbath: which is the secret <note>or "mystical"</note> rest. They must perform nothing for themselves, but simply remain as they are allowed to be.

<column-break/>

3. You shall light no fire in all your dwellings on the day of the Sabbath.

->4. And<-

---

Moses adds further that one should also light no fire: which is not to be understood as meaning they should also make no fire for the melting of metals for the Tabernacle of Testimony, of which he immediately begins to speak; for this was a manual labor, as in other necessities: rather, this can be explained from Chapter 16:23, that they should move the baking and cooking of necessary foods to the previous day, and consume the remainder on the Sabbath, so that they might not spend the day with the ordinary, laborious preparation of food. However, that the necessary lighting of a fire for warmth and light, especially in winter, could not be forbidden thereby: since it is also probable that the necessary preparation and warming of food, especially for the sick, may have been permitted; as can be concluded from Chapter 12:16: such a thing the goodness of God does not let us doubt, as He does not deny us the necessity of the body.
Although this strict ceremony is abolished in the New Testament, one should nevertheless not spend the Lord's Day with such ordinary, laborious provisioning of the body—in order to attend the assembly all the more undisturbed and to pursue the contemplation of divine mysteries all the more diligently—but rather get by with necessities as much as possible; for the day is much more greatly dishonored by large banquets and luxury: as it is well to consider that God has repeated no commandment so often and so earnestly as that of the Sabbath, and has issued warnings against its profanation.
Finally, this is the conclusion of all: If we remain caught in the flesh or the letter, we look at all things only carnally, and stay in a slippery region where many uncertain steps, a partitioning of judgments and opinions, and an endless matter of strife are found. But if we lift ourselves into the spirit, and take the matter in the spirit; then we never err, and also have no need to strive with anyone. And so we will also come closer to the true Sabbath-rest than with much disputing over external circumstances, in which others involve themselves like "Abraham's ram" <note>A reference to Genesis 22:13, used here as a metaphor for being caught in the thicket of worldly details or imagery.</note> in time and in form and images. Our cares are almost always directed toward the "how," and we look past the "essence" of the matter. Let us rightly grasp Jesus Christ, as in Him is pure truth and genuine essence, as the end of the law; thus we will also rightly grasp and seize the Sabbath in its end, and it will happen of itself, and the law of the spirit and of love will explain and drive us, so that we—

<margin>
(a) Hebrews 4:9.
</margin>
**Light no fire**) whereby our rest is disturbed and the Sabbath is broken: no fire of envy against one another, <gloss>Isaiah 11:13,</gloss> nor of legalistic zeal, which arises in so many over the matter of the Sabbath, and burns as unrighteousness like a fire. <gloss>Isaiah 9:18.</gloss> The true Sabbath-observance suffers no such fire. Where the wild nature-fire takes an end, there the still Sabbath-rest finds its beginning.
If we wish to look at it in a better sense, then the lighting of a fire is nothing other than moving the desire a little, in order to warm it on spiritual, sensory, or perceptible love. In other stages this is indeed permitted—namely, those in which one must still be in activity or support oneself with certain testimonies—but it must not happen on the Sabbath day or the rest in God; and he who would nevertheless do it would break the holiness of the Sabbath, in that he would lose the holy rest. Therefore, those who are called to this holy rest, and are also assured of it through their guidance, must enter into it without fear and remain therein, and thereby honor the majesty of God, who wishes to be worshipped entirely in stillness and rest: remembering that this is the Sabbath which has remained for us in the law of grace; a Sabbath which the most chosen people of God must celebrate even in this life and at all times, as soon as they have been led into it, and therein afterward also continue eternally in heaven, according to the interpretation (a) of St. Paul.

<summary>This page concludes the narrative of Moses' radiant face as a symbol of spiritual enlightenment and begins the regulations for the Sabbath, interpreting the prohibition of fire both literally as a domestic rule and allegorically as the cessation of worldly passions and "legalistic zeal."</summary>

### Chapter XXXV. The Second Book of Moses.

4. And Moses spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: This is the word which the LORD has commanded and spoken.

5. Take from among you a <term>heave-offering</term> <note>original: "Hebopffer"; a voluntary contribution lifted up or set apart for God</note> to the LORD. Whosoever is of a willing heart, let him bring it, the heave-offering of the LORD: namely gold, and silver, and bronze;

6. And blue wool, and purple wool, and crimson wool, and fine linen yarn, and goat hair:

<margin>Chapter 25.</margin>
The heave-offering is now requested, just as was previously ordained: so that here too God has given them a sign and a mark of how He has received them back into grace, whereas they had otherwise forfeited it through their sin of idolatry; God intended to promise them His gracious presence among them through such a symbol—indeed, His dwelling in their hearts. Chapter 25:8.

<margin>v. 5. Heave-offering — willingly)</margin>
These first offerings, which God demands, signify the first good works and the beginning of the spiritual life, which the soul, reborn in its love, can then dedicate to Him, because it can act for itself. All its works must flow toward God, without it keeping anything for itself. And through this very voluntary (a) offering of everything within its power, God sanctifies everything else for Himself, because of the very free surrender of the soul's will which it makes to God; He then takes full possession of it, so that hereafter He deals with it as its supreme Commander. And this is the safest and shortest way—indeed, the only means—to attain perfection: namely, to abandon one's heart and everything that depends on it to the power of God, so that He may prepare it Himself as it is pleasing to Him: just as this is praised to us in a Psalm (b). Now, those people who are generous enough to do this, after they have detached themselves from themselves, are rid of the greatest enemy of perfection. And after they have thus happily entered into the Tabernacle of God, they have lost all power over themselves. But they have lost it through nothing other than their voluntary offering which they made of it to God; and they could surely have done nothing more holy, nor more just, nor more beneficial to their freedom, than to give it back and dedicate it to their God, who had graced them with it: although they are still in a state where they might take it back through unfaithfulness, and very few are found who render a complete veneration of the same; for most bring to it either some exceptions or even some retractions. If, however, this perfect sacrifice were to happen all at once, one would instantly be perfect. For it is impossible for any imperfection to exist where God acts and governs without resistance.

The material offerings of the Law are images of the spiritual offerings which God demands of us. And happy are those who see through to the spirit of them, who love the exercise of them, and to whom their truth tastes good!

<margin>Bronze)</margin>
Wherever one reads of "Erz" <note>bronze/brass</note> in the German Bible, the Scripture is speaking of red copper, writes Matthesius (c) <note>Johannes Matthesius (1504–1565), a German minister and mineralogist known for his "Sermons on Mining."</note>.

<margin>v. 6. Crimson)</margin>
Or twice-dipped, high, light-red scarlet wool, which most closely resembles fire, and intends to remind us of the duty of love, in which our entire conduct should be twice-dipped; namely, in the love of God and of our neighbor.

(a) Psalm 54:8 <note>In modern Bibles, Psalm 54:6: "I will freely sacrifice unto thee."</note>.
(b) Psalm 48:14.
(c) J. Berg-Pred. <note>Johannes Matthesius's "Sarepta oder Bergpostille" (Mining Sermons).</note>

7. And red-dyed rams' skins, and badger skins, and acacia wood <note>original: "Sittim-Holz"</note>: <margin>c. 36:29.</margin>

8. And oil for the light, and balsamic spices for the anointing oil, and fragrant spices for the incense:

9. And onyx stones and stones to be set for the ephod <note>original: "Leibrock"</note> and for the breastplate.

10. And all who are of a wise heart among you, let them come and make everything that the LORD has commanded.

<margin>v. 7. Red-dyed rams' skins)</margin>
Bochartus (a) <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar.</note> proves extensively that in the Orient, red—even purple-colored—sheep are found, whose wool is naturally red and purple. Dietericus (b) <note>Conrad Dieterich (1575–1639), a Lutheran theologian.</note> also cites various examples of sheep of different colors, some of which were reddish like minium <note>red lead pigment</note>, some gold-colored, some yellow, and some of other colors.

<margin>Badger skins)</margin>
Or blue-dyed rams' skins, according to another opinion.

<margin>v. 8. Anointing oil)</margin>
This external oil, which Moses had to prepare and with which he consecrated or sanctified the priests and the Tabernacle of the Lord, had its power to sanctify from that oil which our Lord Jesus Christ prepared through His merits, of which it was only a figure; and it also ceased to be holy through that very same thing. For when the new mysteries were introduced, which gave truth and life, the old ones necessarily had to cease, which were only a shadow, sign, and prototype of that truth which they depicted, and in which we now can and should live.

<margin>v. 9. Onyx stones)</margin>
They are said to grow in Arabia and India. They are said to be like a beautiful and white nail of a human being, and have many veins that go around it with milk-colored streaks or circles.

They are said to be found so large that one can even make drinking vessels from them.

<margin>v. 10.</margin>
Wisdom itself must build the house in which the Holy One is to dwell. If Wisdom does not take the direction in the preparations for it, nothing will be established or accomplished according to God's mind: and His soul has a loathing for one's own choices, and does not wish to smell <note>a reference to the "pleasing aroma" of biblical sacrifices</note> such a dwelling.

<margin>v. 11.</margin>
The Dwelling with its tent and covering) By this, only coverings are meant, as is more clearly evident from Chapter 26.

By the **Dwelling** is understood the beautiful, multicolored covering of 10 tapestries, which actually made the dwelling within the walls and the ceiling.

The **Tent** of the same was the camlet covering of goat hair, consisting of 11 tapestries, which made the outer wall and the roof.

And over both was yet the double **Covering** of blue and red skins.

<margin>v. 12. For covering)</margin>
Or the covering <note>the veil</note> of the Holy of Holies.
