# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXV.

34. And whenever Moses went in before the face of the LORD to speak with him, he took the veil off, until he came out. And whenever he came out, he spoke to the children of Israel that which had been commanded him.
35. And when the children of Israel saw the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face shone, Moses put the veil back upon his face until he went in to speak with him again.

One might think that Moses would have had much more reason to place the veil before his face when he spoke with the great God, and conversely, should have taken the veil off when he spoke with the people. But this did not happen without great cause.
Moses is an image of all people enlightened in God, who may stand before the LORD without a veil and naked in their "masculine stature" <note>This refers to a state of spiritual maturity or strength</note>; whereas others, who are still delicate and, like the "female gender," are weak instruments, must have a veil. 1 Corinthians 11:4-5.
He is also at the same time an image of the Jews in the latter times. When he went to the LORD, he took the veil away: and when they shall turn to the LORD, the veil shall be taken away. 2 Corinthians 3:16.
The wise conduct of Moses also teaches us that people of this high spiritual standing must not reveal the mysteries they find, nor what they experience therein, to those who are not yet capable of them, lest such things terrify and drive them back. These things must be known only to God alone and to the leaders, or to those who are on the same "step" <note>original: "Staffel"; a level of spiritual progress</note>. To the rest, everything is covered with a veil which is impenetrable to their spirit, however sharp and pointed it may be; and if this veil were to be uncovered, they would not be able to bear the brilliance that emanates from such sanctified people.

### Chapter XXXV.
->The Sabbath, Heave-offering, and the Master Craftsmen.<-

And Moses gathered the whole congregation of the children of Israel together and said to them: These are the words which the LORD has commanded, that you should do them.
2. Six days shall work be done: but on the seventh day there shall be a holy day for you, the Sabbath of rest to the LORD. Whosoever does any work therein shall be put to death.

<margin>v. 1.</margin> Moses thereupon gathers the whole congregation and proclaims to them what he has accomplished with God (see Chapter 32:30) and what God has commanded him.
<margin>v. 2.</margin> Among which he first makes mention of the Sabbath, and also once again reminds them of the death penalty against those who would profane it with any kind of manual labor. Chapter 31:14-15.
According to the letter, this commandment expresses the rest of those souls whom God has allowed to enter into His holy Sabbath: which is the "secret rest" <note>An internal, mystical state of peace</note>. They must perform nothing of themselves, but simply remain as they are permitted to be.

<column-break/>

3. You shall kindle no fire in all your dwellings on the day of the Sabbath.
4. And

Moses further adds that one should also kindle no fire: which is not to be understood as meaning they should make no fire for the smelting of metals for the Tabernacle <note>original: "Hütte des Zeugnisses"; Tent of Testimony</note>, of which he immediately begins to speak; for that was a manual labor, as in other necessities. Rather, this can be explained from Chapter 16:23: that they should move the baking and cooking of necessary food to the previous day, and consume the remainder on the Sabbath, so that they might not spend the day with the ordinary, laborious preparation of food. Meanwhile, the necessary lighting of a fire for warmth and light, especially in winter, cannot be forbidden thereby: since it is also probable that the necessary preparation and warming of food, especially for the sick, may have been permitted; as such can well be concluded from Chapter 12:16. The goodness of God, which does not deny us the necessities of the body, leaves us no doubt of this.
Although this strict ceremony is abolished in the New Testament, one should nevertheless spend the Lord's Day—and the assembly for the contemplation of divine mysteries—all the more undisturbed and diligently, not spending it with such ordinary, laborious provision for the body, but rather helping oneself with necessities as much as possible. The day is much more dishonored by great feasting and luxury; for it should be well considered that God has repeated no commandment as often and as earnestly as that of the Sabbath, nor warned so strictly against its profanation.
Finally, this is the conclusion of all: if we remain caught in the flesh or the "letter" <note>Literal interpretation</note>, we view all things only carnally, and we stay in a slippery region where many uncertain steps, division of judgments and opinions, and an infinite matter for strife are found. But if we rise into the Spirit and take the matter in the Spirit, we never err, nor do we need to strive with anyone. And so we will also come closer to the true Sabbath-rest than by much disputing over external circumstances, wherein others constantly entangle themselves (like Abraham's ram) in time, forms, and images. Our cares almost always concern the "way" or method, and we look past the "essence" of the matter. Let us rightly grasp Christ Jesus—as in Him is pure truth and righteous essence—as the end of the Law; so we will also rightly grasp and seize the Sabbath in its "end" <note>Its ultimate purpose or fulfillment</note>. It will happen of itself, and the law of the Spirit and of love will explain and drive us, so that we *kindle no fire*,) whereby our rest is disturbed and the Sabbath broken: no fire of envy against one another (Isaiah 11:13), nor of "legalistic zeal" <note>original: "gesetzlichen Eifers"</note>, which arises in so many over the matter of the Sabbath and burns like a fire of injustice (Isaiah 9:18). True Sabbath observance suffers no such fire. Where the "wild nature-fire" <note>Uncontrolled human passions</note> ends, there the quiet Sabbath-rest finds its beginning.
If we wish to look at it in a better sense, kindling a fire is nothing other than moving the desire a little, in order to warm it with spiritual, sensible, or emotional love. In other "stages" <note>Steps of spiritual development</note> this is indeed permitted, namely those in which one must still be in activity or support oneself with certain testimonies. But it must not happen on the Sabbath day or the rest in God; and he who would nevertheless do it would break the holiness of the Sabbath by disturbing the holy rest. Therefore, those who are called to this holy rest, and are assured of it through their spiritual guidance, must enter into it without fear and remain therein, and thereby honor the Majesty of God, who desires to be worshipped through them entirely in silence and rest: remembering that this is the Sabbath which has remained for us in the Law of Grace; a Sabbath which the most chosen people of God must celebrate even in this life and at all times, as soon as they have been led into it, and thereafter continue in it eternally in Heaven, according to the interpretation (a) of St. Paul.
<meta>Catchword: (a) Hebrews 4:9.</meta>

<meta>This page continues the inventory of materials for the Tabernacle. This page lists the specific furniture and garments to be crafted and interprets them as symbols of the internal spiritual life of a believer.</meta>

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXV.

13. The table with its poles / and all its vessels / and the showbread <note>original: "Schaubrode," the twelve loaves of bread set out in the Tabernacle</note>.

14. And the lampstand for light / and its vessels and its lamps: and the oil for light.

15. And the altar of incense with its poles / and the oil of anointing / and the incense of fragrant spices / and the screen of the door at the entrance of the dwelling.

16. The altar of burnt offering and the bronze grate belonging to it / its poles and all its vessels: the basin with its stand.

17. The hangings of the courtyard with its pillars and its bases / and the screen of the gate at the courtyard.

18. The pegs of the dwelling and the pegs of the courtyard with their cords.

19. The garments of service for serving in the sanctuary: the holy garments for Aaron the priest / with the garments of his sons / to minister in the priest's office. <margin>chapter 31:10.</margin>

**v. 13-18.** All the parts of this dwelling are recounted quite orderly / and so that none of them might be omitted / they are all described very precisely with their belonging parts. This should teach us / that also in us / if we wish to be a spiritual dwelling of the Lord / as we ought / nothing must be lacking of all the mysteries / which these images were intended to represent. There must / for example / be the righteousness of faith / signified by the Ark and its accessories / the strengthening of faith / by the table / the enlightenment / by the lampstand / the spirit of prayer / by the altar of incense / the anointing of the gifts of the Spirit / by the anointing oil / the sacrifice of our body / by the altar of burnt offering / and the sanctification in our inner and outer conduct / by the basin / and so forth in the remaining pieces / where it is presented to us / how we should behave in the entire joining together with the rest of the believers / so that we become the one spiritual body of Christ / everything must be present in our inward being. Here, the exhortation of the Apostle must also bring this to our mind / that the God of peace sanctify us through and through / that our spirit entirely together with soul and body be presented blameless: **1 Thessalonians 5:23**. Which happens / if not one of these spiritual pieces is lacking in us.

**v. 19.** The Hebrews divide the priestly garments into 3 kinds: into common priestly garments / into golden garments / and into white garments. Of the common ones there were 4: the breeches / the close-fitting coat / the belt / and the turban. Of the golden ones there were 8: the 4 just mentioned / which the High Priest had in common with all priests / and 4 others / which he alone wore: which they call golden / because they were exceedingly magnificent garments / and gold was partly used for them. These he wore / when he ministered outside the Most Holy Place. Of the white garments there were again 4: breeches / a close-fitting coat / a belt and turban. These the High Priest alone wore / when he entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement.

<column-break/>

20. Then the whole congregation of the children of Israel went out from the presence of Moses.

21. And they came / everyone whom his heart moved / and everyone whom his spirit made willing / they brought the <term>contribution offering</term> <note>original: "Heboppfer," literally a heave-offering or *Terumah*</note> of the Lord for the work of the Tabernacle of Meeting / and for all its service / and for the holy garments.

22. And both men and women came / as many as were of a willing heart / they brought hooks and earrings and rings and bracelets / all being vessels of gold / and everyone who offered a <term>wave offering</term> <note>original: "Web-Opffer," an offering moved back and forth before God</note> of gold to the Lord. <margin>chapter 38:24.</margin>

23.

In this great willingness / where everyone contributed everything according to their ability / the people according to what they had / and the leaders the precious gemstones and fragrances and spices / we have to observe / that we also serve one another / each with the gift we have received / as the stewards of the manifold gifts of God; **1 Peter 4:10.** and as it says there in **v. 11**: If anyone serves / let him serve as out of the ability that God supplies; so that in all things God may be praised through Jesus Christ. See also **Ephesians 4:16.** concerning the supply of his ability for the joining together of the whole body and the assistance of his gifts for its growth. And to this also belongs the charitable contribution for the physical needs of the believers / which the Apostle calls a service to the saints / of which he testifies / how they had given abundantly with all simplicity. For according to their ability / and beyond their ability / they were willing of themselves / and pleaded with us with much exhortation / that we would receive the benefit and fellowship of the assistance to the saints. **2 Corinthians 8:2, 3, 4.** and in the whole **9th chapter**.

We must offer up to the Lord only the firstfruits of our will / and the free power we have over ourselves; so that he can perform the work of the Tabernacle of the Covenant in us. God instructs in this wilderness / and in this rest which his people enjoy therein / through Moses all spiritual people and all leaders under these comprehensible images / how they should go to work / in order to attain a happy progress in their Christian perfection. And whoever has only some light / to glimpse this through the shadows / will see such things with astonishment.

The Tabernacle is the dwelling of God; and it is he himself who erects this dwelling in us / as soon as we have surrendered our rights to him. As soon as a person / through the sweet and strong inward retreat / removes himself from creatures / and **(a)** lives alone in himself with God; and while he raises himself above his frailty / and soars into God / to find therein everything he needs: then God begins his work in him; but with such goodness / that he makes use of all things / to build his internal palace. For he makes / **(b)** that all things must work for the best for those who love him / and who are called to sanctification according to his counsel. The evil will of creatures / who resist him / are so many hammer-blows / which make the exterior of the building smooth through the cross <note>referring to trials or suffering</note> which they cause: while God meanwhile works from within / and erects his Tabernacle. But everything must be offered voluntarily and with a free heart / as the Scripture says / that all had given according to their pleasure: to show / that God does not force freedom; but that he makes the heart fit through his love / so that it may voluntarily give to him that which it is obligated to give.

<margin>**(a) Lamentations 3:28.
(b) Romans 8:28.**</margin>

### Chapter XXXV. The Second Book of Moses.

23. And everyone / with whom was found blue wool / and purple wool / and crimson wool / and fine linen yarn / and goat hair / and red-dyed ram skins / and badger skins <note>original: "Dachs-Felle," traditionally interpreted as badger or dolphin skins</note> / they brought it.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXVI.

## Chapter XXXVI.

->The Abundance of the Heave-Offering / and the Making of the Dwelling and its Tent.<-

Then Bezalel and Oholiab worked / and every man who was wise of heart / into whom the LORD had put wisdom and understanding / to know how to perform all manner of work for the service of the Sanctuary / according to all that the LORD had commanded.

2. And Moses called Bezalel and Oholiab / and all the men who were wise of heart / in whose heart the LORD had put wisdom / even everyone whose heart moved him to come unto the work to do it.

3. And they received from Moses all the heave-offering <note>original: "Hebopffer," referring to the *terumah* or gifts set apart for God</note> / which the children of Israel had brought for the work of the service of the Sanctuary / to perform it. For they still brought a willing gift to him every morning. <margin>chapter 35/29.</margin>

<column-break/>

4. Then all the wise men / who were working on the entire work of the Sanctuary / came / each one from the work he was doing /

5. And spoke to Moses, saying: The people bring too much / more than is necessary for the service of the work / which the LORD commanded to be made.

6. Then Moses gave a command / that they must cause a proclamation to be made throughout the camp, saying: Let neither man nor woman do any more work for the heave-offering of the Sanctuary. Thus the people were restrained from bringing anything more.

7. For the material they had was enough for all the work / to make it; indeed, it was more than enough.

8. Al- <note>The text breaks here to begin the commentary section; "Al-" is the beginning of the next verse, "All the wise men..."</note>

---

The zeal of the people of the Old Testament is here to be praised to the highest degree / since they brought their precious vessels / and whatever else was required for the Sanctuary / so voluntarily and abundantly / that they had to be restrained from bringing more / because everything was sufficient / and even in excess. By this, they wished in some measure to atone for their sin of idolatry <note>A reference to the Golden Calf incident in Exodus 32</note> / in that they had also so readily given up their wealth for that purpose. Chapter 32/3. 

However, this greatly shames the people and the congregations of the New Testament / in that one can only with great difficulty gather resources / when temporal wealth is required for the advancement of a spiritual sanctuary. To be sure, people still spend something on the building of external churches / which are inevitable according to the circumstances of the current state of the church; although all the decoration and preciousness within them is entirely unnecessary / indeed, sinful: But whenever something else is required for those godly institutions / through which people should be prepared from youth up to be such a sanctuary of the LORD; there a great lack and withholding of wealth is felt throughout. 

This also includes what belongs to the care of the poor and otherwise needy members of Christ / through which the sanctuary of the LORD should be maintained in its external form; just as the Apostle praises the zeal of the congregations in Macedonia in this regard / and commends such for the Corinthians to follow / in two whole chapters / 2 Cor. 8, 9. Also 1 Cor. 16.

**v. 1, 2. To know -- to do)** A wise man without work / says a wise heathen (a) / is like a bee without honey.

Most people are indeed anxious to know much / but not to do much / and imagine / it is already enough / if only their understanding is filled with many sciences / even though their will is not constituted in such a way / as God requires.

**v. 3. They still brought a willing gift every morning)** Who is there in our days / when people boast of the Gospel and its great advantages over the Old Testament / who follows this people and their example even from afar / not to say / equals it—much less surpasses it—as the Gospel ought to surpass it! Let no one excuse himself with a lack of opportunity! For God sends such to you in all kinds of ways so richly / to test your willingness / so that / if only you do not wish to be found lazy and sluggish therein / you will find opportunity for it every morning / just as God's goodness is new over you every morning.

**v. 5.** The very best things have their times and hours / when they must cease. Is anything better to be found / than that one offers up what he possesses to God? Why then does the Scripture say / that they had offered more than was necessary? That is: when one has voluntarily offered himself once / yes, when one has given Him his freedom as an irrevocable gift; then it is no longer necessary / that one offer it to Him any further: because it no longer belongs to us; and one would have to take it back / if one wished to offer oneself anew.

But one might say / one can surely always offer new virtues. It is indeed true / that / as long as one possesses the tree / one can always offer new fruits from it. But as soon as one has given away the ground of the tree / it would be something ridiculous / if one still wanted to offer its fruits frequently: because it is clear enough / that the fruits fall to the landlord anyway / and that it is impossible to give them to him again / without in a certain way re-appropriating them to oneself.

Yet if good souls perhaps repeat this gift; as is quite common in the beginning: it happens either because it was not yet done quite perfectly in the beginning; or to cut off any reservations that might be found in that regard; or to renounce the re-appropriations / which might have occurred here; or also through an inclination of love in the heart / which gladly wishes to re-confirm that which it has done for its God's sake; or finally through a movement of God Himself / who gladly sees the frequent renewal of this sacrifice of love.

**v. 6. Then Moses gave a command)** This wise leader / who was very well instructed in secret wisdom / forbade / that neither the men / who represent the strongest and most advanced souls / nor the women / who signify the least purified and weakest souls / should offer any more gifts: because the sacrifice that had occurred should be sufficient in itself / to let God alone work / so that He Himself might erect His sanctuary according to His eternal counsel.

**v. 7.** One had already transgressed the order of God. Namely, because the love for one's own activity generally causes one / to offer oneself out of season. And one would always continue so / if the leaders did not forbid such with a certain patience as force; or if God did not put the soul into a state of weakness / so that it cannot do such things: in that He makes use of the power / which He had obtained over it through its surrender / as He then dries up its ability / and makes its activity wither away.

<margin>(a) Sheikh Saadi in his *Rose Garden* <note>original: "Schich Sadi in seinem Rosenstal"; refers to the *Gulistan* by the 13th-century Persian poet Saadi Shirazi</note>.</margin>

8. Thus all who were of wise heart among the workers on the work made the Dwelling; of ten curtains of twisted fine-linen yarn / and blue wool / and purple wool / and crimson wool: with Cherubim of skillful work they made them.

9. The length of each curtain was twenty-eight cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 inches</term> / and the width was four cubits for each curtain: all the curtains had one measure.

10. And he joined five curtains together / one to another: and again he joined five curtains together / one to another.

11. And he made loops of sky-blue wool on the edge of the first curtain at the end of the coupling. Likewise, he made them on the edge of the outermost curtain in the other coupling.

12. Fifty loops he made on the one curtain / and fifty loops he made on the edge of the curtain that was in the other coupling. The loops were held one to another.

13. And he made fifty golden clasps / and joined the curtains one to another with the clasps / so that the Dwelling became one.

Here now begins the orderly manufacturing of the Tabernacle of the Congregation <note>original: "Hütte der Zusammenkunfft," often translated as the Tent of Meeting</note> related piece by piece / as one after the other was undertaken / and so on in the following 37th and 38th and 39th chapters up to verse 32.

First, the outer pieces were taken in hand; such as the curtains: of which there were four / always to be laid one over the other / along with their loops and clasps.

**v. 8. Ten curtains)** Whereby the fullness of the Law of the ten commandments / which consists in love / according to inward practice can be understood.

**v. 9. The length comes from the Seven-Number of perfection / and at the same time with the width from the Four-Number / as the ground and foundation of all numbers.** <note>The author uses biblical numerology: 7 signifies spiritual perfection, while 4 signifies the material world or foundation.</note>

Five and five)** Our inner and spiritual senses should be gathered / and kept quiet in a holy leisure / in the turning inward toward the truth / which God reveals internally: and thus instructed, we must also betake ourselves outward in this same holy leisure / to contemplate the divine scriptures and the lives of the saints / and also seek to glorify God with our outer senses / and to serve the neighbor in the work of salvation.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chap. XXXVI.

<columns>

20. And he made the boards for the Dwelling of Shittim wood <term>Shittim wood: also known as Acacia, a dense and durable wood found in the Sinai desert</term>, which were to stand upright.

21. Ten cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of measurement, approximately 18 inches</term> was the length of one board, and a cubit and a half was the width of one board.

22. Two tenons <term>tenon: a projecting piece of wood made for insertion into a socket</term> were on each board, joined one to the other. Thus he made all the boards of the Dwelling.

23. So he made the boards for the Dwelling: Twenty boards were for the South side <note>original: "Mittags-Seite," literally "midday side," referring to the direction of the sun at its peak</note>.

24. And he made forty silver bases under the twenty boards; two bases under one board for its two tenons, and two bases under the other board for its two tenons.

---

Schubart writes in his *Spiritual Catechism-Joy* <note>original: "geistlichen Catechismus-Lust"</note> in the first preparatory sermon, citing Arias Montano <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598) was a famed Spanish theologian and editor of the Antwerp Polyglot Bible</note>, that the boards on the walls were crafted so lovely and charmingly that each one looked like a beautiful person clothed in long garments: which appeared as beautiful as if the Tabernacle consisted of nothing but carved human figures. However, the spiritual understanding first sees therein the particular wonders in the Law of God.

**v. 20.** That the boards should stand upright signifies that we should possess a free, upright, and well-ordered mind, and should lift ourselves up to the glory of God with a constant looking-up to His sign and will, as obedient and submissive servants.

**v. 21.** Every resolution of a free mind is so powerful over all its external and internal senses that they must obey it according to the whole will of God, which is contained in the ten-fold number of the commandments; and he can use and apply all ten to the service and honor of God as his instruments to carry out what pleases God. Therefore, every such free resolution is ten cubits long, because a free mind orders and arranges each of the ten senses for its proper effect, but itself surpasses all effects.

**v. 22.** For a person’s resolution to come to pass—to serve the Almighty God with their whole being and all their powers—both the preceding and following inclination of the free will must be present. This free inclination encompasses the whole person—the heart, the senses, the soul, all powers, the free mind, and a sublime spirit—and may be compared to the tenons, by whose help the boards are joined together so neatly and wisely that one can see through nowhere, nor notice any inequality on any side of the wall. And thus every new resolution is born, and joined with the other through an intervening voluntary inclination.

**v. 23.** Every good work is first conceived and intended before it is performed either internally or externally. Now, when we decide to give ourselves over to obedience to the will of God, and also sacrifice ourselves entirely to it according to the instruction of God’s commandments, we have already erected a full ten-fold number of boards to the glory of God. When we do not please or love ourselves in anything, we have a free and empty ground, and can thus sacrifice ourselves to God again in a quiet stillness in which God has chosen to dwell and remain. In this way, we also carry out the will of God according to the Gospel <note>original: "Evangelio"</note>, and manufacture the remaining ten boards. The essence of the Gospel is that we forsake ourselves, overcome ourselves, give ourselves entirely to God as His own, sacrifice ourselves, and follow Him in the strengthening of rest or stillness. However, all of God's commandments aim for the same thing: to give ourselves over entirely for the sake of God's glory to the exercise of all virtues out of true obedience.

**v. 24.** Under every good resolution, we must have a pure conscience and an empty heart. These two pieces are the silver bases that must necessarily be placed under every work or resolution. And so all these bases are then cast when we detach, free, and empty ourselves from vices, sins, and all disorderly inclination toward any creature.

<column-break/>

25. And for the other side of the Dwelling, the North side <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally "midnight side"</note>, he made twenty boards.

26. And their forty silver bases: two bases under one board, and two bases under the other board.

27. And for the sides of the Dwelling toward the West <note>original: "Abend," literally "evening side"</note> he made six boards.

28. And two boards he made for the corner boards of the Dwelling on the two sides.

29. And they were coupled from beneath, and coupled together at the top in a ring. Thus he did to both of them at the two corner boards.

30. So that there were eight boards with their silver bases, namely sixteen bases, two bases under each board.

31. And

---

**v. 25. 26.** We should further form the firm resolution within ourselves to patiently endure, without any refusal or resentment, everything that might happen to us by God’s permission, in whatever way it may be. In this way, we will be strong against the "North"—that is, against everything that could in any way oppress, tempt, and bring us vexation. At the same time, through this very endurance of every tribulation, we fulfill the commandments of God, and thus manufacture the first ten boards on the left side. If we then also wish to obediently follow the Gospel's instruction, we must not only have the resolution to patiently stand through all adversities, but also to sacrifice ourselves entirely to the most free will of the Creator, so that we are even glad to endure more, and are ready and wish to accept what He has decreed over us from eternity, not only with patience but with joy.

If our spirit were thus united with the divine will and could remain in that state, it would certainly be happy and blessed, and almost unchangeable; and we would, in a certain measure, suffer without pain—namely, pain of the mind. For then having comfort or being forsaken, suffering want, and indeed all the changes of time and what falls under it, would gladden our spirit equally; and it would have what it wanted, while conversely being unable to desire or want anything disorderly. And thus we will manufacture the other ten boards of the left side, and worthily occupy our post according to the Gospel; yes, finally possessing all those riches and goods in which all good resolutions have their beginning and end.

**v. 27.** The 6 middle boards of the West side form 6 of the most excellent resolutions of the mind, through which all others are joined together. Namely, there are the so-called 3 theological virtues: Faith, Hope, and Love; which on one side unite us with God, and on the other side are a beginning, origin, and fountain-spring <note>original: "Quelle-brunn"</note> of all other virtues in our duties toward our neighbor.

**v. 28.** And so, through the remaining 2 corner boards—of which each contributed no more than half a cubit to the interior of the Tabernacle to join the two sides of the length with the rear West wall—we may understand our physical nature, which is nothing but an instrument in which and with which we must either work or suffer. And

that we bid goodnight to all vices, overcome them, and give ourselves over to the exercise of all virtues. And

<meta>This page continues the description of the Tabernacle's construction from Exodus 36. Having discussed the boards and bases on the previous page, the text now details the bars that held the walls together and the veil that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy. The commentary continues to interpret these architectural features as allegories for the internal spiritual life and the union of the soul with God.</meta>

### Chapter XXXVI. The Second Book of Moses.

31. And he made bars of Shittim wood <term>Shittim wood: Acacia wood, known for its durability</term>: five for the boards of one side of the Dwelling,
32. And five bars for the boards of the other side of the Dwelling, and five bars for the boards of the Dwelling for the two sides facing the evening <note>original: "gegen Abend," referring to the West, where the sun sets</note>.
33. And he made the middle bar to pass through the middle of the boards from one end to the other.

These bars were large wooden poles that were pushed through golden rings firmly fixed into the paneling around the walls of the hut, intended to surround all the boards as if with a locking mechanism. This was done so that the walls would be firmer and might stand immovable against the violent winds and all other adverse occurrences.

**v. 31. 32.** Our inner person should bind itself to God in an eternal union, and practice and possess the same in three ways: through Faith, Hope, and Love, according to the three sides or walls of the hut. (1) Namely, we should surrender and sacrifice ourselves entirely to God in all obedience to His will, and nevertheless remain in a simple peace and solitude with God. (2) In all tribulation and suffering, we should deny ourselves and leave ourselves to God without wish or choice; whereby we become free from all care and anxiety and become God’s own entirely. (3) Finally, we should cling to God with hope and trust so simply and rely upon Him that the faithfulness we feel and taste in God surpasses all comfort and faithfulness of the creature; also remaining so high with love in His love that God becomes our own again.

When we now firmly resolve to be united with God in this way and to hold fast to Him, we ensure that the free working of God within us becomes our own; and these are our deeds, which we dedicate and give to GOD; in that moment He gives Himself back to us, along with His workings in us. And this reciprocal giving makes GOD and the creature harmonious or in accord, of which one is the cause of the other.

**v. 33.** Truly, the breathing-in or the inspiration of God within ourselves is the middle bar, which always carries the fullness of grace with it into us. Regarding this bar, which went through the middle of the boards so that it could not be seen except at the two ends where it protruded—alongside what was mentioned in Chapter 26, verse 28—it can also be noted that through this, the mystery of the spiritual hut can be presented to us, which is **Christ in us** <note>original Latin reference: Col. 1:27</note>, and that through His Spirit who must be in us <note>original Latin reference: John 14:17</note>: who proves Himself powerful with His inner working for the killing of the old man and the raising of the new man in us <note>original Latin reference: Romans 6</note>; whereby the hidden life of the believers with Christ in God is promoted, and brought to its proper growth and maintained; but the ends thereof must be seen by others from the outside in the abstinence from all vices and earthly vanities, and the practice of Christian virtues <note>original Latin reference: Matthew 5:16</note>. And through this also occurs the right union and strengthening of souls with one another, so that the believers can become one heart and one soul <note>original Latin reference: Acts 4:32</note>. This cannot happen through all the other truths, even if one is already so committed to them; for such things can bring about nothing more than an external union: but Christ and His Spirit, when He is essential in the hearts, unites the hearts rightly and also makes such a connection permanent.

---

->beyond our reason, and is practiced with a freedom in love.<-

The hooks, however, which are to be made at the top, shall be of gold. For in the summit of this ascent, nothing but essential love is felt: namely, when we are stripped and divested of all images—both those we have of ourselves and of all other creatures—and simply enter with GOD into the purity of our spirit.

The 4 silver bases, however, create in us the foundation freed from images, in which God wishes to live and dwell eternally as in Himself.

<column-break/>

34. And he overlaid the boards with gold, but made their rings of gold as places for the bars, and overlaid the bars with gold.
35. And he made the veil of blue wool and of purple wool and of crimson wool and of twisted fine linen yarn: with artistic work he made it with Cherubim.
36. And he made for it four pillars of Shittim wood and overlaid them with gold: their hooks were of gold, and he cast for them four silver bases <margin>(a) ch. 26/32.</margin>
37. And

**v. 34.** Just as the poles had to be overlaid with gold leaf, so must an active love come between us and GOD, which overlays and transforms God's working in us and our affection for the same. This active love is that which makes our spirit live and wake in grace. For God’s love demands our love in return: and just as it brings about in us that hidden longing which passes between us and GOD, as the bond or the connection and union of our love with the love of GOD, in which our spiritual life consists; which essential, quiet, fervent love—having to do with GOD alone—can never work anything else: so it also drives us to an active, outflowing love, with which all gifts of God and all our deeds must be overlaid as if with gold leaf. For GOD bestows no supernatural gifts in vain: He wants us to always answer His grace and meet Him with the same mind. Therefore, if we wish to receive and attain His gifts overlaid with His love, we must give Him all our works overlaid with our love.

**v. 35.** This veil hung down across the width from midday <note>South</note> toward midnight <note>North</note> between the Holy and the Most Holy, and was the division between both, which separated the Most Holy from the Holy and covered the former so that no one could look inside. So that in the same there was no other light than only as much as could penetrate from the front part on the sides of the veil, or through it. And thus GOD dwelt here in the darkness.

**v. 36.** Between the Holy and the Most Holy stood 4 pillars, right under the clasps <note>original: "Häfften," the loops or couplings</note> where the two colorful coverings were joined together above; these coverings were able to rest somewhat on these pillars, because otherwise, with the length of 30 cubits which the dwelling had inside, they would have sunk in the middle.

The **first pillar** is our inward-turned intellect, with which we should always raise ourselves up, free and loose from all hindrance, to simply behold the revelation of the eternal truth shining and dwelling within us.

The **second pillar** is our inward-turned love, through which we always simply ascend into the incomprehensible goodness of the Holy Spirit, who pours His riches and goods—which He Himself is—into the ready elevation of our free will.

The **third pillar** is the simplicity of our spirit, which must constantly ascend to the glorious unity of GOD, which allows no fervent lover to remain within themselves.

The **fourth pillar** is a hidden, essential ascent of our nature into the highest nature of GOD. For it is right that every nature seeks its origin and beginning.

This fourfold ascending remains always in a simplicity...

# The Second Book of Moses. Chap. XXXVII.

37. And he made a screen for the door of the tent of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine-linen yarn, of embroidered work.

38. And five pillars for it with their hooks; and he overlaid their capitals and their rods with gold: along with five bronze bases for them.

---

**v. 37.** A screen) was made for the Holy Place <note>The "Holy Place" was the first room of the Tabernacle, accessible only to priests.</note> to cover it from the view of the people.

The fact that God wanted all kinds of ornamentation woven and embroidered even into this forward curtain signifies that we should also behold and observe the outward customs and works of the saints, so as to do as they have done: so that, just as theirs did, our works may also serve as an example to all people.

If we now find someone who is eager to learn and recognize the truth, we should open and expand our inner selves to them, and teach them the truth according to godliness as we know it; so that they too may learn to know themselves, and see how far they and their actions harmonize with the truth, or not.

However, we should always hang the screen of humility before us and let it down to the ground; and this all the more so when people wish to honor us for our good deeds: so that we do not think more highly of ourselves than is proper. For in truth, too much honor is given to us in this; because all honor belongs to God alone, who is the source of all good. But when we are reviled, or when we are treated poorly, then it is also necessary to hang the screen of humility, behind which we are reminded that we are treated rightly: because we are "unprofitable servants" <note>A reference to Luke 17:10</note> who do not do what is required of them at all.

**v. 38.** Here there are five pillars, and just as many bases. The simple ascent of the spirit draws after it the inner senses, the physical powers, and whatever has feeling and life in nature. Therefore, the senses in us must also be quintuply and simply upright, and constantly united and bound with the spirit.

The capitals, or heads, or foliage upon them are overlaid with gold. For when we follow our spirit with the ascent of our senses, our inner senses are full of the love of God. And so our physical nature is bound with the spirit in and for all spiritual exercises.

Just as the inner veil hung on golden hooks, so also this screen was hung on hooks. For both outward good works and inward virtues depend entirely on the grace of God, which is represented by the hooks.

In general, one can note from this entire chapter that just as they first had to manufacture these outer things of the Tabernacle, and afterwards the inner pieces were made and placed therein, so God also first wanted us to be faithful in external things: such as in outward righteousness, good order in our life and conduct, in outward decency, humility in clothing and otherwise, and peacefulness with everyone; toward which the outward orders in the church assembly also aim, which must necessarily be observed, according to the Apostle’s admonition: *Let all things be done decently and in order.* 1 Cor. 14:40. Then God also wants to give us the inner gifts and treasures of grace, and to unlock and place them within our inward spirit. Christ presents this very thoughtfully in Luke 16:11–12: *If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon <term>mammon: an Aramaic word for wealth or property</term>, who will commit to your trust the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in that which is another's, who shall give you that which is your own?* But the inner gifts of the Spirit are the "true riches," and that which is the property of our immortal spirit, which was robbed from us by sin and the enemy—indeed, which was withdrawn by God Himself in a righteous way.

*I in them, and thou in me: that they may be made perfect in one etc.* John 17:21, 23. Therefore, it is very thoughtfully testified of this Ark of the Testimony that God would unite Himself there with Moses and speak with him from above the Mercy Seat <note>original: "Versöhn-Deckel," literally the "Reconciliation-Cover"</note> between the two cherubim: Cap. 25:22. This now happens in all believers, in whom the inner Word also reveals itself, though in various stages of grace.

<column-break/>

# Chapter XXXVII.

->The making of the Ark, Table, Lampstand, and Altar of Incense.<-

> These four pieces—of which the Ark was in the Most Holy Place, while the Table, Lampstand, and Altar of Incense were in the Holy Place—can represent to us the four chief blessings we have in Christ: that he is made unto us by God for wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption. 1 Cor. 1:30.

1. AND Bezaleel made the Ark of Shittim wood <term>Shittim wood: Acacia wood, prized for being rot-resistant</term>: two and a half cubits was the length thereof, and a cubit and a half the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof.

2. And he overlaid it with pure gold within and without, and made a crown of gold round about it:

3. And he cast for it four rings of gold, for the four corners of it; even two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it.

4. And he made staves of Shittim wood, and overlaid them with gold.

5. And he put the staves into the rings by the sides of the Ark, that the Ark might be carried.

---

**v. 1.** Shittim wood) Wood that resists rot, and to which no worm comes to gnaw it. Such is and was the humanity of Christ, and so we also should have a sanctified heart, wherein the worms of all kinds of shameful lusts may not dwell, so that we also may receive the spiritual body of power from Christ—flesh of His flesh—which is subject to no corruption.

**v. 2.** Overlaid it with gold) The humanity of Christ is anointed with the gold of the Godhead, and clothed with divine attributes.

A golden crown) Partly for ornament, partly so that the cover of the Ark would not fall off, and partly so that one could not see where the cover was joined and fitted onto the Ark.

**v. 3.** Golden rings) These are the powers of the Spirit.

**v. 4, 5.** Staves in the rings) wherein they remained at all times, and were never allowed to be taken out, as happened otherwise with the staves of the other furniture.

Blameless teachers, through whom Christ is presented to the people, must be taken from the precious cedar-wood that does not rot; they must also constantly remain with Christ and His teaching, and not depart or be drawn away from it, but be ready and present at all times to present and proclaim Christ to people.

When a person yearns for the true essential Good, Christ, while living in outward decency and a well-ordered state; then Christ also reveals Himself in him as essential Righteousness, as he feels the effect of the same—the peace of God—in his innermost spirit: for then his spirit is also sprinkled with the blood of Christ, so that he is assured of reconciliation with God in this blood. Rom. 5:1. And that is then the Most Holy Place, which reveals itself in our spirit when we are drawn into the blessed communion with God in Christ, for which Christ still continually prays for His believers:

# Chapter XXXVII. The Second Book of Moses. 425

6. And he made the **Mercy Seat** <note>Also known as the Atonement Cover.</note> of pure gold: two and a half cubits was its length, and one and a half cubits its width.

<margin>(a) chapter 25:18-19. 1 Kings 6:23 and following.</margin>
7. And he made two **Cherubim** (a) of gold; he made them of beaten work at the two ends of the Mercy Seat.

8. One Cherub at this end, and the other Cherub at that end. He made the Cherubim as part of the Mercy Seat, at its two ends.

9. And the Cherubim spread out both wings above: they covered the Mercy Seat with their wings, and their faces were toward one another; the faces of the Cherubim were turned toward the Mercy Seat.

---

**v. 6. Mercy Seat)** Which was at the same time the lid of the Ark, and thus was a golden plate of the exact length and width of the Ark.
This circumstance is well worth noting for the sake of the **mystery**. For just as it is with the Ark and the Mercy Seat—where the Ark was not a self-contained chest that had a separate lid of cedar wood, but rather had this golden plate as its cover, which closed the open part of the Ark and through this union became one thing with it—so it is also with the image of blessing in Christ Jesus, who consists of both divine and human natures.

**v. 7. 8. Two Cherubim)** Which some Hebrew scholars (a) claim were made ten handbreadths high—that is, a little over one and a half cubits.

**v. 9. Wings... above)** With these, they made and presented, as it were, a chair and the seat upon which the Lord sat when He answered the High Priest who sought His counsel. Therefore, it says here and there in the Psalms: *You who sit upon the Cherubim.*
Christ, however, protects His Church under the wings of His Cherubim and covers their sins.
**Dionysius the Areopagite** (b) <note>A Christian theologian of the late 5th century whose writings on the hierarchy of angels were highly influential.</note>, who learned his theology in part from him who had been in the third heaven <note>A reference to the Apostle Paul.</note>, writes that the Cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge and the outpouring of wisdom. This wisdom, along with the power to recognize and behold God and the capacity for an overflowing light which they possess within themselves, they pass on and share with others without envy. They also partake in the fellowship of Jesus, being taught directly by His divinity and raised in an immediate way to God through a power that transcends all things.

**Their faces were turned toward the Mercy Seat)** Jesus Christ is the one upon whom all eyes, all souls, and all spirits must look.
But according to the **secret sense**, we can also understand these two Cherubim—with their faces directed toward one another upon the Ark and the lid—as the contemplation of "enjoying love" in the spiritual life. Here, the two Cherubim signify two qualities of the loving spirit in its highest nobility, where it belongs entirely to divine love and rests from its own works. The first, which can be found in an exalted spirit, is a constant, steady, and precise contemplation in the divine light. The other is a constant "enjoying affection." Both overflow with the wisdom and love of God. And although they are one in unity, they are always two within themselves. They also have two spread-out wings; because they are raised very high in contemplation and enjoyment.
This simple contemplation, directed toward the divine light, and the enjoying affection are constantly turned toward each other, as one lives in the other. Their faces—that is, their loving affections—must be directed toward the Ark and the Mercy Seat, which signifies enjoyable love.
Between these two Cherubim—that is, between our simple contemplation and our enjoying affection—is the seat and the dwelling of God within us. From there, we receive wisdom and grace and learn the commandments and counsel of God. This residence of God within us protects and preserves us from all evil.

<margin>
(a) Rabbi Bechai in Buxtorf’s *History of the Ark of the Covenant*, chapter 9. Rabbi Judah Leo, book 3 on the Temple, chapter 1, sections 3, 19.
(b) *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, chapters 6 & 7.
</margin>

<sig>Hhh</sig>

<column-break/>

10. And he made the **table** of Shittim wood <note>Acacia wood.</note>: two cubits was its length, one cubit its width, and one and a half cubits its height.

11. And he overlaid it with pure gold and made a golden crown around it. 12. And

---

Because the matters concerning the literal meaning were touched upon sufficiently in Chapter 25, we shall focus here more on the **mystery**.
Here, then, the holy table reveals itself. Among other things, this consists of Christ becoming the power of new life as our sanctification, who always provides us with spiritual nourishment and strength to bring forth the fruits of righteousness in the life of faith (Philippians 1:11); that is, the divine power that gives us everything belonging to life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3).
Our love must be common to all people: therefore, this table, as an image of that love, was not placed in the Most Holy Place, but in the front part of the Tabernacle. It stood close before the veil, opposite the golden lampstand on the north side. According to **v. 10**, it was:
**Two cubits long, one cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high)** Thus, this table was half a cubit smaller in length and width than the Ark of the Covenant, but they were both equal in height.
God, out of free goodness, resolved to love us. If we, in turn, resolve to love Him unbreakably, then these two actions are an eternal measure of the **length** of our table.
When we thus expand ourselves in God, our love loses itself and sinks entirely into God, so that His action alone remains in us. Therefore, the **width** of the table is only one cubit.
The **height**, however, is one and a half cubits. Of this, the actions of God in us make up the full cubit; but we find ourselves "too short" in all our works, and feel ourselves to be weak in our part and measure. Such is then the **half-cubit**, which we are unable to make whole. For the more we love, the more we are driven to love, and love can never be satisfied or contented in its works. This is also the reason why love can always grow in this life. And who is he that is so pleased with himself as to think his cubit, which is only half, is whole and perfect in love? Let him be assured that his cubit is false, and his table too wide or too high—he deceives himself with a false imagination.
It is just the same with God's praise, which rises from us to the heights. God works His own praise in all creatures in heaven and on earth: and that is the full cubit. But He is of such incomprehensible greatness and worthy of such great honor that all creatures must necessarily fall short in His praise; and that is the half-cubit.
Thus, a loving soul may love and praise God as much as it desires, yet it can never satisfy its longing, and recognizes continually that it cannot love and praise God according to His worth. Therefore, its cubit remains always half and imperfect, and it constantly holds God worthy of higher and greater honor and praise than it and all creatures can provide.
**v. 11. He overlaid it with gold)** It was heavily plated over and over with golden sheets.

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXVII.

**12. And he made a frame for it of a handbreadth all around / and made a golden crown for its frame all around.**

**13. And he cast for it four golden rings / and put the rings on the four corners that were at its four feet.**

**v. 12. A golden crown)** Love is its own reward / and is adorned and crowned with its own works.

<margin>(a) Explanation of the Tabernacle, this chapter, 117.</margin>
According to the account of Ruusbroec <note>original: "Rusbrochii"; referring to Jan van Ruusbroec, a 14th-century Flemish mystic</note> (a), the Hebrews are said to claim that there were images upon it representing kings / specifically as many as would later reign in Jerusalem from David until Zedekiah: which / if true / must have occurred through divine revelation.

This much is certain / that this crown also depicts the firstborn of the Lamb / the royal generation / which surrounds the twelve loaves of the consecrated twelve tribes / who stand continually before the Lord.

However, just as the crown was twofold / being both above and below the border or the frame; regarding which see chapter 25:24-25, so must the crown of our love be image-less <note>original: "bilder-los"; a mystical term referring to a state of contemplation free from mental concepts or sensory distractions</note> / at least in its highest part or in its most exalted works / where it disposes itself toward the unity of eternal love / which is God Himself; because here no images can be suffered or endured.

Furthermore, as some believe / this double crown signified the future division of the kingdom of Israel. In that case / the lower part must have prefigured the Kingdom of Israel / and the upper part the Kingdom of Judah / to which the priests and Levites belonged / for the sake of the city of Jerusalem and the Temple.

Love also seems to divide its kingdom into two parts. To some, it gives a virtuous life and a right intention / granting them wisdom and the knowledge of God and of themselves. Through this, they become kings in Israel: they then become capable of governing their families / along with the ten tribes; namely, the powers of the soul and the senses / both internal and external. When they do this / they attain the true love of the Law and the ten commandments / and their love is then crowned with all the good works / which they perform for the glory of God: and the more love spreads itself in goodness / the greater this crown becomes; and thus it is great, wide, and beautiful according to the measure of each person's love and virtues.

Above this, love bears another crown / which is far more excellent: which no one can attain except the generation and tribe of Judah / or those who confess, praise, and glorify the greatness of divine love through a disregard for themselves and all their works: namely, through the contemplation of the eternal love which God is Himself; by the sight of which they regard themselves and all their works as far too small. This annihilation <note>original: "Vernichtung"; in mystical theology, the process of emptying the self to be filled with God</note> is the golden crown of the tribe of Judah / which holds the superior place / and from which Christ was born / who as King and Lord lives more in such souls than they do themselves / and dwells in them as in His city and temple in Jerusalem.

Thus, the table of our love is surrounded and adorned with a double crown / as a sign of the conquest of all our enemies / and it is rightly understood what the Psalmist sings: *You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.*

It was a table / and not an altar.

**v. 13.** Therefore it also had to have four feet / upon which it rested.

These four feet signify the Evangelical foundation / upon which our works of love must be grounded. This Evangelical law has four forms / as described by Saint John and the prophet Ezekiel.

The first form is / that through love we overcome everything that is contrary to God / and trample down our animal life. Thereby we receive the face and the spiritual life of the lion / who is a king and conqueror of all beasts.

<column-break/>

**14. Opposite the frame were the rings as places for the poles / so that the table could be carried.**

**15. And he made the poles of acacia wood / and overlaid them with gold / to carry the table.**

**16. And he made the vessels that belonged on the table / its dishes / and its bowls / and its plates / and its cups / with which it was covered / of pure gold.**

**17.**

In the second form, love teaches us / that we should constantly sacrifice ourselves and all our works to God for His honor. When we do this / our inner man receives the form of a calf <note>Or an ox; the sacrificial animal of the Tabernacle</note> / which in the type was customarily offered to God.

In the third form, love teaches us justice / and gives us a rational life adorned with virtues: then our inner life receives the form of a man / and at the same time dominion over the whole world.

The fourth form finally testifies / that love leads some beyond their comprehension into a pure contemplation / and expands their mind into an image-less vastness / where they feel the eye of their understanding to be always open / because it stretches out without ceasing toward the revelation of eternal truth / and contemplates it. From this, love and desire grow, along with a constant yearning to comprehend the incomprehensible God. And in this state, those who are so disposed receive the face of an eagle and a hidden knowledge of God / as well as a clear discernment in all necessary truth. But those who cannot perceive such things in themselves / do well if they follow the light of their faith and their love toward God with a right and simple intention: thus love will eventually lead them to the presence and the sight of God / so that they will attain the fourth form and a truly spiritual life.

But four golden rings also belong here.

**v. 14.** Divine grace is attached to each of the aforementioned forms / because each is pleasing and acceptable to God. This grace of God is quite fittingly compared to a ring / because like a ring, it has neither beginning nor end.

**v. 15. Poles... to carry the table)** But they did not remain in it / when the table stood still. Numbers 4:8.

During transport, it was wrapped in a sky-blue / purple / and scarlet-colored cloth / Numbers 4:7-8 / which are the colors in the rainbow: to indicate / that God’s grace through the blood of Christ covers the table for us.

**v. 16.** For a greater explanation of what was said regarding the vessels of the table in Chapter 25:29 / based on the opinion of the Hebrews / from which there is no reason to depart without necessity in their church customs / because they would have known the ways of their fathers and the vessels of their divine service better than others / it is to be noted / that by the word *Menakkiyot* <note>original: מנקיות; traditionally "bowls" or "jars," but here interpreted as "cleansing tubes"</note> / which is translated here as "plates" / they understand golden branches / which were made like half-tubes and were hollow / just as if one were to cut a long pipe lengthwise down the middle / and thus make two half-pipes out of it. These tubes were longer than the table was wide / and reached over the table. By *Menakkiyot* / which is given here as "cups" / they understand golden forks / each with three golden prongs / of which there were said to be four forks for the table / two for each stack [of bread] / where one stood on this side and the other on the other side of the table / and had pointed feet standing on the ground / like a sharpened stake. These forks towered high above the table on both sides / and between one fork and the other across the table went 14 golden tubes in 5 rows / one above the other. In the four lowest rows, from the three prongs of one fork across to the other three prongs of the other fork, there were 3 tubes in each row; that makes 12 together: and in the top row there were only 2 half-tubes. Thus is also best understood what is said in Leviticus 24:6 / regarding which more will be said.

# Chapter XXXVII. The Second Book of Moses.

### The Making of the Lampstand

**17. And he made the lampstand of pure gold: of hammered work he made the lampstand. Its shaft and its branches / its bowls / its knobs and its flowers / were all of one piece with it.**

**18. And six branches went out from its sides: three branches of the lampstand out of one side / and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side.**

**19. Three bowls shaped like almonds were on the one branch / a knob and a flower: and three bowls shaped like almonds were on the other branch / a knob and a flower. So it was for the six branches that went out from the lampstand.**

---

In this way, Christ is also the lampstand, our wisdom / since through his radiance a bright glow is given to the hearts of the believers regarding all divine truths / according to the measure of grace that God wishes to impart to each person. 2 Corinthians 4:6. At times, these truths are still hidden in the heart / like these **knobs**: which afterwards open into **flowers** / when the truths are first truly born in the heart / and have become ripe, as it were / so that they break forth in public confession / and give off a lovely fragrance of life in all the children and lovers of the truth.

This lampstand, then, signifies the Holy Spirit of our God and of his Anointed / our Lord Jesus Christ / and his enlightenment with which he illuminates his Church / which receives its light and clarity from him: but it also signifies the Church itself / as an offspring of the Spirit. Everything comes forth as an offspring from the lampstand: both the branches and the bowls / both the knobs and the flowers; that is / both the patriarchs of the faith and their children and descendants / who were born from them.

**v. 17** Everything on it is of clear gold / and also all of one piece. The Holy Spirit is and remains one Spirit / even if he, according to—

**v. 18** —spreads out into six branches / and makes the number seven in the center himself / as the Spirit of the Lord / who has precedence over all. Just as in a human being the soul divides itself, as it were / when it manifests in the senses / and sees in the eye / hears in the ear / smells in the nose / etc. though it is and remains one soul as before. Even so, many effects and gifts of light proceed from the one Spirit / which he imparts to men / opening himself in one person through this gift / and in another through that.

**3 and 3 branches)** went out on each side from the shaft / and indeed as high up as the shaft was.

**v. 19** Each branch of these six had three cups or bowls / a knob and a flower / not "knobs and flowers" in the plural / as is found in some translations.

<column-break/>

**20. But on the lampstand itself were four bowls / shaped like almonds / with their knobs and their flowers.**

**21. And there was a knob under two branches of the same / and again a knob under two branches of the same / and another knob under two branches of the same: namely, for the six branches going out from it.**

**22. Their knobs and their branches were of one piece with it: the whole was one piece of hammered work of pure gold.**

**23. And he made its seven lamps with its tongs and its snuffer dishes of pure gold.**

**24. Out of a talent <note>original: "Centner"; a biblical unit of weight for precious metals</note> of pure gold he made it and all its utensils.**
<meta>Chapter 25:39.</meta>

**25. And**

---

**v. 20** The shaft, however, had more ornaments. Exactly how many knobs and flowers there were, however, is not actually reported.

That the bowls were shaped like almonds or like open almond shells / and thus had to be formed / seems to have happened partly because the entire lampstand is presented as a growing thing / where from the shaft or stem the branches come forth as limbs / and from the limbs the knobs / and finally the flowers / emerge and grow out; and thus it is compared to the **almond tree** / which blooms early in January / and already bears fruit in March: as a prototype of the **Oil-children** <note>original: "Oel-Kinder"; a reference to Zechariah 4:14, meaning "anointed ones" or those who produce the oil of the Spirit</note> / as the spiritual births of the Church / who in the midst of the winter of persecution show / that they are of a good kind / and bring forth their blossoms and fruits. All such people are fathered by the one good Spirit of Jesus Christ as chosen **Flowers of Sharon** <note>original: "Blumen Sarons"; likely referring to the Rose of Sharon, a symbol of beauty and Christ</note> / who let their light shine everywhere in good works to the praise of their heavenly Father / and bring forth the firstfruits of the Spirit / when other trees only bud much later.

The almond-shaped bowls were first three times seven / on each of the six branches there were three / which together make eighteen; and then on the middle shaft there were also initially three to match: thereafter, on this shaft / according to the order and command of God / one further bowl had to be made / so that the seventh lamp would have something extra; to indicate the increased power of the Spirit / when the completion of the seventh Church-age <note>An interpretation linking the lampstand to the Seven Churches of Revelation</note> should have come.

**v. 21** Where the branches went out from the shaft / there was a knob on the shaft under the outgoing branches.

**v. 22** The branches were not attached to the shaft from the outside / so that one could take them off and put them on again; rather, the shaft and branches / with all knobs, cups, and floral work / were artistically hammered out of one large piece of gold / so that nothing was joined together from pieces / but everything was firm and whole together.

**v. 23** Regarding the seven lamps, there is so much to say / that it cannot conveniently happen here / but must be saved for elsewhere.

---

This much is to be noted briefly regarding the literal sense / that these lamps were not fixed to the lampstand / but were only placed loosely upon it / and were taken off during the cleaning.

Just as there are seven planets in the heavens / so also in the Church-heaven there are seven stars and seven congregations: and in the upper heaven no fewer than seven throne-angels are counted / over whom the seven Spirits of God are yet raised.

O how great is the sum of the wisdom of God / and its marks everywhere! Even in this at least / that he has presented the greatest mysteries of his kingdom in such graceful and magnificent parables.

The Lord / who is the true light / let his seven lights and spirits shine in us / so that we may also see the wonders in this lampstand / which is so beautiful / and recognize him according to his deep meaning!

# The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXVII.

### 25. And he made the Altar of Incense of Shittim wood <note>original: "Sittimholtz"; also known as acacia wood</note>: its length was one cubit <note>original: "Ehle"</note> and its width one cubit; it was foursquare: and its height was two cubits. Its horns proceeded from the same.

### 26. And he overlaid it with pure gold / its roof and its walls all around / and its horns; and he made for it a golden crown <note>a decorative molding or border</note> all around.

Now that both sides within the Holy Place have been furnished / and the Table of Showbread has taken its place on the side toward the North / and the Lampstand on the side toward the South; we find the Altar of Incense in the middle.

Now, the literal meaning of this is quite clear / so that little needs to be added for its explanation beyond what was already reported in Chapter 30. However, the inner understanding / being the spirit and the most noble part of the matter / is only rightly understood and grasped by those who have grasped its essence / and actually possess it within themselves, standing in the spirit themselves / lifting up holy hands / and offering upon this altar.

Much must depend upon the offering on this golden altar / because it receives its station closest to the Most Holy Place; regarding which see Chapter 30, verse 6 and Chapter 40, verse 5.

Through the Spirit of grace and of prayer / which Christ imparts to His own / and which is represented by the Altar of Incense / He becomes our redemption: in that we could only be redeemed from all evil of body and soul through constant, persistent sighing. Just as the Apostle finally concludes the whole armor of God / with which we can stand against the cunning attacks of the devil / through whom and his instruments all evil is stirred up against us: And pray always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit / and watch thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints. Ephesians 6:11, 18. And through these benefits our soul is rightly prepared for the Holy Place / since its powers are thus enlightened / strengthened / and equipped with the gift of prayer / so that GOD may be recognized, lauded, and praised in this sanctuary.

Blessed is he who, as a royal priest with Aaron, can step before the golden altar / and rightly wield the censer of prayer in the Church of GOD; who is always alert and awake / and has his lamp burning on the golden lampstand: he will find an answer in Christ JESUS / and will truly enjoy His high-priestly prayer. For the entire power of our prayer that is valid before GOD consists in Christ JESUS / when we pray through His Spirit / and let our heart-altar be reconciled with the blood of Christ's atonement-sacrifice. And thus our altar receives its true length and width.

**v. 25.** One cubit its length / and one cubit its width) If one wishes to appear before GOD in the state of a true person of prayer / such an expanding love is required for it / as is also in Christ JESUS / who prayed for those who crucified Him / and worked such expansive love in Stephen also. The length or long-suffering of praying love and its width or expansion are equal / although that which is loved is not equal. For to love, all is one and equal / which in itself is unequal: it looks upon everything as children or creatures of God; it recognizes nothing in all things except what is of GOD and wherein it finds GOD. Therefore, it loves everything in GOD and for God's sake. But if the Spirit of Christ in the believers prays for enemies / how much more will He do it unto perfection for the members / also according to the equality of the high-priestly intercession of Christ in John 17.

It has two cubits in height, because body and spirit with souls and expanded hearts must lift themselves to GOD and lift up holy hands.

Its horns signify its power and authority. The prayer of a righteous man avails much / that which is worked within him. James 5:16. Rabbi Judah Leo <margin>(a) Book 3 on the Temple, chapter 4, section 14.</margin> makes them on this figurative altar foursquare and hollowed out and perforated / as on the Altar of Burnt Offering.

**v. 26. Its roof)** Those who place a grate or network on top / upon which the glowing coals were placed / and where the ashes fell through between the holes / depart herein from the Scripture / according to which everything on top was solid and made of wood / like the walls. The coals were not placed on the roof / but on a coal-pan <note>or censer</note>. Whatever fell off / was always swept up and carried out whenever incense was to be burned again.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<column-break/>

### 27. He also made two golden rings for it under its crown at its two corners on its two sides / as places for the poles to carry it with them.

### 28. And he made the poles of Shittim wood / and overlaid them with gold.

### 29. And he made the oil of holy anointing and the pure incense of sweet-smelling spices according to the work of an apothecary. c. 30 / 23--36.

**v. 27.** Under the crown were rings on two sides / two on each side / which were made fast at both ends.

**v. 28.** Through which poles were thrust / on each of the two sides one pole through 2 rings / so that the altar could be conveniently carried during the departure. But when it stood in the Holy Place / the poles were removed.

**v. 29.** What spices went into the anointing oil / can be seen in Chapter 30, verses 23 and 24. Regarding the weight, however, it is still to be noted for greater clarity / that / because the shekel <note>original: "Seckel"</note> of the sanctuary was as much as 1 Loth <note>approximately 1/2 ounce or 15 grams</note> or half an ounce / (which word "half" was omitted there by oversight) thus 500 Loth of myrrh were added to it / which is 15 pounds / and 20 Loth <note>The author is calculating based on 32 Loth to a pound</note>, of iris root <note>original: "Violen-Wurzel"</note> just as much; but of cinnamon half as much / and of calamus also half as much / namely 7 pounds and 26 Loth: thus from all 4 spices together 46 pounds and 28 Loth. To this was added about 3 measures of olive oil / and they also obtained as much anointing oil in return.

The incense powder was beaten in a mortar until it became as small as dust. That beyond the 4 spices named in Chapter 30, verse 34, still more were added / which were perhaps not all specified and named for that reason / so that it could be imitated all the less / and since the unnamed ones are to be understood under the general word "spices"; is not to be doubted. The Hebrews add besides these: myrrh / cassia / spikenard or lavender / saffron / costus <note>an aromatic root</note>, etc. That calamus was also in this incense powder / is to be seen from Isaiah 43:23, 24.

How much of each was taken / Rittangel <margin>(a) Highly Solemn Ceremonies, page 332.</margin> reports: namely of balsam / onycha / galbanum and frankincense / an equal amount / and 70 Loth of each kind; of myrrh / cassia / spikenard and saffron / 16 Loth of each; of costus 12 Loth; of calamus or Kilupha 3 Loth; of lime-bark <note>original: "Limmet-rinde"</note> 9 Loth. This was the dose of those 11 species. To these were added 2 other species of sweet-smelling things: namely a little of the herb *Maale Alchan* <note>Hebrew: Ma'aleh Ashan, a smoke-raising herb</note>, and a little Jordan amber <note>likely a resin</note> / without a specific dose. Other things were also added / which however had no scent: such as; 9 measures of Carthaginian soap / 3 and a half measures of Cyprian wine / and a quarter of a measure of Salt of Sodom.

The incense powder was afterwards made annually by the priests for burning / because much of it was used / daily in the morning and evening. The anointing oil, however / which was used very rarely / shall / according to the claim of the Hebrews / never have been made again after this time in Moses' day / when the above-mentioned ingredients were given in the prescribed dose with 3 measures / and lasted from then until the time of King Josiah / nearly 900 years / but was not present in the other Temple.

These two pieces / the Holy Anointing Oil and the lovely incense / give us very specifically in the image the Spirit of grace and of prayer.

# The XXXVIII Chapter.
