And he made the Altar of Burnt Offering / of acacia wood <note>original: "Sittimholz"</note>; five cubits <note>original: "Ehlen"; a cubit is approximately 18 inches</note> / was its length and five / cubits its width; it was foursquare; / and three cubits its height.

> We must overcome all the diversity of the 5 senses / and / gather them within us into unity from their divided or / scattered state. We must also bring the desires of our / senses to this unity / and despise and pass over whatever pleases them beyond / necessity. Then our / altar will have a length and width of 5 cubits / and we will / thus stand firm, constant / and as if foursquare / against every / offense.

<term>3 cubits height</term>) This is understood by the Hebrews as the upper / part or the box above the ledge <note>original: "Umgang"</note> / from which the horns / protrude. Indeed / that the entire altar was higher / than 3 cubits / is very believable / as it would otherwise have been quite / misshapen and unsightly. For then the ledge / which reached almost halfway up the altar / would have been about one and a half / cubits high from the ground / and the upper part would also have / had only one and a half cubits. Thus it would then / not have stood much above the knees of the priest / and the priests would have / towered far above the altar.

It was commonly called the Altar of Burnt Offering: / but not as if no other offerings / besides only burnt / offerings / were offered upon it; but because the burnt / offerings were the most distinguished among all offerings.

But the same is to be viewed as

->**A Sign of Christ and His Divinity.**<-

<margin>Exodus 20:24-26. 24:4-8. 27:1-8. Hebrews 9:14. 13:10.</margin>

1. This altar was partly of wood / partly of bronze <note>original: "Ertz"</note>: / to indicate Christ's divinity and humanity. The fire would have / consumed the wood / if the bronze had not been there.
2. It was not to be made according to human art. / Christ was not formed through human help.
3. The altar was foursquare: to indicate / that Christ's / sacrifice would extend to all 4 corners of the world.
4. It was hollow / and / when it was carried / inside the / uppermost part it was quite empty: and when it was to be used / it was not filled with precious material / but with common / earth. And Christ Jesus / although he was in divine form / emptied himself as it were / and took on the / form of a servant. Philippians 2:7.
5. It had horns at the 4 corners / which, sprinkled with blood / were a refuge for wrongdoers: 1 Kings 1. To indicate / that Christ is the strong, mighty God / who through his / accomplished atonement has become our refuge.
6. It had all kinds of vessels and instruments. So / are the believers incorporated into Christ / of whom each has a / certain office and talent / with which Christ is adorned.
7. It had poles in the rings / in order to / be able to carry it. Thus should Christ be carried forth into the world.
8. It was anointed with the holy oil / and had / therefore the glorious name / that it was called the Most Holy / Chapter 29:36,37. Also Daniel 9:24.
9. Upon it fire burned day and night / which had fallen from / heaven / and was maintained by the priests / so that / neither weather nor rain could extinguish it. Leviticus 6. That / is the Holy Spirit in Christ and in his believers / and / heavenly love.
10. This fire consumed the sacrifice. Psalm 69:10 <note>original: Psalm 69:9 in modern Bibles</note>.
11. The sacrifice was sanctified by the altar / which / was more than the sacrifice. Matthew 23:19. Thus has Christ's sacrifice / received its validity from the divinity in one person. / Therefore it is the blood of God. Acts 20:28.
12. The altar was entirely blood-red to look upon / because one / saw nothing but the most beautiful red copper on it; it was also / consecrated with blood / and was always entirely bloody. How Christ / looked in his suffering / we may recognize from the Passion / history.

13. With the blood of the burnt offerings was sprinkled (1) / the altar itself / (2) the people / (3) the book of the covenant. / Thus was Christ sprinkled with his own blood / through which / we are cleansed / and God's Word as it were sanctified / as that which stands upon Christ's blood.
14. The altar stood neither in the Holy nor the Most Holy / Place; as in those places only incense / and no flesh / was offered: but in the court. Christ was offered outside Jerusalem; / and in the Christian church and in heaven / Christ is no longer offered / but only prayer.
15. Just as the altar was a prototype of Christ and his / divinity; just as in the New Testament the word altar / and priest are not used for table and preacher: so / must such things cease / and we must not imagine / that the cross was the altar of Christ.

> Christ is our Altar! (1) He is our refuge in / need. (2) There we must bring the bullocks of our / lips <note>original: "Farren unserer Lippen"; a biblical metaphor for sacrifices of praise</note>. (3) And then / if we eat of him spiritually / we stand in / his community or fellowship / of the divine nature / and become / partakers of his blood and holiness.

(3) It will then sanctify what our hands do / and offer / prayer and alms. (4) And the fire of / love and of the Holy Spirit must not be extinguished by / any tribulation or negligence.

v. 2. **Overlaid it with bronze)** With copper plating. / This copper gave the altar not only a greater decoration / than if it had been only of wood / but / also preserved all the woodwork from the fire / so that it was / not burned by the same.

Our heart should be hollow / that is / empty / of all those things that imprint images upon us / as well as of all disorderly love.

8. And he made the washbasin <note>original: "Waschfaß"; also known as the Laver</note> of bronze / and its base of bronze / from the mirrors of the women who served / who ministered before the door of the Tabernacle of Meeting. <margin>1 Sam. 2:22.</margin>

---

<margin>1 Kings 7:23.</margin> In place of this, Solomon made a molten sea: 1 Kings 7:23. and in the second Temple, there was a hand-basin with 12 pipes.

The word *mar’ot* <note>original: מראת</note> is translated by the Greek interpreters / and most others as "mirrors" / which women especially use / as a certain Jewish Rabbi testifies / that it was the custom among the Jews to adorn the face / and to arrange their head-ornaments every morning before a bronze mirror / or to view their faces in glass mirrors. Thus, some believe / that the women among Israel who feared GOD / and were diligent to please GOD by despising the vanities of this world / offered their mirrors to the Lord / because they no longer had need of them / and they gathered every morning before the door of the Tabernacle / to pray and to hear the commandments of GOD: then it may also have happened / that they otherwise voluntarily offered their necessary labor for the service of the Tabernacle.

<margin>1 Cor. 13:12.</margin> This should then be observed as a lesson by all godly women as well as men / if they should also be devoted to the vanity of viewing themselves in the mirror / so that we may all be moved to look rightly into the mirror of the Word <margin>1 Cor. 13:12.</margin> at our great corruption / and how displeasing we are before the Savior in outward finery / and thus to have a loathing for it / and to cast it off through true holiness / and to walk in humble, simple clothing / in which alone we can please the Lord JESUS / and not in conformity to the world: <margin>Rom. 12:2.</margin> Rom. 12:2. as such is expressly enjoined upon Christian women / and thus outward finery is forbidden as something heathen; <margin>1 Pet. 3:3, 4, 5.</margin> 1 Pet. 3:3, 4, 5. and thus even more so for men / to whom such womanly desire to adorn oneself is much more unseemly / as the clever proverb says: *Forma neglecta virum decet* <note>Latin: "A neglected appearance becomes a man."</note>. See also <margin>Ch. 33:4, 5, 6.</margin> Ch. 33:4, 5, 6.

*Who ministered before the door of the Tabernacle of Meeting* / Or / as others give it / *those assembling in troops* / who came like regiments to the door of the Tabernacle of Meeting. For thus it actually says in the Hebrew / that they formed an army / or approached like an army / or waged war; and the military word may well be used / because they formed a company / and approached in throngs. Indeed—

The Spirit looks even further toward the spiritual war / from which the female gender is not excluded; but / just as there were formerly even among the heathens manly, brave women or heroines / who were famous for their brave deeds; so there were / and still are / and must and will be even from that same gender yet further such brave and capable women / to lead the Lord's wars. This, however, is accomplished by the spiritual and masculine part of the inward man in all believing and holy women; namely, the strength and power of the Spirit and life / which is in all righteous daughters of Sarah / who do not shrink before any terror from their spiritual enemies. <margin>1 Pet. 3:6.</margin> 1 Pet. 3:6.

<margin>Pliny (a).</margin> That in ancient times one used not only mirrors of glass / but also of bronze, steel, and other metal; is to be seen from Pliny (a).

This hand-basin was therefore a very shining vessel / made of nothing but brightly polished mirrors. And because it was of fine, unadulterated, beautiful copper / it was blood-red: therefore the water / that was in it / must also have appeared blood-red.

Just as Christ completes our spirit and soul in those four previously mentioned benefits / so our body also receives through Him / as our Altar of Burnt Offering and Washbasin / power / to kill the old man / who stirs in the members of the body / and to put on the new man in the holiness of His Spirit / that we may present our members for the service of righteousness unto holiness. Rom. 6:19. See also <margin>John 3:5.</margin> John 3:5. And so we present our bodies as a sacrifice / that is living, holy, and well-pleasing to GOD: which must be our reasonable service; <margin>Rom. 12:1.</margin> Rom. 12:1. which must also be able to be observed in our outward life / through moderation, chastity, thrift, justice, humility / and other Christian virtues / in common social intercourse with other people / just as the Altar of Burnt Offering and the Washbasin stood under the open sky / and were seen by all people. See <margin>Matt. 5:16. Phil. 2:15.</margin> Matt. 5:16. Phil. 2:15.

<margin>(a) Book 33 of the Natural History, ch. 9. Book 34, ch. 17.</margin>

9. And he made the courtyard on the south side toward the south: there the hangings of the courtyard were of twined fine linen yarn / of one hundred cubits <note>original: "Ehlen"</note>.

10. With their twenty pillars and their twenty bases of bronze: the hooks of the pillars and their rods were of silver.

11. And on the side toward the north one hundred cubits / with their twenty pillars and their twenty bases of bronze: the hooks of the pillars and their rods were of silver.

12. But on the side toward the west were the hangings of fifty cubits / with their ten pillars and their ten bases: the hooks of the pillars and their rods were of silver. 13.

---

<margin>v. 9. This courtyard was around the dwelling / 100 cubits long / and 50 cubits wide / and was enclosed with hangings and pillars.</margin>

By this is then represented and depicted an externally moral or honorable life / with all that belongs to it.

It should also remind us of the boundaries of our appointed course in our life / that the same is restricted by the LORD in every way. Although He has already earned for us noble freedom / and no law is given to the righteous; <margin>1 Tim. 1:9.</margin> 1 Tim. 1:9. yet believers must not draw this grace and freedom toward wantonness / as if everything were permitted to them: which is a harmful libertinism / that finally robs men of the grace of God entirely / and plunges them into atheism <note>original: "Atheismum"</note>, so that they finally believe nothing at all. And though they say / that they know GOD; which they are accustomed to do to avoid outward shame / and also harm: yet they deny Him with their works / and are thus abominable and disobedient / and unfit for any good work. <margin>Tit. 1:16.</margin> Tit. 1:16. And therefore the Apostle compares the course of life of believers to a race within boundaries / where one must contain oneself / and can deviate neither to the right nor to the left; and concludes: I buffet my body / and tame it; so that I do not preach to others / and myself become a castaway. Therefore, the preachers, like the pillars, must apply themselves before others to walk within these boundaries of an outwardly honorable and orderly conduct / whereby others also may be maintained in order. Otherwise / where these fall through disorderly conduct / all good order falls among the others as well. See <margin>1 Cor. 9:19-27.</margin> 1 Cor. 9:19-27.

<margin>v. 10-12. bases) If Josephus (a) is to be believed / then these were not only pointed all around / so that they could be stuck into the earth / and the pillar stood all the better / but also gilded / and were one cubit long.</margin>

These bases, however, signify an internal firm resolve of the mind toward virtue. And this is a beginning to an orderly life.

Twenty of the same with their pillars shall stand toward the south and twenty toward the north: that is / we should stretch ourselves out with our services of love or exercise of love to the right and left / toward the good and the evil / toward friends and enemies / and be equipped for this with all steadfastness and firmness.

# Ch. XXXIX. The Second Book of Moses.

<columns>

13. And on the east side toward the sunrise, it was fifty cubits. <note>original: "Ehlen"</note>

<margin>c. 27/13.</margin>
14. There were the curtains of fifteen cubits on the one side, with their three pillars and their three bases.

15. And on the other side, on this and on that side of the gate of the courtyard, were the curtains of fifteen cubits, with their three pillars and their three bases.

16. All the curtains of the courtyard all around were of twisted fine-linen yarn.

17. And the bases for the pillars were of bronze; the hooks of the pillars and their rods were of silver, and their capitals <note>original: "Knöpffe"</note> were overlaid with silver. Thus they were provided with silver rods, all the pillars of the courtyard.

---

*Because the courtyard was not on one part or side of the dwelling alone, but rather all around the entire dwelling, and yet was intended to be a court in which one could walk and move about, the question arises: how far were its curtains set back from the dwelling? To this, Philo <note>original: "(a) L. 3. de vit. Mos. p. 517." refers to Philo of Alexandria’s 'On the Life of Moses,' Book 3.</note> gives this answer: that the dwelling was 20 cubits away from the curtains on both the south and the north sides, standing right in the middle. Thus, from each of these two sides of the dwelling to the curtains, there were 20 cubits. Toward the west, there were also 20 cubits from the dwelling to the curtains. At the front, however, from the entrance of the dwelling backward toward the east, following the outermost veil and that wall, it was as the width is described here:*

*v. 13. On the east side toward the sunrise 50 cubits) These very words and the width also indicate at the same time that the measurements from the dwelling must be calculated from the inside. For in this way, there were certainly 20 cubits on each side from the curtains of the south and north sides to the dwelling inside (including the eleven-edged boards), because the dwelling was 10 cubits wide inside, and the court had a width of 50 cubits; this width is exactly made up of the two times 20 cubits on the two sides and the 10 cubits of the dwelling. The entrance to the Holy Place, however, stood right in the middle of the court, because it had 50 cubits out front to the outermost veil, just as the entrance to the courtyard also lay directly opposite it, also toward the east.*

*v. 14. 15. Fifteen cubits - on this and that side of the gate) These together make 30 cubits, and 50 cubits was the entire width. Thus, 20 cubits remained for the gate itself, as mentioned in verse 18.*

*v. 16. The curtains, whose name in Hebrew comes from "engraving," <note>The author likely refers to the mesh-like texture of the fabric.</note> are said by the Hebrews to have been transparent like a net and full of holes everywhere, so that while one could not enter the courtyard through them, one could nevertheless see everything that happened inside.*

*Of fine-linen yarn) One may not unreasonably understand this to signify the sincerity and purity of life: which is to be practiced both outwardly in social interactions and preserved inwardly in intention or purpose, and in such a sense, it must be "twisted."*

*...through the priestly service of the Levites and through a constant attachment to and dependence on God, and a turning away from everything in which God is not found. If we wish to possess a free life in Christ, we must die to ourselves hourly in the humiliation of Christ, and strengthen our spirit above the heights of the earth through the exaltation or ascension of Christ. For through this very act, He has regained for us our freedom in God.*

<column-break/>

18. And the screen for the gate of the courtyard was of embroidered work, of sky-blue wool, and of purple wool, and of crimson wool, and of twisted fine-linen yarn: and twenty cubits was the length, and the height in the width was five cubits, alongside the curtains of the courtyard.

19. With their four pillars and their four bases of bronze: their hooks of silver, and their capitals overlaid, and their rods of silver.

20. And all the pegs <note>original: "Nägel"</note> of the dwelling and of the courtyard all around were of bronze.

21. These are the arrangements of the dwelling, namely the dwelling of the testimony, as they were arranged according to the command of Moses for the service of the Levites under the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest.

---

*v. 18. Of embroidered work) This was therefore equal to the veil of the Holy Place in terms of workmanship.*

*The Hebrews make a distinction between <term>חשב</term> <note>original: "Chosheb," meaning a skilled weaver</note> and <term>רוקם</term> <note>original: "Rokem," meaning an embroiderer</note>: the former being a fabric that has the same appearance on both sides, while the latter was embroidery work made with a needle, having a beautiful appearance on only one side. However, they do not seem to be correct in the latter point, that it was embroidered on only one side. For then the veil of the Holy Place would have looked poor on the other side, whether it hung toward the inside or the outside. One can, however, also embroider with a needle using cross-stitches so that it produces the same figures on both sides.*

*Five cubits) That was the height of the curtains on all sides of this courtyard, and the pillars from which they hung were also that high.*

*All outward manners, by which virtues are brought to light, are performed and practiced through the 5 senses.*

*v. 20. Pegs) These were small iron <note>The text says "eiserne" (iron) here, though the verse says bronze ("Ertz").</note> stakes used to fasten the curtains of the courtyard.*

*v. 21. Ithamar was appointed to receive the voluntary offerings of the children of Israel and then distribute them to the craftsmen.*

*This image and this name indicate something within us that takes in and receives gifts and presents—indeed, in which the greatest goods and spiritual riches gather, from which the tabernacle of God may and should be built. This is the freedom of the spirit, which is like a flat and open hand, always ready only to give away and keeping nothing for itself; as it is generated from the most abundant freedom of God. Therefore, God has made it His treasurer, so that it might distribute what is necessary for the practice of all virtuous and godly undertakings and for the working out of salvation to each and every power working and building on this tabernacle.*

*This freedom we will obtain if we deny ourselves and surrender ourselves to God voluntarily and with joy in all things, even those that are contrary to us and fall heavily upon the spirit or nature. Through this, we will obtain and carry away the victory over sin and all our enemies, and taste the fruits of the same in the sweetest peace of the soul. But this is not attained otherwise than*

# The Second Book of Moses. Ch. XXXVIII.

<columns>

22. And Bezalel / the son of Uri / the son of Hur / of the tribe of Judah / made all that the LORD had commanded Moses;
23. And with him Oholiab / the son of Ahisamach / of the tribe of Dan / a master craftsman and artist / and one who embroidered with sky-blue wool / and with purple wool / and with crimson wool / and with fine linen yarn. 24.

---

This text reveals to us not only the birth and lineage / but also the significance of those who were to build a tabernacle for God, both in symbolic form and in actual deed and truth.

<margin>ch. 31:2, 6; ch. 35:30, 34.</margin>
For certainly it is not to be looked upon lightly / but is indeed noteworthy / that the two most prominent artists and master builders / whom the Lord called by name / are now described for a third time / so extensively according to their lineage and origin: of which it is proper to speak and note more / than the constraints of space allowed in the first instance. Indeed, it is extremely remarkable that the first and most prominent is named

**Bezalel)** Not without a singular providence and promise of **God**. For

What does Bezalel actually mean? Philo <note>original: "(a) L. 2. leg. allegor. p. 68." refers to Philo of Alexandria's 'Allegorical Interpretation.'</note> has perhaps hit upon it best and expressed it most elegantly / so that it accords wonderfully with the work and the truth / when he said in brief words / that it means as much as / **God in the shadow**. For what else does one perceive in the Tabernacle and in all its vessels / as well as in the entire Levitical service / but **God in the shadow** / since the eternal **Son of God** was depicted through all kinds of images and shadows? Thus all the works of Bezalel are pure depictions of **God in the shadow**.

We find the best essence of this within ourselves / when an obedient will is born through the grace of **God** / which **God** chooses for the leading of a righteous and virtuous life / and in which He wishes to reign both in this life and in the next for all eternity. But in the moment / when the will strengthens and fixes itself in that purpose / in that same moment **God** pours His light into the innermost part of the spirit / with which light the spirit is then united. And from this union grace is then born / which from itself begets the obedient will / as the Bezalel or **Shadow of God**.

The shadow, however, represents the likeness or image of that thing / from which it is made / when the object stands correctly between the sun's light and its shadow / and is not transparent / but solid. For in the air / in fire and in water / no shadow can be caught / nor sufficiently recognized. If, therefore, a shadow is to arise and be produced / then three pieces must come together: the light / the medium / and the object that is opposed to the light. The light now / which makes the **shadow of God** / is **Christ Jesus** according to His divinity: the medium / which makes the shadow / is His most worthy humanity / along with the fullness of His graces: and finally the object / which itself becomes a shadow / is our will; provided it is not transparent like air through pride / nor burning like fire through disordered love / nor inconstant like flowing water through the pursuit of the lusts of the flesh: but / if it is fixed and constant with willing and free obedience turned toward the light / then through such a submissive and obedient will it becomes Bezalel. For just as it is ordered in nature / that the shadow imitates the movements of the body / from which it is made / and follows everywhere the body goes: so should we also be God's shadow through an obedient will / and imitate and follow the humanity of Christ in all His teachings or instructions. Then one of those qualities will be expressed by us / which is signified by the name Bezalel / and accompanied by the other / according to which he means as much as a divine shelter. Ps. 91:1. For when the obedient will submits itself to the divine governance / which happens through true serenity and the denial of oneself / then it passes out of itself into **God** / where it is indeed sheltered enough. Such a person speaks with a courageous heart: **The Lord is my light and salvation!** etc. And therefore (see how elegantly it unfolds!) such a person is a

**Son of Uri)** That means as much as "my light" or "my fire." The love of **God** is a fire and light / and this

<note>(a) Book 2 of Allegorical Interpretations, page 68.</note>

<column-break/>

fire and light is the source and origin of every birth of grace.

**God** is a light / in which all things live / and through which everything is created. Now when our spirit turns and holds itself to this light / we become connected and united with it / and are born again from it above nature into grace: and in us, through this very process, His light is brought forth / which is the Son of **God** himself.

**God** is a fire of love / which is kindled between the Father and Son from all eternity and burns unto all eternity. This fire is called the Holy Spirit / and is the most free love of God / which together with the eternal light is the cause both of our creation according to nature / and our restoration according to grace / as well as our calling and invitation to glory. This fire of love / when it is grasped and received by the human mind / becomes in the same a certain foundation and a root of all virtues. And just as fire in nature also has light; although the same is so subtle / that it may not be seen / except in another material <note>original: "(a) Thom. de Aquin. l. de nat. lum. Ignis per se non lucet, sed cum adjungitur alteri corpori." translates to: Thomas Aquinas in his book 'On the Nature of Light': Fire does not shine by itself, but when it is joined to another body.</note>: so also a willing soul receives fire and light together from the generosity of **God** through the **Holy Spirit** as a free gift of grace / and thus recognizes in experience / that her father is named Uri. And that is exactly what she says: You are my light / in the ground of the understanding or the intellectual power; my fire in the ground of the will or the loving power. And because the original source of the Godhead in itself / also considered outside of all time and creaturely existence / is in its nature fire and light; so the grandfather or original father of the fire of the spirit and light of love / which is born in the understanding and will of man through grace / is also called nothing other than Ur / or / as it is expressed here /

**Hur)** For the letter [h] / which is nothing but an opening of the mouth / signifying a vehemence of the spirit / indicates only the great difference between the grace of the Old Testament and that which has appeared to us. As much power or grace as the Jews ever had / they still had to wait for the day of grace as if from afar / which is now present as a day of salvation. Therefore they had to sigh deeply and cry out for it. For the letter *h* <note>The author likely refers to the Hebrew letter 'He' or 'Chet,' interpreting it as a breathy sound of longing.</note> was set between them and **God**; which however is now on this day of grace annihilated and removed through the precious blood of our Savior **Jesus Christ**.

And therefore the spiritual Bezalel or **God**-obedient will is now also much more

**Of the tribe of Judah)** That is / one who praises and glorifies. For the same cannot do otherwise than exalt **God** with praise and thanks in all his works / because he is born of **God** / and inclines himself back into **God** with all his actions. Therefore he is also chosen by **God** as an artist and master builder / to build His tabernacle /

**And with him Oholiab)** That is / our will and understanding / as our two most prominent powers / when they obey the Spirit of **God**. For then we will be filled with all kinds of gifts of **God** / through which we are able to build Him a tabernacle within us consisting of the ornaments and jewelry of virtues.

And indeed there are also two qualities / in which all gifts of God are comprised and enclosed: namely the love of all **righteousness** / and the **knowledge** of all truth. Whoever feels perfect righteousness within / will also find himself driven to all virtues by the fire of love within / as a son of Uri. And whoever has the knowledge of all truth within / the same also feels his light / through whose wisdom the workings of love are also ordered.

Both of these pieces however are aimed for by **God** / and cannot be separated or sundered from one another / as they are, so to speak, two natural brothers begotten by one father / or as two streams springing from one source / which is clearly expressed by the word

**Ahisamach)** That is / a strengthener of my brother / or my brother's strength.

<meta>catchword: When</meta>

### Chapter XXXVIII. The Second Book of Moses.

24. All the gold / that was used for the work / in the entire work of the Sanctuary / that gold from the wave offering was twenty-nine talents / and seven hundred and thirty shekels according to the shekel of the Sanctuary. <note>The "wave offering" refers to items ritually dedicated to God by being "waved" before the altar.</note>

25. And the silver from those numbered of the congregation was one hundred talents / and one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels according to the shekel of the Sanctuary.

26. A half-shekel for every head / being half a shekel according to the shekel of the Sanctuary / for everyone who passed over to those numbered from twenty years old and upward / who were six hundred thousand and three thousand and five hundred and fifty men.

---

This orderly register teaches us / how those things intended for holy purposes / and also whatever else is provided for the needs of the poor / which is customarily called <term>ad pias causas</term> <note>Latin: "for pious causes" or charitable works</note> / should be managed very carefully and with all faithfulness: just as the Apostle notes / that the congregation at Philippi dealt with him in the same way regarding the sharing of contributions for his account of expenses and income; which he also accepts very well: Philippians 4:15. Indeed, when he collected the tax for others / he testifies / that he sees to it / that it proceeds honestly / not only before the Lord / but also before men. 2 Corinthians 8:21. Thus, in all such things dedicated to the honor of God, a very exact account must be kept: which also brings about the blessing of God.

v. 24. 29 talents and 730 shekels) A common gold shekel was half a *Loth* <note>A traditional unit of weight, about 1/32nd of a pound</note> of gold / and a holy gold shekel was one *Loth*.

Some (a) calculate the gold against silver in such a way / that it is worth 16 times as much / and 1 *Loth* of gold is worth 8 Reichsthaler <note>A standard silver coin used in the Holy Roman Empire</note>. According to this calculation, the 730 shekels made 5,840 Reichsthaler or 2,920 Ducats. One talent of gold would thus be 24,000 Reichsthaler or 12,000 Ducats. Therefore, 29 talents would be as much as six hundred thousand and 96,000 Reichsthaler or three hundred thousand and forty-eight thousand Ducats. Thus, the entire sum of the shekels makes approximately seven hundred thousand, one thousand eight hundred and forty Reichsthaler or <unclear>12</unclear>-hundred thousand, fifty thousand, nine hundred and twenty Ducats. Others (b) do not value the gold so high / but rather 12 times as expensive as silver / one *Loth* of gold for 12 *Loth* of silver / or 6 Reichsthaler, and so it would amount to 526,380 Reichsthaler or 263,190 Ducats.

v. 25. One hundred talents) Each talent is worth one and a half thousand Reichsthaler.

And 1,775 shekels) Together with those hundred, they make one hundred and fifty thousand, eight hundred and eighty-seven and a half Reichsthaler.

According to the shekel of the Sanctuary) For a holy shekel was 1 *Loth* of silver or half a Reichsthaler. A common shekel weighed only half as much. (c)

v. 26. A half-shekel) That is as much as one common whole shekel: for they were equal in value.

From --- 20 years --- and upward) Until the 50th year / as Josephus (d) adds.

Totaling 603,550) For every head a quarter-thaler <note>original: "Ortsthaler"</note>: the silver amounted to the sum mentioned in the previous verse.

Every man must pay his half-shekel / in the holiness of life / for redemption from a vain way of life. 1 Peter 1:15, 18. This holiness is at first only half-formed / when one has not long ago come out of Egypt.

<column-break/>

27. And the hundred talents of silver were used for the casting of the sockets of the Sanctuary and the sockets of the veil: one hundred sockets from one hundred talents / one talent for each socket.

28. But from the one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five shekels he made the hooks for the pillars / and overlaid their capitals / and furnished them with rods.

29. And the bronze from the wave offering was seventy talents / and two thousand and four hundred shekels. (a) ch. 35:24.

30. And from it he made the sockets for the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation / and the bronze altar and the bronze grating that belonged to it / and all the vessels of the altar.

31. Furthermore, the sockets for the courtyard all around / and the sockets for the gate of the courtyard / and all the pegs of the dwelling / and all the pegs of the courtyard all around. ch. 27:19. <margin>The</margin>

---

v. 27. Of the sockets of the Sanctuary) For the boards of the dwelling / of which there were 96.

Of the sockets of the veil) For the 4 innermost pillars / on which the innermost veil hung.

One talent) Which makes 3,000 shekels (a).

v. 28. The remaining 887 and a half Reichsthaler were used for the decoration of the pillars / which stood at the front of the entrance to the Holy Place and all around the courtyard.

v. 29. The copper, according to our pounds / where 32 *Loth* go to a pound, weighed approximately 6,637 pounds.

v. 30. From this were made the sockets of the 5 pillars at the entrance to the Holy Place / the altar of burnt offering along with its accessories / etc.

v. 31. All the pegs) Two kinds of copper stakes or pegs are expressly mentioned here / which were used not only for fastening the hangings of the courtyard / but also for fastening the dwelling.

They were driven into the earth / and the pillars and hangings were fastened to them with ropes / so that they would not be tossed about by the wind. Likewise, the outermost coverings of the dwelling were tied to them with ropes / so that no wind or storm could move them / much less the dwelling / from its place. Isaiah 33:20.

In closing this chapter and this page, one should note the distribution and division of the three types of metal according to the 3 parts of the Tabernacle. In the courtyard, everything was red with bronze: in the Holy Place, there was nothing but gold and silver / red and white; yet of another purified redness: and in the Holy of Holies, there was pure gold. Here lies the mystery of the Holy Trinity hidden. Through the red rod and discipline of the Father, we come to the light of the Son and his silver-colored innocence / and attain in and through him the gift of the Holy Spirit. Here is the three-fold path of the <term>Mysticorum</term> <note>Latin: "of the Mystics"</note>: purification / illumination / and union. Through faith / which struggles even unto blood / we are incorporated into Christ / and become partakers of his pure humanity / which is white and red: and through this, we penetrate into the pure Godhead.

### The Second Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIX.

## Chapter XXXIX.

->The making of the holy garments, and a brief account of all the pieces of the Sanctuary.<-

<margin>(a) ch. 39/41.</margin>
1. And from the sky-blue wool, and the purple wool, and the crimson wool, they made the garments of service for serving in the Sanctuary (a); and they made the holy garments that were for Aaron, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

<margin>v. 2. The outer garment <note>original: "Leibrock"</note> was the outermost upper garment, and, as can be seen from the following</margin>
2. And he made the ephod <note>The "Leibrock" or ephod was a waistcoat-like vestment worn by the High Priest.</note> of gold, of sky-blue wool, and purple wool, and crimson wool, and twisted fine linen yarn.

<margin>v. 3. It was made of golden wire, beautiful white Egyptian linen, purple, scarlet, and sky-blue threads, woven with all kinds of floral patterns.</margin>
<margin>Through artistic work) This means it was the same on both sides. Indeed, the Hebrew scholars write that it was 28-stranded; not that 28 threads were twisted into one, but rather: one wire of gold was twisted with six blue threads, one with six purple ones, one with six scarlet ones, and one with six linen ones, which together make 28.</margin>
3. And they beat the gold plates thin, so that they could be cut into threads to be worked in among the sky-blue wool, and among the purple wool, and among the crimson wool, and among the fine linen yarn through artistic work.

<margin>v. 4. It was assembled from two distinct pieces, the front and the back. These two pieces were not woven together, but each stood on its own. They were joined at both sides at the top of the shoulder-blades or shoulders by two golden clasps, which were undoubtedly as long as the shoulders were wide.</margin>
4. They made shoulder-pieces for it, which joined together: at its two ends it was joined together.

<margin>v. 5. From one of these pieces, either the front or the back, there emerged as it were two sleeves or two belts of the same material and woven into the same fabric, with which the High Priest could gird himself, and bind the two pieces—fastened at the shoulders and hanging down front and back—firmly to the body; these belts he wound around his body, tied in a knot in the front, and let the ends hang down.</margin>
5. And its artistic belt that was upon it was attached to it according to the same workmanship; of gold, sky-blue wool, and purple wool, and crimson wool, and twisted fine linen yarn: as the Lord had commanded Moses.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 6. In each clasp, on each shoulder, was an excellent sardonyx, upon which the names of the 12 tribes of Israel were engraved.</margin>
6. And they made the onyx stones, which were surrounded with golden settings <note>original: "Aeuglein," literally "little eyes," referring to the filigree or bezel of the setting</note> all around, engraved as one engraves a seal, with the names of the sons of Israel.

<margin>v. 7. Stones of memorial) Josephus (a) writes that when they reconciled with God through sacrifice, the stone that was on the right shoulder gave off such a brilliance and ray, contrary to its nature, that one could not look upon it even from a distance without wonder. However, for 200 years from the time he wrote this, they had no longer given off any brilliance, because of the people's sin. <margin>(a) Book 3, Antiquities, ch. 9.</margin></margin>
7. And he set them on the shoulder-pieces of the ephod, to be stones of memorial for the children of Israel, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

<margin>v. 8. The breastplate <note>original: "Brust-Schildlein"</note> was an exceedingly precious and priceless jewel, which was the High Priest's highest ornament.</margin>
8. And he made the breastplate of artistic work, according to the workmanship of the ephod, of gold, sky-blue wool, and purple wool, and crimson wool, and twisted fine linen yarn.

<margin>v. 9. Double) So that it would not be torn by the weight of the precious stones.</margin>
9. It was square; and they made the breastplate double: a span was its length, and a span its width, and double. <note>A span is approximately 9 inches, the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the pinky.</note>

11. And the second row was an emerald, a sapphire, and a diamond.

12. And the third row was a hyacinth, an agate, and an amethyst.

<margin>v. 14. Twelve with their names — according to the 12 tribes) So that the priest might draw through them the influences of the 12 stones of the upper world. For there must be a correspondence with one another, and one must draw the other.</margin>

### Chap. XXXIX. The II. Book of Moses. 435

v. 18. With the other end, they were fastened into the clasps on the shoulders, where there was also a ring.
v. 19. At the two bottom corners of the breastplate, there were again two rings on the inside.
v. 20. And on the ephod above the sash there were another two, which had to match those and meet one another.
v. 21. Through these two sets of opposing rings, it was then tied at the bottom with beautiful blue ribbons.
v. 22. The robe was long, yet presumably not so long that it completely covered the under-tunic, but may have reached perhaps to the shins.
v. 23. At the top of the neck was a hole so that the High Priest could put his head through, and around the hole a border was woven.

-> The <-

> In the record of all the pieces of the Sanctuary, a precise account of each is again recorded just as they were manufactured: which should remind us how we ought always to conduct a precise examination within ourselves, whether we find all these goods of grace within us; that we might apply ourselves to godliness and a virtuous life: so that the peace of God may be revealed in our spirit; and then, in our souls, the strengthening of the same to walk in the ways of the Lord, the enlightenment from heavenly truths, the spirit of prayer; the mortification of our lusts and desires, the purification from all works of the flesh, the separation from all common social intercourse with people of the world, in order to keep ourselves strictly within the prescribed boundaries of a true, righteous being, and not to wander through any unseemly freedom: so that we might be found worthy of the previously described priestly adornment. Where we find this in ourselves, then we are made rich in Christ in all things, in all doctrine and all knowledge; and the preaching of Christ has become powerful in us: And thus we have no lack of any gift of grace, and wait only for the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ; 1 Corinthians 1:5, 6, 7. Then we shall also be found worthy of the blessing from our faithful High Priest, just as Moses here blessed the congregation and the workers for their willingness and diligence, wishing upon them the rich grace of God; and we now also receive the blessing with all kinds of spiritual blessings in heavenly goods through Christ, Ephesians 1:3, that we may be translated with Him into the heavenly being. Ephesians 2:6.

<header>Chap. XL. The Second Book of Moses.</header>

# Chapter XL.

->The Setting Up of the Dwelling and the Covering of the Cloud.<-

---

**And** the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
2. On the first day of the first month—namely, on the first of the month—you shall set up the dwelling, the Tent of Meeting.
3. And you shall place therein the Ark of the Testimony, and you shall cover the Ark with the veil.

Here, the setting up of the Tabernacle is again expressly ordained by GOD, specifically designating the time when it should occur, so that nothing might happen by one’s own will, but everything according to the prescription of GOD.
And indeed, one can observe from this timing how Josephus’s account <note>Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian whose works provide extra-biblical details on temple rituals and history.</note> may be quite correct: that they worked for exactly seven months on this artistic construction and the rest of the preparation for the service of God. For in the third month, the giving of the Law was announced. <margin>Ch. 19:1</margin> They had to prepare themselves for three days. <margin>v. 11</margin> Moses was on the mountain for forty days the first time: <margin>Ch. 24:18</margin> and forty days the second time. <margin>Ch. 34:20</margin> And thus the first five months of the first year came to an end.
One can observe from this the zeal in this work, as they were able to bring such an artistic masterpiece to completion in so short a time.
Furthermore, which is also remarkable: just as the Tabernacle was completed in 7 months, so was the Temple of Solomon completed in 7 years. <margin>1 Kings 6:38</margin>
v. 2. *On the first of the month)* Nisan, which most often coincides with our March.
*Set up the dwelling)* O, that it might also come so far with us, and the whole person be prepared for the divine indwelling! But for this, a total transfiguration of our humanity is required, whereby all that is old passes away. The earthly house of this present tent, which man set up through his fall into corruption, must first be melted down if the true divine building—which is not made with hands according to the present form of fallen nature, but is eternal and incorruptible according to heavenly qualities—is to be brought to light. And before this true tent, which the Lord Himself sets up and not man, stands erected in us in such a way that none of its foundation pillars may ever be moved again, we have far less hope or expectation of a saving Presence (which filled the Tabernacle), or that the Deity will or may have its permanent residence and full dwelling in our spirits, in our souls, and in our bodies, for their perfect salvation; this reaches its goal in a truly enjoyable vision of the Triune Majesty, which overshadows and fills the whole person.
So let everyone strive even today that his house be well-ordered, and that a Tabernacle be prepared and set up for Him in us according to GOD’s mind and will, not according to our own choice. And because we have one who is even greater than Moses, who was only a servant in the house of GOD, <margin>Hebr. 3:2, 3, 5, 6</margin>—our Lord Jesus Christ, however, is a carpenter’s son <note>original: "Zimmermanns Sohn"</note> and understands the business of building well, and is well-acquainted with the pattern and original of this tent—let us only surrender the matter and ourselves to Him, so that He may rule and act in us and carry out the work for which He is ordained. Thus our building will be grounded in love and set up as a mutual dwelling, wherein God will remain in us and we in Him eternally. <margin>John 14:23, 1 John 4:16</margin>
v. 3. *That the Lord commanded the veil to be hung before the Most Holy)* this reminds us that what happens in our spirit is for the most part hidden even from ourselves, that our life is hidden with Christ in God. <margin>Col. 3:3</margin>
The longing and the kindling of a good fragrance through the fire of love then constitutes the most noble business.

<column-break/>

4. And you shall bring in the table and arrange its setting; and you shall bring in the lampstand and light its lamps.
5. And you shall set the golden altar (a) for incense before the Ark of the Testimony, and hang the screen in the door of the dwelling. <margin>(a) Ch. 30:8</margin> 6.

Thus, we are also given to understand by the screen before the dwelling—namely, that which covers the Holy Place—how we must also very carefully guard the inner gifts of knowledge, comfort, and prayer, so as not to reveal them before everyone, but only before believers for their edification, who are priests with us and also appear in the Holy Place. And this is also the hidden person of the heart in the incorruptible essence of a gentle and quiet spirit. <margin>1 Pet. 3:4</margin>
Nevertheless, the outward side of this curtain or screen must also stand open before everyone, as much as can and should meet the eye, and our light must shine before men, for the conviction and winning over of everyone, through the remembrance of love and a sincere, blameless walk.
But even if we led such an innocent and holy life, and had such great wisdom that we could instruct all people with words and examples, humility and lowliness must still cover all of this, and we have no reason to become proud or puffed up when GOD makes His goodness and His name known through whomever He wills: because all sound doctrine and virtues come from GOD alone.
This was the reason that during rainy and stormy weather, a coarse and simple covering (a) was hung on the outside of the Tabernacle: not for the sake of the people, so that they might perhaps not see the adornment and beauty of the Tabernacle; but for the sake of the Tabernacle, so that its beauty would not be splashed or stained with impurity. Just so, a truly enlightened person will gladly instruct every eager learner with words and deeds; but he will always despise himself in his own eyes while doing so: and thus he will repel and overcome every attack of pride. And indeed—
The fact that this covering was also hung up at night signifies that we should show nothing but humility even to those who are like the dark night, cold and dark because of their malice.
v. 5. *Set before the Ark of the Testimony)* This is not to be understood as if the Altar of Incense should stand inside the Most Holy Place before the Ark, but rather in the Holy Place, and it is said to distinguish it from the table and lampstand. For these two pieces did not stand in the Holy Place directly before the Ark, or straight across from the Ark outside the veil; but rather to the side, the table toward the "midnight" <note>original: "Mitternacht," an archaic term for North</note> and the lampstand toward "midday" <note>original: "Mittag," an archaic term for South</note>. But the Altar of Incense was to stand directly against the Ark or before the Ark, in the middle between the table and the lampstand; not to the side like the table and lampstand; but in the Holy Place, not in the Most Holy Place. For that is described in the preceding 3rd verse and also covered, or the veil already drawn; in these two verses, however, the Holy Place is included.
Nevertheless, we should stand with our hearts near the Most Holy Place to offer our prayers to our GOD. For we have holy hands to lift up, and therefore we must not linger in nasty sins, but must already be free and clear of them. Therefore, the Altar of Incense represents the life of the righteous and perfect, who have their station, as it were, in the vicinity of the divine oracle <note>referring to the place where God speaks from between the cherubim</note>, who leave behind lower pleasures and are solely and uniquely concerned with the entrance into the kingdom of heaven. For this reason, no flesh was allowed to be sacrificed on this altar, but only incense was to be lit: because the works of the flesh and fleshly lusts have little to do in such a state, and the prayer of the spirit in the presentation of the heavenly—

<note>v. 6. **Before the door**—In the open air; partly for the sake of cleanliness, partly because of the danger [of fire], and partly so they would not be like the heathens. Furthermore, the animal sacrifices were to take place in the presence and sight of the whole people as a sign and testimony that Jesus Christ—who is the door for the sheep and the shepherd, as well as the altar, sacrifice, and High Priest, indeed all in all—would shed His blood and offer Himself up not in a corner, but publicly before the eyes of all people.</note>

<note>v. 7. **Between the tent and the altar**—Facing the morning toward the south, or Southeast. 2 Chronicles 4:10.</note>

<note>v. 8. **All around**—Thus the Tabernacle stood in the middle of the courtyard and was surrounded by it: just as the inner man is surrounded by the outer man.</note>

<note>v. 9–11. **Anoint the dwelling**—Moses did not smear the entire dwelling with the holy oil, nor the entire Altar of Burnt Offering, nor the Laver, nor any other vessel completely over and over (for the small amount of oil made would not have sufficed for that). Rather, Moses dipped his finger into this oil and drew upon the dwelling and all the vessels the shape of a Greek Chi (Χ) <note>original: "griechischen Χ"</note>, in order to point toward Jesus the Crucified and the Anointed.</note>

<note>v. 12. 13. The anointing of the High Priest also took place between the eyebrows.</note>

<note>v. 14. 15. **And his sons... anoint as their father**—After this time, only the High Priest was anointed at his consecration, but the common priests were not. And in the second temple, even the High Priest was consecrated without anointing.</note>

---

<note>Now everything is set up by Moses in the specified time according to the order, just as it was presented in this same order on six different occasions: (1) When GOD commanded it to be made: Chapters 25, 26, 27, and 28. (2) When Moses presented it to the whole congregation and commanded the workers to make it: Chapter 35, v. 4 etc. (3) When the workers completed everything in that order: Chapters 36, 37, 38, 39, up to v. 31. (4) When the workers delivered the finished pieces so orderly to Moses: Chapter 39:32–42. (5) When GOD commanded this Tabernacle to be set up orderly according to all its parts: Chapter 40, up to v. 16. And finally (6) when Moses sets everything up in order according to GOD's command: v. 17–33. So this six-fold account of all the works of this Tabernacle can remind us of the six days of the creation of the world, when everything was created for the sake of man, so that this might become the new heaven and the new earth—and thus the true essential sanctuary in which GOD wished to be glorified for all eternity, when all outward sanctuaries, such as the Tabernacle and Temple, and even the world in its present form, must be destroyed and thus cease. See 1 Corinthians 6:19; Hebrews 3:2–6; 12:26–28.</note>

<note>v. 17. As soon as the new Church-Year began, promptly on the first day of the first month, the start was made here in a suitable place that had been chosen by Moses for this purpose.</note>

<note>v. 18. First, the 96 silver bases <note>term: silver bases <gloss>silberne Füsse</gloss>; the heavy foundations for the Tabernacle walls</note> were placed on the earth next to one another on the south, west, and north sides; likewise the 4 silver bases where the Most Holy Place was to begin; as well as in the front, where the Holy Place was to begin, the 5 copper bases. There, without doubt, the copper stakes were also driven into the ground here and there, to which the coverings were fastened.</note>

<note>Into the 96 silver bases, the 48 large boards were sunk, each board with its two bottom tenons into its 2 silver bases. Whereupon the bars were immediately pushed all around into their gold rings fastened to the boards, as well as the middle bar through the boards, so that the boards could hold together and make 3 walls.</note>

<note>Next, the 4 pillars between the Most Holy Place and the Holy Place, and the 5 pillars at the entrance to the Holy Place, were also sunk into their bases and set up.</note>

<note>v. 19. When that was done, first the two colorful coverings <note>referring to the embroidered linen</note> were stretched over the dwelling, and the interior of the dwelling was covered above. Over this colorful covering, the goat-hair covering was spread, and over the goat-hair covering, the two coverings of skins—the bottom one of reddened [rams' skins], the topmost of bluish [badger/porpoise skins]—which were undoubtedly immediately fastened to the copper stakes.</note>

v. 31. 32. From which—with the water drawn out from the spouts—the High Priest and other priests had to wash their hands and feet whenever they wished to perform their office.

If any man neglected this and performed his office with unwashed hands or feet, his service was void, and he had deserved death before God. <note>(a) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Law*, no. 106.</note>

And because the heathens later imitated the Jews in this, the proverb "to do something with unwashed hands or feet" <note>An idiom meaning to approach a task without proper preparation or reverence.</note> arose from this.

v. 33. Finally, this space was also enclosed; the 56 copper bases were set around, and undoubtedly the copper stakes were driven in, the 56 pillars lowered into the bases, and the hangings fastened all around the pillars, and everything made firm with the copper stakes; also, finally, at the front by the entrance to the Courtyard, the beautiful cloth of the third Veil was hung up.

Thus Moses finished the work. This completion of the Sanctuary or the **Sanctification** is also emphasized and recommended to us. 2 Cor. 7:1. For

God wants to dwell in us as in His tent, in deed and in truth; which was the intention of all these images.

Let each person then earnestly and diligently examine themselves to see if they find, feel, and experience within themselves everything that belongs to this Tent: And if he does not find it in himself, or feels that it is otherwise disposed in him, let him be assured that he is a dwelling for unclean spirits rather than for God.

Moses here serves as a **figure of Jesus Christ**, our predecessor in the new Christian law, who leads all images and figures into the eternal truth and completes them therein. He has, by the command of His heavenly Father, built a spiritual Tent, namely the **holy congregation** <note>The Church.</note>, upon the rock of His name; therefore it shall and must endure eternally.

This Church consists of all the godly whom the Holy Spirit calls and gathers, unites and binds, who are all held together under one law of harmonious and brotherly love in the eternal love of God. To the extent that each person’s life and standing in grace is excellent, so much more or less does he adorn the Tent of God.

Now this Pillar of Cloud—which appeared to them immediately after their departure from Egypt, in which the LORD guided them on their journeys (Chapter 13:21–22), and which afterwards descended upon the Tent, in which the LORD revealed Himself to Moses and gave him commands for the people of Israel (concerning this, see Chapters 33:7 etc. and 34:34–35)—this cloud has now moved from there and has permanently settled upon this Tabernacle of the Testimony in the wilderness.
By this, the great God Himself consecrated the new Tabernacle, as it were.

<margin>verse 35.</margin>
And indeed, it was so majestic that in the very beginning, the glory of the LORD filled the cloud in an extraordinary way—just as happened later with the Temple (1 Kings 8:11)—so that Moses was not able to enter.

<margin>verses 36, 37.</margin>
Meanwhile, it was their constant guide, and indicated how the LORD, with His protection and governance, will never depart from those who have become His true dwelling, but will always assist them with light and comfort (Matthew 28:20).

<margin>Josephus <note>original: "Josephus (a)" referring to the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus.</note> writes that a lovely dew trickled out of the Pillar of Cloud, as a testimony of the gracious presence of God.</margin>
But we observe here, at the very last, regarding this Pillar of Cloud and Fire:

### A Prefiguration of the Incarnation of Christ,
->and a sacrament, a visible sign of His presence.<-

1. Here was something physical and visible; and so it was at Christ's appearance in the flesh.
2. In it appeared the **Angel of the Covenant** <note>A term often used in older commentaries to refer to the pre-incarnate Christ.</note>; so also in the flesh.
3. These were unified and yet distinct: So also the Word and the assumed flesh.
4. This cloud, which the Israelites saw, was to them a sign of that which they did not see, and yet He who was present with His Spirit and power. God was in Christ, He in the Father, and the Father in Him, and to be recognized by the works and signs.
5. Out of this cloud, the Angel spoke to His Church, led His congregation, and performed miracles: And in the fullness of time, God speaks to us through His Son, who promised to be with His congregation every day until the end of the world.

<margin>(a) Book 3, Chapter 9 of the *Antiquities*.</margin>

<column-break/>

38. For the cloud of the LORD was upon the Dwelling by day, and there was fire on it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
<margin>(a) Numbers 14:14.</margin>

6. This Angel-Cloud led the people in the wilderness and was always powerful among them, even though the cloud was above their heads. For though it occasionally came down, it always rose up again. Thus Christ rules and protects us in the New Testament.
7. This cloud was like a pillar, which is a symbol of strength and bravery: And upon Christ rests the Spirit of power and strength.
8. By night it shone and was a Pillar of Fire: Thus the Lord Christ is a light in the darkness, and the light that shines into the darkness (John 1).
9. By day it was a Pillar of Cloud, which demonstrated its presence by giving shade against the heat of the sun (Psalm 121:6).
10. In it watched the Guardian of Israel while they slept (Psalm 121:4).

Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher.</note> writes that by day it gave off a brilliance almost like the sun, and by night it had a fiery form.

Be without fear then, O soul! when you think it is dark within you. Think of the Pillar of Fire that guides God's believers on the path.

> Remain in hidden silence and waiting, so that the Spirit of Life Himself may lift you up and penetrate you in the hidden places, and kindle the sacrifice, so that it may be a pleasing aroma in the joyful Sabbath, which the Lord Himself wishes to celebrate within you.
> Wait in the hidden place and receive the anointing of the Holy Spirit rightly: then darkness shall be to you as the light, and your perceived gloom shall shine like the midday.
> And when the light of day shines for you in the cloud of pure love, then walk only in certainty without fear, and let the full day and light drive out all lies. Your love is light, in which no fear, darkness, or straying from the Holy One is to be found.
> Yet know and remember, that the heat you feel must not burn you; rather, it only softens the hard nature and melts it away, as it were, so that the elements of sin melt away before the glory of the coming LORD, who comes and shall come.

The Tabernacle is no sooner completed according to God's command than He comes immediately to fill it with His presence, and to give visible signs of His majesty there. This is to say that when our inner self is purified to the degree that God desires, He comes immediately into it to set up His dwelling therein, albeit still in the cloud—which is to say, under the darkness of faith <note>original: "Finsterniß des Glaubens," a mystical concept referring to believing without seeing.</note>.
But when this internal Tabernacle, or the center of the soul, is full of God Himself, then nothing else can enter there, not even the most holy things; for everything, as soon as it approaches God and is tasted, melts away without being able to recognize Him; but that which is contrary to Him remains outside entirely. For although this cloud is not God, yet God is in that cloud. Therefore, the inner sanctuary must be so empty <note>original: "ledig," meaning vacant or unattached to worldly things.</note> so that the Majesty of God may rest within it.

<meta>This page serves as the introduction to the Book of Leviticus (the Third Book of Moses). It establishes a thematic bridge from the conclusion of Exodus, where the Tabernacle was completed, to the start of the priestly service and the spiritual interpretation of the sacrificial laws.</meta>

# The Third Book of Moses

<image-desc>A large decorative headpiece consisting of four horizontal bands of intricate woodcut ornaments, including floral, foliate, and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

Though it is, according to its external composition, the smallest among the books of Moses, it is by no means the least in weight. Rather—if all were not to be considered of equal importance—it should be counted among the most distinguished, passing not only for its order but also for its content as the very center of the work.

Indeed, if one wished to see no further, or had no further to see, than the external letter—as it might easily be grasped by the natural man through mere reason and Jewish antiquities—then certainly no special nourishment for our soul-spirit is to be found therein. Much in the Scripture would then appear trivial rather than edifying, just as it is regarded by the wisdom of this world and its followers.

But the foolishness of God is and remains wise against all the pompous wisdom of the flesh, which before God is nothing but wretched folly when measured according to the <term>cubit<note>original: "Ehle"; an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, used here to suggest God’s precise standards.</note></term> and weight of the sanctuary.

In ancient times, when the Church was still weak and in its childhood years, this hidden wisdom—which seems foolish to the world and to those wise in their own eyes—sought to treat them as children. It presented them with all kinds of images to lead them into the sense and essence of the Spirit. It gave them good, hearty nuts with which they could either play or eat, but they first had to learn to bite open the shells before they could reach the kernel.

This is the calling of us all, as well as the Jews and Hebrews, among whom this third book of Moses derives its name from its first opening word <note>original: "Vayikra," meaning "And He called."</note> concerning the glorious and grace-filled calling of man, which had not expressed itself so since the beginning of the world. Among the Greeks and Latins, however, it has its name <note>Leviticus</note> from the tribe of Levi, because of the matters it mostly treats; therefore, it is also called among the Hebrews "the Law of the Priests."

The connection with the preceding book is clear. For what follows more closely in order, since at its end the Tabernacle stands upright, than that the service should now take place within it? Just as this third book of Moses is joined with the second, as that one was with the first, by the little word **And**.

Everything contained in this book was prescribed in one month—namely the first month <term>Nisan<note>The first month of the Hebrew ecclesiastical year, occurring in March–April.</note></term>, of the second year after the departure from Egypt—as is shown by comparing the beginning and end of this book with the last chapter of the preceding and the beginning of the following fourth book.

This consists first of the various sacrifices, of which especially the first seven chapters are full through and through. The Epistle to the Hebrews, however, teaches the purpose and aim most gloriously: which is primarily Christ’s unique and eternally valid sacrifice of atonement, and through this, our purification and holiness. And just as the diligence to strive for this with all earnestness is recommended to us throughout, if we will only pay attention; so we shall also be able to perceive without much trouble how secret theology is perfectly presented to us in this book in the threefold path of salvation, as it is directed by the <term>mystics<note>original: "Mysticis"; refers to spiritual teachers who emphasize the internal stages of the soul’s journey: purification, illumination, and union.</note></term>. For what else does the slaughtering of the sacrifices and the consuming of the same indicate than the work of purification through the steady fire (Chapter 6), which must burn out everything within us?

Where you now let yourself be found faithful in this work, you will learn to recognize through experience how the light arises from this fire, and how you are made fit for true priestly service through the path of illumination or initiation—which in the earliest writings were taken as one and the same—of which the 8th and 9th chapters here treat.

In the meantime, however, purification is not yet brought to an end; rather, it must always be continued simultaneously. And therefore, many chapters follow—namely from the 11th to the 23rd—which partly discover our uncleanness to us, and partly drive us toward purification. In the midst of these, they also point to the right means: the blood of Jesus Christ the Mediator on the Great Day of Atonement. Overall, they mean to say: *Let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God!* (2 Corinthians 7:1).

->❦ ❦ ❦<-

Just as the union with God—and thus the state of the true **Levites**, who derive their name from "clinging" or "adhering" (1 Cor. 6:17)—follows naturally from such proven faithfulness, so too does there follow an eternal feast and celebration, presented under various forms and names in chapter 23. The oil and the anointing of the Spirit do not diminish but increase; and the Bread of Life constantly offers itself as nourishment, strength, and refreshment to be enjoyed (chapter 24). And with that, we have the pleasant **Jubilee Year** <note>In the Old Testament, the Jubilee Year occurred every fifty years; it was a time when debts were forgiven, slaves were freed, and land was returned to its original owners. Here, it symbolizes spiritual liberation.</note> of the Lord (chapter 25).

Choose for yourself now what you will: blessing or curse. For that is set before you in chapter 26. Obedience will fare well. But in your disobedience, look at the reflection of yourself in the two specific judgments in chapters 10 and 24, and take note of God’s earnestness against all **strange fire** <note>A reference to Nadab and Abihu, who were consumed by fire for offering "unauthorized fire" before God (Leviticus 10).</note> of devotion, of the altar, and of all worship—and against all profanation of the divine name!

Therefore, do not neglect to fulfill your vows! (chapter 27).

Let us then pray to God that He may open our eyes to see the wonders in His Law. Thus, in what follows, we shall recognize how much that is glorious is hidden in this book; for certainly, not the slightest detail of all these outward, mostly ceremonial things could have been prescribed to Moses by **Christ the Lawgiver** without having a mystery behind it, even if much of it remains unknown and locked away from us until the time of revelation. And

This is the soul of the entire matter: what is prefigured beneath it. Without this knowledge, everything is certainly meager. But when the internal sense is perceived, the words first receive their proper weight and gladden the heart.

This was also the opinion of **Hesychius**, a pupil of **Gregory of Nazianzus** <note>Gregory of Nazianzus was a 4th-century Archbishop and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" central to early Christian theology.</note> who lived in the 4th century after Christ, when he wrote in the preface to this book: "The present ordinance would seem to me entirely contemptible—indeed, to speak my mind, it would seem a useless and perhaps even harmful letter—if it were robbed of its spiritual understanding and secret interpretation. For certainly, there would be much to find fault with in the literal letter if one did not have recourse to a higher understanding, and could not seek and find satisfaction for the letter therein."

Just as in the last days the Word of God came forth into this world from Mary, clothed in flesh, and one thing was visible on Him externally, while another could be perceived by an opened understanding—for the sight of His flesh stood open to all, but the knowledge of His Divinity was given to few and only to chosen souls—so it is when God's Word is revealed to men through the prophets or the Lawgiver: it does not happen without suitable clothing and coverings. For as it covered itself there with flesh, so here it covers itself with the veil of the letter. Thus, the letter may indeed be looked upon like the flesh, but the internal, hidden meaning, like the Divinity, does not stand open to everyone; yet it is certainly to be sensed and is recognized by a spiritual eye. Such is the nature of this Third Book of Moses, in which the customs and varieties of sacrifices, along with the services and duties of the priests, are described to us. Both the unworthy and the worthy may look upon or hear this according to the letter, which is, as it were, the flesh of the Word of God and the garment of His Divinity. But blessed are the eyes that see the Divine Spirit hidden beneath the veil of the letter; and blessed are those who, to

hear this, bring the pure ears of the inner man! For otherwise, they will clearly perceive only a killing letter <note>original: "tödtenden Buchstaben"; a reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6, "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life."</note> herein. (a)
