<header>Ch. I. The Third Book of Moses [Leviticus].</header>

# Chapter 1.
->The Voluntary Burnt Offerings.<-

AND the LORD called to Moses and spoke to him out of the tabernacle of the congregation, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If any man among you wishes to bring an offering to the LORD, you shall bring your offering of the livestock, even of the cattle or of the sheep.

The first book [Genesis] presented the Seed of the Woman <note>A reference to Genesis 3:15, traditionally interpreted by Christians as the first promise of a Savior.</note> who was to redeem and sanctify the sinner, through various promises; and the second book [Exodus] presented Him in the archetype of a sanctuary and the priesthood according to His benefits. Now, in this third book, the duties of faith and love belonging to that "Seed" as it is sanctified are described (Hebrews 2:11). This is done through various commandments, outward statutes, and ceremonies, and finally through civil laws, which were intended to keep them within the bounds of honor and discipline.

First, the primary duties—of faith, of love toward one's neighbor and toward God, and then of self-denial and repentance—are presented under the symbols of the Burnt, Grain, Peace, Sin, and Guilt offerings. They are presented in this order to show how all such duties flow solely from the power of the single sacrifice of the promised Seed, Jesus Christ, and could only be acceptable to God through Him. See Hebrews 10:5–18. There we can see how the sacrifices, gifts, burnt offerings, and sin offerings—which are the very types mentioned here (and the guilt offerings must also be understood under the latter)—were even then sanctified through the future sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ, and thus made acceptable to God for the forgiveness of sins; as is mentioned so many times here regarding the sacrifices (v. 3, 4, 9, 13, 17, etc.).

Conversely, this very sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ, through the most just duty of the fellowship of suffering and "dying with Him," actually directs faith toward the highly necessary sacrifice of the entire sinful life. This life must be continually brought to God as a burnt offering and be slaughtered and consumed in daily repentance as the "body of sin." For in this way, all outward sacrifices signified essential effects within us: namely, the burning and consuming of sin within us. And the more unpleasant this is to our old nature, the more earnestly both the Scriptures and the godly writers of antiquity have testified of it.

Indeed, as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD) known for his allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> also notes, it is expressed most thoughtfully at the very beginning here:

v. 2. **When a man**) Just as if someone other than a man could bring an offering! Yet, in the following passages, it says: "when a soul," etc.; then "when a priest," etc.; then "when the whole congregation," etc.; then "when a prince," etc. We must not think that such distinctions of persons happen without reason, or that something different is meant by the name "man" than by "soul," "priest," "congregation," "prince," etc. And since it would have been enough to say "when anyone," etc., as is done later, if there were nothing more to signify, we may best understand "man" in this general sense—placed first among those who wish to offer—as representing the whole human race, or the whole person. For God wants the whole person, and for that very reason, among the many types of sacrifices, the burnt offerings (or whole offerings) are placed first.

Since the LORD then promises a gracious acceptance in the Son of His good pleasure, let us all who confess His name be encouraged thereby to come willingly and bring our whole burnt offering—the daily killing of our sin—through the mediation of the High Priest. Thus we and our offerings will find acceptance in the Beloved, and God’s good pleasure will appear over us and within us.

<column-break/>

3. If his offering is a burnt offering of the cattle, he shall offer a male without blemish: he shall offer it at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, that it may be accepted for him before the face of the LORD.
4. And...

The burnt offering was the most excellent sacrifice, where everything—except the blood, parts of the entrails, and the animal's hide—went up in fire and was consumed to the honor of God. Therefore, the Greeks and Romans called it *holocaustum* <note>original: "holocauſtum" - meaning "burned whole."</note>, and the Hebrews called it <term>עולה</term> <note>original: "Olah" – meaning "that which ascends."</note>, an ascending or a going up, because everything ascends toward heaven in fire and smoke. For this reason, it is also called a "whole offering," which is entirely given over to the honor of God.

This burnt offering represents the duty of faith: how one should sacrifice oneself entirely—spirit, soul, and body—to God, and surrender in "yieldedness" <note>A translation of "Gelassenheit," a central term in German mysticism referring to the letting go of self-will to surrender to God.</note> to His holy will in all humility and patience. See 1 Thessalonians 5:23, 24. And thus one loves God with all the heart, with all the soul, with all the mind, and with all one’s strength (Matthew 22:37). And so one yields oneself to God with all one’s capacity, presenting one’s body and its members as a sacrifice that is living, holy, and pleasing to God (Romans 12:1). Just as here the cattle and sheep had to be entirely divided into pieces and burned—except for the hide, which the priest received (Chapter 7:8)—and the entrails and legs had to be washed first; so too must our innermost self and our outward conduct first be purified when we wish to surrender ourselves to God in true faith and love Him.

That the LORD chose cattle for this represents the industriousness and strength they demonstrate with their horns, showing how the person who wishes to surrender to God must be faithful and diligent in their calling and seek their strength for this in God; thus can he lift up his horn in God in the boldness of faith (Psalm 92:11).

It had to be "without blemish" [perfect]: so must believers strive for perfection, that they may be without spot or wrinkle and blameless (Ephesians 5:27), irreproachable (Philippians 2:15).

<margin>(a) Luke 15:23. About which Origen speaks in Homily 1 on Leviticus.</margin>
But who else is this young bull than the "fatted calf" (a), which the Father of Mercy slaughtered for his lost and found son who had squandered all his wealth? The first Adam lost the image of perfection through his disobedience and apostasy; but the Second Adam [Christ] is the "perfect male," the virginal man, who brings it back into life through his death.

And because Christ specifically was prefigured by this sacrifice (Hebrews 9:13, 14), the translators should not have avoided the word "perfect" everywhere, but should have interpreted it as a type of Christ and retained it here and elsewhere.

<margin>(b) Matthew 21:39. (c) Hebrews 13:12.</margin>
**At the door**) For there Christ stands and knocks, but is not easily let in. He came to His own, but His own did not receive Him, but rather thrust Him out (b) and slaughtered Him outside the camp (c).

**Accepted for him before the LORD**) Or, to obtain favor and grace for himself from the LORD.

The whole burnt offering, which was sacrificed to the glory of God, prefigured the "body of sin" that was to be destroyed; and that service was to be made acceptable through Jesus Christ and in the fellowship of His suffering, through whom we must offer up all our sacrifices for that reason (Hebrews 13:15).

Thus the service of God is depicted in the ceremonies of the Old Testament—especially in this mystical book—and is made alive in the New.

And...

### 4. And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the burnt offering; and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.

<margin>Deut. 12:27. 2 Chron. 29:22.</margin>
### 5. And the young bull shall be slaughtered before the face of the LORD; and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall bring the blood, and sprinkle the blood all around the altar that is before the door of the tabernacle of meeting.

v. 4. **Lay his hand upon)** From behind.
The hands had to be washed beforehand. (a)
**Question:** Who laid the hands on? **Answer:** Those who brought the offering, if they were men. If women brought an offering, they did not lay their hands on.
**Qu.:** On which animals were hands laid? **Ans.:** Only on the four-footed ones, not on the birds. (b)
**Qu.:** In all offerings? **Ans.:** Yes; except for the firstborn, the tithes, and the Passover lamb.
Whether only one or both hands were laid on is a matter of dispute, which should concern us all the less because the Scripture does not explicitly report it. Yet, in the Scripture, it almost everywhere mentions only one hand.
It may be of more importance to investigate what the laying on of hands signified.
**Bochartus** (c) <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667) was a renowned French Protestant biblical scholar and philologist.</note> maintains that he who laid on his hand meant to say, as it were: "Whatever I have sinned, let it be upon this animal's head!" That is: "May GOD demand from this animal the punishment I well deserve!" He proves from Herodotus and Plutarch that the heathens also cursed their sacrificial animals and wished all the misfortune that stood before the person onto the head of the animal. The Weimar Bible explains it the same way. This is also the opinion of some of the Hebrews. It is something, but not everything.
In part, as Origen’s thoughts suggest—according to the wonderful fullness of the prophetic word—it may have a view toward the fact that the people of the Law, under the leadership of those of the lineage of Aaron, would especially lay their hands upon Jesus.
Primarily, however, it may designate the work of faith, where the believer must confess himself to the Lord with his hand in all his doing and leaving, and thus lean upon Christ, who is the true burnt offering, who offered Himself entirely to GOD in pure love.
For although all members must suffer, die, and sacrifice themselves with Him, they must nevertheless receive all strength and support for this from the Head, and in His sacrifice, everything must be sanctified.
Thus, we ourselves—in the recognition and confession of our sins, and in the grasping of the merit of Jesus Christ—are the bull or calf presented for sacrifice, which then gives GOD a sweet aroma when we surrender ourselves to GOD entirely without exception and keep nothing back for ourselves. We must entirely strip off our old self and allow ourselves to be put forth quite naked and have the skin drawn off.
In the case of large animals, more than one priest was occupied in catching and sprinkling the blood.

v. 5. **To bring the blood)** At the catching of the blood, the priest's office in the sacrifice first began. (d)

(a) Philo, *On Victims*, p. 648.
(b) Selden, *On the Law of Nature and Nations*, Book 3, Ch. 4.
(c) *Hierozoïcon*, Part 1, Book 2, Ch. 33, p. 323.
(d) Ibid., Ch. 50, p. 577. Lightfoot, *Hebrew and Talmudical Exercitations on Luke 13:1*.

<margin>(a) Ch. 7:8.</margin>
### 6. And the skin shall be flayed from the burnt offering, and it shall be cut into its pieces.

### 7. And the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and lay the wood in order upon the fire:

### 8. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall lay the pieces—namely the head and the fat—in order upon the wood that is on the fire, which is upon the altar.

<margin>Ch. 2:12, 3:16. Exod. 29:18, 25, 41. Gen. 8:21.</margin>
### 9. But its entrails and its legs shall be washed with water; and the priest shall burn all of it on the altar, for a burnt offering and an offering made by fire, of a sweet aroma to the LORD.

v. 6. **The skin shall be flayed)** <note>original: "Man")</note> This was not done by the priests or Levites, as some claim. (a)
**Flay the skin and cut into pieces)** Dr. Majus (b) notes from Rabbi Solomon and Rabbi Bechai that the head was cut off first, and only after its cutting was the skin flayed. By which the fall of the creatures may have been foretold, and the separation of the same from their head, Jesus Christ.

v. 7. **Fire, Fire)** This is the work of the priestly lineage. From this the effect must arise, as with those there who said: "Did not our heart burn?" (c) <note>A reference to the disciples on the road to Emmaus in Luke 24:32.</note>

v. 8. **The priests shall lay the pieces... in order)** As the ancient Hebrews report, in later times 24 priests carried the members and pieces—one this piece, the other that—to the altar; and all such members, the head and the remaining parts, were laid over the wood in the same order as they had previously sat on the body of the bull.
It is certain that everything had to be arranged orderly and <term>nomimos</term> <note>original: *νομίμως* - lawfully or according to the rule.</note> or according to the Law; and that the members of Christ must also be in suffering with Christ, each in the order as and for what GOD ordained it. And through such suffering and the sacrifice of Christ, every member which was previously moved out of its right place through sin will be set back into its right place, as it was in the most beautiful order from the beginning, etc.
And thus, in the mystery of the sacrifices, many very great things are contained!

v. 9. **Entrails)** Heart, liver, lungs, and brain. (d)
**Shall be washed with water)** This was what the one who brought the sacrifice had to do in the preparation of the animals: He laid his hands on the animal, slaughtered it, flayed its skin, hewed it into pieces, and washed the entrails. He did nothing further. The rest was done by the priests alone. Namely:
They caught the blood in the basin, they sprinkled the blood, they prepared the wood and fire on the altar, they brought the sacrificial pieces to the altar, lifted them, salted them, and burned them.
**The priest shall)** Was carried to the altar by a particular priest in a particular bowl.
**Burn all of it)** All the sacrifices of the Law are prototypes of the internal sacrifice, just as the apostles themselves have witnessed (e). However, these are of many kinds: and the creature always keeps something back for itself, both in the one and the other; just as such was depicted in the sacrifices of the Law, in that a part of what was sacrificed to GOD was set aside for the priests and Levites. Of this kind are the sacrifices of all active and suffering states, indeed even hidden ones, from the beginning. The single state of the pure sacrifice, which was represented by the burnt offering, is the only one which keeps nothing left over, but burns everything, even that which was most necessary for the preservation of one's own life. And this very pure sacrifice constitutes the completion of the hidden state.

# Chapter I. The Third Book of Moses.

10. If his offering is of small cattle, from the sheep or from the goats, for a burnt offering; then he shall offer a male without blemish.
11. And it shall be slaughtered on the side of the altar toward the north <note>The original German uses "Mitternacht" (midnight) to mean North, a common archaic orientation</note> before the face of the LORD; and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall sprinkle its blood all around the altar.
12. And it shall be cut into its pieces, along with its head and its fat; and the priest shall lay them in order on the wood that lies on the fire that is on the altar.
13. But the entrails and the legs shall be washed with water, and the priest shall bring it all and burn it on the altar. This is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a sweet savor to the LORD.

---

The sheep represent meekness and patience, an image of which can be observed in them: Isaiah 53:7. These qualities—as found in the "meadow-land" <note>likely referring to the spiritual field of the Church</note>—must especially be found in the believers, as a true mark of the sheep of Christ's flock, of which He is the Good Shepherd. John 10:27. Compared with Matthew 11:29. See Psalm 100:3.

**v. 10. A male without blemish)** But not necessarily exactly one year old, as the old Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note> added, though this is found in neither the Hebrew nor the Greek texts.

**v. 11. Toward the north)** The question arises: why on this side? For GOD does and commands nothing without wisdom.
The North, which is dark and gloomy, is a symbol of death, to which this offering had to be surrendered. Also, this region is the coolest, and therefore most convenient for slaughtering. Finally, the "Type" <note>the symbolic shadow</note> had to agree with the "Antitype" <note>the spiritual fulfillment</note>. For so also was Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb, slaughtered and sacrificed on Mount Golgatha or Calvary, which lay to the north in relation to Zion and Jerusalem.

**Its blood)** The blood was stirred well by the priests with a stick or spoon so that it would not clot or become thick, as animal blood easily curdles. Because of this, the basins did not have a proper flat bottom but were pointed at the base, so that the priests could not set them down out of their hands. <margin>(a)</margin>

**Sprinkle all around)** This was usually done while walking around the altar.

**v. 12, 13.** For the rest, this offering was handled just like the cattle: and whatever is perhaps not mentioned here must be supplemented from the previous section; just as, conversely, one must see in this offering what was not mentioned in the previous one. Thus it has the same meaning: and so also with the goats, which must be an image of contentment; as they satisfy themselves with very little food, namely foliage and other small things. This is what believers also do; they must take no pleasure in dainty foods, as such things easily give birth to the "lust of the flesh" which is sinful and produces many other sins. See 1 Timothy 6:6. Hebrews 13:5.

<margin>(a) Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours* on John 19:43.</margin> <note>John Lightfoot (1602–1675) was an English churchman and Rabbinical scholar.</note>

<column-break/>

14. And if the burnt offering of his gift to the LORD be of birds, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves or of young pigeons. <margin>ch. 5:7.</margin>
15. And the priest shall bring it to the altar and pinch off its head, and burn it on the altar; and its blood shall be squeezed out against the wall of the altar.
16. And he shall take away its crop with its feathers, and cast it beside the altar toward the east, in the place of the ashes. <margin>ch. 6:10.</margin>
17. And he shall split it at its wings, but not divide it asunder: and the priest shall burn it on the altar, on the wood that is on the fire. This is a burnt offering, an offering made by fire, a sweet savor to the LORD.

---

**v. 14.** From the birds, GOD chose the doves to command believers toward chastity and simplicity, in which—along with the aforementioned virtues—one must please GOD alone and sacrifice oneself to Him.

**Of birds)** In this case, it did not strictly have to be a male.

**Bring his offering)** This was always accompanied by a grain and drink offering.

**v. 15. Burn it on the altar)** The head was salted atop the altar and thrown into the fire.
This requirement—that the head had to be pinched off with the [priest's] nails and so burned—shows how it is the specific nature of "simplicity" <note>meaning spiritual singleness of heart</note> that one must kill and stifle all self-will, breaking it off with force, as it were, and letting it be consumed in the fire of the love of God and neighbor.

**Against the wall of the altar)** In the Temple, this was above the red line, and in the Tabernacle, it was above the net or grate of the lower part.

**v. 16.** When one prepares a bird for eating, it is customary not only to pluck its feathers but also to remove the crop and the entrails and throw them away. This is exactly what the LORD wants us to understand when He instructs us how to sacrifice our burnt offering, which is a figure and depiction of our **mortification** <term>Mortification: the spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful desires and worldly attachments.</term>

The crop, which is filled with food, and the feathers, which are like the skin, had to be thrown on an ash-heap: so must believers surrender themselves to GOD without any worry about food, and all fleeting thoughts must always be cast off in the surrender to GOD. See Matthew 10:16. 2 Corinthians 11:3. Song of Solomon 6:9.

**Toward the east in the place of the ashes)** That is, toward the gate of the Tabernacle and Temple.

**Cast)** By which GOD wanted outer and inner impurity to be removed from His sanctuary; because holiness is the beauty of His house forever. Psalm 93:5.

**v. 17.** When men roast their food, they do not let it burn on the outside while remaining raw on the inside; (except for some who want to make their food look beautiful to the eye and have a "fair appearance in the flesh," and are accustomed to devouring it while still raw and bloody); rather, one is used to roasting meat until all the blood is roasted out of it. And if our sacrifice is to be "roasted" enough, the life-blood must be drained, along with all love, desire, pleasure, lust, and inclination toward sin. Hebrews 12:4.

**This is a burnt offering... a sweet savor to the LORD)** Thus, the LORD wanted no wild animals or birds of prey for a sacrifice. This shows that one cannot believe in GOD or please Him while remaining in a wild, unbroken, and fleshly nature.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter II.

# Chapter II.
->The Voluntary Grain Offerings.<-

And when a soul wishes to bring an offering of a grain offering <note>The German "Speis-Opffer" refers to non-animal offerings, usually consisting of flour or grain.</note> to the LORD, his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it and put frankincense upon it;

2. And he shall bring it to the sons of Aaron, the priests; and he shall take from it his handful of its fine flour and of its oil, together with all its frankincense; and the priest shall burn the memorial portion of it upon the altar, for an offering made by fire of a sweet savor to the LORD.

3. But the remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons (a). It is the Most Holy of the offerings made by fire to the LORD.

<margin>(a) Ezekiel 44:29. 1 Corinthians 9:13.</margin>

4. And when he wishes to bring as an offering of a grain offering something baked in the oven, it shall be unleavened cakes of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers smeared with oil.

5. But if your offering is a grain offering from the pan, it shall be of unleavened fine flour mixed with oil.

6. You shall break it into pieces and pour oil upon it: this is a grain offering.

---

<margin>v. 1. This offering could be offered on its own, or as an accompaniment to burnt and peace offerings.</margin>

No grain offering consisted of animals or birds, but solely of the fruits of the earth.

This second type of offering represents specifically the duty of love toward one's neighbor, and especially toward those who are miserable and in need of refreshment and restoration: therefore these offerings consisted of flour, or bread, or something else prepared from flour as food. Of which James speaks: Chapter 2:15, 16. So God wanted to remind His people through these gifts not only of their obligation toward their needy brothers—that they should break their bread for the hungry, Isaiah 58:7—but also toward the priests, to support them with these gifts bestowed by God, both of which the Lord wishes to attribute to Himself. Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord: He will repay him for his good deed. Proverbs 19:17. So also: Honor the Lord with your wealth and with the firstfruits of all your income; so your barns will be filled, and your vats will overflow with new wine. Chapter 3:9, 10. This occurred primarily through the priests, and thus in the maintenance of the sacrificial service.

<margin>v. 2. A handful of it was burned as a memorial offering: which was so named because the Lord wishes to graciously remember such good deeds and reward them abundantly; as previously cited from Proverbs 3 and 19. Just as Christ wishes to remember such deeds on the great Day of Judgment, when He will say to such benefactors: I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in, etc. Matthew 25:35. Therefore, it is mentioned a second time in this offering: This is an offering made by fire for a sweet savor to the Lord, namely in verse 9 again. Just as it says twice, in verse 10 and here</margin>

<margin>v. 3. It is the Most Holy) Whereby God's special pleasure in such benevolence is testified: as such is also testified to believers in the New Testament very emphatically and manifoldly. Do not forget to do good and to share: for such sacrifices please God well. Hebrews 13:16, where it speaks of contributions for the needy believers.</margin>

<column-break/>

<note>This offering had to contain no less than the tenth part of an ephah <note>An ephah is an ancient Hebrew unit of dry volume, roughly equivalent to 22 liters</note>, of which the priest took a handful to offer it to the LORD.</note>

<margin>v. 4. Unleavened) What is purer, more unleavened, more spotless and holier than Christ Jesus, the innocent and spotless Lamb? He Himself had to be offered as unleavened fine flour, or as bread baked by the glow of God's strict justice, or roasted on the grate of the Cross and baked in the pan of His deep humiliation on the high altar of His most holy Divinity, before He could become food for us in the memorial meal of His love.</margin>

<margin>v. 5. From the Pan) Many indeed make of this a dish or a grate: But because the grain offering was prepared in it, and as seen in chapter 6:14-15, was offered in such a way that the priest should not only take his handful of the fine flour of the grain offering but also of its oil; thus it is clear that the vessel in which it was prepared could at least not have been a flat dish, much less a grate: because it had to be a vessel capable of holding the oil as well as the grain offering.</margin>

<margin>But what does it matter whether we know this or not? Yes, dear person who thinks this, consider that the Law is spiritual, and ask God for understanding.</margin>

> This grain offering is beyond all doubt a precious gift, for which a pure and suitable vessel is required: one that has a true depth to contain and hold it. And what can such a thing be other than a sincere and pure heart, capable of receiving the gifts of God through the depth of humility. Such a grain offering and such a pure and convenient vessel will be pleasing to God along with all our persons, devotions, and prayers; because they are sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

<margin>This gift, as such an offering is sometimes called, is offered to God either through Christ Himself or through those who belong to Christ. (1) Christ gave Himself to God as a gift and sacrifice, Ephesians 5:2, and thereby caused the legal offering and gift, which foreshadowed Him, to cease. (2) By virtue of this grain offering of Christ, those who belong to Him also offer their grain offering when they [offer] themselves and their means, according to</margin>

<margin>v. 6. To break into pieces) and to distribute in love, to lay down their lives for the brothers, to break their bread for the hungry, and to share with the needy—even in spiritual matters—the gifts they have also received from the Lord: so that many may be helped out of the error of their ways, converted to the Lord, and become a sacrifice of love to God.</margin>

<margin>Thus shall the converted Gentiles one day be brought to the LORD as a grain offering in a pure vessel: Isaiah 66:20, just as the Apostle, as a priest, offered such. Romans 15:16.</margin>

<margin>And of what, then, does this grain offering consist?</margin>

<header>Chapter II. The Third Book of Moses [Leviticus].</header>

7. But if your offering is a grain offering prepared in a pan, it shall be made of fine wheat flour with oil:
8. And you shall bring the grain offering that is made of such things to the LORD, and it shall be presented to the priest, who shall bring it to the altar.
9. And the priest shall lift up the memorial portion from the grain offering and burn it upon the altar. It is an offering made by fire, a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
10. But the remainder of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons. It is the Most Holy of the offerings made by fire to the LORD.

---

**v. 7. Made of fine wheat flour with oil)** It must be of the finest wheat flour from that same grain of wheat of which our beloved Savior speaks in **John 12:24**, which must fall into the earth and die if it is to bring forth much fruit; and with which he there referred to himself, **v. 20, 21**, as the precious fruit of the earth, **James 5:7, 8**, which must be threshed and ground so that the husks or chaff and bran are separated from it, and it comes out pure. Christ grows up in us according to the flesh and the letter until we have died with him and risen with him. We then reach maturity when he becomes, as it were, invisible according to the flesh, and we begin to recognize him according to the Spirit and become new creatures. **2 Corinthians 5:16, 17.**
Upon this unleavened, pure wheat flour the oil is poured: which was formerly a type <note>In this context, a "type" or "foreshadowing" is an Old Testament person or object that symbolizes a New Testament reality.</note> of the Holy Spirit and the love of God, the perfect gift that descends from the Father of lights. **James 1:17.**
And thus truth springs up from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven. **Psalm 85:11.**
**v. 8. Priest — shall bring it to the altar)** In the New Testament, it is not necessary for us to run after priests; as one is sometimes persuaded elsewhere, that only consecrated priests may offer up Christ: rather, because true believers themselves are made priests by and before God, they too can present such a great gift upon the altar of their hearts, weave the sacrifice <note>The "weaving" or "waving" of the offering refers to a specific ritual movement in the air.</note>, and hold it up and proclaim it to the whole world.
**v. 9. The memorial offering** reminds us quite specifically that we should remember the Lord with every bite of bread and proclaim his death, according to the exhortation of the Apostle, **1 Corinthians 11:26.**
Whoever wishes to bring an acceptable grain offering to the Lord must, in thanksgiving, bring back all the food he takes into his mouth as if to the divine mouth. Oh, what hidden manna or heavenly taste will he then receive in return during such a holy sacrifice, which happens in the deepest silence!
Remember this Sabbath, and sanctify it immediately, and bring forth all the bestowed gifts, and offer them again to the Giver.
**v. 10. The remainder — shall be Aaron's and his sons')** But now all believers—namely those who are true believers and unleavened Christians—have the power, as consecrated priests anointed with God's Spirit, to eat of the grain offering in the holy place. They find and create this place everywhere when they worship God in spirit and in truth and are present to him in his most holy presence. These eat the bread of the Kingdom of God, the heavenly baked goods, which is the flesh of the Son of God, in a hidden and sublime way, so that from it a spiritual, heavenly body of power is conceived and nourished in them, also growing toward divine greatness, so that they become flesh of Christ's flesh and bone of his bones, which is a great mystery. **Ephesians 5:32.**

<column-break/>

11. No grain offering that you wish to offer to the LORD shall be made with leaven. For you shall burn no leaven, nor any honey, as an offering made by fire to the LORD.
12. As an offering of the firstfruits, you shall bring them to the LORD, but they shall not come upon the altar as a pleasing aroma. <margin>ch. 1:9, 3:16. (a) ch. 23:17.</margin>
13. And every offering of your grain offering you shall season with salt, and you shall not let the salt of the covenant of your God be lacking from your grain offering. To all your offerings you shall add salt. 14.

---

That no leaven was allowed to be used in the grain offering indicates that all hypocrisy, **Luke 12:1**, indeed, all malice and wickedness, should be far from good works, **1 Corinthians 5:8**; namely, when there are false intentions in them and they are done to be seen by men, just as Christ punishes such a thing regarding alms in **Matthew 6:1-4**. Rather, they should be done in all purity and sincerity for the Lord's sake: toward the brothers, **Matthew 25:40**; and toward poor natural men, because they are our flesh, **Isaiah 58:7**; yes, even toward enemies, because Christ has so commanded. **Matthew 5:44. Romans 12:20.**
**v. 11. Nor any honey)** By this, the Hebrews understand not only honey properly so-called, but all sweet fruits; such as figs, dates, etc. (a)
This indicates that one should not show kindness to someone with flattery; which is also a part of hypocrisy: where one indeed wants to appear well-meaning but is nonetheless opposed in the heart; or where one only wants to feed someone with sweet words, **James 2:15**. Rather, there should be something substantial and active in the love that one wishes to demonstrate.
**v. 12.** But since the priests received the firstfruits of all fruits as gifts of God, then honey also had to be given among them. **2 Chronicles 31:5.**
When everything is used in its right place, it is good: but otherwise not, if we do not know how to distinguish one thing correctly from the other.
**v. 13. Salt)** Those who had the sacrifice offered did not bring this salt with them; rather, it was procured from the common treasury, like the wood, and there was a specific chamber in the Temple for this salt, called the Salt Chamber.
That salt had to be added to these offerings indicates the quality of true love in general: that it should not smell and overlook the corrupt nature in the beloved, much less approve of it and play the hypocrite to the neighbor therein, but rather should reprove it. To this Christ's exhortation points: "Have salt in yourselves, and have peace with one another," **Mark 9:49**, where this characteristic of the offerings is also cited in **v. 48**. And the Apostle in **Colossians 4:6**: "Let your speech be always gracious, seasoned with salt."
So also, where it is necessary, exhortations and reproofs can be added to good works; yet in such a way that this happens in simplicity and is not thrown back in one's face: just as God is presented to us as an example in **James 1:5**. Otherwise, however, the constancy in benevolence can be pictured here, so that one does not let oneself be turned away by the ingratitude of some; as the Apostle's exhortation goes: "Let us not grow weary in doing good; for in due season we shall reap without ceasing. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith." **Galatians 6:9, 10.** Just as the covenant of God is called a covenant of salt because of such constancy of the promises. **2 Chronicles 13:5.**
(a) <note>original: "R. Lev. Barselon. ap. Hottinger. de ur. Hebr. u. 126. Bochart. hieroz. part. 2. L. 4. c. 12. p. 528. Flac. clav. voc. Mel." — These are scholarly citations referring to Rabbi Levi of Barcelona and the works of theologians Johann Heinrich Hottinger, Samuel Bochart, and Matthias Flacius Illyricus regarding Hebrew customs and the meaning of "Honey."</note>

<meta>This page concludes the commentary on Leviticus Chapter 2 regarding grain offerings and begins Chapter 3, which introduces the peace or thank offerings. It continues the Christological interpretation of the Old Testament sacrificial system, linking the processing of grain to the suffering of Christ and the early Christian martyrs.</meta>

<page-num>448</page-num>
<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chapter III.</header>

14. But if you wish to offer a grain offering of the firstfruits to the Lord, you shall bring the grain offering of your firstfruits from green ears of grain, dried by the fire, from that which is brought forth from fresh ears;

15. And you shall put oil upon it, and lay frankincense upon it: it is a grain offering.

16. And the priest shall burn its memorial portion from what is brought forth from it, and from its oil, with all its frankincense. It is an offering made by fire to the Lord.

That green ears were customarily eaten in the very fertile land of Canaan and contained much nourishment can be gathered from **Matthew 12:1**; and how such were also customarily baked or dried can be seen in **Ruth 2:14, 1 Samuel 17:17, and 25:18**. Therefore, grain offerings had to be brought from these as well, and handled in the previously mentioned manner.

Some, such as the *Weimar Bible* and also some Hebrew scholars, <note>Original: (a) ap. Schindl. Lex. pentagl. in אביב p. 3. (In Schindler's Five-Language Lexicon, under the entry "Abib," meaning fresh ears of grain).</note> interpret this passage as referring to the Wave-Sheaf at the Feast of Passover; which was the special grain offering of the entire congregation, as were the two loaves at the Feast of Pentecost and the weekly Showbread. Others, however, <note>Original: (b) R. Levi Barzelon. ap. Hotting. de jur. Hebr. p. 116. (Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, cited in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Law*).</note> view it as the grain offerings of an individual person, which this chapter addresses. It could, however, be both at once, and this could be a general ordinance for how the firstfruits should be handled in both cases.

**v. 14. Brought forth from the fresh ears)** From this it is concluded that it should not have been in whole grains, but in flour.

**v. 15. Oil upon it)** This signifies the good impulse of the Spirit of God, from which comes pure love toward one's neighbor; which is then also blessed in that same person.

**Frankincense upon it)** Good deeds must be given with grace and friendliness; for then they give off a lovely aroma. For what the Apostle testifies regarding this, see **Philippians 4:18**.

**v. 16.** The priest had to "wave" the grain offering before the Lord, lift it up high, and turn it toward all four corners of the world before throwing it into the fire on the altar. By this it was indicated that the sacrifice of Jesus Christ—the sweet Bread of Heaven, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ—should be offered for all peoples in the entire world. In this, they were to remind themselves, as if by a constant memorial or "remembrance offering," of how much was required for them to be redeemed. Just as the wheat first had to be ground, then baked, and then thrown into the fire as a sacrifice; or as the fresh ears were crushed: so also was the "Firstfruit," Christ, who had to have preeminence in everything—both in suffering and in the glory that followed—crushed through many sufferings, and in his everywhere-bruised body became a lovely aroma to his God and Father. And just as the firstfruits of the grain, freed from all earthly essence by the fiery offering, rose upward and into heaven—after the little grains from which they grew had previously risen from the earth more glorious and fruitful than when they were sown: so also Christ, through suffering, became much more glorious and fruitful in his resurrection and ascension.

And so also must the gifts of grace and the powers of the Body of Christ (**Hebrews 10:5, Psalm 40:6**) be presented, and mixed in the spirits of his members with the oil of joy and the salt of wisdom; indeed, our spirits and qualities themselves must be constantly offered to the Lord as our grain offerings, as food for us in the fire of his burning Spirit.

The holy Ignatius became such a mystical bread and fire-offering, as proof of the fellowship of the sufferings that are in Christ, when he was torn, crushed, and ground by the teeth of lions and leopards by the wrath of the bloodthirsty pagan tyrants. As he then wrote in his Epistle to the Romans: *I am God's grain, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found a pure bread of God.* <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD) was an early Christian bishop and martyr.</note>

(a) See Schindler's *Lexicon pentaglotton* under *Abib*, page 3.
(b) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in Hottinger's *De jure Hebraeorum*, page 116.

<column-break/>

# Chapter III.
->The Peace Offerings.<-
<note>The German "Danck-Opffer" (Thank Offering) is the traditional translation for what is now commonly called the Peace Offering (*Shelamim*).</note>

IF his offering is a peace offering: if he wishes to offer from the herd; whether it be a male or a female: he shall offer such a one as is perfect before the face of the Lord.

2. And he shall lay his hand upon the head of his offering and slaughter it at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall sprinkle the blood all around the altar.

**v. 1.** The third species of offerings were the peace offerings, which took their name from peace, welfare, or happiness, thereby showing how one should be heartily thankful to God for all his benefits. To prove this, they were also to bring a bull, sheep, or goat as an offering: and indeed, here it was to be of equal value whether it was a male or a female; whereas in the burnt offerings only the former was commanded (**Chapter 1:3**), and in the sin and guilt offerings only the latter was commanded (**Chapter 4:32, 5:6**). This can represent how God requires something "masculine" and strong in faith, but in thanksgiving, He does not reject even the weak and imperfect, when a person nevertheless shows some measure of acknowledgment to God, even for outward benefits—such as health, physical blessing, earthly peace, and the like—and praises and glorifies Him for them, and to that end also gives something of his own for the Lord’s sake and offers it to God. Just as this is now commanded in the New Testament through the praise of God: where we should be mindful not only of physical benefits but primarily of the spiritual benefits of God, and constantly praise God that He has blessed us with all kinds of spiritual blessings in heavenly goods through Christ, **Ephesians 1:3**, and thank Him for faith in the Lord Jesus, that we have attained the same through the good working of the Holy Spirit. **Verses 15 and 16** in the same place. Just as the Apostle also exhorts: "Therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually through him, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name." **Hebrews 13:15**, which Hosea calls "the calves of our lips," **Chapter 14:3**.

The cattle had to be older than one year and under three years; these are steers or young oxen: and indeed, those that had not yet been under any yoke. <note>Original: (a) R. Lev. Barzelon. ap. Hotting. de jur. Hebr. n. 131. Bochart. hieroz... (Refers to Samuel Bochart's *Hierozoicon*, a 17th-century study of biblical animals).</note>

And although it was of equal value whether it was of the male or female sex; it must absolutely not be pregnant if it was of the latter kind. <note>Original: (b) Philo lib. de charit. p. 548. Joseph. l. 3. Antiq. c. 10. (Refers to Philo of Alexandria and Flavius Josephus).</note> **Chapter 22:28.**

**v. 2. Of his offering)** Which happened either as thanks for a particular, noticeable benefit; or to receive a future benefit from God; or out of obligation, by a Nazirite. **Numbers 6:14, 17.**

**Sprinkle all around)** The blood was not sprinkled with the finger, but with a silver basin, from which the priest sprinkled and poured some blood against the altar. <note>Original: (c) R. Sal. ap. Lyr. ad Exod. 29. (Rabbi Solomon [Rashi] as cited by Nicholas of Lyra).</note>

This sprinkling was the most important part of all offerings, and was, as it were, the ransom-money of man for his sins. **Chapter 17:11.**

3. And he shall offer from the **thank-offering** an offering made by fire to the **Lord**: the fat that covers the entrails and all the fat that is upon the entrails;
4. And the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks; and the fatty lobe above the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.
5. And **Aaron's** sons shall burn it on the altar alongside the **burnt offering** which is on the wood that lies upon the fire. It is an offering made by fire, a sweet aroma to the **Lord**.
6. And if his offering from the sheep is for a thank-offering to the **Lord**, whether it be male or female, he shall offer one that is without blemish.
7. If he wishes to offer a lamb for his offering, then he shall offer it before the face of the **Lord**;

---

v. 3. 4. Because a portion of the meat from these offerings was given to the priests to eat, and the rest to those who offered it <note>See Leviticus 7:11, 29, etc.</note>, all the internal fat—which is specifically mentioned—had to be burned to the **Lord** as a fire-offering. By this, it was to be understood that thanksgiving should come from the innermost depths of the heart, and indeed with fervent prayer to **God**. See **Psalm 103:1**, where "all that is within me" <note>German: *das Eingeweyde*, literally "the entrails" or "innards"</note> is to praise **God**.

v. 5. A burnt offering also had to be brought at the same time, alongside which this fat of the thank-offering was burned; this was to show how no thanksgiving can be pleasing without faith in *Christ*. Therefore, the *Apostle* requires us to bring *Christ* along in our thanksgivings, as seen in **Hebrews 13:15** and **Colossians 3:17**.
Thus, the Jews may perhaps recognize the outward ceremonies of this offering better and more specifically than the Christians; but what such things signify according to the spirit and inward meaning is revealed only to those who know that, just as all other offerings include *Christ*—the Lamb of **God**—as the heart of all sacrifices, so too in all our praising and thanking, the peace and salvation offering <note>The German *Fried- und Heyl-Opffer* refers to the Peace Offering</note> must take place in *Christ* **Jesus**.
**God** has made His Son so necessary that without Him He will forgive no sin, allow no reconciliation to count, and accept no prayer nor thank-offering, nor anything else, unless we bring this brother of ours, **Benjamin**, along with us. <note>This is a metaphor referencing Genesis 43:3; just as Joseph’s brothers could not see his face without their youngest brother Benjamin, the author argues we cannot approach God without Christ.</note>

v. 6. **One that is without blemish]** Why indeed should **God** ask for a multitude of sacrificed oxen, calves, rams, sheep, and goats? If He were hungry for them, He could have them by the many thousands, for all that walk upon the mountains and in the valleys are His. But He does not hunger for them; rather, what smells so good and sweet to Him in the offerings is *Christ* sacrificed for us, whom the Fathers of the Old Testament took with them in faith to the outward offering.

v. 7. If this Lamb, slain from the beginning of the world, had not been included before **God** in the offerings of the Old Testament, and if the Fathers had not looked upon it in faith, it would all have been in vain. The offerings were, after the manner of the Oriental peoples, a **Picture-Catechism**, <note>German: *Bilder-Catechismus*</note> through which the Jews were instructed in the articles of faith; much like how the Egyptians hid something deeper within their hieroglyphic images. Not only did the holy Fathers of the faith know this for themselves, but they also taught it to the people through their *Kabbalah*, <note>Traditional oral interpretation</note> and held so strictly to it that the smallest circumstance in the sacrificing had to be observed; because every single thing signified and enclosed something special, by which the soul of man—for whose sake everything was done—might be improved.

<column-break/>

8. And he shall lay his hand upon the head of his offering and slaughter it before the Tabernacle of the Congregation: and the sons of **Aaron** shall sprinkle its blood all around the altar.
9. And he shall offer from the thank-offering as a fire-offering to the **Lord** its fat: the whole fat tail, which he shall remove close to the backbone, and the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails:
10. And the two kidneys with the fat that is on them, which is on the flanks, and the fatty lobe over the liver, which he shall remove with the kidneys.
11. And the priest shall burn it upon the altar as the food of the fire-offering to the **Lord**.
12. If

---

v. 8. The peace of **God** could not be maintained except through the reconciling blood of **Jesus**, the innocent and spotless Lamb. For this reason, this peace-offering also had to involve the slaughter of livestock.
**Before the Tabernacle)** Not outside the court <note>Original: (a) As Frantzius argues in *Disputation 13 on Sacrifice*, paragraph 54.</note>, but in the court or the entrance to the Holy Place. See **Leviticus 4:7** and **Exodus 29:11**.

v. 9. In the case of sheep, there was something special: the tail—which is said to be very fatty, large, and heavy on sheep in Eastern lands—had to be removed all the way to the backbone, or to the place where the kidneys lie internally <note>Original: (b) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, cited in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Law*, no. 135.</note>, and thus burned along with the rest of the fat.
This can signify, as some see it, that man should be especially mindful of gratitude toward **God** at the end of his life; just as that is the outermost member of the animal, one should then praise and glorify **God** with all one’s strength for the many benefits He has shown to each person. But especially should one be mindful then of the great benefits **God** has shown to our souls for *Christ's* sake during the entire time of our lives: that this Lamb of **God** has also carried, atoned for, and taken away all our sins with great patience; so that at the end we may rightly enter into the fellowship of His sacrifice through fervent repentance, faith, and love. Thus **David** gratefully remembered all these benefits in **2 Samuel 7:18-19**, and **Jacob** in **Genesis 32:10**.

**The fat that covers the entrails, and on the entrails]**
v. 10. **The 2 kidneys with the fat -- on the flanks, and the fatty lobe over the liver)** All of which belong to the innermost hidden members, and in the symbolic image signify the innermost part of our spirit and heart, which—as the very best that we have—should be given to our **God** in *Christ* **Jesus**, and Him be thanked therewith.

v. 11. **As food -- to the Lord)** The rest was eaten by the priests and those who brought the offering.
When the time finally comes for the great Universal Peace with the whole *Creation*, which was proclaimed in advance by the angel at the birth of *Christ*, and of which this peace and salvation offering (which shall then be experienced by all people) must have been a prototype and impression; then not only the priests and the royal priesthood of the firstborn will come to the enjoyment of it, but also the small and the great shall have a part in it and eat of such a peaceable offering.

<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chapter IV.</header>

**12. If his offering is a goat, then he shall offer it before the face of the Lord.**
**13. And he shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it before the Tabernacle of the Congregation; and the sons of Aaron shall sprinkle its blood all around the altar.**
**14. And from it he shall offer his offering as a fire-offering to the Lord: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails;**
**15. And the two kidneys, with the fat that is upon them, which is on the flanks; and the fatty lobe over the liver he shall remove with the kidneys.**

---

Sheep and goats had to be over one year and under two years old. Otherwise, these animals were no longer suitable for sacrifice if they were older.

v. 12. In a goat, the weakness of our nature can be represented, showing that **God** will graciously look upon even the imperfect praise and "babbling" <note>German: *Lallen*, referring to simple, childlike, or faltering speech</note> of our lips, as long as it comes from the heart and is sent to **God** with fervent sighs.

v. 13. Before the Tabernacle) Not toward the north side of the altar of burnt offering; (for only the most holy offerings were slaughtered there <note>See Leviticus 1:11</note>;) but toward the south, or perhaps toward the east.

v. 14. 15. The question arises: why did **God** always want these three parts—the fat, the kidneys, and a portion of the liver? Answer: The fat can be a symbol of lusts and desires; since fat is, as it were, the concentrated essence of the food, just as the spirit is within the creatures; and these are thus also the outflows of our souls, which we are to "crucify" (**Galatians 5:24**) and thus burn in the fire of **God's** love. The kidneys and the liver also signify passion and longing; we are taught by this that we should kill our fleshly lusts and impermissible desires, just as we should simultaneously follow the example of our great High Priest, **Jesus Christ**, whose highest passion and desire here on earth was to do His Father's will, to whom He sacrificed Himself entirely in obedience.

## The IV. Chapter.
->The Sin-Offerings.<-

**And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:**

The fourth category of sacrifices was the sin-offerings, where sins committed through error or haste had to be confessed before **God** with a sacrifice, thereby asking for His gracious forgiveness. By this, the duty of repentance was imposed, while at the same time forgiveness was promised to the repentant sinner. If, however, the sin had been committed out of malice and with deliberate intent, it had to be punished regardless, and no sacrifice could be brought for it. (**Numbers 15:22 and 30, 31**). The former are the errors and faults that one cannot immediately notice, as human weakness and carelessness are so great that a person does not always properly consider his actions as he rightly should. The latter are the "proud and defiant" sins, from which **David** prays that **God** would keep him back and preserve him through His powerful grace. (**Psalm 19:12–13** <note>German text cites verses 13-14 following the Lutheran numbering</note>).

A fourfold distinction is made here: whether the High Priest, or the whole community, or a prince, or an individual soul should sin; because one sin is greater and more dangerous than another in view of the circumstances.

<column-break/>

**16. And the priest shall burn these things on the altar, as food for the fire-offering for a sweet aroma (*). All the fat is the Lord’s. (a) chapter 2:12, 4:31.**
**17. This shall be an eternal statute for your descendants in all your dwellings: you shall eat no fat and no blood.**

---

v. 16. All the fat is the Lord's) In all sacrifices, **God** received the best. The heathens, however, gave their idols the worst—the gall, the bones—and kept the best for themselves.

Yet some understand this only in regards to these three named animals: cattle, sheep, and goats; and then only of the specified parts, whereas otherwise the remaining fat, with which the meat is marbled in very fertile lands, was not forbidden. Indeed, **God** boasts of the blessing He showed His people, that He let them eat the fat of lambs. (**Deuteronomy 32:14**). So too in **Nehemiah 8:10**: "Go your way and eat the fat."

If everything that is within you is to be purified and raised up for the praise of **God** (**Psalm 103:1**), then your "innards" must be stripped of everything in you that is coarse and fatty like lard; the wanton flesh of lewdness, with all the coarse fatness of corrupt nature, must be removed and handed over into the holy fire of the altar.

Yet we shall be permitted to eat all fat that is marbled through the meat: that is, all taste and spiritual joy associated with good practices shall be free for our enjoyment.

v. 17. You shall eat no fat) Some <margin>(a)</margin> believe it is because it is unhealthy and causes "bad humors" <term>bad humors: in older medicine, these were imbalances in bodily fluids thought to cause disease</term>. Others <margin>(b)</margin> believe **God** wished to separate them from the heathens, who ate the fat of their sacrifices. (**Deuteronomy 32:38**). It could be both, and additionally indicate that they were not yet permitted to see the spiritual meaning of all these ceremonies. Likewise, blood was forbidden to show that the blood had not yet been shed through which the reconciliation had to be brought about.

These statutes were then bound to "eternity," or the hidden long duration of the ceremonies of the Old Testament, with whose conclusion they also reached their end according to the letter. See **Hebrews 7—13**.

<note>original: (a) R. Levi Barselon. ap. Hotting. de jur. Hebr. n. 147. (Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, cited in Hottinger's "On the Laws of the Hebrews")</note>
<note>original: (b) Lyra ad Exod. 29. (Nicholas of Lyra's commentary on Exodus 29)</note>

**2. Speak to the children of Israel and say: If a soul should sin through error against any of the commandments of the Lord, regarding things that should not be done, and has acted against any one of them;** <margin>v. 13, 22.</margin>

---

That should not be done) The commandments of the **Lord** are of two kinds: some want something to be done; others want something not to be done. The latter are also called prohibitions, the former commands. Although only those things "which should not be done" are mentioned here, both types are nevertheless understood. For not only did those sins have to be atoned for where one actually committed something against the **Lord** and His commandment by mistake, but also those which consisted of omitting something that one should have done. It is the same elsewhere. In **Psalm 15**, there are more prohibitions than commands, and yet this Psalm concludes thus: "He who *does* these things shall never fall." **Zechariah 8:16–17**: "These are the things you shall *do*," etc., and yet there are things among them of which the **Lord** says He hates them. And who does not know that, although the Ten Commandments consist of more prohibitions than commands, it is very often said and required by the **Lord** that we should *do* according to His commandments?

### Chapter IV. The Third Book of Moses.

**3. If the priest who is anointed should sin, bringing guilt upon the people; then he shall offer for his sin, which he has committed, a bullock—a young ox without blemish—to the Lord for a sin offering.**

**4. And he shall bring the bullock to the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, before the face of the Lord, and shall lay his hand upon the bullock’s head, and slaughter the bullock before the face of the Lord.**

**5. And the priest who is anointed shall take of the bullock’s blood and bring it into the Tabernacle of the Congregation.**

v. 3. **The priest who is anointed**) This is as much as to say the High Priest, who is called by this name to distinguish him from the common priests; they were not usually anointed, except for what occurred at the initial institution of this priesthood <note>See Exodus 40:15</note>.

A High Priest, who was anointed, was expected to lead others with greater knowledge, holiness, and a cautious way of life, so that he would not, by his example, provoke others to despise God's commandments and thus lead them into sin. In the same way, teachers today should lead everyone with a godly life, refraining from the lusts of the flesh and from conforming to the world. Through their example, others should be corrected, rather than being strengthened in vanities by the teacher’s own conformity to the world—which brings such guilt upon the people that they draw God’s judgments upon themselves.

**To the guilt of the people**) Making them sin and become guilty, either through teaching or by providing an occasion for offense and stumbling by his example. <note>See 1 Samuel 2:17, 24; Isaiah 3:12 and 9:16; Jeremiah 23:15</note>. For example, when many teachers today provide such a meager doctrine regarding the keeping of God's commandments and the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ.

This is not to be understood as referring to something intentional or premeditated. Otherwise, it could not be a sin of error or ignorance, which is the primary focus of this chapter. Rather, that would be a sin of malicious defiance, which allows for no sacrifice <note>Hebrews 10:26</note>.

Bring then—yes, bring without delay—all you teachers of the people, you who ought to be "Anointed Ones" but have also become guilty in this part: oh, dear ones, bring your sin offering for it! Namely, true repentance or remorse and sorrow, a broken spirit and a contrite heart, and humble yourselves before the Lord. Let us confess, forsake, and kill our sins! So that we may be sprinkled by the blood and Spirit of Christ and washed from an evil conscience <note>Hebrews 10:22</note>; and then, a truly divine way of life may win the people over to all godliness. That will then produce truly powerful preachers, who will testify and demonstrate powerfully in word and deed that Christ is the power of God <note>1 Corinthians 1:24</note>, through whom the righteousness of the law may be fulfilled in us <note>Romans 8:3–4</note>. In that passage, as well as here, it is noteworthy that:

**Sin and Sin Offering**) are taken as one and the same word <note>In Hebrew, the word *chattat* refers to both the sin itself and the sacrifice that purifies it</note>.

v. 4. **To the door**) Of the Sanctuary, and thus still within the inner court, where everything was slaughtered.

v. 5. **Bring the blood**) As it were, his ransom money, to offer it to God for reconciliation.

The blood and the Spirit of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, must cleanse us not only from coarse sins but from every single one, even those committed out of error or oversight.

Head, legs, entrails, dung, and thus the entire bullock, had to be taken outside the camp and burned in a special place dedicated to this purpose.

<column-break/>

**6. And the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle of the blood seven times before the face of the Lord, before the veil of the Sanctuary.**

**7. And the priest shall put some of the blood upon the horns of the altar of sweet incense before the face of the Lord, which is in the Tabernacle of the Congregation; and all the rest of the bullock’s blood he shall pour at the base of the altar of burnt offering, which is at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation.**

**8. And all the fat of the bullock of the sin offering he shall take off from it: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat that is on the entrails;**

**9. And the two kidneys with the fat that is upon them, which is on the flanks; and the fatty lobe over the liver he shall tear away with the kidneys:**

**10. Just as it is taken from the ox of the peace offering. And the priest shall burn these things upon the altar of burnt offering.**

**11. But the hide of the bullock with all its flesh, along with its head and its legs, and its entrails and its dung,**

**12. Even the whole bullock, he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place where the ashes are poured out, and he shall burn it on wood with fire. In the place where the ashes are poured out, it shall be burned.**

v. 6. **Dip his finger in the blood**) In no other sacrifice was the blood sprinkled with the finger toward the veil of the Sanctuary except in this one and in the following case in verse 17. However, it was done in such a way that the veil was not actually touched by the blood during the sprinkling.

v. 7. Namely, for sins of greater weight, repentance should be all the more earnest, so that it may penetrate before God into heaven and that these sins might be atoned for through powerful intercession.

v. 8–10. All the fat was specially set on fire, just as in the peace offerings <term>Danckopffer: offerings of thanks or fellowship</term>, to represent more powerfully the burning away of all perverse desires and inclinations.

v. 11–12. Finally, there was something special about this and the following sacrifice: the bullock’s hide, flesh, and the bullock itself had to be taken outside the camp and burned in a special place dedicated to this. The mystery of this is found in Hebrews 13:11–12 <note>This refers to Jesus suffering "outside the gate" to sanctify the people</note>.

<meta>This page continues the specific laws regarding the Sin Offering in Leviticus Chapter 4. Having previously discussed the requirements for an anointed High Priest who sins, it now moves to the requirements for the entire community of Israel.</meta>

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter IV.

13. And if the whole congregation of Israel should err, and the matter remains hidden from the eyes of the assembly, so that they have acted against any of all the commandments of the Lord concerning things which should not be done, and have become guilty;
14. And the sin which they have committed becomes known: then the assembly shall offer a bull—namely, a young steer—for a sin offering; and they shall bring it before the Tabernacle of the Congregation.
15. And the elders of the congregation shall lay their hands upon the bull’s head before the face of the Lord, and the bull shall be slaughtered before the face of the Lord.

Here is presented the sin of the entire congregation of Israel—which at that time was still gathered together, but later, in the land of Canaan, became various assemblies according to their dwellings, each of which could sin individually. Such an error can very easily begin with a few and then be followed by others; or, even if some might see it more clearly, they still cannot resist the multitude: as happened with the sin of idolatry involving the Golden Calf <note>A reference to Exodus 32, where the Israelites worshipped a golden idol while Moses was on Mount Sinai.</note>. Because all are then entwined in the guilt, and the wrath of God is provoked against the whole congregation, they were required to bring a sacrifice similar to that of the High Priest. This was to be handled in the same way: the blood was sprinkled toward the curtain and smeared on the horns of the Altar of Incense; all the fat was burned on the altar, and the entire bull was burned outside the camp. By this, Christ’s blood was also prefigured, which he poured out specifically for the whole congregation of his elect, and through which he desires to bring them into the Most Holy Place by constantly interceding for them before the Father. And this is then the congregation for which Christ gave himself up, that he might sanctify and cleanse it through the washing of water in the word; that he might present it to himself a glorious congregation, not having a spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that it should be holy and without blemish. Ephesians 5:25, etc.

<margin>v. 13.</margin> Furthermore, in order not to fail in applying this to our modern times, one may aptly note the sin of almost the entire outward Christian Church, which consists in the misuse of the holy Sacraments—of Baptism and especially of the Lord's Supper. All are entwined in this guilt, as such misuse is not properly resisted in any congregation. Thus, according to our own confession <note>original: "Bekenntnuß (a)" referencing the Heidelberg Catechism, a Protestant confessional document from 1563.</note>, the covenant of God is dishonored and wrath is provoked against the entire congregation, because such unrepentant, worldly-minded people are not excluded through the Office of the Keys <note>A theological term for the authority of the church to forgive sins or withhold forgiveness, often associated with excommunication.</note> until they improve their lives.

<margin>v. 14. Before the Tabernacle)</margin> In the courtyard, in front of the Holy Place, facing the East.

<margin>v. 15. The Elders)</margin> Specifically, as the Mishnah Sanhedrin <note>original: "Milchn. Sanhedrin (b)"; the Mishnah is a collection of Jewish oral traditions, and 'Sanhedrin' is the volume dealing with legal procedures.</note> states, three of them stepped forward for themselves and on behalf of the congregation; they laid their hands from behind onto the bull’s head between the horns and confessed their sins.

(a) in the Heidelberg Catechism, Question 82. (b) Chapter 1, Section 3.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 16.</margin> Then the priests caught the blood in the basin, which the High Priest—just as with his own sin offering—brought into the Holy Place and sprinkled in the same manner as previously mentioned.

<margin>v. 17. Seven times)</margin> Who does not notice that under this holy number of perfection, a great mystery was indicated!

<margin>v. 18. The wetting of the horns of the Altar of Incense</margin> was something very special in this and the preceding sacrifice, and it teaches us how necessary intercession is for entire congregations, because in them there are always still some who fear the Lord; so that the lampstand of the Word <note>A metaphor for the presence of the Gospel and God's grace in a specific church or location.</note> might not be entirely taken away from a place on account of the sins of some among them.

<margin>v. 19. Fat - lift up and ignite)</margin> When the elders had cut open the bull’s belly and removed all the fat, the High Priest then took it into a bowl, lifted it up to God the Lord, and then brought it to the altar, salted it there, and finally placed it on the fire.

Just as (these are the instructive thoughts of Origen <note>original: "Origenis (a)"; Origen (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar known for allegorical interpretations.</note> regarding the sacrifices in general) all sacrifices pointed toward Christ—so that after he was sacrificed, all sacrifices that prefigured him in shadow reached their end—so too through the fat that was sacrificed (which covered the entrails and was on the kidneys) his holy soul can be understood. This soul covered the innermost parts, such as the secrets of the Godhead; yet with the kidneys—that is, with the bodily matter, which was taken from our humanity in a pure and chaste way—it was connected and placed in the middle between the flesh and God, in order to deify the nature of the flesh and ignite it with the divine fire. Furthermore, the fact that the sacrificial blood had to be sprinkled 7 times before the face of the Lord clearly indicates the sevenfold powers, gifts of grace, and outpourings of the Holy Spirit.

<margin>v. 20.</margin> As with the bull of the sin offering) which was mentioned previously.

<margin>v. 21.</margin> Namely, the carcass with all its appendages was carried on poles outside the camp (or, in Jerusalem, outside the city) and completely burned to ashes.

<meta>This page continues the specific laws regarding the Sin Offering in Leviticus Chapter 4. The previous page discussed the communal offering for the whole congregation; this page transitions to the specific requirements for a "Prince" or leader who sins unintentionally.</meta>

<header>Ch. IV. The Third Book of Moses [Leviticus]. 453</header>

### 22. When a ruler shall sin, and has committed a trespass through error against any of all the commandments of the LORD his God, concerning things which should not be done, and has become guilty;
### 23. Or if his sin, wherein he has sinned, is made known to him: he shall bring for his offering a goat—a male without blemish.

A "ruler" <note>German: *Fürst*. In this context, it refers to a leader or prince.</note> here may be the head of his family, or of an entire tribe—as was common among Israel at that time—or those who later ruled over the whole people as judges and kings. When such a person becomes guilty, whether through specific sins of the flesh that cause others to stumble, or by the abuse of their power to oppress others: then this sin must be presented to them, as happened with David through the prophet Nathan, and as was attempted with Rehoboam (though in vain; see 1 Kings 12), or their conscience must be awakened (see 1 Kings 11:11, etc.). In such cases, they were required to bring a male goat. Through this animal, the "stink" of lustful desires was acknowledged before God, as well as a "butting" or aggressive nature—meaning the misuse of one's prestige and power to the harm of others, or attacking them improperly in anger. They were to visualize the putting to death of their own lusts and desires through the killing of the animal and the burning of its fat, so that they might plead with God for reconciliation and forgiveness through the shedding of blood and the sprinkling of the Altar of Burnt Offering.

May the Lord also grant the rulers among His people of the New Testament to recognize this well, so that the measure of sin does not become too full, and the Lord does not awaken over them with the punishment of the Sixth Seal <note>A reference to Revelation 6:12-17, describing divine judgment upon the kings and great men of the earth.</note>. They would do well to take to heart what is written in Ezekiel 45:8–9 and Revelation 6:15, so that some might yet escape the coming wrath through true repentance. (Psalm 2:10, etc.)

**v. 22. A ruler)** By this is understood any prominent, respectable, and honored man. The priests are also included under this term, as is commonly held, because they are not otherwise specifically named here.

Great lords often persuade themselves that they are permitted more than other people, and they assume an unfounded freedom to transgress God's commandments without much thought—getting drunk, whoring, keeping concubines, and the like—as if they had a special privilege for it and it were part of their high status. But the holy God, before whom they are nothing but miserable creatures, will have none of it. He indicates here that their dignity grants them no license or permission for sin; rather, it makes them all the more criminal in His sight. God requires that they should mistreat no one, just like all others and their own subjects.

**Against any of all the commandments of the Lord)** This is expressed here for the second time, and is all the more noteworthy because of the almost universal contempt for God's commandments today, as well as the common delusion that it is impossible for a person to keep them, even through God's grace. Here, however, something else is shown: for the Lord requires from priest and people, from ruler and all subjects, a universal regard for each and every one of His commandments. Should Christians have any less care and observation of every one of God's commandments than was required of the people under the Law? Some persuade themselves so, dreaming of an "Evangelical obedience" that effectively sets men free from the Law. But such a delusion and doctrine has no foundation, even if it finds much belief and approval among men because it makes the path easy and comfortable. For people love an easy religion and a comfortable life because they love pleasure more than God.

It is our duty—and it should also be our delight, if we desire to honor and fear the Lord—that we conscientiously observe each and every commandment of God, and guard ourselves precisely so that we do not transgress any of them. For whoever breaks one commandment is guilty of them all. (James 2:10).

**v. 23. A goat)** In ancient times, goat meat was held in very high regard among the Hebrews. When they wanted to treat their guests well or send someone a delicacy, goat meat was used. (Genesis 27:9, 14; Judges 6:19; 13:15; 19:etc.)

<column-break/>

### 24. And he shall lay his hand upon the goat’s head, and slaughter it in the place where they slaughter the burnt offering before the face of the LORD. This is a sin offering.
### 25. And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, and put it upon the horns of the Altar of Burnt Offering, and shall pour out its blood at the base of the Altar of Burnt Offering.
### 26. And he shall burn all its fat upon the altar, like the fat of the sacrifice of the peace offering. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him regarding his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.
### 27. And

**v. 24. Slaughter)** Their method of slaughtering was not always the same. Sometimes they struck through the nape and neck of the sacrificial animal, just as the pagans used a slaughtering knife or sacrificial axe to cut off the neck. The most common method among the Jews was this: they took a large and sharp sacrificial knife, placed it at the animal's neck, and pulled it back and forth through the neck, cutting the animal's throat or gullet along with the windpipe. If even one of these was not cut through, it was not considered a proper or perfect slaughtering. (a)

**Before the face of the Lord)** A prince or ruler, or any other prominent person in the world, must likewise perform true repentance before the eyes of all if he wishes to receive reconciliation with God. If they do not do this, their sins remain written upon their hearts with iron styluses.

**v. 25. Blood—on the horns of the Altar of Burnt Offering)** In this case, none of the blood was brought into the Holy Place. Nevertheless, in all sin offerings, some of the blood was placed on the horns of an altar, which did not happen with other sacrifices. And because the priest ascended from the east toward the circuit of the altar, he began at the southeast horn. From there he went to the northeast, then around to the northwest, and finally to the southwest. When he had placed blood on each horn with his finger and let it run down the length of the horn, he then descended the small ramp toward the west with the remaining blood and poured it at the base of the altar in the southwest corner. He did not pour it into the pipe that faced west (where the blood remaining from the Holy Place was poured), but right nearby into the pipe that faced south.

**v. 26. Thereupon)** the ruler or his assistants stripped the skin from the slaughtered young goat, cut open the belly, and took out the entrails. The priest took all the fat into a bowl, and after he had salted it, he brought it to the altar where he salted it again and then placed it on the fire.

When God had received what was His—namely, all the fat and a piece of the liver—then all the rest of the meat, as well as the entrails such as the heart, liver, lungs, and brain (which were only burned entirely in the Burnt Offering), belonged to the priests, as seen in Chapter 6:26, 30.

(a) <note>original: "Bochart. hieroz. part. 1. l. 2. c. 50. p. 586. Saubert. de sacrif. vett. c. 19."</note> These refer to scholarly works: Samuel Bochart’s *Hierozoicon* (concerning animals of the Bible) and Saubert’s *On the Sacrifices of the Ancients*.
