### 454 The Third Book of Moses [Leviticus]. Ch. IV.

### 27. And if any soul shall sin through error from among the people of the land, by doing somewhat against any of the commandments of the LORD which ought not to be done, and be guilty;
### 28. Or if his sin, wherein he has sinned, come to his knowledge: then he shall bring for his offering a young goat, a perfect female, for his sin which he has sinned.
### 29. And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering, and slay the sin offering in the place of the burnt offering.
### 30. And the priest shall take of the blood thereof with his finger, and put it upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar.
### 31. And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat is taken away from off the sacrifice of peace offering; and the priest shall burn it upon the altar for a sweet savor unto the LORD. And the priest shall make an atonement for her, and it shall be forgiven her.

---

Every individual person who became mindful of a sin committed through error or haste—perhaps being corrected by others or rebuked by their own conscience—was required to bring a goat or a sheep-lamb (a female). They were to confess their sin by laying their hands upon the head of the sacrifice. Through the shedding of blood, the smearing of the horns of the Altar of Burnt Offering, and the burning of all the fat, they were to plead for reconciliation and the forgiveness of their sin, and for the destruction of all their sinful lusts and desires. In this context, the female gender <note>German: *weiblichen Geschlecht*. The commentator suggests that the use of a female animal symbolizes human frailty.</note> represents the weakness and powerlessness of our corrupted nature. However, in the previous sacrifices for the High Priest and a Prince, a male animal was ordained; this showed that those individuals should prove themselves more manly and stronger in spirit, as they have often received more natural ability and other gifts of the Spirit than others.

**v. 27.** This sacrifice was brought by one who erred in matters not concerning divine service. For if someone erred in matters concerning divine service <note>referring to ritual or ceremonial laws</note>, he had to bring a year-old goat as a sacrifice. This applied equally to the High Priest, other priests, the Prince, and the common man; it was sacrificed in the same way as this offering of sheep or goats, as seen in Numbers 15:27.

**v. 28. A perfect female)** A symbol of Heavenly Wisdom, in which Jesus Christ, through the Holy Spirit, also makes Himself known, shares Himself, and allows Himself to be recognized and enjoyed in a "feminine" quality <note>This is a mystical interpretation common in some 17th-century Pietist traditions, identifying Christ with Sophia or Divine Wisdom.</note>. For where else is a "perfect little woman" to be found among thousands, if not this "wife of our youth"?

**v. 29. Slay in the place of the burnt offering)** Toward the north <note>German: *Gegen Mitternacht*, literally "toward midnight," a traditional term for the North, which was the location for slaughtering most sacrifices.</note>, as was customary.

**v. 30. 31.** This sin offering was sacrificed with the same ceremonies as that of the Prince.

<column-break/>

### 32. And if he bring a lamb for a sin offering, he shall bring it a perfect female.
### 33. And he shall lay his hand upon the head of the sin offering, and slay it for a sin offering in the place where they kill the burnt offering.
### 34. And the priest shall take of the blood of the sin offering with his finger, and put it upon the horns of the altar of burnt offering, and shall pour out all the blood thereof at the bottom of the altar:
### 35. And he shall take away all the fat thereof, as the fat of the lamb is taken away from the sacrifice of the peace offerings; and the priest shall burn them upon the altar, according to the offerings made by fire unto the LORD: and the priest shall make an atonement for him for his sin that he has committed, and it shall be forgiven him.

---

The only difference in this case, as we can see here, was:
**v. 32. A female)** whereas there <note>in the case of the ruler</note> a male is required, according to the distinction between persons.
**v. 33.** In the laying on of hands and in the slaughtering, however, as well as
**v. 34.** in the treatment of the blood, they were the same. In every sacrifice of an animal made for sin, one had to
->**Pour all its blood at the bottom of the altar**<-
This brings repentance with it, so that we humble ourselves before GOD and lower ourselves with a contrite spirit even into the dust.
Finally, there was also a difference compared to the sacrifice of a Prince: when a common man sacrificed a sheep, the tail <note>German: *Schwantz*. In Middle Eastern fat-tailed sheep, the tail was considered a choice part consisting almost entirely of fat.</note> also belonged to the fat that was placed on the altar. Therefore it says:
**v. 35. Just as the fat of the lamb is taken away from the peace offering)** What was taken from the fat of the sheep or lambs at the peace offering can be seen in Chapter 3:9.
The Hebrews call these described sin offerings, which consisted of four-footed animals, (a) "steadfast," "firm," or "immovable" offerings <note>original: *standhaffte, veste oder unbewegliche Opffer*</note> because no change was allowed in them; rather, everyone had to give what they owed, whether they had much or little to pay. They also write that these sin offerings were certainly for those sins committed unknowingly and unintentionally which, had the person committed them knowingly and intentionally, would have deserved "cutting off" <note>excommunication or death</note> from the people of God.
However, the sin offerings were not always sacrificed immediately, but were often postponed until the festivals.
Furthermore, not everyone always brought the animal themselves, but instead gave money to the priests, who bought a sin offering and placed the remainder in the God-chest <note>the treasury</note>.
And because the priests received a significant portion of this, God frequently complains about their greed, noting that they were happy to see the people sinning just so that many offerings would come in. (Hosea 4).
One also sees here and there in the Scripture that a sin offering was sacrificed not only for certain named sins and cases, but also sometimes in cases where there was actually no sin: as seen in chapters 12:6, 8; 9:2; 15:27; Numbers 6:10, 11, 14; 8:8, 12; Ezra 6:17; 8:35.

<meta>This page transitions from the general Sin Offerings of Chapter 4 to the specific "Trespass Offerings" or "Guilt Offerings" described in Chapter 5. It focuses on sins of omission (failing to testify), ritual impurity (touching carcasses), and rash oaths.</meta>

### Chapter V.

->The Trespass Offerings.<-

<margin>
In addition to the Sin Offerings of the previous chapter, there was another Sin Offering brought in the cases recounted here, as a fifth category of sacrifice: the Trespass Offering <note>German: *Schuld-Opffer*; often translated as Guilt Offering.</note>.

In all sins there is also guilt; namely, because through sin one has made oneself liable for punishment before GOD: See Chapter 4:13, 22, 27. However, several sins are recounted here that bring about a special guilt before GOD.

The voice of a curse) This refers specifically to that type of adjuration whereby a person, upon hearing it, is bound to say or do something—which is otherwise called an oath or summons. For

The Jews permitted in their courts of law an adjuration to be placed upon all persons present to investigate and bring out the truth hanging in dispute; so much so that, even if a man were not personally cited and sworn to confess his knowledge in the matter, he nevertheless—if he heard the adjuration or curse and concealed the truth—made himself guilty according to this law. How much more so, then, if someone had been personally sworn to speak their knowledge and had yet remained silent; in which case he was obligated to answer the adjuration, even if his statement resulted in his own disadvantage.

So false is the pretense that no one is obligated to accuse themselves. This law binds a person to reveal what he knows of a matter, even if he were only cited generally, along with all who hear the adjuration, regardless of whether his own interests suffered disadvantage thereby. Otherwise, the law makes him guilty. How much more so when the judge himself adjures him specifically and in person to speak the truth, as happened to Christ. Matthew 26:59–64.

Note how sharply and precisely the Lord requires the discovery of sin, so that the truth may be brought to light and to judgment; and this under a ceremonial service: so that he who concealed what he knew made himself guilty. Silence and consenting to evil were one and the same in this case.

Should we then, who wish to be Christians—who should deviate from every evil way and from every transgression and sin, hating them and having a loathing and abhorrence for them within ourselves—conceal and preserve another’s sin as something "sweet under our tongue"? In such a case, it befits a Christian understanding and light to investigate well what is most useful for our brother’s improvement. If we overlook our brother's sins and do not point them out or present them to him—not merely remaining silent for a time to wait for a more convenient time for his correction—we make our brother’s sin and guilt our own, and our kindness toward our brother is interpreted as nothing other than disobedience toward GOD.
</margin>

And if a soul shall sin, in that she hears the voice of a curse <note>A public summons to testify under oath.</note> and is a witness thereof; whether he has seen it or learned of it: if he does not report it <note>(a) Proverbs 29:24.</note>, then he shall bear his iniquity.

<column-break/>

2. Or if a soul shall touch any unclean thing; whether it be the carcass of an unclean wild beast, or the carcass of unclean cattle, or the carcass of an unclean creeping thing: if it were hidden from him, yet he is unclean and has become guilty.

3. Or if he shall touch the uncleanness of man, according to all his uncleanness whereby he may become unclean, and it were hidden from him; but when he comes to know it, then he has become guilty.

4. Or if a soul swears, uttering with the lips to do evil or to do good, according to all that a man may utter with an oath, and it were hidden from him, and he comes to know it, that he has become guilty in one of these things.

5. And...

---

<margin>
v. 2. Touching an unclean thing—a carcass) What was signified by this other than "dead works" (Hebrews 6:1), from which we should abstain and have no fellowship with them (Ephesians 5:11).

If it be hidden from him, he is unclean) Note how earnestly GOD searches everything in us, and places even our unrecognized sin into the light before His face, and simply wants it to be atoned for or punished.

If then he was punishable under the Old Testament who had only touched something unclean; how much more then will he be punishable before GOD who himself does unclean things and wallows like a sow in the mire of sin.

v. 3. If he shall touch the uncleanness of man) The Hebrews do not understand both laws regarding the unclean simply, because such an unclean person could be restored by bathing; rather, they interpret it as those who have become unclean through contact and, in their uncleanness, ignorantly entered the Temple or ate of the holy things <note>(a) original Latin: *Hottinger, de jur. Hebr. n. 121. & 119. 171.* (Hottinger, On Hebrew Law).</note>.

v. 4. If a soul swears) Whereby GOD wished to rebuke the profanation of His name in a special way, so that such sins had to be given up with great repentance. Proverbs 29:24. For here, such cursing and swearing is meant even more than in verse 1, though some take it to mean that as well.

However, swearing was not entirely forbidden to the Jews, neither in nor out of court: but only swearing frivolously, vainly, and falsely. Chapter 19:12; Jeremiah 7:9.

Hidden, and he becomes aware of it) For it can indeed become manifest through the conscience. How often one considers something to be no sin! But when GOD afterwards visits one with heavy tribulations, so that one must humble oneself before Him with fear and trembling; then it dawns upon the inner man through the Spirit of GOD that one has incurred guilt before GOD in this or that. And these are the hidden faults for whose forgiveness David prays to GOD in Psalm 19:12. They are the unrecognized sins that GOD sets in the light before His face (Psalm 90:8). This should teach us to perform a careful daily rebuke and examination of our conscience, to ask GOD for forgiveness for whatever may trouble us in our conscience, and to improve it. For this reason, Christ also teaches us to pray generally: Forgive us our debts!
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Trespass" or "Guilt Offering" (Schuld-Opffer) from the beginning of Chapter 5. The previous page established that even unintentional sins or sins of omission (like failing to testify) require an offering to address the guilt before God.</meta>

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter V.

5. And it shall come to pass, when he shall be guilty in one of these things, that he shall confess that in which he has sinned.
6. And he shall bring his trespass offering unto the LORD for his sin which he has committed: a female from the flock, namely a lamb or a young goat, for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin.

---

<margin>v. 5. Confess)</margin> Drusius <note>original: "ad loc. diss. Lev. c. 13." - Johannes Drusius was a Flemish Protestant 16th-century scholar of the Old Testament.</note> cites this confession as follows: Whoever had sinned would lay his hand between the animal's horns and say: "Ah, Lord! I have sinned, transgressed Your commandment, and done evil before You in this or that way. See, I am sorry, and I am ashamed of my deeds; I will do it no more!"

<margin>v. 6. Bring a trespass offering)</margin> In these cases, however, the sacrifice was not a fixed, unmovable, and certain requirement, but was instead according to one's means. It was established that whoever was able to give was required to give either a

<margin>female from the flock, or a goat)</margin> Not a mother goat that has already borne young, as it is given in several of Luther’s translations, but a nursing goat or a year-old sheep; this was intended to acknowledge the great weakness and corruption of nature, with which they then dealt just as they did with the sin offering.

<margin>Atonement)</margin> or cleansing from one's sin. For by "atonement" nothing else is to be understood but reconciliation or unity with God—when God and man are at one. This, however, cannot happen or be effected as long as sin comes between them and separates man from God. Isaiah 59:2.

Now, the Spirit of God certainly includes two meanings under the word "atonement" or "cleansing": 1) to cover, and 2) to cleanse, wash away, or reconcile. Yet, a "cloak for vice" (1 Peter 2:16) is by no means intended when it signifies "covering"; nor is it to be understood as a mere hiding of sin. Rather, it is just as a plaster is laid over a wound to cover it, and thus to cure and heal it. In this way, one meaning unites with the other.

To be sure, the Jewish actions in this matter were "ceremonial and beggarly elements" <note>A reference to Galatians 4:9, describing the Old Testament laws as elementary stages of faith.</note>. Nevertheless, the precious and dear truths of God concerning reconciliation with God and cleansing from sin were prefigured through them. The essential cleansing from our sins through Christ is meant and indicated by this ceremonial cleansing. Hebrews 9:13–14.

But if sin were only covered in such a way that it nevertheless remained always within us, what kind of extraordinary benefit would reconciliation or cleansing be? It would be nothing more than a foul and stinking ulcer being covered over with a skin; the gnawing and accusation of the guilty conscience would be stilled and satisfied for a time; the evildoer would be given a short reprieve, and his punishment merely postponed for a while. Oh, what a wretched reconciliation that would be! For the sore covered with a crust will and must break out again, and judgment and vengeance will pursue the sinner until the sin is taken away! Thus it will finally become manifest, when it is too late to heal, what kind of "worthless physicians" (Job 13:4) those were who healed the wound of the people superficially and said: "Peace, peace!" when there is no peace. Jeremiah 6:14.

The ancient Jews called the Messiah a "Man of Atonement" or "Cleansing": as the only true priest who should finish the transgression and make an end of sins. Daniel 9:24. Now, if such a thing had happened in all the world, but not in you and me, how would the greatest of all the works of God and Christ help us!

<column-break/>

7. And if his hand is not able to reach as far as is enough for a small animal, then he shall bring for his trespass, which he has committed, two turtledoves or two young pigeons unto the LORD; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.
8. And he shall bring them unto the priest, who shall offer that which is for the sin offering first, and nip off its head near its neck, but shall not divide it asunder.
9. And he shall sprinkle of the blood of the sin offering upon the side of the altar, and the rest of the blood shall be wrung out at the bottom of the altar. It is a sin offering.
10. And he shall prepare the second for a burnt offering, according to the ordinance. So shall the priest make atonement for him for his sin which he has committed, and it shall be forgiven him.

---

<margin>v. 7. If it was)</margin> that someone did not have the means to give a sheep or goat, as he was required to do in the fixed and unmovable sacrifice, he could also give a lesser offering according to his means. Nonetheless, the poor were not to be spared from making amends for their guilt: if he could afford birds, he gave those: namely, two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

<margin>One for a sin offering, the other for a burnt offering)</margin> Because the latter always had to accompany the former.

<margin>v. 8. For the pigeon that was to be a sin offering,</margin> the priest—at whichever part of the altar he wished—used his nails against the nape of the neck to cut into the throat, and thus opened the veins. However, in this case, the head of the bird was not torn off, as in the burnt offering, but remained on the torso for the "adornment of the sacrifice," as Rabbi Levi Barzel writes <note>original: "ap. Hottinger. de jur. Hebr. n. 128." Refers to Levi ben Gershom as quoted in Hottinger’s *On Hebrew Law*.</note>. We note here briefly regarding the

<margin>nipping off of the head)</margin> what has not found a place elsewhere <note>original: "(a) nicht Platz gefunden."</note>. According to the Weimar Bible, the Hebrew word <term>מלק</term> <note>Melaq: A technical term for a specific way of killing sacrificial birds using the thumbnail.</note> means as much as "to wring" or "turn," but not to tear off entirely. And so it should be here. Otherwise, Buxtorf writes in his Lexicons that it normally means to tear off the head with the nail or to cut into it; all Hebrews agree with this and consider it one of the most difficult tasks in the entire Levitical priesthood. <note>original citations: Buxtorf’s Lexicons; Bochart’s *Hierozoïcon*; Saubert’s *On Ancient Sacrifices*.</note>

<margin>v. 9. Of the blood,</margin> the priest sprinkled some below the ledge of the altar and let the rest bleed out at the base of the altar.

As soon as the blood was out, the bird was not burned; rather, the whole bird belonged to the priest and was for his food, as Josephus reports <note>original: "l. 3. Antiq. c. 10." - Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3.</note>. For from all sin offerings of private individuals, the priests had the remainder.

<margin>v. 10. The other pigeon</margin> was offered as a burnt offering, in the manner and fashion prescribed for the burnt offering of birds in Chapter 1:15, 16.

### Ch. V. The III. Book of Moses (Leviticus). 457

11. But if his hand cannot reach to two turtledoves or two young pigeons, then he shall bring for his offering, for that in which he has sinned, a tenth part of an ephah <note>An ephah was a standard dry measure, roughly equivalent to 22 liters; a tenth part is about 2.2 liters.</note> of fine flour for a sin offering. He shall put no oil upon it, nor shall he put any frankincense thereon: for it is a sin offering.
12. And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest shall take his handful of it as a memorial offering thereof, and burn it on the altar alongside the offerings made by fire to the LORD. It is a sin offering.
13. And the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin, which he has committed in any of these things: and it shall be forgiven him, and it shall belong to the priest as the grain offering.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> If, however, one was so poor that he could not even buy pigeons, he was still required to bring at least as much flour as was necessary for daily sustenance, as if they were to be punished, as it were, with a one-day fast. And

Since no oil or frankincense was permitted with this flour, as is usually done with the grain offering, this served as a testimony to how sins deprive us of the joy of the Spirit and its influence, especially in prayer. Ephesians 4:30.

The Hebrews therefore call this sin offering, in the specific cases mentioned above, an "ascending and descending offering" <note>original: *auf- und niedersteigendes Opfer*, likely referring to the *Korban Oleh ve-Yored*, an offering whose value fluctuates based on the petitioner's financial status</note>, which GOD in His goodness ordered so that for these four specific sins, such small offerings could be made, so that everyone could easily bear the cost—because one could fall into these four sins much more easily than any others. (a)

<margin>No oil nor frankincense on it)</margin> For how should the oil of joy and the incense of sweetness be fitting where it instead says: *I go crooked and very bowed down; I go mourning all the day long. My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness?* <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 38:6-7.</note> Consideration is also given here to poverty, which does not have much to give.

<margin>v. 12.</margin> Otherwise, it was offered just as the grain offerings were usually offered: the priest lifted it up to the LORD and brought it to the altar, taking a handful after he had salted it with the salt that was up by one of the horns of the altar, and threw it into the fire along with the salt, but kept the remainder for himself. Lev. 7:10. For

GOD and the priests shared all sin offerings between them, except for the "standing" offerings of the High Priest and the entire community, and those where some of the blood entered the Holy Place; from these, they received nothing, but everything was burned.

<margin>v. 13. Shall make atonement for him concerning his sin)</margin> But if the sin remains, how can or should an atonement occur? For sin is the only disturber of peace that disrupts everything and separates us from our GOD. Therefore, whenever and wherever sin remains and is not effectively and truly removed and extinguished, the wrath, condemnation, guilt, and bond to death must necessarily remain with it.

<note>(a) Hotting. *de jur. Hebr.* n. 121. (Hottinger, *On Hebrew Laws*, no. 121).</note>

<column-break/>

14. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
15. If a soul commits a breach of trust <note>original: *Untreu*, often translated as "sacrilege" or "trespass"</note> and sins through error in the things which are holy to the LORD; then he shall bring for his trespass offering to the LORD a ram without blemish out of the flocks, according to your valuation in silver shekels, after the shekel of the sanctuary, for a trespass offering.
16. And he shall make restitution for the harm that he has done in the holy thing, and shall add the fifth part thereto, and give it to the priest; and the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering: and it shall be forgiven him.
17. And

Here, some specific trespasses are now recounted. When someone has trespassed against things consecrated to GOD—such as firstfruits, tithes, and the like—and acted unfaithfully by withholding such things from the priests, provided it happened through error and not by intent (which would have been theft); then he had to offer a ram as a sacrifice, along with the value of what was withheld (as the priest would estimate it), and additionally give a fifth part of the estimated value as a penalty. This was so they might learn to act cautiously and faithfully pay their dues to the priests, lest they lose GOD’s blessing and instead draw GOD’s righteous curse upon themselves; the prophet Malachi deals with this at length in Chapter 1:8, 14 and 3:8–11. Believers in the New Testament are also warned at length about such unfaithfulness, that they should not shorten the sustenance appointed for the ministers of the Gospel, or provide it too sparingly, which also brings them into debt before the LORD. See 1 Cor. 9:4–14 and 2 Cor. 9:6-7.

<margin>v. 15. Through error)</margin> This is therefore to be understood as one who did it out of ignorance. If someone did it intentionally, he was scourged for it, and after enduring the punishment, he was not bound to return the principal or the fifth part.

<margin>v. 16. He shall make restitution)</margin> If the item was still at its original value and undamaged, he had to give back exactly what he had taken. But if it was no longer in his power and could not be recovered, he paid for it, and always added the fifth part as a penalty.

<margin>Atonement with the ram)</margin> This was presented to the LORD in the inner court toward the north side of the altar; the one who brought it laid his hands between its horns and confessed his sin and guilt. Thereupon he slaughtered the ram, and the priest caught the blood, stirred it well, and sprinkled it with the silver basin all around the base of the altar, etc.

<margin>So it shall be forgiven)</margin> Otherwise not. Reflect on this, O soul, you who may not be precisely malicious but yet harbor many unrecognized sins; learn here to examine your Pharisaical mind. How often do you trespass with false judgment against things consecrated to the Lord, and yet think you do well because the Lord acts for a while as if they do not concern Him, veiling them with a dark shroud of uncomeliness so that the foundation and thoughts of many hearts may be revealed. But God will look into it at the right time and will know how to care for what is consecrated to Him: and then He will also set before your eyes your impropriety, so that you will be ashamed of your conduct.

So see to it now that you rectify this fault, and rather add a contribution of your valuation than hold back your hand.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter V.

5. And it shall come to pass, when he shall be guilty in any of these things, that he shall confess that in which he has sinned.
6. And he shall bring his guilt offering to the LORD for his sin, which he has committed: a female from the flock, namely a lamb or a young goat, for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin.

**v. 5. Confess)** Drusius <note>Johannes Drusius (1550–1616) was a renowned Flemish scholar of the Old Testament and Hebrew language.</note> (a) describes this confession as follows: Whoever had sinned would place his hand between the horns of the animal and say: "O LORD! I have sinned, I have transgressed Your commandment, and have done evil before You in this or that way. See, I am sorry, and I am ashamed of my deed; I will do it no more!"

**v. 6. Bring a guilt offering)** In these cases, the offering was not a fixed, immovable, or strictly set sacrifice; rather, it was set according to one's means. It was established so that whoever was able to give, necessarily had to give either a

<margin>Female from the flock, or goat)</margin>
Not a mother goat that has already borne young, as it is given in some of Luther's translations, but rather a nursing goat or a year-old sheep; this was intended to acknowledge the great weakness and corruption of human nature, which they then treated in the same manner as the sin offering.

<margin>Atonement)</margin>
or cleansing from his sin. For by "atonement," nothing else is to be understood but "at-one-ment" or unity with GOD, when God and man are as one. This, however, cannot happen or be brought about as long as sin comes between them and separates man from God. Isaiah 59:2.

Now, the Spirit of God has indeed hidden two effects under the word "atone" or "cleanse": 1) to cover, and 2) to cleanse, wash away, or reconcile. However, this does not mean a "cloak for vice" (1 Peter 2:16) when it signifies "covering," nor should it be understood as a hiding of sin. Rather, it is like a plaster laid over a wound to cover it, and thus to cure and heal it. In this way, one meaning unites with the other.

Admittedly, the Jewish actions in this matter were ceremonial and "poor elements" <note>A reference to Galatians 4:9, describing the temporary nature of Old Testament rituals compared to the Gospel.</note>. Nevertheless, they prefigured the precious and dear truths of God regarding reconciliation with God and the cleansing from sin. The essential cleansing from our sins through Christ is meant and indicated through this ceremonial cleansing. Hebrews 9:13-14.

But if sin were only covered in such a way that it nevertheless remained always within us, what kind of extraordinary benefit would reconciliation or cleansing be? It would be nothing more than a foul and stinking abscess being covered with a skin; the gnawing and accusation of the guilty conscience would be stilled and satisfied for a time; the wrongdoer would be given a brief respite, and his punishment merely delayed for a while. O, what a miserable atonement that would be! For the sore covered with a crust will and must break open again, and judgment and vengeance will pursue the sinner until the sin is taken away! Thus, it will finally be revealed, when it is too late to heal, what kind of "worthless physicians" (Job 13:4) those were who healed the wound of the people superficially and said: "Peace, peace!" when there is no peace. Jeremiah 6:14.

The ancient Jews called the Messiah a "Man of Atonement" or "Cleansing," as the only true Priest who would finish the transgression and make an end of sins. Daniel 9:24. Now, even if such a thing happened in all the world, but not in you and me, what would the greatest of all the works of God and Christ help us!

<margin>(a) On the location, dissertation on Leviticus, chapter 13.</margin>

<column-break/>

7. And if his hand cannot reach as much as is sufficient for a small animal, then he shall bring for his guilt offering, for that in which he has sinned, two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the LORD; one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering.
8. And he shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer that which is for the sin offering first, and pinch off its head near its neck, but shall not divide them asunder.
9. And he shall sprinkle of the blood of the sin offering upon the side of the altar, and the rest of the blood shall be drained out at the base of the altar. It is a sin offering.
10. And he shall prepare the second for a burnt offering, according to the law. Thus the priest shall make atonement for him for his sin which he has committed, and it shall be forgiven him.

**v. 7. If it were that someone did not have the means)** to give a sheep or goat, as he was required to do in the fixed and immovable offerings, he could also give a lesser offering according to his ability. Nevertheless, the poor were not to be spared from making amends for their guilt. If he could afford birds, he gave those: namely two turtledoves or two young pigeons.

<margin>One for a sin offering, the other for a burnt offering)</margin>
Because the latter always had to accompany the former.

**v. 8. From the pigeon that was to be a sin offering,** the priest—at whatever place on the altar he wished—used his fingernail against the neck to cut into the throat, and thus opened the veins. However, the head of the bird was not torn off here, as it was in the burnt offering, but remained attached to the torso for the "adornment of the sacrifice," as Rabbi Levi of Barcelona (b) writes. We note here briefly concerning the

<margin>Pinching off the head)</margin>
what Placcius <note>Vincent Placcius (1642–1699), a German jurist and writer.</note> did not find. According to the Weimar Bible, the Hebrew word <term>מלקה</term> <note>Melikah: The specific sacrificial method of killing a bird with a fingernail.</note> means as much as "to turn around," but not to tear off entirely. And so it was supposed to be here. Otherwise, Buxtorf <note>Johannes Buxtorf (1564–1629), the preeminent Hebraist of his time.</note> writes in both Lexicons that it normally means to tear off the head with the nail or to cut into it; all Hebrews agree with this and consider it one of the most difficult tasks in the entire Levitical priesthood. (b)

**v. 9. From the blood, the priest sprinkled some below** the rim of the altar, and let the rest bleed out at the base of the altar.

As soon as the blood was out, the bird was not burned, but the entire bird belonged to the priest and was for his food, as Josephus (c) reports. For the priests received the remainder from all sin offerings of specific individuals.

**v. 10. The other pigeon was sacrificed as a burnt offering,** in the manner and way prescribed for the burnt offering of birds in chapter 1, verses 15 and 16.

### The Third Book of Moses. Ch. V.

17. And if a soul shall indeed sin, in that he has acted wrongly against any of all those commandments of the LORD concerning things which should not be done; and he did not know it, so that he has become guilty: then he shall bear his iniquity.
18. And he shall bring a perfect ram from the flock, according to your valuation, for a guilt offering to the priest, and the priest shall make atonement for him regarding his error, wherein he strayed while he did not know it: so it shall be forgiven him.
19. It is a guilt offering; he has certainly become guilty before the LORD.

---

v. 17. Also, a guilt offering had to be given by one who stood in doubt as to whether he had committed so great a sin that, had it been done knowingly and intentionally, would have deserved extirpation <note>The Hebrew term is 'Kareth,' referring to being "cut off" from the community or divine favor.</note>: it is these doubtful sins that are spoken of here.
3. E. <note>likely "3rd Explanation"</note> If someone has two kinds of fat before him, one of which is permitted to be eaten and the other forbidden <note>The forbidden fat is 'chelev,' which was reserved for the altar.</note>: and he eats one, but the other goes missing; yet he does not know which of the two he had eaten, and thus stands in doubt: he had to bring his guilt offering.
v. 18. In all these cases, this guilt offering had to be a ram, worth two shekels of silver, according to the shekel of the sanctuary—that is, according to our currency, 1 Reichsthaler <note>original: "Rthlr."; a large silver coin used in the translator's time to help readers visualize the value.</note>. It could not be of lesser value, but certainly could be of better quality (a).
But what if someone is poor and does not have enough to buy a ram? See to it then that you become rich. God must have His ram in such a case, and being poor does not count here.
How everything in this doctrine of offerings is so full of deep mysteries! See how necessary Christ is to you! Just as all offerings overshadow Him, so much more does the ram, which was also once appointed by God in the place of Isaac.
Thus must we acquire Christ for ourselves with the shekel of the sanctuary, so that He may take away our sins. The holy shekel, however, has the form of our faith. This you must have, otherwise no reconciliation is to be had.
v. 19. Furthermore, it should be noted regarding this and the preceding offering how they are explicitly spoken of in relation to Christ. Namely, that God sent His Son as an offering for sin; that is, as a sin offering (Romans 8:3). For He, who knew no sin, was made sin for us; that is, a sin offering, according to the Greek way of speaking <note>The Greek word 'hamartia' can mean both "sin" and "sin offering."</note> which follows the Hebrew (2 Corinthians 5:21). And how He gave His soul or His life as a guilt offering (Isaiah 53:10). Thus, Christ had to atone and make satisfaction for our known sins—indeed, for our debts, whereby we have sinned either unknowingly and out of error, or even grossly—and had to reconcile us: provided that one does not sin willfully, by persisting in unbelief and letting sin reign within. For then no further sacrifice remains for sin, but a terrifying expectation of judgment and fiery zeal that will consume the adversaries (Hebrews 10:26-27; see also Numbers 15:30-31).
Therefore, O you immortal souls, because your errors and your ignorances are already far too many, do not add—O do not add—willful transgressions to them, lest the guilt of your sins grows over your head and, as a heavy burden, presses you down into the lowest hell!
(a) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona <note>original: "R. Levi Barselou."</note> cited in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Law*, number 122 <note>original: "ap. Hotting. de jur. Hebr. n. 122."</note>.

20. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
21. When a soul shall sin and commit a breach of faith against the LORD, such that he denies to his neighbor <gloss>(a)</gloss> what was entrusted to him, or what was placed in his hand, or what he has robbed, or where he has wronged his neighbor;
<margin>(a) Leviticus 19:11, 13.</margin>
22. Or has found something lost, and denied it and sworn falsely, in any of all those things which a person can do to sin in such matters:
23. <unclear>S</unclear> <note>The letter "S" likely begins the next verse "So it shall be," but is cut off or abbreviated.</note>

For the rest, they were to deal faithfully with their neighbor’s goods: whether something was given to someone for safekeeping, or lent for use; or if something was found; or in whatever way one deals with a neighbor regarding temporal goods and perhaps does him wrong therein, by force or by false affirmation. Whatever the circumstances of such a thing, the damage was to be restored, and beyond that, a fifth part was to be given as a penalty, and a ram brought and sacrificed as a guilt offering and atonement for the sin. Just as it is strictly forbidden to believers in the New Testament to commit even the slightest infidelity in such earthly matters—that is, that no one should overstep and take advantage of his brother in trade, for the Lord is the avenger of all these things. For God has not called us to uncleanness, but to holiness (1 Thessalonians 4:6-7).
v. 20. (The LORD spoke) And must not the words of the LORD be understood more according to the majesty of the Speaker than according to the incapacity of the listeners and readers? But the Lord is the Spirit. Thus, what He speaks is to be received and understood more according to the spirit than according to the letter. Indeed, it is not only spiritual, what He tells and speaks, but is itself Spirit and Life (John 6:63).
v. 21. (Wronged) It may have happened knowingly and intentionally, or unknowingly.
v. 22. (Which a person can do) That a thing is possible does not yet prove that it is actual. But if a thing is actual, then it is established that it is also possible and can happen; and where the facts themselves appear and speak, no proof of that is necessary.
(In such things) A great multitude of sins from various kinds of offenses, which people are accustomed to inflicting upon one another, are summarized and indicated in these words. These may be condensed into two main sources, which are called Violence and Fraud.
Now, whoever is weak and incapable of the deeper mystery must build themselves up from the letter as best they can in such things, and envision the abominableness of all these types of sins.
Origen <gloss>(a)</gloss>, however, cannot believe that such a sin according to the letter could occur among the people of God, especially in the Christian Church, because one should have learned Christ differently. But will our modern Christians remain so? They who fail the test in this way, neither according to the spirit nor the letter.
Since, therefore, such coarse and abominable sins do not concern the Church of Christ according to the letter (one canceling the other out), the learned and pious Church teacher <note>referring to Origen</note> applies this law spiritually to the Church of Christ.
(a) Origen, Homily 4 on Leviticus 6 <note>original: "hom. 4. in Lev. 6."</note>.

### Chapter V. The Third Book of Moses.

23. So shall it be, when he has sinned and become guilty, that he shall restore the stolen thing which he has robbed, or the wrong in which he has acted unjustly, or the thing entrusted which was committed to him, or the lost thing which he has found;

24. Or anything for which he has sworn falsely: and he shall restore it in its principal sum, and shall add the fifth part more to it <gloss>(a)</gloss>. To the one to whom it belongs he shall give it, on the day of his guilt offering. <margin>(a) Numbers 5:6, 7.</margin>

->The<-

---

**restore)** This sin of fraud (say the Hebrews <note>original: "Hebräer (a)"</note>) will not be forgiven him in eternity if he does not restore what is owed. He must also reconcile with the other person whom he has wronged and ask them for forgiveness. If the other person will not forgive him, he should ask them three times through three different people. — If the other person dies before he has received forgiveness, he takes ten people with him to the grave and says: "I have sinned against the LORD, the GOD of Israel, and against this person [N.] in such and such a way." If he owes him money, he gives it to his heirs. If he does not know who his heir is, he deposits it with the court.
As long as such a person, who has cheated his neighbor of something, does not return such ill-gotten goods, his guilt offering was not accepted. <note>original: "(b)" refers to later footnote for Lightfoot</note>
Violence and fraud break the bond of human **society**, indeed the bond with GOD; they make the soul desolate, waste, and lonely, without GOD and man. These bonds cannot be reunited until full restitution has occurred. The sin of fraud and violence is not forgiven until that which was taken has been returned. Should this not be a hard word for many?
In the meantime, notice the wisdom and goodness of the most-just GOD, the Judge of all the world, who removes all obstacles and stumbling blocks from among us, so that His royal law may find room in their hearts, and we may owe no man anything but love. What is more just than the rule of the most-just Judge of all the world?
**The stolen thing)** This robbery is also committed when people take and appropriate for themselves all the promises of God which do not yet belong to them, and thereby lay violent hands on the Kingdom of GOD before the day of John the Baptist has begun to dawn within them. *Matthew 11:13*. For he who does not enter the sheepfold through the door of the death and life of Christ, but by another way, is a thief and a robber. *John 10:1*.
Otherwise, the word **restore** is properly applied to that very thing which was secretly taken or stolen: *Judges 17:13*. Just as **paying back** or **replacing** is more properly understood as the price or value of a thing. And what then might be
**The thing entrusted)** Let us search a little deeper here and go to the foundation which is closest to us, so that we may have more benefit from the Scripture and its contemplation: thus we will find that to each of us a **deposit** <note>original: "Depoſitum," a legal term for property held in trust</note> has been entrusted to trade with; namely our precious soul and body, and the **Image of GOD** stamped therein: which is to be used for our LORD's purpose.
This pledge, this good thing deposited with us for safekeeping, must be restored entirely to our GOD. No replacement in value can be given for it: it must be returned to GOD Himself.

<margin>v. 24. The 5th part more)</margin> If one confesses his guilt voluntarily. But where witnesses were present who first had to convict him, he had to give double, namely two fifth-parts. <note>original: "(a)" referring to Drusius</note>
<margin>along with your valuation for a guilt offering. v. 18.</margin>
But how this is to be understood spiritually, let us see. The number five is very often, indeed almost always, taken for the **five senses**. These must be withdrawn from misuse in worldly affairs and restored to the LORD in repentant and holy works. Indeed, we should add another five to these, namely the senses of the **inward man**: whereby we then, with a pure heart, shall either see GOD, or have an ear to hear the teaching of Christ, or perceive the fragrance of which the Apostle speaks in *2 Corinthians 2:14-16*, or taste how friendly the LORD is, or touch the Word of Life with our hands.
<margin>To the one to whom it belongs)</margin> If there was no one there to whom it could be given, then such unjust goods were forfeited to the LORD and given to the priests, who then performed the service. <note>original: "(b)"</note>

The perfect ram, the head of the sheep—Christ outside of us—does not accomplish it alone. **Christ in us**, the faith that is active through love, the faith which purifies the heart (*Acts 15:9*), must give you the weight.
<margin>v. 26. Thus shall he—make atonement—and he shall be forgiven)</margin> Since we still have time, let us strive for such an atonement, which will most certainly follow a preceding purification. While godless men and hypocrites, out of self-love and fear of punishment, only plead for the forgiveness of sins, let us, out of true hatred for the same, kill our sin in sincere daily repentance, and pray that the LORD would take it away.

### The Third Book of Moses. Ch. VI.

# Chapter VI.

->The perpetual fire upon the altar / Grain offerings of the priests / and the consumption of the sin offerings.<-

And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Command Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the burnt offering. It is that which goes up in the fire upon the altar all night until the morning, where the fire of the altar shall be kept burning upon it.

Through the daily burnt offering of the two lambs, one of which had to be offered in the morning and the other in the evening, the fire was to be kept constantly burning on the altar, even throughout the entire night until the morning. At that time, the ashes first had to be gathered while wearing the holy garments and placed beside the altar; then the first morning offering was prepared and ignited along with the fat from the peace offering. Afterward, however, the priest had to put on his ordinary, regular garments to carry the ashes out to a clean place dedicated for this purpose.

v. 2. **That which goes up in the fire)** The fire, by completely consuming the offering, took it up with itself and, as it were, transformed it into itself: a depiction of the most intimate communion during the purification, which is promoted by fire and completed by the blood of the lamb.

The nature of fire is to shine, and as a burning light, to penetrate, search through, refine, and purify everything—to consume what is foreign, and to transform into itself whatever is capable of its nature, taking it up with it into the heights.

Therefore, this offering also takes its name from <term>Olah (עלה)<note>meaning "to ascend" or "that which goes up"</note></term>: whereby we lose nothing, but rather rise through the fire into the heights and unite ourselves most intimately with God. For according to the spirit, this kind of offering puts on the divine nature, which is a fire, and conversely puts off the earthly nature, which cannot endure the fire at all. For everything desires to be with its own kind: and it is no wonder that God was reconciled through the fire offering, since the world itself is to be renewed through fire.

**The fire of the altar)** is called thus because it was to be everlasting, and the offerings were not to be lit with any other fire.

By this, it was depicted that our hearts should always stand in fervent love toward God and our neighbor: which fire of love can be maintained in no other way than through constant prayer, as one should pray without ceasing; also through fervent meditation on the law of the LORD day and night, Ps. 1:2, where one should also speak and wait with one's heart upon one's bed at night, Ps. 4:4 <note>The original cites Ps. 4:5, following the German numbering</note>, namely for a revelation of the divine mysteries, which one should preserve well in the morning in a pure heart.

The early Christian church learned from the true Jewish church to hold no divine service without fire or burning candles. And although something of this sort is still practiced here and there today, it is nonetheless only a dark shadow of a mimicked custom, wherein the divine fire has long since been extinguished.

<column-break/>

3. And the priest shall put on his linen garment, and he shall put linen breeches over his flesh, and shall take up the ashes after the fire has consumed the burnt offering on the altar, and he shall lay them beside the altar. c. 1:16.
4. Afterward he shall take off his garments and put on other garments, and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place.
5. And the fire on the altar shall be kept burning by it; it shall not go out; but the priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and arrange the burnt offering on it, and burn the fat of the peace offerings on it.
6. A perpetual fire shall be kept burning on the altar; it shall not go out. 7. And

v. 3. When the altar was to be cleaned early in the morning, the priest who was found worthy of this through the lot had to wash himself and sanctify his hands and feet. Once he had washed, he took the silver fire-pan and climbed up the altar with it, took some of the glowing coals consumed in the middle of the fire, as well as some ash (no less than a handful), in his fire-pan, and went down from the altar again to the ground, about 10 cubits <note>approx. 15 feet</note> toward the north <note>original: "mitternachtwärts" (midnight-wards), an archaic term for North</note> to the ash heap, which was there toward the east <note>original: "Morgen des Aufgangs"</note> three hand-breadths from the ascent, and poured the ash and glowing coals there. His brothers, the other priests, ran toward him, brought hands and feet <note>to assist</note>, took brooms and shovels with them, went up the altar, and swept the ash of the burnt wood and the offerings from all sides into a round heap in the center of the altar’s hearth, shaped like an apple: partly for the decoration of the altar, and partly so that the fire would burn better when the ash was removed. Now, when this heap grew and the ash became plentiful and finally had to be removed, they took a large ash-pot, so large that about half a malter <note>a historical dry measure</note> might fit in it, and put a little of the much ash into it, which remained there until they had filled all other ash with shovels into other ash-pots and carried all the ash away. (a) After which, the ash in the large ash-pot was doubtless put back on the altar, so that it would never be without ash.

This cleaning of the altar was performed by the priests in holy priestly garments and was thus likewise

---

a piece of the divine service just as the offering itself.

v. 4. But when the ash had been brought down and was to be carried out of the Tabernacle and outside the camp; the priests who carried out such ash had to take off their holy garments and carry it out in their own common clothes; yet to a clean place. And

When we have presented our bodies to God as a sacrifice and consumed our strengths in His service, then the ashes of our decayed bodies will also be in good keeping, from which they shall be awakened again.

v. 5. 6. Thus, three piles of fire were made daily on the altar and maintained with wood (b): the pile for the offering, toward the east; the pile for incense, toward the south and west; and the pile of perpetual fire, which was undoubtedly toward the north, from which the other piles, if they had burned out, were renewed and ignited. Paul undoubtedly refers to this perpetual fire in 1 Thess. 5:19 <note>"Quench not the Spirit"</note>.

(a) R. Levi Barzelon. in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Laws*, p. 131. R. Judah Leo, book 2, *On the Temple*, ch. 13, § 82 & ch. 14, § 90.
(b) R. Judah Leo, book 2, *On the Temple*, ch. 13, § 76. R. Levi Barzelon. in Hottinger's *On Hebrew Laws*, p. 132. Cunaeus, book 2, *On the Hebrew Republic*, ch. 11. Buxtorf, *History of the Sacred Fire*.

### Ch. VI. The Third Book of Moses.

7. And this is the law of the grain offering: the sons of Aaron shall bring it before the face of the Lord, in front of the altar.
8. And he shall lift up a handful from it; from the fine flour of the grain offering and from its oil, and all the frankincense that is upon the grain offering: and he shall burn it upon the altar for a pleasing aroma, as a memorial offering for the Lord.
9. But the remainder of it shall Aaron and his sons consume: it shall be eaten with unleavened bread in a holy place: they shall eat it in the courtyard of the Tabernacle of the Congregation. <note>The "Tabernacle of the Congregation" is often called the Tent of Meeting.</note>
10. It shall not be baked with leaven. I have given it as their portion from my offerings made by fire. It is most holy, like the sin offering and like the guilt offering.
11. Every male among the sons of Aaron shall eat it. This shall be an everlasting statute among your descendants regarding the offerings of the Lord made by fire. Everything that touches them shall be holy.

<note>The grain offerings of the people were already treated in greater detail in Chapter 2.</note>
<note>v. 8. When it says, "his handful," it is not to be understood as a large handful. For the priest would rather defile the grain offering if he stretched his hand out too far. Rather, it was a very small amount that he took, whereby the tips of the fingers rested against the middle of the flat palm. <margin>(a) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, cited in Hottinger, *On Hebrew Law*, no. 133.</margin></note>
<note>v. 9. What remained of the fine flour and oil was sanctified by the burning of the handful and belonged to the priests. Of the frankincense, however, the priests received nothing.</note>
<note>In a holy place, in the courtyard of the Tabernacle, toward the North <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally midnight, used historically to mean North</note>, where the dining chambers were located.</note>
<note>This was to remind the priests how they should enjoy their nourishment in the fear of God with moderation, as if before the face of the Lord; and since they received it because of their service at the altar, they should attend to that service carefully. Furthermore, since it had to be eaten with unleavened bread, it showed how, especially during the enjoyment of food, all corrupt old nature and evil desires should be far away, since sin entered the world through the eating of forbidden fruit.</note>
<note>Believers in the New Testament, since they are all called to be spiritual priests, should remember that they are to view all food as being blessed again in Christ, as a gift of grace. Since God's honor is present wherever they eat or drink, they must do so to the glory of God (1 Cor. 10:31). This should be done before the face of God, where one should refrain from all immoderate pleasure and all vain talk, and instead speak of useful and edifying things. See Col. 4:6; Eph. 4:29.</note>
<note>v. 11. Every male) Not the wives or daughters of the priests.</note>

12. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
13. This shall be the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when he shall be anointed: a tenth part of an ephah <note>An ephah was a standard dry measure, roughly 22 liters; a tenth part is about 2.2 liters.</note> of fine flour for a perpetual grain offering, half of it in the morning and half of it in the evening. <margin>Sirach 45:17.</margin>
14. It shall be prepared in a pan with oil: there you shall bring it roasted. You shall offer the grain offering in baked pieces for a pleasing aroma to the Lord.
15. And the priest who is anointed in his stead from among his sons shall do this. This is an everlasting statute: it shall be entirely burned to the Lord.
16. For every grain offering of a priest shall be a whole offering; it shall not be eaten. <meta>v. 17.</meta>

<note>This was the High Priest’s first offering with which he entered his office; the same applied to the common priests.</note>
<note>v. 13. For a perpetual grain offering) He had to make this offering daily from his own means and at his own expense. <margin>(a) Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3, Ch. 10. Rabbi Judah Leo, *On the Temple*, Book 3, Ch. 18, f. 107.</margin></note>
<note>Half in the morning and half in the evening) Simultaneously with the daily burnt offering, following the daily grain offering and before the daily drink offering.</note>
<note>The law of the Lord, with which the souls of men are to be fed, also had to be divided into two parts by the priest: namely, into the Letter and into the Spirit. One half, that of the Letter, was to be presented in the morning, in the early time of the Law, and brought at that time a new light and a new day. In the evening, however, the Spirit was to be poured out, leading everything into and toward the Spirit.</note>
<note>v. 14. You shall... offer) It was not necessary, however, for the High Priest to always do this himself in person; he could also have it done by the other priests.</note>
<note>v. 15. In his stead) From this, the Hebrews likewise prove that this offering of the High Priest had to occur and be repeated daily.</note>
<note>v. 16. What is special here is that while a handful of the people's grain offering was burned as a memorial, here the entire grain offering had to be burned. Therefore, it was called a "whole offering" (Deut. 33:10). This gives rise to the thought that while believers in their common calling may take something with their hand from their earthly wealth for charitable gifts and scatter it among the poor (see Ps. 112:9), those who dedicate themselves to the service of the Gospel should apply whatever comes to them—and is not necessary for their own or their family's maintenance—entirely to the service of their neighbor, whether in bodily or spiritual matters. For what is collected from this and held back, rather than being entirely sacrificed, usually carries no blessing. The example of Paul is well worth noting here (Phil. 4:10–19). It was also a prototype of the sacrifice of righteousness and the "whole offering" which was to be offered by Christ when the Lord began to do good to Zion (Ps. 51:21).</note>

### The Third Book of Moses. Ch. VI.

17. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:

18. Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering. In the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the sin offering shall be slaughtered, before the face of the **LORD**. It is the Most Holy.

19. The priest who offers it for sin shall eat it. It shall be eaten in a holy place in the courtyard of the Tabernacle of the Congregation. <note>The "Tabernacle of the Congregation" refers to the Tent of Meeting, the portable sanctuary of the Israelites.</note>

20. Everything that touches its flesh shall be holy; and whoever splashes any of its blood upon a garment, that upon which it was splashed you shall wash in a holy place.

---

<margin>v. 17.</margin> The **LORD** spoke to Moses and said.) And the Holy Spirit speaks to us and says through the Apostle Paul in Hebrews 10:26: "If we sin willfully after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remains no more sacrifice for sins." <note>original: "Hebr. 10/26. So wir muthwillig sündigen / nachdem wir die Erkenntniß der Wahrheit empfangen haben; so ist weiter kein Opffer mehr für die Sünde."</note> Thus it is now, that we continue on—

<margin>v. 18.</margin> This is the law of the sin offering.) that we should be planted with Christ in a death like his, so that our old self should be crucified with him; in order that the body of sin might be done away with, and that we should henceforth not serve sin. Romans 6:5-6.

<margin>v. 19. 20.</margin> "If these things are grasped only according to the letter," (writes Origen here once again (a)) "then we shall be more of a hindrance to the Christian religion and ruin it, rather than creating edification. But if they are properly noted and accepted, in a manner worthy of God, then from the hearing of them such a Jew will arise as Paul (b) describes, who is hidden within. Many do not understand this distinction between a visible and an invisible Jew, and for that reason, they not only find such Scriptural texts loathsome, but they also turn away from God himself, who gave such laws and Scripture to men, and they devise for themselves another god of their own.

"Just as visible and invisible things generally have a great relationship with one another, and the world consists of their connection; so must one also look upon Holy Scripture, as it consists of visible and invisible things: like a body, namely the letter which is seen; and then further a soul, the hidden inner meaning; and indeed even a spirit, in those heavenly and divine things which it contains within itself. And since this is so, let us—calling upon God, who himself gave the soul and the body and the spirit to the Scripture—leave the body to those who were before us, and the spirit to those who come after us and will reach the Kingdom of Heaven, but let us keep for ourselves the soul of the law, as much as is fitting for the present.

"Just as the Jew must therefore be hidden within, so also his sacrifice and the eating of the sacrifice happen not in the flesh, but in the spirit. Since the sacrifices are also different—some belonging to God alone, others of which Aaron and his sons the priests might eat, others their daughters and wives, and others the sacrificing Israelites—you, who are a hidden Jew, must not seek all these sacrifices in visible animals, nor expect to find them in mute cattle: but in yourself and in your soul. There you will encounter whole herds of cattle and sheep and goats, and even birds of the heaven, because you are indeed a small world <term>microcosm|The idea that a human being is a "little world" reflecting the entire universe.</term>.

<margin>(a) In Leviticus chapter 7, homily 5. <note>original Latin: "in Lev. c. 7. hom. 5."</note> (b) Romans 2:28-29.</margin>

—to recognize: as James has made mention of the elders.

<column-break/>

21. And an earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken. But if it was cooked in a bronze vessel, it shall be scoured and rinsed with water.

22. Every male among the priests shall eat of it. It is the Most Holy.

23. But no sin offering whose blood is brought into the Tabernacle of the Congregation to make atonement in the Holy Place shall be eaten; it shall be burned with fire.

---

"But consider only what great goodness and mercy of God it is, that he commands the sin offering to be slaughtered at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, which belongs to God alone. This is to give the repentant sinner—who brings the sacrifice of a contrite and broken spirit in true repentance and conversion to the Lord—to understand that he already stands in a holy place, under the fellowship of that which belongs to God.

"Who then is the one who sacrifices before the face of the Lord? Without doubt, it is he who does not go away from the face of God like Cain (Genesis 4:14–16), but rather seeks His face with confidence.

"Where is the Most Holy to be sought in this, if not in the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who alone became a sacrifice for sin?

"He who is the sacrifice is the very same who is also the priest who offers the sacrifice. The very same shall also eat the sin offering—or, as it is often and properly called, the sin itself of the one sacrificing. And how does that happen? How is our Lord and Savior the sins of the people? Hear what the Scripture says: The Lord our God is a consuming fire. What now does this divine fire consume? We shall not be so foolish as to think it consumes wood, straw, or iron. Rather, it consumes sins and cleanses from them.

"Now it follows that according to the image of Him who instituted the priesthood of the Church, His servants should also be.

Thus, by the fact that the sin offerings had to be eaten at a holy place by the priest who made atonement with them, and that he was thereby to bear the iniquity of the sinner to atone for him (Chapter 10:17), it is also represented in a spiritual sense how the faithful should reveal their sins to the elders and other holy ones, to souls visible in the fellowship of God, so that these may carry the soul's sins in prayer and pray for them, so that the sins may be forgiven them (James 5:14-16).

"For what else is the holy place in which the same shall be eaten, other than unfeigned faith and a heart of pure heart and good conscience? Whoever dwells therein certainly stands in a holy place. For otherwise, no holy place is to be sought on earth, over which the decree of God once went forth: 'Cursed be the ground for your sake!' But a pure, upright faith and holy conduct is a holy place.

<margin>v. 21.</margin> It is remarkable, however, that the pots in which the meat of the sin offering was cooked, if they were earthen, were broken as soon as the meat was cooked.

By which one can understand in a spiritual sense, according to the above, that in the case of such sins as have been confessed to one in secret—which one has also taken into one's own heart out of sincere compassion and carried in prayer—the vessel of our memory should be, as it were, broken and rinsed out through love, so that one forgets such sins and does not spread them further to the shame of the neighbor.

<margin>v. 22.</margin> But there must also be masculine souls and beings in the spirit (1 John 2:13–14) and thus spiritual priests, to whom this confession can be entrusted, who thereby [bring] their plea into the fellowship of sins for their atonement—

<margin>
v. 1. When the guilt offering, as well as other parts of the Levitical service, are called the Most Holy, it is to be understood that all those parts had a special holiness above others, and were to be handled very precisely and with great reverence.

<column-break/>

Just as the guilt offering is compared here with the sin offering, the difference between them is also difficult to find. One can only say that some sins carry a greater weight of guilt; and also that sins committed unknowingly still make us guilty before **God.** This might be perceived when the conscience feels a peculiar pressure, or when one experiences no blessing or progress in a certain action or undertaking. From this, one should judge that they may have unknowingly incurred guilt, for which one should heartily ask **God's** forgiveness, or call upon **God** to graciously reveal such a fault and guilt to us.

The Hebrew words used for "sin offering" and "guilt offering" actually mean "sin" and "guilt" themselves in their most literal sense. This is also how they are rendered in the translations of Hosea 4:8 and 2 Corinthians 5:21. Whether they are distinct from one another, and how, is a matter where opinions have greatly diverged. That there is a difference between them is undeniably proven by this passage. How they differ, however, is hard to recognize. One scholar places the difference in this: that sin is the *commission* of evil, while guilt or transgression is the *omission* of good. Another makes the first a knowing sin of awareness, and the other a sin of ignorance by which a person is overtaken. Perhaps the observation of the following distinction may also be useful: according to this, the first, *chataah* <note>Hebrew: חַטָּאָה, meaning sin or miss the mark</note>, is that sin into which a person falls by themselves; *ascham* <note>Hebrew: אָשָׁם, meaning guilt or trespass</note> is the sin into which one falls through the offense and provocation of another. Examples of this distinction exist in chapter 4:3, Genesis 26:10, 1 Chronicles 22:3, and Proverbs 30:10. Although it cannot be denied that the other term may also be used in such cases.

However, it does not matter so much, and we should not remain hung up on this or dwell on it too long. Rather, from the distinction of sins and their various names, we should learn to recognize that a general and common confession before **God**—simply saying we are poor sinners—is not sufficient. Instead, just as specific gifts were offered for specific sins, a more precise recounting of our sins is necessary. Despite the fact that the Hebrew language, in comparison to others, is very meager and deficient in words, it nevertheless has many words to express sin and godlessness.

But praised be **God** that, although our sins are many, even countless, He has given us—who believe and are obedient to Him—a High Priest whose blood and Spirit cleanse us from all sins! This eternal High Priest now also makes his believers and those who love Him into priests, to cleanse and sanctify others. **And**

**The priest who makes atonement with it shall have it)** Or: To the priest who performs the atonement belongs the sin and transgression. But is this not a hard saying? How does the sin and transgression belong to him? Answer: He shall eat it (chapter 6:26, 29). But how and why? Answer: So that they might bear the iniquity of the congregation (chapter 10:17). It was the priest's office to eat the sins of the people (Hosea 4:8). To "eat sin" is therefore as much as to consume it, and thus to destroy it. By making atonement for it, you eat it; and when you eat it, you make atonement for it. When you take an interest in a sinner—moving him to repentance through reminding, admonishing, teaching, and instructing, turning him from the error of his way, and leading him to an earnest improvement and change of his mind and vicious life—when you have brought him so far that **God** can be gracious to him upon true conversion, it can be said that you have "eaten" him. For the duty to remind, bear, and improve one another in love has long been out of fashion. Therefore, it is also difficult to recognize from *practice* that this is the Law of Christ (Galatians 6:2).

Whoever has been made a priest of the holy priesthood by the High Priest of our confession <note>Referring to Jesus Christ</note>, let him consider his office, and not make himself unworthy of the priest's portion that the **Lord** has assigned to him. When we bear our brother's sins, instruct him, admonish him, warn him, remind him, have compassion for him and suffer with him, pray and sigh for him, and thus seek to consume his sins in every way; then Wisdom has assured us that we shall be satisfied by the fruit of our mouth (Proverbs 12:14).

v. 17. The **LORD** spoke to Moses and said). Thus it is now, that we continue on—

v. 18. This is the law of the sin offering) that we should be planted with Christ in a death like his, so that our old self might be crucified with him; in order that the body of sin might be done away with, and that we should henceforth not serve sin. Romans 6:5-6. <note>original: "Röm. 6/5.6"</note>

"v. 19, 20. If these things are understood only according to the letter," (writes Origen here once again (a)) <note>referring to Origen's Homilies on Leviticus, a series of sermons explaining the spiritual meaning of the Law.</note> "then we shall be more of a hindrance to the Christian religion and bring it to ruin, rather than creating edification. But if they are properly noted and accepted, in a manner worthy of **GOD**, then from the hearing of them such a Jew shall arise as Paul (b) describes, who is hidden within. Many do not understand this distinction between a visible and an invisible Jew, and for that reason, they not only feel a loathing toward such scriptural texts, but even turn away from **GOD** himself, who gave such laws and scriptures to men, and they devise for themselves another god of their own.

"But just as visible and invisible things generally have a great kinship with one another, and the world consists of their connection; so also must one look upon the Holy Scripture, as it consists of visible and invisible things: like a body, namely the letter, which is seen; and then further a soul, the hidden inward meaning; and indeed even a spirit, in those heavenly and divine things which it contains. And since this is so, let us—calling upon **GOD**, who himself gave the soul and the body and the spirit to the Scripture—leave the body to those who were before us, and the spirit to those who come after us and are caught up into the kingdom of heaven, but keep the soul of the law for ourselves, as much as is fitting for the present.

"Just as the Jew must therefore be hidden within, so also his sacrifice and the eating of the sacrifice does not happen in the flesh, but in the spirit. Since the sacrifices are also different—some belonging to **God** alone, others which Aaron and his sons, the priests, might eat, others also their daughters and wives, and others also the sacrificing Israelites—you, who are a hidden Jew, must not seek all these sacrifices in visible animals, nor expect to find them in mute cattle: but rather in yourself and in your soul. There you will encounter—since you are indeed a small world <note>The concept of "Man as Microcosm" (a little world), a common philosophical idea that the human soul contains the essence of the entire universe.</note>—whole herds of cattle and sheep and goats, and even birds of the sky.

### 23. But no sin offering, from which any blood is brought into the Tabernacle of Meeting to make atonement in the Holy Place, shall be eaten; it shall be burned with fire.

"Consider only what great goodness and mercy of **God** it is, that he commands the sin offering to be slaughtered at the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered, which belongs to **God** alone: to give the repentant sinner—who in true remorse and conversion brings the sacrifice of a contrite and broken spirit to the **Lord**—to understand that he already stands in a holy place, and in the fellowship of that which belongs to **GOD**.

"Who then is he who sacrifices before the face of the **LORD**? Doubtless he who does not go away from the face of **GOD** like Cain, Genesis 4:14—16, <note>original: "1. Mos. 4/14—16"</note> but rather seeks His face as his trust.

"Wherein is the Most Holy to be sought here, if not in the only-begotten Son of **GOD**, our **Lord JESUS** Christ, who alone became a sacrifice for sin?

"He who is the sacrifice is the very same who is also the priest who offers the sacrifice. He himself shall also eat the sin offering, or—as it is often and properly called—the sin itself of the one sacrificing. And how does that happen? How is our **Lord** and Savior the sins of the people? Hear what the Scripture says: The **LORD** our **GOD** is a consuming fire. What does this divine fire consume? We shall not be so foolish as to think it consumes wood, straw, or iron. Rather, it consumes sins and cleanses from them.

"It follows now that after the image of him who dies as the sacrifice, his ministers are also appointed to the church.

Thus, through the fact that the sin offerings had to be eaten at a holy place by the priest who made atonement with them, and that he was thereby to bear the iniquity of the sinner so that he might atone for him (Chapter 10:17), it is also represented in a spiritual sense how the faithful should reveal their sins to the elders and other saints in the fellowship of **GOD**, and to those souls, so that they may bring the souls before God in prayer and intercede for them, so that their sins may be forgiven. James 5:14, 15, 16. <note>original: "Jac. 5/14. 15. 16."</note>

"For what is the holy place in which the sacrifice is to be eaten, other than unfeigned faith and love from a pure heart and a good conscience? Whoever stands therein, surely stands in a holy place. For otherwise, no holy place is to be sought on earth, over which the decree of **GOD** once went forth: 'Cursed be the ground for your sake!' But a pure, upright faith and a holy walk is a holy place.

v. 21. It is noteworthy, however, that the pots in which the flesh of the sin offering was cooked, if they were earthen, were broken as soon as the flesh was cooked.

By which one can understand in a spiritual sense, according to the above, that in the case of such sins as have been confessed to one in secret—which one has also taken into one's heart out of sincere compassion and brought before God in prayer—the vessel of our memory should be, as it were, broken and extinguished through love, so that one forgets such sins and does not spread them further to the shame of one's neighbor.

The Hebrew words used for "sin offering" and "guilt offering" otherwise most properly mean sin and guilt themselves. And so it is translated in Hosea 4:8 and 2 Corinthians 5:21. Whether they are distinct from one another, and how, is a matter of much debate. That there is a distinction between them is undeniably proven by this passage. How they differ, however, is difficult to discern. One defines the difference by saying that sin is the commission of evil, while guilt or transgression is the omission of good.
