->### The Third Book of Moses. Chap. X.<-

12. And Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and to Ithamar, his sons who were left: Take the grain offering <note>The original "Speis-Opffer" refers to a non-meat offering, typically fine flour mixed with oil.</note> that remains from the offerings of the Lord made by fire, and eat it with unleavened bread beside the altar. For it is the most holy thing.
13. But you shall eat it in a holy place. For it is your allotted portion and your sons' allotted portion of the offerings of the Lord made by fire. For so I have been commanded.
14. Also the breast of the wave offering <note>The "Web-Opffer" was moved horizontally toward the altar and back, symbolizing a gift to God that is returned to the priest.</note> and the shoulder of the heave offering <note>The "Heb-Opffer" was lifted vertically to designate it for God's service.</note> you shall eat in a clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you. For they are given as your allotted portion and your sons' allotted portion from the peace offerings of the children of Israel.
15. They shall bring the shoulder of the heave offering and the breast of the wave offering along with the fire offering of the fat, to wave it as a wave offering before the face of the Lord: and it shall be yours and your sons' with you as an eternal statute, as the Lord has commanded.

---

The Lord intended to provide for his servants' nourishment and that of their families before their service; and indeed the most tender of all meat: so that he granted them a refreshment in their laborious ministry.

v. 12. Which they must enjoy with unleavened bread: which shall remind them and all of us who share in the benefits of God in our labor, that one should use earthly gifts without the leaven of the perverse plague of lust and sinful excess.

The nature of leaven is that it sweetens the dough, yet has a sharpness within it whereby the sweetness is soured. The holy grain offering of the Lord shall not be performed with a turgid and haughty heart like that of the Pharisees, nor should the participation in the Lord’s table occur in the old nature, which makes all sweetness sour.

<margin>(a) Origen, Homily 4 on Leviticus 6.</margin>
v. 13. 14. In a holy place / in a clean place) Note, (calls out the zealous teacher Origen <gloss>(a)</gloss>) you who cause divisions in the churches by introducing foreign and perverse doctrine, and think that the holy flesh "of the Word of God may be eaten outside the temple and the courts of God! Your offerings are unclean because they are not according to the law! It must be eaten in a holy place; in the courts of the Lord! But what else are these courts than those which the wall of faith surrounds, which the pillars of hope hold together, and the expansion of love enlarges? Where these are not, there is no holy flesh to be had, much less to be eaten.

v. 15. It shall be yours — as an eternal statute) Thus this ordinance remains generally under the New Testament as the Apostle presents it: that the Lord has commanded that those who preach the Gospel should also live from the Gospel: 1 Corinthians 9:13, 14, where this provision was also intended.

<column-break/>

16. And Moses diligently sought the goat of the sin offering, and behold, it was burnt. And he was angry with Eleazar and with Ithamar, Aaron's sons who were left, and spoke:
17. Why have you not eaten the sin offering in a holy place? For it is most holy, and he has given it to you that you should bear the iniquity of the congregation, to make atonement for them before the face of the Lord.
18. Behold, its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary. You should indeed have eaten it in the holy place, as I commanded.
19. But Aaron spoke to Moses: Behold, today they have offered their sin offering and their burnt offering before the face of the Lord, and such things have happened to me; if I had eaten the sin offering today, would it have been good in the eyes of the Lord?
20. When Moses heard that, he let it be good in his eyes.

<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

---

Moses rightly insisted on the observation of God's order, as the priests were to eat of the sin offering to show how they, as it were, took the guilt of the sinner upon themselves, and entered into the fellowship of the sacrifice, as if they had atoned for the sin with the blood; which came to its true essence in Christ: in that he took our sins upon himself, and presented himself as a sin offering, and actually shed his blood for sin, and truly reconciled Israel, which the prefigurations <note>The "Fürbilder" are Old Testament symbols or types that foreshadow New Testament realities.</note> could not do. See Isaiah 53:4, 12. Now, when we eat of his flesh and drink of his blood according to his command, we enter into the fellowship of his body sacrificed for us for our reconciliation. John 6:53, 54. Matthew 26:26, 27.

v. 17. The most holy) There was a difference in the offerings. The most holy and noble were burnt offerings, grain offerings, sin offerings, guilt offerings, and the thank offerings of the whole congregation. The holy offerings were the thank offerings of individual persons, as well as all other offerings not included in these five.

The most holy were slaughtered to the north of the altar of burnt offering; but the holy ones were not.

v. 18. Its blood was not brought into the inner part of the sanctuary) Therefore the meat should have been eaten. chapter 4:5, 6:30.

You should have eaten it) Whatever of the most holy could be eaten was eaten only in the inner court, and only by priests alone.

God had the blood and fat from it; everything else belonged to the priests: to those who offered it before all others; though they could well invite their sons and other priests to it.

It had to be eaten the same day it was offered, or that same night. <gloss>(a)</gloss>

<margin>(a) Philo, Book on Victims, page 653.</margin>
v. 19. 20. Since Aaron excused the oversight of his sons, saying they would certainly not have eaten it with pleasure in such sadness; Moses overlooks such a transgression. Just as such a thing deserves a sharper punishment when it happens out of insolence—as the crime of the previous sons <note>Referring to Nadab and Abihu's "strange fire."</note> is to be seen—so it is viewed differently when it happens out of melancholy, where one can easily fail. See Chapter 6:19, 23.

<summary>Moses instructs Aaron and his sons on the proper consumption of sacrificial portions, but a conflict arises when they burn a sin offering out of grief rather than eating it. Moses ultimately accepts Aaron's explanation that their mourning made them unfit for the celebratory aspect of the meal.</summary>

# Chapter XI.
## The Distinction Between Clean and Unclean Animals.

> 1. And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them:
> 2. Speak to the children of Israel and say: These are the animals which you shall eat among all the beasts that are on the earth.
> 3. Everything that divides the hoof, and is wholly cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the beasts; that you shall eat.
> 4. Nevertheless, you shall not eat these among those that chew the cud or those that divide the hoof: the camel; for it chews the cud indeed, but it does not divide the hoof: it is unclean to you.
> 5. And the rabbit <note>The German "Caninchen" (rabbit) likely refers to the rock hyrax or coney mentioned in modern translations.</note>; for it chews the cud indeed, but it does not divide the hoof: it is unclean to you.

---

Regarding what the situation was before the Great Flood concerning clean and unclean animals, one may look back at the notes on Genesis 7:2. However, at that time, nothing was expressly forbidden to be eaten, but rather everything was permitted, as seen in Genesis 9:3–4. But now, God wished to forbid the eating of many animals, as well as fish, birds, and creeping things, since they already had a sufficient supply of permitted animals and livestock in such a good and fruitful land. And indeed, God undoubtedly looked—though not so much upon the health or unhealthiness of the meat of the forbidden animals—rather toward the accusation of the impurity of man, who had not yet been reconciled through the blood of the Mediator <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as the "Mittler" or Mediator between God and humanity.</note>, who alone can cleanse us from sin. Therefore, they were meant to notice the characteristics of the forbidden animals and how they shared commonalities with the unclean lusts and vices of men. Thus, they should hate and avoid such vices, not only in themselves but also in others, and therefore carefully flee from their common company. See Psalm 1:1, 26:4–5, and 101:3–5.

v. 2. **These—animals which)** The animals were indeed all created good by God, but through the Fall, many came to the "left side," where the poison of nature prevails. Therefore, unclean spirits find their influence and seat more easily in such creatures.

v. 3. As a sign of purity, the splitting of the hoof and chewing of the cud are established, and such animals are permitted and ordained as good and convenient for food.

However, it is beyond doubt that the intention here pertains to man himself.

Thus, chewing the cud and splitting the hoof can represent reflection and constancy in one’s actions; for one considers everything well, and thereafter remains constant in it. The opposite of this is thoughtlessness, frivolity, and inconstancy in one's dealings and undertakings.

v. 4. And so, using the animals named here as examples, one can notice the characteristics of unclean men: those who are inconstant in all their ways (James 1:8), forgetful hearers of the Word (v. 26). They are like camels, burdened with the goods and cares of this world, so that they cannot easily enter through the narrow gate of the Kingdom of God (Matthew 19:24).

v. 5. Like rabbits, they burrow only into earthly things and the worries of sustenance. See 1 Timothy 6:9.

<column-break/>

> 7. And the pig; for it divides the hoof indeed, so that it is wholly cloven-footed, but it does not chew the cud at all: it is unclean to you.
> 8. Of their flesh you shall not eat, nor shall you touch their carcass: they are unclean to you.

v. 6. They are fearful and despondent in doing good, failing to take hold of it. See Revelation 21:8 and Proverbs 22:13.

v. 7. They wallow with the pigs in the filth of fleshly lusts (2 Peter 2:22) and are of the same nature as a pig, which—according to the depiction of St. Barnabas <note>Referring to the Epistle of Barnabas, an early Christian text that uses allegorical interpretations of the Law.</note>—does not know the Lord when it eats, and when it hungers, it only cries out, but is satisfied once it has eaten its fill. Indeed, as Lactantius Firmianus (a) expresses the matter even more clearly:
" [It is] an unclean, foul, and filth-loving
" animal that never looks toward heaven, but
" with its mouth constantly cares only for its
" belly and fodder; yes, it stretches itself out
" on the earth into the mire; also, as long as it
" lives, it provides no use like other animals, which
" serve either for riding or for agriculture, or
" pull wagons, or carry loads, or are useful for
" clothing and other things with their hides,
" or provide milk, or guard the house, etc.
" So God, under the prohibition of pig's
" flesh, wanted to forbid the swinish life, where
" one serves only one's belly and lusts, and lets
" oneself be fattened like pigs for the day of 
" slaughter, but has no qualities for the 
" exercise of righteous works. For these are 
" certainly true 'swine-people,' who can give 
" their spirit nothing high or noble to do, 
" but throw it down into the mire of animalistic 
" nature, where it must fatten itself in the 
" company of pigs with filth."

Those among the blind "name-Christians" who vex and torment Jews with pig's flesh should know that they are not dealing only with Jews, but are treating the Law of God with contempt. They also only make the Jews more stubborn, as the Jews imagine they are suffering as martyrs for the Law and the honor of God. Though such a law no longer binds us in its strictness, the foundation of the Law binds us all the more in the New Testament. And although the distinction of foods has been abolished, there is—as mentioned—a deep ground hidden beneath it, which, alongside the sense and intention of God, is not abolished at all; therefore, such and similar laws remain unchangeable in that regard. Accordingly, it behooves us to speak with reverence of all and every law of Moses, because they have as their author the holy and unfathomable God, who looks much further than the letter. Rather, many "swinish-minded" people have more need to examine themselves to see if they, like the Gadarenes, do not love their swine more than Christ.

v. 8. Also belonging here are the wild animals, such as lions, bears, tigers, and the like; as well as horses, donkeys, dogs, and the like: in which cruelty, unruliness, laziness, malice, envy, and similar vices can be noted. See Ezekiel 32:2 and Daniel 7:4–7, where kings in these world-empires were represented under the image of wild animals. Psalm 32:9, etc., etc.; Matthew 7:6.

So too belong here the greed and cruelty of wolves (Zephaniah 3:3, Matthew 7:15) and the cunning and stalking of foxes (Ezekiel 13:4, Song of Solomon 2:15, Luke 13:32).

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XI.

9. These you shall eat of all that are in the waters: everything that has fins and scales in the waters, in the seas, and in the rivers, those you shall eat.

10. But everything that does not have fins and scales in the seas and in the rivers, of all that teem in the waters and of every living creature that is in the water, that shall be an abomination to you;

11. Yes, they shall be an abomination to you: you shall not eat of their flesh, and you shall have their carcasses in detestation.

12. Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales shall be an abomination to you.

---

God the Lord had to deal with the Jews as with weak children, to whom the first letters of divine teaching had to be presented under images, so that they might thereby be gradually led to something greater. But after the time of childhood and youth has been put aside, and the true Man of Wisdom has come forth in Christ: then indeed the "beggarly elements" <note>original: "dürfftige Elementen"; a reference to Galatians 4:9, referring to the basic religious rituals that are superseded by Christ.</note> have fallen away, but the essence of the matter remains and must remain, which is now set forth only in stronger foods and mysteries with a much higher expression of discourse.

<margin>v. 9.</margin> In the clean fish, it can be observed how they raise themselves up with their fins and lean upon the water, and are covered with scales: so that these can represent the wings of faith in the believers, with which they always soar upward again in the waters of tribulation and rely on the gracious help of God; whereby they are covered with the whole armor of God, as if with scales and shields. Conversely, the unclean fish mostly have the nature of serpents and commonly hide themselves in hollow holes. And this is also the nature of unclean people: they hide themselves in all their doing and use a serpent-like cunning therein. The whales and crocodiles and other sea-monsters are also very treacherous and cruel, and are therefore an image of tyrants. Isaiah 27:1. And the Leviathan is used as an image of the Antichrist and false prophets in Job 40:20 and 41.

One has, therefore, the testimony and authority of Scripture before them when one also understands humans by these: in which the Savior Himself compares the Kingdom of God to a net, with which all kinds of fish are caught, good and bad, clean and unclean.

<margin>v. 10.</margin> What does not have fins and scales) That is, as it were, nothing but flesh or entirely fleshly, and cannot rise into the heights, as those provided with them may soar and come closer to our air, like those who seek, as it were, the freedom of the spirit.

<margin>v. 11, 12.</margin> Those others, however, who are not at all suited for swimming, and therefore mostly find themselves down at the bottom where the mud is greatest, and thus nourish themselves in filth and darkness, therefore provide an image of unclean sinners, with whom one should have no fellowship, nor even eat with them. 1 Cor. 5:11.

**Owl:** just as in the two preceding verses, mention of other species of the same has already occurred.

**Bittern)** The Jews understand by this what is otherwise called the Cuckoo, and prove it from the Talmud, where it is called *Kuk*.

**Pelican)** The Hebrew word is <term>Racham</term> <note>Hebrew: רָחָם, referring to a carrion vulture or similar bird</note>, and signifies in its linguistic origin to love heartily and inwardly, to be merciful and to have compassion for someone, so that the bowels are moved by it. Thus, it is understood as such a natural love as exists between parents and their children. Now, because the vulture is said to have such a love for its young that—as Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani, a 16th-century Italian humanist known for his work on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> relates from the Egyptian monuments—she wounds herself so that she may nourish the young with her blood; some therefore place this bird here. Others, however, place the Pelican, because precisely the same is said of them. And the next following bird

<margin>v. 13-15.</margin> These are then mostly birds of prey that nourish themselves on carcasses: and are thus an image of the greedy, who look around in all places for a profit, and with whom one can keep no contented friendship; they are also something detestable in the eyes of God as idolaters, and therefore should be fled from by the believers. You shall detest—the eagle, the hawk, and the ravens etc.) than, as Saint Barnabas likewise gave it briefly and beautifully: Do not associate with and do not make yourself like such people who do not know how to provide food for themselves through their own sweat and labor, but live solely on what they take from others by force, and to that end keep a sharp eye on those who walk in simplicity, in order to make them their prey. <note>A reference to the Epistle of Barnabas, an early Christian treatise that provides allegorical interpretations of the Mosaic Law.</note>

<margin>v. 16. Cuckoo)</margin> Among the Germans, its meat is not eaten as it is considered unclean; whereas the Italians, especially, consider the young to be a rare meal. It is the most fearful among all birds, and yet is feared everywhere by all small birds because it resembles the falcon.

This bird is forbidden for the Israel of God to eat not without reason. For it is not only accused of common ingratitude toward its mother, but also that it even kills her and eats her along with its own young. Furthermore, it is said never to make a nest itself, but to lay its eggs in other birds' nests and let them be hatched by them. Further, this bird has only one tone, from which it received its name in many languages, and with which it thus always calls itself out, thereby illustrating and representing the vain boasters. Thus pride and vain honor, ingratitude, fear, and cruelty are this bird's evil qualities, which shall be a horror and abomination to you, O Israel!

### Chapter XI. The Third Book of Moses.

19. And the stork, the heron after its kind, and the hoopoe, and the bat.
20. Everything that creeps among the birds, that goes on four legs, that shall be an abomination to you.
->21. Yet<-

---

<margin>(a) Aelian, Book 3, Chapter 23.</margin>
**v. 19. The Stork)** Naturalists (a) praise this bird for the intense natural love between the old and the young; it even derives its name in Hebrew from "godliness." <note>original: "Chasidah" (חֲסִידָה), which is related to "Chesed," meaning kindness or piety.</note>

Both the stork and the pelican migrate before winter, and when they return, they bring joyful news of the approaching spring, etc.

But why then are these birds reckoned among the unclean? Answer: Because their flesh is hard, tasteless, foul, and unhealthy to eat, etc. This is the natural cause, which pertains to the body.

But why should they be an abomination, since naturalists tell of so much good regarding especially the pelican and the stork; yet here the typological vice of the birds—as with the beasts—renders them actually unclean to Israel? Answer: The Lord did not want the mercy and natural love of the pelican and stork to be abolished, but rather preserved together, so that they might serve as living examples and witnesses among the birds of the air. To these, the Lord might point those humans who do not wish to increase and grow in the school of true knowledge. Thus, parents and children between whom communal love and affection is not great may see and learn it from the stork and the pelican. From the former, we may recognize our time and learn to face the judgment. Jeremiah 8:7.

These birds, and those like them, the Lord did not want killed, eaten, or consumed; indeed, to eat and consume them is an abomination. Rather, the Lord wanted them to proclaim or display their virtues, and to be perpetual reminders to humans, to remind them of their duties. For this reason, they also live for a very long time.

Both of these birds have no tongue, whereby they might chatter out their praise or let themselves be heard with singing. Just as one does not read that the most excellent saints spoke much, except for what they left behind in their writings. They all passed through this world in great silence and declared the praise of God with their lives and deeds, Psalm 63:4, and not their glory with their words. Everything known that Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob spoke could be written on very little paper. Of Abel, one does not read that he spoke a single word all the days of his life. Nevertheless, they were all righteous and full of faith. Hebrews 11. And whom may one place alongside them in this feeble age of time? When most cry out their own goodness, but few of the faithful or people of truth are found among the children of men.

If it should nevertheless seem strange to anyone that these birds are reckoned among the unclean, despite having no evil qualities themselves; let him know that, nevertheless, the vulture and pelican are exceedingly gluttonous birds; just as the pelican also has a double crop. Pliny calls it an insatiable animal. Yet it is always lean: either for the sake of its rapid digestion, or because its intestines have no capacity for retention, or because it has a kind of "eating-sickness" and "hound-hunger" <note>original: "Hunds-Hunger," an old term for bulimia or insatiable appetite.</note>, just as many churchgoers are insatiably eager listeners, and yet do not increase from their spiritual food.

**Heron)** Though others consider this more properly to be the bittern. Opinions are very divided.

According to the accounts of naturalists, the heron is one of the most virtuous among all birds, of singular temperance and moderation, wisdom and foresight, piety and love between the old and young toward one another. (b) In particular, the wisdom and prudence of this bird is most remarkable above all others; when it foresees a change in the weather or a storm, it soars above the clouds, and thus wisely and cautiously seeks to escape it.

<column-break/>

Who will now say that these are the qualities of unclean birds? Or who can therefore claim with certainty that the heron is meant here?

It would therefore be handled more correctly if one understood another bird here than the so chaste, temperate, pious, and loving, wise and cautious heron: so that through the translation one does not do him as much injustice as the world does to the generation of the righteous, when it regards and esteems them as unclean birds. One should not wonder that he is esteemed a godless person and a blasphemer who is loving and godly: that those are fashioned into fools in this world who are wise in God and cautious for a better world.

However, the bittern is also counted among the herons, because of some similarity in its external form and shape. But in its internal nature, there is likely little other agreement than that they are both birds: just as they also do not have the same feathers. The bittern is called a "star-heron" in Greek and Latin <note>original: "Asterias" in Greek, "Ardea stellaris" in Latin.</note>, because of its many star-like speckled spots. This bird is easily provoked to anger and fury, and then it goes for the eyes of those by whom it considers itself offended. It gives off a terrifying voice, like an ox. It is one of the laziest and most predatory of birds, so lazy that it can hardly fly for laziness.

What wonder is it then, if this is reckoned among the unclean birds! It does not want to soar to holy thoughts and inclinations, to heavenly things; but sits still in the nest of its old principles of vanity and laziness, and hatches others who are of its own understanding and judgment: lazy toward what is good, active in what is evil; it seeks to deprive man of the inner eye of faith, of understanding, of judgment, and of conscience.

From such birds of prey, guard and preserve yourself with great diligence, O Israel of God, you who are a prey and booty to every bird of prey, and let them be an abomination to you! Yet punish and instruct them in love and the fear of God. Through divine wisdom, teach all unwise and incautious birds to flee the judgments of God that shall come upon the earth: and be yourself a true heron, who soars above the clouds. Colossians 3:1.

**Bat)** That the Lord forbids you, O Israel, to eat of the night-birds or to have fellowship with them, is also no wonder. For your God wanted you to be like Him. This is the chief end of pure and undefiled religion. Now, however, He is Light, and in Him is no darkness at all. 1 John 1:5. But the devil is darkness and the prince thereof. Therefore, St. Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 2, compares the bat to the devil, who hates the light and loves the darkness. Now, as our Lord said of him: "The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me": so guard yourself, so that he may not, when he comes, find anything of his own in you; so that he may not find his lusts—which through your agreement and consent have become yours—living in you: so that he may not take both them and you away together, because you do not want to part from them! Isaiah 2:20.

Therefore, be not like the owls and bats, which have eyes and yet in truth do not see: who are sharp-sighted in judging the hidden things of darkness, but have no sight, no discernment of the clear daylight of life, the Sun of Righteousness, not at all; nor of the morning star, which rises in the hearts of the children of light. They have wings of contemplation and meditation, with which they give the appearance as if they were raising themselves and soaring toward heaven: but their entire speculation is directed solely toward earthly, worldly, and temporal things. Just as bats indeed have wings, yet cannot soar much above the earth. They are, in a wondrous way, enlightened by darkness and blinded by the light; says Ambrose.

v. 20. All these night-birds shall be an abomination to you, O Israel!

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XI.

**21.** Yet these you may eat of every flying creeping thing that goes on all fours, which has legs above its feet with which to hop upon the earth;
**22.** These of them you may eat: the locust after its kind, and the singing locust <note>likely referring to the bald locust or 'soleam'</note> after its kind, and the beetle after its kind, and the grasshopper after its kind.
**23.** But all other flying creeping things which have four feet shall be an abomination to you,
**24.** And by these you shall become unclean. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening.
**25.** And whoever carries any of their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.
**26.** Concerning every beast which divides the hoof but does not split it completely, and does not chew the cud; these shall be unclean to you. Everyone who touches them shall be unclean.

---

<margin>v. 21.</margin> Since, moreover, one cannot know for certain the specific species of all the birds named here—as there may well be many more and different species in the Eastern lands—one has partly followed the opinions of other translators in this matter, as they are given according to the species found in our own countries.

<margin>v. 22.</margin> Thus, the first general word *Arbeh* <note>Hebrew: אַרְבֶּה, the common migratory locust</note> is rendered here as "locusts"; the three following words, however, are set down by most translators with their Hebrew names. The English translation, however, makes three certain species of locusts out of them, which we have chosen to follow. Otherwise, such insects as frequently stay in the deserts are eaten, as is written of John the Baptist in Matthew 3:4. And so the famous naturalists Aristotle and Pliny testify of certain peoples, such as the Moors and Parthians, that these are used among them for food.

<margin>v. 23-25.</margin> But away with all those birds that claim the heavens and yet love the earth! Those may well be true "creeping birds," which indeed have wings, but only use them to fly into a manure pile like dung-beetles and wallow in the filth of the earth. And despite all this striving and wallowing, such unclean "manure-finches" <note>a derogatory term for those preoccupied with worldly vice</note> may nonetheless say: "Hey, we want to go to heaven too!"

<margin>v. 26.</margin> He who contemplates the Lord’s law and will day and night, who applies himself to prayer, and who thoughtfully considers the good he sees, hears, or reads within a prayerful spirit—so that he may transform it into his flesh and blood, that is, into his very essence and life—he stands in the quality of "chewing the cud."
But those who walk in the distinction between good and evil, such that they grasp the former and avoid the latter; they "split the hoof" rightly.
In the same way, our works must also have split hooves; so that in all our doing we direct ourselves toward both God and our neighbor, that we enter into God with all people, and in turn go out to all people with God. Thus are the works pure, in which we purely seek God’s honor and our neighbor’s salvation and benefit. And so it is to the contrary.

<column-break/>

**27.** And whatever goes on its paws, among all the animals that go on all fours, those shall be unclean to you. Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening.
**28.** And he who carries their carcass shall wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening. These shall be unclean to you.
**29.** Un

<insert>
All those works in which we think we seek God but neglect our neighbor are unclean. For though they may "chew the cud," they do not "split the hoof."
Likewise, those works in which we seem to care very much for our own well-being and the benefit of our neighbor, but do not observe God’s honor therein as we are bound to do, are also unclean. For though they may "split the hoof," "chewing the cud" is missing.
Thus, both must necessarily be together if our works are to please God and be spiritual nourishment for us.
We should indeed rightly serve one another and show faithfulness and help to one another in all spiritual and physical need; but we must also stand upright with Christ our Head for the glory of God. Then our works will be pure and nourish us for a holy life.
To such pure ones, all things are pure; but to the unclean and disobedient, who confess God with their mouths but deny Him with their works, nothing is pure—not even that which is clean—because their mind and conscience are unclean. For this reason, they shall be an abomination to God as well as to His people. Titus 1:15-16.

<margin>v. 27.</margin> And indeed, that such knowledge of this was held even in the Old Testament, the history of Aristeas <note>The *Letter of Aristeas*, an ancient account of the translation of the Septuagint</note> teaches us. At the time when the 70 interpreters under King Philadelphus translated the Bible from Hebrew into Greek, the High Priest Eleazar answered Aristeas and Andreas, who had put several questions to him: "So that we might not be infected through fellowship with any godlessness, nor corrupted by association with the godless, God has hedged us about with an established purity in food, drink, touch, sight, and hearing. For everything He has ordained for us, whether we use it or abstain from it, has its deep reason and cause. Therefore, one must not have such contemptuous and lowly thoughts of our Lawgiver, as if He were concerned about mice and weasels; rather, believe that everything was holily ordained by Him for the sake of righteousness, for the improvement of our lives and the preparation of our minds for holy thoughts. For example, the poultry which we may use are all tame and the purest of all, living on herbs and grains: such as doves, turtledoves, chickens, partridges, geese, and the like. But you will find that those forbidden to us for the most part eat meat, devour others, and prey upon those tame ones; indeed, they show themselves hostile not only toward them, but even fly at sheep and lambs, yes, and at humans themselves, not only the dead but also the living. Therefore, God attaches to them the noticeable mark of calling them unclean, and thereby teaches those to whom He gave the laws that they should be devoted to righteousness in their minds, oppress no one with violence, nor rob or take anything away, but rather arrange their whole life after the example of those tame animals that draw their nourishment from the plants of the earth and do not assume any violence against others of their kind. Thus, the Lawgiver wanted to bring to the minds of the understanding through these signs that they should love righteousness, oppress no one, and do nothing with violence. For since He did not want to permit the touching of the named animals because of the indwelling drive and inclinations that each of them has; how could He not have intended to show thereby how one should take care that our customs and life not be formed in a perverse way according to their nature?"

### Chapter XI. The Third Book of Moses. 481

**29.** And these shall be unclean to you among the creeping things that creep upon the earth: The weasel and the mouse and the toad, after their kind.
**30.** And the hedgehog, and the newt, and the lizard, and the snail, and the mole.
**31.** These are unclean to you among all the creeping things. Every one who touches them when they are dead shall be unclean until the evening.
**32.** And everything upon which any of them falls when they are dead shall be unclean, whether it be any wooden vessel or clothing or skin or sack. Any tool with which work is done must be put into water and is unclean until the evening; and so it shall be clean.

<margin>v. 29.</margin> These creeping animals can be an image of sloth;
<margin>v. 30.</margin> And those that burrow in the earth, as the moles do, can represent earthly-minded people who likewise only burrow in the things of this earth, lying as it were entirely buried in the terrestrial, and in heavenly things are quite foul and lazy, and as blind as moles. Hence we have the proverb, <term>Blinder than a mole</term> <note>original: "Talpa cæcior"</note>. This is used for ignorant, dull people, with whom alas! outward Christianity is filled in these final, difficult times, when the hearts of most are weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness, and with the cares of survival. Luke 21:34.
<margin>v. 31.</margin> These) 8 creeping animals. For others, such as for example snakes, scorpions, and the like, do not defile: even these eight do not defile through touch, except after their death.
This indicates how one should have no fellowship with the barren works of darkness of people who are dead in sins, but rather should rebuke them. Ephesians 5:11. To this also pertains the exhortation of the Apostle that one should carefully avoid the common company of such sinful people. 1 Corinthians 5:9-13. For here their evil tastes also corrupt good morals.
The lusts and vices are therefore what God’s people should neither touch nor defile themselves with, in either the Old or New Testament. Which conclusion they could easily have made for themselves in the Old Testament: If I am to abstain from such external things, how much more then must I abstain from sins? What cause would God otherwise have to forbid this and that, especially in food, if the great and wise God had not hidden something deeper and secret beneath it, with which we should not defile ourselves?
Concerning this, the aforementioned Eleazar <note>Likely referring to the High Priest Eleazar from the Letter of Aristeas, who provided allegorical explanations of the Law</note> speaks thus:
> "Just as God made an ordinance regarding food and drink, so he also diligently commanded how one should behave in things concerning hearing and touch, so that we neither do nor hear nor speak anything that is unbecoming. And so, likewise, these things and the causes for them are to be found in the natures of the animals which God has forbidden here. For the nature of these animals is only harmful and inclined to do damage. Just as mice devastate and ruin everything, and are not satisfied with seeking food for themselves, but handle everything they encounter to the detriment of humans. The nature of the weasel, however, has something peculiar in this regard: that such an animal, besides this property and inclination to do harm, has this unique trait: that it conceives with its ears and gives birth to its fruit through its mouth. <note>This reflects a common ancient and medieval folk belief about the biology of the weasel, often used as an allegory for speech and hearing.</note> By which then the so unclean nature and habit of humans is signified, as they spew out again through their unclean mouth what they received with unclean ears, and thus unceasingly defile and contaminate themselves and others through their ungodly being and life."

<margin>v. 32. 35.</margin> Not only was a person defiled by the unclean carcass of these eight creeping things, but also everything upon which it fell.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XI. 482

**41.** Indeed, every creeping creature that creeps upon the earth shall be an abomination; it shall not be eaten.
**42.** Everything that goes on its belly, and everything that goes on four feet, up to everything that has many feet, of all creeping creatures that creep upon the earth, these you shall not eat; for they are an abomination.

There is no doubt that although the New Testament contains no explicit prohibition of certain foods, it would not be harmful to our bodies to abstain from those things; for such abstinence contains within itself a counsel for health. Just as it is healthy for our souls to abstain from the vices and lusts that are represented by these creatures.

Man is dearer to God than he is to himself. Therefore, He cares not only for our soul, but also simultaneously for the well-being of the body, so that <term>a healthy mind may dwell in a healthy body</term> <note>This is a reference to the Latin phrase "mens sana in corpore sano."</note>. To that end, for our own benefit, He desires abstinence from certain things. In this, however, He certainly aims further, and has simultaneously bound Israel to abstain from fellowship with the Gentiles, which He commanded in so many other places with express words; just as He also gives a clear understanding of His meaning in Chapter 20, verse 24.

But what shall we say now, after the distinction between Jews and Gentiles has been removed? Should this Scripture, like a long-outdated letter, have become entirely useless? Far be it! How would that stand with the truth that "all Scripture is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness"? <note>2 Timothy 3:16</note>. Thus, this Scripture, as well as all others, must still have its spiritual use to this day. And who knows whether it might not also have a physical use, if it were so applied. For

Just as it is beyond all doubt—and also confessed and confirmed by experienced physicians after mature investigation—that all the things God forbade to eat do not harmonize with the health of our body, and for that reason, among others, the eating of blood and fat is forbidden; so it is also right and certain that God, who as the Creator knows the nature of all flesh best, and in this sense may be called a "Lord and God of all flesh" <note>Jeremiah 32:27</note>, has cared for human nature therein. Thus, we too can make use of the Scripture and the counsel of God within it for this reason.

And although the dividing wall of carnal ordinances between Jews and Gentiles is broken down, the heathen lifestyle—which constitutes true heathendom—is still spread everywhere; not only among Jews and Gentiles, but also among so-called Christians. It expresses itself in lewdness, lusts, and all the things which are listed one after another in 1 Peter 4:3.

That is therefore what defiles man and his soul! Those are the unclean animals, birds, and fish that shall be an abomination! namely, the abominations of sin prefigured by them. Just as, on the other hand, it is the salvation of our souls when we gladly act according to God’s commandments: which are good, sweet, righteous, pure, clear, and a healthy food.

With this, the answer is simultaneously given to a double question: namely, why did God forbid in the Old Testament what is not forbidden in the New Testament? and then, why were such animals declared unclean, when they were all created by God? The animals are only images of those vices which are primarily intended. These, however, are forbidden just as much—and even more so—in the New Testament than in the Old. And just as they arose through the Fall, so something has also penetrated through the Fall into the entire creation, and consequently also into the animals, which God did not create.

The creeping creatures, which draw their nourishment from the slime of the earth, are therefore actually the carnal vices and the people who wallow in them: such as, primarily, the lust for gluttony and drunkenness, unchastity, and the accompanying laziness, listlessness, and incapacity for good. All of this is unclean and makes unclean whoever does not guard themselves against it.

<column-break/>

**43.** Do not make your souls an abomination with any kind of creeping creature that creeps, and do not defile yourselves with them, that you should be defiled by them.
**44.** For I am the Lord your God: Therefore you shall sanctify yourselves, that you may be holy; for I am holy: and you shall not defile your souls with any creeping creature that slinks upon the earth.
**45.** For I am the Lord who brought you up out of the land of Egypt, that I may be your God. Therefore you shall be holy, for I am holy. <margin>Luke 6:36</margin>

<margin>v. 44.</margin> Since God now so earnestly cites His holiness as the basis of this law, and that they therefore must also be holy, He wanted to bring to their minds that, just as their bodies would be an abomination before Him if they ate of such animals declared unclean by Him or were touched by them, so much more would the uncleanness of their souls be an abomination before Him if they were defiled through association with the Gentiles, who defiled themselves in all sinful lusts. By this, He also wanted to withdraw them from all Gentile customs and ways of life; of which they later had a sorrowful experience in their dealings with the Moabites. <note>Numbers Chapter 25</note>.

I am holy) He is <term>kadosh</term> <note>original: "kadosch," Hebrew for holy or set apart</note>, that is, unmixed or set apart. He is set apart in His nature from all His creatures; yet in such a way that He is in them all: like the light in the whole air, which is yet not the air; like the soul in the body and in every part thereof, and is yet not the body. In this sense and understanding, we must be holy as God is holy. <note>2 Corinthians 6:17</note>.

The holiness which God demands is a holiness consistent with His own holiness. Now, the holiness of God is in Himself, from Himself, and before Himself. Thus, the holiness of the soul must be in God, from God, and before God. It must be in God, in that it consists only in Him; otherwise, it would be one's own holiness and would also rob Him of something. And from God, the pure holiness, which has not been accepted by God as holiness, can be so named. And before God, in that it is given back to Him, as to its end-goal and center-point, and must serve Him for His glorification. Thus, a soul that has arrived in God has nothing of itself, from itself, or for itself; but everything is taken up into God through the loss [of self] into Him. And just as what she has is not for her, so also it does not come from her. But since everything has come from God, so it has all flowed back there again. This then is the holiness which is peculiar to this level.

<margin>v. 45.</margin> This is the interpretation of the previous verse, and explains it even more clearly. God testifies that He has redeemed His people from captivity—which were their own inventions—so that He could make them lose themselves in Him.

The word, "that I may be your God," means as much as: so that I <margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 15:28</margin> might be everything in all things for you, in myself, and before myself. He does not say more; such as "that I may be in you" or "in your midst"; for that would be too little. Nor "that I may be before you"; but "that I may be God to you"; not before you, but in myself and before myself. Therefore you shall be holy, for I am also holy. Or, holy with this holiness, for it is My holiness.

# Chapter XI. The Third Book of Moses. 483 <note>original: "III. Buch Mose" refers to the book of Leviticus.</note>

**46.** This is the law of the livestock, and the birds, and every living soul that moves in the waters, and of every soul that creeps upon the earth.

**47.** That you may make a distinction between the unclean and the clean, and between the animal that is eaten and the animal that shall not be eaten.

---

Through this you should judge everything that lives: namely, what is perfect or imperfect. And through this very thing, you should recognize that I demand from you only the pure and right love. It is not that a less-perfect law was not given to those souls living within themselves—which they can and must follow, as they recognize no other. But the souls living in **God** must make this distinction. For that which is still good enough for others would be unclean to them; and for this reason, light has been given to them to recognize what they must accept and what they must reject. Others, however, do not yet have a complete discernment of this.

Now, although in the present day the distinction of foods has been abolished, *Colossians 2:16, 17*, and every creature of **God** is good and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving, *1 Timothy 4:4*; toward which also the vision given to **Peter** pointed—that through such animals the heathens in former times were depicted, and that they should now strive to join themselves to such people and bring them to the faith, and that all animals were now purified again so that they could be eaten, *Acts 10:11–15*. Yet believers of the New Testament must mostly guard themselves against a lust for such unhealthy animals, since **God** has provided enough healthy food for our necessity. Above all things, however, we must look much more toward distancing ourselves from common fellowship with such earthly and vice-ridden, unclean people, as such is very earnestly forbidden to us in *1 Corinthians 5:9, etc.* To this end also goes the warning of **Christ**, that one should not throw that which is holy before dogs or pearls before swine: because believers should only speak edifying things with others, whereas such things are despised by unclean and wicked natural "world-people" to their own harm, and they only mock them for it. *Matthew 7:6.* See also *Proverbs 23:6–9.*

Every human is either clean or unclean: and every person becomes food for their neighbor according to what they are. If a person is pure, upright, and of a good spirit, they will become a good and healthy food for their neighbor through fellowship, like an innocent sheep. But if they are evil and bring forth evil from the evil treasure of their heart, their neighbor will have little benefit from them.

In case someone should shake their head at this and—following the sense of those who said: "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?"—consider such an explanation forced and tasteless: let them first become better acquainted with the Scripture. Let them see whether that which is said of animals is not interpreted as referring to humans here and there throughout; and take *Acts 10* as an example. Then, once they are better grounded and instructed in the Evangelical mysteries, and the Word has become flesh and dwells within them, they will surely recognize that this is the **Lord’s** meaning in what is written here.

The reason, however, that the language of **Moses** is understood so differently is our own unequal condition.

<margin>(a) 2 Corinthians 3:16.</margin>
The Apostle says (a) that in the conversion to the **Lord**, the veil of **Moses** from the Old Testament and from our hearts is taken away. By this, he simultaneously gives us to understand that the less the understanding of these things lies open to us, the less we are yet converted to the **Lord**. If we, therefore, truly wish for the wonders in the law of the **Lord** to be opened to us, we must first of all be intent with all earnestness on renouncing all worldly ways and transitory lusts; seeking our delight instead in **God’s** law day and night, and converting to the **Lord** with our whole heart. Without this, we are not fit to understand the language of the Spirit—indeed, hardly even the letter in its entirety—and an atheistic mocker should blame himself that these things appear foolish and ridiculous to him.

## Chapter XII.
### The Purification of Women after Childbirth.

1. **AND** the **Lord** spoke to **Moses**, saying:

2. Speak to the children of **Israel** and say: When a woman brings forth seed and bears a son, she shall be unclean for seven days; according to the days of uncleanness for her sickness, she shall be unclean.

3. And on the eighth day, the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised.

<margin>(a) Psalm 24:4.</margin>
4. And she shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification: she shall touch no holy thing, nor shall she come into the sanctuary (a) until the days of her purification are fulfilled.

5. When...

---

After the atonement for sins was presented in the sacrifices, and in the previous chapter the various vices were depicted under the symbol of unclean animals—which one should not eat, and thus not take their characteristics upon oneself or absorb them through fellowship with such people—now in this chapter, our sinful birth, and in the following, our great and manifold corruption of nature, is presented under the illness of leprosy and other weaknesses of nature.

v. 2. Our unclean birth then had to be felt by the mother; in that we are conceived in lust, and the mother is specifically mentioned: "See, I was conceived from sinful seed, and my mother conceived me in sin." *Psalm 51:7.* <note>This citation follows the numbering in the author's Bible; in modern English Bibles, this is Psalm 51:5.</note>

She was declared unclean for seven days, and that undoubtedly along with her child, who was her flesh and blood, and she had to live set apart. On the evening of the 7th day, as the 8th day began, she bathed herself.

The 7 days, which make up a week, can indicate the time of this present life which we spend in this world, which also reached its completion in 7 days. As long as we live in this flesh and time, we have to do with our purification, which does not reach its completion until the 8th day of the coming world arrives. When something masculine is born in us, then everything is cut away from it that could still hinder the participation in and enjoyment of the covenant of union with **God**.

v. 3. On the eighth day, even if it fell on a Sabbath, the little boy was circumcised and thus accepted into the covenant of **God**, and so was declared cleaner along with the mother.

On the last great and glorious day of the Feast of Tabernacles, *John 7:37*, as on the eighth day, the foreskin of the heart of all those who fear **God** is cut away, and all true seed of **Abraham** is circumcised. This is the true circumcision on the 8th day.

v. 4. For her complete purification, the mother had to remain at home for 33 more days beyond the 7—thus 40 in total, or 6 weeks minus 2 days—and was not allowed to touch any holy things, such as the thank-offering, nor appear in the sanctuary for the sacrificial service until she had brought her offering.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

5. But if she bears a girl, she shall be unclean for two weeks, as in her impurity, and she shall remain in the blood of purification for sixty-six days.

For a girl, she had to be unclean for just as long—namely 14 days—and stay at home for 66 days. This may well point to the first source of sin, as the Apostle notes: **Adam** was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression; 1 Timothy 2:14. Thus, she, as it were, introduced sin, since it originated through her. But so that we do not bear a grudge against the female sex, we should remember how a woman, in turn, was to bring about salvation and life through the blessed birth of the Savior. Therefore, **Adam** immediately named his wife **Eve** <note>original: "Heva"</note>, that she might become a mother of all living. From this we can draw comfort again, and thus each person has cause to complain only about their own sin and corruption if they will not gratefully acknowledge and accept the offered grace in the blessed seed of the woman.
<gloss>two weeks: That is 14 days</gloss>
<gloss>And 66 days: That is a total of 80 days, or 12 weeks minus 4 days.</gloss>
We may certainly believe that nothing was ordained without the great wisdom of the Lawgiver in this matter, as in others.
Not only is a distinction made in the time of purification between a boy and a girl, but also for both between the first and subsequent time; between the first 7 and the following 33, and between the first 14 and the following 66 days. After the passing of the first 7 or 14 days, the woman <term>Kindbetterin: a woman in childbed or the postpartum period</term> was already purified in a certain way and was only forbidden from coming to the sanctuary. This may serve as a lesson to us: that we should not only seek to be purified to a certain degree, but must continue in it, and should cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and the spirit if we wish to attain and perfect holiness in the fear of **God**. 2 Corinthians 7:1. He who is righteous must become more and more righteous; and he who is pure must become more and more pure; Revelation 22:11, until the 40 spiritual days—after which Christ ascended to heaven—are fulfilled in us, and we are taken up into heaven with Him, once we have made our clothes thoroughly bright and white in the blood of this spotless Lamb. Just as we will then be raised in glory from one degree to another and go from clarity to clarity.
And although more time for purification was required here for a girl, this only serves as a testimony that ultimately the various births and creatures will be freed from all their impurities, even if more time belongs to some than to others. But **God** has already ordered everything in measure, number, and weight, and knows best how much and how long He should set for every unclean creature to end the days of its purification.
The 7 great days are ordained for the boy or the male image, which the Bride of the Lamb bears here in the spirit; thereafter the rest, each in its order.
Whoever has carried nothing masculine within themselves against sin, but has been womanish and soft in their conduct, will not attain forgiveness or purification from sins in two weeks, neither in this world nor the next. The rest is left to **God**, what He wishes to do in eternity.

<column-break/>

6. And when the days of her purification are fulfilled, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a lamb of one year old for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering, to the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation to the priest.
7. And he shall offer it before the face of the **LORD** and make atonement for her; thus she shall be clean from the fountain of her blood. This is the law for her who bears a boy or a girl.
8. But if her hand does not find enough for a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and one for a sin offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her: so she shall be clean.

Therefore, only one kind of offering was ordained for a son as well as for a daughter; namely, a 1-year-old lamb and a young pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering: to show through this that in the attainment of grace they would all be considered as one, whether man or woman. See Galatians 3:28.
v. 6. As soon as the full 40 or 80 days were over, the woman was indebted to the **LORD** for an offering, and she delivered it the following day if she was nearby; or, if she was far from the Tabernacle or the Temple, whenever it suited her best, or when she went up for the feast days. Most people postponed these offerings until then and went in groups (1 Samuel 2:22) to deliver their offering to the priest. But before the time when the full 40 or 80 days were ended, it could not happen, and if it did, it was not valid. As long as the sacrifice was not offered, she had to abstain from everything holy and could eat of nothing holy at all; she was also not fully purified until she brought her offering.
**Bring — to the door**) When the woman wished to be purified, she came very early to the Tabernacle or the Temple; and when it was time for the incense to be burned and the bell rang for prayer, the "Stationary Man" <note>The "Stationary Men" or *Ma'amadot* were lay Israelites who represented the people at daily sacrifices.</note> placed her by the Gate of **Nicanor**, by the small side-door that was there next to the great gate and was opened daily, so that she might be purified there. Then, when the daily burnt offering was sacrificed, her offering was slaughtered and sacrificed, and she was sprinkled with the blood of her sin offering and thereby fully purified.
v. 8. The poor had only to bring a pair of pigeons, which could be obtained for a small price; this offering was also brought by the mother of our Savior, Luke 2:24, and she thereby made known her physical poverty.
Where pigeons or turtledoves were brought for sacrifice, the older ones were taken for turtledoves—and the young ones for other pigeons; as both are then most pleasant and delicate to eat. The turtledoves were fit for sacrifice as soon as they began to shine and shimmer like gold. But when the [other] pigeons began to shimmer, they were unfit for it. (a)

---

In this sacrifice, they should long for the Lamb's innocence and gentleness and the dove's simplicity, through which the sins were lost.
This impurity of women in childbed is now taken away through **Christ's** blood, pure conception, and birth; and this blessing primarily benefits the believers, of whom it is said: She will be saved through childbearing, if she remains in faith and love and holiness with modesty. 1 Timothy 2:15.
All purification must be accomplished through the blood of the Lamb and through His spotless Dove-Spirit, which blood must be accepted in faith and applied for actual atonement.

# Chapter XIII.

->The various types of leprosy in humans and clothing.<-

AND the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:
2. When a person has a swelling, or a scab, or a bright spot on the skin of his body, and it appears to be the mark of leprosy on the skin of his body, then he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons, the priests.
3. And the priest shall examine the mark on the skin of the body: if the hair at the mark has turned white, and the appearance of the mark is deeper than the skin of his body, it is a mark of leprosy. When the priest has examined him, he shall declare him unclean.

---

Leprosy was formerly very common in the Promised Land, as can be seen here and there in the Scriptures. However, as many also believe, it seems to have been quite different from the modern kind—which covers the entire body with scales and is almost like the skin of an elephant <note>This refers to elephantiasis, a condition often confused with biblical leprosy in early modern medical thought.</note>. It was a special plague sent by God, with which He often punished the people of Israel in the otherwise very blessed and healthy land of Canaan for their stubbornness and disobedience. This is seen with Moses' sister, Miriam, in Numbers 12:10, and with King Uzziah in 2 Chronicles 26:20. Furthermore, not only humans but also houses and clothes became "leprous," a plague of which nothing is known today.

It was, however, such a great corruption of the blood that it broke out in a foul moisture or heat in the skin, and was therefore visible in such flowing and stinking matter <term>Epter: an archaic term for pus or discharge</term> and similar disgusting external damage to those persons. See Psalm 38:5-6.

v. 2. The judgment of this matter did not belong to the physicians, but to the priests, who were to judge between the clean and the unclean. This was for the purpose that such a person might be excluded from the community during the service in the Tabernacle of the Congregation.

Three types of conditions are recounted here: a swelling, which arises from great heat and finally breaks out on the skin as an ulcer or similar; a scab, which comes from foul moisture and breaks out into such pussy damage; and a bright spot, which may come from both foul moisture and heat. All of these affected the blood so much that it fell into total decay, thereby making the person completely incurable and repulsive to himself and others.

v. 3. A sign was also given to them by which leprosy could be recognized: when the hair changed its natural color to white, and the skin appeared deeper, meaning that the flesh had been eaten away and disappeared due to such a plague.

<column-break/>

4. But if it is a white spot on the skin of his body, and its appearance is not deeper than the skin, and its hair has not turned white, then the priest shall isolate the mark for seven days.
5. Then the priest shall examine him on the seventh day. Behold, if the mark remains the same in his eyes and the mark has not spread further on the skin, then the priest shall isolate him for another seven days.
6. And when the priest examines him a second time on the seventh day, and behold, the mark has faded and has not spread further on the skin, the priest shall declare him clean; it is a scab. And he shall wash his clothes, and he shall be clean.
7. But

---

v. 4. **Isolate for 7 days:** This happened in doubtful cases, so that they would not be overhasty in their judgment.

v. 5. **Examine on the 7th day:** The 7th day is among physicians a <note>original: "dies criticus"</note> critical day, a day of recognition or judgment, on which the disease usually reveals itself so that one can judge it.

If the mark had spread further, he declared him unclean immediately, even if he noticed no other sign.

But if the priest noticed no change, and none of the signs of impurity appeared, he isolated him

**Another 7 days:** Thus until the 14th day, which is likewise a <note>original: "dies criticus"</note> critical day among physicians.

v. 6. If one of those signs then appeared, he promptly declared him unclean.

On the flesh, skin, or body of a person, leprosy was a white mark, where one or more places on the person's flesh became as white as an eggshell, or even whiter. As long as they were not that white, but darker (which darkness Luther often translates as "fading"), it was not leprosy, but a kind of itch or scurvy. But if they were as white as an eggshell, or even whiter—perhaps like white wool, or the lime on the Temple, or even like snow—then it was certainly leprosy.

If, however, the mark had become darker than an eggshell, or no change was to be felt, he was not isolated further after he had endured his 14-day trial period.

Thus, if something had indeed shown itself but afterwards contracted and had not spread, it was recognized as a scurvy or itch, which only breaks out and soon passes away again; it is like a cleansing of nature, where it casts out something impure and then recovers. And this examination had to happen every seven days.

During the time he was isolated, he was not required to do what those recognized as lepers had to do; he did not have to let his hair grow wild, nor tear his clothes. And when he was declared clean, he did not have to be shaved or have his nails cut as the lepers had to; rather, he bathed in water and washed his clothes like other unclean persons: thus he became clean.

But if one of the signs of impurity appeared after he had been pronounced clean, he was immediately recognized as unclean. For if these signs were found, he was always unclean.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XIII.

7. But if the scab spreads further in the skin after he has shown himself to the priest for his cleansing, he shall be seen by the priest a second time.

8. And if the priest sees that the scab has indeed spread further in the skin, the priest shall declare him unclean: it is leprosy.

<note>v. 7. Such spreading was one of the definitive signs, alongside others.</note>

<note>v. 8. (It is leprosy) Thus, not everything that appeared to be leprosy was actually so. It seems that neither the Scripture nor the Hebrew scholars agree with Luther’s marginal gloss—which follows the Weimar interpretation <note>The Weimar Bible, also known as the Ernestine Bible, was a highly influential 17th-century Lutheran study Bible.</note> and others—suggesting that Moses meant all kinds of scabs, smallpox, or marks by "leprosy." Rather, true leprosy is clearly distinguished from common scabs, the itch <note>scabies</note>, heat-blisters, and similar malignant boils or swellings.</note>

There is no doubt, however, that just as with other parts of the Law, there is a hidden mystery contained within leprosy and its specific recognition, cleansing, and healing. The spiritually-minded Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretation of the Bible.</note> perceived so much in this that, in his judgment, what a person finds and recognizes—once God has removed the veil from the reading of the Old Testament—could hardly be contained in many books.

There is also no doubt that in its power, leprosy signifies not only original sin but also "reigning sin"—that which consumes the entire conduct and the whole heart of a person. It is a sickness from which all must die and perish in their impurity if they do not attend to it in time and allow themselves to be cleansed and healed through the blood of Christ.

God intended to teach us here the great corruption of our souls through original sin, which can be seen either in a swelling—that is, a "swollen" pride and an outward haughty nature, to which those of a "biting" or hot temperament are very prone; or in a scab—that is, a greedy nature glued to created things, where a person seeks only to become rich and thereby sinks into the mire of earthly things; or in pustules—that is, all kinds of fleshly lusts of anger or pleasure, breaking out in "gluttony and drunkenness, in chambering and wantonness, in strife and envying" (Romans 13:13). These are the three main sources of all vice: namely, the pride of life, the lust of the eyes, and the lust of the flesh (1 John 2:16).

When any outbreaks of these lusts appear, believers, acting as spiritual priests, should first warn and rebuke them according to Christ’s admonition: "If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother" (Matthew 18:15). In such a case, it is merely a sin of weakness or haste that does not put the person outside of God’s grace, because it is recognized and repented (See Galatians 6:1). But if he continues to sin and breaks out in such vices, and does not listen, Christ says, "take one or two more with you, that every word may be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses." In this way, such a person is inspected, examined, and rebuked a second time—that is, with greater earnestness by more people. And if he does not listen to them, tell it to the church. If he does not listen even to the church, then regard him as a heathen and a tax collector (Matthew 18:15–17). This means nothing else than that he should then be declared a "leper," one who is entirely in the bondage of sin and, as an unrepentant person, has no part in Christ or His goods. Concerning this, the Apostle also says that the spiritual ones, as priests, shall judge all things (1 Corinthians 2:15). Namely, "if anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or an extortioner—with such a person do not even eat" (1 Corinthians 5:11). "Put away from yourselves that wicked person" (v. 13).

<column-break/>

9. When a mark of leprosy is on a person, he shall be brought to the priest.

10. And the priest shall see it; and behold, if there is a white swelling on the skin, and it has turned the hair white, and there is fresh raw flesh in the swelling;

11. That is an inveterate <note>meaning old or deep-seated</note> leprosy in the skin of his flesh; therefore the priest shall declare him unclean: he shall not shut him up <note>quarantine him</note>, for he is already unclean.

12. And if the leprosy breaks out all over the skin, so that the leprosy covers all the skin of the mark from his head to his feet, everywhere the priest’s eyes look;

13. And...

<note>v. 9. If a heat-blister, an angry swelling, a scabby area, or something pussy or reddish-white appeared on a person's skin, and it was not known whether it was leprosy or might break out into it, that person had to go immediately either to the High Priest or another priest nearest to his home to show the damage for inspection.</note>

<note>v. 10. So that the priests would err less in identifying leprosy, they had several signs to recognize it: if the hairs in the mark had turned white, and the mark appeared lower than the surrounding skin—not protruding but sunken into the skin—the priest could both see and feel these signs.</note>

If there was healthy flesh in the middle of the mark, so that healthy flesh was mixed and mingled with the ulcer and the white mark, it was much worse; it was a sign that the leprosy was already quite deep-rooted.

<note>v. 11. This "fresh raw flesh" found in the ulcer, which would not heal over with skin, had to be declared an "old leprosy" immediately without further investigation. This indicated that a bold, raw sinner who is not ashamed of his sin, but rather boasts of it, should be avoided immediately without further warning, and declared as one who is outside the Christian community. Of this the Apostle says: "What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But those who are outside, God judges" (1 Corinthians 5:12–13).</note>

<note>v. 12. If the entire skin turned white everywhere, so that the whole body and everything on it was changed to white—which the priest had to inspect by seeing the person entirely naked—then he was not declared unclean or leprous.</note>

v. 24. **A burn from fire)** arises in the soul when one stands open to the fiery darts of the wicked one <note>A reference to Ephesians 6:16</note> and gives them space to penetrate within; or also on the skin of the flesh, where the lust of the flesh and carnal love burn in the will.

# Chapter XIII. The Third Book of Moses.

34. And when the priest shall examine the scab <note>original: "Krätze" – in a biblical context, this refers to a "scall" or an itchy infection of the scalp or beard</note> on the seventh day; and behold, the scab has not eaten further into the skin, and its appearance is not deeper than the skin; then the priest shall declare him clean, and he shall wash his clothes, and he will be clean.
35. But if the scab shall have eaten further and further into the skin after his cleansing;
36. And the priest shall have examined him, and behold, the scab has eaten further into the skin: then the priest shall not seek for the yellow hair; he is unclean.
37. But if the scab has remained the same before his eyes, and black hair has grown upon it: then the scab is healed; he is clean: therefore the priest shall declare him clean.

It is otherwise difficult to find the distinction between the three or two words in verse 2, verse 6, and here; since the corruption of the blood is so varied, and such distinction must be better known to the physicians. As to what it may actually be on the head, whether it be a crust or a scab—as it can be named to distinguish it from the previous cases—and is not to be judged as that very wicked scalp-rot <note>original: "Erbgrind" – likely referring to *Favus*, a severe fungal infection that causes permanent baldness</note>, which could indeed be recognized immediately without examination; so this can represent to us in a spiritual sense the erroneous opinions that are outpourings of proud and presumptuous reason. When such things would overturn the foundation of salvation, and thus the fundamental truths, and otherwise be dangerous, whereby people might be led into a false freedom of the flesh, so that they might turn the grace of God into wantonness <note>A reference to Jude 1:4</note>; then their self-willed nature is to be avoided, as was previously cited from Titus 3:10–11. Paul also warns against such people in 2 Timothy 2:14–18, where he testifies of them that their word eats away like a cancer <note>original: "Krebs" – often translated as gangrene or canker in biblical texts</note>, because they had perverted thoughts regarding the fundamental truth of the resurrection of the dead.

<margin>v. 34.</margin> If he found no sign on the 14th day, but the mark had stood still and the hair had become black; he declared him clean.
<margin>v. 35. 36.</margin> But if on this 14th day, or even afterward, when he had been declared clean, he found the appearance deeper and the hairs gold-colored, or that the mark had eaten further—which eating-away made one just as unclean as the other signs—then he was declared unclean.
<margin>v. 37.</margin> **He is clean:** therefore the priest shall declare him clean. Here we see the ground upon which the priest’s absolution, and the declaration of being clean and saved, must be based. But those who justify the godless for the sake of a reward, and deny justice to the righteous; and those who thus call evil good and good evil, darkness light and light darkness: upon their necks the "Woe" is laid in Isaiah 5:20, 23, and they shall bear the curse of uncleanness and the ban which they wish to take away from others. They should also by right be publicly recognized and declared clean and innocent by the priest.
<margin>v. 40.</margin> Such natural defects, when the hair fell out, because of which one became bare-headed or got a bald spot <note>original: "Glatze" – specifically baldness at the forehead or crown</note>, these defiled no one. Which can then also be understood of bodily weaknesses, for which no one can be blamed, but rather one should have compassion for such. Therefore it was a heavy sin when those small boys mocked the prophet Elisha and cried: "Go up, thou baldhead! Go up, thou baldhead!" which they then had to pay for with their lives, being torn apart by bears. 2 Kings 2:23 etc.
<margin>v. 41.</margin> Because women otherwise practiced pride with braided hair, they were threatened with baldness as a punishment for it. Isaiah 3:24.
When a soul puts off and throws away that which has died in its nature; it is clean.
<margin>v. 42-44.</margin> But if it takes back up that which it had put off, and indeed with signs of a worse kind and the sickness of a relapse <note>original: "Recidivs"</note> than it previously carried; such a soul is rightly to be considered leprous.

<column-break/>

38. And when a man or woman has spots <note>original: "Blattern" – white pustules or bright spots</note> on the skin of their flesh, namely white spots;
39. And the priest shall see it, and behold, in the skin of their flesh are spots that have contracted and are white: that is a blister <note>original: "Blase"</note> that has blossomed in the skin; he is clean.
40. And when a man’s hair falls out from his head, he is bare-headed, he is clean.
41. And when the hair falls out from the front of his head, he has a bald spot, he is clean.
42. But if there is a white-reddish mark where he is bare-headed or on the bald spot, that is a blossoming leprosy on his bare head or on his bald spot.
43. And if the priest shall have examined him, and behold, the swelling of the mark is white and reddish on his bare head or on his bald spot, the skin of the flesh is to be looked upon as leprosy:
44. He is a leprous man, he is unclean, the priest shall declare him utterly unclean; since he has his mark upon his head.
