<meta>This page continues the examination of leprosy (tzara'at) in Leviticus 13. While the previous section categorized various skin eruptions and infections of the head, this page details the social and ritual requirements for those confirmed as lepers, as well as the laws regarding "leprosy" found in fabrics and leather.</meta>

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XIII.

45. And the leper in whom the plague is, his clothes shall be torn, and his head shall be bare, and he shall cover his upper lip, and shall cry out: Unclean! Unclean!
46. All the days that the plague is upon him, he shall be unclean; he is unclean: he shall dwell alone; outside the camp shall his dwelling be.

---

**v. 45.** Once a person was recognized as a leper by the priest, he was required to tear his clothes at the seams and at the sides, provided he was a male. Women, however, were exempt from this requirement of tearing their garments. <note>original: "(a) Mischn. Sotac. 3. lect. 8." — A reference to the Mishna, specifically the tractate Sotah regarding laws for women.</note>
He was also required to let his hair grow long, according to the Hebrew interpretation of what is otherwise described as "baring the head" <note>original: "(b) Lund. J.H. 3. B. 51. C. n. 27." — Refers to Johann Lund’s scholarly work on Jewish antiquities.</note>: though in practice, both often occurred.
He also had to cover his mouth, so that he might not poison or infect anyone with his breath.
If anyone approached him, he cried out: I am unclean! I am unclean! I am unclean! so that every person could step back from him. All other unclean persons who could transmit defilement were also required to do this.
Such a wretched outward appearance, and the necessity of warning all others not to approach to avoid infection, was intended to represent the **abominable nature of sin** in the eyes of God, and how believers should likewise loathe sin in themselves and others, since such vanities, malice, and earthly-mindedness can so easily infect the soul. Therefore, the spiritual book of Psalms begins with this healthy warning in Psalm 1:1: *Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.* Indeed, how the corruption of the Church is compared to such a leprosy can be read in Isaiah 52:11 and 2 Corinthians 6:17.
Furthermore, a "leprous soul" should take great care not to cover its shame or seek to hide or excuse it, but should rather willingly expose its true condition through free confession: so that it does not appear outwardly beautiful and pure before men like a **whitewashed tomb**, after the manner of ancient hypocrites, while being found inwardly full of dead men’s bones and uncleanness before God.
Nothing should be covered but the mouth. For to the wicked God says: *What hast thou to do to declare my statutes, or that thou shouldest take my covenant in thy mouth? seeing thou hatest instruction, and castest my words behind thee* (Psalm 50). For he who does not teach himself should also keep his mouth closed toward others. Thus, he who lives in sin forfeits the freedom to speak.

**v. 46. Unclean—unclean)** Lepers were the most unclean of all the unclean, and the priests had more to do with them than any other category of impurity, both inside and outside the Temple.
A leper was not permitted to live among healthy people but had to exist alone, or stay with other lepers: specifically outside the city, or outside the village and all camps, so that he was permitted to enter neither the Court of Israel, nor the Outer Court, nor the Court of the Gentiles, nor even the city itself—neither Jerusalem nor any other city or village.
Thus King Uzziah <note>original: "Usias"</note>, when struck with leprosy, was also required to dwell alone (2 Kings 15:5, 2 Chronicles 26:21).
If such a person wished to attend school <note>likely referring to the synagogue or house of study</note>, it was not forbidden, but a special partition was made for him, ten handbreadths high and four cubits wide. He also had to be the first to enter the school and the last to leave, so that he would not infect anyone (c). <note>original: "(c) Lightfoot. hor. hebr. ad Luc. 17. 12." — John Lightfoot’s "Hebrew and Talmudical Exercitations" on Luke 17:12.</note>
Lepers could associate with one another, but other unclean persons had to abstain from them.
The Hebrews therefore counted them among the dead, and they certainly provide us with a picture of the **living dead**, who are not numbered among the living in Jerusalem and have no part in the City of God.

<column-break/>

47. And when there is a plague of leprosy in a garment, whether it be a woolen garment or a linen garment;
48. Whether it be in the warp or in the woof <note>the vertical and horizontal threads of a weave</note> of linen or of wool, or in a skin, or in anything made of skin:
49. If the plague be greenish ->(a) chapter 14:37<- or reddish in the garment or in the skin, or in the warp or in the woof, or in any vessel of skin; it is a plague of leprosy: therefore it shall be shown to the priest.
50. And when the priest has seen the plague, he shall shut up the plague for seven days.
51. But if he sees the plague on the seventh day, that the plague has spread further in the garment, or in the warp, or in the woof, or in the skin, for whatever purpose the skin is made; the plague is a consuming leprosy; it is unclean.
52. And he shall burn the garment, or the warp, or the woof, of wool or of linen, or any vessel of skins wherein the plague is: for it is a consuming leprosy; it shall be burnt with fire.
53. But if the priest shall see it, and behold, the plague has not spread further in the garment, or in the warp, or in the woof, or in any vessel of skin;
54. Then the priest shall command that they wash the thing wherein the plague is, and he shall shut it up a second time for seven days.
55. And...

---

**v. 47. 48.** Just as humans could be afflicted, so too could the garments of men and women, whether they were linen or wool, as well as all types of skin (leather), prepared or unprepared, and things made from skins, such as shoes and the like, become leprous and infect people.
**v. 49. In the garment)** Whether old or new, on one side or the other, or on both at once.
**v. 50. Shall shut up the plague)** In order to see whether it would consume further or not, or if it were merely a common stain.
**v. 51. 52.** If it spread, it was immediately declared unclean and burned: so that no one would receive it and potentially be infected by it.
**v. 53. 54.** But if it had not spread, the priest had it thoroughly washed and shut up even further.

### Chap. XIII. The Third Book of Moses. 491

55. **And when the priest shall see / after the mark is washed / and behold, the mark has not changed its appearance / and the mark has not spread further; it is unclean / you shall burn it with fire: it is something deeply eaten-in / whether it be bald on the inside or smooth on the outside.** <note>The German text uses "kahl" (bald) and "glatt" (smooth) to refer to the front and back sides of the fabric or leather.</note>

56. **And when the priest shall examine it / and behold, the mark has shrunk / after it has been washed; then he shall tear it out from the garment / or from the hide / or from the warp / or from the woof.** <note><term>Warp and woof</term> refer to the vertical and horizontal threads in a loom, indicating that the infection could live within the very structure of the cloth.</note>

57. **But if it shall still be seen further on the garment / or on the warp or on the woof / or on any vessel of hides: it is something breaking out / you shall burn it with fire / that on which the mark is.**

58. **But the garment or the warp or the woof or any vessel of hides / which you shall have washed / and the mark has departed from them / shall be washed a second time; then it shall be clean.**

59. **This is the law of a leprosy-mark on a woolen or linen garment / or on the warp or on the woof / or on any vessel of hides / to declare it clean or unclean.**

---

<note>
For this purpose / as can be easily recognized from all the above / a great science was required / to rightly know leprosy of so many kinds / and to distinguish it from something else (a).
v. 55. If the mark had not lost its previous green or red color after washing, it was promptly declared unclean, even if it had not spread further, because the persistence of the color was a sign of the leprosy.
v. 56. But if, upon inspection on the 7th day after washing, it had disappeared / or at least the color had changed; the priest tore the place where the spot was from the garment / and burned that specific piece.
v. 57. If, after tearing out this piece, such a spot appeared again on the garment / or a trace of it; the priest judged that it must not have been completely removed / but a decaying power remained behind / and he had the entire garment or hide burned / so that no one might suffer harm from it.
v. 58. But when the mark completely disappeared after washing, it was not yet clean through that single washing / but had to be washed anew / only then was it clean.
v. 59. This was also a particular plague upon the Jewish people / by which GOD undoubtedly intended at times to punish their pride in clothing / to which they were also devoted in such a blessed land / just as these judgments are also interpreted in Isaiah 3, 16. etc. It is to be noted here / however, that in a spiritual sense one must primarily look to one’s association with others / with which a person, as it were, clothes, warms, and refreshes his soul. This is where the exhortation of the Apostle points in 2 Corinthians 6, 14.

## The XIV. Chapter.
->The Cleansing of the Leper / and Leprosy of Houses.<-

1. And the **LORD** spoke to **Moses**, saying:

2. This shall be the law of the leper on the day of his cleansing: he shall be brought to the priest;

3. And the priest shall go forth out of the camp. If the priest shall see, and behold, the mark of leprosy is healed on the leper:

4. Then shall the priest command / that for him who is to be cleansed, two living birds be taken / which are clean / and **cedar-wood** and **scarlet-wool** and **hyssop**. 4 Moses 19, 6. <note>Refers to Numbers 19:6.</note>

5. **And**

---

<note>
Here the cleansing and reconciliation of a leper / who had become healthy again / is commanded and arranged with various sacrifices. For although leprosy in itself was not a sin / yet it served as an indictment of the corruption of our nature through original sin; and thus it will mostly have been a divine judgment because of committed sin / as can be seen with Miriam and King Uzziah: and therefore this cleansing and reconciliation was imposed with the prescribed sacrifices.
Regarding the cleansing of a leper, it proceeded as follows:
v. 2. When the mark and the plague faded or darkened on such a person; he had to present himself again to the priest for inspection; and indeed to the very same priest / by whom he had been declared unclean.
v. 3. He went to him outside the camp / or outside the gate of the city / or out in front of the village; there the leper came out of his dwelling to meet him / and allowed himself to be inspected by him.
If the mark had completely disappeared / or had become darker than an eggshell; he pronounced him clean / because it was no longer leprosy / and received him back into the community of other people with special ceremonies.
v. 4. That one should — take) The leper had to provide everything.
Two living birds) There are indeed many (a) and among them the Hebrews generally / who believe that sparrows are meant here: which Jerome and Origen, however, make into "hunters" <note>likely referring to wild birds</note>. And those may well come closest to the mark who (b) hold that it did not matter / what kind of birds were taken / as long as they were clean.
These two clean birds / which one was allowed to eat / along with the cedar-wood, scarlet-wool, and hyssop / then represented Christ’s sacrifice / through which we are cleansed and reconciled from original sin as well as from actual sins / not only that such are not reckoned against us / but that they may also be increasingly blotted out / and we may be cleansed and redeemed from them.
Because Christ’s two states, namely death and life, were distinct / it was not possible to prefigure them in a single creature alone. But Christ in the antitype or true essence performs alone / that which in his type in the Scripture was mostly signified by death and life in two creatures.

<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chap. XIV.</header>

### 5. And the priest shall command that one of the birds be killed in an earthen vessel over fresh water.
### 6. As for the living bird, he shall take it, and the cedar wood, and the scarlet wool, and the hyssop, and shall dip them and the living bird in the blood of the bird that was killed over the fresh water;

v. 5. When Christ is presented here under the image of a bird, it signifies his condition here on earth, where, because of the pursuit of his enemies—Herod and the Jews—he had to flee from one place to another from his childhood onward, and often had to hide himself where he could not walk freely in public. See Psalm 11:1, which also applies to Christ in the spirit: *In the Lord I put my trust; how say ye then to my soul: Flee as a bird to your mountain?* And how this was fulfilled can be seen in Matthew 2:13, 22; 4:12; John 7:1, 10; 8:59; 10:39; 11:54.

The bird that was killed signified his death, and the one that was let go free into the field, so that it flew away, signified his resurrection and ascension.

**Cedar Wood)** This had to be a fairly thick stick, one cubit <note>The "Elen" or ell was a historical unit of length, roughly 18–24 inches.</note> long, and as thick as the fourth part of a bedpost.

**Scarlet Wool)** This band had to be neither crimson nor any other red, but a deep scarlet, weighing one shekel or one loth. (a) <note>original: "Seckel oder 1 Loth"; a "Loth" was a historical German weight of about 15 grams.</note>

**Hyssop)** Because of its similarity to the Hebrew word <term>אזוב</term> <note>original: *ezov*</note>, most consider it to be this herb (b): especially since the 70 translators <note>The "70 translators" refers to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> and Paul in Hebrews 9:19—who knew best what kind of herb it was and what was used in the Levitical service, as they wrote while it was still in full practice—rendered it as such. Yet there are others who, with irrefutable reasons, substitute rosemary for it: of which more may perhaps be mentioned on another occasion.

Three stalks of this hyssop were taken, each a hand-breadth long, as others (c) cite from the Hebrew writers.

The cedar wood signifies, because of its durability and dense nature, Christ's divine nature, in which is also the source of all gifts of the Spirit; and the hyssop signifies his human nature, for which the note on Exodus 12:22 should be consulted for more detail.

The scarlet wool, or the thread spun from it, with which the hyssop was tied to the cedar stick, signified our blood-red sins laid upon Christ, which He, as our guarantor, had to bear and atone for according to His divine and human nature.

That this bird's blood had to be let into an earthen vessel with fresh, flowing water and thus mixed, testified how Christ came with water and blood; not with water alone, but with water and blood: 1 John 5:6. To confirm this, blood and water also flowed out of his side when it was opened with the spear, as the Apostle John himself testifies in John 19:34. Thus, both atonement and cleansing or sanctification were envisioned here at once.

**In fresh water)** It had to be flowing or spring water, which the original language calls "living water."

The priest poured some of this water into a new earthen bowl, then took the two clean birds, chose the best and fattest among them, and slaughtered it over the water in the earthen bowl, letting the blood drip into the water so that the blood could be recognized in the water; then he dug a pit and buried the slaughtered bird in it.

v. 6. Afterward he took the cedar stick, tied the hyssop or rosemary stalks with the scarlet band around the end of the stick, and placed around these tied stalks the outermost part of the wings along with the tail of the living bird, dipping all four pieces into the water mixed with blood.

<column-break/>

### 7. And he shall sprinkle seven times upon him who is to be cleansed from the leprosy, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird go into the open field.
### 8. And he that is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes, and shave off all his hair, and wash himself with water; then he shall be clean: and after that he shall come into the camp; but he shall stay outside his tent seven days.
### 9. And it shall come to pass on the seventh day, that he shall shave off all his hair, namely his head and his beard and his eyebrows, even all his hair he shall shave off, and he shall wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in water: then he shall be clean.

v. 7. And with this, he sprinkled the back or top of the leper's hand seven times.

When all seven sprinklings were performed, he released the living bird and let it fly away into the open air. If the priest stood within the walls, he threw the bird over the walls and turned his face toward the wilderness. If the bird came back, the priest had to throw it out again, even if he had to repeat it a hundred times.

v. 8, 9. When this was done, the priest was not yet to release the leper who had been declared clean, but first had to shave him; he shaved away all the hair on the entire body smoothly with a razor, so that he became entirely bald over his whole body. His nails were also cut and buried.

As soon as this was done, the one who had been a leper bathed, washed his clothes, and was thus clean to the extent that no one was forbidden from interacting with him anymore, because he could no longer infect anyone; rather, anyone could freely sit or lie near him. He could also enter the city immediately, but he still had to count seven days, during which he was not yet allowed to come to the Temple, nor even into his own house. And although anyone could interact with him without danger of infection during that time, he was not so completely clean during these seven days that everyone who touched him was not unclean for the rest of the day.

But as soon as the seventh day dawned, the priest had to act as a barber again and shave all the hair of the former leper for a second time with a razor, just like the first time; and after he had washed his clothes and bathed, he was entirely clean before men and no longer defiled anyone.

The slaughtering of the bird, the sprinkling, and the shaving had to be performed by the priest alone, whether upon the leper or others.

However, the shaving of all hair on the body, which had to be done twice, indicates the diligent examination of our sins; because impurity is easily found in the hair from sweat, and thus all our laborious occupations are soiled with much defilement. And this examination must occur with all diligence both at the beginning of repentance and in its progress, and especially at the end of our lives, striving to cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and spirit, and thus to perfect our sanctification in the fear of God. 2 Corinthians 7:1. For all of which David constantly pleaded in Psalm 51:9.

---

<page-num>493</page-num>
<header>Chapter XIV. The Third Book of Moses.</header>
<sig>Q q q 3</sig>

10. And on the eighth day he shall take two lambs without blemish, and one ewe-lamb of the first year without blemish, and three-tenth deals of fine flour for a grain offering, mingled with oil, and one log of oil.
11. And the priest who cleanses him shall present the man who is to be cleansed, and those things, before the Face of the Lord, at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation.
12. And the priest shall take one lamb, and offer it for a guilt offering, with the log of oil, and wave them for a wave offering before the Face of the Lord.
13. And he shall slay the lamb in the place where the sin offering and the burnt offering are slain, in the holy place. For as the sin offering is the priest's, so is the guilt offering: it is most holy.

---

**v. 10.** As soon as one who had been a leper was cleansed before men with the aforementioned ceremonies, he had to bring his sacrifice on the following 8th day—provided he was near Jerusalem or the Tabernacle, or else at a later time—and also be purified before God and reconciled with Him in a special manner.
As long as this did not happen, he was "one lacking atonement" <note>German: *Versöhnungs-fehlender*</note> and was not permitted to eat of any sacrifice or holy thing, even though he had already been declared clean before men and received back into the society of the clean through the previously mentioned ceremonies.
(**2 lambs &c.**) provided, of course, that he was able to afford so much.
**A ewe-lamb of the first year**) The "yearling" status was calculated from the 8th day of its birth until the last day of its first year. For before the 8th day, God did not desire to have any animals. See Chapter 22:27. Anything that was still in its first year, and not yet a full year old, Scripture calls "of the first year," provided it was over 7 days old. See Chapter 23.
The three types of offerings—the guilt, sin, and burnt offerings—which were made from the two lambs and the one sheep, signified primarily how guilt must be acknowledged. This was specifically understood as original sin, on account of which God might well send such a plague of leprosy, even if the person was not aware of being guilty of any particularly notable great sin. Because many actual sins flow from this source, the sin and burnt offerings were also necessary as a testament of repentance and faith. Therefore, David presented himself most humbly before God as such a leper on account of his original sin—in which he was conceived and born—and later on account of his coarse adultery, and prayed that God would purge him with this sprig of hyssop and wash him, so that he might become whiter than snow. Psalm 51:9.
**For a grain offering**) for each individual sacrifice.
**A log of oil**) About as much as could fit in 6 empty eggshells. <note>A "Log" is a small biblical liquid measure, roughly equivalent to 0.3 liters.</note>
The grain offering was intended to remind one of active love toward the needy neighbor, and the oil of the alertness and anointing of the Spirit, in order to practice obedience to God's commandments in all dealings and conduct.
**v. 11. The man who is to be cleansed**) arrived very early at the Temple and went to the Court of the Lepers, which was at the Temple in the northwest corner, where he bathed himself once again.
**v. 12.** Thereupon a priest took the leper's guilt offering alive and waved it before the Lord alongside the log of oil.
**v. 13.** Then he brought the guilt offering to the gate, where the leper laid his hands upon it. For because his atonement had not yet occurred, he was not permitted to enter into the Court of Israel.

<column-break/>

14. And the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering, and the priest shall put it upon the lobe of the right ear of him who is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the great toe of his right foot.
15. And the priest shall take some of the log of oil, and pour it into the palm of the priest's own left hand:
16. And the priest shall dip his right finger in the oil that is in his left hand, and shall sprinkle of the oil with his finger seven times before the Face of the Lord. 17.

---

**v. 14.** Two priests caught the blood of this lamb during the slaughter: one in a vessel; the other in his right hand, and poured it into his left hand. Had he taken it in his left hand first, it would have been unclean.
The blood in the vessel was sprinkled around the altar of burnt offering, and the remainder was poured at the base of the altar.
But the one who had the blood in his hand went with it by the Temple toward the Gate of Nicanor, where the former leper stood, and was accompanied there by another priest with the log of oil. Then the former leper first stretched his head, then his right hand, and finally his right foot into the inner court, but remained standing with his body on the outside; for he was not permitted to enter the inner court, and yet the blood was not allowed to be carried out of it. The priest, who had the blood in his left hand, then dipped his right finger into it and moistened first the bottom of the right ear, then the right thumb, and finally the right toe with the blood; as a memorial and reminder that the cleansed person should in the future keep his ear from all foul gossip, let his hands perform good works, and conduct his life cautiously. For
This manner of cleansing indicates that the soul, which is clean and pure enough to embark upon a more perfect path of the spirit, must have its ear dedicated to God alone in order to listen to Him. For she now uses no more words toward GOD: namely, in general, until He Himself brings her to utter some words; which, however, happens very rarely. Therefore, the ear is cleansed, and not the tongue: so that she may be silent before God and, conversely, be faithful in listening. The thumb of the right hand is also cleansed: which signifies that all works of these souls must be dedicated to God and must all occur in the rectiness of His Spirit. For God is the Master and Author of the same, just as He is of the inclinations of the heart and the conduct, which are represented by the feet, which must be entirely clean. But only the right foot is sanctified; because the soul must always offer everything to God, without ever doing anything out of self-interest or for itself. For this reason, David also (a) made this prayer: *Teach me thy way, O Lord, and lead me in thy truth.* He meant to say: in God Himself. For God is the truth, just as He is love: from which we must never turn away.
**v. 15. 16.** Hereupon the same priest poured some oil from the log into the other priest's left hand, or else into his own, dipped his right forefinger into it, turned toward the Temple and the altar of burnt offering, and sprinkled seven times in that direction.
(a) Psalm 86:11.

The commentary interprets these physical acts as a spiritual commitment to silence before God and the performance of holy works.</summary>

<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chap. XIV.</header>

17. And of the rest of the oil that is in his hand, the priest shall put upon the tip of the right ear of him that is to be cleansed, and upon the thumb of his right hand, and upon the big toe of his right foot, on top of the blood of the guilt offering.
18. And what remains of the oil that is in the priest's hand, he shall put upon the head of him that is to be cleansed, and the priest shall make atonement for him before the face of the LORD.
19. And the priest shall prepare the sin offering, and make atonement for him that is to be cleansed, because of his uncleanness; and afterward he shall slaughter the burnt offering:
20. And the priest shall offer the burnt offering along with the grain offering upon the altar, and the priest shall make atonement for him; so shall he be clean.

---

<margin>v. 17.</margin> He then turned back to the one who had been a leper, dipped his finger into the oil, and wherever he had previously placed blood, he now placed oil—on top of it.
*Upon the blood* or perhaps next to the blood, which he could well have wiped away beforehand.
Since all our deeds must first be purified solely in the blood of Christ, and thus can only be acceptable before God in this blood that cleanses us from sins, the ears, hands, and feet of the person being cleansed had to be smeared first with blood and afterwards with oil. See v. 14.
<margin>v. 18.</margin> If anything was overlooked or neglected during this ritual, the entire purification was worth nothing.
Whatever oil remained in the <term>log<note>A log is an ancient Hebrew liquid measure, approximately equal to the volume of six eggs or about 0.3 liters.</note></term> belonged to the priests.
Otherwise, the proceedings with the guilt offering continued in the usual manner.
<margin>v. 19.</margin> Following this, the sin offering—namely the female lamb—was also offered in the customary way; and finally the second lamb as a burnt offering.
<margin>v. 20.</margin> Whereupon the grain offerings followed. And this was something special about these sacrifices: for those of means, not only the burnt offering, but also the sin and guilt offerings had a grain offering attached, which was otherwise not customary.
As soon as these sacrifices were performed, the former leper was fully reconciled with God and also clean before Him, and could thereafter, if he wished, enter the inner court and bring his thank-offering to God the LORD there.
The fact that all types of sacrifices except the thank-offering had to be brought for the leper is intended to teach us that in our penitent devotions—wherein we confess our great corruption before God—we must first acknowledge the countless faults we commit (which the guilt offering aimed at) and then also the specific sins of which we are conscious (which the sin offering represented). See Psalm 19:13, 14 and 38:19. Then we must also lift ourselves to God in faith and, whenever the opportunity arises (which is never lacking), be mindful of the poor: which the burnt and grain offerings represent. See Daniel 4:27.

<column-break/>

21. But if he is poor and his hand cannot afford it; then he shall take a single lamb for a guilt offering and for a wave offering, to make atonement for him, and one tenth part of fine flour mingled with oil for a grain offering, and a log of oil;
22. And two turtledoves or two young pigeons, such as his hand can afford; and one shall be a sin offering, and the other a burnt offering.
23. And he shall bring them on the eighth day of his cleansing to the priest, to the door of the tent of meeting, before the face of the LORD.
24. And the priest shall take the lamb of the guilt offering and the log of oil, and the priest shall wave these things for a wave offering before the face of the LORD.

---

<insert>There was no further difference between this and the previous sacrifice, except that it appeared somewhat lesser in value according to one's means.</insert>
If someone wanted to pay the sacrificial costs for the former leper, and he was content with it, that was permitted. If a wealthy person chose to do it, he would give the sacrifice of a man of means.
<margin>v. 21.</margin> Otherwise, the LORD wished to spare the poor in their sacrificial gifts, yet in such a way that they were still bound to bring something as an acknowledgment of their duty. And through this, God wanted to teach that those who are also small and lacking in gifts of the intellect must nonetheless have in their hearts the simple knowledge of Christ—as the innocent Lamb who bore and wishes to take away their sins—and must be led to this: for it should not be expected of them to perceive the knowledge of the mysteries of the Gospel in its length and breadth, depth and height. If such souls only reach the knowledge of the core verse: *For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life* (John 3:16), then they can already comfort themselves in faith with this Lamb as their guilt offering and be built up by it in their soul's distress.
Only one tenth of flour was required, to show that even the poor are bound to give their gift of love according to their ability, just as the Savior praised the two small coins or farthings which the poor widow cast in, even out of her poverty, indeed her whole living. Luke 21:2, etc.
They were also required to give a <term>log of oil<note>A 'log' or 'Mössel' was the smallest liquid measure used in the sanctuary.</note></term>, which the wealthy also brought: to show how they too must stand in the communion of the One Holy Spirit, who is one and the same for the poor and the rich.
<margin>v. 22.</margin> And then they had to bring a pair of pigeons, one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering, to show how the poor especially should apply themselves to the simplicity and true uprightness of spirit for true repentance and faith in Christ, in order to walk before God therein, so that they too might be brought to obedience before God and to a holy way of life.

<header>Chapter XIV. The Third Book of Moses <note>The Third Book of Moses is the traditional name for the book of Leviticus.</note></header>
<meta>catchword: When</meta>

25. Afterward, he shall slaughter the lamb of the guilt offering, and the priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering and put it on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot.
26. And the priest shall pour some of the oil into the priest's own left hand:
27. And the priest shall sprinkle with his right finger some of the oil that is in his left hand seven times before the face of the LORD.
28. And the priest shall put some of the oil that is in his hand on the lobe of the right ear of the one being cleansed, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot—on the same place where the blood of the guilt offering was placed.
29. And what remains of the oil in the priest's hand, he shall put on the head of the one being cleansed, to make atonement for him before the face of the LORD.
30. Afterward, he shall prepare one of the turtledoves or of the young pigeons, according to what he is able to afford.
31. Of that which he is able to afford, one shall be a sin offering and the other a burnt offering, along with the grain offering; thus the priest shall make atonement for the one being cleansed before the face of the LORD.
32. This is the law for him in whom there is a mark of leprosy, whose hand cannot afford the standard requirements for his cleansing.

<column-break/>

33. And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:
34. When you come into the land of Canaan, which I give to you for a possession, and I put a mark of leprosy <note>In the context of a house, "leprosy" likely refers to spreading mold, rot, or fungal growth that made a dwelling unhealthy.</note> in a house of the land of your possession;
35. Then the one who owns the house shall come and tell the priest, saying: It seems to me as if there is a mark in the house.
36. And the priest shall command that they empty the house before the priest goes in to inspect the mark, so that everything in the house does not become unclean; and after this, the priest shall go in to inspect the house.
37. If he sees the mark, and behold, the mark on the walls of the house consists of greenish or reddish hollows, and their appearance is deeper than the wall;
38. Then the priest shall go out of the house to the door of the house and shut up the house for seven days.
39. And the priest shall come again on the seventh day, and if he inspects it and sees that the mark has spread further on the walls of the house;
40. Then the priest shall command that they break out the stones in which the mark is found and throw them in an unclean place outside the city.
41. And the house shall be scraped inside all around, and they shall pour the dust they have scraped off into an unclean place outside the city.
42. And they shall take other stones and put them in the place of those stones, and they shall take other mortar <note>The original German uses "Laymen," referring to Lehm or clay-based plaster.</note> and coat the house.

---

<margin>v. 25. 28.</margin> Therefore, here too, their ears, hands, and feet had to be sprinkled with the blood and oil: this was intended to remind the poor as well as the rich of the cleansing through the blood of Christ and in the Holy Spirit. See John 3:5, 1 John 1:7, 2:20.

When someone noticed a green or red spot in his house, he had to go quickly to a priest—whoever was nearest to him—and reveal it to him; then the priest immediately commanded him to empty the house and take everything out, so that if the priest declared the house unclean, everything inside would not also be rendered unclean.

When all the furnishings were out, the priest went in and inspected the mark. If he noticed greenish or reddish hollows in the wall, the appearance of which was deeper than the rest of the wall, he had the house closed for 7 days to see whether the mark would spread or if the spots might have originated from something else. During these 7 days, no one was allowed to remain in the house, eat in it, or lie down in it; otherwise, they became unclean.

On the 7th day, the priest inspected the house again, and if he noticed that the mark had spread further, he saw clearly that it was leprosy; however, before the total demolition of the house, he attempted one more remedy to see if perhaps the leprosy in the house could be removed by it, and the house might be allowed to stand.

<meta>This page continues the instructions from Leviticus 14 regarding the "leprosy of the house" (likely a form of malignant mold or fungal growth). It transitions from the physical laws of demolition to a spiritual commentary on God's judgment, followed by the specific ritual for purifying a house that has been cleared of infection.</meta>

<page-num>496</page-num>
->### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XIV.<-

43. But if the mark shall return and break out in the house after the stones have been pulled out, and after the house has been scraped, and after it has been plastered;
44. Then the priest shall go in: and if he sees that, behold, the mark has eaten further into the house; that is a malignant leprosy <note>The term "leprosy" is used here for a spreading growth or mold in the walls of a building.</note> in the house; it is unclean.
45. Therefore, the house shall be demolished: its stones and its wood and all the mortar of the house; and it shall be carried out of the city to an unclean place.
46. And whoever goes into the house during the entire time that it is closed up shall be unclean until evening.
47. And whoever lies in the house shall wash his clothes: and whoever eats in the house shall wash his clothes.
48. And when the priest shall have come back and inspected it, and behold, the mark has not eaten further in the house after the house was plastered; then the priest shall declare the house clean: for the mark has been healed.

---

If the mark returned and had eaten further around itself, the priest had the entire house demolished so that no one would be infected by it.
By this leprosy of the houses—with which **God** also wished to visit the people of Israel because of their great obstinacy and earthly-mindedness in the blessed land of Canaan, and to plague them because of the luxury practiced in the houses—**God** showed the great corruption of his whole people. This would one day break out in the rejection of the Rock of Salvation <note>A traditional title for Jesus Christ.</note> during the crucifixion of Christ, within the greenish-bitter, envious, and blood-red or bloodthirsty council of the high priests and elders of the people. This would infect the whole people like a leprosy, so that not only did their Temple have to be demolished, but they were also driven out of the Land of Promise. Concerning this, the Savior said: Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate! Matthew 23:38. And of the Temple: There shall not be left here one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down! Matthew 24:2.
So also the **Lord** threatens the curse that shall come over the house of the thief and of him who swears falsely by His name, and it shall remain in that house and consume it along with its wood and stones: Zechariah 5:4. This will strike the entire following of the Beast and the false prophet, so that many palaces will be destroyed like such leprous houses: just as this often strikes many houses of the great and rich of this world built with injustice. So also belong here the various houses of drinking and harlotry, and the comedy-houses and other houses of pleasure built rather for useless pastime or waste, in which so many sins are committed that will draw divine judgment over many cities and lands, so that **God** will know how to destroy them in His own time.

How careful one should then be in all large and small assemblies of people to watch over offensive families and houses where strife, impurity, laziness, and gluttony are in vogue, to check such things, through which they must finally and certainly go to ruin.

<column-break/>

49. And to cleanse the house, he shall take two birds, and cedar wood, and scarlet wool, and <term>hyssop</term> <note>A small aromatic plant used in ancient purification rituals for its cleansing properties.</note>;
50. And he shall kill one bird in an earthenware vessel over fresh water.
51. Afterward, he shall take the cedar wood and the hyssop and the scarlet wool and the living bird, and shall dip these things into the blood of the killed bird and into the fresh water, and sprinkle the house seven times.
52. Thus he shall cleanse the house with the blood of the bird and with the fresh water, and with the living bird, and with the cedar wood, and with the hyssop, and with the scarlet wool;
53. And he shall let the living bird fly out of the city into the open field, and make atonement for the house: so it shall be clean.
54. This is the law for every kind of mark of leprosy and for scabs;
55. And for the leprosy of clothes and of houses;
56. And for swellings, and for crusts, and for spots:
57. To teach on which day something is unclean, and on which day something is clean. This is the law of leprosy.

---

Where the house was recognized as clean, the master of the house, or he who lived in the house, had to have it consecrated again and made fit for dwelling with certain ceremonies, just as with the cleansing of a leper.
Just as all this Levitical system looks throughout toward **Jesus**, so we note here briefly the lovely prefiguration now occurring for the second time in the cleansing of leprosy:

->### The Prefiguration of the Two Birds.<-

1. There were two of them, pointing to the two natures of Christ <note>The theological concept that Christ is simultaneously fully human and fully divine.</note>.
2. Just as both birds had to be clean, so also is Christ entirely clean and without sin according to both natures.
3. One of them was killed and had to give blood: thus the human nature in Christ had to die and shed blood.
4. The other remained alive but was dipped into the blood of the one killed. The divine nature did not die and could not die; but it was, as it were, dipped into the blood of the human nature, and adds all the power to cleanse to the same. Therefore it is also **God's** blood. Acts of the Apostles 20:28.

# The 15th Chapter.

->All kinds of uncleanness of men and women.<-

And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When any man has a discharge <note>original: "Fluß"; referring to a bodily emission or flow, often interpreted in a medical or ritual context</note> from his flesh, he is unclean because of his discharge.
3. And this shall be his uncleanness from his discharge: whether his flesh lets his discharge run like spit, or his flesh is stopped up by his discharge; that is his uncleanness.
4. Every bed on which he lies who has the discharge shall be unclean; and every household item on which he sits shall be unclean.
5. And whoever touches his bed shall wash his clothes and bathe himself with water, and be unclean until the evening.

Just as the corruption of nature through **original sin** was particularly represented by leprosy, so through this weakness of nature, the outflow of all evil—and especially the unclean—thoughts and desires is made known, toward which man is inclined even from tender youth. Therefore, under the "unclean lust for the neighbor's wife," the lust for all women is forbidden; indeed, even the gruesome uncleanness of the so-called **silent sins** <note>original: "stummen Sünden"; a historical term for "sins not to be named," typically referring to homosexual acts or other non-procreative sexual behaviors</note>, where men burn in unclean lust toward one another, of which more is said in Romans 1:26-27.
v. 2. It is also probable that **GOD**, in the fertile land of Canaan, may have visited the Jews with this weakness of the body because of their abuse of **GOD’s** gifts through intemperance in eating and drinking. And if this was a punishment, then the intentional provocation of uncleanness is an even heavier sin; thus, parents should apply themselves to keeping their children from youth toward temperance, industriousness, and the avoidance of all sorts of bad company, so that unclean lust—which increases with the years—is not awakened in them.
v. 3. The **ceremonial uncleanness** <term>ceremonial uncleanness: a ritual state that prohibited a person from participating in communal worship or entering sacred spaces</term>, which made a person unfit to come to the Tabernacle or the Temple and to touch holy things, was not of a single kind. Some was great and coarse, some moderate, and some minor. That which is spoken of here belongs to the coarse kind.
v. 4. Everything such a person touched, or whatever touched him, became unclean; not only people, but also vessels and other things.
v. 5. Minor uncleanness was mostly found in those who became unclean only through the touching of unclean things; they were required to remain unclean for no longer than one day and did not contaminate others through touch.
Those who touched one of the "coarsely unclean" persons, or what was used by them, were afflicted with such uncleanness.
These persons afflicted with minor uncleanness might well enter the outer courtyard of the Temple, but could go no further in until they had been purified.

<margin>v. 20. Unclean)</margin> All our own righteousness and holiness is compared to this uncleanness and accused of being the same in Isaiah 64:6. <note>The prophet Isaiah uses the image of "unclean rags"—specifically menstrual cloths—to describe human efforts at righteousness compared to God's holiness.</note>

<margin>v. 21. The washing of clothes)</margin> Some (a) interpret this not as all clothes, but only the undergarments that cover the body, and specifically if they were woolen or linen; because leather garments and the like would have been ruined by washing. Also, the clothes had to have colors that could not be washed out; therefore, they preferred to wear white clothes.

<margin>v. 22. With this bathing and washing)</margin> Those who were afflicted with minor uncleanness could still approach, provided they had not inadvertently entered the Temple further than was permitted while in their uncleanness.

<margin>v. 23. Unclean until the evening)</margin> These were not unclean longer than that one day, provided they washed themselves.

The washing, however, was left to their discretion to do or leave undone, as long as they did not intend to go into the Tabernacle or the Temple. For

All purity and impurity—both for those afflicted with minor and with gross or moderate uncleanness—depended solely on the Tabernacle or the Temple, according to whether they wished to visit the Temple or not.

<margin>v. 24. The moderate uncleanness, </margin> of which this verse gives an example, did not pass with simple bathing alone, nor did it last only until evening. However, it was distinguished from gross uncleanness in that, while with gross uncleanness not only the furniture and bed were made unclean, but one could also be made unclean again by touching them; this was not the case with moderate uncleanness. Meanwhile, God intended with all these images to reveal the poison of uncleanness—how it creeps in and propagates in every way—and how the defilement of the world cannot be avoided or prevented carefully enough by all God-fearing souls. See James 1:27.

<margin>v. 25. Many days -- beyond -- the days)</margin> And thus, unnatural.

<margin>v. 26. Everything)</margin> that she touched was defiled by her.

<margin>v. 27. With water)</margin> Which belonged to all purifications, and without which no unclean person could become clean. This presents to us both the necessity and the excellence of this pure and purifying element, both in the earthly and the heavenly, in the physical and the spiritual. Therefore, we should desire all the more to be washed with pure water.

<margin>v. 28. When a woman with a discharge of blood</margin> was freed from her ailment, she was not immediately clean, but first had to count 7 days to see if the discharge had truly stopped; and if that were the case, then she was

**Clean)** This entire chapter indeed contains external legal purity, but God's command for the strict keeping of the same would be disparaging to God if it did not represent God’s intent to instruct a <term>coarse people</term><note>A common term in 18th-century theology referring to the ancient Israelites as people who needed physical rituals to understand spiritual concepts.</note> and to give them a great idea of purity (according to what they were). For this external cleansing, shown through the frequent washing of clothes—which could give no purity to the soul—was only an external sign of that purity which God demanded of the soul. Since God had established this external law of cleansing because of the coarseness of this people, He shows in the Gospel how lightly such a thing is esteemed (a) by rebuking the Pharisees, saying that they only cleaned the outside of their dishes and cups, while their inside remained full of robbery. Today's Christians do the very same: and even of those, there are few. They are content to clean and wipe the outside; namely, to lead a respectable life from the outside, even though the inside is full of robbery and self-interest against God.

Thus, it is to be believed that all the benefit one can draw from this chapter is to show the purity which God requires of those who belong to Him, both inward and outward—of which the latter was only a coarse image. We are no longer washed with water, but with the blood of Jesus Christ, into which we can incessantly immerse ourselves. And we must do this immediately, as soon as we realize that we have committed some faults or haste: either by the will, through a conversion that is sincere and simple toward Jesus Christ, more or less effective (according to the stage of the soul) as her prayer is more or less effective; or through a simple turning, in an <term>immersion in God</term><note>original: "Einer-senkung in GOtt"; a mystical term for the soul sinking into or becoming absorbed in the divine presence.</note>, into this sea of love, which will cleanse us of all defilements far more than all the waters of the whole world.

(a) Matthew 23:25. Mark 7:4.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XV.

29. And on the eighth day she shall take for herself two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and she shall bring them to the priest at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation.

30. And the priest shall prepare the one for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make atonement for her before the face of the LORD for the discharge of her uncleanness.

---

<margin>v. 29. What one was accustomed to offer after purification were pigeons or turtledoves: indicating that no sacrifice is more pleasing to God than simplicity. A simple soul is immediately restored to grace and the pure love of God; and this happens as swiftly as a straw is consumed in a great fire—provided the soul does not stray from that simplicity.</margin>

**On the 8th day)** Or afterward, whenever she was able to come there.

**2 Pigeons)** Not 2 female lambs, as Josephus writes. <note>original: "Josephus writes (a)"; referring to the Jewish historian Flavius Josephus in his work *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3, chapter 10.</note>

The same sacrifice was ordained for both men and women to show how in Christ there is no distinction between man or woman, but that they are both one in Christ Jesus, *Galatians 3:28*, and thus both share in His sacrifice. By the power of this sacrifice, they must strive from the heart toward sanctification, simplicity, and chaste, pure love. However, only the believers may take comfort in this, not the unbelievers and natural, fleshly people who remain stuck in their carnal lusts and lewdness, inciting others to do the same (*2 Peter 2:18*). These will die in their uncleanness because they have defiled the holy faith of the Gospel, which was preached among them, with their unholy and unchaste conduct, as much as lies within them.

**Shall bring them to the priest)** She only needed to place as much money as was necessary into the appropriate chest, and by evening she was permitted to eat of the holy things,

<margin>v. 30. Meanwhile, the priests offered the pigeons purchased with that money. For the priests did not leave until the designated chest was empty and birds had been sacrificed for all the money provided.</margin>

**The one for a sin offering, the other for a burnt offering)** There are two kinds of surrender. The first is simply offered to God: this represents the purity that comes through the simple turning back to God after committing errors of oversight or genuine weakness. The burnt offering made from the second turtledove signifies the purity of a higher stage, which occurs through sanctified love. Here, the soul is always like a burnt offering—not only to be purified but to be entirely consumed in that same love. It then seems as if the soul changes its form and nature, so that it might have no other nature than that of spiritual fire. This is the thorough and deepest purification, which occurs through nothing other than pure love.

**Atonement)** No one among the unclean who required atonement was reconciled with God, nor pure before Him, nor permitted to eat of the holy things as long as they did not bring their sacrifice—even if he or she had washed with water and was cleansed before men, and even if the sun had set upon them on the 7th day.

Just as the priests under the Law purified or atoned for those who carried guilt through these sacrifices, so the priests of the New Covenant of Christ can much more cancel debts through their holy sacrifices and prayers. Ephrem <note>original: "Efrem (b)"; referring to Ephrem the Syrian, a 4th-century theologian. The Latin citation (b) refers to "in his Testament, p. 790."</note> concludes this from a sound basis, which is primarily to be found in the intercession of the Spirit of Christ.

<column-break/>

31. Thus shall you separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness, that they die not in their uncleanness when they defile my dwelling that is in the midst of them.
> 2 Exodus 29:45, 46. 1 Kings 8:27. 1 Corinthians 3:17.

32. This is the law for him that has a discharge, and for him whose seed of copulation goes from him, so that he is defiled thereby;

33. And for her that is weak in her separation; and for whoever has a discharge, whether it be man or woman; and when a man shall have lain with an unclean woman.

<margin>v. 31. Separate from their uncleanness)</margin> This the priest does when he understands true spiritual uncleanness and cleanses from it.

**But who does this?** Answer: The priest of the Old Testament did it symbolically, as a figure of the High Priest <note>Jesus Christ</note> who has made the purification of our sins through Himself, and truly still makes it, essentially separating us from uncleanness. And although it is also said of Protestant <note>The German "Evangelischen" refers to the Lutheran or Reformed clergy of the author's time.</note> priests that they loose and absolve as God’s substitutes on earth, these actions are nonetheless often performed in great ignorance and presumption. This is especially true of those who, for the sake of physical livelihood or some other side-motive, and out of the impulse of their own spirit, have taken the honor of the priestly office upon themselves or had it bestowed by others without the impulse and calling of God the Holy Spirit. What wonder is it then if neither wit nor understanding, neither diligence nor zeal, is shown in distinguishing the clean from the unclean?

But just as the priests here had to watch over this uncleanness to separate such unclean persons from the community of the sanctuary, so much more must the ministers of the New Testament oppose all uncleanness of the flesh and the spirit with great earnestness. They must lead such unclean people away from sinful lusts through the testimony of the Spirit, since in Christ a pure and chaste being must be sought (*Ephesians 4:19 etc.*). Indeed, those found in the outbursts of such fleshly lusts must be separated from the community of believers, just as Paul earnestly testified against fornication and excluded the man guilty of incest (*1 Corinthians 5:1 etc., 6:9 etc.*).

**In the midst of them)** Or more accurately, "within them."

The true Israel of God should and must be clean for this very reason: because he is such (*Psalm 73:1*), and because the most pure and holy God has His Tabernacle and Temple in the midst of them. For He prepares to set it up there when we keep and do His commandments (*Chapter 26:3, 11-13*). The holy place and site where the most holy God wishes to dwell must be holy and pure! He can be touched by no one who is unlike Him, nor can anyone draw near to Him (*1 John 3:3*). This dwelling is your heart, O Israel! (*2 Corinthians 6:16, 17; 7:1*).

<margin>v. 32. This is the law).</margin> The priests were subject to this law of uncleanness just as much as others. Thus, if such a thing happened to a priest in his sleep, he went out of the Temple in the morning and was not allowed to perform any priestly office in the inner court.

<margin>v. 33. Finally, the Jews added many more such uncleannesses, as the Savior laments in Mark 7:4, 5.</margin>

# Chapter XVI.
->The Day of General Atonement.<-

**And** the Lord spoke to Moses after the two sons of Aaron had died, when they had come before the face of the Lord and died;
2. And the Lord spoke to Moses: <margin>(a) Numbers 8:1, 2.</margin> Speak (a) to your brother Aaron, that he should not go at all times into the Sanctuary inside the veil, before the Mercy Seat that is upon the Ark; so that he does not die.

---

<margin>v. 1. The time is named when GOD made this arrangement.</margin>
<margin>Died) Were killed by the Lord because of the strange fire they brought.</margin>
This chapter is one of the most remarkable that may ever occur, for the understanding of which, according to the true sense of the Spirit, the wisdom from above especially belongs. Initially, it is stated:

There is nothing of greater importance for a soul which GOD draws to Himself than that it brings no "strange fire" before Him. Its fire must be pure, clean, rising straight upward, and inviolably sanctified to GOD: without which, the same brings death after it.

There are two kinds of strange fire. One is coarser, but the other is more subtle and thus also more dangerous. The first is attachment to any of the creatures outside ourselves: such as goods, honor, fortune, persons, etc.—in summary, to everything that is not GOD Himself. The other strange fire is self-love and one's own will, which are rooted in us and have, as it were, become one being with us. This is then called bringing a strange fire when we burn our incense on this unholy fire. The incense represents petition and prayer, as the Revelation of John (a) indicates when it says that each of the twenty-four elders held a censer before the throne of GOD, and that these were the prayers of the saints. If prayer is to be perfect, it must emerge from pure love, which melts the soul and makes it fluid, just as the gum of the incense is melted and becomes fluid in the fire; so that (if it is permitted to speak in such a way) this soul, having been melted through the abandonment of selfhood <note>German: *Eigenheit*, a term used in mystical theology to describe the ego-centered nature that resists God</note>—which it held entirely hard within itself and prevented from flowing out and losing itself in God—may be completely freed from all selfhood through pure love, which alone can do it, and lose itself entirely to itself, and thereafter in God its ultimate goal.

<margin>v. 2. It was therefore necessary that Aaron be further instructed with heavenly teaching on how to approach the altar and in what manner he should atone to GOD, so that what happened to his sons would not also happen to him, as they brought strange fire and not that which had come from heaven.</margin>
<margin>Not at all times) He was allowed to go in there only once a year and on a certain day of the year (v. 29, 30), yet several times. For it was impossible for him to carry and take in with him everything he needed all at once.</margin>
Why, however, did God not want the High Priest to be allowed into the Most Holy Place at all times? This happened so that GOD would be made all the more venerable at that time to these peoples, who then had only a very poor and coarse concept of God, since they had been led only through terror, through extraordinary things, miracle-works, and unheard-of matters. After the birth of Jesus Christ, this so great GOD made Himself entirely accessible to men. But alas! how much have they not misused this! Perhaps fear was more advantageous to them than this overflowing goodness. This is indeed so in consideration of those desolate hearts: But the good hearts are moved much more by His love than by all His imaginable miracle-works. Oh, how such goodness is so rare!

<margin>(a) Revelation 5:8.</margin>

<column-break/>

For I will appear in a cloud upon the Mercy Seat. <margin>Numbers 9:15.</margin>

**3. Herewith Aaron shall go into the Sanctuary, with a bullock, namely a young ox, for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering.** <margin>ch. 9:7.</margin> **4. He**

---

<margin>God covers and, as it were, veils His majesty with a cloud.</margin>
There is, however, another thing to consider: namely, that God says He will appear in a cloud upon the Mercy Seat. For it is certain that the soul has no free and constant access to God in the center of its soul, wherein God dwells, except through faith, and indeed the very purest faith. GOD covers and, as it were, veils His majesty with a cloud. Everything thus occurs in this spiritual darkness and is also worked in the same: in that the soul feels, sees, knows, nor distinguishes anything else but a deep silence. Yet it is assured through faith that it is God: it also cannot doubt it; because He, as He Himself said elsewhere, (a) has chosen the darkness for His hiding place. This worshipful majesty of GOD, hidden in the cloud, has something much greater and more certain in itself than all that which can be perceived through the senses and powers, such as taste, visions, revelations, ecstasies, and the like, which are felt through the senses because they are much coarser; or through the powers, which are indeed not so coarse, but yet very slight in comparison to this holy darkness, which in this life must serve for the communication of GOD Himself, just as the light of glory must serve in the next life.

Since God also wanted to appear here in a cloud, namely on this day, in order then to accept the atonement of the people, and because this place should be singularly honored with the appearance of the Lord; so no man should come here out of reverence for this place until He would have come who acquired access to God for us, so that we might one day appear before His face.

<margin>v. 3. The High Priest had to be completely purified when he wanted to go into the Most Holy Place, according to the complete purification of the law, which occurred through the shedding of the blood of animals—a purification even more extensive than that of water: because it served not only (like water) for legal purity, but also for sins; although this blood of itself had no worth: For all its merit consisted in the blood which JESUS Christ was to shed. Therefore, the High Priest had to be purified through blood before he went into the Most Holy Place, which was then covered with clouds.</margin>
The soul must also be purified from all its defilements through the blood of Jesus Christ, after it has been previously washed through the water of the tears of repentance, so that it can be received into the cloud wherein GOD is. What a purification it must endure! JESUS Christ can only give the soul true purity through His blood. It must not only be sprinkled with the same, but entirely washed. O You worshipful Savior! nothing happens except through You. And although You are then hidden from the soul according to Your purpose, it finds afterward, when it has come a little further, that Jesus Christ has done all these things. (b) All things were made through Him, and nothing without Him. Thus Jesus Christ cleanses and prepares the soul until He has made it pure enough to be able to lose it in God and hide it with Himself.

And this true High Priest, the prefiguring <note>German: *fürbildende*, referring to the Old Testament types that point toward Christ</note> High Priest from among men had to represent with the ordained sacrifices for himself and his house, which was the tribe of Levi, and then for the people, which were the other tribes.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XVI.

4. He shall put on the holy linen **tunic**, and have the linen **undergarments** <gloss>(a)</gloss> upon his flesh, and gird himself with a linen **sash**, and wear the linen **turban**; these are the holy garments: and he shall bathe his flesh in water, and put them on.

<margin>(a) Exodus 28:42.</margin>

---

And indeed, since he was to appear only in linen clothes, and was not permitted to wear the high-priestly finery here—the robe, the breastplate <note>original: "Amt-Schildleins," the breastplate of judgment set with gemstones</note> with the precious stones, and the golden crown—this points toward the state of **Christ's humiliation** in His weak humanity, in which He had to perform the sacrifice of atonement.

For linen comes from the earth: and so the true High Priest JESUS Christ puts on the holy linen tunic when He assumes the nature of the earthly body.

But it is not without reason that this linen tunic is called **holy**: because the tunic of Christ's flesh was not produced from the will or seed of a man, but from the Holy Spirit.

It is well to note, however, that the High Priest certainly wore his full ceremonial regalia on the Day of Atonement: but only when he was outside the Most Holy Place, either in the Holy Place or in the inner courtyard, dealing with sacrifices whose blood did not enter the Most Holy Place. But when he entered the Most Holy Place, or dealt with sacrifices whose blood entered the Most Holy Place, he did not wear his ceremonial regalia at all, but rather white **mourning clothes**, and thus he had to change his clothes often on this day.

Furthermore, these four linen garments were not the ones he usually wore under his other clothes, which he had in common with the other priests: rather, they were special garments made of plain white six-strand linen, mixed with no other color, unlike the sashes the priests usually wore.

This linen clothing, with which the High Priest was to be arrayed, beautifully signifies a pure, simple, and outwardly innocent life, which observes all rules of decency and modesty externally (to edify one's neighbor and not to cause offense), hides the interior, and covers it with this veil of simplicity and innocence. Nothing is more common than linen: nothing is more common than the life of these simple, innocent, small, and childlike souls.

**Shall bathe his flesh with water, and put them on)** As soon as the dawn of this day broke, and the time approached to slaughter the daily morning sacrifice, they brought the High Priest to the bathing chamber so that he might bathe. Between the High Priest and the people (who could look up through the windows in the Court of the Gentiles) a beautiful white linen curtain was drawn, so that no one could see him.

If the High Priest was old or weak, they would heat various iron plates the evening before and thrust them into the cold water so that the bath would become somewhat lukewarm.

Once he had bathed his whole body and dried himself again, the priests brought him his magnificent ceremonial clothes, which they called the **golden garments**. With these, he went into the inner courtyard. Before he began anything, he first washed his hands and feet again, specifically from a golden basin. When that was done, he began his service with the daily morning sacrifice, which he slaughtered even before sunrise, and then left to another priest to prepare further. He, however, then entered the Holy Place, burned incense, and extinguished the lamps: and after he had said his prayer and come out again, he offered each thing that was customary for the daily sacrifice.

After the daily sacrifice had been offered, the High Priest was taken back to the bathing chamber, and there a linen curtain was likewise drawn. He washed his hands and feet again, took off his magnificent clothes, and stepped into the bath; after he had stepped out again and dried himself, instead of the eight magnificent garments in which he had offered the daily sacrifice, four other snow-white linen garments were handed to him, made of precious **Pelusian linen** <note>Linen from Pelusium in Egypt, famous in antiquity for its superior quality</note>, the value of which was estimated at one and a half hundred Reichsthaler <note>A historical German silver coin; 150 Rthlr. was a very large sum</note> by our calculation.

<column-break/>

5. And he shall take from the congregation of the children of Israel **two male goats** for a sin offering, and one **ram** for a burnt offering.
6. And Aaron shall offer the **bull** <note>original: "Farren," a young bull or steer</note> of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and his house.
7. Afterward, he shall take the two goats and set them before the face of the LORD before the door of the Tabernacle of the Meeting.
8. An<unclear>d</unclear>

---

**v. 5.** [Two male goats] And indeed very tender young ones, as the text indicates, which are still with their mothers and are taken from them; two young kids.

These were not unclean animals that were forbidden from God's altar; rather, they were certainly clean and accustomed to being sacrificed: so that you may know that they bear the image not of those who are outside, apart from the church and the most holy faith, but of those who have entered the fellowship of faith.

These two goats represent **two kinds of people** who are called by GOD to be sacrificed to Him in different ways. The first through the losing of themselves in GOD: these belong to Him especially, because He also dedicates them to the highest grace, which is to be reserved for Him alone, to be sacrificed without exception, and without any means of preservation remaining to them. The others are those dedicated to good works, such as the service of the people and spiritual gifts: and they save their souls.

Also prefigured here were the persons who are to be established by the LORD. These are of two kinds and shall be separated from one another, just as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.

But how can goats become sheep? **Answer:** When they free themselves from their sins through righteousness, and from their iniquities through mercy (Daniel 4:24); when they make friends for themselves with the "unrighteous mammon," while the others keep their unrighteous mammon, perish with it, and remain goats.

**Ram for a burnt offering)** This is the final purification, which cannot happen except through pure and holy love. For this burns and consumes everything, so that nothing can remain. Therefore, pure love is actually the true **burnt offering**, in which all self-interest <note>original: "Eigenheit," self-will or ego</note> has been consumed.

**v. 6.** After the High Priest had put on the snow-white linen garments and again washed his hands and feet, he went back into the inner courtyard to the bull; he stood facing East behind the bull, which stood with its head toward the South and its face turned Westward; and his own face was also turned Westward toward the Temple. He laid both his hands on the bull’s head and made confession of sins for himself and his family.

**v. 7.** Thereupon he left the bull standing and went Eastward to the North side of the altar of burnt offering, where the two young goats stood.

The Deputy <note>original: "Statthalter," likely referring to the Sagan or second-in-command to the High Priest</note> was always at the High Priest’s right hand for honor’s sake, and the head of the paternal house at his left.

They saw to it that they obtained two identical goats, which were alike in color—either both black or both white—and also of equal size and value, if possible.

**They set)** Both goats had their faces turned Westward toward the Temple and their backs toward the East; one goat stood at the High Priest’s right, and the other at his left. <gloss>(a)</gloss>

# 8. And Aaron shall cast lots upon the two goats: one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for the goat that goes away.
