->(Casting the Lots)<-

There were two plates <note>likely small tablets or tokens</note> that lay in a wooden box, which was wide enough at the top so that one could put both hands inside; these he would rattle and shake.

Otherwise, it did not matter what material the lots were made of, as long as they were identical and made of the same substance. In the First Temple, they were made of wood; in the Second, they were made of gold. On one plate or tablet was written: ליהוה <note>original: "La-Adonai," meaning "To the LORD"</note>: and on the other: לעזאζל <note>original: "La-Azazel," meaning "To Azazel"</note>.

Once he had shaken the box, he reached in with both hands and grasped the plates. If he grasped the lot "To the LORD!" in his right hand—which they considered a good omen—the Deputy <note>original: "Statthalter," likely referring to the Segan, the assistant High Priest</note> standing at his side would say: "Lord High Priest, raise your right hand high!" But if he received it in his left hand, the Head of the Father’s House standing at his left would call out: "Lord High Priest, raise your left hand high!"

He then placed both lots upon the goats: on the goat to his right, the lot he had grasped with his right hand; and the one he had grasped with his left hand, he placed on the goat to his left. When he placed the lot with the name of the LORD on the goat upon which the LORD's lot had fallen, he would say: "To the LORD!" or "To the LORD for a sin offering!" Then the priests, Levites, and all the people—as soon as he uttered the most holy name of God, יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God</note>, which he spoke on this day alone exactly as it is pronounced—would kneel and say: "Blessed be the glorious name of His kingdom forever and ever!" <gloss>(a)</gloss> which they always did upon the naming of this name on this day.

If one of these two goats died by accident before the lots were cast, another was brought in its place. However, if it happened after the lots were cast, another pair was purchased from the public treasury, and the lots were cast anew. If the goat belonging to the LORD had died, the High Priest would say: "The goat upon which the LORD's lot falls shall stand in the place of the previous deceased one." But if the other had died, he said: "The goat upon which the lot for Azazel falls shall stand in the place of the previous deceased one."

The question arises, however: what is Azazel? Concerning this, one may cite several opinions without necessarily adopting them, leaving the judgment to the reader.

Some Hebrews maintain it is a certain devil <note>or demon</note> to whom they gave a goat on this day so that he would do them no harm.

The Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as <term>apopompaion</term> <note>original: "αποπομπαιον"</note>, which some explain as a goat sent away or dismissed; however, it seems they were looking toward the custom of the heathens, among whom there were certain <term>theoi apopompaioi</term> <note>original: "θεοὶ αποπομπαιοι"</note>, or <term>Dii averrunci</term> <note>Latin: "Averting gods"</note>, which are gods who turned evil away from the land. Emperor Julian therefore mocked this greatly, claiming God allowed an offering to be given to the devil <gloss>(b)</gloss>.

Other Hebrews claim it is the name of a place, specifically a mountain in the desert of Juk, where this goat was taken; many Christians also agree with this <gloss>(c)</gloss>. However, others have been unable to find this mountain anywhere in geography or on maps, though they have searched thoroughly.

Others <gloss>(d)</gloss> also want the goat itself to be so named, namely the "going-away goat": which others refute based on this very verse and its logic, because if one goat were to be Azazel itself, the other goat would have to be "the LORD" (ליהוה); for the text clearly states in a balanced contrast: one lot for the LORD, the other for Azazel.

---

(a) Rabbi Judah Leo, Book 3 on the Temple, Ch. 6, §. 22. Bochart, cited above, p. 656.
(b) see Dieteric, Biblical Antiquities on Psalm 50:10. Vol II, p. 451. Reitz, note 1 on Goodwin's Moses & Aaron, Book 3, Ch. 8. Momma, on the state of the Church under the Patriarchs, Vol 1, Book 2, Ch. 11, §. 31 ff. Bochart, Hierozoicon, Part 1, Book 2, Ch. 54, p. 650 ff.
(c) see Leigh in Lexicon, p. 166. Glass, Sacred Grammar, p. 763. Cunaeus, On the Hebrew Republic, Book 2, Ch. 6.
(d) Quistorp on this passage. Goodwin, cited above.

<column-break/>

->(One lot for the LORD, the other for Azazel)<-

From this one also sees that, just as all five books of Moses are in fact very mysterious, so too is this third book in particular: and all the more so in those parts which the Spirit of God seems to hide with all diligence, and which are therefore of such a nature that they require our special diligence, humility, and teachability to investigate. For if they were not meant to be searched and explored, why would they have been written? Especially since in this final age in which we find ourselves, nothing shall remain covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be made known. Matthew 10:26.

Franciscus Georgius Venetus, Cornelius Agrippa, Reuchlin, and other learned men, especially Cabbalists—who have written with great confidence about good and evil angels—make this Azazel the overseer of the desert: this we leave to their credit, though we have no reason to doubt that just as there are hierarchies and orders among the good angels, there are also overseer-ships and distinctions or grades among the evil angels, as Holy Scripture itself points to here and there. Matthew 12:24, Job 12:31, Ephesians 2:2, 6:12, Colossians 2:15.

Accordingly, the opinion is not so absurd or rejectable that by Azazel the devil is understood. It is also notable that in Hebrew, a goat and the devil share the same name; as can be seen from verse 7 of this chapter and the following chapter 17:7, 2 Chronicles 11:15, Isaiah 13:21, 34:14. And whenever one of the two goats is mentioned in this chapter, it is always called by the name <term>Seir</term> <note>a shaggy goat or demon</note>, and not <term>Ez</term> <note>a standard goat</note>, as is usual elsewhere and from which the word "Azazel" is derived. From this, some conclude that the word Azazel, which appears four times in this chapter, must be left untranslated; they also rely on the clear and distinct separation in this verse where, just as the two goats are contrasted, so also the LORD and Azazel are set against each other, rather than the LORD and a goat; and they argue that such a translation would create ambiguity instead of the distinction made between the two goats by lot.

There are two things in man: one is spiritual, the other is animalistic or sensual; and in this latter part there are again two distinct things, one of which is left to the devil, while the other is transformed into the spiritual.

What then are these two lots other than the sheep on the right, whom the LORD has chosen for His inheritance, and the goats on the left, who retain the "goat-nature" of their father, the devil? Over these, Christ the High Priest, as the judge of all flesh, casts the lot; He can surely strike the sinful goat, or bring out the guilty Achan by lot.

Thus, the lot of the LORD (or for the LORD) represents the believers and the pious, who have stepped onto God's side and clung to the good; they are therefore also called the lot of His inheritance. The lot of Azazel, however, by clear contrast, represents the devil's followers, or those who are of his part, as they are called in Wisdom of Solomon 2:25; just as they find their portion with him in the eternal wilderness where there is howling. For if there is nothing absurd in ascribing a kingdom to him as well as to God the LORD, then there can be nothing absurd in the idea that, just as one lot falls to the LORD, so in contrast the other goat—and under its image, his lineage and the serpent’s seed—should fall to the devil. This contrast between God and the devil is indeed established so often and in so many parts of Scripture.

Meanwhile, we have here a clear and obvious proof that we are saved by grace. We all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, just like the two goats that were taken for the whole congregation of Israel and presented here to the LORD. The different lots give us: one for the LORD, the other for Azazel. Who among us knows which lot will fall upon him? For we all fall short of the glory of our God (Romans 3:23). And the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). And those who are blessed and called to inherit the kingdom of God want to know nothing of the good that is praised in them. Matthew 25:37–39.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XVI.

<margin>(a) Exodus 28:42.</margin>
**4. He shall put on the holy linen tunic, and have the linen undergarments (a) upon his flesh, and gird himself with a linen sash, and have the linen turban on; these are the holy garments: and he shall bathe his flesh with water, and put them on.**

Indeed, since he was to appear only in linen clothes and was not permitted to wear the High Priestly finery—the ephod, the breastpiece of judgment with the precious stones, and the golden crown—this points toward the state of Christ’s humiliation in his weak humanity, in which he had to perform the sacrifice of reconciliation.

For linen comes from the earth: and so the true High Priest JESUS Christ puts on the holy linen tunic when he takes on the nature of an earthly body.

This linen tunic is not called holy without reason: for the "tunic" of Christ's flesh was not begotten of the will or seed of a man, but of the Holy Spirit.

It is well to note that the High Priest did indeed wear his full regalia on the Day of Atonement, but only when he was outside the Holy of Holies—either in the Holy Place or in the inner courtyard—dealing with sacrifices whose blood was not to be brought into the Holy of Holies. However, when he entered the Holy of Holies or dealt with the sacrifices whose blood did enter the Holy of Holies, he did not wear his regalia at all, but rather white mourning clothes, and thus had to change his clothes often on this day.

Furthermore, these four linen garments were not the ones he usually wore underneath his other clothes or those he had in common with other priests; rather, they were special garments made of plain, white, six-threaded linen, mixed with no other color, unlike the usual sashes of the priests.

This linen clothing, which the High Priest was to be dressed in, beautifully signifies a pure, simple life, innocent on the outside, which outwardly observes all rules of propriety and modesty (to edify one's neighbor and not to cause offense), while hiding the inner self and covering it with this cloak of simplicity and innocence. Nothing is more common than linen: likewise, nothing is more common than the life of these simple, innocent, small, and childlike souls.

**Shall bathe his flesh with water, and put them on)** As soon as the dawn of this day broke and the time approached to slaughter the daily morning sacrifice, they brought the High Priest to the bathing chamber where he bathed. Between the High Priest and the people (who could look up through the windows in the Court of the Gentiles), a beautiful white linen curtain was drawn so that no one could see him.

If the High Priest was old or weak, they would make various iron plates very hot the evening before and thrust them into the cold water so that the bath would become somewhat lukewarm.

Once he had bathed his whole body and dried himself, the priests brought him his magnificent garments of state, which they called the "golden garments." With these, he went into the inner courtyard. Before he began anything, he washed his hands and feet again, specifically from a golden basin. When this was done, he began his service with the daily morning sacrifice, which he slaughtered even before sunrise, leaving it to another priest to prepare further. He, however, then entered the Holy Place, burned incense, and extinguished the lamps; and after he had said his prayer and come out again, he offered everything that was customary for the daily sacrifice.

After the daily sacrifice was offered, the High Priest was brought back to the bathing chamber, and a linen curtain was again drawn. He washed his hands and feet once more, took off his magnificent garments, stepped into the bath, and after climbing out and drying himself, instead of the eight magnificent garments in which he had offered the daily sacrifice, he was handed four other snow-white linen garments made of precious Pelusian linen <note>A high-quality fine linen from Pelusium, Egypt</note>, the value of which was estimated at one hundred and fifty Reichsthalers <note>An early modern silver currency</note> by our calculation.

<column-break/>

**5. And he shall take of the congregation of the children of Israel two kids of the goats for a sin offering, and one ram for a burnt offering.**

**6. And Aaron shall offer his bullock of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make an atonement for himself, and for his house.**

**7. And he shall take the two goats, and present them before the LORD at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation.**

**8. An-**

**v. 5. Two kids of the goats)** Specifically very tender young ones, as the text indicates, which are still with their mothers and are taken from them; two young kids.

These were not unclean animals that were forbidden from coming upon the altar of God; rather, they were certainly clean and accustomed to being sacrificed: so that you may know that those who bear the "Image" <note>likely referring to the image of God or the mark of the faithful</note> are not those who are outside, apart from the Church and the most holy faith, but those who have entered into the communion of faith.

These two goats represent two kinds of people who are called by GOD to be sacrificed to Him in different ways. The first kind through the denial of themselves in GOD: these belong to Him especially, and He subjects them to the highest grace, which is to be separated by the Shepherd who divides the sheep from the goats.

The others are those dedicated to good works, such as the service of the people and spiritual gifts: and these save their souls.

Also, the persons who are to be judged by the Lord were prefigured here. These are of two kinds and shall be separated from one another, just as the Shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.

But how can sheep be made out of goats? Answer: When they free themselves from their sins through righteousness, and from their iniquities through mercy (Daniel 4:24); when they make friends for themselves with the "unrighteous mammon" <note>wealth/money</note>, while the others keep their unrighteous mammon, perish with it, and remain goats.

**Ram for a burnt offering)** This is the final purification, which cannot happen except through pure and holy love. For this love burns and consumes everything so that nothing can remain. Therefore, pure love is actually the true burnt offering, in which all self-interest has been consumed.

**v. 6.** After the High Priest had put on the snow-white linen garments and washed his hands and feet yet again, he went back into the inner courtyard toward the young bull. He stood facing East behind the bull, which stood with its head toward the South and its face turned toward the West. He also had his face turned toward the West toward the Temple, laid both his hands on the bull's head, and made confession of sins for himself and his family.

**v. 7.** Thereupon he left the bull standing and went back toward the East to the North side of the altar of burnt offering, where the two young goats stood.

The Deputy <note>original: "Statthalter," the Segan or assistant priest</note> was always at the High Priest’s right hand for the sake of honor, and the Head of the Father’s House was at his left.

They saw to it that they obtained two identical goats, which were similar to each other in color—either both black or both white—and also equal in size and value, if possible.

<margin>(a) See Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, part 1, book 2, chapter 54, page 655.</margin>
**They presented)** Both goats had their faces turned toward the West toward the Temple, and their backs toward the East; one goat stood at the High Priest’s right, and the other at his left. (a)

->Chapter XVI. The Third Book of Moses (Leviticus). 503<-

## 8. And Aaron shall cast lots over the two goats:

(Casting the lots) These were two plates, kept in a wooden box that was wide enough at the top for someone to put both hands inside, which he then shook and rattled.

Otherwise, it did not matter what material the lots were made of, as long as they were identical and made of the same substance. In the first Temple, they were made of wood; in the second, they were made of gold. On one plate was written: **For the LORD** <note>Hebrew: *la-Adonai* (ליהוה)</note>: on the other: **For Azazel** <note>Hebrew: *la-Azazel* (לעזאזל)</note>.

Once he had shaken the box, he reached in with both hands and grasped the plates. If he caught the lot "For the LORD!" in his right hand, they considered it a good omen. The deputy standing at his side would then say: "Lord High Priest, raise your right hand high!" But if he caught it in his left hand, the head of the ancestral house standing to his left would cry: "Lord High Priest, raise your left hand high!" He then placed both lots on the goats: on the goat to his right, the lot he had grasped with his right hand; and the one he grasped with his left hand, he placed on the goat to his left. When he placed the lot with the name of the LORD on the goat designated for the LORD, he would say: "For the LORD!" or "For the LORD as a sin offering!" At that moment, as soon as he spoke the most holy name of God, **YHWH** <note>The Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God, which was only pronounced by the High Priest on this specific day</note>—which he alone pronounced on this day exactly as it sounds—the priests, Levites, and all the people would kneel down and say: "Blessed be the praiseworthy name of His kingdom forever and ever!" <margin>(a) Rabbi Judah Leo, *De Templo*, Book 3, Chapter 6, Section 22.</margin> (a) This they would always do whenever that Name was mentioned on this day.

If one of these two goats died by accident before the lots were cast, another was brought to take its place. However, if it happened after the lots were cast, another pair was purchased from the public treasury, and the lots were cast anew. If the goat to be killed for the LORD died, the High Priest would say: "The goat upon which the lot of the LORD falls shall stand in the place of the previous deceased one." But if the other died, he said: "The goat upon which the lot of Azazel falls shall stand in the place of the previous deceased one."

The question arises: what is Azazel? Several opinions can be cited here, without necessarily endorsing them, leaving the judgment to the reader.

Some Hebrews maintain that it is a certain devil to whom they gave a goat on this day so that he would do them no harm.

The Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translates it as *apopompaion* <note>Greek: αποπομπαῖον, meaning "the one to be sent away"</note>, which some explain as a "sent-away goat"; however, it seems they were looking toward the customs of the heathens, who had certain *Theoi apopompaioi* <note>Greek: "Averting gods"</note> or *Dii averrunci* <note>Latin: "Gods who turn away evil"</note>, which are gods who turned evil away from the land. The Emperor Julian <note>Known as "the Apostate" for rejecting Christianity</note> mocked this greatly, claiming that God allowed an offering to be given to the devil. <margin>(b) See Dietericus, *Antiquitates Biblicae* on Psalm 50:10, Volume II, page 451. Reitz, note 1 on Goodwin’s *Moses and Aaron*, Book 3, Chapter 8. Momma, *The State of the Church under the Patriarchs*, Volume 1, Book 2, Chapter 11, Section 31 and following. Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, Part 1, Book 2, Chapter 54, page 650 and following.</margin> (b).

Other Hebrews claim it is the name of a place, specifically a mountain in the desert of "Zuck," where this goat was taken; many Christians also agree with them (c). However, others have been unable to find such a mountain in any geography books or maps, even though they have searched diligently.

<margin>(c) See Leigh in *Lexicon*, folio 166. Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, page 763. Cunaeus, *The Hebrew Republic*, Book 2, Chapter 6.</margin> Others (d) also argue that the goat itself was called by this name, namely "the goat that goes away." However, others refute this based on this very verse and linguistic logic; for if the goat itself were meant to be called Azazel, then the other goat would have to be called "the LORD." <margin>(d) Quistorp on this passage; Goodwin, as cited above.</margin> (d) For the text clearly states in the balance of the opposition: <note>Bochart, part 1, book 2, chapter 54, page 656.</note>

<column-break/>

## one lot for the LORD, and the other lot for the goat that goes away.
## 9. And

(One lot for the LORD, the other for Azazel) From this also, one can see that just as all five books of Moses are in fact full of mysteries, this third book in particular is a very mysterious book. This is especially true in those parts which the Spirit of God seems to hide with all diligence, and which therefore require our extraordinary diligence, humility, and teachability to investigate. For if they were not meant to be investigated and explored, why were they written? Especially since in this final age in which we find ourselves, nothing shall remain covered that shall not be revealed, nor hidden that shall not be made known (Matthew 10:26).

Franciscus Georgius Venetus, Cornelius Agrippa, Reuchlin <note>Prominent Renaissance scholars and Christian Kabbalists who studied Jewish mysticism</note>, and other learned men, especially the Kabbalists, who have written with great confidence about good and evil angels, make this Azazel the overseer of the desert. We leave this to their credit, though we have no reason to doubt that just as there are hierarchies and orders among the good angels, there are also overseer-ships and distinctions or grades among the evil angels, as Holy Scripture itself points to this here and there (Matthew 12:24, John 12:31, Ephesians 2:2, 6:12, Colossians 2:15).

Accordingly, the opinion that Azazel refers to the devil is not so absurd or rejectable. It is also notable that in Hebrew, a "goat" and the "devil" share a name, as seen in verse 7 of this chapter and the following chapter 17:7, 2 Chronicles 11:15, Isaiah 13:21, and 34:14. And whenever one of the two goats is mentioned in this chapter, it is always called by the name *Seir* <note>meaning "hairy" or "shaggy"</note>, and not *Ez* as is otherwise common (from which the word *Aza-el* originates). From this, some conclude that the word Azazel, which appears four times in this chapter, must be left untranslated. They also appeal to the clear and distinct contrast in this verse: just as the two goats are contrasted, so too are the LORD and Azazel contrasted—not the LORD and a goat. Using a translation like "scapegoat" instead of the distinction God made between the two goats would create an ambiguity.

There are two things in man: one is spiritual, the other is animalistic or sensual; and in this latter part, there are again two distinct things, one of which is left to the devil, while the other is transformed into the spiritual.

What then are these two lots other than the sheep on the right, whom the LORD has chosen for his inheritance, and the goats on the left, who retain the "goat-nature" of their father, the devil? Over these, Christ the High Priest, as the Judge of all flesh, casts the lot; He can surely strike the sinful goat or bring out the guilty Achan through the lot.

Thus, the lot of the LORD, or for the LORD, represents the believers and the godly who have taken God's side and clung to the good; they are therefore called the "lot of His inheritance." But the lot of Azazel, following the clear contrast, represents the devil's followers, or those who are of his portion, as they are called in Wisdom 2:25; just as they will find their portion with him in the eternal wilderness where there is wailing. For if it is not absurd to attribute a kingdom to him as well as to God the LORD, then it cannot be absurd that just as one lot falls to the LORD, the other goat likewise falls to the devil as a contrast—and under the image of that goat, his lineage and the "seed of the serpent" are included. This contrast between God and the devil is established by Scripture so often and in so many parts.

Meanwhile, we have here a clear and obvious proof that we are saved by grace. We all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, just like the two goats which were taken for the entire congregation of Israel and presented here to the LORD. The different lots are cast for us: one for the LORD, the other for Azazel. Who among us knows which lot will fall upon him? We all fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23). And the wages of sin is death (Romans 6:23). And those who are blessed and called to inherit the kingdom of God want to know nothing of the good that is praised in them (Matthew 25:37–39).

### 9. And Aaron shall bring the goat upon which the lot fell for the LORD and prepare it as a sin offering.

The lot creates the distinction: and the eternal inheritance is called a distribution "by lot" in Acts 20:32, an inheritance "obtained by lot" in Ephesians 1:11. And the means that qualifies us and makes us fit or capable of receiving this inheritance is expressed in 2 Peter 1:1.

What, then, is more doubtful or uncertain than a lot? And yet, the same must decide who is for the Lord, so that he may receive the Kingdom; and who, on the other hand, is for Azazel <note>The Hebrew term *Azazel* is often translated as "scapegoat," but here the author treats it as a destination or a spiritual entity opposing the Lord</note>, so that he may depart from the Lord and be sent to Azazel.

But praised be God the Lord and eternally exalted, who holds the governance of the lot in His hand and reserves it for His own power, as in Proverbs 16:33. For this is so far from introducing some fatalistic necessity <note>original: "fatalen Nothzwang," referring to the idea that humans have no free will</note> that such a thing can find even less place here. Therefore, it has been shown to you, O man, what is good! (Micah 6:8).

Just as a lot from these two is certain for each among us, so it is also certain that when we do good, we belong to the Lord’s lot; and conversely, if we do evil, our lot brings us toward the wilderness. If you have lived for the Lord, broken your bread from the heart for the hungry, clothed the naked, judged with a righteous judgment, hated evil, and had no fellowship with it—then you make the Lord Himself your lot and choose the "better part" <note>An allusion to Luke 10:42</note>. But if you serve your lusts and love the world and yourself more than God, then you step of your own accord to the side and into the lot of Azazel.

Thus, the lot is not to be understood as it occurs among men by chance and without understanding or judgment; rather, the "lot of the Lord" is as much as to say the Lord’s choice or portion. Conversely, that lot by which one must wander into the wilderness is to be seen as that portion which is despised and rejected by God because of its unworthiness.

The ultimate purpose that the Lord has in this also indicates that not all purified souls are called to the Apostolic life. There are excellent souls of whom one has no knowledge at all, who are secretly sanctified and will not be recognized until the future life. And these are the saints dedicated to the Lord, just as this goat was also sanctified to the Lord.

The lot represents clearly enough the peculiar and powerful calling of God, both of the first and the second kind of these paths. Those who are called to good works end their lives in such a way, and indeed holily, that they receive great rewards from God as fruits of their toil and labor, and for the services they rendered to souls. But those who are dedicated to God Himself even in this life—oh, they must give up their lives for it and be sacrificed without mercy! Everyone must therefore be faithful in his calling and path, and hold the calling of another in high esteem, without judging or despising it, considering that <margin>(a) each has received his own gift from God, and that all the worthiness of every station comes from the will of God—by which one is in that station—and from the faithfulness with which one remains in it; just as it is that which works our perfection.</margin> (a) each has received his own gift from God, and that all the worthiness of every station comes from the will of God—by which one is in that station—and from the faithfulness with which one remains in it; just as it is that which works our perfection.

The goat upon which the Lord’s lot fell had to be sacrificed. And if we are of the Lord’s lot, then we must be such as He is; namely, put to death in the flesh, that we may be made alive in the spirit (1 Peter 3:18).

If all the people of the Lord were holy, writes Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–253 AD)</note>, then there would be no need for two lots to be made, nor for one goat to be sent into the wilderness while the other was sacrificed to the Lord; rather, there would be only one lot and one sacrifice. But now, since among the multitude of those who come to the Lord some are of the Lord and others deserve to be cast away and separated, only one goat is sacrificed to the Lord.

(a) 1 Corinthians 7:7.

But / and all those who do not depart from it and are at odds with it—

<column-break/>

### 10. But the goat on which the lot fell to be a departing goat shall be presented alive before the face of the LORD.

Because he who is found in the Lord’s lot places his hope in the future world and not in the present one, and therefore "dies daily" so that the Lord remains his portion, the goat on which the Lord’s lot fell is slaughtered so that it might purify the people of God through its blood. But he who belongs to the other lot is not worthy to die. For whoever is in the lot of the Lord is not of this world; but the other is of this world, and therefore he is left in the world and for the world, because "the world loves its own." Thus, this goat—at least in such a sense—cannot well be seen as a prefiguration of Christ, as some wish; but rather and much more as an image of Barabbas <note>The prisoner released by Pilate instead of Jesus</note>, and thus of what happened with him and Christ when Pilate said: "Whom will ye that I release unto you? Jesus, who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release Barabbas (leaving him alive and sending him into the world) but bring Jesus to His death. Here we have, in person, the goat that was actually left alive in the wilderness.

To guide us a little into the knowledge of the practices of the modern Jews and their Jewish ceremonies: those who live near them will notice that around this time—namely, toward the end of September—they slaughter many roosters. For as soon as they come home from the "school" <note>The synagogue (from the Yiddish/German *shul*)</note> on the day before the Feast of Atonement, every man and every boy takes a rooster, and the women each take a hen. They prefer white birds and consider them purer, whereas red roosters are despised as unclean among them. A pregnant woman takes a rooster and a hen for herself and her child. Meanwhile, they pray Psalm 107:10, 21 and then speak from Job 33:23-24, swinging the rooster or hen three times around their head, saying each time: "This rooster shall be a substitute for me; let it come in my place; let it be the atonement (<term>Capporah <note>The Kapparot ritual, still practiced by some Jewish communities today</note></term>) for me; let death come to this rooster, but to me and all Israel a happy life!" Then they press their hands on the rooster's neck, and it is slaughtered, roasted, and eaten; though they give as much in alms to the poor as the rooster cost. They also commonly throw the entrails onto the roofs so that the ravens might carry them away, and take their sins with them.

However, one must notice a confusion here, as in so many interpretations of the two goats, in which no distinction is made regarding the "sin-goat" and the "sin-offering for atonement" (which alone had to be slaughtered), even though these are very different from each other.

A scarlet band was tied around the neck of the goat for the Lord, and it alone was actually used for the sin offering, although according to verse 5, both were required before the Lord for that purpose. For to this sin offering belonged death and the shed blood, which atoned for and reconciled sins.

The creature of God that is to be purified is defiled and contaminated by two types of sin: one is manifest and known (Galatians 5:19), the other has an appearance and outward show of righteousness (John 16:8), which together make up the "body of sin" (Romans 6:6). Now, it is not the Lord's will that His creature should perish in sins. But it is also not His will, nor is it possible, that His creature should be saved *in* its sins: because being "saved" is the same as being "delivered from sins" (Matthew 1:21). And therefore, the sinful man—signified by the goat that is for the Lord—must die to sin; he must be killed, and the will to sin in him must be completely and utterly dead. He must be separated from the other through death. Just as with a seed—for example, a grain of wheat—when it is cast into the earth, the earthly part falls away and something of it returns to the earth, while the other part (after being improved by the <term>quintessence <note>In alchemical terms, the most essential or purest part of a substance</note></term> or natural balsam) becomes part of the plant. So Christ takes the animal or "soulish" man, who was crucified with Him, into Paradise; the sinful souls who wish to remain such, He sends away to Azazel. For

...to make atonement for him, so that the same goat, which has become the departing goat, may be led out into the wilderness.

11. Afterward, Aaron shall bring the bull of the sin offering, which is for himself, and make atonement for himself and his house, and shall slaughter the bull of the sin offering that is for him.

<margin>Others translate the latter words of the 10th verse thus: Send him to Azazel.</margin>
But if this word is indeed to be translated, as has been done here with diligence, then such a translation may still provide the best sense. It is represented by the twofold lot that a distinction would appear among all those who would be outwardly called to the grace of God, first under the Old Testament and then also under the New. In both, many would be called, but few would be chosen.

As for the chosen ones, the lot has fallen for them in pleasant places with Christ, and a beautiful heritage has become theirs (Psalm 16:6). They have thus fallen to the Lord; therefore they can say: "The Lord is my portion and my share; you maintain my inheritance" (verse 5). And they have, as it is properly called, obtained a faith of equal value with the Jews through the lot (2 Peter 1:1).

The others, however, as unbelievers—first among the Jews and afterward among the Gentiles—have become like an Azazel or a departing and straying goat, which has been banished into the wilderness of misery. This is what happened to the unbelieving Jews, who were thrust out from their land into the "separated land" (verse 22) of the Gentiles far and wide; of whom it is written in Psalm 68:7: "He lets the rebellious dwell in a parched land."

Atonement has also been made for these, as is clearly to be noted here from verse 10; thus, the salvation of the Jews in the latter days is quite clearly promised through this. And this is what Paul says: "Hardening has happened to Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in; and so all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25-26). For this rebellious Israel, atonement was made first; and then, according to the conviction of many precious believers, it will likewise happen that Christ will become the actual atonement for the sins of the whole world.

Thus, the second goat receives atonement through the first goat, which alone prefigures Jesus Christ and His bloody sacrifice. The other goat prefigures instead the "goats on the left hand" <note>A reference to the Last Judgment in Matthew 25:33, where the righteous are sheep and the unrighteous are goats</note>, to whom it will one day be said: "Depart from me!" because they had previously departed and gone away from God.

And so, those upon whom the Lord’s lot falls are saved through mercy; but those upon whom Azazel’s lot falls perish through justice.

O, that the whole congregation of Israel—for whom these two goats are taken—while the matter can still be helped, and while there is still time to work out our salvation before the evil days come, might strive! May each of us seek to kill his sin, to crucify his flesh along with its lusts and desires, before it is too late! What is better and safer than to use the time we still have for the daily <term>mortification</term> <note>The spiritual practice of "putting to death" sinful desires and the "old self"</note> and killing of our sins, and to let this be our chief work? This is so that on the Day of Atonement, when a precise decision shall be made "between the righteous and the wicked, between those who serve God and those who do not serve Him" (Malachi 3:18), we may be found in this occupation. Blessed is that servant whom his Lord, when He comes, finds so doing!

<margin>v. 11.</margin> When both goats had been separated by lot, the High Priest went again in his white linen garments to his bull, which stood between the Temple and the Altar. He laid both hands upon its head for the second time; and just as he first confessed for himself and his house as poor sinners, he now did it for himself and his brothers, the other priests.

Thereupon he slaughtered this bull and caught the blood in a basin, giving it to another priest who stood a short distance away to stir it well, so that it would not clot.

12. And he shall take a censer <note>original: "Kohl-Pfanne," literally a coal-pan or brazier</note> full of burning coals of fire from off the altar <margin>(a) Numbers 16:46.</margin> that is before the face of the Lord, and his hands full of finely ground incense of sweet spices, and bring it inside the veil:

13. And

He himself took a censer and went up to the Altar of Burnt Offering. He took some of the innermost glowing coals from the pile of fire specially designated for this purpose, placed them in his censer, climbed back down, and set it on the floor.

This censer was very different from the others used daily. For while a silver one was used daily for this, and the coals were placed in it and afterward transferred from the silver into a golden censer, here he used only one, and specifically a golden one. This one was much lighter than those used daily and was made of much finer gold than the daily ones; it also had a longer handle so that he could hang it over his arm if necessary. All of this was done to make the great labor the High Priest had on this day somewhat more bearable and easier.

A vessel full of incense powder was then brought to him. This was much finer than that which was burned daily in the evening and morning, as the High Priest had ordered three pounds of the powder they used daily to be put back into the mortar the day before to be ground very small.

From this incense powder brought to him, he took a handful. To be sure, as he was a large and strong man, it was a large handful. As the person was, so was the handful. They considered taking this handful to be a difficult task; for this reason, the other priests—if the High Priest did not know how—would instruct him in this beforehand. This happened especially during the time of the Second Temple, when there were often unskilled High Priests who knew little of what a High Priest’s office was. Then the most prominent and the elders from the High Court would hand him over to the old priests, who showed him how to grasp a handful of incense. He thrust his hand into the powder, squeezed it with the three middle fingers, and what he could hold between them was a "handful." What stuck out above the three fingers he pushed back with his thumb, and what remained below, he pushed back with his pinky finger. Thus, it was only a small amount that he kept in the hollow of his hand between the three fingers. For less than half a pound went into the incense-burning in the Most Holy Place, whereas that much was always used in the Holy Place. And he put this into the golden vessel brought to him from the vessel chamber.

He then took the golden censer with the glowing coals in his right hand and the golden vessel with the incense powder in his left hand, and in his white garments, he walked reverently toward the Temple and the Most Holy Place. For he was not permitted to atone before God with blood until he had first performed the incense offering.

Happy is he in whom the eternal High Priest finds something of living and glowing coals, which He may deem fit and worthy to bring before His Father! Blessed is he in whose heart He finds such fine and spiritual incense-powder of devotion, which He may deign to fill His hand with and make a pleasing aroma for the Father! But unhappy is the soul whose fire of faith and warmth of love have so gone out and grown cold that this High Priest can find nothing but dry and cold ash instead of glowing coals! But where shall this fire, where shall the glowing coals come from, if you never let yourself be ignited by the Word of the Lord or by the Holy Spirit, but rather by anger and false love?

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter 16.

### 13. And he shall put the incense upon the fire before the face of the Lord, so that the cloud of incense may cover the atonement cover <note>The "Versöhn-Deckel" or Mercy Seat is the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, where God’s presence was said to dwell.</note> which is upon the testimony (a); so that he does not die.

### 14. And he shall take some of the blood of the bull and sprinkle it with his finger against the front of the atonement cover: and before the atonement cover he shall sprinkle of the blood with his finger seven times.

---

*verse 13. In the Holy of Holies, he set the coal pan down between the poles of the Ark of the Covenant, and poured the incense powder from the golden vessel onto the coals. For the incense powder was not poured out or lit until he had entered the Holy of Holies and set down the coal pan.*

*Just as the sacrifice of the bull and the goat represented Christ's high-priestly office in the atonement, so the burning of incense, which likewise had to occur, represents the intercession that Christ now performs in heaven for the believers, where he himself now appears before the face of God for us as an advocate who represents the saints there. Romans 8:27, Hebrews 9:24, 1 John 2:1.*

*This is now another sacrifice, which is performed only in the Holy of Holies: because it is entirely internal, and the soul must have almost reached its end so that it can be sacrificed. This is the incense offering, by which the sanctified fire of love was melted; there, prayer is nothing more than a smoke of incense, where the soul is made liquid, as it were, in holy love, and does nothing but flow into God. There, the smoke and the good scent of the entire inner being constantly rises to the Lord without bowing down again, and the soul—possessing nothing more than the glory of God alone, and having nothing of itself in any way—constantly ascends.*

*This sacrifice has an excellent scent that rises to the throne of God, who also gladly accepts it. It is the sacrifice of praise of which David speaks (a), in which the soul has no other intention than God. She desires only that He alone may be loved and praised. She also knows that He alone is worthy of such; she sends everything to Him. It is also the sacrifice of total divestment. Nothing remains of the incense after it has melted but a sweet scent, after all the smoke has flown away. And this may well be the most correct sense of what Paul calls the "good aroma in Jesus Christ" (b).*

*The smoke had to cover the atonement cover so that the high priest would not die. In this state, everything is covered with the darkness of this fragrant smoke, so that the soul (since everything is covered with darkness, and faith is the true light of this life) can distinguish nothing of God and cannot even see itself. For seeing oneself causes us death, just as curiosity does in those things which God himself does not reveal to us.*

*verse 14. As soon as he had come back into the court, he took the basin with the bull's blood from the one to whom he had given it to stir, and went with it also into the Holy of Holies, dipped his finger into the blood, and swung it once upward and then seven times downward.*

*The entire power of our prayer, valid before God, consists in Jesus Christ, when we possess the holy number seven <note>The number seven signifies spiritual perfection or the fullness of the Holy Spirit.</note> through His Spirit and let our heart's altar be sprinkled with the blood of Christ's atonement sacrifice, which atonement sacrifice had to be offered in the God-man through His blood.*

*Against the atonement cover) But not so that the blood actually touched the atonement cover.*

<margin>(a) Psalm 116:17. (b) 2 Corinthians 2:15.</margin>

<column-break/>

### 15. Afterward, he shall slaughter the goat of the sin offering, which is for the people, and shall bring its blood inside the veil, and shall do with its blood as he did with the bull's blood, and shall sprinkle it over the atonement cover and before the atonement cover.

### 16. And he shall thus atone for the sanctuary from the uncleanness of the children of Israel, and from their transgressions according to all their sins. And so shall he do at the Tent of Meeting, which dwells among them in the midst of their uncleanness.

### 17. An... <note>Original text cuts off mid-sentence; likely "And no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting."</note>

---

*verse 15. When the sprinkling was finished, he went backward out again into the Holy Place and set the basin with blood on one of the golden pillars.*

*Then he went out into the court, where they brought him the goat upon which the Lord’s lot had fallen, and which was the sin offering for the people. This he slaughtered, caught the blood in the basin, and went with it also into the Holy of Holies and did as before. Thus, he entered the Holy of Holies more than once on that day; whereas the first time, a thick smoke of crushed incense powder had to be made so that the Ark could not be strictly observed by him. Which, according to the explanation of the Apostle in Hebrews 9, represented how Christ’s blood was first brought into heaven according to its worth when it was shed, by which he then found and brought about an eternal redemption (verse 12). And indeed, so that the sacrifice for the priests, which happened first, represents the atonement for the believers and the firstborn, whom he has made into priests and kings, who were distinguished first, as it were, to enjoy the glorious effect of the same. For Christ had no need to offer a sacrifice for himself.*

*The other sacrifice, however, for the people, may represent the atonement for those born later, who will afterwards be saved on the great general Judgment Day of the Last Day, and thus only then attain the effect of the atonement. And here also belongs the meaning of the words found in other verses: that Christ is the Savior of all men, but especially of believers. 1 Timothy 4:10. And the same is the atonement for our sins, but not only for ours, but also for those of the whole world. 1 John 2:2.*

*verse 16. It seems as if the sins of the people defiled the sanctuary of the Lord. This is so true that even the destruction of the Temple happened only because of the sins of the people of Israel, just as they had been threatened: (a) I will make my sanctuary common; I will annihilate it, along with the Sabbaths, etc. Thus, the sanctuary had to be cleansed from the sins of the peoples.*

*Today, it is just the same. The Church is in itself—just as the Tabernacle also was—entirely pure, but we defile it through our misdeeds. How should it be cleansed again from our impurities if we do not repent? If we ourselves are not cleansed, then through our sins we are to blame for all the misfortunes that continually befall her. It is in vain to want to "renew the Church." Let us all turn to the Lord; let us renew ourselves: then she will be renewed again! She is without spot or wrinkle: but we cover her with filth and mockery. Lord, renew our hearts! For this is the only correct renewal.*

<margin>(a) Leviticus 26:31. Ezekiel 24:21.</margin>

It emphasizes that while the Church is inherently pure, it is defiled by the sins of the people, necessitating internal spiritual renewal.</summary>

## Chapter 16. The Third Book of Moses. 507

17. And no man shall be in the Tabernacle of Meeting when he goes in to make atonement in the sanctuary, until he comes out: and he shall thus make atonement for himself and his house, and the entire assembly of Israel.

18. Afterward he shall go out to the altar <margin>(a)</margin> which is before the face of the Lord, and make atonement for it, and shall take of the blood of the bull and of the blood of the goat, and put it on the horns of the altar all around. <margin>ch. 4:7, 18.</margin>

<margin>(a) Exodus 30:6, 10.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 17.</margin> During all the time that the High Priest had to work in the Holy of Holies and the Holy Place, no person—not even a priest—was permitted to enter the Temple. This was to ensure that no one might catch a glimpse into the Holy of Holies when the curtain was lifted.

According to the hidden spiritual meaning, however, this indicates to us that when God enters His sanctuary—which is the innermost ground of our heart—the soul must be entirely released and freed from all coarse earthly distractions <note>The original German "Vorwürffen" here refers to objects of thought or external distractions.</note>, and even from itself. For no attachment—indeed, nothing to which the heart might cling—can enter into this sanctuary.

Good souls, upon hearing this, might become troubled that they still have, against their will, certain distractions and vain thoughts which they cannot prevent. They must not let this trouble them, however, because all of this does not enter the sanctuary; it remains only in the outer court of the Temple. God permits this so that He Himself may take away our awareness of what is happening in the Holy of Holies, just as He hid from the eyes of the people everything that took place there. Once the heart is free and detached from everything, such distractions can do no harm. But all those things that arise from any attachment must be improved by cutting off all inclinations of the mind, through a total death to all things.

<margin>v. 18. Afterward he shall go out)</margin> When both types of sprinkling in the Holy of Holies were completed, he walked backward out into the Holy Place, set the basin on the other golden pillar, and then took the basin with the bull’s blood. He sprinkled it against the curtain that was between the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies; in the second Temple, where there were two curtains, he sprinkled against the outermost curtain hanging toward the Holy Place, though he did not touch the curtain.

He then did the same with the blood of the goat, setting the bull’s blood back on its pillar and taking up the goat’s blood.

Following this, he poured the bull’s blood into the goat’s blood, and then poured the full basin back into the empty one several times to mix both types of blood. He then stepped toward the Altar of Incense and let the blood drip from his finger onto its four horns, dipping his finger into this mixed blood for each horn and letting it run down the horn from the top. If he neglected this, all his deeds and labor were in vain. Everything had to follow a specific order, each thing exactly as it should be; otherwise, it was all for nothing.

This was to show how Christ, after His ascension to heaven, sent down the Holy Spirit, who works prayers in the hearts of the faithful and awakens in them those "unspeakable groans" <note>A reference to Romans 8:26, describing the Holy Spirit interceding for believers.</note> which He also sanctifies, so that they rise to Christ and are presented by Him to the Heavenly Father. See Romans 8:23, 26, 27; Revelation 8:3.

<column-break/>

19. And he shall sprinkle of the blood with his finger seven times upon it, and shall cleanse it and sanctify it from the uncleanness of the children of Israel.

20. And when he has finished making atonement for the sanctuary and the Tabernacle of Meeting and the altar, then he shall bring the living goat.

21. Then—

---

<margin>v. 19.</margin> After the horns of the Altar of Incense were moistened with blood, he pushed aside the ashes and coals on this altar and cleaned the spot; on this cleaned and wiped spot, he also sprinkled seven times with this blood.

This indicated that such atonement shall demonstrate its power across seven great ages and cycles of time, and thus the shed blood of Christ will reveal a seven-fold power.

This annual atonement for sins, which is presented to us in outward and figurative words—which must have their truth if they are ever to be blessedly fulfilled in us—is the great work of this chapter. And:

Just as the most remarkable prototype of Christ in the First Book <note>Genesis</note>—specifically of His sacrifice in death—was the commanded sacrifice of Isaac (Chapter 22); and in the Second Book <note>Exodus</note> the chief prototype was the Passover Lamb (Chapter 12); so in this book, the greatest sacrifice and prototype of Christ's sacrifice are those offerings that occurred on this Day of General Atonement once a year with special ceremonies.

<margin>v. 20. Sanctuary — Tabernacle — Altar)</margin> The Holy of Holies, the Holy Place, and the Outer Court, as the three parts of the Tabernacle, are indicated by these terms.

<margin>Bring the living goat)</margin> So that the two goats would not be confused with one another, the High Priest tied a scarlet-red woollen rag, shaped like a tongue—or, as some call it, a scarlet band—weighing two shekels, to the head or horns of the goat that was to go out into the wilderness. Immediately after the drawing of lots, he brought it toward the east, toward the Eastern Gate, from where it would later be led out.

Now, concerning the meaning itself, it is again exceedingly noteworthy that it says: when the atonement was completed, only then should this goat be brought forward. For the Day of Judgment (Hebrews 10:26, 27) shall occur only after everything belonging to the LORD has been marked and sealed with the blood of atonement. Then the living goat—whose goat-like nature <note>The commentator uses "Bocks-Art" to refer to the stubborn, unrepentant nature of the "old man" or the flesh.</note> did not wish to die—shall be placed before the Lord (before whom no living person is righteous except through Christ) to receive his sentence and what his deeds are worth. In this regard, it is no less noteworthy what is testified particularly concerning the Beast and the False Prophet in Revelation 19:20: that they shall be cast alive into the lake of fire, as a true wilderness. Similarly, 4 Ezra 12:33 says of their followers, as the "goats of the world," that they shall be placed alive before the judgment. Thus, the process of judgment is clearly indicated in this verse, according to the same order by which it proceeds spiritually in every individual soul when it is to be sanctified to the Lord. For although the atonement accomplished by Jesus Christ on the cross was finished all at once, laying the foundation for the internal cleansing of the soul, this work is not done all at once in us, but requires time.

For the goat—the old man—still lives, and it is over him that judgment must first begin and be carried out for the destruction of the flesh, so that the body of sin, or the entire body <note>original: "corpus"</note> and the whole collection of sins (like the sins of the entire congregation) may be removed in and from the person. In this process, one also enters into an unpleasant wilderness.

Oh, how many are the wonders in the law of the LORD!

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter 16. ###

**21. Then Aaron shall lay both his**
**hands upon the head of the live goat,**
**and confess over him all the iniquities**
**of the children of Israel, and all their**
**transgressions according to all their sins,**
**and shall put them upon the head of the goat,**

Confess) Thus:
> O Lord! Your people, the house of Israel, have erred. They have been rebellious and have sinned before you. O Lord! Forgive now the error, the rebelliousness, and the sin with which they have erred, wherein they have been rebellious, and with which they have sinned before you; your people, the house of Israel; as it is written in the Law of Moses your servant, where he says: (v. 30.) On this day shall your atonement be made, that you may be cleansed. From all sins you shall be cleansed before the Lord.

This was the third confession on this day, as he first confessed for himself and his house, then for his brothers, the priests, and finally for the entire people and their transgressions and iniquity.

If this action and this goat are also to be interpreted as pointing toward Christ <note>This is a "typological" interpretation, common in older commentaries, which sees Old Testament rituals as "shadows" or "types" of Jesus Christ's later life and sacrifice.</note>, then this confession of sins may represent how the Eternal Father, by laying His justice upon His Son, burdened him with the multitude of our sins, the ugliness of which He had shown to him. Therefore the Prophet says (a), he was burdened with our iniquity, and that by his wounds we have been healed.

Shall put them upon the head of the goat) For this reason, some interpret this action and this goat as referring to Christ, who also took upon himself and bore the sins of the whole world. For it is certain that Jesus Christ felt the entire weight of God, which is the weight of His justice. Job, the most patient among all men, desired (b) that one should have compassion for him, because the hand of the Lord had struck him. If this mere touch was so painful, what must the heaviness of that mighty hand be? And is not the holy Savior become a curse for his people, just as this goat was loaded with curses, as we shall soon hear? As it is written: (c) He became a curse for our sake. And further: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. Was he not driven away from among the men whom he had come to redeem? Was he not in the wilderness with no other company than the animals? Thus, if the other circumstances of the text allowed it, an image of Jesus Christ, burdened with the sins of all men, could be made from this goat.

But because this goat was not killed, but remained alive, and even required atonement himself (as seen in v. 10): according to the judgment of others, he cannot be an image of the sins of the world being laid upon Christ. Instead, they consider what was prefigured there to be of a completely different nature, and understand by such a goat those among the Jewish people who did not accept the atoning blood of the holy sacrifice of Christ, but remained in unbelief, just as the entire multitude is still stuck in it to this day. So long as they are unbelieving, their sins remain upon them, as well as the sins and iniquities of their fathers and all other Israelites, which they must bear as a great burden and curse. Of which curse Jeremiah chapters 24 and 25 testify, as do all the other prophets. See also Exodus 20:5, Matthew 23:35, Revelation 18:24.

And thus, according to Origen's explanation (d), all those for whom the lot was determined for the wilderness must also take upon themselves and their own heads the sins of those who have repented and abandoned wickedness; as those who have made themselves worthy of such a service and lot. And this also applies, in reverse, to what is said in another sense: To him who has, more will be given. He who loves sin, so that he is found in the lot of the scapegoat, to him will also be added those sins which are taken away from the saints: so that in them also may be fulfilled what is written: But from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away, so that it may be given to him who has much (sin).

---

(a) Isaiah 53:5. (b) Job 19:21. (c) Galatians 3:13. 2 Corinthians 5:21.
(d) <note>original: "in Levit. c. 16. hom. 9."</note> Origen, Homilies on Leviticus, chapter 16, homily 9.

<column-break/>

**and shall send him away by the hand of a fit**
**man into the wilderness:**

**22. The**

---

When these or those people turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, then all their sins fall back upon the Devil, the author of sin; who then, as the true goat, will one day have to feel upon himself, in a living and powerful way, all the sins he introduced into the world. Oh, what a burden that will be, when all sins finally concentrate upon him! It would be a wonder if he were not crushed by it.

A fit man) A man of the time <note>The German "bequemen Manns" literally means a "convenient" or "suitable" man, but the commentator links it to the "fullness of time."</note> by which some also understand, in the counter-image, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; John 1:29; as the Redeemer who came in the fullness of time. Galatians 4:4.

Otherwise, anyone who wished could perform this leading out, provided they knew how they should conduct themselves. For this reason, the High Priest previously appointed a certain person for this and had him well instructed, so that he knew what he should do.

They did not like to use Israelites for this, but rather foreigners; though sometimes Israelites did it.

Whether he was clean or unclean did not matter much. For in this case, even an unclean person might enter the inner court (a).

Now, whoever knows how to cast out from his heart at the right time—that is, in good time—all that belongs to the lot of Azazel, such as evil thoughts, all evil desires, all anger, all envy, all malice, all deceit and falsehood, etc., he is fit for the kingdom of God, and a truly "fit man."

Into the wilderness) Juck <note>Likely referring to "Zuk," the traditional site of the scapegoat's precipice.</note>, which was 12,000 steps from Jerusalem and full of rough stone cliffs (b).

Send him away) Everyone pressed for him to hurry away quickly with the goat, as a curse and a curse-offering for the whole land. As Tertullian (c) also writes, that this goat was cursed, spat upon, tormented, and torn at by the people.

And because at the time of the Second Temple, various Jews and Jewish proselytes from Alexandria plucked the hair of the man himself when he was to leave with the goat, and called out to him: "Go forth! Go forth! Get out! Why do you tarry so long? Our sins are not yet atoned for!" Therefore, so that he might remain unmolested and no one could further reach him or the goat, they had to have a wooden walkway <note>original: "Stellache"</note>, knocked together from boards and beams, built beforehand, leading out both to the Temple and out to the city, which was built at the expense of the treasury box in the Temple, upon which he went out to the Temple and the city (d).

The most prominent men of Jerusalem accompanied the leader of the goat as far as the first hut. For between Jerusalem and the wilderness, 10 huts had been previously set up, one of which stood 1000 steps from the other, where one or several people had gone the day before to each hut, having water and food with them. They were not allowed to go further with him than 1000 steps and then back again—that is, a Sabbath day's journey <note>A traditional Jewish limit on travel distance during holy days, roughly 2,000 cubits.</note>—because it was a holy feast day. Those in this first tent offered the leader of the goat food and drink, if he pleased, and accompanied him to the second tent; and so the people from each tent continually accompanied him to the next, besides having offered him food and drink. However, the one in the last tent did not accompany him the remaining 2000 steps into the wilderness: because he would then not have been able to come back again, as he was not allowed to walk more than a Sabbath day's journey on this highly solemn day; instead, he accompanied him only half the way, and then stood still and watched from afar what the leader would do with the goat of Azazel.

### 22. So that the goat shall bear all their iniquities upon itself into a solitary land, when the goat shall have been led out into the wilderness.

<margin>1 Corinthians 4:13</margin>

This arrangement was highly necessary because much depended on this journey, and something could easily have happened to the leader if he had been alone, which would have prevented the execution of the task. He otherwise had the freedom to travel as far as needed on this day because God’s express command was there; likewise, he was permitted to eat something so that he would not grow faint. Yet the Hebrew scholars write that there is no recorded example of the goat’s leaders ever taking anything for refreshment on this journey.

As soon as he reached the wilderness and brought the goat to the high cliff, he took the scarlet band that was tied to the goat's horns and divided it. He tied one half of it to the rock and the other half between the goat's horns, and pushed it backward with all his might down the cliff, so that it tumbled over and over and was dashed to pieces against the crags before it was even halfway down (a).

The Hebrews claim that if God was gracious to the people, the red band would turn white. Then the leader of the goat would immediately blow the horn; and when the person who had last accompanied him heard this, he would also blow his horn, followed by the others, one after another, all the way to Jerusalem. Throughout the entire land, from the wilderness onward, horn-blowers were stationed at such distances that one could hear the other, so that within an hour the whole land knew that God was gracious to them. Indeed, they say that forty years before the final destruction of Jerusalem <note>Referring to the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 AD.</note>, the red band never turned white again; initially, it was said to be hung over the door of the Temple.

The man who had led the goat out remained in the last tent overnight.

v. 22. That through this living goat, which became the departing goat by lot, the apostates among the Jews are primarily understood; this opinion is held among others by the godly Cocceius <note>Johannes Cocceius (1603–1669), a prominent Dutch theologian known for his "Covenant Theology."</note>, where he speaks at this place:
> "That those are understood here who contradicted Christ's
> "priesthood, office, and righteousness; who were therefore
> "separated from all the tribes of Israel, and were burdened
> "with all their sins and with every curse, and thus sent
> "into the world, that they themselves might be hardened by
> "Satan until the time of their mercy should come. For in
> "verse 10, it is said of the living goat that it also
> "should be reconciled. Therefore the Apostle calls them
> "beloved for the sake of the fathers, because of the
> "election, Romans 11:28, because they too would obtain
> "mercy."

v. 31. According to this sense, the solitary land and the wilderness can signify the lands and places of the Gentiles separated from the land of Canaan, where the then-living goat was led into a rough wilderness separated from the camp of Israel by a suitable man, who was fit to perform this faithfully, and was thus delivered as a prey to wild beasts.

That the Spirit aims even further with this matter is beyond doubt; this is left to the reflection of the searching reader. And

If an interpretation referring to Christ finds a place here, then it is certain that He also leads our sins into a land of separation: namely, as far as the East is from the West, so far does He remove our sins from us (Psalm 103:12) and delivers them to Azazel, thus giving the Devil his due.

Into the wilderness) The destination of this lot is the wilderness, that is, a forsaken place—forsaken by God, forsaken by righteousness, forsaken by Christ, forsaken by everything good.

<note>(a) John Lightfoot, *The Temple Service as it Stood in the Days of our Saviour*, chapter 54. Samuel Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, page 658 and following. Although God's command rather implied that the goat should be left free and loose in the wilderness, as many Hebrews also confess; but because the goat occasionally came back alive from the wilderness, they eventually suspected something evil from this and therefore ordained this [pushing it off the cliff].</note>

<column-break/>

### 23. And Aaron shall go into the Tabernacle of the Congregation, and put off the linen garments, which he put on when he went into the sanctuary, and shall leave them there.

### 24. And he shall wash his flesh with water in the holy place, and put on his garments: and afterward come forth, and offer his burnt offering, and the burnt offering of the people, and make an atonement for himself, and for the people.

### 25. And

Meanwhile, as the man brought the goat out toward the wilderness, the High Priest went to his slaughtered bull and the slaughtered goat, cut open the bellies of the bull and goat, took out all the fat along with the kidneys and what belonged to them, and placed them in a dish. He then made several large, sharp cuts in their carcasses—yet so that everything held together—and had them carried out to the place of burning.

However, so that the High Priest could know when the goat had reached the wilderness, they had set up various watch-posts along the way to the wilderness from Jerusalem, erecting large stones at such distances that one could see from one to the other. When the man arrived in the wilderness with the goat, the one closest to the wilderness waved a large linen cloth that he had in his hand. As soon as the second saw this, he did the same with his linen cloth, and so on, one after another. As soon as the High Priest thus learned that the goat had arrived in the wilderness, he prepared himself for the reading, which he could perform either in the white garments or in his own clothes. For this purpose, he went into the outer court, or the Court of the Women, where the entire congregation gathered to him. There he read this 16th chapter of the 3rd Book of Moses, as well as Chapter 23:27-32. He then rolled the Law back together, pressed it to his chest, and recited the passage from Numbers 29:7-10 from memory, following this with various prayers and blessings.

During the time that this was happening in the court, the bull and goat that had been taken out were burned outside the city.

Thereupon, the High Priest went out from the Court of the Women again and into the inner court to bathe himself once more, because he was now to put on his magnificent robes of state <note>The "Golden Garments" of the High Priest, as opposed to the simple white linen used for the Atonement ritual.</note>.

v. 23. The linen garments — which he put on, etc.) Never in the whole year did he wear these, except on this day alone; and indeed not for the whole day, but only when he entered the Most Holy Place and performed what was required there.

Put off and leave them there) These white garments never again touched the body of the High Priest or anyone else, and were never used again for eternity, but only on that single day, and indeed only once, and not again the following year (a).

v. 24. Wash) If he had read the Law in his own common clothes, he did not wash his hands and feet before the bath, because that had already been done when putting off the linen clothes, but bathed himself immediately. But if he had read in the holy garments, he first washed his hands and feet, then took off the linen garments and bathed. For

He had to bathe quite often during this festival—namely five times—and wash his hands and feet ten times, twice at every change of clothing.

However, he did not bathe in the same place all five times; rather, the first time was only in a common place, but the other four times were in a holy place.

<note>(a) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in Hottinger’s *On Hebrew Law*, page 99.</note>

<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XVI.</header>

### 25. And he shall burn the fat of the sin offering upon the altar.
### 26. And he who led out the goat that is the outgoing goat <note>The scapegoat or Azazel</note> shall wash his clothes and bathe his flesh with water, and afterward he shall come into the camp.

After he had now stepped out of the bath and dried himself, they brought him his magnificent state garments <note>The "golden garments" of the High Priest, distinguished from the simple white linen worn in the Holy of Holies</note>, which he put on. Afterward, he washed his hands and feet and went into the inner court. There he offered a ram for himself (which, as Josephus writes in <margin>(a) Book 3, Antiquities, chapter 10.</margin> he had to provide at his own expense, just as he did previously with the bull for the sin offering) and a ram for the people, and seven year-old lambs for a burnt offering, along with the grain and drink offerings belonging to them. None of these entered the Most Holy Place.

**v. 25.** At the same time, he brought up and burned the fat which he had previously placed in the bowl from his own sin offering and the people's sin offering—the bull and the goat.

When it finally drew near the time of the evening sacrifice, the High Priest offered yet other sacrifices, slaughtering again a bull for a burnt offering with its grain and drink offering, as well as a goat for a sin offering, in addition to the previous sacrifices. Whereupon finally followed the last offering of this day, namely the daily evening sacrifice. Thus, besides the goat of atonement, fifteen sacrifices were offered on this day: two lambs for the daily offering, one bull for the sin offering of the High Priest and his brothers, one goat for the sin offering of the people, one bull, two rams, seven year-old lambs, and one male goat for the festival offering; the bulls, rams, and lambs as burnt offerings, and the male goat as a sin offering.

After the evening sacrifice was complete, he washed his hands and feet, undressed, stepped into the bath, and after he had dried himself, they brought him other linen clothes—not of Pelusian linen as before, but of Indian linen, which by our calculation cost over 200 Reichsthaler <note>A significant sum of money in the early modern period, emphasizing the transition to even finer garments</note>. He put these on, washed his hands and feet, and then entered the Most Holy Place for the fourth time, where he retrieved the golden censer and the golden vessel he had left there in the morning.

Thus, the High Priest entered the Most Holy Place four times during this festival: once with the incense powder and censer, then with the blood of the bull, then with the blood of the goat, and finally now, when he fetched the vessels.

When the High Priest had come out for the last time, he washed his hands and feet again and undressed. After he had bathed and dried himself, he put on his magnificent state garments again, washed his hands and feet, and then went into the Temple to burn the customary evening incense and to light the lamps.

After he came out again, offered the drink offering, and had now performed everything—doubtless including the blessing—he washed his hands and feet once more, took off his magnificent official garments, put on his own clothes, and went home.

**v. 26. Who led out the goat that is the outgoing goat)** Or, as others prefer, brought it to Azazel.

**Shall wash his clothes)** He was therefore regarded as unclean. This is also cited as a reason by those who do not wish to admit that this figure <note>The scapegoat</note> may be interpreted as Christ. From this, it is rather to be taken that common association with unbelievers defiles us and must therefore be avoided. See 1 Corinthians 5:9, 10, 11.

...because of sins, as David gives an example of this in the 38th Psalm.

...fasting and abstinence from food and drink. See Psalm 35:13 and Acts 27:9, where this day is called "the Fast."

This should indeed be taken as an image of real repentance, were it not added: "you shall

**Do no work)** For there are two kinds of effective repentance. The first consists in disciplining the flesh through fasting, chastisement, abstinence, and restraint, so that this very flesh may be brought into subjection. The second requires a broken heart, as it is written <gloss>(a) <note>original: Psalm 51:19</note></gloss>: namely, a heart broken through sorrow, because of the regret and the grief one has for offending God; for this God deserved all our love and gratitude, and yet we have paid Him only with pure ingratitude.

There is yet another kind of repentance, which one can properly call a "passive repentance," such as when our soul is grieved by the withdrawal of comfort and all perceptible support. We grieve our soul to the utmost by reflecting on the graces which we believe we have lost, because we can no longer feel or comprehend them. In that same time, one must do no work, but wait in the peace of the Lord until He reveals Himself.
