### 27. And the bull of the sin offering and the goat of the sin offering, whose blood was brought in to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall be carried out outside the camp; and they shall burn their hides, their flesh, and their dung with fire.
### 28. And he who burns them shall wash his clothes and bathe his flesh with water, and afterward he shall come into the camp.
### 29. And it shall be a perpetual statute for you: in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, you shall humble your souls and do no work, neither the native nor the stranger who dwells among you.

**v. 27. Shall be carried out)** Four persons carried them on two poles. Two went in front and two behind, and they had the poles on their shoulders, while the bull and the goat hung across and under one another on these poles.

**Outside the camp — burn)** Which the Apostle <note>The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews</note> interprets as Christ; "Therefore Jesus also, that He might sanctify the people with His own blood, suffered outside the gate" (Hebrews 13:12), where He allowed Himself to be entirely consumed and, as it were, burned by the fire of God's wrath over sin.

**v. 28.** As soon as the first carriers had come out of the inner court, their clothes were unclean; however, the clothes of the two priests were not until they also had come out, at which point all four became unclean. Then they committed this bull and goat to the full flames.

**v. 29. A perpetual statute in the 7th month)** This was the month of Tishri, which corresponds to our September, and was the beginning of the year. On the tenth day of it—and thus toward the end of our September—this atonement had to be made for everyone in general. It indicated how a new time should begin after this true general atonement had occurred: which was the "acceptable year of the Lord," when the Gospel was to be preached to all the wretched, to bind up the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and an opening to the bound (Isaiah 61:1-2). This was brought about through the true atonement obtained through Christ, which must now be recognized and praised with a grateful heart at all times and for all eternity; whereas the prefiguring atonement on the annual tenth day of the first month in the civil year (which was reckoned from the creation of the world) had only to be observed in the "eternity" or hidden duration of the Old Testament. See also Daniel 9:24, where this general atonement for iniquity in the death of Christ is also spoken of, the memory of which the Jews celebrated annually with this figure <note>This "figure" or "type" refers to the ritual of the Day of Atonement</note>.

<header>Chapter XVI. The Third Book of Moses.</header>

## 30. For on this day he will atone for you, to cleanse you: that you may be clean from all your sins before the face of the Lord.

## 31. It shall be a Sabbath of rest unto you, and you shall humble your souls: it is an eternal statute.

---

**v. 30.** At that time, the soul passes through all the purifications of which we have spoken, which are indicated by this expression: that all [human] activity must cease. For the ever-busy nature of man, which constantly seeks support, comfort, and whatever might please it, tries in every way to regain what it thought it had lost—and yet, in doing so, it only dries itself out all the more.

Therefore, at this time it is most necessary not to act through our own strength, but to let ourselves be gradually consumed by sorrow, so that such sorrow may have its effect and cleanse us according to the will of God. Our own busyness hinders the work of Divine Justice. Only stillness allows it room to work.

Just as the Scripture assures us, after this time of purification, one shall stand cleansed of all sins before God; this can happen in no other way than through a total emptying of the self.

There is a great difference between the purity that appears good before men and that which is truly so before God. Active purification <note>The author distinguishes between "active" purification (human effort) and "passive" or "suffering" purification (submitting to God's work).</note> alone makes us appear clean to men, and one may truly be so in a sense; but one is still far from being seen as such in the eyes of God. Nothing but passive purification and total emptying can bring this about.

**(On this day)** This day, which lasts until the sun goes down—that is, until the world reaches its end—is necessary for all who have sinned. And therefore in the Law, which contains the shadow and the image or the figure of future goods and heavenly things and mysteries, a solemn ceremony had to be ordained, which was called the Day of Atonement.

All the days from the New Year or from the first of Tishri <note>original: "Tiſri"; the first month of the Jewish civil year.</note> until this feast were days of repentance.

**v. 31.** Since this day also had to be a Sabbath of rest, it shows how, with the death of Christ, the great Sabbath of rest for our souls has dawned, which will last into all eternity.

For this feast was called the "Great Sabbath," the great day of rest. Just as they were permitted to cook food on other feasts, they were not allowed to do so here; rather, they had to refrain from all cooking as they did on the Sabbath. Indeed, while eating was permitted on the regular Sabbath, it was not to happen on this day; instead, they were to fast entirely.

After the soul is purified before God, it enters into this Great Sabbath, which is not our Sabbath or rest, but the Lord's Sabbath. There, when the soul enters into God, it finds in Him this complete rest and eternal satisfaction, because it is used entirely for Him and by Him, and can be moved by no other thing. This divine service is performed in God and before God Himself. May one well say that it is the worship of God in God, and not in us? This highest adoration is as sublime as a refined creature, elevated in God, can possibly perform.

But, one might say: when the soul is in this perfect rest, by what can it then be troubled? **Answer:** By nothing that concerns itself. This eternal service troubles the soul only because it recognizes what is due to God and how little it has fulfilled it. In this eternal service, God imposes sorrow upon the soul: either to make it more like Jesus Christ, or for the sake of someone else; or perhaps there are many creatures to whom one must respond and with whom one must harmonize during this state of pilgrimage. This sorrow may well occupy the soul, but it cannot enter into its deepest ground—which is the sanctuary that God has designated for His Sabbath or His rest.

<column-break/>

## 32. And the priest, who shall be anointed, and whose hand shall be filled to minister in the priest's office in his father's stead, shall make the atonement: and he shall put on the linen clothes, the holy garments;

## 33. And he shall thus atone for the holy sanctuary, and for the tabernacle of the meeting, and he shall atone for the altar, and he shall atone for the priests and for all the people of the assembly.

## 34. And

---

**The Priest — shall atone)** Not a common priest, but the High Priest.

To this end, he was separated seven days before the feast and led from his house up to the Temple.

During these seven days, he waited in the Temple and in the courtyard, sprinkled the blood of the daily burnt offering, burned incense in the Holy Place, trimmed the lamps, and did whatever else was to be done, so that on the Day of Atonement he would be all the more quick and skilled in all things.

On the day before the feast, as on the holy eve, the most prominent members of the High Court <note>The Sanhedrin</note> accompanied him in the morning to the Eastern Gate, where bulls, rams, and lambs were brought forth, which he then slaughtered and offered, so that he would know how to handle them more quickly the following day.

On that same ninth day, he ate a good meal at noon so that he would not become faint on the following day, when he was forbidden from eating and yet had much work to do.

But on the evening of the ninth day, he was not allowed to eat much, so that he could stay awake more easily; he also had to abstain entirely from certain foods.

To ensure that the High Priest kept sleep from his eyes as night approached, various young apprentice priests were left with him to read to him from the Holy Scriptures. If he began to fall asleep over this, the young priests would use their fingers—namely, on a certain pipe <note>Perhaps a musical instrument or a signaling device to startle him awake</note>—or they sang, or held conversation with him, thus keeping him from sleep until it was time to slaughter the daily morning sacrifice.

But who is portrayed under this High Priest, and who is the one who in truth had to perform the atonement? Who else but the excellent Priest after the order of Melchizedek <note>A reference to Jesus Christ as described in the Book of Hebrews</note>. To Him it is given to do such things, and no one but He can perform them. He was set apart among His brothers by the holy anointing, which He received more than they all. And since He became man, He is also our brother. He was sanctified through the anointing so that He might sanctify others, and He performs the office of a High Priest in His Father's stead for atonement. God the Father, in His justice, owed the punishment to sinners: our sins had to be punished out of respect for His essence, so that His justice, which would not waive its right, might be satisfied. But this well-beloved Son, this excellent Priest, has received the anointing for atonement: He took the blows of Justice upon Himself and showed mercy to men. For them, He obtained a grace of mercy, which would have been a useless attribute of God had no sinner been found upon whom He could exercise such mercy. Justice has obtained a far more glorious satisfaction in and through Jesus Christ than it would have received even if all men had been punished.

When Jesus Christ became man, He clothed Himself with the linen robe and with holy garments. He has cleansed both the Tabernacle and the people by transforming a symbolic divine service into a most holy service. He has sanctified the people, not with the blood of sacrificial animals, but through His own blood.

34. And this shall be an eternal statute for you: that you make atonement for the children of Israel for all their sins once a year. And he did as the LORD had commanded Moses.

<margin>Once a year</margin>
->As a<-
### Foreshadowing of the Great Day of Atonement,
which Jesus Christ, the end of the Law, was to hold on the so-called Silent or Good Friday: <note>The original uses "Char-Freytag," an older spelling of Karfreitag (Good Friday). The "Silent" Friday refers to the solemnity of the day.</note> of which we shall note here in conclusion only a few points of comparison.
1. On this day, the High Priest made atonement not just for one or another, but for himself, the priests, and the entire people. Jesus, however, atoned for the whole world with God. <margin>Colossians 1:19 etc.</margin>
2. The High Priest had to perform the atonement alone, and no man was permitted to be in the Holy Place while he atoned for the people. Jesus alone has atoned us with God. No man, no angel, no archangel, no creature, neither in heaven nor on earth, helped him in this work. <margin>1 Timothy 2:5-6; Isaiah 63:3.</margin>
3. The High Priest had to begin the atonement with a special offering of incense. Jesus began the atonement with God with the incense of prayer. How he prayed to God before his passion began! <margin>John 17; Luke 22:44.</margin>
4. For the High Priest, the Day of Atonement was a long, bitter, and difficult day, the likes of which he did not have in the whole year; for he had to perform great labor and received neither food, nor drink, nor rest. So too for the High Priest Jesus, Good Friday was a long, bitter, and difficult day, the likes of which he never had in his whole life; <margin>Isaiah 43:24; 53:11.</margin> during which he also had neither food, nor drink, nor rest.
5. On this day, the High Priest had to change his clothes often: and Jesus did as well. Now Herod clothed him in white, now the soldiers clothed him in red, now they put his own clothes back on him. <margin>Luke 23:11; Matthew 27:27, 28, 31, 35.</margin>
6. The High Priest let the blood of the bullock and the goat out in the forecourt, but did not remain there with it; rather, he went with it into the Most Holy Place and appeared there with this blood before God. So also Jesus on earth—as if in the forecourt—let all his blood be drained, but did not let it remain on earth; rather, he took it back to himself in the Resurrection and with him into heaven. <margin>Hebrews 9:12, 24.</margin>
7. The atonement happened only once a year: and Jesus has redeemed us once and for all, and atoned God with us. <margin>Hebrews 9:12.</margin>
> See, however, how much more glorious the High Priest Jesus is compared to that Levitical High Priest, and so also his atonement is infinitely higher and more glorious than that one, since:
> 1. The High Priest could not atone for the people before he had brought a bullock as a sin offering for himself and had atoned for himself; because he was just as much a poor, miserable sinner as the people. Not so the High Priest Jesus. <margin>Hebrews 7:26-27.</margin>
> 2. The High Priest atoned only for the people of Israel: Jesus for the whole world. <margin>1 John 2:2.</margin>
> 3. The High Priest had nothing other than the blood of bullocks and goats: <margin>Hebrews 9:12.</margin> <note>Implied: Jesus offered his own blood.</note>
> 4. The High Priest entered only into the Most Holy Place made with hands: Jesus into heaven. <margin>Hebrews 9:24.</margin>
> 5. The High Priest had to repeat the atonement every year. <margin>Hebrews 9:12, 25, 26; 10:1, 2, 14.</margin>
> 6. The High Priest atoned only by way of foreshadowing: Jesus in the essence of truth. <margin>Hebrews 10:1–4, 10 etc.</margin>

> The Jews were very lustful for the sacrifices and customs of the heathens, and quite inclined toward idolatry: therefore it was all the more necessary to strengthen the faith in one single God in their hearts:
> v. 2. Whereby at the same time the obedience of faith toward his word is always included.
> v. 3. (Whoever -- shall slaughter) This must be understood as referring to those animals which they intended to slaughter as a thank-offering; that they should not do such a thing according to their own pleasure in the field, as they may have done in Egypt. <margin>Deuteronomy 32:17; Ezekiel 20:7-8.</margin> where it is said how they had served the "dung-gods" in Egypt, <note>The original "Dreck-Götter" is a derogatory term for idols, likely referencing the Hebrew 'gillulim'.</note> which are here in v. 7 called devils, or actually hairy or shaggy goats, from the long hair that large goats have; just as elsewhere they also appear under the name of "field-devils": which are then nothing other than the heathens' Fauns and Satyrs, in whose form the devils appeared to their idol-worshippers, and thereby had to make known their nature, which stinks of nothing but vices.

This is what man does out of self-will in religious duties, which must be arranged according to the will of God alone. See Colossians 2:20-23.

6. And the priest shall sprinkle the blood upon the altar of the LORD at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, and burn the fat for a pleasing aroma to the LORD.
7. And they shall no longer offer their sacrifices to the <term>devils</term><note>The German "Teufeln" (devils) here refers to the goat-idols or "satyrs" mentioned in the original Hebrew text.</note> after whom they go whoring. This shall be an eternal statute for them among their descendants.
8. Therefore you shall say to them: Any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who dwell among them, who wishes to offer a burnt offering or sacrifice;
9. And does not bring it to the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation to prepare it for the LORD: that man shall be cut off from his people.

---

v. 6. **Burn the fat for a pleasing aroma**) God desires that all the best within a human should be consumed by the holy fire of His love, serving Him as an acceptable burnt offering. This holy fire consumes all "selfness" even in good deeds.
v. 7. **They shall no longer sacrifice to devils**) Truly, to sacrifice to devils is to sacrifice to one's own <term>self-love</term><note>A key concept in Pietist theology: the idea that doing things for one's own ego is a form of idolatry.</note>. All works that are not offered through pure love alone for the glory of God, and which have goals other than God Himself, are dedicated to self-love.
<margin>(a) Psalm 73:27.</margin>
But how can what God says—that all people who sacrifice to the devil, or to self-love, give themselves over to whoredom—be understood? In the very same sense as it is written: (a) *You will destroy those adulterous souls who have turned away from You.* God is the Creator of souls, their Redeemer, and their Bridegroom. Thus, it is adultery or whoredom to turn away from God to love something outside of Him, or something that does not harmonize with Him.
v. 8. Why does God demand with such earnestness that all animals slaughtered for sacrifice should be dedicated to Him? Especially since He asserts that such types of sacrificial animals and burnt offerings do not please Him? It is because they truly had no power in themselves other than that which they borrowed from the future sacrifice of Jesus Christ; for all their worthiness consisted not in themselves, but in that which they <term>foreshadowed</term><note>Original: "vorbildeten." This refers to the "Type/Antitype" relationship where Old Testament events pre-figure New Testament truths.</note>.
v. 9. God requires this ceremony to instruct future generations that they are obligated to give back to God through Jesus Christ that which they have received from Him. Even then, He taught the Israelites the proper discharge of duty according to the state in which they stood. For it is not to be believed that God received any glorification from this great mass of blood poured out at the entrance of the Tabernacle in any other way than insofar as such pouring out represented the blood of the <term>significant Lamb</term><note>Referring to the "Lamb of God," Jesus Christ.</note>, which had to be shed before His Father’s face for the salvation of His people.
That believers occasionally performed their sacrifices in other places than the Tabernacle by a special prompting of the Spirit of God, and were therefore pleasing to God, can be seen in Manoah, Judges 13:16, 19, 20; in Samuel, 1 Samuel 7:9, 11:15, 16:2, etc.; in David, 2 Samuel 24:18; and in Elijah, 1 Kings 18:23.
Whatever promptings of the Spirit one might feel today, when two or three gather together as a testimony against the decay of public assemblies, these should not be disturbed, but rather taken to heart in the fear of the LORD for the improvement of the general congregation.

<column-break/>

10. And any man of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who dwell among them, who eats any kind of blood, I will set My face against the soul that has eaten the blood, and will cut him off from the midst of his people.
11. For the soul of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls. For it is the blood that shall make atonement for the soul.
12. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel: No soul among you shall eat blood; nor shall any stranger who dwells among you eat blood. <note>1 Samuel 14:32.</note>
13. And any man of the children of Israel, or of the strangers who dwell among them, who catches any wild animal or bird that may be eaten while hunting; he shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. <note>Deuteronomy 12:24.</note>
14.

---

v. 10. **I will set My face against the soul**) <margin>(a) Maimonides, Guide for the Perplexed, part 3, chapter 46.</margin> Maimonides (a) notes that such words are used in all of Holy Scripture for no other sin than this one and the burning of children to Moloch in chapter 20:3.
v. 11. **The soul of the flesh is in the blood**) Meaning in the movement of the blood. Otherwise, the body has no soul or life.
v. 12. The prohibition of blood is very often repeated in the Law: Chapter 3:17, 7:26-27, 19:26; Deuteronomy 12:16, 15:23. With this, God intended to impress upon them how the lives of men were forfeited to Him because of sin, and that they should therefore long in faith for the blood which could bring about the true forgiveness of sins. This was the blood of the promised <term>Seed of the Woman</term><note>A traditional Christian reference to the Messiah, based on Genesis 3:15.</note>, which was to be shed through the serpent’s bruising of His heel (or the killing of His flesh). Thus He gave His blood or His life as a guilt offering: Isaiah 53:10. Regarding this foreshadowing blood-shedding for the forgiveness of sin, and its connection to the blood of Jesus Christ which brought eternal redemption, the Apostle treats more fully in Hebrews 9:12–26.
Furthermore, God also intended to testify forever how He has a particular horror of all bloodthirsty people: Psalm 5:7. Not only murderers who shed innocent blood, but all unmerciful people who, through exploitation, greed, usury, and all other ways, seize people's goods and the sweat and blood of the poor. The Prophet notes this as the reason why God would not hear the prayers of such people, because their hands were full of blood, Isaiah 1:15; and they eat it like their bread, as it is literally said in Psalm 14:4.
v. 13. **Cover it with earth**) In doing so, they spoke this special blessing or prayer: *Blessed be the LORD our God, King over all, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to cover the blood (b).* <margin>(b) Hottinger, On Hebrew Law, note 185. Wagenseil, note 6 on Gemara Sotah, chapter 2.</margin>

14. For it is the life of all flesh; its blood is for its life. Therefore I have said to the children of Israel: You shall eat the blood of no flesh. For the life of all flesh is its blood: Whoever eats it shall be cut off.

<note>Commentary on Verse 14</note>
**You shall eat the blood of no flesh**) This prohibition indicates to us that we should not dwell upon that which is fleshly, sensory, and worldly, but rather return to the earth that which belongs to it. In this way, the spirit—now unburdened and free—may approach God and be reunited with Him, for He is the ultimate purpose of its creation.

...then bear his uncleanness and wash himself with water. This teaches us once again to [not] associate with people who are dead in sins; and if one has come into their company by mistake or where it could not be helped, one must carefully wash oneself again in the <term>water of repentance</term><note>A common Pietist metaphor for the cleansing power of contrition and turning back to God.</note>. See Psalm 26:4, 5, 6.

### Chapter XVIII.
->The forbidden degrees of kinship and sins of the flesh.<-

And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: I am the LORD your God.

<note>Commentary on Verses 1-2</note>
Because the great mass of the heathens have willfully alienated themselves from the life that is from God, and because they have disregarded the knowledge of God—which God placed in them through Christ as the universal light that wishes to enlighten all people—they have therefore been given over to a perverted mind to do what is not proper. Thus, God warned His people (whom He chose from all nations to be a people for Himself, as the seed of His dear friends Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob) against all such abominations of the heathens. Furthermore, they were to enter the land of Canaan, which was inhabited by those living under the curse and thus walking in all manner of lusts and abominations, whose works would be sufficiently revealed. In contrast, the Israelites were to arrange their conduct according to the holy commandments of God: partly to observe the <term>mysterious statutes</term><note>The "ceremonial laws" of the Old Testament, seen by this commentator as "shadows" or symbols of the coming Christ rather than having holiness in themselves.</note> which God established as shadows of His dear Son (in which otherwise no essential holiness was contained through which one could have had life: Ezekiel 20:25); but partly also such laws in which true holiness consisted—in the love of God and of man—through which a person would be able to live, if he were able to keep them (Ezekiel 20:11). Through this, however, the impotence of the flesh was actually revealed, so that one might long for the true Redeemer, who was able to satisfy the Law for us in every way. Romans 8:3.

Therefore, those whom Christ has wished to call as His people must not conform themselves to this world, which (as far as the great mass is concerned) always lies in wickedness, even if they confess Christ with their mouths; for they do not do the will of the heavenly Father revealed through Christ. Romans 12:2; Matthew 7:21. See also Ephesians 4:14-20, where believers are earnestly warned against such heathen conduct. But how heathen customs are spreading far and wide again under other names among all religious parties—and how burdensome times filled with all vices have appeared, in which people heap up the wrath of God for the day of wrath and the revelation of His righteous judgment—that is entirely evident to the eyes of god-fearing souls. See 2 Timothy 3:1 etc.; Romans 2:5.

v. 2. God begins this chapter with the words repeated several times: **I am the LORD your God!** It is as if God said: "Hear my words, so that you also obey me. I have every right to command you, and you cannot withdraw from my commands without becoming rebels and worthy of death."

<column-break/>

15. And every soul that eats <term>carrion</term><note>Animals that died of natural causes or were killed by other beasts, rather than being ritually slaughtered.</note> or what is torn, whether he be a native or a stranger, he shall wash his clothes and bathe himself in water, and be unclean until the evening: then he shall be clean.
16. But if he does not wash them, nor bathe his flesh, then he shall bear his iniquity.

<note>Commentary on Verses 15-16</note>
Because the blood was not poured out from a carcass, and it is moreover a disgusting thing to eat from such carrion or a torn animal (as was also forbidden above in Exodus 22:34), it is here further commanded that if one has eaten such a thing by mistake, how he should...

3. You shall not do according to the works of the land of Egypt, wherein you dwelt; neither shall you do according to the works of the land of Canaan, where I will lead you. Neither shall you walk in their statutes.
4. You shall do my judgments and keep my statutes, to walk therein: I am the LORD your God.
5. Therefore you shall keep my statutes and my judgments. Which if a man do, he shall live by them. I am the LORD.

<note>Commentary on Verses 3-5</note>
v. 3. Thus I command you then as your LORD and God, that you do not follow the customs of other nations or of the Egyptians. As if He said: Do not follow the way of the world. For if you are mine, then you may no longer belong to the world. Leave the "multiplicity" of Egypt to enter into the "simplicity" of my children. Cling to me alone. Flee the world as my enemy.

v. 4. I command you to follow me and give ear to me, I who am your only God and LORD. One must follow my commandments and walk in my ways, performing everything that I command; that is, to lose all one's own will so completely that you retain no other will but mine.

v. 5. If you will always do my will and that which I command, so that you lose all your own will in mine: then you will find life. In the loss of our will into the will of God, we find the right and true life. For Jesus Christ becomes our resurrection and our life. He who is not in God remains in death. For can one live without You, O You true and only Life? You are our God and a mighty LORD, to give back to us an infinitely more perfect life than we lost in Adam: namely, if we are willing to die to ourselves completely, to live only in You and through You.

<header>Chapter XVIII. The Third Book of Moses.</header>

6. None of you shall approach any who are near of kin <note>original: "Fleisch von seinem Leibe" (flesh of his body)</note> to him, to uncover their nakedness: **I am the LORD.**
7. The nakedness of your father and the nakedness of your mother you shall not uncover: she is your mother; you shall not uncover her nakedness.
8. The nakedness of your father’s wife <margin>(a) 1 Corinthians 5:1.</margin> you shall not uncover: it is your father’s nakedness.
9. The nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother, whether she was born at home or born elsewhere, their nakedness you shall not uncover.

---

<margin>Although all human beings are of one flesh with one another (see Isaiah 58:7), so that no marriage could be found where one did not approach "their own flesh"—especially since the woman is expressly called "flesh of his flesh" in relation to the man in Genesis 2:23—nevertheless, here...</margin>
**v. 6. flesh of his body)** among the already expanded and multiplied human race, this is to be understood as the very closest degrees of birth, as is explained in Chapter 21:2. Out of the naturally implanted sense of modesty, God willed to forbid such marriages with the closest blood-relatives. And if this reason were not enough, God willed to press His seal upon this and all following commandments when He speaks and repeats—so often here and in the following chapter, sixteen times in total:
**I am the LORD.** This must be enough for us humans: that it thus pleased the Lord and was His good will. Conversely, humans should not dare to imitate this without offending God, but must give rational causes for their own commands.
**v. 7. 8. etc.** First, marriages are forbidden in the ascending and descending lines, and in the first collateral line: between parents and children, whether they be grandparents or grandchildren, by whatever name they may be called; and then between siblings, whether they be full siblings or half-siblings, because they are always the flesh of our parents as well.
**v. 9. Sister -- not)** According to the sense of the letter and the Law. But according to the sense of the Gospel, a disciple of Christ who wishes to enter into physical marriage should take a "sister" <note>Referring here to a fellow believer, as in "sister in Christ."</note> as a wife. 1 Corinthians 9:5.
**The People** whom God shall accept and recognize as His own possession must be a holy people, and must therefore cleanse themselves from all defilement of the flesh and spirit.
**If God has now** forbidden close blood-relationship in matters of marriage, He has forbidden even more that we should love ourselves improperly and bind ourselves to our own will. For who is closer to us than ourselves, and what we have in our own souls? If we now love ourselves with an improper desire and devote ourselves to our own will as if in a blood-relationship—seeking our own honor and our own profit, and not holding purely to our God in Christ—then we have sinned more than if we had physically held to our closest blood-relative. And whoever wishes to keep only the "outside of the cup" clean in this matter, but does not care much for the internal state, is a <term>Pharisee</term><note>A reference to Matthew 23:25-26, highlighting the difference between outward legalism and inner purity.</note>.
**We should not** live according to our fleshly will, but according to the will of Christ our Lord, as the Bridegroom of our souls, and unite ourselves with Him. In that union, we cannot be too closely joined. He also seeks no other bride than the one who is of His kin, who is of His flesh and bone, and who is found in His blood-relationship; that is, one who has cleansed herself in His blood and allows no foreign lover, but finds enough in her Beloved.

<column-break/>

10. The nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s daughter, their nakedness you shall not uncover, for theirs is your own nakedness.
11. The nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, begotten of your father, she is your sister; you shall not uncover her nakedness.
12. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister: she is your father’s near kinswoman <note>original: "Fleisch" (flesh)</note>.
13. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister: for she is your mother’s near kinswoman.
14. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother: you shall not approach his wife; she is your aunt <note>original: "Baase" (a term for a female relative, here specifically an aunt by marriage).</note>.
15. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law <note>original: "Schnur".</note>: she is your son’s wife; you shall not uncover her nakedness.
16. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife: it is your brother’s nakedness.
17. You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter; you shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter to uncover her nakedness: they are near kinswomen; it is wickedness <note>original: "Schandthat" (a shameful act or crime).</note>.
18.

---

**v. 12. 13. The father's and mother's sisters are** the flesh of our grandparents, and for that reason are forbidden to be married. But those who already come from the grandparents through their children, and share a grandfather or grandmother with us <note>i.e., cousins</note>, their marriages God did not wish to forbid.
**Therefore, no one** should take the liberty of forbidding degrees in marriage which God’s holy and righteous Law has left free; for one should not restrict marital love where God has allowed it to blood-relatives who descend from a still-known patriarch, even if it were the grandfather. Thus, children of siblings <note>first cousins</note> can marry with all right, as the Roman laws also expressly permit. (a) <margin>(a) Justinian's Institutes, Book 1, Title X, Paragraph 4. <note>original: "Instit. Lib. 1. Tit. X. §. 4."</note></margin>
**The 14th verse has caused some difficulty:** for some thought it was forbidden here to marry the daughter of one's brother or—since there is an equality here—the daughter of one's sister. However, the following words explain and restrict the prohibition to marriage with the father’s brother’s wife, because she is the closest aunt; for one must honor the father’s brother like a father, and thus his wife like a mother.
**v. 15. Your daughter-in-law, not)** Our son’s wife has become our daughter, and this would be equal to the incest which is forbidden with one's own children.
**v. 16. Just as siblings may not marry, so** it is the same case with their spouses. This is why John [the Baptist] rebuked Herod for having taken his brother’s wife. Matthew 14:3, 4.
**v. 17. When we take one as a wife who** has children from her previous husband, then these are our stepchildren, and they must also bear filial reverence toward their parents' spouse. Wishing to marry such a person is denounced as an act of wantonness, because parental reverence is thereby set aside.

<page-num>516</page-num>
<header>The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XVIII.</header>

18. Also you shall not take one wife beside another, to provoke enmity, to uncover her nakedness beside her during her lifetime.
19. You shall also not approach a woman in her separation because of her uncleanness, to uncover her nakedness.

---

<margin>v. 18. One wife beside another — during her lifetime</margin> This is otherwise understood and accepted as referring to two sisters; from this, both Jews and Christians conclude that when a man’s wife has died, he is permitted to marry her sister after her death (a); because it then provokes no enmity, and the circumstance is expressly added here, **during her lifetime**. Against this, however, others consider it better to avoid such a case and marry elsewhere; because the world is now large enough, and people commonly seek such close marriages for carnal reasons—either so that property remains within the family <note>original: "Freundschaft," which in this context refers to the extended family or kin-group</note>, or for other no better intentions. Indeed, some also believe that this is forbidden by virtue of verse 16, due to parity: just as a man could not take his brother’s wife, so too a woman should not marry her sister’s husband.

However, if one looks at the matter in the right light and examines the text closely, it does not even speak of two sisters (at least it is not necessary to understand it so). Instead, according to the current well-founded translation, it rather forbids polygamy <note>original: "Vielweibery"</note>. For according to the Hebrew idiom, as is well known, "another man" is expressed by the word **brother** and "another woman" by the word **sister**; just as such terms are used for inanimate things: such as the curtains in Exodus 26:3, or the wings in Ezekiel 1:9, where one is called the "sister" of the other in a figurative sense.

**God** had already forbidden this in the beginning at the institution of marriage, by making one man and one woman to be one flesh. For this reason, Christ also rejected the divorcing of one wife—and thus also the taking of another wife alongside the first—as it would be contrary to the first institution of **God**. Matthew 19. See Malachi 2:14, 15.

Now, if this was forbidden in the Old Testament after the Law was given, it is certainly much less permitted in the new, holy, and pure Covenant, which is as different from the old as the state of innocence is from the Fall. And although some lustful people wandering about today have a gloss or appearance of wisdom about them, they look with an earthly eye upon Solomon’s luxury rather than upon Christ’s death, from which alone a new life must grow.

No greater blessedness or glory is to be expected in this world or the next than the one pure, most holy marriage of **God**, which He creates anew in the restoration; just as the Fall lies solely in multiplicity and distraction.

<margin>v. 19.</margin> Through this, immoderation in marital intercourse is forbidden; a sin which the prophets also placed and punished among the widespread abominations <note>original: "Blut-Schanden," literally blood-shames or incestuous acts</note>. Ezekiel 22:10.

According to the spirit, this prohibition means that we should not defile ourselves through intimate association with an unclean soul that sins against the **Lord**; rather, one should abstain from such a person until they have been released from their uncleanness and can be most closely reunited with us.

<margin>(a) see Selden, *On the Law of Nature and Nations according to the Hebrews*, book 5, chapter 10, p. 615 and following.</margin>
<gloss>The famous **Dr. Wagenfeil** is also of this opinion and approves this as a marriage that conflicts with neither natural nor divine law—but is permitted to everyone with the dispensation of the Supreme Bishop <note>original: "Supremi Episcopi," likely referring to the sovereign as the head of the church</note>—in a special treatise: *Whether Holy Scripture allows a man to marry two sisters in succession?* which is appended to the back of his *Instruction on the Jewish-German Way of Speaking and Writing*, **Königsberg, Anno 1699, in quarto.**</gloss>

<column-break/>

20. You shall also not lie with your neighbor’s wife for insemination, to defile yourself with her.
21. You shall also not give any of your seed to let it pass over to **Molech**; and you shall not profane the name of your **God**: **I am the LORD.**

---

<margin>v. 20.</margin> Here adultery is forbidden: which consists not only of a man sleeping with another’s wife—which is a double adultery also committed by the wife—but **Christ** also extends this to mean that if someone marries a divorced woman, he also commits adultery. Matthew 19:9. For a man’s unjust act cannot sever the bond that is made according to **God's** providence between him and his wife.

It is also adultery if a married man lies with an unmarried person. For he commits unfaithfulness against his wife; just as a woman who has to do with an unmarried man commits adultery and can be left by her husband. Matthew 19:9. This is specifically counted as a shameful deed, as it is termed in Deuteronomy 24:1.

We should avoid all foreign love that can keep us from the pure marital love for our heavenly Bridegroom, and not lust after this or that external beauty or wisdom.

The lovely heavenly Wisdom, the wife of your youth, should be enough for you: you should remain with her alone and love all else in her, without attachment to creatures, however beautiful they may be, for love of them in self-will <note>original: "Eigenheit," a Pietist term for the ego or self-centered nature</note> will surely defile you.

<margin>v. 21.</margin> This refers to the cruel idolatry where the heathens, through the suggestion of the Devil (who was a murderer from the beginning), had their firstborn sons burned in the arms of a glowing copper image that had an ox's head. In later times, they were said to have only passed them through the fire in honor of this idol, so that they might experience a blessing upon their other children. This was very sharply forbidden by **God**, especially because His name would be profaned by the observation of such terrible customs, which were an abomination before Him. See Leviticus 20:2-5, Deuteronomy 18:10, and Ezekiel 20:26, 31. See also Lactantius, Book 1, Chapter 21.

**Molech** was the idol of the Ammonites; according to some descriptions, his image was hollow inside and had seven chambers or small chapels. Anyone wishing to sacrifice a bird would place it in the first chamber after a fire was lit inside the image and it became red-hot. In the second chamber, a sheep or lamb was sacrificed; in the 3rd, a ram; in the 4th, a calf; in the 5th, a young bull; in the 6th, an ox; in the 7th, a human. This last was the most prominent sacrifice, and he who wished to burn his child would first kiss **Molech** before the fire was lit.

Others relate it somewhat differently: namely, that in the first chamber, fine flour was offered; in the second, birds, and so on, omitting the young bull in the 5th.

Others doubt the seven chambers and say the children were placed directly into the arms of the fiery, glowing idol. (a)

As soon as the poor children were handed over to the glowing **Molech**, drums and cymbals were immediately and joyfully struck and dances performed, so that the children’s pitiful cries would not be heard and the parents would not be moved to compassion. (b)

But so that we do not stray too far from ourselves: what else do all those do who sacrifice the fruit of their womb to the world and its pride and vanity, raising them in heathen vices and sins, and teaching them things through which their souls suffer harm?

<margin>(a) A copperplate engraving of both versions can be found in Lundius, *The Jewish Tabernacle*, Book 3, Chapter 33, p. 564.</margin>
<margin>(b) See more at Jeremiah 7:31 in Luther’s gloss; likewise in Selden’s *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma 2.</margin>

22. You shall not lie with a male as one lies with a woman: that is an abomination.

23. You shall also not lie with any beast to defile yourself with it; and no woman shall stand before a beast to lie down before it. That is a shameful perversion.

24. You shall not defile yourselves with any of these things: for by all these things the heathens <note>original: "Heyden," referring to the non-Israelite nations</note> have been defiled, whom I will cast out before you;

25. And the land is defiled. Therefore I will visit its iniquity upon it, so that the land spews out its inhabitants.

26. So now you shall keep my statutes and my laws, and do none of these abominations: neither the native nor the stranger who dwells among you.

Such shameful and unnatural lust has become prevalent among the heathens through the devil’s cunning. Because they did not highly value the knowledge granted to them by God, nor searched for His holy essence and will, they became a prey to Satan. He can pull a person’s mind toward the most terrifying abominations and finally actually seduce them into doing them: Romans 1:25 etc. <note>original: "2c." is an old abbreviation for "etc."</note> These abominations should be heard of least of all among those called to the knowledge of Christ. But because even this glorious benefit is treated with punishable contempt by many, it is no wonder that Satan sometimes gains such power over some such despisers and foolish people. See Ephesians 4:19; Colossians 3:5–7.

God also wants us not to be beastly minded in other ways, nor to harbor such disorderly lusts through which we become an abomination before God. For the pure God only wants to receive and accept "God-men" <note>spiritually renewed people</note>—and not a beast—into His fellowship.

<column-break/>

27. For the people of this land who were before you have done all these abominations, and the land is defiled.

28. Lest the land also spew you out when you defile it, just as it spewed out the nation that was before you.

29. For whoever does any of these abominations, the souls that do them shall be cut off from among their people.

30. Therefore you shall keep my charge, that you do none of the abominable customs that were done before you; that you do not defile yourselves with them. I am the Lord your God.

A land is defiled by abominable sins, so that such sinners are finally destroyed by God’s judgment in a land, or driven and cast out from it. They are spewed out of a land as harmful despisers of God, like a bad and indigestible food that cannot remain in the stomach and must therefore be vomited out. See also Revelation 3:16. One should strive to remove such sinners who do not want to improve their lives—either by taking them out of common society through houses of correction <note>original: "Zucht-Häuser," early modern institutions for reform and punishment</note> or otherwise removing them from the lands. See Psalm 101:8.

However, if everything that is an abomination before God were to be viewed this way, then sadly the Christian world might be left quite deserted by its inhabitants. For can it not also be said of the great multitude among us that they all follow unrighteousness together with lies, and thereby distance themselves ever further from God? Oh, how it is to be feared that such a generation might indeed be punished in the same way, when they least expect it! Punishments befall us daily, and yet we do not think that such things happen for the sake of our sins. If we imitate the sins of those whom God punished so harshly, how do we then think we can escape those punishments? But if we desire to escape them, let us turn to our Lord and God with all our heart and all our soul: then we shall find life. For He is our God, who wants to make us into new creatures in Himself.

# The XIX. Chapter.
->Various commands of holiness and ceremonial statutes.<-

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

2. Speak to the entire congregation of the children of Israel and say to them:

<column-break/>

You shall be holy, <margin>(a)</margin> for I the Lord your God am holy. Isaiah 6:3. (a) ch. 20/7.

<meta>catchword: 3. A</meta>

---

In this and the following chapter, the Lord presents various commandments from the Ten Commandments and other statutes and laws, most of which are repeated to further impress all His commandments upon them.

v. 2. And so a general preface regarding the holiness of God is repeated here, as it should be the pattern for all our actions. And since this is so often impressed in the Old Testament, it should be observed all the more in the New Testament, as this is the will of God: our sanctification. 1 Thessalonians 4:3; 1 Peter 1:15–16; Hebrews 12:14.

This is what God demands of His people and the entire congregation of Israel:

To let Him have His holiness without unrighteously claiming it for themselves; but on the other hand, to become pure enough to be able to approach Him and to lose oneself in Him as in the abyss of holiness. In this state—where we then no longer have any holiness of our own—we become partakers of God’s holiness (b), not indeed for ourselves, but in Him and through Him.

> Be holy, O my God! And cleanse us so that we do not, through our impurity, resist that purity and infinite holiness which flow out like small streams upon the blessed and upon the faithful people of the Lord.

<margin>(a) Exodus 28:36. (b) Hebrews 12:10.</margin>

<column-break/>

As soon as one stops being holy, one falls back from the rank of being God’s people. For there must be some similarity between the people of God and the so holy and pure God.

But what kind of holiness does God demand from those who belong to Him? We must not believe it to be a merely assumed holiness, as if we were to claim for ourselves what we only find in God Himself. What God demands is a complete outward and inward purity of heart and spirit, so that we may approach such a holy and pure God, whose holiness is so terrifying to the sinners spoken of above. For the same Holy Scripture—or rather God Himself—who says: "you shall be holy, because I also am holy," also tells us (a) that holiness belongs to Him who exists. <note>likely a reference to Psalm 93:5 or a similar ontological claim about God's nature</note> Therefore one must

<header>The Third Book of Moses. Ch. XIX.</header>

### 3. Every one shall fear his mother and his father, and shall keep my Sabbaths (a): I am the Lord your God.
<margin>(a) Lev. 26:2. Exod. 31:13.</margin>

### 4. You shall not turn to idols, nor make for yourselves cast gods: I am the Lord your God.

->Four of the Ten Commandments flow together in these two verses.<-

From the fifth commandment, the **mother** is placed first to show that God has laid the reverence for her upon children just as much as for the father. In this, the perversity of humanity is revealed, among other things, in that children often do not have such fear for their mothers; because mothers have interacted more familiarly with children from tender infancy, fear of them is seldom found. There is, however, more fear for fathers because of their often strict discipline.

From the fourth commandment, the **keeping of the Sabbaths** is drawn—and thus all ordained festivals, which must also be celebrated with such rest—and it is secured with the seal that it is the Lord who commands it. He, in the very first commandment, introduces <note>original: "insinuiret"</note> his sovereign dominion and sole true divinity.

**Fear mother and father)** one should, because they represent God's place on earth, and because He has used them to give us this fleshly life, without which we could not have had an existence and would have been deprived of the blessedness of knowing God.

But how poorly this commandment is observed! Children despise their fathers: their life is a burden to them, and they kill them a thousand times over through the heartache they inflict. Parents must often endure unheard-of tribulations from their children! But this frequently does not remain unavenged even in this life; for children often experience that they are treated in exactly the same way they treated their own parents.

**Keep my Sabbaths)** These Sabbaths of the Lord are not a mere resting from some external works, as some imagine; rather, they are primarily a resting from all works of unrighteousness. Furthermore, they are a resting from our own works, so that God Himself can work in us, in order for us to reach the true Sabbath—which is the rest of the soul in its own domain—and finally in God Himself as its end. This latter is the eternal Sabbath, a perpetual rest, which begins here in order to continue for all eternity.

**v. 4. The first and second commandments are also drawn in,** and the idols are called "nothings" <note>original: "nichtige Dinge," meaning empty or vain things</note> with an emphatic word, because an idol is nothing in the world (1 Cor. 8:4), and their casting from metals is forbidden. See Psalm 115:4, Isaiah 40:19.

**Turning to idols)** This is what we do when we turn away from God and toward any creature, whatever it may be. When we prefer a creature over God, we make an idol out of that creature. Is it not written (a) that greed is idolatry? We commit idolatry in everything that we love excessively. How many idol-worshipers are there not among the Christians!
<margin>(a) Col. 3:5.</margin>

<column-break/>

### 5. And when you will offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Lord, you may offer it according to your own will.

### 6. It shall be eaten the same day you offer it, and on the next day: but what remains on the third day shall be burned with fire.

### 7. But if any of it is eaten on the third day, it is an abomination; it will not be accepted.

### 8. And he who eats of it shall bear his iniquity, for he has profaned the sanctuary of the Lord: and that soul shall be cut off from among his people.

---

With this, it is strictly commanded that the <term>thank-offering</term> <note>German: "Danckopffer." In modern Bibles, often translated as a "peace offering" or "fellowship offering."</note> should no longer be eaten on the third day, but burned, as in Lev. 7:17, 18. This gives us occasion for the following reflection: The time before the appearance of Christ can be divided into two parts, or two great "days." These represent the two great divine dispensations: the approximately 2,000 years under the Promise, and the approximately 2,000 years under the Law (reckoning from Abraham, when the covenant of circumcision was established, until the coming of Christ). During these two days, thank-offerings of slaughtered animals were customary and ordained. But whoever would still use animals for a thank-offering and eat of them on the "third day" of the New Testament, he would be—if he slaughtered an ox—as if he slew a man; and if he sacrificed a sheep, as if he broke a dog's neck, etc. Isaiah 66:3. See also Daniel 9:27.

**v. 5. Once the soul has reached its deepest rest,** one can rightly say that it offers sacrifices of thanksgiving to God. For it is like a sacrificial animal offered to God in its suffering state, bearing everything, both internally and externally: namely, the internal workings of God, both the crucifying and the gracious ones; and externally all crosses, sorrow, and suffering—indeed, everything that happens to us from God, from people, from devils, and from ourselves through our failings and carelessness.

**v. 6. Why did the thank-offering have to be eaten the same day, or the following morning?** To teach us that the soul, submerged and rested in God, is satisfied with the <term>holy moment</term> <note>German: "heiligen Augenblicke," a key concept in mystical Pietism referring to living in the immediate presence of God without anxiety for the future.</note>, without preparing anything for the future. Its nourishment is the present moment of God's command over us. What remained had to be burned and consumed by fire. What are the remains? After one has surrendered to the holy moment, and yet still prepares something for the future, reversals and over-reflections return; these one must immediately set aside and let them all be burned in this fire of holy love.

**v. 7. If one ate of this thank-offering in the following days, one was an abomination.** This indicates how foresight for the future is contrary to <term>yieldedness</term> <note>German: "Gelassenheit," meaning a state of surrender to God's will.</note>; and that there is a certain time in which one must make use of the present light. For after that time has passed, one cannot reach it again. Jesus Christ Himself said this: (a) Walk in the light while it is still day. Thus, the present moment must be the life of the thankful soul.
<margin>(a) John 12:35.</margin>

**v. 8. In short: One should not postpone the thank-offering, but eat of it soon,** applying it to oneself for the best, moving it well in the heart, and thus ruminating upon it; because by postponing, one very easily and ungratefully forgets to praise and thank.

Just as the first day may be understood as the active life and the second day as the contemplative life, so must what is to be done be done in these two days. If it is postponed further to the third day, then divine judgment arrives, when man can no longer work the good which he neglected to work here while it was day. For then there will be no time to work, but to receive what we have dealt with during our physical life, whether it be good or evil. (a) John 12:35.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Leviticus 19, moving from the foundational commandments of the Decalogue (respect for parents and the Sabbath) toward social justice and ethical behavior toward one's neighbors, specifically the poor and the disabled.</meta>

### Chapter XIX. The Third Book of Moses. 519

9. And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, nor shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest. <margin>ch. 23:22. Deut. 24:19.</margin>

10. You shall not glean your vineyard, nor shall you pick up the fallen grapes of your vineyard; you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger. I am the LORD your God.

11. You shall not steal; and you shall not lie, nor deal falsely every one with his neighbor. <margin>ch. 6:2.</margin>

---

First, generosity and benevolence are commanded here, so that they should leave something of the harvest bestowed upon them by God for the poor and strangers. The elders of the Jews determined that this should be at least the sixtieth part. <note>The "sixtieth part" refers to the *Pe'ah*, a Rabbinic tradition defining the minimum amount of a field to be left for the poor.</note>

God gave the Jews this commandment to turn them away from all greed and to move them to leave a portion of what God had bestowed upon them for the poor.

v. 9. **Not wholly reap** / What does this point to but a double harvest? You should learn to sow your harvest once more for increase <note>original: "auf Wucher," implying a spiritual investment or "interest" paid by God</note>; you should open your heart to the needy and do good to everyone from what is yours, while you still have time and are still master over your things: then you will reap in due time without ceasing.

v. 10. **Leave for the poor** / He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. This is in accordance with divine justice and love. All those who wish to be diligent workers and restorers <note>original: "Ausheiler," meaning those who bring healing or wholeness to a task</note> in God's vineyard and field-work will experience this. Oh, that the Lord of the harvest would send out many such faithful workers into His harvest!

And so, these two verses contain a good moral lesson according to the letter: that one should leave something from one's abundance and blessing for the poor and strangers, and not seize and keep everything for oneself through greed, which God the Lord has given in the physical realm. However, there is also a spiritual meaning within it: that one should not keep the divine gifts of the Spirit for oneself alone, but should also share what one has received from God with others who are lowlier.

v. 11. Following this, the opposite of the eighth commandment—theft—is forbidden: which among other things consists of postponing the hard-earned wages of the poor day laborer, because he must feed himself daily from hand to mouth. See also v. 13. Job 24:10, 11. Mal. 3:5. James 5:4.

So also is the ninth commandment explained, showing how one sins against it: partly when one remains silent about the known truth, and partly when one even speaks lies and deals falsely with one's neighbor.

God forbids theft all the more earnestly so that, while we are encouraged to observe justice toward men and not take away what is theirs, we might thereby also learn to observe justice toward God, and not steal anything from Him, nor rob Him of His rights. Therefore, it is immediately added:

**You shall not lie.** For (a) he who imagines himself to be something, when he is nothing, is a liar. He who wishes to be highly esteemed by men is a deceiver. Among all deceivers, thieves, and liars, none is greater than the hypocrite. He steals God's honor: he constantly deceives people by appearing to be what he is not: he deceives himself; and is full of robbery and injustice. <margin>(a) Gal. 6:3.</margin>

Oh, how many such false deceivers seek to practice their lusts under the appearance of God's name, and deceive those souls in whom there is no falsehood and who therefore suspect nothing! They work their wickedness in the appearance of godliness: and that is the worst deception, with which they catch and destroy souls. Therefore, they are of the devil's portion; they help him in his murder and lies and use his art; for in him there is no truth, just as in Christ there is no lie.

<column-break/>

12. And you shall not swear falsely by my name, so that you profane the name of your God. I am the LORD.

13. You shall not do wrong to your neighbor nor rob him. The wages of a day laborer shall not remain with you overnight until the morning.

14. You shall not curse a deaf person; and you shall not place a stumbling block before a blind person; but you shall fear your God. I am the LORD.

---

v. 12. The third commandment is explained: how the name of God is especially misused and profaned with false swearing, when one does not fear the omniscient and jealous God.

Many people swear falsely by promising God with an oath that they will no longer be disobedient to Him, yet they always do it again. Others use the oath to deceive their brothers. Such people profane the name of God by using it for deception. These people are already condemned. They always have the name of God in their mouths to fool and deceive people: and by using it for deception and trickery, they defile or profane it.

v. 13. The eighth commandment is further explained regarding injustice and overt violence. See 1 Thess. 4:6.

Slander <note>original: "Das Affterreden"</note> is very common nowadays. Hypocrites make use of it, thinking to exalt themselves greatly through the harm of their neighbor; partisan people do the same, believing everything is permitted to them if they can only reach their goal through it. Both use force to suppress those whom they have slandered: and that is indeed the greatest wickedness.

The commandment that one should not withhold the wages of a day laborer is also a matter to which few pay attention. One is thereby guilty of causing their families to struggle because their payment is withheld, forcing them to borrow and thereby go to ruin.

If it is such a great sin to withhold the laborer's wage, how great a sin must it be to keep his daily wage entirely, or to cheat him out of it altogether?

There are people who give alms from the property of others: by depriving poor craftsmen of their earnings so that they may distribute more magnificent alms. All this is an abomination before God. God demands fairness <note>original: "Billigkeit," or equity</note> in all things.

v. 14. This commandment is directed against all spiteful nature in men, where one seeks to harm another if only he can hide it from people; which also happens through evil gossip in one's absence: whereby man disregards the fear of the all-seeing God who avenges injustice.

However, besides the external literal meaning, this also has a spiritual sense, according to which those

**Curse a deaf person, and place a stumbling block before a blind person** / who not only despise those who do not yet have insight into divine things and leave them to go on in their blindness, but even give them an offense <note>original: "Aergerniß," meaning a cause for stumbling or sin</note> so that they fall over it; indeed, treating them with harshness because they do not understand what they should understand: whereas they should much rather help them aright.

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XIX.

15. You shall not act unjustly in judgment: You shall not partial to the person of the lowly, nor honor the person of the great: You shall judge your neighbor with righteousness.
16. You shall not go about as a slanderer among your people. You shall not stand up against the blood of your neighbor. I am the LORD.
17. You shall not hate your brother in your heart: you shall earnestly rebuke your neighbor, so that you do not have to bear a sin on his account.

<margin>v. 15. In the courts, God desires justice to be administered by judges without respect of persons: they should not take the side of the poor man at the wrong time against the rich, namely if the poor man is in the wrong; for one can show him mercy in other ways. Nor should one be blinded by the status of the great and powerful to grant him right in an unjust cause by striving to gloss it over in every way.</margin>

There is almost no justice left on the earth. Either the judges are partisan, and by falling in with one side, they are so biased that injustice appears to them to be justice. Others, however, allow themselves to be bribed. It is very rare that a poor man who has a good cause wins against a rich man, even if the latter pursues an evil cause. Would one even dare to solicit judges, except when giving them instruction on one's case? There are indeed honest people in all places, and the world is not entirely bare of good judges: but they are rare! And how many are there who do not oppress the innocent when their own reputation is involved!

<margin>v. 16. This is a further explanation of the Ninth Commandment, that one should not seek to plunge one's neighbor into all kinds of harm and even danger of life through false accusation.</margin>

There are two kinds of slanderers. Some who invent new sins, or boast of such sins which they have not even committed; others, however, who attribute sins to their brothers so that they may be insulted and persecuted, taking away their good name. And secret slanderers are a thousand times worse than open ones, to whom one gives only light credit. But these secret slanderers give their slander and blasphemy some weight, and thereby make them infallible. Those who make no difficulty of inventing and spreading the most lying things, taking the honor of honest people so that they might make their slanders immortal, as it were, through their writings; oh, how harshly will all these be punished one day!

<margin>v. 17. Love of neighbor is commanded here in general, as man must first clear all hatred and ill-will against his neighbor from his heart, and then walk toward him in all friendliness.</margin>

But because one is accustomed to use the neighbor's bad behavior, or even our own injury, as a pretext for hatred; so God wants us to rebuke him for it, yet out of the foundation of love, to see if he might be won over, as Christ also commanded us in Matthew 18:15. For God also wants the evil to be rebuked, so that one does not become a partaker of such sins through silence, and thereby seem to approve of them. See Romans 1:32.

Brotherly rebuke is something very delicate, and very little in use. Some rebuke their brothers publicly, not because they have sinned, but because they hate them. Others cry them out and reveal such faults of their brothers to others which they have even invented themselves. When one wants to improve his brother, he must first be without passions <note>original: "affecten," referring to being emotionally compromised or biased</note> himself, or he must have the authority to do so. When one has no power to rebuke him, he must leave him to the hand of God without crying him out.

<column-break/>

18. You shall not take vengeance, nor bear a grudge against the children of your people: but you shall love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.
19. You shall keep my statutes: You shall not let your cattle breed with a different kind: You shall not sow your field with two kinds of seed, and no garment made of two kinds of thread shall come upon you.

<margin>v. 18. One should also keep no hidden hatred against his neighbor, but be inclined toward forgiveness and reconciliation, and thus love the neighbor as one would want him to act toward us and love us: which commandment Christ cites as the second commandment, which is like the first and most eminent commandment of the love of God; Matthew 22:39–40. Thus God intended to place the highest duties of man in the required love toward Him and toward the neighbor, so that they might comfort themselves in His grace and lead a contented life with one another.</margin>

It is forbidden to us that we should take revenge ourselves. Who is there who does not seek to avenge himself with all his strength, and who does not say that nothing is sweeter than one's own revenge? Both Testaments have commanded that one should forget injuries: But who puts this into practice?
**Against the children of your people — your neighbor.** From this the Jews conclude that they should hate their enemies (Matthew 5:43), especially those whose hearts were more inclined to hate than to love.
But the neighbor is he who is of one flesh with us, since we all come from one. See Isaiah 58:7.
**As yourself)** And thus not all self-love is forbidden.
Namely, there are two kinds of self-love: a good one and an evil one. The good kind, which Adam also had and which is reordered in believers, must not be set aside or denied; rather, only the evil, disordered love of ourselves that arose from the Fall. The former, however—where man loves himself for God's sake and in God <note>original: "Thom. Aquin. 2. 2. quæst. 19. art. 6. & quæst. 25. art. 4. & 5." Referring to Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 19, Article 6, and Question 25, Articles 4 and 5.</note>—is much more commanded here alongside the love of neighbor; and is consequently to be regarded as an error if someone wished to reject it.

<margin>v. 19. **Not sow with two kinds)** They were not allowed, for example, in the Promised Land to sow wheat and barley, or beans and lentils, or similar diverse seeds that served as food for man, mixed together; nor in a hollow vessel filled with earth; nor to graft or bud different trees into one another, e.g., a fig branch into a lemon tree, or the like: although the Hebrews allow the sowing of seeds of trees with other things; also two kinds of seeds in one field, if each is sown separately for itself, so that there was a space of 3 furrows between the two kinds of seeds.</margin>

With these commandments, God intended to command simplicity <term>simplicity: here meaning purity or singleness of purpose, avoiding "mischmasch" or dilution</term>, so that they should not mix the order of nature, nor take occasion for all kinds of disordered lusts through manifold mixing. This commandment, however, is much neglected; as the fields are sown with many kinds of fruit, and fabrics mixed with wool, woolen and linen, or even silk are entirely in vogue, to which also belongs the usual mixing of many kinds of food for the gratification of the disordered appetite: all of which shows how rarely simplicity has remained, which yet should be so carefully observed among the people of God.
The same should also happen in matters of religion, and there is no doubt that something deeper is represented here against all "mischmasch" <note>original: "Mischmasch," meaning a confused mixture or hodgepodge</note> in the work of salvation: just as one should confess all the truth purely and in divine simplicity.

<note>Footnote reference to Thomas Aquinas.</note>
(a) Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica*, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 19, Article 6, and Question 25, Articles 4 and 5.

### Chapter XIX. The Third Book of Moses.

20. And when a man lies with a woman with carnal intercourse, and she is a maid-servant who has been rejected <note>German: *verschmähet*; in this context, it refers to a servant betrothed or assigned to another man but not yet fully redeemed.</note> by a man, such that she has not been redeemed at all, or freedom has not been given to her; there shall be a punishment. They shall not be put to death, because she was not made free.

21. But for his guilt, he shall bring a ram as a guilt offering to the LORD, to the door of the Tent of Meeting. <margin>chapter 5, verse 15.</margin>

22. And the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the guilt offering before the face of the LORD for his sin which he has committed: thus he shall obtain forgiveness for his sin which he has committed.

23. And when you come into the land and plant all kinds of trees from which you eat; then you shall circumcise <note>original: *beschneiden*</note> their foreskin, their fruits. For three years they shall be as uncircumcised to you: they shall not be eaten.

---

<margin>v. 20.</margin> The case in this commandment seems to be this—which is otherwise interpreted variously by commentators because they translate the word *rejected* differently, though this is the actual meaning of the Hebrew word: When a man married his maidservant, but afterwards rejected her so that he did not live with her, yet had not actually divorced her: if she then allowed herself to be slept with by another, they were not punished with death as adulterers, precisely because of this rejection and because she was a maidservant; nevertheless, the matter had to be investigated so that they could be punished according to the findings.

This commandment also seems to mitigate the death penalty in cases where someone withdraws the rightful affection from his wife and thus rejects her, thereby giving her, as it were, an occasion to fall with another: who otherwise must be punished according to the circumstances.

<margin>v. 23.</margin> In this prohibition, God intended to restrain the curiosity that people tend to have toward new plants, so that the appetite should also be sacrificed to the will of God, who had otherwise bestowed an abundant supply of food upon them in such a fruitful land.

*Shall circumcise their foreskin, their fruits)* You shall break off the first fruits as soon as they emerge and not eat them, but throw them away, just as one throws away the foreskin in circumcision as something useless.

*Three years)* they should thus be to them as uncircumcised, and the fruits of the first three years should be counted as a foreskin.

Josephus <note>original: *Antiq. l. 4. c. 8.* refers to *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 4, Chapter 8.</note> (a) gives the reason that the fruit of the first three years is premature, or imperfect, as Philo <note>original: *L. 3. de charit. p. 551.* refers to *On Charity*, Book 3.</note> (b) expresses it.

<margin>
(a) Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book 4, Chapter 8.
(b) Philo, Book 3, *On Charity*, page 551.
</margin>

<column-break/>

24. And in the fourth year, all their fruits shall be a holy offering of praise to the LORD.

25. But in the fifth year, you shall eat their fruits, so that you may increase their yield for yourselves. I am the LORD your God.

26. You shall eat nothing with the blood. You shall not practice divination, nor choose auspicious days.

27. You shall not round off the hair at the edges of your head, nor completely remove the edges of your beard. <margin>chapter 21, verse 5.</margin>

28. And

---

<margin>v. 24.</margin> In the fourth year, the fruits were brought to the LORD, just as children, as the fruits of the body, had to be presented to the LORD at their time with an offering. <margin>Chapter 12.</margin>

Some have concluded from this that they belonged entirely to the priests. <note>original: (a) *vid. Schindl. Lex. pentagl. in תלל p. 573. & ערך p. 1390.* refers to Schindler’s *Pentaglot Lexicon* under the entries for *hillul* (praise) and *arak* (valuation).</note> (a)

However, as Josephus reports—who had the best knowledge of this—they were only to be consumed in Jerusalem and not at home, together with friends, widows, and orphans.

One could also redeem them for money, which had to be brought to Jerusalem, and one had to add a fifth [of the value] to it. The value, however, was then determined by three wise men, among whom there had to be a priest.

One could also sell them and bring the money to Jerusalem, in which case the fifth did not have to be added. <note>original: (b) *Hotting. de jur. Hebr. num 220.* refers to Hottinger’s *On Hebrew Law*, number 220.</note> (b)

<margin>v. 25.</margin> In the fifth year, they were allowed to freely enjoy God's blessing: which was promised to them insofar as they behaved obediently in this matter; since obedience to God's commandments is the source of all blessing. <margin>Leviticus 26.</margin>

This can also represent how man, as a sinner, has no right to all the growths of the earth, but that he must first seek the enjoyment of them again in the reconciliation of God through Christ, in which he can then enjoy everything primarily with thanksgiving, and it is pure to him; whereas to the impure, everything is impure. <margin>Titus 1:15 and 1 Timothy 4:3, 4, 5.</margin>

<margin>v. 26. 27.</margin> In these prohibitions, the LORD intended to forbid His people from pagan customs that occurred out of sheer idolatry to honor idols; which one does not necessarily need to know exactly, how and why the pagans behaved so. Israel, however, as a people of God, should apply themselves to all simplicity in their entire conduct.

They should not worry about knowing future things through divination but should daily leave themselves to the providence of God and commend themselves to His government: then everything will turn out well.

<margin>v. 27. Nor completely remove the edges of your beard)</margin> Or: and you shall not destroy the corner of your beard. The Jews must observe this commandment as soon as they are married. Therefore, they allow no razor to come upon five corners—on the upper and lower jawbone on each side and under the chin—but only allow themselves to be trimmed with shears <note>original: *zwicken*, referring to the use of scissors or tweezers rather than a razor blade.</note>.

In such matters—as in taking away the beard entirely, or leaving something standing, just as the Jews were to leave the extreme ends as a sign of manhood, perhaps to behave to some extent according to the external practices of the Oriental peoples—one can indeed yield somewhat to the customs of men that remain in freedom: since one should otherwise strive to prove manhood not in the beard, but in wisdom and prudence, and manly bravery rather in Christian patience and steadfastness.

(b) Hottinger, *On Hebrew Law*, number 220.
