### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XIX.

28. And you shall not make any incision <note>original: *Riß*; refers to ritual scarring or lacerations</note> in your flesh for the sake of a dead person, nor shall you make any incised writing (*) on yourselves. I am the LORD. <margin>(a) chapter 21, verse 5.</margin>

29. You shall not profane your daughter by keeping her for prostitution, so that the land does not practice harlotry and the land becomes filled with vices.

30. You shall keep my Sabbaths and fear my sanctuary. I am the LORD.

31. You shall not turn to soothsayers nor to interpreters of signs (*): you shall not seek them out, lest you be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God. <margin>(a) Deuteronomy 18, verse 10.</margin>

32. You shall rise before a gray head and honor the face of an old man. For you shall fear your God: I am the LORD.

---

v. 28. One should not make strange figures on one’s head and body: this arises from pagan madness, where people indulge in all sorts of foolish imaginings; just as they also used to do to show their mourning for the dead: see Jeremiah 41:5. Instead, one should strive for simplicity, as well as dignity and decency, according to which one should neither shave the head entirely nor let the hair grow completely wild, but rather cut it modestly. See Ezekiel 44:20; 1 Corinthians 11:14.

<gloss>make an incision in your flesh, nor incised writing)</gloss> So great is the power of superstition that a person can be unmerciful toward their own flesh without necessity, as the priests of Baal also did. 1 Kings 18:28. But to crucify one's flesh with its passions and desires according to the will of God—wherein only the perverse self-will suffers by being broken and thus killed—that is something people do not want to approach, even though it would be for the well-being of both body and soul.

v. 29. The pagans also did not consider prostitution a sin, but rather encouraged their daughters to engage in it to honor their unclean idols: therefore the Apostles also wished to forbid such things through a general decree in Acts 15:20 <note>The original cites 15:15, likely a typo for the Apostolic Decree in 15:20/29</note>, as Paul later urged with more detail in 1 Corinthians 6:15 and 1 Thessalonians 4:3, 4, 5, etc.

v. 30. They should also have a reverence for the sanctuary as a sign of the divine presence among them: which one should always have wherever divine matters are handled.

v. 31. They should not turn to extraordinary means to seek help; but rather call upon God in times of need and for all concerns for help and counsel. Psalm 91:14, 15.

v. 32. Because the perversity of youth consists, among other things, in the fact that they have little regard for the elderly and desire to live according to their own stubbornness, God wished to command us to show respect for the elderly under the threat of His punishments. For God will hear their sighing, not only when children and grandchildren treat their parents poorly, but also when the elderly in the community at large are despised, which is an indication of the great corruption of men, who thereby only heap up divine judgments upon themselves. See also 1 Timothy 5:1, 2.

<column-break/>

33. And when a stranger stays with you in your land, you shall not oppress him.

34. The stranger who stays with you shall be among you like a native of your own; and you shall love him as yourself. For you were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.

35. You shall practice no injustice in judgment, with the ell <note>original: *Ehlen*; a unit of measurement for length, roughly the length of an arm</note>, with the weight, or with the measure. <margin>Micah 6:11.</margin>

36. Just balances, a just pound, a just Ephah, and a just Hin <note>biblical units of dry and liquid volume</note> shall be among you. I am the LORD your God, who led you out of the land of Egypt.

37. Therefore you shall keep all my statutes and all my judgments and do them. I am the LORD.

---

v. 33. Mercy and kindness are especially fitting for the people of God, such that one does not envy those who come to us and wish to sustain themselves among us. Since they possess nothing of their own among us, they are also not obligated to bear the common burdens <note>i.e., taxes or civic duties tied to land ownership</note> which should primarily be paid on account of property.

v. 34. We should then show all friendliness to such people, especially when they have had to leave their own for the sake of conscience.

v. 35. Among the people of God, under the present constitution, there should also be a good civil order <note>original: *Policey-Ordnung*; refers to the regulation of public life and trade</note>, where all things are arranged according to their right measure and weight, and the just price of the way: because due to great imperfection, men cannot otherwise manage, as the state of trade must be conducted in such an order established by the authorities. See also Ezekiel 45:10, 11.

v. 36. <gloss>Ephah, Hin)</gloss> A Hin was the 6th part of an Ephah, and held as much as 72 eggs might contain.

v. 37. <gloss>All my statutes and judgments)</gloss> The entire chapter is full of nothing but prescriptions of equity, which God commands to be kept.

One must also take note that in all the commandments the LORD gives in this chapter, He adds a supplement to almost every single one:

**I am the LORD!** And this is for two reasons. Firstly: to stir up the attention of this people and to keep them in obedience. Secondly: to show that He desired obedience and was entitled to demand such blind obedience from this people. For what GOD demands of us is total obedience and the dying away of our own will. And one may well believe that when God imposes so many commandments on this people—and that in such small and minor matters that it might almost seem belittling to the great God to command such things, which seem very insignificant, in such piecemeal fashion—this happens to teach them and us this blind and unquestioning obedience. It is enough that He who is our LORD and our God commands us a thing: so we must carry it out without looking at the importance of His commandment. For obedience in smaller things is more perfect than in larger ones, which carry their worthiness in themselves. Moreover, small opportunities occur daily, and thus do not let the flexibility of the soul fall asleep.

The multitude of these commandments, their repetition, and their minor nature gradually make the soul supple and agile. Although we are not under the Law of severity <note>referring to the transition from the Old Covenant to the New Covenant/Grace</note>, God nevertheless demands our obedience no less. People today have only ten commandments, which they constantly transgress; yet the Jews were precise in such a great multitude of them. Yet it is true that they feared the punishment and did not have the obedience of love that God demands of us, His children.

### Chapter XX. The Third Book of Moses.

## The XX. Chapter.

->Various Death Penalties and Israel’s Separation.<-

AND the LORD spoke to Moses, and said:
2. You shall also say to the children of Israel: Anyone from the children of Israel, or from the strangers residing in Israel, who gives his offspring to Molech <note>Molech was a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice</note>, shall certainly be put to death; the people of the land shall stone him.
3. And I will set my face (*) against that man, and will cut him off from the midst of his people, because he has given his offspring to Molech, thereby defiling my sanctuary and profaning my holy name. <margin>(a) chapter 17:18.</margin>
4. And if the people of the land should in any way hide their eyes from that man when he gives his offspring to Molech, so that they do not kill him:
5. Then I will set my face against that man and against his family, and I will cut him off, along with all those who followed him in whoring after Molech, from the midst of their people.

> Since the corruption and stubbornness of mankind is so great that they will not be deterred from even the most unjust and godless deeds by good laws—even though they should test and observe what is best for them—God has chosen to show His seriousness regarding certain very abominable acts and has commanded that such be punished with death.
> v. 2. First and foremost, the cruel idolatry performed by sacrificing children to Molech, which was discussed above in Chapter 18:21.
> **He shall be put to death — the people shall stone him, v. 3-5. Cut off — where the people did not kill him.** Being "cut off" from the midst of the people and the "capital punishment" <note>original: *Hals-Strafe*, literally "neck-penalty"</note> to be carried out by the authorities are sometimes placed together in Scripture, just as happens here. From this, however, it does not follow that they are the same punishment, as some suggest (a); rather, it is to be understood as follows: if someone commits a sin worthy of death and a capital penalty is set for it, but the authorities do not find out and it remains secret; or, even if the authorities do find out but "look through their fingers" <note>an idiom meaning to intentionally ignore a crime</note> and do not perform their duty: in such a case God threatens that even if such a person escapes the punishment of the authorities, he shall not escape His divine punishment. He will then punish the person Himself and avenge what men did not avenge. Thus, "cutting off" is a punishment where God Himself snatches the person prematurely from the world—the vengeance of God striking the person by God's own hand (b): (see Exodus 30:38) and is therefore not the same as the civil capital punishment. The authorities should punish what is to be punished and take the lives of those under the Old Covenant law who had forfeited their lives. If they would not do so, then God Himself would be the judge. Hebrews 13:4.

<column-break/>

6. And the soul that turns to soothsayers and to interpreters of signs, to go whoring after them; I will set my face against that soul and will cut it off from the midst of its people.
7. Therefore you shall sanctify yourselves, that you may be holy: For I am the LORD your God. <margin>chapter 19:2.</margin>
8. And you shall keep my statutes and do them: I am the LORD who sanctifies you. <margin>chapter 22:9.</margin>
9. When

> v. 6. **The soul that turns to soothsayers)** If someone should willfully follow the unclean spirit and seek help and counsel from it, as the blind heathens let themselves be led astray by Satan's cunning—abandoning the true God and turning to worthless idols in which Satan allowed himself to be worshipped. After the revelation of the true God among the people He had chosen as His own, this was highly shameful and was therefore to be punished with death. See verse 27 here.
> v. 7. God then commands sanctification once again, that they should strive for it as a people of the holy God, by abolishing all such abominable idolatries and taking refuge in God, so that He might sanctify them and redeem and cleanse their hearts from all such abominable and shameful inclinations. See Ezekiel 36:26, 27.
> **Holiness indicates two things:** 1) a separation or division from something; as here from Molech, from soothsayers, and from those who have *spiritus familiares* <note>original Latin: "familiar spirits" or "guiding spirits" used in divination</note>; 2) a dedication and devotion to the LORD in the observation of His commandments.
> **Why is this required?** Because He is the Holy One of Israel; therefore He separates His people from all other gods and their defiled services, and claims them for Himself and His pure and holy service, so that they may be holy just as He is holy.
> God also repeats to the soul once more that He desires it to be holy, to signify that it must continually walk in purity: which happens as the soul increasingly goes out from itself to lose itself in Him.
> v. 8. He also assures them that He is the one who sanctifies them: so that they may learn not to seek holiness in the law-book anymore, nor perfect purity in any created means; because such is found in God alone.
> Here we also learn the only source of obedience to God's commandments so that one may fulfill them: namely, not our own powers which might remain from the light of nature—for by nature we are dead to all that is good—but rather the sanctifying power of the Holy Spirit, who works in us both the will and the deed according to His good pleasure. Philippians 2:13. To this belong the promises of the New Testament. Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 11:20; 36:27.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XX.

### 9. If there is anyone who curses his fa-
### ther or his mother /
### he shall certainly be put to death :

Curses uttered in anger against one’s parents were to be punished with death: Exod. 21:17. The reason is added here: because he has cursed his parents. This constitutes the most shameful ingratitude and the most disgraceful mistreatment of parents through both words and deeds.

These words contain the announcement of punishment for a specific vice; to make the matter even more serious, the words are repeated and the punishment is reaffirmed.

**or)** This distinguishing translation is confirmed by the authority of the Lawgiver Himself in Matthew 15:4. <note>Jesus cites this law when rebuking the Pharisees for prioritizing their traditions over the commandment to honor parents.</note>

Thus, even one who curses only one of his parents is guilty of death; otherwise, if it were phrased differently, one might try to escape the law's reach.

**Cursing)** The Hebrew word <note>original: *qillēl*</note> does not only mean to speak evil against or of someone, or to wish them harm, as it is commonly understood; rather, it more precisely means to disparage, to hold in contempt, and to dishonor. 1 Sam. 2:30.

**Father -- Mother)** These are not only to be understood as those who conceived and gave birth to us; Prov. 23:22; nor only those whom the law makes such to us: Ruth 3:1–6. Instead, they also refer to rulers and authorities, according to the usage of Scripture. Isa. 22:20–21; 2 Kings 5:13; Judges 5:7. Also, those through whom God begets us are called our fathers. Gen. 45:8; 1 Cor. 4:14–15. Therefore, all those who are treated with contempt or cursed—who by analogy are called "children" in their relationship to these figures—are guilty of the same punishment.

Just as the duty to honor one's parents is righteous and fair (as discussed elsewhere), so the crime and transgression of this duty—consisting of contempt or dishonor—must necessarily be highly unfair and unjust. This applies whether it occurs through words, gestures, or deeds, such as when one refuses obedience to their commands or fails to provide for their necessities, even under the outward pretext of honoring God, as seen for example in Matthew 15:4–5.

But what if my father is a godless man? May I not then despise him and speak ill to or about him? By no means! The godlessness of parents does not release any child from the duty owed to them. It does not say, "Honor your *good* father and your *good* mother," but simply, "Honor your father and mother." Nor does it say here: "If someone curses his *pious* father," but rather, "his father or mother."

Meanwhile, parents must not think that there is no lesson here for them as well. He who does not wish to be held in low regard and despised must not be contemptible or worthy of contempt; as Paul writes to Titus regarding spiritual fatherhood: "Let no one despise you." Titus 2:15. Most parents lose their authority and respect through a lack of proper seriousness, through negligence in raising children, through unwise and crude conduct, and through the example of their own ungodly way of life.

However, children are not thereby excused if they fail to fulfill God's will and their duty in this matter. Nevertheless, this is a sin so common among us that it must rightly be counted among those that bring God's wrath upon us in these final days. Ezek. 22:7. May God avert from us the judgment that He threatened against His ancient people for this sin and executed upon them! v. 19–22. For it is a sin worthy of the punishment the Lord has placed upon it. Exod. 21:15, 17; Deut. 21:18–21, 27:16; Prov. 30:17. Therefore, it is as if the Lord God appeals to our own sense of justice, asking whether His decree is good or not, when He repeats and confirms the matter once more:

<column-break/>

### er; his blood is upon him!

### man’s wife shall have committed adultery,

**He has cursed; his blood is upon him! )** The visibility of the deed justifies God's judgment. Thus Jacob also appeals against Reuben in Genesis 49:4 through a repetition, calling as it were upon anyone who should judge whether his sentence was just or not.

But because the Law is spiritual, the words must also have their spiritual sense and meaning. The name of the Father contains a great mystery, and the name of the Mother a secret reverence. God is your Father according to the Spirit, and the heavenly Jerusalem is your mother. You can learn this, if you wish, from the prophetic and apostolic testimonies. "Is God not your Father, who bought you? Has He not made and established you?" asks Moses himself in Deut. 32:6. Is not Christ the "Father of the future world"? <note>Often translated as "Everlasting Father"</note> Isa. 9:6. And who is your mother but the Wisdom that comes down from above? James 3:17; Gal. 4:26; Rev. 21:9–10; Matt. 12:49–50; she who is so often introduced speaking in the Proverbs of Solomon.

As earthly fathers give their children being, nourishment, upbringing, and inheritance, so the Father of Spirits gives His children His divine nature. 2 Pet. 1:4. He nourishes them with flesh and blood, the Word and Spirit of His Son. He instructs them and gives them the anointing from the Holy One, through which they know and recognize all things. 1 John 2:20, 27. He punishes and disciplines us as our loving Father, so that we might partake in His holiness. Heb. 12:10. He prepares for us an incorruptible and undefiled inheritance. 1 Pet. 1:4. Meanwhile, He carries us and is patient and long-suffering toward us, just as a father carries his children. Deut. 1:31; Ps. 103:13.

Since the name of the Father is so hallowed and venerable—and the same is to be understood of the Mother, through whose labor, care, diligence, service, and toil you were born and raised—all dishonor and contempt directed at them falls back upon the spiritual Father and Mother. And therefore, you shall not offend against father and mother in any way, not even with a word, as Origen <margin>(a)</margin> reminds us. It is the father, it is the mother; they may act, behave, or speak as they see fit.

If such respect is required for fleshly and physical parents, who only bear the image, how much more so for the original Father and Mother. Yet what happens more often? And what is it other than the greatest contempt when one despises a father’s commands? And what else do those do who refuse to keep the commands of the heavenly Father <margin>(b)</margin>? What else do those do who prefer the wisdom of the flesh over the Wisdom of God? By this, you hold in low regard Him who gives all things their being! Do you think you will succeed? Choose rather to "die" in good time—to kill the members of sin on earth—so that you may escape the eternal death announced to all who despise God, alongside ungrateful children, with temporal punishment here!

**v. 10.** Adultery was to be punished with death for both the man and the woman; by this, God intended to testify to the holiness of the state of marriage, that it should be conducted in unbreakable love and faithfulness.

The reason that moved the Savior not to pronounce such a death sentence over the woman caught in adultery in John 8 is of great importance. It can certainly be applied to all death sentences, as He wished to give an example to all His servants of how they should press more for the conversion of sinners than for their condemnation to death.

Those who therefore possess such a bloodthirsty temperament show that they do not have the mind of Christ.

There were also several forms of incest <note>German: *Blut-Schanden*, literally "blood-shames"</note> and abhorrent, unnatural carnal minglings that were to be punished with death; since without doubt, in that fertile land <note>Canaan</note>, such shameful lewdness may have been very widespread / which God intended to root out with such heavy death-penalties. See also Exodus 22:18 and here in Chapter 18:22 etc.

Note, however, the order of divine wisdom in this: although God had given these same commandments shortly before in Chapter 18, He did not immediately attach a punishment to them as He does here. For He desires that we keep the Father’s commandments not out of fear of punishment / but out of a love for the fear of God. But if you despise them / then the punishment is dictated to you not as one of His people / but as a despiser. Thus, you are first reminded of obedience with goodness and friendliness as a son and child. But if you will not be an obedient child / you will be punished as a servant and a despiser of God’s will.

Burned with fire)** Regarding the method / some conclude from this passage and from the case in Chapter 21:9 <margin>(a) See Drusius on the difficult passages of Leviticus, chapter 74. <note>original: "vid. Druf. ad loc. dific. Lev. c. 74."</note></margin> (a). That otherwise, the burning did not happen / as it does today / on a lit pyre of wood / but rather the one condemned to burning was lowered into manure up to his knees. A linen cord wrapped in a towel was wound around his neck / which was pulled from both sides / so that he opened his mouth and throat / and / if he did not open his mouth / it was forced open with tongs / and then hot melted lead or tin was poured down his throat /

**v. 15. Shall certainly be put to death)** Where the Scripture does not name a specific type of death / the Hebrews understand it to mean suffocation or strangulation / which did not happen on a gallows / as is common among us / but the criminal stood in manure up to his knees / and a linen cord in a towel was wound around his neck / the throat was constricted / and he was thus executed.

**v. 16. Their blood is upon them!)** Wherever these words appear / the Hebrews say / that the punishment of stoning is indicated in the Scripture.

**20. And if a man lies with his aunt / he has uncovered his uncle’s nakedness: they shall bear their sin; they shall die childless.**

<margin>v. 20, 21.</margin> To some, the blessing of the married state was to be withdrawn / so that they would neither conceive nor raise children: this is threatened against those marriages undertaken against God’s express command / and is not to be applied further / unless God has other holy reasons to withdraw the blessing / both from physical relatives who marry where God has not forbidden it / as well as from other married couples. Although in the New Testament / childless marriages are not always to be viewed as a punishment from God; because God has not promised physical blessing there / and therefore other natural causes / or even hidden ones / may take place. And thus one must refrain from judging here beyond the foundation of God’s Word. Matt. 7:1.

<margin>v. 22.</margin> So that the land does not vomit you out) The LORD already knows how to root out the godless and wicked / not only from the congregation of the righteous / but also from the land / at the right time / and conversely to grant the land to the pious and gentle / and to preserve them in it. Ps. 1:5–6, 37:9–11.

<margin>v. 23.</margin> All heathen abominations shall be rooted out from among the people of God with all earnestness; and how much more so among Christians / since the holy Savior, unstained by sin, desires to have such a holy life among His own / whom He willed to redeem from all unrighteousness / and to purify for Himself a people of His own possession / who would be entirely zealous for good works.

But when all kinds of heathen abominations break in again in abundance / in a luxurious / voluptuous / magnificent / greedy / and unjust life of those who wish to bear the name of Christians; and thus such abominations are found in the holy place: then one may certainly conclude / that the abomination of desolation is drawing ever closer / which stood before the people of the Old Testament and was fulfilled / Matt. 24:15. and even more so stands before the people of the New Testament / who through these same abominations have become a spiritual Sodom / Egypt, and Babylon / over which the Lord is angered / and has conceived a loathing for it / so that the judgments threatened in the Revelation will certainly come upon them.

<column-break/>

**25. Therefore you shall make a distinction between the clean cattle and the unclean / and between the unclean birds and the clean / and you shall not make your souls an abomination by the cattle or the birds or by anything that creeps on the earth / which I have separated for you / to declare them unclean.**
**26. And you shall be holy to me; for I the LORD am holy: Therefore I have separated you from the peoples / that you should be mine.**
**27. And if there be a man or woman in whom is a spirit of sorcery or fortune-telling / they shall certainly be killed; they shall be stoned: their blood is upon them!**
<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

---

The believers in these last times must then be all the more careful to take the warning of Christ to heart / and to guard themselves against such heathen high-living and worries about sustenance / and the striving for the goods of this earth / Luke 21:34. and to go out from such people and separate themselves / and touch nothing unclean: so that we may be accepted by the LORD / that He may be our Father / and we His sons and daughters / whom He, as the Almighty God, will protect and preserve in the destruction. 2 Cor. 6:14–18.

<margin>v. 25.</margin> For this, however, a good judgment of discernment is indispensably required. "For whoever wishes to lead a Christian life with great caution," says an ancient, godly teacher <margin>(a)</margin> <note>original: "alter gottheiliger Lehrer" referring to Macarius the Egyptian, a 4th-century monk</note> / "he must especially care for that part of the soul / which has the power to understand and to discern: so that / when he has attained the power to discern exactly what is good or [not] good / and can discern well what / outside of nature / seeks to be introduced into the pure essence / he may thus walk rightly and straightly."

<margin>v. 26.</margin> These God Himself wishes to sanctify in such a way / that they do not only become holy like others / nor before others; but they shall be holy before Him Himself and the LORD. Why? Because

**The LORD is holy)** Holiness is / as thought above / a separation from the one / and a dedication toward another.

**GOD** is in nature and essence separated from all His creatures / and yet He carries them all / and all move and have their being in Him. He is devoted and turned toward Himself / as the First and the Last / from whom and to whom all things are.

**Separated -- mine)** All other people can strive for holiness for themselves; but these are more distinctly holy to be before GOD. And therefore they are holy with the holiness which is from GOD / and accepted before Him Himself.

<margin>v. 27. Stoned)</margin> This was carried out in the following way. When the evildoer came so close to the place of stoning that he was 10 cubits <note>approx. 15 feet</note> away from it / he had to make his confession / and reveal his misdeed himself. If he came closer / and was still 4 cubits <note>approx. 6 feet</note> away / his clothes were removed. A male person was stoned naked / but a woman was not.

The place of stoning was two men high <note>approx. 10-12 feet</note> / which the evildoer climbed with bound hands / accompanied by the witnesses. One of the witnesses pushed him down / so that he fell on his loins. If he fell on his chest / he was turned over / so that the chest lay upward. If he died from the fall / then the law was satisfied. But if he did not die / the second witness took a very large stone / and threw it upon the evildoer's chest. If he died from this throw / it was enough. If he did not die / then all those present pelted him with stones / until he died. See Deut. 17:5. This was considered the most terrible punishment among the Jews.
<margin>(a) Macarius, Homily 4, § 8.</margin>

# Chapter XXI.
->The Purity of the Priests and the High Priest.<-

And the LORD spoke to Moses: Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: None shall defile himself for a dead person among his people.
2. Except for his closest blood relatives; for his mother and for his father, and for his son and for his daughter, and for his brother: <margin>(a) Ezekiel 44:25.</margin>
3. And for his sister who is a virgin and is closest to him, who has had no husband; for her he may defile himself.
4. He shall not defile himself as a husband <note>The Hebrew word used here is *Baal*, meaning master or husband.</note> among his people, to profane himself.
5. They shall not shave a bald spot on their head, nor shave off the corners of their beard, nor make incisions in their flesh. <note>Cross-reference to Chapter 19:27-28.</note>

<column-break/>

6. They shall be holy to their GOD, and not profane the name of their God. For they offer the fire offerings of the LORD, the bread of their God: therefore they shall be holy.
7. They shall not take a wife who is a harlot (a) or one who is defiled <note>The German *Geschwächte* refers to a woman whose virtue has been compromised.</note>, and they shall not take a wife who is divorced from her husband. For he is holy to his God. <margin>(a) Ezekiel 44:22.</margin>
8. Therefore you shall hold him holy: for he offers the bread of your God. He shall be holy to you; for I the LORD, who sanctifies you, am holy.
9. And if any priest's daughter begins to play the harlot, she has shamed her father; she shall be burned with fire. 10. And

---

This section deals with the purity of the priests, intended to represent the holiness of the soul, which the priests should especially strive for, so as to lead others not only with the doctrine of holiness but also with a holy life itself.
**v. 1. None shall defile himself for a dead person)** by coming to a dead person, touching them, or being near them; also not entering any house where a dead person was inside; nor coming within 4 cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches.</note> of a grave.
**Among his people)** They were permitted to walk over a heathen grave and enter a heathen house where a dead person was.
A priest of GOD should, above all others, not defile himself with dead works, nor have fellowship or interaction with those who have the name of being alive but are dead.
**v. 2.** They were allowed to show their love to the six closest relatives, to remember the soul even in the dead corpse that has left this dwelling, the body, and thus to see it and follow it to the burial.
And these were the dead of their 6 closest blood relatives: father, mother, son, daughter, brother, sister:
**v. 3.** And specifically the sister, if she was still unmarried: or if as a widow she regained her old right, the same as when she was a virgin, according to Chapter 22:13.
**v. 4.** Aside from these six, they must not even come near their grandfather or grandmother, and indeed—what is more—not even to their own dead wives.
This verse is translated in various ways, but one remains with good reason by the common meaning of the word *Baal*, which means a husband. See Genesis 21:3. Thus, the relatives of his wife are specifically forbidden here, such as parents-in-law and siblings-in-law, because they belong to a different family.
**v. 5.** In mourning, they must not behave in an unruly manner, nor make themselves bald-headed; not shave away their beard or eyebrows; also not pinch any mark into their bodies, or wound, cut, or scratch themselves with nails, awls, or knives; or cut or etch certain letters, signs, or strokes into the flesh and fill them with ink or other color, and thus make marks on their bodies, as the heathens were accustomed to do (a).
A priest of GOD shall walk simply before the LORD and not take on anything peculiar to show an external holiness.
<margin>(a) See <note>original: "vid."</note> Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book 5, Ch. 39. Geier, *On Hebrew Mourning*, Ch. 10.</margin>

<column-break/>

**v. 6.** Rather, they should sanctify themselves to the LORD alone and present themselves as approved in secret.
**v. 7.** They were free to marry into whatever tribe they wished, just like the High Priest; but they had to take great care in doing so. For
It was forbidden for them to take a harlot, or a "common" woman, as some prefer to read instead of "defiled": regarding which see verse 14.
Also, they must not take a woman divorced from her husband by a letter of divorce, nor—as the Hebrews maintain—a woman rejected by the brother of her deceased, childless husband <note>Referring to the levirate law where a brother-in-law refuses to marry the widow.</note>.
The daughters of all lowly people were also forbidden to them. All foreign heathen women and their daughters were strictly forbidden to them.
And this was because they were sanctified to the LORD and set apart from the common masses for His service, to administer it holily.
**v. 8.** For they draw near to the LORD to bring that in which GOD testified He took pleasure, which was, as it were, His nourishment; this consisted in the delight in the obedience of His dear Son, who constantly presented Himself in spirit as a sacrifice for sin, and allowed this to be prefigured in physical sacrifices. See Genesis 8:20-21, Hebrews 9:14.
And therefore they should also be held holy by others—that is, held in honor—so that one should imagine the presence of GOD all the more powerfully in the presence of His servants, to avoid doing anything unseemly. Whereby, however, the servants themselves must remember not to do or say anything that is unseemly for the servants of GOD. See 1 Timothy 5:17.
This frequently repeated command of GOD shows sufficiently that GOD’S people cannot claim they can sanctify themselves, nor should they be satisfied with a mediocre holiness. He wants to sanctify them himself, so that they might possess the full holiness, which is the holiness of GOD; in that He sanctifies them through His own holiness.
**v. 9.** A priest's daughter who has shamed her father with her disobedience, and thus made him unedifying, and has thereby also sinned heavily against GOD, should be punished with a heavy judgment of burning, to be an abomination to others. Which teachers must take to heart, so that they rule their own house well, that they may have obedient children with all honesty, 1 Timothy 3:4, who are kept from the vanities of the world with all earnestness.
The Hebrews understand this place not as referring to an unbetrothed daughter, but to a betrothed or already married daughter of a priest (a).
<margin>(a) Lightfoot, *Hebrew Hours* <note>original: *hor. hebr.*</note> on John 9:13.</margin>
<margin>Quenstedt, *On Ancient Burials*, Ch. 6.</margin>

10. And the High Priest among his brothers, upon whose head the anointing oil was poured and whose hand was filled <note>This "filling of the hand" is a Hebrew idiom for ordination or consecration to office.</note> to put on the [sacred] garments, shall not bare his head (a) nor tear his clothes. <margin>(a) ch. 10:6.</margin>

11. He shall not go near any dead body; he shall not defile himself even for his father or his mother.

12. And he shall not leave the sanctuary, so that he does not profane the sanctuary of his GOD. For the crown of the anointing oil of his GOD is upon him. I am the LORD.

---

Since the High Priest was a special prototype of Christ, he had to represent the essential holiness of Christ at a higher level, such that he was not allowed to defile himself by any dead person. Whereas the permitted defilement of the other priests for their closest kin can represent their "sins of weakness" with which they were still surrounded, here Christ was to be prefigured—He who was holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens. Hebrews 7:26.

v. 10. **The High Priest had to, when he entered mourning,**

<margin>(a) Thus Luther, the Vulgate, Münster, Junius, Geier in *On Hebrew Mourning*, ch. 11, § 4, Osiander, the Weimar [Bibles], and others.</margin>
**not bare his head)** As many interpret it (a): although the Hebrews understand it quite differently (b), namely that he was not allowed to let his hair grow freely, but had to have his hair cut every Friday evening before the Sabbath, as was otherwise done. However, both interpretations are valid, as it was customary in mourning to set aside head coverings and walk with bare heads: which GOD did not want from the High Priest. He should also

<margin>(b) Selden, *On the High Priests*, book 2, ch. 5.</margin>
**not tear his clothes)** Which the Hebrews again do not understand as a total ban on tearing, but only as a restriction on the *manner* of tearing: namely, that he should not tear his own clothes (for he was absolutely never allowed to tear the holy garments) from the top and around the chest downwards like others, but from the bottom at the feet upwards (c).

<margin>(c) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona, in Hottinger’s *On Hebrew Law*, p. 156; Cunaeus’ *On the Hebrew Republic*, book 2, ch. 12.</margin>
v. 11. **He had to approach no dead person at all;** and even if it were his own father or mother, he must

**not defile himself)** Because such a ritual defilement lasted seven days, and the High Priest had to enter the temple at all times—at least every Sabbath—and thus always remain pure, he had to guard himself against all impurity that could be contracted from the dead.

All these things point to something deeper, which may be tracked and excavated through the light of the Spirit. He whose image the High Priest bore [Christ] was certainly not defiled by either father or mother, just as all other men become partakers of impurity through the unclean, sinful birth, by virtue of the death that has permeated all people. So He, as the Wisdom of GOD, does not enter into a malicious soul subject to sin (Wisdom 1:4), which is dead while alive. For what fellowship has light with darkness, or life with death? And we should also let the dead bury their dead and follow Christ.

v. 12. **Even in the case of death among his closest blood-relatives,** he was not permitted to leave the Tabernacle or the Temple to attend the burial upon hearing the news; rather, he had to perform his office as if nothing had happened, whereas other priests were released from their duties when mourning occurred.

Meanwhile, we have a much greater High Priest who never and at no time leaves the Sanctuary, but is always found in that which is His Father's, in a constant holiness that could never be interrupted by any sin or sinful thought. See John 8:46.

Whoever sins, leaves the Sanctuary. But Christ, who is separated from sinners, remains holy at all times in all His speech, holy in all His works, holy in His entire will and all His intentions, and thus never leaves the temple of the true Sanctuary. And if you follow Him faithfully and remain in His teaching, you also do not leave the Sanctuary, wherever else you may be, whether at home or in the market.

<column-break/>

13. And he shall take a wife in her virginity.

14. A widow, or a divorced woman, or a defiled harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take a virgin of his own people as a wife:

15. So that he does not profane his offspring among his people. For I am the LORD who sanctifies him.
<margin>Exodus 29:6, 16. And</margin>

---

v. 13. In marriage, he had to take a pure virgin who was also from untainted parents.

v. 14. He was not allowed to have a widow, unless he had married her before he became High Priest.

**Divorced)** Namely, a woman whom a husband has cast off with a certificate of divorce.

**Defiled harlot)** If one wants to make two forbidden categories out of this, as Luther does, then what he rendered as "Defiled" should rather be called "Common" or "Made-common" <note>This refers to the *chalalah*, a woman disqualified from the priesthood through her birth or past conduct.</note>.

However, the word <term>זונה</term> <gloss>harlot</gloss> refers not only to a common prostitute, but according to the Hebrew reports, also to a woman who is not of Israelite descent; likewise an Israelite woman who has had dealings with a man whom the law forbids her to have (ch. 18, Deut. 23, Exod. 23:34, 16, 20).

A "common woman," <term>חללה</term> <note>original: *chalalah*</note>, was either common by birth or became common through illicit cohabitation. By birth, "common" children of both sexes were those born either from a harlot as described above, or from a divorced woman, or otherwise begotten from a forbidden marriage.

**A virgin from his people)** No foreigner, even if she had already converted to the Jewish religion.

Otherwise, he was free, like the other priests, to marry from whichever tribe of the children of Israel he wished.

Our royal High Priest Jesus Christ must also have a pure virgin for a wife (2 Cor. 11:2), specifically one who has no spot or wrinkle or any such thing (Eph. 5:27), who does not defile herself with the world or treat worldly things as paramours to whom she devotes her love. See Rev. 14:4, Hos. 2:4, 20. He will not and cannot accept a sinful soul that stands open to evil, unclean spirits.

This is a common harlot—take note!—one who allows access to the devil and his angels. The soul was created very beautiful by GOD, and the devil is in love with this beauty and lusts after it. If you now admit this unclean spirit—the spirit of wrath, envy, and resentment, of pride, arrogance, and impurity—and willingly and with pleasure accept and receive the poisonous seed of his inspirations, then you are playing the harlot with the devil. Away with such a harlot! She is not fit to be a bride for Jesus.

v. 15. **Profane his offspring)** Since "offspring" elsewhere also prefigures the Word of GOD, let teachers who wish to be priests of the Most High GOD see to it that they do not profane such [Word] through an improper fellowship and mixing with unclean, unrepentant souls.

<margin>(a) in Selden, *On the Succession of the High Priests*, book 2, ch. 2.</margin>

<page-num>529</page-num>
<header>Ch. XXI. The Third Book of Moses <note>The Third Book of Moses is the traditional name for the Book of Leviticus.</note></header>

16. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
17. Speak to Aaron and say: If anyone of your descendants throughout their generations has a blemish, he shall not approach to offer the bread of his GOD.

---

There is no doubt that the literal sense here actually concerned the sons of Aaron and the Levitical priesthood and its services for as long as they lasted. However, because "all these things happened to them as an example" <note>quoting 1 Corinthians 10:11</note>, it may be concluded from this that the defects, excesses, and deformities arising from them in poorly-qualified persons also indicate something spiritual, for which reason one should still be excluded from the service of God today. The Jewish philosopher Philo himself recognized this and expressed it thus: "These things seem to me to typically aim at the perfection of souls. For if such close attention had to be paid to the mortal body of the priest, so that no ill accident might defile him, how much more should the immortal soul be shaped according to the image of the true God."

Indeed, this ordinance indicated what the community of believers should be like, since Christ wanted to "sanctify, cleanse, and present to himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish." Ephesians 5:26, 27. Thus, all such spiritual defects—blindness in understanding and the rest—must not be found among believers, and especially not among the "firstborn" whom Christ has willed to raise to the high dignity of "kings and priests before his heavenly Father." Revelation 1:6; 1 Peter 2:9. But teachers especially should take this to heart: they must strive above others to be blameless, shining before others as examples in all Christian virtues, and carefully avoiding and being free from all such defects of the spirit. 1 Timothy 3:2, 3 etc.; 1 Peter 5:3. These spiritual defects alone make one unfit for the ministry of the Gospel, and not physical infirmities; because in the Old Testament, these were only ordained as a "type" or symbol. If, however, in the New Testament someone were endowed with special gifts of the Spirit, these could easily compensate for physical defects, which believers ought to overlook, looking only to the gifts of the Lord.

**v. 17. A blemish)** By this, all external bodily defects are understood, but not the internal ones that cannot be seen, which did not hinder one from the priesthood.

<margin>(a) John Selden, *On the Succession of the High Priests*, Book 2, ch. 5.</margin>
Seldenus (a) <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of Jewish law.</note> cites from the Hebrew teachers 142 blemishes and defects, which they divide into three classes or types. The first type defiled both the priests and the sacrificial animals to such an extent that neither could the animals be sacrificed, nor could the priests perform their office. The second type defiled only the priests. The third type consisted of only 2 to 10 things that were considered unseemly for a priest if they were seen. Whoever wants to know them all by name can read them in the place mentioned. It is enough to recognize from this—which Josephus (b) also confirms—that even the slightest blemish that could be noticed on them excluded them from the priestly office. Therefore, no priest was admitted to service until he obtained clearance from the High Court or the Great Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, which held the judgment in this matter. If someone was found unfit, he was dressed in black and left the court chamber. But whoever was found fit, they let him put on white priestly garments and enter the inner court to wait with the other priests, and thus he entered his service.

<column-break/>

18. For no man who has a blemish shall approach: be he a blind or a lame man, or one who is mutilated in his limbs, or has a limb too long;
19. Or a man who has a broken foot or a broken hand;
20. Or

---

As already mentioned, there is no doubt that through Moses, internal deformities and ugliness were also primarily meant and forbidden, which made one unfit for the priestly office. Thus, there are many more corresponding spiritual defects which, for the same reason, make men unfit to serve in the Gospel ministry.

**v. 18.** Thus, for example, no Gospel priest must be:
**A Blind Man)** And he is spiritually blind, says Gregory the Great <note>original: "Gregorius M.", referring to Pope Gregory I</note>, who does not know the light of heavenly contemplation; who, for lack of love for the future life, is wrapped in the darkness of this present life, and thus, according to 2 Thessalonians 2:10–12 and 2 Peter 1:5–9, does not see.

That such a person is unfit for office is clear in itself. For their office requires that they should "open the eyes of men." Acts 26:18. And how can someone do that if he himself is blind to God and His mysteries? They are supposed to be leaders and guides of the people. But how poorly do these things fit together: a blind guide? Can one blind man show the way to another? But even more irrational is it if the blind guide is also a

**Lame Man)** And who is lame? Answer: It is certainly he who cannot walk or progress on the path of life because of the instability of his inclinations; who either limps on both sides, wanting to serve God and the world at the same time and satisfy everyone; or who loves pleasure and wealth more than God, and is thus "lame on the left side"; or at least stands on his own strength and has himself as the end goal in his actions, doing everything like a day-laborer for the sake of the reward, and would by no means serve God if he did not expect to obtain a reward from Him. These are then "lame on the right side," and all together are therefore unfit and unworthy to receive the Holy Spirit, and consequently, necessarily unfit for office.

**Mutilated in his limbs)** Various translators, including Jerome and Luther, as well as the Jewish teachers, interpret this as a defect of the nose. However, the word *Charum* <note>Hebrew term for 'mutilated' or 'flat-nosed'</note> signifies much more—as the Arabic and Samaritan translations, as well as the Chaldean interpreter, understand it—alongside the following word *Saruah* <note>Hebrew term for 'extended' or 'having an extra limb'</note>: a deficiency or excess in the parts of the body. This clearly indicates that the priest must have a perfect body, and even more so a perfect soul, following the correspondence between the exterior and the aforementioned testimony of Philo. For that thing is perfect which lacks nothing, nor has anything

**Too much)** Being too bold and impudent, without fear and humility.

**v. 19. A broken foot or a broken hand)** One who is without hurrying, compassionate, and sharing love or helpfulness.

Indeed, what is the "break of the foot" other than the rebellion of the heart and the inclinations that have broken away from the ways of God? And the "break of the hands" other than the ceasing from doing good?

---

Even if these named infirmities do not, according to the letter of the law, extend to the Gospel priesthood, the reason and fairness of this ceremonial law may still apply in the times of the Gospel. It should deter parents from designating those of their children for the teaching office who have a visible blemish; and often for the quite irrational reason that their children are so deformed that they consider them "unfit for other duties." Such intentions are certainly evil, base, and shameful, ungodly and unworthy of the Gospel of Jesus Christ. They clearly prove that such parents have a poor opinion of Christ's servants, and even low and contemptuous thoughts of the Most High GOD, to whom, in view of His highness and majesty, the very best that one has is rightfully due. Malachi 1:14. Without doubt, these people "seek only their own, and not that which is Jesus Christ's," and view the Gospel teaching office only as another trade or profession by which one may earn his bread—just as it is, alas, pursued by many with no other aim.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chap. XXI.

->**20. Or a hunchback, or a dwarf, or one who has a film on his eye, or is scabby or scurvy, or who is broken.**<-

**21. No [man of the descendants of Aaron the priest who has a blemish...]**

**Hunchbacked)** Rich, greedy, or burdened with the cares of sustenance; these are crooked souls, pressed down toward the earth and empty of heavenly things.

When wealth and greed exist together in a person, they create a spiritual "hunch" or hump, which over time becomes so natural that it can hardly be lifted. It is just as it is with a natural hunchback: when the condition is old and long-rooted, the nerves and veins have already contracted, making it difficult to raise oneself. Such people walk bent down toward the earth and can never turn their gaze straight up to heaven. Therefore, the Savior says (a) not without reason: *How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!* For the gate of heaven is narrow, and a hunchback may not pass through it.

<margin>Hebrews 12:1</margin>
God’s priest must lay aside every weight that presses him down.

<margin>Lamentations 2:20</margin>
Furthermore, he must not be a dwarf, or hinder his spiritual growth, remaining only the stature of a span long.

**A film on his eye)** This occurs when the white of the eye has mixed and mingled with the black of the eye.

The black of the eye <note>The pupil.</note> is that with which we see. It is God’s great blessing and wonderful work—both in nature and in grace—that He causes sight and light to shine out of blackness and darkness. Now, when imagined knowledge, ambition, greed, envy, etc., hinder one's vision, a "film" has grown over the eyeball of the hidden "new man" of the heart, through which alone we may see God (Matthew 5:8). Man sees and recognizes something of the divine light through the "black"; but this light is darkened by the intervention and mixing of the "white"—namely, the delusion of one's own wisdom and holiness, in which one puffs oneself up.

From this, one can learn the nature of the true "Babel," which derives its name and origin from "mixture" or "confusion."

Do not look here or there, but turn your eyes inward into yourself, and see if the "beam" of proud knowledge is not in your own eye—a false light that renders you unfit to be the Lord’s priest.

**Scabby)** Through the word <term>Garaf <gloss>Hebrew: garab, referring to a chronic skin eruption</gloss></term>, as is clear from Deuteronomy 28:27 (where the "itch" is called incurable), we should not understand common scabs. Rather, it refers to a moist or purulent scurvy, where the corrupt and putrid blood is so excessive that it breaks out and makes the flesh deformed and hideous. And

What else is this but manifest and known sin—the obvious "works of the flesh" (Galatians 5:19) which proceed from the abundance of a corrupt heart and defile the person (Matthew 12:34, 15:19-20). This refers especially to the lust of the flesh, which makes a person "scabby" and unclean when it overcomes and occupies the mind.

**Scurvy)** The word <term>Jallephet <gloss>Hebrew: yallephet, usually interpreted as a scaly skin disease or ringworm</gloss></term> signifies dry scurvy or lichen, although many interpreters reverse these two and place the purulent scurvy here.

Saint Gregory attributes this to greed, which seizes our soul just as dry scurvy seizes the body, spreading without pain. For while it pleases or amuses the heart of the one seized by it, it eats away and corrupts him without any sensation of pain. The pain is removed by the "tickling" and "itching" of the hope for gain. But just as this scurvy makes the body hideous, so greed stains the beauty of the soul, and for this reason, it is called "shameful gain" (Titus 1:11; 1 Peter 5:2).

(a) Mark 10:23.

<column-break/>

This dry scurvy may also arise from a "Pharisaic humor" or evil fluid: for example, when people itch for honor and praise (Matthew 23:5), infecting others with this "itching scurvy" (John 12:43). It can also point to the desire to propagate and spread one's own opinions, which is so violently "itchy" that one often travels over sea and land to make a fellow believer in one's own delusions and opinions (Matthew 23:15). The Pharisees have always had such a hot, itching scurvy; their chief pursuit is to poison others with their infectious opinions rather than to rescue them or make them blessed and win them for the life of God. Just as such people have an "itch on their tongues," the people have an "itching in their ears" for it, as the Apostle explicitly calls it in 2 Timothy 4:3.

**The broken)** Whereby the bowels fall apart. <note>In the biblical context, this likely refers to a hernia or crushed testicles, but the author interprets it as a "broken" internal state.</note>

Who can be better understood by this than the angry and the envious? In them, their "bowels" <note>The "bowels" were historically considered the seat of compassion and deep emotion.</note> fall apart, and their neighbor—with whom they should always be joined by the bond of love—falls out. Whoever allows this separation, letting his neighbor escape from the bond of love rather than embracing him with love, has "broken" the bond of love.

But just as all people, both evil and good, are our neighbors, so must all generally live and be contained within our "bowels," so that we carry them in our hearts and wish and grant that they might be united in the "bowels" or heart of Christ. Indeed, a priest must especially be a "perfect man" in this regard, and capable of birthing others for God (1 Corinthians 4:13).

From all these defects which a priest of the Lord must not have, one can conversely recognize what qualities the Evangelical <note>In this context, "Evangelical" refers to the Gospel-based or New Testament priesthood of all believers.</note> priesthood should specifically possess. Namely, they should not be blind and ignorant, but on the contrary, understand what the will of the Lord is (Ephesians 5:17). And when they know the Lord's will and the way, they should also walk in it. They should present themselves as leaders to others, so that others may walk as they have them for examples. They should lay down the weight of all unnecessary cares; nor should they restrict their growth in grace contrary to Scripture, nor imagine for themselves an unfounded limit in holiness, but rather strive for its "perfection in the fear of God" (2 Corinthians 7:1). They should have eyes to see and to avoid the confusion of Babel. They should lay aside all filthiness and "overflow of wickedness" (James 1:21) and possess a certain perfection of the soul, just as the priests of the Law had to possess a perfection of the body: so that they may also win others for God and "present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Colossians 1:28).

Regarding these qualities required here for a priest, a famous teacher of the English Church (a) <note>Robert Gell (1595–1665), an English chaplain known for his kabbalistic and perfectionist interpretations of the Bible.</note> makes the following lamenting conclusion:

> "Into what times have we fallen! When every blind 'Blocker' <note>Original: *Blocker*, likely meaning a dullard or one who obstructs.</note> who sees only with other people's eyes, and is taught only with other people's knowledge, is expected to be a seer, a prophet, and a priest to the people. When those who limp between God and Satan, between Christ and Belial, dare to be leaders of the people—walking in God's ways as cripples with their broken feet, and with their broken teeth instructing others to do the commandments of God, which they nevertheless cry out is 'impossible' to do. — Oh, how far we are in this 'dregs of time' from the spiritual growth and godly earnestness of the first holy Fathers in their striving for a perfect life! Now, every dwarf presumes to be a grown man, or to be as perfect as he 'needs' to be; every novice in the immaturity of the Christian life thinks himself as fully capable as a grown man in Christ, or as the most perfect scribe taught for the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:52). Since, according to Ephesians 4:13, believing that a capability for perfection can be reached in this life is considered as great an error in a priest under the Gospel as being blind or lame, scabby or scurvy, etc., was considered a defect in a priest under the Law. Since teaching perfection makes a priest an 'unfit man' and—despite it being presented so often in Holy Scripture—is considered a sufficient reason to remove a church minister from his service, etc."

(a) R. Gell, *Remarks on the Third Book of Moses*, p. 345.

### Chap. XXI. The Third Book of Moses.

**21. No man of the descendants of Aaron the priest who has a blemish shall come near to offer the offerings of the Lord made by fire: he has a blemish; therefore he shall not come near to offer the bread of his God.**

**No man of the descendants of Aaron who has a blemish shall come near)** Anyone who could not prove with sufficient witnesses and evidence that he was of the pure lineage of Aaron was not only removed from all priestly duties but also from all priestly rights and was not counted among the priests at all. However, those who were merely physically infirm were indeed excluded from all priestly duties, yet they were allowed to enter the inner court. They did not wear the white holy garments, but common clothes, as Josephus writes (a): they were also forbidden from approaching the altar or proceeding further toward the Temple. This rule was also observed regarding those who suffered a temporary infirmity, as long as it lasted (b).

When it was the turn of such infirm or unfit priests to serve, their duty was in the outer court, in the so-called **Wood Court**, to separate worm-eaten, useless wood from the good wood and to split wood for the altar. 
<note>a) Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book 6, Chapter 6. b) Josephus, *Against Apion*, Book 1.</note>

**24. And Moses told it to Aaron, and to his sons, and to all the children of Israel.**

**v. 24.** Since Moses tells this not only to Aaron and his sons but also to all the children of Israel, one may well conclude that just as this divine law concerns those in the priestly office who teach the people and offer prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings for them, it also concerns those among the people who are to be made priests in a spiritual sense to God. <note>original: 1. Peter 2:5</note>

## The XXII. Chapter.

**And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:**

**2. Speak to Aaron and to his sons, that they separate themselves from the holy things of the children of Israel (lest they profane my holy name) which they sanctify to me. I am the LORD.**

**3. Say to them: Whoever of all your descendants throughout your generations who goes near the holy things which the children of Israel sanctify to the LORD, while he has his uncleanness upon him, that soul shall be cut off from my presence. I am the LORD.**

Anyone who wishes to know the connection and context of this chapter with the preceding one need only look at the 22nd verse of the previous chapter; there they will see it immediately, as it also speaks of the **holy things** (v. 2) which were assigned to the priests for food.
The priests were to be careful when using the things sanctified for sacrifices by the children of Israel, so as not to eat them while in any state of ceremonial uncleanness (of which the previous chapters 11–15 have treated); otherwise, they would make themselves guilty of being "cut off" and would thus have to die in the guilt of their sin.
**v. 3.** The priests were permitted neither to perform their office nor to eat of the holy things when they had defiled themselves. If they did so, the young priests would drag them out of the court and dash their brains out with clubs. (a)
<note>a) Lundius, *The Ancient Jewish Sanctuaries*, Book 3, Chapter 57, no. 3, p. 715, citing the Mishnah.</note>

<column-break/>

**22. He may eat the bread of his God, both of the most holy and of the holy.**

**23. Only he shall not go in to the veil, nor come near the altar, because he has a blemish; that he profane not my sanctuaries. For I the LORD do sanctify them.**

**v. 22.** When it was time to eat of the Holy or Most Holy things, if they were not otherwise unclean, they had the same access as those on duty; they went with them into the inner court and ate of it just as well.
**Most Holy)** The noblest and most holy offerings were burnt offerings, grain offerings, sin offerings, guilt offerings, and the thank offerings of the whole congregation.
**Holy (or sanctified))** were all others besides these, including the thank offerings of individual persons.
**v. 23. Shall not go in to the veil, nor come near the altar)** That is: He shall perform neither the office of the High Priest nor that of the other priests; he shall neither enter the Most Holy Place nor offer sacrifice.

**4. Whatever man of the seed of Aaron is a leper, or has a discharge, he shall not eat of the holy things until he be clean. And whoever touches any thing that is unclean by the dead, or a man whose seed goes from him;**

**5. Or whoever touches any creeping thing whereby he may be made unclean, or a person by whom he may be made unclean, according to all his uncleanness:**
<note>a) chapter 11:29 etc.</note>

**6. The soul which has touched any such shall be unclean until evening, and shall not eat of the holy things, unless he wash his flesh with water.**

**7. And**

**v. 4.** By the **holy things**, one specifically understands the wave-breasts and the heave-shoulders of the thank offerings, which no one but the pure priests along with their pure household might eat; in this regard, the great first-fruits were also like them.
**v. 6. Wash with water)** This every priest had to do before his service, even if he was already clean, otherwise he was not permitted to enter the inner court. (a)

v. 8. 9. Since these sanctified offerings partly represented the sacrifice of Christ—in whose communion the priests stood on behalf of the people by eating of them (1 Cor. 10:18)—it teaches us that we can have no part in the sacrifice of Christ while in the spiritual impurity of sin, if one does not strive to keep oneself unspotted from the world (James 1:27).
On the other hand, it also represents believers, how they must present themselves, and thus their bodies, as a sacrifice that is living, holy, and pleasing to **God** (Rom. 12:1), in order to have a part in Christ. Whoever presumes to do this in his sinful impurity, or is still a stranger to the life that is from **God**, and yet thinks to have a part in Christ through his historical, dead faith, he will also die in his sins and experience the cutting off of his soul. See 1 Cor. 11:29-30.
Just as Christ alone may approach **God** (Jer. 30:21), so too it is only those who stand in His Spirit who may approach all the acquired goods of salvation—such as the eating of the **Lord** or His gifts—and dare to enjoy them (Jer. 31:12); for the **Lord** has sanctified and set them apart through faith in His Son. Therefore, believers are called the "called saints" (Rom. 1:7; 1 Cor. 1:2, etc.).
v. 10. Furthermore, all strangers were to abstain from these sacrificial foods, even if they lived with the priests or worked for them for wages.
v. 11. But those who were bought as servants for money, or were born to such in their house, were esteemed the same as their children, to whom these offerings were also granted for their nourishment.
Just as there is a distinction in foods according to purity and impurity, so too there are degrees regarding those that are pure and permitted, and therein a distinction among those who may enjoy them. Thus, there are common, there are holy, and also most holy foods and sacrifices; and that which is holy does not belong to the dogs (Matt. 7:6).
v. 12. If a priest's daughter married an Israelite and thus left the priestly order and status, she was no longer permitted to eat of it.

<margin>v. 20. **Anything that has a blemish**) The Hebrews count 46 defects and infirmities that disqualify an animal from sacrifice (a).</margin>
<margin>v. 21. **There shall be no blemish in it**) Therefore, every sacrificial animal had to first be inspected and tested by the priests (ch. 10:10). This occurred during the delivery, where they began with the hooves and thoroughly inspected the entire body over and over.</margin>
<margin>v. 22. This is where the entire teaching of the Gospel is directed: that believers must let themselves be healed, purified, and sanctified by Christ the Physician from all innate flaws and infirmities of their corrupt nature. God expressly forbids this even for freewill offerings in verses 18 and 19. The priests would sell such an unfit animal presented to the **Lord** and use the money for the service of the Tabernacle or the Temple.

### The Third Book of Moses. Ch. XXIII. 534

# The XXIII. Chapter.
->The Festivals of the Old Testament.<-

AND the **Lord** spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: Concerning the appointed gatherings of the **Lord**, which you shall proclaim as holy convocations, these are my appointed gatherings.
3. Six days shall work be done, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of rest, the holy convocation: you shall do no work of any kind; it is the Sabbath to the **Lord** in all your dwellings.

v. 1. Those who are perfect—these are the words of Origen (a)—will be taught by God Himself concerning the festivals and the manner of their celebration, so that they need no human being as a teacher to learn these things, if they can perceive the voice of God Himself.
v. 2. But those who are lesser, or stand lower, learn from those who have learned it from God.
This is a twofold way of teaching. One, where the prophetic mind is enlightened and taught by the Spirit, more through the contemplation of the soul than through the sound of a voice; whereby truth itself—and not merely a shadow or image of the truth—is recognized. Those who cannot grasp or endure the clarity of God Himself, nor behold the full radiance of the truth with a steady eye of the soul, listen on the "second bench" to those who learned it on the first. And while the truth of the matter itself appeared to the latter through actual insight, for the former, mere hearing brings only its shadow.
In this chapter, the Lord wished to determine certain times when they should hold a holy convocation, which was to be publicly proclaimed; thus the congregation of the children of Israel was called to a holy assembly, in which they were to take to heart the most excellent blessings that God had shown them in the physical realm. However, the enlightened among them—and especially now the believers in the New Testament—should regard these as shadows of the spiritual blessing in the eternal heavenly goods in Christ.
There are seven of these festivals: which undoubtedly points toward the seven secret ages of the New Testament Church.
Indeed, three among these were special festivals at which every male had to appear before the Lord: namely, where He would specifically establish the memorial of His name, which later occurred at Jerusalem, as was discussed in Exodus 23:14–17.
v. 3. The first appointed time for a holy convocation was according to the fourth commandment, Exodus 20:8 etc., on every seventh day, when they were to contemplate the memorial of the Creation and the Rest of God in all their dwellings. For this purpose, they built schools <note>A reference to synagogues</note> in all places for such holy assemblies, to come together in them, to contemplate the law of the Lord, and to offer their prayer and thanksgiving to God.
Believers of the New Testament should, in doing so, envision the new creation and the eternal rest of the soul earned in Christ.
(a) <note>original: "hom. 13. in Lev. c. 23"</note> Origen’s 13th Homily on Leviticus, chapter 23.

<column-break/>

4. These are the appointed gatherings of the **Lord**, the holy convocations, which you shall proclaim at their appointed time.
5. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, between the two evenings, is the Passover to the **Lord**.
<margin>2 Chron. 30:2, 15.</margin>
6. And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the Feast of Unleavened Bread to the **Lord**: then you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days.
<margin>Ex. 13:6–7, 23:15.</margin>
7. On the first day there shall be a holy convocation among you; you shall do no servile work <note>original: "Dienst-Arbeit"</note> of any kind.
<margin>Ex. 12:16, Num. 28:18.</margin>
8. And you shall offer a fire-offering to the **Lord** for seven days (a). On the seventh day is the holy convocation; you shall do no servile work of any kind. (a) Num. 28:19–24.
9. A<insert>nd the Lord spoke...</insert> <meta>Catchword for next page</meta>

---

The second appointed time was the Feast of the Passover or Easter Lamb, and the associated Unleavened Bread, which had to be eaten for seven days. On the first and seventh day, there was a holy convocation, during which they contemplated with thankful hearts the great blessing of the exodus from Egyptian servitude and were to praise God for it.
The Passover lamb and other sacrifices were discussed in Exodus Chapter 12: and how believers must envision themselves through the single sacrifice in the death of Christ, and how they shall be rescued from the spiritual servitude of sin and Satan.
v. 5. **Between the two evenings**) The daily evening sacrifice had to be offered before the blood of the Passover was sprinkled; for this reason, it was offered earlier on this day than usual.
**7 Days**) In all these 7 days, none of the ash was removed from the altar of burnt offering, but everything was swept together in the middle as an ornament of the altar.
**On the 7th Day**) This was the 21st of Nisan <note>Nisan: the first month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly March/April</note>.
**The holy convocations**) are most truly present where the saints are gathered in God Himself, the City of Peace, the true Jerusalem, of which it is said: *Here is the Lord.* Everything external—including what is contained in these ordinances—is an image of the "letter," which is primarily intended in a spiritual sense. It is so grasped and understood by those who are spiritually minded. For in the inward parts lies the ground of all things, both of God and of the Devil, hidden.
But as far as external gatherings are concerned: since the Lord demanded such external and internal purity and holiness from His people in the Old Testament, how much more then should the blood of Christ now in the New Testament cleanse us from all sins and defilements of the flesh. However, when unseemly customs have crept into such gatherings, He has long since accused them through His Spirit. As it is recorded with Him, He gave enough to understand through the words of the prophet Amos, ch. 5:21: *I hate your feast days, and I despise them, and I will not smell the aroma of your assemblies!* And what wonder is it then if some find themselves driven in conscience to avoid such gatherings and to bear witness by their absence.

The commentary provides a mystical interpretation, distinguishing between the external "shadow" of the law and its internal "spiritual" reality in Christ.</summary>

The third appointed time was the day after the Sabbath <note>specifically, the day after the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread</note>, namely after the first day of the unleavened bread, since that was a Sabbath of a holy convocation: when the first sheaf of the harvest, which could already occur at the beginning of April, had to be brought, in order to entreat the blessing of the harvest from God, and to bring the firstfruits of the fruits to the Lord before they were permitted to enjoy them.

In a spiritual sense, however, this was intended to foreshadow Christ’s resurrection from the dead, which also occurred on the first day after the Sabbath, whereby He became the firstfruits among those who sleep, *1 Corinthians 15:20*, and the beginning and firstborn from the dead, *Colossians 1:18*, through whom all who are chosen for eternal life have been sanctified, as the first harvest of God’s rational creatures who are to be brought into the house of God, which is heaven.

v. 10. A sheaf) Not every individual Israelite or father of a house brought one, but one was cut in the field of Jerusalem and brought in the name of the entire community.

This sheaf was of barley (a), as that was the first to become ripe in the land of Canaan.

On the evening of the first day of Passover, as the second day of Passover (the 16th of Nisan) began, those appointed by the High Court went out into the field with a sickle and basket, accompanied by a great crowd of people; and as soon as the sun had set and it began to grow dark, the one who was to cut the barley said: "The sun has set." To which the present people answered: "Yes." Then he said: "Shall I cut?" They said: "Yes." He asked: "With this sickle?" They said: "Yes." He asked further: "Into this basket?" and they also answered: "Yes." If it was a Sabbath that was just beginning, he asked: "Shall I do it on the Sabbath?" To which the people again said yes. For the Sabbath had to give way to this work. He asked each question three times in succession, and the people answered "Yes" every time. Then he cut as much as was sufficient for the prescribed measure. As soon as they returned home, the cut barley was dried by the fire, stripped, made into meal, sifted 13 times, and thus an Omer <note>a Hebrew unit of dry measure</note> of the finest, most pure meal was taken from it and handed over to the priests on the following day.

v. 11. Through these firstfruits, the entire harvest and the whole field, with everything upon it, was sanctified, and thanks were given to God the Lord, and further blessing was requested.

The day after the Sabbath) Not after the next weekly Sabbath, or the 7th day of the week, as the Sadducees <note>a Jewish sect that interpreted the law literally and rejected oral tradition</note> wanted; but after the first day of Passover, which was a Sabbath and day of rest, just as all festivals are called; and thus it had to happen on the second day of Passover, whether it fell on a Sabbath, or Sunday, or Monday, etc. (b).

As soon as it was past midnight, the gates of the Temple were opened; and before the cock crowed toward daybreak, the forecourt was again full of Israelites who were attending to their burnt offerings, which they were to offer on the second day because of the Appearance <note>the requirement to appear before the Lord at the festivals</note>.

(a) <note>original: "Joseph. l. 3. c. 10. antiq."</note> Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 3, Chapter 10.
(b) <note>original: "Lightfoot. hor. hebr. ad Matth. 12, 1. & Luc. 6, 1. & Act. 2, 1. Selden. de ann. civil. Judæor. c. 7."</note> Lightfoot, Hebrew Hours on Matthew 12:1, Luke 6:1, and Acts 2:1. Selden, On the Civil Year of the Jews, Chapter 7.
