v. 12. In honor of this firstfruit, a special sacrifice was also offered alongside it: namely, a lamb for a burnt offering.

v. 13. Along with the corresponding grain and drink offerings: of which the grain offering was something special and had a double measure, whereas otherwise only one-tenth of fine flour and a quarter Hin of oil was added to a lamb.

v. 14. As soon as this firstfruit was offered, everyone might enjoy the new grain: but not before. And does God not indicate by this that He wants to have the honor from us, that everything be offered to Him first, and that man possesses nothing as his own property, but gives everything back to the Source, remaining only as a steward over it?

v. 15. The fourth appointed time was the Feast of the Harvest of the firstfruits of their labor, which, calculated as seven weeks from the Passover Feast, had to be held on the fiftieth day, when they had to bring two loaves of bread—just as they had previously brought the sheaf—from such firstfruit. This was done from all the dwellings of the children of Israel, but only two were moved to and fro before the LORD as a wave offering, so that the harvest bestowed by God might be blessed for their nourishment.

This festival represented the first outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, of which it is written in *Acts 2*, which was, as it were, the first harvest of the promised gifts of the Holy Spirit, prophesied in *Joel 2* and *Ezekiel 36* and other places; however, such prophecies were not yet fully fulfilled by this, but will attain such fulfillment at the end of days in Christ’s glorious kingdom. Therefore, the gifts of the Spirit imparted at the beginning of the New Testament are emphatically called the firstfruits of the Spirit, *Romans 8:23*.

v. 15. From the day after) Namely, from the day after Passover.
7 complete Sabbaths) Or 7 full weeks, or 49 days.

v. 16. Until the day after) Thus it always fell on the same day of the week as the second day of Passover, and in the 3rd month, Sivan.
50 days) The fiftieth day was the festival day, from which number the festival also received its name, and from which the German word *Pfingsten* <note>Pentecost</note> also has its origin.

The sixth appointed time was the Day of Atonement / which was celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month / of which we dealt extensively above in Chapter 16.

v. 27. On the 10th of the 7th month) From the previous festival until this one, every day was a day of penance.

v. 28. The Day — that you may be reconciled) Reconciliation occurred / yet under the condition of repentance / for all sins, even the coarsest / provided they had not broken out into public scandal.

Sins committed against one's neighbor were likewise forgiven / but also under the condition / that they had first reconciled with their neighbor. For this reason, they took great pains / to reconcile with their enemies before this day.

v. 29. Since all other festivals were held in joy / on this one they were not permitted to eat or drink even the slightest thing / but rather had to chasten the body.

Minor children were exempt from this. However, as soon as a boy was 13 years and one day old / and a girl was 12 years and one day old; they were fully bound to fast.

And this fasting is also the only one / that **GOD** commanded the children of Israel through Moses.

Men and women wore their burial shrouds <note>German: *Todtenhemder*; literally "death-shirts," worn as a sign of humility and mortality.</note> during this festival. The young women in Jerusalem also went about in snow-white on this day.

The Jews today reduce this command to 5 points: namely / that on the same day they do not wash / do not anoint themselves / do not eat / do not drink / and do not wear leather shoes in the synagogue / but rather go and stand either in bare stockings / or have wooden shoes on their feet. The men often strike their breasts with their fists during prayer. They especially hold standing in high regard / and / to truly discipline themselves / the most pious stand in one spot in the synagogue for the entire festival, day and night / without eating / drinking / or sleeping.

v. 30. Doing work on this day) is forbidden / because atonement has its focus on rest.

v. 31. An eternal statute) From this, the Jews seek to maintain / that the Sabbath and this day of rest have not yet been abolished. But where have other things gone among them / which were called by the same name? Yet if one carries the matter into the spirit and the inner life / then it has its certain path / and this statute still applies.

However, the believers of the New Testament have been taught through these 2 points / the humbling of souls through fasting and the refraining from all work / that / now that the atonement of their souls has happened through the blood of Christ / they must constantly humble their souls in the denial of themselves and the willing taking up of his cross / namely the yoke of Christ / and in abstaining from fleshly lusts / which war against the soul. 1 Peter 2:11.

v. 32. From evening until evening) This indicates / that in the festivals of the Church, the beginning would be from the lesser light / and would proceed to the greater light / from the moon and stars of the dark night and shadows of the Old Testament / to the bright light of the sun in the New Testament / and that until the bright noon in the great light of the glorious kingdom of Christ.

v. 33. etc. The 7th appointed time was the Feast of Tabernacles <note>Also known as *Sukkot*, where booths are built to remember the wilderness wanderings.</note> / which they were to hold in remembrance of the arduous dwelling in huts for 40 years in the desert, now overcome / in their cities and houses with joy over all the physical blessings / which **GOD** had now bestowed upon them in the promised fruitful land.

v. 34. Therefore this fell at the time when the final harvest of the vineyards and other late fruits had occurred / which happened at the end of the civil year. Exod. 23:16.

On the 15th day of the 7th month) Occurs at the beginning of our October.

v. 35. Of all 7 days, the first day alone was entirely holy / but the other 6 / and thus also the 7th / were not / as some (a) claim. v. 36. On this festival, the reading of the Law and the Prophets was finished / and on the next following Sabbath, the beginning was made again in reading: although later this finishing seems to have been moved to the 9th day / which the Jews celebrate nowadays as well.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII.

**Left Column**

17. You shall bring from your dwellings bread for a wave offering; they shall be two tenths of fine flour: they shall be baked with leaven, as firstfruits to the **LORD**.

<margin>chapter 2:12.</margin>
18. And you shall bring with the bread seven lambs that are without blemish and one year old, and one young bull and two rams: they shall be a burnt offering to the **LORD**, along with their grain offering and their drink offerings, as a fire offering of a sweet aroma to the **LORD**.

19. And you shall prepare one male goat for a sin offering, and two lambs that are one year old for a peace offering <note>original: *Danckopffer* — literally "thank offering," though in this ritual context it refers to the communal peace offering</note>.

20. And the priest shall wave them together with the bread of the firstfruits as a wave offering before the face of the **LORD**, along with the two lambs: they shall be holy to the **LORD** for the priest.

21. And you shall proclaim on that very day that there shall be a holy assembly among you; you shall do no servile work at all: it is an eternal statute in all your dwellings throughout your generations.

---

<margin>verse 17.</margin> As soon as the daily morning sacrifice and the special festival sacrifices were offered on that day, two loaves of bread made from the new grain were brought to the **LORD** in gratitude for the successful harvest. This was done on behalf of the entire community, not by each individual head of a household.

The priest waved these toward the one who presented them, but he did not place them upon the altar—where nothing containing leaven was permitted to go—but rather kept them for himself.

<margin>verse 18.</margin> In addition to these two loaves, special offerings had to be brought to the **LORD** by the congregation.

<margin>verse 19. One year old)</margin> As soon as a lamb was over a year old—even if only by a single hour—it was no longer considered a lamb and could not be sacrificed as one.

Peace Offering) Because these were peace offerings for the entire congregation, and the whole community could not eat from only two lambs, they were sacrificed almost like sin offerings, where the blood and fat were brought to the altar.

<margin>verse 20.</margin> The meat, however—after being waved to the four winds <note>A ritual gesture symbolizing God's omnipresence over the earth</note> before the **LORD**—belonged entirely to the priests, who had to consume all the meat that same day as something "Most Holy."

Everything was provided from the communal treasury of the half-shekel <note>A standard tax paid by all adult males for the upkeep of the sanctuary</note>.

<margin>verse 21. On this day)</margin> This festival lasted only one day (Numbers 28:26) and was therefore called a "holiday" by the Jews. Modern Jews, however, celebrate for two days because they no longer know the exact day, as there is no longer a High Court <note>The Sanhedrin</note> to determine the appearance of the new moons.

A holy assembly) The foreigners and strangers who could not all fit in the Temple stayed meanwhile in their "schools" <note>synagogues</note>; the inhabitants of Jerusalem did the same after they had finished their duties in the inner court.

<column-break/>

**Right Column**

22. And when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field, nor gather the gleanings of your harvest: you shall leave them for the poor and for the stranger. I am the **LORD** your **God**.

23. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:

24. Speak to the children of Israel, and say: In the seventh month, on the first of the month, you shall have a day of rest, a memorial of blowing <note>original: *Blasen* — referring to the sounding of the Shofar or trumpets</note> (a), a holy assembly.

<margin>(a) Numbers 29:1.</margin>
25. You shall do no servile work at all, but offer fire offerings to the **LORD**.

26. An- <note>This marks the beginning of the next section, "And the Lord spoke..."</note>

<margin>verse 22.</margin> Charity toward the poor was already addressed above in Chapter 19:9–10.

<margin>verse 24.</margin> The fifth appointed time was the "Sabbath of Blowing," where on the first day of the seventh month, Tishrei, a signal had to be given by blowing horns throughout the entire land. This served as a memorial of the beginning of a New Year in civil matters, as it was believed the years began then at the creation of the world. Otherwise, in religious matters, they were commanded to make the month of Abib <note>Aviv/Nisan</note> in the spring (which corresponds to our April) the beginning of the year, as that was the time they were led out of Egypt (Exodus 12:2). However, this reminder of the old creation should also remind believers of the "new creation" that began with the birth of Christ, which the angels also "trumpeted" when they said: *Behold, I bring you tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people,* etc. (Luke 2:10–11). This is emphatically the day of the appointed time, and the day of the feast of the **LORD** (Hosea 9:5), the year of the **LORD** to redeem His own (Isaiah 63:4), the favorable year of the **LORD** (Isaiah 61:2), the acceptable year of the **LORD** (Luke 4:19). With this, Christendom also began to count its years—namely, from the birth of our **LORD** and Savior **Jesus Christ**.

In the seventh month) Counting from Nisan.

On the first of the month) This civil New Year's Day was thus a double festival, because it was also the New Moon.

A memorial of blowing) The priests blew horns <note>shofars</note> in the Temple at Jerusalem. After the destruction of the city and the Temple, it later took place in all cities, just as they still blow the horns in their schools <note>synagogues</note> today.

The blowing occurred throughout the entire day, from the dawn until the setting of the sun (a).

<margin>verse 25.</margin> Along with the daily morning sacrifice, the New Moon offerings were sacrificed, followed by the special festival offerings of the Feast of Blowing. See Psalm 81:4–5 regarding this.

The entire country was not required to come to Jerusalem for this; rather, they could celebrate the festival at home, which also lasted only one day.

Eventually, they began celebrating for two days and considered both as a single day (b), which still happens today.

<margin>(a) Thomas Goodwin, *Moses and Aaron*, Book 3, Chapter 7.
(b) Johannes Buxtorf, *The Jewish Synagogue*, Chapter 24.</margin>

### Chapter XXIII. The Third Book of Moses.

26. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, 
and said:
27. On the tenth day of this seventh month, which is the Day of Atonement, there shall be a holy assembly among you; and you shall humble your souls, and offer a fire offering to the **LORD**.
28. Also, you shall do no work at all on this very day: For it is the Day of Atonement, that you may be reconciled <note>original: *versöhnet* — to be atoned for or made at one with God</note> before the face of the **LORD** your **GOD**.
29. For every soul that will not humble itself on this very day shall be cut off from among its people.
30. And every soul that does any work at all on this very day, that same soul I will destroy from the midst of its people.
31. You shall do no work at all: This is an eternal statute among your descendants in all your dwellings.

---

The sixth appointed time was the Day of Atonement, which was celebrated on the tenth day of the seventh month, of which a detailed account was given above in Chapter 16.
**v. 27. On the 10th of the 7th month)** From the previous festival until this one, all the days were days of repentance.
**v. 28. The day -- that you may be reconciled)** Reconciliation occurred, yet under the condition of repentance, for all sins—even the greatest—provided they had not broken out into public scandal.
Sins committed against one's neighbor were likewise forgiven, but only on the condition that they had first reconciled with that neighbor. For this reason, they took great pains to reconcile with their enemies before this day.
**v. 29.** Since all other festivals were held in joy, they were not permitted to eat or drink the slightest thing on this day, but rather had to mortify the body.
Underage children were exempt from this. However, as soon as a boy was 13 years and one day old, and a girl 12 years and one day old, they were fully obligated to fast.
And this fast is also the only one that **GOD** commanded the children of Israel through Moses.
Men and women put on their burial shrouds <note>original: *Todten-Hemder* — referring to the white *kittel* worn on Yom Kippur to symbolize purity and mortality</note> for this festival. The young women in Jerusalem also went about in snow-white on this day.
The Jews today reduce this command to 5 items: namely, that on this day they do not wash themselves, do not anoint themselves, do not eat, do not drink, and do not put on leather shoes in the synagogue; instead, they go and stand either in their bare stockings or wear shoes made of wood on their feet.
The men often strike their breasts with their fists during prayer. They especially hold standing in high regard; to truly afflict themselves, the most pious stand in one spot in the synagogue for the entire festival, day and night, without eating, drinking, or sleeping.
**v. 30. Do work on this day)** is forbidden because reconciliation has its aim in rest.
**v. 31. An eternal statute)** From this, the Jews seek to maintain that the Sabbath and also this day of rest have not yet been abolished. But where have other things gone among them that are named in the same way? Yet if one leads the matter into the spirit and the inner life, it has its certain use, and this statute still applies.
However, believers of the New Testament <note>original: *N. T.*</note> are taught through these two parts—the humbling of souls through fasting and the refraining from all work—that since the reconciliation of their souls has now occurred through the blood of Christ, they must constantly humble their souls in the denial of themselves and the willing taking up of his cross—namely, the yoke of Christ—and in refraining from the fleshly lusts that war against the soul. 1 Peter 2:11.

<column-break/>

32. It is a Sabbath of rest for you, that you may humble your souls. On the ninth day of the month at evening, from evening until evening, you shall rest on your Sabbath.
33. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, and said:
34. Speak to the children of Israel and say: On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: *Laubhütten* — literally "booths" or "leafy huts"</note> for seven days to the **LORD**.
<margin>Numbers 29:12 etc. Nehemiah 8:14-18.</margin>
35. On the first day there shall be a holy assembly: you shall do no servile work at all.
36. Seven days you shall offer fire offerings to the **LORD**; on the eighth day there shall be a holy assembly among you, and you shall offer fire offerings to the **LORD**: it is a festival day (a); you shall do no servile work at all.
<margin>(a) Numbers 29:35.</margin>

---

**v. 32. From evening until evening)** This indicates that in the festivals of the Church, the beginning would be from the lesser light and proceed toward the greater light; from the moon and stars of the dark night and shadows of the Old Testament <note>original: *A. T.*</note> until the bright light of the sun in the New Testament <note>original: *N. T.*</note>, and that until the bright noon in the great light of the glorious kingdom of Christ.
**v. 33. etc.** The 7th appointed time was the Feast of Tabernacles, which they were to hold in memory of the now-passed arduous dwelling in huts for 40 years in the wilderness. They were to keep it in their cities and houses with joy over all the physical blessings that God had now bestowed upon them in the promised fruitful land.
**v. 34.** Therefore, this fell at the time when the final harvest of the vineyards and other late fruits had occurred, which happened at the end of the civil year. Exodus 23:16.
**On the 15th day of the 7th month)** Occurs at the beginning of our October.
**v. 35.** Of all 7 days, the first day was entirely holy; the 6 others, however—and thus also the 7th—were not, as some (a) would have it. They were indeed not proper workdays, but also not full festival or rest days; rather, they were intermediate days, like those in Exodus 12:16, though everyone refrained from work as much as possible.
**v. 36. But the eighth day)** namely, the 22nd of the 7th month, which was called the greatest day of the festival, John 7:37, was a glorious day, and as it were a special feast that had little or nothing in common with the previous one. At this feast, the Law and the Prophets were concluded, and on the next following Sabbath, the reading was begun again: although later this conclusion seems to have been moved to the 21st day, which the Jews also celebrate today.
<margin>(a) Thomas Goodwin, *Moses and Aaron*, book 3, chapter 6. Leyden, *Miscellaneous Hebrew Philological Disputations*, 39.</margin>

### The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>v. 37.</margin> 37. These are the appointed gatherings of the **LORD**, which you shall proclaim as holy assemblies, to offer fire-offerings to the **LORD**: burnt offerings and grain offerings, sacrifice-offerings and drink offerings, each on its designated day:

<margin>v. 38.</margin> 38. Besides the Sabbaths of the **LORD**; and besides your gifts, and besides all your vows, and besides all your voluntary offerings, which you shall give to the **LORD**.

<margin>v. 39.</margin> 39. But on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered in the harvest of the land, you shall celebrate the feast of the **LORD** for seven days. On the first day is a day of rest, and on the eighth day is a day of rest.

<margin>v. 40.</margin> 40. And you shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of stately trees, palm branches, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook; and you shall rejoice for seven days before the face of the **LORD** your **GOD**.

<margin>v. 37.</margin> **These are the appointed gatherings)** Here it is also worth considering that in the first month of the ecclesiastical year, the two festivals of Passover and the First Sheaf <note>signifying Christ's death and resurrection</note> occur, and in the seventh month, the last three festivals follow closely upon one another. These latter feasts represent the proclamation of the Kingdom of God throughout the world in the end times, the great persecution by the Antichrist, and the subsequent redemption in the glorious Kingdom of Christ. Thus, the beginning and the end of the New Testament era were very rich in mystery, while in the middle time, the firstfruits of the Spirit—the antitype <note>the spiritual fulfillment of a symbolic shadow</note> of the middle festival of Pentecost or Firstfruits—were poured out upon the believers in the Church.

**Of the LORD)** Those which are directly commanded by Him. To these, however, the Jews subsequently added several others of their own free will: such as the Feast of Dedication <note>Hanukkah</note> known from John 10:22, the Feast of Purim mentioned in the Book of Esther, and several others found in the Books of the Maccabees and in the writings of the Jewish historian Josephus.

<margin>v. 38.</margin> **Besides)** Those offerings which are already set for the Sabbaths, should such a festival fall on a Sabbath; or those which you wish to bring to the **LORD** out of free will, or are obligated to give due to a vow.

<margin>v. 39.</margin> **On the first and 8th a day of rest)** This occurs when man returns to **GOD**; when, as it was in the beginning, so it is now again; when one extreme is **GOD**, and the other is man made most like unto **GOD**, and both form a most harmonious and peaceful octave <note>a musical metaphor for perfect spiritual harmony</note>. There, in both, is only one mind, one heart, one will, and **GOD'S** will is done on earth as it is done in heaven. O most perfect, most blessed day of rest!

<margin>v. 40.</margin> **Of stately -- and thick trees)** The Hebrews unanimously hold that although the words in the original text do not name specific trees, they are understood to be the stately citron trees <note>the Etrog</note> and the thick myrtle trees. (c)

(c) <note>original: "Buxtorff. synag. Jud. c. 21. Ursin. arboret. bibl. c. 2. n. 24." — References to Johannes Buxtorf's 'Jewish Synagogue' and Johann Ursinus's 'Biblical Arboretum,' standard scholarly works on Jewish customs and plants in the 17th century.</note>

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 41.</margin> 41. And you shall celebrate this feast of the **LORD** seven days in the year. This is an eternal statute among your descendants; in the seventh month you shall celebrate it.

<margin>v. 42.</margin> 42. Seven days you shall dwell in booths: All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths.

<margin>v. 43.</margin> 43. So that your descendants may know that I made the children of Israel dwell in booths when I led them out of the land of Egypt. I am the **LORD** your **GOD**.

<margin>v. 44.</margin> 44. And Moses spoke of the appointed gatherings of the **LORD** to the children of Israel.

<margin>v. 41.</margin> This festival was intended to remind believers of the great final festival of the New Testament in the glorious Kingdom of Christ; when the seven secret periods of the Church shall have passed, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has become believing. Then the joy will appear of which the prophets speak in so many places—how the mourning of the believers under the persecution of the last Antichrist will be turned into pure joy, as dealt with more extensively in Isaiah 60 to 66 and chapter 12, and Jeremiah 31:11-14, 20. And this time is also expressly called the Feast of Tabernacles by Zechariah, which shall be celebrated in the latter days, and no other, Zechariah 14:16, 18.

<margin>v. 42.</margin> The booths <note>or "tabernacles"</note> had to be made under the open sky, not under a roof or under trees. Also, they were not to be covered over with cloth on top, nor made too dense with branches; rather, holes were left so that they could see the sun and stars through them, and the rain could also fall through. A tapestry could certainly be drawn over for decoration, or the walls could be lined with it.

In these booths they had to have their being and dwelling for 7 days, cooking, eating, sitting, reclining, and sleeping therein. Therefore, they also decorated them with all kinds of household items and tied citrons and other fruits to the branches.

Only the sick were permitted to remain in the house.

If a very heavy downpour fell, they might eat and sleep in houses for as long as it took for the weather to pass.

Many of the people also built their booths outside the city of Jerusalem—since there was not enough room for everyone in the city—but no further than a Sabbath day's journey away <note>a traditional distance permitted for travel on the Sabbath, roughly 2,000 cubits</note>.

<margin>v. 43.</margin> Today, the descendants of the children of Israel—especially the wealthy—not only have ornate tapestries in them, but also golden stars, all kinds of decorative fruits, even pumpkins; and in every booth hangs a thick onion in which 4 goose feathers or other feathers are stuck. By this, according to the opinion of the Jews, all evil is to be kept away from these booths. They also have a white chicken egg hanging in every booth, which is blown out and empty, upon which they write the words of this verse in Hebrew: <term>בסכות תשבו שבעת ימים</term> <note>original Hebrew: "You shall dwell in booths seven days"</note> (a)

The purpose, however, was to stir them to gratitude, in consideration of their lack in the wilderness when they were without houses, and their abundance in the land of Canaan when they dwelt in houses they had not built.

<margin>v. 44.</margin> Just as Moses revealed these appointed gatherings of the **LORD** to the children of Israel, so Paul teaches us of one toward which all the others pointed, Hebrews 12:22-23. To that one we should and will strive, and not let up until we have reached it!

(a) <note>original: "Schudt. Jüd. Merckw. P. II. l. 6. c. 35. n. 25." — Referring to Johann Jacob Schudt's 'Jewish Remarkabilities,' a famous 18th-century compendium of Jewish life and folklore.</note>

# The XXIV Chapter.

->The Light and Bread in the Sanctuary / and the Punishment of a Blasphemer.<-

And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Command the children of Israel that they bring to you pure, beaten olive oil for the light, that the lamps may be kept burning continually.
3. Outside the veil of the testimony in the Tabernacle of Meeting, Aaron shall prepare them continually from evening until morning before the face of the **LORD**. This shall be a perpetual statute among your descendants.
4. He shall set the lamps upon the pure lampstand continually before the face of the **LORD**.

> This commandment has already been given and considered in this way in Exodus Chapter 27:20, 21. It reminds the believers that they should continually keep the light of the Holy Spirit burning within themselves through watching and prayer. Regarding the lampstand, see Exodus 25:31, etc.
> <term>v. 2. Beaten</term>) Crushed with an oil-pestle. For that which is ground and pressed is not as pure.
> <term>v. 3. Aaron</term>) is taken here not only for the High Priest, but for the entire priestly order. For the preparing of the lamps was not performed by the High Priest alone—indeed, very rarely—but mostly by the common priests.
> <term>v. 4. Prepare</term>) This was done as follows: The priest took a vessel of glowing coals from the incense-fire on the altar of burnt offering into the sanctuary; he took the lamps and cleaned them first. Thereupon he took out what remained of the wick, likewise all the old oil that was still inside, using the small golden spoon, and from the nearby oil jar he poured in fresh oil, a half-log <note>A "log" is an ancient liquid measure; a half-log is approximately the volume of three empty eggshells</note> into each lamp. Following this, he took seven fresh wicks from the golden vessel where the snuffers, small golden spoons, and wicks were kept; he grasped one with the snuffing-tongs, lit it from the aforementioned fire, and with this one he lit the other six. Then he said his prayer, after which he took the ashes and the refuse out with him and threw them into the ash-heap on the east side of the altar.
> This lighting occurred in the evening, when the evening sacrifice was placed upon the altar, before the drink offering was sacrificed.
> The people of Israel had need of the lamps because the sun did not rise for them until the **LORD** **JESUS** Christ came. This light of the lamps among them was the Law and the Prophets: which was enclosed within narrow walls and did not radiate its light into all the world, but only within the narrow borders of the Jewish land. But now that the Sun of Righteousness has risen in our Savior, do we still have need of the oil? Yes, indeed! For it has become evening again, and the day has declined: indeed, it is night, and it will likely remain night until the new day of the future world breaks forth with the new radiance from Zion. Therefore we have great need of the oil, and without it we shall walk in darkness with the daughters of the foolish woman <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins</note> and remain excluded from the light of life.

<column-break/>

5. And you shall take fine flour and bake twelve cakes from it. Two tenths <note>Two tenths of an ephah, a dry measure</note> shall be in one cake.
6. And you shall set them in two rows, six in a row, upon the pure table before the face of the **LORD**. <margin>Exodus 25:30.</margin>
7. And you shall put pure frankincense upon the row, which shall be with the bread for a memorial offering, a fire-offering to the **LORD**.
8. Every <note>The text breaks here at "An", referring to the beginning of the Sabbath instruction</note>

> <term>v. 5. Fine flour</term>) Which, as Rabbi Judah Leo (a) writes, was bolted through eleven sieves.
> <term>Twelve</term>) According to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel, in whose image, as some believe (b), the form of the entire rational creation was comprised. For it is held that there are twelve general orders of the rational creation, whose figure the twelve tribes bore. Among which there was also a royal order, which was called Judah. Another order was priestly and called Levi. Another was close to Judah and called Benjamin, in which order the Temple of God and the Altar also found their place. Of which no more is to be said now. And although one tribe or another does not originate from the free woman but from the maidservant <note>Referring to the sons of Jacob born to Zilpah and Bilhah</note>, and is thus only partly free and partly servile, yet a loaf of bread is placed before God's face for every one.
> <term>Cakes</term>) The shape, according to the description of the Jews—who can give the best account of these things—was not round but oblong: six handbreadths long, five handbreadths wide, and one finger thick; thus thin and flat like cakes.
> They were unleavened, as Josephus reports.
> They were kept warm in a hot oven before they had to come before the face of the **LORD**, until the Sabbath began. For they were set out while warm. 1 Samuel 21:6.
> <term>v. 6. In 2 rows</term> — 6 in one) Five upon fourteen tubes of the two three-pronged forks, and the sixth beneath the tubes on the table itself; and likewise the other layer: according to the explanation of the Hebrews. Then, of the two that lay on the table, each took up half the table except for one handbreadth, because of their length and breadth. For the length of a cake was six handbreadths and the width was five: And the length lay across the width of the table, but the width lay along the length of the table.
> <term>v. 7. Each of these 2 rows</term> with cakes had a golden vessel, shaped like a hollow hand, with the finest and purest frankincense, each vessel filled with a handful.
> <term>Upon</term>) Or, because the Hebrew word <note>original: "עַל" (al)</note> also means "by" or "beside," this may give a better sense here. For otherwise it would seem as if they had stood on top of the two uppermost cakes.
> <term>Pure frankincense</term>) Vigilance and the purity of prayer must be joined with the cakes of faith. But that is a pure prayer where one lifts up pure hands, without anger or doubting. 1 Timothy 2:8. Therefore, if one prays and yet does not have a pure conscience, he may indeed lay on frankincense, but it would not have been necessary to require "pure" frankincense. God does not mean the kind from Arabia: rather, the prayers from a pure heart and a good conscience are the frankincense that he gladly smells.
> <term>Memorial Offering — Fire-Offering</term>) it is called, because the frankincense that was placed upon it had to be lit and burned when the bread was changed. It was brought to the altar of burnt offering with the daily morning sacrifice on the Sabbath, salted, and instead of the removed bread, it became a "fire to the **LORD** for a memorial," as it may properly be called. (c)

This shall also represent the Word of God as the food of the soul, which must be presented and heard with prayer, and which is renewed, as it were, every Sabbath in various preachings.

(c) See Josephus, Book 3, Antiquities, chapter 10, and Rabbi Judah Leo, Book 2, On the Temple, chapter 12, section 75. Where one also finds this: that the frankincense was scattered upon the special fire-heap from which the coals for the incense-burning in the Holy Place were taken.

### The III. Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII.

37. These are the appointed feasts of the **LORD**, which you shall proclaim to be holy assemblies, to offer fire-offerings to the **LORD**, burnt-offerings and grain-offerings, sacrifices and drink-offerings, each on its own day:
38. Besides the Sabbaths of the **LORD**; and besides your gifts, and besides all your vows, and besides all your voluntary offerings, which you shall give to the **LORD**.

On the first and 8th a day of rest) This occurs when man returns to God; when, as it was in the beginning, so it is now; when the one extreme is God, and the other is man made most like unto God, and both create a most harmonious and peaceful octave. 41. And you shall keep this feast of the **LORD** seven days in the year. This is a perpetual statute among your descendants; in the seventh month you shall keep it.
42. Seven days you shall dwell in booths <note>original: "Laubhütten," literally "leaf-huts."</note>; all who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths.

<margin>v. 41. This festival was to remind the believers of the great final feast of the New Testament in the glorious Kingdom of Christ, when the seven secret epochs of the Church will have passed, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has become believing. Then the joy will appear of which the prophets speak in so many places—how the mourning of the believers during the persecution of the final Antichrist will be transformed into pure joy, which is treated more extensively in Isaiah 60 to 66, and chapter 12; Jeremiah 31:11-14, etc. And this time is also explicitly called the Feast of Tabernacles by Zechariah, which shall be celebrated in the latter days, and no other: Zechariah 14:16, 18.</margin>
<margin>v. 42. The booths had to be made under the open sky, not under a roof or under trees. Also, they were not to be covered with cloth on top, nor made too dense with branches; rather, holes were left so that they could see the sun and stars through them, and the rain could also fall through. A tapestry for decoration might indeed be pulled over or the walls adorned with it.
In these huts, they had to conduct their lives and dwelling for 7 days, cooking, eating, sitting, lying, and sleeping therein. Therefore, they also decorated them with all kinds of household items, and tied citrons and other fruits to the branches.
Only the sick were permitted to remain in the house.
If a very heavy downpour fell, they might eat and sleep in houses until the weather passed.
Many of the people also built their huts outside the city of Jerusalem, because it was impossible for everyone to have space within the city, yet they were not to be more than a Sabbath-day's journey away.</margin>
<margin>v. 43. Nowadays, the descendants of the children of Israel, especially the wealthy, have not only elegant tapestries inside, but also golden stars, all kinds of decorative fruits, even pumpkins; and in every hut hangs a thick onion in which 4 goose feathers or other feathers are stuck. By this, according to the opinion of the Jews, all evil is supposed to be kept away from this booth. They also have a white chicken egg hanging in every hut, which has been blown out and is empty, upon which they write the words of this verse in Hebrew: <term>בסכת תשבו שבעת ימים</term> <note>original: "Basukkot teshvu shiv'at yamim"</note> "Seven days you shall dwell in booths." (a)</margin>
<margin>The purpose, however, was to stir them to gratitude, considering their lack in the wilderness when they were without houses, and their abundance in the land of Canaan, where they lived in houses they had not built.</margin>
<margin>v. 44. Just as Moses revealed these appointed feasts of the **LORD** to the children of Israel, so Paul teaches us of one assembly toward which all others aimed, Hebrews 12:22, 23. Toward that we should and will strive, and not let up until we have reached it!
(a) Schudt, *Jewish Remarkabilities*, Part II. book 6. ch. 35. n. 25.</margin>

### The XXIV Chapter.

#### Chapter 24. The Third Book of Moses.

->The Light and Bread in the Sanctuary / and the Punishment of a Blasphemer.<-

And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Command the children of Israel that they bring to you pure, crushed olive oil <note>original: "Baumöl"; literally "tree oil," commonly used for olive oil in this period</note> for the light, so that the lamps may be kept burning continually.
3. Outside the veil of the testimony in the Tent of Meeting, Aaron shall arrange them continually from evening until morning before the face of the **LORD**. This shall be a perpetual statute among your descendants.
4. He shall arrange the lamps on the pure lampstand <note>the Menorah</note> continually before the face of the **LORD**.

<margin>Exodus 27:20–21</margin> This commandment has already been given and considered in Exodus Chapter 27:20–21. It reminds the believers that they should continually keep the light of the Holy Spirit burning within themselves through watching and praying. Regarding the lampstand, see Exodus 25:31, etc.

**v. 2. Crushed)** With an oil-pestle. For that which is ground and pressed does not become as pure.

**v. 3. Aaron)** is taken here not only for the High Priest, but for the entire priestly order. For the arranging of the lamps was not done by the High Priest alone—indeed, only very rarely—but mostly by the common priests.

**v. 4. Arrange)** This was done as follows: The priest took a vessel with glowing coals from the incense-fire on the Altar of Burnt Offering with him into the Holy Place; he took the lamps and cleaned them first. Then he took out what remained of the wick, as well as all the old oil that was still inside, using the small golden spoon, and poured fresh oil from the standing oil-jug into each lamp—half a *log* <note>A 'log' is an ancient liquid measure; half a log is roughly the volume of three eggshells</note>, or as much as may go into three empty eggshells. Hereupon he took out seven fresh wicks from the golden vessel—in which the snuffers and small golden spoons, as well as the wicks, were kept—seized one with the tongs, lit it from the aforementioned fire, and with this lit the other six. He then said his prayer, after which he took the ash and the refuse out with him and threw it into the ash-heap on the east side of the altar.

This lighting took place in the evening, when the evening sacrifice was placed on the altar, before the drink offering was sacrificed.

The people of Israel had need of the lamps because the Sun <note>referring to Christ as the Sun of Righteousness</note> did not rise for them until the Lord **JESUS** Christ came. This light of the lamps was, for them, the Law and the Prophets: which was enclosed between narrow walls and did not radiate its light into all the world, but only within the narrow borders of the Jewish land. But now that the Sun of Righteousness has risen in our Savior, do we still have need of the oil? Yes, indeed! For it has become evening again, and the day has declined: indeed, it is night, and it will likely remain night until the new day of the future world breaks forth with the new radiance from Zion. Therefore, we have great need of the oil, and without it, we will walk in darkness with the daughters of the foolish woman <note>a reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins</note> and remain excluded from the light of life.

<column-break/>

5. And you shall take fine flour and bake twelve cakes from it. Two-tenths <note>of an ephah</note> shall be in one cake.
6. And you shall place them in two rows, six in a row, upon the pure table before the face of the **LORD**. <margin>Exodus 25:30</margin>
7. And you shall put pure frankincense on each row, which shall be with the bread as a memorial offering, an offering made by fire to the **LORD**.
8. Every

**v. 5. Fine flour)** Which, as Rabbi Judah Leon (a) writes, was bolted <note>sifted</note> through eleven sieves.

**Twelve)** According to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel, in whose image—as some believe (b)—the form of the entire rational creation was comprised. For it is held that there are twelve general orders of the rational creation, whose figure the twelve tribes bore. Among which was also a royal order, which was called Judah. Another order was priestly and called Levi. Another was near to Judah and called Benjamin, in whose order the Temple of God and the Altar also found their place. Of which no more is to be said at this time. And although one or another tribe does not originate from the free woman, but from the handmaid <note>referring to the sons of Jacob born to Bilhah and Zilpah</note>, and is only partly free but partly servile; yet a loaf of bread is placed before God's face for every single one.

**Cakes)** According to the description of the Jews, who can give the best account of these things, the shape was not round, but oblong: six handbreadths long, five handbreadths wide, and one finger thick: thus thin and flat like cakes.

They were unleavened, as Josephus reports.

They were kept warm in a hot oven before they had to come before the face of the **LORD**, until the Sabbath began. For they were set out while still warm. <margin>1 Samuel 21:6</margin>

**v. 6. In 2 rows — 6 in one)** Five upon fourteen tubes of the two three-pronged forks, and the sixth under the tubes on the table itself; and so the other stack: according to the explanation of the Hebrews. Then, of the two that lay on the table, each took up half the table (save for one handbreadth) because of their length and width. For the length of a cake was six, and the width five handbreadths: And the length lay across the width of the table, while the width lay along the length of the table.

**v. 7. Each of these 2 rows** of cakes had a golden vessel, shaped like a hollow hand, with the finest and purest frankincense, each vessel filled with a handful.

**Upon) Or, because** <term>עַל</term> <note>Hebrew: 'al'</note> also means "by" or "beside," this may give a better sense here. For otherwise it would seem as if they had stood on top of the two uppermost cakes.

**Pure frankincense)** Vigilance and purity of prayer must be combined with the cakes of faith. But that is a pure prayer where one lifts up pure hands, without wrath or doubting. 1 Timothy 2:8. Accordingly, if someone prays and yet does not have a clean conscience, he may indeed lay down frankincense, but it would not have been necessary to require "pure" frankincense. God does not mean the kind from Arabia: rather, the prayers from a pure heart and a good conscience are the frankincense that he loves to smell.

**Memorial offering — Fire offering)** it is called so because the frankincense placed upon it had to be lit and burned when the bread was changed. It was, however, brought to the Altar of Burnt Offering with the daily morning sacrifice on the Sabbath, salted, and instead of the removed bread, it became a fire to the **LORD** for a memorial, as it may actually be called. (c)

This shall also represent the Word of God as the food of the souls, which must be presented and heard with prayer, and which is, as it were, renewed every Sabbath in various preachings.

---

**v. 41.** This feast was meant to remind believers of the great final feast of the New Testament in the glorious Kingdom of Christ, when the seven secret epochs of the Church will have passed, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel has become believers. Then the joy will appear of which the prophets speak in so many places; how the mourning of the believers under the persecution of the final Antichrist will be turned into pure joy: this is discussed further in Isaiah 60 to 66 and chapter 12, Jeremiah 31:11-13, etc. And this time is also explicitly called the Feast of Tabernacles <note>Sukkot</note> by Zechariah, which shall be celebrated in the last times, and no other, Zechariah 14:16, 18.
**v. 42.** The booths <note>original: "Laubhütten"</note> had to be made under the open sky, not under a roof or under trees. Also, they were not to be covered over with cloth at the top, nor closed too tightly with branches; rather, holes were left so that the sun and stars could be seen through them, and rain could also fall through. A tapestry could certainly be pulled over for decoration, or the walls could be covered with one.
In these huts they had to have their being and dwelling for 7 days, cooking, eating, sitting, reclining, and sleeping in them. Therefore, they also decorated them with all kinds of household items and tied citrons and other fruits to the branches.
Only the sick were permitted to remain in the house.
If a very heavy downpour fell, they were allowed to eat and sleep in houses until the weather had passed.
Many of the people also built their huts outside the city of Jerusalem, because it was impossible for everyone to have space in the city, but no further than a Sabbath day's journey away.
**v. 43.** Nowadays, the descendants of the children of Israel, especially the wealthy, have not only decorative tapestries inside, but also golden stars, all kinds of decorative fruits, even pumpkins, and in every hut hangs a dried onion in which four goose feathers or other feathers are stuck. By this, according to the opinion of the Jews, everything evil is kept back from this booth. Likewise, they have a white chicken egg hanging in every hut, which is blown out and empty, upon which they write the words of this verse in Hebrew: <note>original: "בסכת תשבו שבעת ימים"</note> *In booths you shall dwell seven days.* (a)
The purpose, however, was to stir them to gratitude, considering their lack in the desert, when they were without houses, and their abundance in the land of Canaan, when they lived in houses that they had not built.
**v. 44.** Just as Moses revealed these appointed gatherings of the Lord to the children of Israel, so Paul tells us of one toward which all others have aimed, Hebrews 12:22, 23. To that one we should and will strive, and not let up until we have reached it!
(a) <note>original: "Schudt. Jüd. Merckw. P. II. l. 6. c. 35. n. 2. 2c."</note> Johann Jakob Schudt, *Jewish Memorabilia*, Part II, book 6, chapter 35, no. 2, etc.

# Chapter XXIV. The Third Book of Moses.

## The XXIV. Chapter.

->The Light and Bread in the Sanctuary, and the Punishment of a Blasphemer.<-

1. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Command the children of Israel that they bring to you pure, beaten olive oil for the light, so that the lamps may be kept burning continually.
3. Outside the veil of the testimony in the Tent of Meeting, Aaron shall arrange them continually from evening until morning before the face of the Lord. This shall be a perpetual statute among your descendants.
4. He shall arrange the lamps on the pure lampstand continually before the face of the Lord.

<margin>
This commandment has already been given and considered in Exodus 27:20-21. It reminds the believers that they should always keep the light of the Holy Spirit burning within themselves through watching and praying. Regarding the lampstand, see Exodus 25:31, etc.
</margin>

**v. 2. Beaten)** With an oil-stamper. For that which is ground and pressed is not as pure.

**v. 3. Aaron)** is taken here to represent not only the High Priest, but the entire priestly order. For the arranging of the lamps was not done by the High Priest alone—indeed, it was quite rare—but mostly by the common priests.

**v. 4. Arrange)** This happened as follows: The priest took a vessel with glowing coals from the incense-fire on the Altar of Burnt Offering into the Holy Place, took the lamps, and cleaned them first. Then he took out what remained of the wick, as well as all the old oil that was still inside, using a small golden spoon, and poured fresh oil from the nearby oil jug into each lamp—half a <term>log</term> <note>A biblical unit of liquid measure, roughly 0.3 to 0.5 liters.</note>, or as much as might fit into three empty eggshells. Then he took seven fresh wicks out of the golden vessel where the snuffers, small golden spoons, and wicks were kept. He took one with the snuffing-tongs, lit it at the aforementioned fire, and used it to light the others. Then he said his prayer, after which he took the ash and the refuse out with him and threw it onto the ash-heap on the east side of the altar.

This lighting occurred in the evening, when the evening offering was laid upon the altar, before the drink offering was sacrificed.

The people of Israel had need of the lamps because the sun did not rise for them until the Lord Jesus Christ came. This light of the lamps was for them the Law and the Prophets: which was enclosed within narrow walls and did not radiate its light into all the world, but only within the narrow borders of the Jewish land. But now that the Sun of Righteousness has risen in our Savior, do we still have need of the oil? Yes, indeed! For it has become evening again, and the day has declined: yes, it is night, and will likely remain night until the new day of the future world breaks forth with the new brilliance from Zion. Therefore, we have great need of the oil, and without it, we shall wander in darkness with the daughters of the foolish woman <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25.</note> and remain excluded from the light of life.

The incense that was placed upon it had to be lit and burned when it was changed. It was, however, brought to the Altar of Burnt Offering with the daily morning sacrifice on the Sabbath after the burnt offering, salted, and instead of the bread that was removed, it became a fire-offering to the Lord, as it may actually be called. (c)

This shall also represent the Word of God as the food of the soul, which must be presented and heard with prayer, and is, as it were, renewed every Sabbath in various proclamations.

<column-break/>

5. And you shall take fine flour and bake twelve cakes from it. Two tenths <note>Two tenths of an ephah, approximately 4.5 liters.</note> shall be in one cake.
6. And you shall set them in two rows, six in a row, upon the pure table before the face of the Lord. <margin>Exodus 25:30.</margin>
7. And you shall put pure frankincense on each row, which shall be with the bread for a memorial offering, a fire-offering to the Lord.

<margin>
**v. 5. Fine flour)** Which, as R. Judah Leo (a) writes, was bolted <note>Sifted through a cloth or sieve.</note> through a sieve.
</margin>

**Twelve)** According to the number of the twelve tribes of Israel, in whose image, as some believe (b), the form of all rational creatures was comprised. For it is held that there are twelve general orders of rational creatures, whose figure was carried by the twelve tribes. Among these was a royal order, which was called Judah. Another order was priestly and called Levi. Another was close to Judah and called Benjamin, in which order the Temple of God and the Altar also found their place. Of which no more can be said now. And although one or another tribe did not originate from the free woman but from the maidservant, and is only partly free and partly servile, nevertheless a bread is laid before God's face for every one.

**Cakes)** The shape, according to the description of the Jews—who can give the best report in these matters—was not round, but oblong, six handbreadths long, five handbreadths wide, and one finger thick: thus thin and flat like cakes.

They were unleavened, as Josephus reports.
They were kept warm in a hot oven before they had to come before the Lord's face, until the Sabbath broke. For they were set out while warm. 1 Samuel 21:6.

**v. 6. In two rows—six in one)** upon fourteen tubes of the two three-pronged forks, and the sixth one under the tubes on the table itself; and so with the other stack, according to the explanation of the Hebrews. Thus, of the two that lay on the table, each took up half the table, except for one handbreadth, because of their length and width. For the length of a cake was six, and the width five handbreadths: and the length lay across the width of the table, while the width lay along the length of the table.

**v. 7. Each of these two rows of cakes had a golden vessel, shaped like a hollow hand, with the finest and purest frankincense, each vessel filled with a handful.**

**Upon)** Or, because the word *al* <note>original: "על"</note> also means "by" or "beside," this may give a better sense here. For otherwise, it would seem as if they stood on top of the two uppermost cakes.

**Pure frankincense)** With the cakes of faith, the vigilance and purity of prayer must be joined. But that is a pure prayer where one lifts up pure hands, without anger or doubting. 1 Timothy 2:8. If, therefore, someone prays and yet does not have a pure conscience, he indeed lays out frankincense, but not pure frankincense. If all frankincense were pure, there would have been no need to demand *pure* frankincense. God also does not mean the kind from Arabia: but the prayers from a pure heart and good conscience; those are the frankincense he loves to smell.

**Memorial offering—fire-offering)** It is called this because the frankincense that was placed upon it had to be lit and burned when the bread was changed.

<margin>v. 8. On the</margin>

### 540 The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XXIV.

8. On every Sabbath day <margin>(a) 1 Chronicles 9:32.</margin> he shall prepare it continually before the face of the Lord, on behalf of the children of Israel as an everlasting covenant.
9. And it shall belong to Aaron and his sons <margin>(a) Matthew 12:4.</margin> and they shall eat it in a holy place. For it is the most holy thing for him from the offerings of the Lord made by fire, by a perpetual statute.

<margin>v. 8. On the Sabbath day) In the rest of the soul. And in what does a believing soul find greater rest than in the remembrance of God, and in</margin>
<margin>Before the face of the Lord) walking and persisting in constant prayer and the practice of the presence of God?</margin>
<margin>v. 9. The removed loaves belonged to the priests, not to the High Priest alone; he only took his portion first, as much as he wanted: the rest the priests had.</margin>
<margin>In a holy place) In the courtyard; because they were among the most holy things.</margin>

But I, says Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar who often interpreted the Old Testament allegorically.</note>, seek no holy place on earth, but rather in the heart. Thus, my soul is a place for the devil if I do evil; and if I do good, it is a place for God. Therefore, the holy place is a pure soul which receives the bread that comes down from heaven to eat. And is not something better understood by the "holy place" than when we imagine that a heap of unfeeling stones is called such?
**It is the most holy thing for him)** The secret bread and Word do not fit everyone, but only those to whom it is given.
**As a perpetual statute)** That which is spiritual is eternal. The visible is temporal and soon comes to an end. The fashion of the world passes away, and the letter [of the law] undoubtedly does as well; but the eternal remains, and that is the spiritual sense of the Word. Let us also note this briefly here at the conclusion regarding the loaves, how they are a

->Prefigurement of Christ.<-

1. The cakes are called the Loaves of the Face <note>original: "Brode des Angesichts" — often translated as "Showbread" or "Bread of the Presence."</note>. Christ is the essence of all bread (John 6) and is Himself the face of God; He also appears without ceasing before the face of God for us (Hebrews 9:24).
2. They were unleavened. The Bread of Life, Jesus Christ, is pure and clean, and as free and far from the leaven of false doctrine as He is from sin.
3. Added to this was the finest, most subtle, and most nourishing semolina flour. In Jesus, we find the true nourishing flour from the best wheat of the purest God-humanity.
4. There were 12 of them in two rows: to indicate that God prepares food for the two Testaments, one of which consisted of 12 tribes, and this one which is founded upon 12 apostles.
5. They were not set out raw, but first baked in a hot oven. So Christ was baked in the fiery oven of God's wrath, and as it were roasted, before He entered into heaven to appear before the face of God for us.
6. It was served in golden dishes. Jesus Christ is presented to us in the Law and the Gospel, which is more precious than gold and much fine gold (Psalm 19:10).
7. They had to lie on the table at all times: to indicate that Christ is our daily food at all times and for eternity.
8. They had to be brought out fresh and new at all times. So Christ could easily seem moldy to us if He were not always presented fresh.
9. They lay before the eyes for 7 days, and were fresh on the Sabbath. Thus on the great Sabbath <note>A reference to the eternal rest in the afterlife.</note>.
10. Only the priests were allowed to eat of them. No one should approach the table of the Lord except true believers (1 Peter 2:9). Also, in the Kingdom of God in the church above, no one will eat the glorified bread at His royal table except the royal priests (Luke 13:28-30).
11. Upon and beside them lay incense in golden bowls. We must receive Christ with prayer and thanksgiving.

<column-break/>

10. And the son of an Israelite woman, who was the son of an Egyptian man, went out among the children of Israel, and the son of the Israelite woman and an Israelite man fought in the camp.
11. And the son of the Israelite woman blasphemed the Name and cursed; so they brought him to Moses. His mother's name was Shelomith, a daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan.
12. And they put him in custody, so that a declaration might be made to them through the mouth of the Lord.

<margin>From such unequal marriages with unbelievers, such crude spirits can be born, who then follow evil much sooner than good.</margin>
<margin>v. 10. Went out) He who sins "goes out" in a double way. He goes out from the purpose of good and the uprightness of the heart, from the truth and fear of God, from love, from the way of righteousness, and from the bounds of the law and the will of God. And when he is punished for it, and the fear of God is slight in him, he also goes out and departs from the fellowship of the believers. Thus it is said of Cain in Genesis 4: that he went out from the face of the Lord.</margin>
<margin>But there is also a "going out" which is commanded by the Lord, and for which one is much more to be called blessed if one obeys it: of which mention is made in 2 Corinthians 6:17 and Isaiah 52:11.</margin>
<margin>The son of an Israelite woman -- an Egyptian man) He who is entirely outside the faith is completely an Egyptian. But he who professes the faith and yet sins is, as it were, of Israelite descent on the side where he believes God, and on the side where he sins, he has his origin from an Egyptian. But he who both confesses with the mouth and believes with the heart and proves it in deed, he is of Israelite lineage on both sides. Also,</margin>
<margin>When someone reads the Scripture, writes Origen (a), and follows the letter indeed, but despises and rejects the spiritual understanding, he has an Israelite mother—that is, the letter. But because he neglects the nobler part and follows his fleshly sense of darkened reason, he has an Egyptian for a father.</margin>
<margin>And what comes of it? He who is born according to the flesh hates, envies, and persecutes him who is born according to the Spirit (Galatians 4:29). Therefore he stirs up nothing but strife against the Israelite) Who is an Israelite from both parts, both according to the letter and according to the Spirit; because he [the fighter] is an Israelite only according to the letter, but an Egyptian according to the Spirit.</margin>
<margin>Note, however, how the Scripture speaks so wisely and deliberately in everything. He who was an Israelite by both father and mother is called</margin>
<margin>An Israelite man) The other, however, is not called a "man." Does this happen by chance? Oh no. In the words of the Holy Spirit, nothing is placed without a deep reason. He who is only half an Israelite and half an Egyptian, and thus a double-minded hypocrite, is not worthy to be called a man. But he who is a whole and complete Israelite is a "man" for the sake of the inward man, who is created according to the image of God and Christ.</margin>
<margin>v. 11. Blasphemed the Name and cursed) Thus anger revealed the evil ground of the heart, that he had no reverence before the wrath of God, and therefore named Him so explicitly and cursed therewith. The "how" is not reported, to show that such shameful words should not be repeated.</margin>
<margin>v. 12. Although such a sin against parents was also to be punished with death (Chapter 20:9), they did not yet know how this one, which was much heavier, should be handled. Therefore Moses sought the Lord to reveal His will to him.</margin>
<margin>In which all authorities should take an example: to call upon God for counsel and the revelation of His will in difficult cases; He would then not leave Himself without witness to them. See also Numbers 15:34.</margin>

### Chapter XXIV. The Third Book of Moses.

13. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
14. Bring the one who cursed outside the camp; and let all who heard him lay their hands upon his head, and let the entire congregation stone him.
<margin>Chapter 20:27.</margin>
15. And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin;
16. And whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death: the entire congregation shall surely stone him. As with the foreigner, so shall it be with the native-born: when he blasphemes the Name, he shall be put to death.

---

God reveals to us always and everywhere that in His nature He is Fire and Light. To Moses and to every born soul, He is a Light which reveals to them all His counsel and will from time to time according to all their needs, and gives teaching and instruction in all doubtful cases, so that they may know how to conduct themselves. But to sinners and to all sinful beings, He is a consuming fire and a just, jealous God, whose wrath kindles against all the godless nature of the disobedient at the proper time.

**v. 14. Lay their hands upon his head)** The laying on of hands by the judges and witnesses occurred before all others at the execution of a blasphemer, with these words: "Your blood be upon your own head! For you yourself are the cause of this." (a) And therefore the Hebrews also say that the punishment of stoning is indicated in the Scripture whenever it is said: "His blood be upon him!"

**v. 15. 16.** These two verses may perhaps best be explained by the saying of the Savior: "Whoever speaks a word <note>specifically as a blasphemy, which He is speaking of there</note> against the Son of Man, it will be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come" (Matthew 12:32). For otherwise, it is difficult to say how cursing one's God and blaspheming the name of the LORD are so different that the former is to be considered minor compared to the latter. However, Origen <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar known for his deep, often allegorical, interpretations of the Bible.</note> reverses this, and regarding these two expressions and the two different punishments appointed, he has this particular observation:

> It is a much heavier thing to "bear one's sin" than to be put to death. Death, which is inflicted as a punishment for the sake of a crime, is itself a cleansing of the sin for which it is endured. Thus, the sin is forgiven through the punishment of death (because it is, so to speak, paid for in a certain way), and therefore <note>so easily</note> nothing remains of this wrongdoing for the day of judgment and the eternal fire. But he who must "bear his sin," it remains upon him and goes with him even after death: and because he has not paid for it in time, he must take eternal punishments upon himself there. — Thus, it is indeed a heavier thing to take sin with oneself into hell than to endure something for it here in this time. Paul also looked to this when he handed that incestuous man (1 Corinthians 5) over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved on the day of the LORD JESUS.

So let us now voluntarily take upon ourselves the destruction of the flesh in this time, so that our spirit may be thoroughly cleansed in the present life, and thus pure and clear, may pass over from death into life to our LORD Jesus Christ!

(a) <note>original Latin: Maimon. c. 2. de idololatr. sect. 14. This refers to the "Mishneh Torah" by the Jewish scholar Maimonides, specifically the section on "Laws concerning Idolatry."</note>

<column-break/>

17. And when anyone strikes down any soul of a man, he shall surely be put to death.
18. But whoever strikes down the soul of a beast shall make it good; soul for soul.
19. And when anyone causes a blemish in his neighbor, as he has done, so shall it be done to him.
20. Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth: as he has caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him.
21. And he who kills a beast shall make it good: but he who kills a man shall be put to death.
22. There shall be one law among you: so shall it be for the foreigner as for the native-born. For I am the LORD your God.
23. And Moses spoke it to the children of Israel, that they should lead the curser outside the camp and stone him to death. And the children of Israel did as the LORD had commanded Moses.

---

**v. 17.** On this occasion, the death penalty against murderers is renewed. Exodus 21:12; Genesis 9:6.
**v. 18. Soul for soul)** Ox for ox, donkey for donkey.
**v. 19. 20.** Whenever harm was done to the body, it had to be investigated according to judicial findings, and the right of retaliation <term>lex talionis; "an eye for an eye"</term> was to be observed by the judge; regarding which see Exodus 21:23, etc.
**v. 21.** Damage to livestock should—or at least could—be compensated with money.
**v. 22.** Foreigners have a mighty patron who faithfully takes up their cause everywhere. This is for all judges and rulers to note, so that they may demonstrate toward them what is right and equal, and remember that they also have a Master in heaven, and with Him there is no respect of persons. It is the LORD our God—yes, even the LORD your God—and our common Creator, O you gods of the earth! <note>"Gods of the earth" is a common historical reference to earthly judges or rulers based on Psalm 82.</note>
**v. 23.** If authorities ever wanted to show any just zeal and uphold the law of justice, there would be something to learn here in this case <note>original: casu</note>. For

One must be astonished when one considers the many kinds of cursing and notices how every nation among Christians has its own particular inventions in this regard: and yet there is nothing more surprising than that authorities usually punish all other misdeeds sooner than cursing and blasphemy. A common person is indeed punished with the iron collar or the like—which in itself is not unjust—when he has stolen a few apples or pears from a garden, or a few sheaves of grain from the field. But when he curses every day during his work or otherwise and shames the holy name of God, it is overlooked, as if no one needs to concern themselves with it.

# The Third Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.

## The 25th Chapter.

->Regarding the Sabbatical and Jubilee Years, and the Poor.<-

And the LORD spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land that I give you, the land shall keep a Sabbath rest unto the LORD.
3. Six years you shall sow your field, and six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather in its fruit.
4. But in the seventh year, the land shall have a Sabbath of rest, a Sabbath unto the LORD: you shall neither sow your field nor prune your vineyard.

---

This commandment regarding the Year of Rest was already briefly introduced in Exodus 23:10–11, where it was specifically mentioned that the poor among them should then eat what grew of its own accord—namely, from the seeds that fell naturally and from the unpruned vines. These vines had to be allowed to grow freely and are specifically called "separated" here <note>The German text uses "abgesonderte," referring to the Hebrew term *nazir*, meaning "unpruned" or "consecrated" like a Nazirite</note>, because they were not properly tended or pruned, just as the Nazirites had to do with their hair. Here, however, the fruits are still left to the owners and their families, provided that, according to the previous commandment, they also granted the poor a free right to enjoy such fruits according to their needs.

**v. 2. Into the land — that I give you)** The Jews who lived elsewhere, outside the land of Canaan, were not obligated to let their land rest (a).

**The land)** This does not seem to favor the opinion that gardens were exempted from this law, as some suggest (b).

**v. 3. Six years)** Just as God worked for six days in His creation and assigned the same number of working days to man, He also allows something visionary <note>The author uses "perspectivisches" to mean a prophetic foreshadowing</note> to be seen here; for by ordering the number of years according to the number of days, He makes the latter an image of the former. For:

In this consists the wisdom of God: that He first allows certain images to go before, in order to represent something greater and more secret through them; as He, in His works, according to the order of time, becomes greater and greater—not that He can become greater in Himself, but in His effects which He demonstrates in the creature, in which He and His eternal Son (through whom He brought forth all things) continue to work.

**v. 4.** Just as the seventh day of the week was holy to the LORD God and was a Sabbath or Day of Rest, so every seventh year also had to be holy to the LORD God and be a Sabbatical or Year of Rest, in which both the land and those who cultivated it were to rest.

**In the seventh year)** This year did not begin with the month of Nisan <note>The first month of the religious calendar, roughly March/April</note>, according to which all other festivals in the year were directed; rather, it began with the month of Tishri <note>The first month of the civil calendar, roughly September/October</note>, when the civil year began. This was for the benefit of the land; for in Nisan, the grain everywhere only begins to truly ripen. Thus, in many places, the fruits of the sixth year—which was supposed to provide so abundantly for the following year—would have remained standing if the rest had begun in Nisan. The month of Tishri was also most suitable because the Jubilee year was to begin in that same month.

(a) <note>Latin: "See Hottinger, *On Hebrew Laws*, no. 69."</note>
(b) <note>Latin: "Vinarius on this passage. Quistorp on Exodus 23:10. Hottinger, as cited above."</note>

<column-break/>

5. What grows of its own accord after your harvest you shall not reap, and the grapes of your unpruned vines you shall not gather; it shall be a year of rest for the land.
6. But what the Sabbath of the land produces shall be for food for you: namely for you, and for your male servant, and for your female servant, and for your hired laborer, and for your guest who stays with you. <margin>Exodus 12:45.</margin>
7. And for your cattle, and for the wild animals that are in your land, all its produce shall be for food.

---

**v. 5. What grows of its own accord after your harvest)** This refers to grain from the sixth year that fell out during cutting, binding, stacking, loading, or transport, took root in the earth, and then shot up in the seventh year, as often happens.

**v. 6, 7. All of this was made free for everyone.**
The head of the household was allowed to eat what grew on his land, and could also take some home and keep it with him, and share it with his family, as long as some of that fruit still remained on the land or on the trees. However, if there was nothing left in the field, he had to give away what he had at home for the common good. If someone had sold any of it, the money received also had to be given for the common good (a).

If someone kept something for himself alone and sought to seek his own profit with it, he was regarded as if he were dishonest and considered unfit to give testimony before a court.

No one had anything of their own from the land here; rather, everything was common property. The poor, strangers, widows, and orphans—indeed, even the cattle and the wild animals in the field—had just as much right to consume all fruits and plants as the person on whose land they grew. If, for example, someone picked a grape from his own vineyard, this did not happen from "his own" grapes that belonged to him, but from the "common" grapes that belonged to everyone.

Just as the Lord wished to free them from all otherwise imposed labor of cultivating the land in the seventh year, so in this Sabbatical Year He wished to give the believers an image of the desired rest of the people of God in the glorious Kingdom of Christ in the final seventh millennium from the creation of the world (Hebrews 4:9; Revelation 20:6). Since we are now in the sixth millennium and have already put over seven hundred years behind us <note>This indicates the author is writing in the late 17th or early 18th century (the 1600s or 1700s AD)</note>, and things must be fulfilled precisely according to the number the prophets indicated, one should rightly be encouraged to contemplate this in faith. As this is described, among other places, in the final chapters of Isaiah from Chapter 60 onwards, they will build houses there, plant vineyards, and otherwise work (Chapter 65:21, etc.); but this will not happen with such toil and under this curse, but with pure delight and much blessing, which they will have in all their labor. See v. 21.

Then the creature, which is subjected to futility—not willingly, but because of Him who subjected it, and that in hope—will be set free from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God (Romans 8:20, 21; and Chapter 13:5). Thus, the heavy servitude among men, where life is made bitter for farmers and others (Job 31:39), shall cease, and everyone will dwell in quiet rest under his vine and fig tree (Micah 4:4).

(a) <note>Latin: "See Lightfoot, *A Chorographical Century on Matthew*, Preface, ch. 1. Buxtorf, *Talmudic Lexicon* under the word <term>עבר</term> (transgression or intercalation)."</note>
