<margin>v. 40, 43. Males) This is how all the firstborn are to be understood.</margin>

<margin>v. 41. I am the Lord) He who has the right and power to demand it.</margin>

The cattle of the Levites) Not that it should be sacrificed, but that it, along with the Levites and for their sake, should be His.

<margin>v. 42. Moses numbered) In simple obedience, through which he was surely granted the ability to recognize the meaning and the mysteries of the Lord hidden within it.</margin>

<margin>v. 44. The Lord spoke and said) for herein out of His law emerge pure, deep wonders of mysteries, for the opening of which David prayed with good reason. Psalm 119:18.</margin>

<margin>v. 45. The exchange of the firstborn of Israel was a sign of wrath, as noted in Ezekiel, where it actually says: "And I defiled them with their own gifts, in that they set apart all that opens the womb." ch. 20:26. From this, one can conclude that the firstborn were rejected from the sacrificial service, as noted in Exodus 24:5, and now here all the Levites were chosen for the service of the Lord, while the descendants of Aaron alone were chosen for the priesthood out of all Israel. This also points toward the wonderful separation at the end, when the firstborn of the Spirit—as true Levites who, according to the meaning of the word, have clung to the Lord and become one spirit with Him, 1 Corinthians 6:17—shall also be assigned to the Lord from the whole multitude as the firstfruits of God’s creatures, James 1:18. They shall be with the Lord always, 1 Thessalonians 4:17, and thus serve the Lord in the essential sanctuary for all eternity, as the congregation of the firstborn who are written in heaven, and thus also numbered by name and inscribed in the Book of Life. Hebrews 12:23, Philippians 4:3. In this context, the correspondence of the 22,300 (the actual number of Levites) with the 22,273 firstborn in Israel—differing by only 27—may contain something mysterious regarding the wonderful providence of God in the births of men, and especially His own people. See Isaiah 40:26.</margin>

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter IV.

46. But as for the two hundred seventy-three who must be redeemed, who are in excess of the Levites from the firstborn of the children of Israel;

47. You shall take five shekels per head: according to the shekel of the sanctuary you shall take it. The shekel is twenty gerahs.

48. And you shall give the money to Aaron and his sons from those redeemed who were in excess of them.

49. So Moses took the redemption money from those who were in excess over those redeemed by the Levites.

50. From the firstborn of the children of Israel he took the money, one thousand three hundred and sixty-five, according to the shekel of the sanctuary.

51. And Moses gave the money from those redeemed to Aaron and his sons according to the command of the Lord, as the Lord had commanded Moses.

---

v. 46. Origen <note>original: "Origenes" (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar.</note> (a) gives some traces of this with these words: "Do you think that Moses intended to report through this the mere history of the census, and that under this diversity of numbers no mystery is hidden, as he is otherwise accustomed to do? Should there be no secret cause behind why the number of the firstborn of Israel exceeds by only 273, and for the Levites it is set exactly at 22,000? Once one pays attention, they will find that the number 22 in Holy Scripture is often attributed to principal matters. Just as among the Hebrews there are 22 letters in the alphabet. So it is also reported that from the first father Adam until Jacob, from whose seed the 12 tribes have their origin, 22 fathers or generations were counted. It is also held that the species of all God's creatures are comprised in the number 22. And many other things will be discovered rich in mystery under this number in Scripture by anyone who pays close attention.
"But the birth of the human race in the flesh is also (as those experienced in such things confirm) hidden for 9 months in the mother, and is said not to move toward birth until another 3 days in the 10th month have passed. And thus it becomes evident that the number 273 indicates those days which come out of 9 months and 3 days, and thus from that become the 273 days after which the human race is permitted entrance into this world. Thus, in this surplus found among the firstborn of Israel, the mystery of human birth is expressed." <note>Origen is using "biblical numerology" to link the 273 extra people to the typical number of days in a human pregnancy.</note>

v. 47. 5 shekels of the sanctuary) Is two and a half Reichsthaler. <note>The Reichsthaler was a standard silver coin in the Holy Roman Empire at the time of this translation.</note>
Gerah) Was approximately as much as 9 Heller. <note>The Heller was a small German copper coin of low value.</note>

v. 49. From those who were in excess) The question arises: how could Moses have known which ones they were? For every man, upon the demand for redemption money, could have said he was one of those redeemed by a Levite. To this, the Hebrews (b) give the report: Moses made 22,000 slips and on each wrote: **Levite.** Similarly, he made 273 slips and wrote upon them: **Five Shekels.** All these slips he put together in a pot and let each of the firstborn draw out one slip. Whoever got one where "Levite" was written, him he declared free. The others, however, had to give their redemption money.

v. 50. 1365 shekels) makes 682 and a half Reichsthaler.

## Chapter IV.
->The Service of the Levites at the Tabernacle during Travel.<-

1. AND the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:

2. Take the sum of the sons of Kohath from among the sons of Levi, by their families, by the house of their fathers;

3. From thirty years old and upward, and even to fifty years old, all who come to the service to do the work in the Tabernacle of the Meeting. (a) ch. 8:25.

4. This shall be the service of the sons of Kohath in the Tabernacle of the Meeting: namely, the Most Holy things.

---

The service of the Kohathites at the Sanctuary during travel is the first thing described here.

v. 2. Take the sum) Again, by another method of counting. <note>This census was specifically for those eligible for physical labor, rather than just a general count of the tribe.</note>

v. 3. From 30 years) Namely, for this specific service; but from the 25th year onward, they were trained in other Levite duties. ch. 8:24.
For carrying, no one was to be accepted before he had full strength. Which teaches us how teachers should also rightly have reached their mature years before they enter such an important office: just as Christ also did not begin his teaching office until His 30th year. Luke 3:23.
Practiced senses are required to worthily manage the great office of the Lord and His service. And how few, a still-living theologian cries out, are fit for it! Oh, how many are the unfit who yet press themselves into it, or are so disorderly chosen for it by others! What else has become of it but a great disorder and a wild, desolate wasteland! Should not the lowliest layman, who has the anointing from GOD and is anointed with His Spirit, be better and more skilled for the service of GOD than the fleshly priest who is ignorant in the ways of GOD and only externally learned according to the letter? <note>This is a critique of the established clergy of the author's time, contrasting academic learning with spiritual "anointing."</note>

v. 4. The Most Holy) The Ark, the Table of Showbread, the Lampstand, the golden and iron altars, along with the vessels of the Tabernacle. Which, however, are not to be considered solely externally according to the letter, but rather how they point us to higher things than they themselves are, of which they were only figures and images. Heb. 8:5, 9:23. The Ark is the Glory, that is, the Son of God. 1 Sam. 4:22, Heb. 1:3, Luke 2:32. The golden altar of incense signifies the Spirit of prayer, Zech. 12:10, which teaches us to light incense, that is, to pray to the Father. Ps. 141:2, Rom. 8:26. The Bread of the Presence <term>Showbread</term> points to the presence of GOD in and with His people, and His people in Him. The Lampstand holds before us the Word and light of life, which is held and presented by the Church; which is therefore also called a lampstand. The iron altar signifies the spirit of patience, through which we mortify the deeds of the body. Rom. 8:13. Christ Himself is explicitly called the "Most Holy" in Dan. 9:24.

### Chapter IV. The Fourth Book of Moses. 569

5. Then Aaron and his sons shall go in when the camp sets out, and they shall take down the covering veil and cover the Ark of the Testimony with it;

6. And they shall put upon it the covering of badger skins, and spread over it a cloth entirely of sky-blue, and insert its poles.

7. And over the Table of Showbread they shall spread a sky-blue cloth, and place upon it the dishes, the bowls, the plates, and the flagons for the drink offering; and the continual bread shall remain upon it.

8. And they shall spread over them a crimson cloth, and cover it with a covering of badger skins, and insert its poles.

9. And they shall take a sky-blue cloth and cover the lampstand of light and its lamps, with its snuffers and its snuff-dishes, and all its oil vessels with which they tend to it:

10. And they shall put it and all its vessels into a covering of badger skins and place it upon a carrying bar.

**v. 5. And his sons)** As long as they were in the desert, where they often traveled from one place to another and had to take down, pack up, and set up the Tabernacle again, the priests were permitted—when this was to happen—to enter the Most Holy Place to cover or uncover the Ark of the Covenant. Except in this case, however, no one entered, not even the High Priest himself, except on the Day of Atonement.

**The covering veil)** This was the curtain between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place.

**v. 6. Insert its poles)** or lay them upon. Because the poles were never to be removed from the rings, nor were they to be pushed back in upon departure like the other equipment; according to the clear command in Exodus 25:15. Thus, some <note>original: "Aben Esr. ap. Buxtorff. c. 8. hist. arc. foed. quaest. 4. R. Lev. Barzelon. ap. Hotting. de jur. Hebr. n. 97." Translation: Abraham ibn Ezra as cited by Buxtorf in "History of the Ark of the Covenant," chapter 8, question 4; and Rabbi Levi of Barcelona as cited by Hottinger in "On Hebrew Law," number 97.</note> understand this to refer to the shoulders of the bearers, upon which the poles (which always remained in the rings) were to be placed at the time of departure.

**v. 7. Bowls)** For the incense. Luther translates this as "spoons" here, and in Exodus 25:29 as "cups," where all these pieces are discussed in more detail.

**v. 8. Crimson)** According to other opinions, scarlet or nacarat <note>A pale red or orange-red color, similar to mother-of-pearl.</note>.

**Badger skins)** Or, if according to another opinion <term>תחש</term> <note>Hebrew: "Tachash," a term of uncertain meaning; historically translated as "badger" or "seal," though modern scholars often suggest it refers to the color violet or the hide of a sea cow (dugong).</note> is the name of a color: beautiful sky-blue skins.

**v. 9. 10.** Only the Ark of the Covenant and the Table of Showbread were wrapped in three covers; the other vessels each had only two covers.

<column-break/>

11. And over the golden altar they shall spread a sky-blue cloth, and cover it with a covering of badger skins, and insert its poles.

12. And they shall take all the utensils of the service with which they serve in the sanctuary and put them in a sky-blue cloth, and cover them with a covering of badger skins, and place them on carrying bars.

13. They shall also remove the ashes from the altar and spread a purple cloth over it:

14. And they shall place upon it all its utensils with which they serve upon it: the firepans, the tongs, the shovels, and the sprinkling basins; all the utensils of the altar: and they shall spread over it a covering of badger skins and insert its poles.

15. When...

**v. 11—14.** Some believe that the same coverings used to cover the top of the dwelling (which served as the roof) were also used here. However, this can hardly be the case, because the Gershonites <note>The branch of Levites responsible for the curtains and coverings of the Tabernacle.</note> had those in their keeping and on their transport wagons. Furthermore, the colorful tapestries were sewn together and made only two large coverings, which could not have covered so many separate items, any more than the others could. Indeed, these coverings were not floral or multicolored like those, but only of a single color. Therefore, they were likely special covers made expressly for this particular service, so that the holy vessels would be wrapped in them upon departure; Luther calls these "garments of service" <note>original: "Amts-Kleider"</note> in Exodus 31:10, 35:19, and 39:1, 41. Josephus <note>original: "Josephus (a) l. 3. Antiq. c. 9." Referring to Flavius Josephus, "Antiquities of the Jews," Book 3, Chapter 9.</note> agrees with this when he says: "Whatever materials remained from the construction of the Tabernacle, Moses commanded that they all be used for the covers of the Tabernacle, the lampstand, the incense altar, and other vessels; so that they would not be damaged or made desolate by dust or rain during the journey."

Now, while this wrapping certainly served that purpose, this figure surely looks further: namely, that when traveling to other places in the wilderness that are not yet sanctified, one should not show and reveal the mysteries of God to everyone, but should cover them.

The Savior wants holy things to be kept holy, so that they are not made common among impure souls. Matthew 7:6 <note>"Do not give what is holy to the dogs; nor cast your pearls before swine."</note>. A priest of Christ, to whom the holy vessels—that is, the hidden mysteries of wisdom—are entrusted, can take note here of how he must preserve and veil these in the "covering of the conscience" and not immediately make them known publicly; so says Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 185–254 AD).</note>. Yet it can also happen that one might publish something of certain mysteries in general, so that it might be revealed to those to whom it belongs; just as they then soon recognize it from the spirit of prophecy given to them. Conversely, for others—and indeed for most—it remains closed and sealed, so that they do not see it although they see it, and do not understand it although they read or hear it.

In the Greek translation of the 70 Interpreters <note>The Septuagint (LXX).</note>, these words are still read in the text at the 14th verse: "And they shall take a purple cloth and cover the washbasin and its base, and shall wrap it in a covering of blue skins, and place it on poles."

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter IV.

15. **And when Aaron and his sons have finished covering the sanctuary and all the vessels of the sanctuary, when the camp sets out, after that the sons of Kohath shall come to carry them; but they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die.**

What is to be understood by the "sanctuary" or the "holy things" was partially mentioned in verse 4. <note>The author is referring to the most sacred objects like the Ark and the Altar.</note>

However, there are grades and levels of holy things, just as there are of the persons who may approach them. Some are within the veil and in the Most Holy Place; others are outside the veil. Some are great mysteries, such as the mystery of the union with GOD (Ephesians 5:32; 1 Timothy 3:16). These are called "wisdom among those who are perfect" (1 Corinthians 2:7).

Just as there were two types of holy things, so there were also two types of holy persons who were permitted to enter, draw near, and see the holy things: the High Priest and the priests of the second order. Thus, there are grades of holy persons. Some are young and weak, inexperienced in the word of righteousness; others are grown and practiced.

But why then must the holy things be covered? Answer: To some extent, there is a necessity that holy things must be hidden because they have no specific name of their own, nor any outward likeness that is unique to them, as **Dionysius the Areopagita** <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th to early 6th century.</note> says; they must borrow these from things known to us if we are to recognize anything of them. And it is an honor to divine truths that they are thus hidden in mystery. Nature has hidden its treasures from open view. The fact that gold and silver are hidden under the earth only makes them more precious and worthy. In the same way, pearls are hidden in shells under the water. And so also the Kingdom of Heaven is a precious pearl (Matthew 13:46), a treasure in "mussel-shell" vessels <note>The author uses a metaphor for "earthen vessels" here, referencing 2 Corinthians 4:7</note>, a hidden treasure in a field (Matthew 13:44), and for that reason, it is only the rarer and more valuable. Jewels and gemstones are not usually delivered openly, but in small boxes and other coverings. This is the most useful and pleasant way to convey the precious jewels of divine truth to mankind.

However, there are two kinds of coverings by which the sanctuary or holy things are covered and hidden from us. One kind was upon the holy things themselves: such as the ceremonial services in figures and types. These are the various coverings over the Ark of the Covenant, the Table of Showbread, the Altar, etc., all of which are models of heavenly things. And there, in turn, are internal and immediate coverings—such as riddles, parables, and numbers—and more external ones, like the outer coverings of the worldly sanctuary.

But there are also coverings upon *us*, by which the holy things are covered and hidden from us: partly inborn (1 Corinthians 2:14) and partly assumed and self-made. These are again of two kinds: one kind is drawn over the minds, namely the "covering of falsely-named knowledge"; the other is stubbornness and unbelief, which lies covered over the heart (2 Corinthians 3:15). From these two is braided and woven the far-reaching, thick black shroud that covers all nations (Isaiah 25:7). These coverings are patched together with great skill through the cunning of the "old serpent" <note>A biblical reference to Satan.</note>, who has invented a world full of "distinctions" through a slippery art of differentiation to hide and protect himself, without any basis in God's Word.

And what else is the ground and material of all, or at least most, disputes in the Church of GOD? Over things that are publicly known, there is no dispute among men. Whether it is day or not, no one will dispute when the sun shines clearly and brightly at high noon, except perhaps a madman or a person blind with cataracts. So there are divine truths that give testimony of themselves and therefore need no other proof. These cut off all disputes. Others, however, are secret and hidden. And over these arise so many disputes which have confused the Church of Christ at all times. The truths must therefore be "unknown" over which they dispute. For if they were known, there would certainly be no dispute about them.

<column-break/>

**This is the burden of the sons of Kohath in the Tabernacle of the Congregation.**

16. **And to the office of Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest pertain the oil for the light, and the sweet incense, and the daily grain offering, and the anointing oil: the oversight of all the tabernacle and of all that is therein, in the sanctuary and in its vessels.** (a) Chapter 3:32.

Accordingly, there is no need to quarrel over whether the Scripture is as plain and clear as many wish to claim, or not. For if it were so entirely clear, there could be no dispute at all over its subject matter. But both are true. To one, it is clear and revealed; to the other, it is dark and covered. Nevertheless, the complaint of **Jerome** <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> also has merit: that while the simplest and easiest crafts require a long time to learn the secrets contained within them, many nevertheless form such a miserable concept of the most secret "art of life" <note>Theology or spiritual living.</note>, as if it could be learned so easily.

Furthermore, it is therefore neither a defect of the Holy Scripture, nor unfounded or wrong, if one discovers within it—alongside the "letter" of external understanding—a mystical or secret, spiritual, and allegorical sense, both in the Law and the Gospel. Indeed, it is rather a great honor to follow the Lord, who speaks to us through Moses and the Prophets in this figure, and who even in the days of His flesh spoke in parables (Mark 4:34). Thus, the writings of the Apostles are also full of such explanations and interpretations; and so the dishonor and "burden" of the sons of Kohath will fall more upon those who hang solely on the "letter" and yet consider and present themselves as stewards of the mysteries of GOD (1 Corinthians 4:1).

**Kohath** means "bluntness" or "stupidity" (Ecclesiastes 10:10) and indicates metaphorically an inborn awkwardness, and even a self-caused animalistic stupidity in hearing, understanding, and perceiving spiritual things; which is described in Hebrews 5:11 and 6:12 as being "dull of hearing" and "sluggish." With such ears, eyes, and hearts, it is easy for something—or even everything—to be mystical, dark, and covered.

However, teachers, and likewise all believers as priests, should possess the mysteries of the Lord in heavenly light within their hearts. In contrast, they may have a lowly appearance from the outside because of the simplicity and renunciation of the world required of them; they carry this treasure in earthen—but not "earthly" or "earthly-minded"—vessels, which look very distorted and insignificant due to bodily tribulations (2 Corinthians 4:7, 8, 10). See also Colossians 3:3.

Although these heavenly goods of grace are not hidden for the reason that we walk here by faith and not by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 13:12).

In this, teachers must bend their shoulders under the heavy burden of the office, of which an ancient teacher once said that it would be too heavy even for the shoulders of angels. Therefore, one must work in "dark faith" and commend the success to GOD. There, "blind obedience" has its place—not as the Roman Church teaches much of it—but an obedience that must be rendered not to men, but to God and Christ, also by believers in general (Galatians 1:15, 16; 2 Corinthians 10:5).

**v. 16. The oversight of Eleazar shall be:**

Thus, the congregations always have need that the oversight of holy things be observed by capable supervisors, so that there is no lack of the light of knowledge, the spirit of grace and prayer, the care of the poor, and the various gifts of the Spirit. Therefore, believers should be concerned that capable teachers are drawn to and called into the congregations, so that they do not become as if rooted out—which happens when Christians have become "salt that has lost its flavor" (Matthew 5:13), "foolish shepherds" (Zechariah 11:15, 16), and "prophets who prophesy out of their own heart" (Ezekiel 13).

### 17. And the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:

### 18. Do not let the tribe of the families of the Kohathites be cut off from among the Levites.

### 19. But do this for them, that they may live and not die when they approach the Most Holy Place: Aaron and his sons shall go in and appoint each of them to his service and to his burden.

> GOD cares and desires care to be taken for the tribe of the Kohathites, so that the wrath of the LORD is not provoked to wipe them out through negligence or a lighthearted, improper handling of holy things. He wishes to prevent something happening similar to what already occurred in Leviticus 10:1–2 <note>This refers to Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, who were consumed by fire for offering "unauthorized fire" before the Lord.</note>, where the consequences of their burden might fall upon the heads of the others.
>
> Now, once you have understood what the order of the history intends to say, rise up to the splendor of the mystery and behold the light of the spiritual law, provided the eye of your mind has been purified for it.
>
> Whoever among those standing in the service of GOD is worthy and capable of grasping and seeing the divine mysteries—of which others are not capable—that person is a "son of Aaron." He is one who can enter where others are not permitted to go.
>
> **v. 18.** The Kohathites, however, represent people who are either in their natural state or under the Law. Therefore, they are not yet sanctified, and consequently, they are unsuited to see the covered holy things and unqualified to behold the divine mysteries (1 Corinthians 2:14). Thus, the Law and the legal services and ministers of the Law always have a view toward the Gospel.
>
> To be sure, it cannot be denied that the senses, the imagination, and the reason of "flesh and blood" <note>A common biblical idiom for human nature apart from divine grace.</note> may know much of divine truth—indeed, may even see further than some who are truly spiritually minded. But there always remains a veil over the divine matters they see, so that they cannot see the end or the innermost truth of the things they behold (2 Corinthians 3:13). They are much more like the posts and couriers who carry state secrets but have no personal knowledge of them; just as the Kohathites carried the secret holy things but did not see them.
>
> Is this not the condition of many today who wish to be teachers of the Law and the Gospel, yet do not understand what they say or affirm? (1 Timothy 1:7). Do not many read the Gospel and preach Christ—that He was born, crucified, died, buried, resurrected, and ascended—and yet understand no more than the bare letter of all these articles of faith? What more do they understand of Christ than the "stupid Kohathites" (according to the letter) recognized of the holy things they carried, which they neither touched nor saw? For what is the "letter"—which hides the Spirit from them—other than the many and various coverings of the holy things among the Kohathites? They have no spiritual, tangible, or experimental knowledge of the things they speak of (1 John 1:1).
>
> **v. 19. Aaron shall appoint them to their burden)** The wisdom and equity of the High Priest assigns to each his burden according to his strength or power and ability to carry it, so that one is not relieved while another is burdened, but that there might be an equality. This ensures there is no disorder, but that everyone may know his duty, and that no one may meddle or intrude into the work of another.

<column-break/>

### 20. But they shall not go in to see when the sanctuary is being covered, lest they die.

### 21.

> If these [the Kohathites] are not permitted to enter to see the holy things, where then shall the ungodly and the sinner remain? GOD does not throw His sanctuary or His pearls before swine. The secrets of the Kingdom and the State are not made known to strangers, much less to enemies and rebels. It does not matter that the Pharisees imagine themselves and others to be seeing, saying: "We see" (John 9:41). For this reason, they remain blind leaders.
>
> Since such people nevertheless sit in the seat of Moses and in power, the disaster caused by them is truly indescribable. For they take away the key of knowledge and do not let others enter where they themselves are not permitted to go. And because of this, it unfortunately reaches a point where
>
> **The sanctuary is covered)** <note>original: "Heiligthum einwickelt"</note>—indeed, even devoured, swallowed up, and destroyed, according to the literal meaning of the word used here. <note>The author is arguing that the Hebrew word used here for "covering" also implies consumption or destruction.</note> This word is used nowhere else in Scripture for "covering" except in this place; however, this sense is reinforced by the word used in verse 15.
>
> Both are true: Holiness, as it is properly called, is covered; and holiness is also swallowed up.
>
> But can holiness then be eaten and swallowed? Yes, can it not? If it cannot, what has become of it? Much questioning and research has been conducted regarding where the Ark of the Covenant, the golden altar, and other symbols of holy things have gone. But who searches for the holy things themselves? Who asks after GOD? Where, oh where, has the glory of GOD, the beauty of holiness, gone? It has been taken captive by the Philistines! The earthly spirits have swallowed up and buried the beauty of holiness! Is not the Son of GOD, the Holy and Most Holy One, swallowed up in the heart of earthly man? An "evil beast" has devoured Joseph (Genesis 37:33), or the perfection of life! Satan has had his servants in all ages who have eaten and swallowed up holiness and GOD's holy people. And what they do not destroy, they dismiss as error, heresy, and false doctrine, robbing us of our good name and credit. Thus, holiness and those who carry it—that is, those who teach that Joseph or perfection still lives, that the life of GOD from which we were alienated is to be regained, that the Most Holy One, namely Jesus Christ, should appear in our mortal flesh (2 Corinthians 4:11)—must walk under a cloud of harsh discipline, shame, and blasphemy. It is a great mercy of GOD if they are not entirely swallowed up and devoured by liars, evil beasts, and "lazy gluttons" (Titus 1:12).
>
> Because that which has been thus "devoured" is hidden from our eyes, the word also means "to cover." Regarding the matter itself, enough was said at verse 15. Here the only question remaining is: Can holiness and holy things be seen again, and how does one attain and reach them? Answer: Not through innate cleverness or the eager searching of one's own power and ability. No one may see the holy things unless the Holy One grants them to be seen and reveals them. And the great Distributor of secrets hides them from the wise and prudent and reveals them to babes. When we turn to the Lord, when we allow ourselves to be born again through the Word of life and the Spirit of the Son, then the veil is taken away (2 Corinthians 3:16). But we must first and above all things
>
> **Die)** The Most Holy GOD and His "Holiness of Holinesses" cannot be seen by any others than those who are like Him. This is the primary purpose of true religion: that it wishes to make us like GOD. and in what else but in holiness and righteousness? Otherwise, we cannot see the Most Holy GOD and His holiness within ourselves. Just as GOD is Light and Life, so the Light and Life of GOD is required to see GOD and divine things. As GOD is pure and holy, only those who are pure in heart can see Him. Therefore, holiness is required above all things. The first part of holiness is the separation from all uncleanness of the flesh and spirit. When this has happened, the second part takes its place. This consists of spiritual dying. When the sinful life is killed, only then do we see our GOD (Exodus 33:20). This is a death that must necessarily precede the beholding of the Most High GOD and His most holy things. Through this "dying with Christ," the curtain is torn, and we see the Most Holy Place.

<insert>
From this it appears sufficiently clear that there were orders and ranks of the servants of the Temple in the Old Testament; some who assigned the loads, and others who carried the loads assigned to them. And because the Law was pregnant with the Gospel, there must also be ranks and orders among the servants under the Gospel: because both represent the ranks and orders found among the angels. However, those who have improperly forced themselves into these services, or who stand unworthily within them, should not presume to claim these ranks for themselves.

Just as this service and office of the Levites was a permanent thing among the clans in the Old Testament, so too in the New Testament, those who hold the lesser offices—especially the instruction of children and the youth, which is a very laborious task—can, if they serve well, "purchase to themselves a good degree" and "great boldness in the faith which is in Christ Jesus" (1 Timothy 3:13): namely, to also serve in the precious office of an overseer <note>The term "overseer" here relates to the biblical "Episkopos" or Bishop.</note> and teacher in the congregation.

<insert>
Just as the Gershonites and Merarites had their different duties for the Tabernacle and had to attend to the lesser things, so it should also be arranged in the congregations: that the instruction of youth by servants or capable schoolmasters, and the temporal wealth—without which the service of the Gospel and its requirements cannot be managed, especially in the currently still imperfect state of the congregations—may be administered by faithful stewards.

**v. 30. The service to perform the work of the Tabernacle)** This must not be understood as if they had anything to do inside the Holy Place like the priests once the Tabernacle was set up. For there was nothing for the Levites to do in the Holy Place, except only during the departure, after everything had first been wrapped up. In the courtyard, however, once the Tabernacle was set up and the divine service was in full swing, they had much to do and had to assist the priests. Regarding the rest of the dwelling, they indeed had enough to do inside and out, but only during the departure and the re-erection of the Tabernacle; for then they had to perform everything and take everything apart or put it together.

**v. 31. Oversight of their load)** It is indeed said in verse 25 of the Gershonites that they "carried" their things; which word was also inserted here by Luther: but this cannot be understood otherwise than carrying things from the Tabernacle to the freight wagons. For the Kohathites alone carried their items the whole way <note>The Kohathites carried the most sacred objects on their shoulders, while the other clans used wagons for the heavy boards and curtains.</note>.

**v. 32. Assign by name)** To each man, during the departure, his specific items were assigned and written down, and upon the re-erection, everything had to be delivered again exactly and completely.
The boards of the sanctuary were also marked with letters during the departure—each board with a specific letter—so that upon re-erection they would know where the boards belonged together and where each one should stand.

> The Levitical office is a laborious office, a service, and a burden; and in this, it is an image of Christianity, in which all and everyone who confesses it in deed and truth must take up no small burden, toil, and labor through the wilderness of this world, and must carry the dear Cross, nor can they be rid of it until they come into the promised land of the heavenly Canaan. On one hand, they must be like the Kohathites, **Christ-bearers** <note>original: "Christophori"</note>, and carry Christ, the Holy and Most Holy, in their hearts: on the other hand, like the Gershonites and Merarites, they must be **Cross-bearers** <note>original: "Crucigeri"</note>.
>
> There is neither equality nor fairness in a situation where one man must carry the burden of two men. Therefore, better services are nowhere to be sought or found than with Christ, whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light. Matthew 11:30.

> Since over eight and a half thousand <note>original: "neunthalb-tausend"; an archaic German expression for 8,500, approximating the total of 8,580</note> Levites served at this Tabernacle of Meeting; and indeed an entire people, which was over six hundred thousand men of war alone, had to be served in the sacrificial worship and other holy things imposed by God, they certainly had their share of work. Thus, one should also observe a consistent and sufficient provision for the congregations in spiritual service; however, a great negligence is mostly found therein, so that often a spiritual pastor or teacher has to serve several hundred souls, and some "Gershonite" or school-servant <note>The author compares modern school assistants to the Gershonites who assisted the priests</note>—of whom very few are truly capable, as is the case with the former—has to serve over fifty or more children, who cannot possibly all be cared for in spiritual matters as would be fair. Thus, the complaint of our Savior has also come to fulfillment here: The harvest is truly great, but the laborers are few. <header>The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter V.</header>

# The Fifth Chapter.

->The purity of the camp, the restitution of guilt, and the law of jealousy regarding a suspected wife.<-

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Command the children of Israel that they put out of the camp every leper, and everyone who has a discharge, and whoever is defiled by a dead body.
3. Both male and female you shall put out; outside the camp you shall put them, that they do not defile their camps, where I dwell in the midst of them.
4. And the children of Israel did so, and put them outside the camp; as the Lord spoke to Moses, so the children of Israel did.
5. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
6. Speak to the children of Israel:

From this it now becomes even more clear that the word given through the numbers in the preceding chapters can and must be understood just as much, and even more so, as a "mustering" and "inspecting" or "visitation." <note>The author argues that the census was not just for counting people, but for assessing their spiritual and ritual fitness.</note> For, after this has occurred, the Lord now gives the command on how the camp is to be purified, both from physical defilement and from the defilement of the soul; which is then partly ceremonial and partly moral, concerning the conduct of one's life.

The Lord desires to keep his militant Church here below on earth pure, so that she permits no access to the fellowship of the mysteries of the Gospel to those who are spiritually leprous, those stuck in blood-guilt, or those who have fellowship with the dead works of darkness. Just as the Apostle enumerates various kinds of such unclean people with whom one should not even associate or eat; and therefore makes the conclusion: "Put away from yourselves that wicked person!" 1 Cor. 5:9–13.

v. 2. **Outside the camp)** The lepers were cast out of the entire great camp, which consisted of three different camps, and were not permitted to approach the camp of the children of Israel, so that they would not infect anyone; much less the camp of the priests and Levites, and least of all the camp of God or the Tabernacle of Meeting.

v. 3. **Outside the camp)** Those who were afflicted by a discharge with coarse impurity were excluded from the two inner camps and were not allowed to come into the camp of the Levites or to the Sanctuary, though they could remain in the camp of the 12 tribes of Israel, because they did not infect others.

v. 4. **Outside the camp)** Whoever had defiled himself by a dead body, or was otherwise afflicted with a minor impurity, was excluded only from the camp of God. The other two camps, however, were not forbidden to him. This is how these words are to be understood.

According to this division, they later divided Jerusalem into three parts, and as it were into three camps: so that every unclean person would know how far he was permitted or forbidden to come. The Temple itself, with the courts of the priests and of Israel up to the gate facing east, was called the "Camp of the Divine Majesty." The outer court and the Temple Mount were called the "Levites' Camp." The third part was the city of Jerusalem itself and was called the "Camp of Israel." (a)

<margin>(a) Selden, *On Natural Law and the Law of Nations among the Hebrews*, book 3, chapter 6. <note>original: "Selden. de J. N. & G. l. 3. c. 6." refers to John Selden's 1640 work on Jewish law.</note></margin>

<column-break/>

When a man or woman shall have committed any sin against a person, acting unfaithfully against the Lord, and that soul has become guilty;

7. Then they shall confess their sin which they have done, and he shall restore his guilt in its principal sum, and add the fifth part more to it, and give it to the one against whom he has trespassed.
<margin>Leviticus 5:21–26.</margin>

Although human weaknesses are not to be understood here—by which one might sin against God alone in particular, Ps. 51:6, even if one had not trespassed against any person—it is clear enough that sins committed against people are to be understood here. Yet, certainly, with all sins against one's neighbor, unfaithfulness is simultaneously committed against God, who has so earnestly commanded us to love: to love one's neighbor as oneself. 1 Cor. 10:24.

v. 6. **Sin committed against a person)** is either through violence or fraud.

O, that men and women would let themselves be advised against their profit-seeking sins, which the Lord watches so closely! For commonly, he who does wrong to his neighbor has the intention of increasing his own goods.

**Acted unfaithfully against the Lord)** The two tables of the Law are not so separated and divided that only the first contains our duties and obligations toward God, while the other aims merely at our neighbor and the duties of men toward one another. Rather, the second table also certainly contains duties toward God and forbids the transgression of them. The heavenly Father must be honored according to the 5th Commandment as much as the physical father—indeed, above all things. Spiritual murder and "crucifying Christ in us" is certainly also forbidden in the 5th Commandment. And through the 7th, spiritual adultery against God is forbidden just as much as physical adultery against our neighbor. For this very reason, the tables were written on both sides. Exod. 32.

How highly the Lord God prizes brotherly love, faithfulness, and the resulting sincere dealings of one person with another can be gathered from the fact that He counts the breach of these—through unjust dealing—as being done to Himself.

v. 7. **He shall restore his guilt)** A person may well fall into debt/guilt: but how he should extricate himself from it and how he should pay it; that is the question. We can quickly go astray and sink down to hell: but how we shall come up again is another question.

What then should the unfaithful sinner do? Alas, he is bankrupt, just as he is wretched, poor, and needy! And what answers to this, according to which it is meant in the most literal and deepest sense:

**In his Head [principal sum])** <note>The author makes a theological pun on the German word "Hauptsumma" (principal sum). Since "Haupt" means "head," he links the repayment of the debt to Christ, who is the "Head" of the Church.</note> And who else is this but Christ? 1 Cor. 11:3, Eph. 1:22, 5:23, Col. 1:18. This is the ransom money which God finds upon man's recognition and confession of his sins. Job 33:23–24, Rom. 3.

**The 5th part more)** By which we may understand everything that is above that which is elementary, visible, and of the lower world; everything that is holy, righteous, good, wise, merciful, gentle, kind, venerable, and excellent. <note>In traditional cosmology, there were four physical elements; the "fifth part" or "quintessence" represented the spiritual or heavenly realm.</note> Yes, and infinitely more is to be attributed to Him against whom we have sinned. To Him be glory, majesty, and splendor, in and among all His creatures, and may all lands be full of His glory!

**v. 14. The spirit of jealousy comes upon him)** The question arises: how do the Jews today deal with suspicious wives? Answer: If today a Jew says to his wife, "Beware that I do not see you with so-and-so again!" and he encounters them both despite his prohibition, or hears of it from others, then he divorces her, and she may marry whom she wishes, except for the one with whom she was under suspicion (a).

But if she was with him in secret, the husband no longer associated with her alone, but rented her a separate house and let her eat there by herself, being near her only in the presence of his children or household members. As soon as the complaint was received, the man was told to step aside, and they spoke to the woman very movingly, saying that if she were guilty, she should confess openly and not let it come down to the drinking [of the bitter water]. "Dear daughter!" they would say, "perhaps wine is to blame for your slip, or your childish youth. Perhaps godless neighbors gave you the occasion for it. All who were present also surrounded her to frighten the poor woman, so that she would not know which way to turn.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter V.

17. And the priest shall take holy water in an earthen vessel; and the priest shall take of the dust that is on the floor of the Tabernacle and put it into the water.

18. And the priest shall set the woman before the face of the **LORD**, and shall uncover the woman’s head, and shall put the grain offering of memorial, which is a grain offering of jealousy, into her hands: and the priest shall have in his hand the bitter water that brings the curse.

19. And the priest shall charge her by an oath, and say to the woman: "If no man has lain with you, and if you have not gone aside to uncleanness while under your husband’s authority; may you be free from this bitter water that brings the curse!"

<column-break/>

20. "But if you have gone aside while under your husband’s authority and if you have been defiled, so that some man has had sexual intercourse with you besides your husband;"

21. "Then the priest shall charge the woman with an oath of cursing, and the priest shall say to the woman: 'The **LORD** make you a curse and an oath among your people, when the **LORD** shall make your thigh fall away and your belly swell!'"

22. "'That this water that brings the curse may enter into your bowels, to make the belly swell and the thigh fall away.'" And the woman shall say: "Amen, Amen!"

23. And the priest shall write these curses on a scroll, and wash them off into the bitter water;

24. And he shall give the woman the bitter water that brings the curse to drink, so that the water that brings the curse enters into her for bitterness.

<meta>catchword: 25. An-</meta>

---

<margin>**v. 17. Holy Water)**</margin> The priest had to take this from the bronze sea <note>The "bronze sea" or "laver" was a large basin in the Temple court used for ritual washing.</note> or the washbasin, and pour it
<margin>**Into an earthen vessel)**</margin> a new earthen bowl.
<margin>**Of the dust on the floor of the Tabernacle)**</margin> In the Temple, there was a small pit on the right side in the Holy Place covered with a marble stone; he would lift it by its ring and take some dust from it. If there was none inside, he could put some in, provided it came from that spot.
<margin>**Put it into the water)**</margin> He scattered just enough on top of the water so that it could be seen, yet she could still drink it. He could also put the dust into the bowl first.

<margin>**v. 18. When the woman had come directly opposite the Temple,**</margin> the priest appointed for this task would seize her clothes and uncover her to her shame, even down to her bare breast; it did not matter if the clothes were torn in the process. He also removed her veil and her bonnet from her head and unbraided her hair, so that she stood there with her hair flying about, looking quite ghastly and abominable. She was also dressed in black, and all her jewelry and finery were removed. If she had been wearing clean black clothes before, they were replaced with ugly ones. He girded her torn clothes over her breasts with bast <note>A strong plant fiber often used for rope.</note> or a willow band so they would not fall off. All this happened publicly in the presence of all the people; indeed, the women had to be there and watch, so they might see her as a mirror for themselves. Only the servants of the accused woman were not permitted to watch, so that the woman would have no comfort or refreshment from their sight: for this reason, they also never gave the drink to two such suspected women at the same time.
<margin>**Put the grain offering into her hands)**</margin> The husband brought it in a willow basket: he gave her the basket with the flour into her hands; the woman then had to hold it in her hands the entire time, so that she would also be exhausted by it.
<margin>**The bitter water)**</margin> Which, according to the most thorough judgment, was so named because of its bitter and terrifying effect. Naturally, it could not have tasted well because of the dust and the ink that was mixed into it.

<margin>**v. 19. Here the priest admonished her once more,**</margin> that she should consider what she was doing, etc. If even this did not help, he swore her in her mother tongue with the words of this verse.

<margin>**v. 20. Under your husband)**</margin> The oath did not include anything she might have committed before her betrothal; nor if she had been cast out by a bill of divorce and he later desired her back, being unaware that she had behaved improperly in the interim.

<margin>**v. 21. Belly swell)**</margin> Josephus <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>original: "L. 3. Antiq. c. 10." Referring to Josephus’ *Antiquities of the Jews*.</note> understands this to mean that she became dropsical <note>Suffering from "dropsy" or edema, an accumulation of fluid in the body.</note>.

<margin>**v. 22. The woman shall say: Amen! Amen!)**</margin> With this double "Amen," she cursed herself if she were guilty.

<margin>**v. 23. On a scroll)**</margin> Not on paper, but on a piece of parchment prepared from a clean animal.
<margin>**Write)**</margin> With a unique ink made from the smoke of oil, pitch, or wax, which was allowed to smoke into a glass vessel and collected; this was worked through with honey until it could be broken into small pieces and dried, and then softened and dissolved again with gall-apple water. No vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate often used in permanent inks.</note> or anything of the kind was to be added, so that the writing would not eat into the parchment, but could be easily erased and rinsed off. The priest was not to write until after the oath had been taken: nor was he to write as they usually do, from the right hand to the left, but vertically in a long way down. There are a total of 54 words in this Hebrew oath, arranged in three columns side by side, with 18 words in each column <gloss>(b)</gloss> <note>original: "vid. Wagenfeil. Mischn. Sot. c. 2. p. 363." Referring to Johann Christoph Wagenseil’s commentary on the Mishnah tractate *Sotah*.</note>.

<margin>**v. 24. Give the bitter water to drink)**</margin> It is said to also be the custom on the Gold Coast of Guinea that if a man or woman is suspected of some vice, primarily adultery, and there is no certain or convincing evidence, then their <term>Fetissero</term> <note>A priest or sorcerer; the term comes from the Portuguese word for "fetish" or "charm."</note> or priest performs a special test to bring out the truth, also using a bitter water he has prepared. If the person refuses to take this water, they are immediately declared guilty. But if they take it and are guilty, their belly swells so much that it bursts. If they are innocent, no harm comes to them. Meanwhile, those who must undergo this test are usually so fearful that they would rather take the usual punishment and allow themselves to be sold to Europeans as slaves <gloss>(c)</gloss> <note>original: "Dampier Tom. III." Referring to the explorer William Dampier’s account of his voyages.</note>.

<note>Footnotes at page bottom:</note>
<gloss>(a) Book 3, Antiquities, chapter 10.</gloss>
<gloss>(b) For how it was written, see Wagenseil, Mishnah Sotah, chapter 2, page 363; and from him, Lund, Jewish Sanctuaries, book 3, chapter 55, number 40.</gloss>
<gloss>(c) Dampier, Volume III of his Voyage Around the World.</gloss>

### Chapter V. The Fourth Book of Moses.

25. And the priest shall take the grain offering of jealousy from the woman’s hand, and wave the grain offering before the face of the **LORD**, and offer it upon the altar.
26. And the priest shall take a handful of the grain offering as a memorial offering, and burn it upon the altar, and afterward give the woman the water to drink.
27. And when he has given her the water to drink, it shall happen, if she has been defiled and has acted unfaithfully toward her husband, that the water that brings the curse shall enter into her for bitterness, so that her belly shall swell and her thigh shall fall away; and the woman shall become a curse among her people.

<margin>v. 25.</margin> The husband took the barley meal from the woman’s hand and placed it in a holy vessel; he then gave it back into the woman’s hand. At that point, the priest placed his hand beneath the woman’s hand and waved it with her before God the **LORD**.
<margin>v. 26. Handful)</margin> Whatever remained belonged to the priest, unless the husband himself was a priest, in which case it was entirely burned.
<margin>Afterward—give to drink)</margin> From this, some conclude that the offering came first, by which the woman was exhorted one last time to confess, and the husband was given a chance to see if he might set aside his spirit of jealousy.
When the offering was completed, the priest took the water mixed with dust back into his hand and rinsed the written curse from the parchment into it, so that not a single letter remained on the parchment.
However, if the woman finally confessed before the drinking and the offering, the offering was burned on the ash heap, and the writing was set aside and preserved; yet it could not be used for any other woman, for a specific scroll was written for each individual. If she confessed after the writing had been rinsed away, the water was poured out. But if she refused to confess or drink even then, she was compelled to do so by force.
<margin>v. 27.</margin> If she was indeed guilty, she felt **God’s** visible punishment immediately after drinking. Even before she finished drinking, her face would turn blue, her eyes would begin to swell, her cheeks would puff up and become full of veins, and her whole flesh became wrinkled. Whereupon they cried out: "Thrust her out! Thrust her out, so that she does not defile the courtyard!" for she usually did not survive much longer.
The Hebrew scholars also write that the adulterer with whom she had sinned died at the very same hour she died, no matter where he happened to be, suffering exactly what she suffered.
Since the question is asked why the woman did not have the same right to accuse her suspicious husband, it is answered—not without reason—that a woman's adultery is far more detrimental to the marriage state, because through it, children may be brought to the husband of whom he does not know, nor can be certain, that they are his own.

<column-break/>

28. But if the woman has not been defiled and is clean, she shall be free and shall be able to conceive children.
29. This is the law of jealousy, when a woman goes astray under her husband and is defiled:
30. Or when the spirit of jealousy comes upon a man, and he is jealous of his wife, and sets the woman before the face of the **LORD**, and the priest performs all this law upon her.
31. And the man shall be guiltless of iniquity, but the woman shall bear her iniquity.

<margin>v. 28. But if the woman—is clean)</margin> Nevertheless, she was not permitted to be found again with the suspect in a secret place against her husband's prohibition; otherwise, she was still cast out. And if it happened with another man against her husband's prohibition, she had to drink again. <note>original: "(a) Selden. ux. Ebr. l. 3. c. 13." Referring to John Selden's "The Hebrew Wife," Book 3, Chapter 13.</note>
Meanwhile, even innocent women did not like to drink this water, and many would have preferred death to such public shame, had it been up to them.
<margin>She shall be free)</margin> What is particularly remarkable is that, as the Hebrew scholars likewise report, such bitter waters did not manifest their power even on an unchaste woman if the husband himself was not chaste but was himself given to unclean ways. Therefore, when adulterers became numerous in Israel, a certain Rabbi—with the consent of the high council in Jerusalem during the time of the Second Temple—abolished the use of the bitter waters. <note>original: "(b) Wagenseil. Sota p. 594. sqq. & 928. sqq." Referring to Johann Christoph Wagenseil's commentary on the Talmudic tractate "Sotah" (The Suspected Adulteress).</note>
<margin>v. 29. 30. Husband and wife)</margin> Some note regarding the Hebrew words that *Isch* <note>original: "Isch" (אִישׁ), meaning man.</note>, the man, and *Ischah* <note>original: "Ischah" (אִשָּׁה), meaning woman.</note>, a woman, contain the letters *i* and *h* within them; these two together make up *Jah* <note>original: "Jah" (יָהּ)</note>, the name of the **LORD**. As long as the husband and wife have the name of the **LORD** within them—meaning they fear **GOD** and love one another—the **LORD** is with them and helps them. But if they forget the **LORD** and hate one another, the name *Jah* is lost, and what remains for each is only *esch*, *esch*; fire, fire <note>original: "esch" (אֵשׁ), meaning fire</note>—the fire of quarrel and strife, and the fire of the fierce wrath and displeasure of **GOD** in and upon them.
<margin>v. 31.</margin> However, since **GOD** nowadays no longer desires such visible demands for His vengeance, no such signs are ordained for it. Rather, the trials ordained in corrupt times—such as by boiling water or glowing iron and the like—are instead "temptations of **GOD**," through which innocent people may lose their lives due to hidden causes. Therefore, in such doubtful cases, one should leave vengeance to **GOD** and be more inclined toward forgiveness than toward strict investigation; especially since all sins, even those that slip through here, will be rebuked in eternity! It would be enough if only the manifest sins were properly punished here.
Furthermore, since the Jews in Christ’s presence cried out: "We have no king but Caesar!" (John 19:15) and thus made themselves guilty of spiritual adultery, the righteous spirit of jealousy surely entered into their lawful King and Husband. He gave them such a bitter cup of the water of tribulations to drink, by which all the curses written in the Law entered into them, so that their loins and all their strength vanished, even though their "belly" swelled—meaning they became a great multitude upon the earth.
But all those who love the world while professing Christ must also take note of this with terror (James 4:4). When tribulations come, they bring the curse: and the great wealth with which one has filled the belly, while the strength of the spirit has vanished, will then reveal a great feebleness.

<header>The IV. Book of Moses. Chapter VI.</header>

# Chapter VI.

->The Law of the Nazirites and the Blessing.<-

1. AND the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When a man or woman shall make a special vow of a Nazirite <note>The term "Nazirite" comes from the Hebrew *nazir*, meaning "consecrated" or "separated."</note> to separate themselves unto the **LORD**;
3. He shall abstain from wine and strong drink <margin>(a) Judges 13:14.</margin>: He shall drink no wine vinegar nor vinegar of strong drink; nor shall he drink any juice of grapes: and he shall eat neither fresh nor dried grapes.

---

This Nazirite state was a voluntary way of life, which God did not expressly command, but which He nevertheless took pleasure in when it was done out of a pure and good intention, so that some might present themselves blameless and chaste in body and spirit.

However, so that they would not fall into a self-chosen form of worship, He gave certain rules for it.

Namely, if someone wanted to vow a particularly holy life to God, three things were required of him: abstinence from wine and everything that came from it; that no razor should come upon his head; and that he should not come near any dead person in the slightest. If someone died unexpectedly beside him, the vow had to be renewed with certain sacrifices. And since the vows were made for a certain time, they had to bring almost all types of sacrifices upon their completion, in order to be publicly released from their vow by the priest.

<term>v. 2. Man or Woman)</term> A male person was not permitted to make a vow before his 13th year; a female person, however, could do so when she was 10 years and one day old (a).

A father could also overturn the vow of his son, and a husband the vow of his wife.

Similarly, parents could vow their children, as happened with Samuel: 1 Sam. 1:11. And some were set apart for His service by an extraordinary revelation from the **LORD**, who were thus the "Set-Apart" or "Vowed ones of the **LORD**"; such as Samson, Judges 13:5, and John the Baptist, Luke 1:15.

According to the report of the Hebrews, if a father wished to vow his minor son (before he reached his 13th year and one day) to the **LORD**, and said in the presence of his relatives, "This my son shall be a Nazirite," or addressed the son himself, "You, my son, shall be a Nazirite," and the relatives remained silent, the son was bound to the **LORD** and had to keep the vow made by the father. The mother, however, did not have this power.

<term>Nazirite</term> <note>original: "Naziräer"</note> is, according to the word, the same as "one who is set apart" in German. It generally signifies a person who is separated from the common way of life and spends his time in a sober, secluded, and pure life, in contemplation of the divine will, the works, and the blessings of God, serving his God in a quiet manner, and thus is holy to the **LORD**. (v. 8).

<term>Shall vow)</term> Many did this in times of need, such as when someone became ill or had some other distress (b).

<term>v. 3. From Wine)</term> Which is a figure of earthly lust and joy, and also of earthly human wisdom.

<term>From strong drink)</term> Which the Karaites <note>A Jewish sect that follows the written Torah strictly, rejecting the oral tradition or Talmud.</note> or Sadducees understand to mean all intoxicating drinks, including mead or cider; other Hebrews, however, understand it only as that which comes from the grapevine.

<term>Juice of grapes)</term> Since wine itself is nothing other than the juice of grapes, and was already mentioned, others understand this word to mean water in which grapes have been soaked and thereby colored. And what else is forbidden by this, except that along with the use of wine, everything attached or belonging to it is also forbidden?

<meta>(a) Drus. ad loc. diffic. Num. 6. 21.</meta>

<column-break/>

4. All the days of his separation he shall eat nothing that is made of the grapevine, from the seeds even to the skins.
5. All the days of the vow of his separation no razor shall pass over his head: until the days are fulfilled in which he has separated himself to the **LORD**, he shall be holy, and shall let the locks of the hair on his head grow.
6. All the days that he separates himself to the **LORD**, he shall go to no dead body.
7. <unclear>...</unclear>

---

<term>v. 4. Separation)</term> <note>original: "Enthaltung"</note> was that in which the entire order of the Nazirites consisted. And although it required the ceremony of abstaining from certain things, the substance and essence indicated the sanctification and dedication of a person who gave themselves to God.

<term>Skins)</term> Raisins.

<term>v. 5. All the days of the vow)</term> There were two kinds of Nazirites. Some were so for their entire life; others only for a certain time. Of the former, the Old Testament Scripture names two: Samson and Samuel. In the New Testament, there is John the Baptist.

Those who were so only for a certain time often set themselves apart by a vow: which, if no specific time was named, lasted 30 days. If one wished to vow for longer, they were free to choose as long as they wanted: but not under 30 days. (a)

This number of days should, as the learned Jews interpret, be meant in the word <term>jihjech</term>. <note>Hebrew: "He shall be." The numeric value of the letters in this Hebrew word (Yod-He-Yod-He) is often interpreted kabbalistically, though the commentator here links it to the duration of the vow.</note>

<term>He shall be)</term> Because in such a word the number 30 is contained.

<term>Let the locks of hair grow)</term> Thus, the Nazirites of Israel otherwise did not wear long hair, but while they did not shave it completely smooth, they cut it quite short, so that it did not even peek out from under the hat or turban.

But when someone wore long hair, it was a sign that he was a Nazirite. (b)

By this wearing of hair, the Nazirite had power upon his head, like the woman in 1 Cor. 11:10, and thereby testified his submission to God. These respected the will of God and are therefore occupied in contemplation of the law day and night. Ps. 1:2.

Some also surmise from various places in Scripture, and especially from the example of John the Baptist, that they had their outer garments made of coarse, rough, and hairy material, even black in color, like Elijah in 2 Kings 1:8 and other prophets. Zech. 13:4, Heb. 11:37.

<term>v. 6. To no dead body)</term> This does not seem to have been forbidden to the lifelong Nazirites, but only to the others. For the former did not observe it, as for example Samson in Judges 14:8, 9, 19, and Samuel in 1 Sam. 15.

Strictly speaking, it says: "to no dead soul": and it follows from this that there are dead souls. And indeed all too many. Namely, just as natural death is the separation of the soul from the body, so spiritual death is nothing other than the separation of the spirit of life from the soul.

> (a) see Josephus, in the cited place; Selden, on succession in the high priesthood, book 2, chapter 6; Leusden, Hebrew philology, miscellaneous dissertation 22.
> (b) Geier, on Hebrew mourning, chapter 8, §. 6 and following.
> (c) Fuller, sacred miscellany, book 4, chapter 7; Hottinger, philological treasury, book 1, chapter 1, section 5, number 1; Leusden, in the cited place.

<meta>(b) Josephus, book 2 of the Jewish War, chapter 15.</meta>

<header>Cap. VI. The IV. Book of Moses.</header>

7. For his father or for his mother, for his brother or for his sister, for these he shall not defile himself when they die: For the abstinence <note>The German *Enthaltung* here refers to the Nazirite's state of being set apart or consecrated.</note> for his GOD is upon his head.

-> Father -- Mother -- Brother -- Sister -- not) <-

And thus, such a person truly had to keep himself more strictly and live a more secluded life than even the priests of the other order, who, just as they were allowed to drink wine outside of the Tabernacle and the Temple, might also well defile themselves for such deceased relatives; but this man could not, for in this he was made entirely equal to the great High Priest.

One might have thought that in this case, it would have been allowed first of all, and the aforementioned persons would have been excepted. Father and mother, brother and sister, are certainly close and dearly beloved relatives who mean much to us. But no, there lies precisely the greatest danger regarding old parents: because love for the closest relatives overlooks much that should not be; and the respect or honor which one owes to parents draws many things, and consequently much evil, to itself. One gladly takes from them an example for imitation in those matters toward which one is already naturally inclined anyway.

The dearest relatives make the most claim on our best inclinations: but GOD wants these natural inclinations, love, and desires, which are directed toward them, to be called back and directed toward Himself.

We should have no fellowship with anyone in their dead works, no matter how closely related they may be to us, and we must not defile ourselves spiritually through natural affection and overlooking [of sin]; not even for the sake of our fathers and mothers. Genesis 33:9. <note>This likely refers to the Levites in Exodus 32 or Deuteronomy 33:9, who chose God's covenant over their own family ties.</note>

**The abstinence -- is upon his head)** The Chaldean translator and others following him render this as "a crown," similar to Psalm 132:18.

The true Nazirite is in an excellent way in covenant with his GOD. Therefore he wears this crown to the honor of his GOD, who in turn honors him by making him a king and priest in the spirit, and allows him such questions <note>The author refers to the spiritual inquiries or status granted to the consecrated.</note> as a sign that he is of royal lineage.

But the head of every man is Christ. 1 Corinthians 11:3. And what else is the crown then but the Spirit, the mind, and the will of Christ, in and through which the thoughts and inclinations of the true Nazirite are within his power. For this reason, others give the word "abstinence"; namely, from all vain lusts and desires, and from all corrupt inclinations. He who sets the crown upon his head gives him power to tread on serpents and scorpions. These are those whom GOD has made to be kings and priests. Just as it does not befit kings to drink wine, Proverbs 31:4, nor priests strong drink, Leviticus 10:9, so it is also not fitting for spiritual kings and priests to mingle and defile their souls with the joys and lusts of earthly life: rather, it behooves them, and their status brings with it, that they subject themselves entirely to their GOD and live solely for His will, to which they have surrendered and separated themselves, and whose crown they wear.

Thus, in this vow, the state of perfection was prefigured, just as it was in the High Priest, upon whose forehead was the golden plate or holy crown: which prototype is essentially fulfilled in Christ, the true Nazirite and High Priest; who is now in turn presented as a prototype and model of the perfect life to all, and to follow Him therein is required of all who wish to be Christ’s and belong to Him. For is it not the very thing that the Lord wants from all of us through the Apostle in 2 Corinthians 6:17 when he says: Separate yourselves, be true Nazirites; touch nothing unclean, come near no dead soul, do not love father or mother, brother or sister, in such a way that if they are dead in transgressions and sins, you might be defiled for their sake; rather, He recognizes no father or mother, no brother or sister on earth in such a case! Then I will be your Father, and you shall be my sons and daughters, yes, even my mother, brother, and sister. Matthew 12:50.

<column-break/>

8. All the days of his abstinence he is holy unto the LORD.

9. And if any man die very suddenly beside him, he hath defiled the head of his abstinence: and he shall shave his head in the day of his cleansing; on the seventh day shall he shave it.

10. And

**v. 8. All the days of his abstinence)** But since these were mostly and ordinarily set at only 30 days, the Christian vow of spiritual Naziriteship surpasses the vow of the Law, as it extends to all the days of one's life; just as it is also otherwise a vow of far greater abstinence: wherein we have renounced the devil and all his works, the pomp and vanity of the godless world, along with all its spiritual desires, as well as all sinful lusts of the flesh; and in return have bound ourselves to be faithful to the Lord forever and for our whole life, and to fulfill God's holy will as obedient children. This way of life is also not at all voluntary, like that of the Old Testament, but rather everyone who bears the name of a Christian is bound to it by virtue of the vow made at his baptism, through which he was initiated into the Christian Naziriteship. And even if he, as a child then, did not understand what happened and others vowed in his place; yet every Christian soul is bound to such duty and is obligated to make this vow even at this hour, if it had not happened before: or else one must rather renounce Christianity, just as one renounces it in works. Thus, every Christian must be a Nazirite according to the spirit and can be nothing else; indeed, a Christian and a Nazirite are as much as one and the same. For here it must be said even more: He

**is holy unto the LORD)** Such a true Nazirite must be separated in a special way from all defilements of the creatures, so that he becomes a wonder because of it and a person at whom the frivolous world marvels, shakes its head, and looks upon his actions with much estrangement; just as the word for "separate" or "abstain" in Hebrew implies "wonder": <note>The Hebrew root *pala* can mean both to make a special vow and to be wonderful/extraordinary.</note> and in contrast, he must be devoted and joined to the LORD.

The secret sense therefore indicates that he who has dedicated himself to the LORD in a special way (which everyone does who confesses himself to Christianity; since in the New Testament no distinction of persons applies, nor does any exception find a place therein) must also cleanse and sanctify himself from all defilement of the flesh and spirit, 2 Corinthians 7:1, and, as the Scripture says, must abstain from all things, 1 Corinthians 9:25, so that even that which is not so punished in another who is not under such a vow, is a sin and reckoned to him. The souls who have dedicated themselves to GOD and wish to be virgins of the Lamb must be pure in body and spirit above all others. The Lord’s will is that all joy and lust of our souls should not run out to any of the creatures, but should be entirely centered in His love, which is better than wine. Song of Solomon 1:2.

But where then will the wineskins <note>Likely a metaphor for those filled with earthly spirits or excess.</note> remain among the Christians, and all those who love strong drink? Indeed, what can be thought of those who refuse to be subject to GOD in a holy life, and instead defile themselves with dead works without ceasing and without shame? These have lost their crowns! They have broken the vow! And what then will become of those who are not only thus constituted themselves, but also dare to corrupt others and take their crown from them! Amos 2:11, 12.

**v. 9.** The Nazirite vow requires such precise observance, and could be so easily defiled in the prototype, that even if someone died suddenly beside a Nazirite, such that he could do nothing about it, that did not excuse him, but his vow thereby became invalid, and he had to be unclean for 7 days.
