### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter VI.

10. And on the eighth day he shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, to the door of the Tabernacle <term>Tent of Meeting</term>.

11. And the priest shall offer one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, and make atonement for him, because he sinned by reason of the dead body; and he shall sanctify his head on that same day.

12. And he shall consecrate to the LORD the days of his separation, and shall bring a lamb a year old for a guilt offering. But the previous days shall be lost, because his separation was defiled.

13. And this is the law of the <term>Nazirite</term> <note>From the Hebrew 'nazir,' meaning 'consecrated' or 'separated'; a person who took a special vow of devotion to God.</note>: On the day when the days of his separation are fulfilled, he shall be brought to the door of the Tabernacle.

14. And he shall offer his gift to the LORD: one male lamb a year old without blemish for a burnt offering, and one ewe lamb a year old without blemish for a sin offering, and one ram without blemish for a thank offering <note>Also known as a peace offering.</note>:

15. And a basket of unleavened bread, namely cakes of fine flour mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, along with their grain offering and their drink offerings.

---

v. 10. **On the 8th day he shall—bring)** After he has also previously let himself be sprinkled with the cleansing water at the proper time, as discussed in chapter 19.

v. 11. **Sanctify his head)** For a new renewal of the vow.

v. 12. **All the previous days, however, were lost and were in vain:** so that even if he had already spent 29 days in his vow and became defiled on the 29th day, or if he had vowed 100 days and became defiled on the 99th, all the past days were of no help; rather, he had to count anew as many days as he had vowed, and start his vow over from the beginning and endure it entirely. However, if he were defiled on the 30th or hundredth, or precisely on the last day, then the previous days were not lost.

So it is also with us; when we defile our souls through fellowship with dead works, all our previous labor is completely lost. <note>original: "Ezech. 18 / 24"</note> <note>Ezekiel 18:24 warns that if a righteous man turns to sin, his former righteousness will not be remembered.</note>

v. 13. When the time was now over and correctly endured, as the person had vowed, then he had to be publicly released from it.

v. 14. To that end, he had to bring his offering:

v. 15. **Moistened cakes and wafers,** which were to be eaten during the consumption of the thank offering.

<column-break/>

16. And the priest shall bring them before the LORD, and shall prepare his sin offering and his burnt offering.

17. And he shall prepare the ram as a thank offering to the LORD, along with the basket of unleavened bread; then the priest shall prepare its grain offering and its drink offering.

18. And the Nazirite shall shave the head of his separation at the door of the Tabernacle, and shall take the hair of the head of his separation and put it on the fire which is under the thank offering.

19. And the priest shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, and one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them upon the hands of the Nazirite, after he has shaved his Naziriteship.

20. And the priest shall wave them for a wave offering before the LORD; this is holy for the priest, together with the breast of the wave offering and the shoulder of the heave offering: and after that the Nazirite may drink wine.

21. This <note>The text cuts off here.</note>

---

v. 16. The meat of the sin offering was cooked in the inner courtyard.

v. 17. The meat of the thank offering, however, was cooked in the outer courtyard, where there was a specific so-called **Court of the Nazirites** in the Temple.

v. 18. In this small court, the Nazirite also shaved himself with a razor, very close to the head.

Luther indeed translates it as if the priest had shaved him; but the Hebrews interpret it as the Nazirite doing it himself.

v. 19. When this was done and the meat was cooked, the priest took the shoulder <note>literally "the leg" or "joint"</note> along with a cake and wafer, placed it on the Nazirite's hands, and placed his own hands underneath.

v. 20. He waved it thus together with him toward the four winds.

**This is—for the priest, together with)** This was something special in the thank offering of the Nazirite: that the priest had to not only heave the right shoulder and wave the breast, but also wave the cooked joint or the left shoulder, which belonged to him here, which did not happen in other thank offerings.

**After that he may drink wine)** He who completes his vow in this way and walks with constancy, finally arrives—after an appropriate earnestness and strict order of life, which is often regarded as legalistic—into a greater **freedom of the spirit**, through which the use of all things becomes free to him. But not before; and otherwise, everything is a presumed, false freedom of self-will, which one takes for oneself, and also vainly appeals to and relies on the examples of others, whom one should first have followed in other matters. The desires must first be laid aside, and one must prove that one is truly dead to this or that pleasure in food and drink, to vanity in clothing, and the like, and that the heart does not cling to such things. There, earnestness is required beforehand, to crucify the flesh with its lusts and to deliver it into the grave through the power of Christ's death, before one can use things as if one did not have them. Then the LORD Himself will surely turn our water into the wine of joy, and pour for us abundantly from His cellar of love.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws of the Nazirite from the previous page and introduces the famous Priestly Blessing from Numbers 6:24-26. The commentator links these Old Testament rituals directly to Christ and the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</meta>

<page-num>581</page-num>
<header>Ch. VI. The Fourth Book of Moses.</header>

21. This is the law of the <term>Nazirite</term> <note>One who has taken a vow of separation and devotion to God.</note> who has vowed his offering to the LORD because of his separation, beyond what his hand is able to afford: according to the content of his vow which he shall have vowed, so shall he do, according to the law of his separation.
22. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
23. Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and say to them;

<margin>v. 21.</margin> This law of the Nazirite) aimed now—as has already been partly mentioned—primarily at Christ, who was entirely set apart from sinners, <note>Hebrews 7:26</note> and was thus a true Nazirite of the LORD; and as the angel calls him, the Holy One, who was to be born of Mary and called the Son of GOD. <note>Luke 1:35</note> He abstained from the essential things prefigured in these ceremonies: from the pleasures and goods of this world, <note>Matthew 8:20</note> from all pomp and prestige among men, <note>Isaiah 53:2</note> and from all sins. <note>John 8:46</note> And in this, he has gone before all his true believers, who in him and in the fellowship of his Spirit shall renounce all lusts of the flesh and the desire for the goods of this world, <note>Matthew 6:19</note> all pomp and vanity of the world, and indeed die to all sins, having no fellowship with the dead works of darkness. Peter emphatically describes this Nazirite-state: "Dear brothers, I exhort you as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul," <note>1 Peter 2:11</note> namely against the spirit enlightened by Christ. See Galatians 5:24. Therefore, all such fleshly delights—great banquets, dances, games, comedies, and whatever they may be named—are entirely contrary to the Nazirite-state incumbent upon Christians. See 1 Corinthians 10:7.

The special vows, however, such as abstinence from marriage, from food on certain days, and from possessing any property—which some have sought to introduce through laws and wish to hold as Nazirites in the New Testament—are against the word of the LORD and have been expressly rejected by the Spirit of GOD. <note>1 Timothy 4:3; 1 Thessalonians 4:11-12; 2 Thessalonians 3:10-12.</note>

<margin>v. 23. Thus)</margin> With uplifted hands; <note>Leviticus 9:22</note> whereby the fingers were stretched apart in such a way that the thumb stood alone, and then the others were in pairs (2 and 2) close together, but with a space between them, so that on both hands there were 5 spaces. For this reason, this blessing was also called the "lifting up of the hands." It was also given and received with downcast eyes, during the singing.

For this speaking of the blessing, the Hebrews require 6 necessary parts: (1) that it be sung in the holy language <note>Hebrew</note>; (2) that the priest stands for it; (3) that he lifts up his hands; (4) that he speaks the blessing with a loud voice; (5) that his face is turned toward the people; (6) that the blessing is spoken with the name יהוה <note>The Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God, often rendered as 'LORD'</note> (a).

<margin>You)</margin> No one was permitted to speak this blessing except the priests alone. <note>Sirach 45:19</note>

This occurred every morning after the sacrifice (b).

Even today they bless in their synagogues and schools where they have priests from Aaron’s lineage: there the priests cover their faces, and the people hold their hands before their eyes. Also, they do not speak the blessing without the presence of at least 10 persons, including the priest.

<margin>(a) Schindler’s Lexicon Pentaglotton <note>A dictionary of five languages</note> under יהוה, p. 431.</margin>
<margin>(b) Rabbi Judah Leon, Book 1 on the Temple, ch. 21, §. 174.</margin>

<column-break/>

24. The LORD bless you and keep you!
25. The LORD make his face shine upon <margin>(a) Ps. 119:135.</margin> you, and be gracious to you!
26. The LORD lift up his face upon you, and give you peace!
27. Thus shall they put my name upon the children of Israel, and I will bless them.

->The<-

THERE is a mighty revelation of the divine majesty hidden in these words of blessing, which GOD commanded to be spoken over the people already in the Old Testament: since they should be promised in God’s name—when they walk in all his commandments throughout their lives and are thus obedient to GOD—that GOD would take them into his gracious protection, let his light shine in their souls, and thereby make them partakers of divine peace, which is higher than all understanding, both inwardly and outwardly.

The frequent, and especially the threefold, repetition of the divine name certainly indicates a deep mystery of the Godhead: as here, so also in Psalm 67:7-8 and 80:4, 8, 20. And what else should be revealed to us by this, than that the most holy Trinity is the sole and perfect source of all blessing and all good. This blessing from this triune GOD is now quite clearly expressed in the New Testament: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all." <note>2 Corinthians 13:13</note>

<margin>v. 24. The LORD)</margin> Here the name of GOD יהוה <note>Yahweh</note> was pronounced according to its letters as it actually sounds; and so every day, even by the common priests when they spoke the blessing: but nowhere else except in the Temple; and not very loudly, as the Hebrews report, although otherwise the entire blessing was given with a clear voice.

Bless and keep) There is a wonderful connection and union in the words of this glorious blessing, where the following word always explains the preceding one. Thus, for example, here the blessing is revealed through preservation, as GOD maintains his creature in being, and does all kinds of good for them in body and soul, also powerfully preserving them from all evil.

<margin>v. 25. His face)</margin> Which is attributed to GOD here and in the following verse—actually in the plural number, as "faces": so that 3 faces are to be found in the distinct properties of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which are distinct from one another, though they are and remain one; which can give cause for notable reflection.

Shine) The light of his face is, like the sun, the means of preservation for all things, by which all things grow, are maintained, and preserved.

Be gracious to you) With this he looks upon us graciously, as Christ looked upon Peter in grace and had mercy on him in his fall. And

Because GOD created everything through Christ Jesus, the true light, and maintains everything through this almighty word; so it is also pure grace that he lets the light of his faces shine in him, and appears to us graciously in the Son even after the Fall and has mercy on us. <note>Psalm 77:2</note>

But it does not stop at the mercy of GOD; rather, he lets his light and grace shine and rise even higher.

<margin>v. 26. He lifts up his faces over Israel, and grants them</margin> Peace) So that they have to fear no enemy, whether bodily or spiritual.

The peace of GOD comes and springs forth, as the last among the benefits of God, from the granted light and mercy, wherein the elevation and the abundance of his love becomes great, and spread first over the Israel of GOD, and thereafter also over every creature, which is included in that same peace of GOD.

Therefore, when the priest in the blessing said "gracious to you" or "lift up over you" <note>original: "sey gnädig dir / erhebe über dich"</note>: these words in Hebrew are twice the last ones; so he held out the voice for a long time and—which is very notable—turned toward midday <note>South</note> and midnight <note>North</note>, so that this blessing would spread toward all parts of the world: wherein he finally concluded with peace.

<margin>v. 27. My name)</margin> As one that nevertheless comes three distinct times in the blessing. Therefore, the name of GOD is also written by many Rabbis with 3 Yods "ייי".

## Chapter VII.

->The Offering of the Princes, and Moses’ Speaking with GOD.<-

And it came to pass on the day when Moses had fully set up the Tabernacle, and had anointed and sanctified it, with all its furnishings, and the altar with all its utensils, and had thus anointed and sanctified them;

2. Then the princes of Israel, the heads of their fathers' houses, offered. These were the princes of the tribes, those who stood over those who were numbered.

3. And they brought their offering before the face of the LORD, six covered wagons and twelve oxen, one wagon for two princes and one ox for each; and they brought them before the Tabernacle.

4. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

5. Take it from them, that it may be for performing the service of the Tent of Meeting; and give them to the Levites, to each according to the requirement of his service.

6. Then Moses took the wagons and oxen, and gave them to the Levites.

7. Two wagons and four oxen he gave to the sons of Gershon, according to the requirement of their service.

8. And four wagons and eight oxen he gave to the sons of Merari, according to the requirement of their service, under the hand of Ithamar, the son of Aaron the priest.

<column-break/>

9. But to the sons of Kohath he gave nothing: for the service of the sanctuary was incumbent upon them, as they had to carry it upon their shoulders.

10. And the princes brought the dedication of the altar on the day that it was anointed; then the princes offered their offering before the altar.

11. And the LORD spoke to Moses: Let each prince bring his offering for the dedication of the altar, each on his own day.

12. And it came to pass, that he who brought his offering on the first day was Nahshon, the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah.

13. And his offering was one silver charger <note>original: "Schüssel" — a large, deep plate or platter</note>, the weight of which was one hundred and thirty shekels; one silver sprinkling bowl of seventy shekels, according to the shekel of the sanctuary: both of them were full of fine flour mixed with oil for a grain offering.

14. One spoon of ten shekels of gold, full of incense.

15. One young bull—namely, a young steer—one ram, one lamb of the first year for a burnt offering.

16. One male goat for a sin offering.

17. And for a sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, five lambs of the first year. This was the offering of Nahshon, the son of Amminadab.

---

After the Tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting had been set up at the very beginning of the second year (Exodus 40:2, 17) and immediately afterward was also anointed by Moses (Leviticus 8:10), the princes now made the beginning by presenting gifts for the Tabernacle.

<margin>v. 2.</margin> Offered) These were voluntary offerings.

<margin>v. 3.</margin> Covered wagons) So that no rain could get through, nor the things loaded upon them be spoiled.

<margin>v. 4.</margin> The LORD — said) Either as an answer to Moses, who did not know what to do with the wagons, or whether he should accept them, as they were things that did not belong to the sacrifice, and therefore asked for counsel, as some believe; or also of His own accord, from the counsel of His wisdom and understanding, and likely not without mystery.

<margin>v. 5.</margin> Give them to the Levites) To load the majority of the Tabernacle upon them when traveling.

<margin>v. 6.</margin> Then Moses took) After he understood from the LORD what was to be done with them.

<margin>v. 7.</margin> Two wagons) Thus only half as many as the following; because they <note>The Gershonites</note> had lighter things to carry, which also did not take up as much space.

<margin>v. 8.</margin> Those who have heavy, hard, and coarse services to perform require more animal strength for it.

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 9.</margin> The sons of Kohath, although they were not priests, were nevertheless closest to the priests, and for that reason have stronger shoulders for carrying.

No animalistic person <note>The commentator contrasts the "animal strength" of the wagons/oxen with the spiritual or "human" dignity of the Kohathites' task</note> may approach the Holy [place], which is covered and stands open only to the priests: much less does it belong to him to carry it.

<margin>v. 10.</margin> The princes brought near) In this way, princes and persons of standing should lead others with a good example through foundations for godly works—since the salvation of men and, through this alone, the honor of GOD is promoted—so that in this way they may make friends for themselves from the unrighteous <term>Mammon</term> <note>A biblical term for wealth or property, often used to suggest that material riches should be used for spiritual or charitable ends</note>; which can keep their memory in blessing for eternity, in that such shall stand recorded in the book of the LORD (see Matthew 26:13); whereas the monuments of vanity will rot along with the names of the glory-seekers. Proverbs 10:7, 1 Samuel 15:12, 2 Samuel 18:18.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> Each prince) According to the order of the camp, as it was arranged by the LORD.

On his day) Each should have his own special day for that which they further wished to offer. For the transport wagons and oxen were all brought on one day and presented to the Tabernacle.

<margin>v. 12.</margin> On the first day) Also of the first month, as on the day of the dedication. (v. 10). The setting up and dedication of the Tabernacle, the priests, and the presentation of the princes all occurred at the same time and in the first 12 days of the first month, of which 7 were counted toward the dedication.

<note>Commentary on the values and vessels mentioned above:</note>

v. 19. 25. **130 Shekels**) According to our coinage, worth 65 Reichsthaler. <note>The Reichsthaler was a standard silver coin used in the Holy Roman Empire during the time this translation was written.</note>
**70 Shekels**) make as much as 35 Reichsthaler.

v. 20. 26. **A bowl**) or an incense vessel, which was shaped like a spoon or a hollow hand. Two of these, full of incense, were placed weekly upon the Table of Showbread.

**Of 10 shekels of gold**) Which, according to the calculation of those who value gold 16 times higher than silver, was worth 80 Reichsthaler; but according to others who set it 12 times as high, it was worth 60 Reichsthaler.

v. 21-23. 27-29. In addition, each prince honored the occasion with 21 sacrificial animals for himself.

<note>Commentary on the animals used for peace offerings:</note>

For a peace offering, as is known, all three kinds of animals—oxen, rams, and goats—could be taken; indeed, not only the male but also the female sex, sheep and goats, provided they were otherwise without flaw or blemish. And because lambs a year old were also brought here, it is evident that both small and large livestock could be offered for a peace offering. In this matter, Josephus (a) <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> contradicts the Holy Scripture, as he writes that the animal for a peace offering must have been over a year old.

(a) Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 3, Chapter 10.

### 588 The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter VIII.

### 23. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:
### 24. This is what pertains to the Levites: From twenty-five years old and upward, one shall go in to perform the duties of the service in the Tabernacle of Meeting.

<margin>According to the letter, this refers to the Levites of the Old Testament; according to the mystery, it refers to all people who cling to God through faith and good will.</margin>
<margin>These words contain the common time between the Levites' heavy labor and their holy or venerable service.</margin>
<margin>v. 24. Nowhere before the time of David does Scripture clearly and expressly state what their service consisted of specifically, other than keeping watch, carrying, and lifting. Above in Chapter 4, verse 3, etc., they were numbered from the thirtieth year onward and thus actually placed in the administration of their service; here, however, they are already appointed to it.</margin>

**From 25 years old)** How does this reconcile? Answer: For the work of carrying, no one was accepted until he was 30 years old and thus had full strength. For other Levitical duties, however, they were accustomed and instructed from the 25th year, and thus were first trained in their service for 5 years, during which they were used for the lesser services, such as running errands, singing, and keeping watch.

Regarding the number, Origen has his mystical thoughts, as is his custom. "In the number 25," he writes, "is given to understand the perfection of the five senses; since 5 times 5, each multiplied by itself, makes 25: and this indicates that he who is called to the service of God must be rich and pure in his senses, indeed, perfect."

**And upward)** As long as our full power and strength lasts, which the Lord wants to see applied entirely in His service. Everyone who has a healthy understanding of this will also easily recognize that all time is certainly lost which is spent in any other service besides this one. Whereas, in this service, faithful servants of God bring forth fruit even in old age, and they are and remain flourishing and fresh. Psalm 92:15.

**Go in)** In temporal and fleshly wars, kings go out to battle: 1 Chronicles 21:1. But in the spiritual war, one must go in.

**To perform the duties of)** Or, as others translate it, *to wage the war* in the service <note>original: "zu kriegen den Krieg im Diensttext." The Hebrew word *tsaba* refers to both a military host and a period of service.</note> according to the actual meaning of the words, and following the similarity with Exodus 38:8 and 1 Samuel 2:22.

**Why the service of GOD is called a war** will be easily understood by the one who has a desire and longing to draw near to God and cling to Him, when he finds and feels the law of his members warring and struggling against the law of his mind; Romans 7:23. **It is a shame, however, when a spiritual Levite spends his prime time, power, and strength—from 25 to 50, or even to 60 and 70 years—in the war of his members, and yet does not finish with it, because he follows his fleshly lusts, which war against the soul.**

**Service)** The word in Hebrew signifies the greatest toil and labor that men undertake in times of peace: the labors of the earth, in plowing, sowing, harrowing, and fallowing—and that for the 2nd and 3rd time, etc., and every year again. For the work and labor of the farmer returns every year as if in a circle.

The spiritual Levite has his great and heavy work, toil, and labor, surrounding a worldly tabernacle of earthly-planted people. He plows the desolate and waste-lying fields—the earthly hearts of men—which have long lain unbroken. He sows the seed of the Word; and it is a great deal if a fourth part of the earth proves good and fruitful: Matthew 13:8, 23. Thus, the greatest part of his labor is certainly lost, and he applies his strength in vain. Hence it is that the spiritual Levite is compared to a hardworking ox. Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9. But

The greatest labor of the spiritual Levite is the carrying of the Tabernacle in which Christ dwells: a burden about which Moses, as a Levite, also complains in Deuteronomy 1:9. To bear the burdens of the weak, their manifold infirmities and weaknesses, their murmuring and discontent, their rebelliousness and stubbornness: while meanwhile, in great patience and long-suffering, they seek and await their repentance and improvement.

<column-break/>

### 25. But from fifty years old one shall retire from the administration of the service and serve no more.
### 26. But he shall serve his brothers in the Tabernacle of Meeting, that he may attend to the guard, but he shall perform no service. Thus shall you do to the Levites in their watches.
<sig>D</sig>

<margin>v. 25. But from 50 years—no more) Regarding carrying and lifting. For</margin>

They were not entirely dismissed because of this, but served their brothers by singing, forming choirs, and keeping away those who had no business in the Tabernacle (a), and were thus used in lighter works according to their strength, and freed from the toilsome and heavy labor.

The reason is clear: because nature, gradually exhausted and tired of strength, then demands ease and rest. For the Levites, like others, dwell in houses of clay, Job 4:19, which are weak and fragile. And although the soul is strong and capable of action in its other house, the starry body <note>original: "Stern-Leib." A Paracelsian or mystical term for the astral body or spiritual essence of a person.</note>; yet in the action which must happen through an elementary body, which daily goes toward decay, the spirit is more willing, and the flesh more weak.

It is not the will of God that His soldiers should war and struggle forever and ever. No man struggles except in hope of victory. And there must rather be for us a goal and end of the struggle and war, when the Lord of Hosts accepts us; because He takes some delight in our insignificance.

Since the Lord had such foresight for the Levites in the time of the Law, how should those who have served in the time of the Gospel and fought a good fight not also become retired soldiers who may rest from all their labor? Or should the Lord have entirely forgotten His spiritual Levites when their power and strength fail them? Certainly, God intended to show and indicate by such an ordinance how He has no pleasure in straining His servants beyond the time and strength of old age, but rather allows them some rest then. This should be observed all the more in the New Testament: that old, exhausted servants should be given such rest, releasing them from some of the more toilsome duties; yet they could otherwise assist the younger ones with good counsel and especially persevere in prayer for the congregations.

The fiftieth year is the year of freedom and release, of the putting away and removal of sin: just as we recently observed a notable prefiguration of this in the Jubilee Year.

The actual time of rest from spiritual warfare is the age of 50 years; this is the time of the Spirit. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. A son of 50 years is a son born of the Spirit. Therefore, David, who had zealously conducted the Lord's wars, was followed by a son of peace and rest <note>Referring to King Solomon.</note>.

So then, let us hasten the coming of this great year, the year of redemption from our hard service, so that the approach of the acceptable year of the Lord, the day of the Lord, may also be hastened for us! 2 Peter 3:12.

v. 26. How graciously the Lord proves Himself toward those who work in His service! They shall rest from their labor, toil, and burden when they have applied and consumed their power and strength in the service and war of the Lord: but they shall not therefore be idle, but shall then serve in a lighter and more honorable service. For there is no part of time which entirely frees a man from God's service. When the enemies in the spiritual war are overcome, and we are delivered from the hands of our enemies; then we must serve Him in holiness and righteousness all the remaining days of our lives. Luke 1:74, 75. Therefore, there is a distinction in the words of the Hebrew, just as there is a distinction between service and service. After the time of servile labor follows the time of waiting upon the Lord, which is also spoken of in Genesis 39:4.

<margin>Selden, Book 1, *On the Succession of the Pontiffs*, Chapter 4.</margin>

5. And they kept the Passover in the first [month], on the fourteenth day of the month between the two evenings, in the Wilderness of Sinai. According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so did the children of Israel.
6. And

---

These words contain the law regarding the proper observation of the Passover, stating that it should be kept at the right appointed time and according to the prescribed manner.
vv. 2–3. And a specific command is given regarding the appointed time, which is mentioned twice.
v. 4. Concerning the matter itself, the command is given to us, as well as to the children of Israel through Moses, by the ministers of the New Covenant according to the Gospel sense, that we should keep Easter <note>original: "Ostern" — in German, the word for Passover and Easter is the same, reflecting the theological connection between the two</note>: namely the passage from the flesh into the spirit, or from death into life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ (John 5:24); or the Feast of Unleavened Bread: in complete abstinence from the old Adam-like leaven of malice, lusts, hypocrisy, and error; and in the eating of the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:7–8). For we also have a Passover Lamb, says Paul, and points as if with fingers how

### the Passover Lamb of the Old Testament is a glorious archetype <term>archetype|Fürbild: a prophetic symbol or foreshadowing in the Bible</term> of Christ, and especially his death: being at once a sacrifice and a sacrament.

<columns>2</columns>
1. It was a lamb, an <term>emblem|emblema: a symbolic representation</term> of the gentleness and humility which one can and should learn from Christ Jesus (Matthew 11:29).
2. A lamb benefits man with everything, providing food and clothing: and Christ is everything himself.
3. It was to be a male (Revelation 12:5).
4. There was to be no blemish in it: because we required such a sacrifice and High Priest.
5. It was to be one year old, neither too young nor too old, when the meat is most flavorful: Christ was crucified in the flower of his age and became the most delicate food for our souls. And just as one was not allowed to eat a lamb while it was still on its mother’s milk, so Christ, while he was still at his mother's breast, could not be slaughtered by Herod.
6. It was to be slaughtered in the month of Abib, in the spring, which corresponds to our March and April: so too Christ was sacrificed at Passover.
7. It was when the children of Israel were to leave the house of bondage; and we from the yoke of the Old Testament.
8. On the 4th day after it was separated from the flock, or on the 14th day of the month of Abib: Christ in his 34th year, and in the 4th year of his preaching ministry; and on the 10th day of Nisan or Abib, Christ came to Jerusalem and was crucified on the 14th (John 12:1, 12).
<column-break/>
9. Death occurred in the evening for both.
10. The Jews ate it at night: in the night Christ also ate with his disciples and offered his own body as food.
11. One lamb was enough for many: many become partakers of one lamb, who gave his life as a ransom for many.
12. The entire congregation of Israel was to slaughter it. All Jews are guilty of Christ’s death, indeed all people.
13. After it was slaughtered, it was hung up; to be an image of the hung Christ.
14. First in Egypt; later in Jerusalem (Revelation 11:8).
15. It was only allowed to be eaten there. Outside the Church, Christ is not consumed.
16. Both doorposts and the lintel were struck with its blood. Christ is the door sprinkled with his own blood.
17. In the house whose posts were so struck, the inhabitants were free: and whoever’s heart-door is sprinkled with the blood of Jesus, the destroyer cannot touch.
18. Not the threshold, but the lintel and posts were struck. This signifies Christ’s cross, and teaches that the blood of Christ must not be trampled underfoot: we must not disregard the blood of the New Testament.
19. A bunch of hyssop was dipped into the blood, and the houses were sanctified with it. This signifies Christ's body, which was dipped in blood, and thus our bodies were sanctified through it.
20. It had to be eaten—that is, bitten with teeth, swallowed, and digested or completely united. Thus it happens with Christ through faith.
21. It was eaten roasted. The heat of the sun, of God’s wrath and zeal, consumed Christ; so that he would become sustenance for his believers, roasted in hot love.
22. It was not to be eaten raw: Christ must not be grasped crudely or carnally.
23. Nor boiled in water, where much strength is lost. We must not add our own righteousness to Christ, nor say that he uses his "juice" to make our works merit anything; otherwise, he loses his power.
24. But it had to be roasted on a spit so that the blood and fat dripped out. Indeed, this is what happened to Christ.
25. It had to be eaten whole, with head, legs, and entrails. Nothing in Christ must displease us. We must accept him entirely, both his members and the head.
26. Nothing was to remain until morning. Christ (1) did not remain on the cross. (2) Faith must not be postponed: Today is the day of salvation. (3) Christ's sacrifice is not repeated.
27. No bone of it was to be broken. This excluded all negligence (John 19:36). We must not separate in Christ what belongs together.
28. They had to eat it with bitter things. One becomes a partaker of Christ’s benefits through suffering with him (Romans 8:17).
29. They were to eat it as travelers, girded, with shoes on their feet and staves in their hands. We must be ready to leave this "Egypt" when we wish to accept Christ.
30. With unleavened new bread: with a new heart and a new spirit.
</columns>

v. 5. In the Wilderness) And because we read of no further Passover in the wilderness, this may have been a foreshadowing of the stubbornness in the current long-lasting captivity of the Jews, wherein they have no part in Christ.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter IX.

6. And there were men who had become unclean because of a human corpse, so that they could not keep the Passover on that day; and they came before Moses and before Aaron on that day;
7. And those men said to him: We are unclean by a human corpse; why should we be kept back, so that we cannot bring the offering of the **LORD** at its appointed time among the children of Israel?
8. And Moses said to them: Stand still, that I may hear what the **LORD** will command concerning you.
9. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses, saying:
10. Speak to the children of Israel and say: If any man among you or your descendants shall be unclean by a corpse, or is on a distant journey; he shall nonetheless keep the Passover to the **LORD**.

<column-break/>

11. In the second month on the fourteenth day, between the two evenings, they shall keep it: with unleavened bread and bitter things <note>referring to bitter herbs, such as horseradish or lettuce, symbolizing the bitterness of slavery</note> they shall eat it. <margin>Exodus 12:8.</margin>
12. They shall leave none of it until morning, nor break any bone of it(a): they shall keep it according to all the statutes of the Passover. <margin>(a) John 19:36.</margin>
13. But the man who is clean, and is not on a journey, and neglects to keep the Passover, that same soul shall be cut off from among his people; because he did not bring the offering of the **LORD** at its appointed time: that man shall bear his sin.
14. And if a stranger dwells among you, he shall also keep the Passover to the **LORD**: according to the statute of the Passover and according to its right, so shall he keep it. There shall be one statute for you, both for the stranger and for the native of the land.

---

vv. 6-11. Consider then the incident that occurred: some had become unclean because of a dead person and thus could not keep the Passover, yet they were eager to bring their Passover Lamb to the **LORD** and to praise the **LORD** for their deliverance from Egypt. This prompted Moses to ask the **LORD** what His gracious will would be. The Lord then commanded that they should keep it the following month on the same day, according to all its rites, just as it should have been in the first month. This may be a hidden type <note>a "type" is a prophetic symbol or person in the Old Testament that foreshadows something in the New Testament</note> of how the first-fruits of the believers from among the Jews would be the first to keep the true Passover in spirit, through faith in the Easter Lamb <note>original: "Oster-Lamm" — in German, the word for Passover and Easter is the same</note>, Christ, sacrificed for us: 1 Corinthians 5:7. However, the unbelievers—who were the greater multitude at that time and who defiled themselves with the death of the **Lord** when they cried: "His blood be upon us and upon our children!" (Matthew 27:25)—they would only keep this Passover feast in the second time, in the glorious kingdom of Christ, when all Israel shall be converted and the fullness of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:26). At that time, they shall share in all the graces that the first believers enjoyed. See also 2 Chronicles 30:2 etc.
It is noteworthy, exclaims Herberger (a) <note>Valerius Herberger (1562–1627) was a famous German Lutheran preacher and writer known for his "Magnalia Posthuma."</note> regarding this, that **Jesus** allows a comforting "After-Easter" for those who confess their uncleanness or are far away in a foreign land. Thus He also provided a gracious "After-Easter" for Thomas—who had defiled himself with thoughts over Christ's corpse and was delayed in his Easter joy—eight days after His resurrection. John 20:26.
This "After-Easter" was not kept for seven days, but for only one day. (b)
<margin>(a) Herberger's *Great Deeds*, Part II, on this passage.</margin>
<margin>(b) Buxtorf, *Lexicon Chaldaicum, Talmudicum et Rabbinicum* under the word: Passover <note>original Hebrew: פסח</note></margin>

<column-break/>

v. 11. Between the two evenings) Because the Scripture explicitly speaks of "two evenings," not only here but also in Exodus 12:6, the translators should have remained faithful to the Scripture here and followed its expression; they should not have followed the common image we have created, where we only know of one evening in a day when the sun goes down. Our understanding, will, inclinations, deeds, life, and essence must all be formed and shaped according to the rule and plumb line of God's Word: the Word must not be modeled after our understanding, will, inclinations, life, and essence.
The first evening is the turning of the sun from its noon point <note>the decline of the sun after midday</note>, and the other is the setting of the sun.
There had to be an accurate correspondence between the type and the truth, between the slaughter of the Passover and the crucifixion of Christ.
When we are with the Sun of Righteousness, it is with us; but when we depart from our obedience, become apostate from the light, turn away from the **LORD**, follow the prince of darkness, and do his lusts; then these are two spiritual evenings between which the Passover lamb is slaughtered. Sin consists in turning away from GOD and turning toward the creature. These are the very two evils of which the prophet speaks in Jeremiah 2:13. Between these two spiritual evenings, a person dies to their spiritual life or the life of GOD. Proverbs 1:32. And just so, the Lamb of GOD dies to the sinful man between the two evenings. Romans 5:8. See, however, how the sun sets through the aforementioned spiritual death, so it may also rise again through death, when we die to sin with Christ.
v. 13. Neglects) Out of lightheadedness and negligence, or even contempt, failing to follow the **LORD's** will.
v. 14. Stranger) A "stranger of righteousness" <note>often called a "Proselyte of Righteousness," a gentile who fully converted to Judaism</note>; those who, out of love for GOD and righteousness, accepted the entire Law of Moses along with the children of Israel and obligated themselves to keep it: these are sometimes simply called strangers or foreigners. Exodus 12:48, 49.

### Ch. IX. The Fourth Book of Moses (Numbers).

15. And on the day that the Tabernacle was set up, the cloud covered the Tabernacle of the Tent of Testimony: and in the evening it was over the Tabernacle like the appearance of fire until the morning.
16. So it happened continually, that the cloud covered it, and by night the appearance of fire.
17. And when the cloud was taken up from the Tent, then after that the children of Israel journeyed: and in the place where the cloud settled, there the children of Israel camped.
18. At the word of the **LORD** the children of Israel journeyed, and at the word of the **LORD** they camped: All the days that the cloud remained upon the Tabernacle, they remained in camp.

This pillar of cloud and fire, and what was symbolized by it and has been continually promised to the Church of Christ, has already been treated in Exodus 13:21, 22 and Chapter 40:34, etc.

v. 15. **Covered the Tabernacle)** Up over the Most Holy Place, and especially that part where the Ark was located.

<margin>
That it was also inside the Most Holy Place between the Cherubim over the Mercy Seat <note>The "Versöhn-Deckel" or Mercy Seat was the gold lid of the Ark of the Covenant, considered the earthly throne of God</note>, and thus drew itself down through the roof or the tapestries, is to be seen in Leviticus 16:2.
</margin>

**Tent of Testimony** the dwelling—which otherwise is mostly called the Tent of Meeting—is called this because the most excellent thing kept within it was the Law, or the Testimony of the Will of God: Exodus 25:21.

v. 16. **Appearance of fire)** At night it appeared as a fire and was thus seen by the children of Israel, which could not be seen during the day because of the cloud.

v. 17. When the pillar of cloud drew upward from the Tent, this was a sign that they should break camp and prepare for the journey. As soon as the priests noticed this, they went into the Tent, took down the innermost curtain, and covered the Ark of the Covenant, the Table of Showbread, the golden lampstand, the Altar of Incense, and outside in the court, the Altar of Burnt Offering and the washbasin, with the appropriate coverings. The Levites quickly dismantled the Tabernacle and took everything apart.

v. 18. **At the word of the LORD they journeyed and camped)** Just as they directed themselves so carefully according to this guide and compass, arranging their journeys and campsites accordingly whether for a short or long time; so must the believers hold themselves very closely to their promised Guide in this pilgrimage on earth. Our Savior first offers Himself thus: *I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me:* John 14:6. And then He also promises the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of Truth, who is to remain with us, indeed to be in us, and thus not depart from this Tabernacle of our souls and spirits consecrated to the Lord (John 14:16, 17), but is to lead us into all truth (Chapter 16:13).

Thus we must always be mindful of that glorious prayer, that we may commend ourselves therein to this guidance of the Spirit: *Teach me to do according to your good pleasure; for you are my God: let your good Spirit lead me on a level path!* Psalm 143:10 <note>Original text cites Ps. 143:9</note>. See also the glorious wish aiming at this in 1 Thessalonians 5:23.

So this cloud is also always present to those who are children in the Spirit, and leads them through the wilderness of this world, so that they may be certain of how they ought to walk.

v. 19. Without God’s Spirit, one must not move. According to His signal, we must let ourselves be moved, and also rest again as it pleases Him.

v. 20. This is the quality of a very resigned soul <note>German: "sehr-gelassenen Seele." Gelassenheit refers to a state of surrendered equanimity or letting-go, central to German mystical and pietist thought</note>: to let oneself be led by God so that she undertakes not the slightest thing except through the movement of His Spirit; to be ready for everything and prepared to leave everything (since everything is the same to her) as she finds herself moved to it by God. And this is all that is required for it.

v. 21. These faithful, resigned ones also do not look to see whether it is day or whether it is night; whether they find themselves in the light or in the darkness.

v. 22. They have for themselves no certain hours nor times, but they let themselves be led without wavering and without doubt, in that they go or remain standing according to the command of God with a wonderful speed, and do not worry about their journeying forth nor about their resting, since everything in the ways of God is equal to them.

v. 23. **At the word of the LORD)** Which is Christ. John 1:1.

Moses heard it from Christ Jesus, God the Word: and through Moses it was made known to the congregation; which, besides the command through Moses, had the visible sign of the cloud, both in its settling and its rising.

Oh, that we might follow this mysterious image according to God and His movement, not running ahead with our own spirit, but waiting upon it until He moves our spirit to call or to go forth, to speak or to remain silent! Romans 15:18. How necessary this will be, especially in the present time! So that one may learn to keep the right measure in all things, and be certain of what one does or leaves undone; so that one is not moved by every spirit, nor even by one's own spirit and wind of doctrine, but knows well how to distinguish the voice of the stranger from the voice of the friend, and thus then goes forth and does not let oneself be stopped when one is divinely <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence</note> convinced in this or that matter: where so many spirits wander in uncertainty according to the impression of their own spirit.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter X.

## Chapter X.

->The two trumpets / the journey from Sinai / Hobab’s company /
Moses' prayer for the journey.<-

And the **LORD** spoke to Moses and said:
2. Make for yourself two silver trumpets; you shall make them of a single piece, so that you may use them to call the assembly together and for the breaking of camp.
3. And when they blow with them, the whole assembly shall gather before you at the door of the Tabernacle of the Tent of Meeting.
4. And when they blow with only one, then the leaders, the heads of the thousands of Israel, shall gather before you.
5. And when you blow a signal with a joyful shout <note>The German *Jauchzen* here refers to the Hebrew *teruah*, a broken or alarm-like blast distinct from a steady tone</note>, then the camps that are stationed toward the east shall set out.
6. And when you blow a signal with a joyful shout a second time, then the camps that are stationed toward the south shall set out; they shall blow a joyful shout for their journeys.

---

How the departure—of which the latter part of the previous chapter treated—was to be conducted is further organized here with more detail.
**v. 2. Two trumpets** are commanded to be made, specifically of silver, because this metal produces a very bright tone.
**Of a single piece)** Just as the lampstand was made (Chapter 8:4): not assembled piece by piece, but hammered out of a single piece of silver, and quite thick, as Josephus (a) describes them, and less than a full cubit in length. <note>original: Josephus (a) L. 3. Antiq. c. 11. / Flavius Josephus was a 1st-century Jewish historian; his *Antiquities of the Jews* provides physical descriptions of Temple artifacts.</note>
These two trumpets were ordained in the wilderness for the calling of either the leaders or the entire assembly, and then as a signal for departure, so that the march might proceed in an orderly fashion.
**v. 3. When the whole assembly** was to gather, both trumpets were blown.
**v. 4. But when only one** was blown, it signified the leaders alone, who were to take notice that they were being called.
Their tents must therefore have been the closest to the camp of the priests and Levites, for otherwise they could hardly have heard the sound.
**v. 5. The blowing with a joyful shout)** which is what the word actually means, indicates a broken and often repeated tone, just as one is accustomed to do with the mouth when shouting for joy; this may also have occurred during times of war. See Judges 7:20.
**The camps toward the east)** The tribe of Judah with its standard, and the two tribes belonging under it, Issachar and Zebulun.
**v. 6. Those toward the south)** Reuben, Simeon, and Gad. **Blow with a joyful shout)** Where the sound rises and falls and changes manifoldly. This signified the march.

(a) Book 3, Antiquities, chapter 11.

<column-break/>

7. But when you gather the assembly, you shall blow, but not with a joyful shout.
8. And the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets; and they shall be to you for an eternal statute throughout your generations.
9. And when you go into battle in your land against the enemy who oppresses you, then you shall shout with the trumpets; so you will be remembered before the face of the **LORD** your God, and you shall be delivered from your enemies.
10. And on the day of your gladness—namely at your appointed times and at your new moons—you shall blow the trumpets over your burnt offerings and over your thank offerings, so that they may be a memorial for you before the face of your God: I am the **LORD** your God.

---

**v. 7. But when they were only to gather** and not to journey, both trumpets were sounded in a single, continuous tone.
**v. 8. The priests shall blow)** This was an image of the proclamation of the favorable year of the Lord, which was to be preached not with trumpets, but through the voices of the good messengers of the Gospel. See Isaiah 61:1 etc. and Chapter 40:1 etc.
Conversely, however, the trumpeting angels in the New Testament are used for the sounding of the judgments of God (Revelation 8 and 9); therefore, the judgments are proclaimed as if with a trumpet far and wide by the witnesses of truth (Isaiah 58:1). This is also an image of the battle cry and the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God with which the Lord Jesus will come for judgment (1 Thessalonians 4:16).
When, therefore, in the future such bright trumpets are heard publicly, announcing the departure of the Lord to the assembly and refusing to let their mouths be stopped: then know how you should conduct yourself. See to it that you then go with Israel without contradiction or doubt, lest you remain behind and become the portion of the wild beasts in the wilderness of this world. For the Lord will also show His little flock in the latter time a wilderness wherein He will nourish them before the face of the serpents and preserve them from the three remarkable beasts: the lion, the wolf, and the leopard. (Jeremiah 5:6).
**v. 9. 10. In the land of Canaan** the Jews used these trumpets during their festivals to witness their joy over all the blessings of God (Psalm 81:4), and also in times of war to give courage to the people, that they would be remembered by God to deliver them from their enemies—provided they stood in the grace of God and had not sinned through impropriety. See Joshua 7.

### Chapter X. The Fourth Book of Moses.

11. And it happened in the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, that the cloud lifted from the Tabernacle of the Testimony.

12. And the children of Israel set out on their journeys from the Wilderness of Sinai; and the cloud settled down in the Wilderness of Paran.

13. So they set out for the first time according to the word of the Lord by the ministry of Moses.

14. And the standard of the camp of the children of Judah set out first according to their armies: and over its army was Nahshon, the son of Amminadab.

15. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Issachar was Nethanel, the son of Zuar.

16. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Zebulun was Eliab, the son of Helon.

17. Then the Tabernacle was taken down; and the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari set out, carrying the Tabernacle.

<margin>v. 11. 12.</margin> In the second year, in the 2nd month, on the 20th day, the cloud lifted — and settled down) They had therefore remained in the Wilderness of Sinai for one year minus 13 days, as can be gathered from Exodus 19:1; during which time the Sanctuary was completed and erected, and for the first time it stood only until the 20th day, when it was taken down again and moved into the

<margin>Wilderness of Paran)</margin> Which is the general name of the wilderness from Mount Sinai to Kadesh-Barnea or to the land of Canaan, an eleven-day journey long. Deuteronomy 1:1, 2, 8.

It is said to be such an untracked, arid region that one sees neither huts nor people, neither animals nor birds, neither trees nor shrubs, but only high mountains and rocks.

<margin>v. 13.</margin> So they set out for the first time) And so many believers in their pilgrimage also have various camping places here on earth, as we have no lasting city, but seek the one to come. Hebrews 13:14.

<margin>v. 14 – 16.</margin> They also marched in their finest order: with the Ark of the Covenant going before them under the pillar of cloud, as concluded from v. 33 and Joshua 3:6, and being carried by the Kohathites; whom the tribe of Judah with its regiments followed at a distance of a quarter-mile.

<margin>v. 17.</margin> As soon as these had passed, the Gershonites and Merarites followed between the two banners of Judah and Reuben with their six wagons, upon which were packed the coverings of the Tabernacle, the two inner curtains and the hangings for the courtyard, the boards and bars of the Tabernacle, the pillars and bases of the Tabernacle and the courtyard, the pegs, ropes, and everything belonging to them; all the Levites belonging to these two families also followed.

<column-break/>

18. Then the standard of the camp of Reuben set out according to their armies, and over its army was Elizur, the son of Shedeur.

19. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Simeon was Shelumiel, the son of Zurishaddai.

20. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Gad was Eliasaph, the son of Deuel.

21. Then the Kohathites set out, carrying the holy things: and the others set up the Tabernacle before these arrived.

22. Then the standard of the camp of the children of Ephraim set out according to their armies, and over its army was Elishama, the son of Ammihud.

23. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Manasseh was Gamaliel, the son of Pedahzur.

24. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Benjamin was Abidan, the son of Gideoni.

25. Then the standard of the camp of the children of Dan, which gathered all the camps together, set out according to their armies: and over its army was Ahiezer, the son of Ammishaddai.

26. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Asher was Pagiel, the son of Ochran.

27. And over the army of the tribe of the children of Naphtali was Ahira, the son of Enan.

28. These were the departures of the children of Israel according to their armies, as they set out.

<margin>v. 18 – 20.</margin> Then came Reuben with his subordinate tribes: so that the first six tribes, according to their two camps, had the Gershonites and Merarites with the outermost parts of the Tabernacle in their midst; who would then first set it up when the first camp of Judah had settled down.

<margin>v. 21.</margin> Until the other camp arrived later, then the Kohathites came with the most holy things, the table, lampstand, incense altar, etc., which were placed into the Sanctuary: the rest of the Kohathite family stayed with these, and Aaron and the priests, as well as Moses, also walked with them in the midst of the 12 tribes, who surrounded them from front and back, and all had an equal share in it.

<margin>v. 22 – 24.</margin> Following this was the camp of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin; which David refers to in Psalm 80:2, 3.

<margin>v. 25 – 27.</margin> Finally, the last three tribes brought up the rear of the troops.

<margin>v. 28.</margin> Thus they did not march as they had camped, in a square, but in a beautiful long order one after another through the wilderness when they traveled; so that the three most populous camps were in the front and back, with Judah making the beginning and Dan the conclusion.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter X.

¶ 29. And Moses said to Hobab, the son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses' brother-in-law: "We are traveling to the place of which the LORD said, 'I will give it to you.' Come with us, and we will do you good; for the LORD has promised good things concerning Israel."

¶ 30. But he said to him, "I will not go; rather, I will depart to my own land and to my own kindred."

¶ 31. Then Moses said, "Please do not leave us! For you know how we are to camp in the wilderness, and you can be our eyes." <note>Moses is asking for Hobab’s practical knowledge of the desert landscape, despite having divine guidance.</note>

¶ 32. "And it shall be, if you go with us—whatever good the LORD does for us, the same we will do for you."

---

<margin>v. 29. It appears that the person mentioned here is not Moses' father-in-law (who is called Reuel and Jethro in Exodus 2:18 and 3:1, and Jethro in Chapter 4:18), but rather Moses' brother-in-law, who is called the son of Reuel and named Hobab. For the father-in-law had already returned to his own land (Exodus 18:27), but the brother-in-law remained with Moses at his request. Consequently, his descendants lived among Israel and enjoyed the blessings promised here. See Judges 1:16, 4:11, and 1 Samuel 15:6.</margin>

<margin>v. 30. *I will go to my own land and my kindred*) This represents loving wife, child, father, mother, sister, or brother more than the Cross of Christ.</margin>

<margin>v. 31. *That you might be our eyes*) This reason for the entreaty can be understood in two ways: partly that he should not leave their sight, so they could continue to care for him as they had before; and partly that he could provide them with good intelligence in this wilderness, as he likely knew the area well from living in the neighboring region of Midian.</margin>

Otherwise, the Pillar of Cloud and Fire had to show them the way, and they did not strictly need him as a guide. However, he could still be useful to them in many matters. He knew all the opportunities and dangers of these wildernesses. When they wanted to pitch their camp, he knew where the surrounding enemy might first break in, and where the camp therefore required the most fortification. When they needed supplies and wanted to purchase them from the surrounding pagans, he knew where they could get them best and most conveniently. In many such matters, he could provide excellent assistance. Indeed,

Hobab is so necessary to Israel that they can do nothing without him. For Hobab means "Beloved," and signifies the love of God and neighbor, in which all things should be done (1 Corinthians 16:14). Everything that the true House of Jacob does must have Hobab—or the love of God and neighbor—as the doer. Otherwise, they are not the true Israel.

<margin>v. 32. It is only fair that those who bear the burden and heat of the day with us should also enjoy the refreshment and the good things with us.</margin>

...the friendship of this world is enmity against God.

<margin>v. 36. Arise then, O Israel, and begin your journey! The Ark of the Strength of the LORD will set out, scatter your enemies, and put them to flight. Ten thousand thousands of Israel have traveled this same path of the LORD before you. And since we have such a great cloud of witnesses before us, let us run the appointed race without weariness, and choose Jesus as our leader in our movements, our travels, and in our resting places, that he may lead us out and bring us in until the end.</margin>

<column-break/>

¶ 33. So they departed from the mountain of the LORD on a three days' journey; and the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD went before them (a) for the three days' journey, to search out a resting place for them. <margin>(a) Joshua 3:6.</margin>

¶ 34. And the cloud of the LORD was over them by day when they set out from the camp. <margin>Psalm 105:39.</margin>

¶ 35. And it happened, when the Ark set out, that Moses said: "Rise up, LORD! Let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before your face!" <margin>Psalm 132:8.</margin>

¶ 36. And when it rested, he said: "Return, O LORD, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel!"

---

<margin>v. 33. *Before them a 3 days' journey*) This should not be understood as the Ark being three full days ahead of the people, but rather that the journey lasted for three days before they set the Ark down and the Pillar of Cloud stood still.</margin>

Furthermore, it is to be concluded from this that the Ark of the Covenant went before all the people, rather than being carried in the middle of the twelve tribes with the other most holy items, as some Hebrews and others among us contend.

<margin>v. 34. The Pillar of Cloud served them not only as a guide but also protected them from the great heat.</margin>

They certainly had need of such a screen in the Arabian wilderness, where it is said there is nothing but barren sand which, when ignited by the vapor of the sun, and as the scorching sun burns the soles of the feet, creates an unbearable heat (a).

<margin>v. 35. Just as the LORD commanded a formal blessing to be spoken over His people (Chapter 6:23), Moses here used a customary prayer for the breaking of camp and the settling of camp. It was very short, emphatic, and pithy. David also aimed for this in several Psalms: Psalm 3:8, 7:7, 9:20–21, 10:12, etc., and especially Psalm 68:2, where this prayer appears with almost the same words and is interpreted for the final times, when the Ark of the Covenant will cast down Dagon <note>Dagon was a Philistine deity; the author uses this as a symbol for the fall of false idols.</note>. And David speaks of the return to rest among his people in Psalm 132:8, where he makes special mention of the Ark. Both should also be the wish of all believers in all their undertakings: that the LORD would help and come to rest with us as well. Psalm 118:25.</margin>

*Let your enemies be scattered*) If ever a nation or people has been scattered, it is the Jews themselves, even to this day. Thus, that which was once prayed *for* them has been fulfilled *against* them, because they showed themselves to be enemies of the LORD and did not want Him to rule over them.

However, when these words of prayer are directed against people who are of a different opinion than we are—whether they be Jews, Turks <note>In the 18th century, "Turks" was often a general term for Muslims.</note>, or professing Christians—it is often done out of partisanship. People taken with self-love imagine in their fantasy that they are dear and precious to Christ as His friends above all others; but others, who do not walk their path, they view with secret hatred as enemies of God and Christianity, though it may be quite different in God's eyes. Meanwhile, they fail to consider that being carnally minded is enmity against God, and that our carnal lusts are the true enemies of God. It is for this that we should pray: that He might rise up within us and scatter these, which are His and our most truthful enemies.

v. 1. The people complained greatly) This complaining may well have arisen from several causes; for example, because of the difficulty of the journey / in such a terrible wilderness: but ultimately it was the perverse craving for meat and other pleasant fruits of the earth in Egypt / where they may have had an abundance of everything. Since they were now unmindful of the great benefits of God / who had delivered them from such an oppressive bondage / and had already shown so many wonders to their enemies and to themselves / and also wished to lead them into a fruitful land; so they did not wish to endure for a little while longer / and be content with the pleasant bread / the Manna / which was provided for their necessity / but expressed their displeasure in every way. Thus God let them feel the fire / in which He had appeared to them at the giving of the Law on Mount Sinai. See Exodus 19:16, 18. Deuteronomy 33:2.

It is such a strange thing concerning the "bite" and the wilderness of faith / which is stripped of all supports / that it becomes very bitter for the soul / to remain satisfied and faithful within it / without regretting that it has embarked on such a journey so rough and long to the senses. For although God is its guide / it still cannot rely on that / because everything appears as mere clouds. The greatness of such anxiety causes one to murmur / as if one were complaining against God. But this is accompanied by an even greater anxiety; because the soul is shrouded in such a cruel internal burning / that it suffers death-pains over it. And this fire consumes a part of the camp / which is the soul's place of rest. But it is only the outermost part; namely the peace that it sought in itself / or in the gifts of God: which must be taken away / so that it can rest unchangeably in God alone and in His will.

v. 2. This is the verse / with which the Jews even today try to appease, stop, and extinguish fire. But
The prayer of Moses / or the returning of the soul into its surrender / better stills the wrath of God.

The fire of the LORD) from that time until today, not only individual people / but also entire murmuring nations / have experienced this: and it is not just one Taberah that stands as a testimony and an example of a site of burning before our eyes / but almost countless voices cry out and testify to the kindled wrath of God; so that / since we do not recognize God from His benefits / we must recognize Him from His judgments and punishments. For we ourselves kindle the fire of divine wrath / and cause it to burn so often among and near and within us. Thus / as often as such evil befalls us / the rebuke of the prophet in Isaiah 50:11 (a) rightly strikes us.

# Chapter 11. The Fourth Book of Moses.

16. And the LORD said to Moses: Gather for me seventy (a) men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be the elders of the people and its officials; and bring them before the Tabernacle of Meeting, so that they may stand there with you.
<margin>(a) Genesis 46:27.</margin>

---

Moses had previously, following Jethro’s advice, selected such upright men to help him carry the burden of government. Exodus 18:25. These were the elders and officials of the people, from whom he was now, according to God’s decree and for the further easing of his office in all occurring matters, to choose seventy men. God intended to assign them to him and provide them, like him, with the necessary gifts of the Spirit.

Thus God often chooses to relieve upright leaders of part of their burden by joining such people to them who must help them carry this yoke.

**Gather for me 70 men from the elders)** The Hebrews unanimously—and many scholars among the Christians (a) with them—set this decree as the foundation and origin of the Great Sanhedrin or *Synedrium* <note>The supreme judicial and ecclesiastical council of the ancient Jews.</note> at Jerusalem. This great council of the Jews consisted of priests, Levites, and godly Israelites. 2 Chronicles 19:8. This spiritual council, which judged all divine and human, civil and capital matters, remained among the Jews until the time of Christ (see Mark 15:1). Furthermore, Christ also appointed seventy disciples according to this model, whom he assigned to his Apostles for the proclamation of the Gospel. Luke 10:1.

**Whom you know to be elders)** Accordingly, this office of elder is not to be understood as referring to natural age in this external world, but in regard to wisdom, or Christ himself, who enters into holy souls according to their "ages"; Wisdom of Solomon 7:27. <note>The author quotes the apocryphal Wisdom of Solomon to argue that "age" refers to spiritual maturity and the indwelling of Christ.</note> Thus, it refers to the age of the Spirit. To such as these alone, according to God’s intent, belongs the care and governance of his Church. Therefore, wise, God-fearing, loving, gentle, merciful, patient, and humble people are required—those who are like Moses; even more so after they have received a portion of his excellent Spirit.

However, in the following times, little regard was given to this "age of wisdom," and men from the priests, Levites, and other Israelites were chosen who indeed exercised the same power and authority, but did not possess the same Spirit and life of God. Therefore, their authority was like a sword in the hand of a madman, and they abused it to satisfy their desires and lusts and to suppress the Truth itself; so much so that they would not allow anyone to teach the people who was not appointed by them, even if he were called and sent by God. Jeremiah 29:26, 27; Matthew 21:23; Acts 4:7. Neither God the Son, nor his disciples and apostles—though they were full of the Holy Spirit—were permitted to present divine doctrine or perform any good work except by the permission of the elders. So corrupted was this government in later times, having degenerated from its initial purity of divine decree.

How things stand in this regard today, and whether the right "age" is greatly considered, experience may best testify. It is certain that there should be spiritual men in the Church who are fit and capable of judging spiritual things. Certainly, there is also no lack of material upon which to pass judgment.

<margin>(a) <note>This margin list cites several 17th-century scholars: Pietro Galatino, *On the Secrets of Catholic Truth*, book 4, ch. 5; Wilhelm Schickard, *On the Royal Law of the Hebrews*, ch. 1, theory 2; Petrus Cunaeus, *On the Hebrew Republic*, book 1, ch. 12; Johannes Leusden, *Mixed Hebrew Philology*, dissertation 46; John Selden, *On Natural and International Law*, book 5, ch. 9; Hugo Grotius, *On the Law of War and Peace*, book 1, ch. 3; Matthias Flacius, under the terms *Synagogue* and *Sanhedrin*, etc.</note></margin>

...you shall eat; so that you may recognize the preciousness of the previous food.

**You have -- spoken -- therefore the LORD will give to you)** When God wants to help souls forward with strength, so that the higher part of the soul has no share in such complaints, he gives them nothing: so that no perceived relief prevents them from passing through all things to draw near to him alone. But as soon as the [human] will meddles in it, he gives them meat, which can satisfy them sufficiently. Such souls do not see that it is a punishment for their sin; instead, they think it was sent to them as a great grace, in which they find themselves very well. Indeed, self-interested people even say that God performs wonders for their sake and gives them whatever they desire.

<column-break/>

17. Thus I will come down and speak with you there, and take of the Spirit that is upon you and lay it upon them; so that they may bear the burden of the people with you, that you might not have to bear it alone.

18. And to the people you shall say: Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, that you may eat meat. For you have wept in the ears of the LORD and said: Who will give us meat to eat? For it went well with us in Egypt. Therefore the LORD will give you meat, so that you may eat.

19. Not

---

v. 17. **Take of the Spirit that is upon you and lay it upon them)** Just as the two final witnesses shall walk in the spirit and power of Moses and Elijah.

**That they)** might be strengthened by that same excellent Spirit of judgment, and made fit and capable for the government of the

**Burden of the people)** their weakness and stubbornness, to

**Bear)** This shall be the foremost office and work of regents and authorities.

And thus, the spiritual ones are the strongest and most fit for an office and duty. Romans 15:1; Galatians 6:1. And the Spirit, which is so strong that it bears all things, is the Spirit of Love. 1 Corinthians 13:7. Whoever has this excellent Spirit becomes capable through it to endure and bear all the weaknesses, recalcitrance, murmuring, and impatience of the people. This excellent Spirit of Christ, which is also recognized by other fruits (Galatians 5:22), sufficiently qualifies all spiritual rulers.

Therefore, there is no need for much questioning and arguing about the government of the church, as to whom it actually belongs and is due. For without doubt, the best government in both Church and State must necessarily be where the Spirit of God governs those who hold the government; and that same church will undoubtedly be the best Reformed and Evangelical church. But if this excellent Spirit does not rule in the regents, then it matters little who has the government in the church. For then it is no spiritual and divine government, as Christ’s government should be, even if it were otherwise rational and just. For Christ, the head of the church, must—as the Son in the house—have even better regents than Moses the servant. Hebrews 3:5, 6.

Oh, if only one would first take the lowest place and allow oneself to be instructed and disciplined by the Law of God; and thereby be brought to the Son and bear the yoke of Christ; then his Spirit of life and resurrection would not fail to appear, by which one would be made fit to bear the burdens of others. One would thus be taught to first govern oneself and one's house in a godly manner, and then become fit to be a ruler and overseer of the Church of Christ.

v. 18. **Sanctify yourselves, that you may eat meat)** Because you did not want the LORD to sanctify you, now sanctify yourselves; return to your own exercises. Then you will eat meat—that is, you will enjoy the pleasure of the senses, which you indeed recognize as spiritual (which is nothing other than satisfying the "sweet tooth" of the spirit). Indeed, you will eat so much of it that you will not only be full, but even grow weary of it.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XI

7. The manna was like coriander seed, and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium. <margin>Genesis 2:12.</margin>

### Type of Christ.

10. On the 7th day it was not seen, but again on the 8th or first. Thus Christ was hidden in the grave and rose again.

12. The Israelites ate of it until they came to Canaan. Christ is the food for eternal life.
13. They had a loathing for the manna and called it a "light food." And in what low esteem is Christ held among his people!
14. In a small golden jar, a gomer was kept before the LORD in the Tabernacle, where it remained until the destruction of the first Temple, after which it was no longer found on earth. Thus Christ is also taken up into heaven and is no longer seen on earth: nevertheless, he is and remains our hidden manna, of which we can eat. Revelation 2:17.
