# Chapter XI. The Fourth Book of Moses. 597

16. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses: Gather for me seventy <margin>(a)</margin> men from the elders of Israel / whom you know / to be the elders of the people and its officials; and bring them before the Tabernacle of Meeting / so that they may stand there with you. <margin>(a) Genesis 46:27.</margin>

<note>Moses had previously, following Jethro's advice, selected such upright men / who were to help him carry the burden of government. Exodus 18:25. These were the elders and officials of the people / from whom he was now, according to **God’s** decree for the further easing of his office in all occurring matters, to choose seventy men / whom **God** would assign to him and provide with the necessary gifts of the Spirit just like him.

Thus **God** often chooses to relieve upright leaders of part of their burden / by joining them with such people / who must help them carry this yoke.</note>

<note>Gather for me 70 men from the elders) The Hebrews unanimously view this decree / and many scholars among the Christians (a) with them / as the foundation and origin of the Great Sanhedrin or Council in Jerusalem / the great council of the Jews / which consisted of priests / Levites / and godly Israelites. 2 Chronicles 19:8. This spiritual council / which judged all divine and human / civil and capital matters; remained among the Jews until the time of Christ: (see Mark 15:1) and Christ also, according to this, appointed seventy disciples / whom he joined to his Apostles in the proclamation of the Gospel. Luke 10:1.</note>

<note>Those whom you know / to be elders) Accordingly, this office of elder is not to be understood as natural age in this external world / but in view of wisdom / or Christ himself / who enters into holy souls according to their ages; <note>original: "nach den Altern"</note> Wisdom of Solomon 7:27. and thus refers to the age of the Spirit. To such alone, according to **God's** intent, belongs the care and governance of his Church. Thus there are required for this wise / God-fearing / loving / gentle / merciful / patient, and humble people / such as Moses was; even more so / after they have received a portion of his excellent Spirit.</note>

<note>However, in the following time, little regard was paid to this "age of wisdom" / and men from among the priests / Levites, and other Israelites / were chosen for it / who indeed exercised the same power and authority / but did not have the same Spirit and life of **God**. Therefore, their authority was like a sword in the hand of a madman / and they misused it to satisfy their desires and lusts and to suppress the truth itself; so much so that they would not allow anyone to teach the people / who was not appointed by them / even if he was already called and sent by **God**. Jeremiah 29:26-27. Matthew 21:23. Acts 4:7. Neither **God** the Son / nor his disciples and apostles / though they were full of the **Holy** Spirit / were allowed to present divine doctrine / nor do any good work / except with the permission of the elders. So corrupted was this government in following times / and it deviated from its initial purity of divine decree.</note>

<note>How it stands today / and whether great attention is paid to the right "age" [of the spirit] / experience may best bear witness. That spiritual men should be in the Church / who are fit and capable of judging spiritual things / is established. Thus there is certainly no lack of matters / about which to judge.</note>

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chap. XI. 598

<margin>19.</margin> Not for one day shall you eat, nor for two days, nor for five days, nor for ten days, nor for twenty days.
<margin>20.</margin> But for a whole month, until it comes out of your nostrils and becomes a loathing to you. Because you have rejected the **LORD** who is among you, and have wept before His face and said: Why did we ever leave Egypt?
<margin>21.</margin> And Moses said: The people among whom I am are six hundred thousand on foot; and you say: I will give them meat, that they may eat for a whole month!
<margin>22.</margin> Shall sheep and cattle be slaughtered for them, to be enough for them? Or will all the fish of the sea be gathered for them, to be enough for them? <margin>(a) 1 Cor. 15:39.</margin>
<margin>23.</margin> But the **LORD** said to Moses: Has the **LORD's** hand then become too short? Now you shall see whether my word can come to pass for you, or not.

**v. 19. Not for one day)** **God** indeed sometimes gives a soul what it desires for a few days, satisfying its taste through certain sensible gifts; sometimes even longer. This then makes the soul believe that everything is accomplished and that it has entered a new life, even though such a state is merely one of pure sensuality and self-love. <note>The commentator warns that spiritual "good feelings" are not the same as true spiritual maturity.</note>

**v. 20. God wanted** to satisfy the people’s appetite not for a short time, but for a long duration, until that very thing for which they previously had such an immoderate craving would arouse a loathing in them. Thus, both Moses and the people were to be heard in their concerns, though the people’s request was granted as a punishment.

**v. 21. Here, however,** Moses was again overtaken by his weakness, in that he wanted to form a human conception of divine help, the manner of which he should have left to **God**. For this reason, he was also rebuked by **God**. See 2 Kings 7:2.

**v. 22. He doubts** the divine omnipotence, even though he had received so many assurances of it. This, however, is recorded for our instruction. **God** allows such doubts in His servants in order to draw forth infallible truths from them, which He Himself speaks when He answers them. An example of such an oracle <note>original: "Oraculum"</note> was the doubt of the Apostles (a) regarding the multiplication of the bread. But **Jesus** took that opportunity to instruct them and to perform His miracles.

**v. 23. God shows** how easy everything is for the arm of His power, and how nothing surpasses His strength, which is infinite. He who tries to measure **God’s** power with his own weak understanding offends Him.

He also assures therein that His word—which often seemed so incredible in the mouths of His servants—should become true through His works, and that one would eventually see the effect of His power in those things which had been considered entirely impossible.
<margin>(a) John 6:9.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>24.</margin> And Moses went out and spoke the words of the **LORD** to the people, and gathered the seventy men from the elders of the people, and placed them around the Tabernacle.
<margin>25.</margin> Then the **LORD** came down in the cloud, and spoke to him, and took of the Spirit that was upon him, and put it upon the seventy men, the elders. And it happened, when the Spirit rested upon them, that they prophesied; but they did so no more. <margin>26. v.</margin>

**v. 24. Moses went out)** As long as Moses hears the word of the **LORD** and is taught by Him, he is "inside" and remains in the interior, where the most hidden mysteries are revealed to him in the secret chamber of **God**. But when he speaks to the people and serves those who cannot stand within, it is said of him that he "goes out."

Similarly, when a theologian ponders the hidden mysteries in his heart, or brings forth some secret of **God’s** wisdom among the perfect (1 Cor. 2:6), and as long as he remains in the depths of the spirit, he is "inside." But when he speaks to those who are "outside," telling them what is sufficient and conducive to their salvation, and expressing things the common people can hear and grasp, it is also said of him that he has "gone out."

**Gathered the 70 men)** In the Gemara Sanhedrin <note>The Gemara is part of the Talmud, a collection of Jewish rabbinical teachings.</note> (a) it is recounted how Moses chose the 70 elders. He thought to himself: "If I choose 6 from each tribe, there will be 72, which is two too many. If I choose 5 from each tribe, I will be ten short. If I take 5 from some and 6 from others, I will stir up resentment among them." What did he do then? He chose 6 from every tribe, then he took 72 slips of paper. On 70 of them was written: "Elder." Two were left blank. He threw these into a pot together and had each of the 72 chosen men take a slip. To him who got a slip with the word "Elder," Moses said: "**God** has gently sanctified you." But to him who got a blank slip, he said: "**God** does not desire you."

**v. 25. Took of the Spirit that was upon him)** Everyone who rests in **God** alone is so free and detached from his own "goodness" that he allows everything previously given to him to be taken away without resistance; he is even happy that **God** shares it with others, because he seeks not his own honor, but the honor of **God**.

**Put it upon the 70)** But this, writes Origen, <note>Origen was an early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> 
> "is not to be understood as if He took a physical substance from 
> him, divided it into 70 parts, and gave a small piece to each. 
> It is impious to have such a concept of the nature of the **Holy Spirit**. 
> Rather, you should consider the figure of this secret speech: 
> it is as if Moses and the Spirit in him were a lamp with a very 
> bright light, from which **God** lit 70 others; the radiance of this 
> principal <note>original: "principalen Haupt-Lichts"</note> light was 
> added to them in such a way that the original light suffered 
> no lack whatsoever."

**When the Spirit rested upon them)** The Spirit is not said to rest upon all kinds of people, but only upon the holy and those of pure heart. For what fellowship should the **Holy Spirit** have with the unclean spirit that dwells in every heart devoted to sin? As soon as the latter is let in through evil thoughts and desires, the **Holy Spirit** flows away as if driven out. Thus, it is admitted that the resting of the Spirit indicates the pure and virtuous life of these 70 men. But what does it help us to know this if we do not also prepare a resting place for Him?

**They did so no more)** Luther indeed translates it as "and they did not stop," as if they had kept the prophetic spirit; but in the Hebrew, the opposite is more clearly stated, meaning: they did not continue, namely, they did not continue to prophesy, but stopped after that day. **God** intended to set them apart from others through this prophesying and to initiate them into this high office, as well as to awaken authority and prestige for them in the eyes of others.
<margin>(a) chapter 1, section 17. (b) homily 6 on Numbers.</margin>

### Chap. XI. The Fourth Book of Moses.

26. And two men remained in the camp; the name of one was Eldad, and the name of the other was Medad: and the Spirit rested upon them. For they were among those who were registered, but they had not gone out to the Tabernacle; and they prophesied in the camp.

27. Then a young man ran and told Moses, saying: Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.

<note>Eldad and Medad were, by all appearances, the two men who remained from the seventy-two mentioned in verse 24.</note>

Now, since these two who stayed behind were also graced with the gifts of the Spirit and, like the others before them, spoke for the first time with a remarkably holy eloquence concerning the ways of **GOD** (see Acts 2:11), through which the communication of the Spirit could be perceived by everyone; and since this was no longer necessary for the future and therefore did not happen again: Joshua was seized with a spirit of zeal, as if his master’s reputation might suffer if anyone dared to take up such eloquence to instruct people in the ways of **GOD**. Moses, however, showed his humility by wishing this divine gift upon everyone, so that they might speak of the **LORD’S** ways and thus walk in them. In such a case, there would be no special need for prophets and rulers, who are often more burdened by this office than made particularly happy by it, especially when one must serve so many in this way.

It surely does not happen without a special divine wisdom that only these two are mentioned by name. For within both their names lie two glorious qualities hidden, which all authorities and judges should possess. Namely:

**Eldad** signifies the **Love of GOD**, and indicates that rulers must be adorned with a rich measure of divine mercy, kindness, and love, so that they do nothing out of cruelty or thirst for revenge, but rather show mercy and compassion to all those in need of it: so that in this way they may represent **GOD** the **LORD** as much in goodness as in power and in the execution of their office.

Just as Eldad signifies the love of **GOD**, so **Medad** means a **Measure**, and points toward **Justice**, in which those in authority should shine before others, so that in this as in all their works they provide a measure and a model for others. Indeed, according to a deeper and cabalistic <note>A reference to Jewish mystical interpretation (Kabbalah), which often looks for hidden meanings in the numerical value or spelling of Hebrew names.</note> yet scripturally grounded method of interpretation, Medad may mean **GOD’S Measure**, because in the original language the Hebrew letter *Yod* is included in the name; this is the initial letter of the names **Jah** and **Jehovah**, and these two names are two of the great names of **GOD**. And so it represents an unmixed justice, and thus another great quality of a ruler, who should follow **GOD** the **LORD** in impartial justice as well as goodness and mercy, and measure out to each man his due, whether reward or punishment. In this way, the **LORD** Himself describes a person in authority in 2 Samuel 23:3.

O, if only Christian nations were blessed with such rulers who gave a good example to others, and who strove to become like Him who calls Himself the Prince of the kings of the earth—not only in authority, but also in goodness, fairness, and humility, out of which (as is likely) these two remained in the camp; then one would certainly have reason to hope that the **LORD** would also pour out a measure of that excellent Spirit upon them: and they would then be so far from suppressing prophecy that they would practice it themselves. Thus, no honest man would envy them for such a privilege, but would all the more fear and hold them in honor, mindful of the answer which Moses gave here to Joshua.

as if to be so many joyful echoes of this voice, which from...

<note>v. 30. He and the elders) Presumably the seventy,</note>

<column-break/>

28. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen ones, answered and said: My lord Moses, forbid them! <margin>1 Thessalonians 5:19-20.</margin>

29. But Moses said to him: Are you jealous for my sake? Oh, that all the **LORD’S** people were prophets, and that the **LORD** would put His Spirit upon them!

30. So Moses returned to the camp, he and the elders of Israel.

<note>v. 28. Joshua said: Forbid them!) Just as this blind zeal also seized the disciples of Christ. Mark 9:37 etc. Luke 9:49.</note>

And is this not the very mindset that one sees displayed so frequently today? And this after we already have the mind and thoughts of Moses and others before us. **GOD** lets His sun rise over the evil and the good; yet we always want to forbid one another from letting their light shine, and instead prefer that it be placed under a bushel. Why is the eye so squinted and envious when **GOD** does not bind His calling and gifts solely to us? Why does one always seek to close the windows of heaven and build a dam before the great river Euphrates, so that its living streams from the throne of **GOD** and the Lamb may not flow down over the parched desert of our souls?

v. 29. If only one would take Moses' answer a little more deeply to heart, even today when **GOD** equips certain persons—who may not hold a public office—with something special, and makes known His will through them in prophecy and the proclamation of future things, or places in them some other gift of edification! Why does one now—and under the Gospel, no less—speak an entirely different language than Moses, whereby one separates oneself into the teaching office to the exclusion of one's brothers? Why is the prophet and the man of the Spirit now regarded as so foolish and insane? Must we not all be taught by the **LORD**? Shall not the knowledge of the **LORD** be as abundant as the waters that cover the depths of the sea? Certainly Moses, in this wish, looked simultaneously as a prophet toward the times of the Spirit and the New Testament, when it should and would be so, when **GOD** promised to pour out His Spirit upon all flesh. Why, then, is one so eager to always quench the Spirit? Why does one now seek in the New Testament to make a monopoly out of the prophetic office, and dare to reject the gifts of the Spirit—which manifest in everyone for the common good—and bind them only to consecrated priests? Have those who have the key of knowledge received it to lock knowledge away, or to open the door to all the people?

The very pure zeal for the honor of **GOD** is what caused Moses to give Joshua such a beautiful answer. The most truly rational people do the same when graced souls take up their own honor. They care nothing for it, even if they should lose everything for the sake of **GOD** and souls. Why, they say, are you jealous on our behalf? One must only be jealous with the jealousy of **GOD**, who is jealous only for His own honor. We too must be zealous for nothing but the honor of **GOD**. O, how beautiful are these words of Moses, and how vividly should they be impressed upon the hearts of all those who assist souls through the ministry of the Word of **GOD**! Would to **GOD** the whole world could prophesy, and that the **LORD** would give them His Spirit! Saint Paul was of this same opinion when he said: <margin>(a) Philippians 1:18.</margin> (a) what does it matter, as long as Christ is proclaimed in every way? I will rejoice in it more and more. All true lovers of **JESUS CHRIST** must flow with an disinterested love.

<note>whom he had previously gathered at the Tabernacle according to verse 24.</note>

<margin>v. 19. *Not one day*) **GOD** does indeed sometimes give a soul what it desires for a few days, satisfying its taste through certain sensory gifts; sometimes even longer. This then makes the soul believe that everything is accomplished and that it has entered a new life; even though such a state is merely one of pure sensibility and self-love. <note>Sensory gifts: Refers to emotional or physical spiritual "feelings" that can mislead a believer into thinking they are more spiritually advanced than they are.</note></margin>

<margin>v. 20. **GOD** wanted to satisfy the people’s appetite not for a short time, but for a long duration, until they themselves would feel a loathing for that which they previously had such an immoderate craving for; thus, both Moses and the people were to be heard in their concerns.</margin>

<margin>v. 21. Here, however, Moses was again overtaken by his weakness, for he immediately wanted to form a conception of divine help, the manner of which he should have left to **GOD**; and for this reason, he was also rebuked by **GOD**. See 2 Kings 7:2.</margin>

<margin>v. 22. He doubts divine omnipotence, even though he had received so many assurances of it. This, however, is recorded for our instruction. **GOD** permits such doubts in His servants in order to draw forth infallible truths from them, which He Himself speaks when He answers them. One such oracle was the doubt of the Apostles (a) regarding the multiplication of the bread. Jesus, however, took that opportunity to instruct them and to perform His miracles.</margin>

<margin>v. 23. **GOD** shows how easy everything is for the arm of His power, and how nothing surpasses His strength, which is infinite. He who tries to measure **GOD'S** power with his own weak understanding offends Him.</margin>

He also assures therein that His word—which often seemed so unbelievable in the mouths of His servants—should become true through His works, and that one would one day see the effect of His power in those things which were considered entirely impossible.
<margin>(a) John 6:9.</margin>

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

24. And Moses went out and spoke
the words of the **LORD** to the people,
and gathered the seventy men
from the elders of the people, and
placed them around the Tabernacle.

25. Then the **LORD** came down in
the cloud and spoke to him, and
took of the Spirit that was upon him
and put it upon the seventy
men, the elders. And it happened
that as the Spirit rested upon them,
they prophesied: but they did so no further.

---

<margin>v. 24. *Moses went out*) As long as Moses hears the word of the **LORD** and is taught by Him, he is "inside," remaining in the inner being where the most hidden mysteries are revealed to him in the secret chamber of **GOD**. But when he speaks to the people and serves those who cannot stand within the interior, it is said of him that he "goes out."</margin>

Thus, when a theologian ponders hidden mysteries in his heart, or when he brings forth something rare from the wisdom of **GOD** among the "perfect" (1 Cor. 2:6), and as long as he stays in the depths of the spirit, he is "inside." But when he speaks to those who are "outside," telling them what is good and sufficient for their understanding—speaking of things the common people can hear and grasp—it must also be said of him that he has "gone out."

*Gathered the 70 men*) In the *Gemara Sanhedrin* (a) it is recounted how Moses chose the 70 elders. He thought to himself: "If I choose 6 from each tribe, there will be two left over; if I choose 5 from each tribe, I will be seven short." What did he do? He chose 6 from every tribe, then he took 72 slips of paper. On 70 of them was written: *Elder*. Two were blank. He threw these into a pot together and told each of the 72 chosen men to draw a slip. To whoever drew one with the word *Elder*, Moses said: "**GOD** has already sanctified you long ago." But to whoever drew a blank slip, he said: "**GOD** does not desire you." <note>Gemara Sanhedrin: A section of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism, which discusses the appointment of the biblical judges.</note>

<margin>v. 25. *Took of the Spirit that was upon him*) Anyone who rests in **GOD** alone is so detached and free from all possessions that he allows everything previously given to him to be taken back without resistance; he is even happy that **GOD** shares it with others, because he seeks not his own honor, but the honor of **GOD**.</margin>

*Put it upon the 70*) Regarding this, Origen writes (b): "This is not to be understood as if He took a physical substance from him, divided it into 70 parts, and gave each a small piece. It is ungodly to form such a concept of the nature of the Holy Spirit. Rather, you should consider the figure of this secret speech: as if Moses and the Spirit in him were a lamp with a very bright light, from which **GOD** lit 70 others; and the radiance of this principal main light increased such that the original light suffered no loss thereby." <note>Origen: An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) who often used light and fire as metaphors for spiritual concepts.</note>

*As the Spirit rested upon them*) The Spirit is not said to rest upon all kinds of people, but only upon the holy and those who are pure in heart. For what fellowship could the Holy Spirit have with the unclean spirit that dwells in every heart devoted to sin? Where the latter is let in through evil thoughts and desires, the Holy Spirit flees as if driven away. Thus, the pure and virtuous life of these 70 men is indicated here.

---

<note>The following text spans the bottom of both columns.</note>

But what does it help us to know this if we do not also prepare a resting place for Him?

*They did so no further*) Luther, it is true, renders this "and did not stop," as if they had retained the prophetic spirit; but in the Hebrew, the opposite is actually written, which others translate as: they did not continue—namely, to prophesy—but stopped that day. **GOD** intended, through this prophesying, to set them apart from others and initiate them into their high office, and also to awaken authority and respect for them among the others.
<margin>(a) 1 Sam. 10:10. <note>Correcting the original margin note (a) which likely intended a different reference, as 1 Sam 10:10 refers to Saul prophesying.</note></margin> <margin>(b) Homily 6 on Numbers.</margin>

# Ch. XI. The Fourth Book of Moses. 599

**26. And there remained two men in the camp; the name of the one was Eldad, and the name of the other Medad: and the spirit rested upon them. For they were among those who were registered, but they had not gone out to the Tabernacle: and they prophesied in the camp.**

**27. Then a young man ran and told Moses, and said: Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.**

---

Eldad and Medad were, by all appearances, the two men who remained from the seventy-two mentioned in verse 24. <note>While Moses was told to gather seventy elders, it was traditional to select six from each of the twelve tribes, totaling seventy-two; two would then be "left over" to maintain the number seventy.</note>

Since these two who stayed behind were also graced with the gifts of the Spirit, and spoke with the others for the first time with a special holy eloquence concerning the ways of God (see Acts 2:11), the communication of the Spirit could be perceived by everyone. This was no longer necessary for the future, and therefore did not happen again. However, Joshua was seized with a spirit of zeal, as if something were being taken away from his master’s authority if anyone were allowed to take up such eloquence to instruct people in God’s ways. But Moses showed his humility, wishing that this divine gift were given to all so that they might speak of the Lord's ways and walk in them. If that were so, there would be no special need for prophets and rulers, who are more burdened by this office than made particularly happy by it—especially when one must serve so many.

It certainly does not happen without special divine wisdom that only these two are mentioned by name. For in both their names lie two glorious qualities hidden, which all authorities and judges should possess. Namely:

**Eldad** signifies the "Love of God," and indicates that rulers must be adorned with a rich measure of divine mercy, kindness, and love, so that they do nothing out of cruelty or thirst for revenge. Rather, they should show mercy and compassion to all who need it, so that in this way they may represent God the Lord in His goodness, power, and the conduct of His office.

Just as Eldad signifies the love of God, so **Medad** signifies a "Measure," and points to justice, in which authoritative persons should shine before others in such a way that they provide a measure and an example to others in this, as in all their works. Indeed, according to a deeper and cabalistic—yet scripturally grounded—interpretation, Medad may mean "God’s Measure," because in the original language the Hebrew letter *Yod* is included in the name. This is the first letter of the names *Jah* and *Jehovah*, both of which are among the great names of God. <note>In Hebrew, the letter Yod (י) is often used as a shorthand for the divine name. The author suggests that the name Medad (מידד) contains this divine "measure" within its structure.</note> Thus, it represents an unmixed justice, and with it, another great quality of a ruler, who should follow God the Lord in impartial justice as well as goodness and mercy, measuring out to each what is theirs, whether reward or punishment. In this way, the Lord Himself describes an authoritative person in 2 Samuel 23:3.

Oh, if only Christian nations were blessed with such rulers who gave others a good example! Rulers who strove to become like Him who calls Himself the Prince of the Kings of the Earth—not only in authority but also in goodness, fairness, and humility (out of which, likely, these two remained in the camp). Then there would be reason to hope that the Lord would pour out a measure of that excellent Spirit upon them; and they would be so far from suppressing prophecy that they would practice it themselves. No honest person would envy them for such a privilege, but would rather fear and honor them all the more, mindful of the answer Moses gave to Joshua here.

<column-break/>

<margin>1 Thess. 5:19–20.</margin>
**28. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Moses, one of his chosen, answered and said: My lord Moses, forbid them!**

**29. But Moses said to him: Are you jealous for my sake? Would to God that all the Lord's people were prophets, and that the Lord would put His spirit upon them!**

**30. And Moses returned to the camp, he and the elders of Israel.**

---

v. 28. *Joshua said: Forbid them!*) This same blind zeal also seized the disciples of Christ. <note>original: "blinder Eifer" — an emotional, protective jealousy that lacks spiritual insight.</note> Mark 9:38, Luke 9:49.

And is this not the very mindset that is seen so frequently today? Even now, after we know the mind and thoughts of Moses and others. God lets His sun rise over the evil and the good; yet we always want to forbid one another from letting their light shine, wanting instead to put it under a bushel. Why is the eye so squinted and envious when God does not bind His calling and gifts solely to us? Why do we always seek to close the windows of heaven and build a dam against the great river Euphrates, so that its living streams might not flow down from the throne of God and the Lamb over the parched wilderness of our souls?

v. 29. Would that people would take Moses's answer a little more deeply to heart today, when God equips certain persons—who perhaps do not hold a public office—with something special, and makes known His will through them in prophecy and the declaration of future things, or places some other gift of edification within them! Why do people now, especially under the Gospel, speak a completely different language than Moses? Why do they separate themselves into a "teaching office" while excluding their brothers? Why is the prophet and the man of the spirit now regarded as so foolish and insane? Must we not all be taught by the Lord? Should not the knowledge of the Lord be as abundant as the waters that cover the depths of the sea? Certainly, in this wish, Moses saw as a prophet into the times of the Spirit and the New Testament, when it should and would be so, for God promised to pour out His Spirit upon all flesh. Why, then, do people want to quench the Spirit so willingly? Why do they now seek to make a monopoly out of the prophetic office in the New Testament, and dare to reject the gifts of the Spirit which manifest in everyone for the common good, binding them only to ordained priests? Have those who hold the key of knowledge received it to lock up knowledge, or to open the door for all the people?

A very pure zeal for the glory of God caused Moses to give Joshua such a beautiful answer. The most righteous people do the same when graced souls take care of their own honor. They care nothing if they should lose everything for the sake of God and souls. Why, they say, are people jealous for our sake? We must only be jealous with the jealousy of God, who is only jealous for His own honor. We should be jealous for nothing but the glory of God. we should rightly wish with Moses that everyone might attain to that same state and have the same Spirit of God. Oh, how beautiful are these words of Moses, and how vividly should they be imprinted on the hearts of all those who assist souls through the ministry of the Word of God! Would to God the whole world could prophesy, and that the Lord would give them His Spirit! St. Paul was of this same opinion when he said: <margin>(a) Phil. 1:18.</margin> (a) What does it matter, as long as Christ is proclaimed in every way? I will rejoice in it more and more. All true lovers of Jesus Christ must be like so many faithful echoes of this voice, which flows out of an disinterested love.

v. 30. *He and the elders*) Presumably the same seventy whom he had previously gathered at the Tabernacle according to verse 24.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Ch. XI.

**31. Then a wind went out from the Lord, and swept quails from the sea, and they spread out around the camp, here a day's journey and there a day's journey all around the camp, and about two cubits <note>About three feet</note> above the earth.**

**32. Then the people rose up that entire day and the entire night and the entire next day, and gathered the quails. He who gathered the least had gathered ten homers <note>A homer was a large dry measure, roughly 6 to 11 bushels</note>: and they spread them out neatly for themselves all around the camp.**

---

<margin>v. 31. They had already been fed with this food once at the beginning of the manna, but only for a short time. Exodus 16:13.</margin>
By means of the east and south winds, God allowed an indescribable multitude—which some translate as quails, while others say locusts (a)—to fall upon their camp from the Persian and Arabian Seas. These spread for an entire day's journey in every direction, lying about two cubits deep upon the earth, for they were so exhausted from their long flight that they could no longer move.

<margin>v. 32. One can conclude what an unspeakable quantity this was from the fact that the largest measure, a homer, was used, and each family gathered at least ten. Psalm 78:26-28.</margin>
A homer is equal to 10 ephahs or bushels; thus, 10 homers would be a hundred bushels. And if the one who gathered the least collected that much, how much must the one who gathered a lot have collected? Therefore, others believe the word *homer* here should be rendered as "heaps," which the word also signifies in Exodus 8:14 and Judges 15:16, referring to how birds are typically gathered into piles.

By spreading them out in the open air, they dried them, thereby preserving them from rotting.

(And the entire night and the entire next day) How hot and greedy is man for earthly things! They were not satisfied with one day's supply, nor with a provision for the immediate needs of the present day. It seems they did not believe that God could or would provide the same nourishment on the remaining days—even though He sent them manna daily—and so they worried about the next morning, and indeed for an entire month all at once.

The Lord had promised them meat for a month, and they made such provisions for themselves as if every day were a month. But if we condemn these people, how can we justify ourselves, we who make provision for children and grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation? It is as if God were only our God, and not also the God of our offspring. This is a story that happened in Moses' time, happened in later times, and still happens today.

Now, when wise people read histories to benefit from them, they look primarily at two things: the deed that occurred, the counsel taken, and the outcome. Here, the deed was the grumbling and the testing of God, and the belly was their counselor. What followed from this evil deed and foolish counsel is found in:

(a) That these could not have been quails has been clearly proven from the circumstances of the text by Job Ludolf, who conversely showed it very likely that they were locusts, the kind John the Baptist later ate in the wilderness. <note>original: "comm. ad Hist. Æthiop. l. 1. c. 13. n. 96. f. 168. sqq. & in append. 2. ad hist. Æth. diss. de locust. fol. 1. sqq." — These are references to Ludolf's *Commentary on the History of Ethiopia* and his *Dissertation on Locusts*.</note> Paulini also agrees with this opinion in his *Timely Edifying Delights*, Part 2, number 108, page 564, and Part 3, number 124, page 775 and following.

<column-break/>

**33. The meat was still between their teeth, it was not yet chewed, when the anger of the Lord burned against the people, and the Lord struck the people with a very great plague.**

**34. Therefore the name of that place was called Graves of Craving, because there they had buried the people who had been lustful.**

**35. From the Graves of Craving, the people moved on toward Hazeroth, and they remained at Hazeroth.**

---

<margin>v. 33. The meat — still — when) This truly means: reaping destruction right from the meat! Thus does the Lord’s anger flare up when one loves the flesh and holds the Word and Bread of Life in forgetfulness!</margin>
Because this food was consumed with sensory desire rather than with the proper holiness and preparation of heart that was required (v. 18), it seems God struck them—especially the transgressors—with a sudden, heavy plague at the end of the month, even as they were eating. The meat was not yet properly chewed or cut with the teeth (as the word actually means), and thus had not yet reached the stomach, when He struck them for their immoderate craving. See Psalm 106:14-15.

The question arises: why is the people punished so severely for this sin here, when they got off so easily in Exodus 16? It is because this is what happens when one despises God's goodness, patience, and long-suffering. Since then, they had received many more proofs and wonders of God's faithful guidance and care. There, they lacked everything and had nothing to eat; but here, they were weary of the heavenly food.

They should have remembered with fear that this food was given to them in anger; and therefore, they should not have misused it for their pleasure. See 2 Samuel 23:15, etc.

O poor souls, you who taste new refreshments—which you all regard as great graces, but which are nothing other than the object of your spiritual greed—you make God pay dearly enough for this small pleasure! You are so full of these apparent sweetnesses, while meanwhile, through a grace of His mercy and justice, He allows a great and terrifying wound to come upon you. If one knew with what a dreadful, deadly wound God punishes spiritual gluttony and the vanity of those souls who, after tasting the manna of pure faith, nevertheless return to sensory feelings, one would be terrified. Oh, how much better it is to experience the first punishment of His mercy in our stripping bare, than to feel the severity of His justice, which one has brought upon oneself by mixing a received benefit with the sensuality of the spirit!

<margin>v. 34. The region of the burial site was named Graves of Craving <note>Hebrew: Kibroth-hattaavah</note> because of the many buried there; however, the entire place was called Taberah because of the fire.</margin>
Just as God has nothing for us but pure merciful justice, even in His greatest severity, so such a chastisement of such souls is generally the grave of craving. For through such long-lasting and terrible chastisements, they lose their fleshly desires in divine things.

<margin>v. 35. And by leaving all desires behind there, they departed from that place without hesitation to stay in another location further along. And that is</margin>

->**Hazeroth)** The Forecourt.<-

When one leaves behind lust, and when the lusts and cravings have died, then one comes to the forecourt and the entrance to the heavenly Jerusalem.

# Chapter XII. The Fourth Book of Moses.

### The XII. Chapter.
->Miriam and Aaron’s Murmuring against Moses.<-

AND Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of the woman, the Ethiopian, <note>German: *Morin*. Historically referring to a woman from Cush or Ethiopia; likely Zipporah, though the text debates this.</note> whom he had taken; for he had taken an Ethiopian woman as a wife;

2. And they said: Does the LORD then speak only through Moses alone? Does he not also speak through us? And the LORD heard it.

<margin>v. 1. Miriam and Aaron)</margin> In the Hebrew, through the Spirit of God, it is indicated even more clearly that Miriam was offended first and drew her brother Aaron into the sin: for it might most properly be read; "and Miriam spoke, and also Aaron, against Moses": thus Miriam bore more guilt. In this way Eve sinned first, and then Adam. And for that reason, Aaron was not struck with leprosy, but Miriam alone. Likewise, Adam was not punished as severely or harshly as Eve.

<margin>Ethiopian woman)</margin> Some believe the land of Midian belonged to the land of the Moors in Egypt as a part of its dominion beyond the Red Sea; therefore they called her an Ethiopian, though she was a Midianite. Exodus 2:15, 21. Although in the Hebrew she is specifically made out to be a Cushite, which does not necessarily mean an Ethiopian, but rather an Arabian. Just as the land of Cush in Arabia bordered the land of Canaan (a). See Genesis 37:28, 2 Chronicles 14:8, Isaiah 20:5. Because the nation of the Arabs was especially highly despised, as seen in Amos 9:7, this also seems to have made her contemptible in the eyes of Miriam, who was a prophetess, and therefore might have wished to exalt herself over her sister-in-law, and also incited her brother Aaron to do so, in order to oppose Moses under the pretense that they were equal in gifts, and thus oppose his wife all the more.

However, this is a prototype of the Jewish Church and the Aaronic priesthood, who also rose up against Christ when he first wished to accept the Gentiles—who in their eyes were sinful "Moors"—as his bride. See Acts 13:44, etc.

<margin>Had taken)</margin> Moses was a witness to those things which were to be spoken of afterward, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 3:5, so that through what he did and commanded to be done, as well as what he wrote and taught, he might bear witness to the will of God. What he did, wrote, and taught more obscurely with a veil over his face was afterward to be explained more fully according to the degrees of divine revelation to those capable of receiving such things. Thus, he prefigured here the one who was to be like Moses, and who would reject his disobedient, impenitent, and hardened people—who did not desire to reform—and would take a people from the Gentiles for his name, Acts 15:14, so that they might be called by his name, just as a wife is called by her husband's name. This was an occasion of great contradiction against the spiritual Moses: John 7:35, Acts 22:21, 22. And to this very day, the Synagogue of Satan speaks ill of Moses, as the image of the spiritual law, because he does not teach his "Ethiopian"—the circumcision of the flesh, the observation of the Sabbath, the new moons, and all kinds of feast days, or the sacrifices of the flesh; but instead drives toward the circumcision of the heart, the rest from sin, the feast days of the spirit, of purity and truth, and toward the thank-offerings of the heart and the slaughtering of animal lusts.

<margin>v. 2. Does the LORD speak alone --- not also etc.)</margin> Envy and ambition are hidden enemies against which even the best and most gifted souls must watch, so as not to be overtaken by them when the opportunity arises.

<margin>Through us)</margin> Or more precisely, *in* us.

It is common for suffering souls, when they stand in the peace of this state, to believe that they have now overcome all states; and because they have a quite natural desire to speak and write of divine things, they imagine they stand on the level of perfection. But they are still far removed from it. And though they say they have the same spirit as Moses (or like those souls who have already reached God alone) and that God lets them hear that very same voice, they deceive themselves very grossly.

<note>(a) See Pliny, Book 5, Chapter 1.</note>

<column-break/>

3. But the man Moses was very meek, <note>German: *sanftmüthig*. Referring to a humble, gentle, and patient disposition.</note> more than all the men who were on the earth.

4. Then the LORD spoke suddenly to Moses and to Aaron and to Miriam: Go out, you three, to the Tabernacle of Meeting! And the three went out.

5. Then the LORD came down in the pillar of cloud and stood at the door of the Tabernacle, and called Aaron and Miriam: and they both went out.

6. And he said: Hear now my words! If there is a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known to him in a vision, I will speak with him in a dream.

<meta>Catchword: 7. Not</meta>

<margin>v. 3.</margin> After God sees this abuse, he himself takes up the cause of these people who are so holy and so perfect in him: because they then possess such meekness that the like is no longer to be found on the whole earth; for it is no longer the goodness of the earth, but of heaven, yes, of God himself. This friendliness is not placed here in vain; for it is one of the most prominent signs that distinguishes the souls belonging to God from the rest.

All rulers should take an example from the great meekness of Moses; thus they would best be powerfully protected by the LORD against all who wish to rise up against them. To this end, Christ also presents his meekness to us all as an example in Matthew 11:25.

<margin>v. 4. 5. The LORD --- came down)</margin> To hold judgment over the two parties.

<margin>v. 6. Hear my words)</margin> These words of God contain so beautifully, even according to the letter, the distinction that exists between the suffering and enlightened states and between the state of God himself; one need only repeat such words to grasp this. God communicates with enlightened souls through visions and dreams, under shadows and images, which create some distinction between him and them: But with divinely-made souls he speaks mouth to mouth, and as it were from being to being, through inflow, <note>German: *Einfliesung*. A mystical term for direct divine influence or "infusion" without external media.</note> and not otherwise. And this essential word is manifest; it can only be received into the essence of the soul, from whence it pours out into the faculties when it is to be brought forth.

<margin>Vision)</margin> Is an appearance through an image or form while awake: and is thereby contrasted with

<margin>A dream)</margin> Which, when God reveals something through it, cuts into the heart in such a way that not only the understanding but also the will is moved in an unusual manner, and by this, it is recognized as being divine. (a)

<note>(a) Luther, Vol. 10, Wittenberg edition, folio 322.</note>

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XII.

7. <margin>Hebrews 3:2.</margin> My servant Moses is not so; he is faithful in all my house.
8. <margin>(a) Deuteronomy 34:10. (b) 1 Corinthians 13:12. (c) Exodus 33:11.</margin> I will speak with him from mouth to mouth, even face to face <gloss>(a)</gloss>, and not through dark words <gloss>(b)</gloss>; and he beholds the form of the LORD <gloss>(c)</gloss>. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant, against Moses?
9. <margin>Genesis 8:3, 5; 26:13. Exodus 19:19.</margin> And the anger of the LORD was kindled against them, and it increased.
10. And the cloud departed from the Tabernacle <note>German: *Hütten*. Refers to the Tent of Meeting or Tabernacle.</note>: and behold, Miriam was leprous, white as snow;

---

**v. 7. Moses is — faithful)** Behold what the slanderers and those who so readily engage in the belittling of others actually achieve for them! Never did God bestow greater praise upon Moses than when people—and indeed his own closest relatives—confronted him with useless words.
**v. 8. He beholds the form of the Lord)** This is certainly a manner that belongs to no one but Christ, as the only-begotten Son who is in the Father's bosom; John 1:18. He far surpassed Moses, yet even in this, He wished to take Moses as a prototype <note>Theologians often see Old Testament figures as "types" or "pre-figurations" of Christ.</note> and compare Himself with him. Hebrews 3:2-6.
This "form of God" contains something great within it, which the believers will also get to behold in eternity. Psalm 17:15.
God Himself, as the All-Wise, must know best which things are great and excellent, or not. Since He here makes it a special sign of His love for Moses and the high esteem of his person that He lets him see the form of the Lord, it must truly be a high enjoyment or grace to behold Him in that glorious spiritual form which He Himself assumes to appear in.
Before Moses had taken the Ethiopian woman <note>German: *Morin*. Referred to previously as the Cushite woman.</note>, it is not written that he saw God in His form. But after he took the Ethiopian woman, He no longer speaks through dark words. When Moses unites himself with the Ethiopian woman <note>In this mystical interpretation, the "Ethiopian woman" represents the Gentile Church joining with the Law (Moses).</note>, the Law is no longer recognized and fulfilled under coverings, shadows, images, and figures, but in spirit and in truth.
**Why then were you not afraid)** The more someone stands in grace with God, whether through gifts or through virtue, the more one ought to fear offending such a person. Psalm 105:15.
**v. 9.** Let no one open their mouth to speak evil of their neighbor, and do not despise or belittle your brother! For the Lord is a revenger of all such things, and His anger burned against those who so readily have to do with evil rumors.
**The Lord's anger increased)** in that God did not let the matter rest with a verbal rebuke:
**v. 10.** Rather, the pillar of cloud also withdrew as a sign of the divine presence, so that the people might also recognize the unjust conduct of Miriam and Aaron by this, and take it to heart as a warning.
**Miriam was leprous)** This was to make the loathsomeness of her soul’s condition before God sensibly apparent to the eyes, which is always of such a nature wherever one wishes to oppose God's holy providence through stubbornness.
First the cloud departs, and then the leprosy becomes manifest. The grace of the Holy Spirit departs, where it is, when the tongue breaks out in belittling and contempt of one's neighbor, and then the soul stands naked in its own leprous form.
So also had the Jewish people formerly had God's grace in our Lord Jesus Christ, their brother according to the flesh; it departed from them and left their house desolate: which

and Aaron turned toward Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. <margin>Exodus 4:6. 2 Chronicles 26:19.</margin>

**She was leprous)** This punishment of Miriam shows that God does not fail to punish people who are full of self-conceit with the leprosy of a thousand-fold weaknesses, and (just as was said above (a)) this is the common punishment for such types of souls.
**v. 11. Aaron had a soft heart)** therefore a fine repentance and confession of their sin and folly followed immediately from him, whereby he asked Moses for forgiveness and at the same time for his intercession for their sister.
**v. 12. When it comes out / half is consumed)** This secretly points to the poor progress of the offspring of Israel, because of the intervening sins, whereby it comes slowly or not at all to a perfect birth. Sin consumes the half.
**v. 13. Moses said: Oh God, heal her!)** How easily he also did this for the Jewish people in the conversation with Christ on the mountain, so that all Israel might be healed and saved; so says Origen <note>A 3rd-century Christian scholar and theologian.</note>.
**v. 14.** Although Moses was quite inclined toward forgiveness, the Lord shows him that as a disobedient daughter she well deserved such shameful discipline, and therefore should be shut away for seven days just like any other leper. See Leviticus 14:8.
**v. 15. Miriam shut out 7 days — and received again)** Behold the people of the Jewish Church in its leprous state and piteous sight! This leprosy will not last forever, but when the time of 7 days or the "great week of the world" <note>An allegorical interpretation where 7 days represent 7,000 years of human history.</note> is fulfilled, then she shall be received again; and at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, all Israel shall be saved.
**v. 16. Wilderness of Paran)** took its name from Mount Paran, Deuteronomy 33:2, and it was already spoken of in Chapter 10:12. The specific place in this great wilderness was called Ricmah, Chapter 33:18, where they had now camped.

# Chapter XIII. The Fourth Book of Moses.

### Chapter XIII.

->The Sending Out of the Spies.<-

1. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
2. Send men out for yourself, that they may scout the land of Canaan, which I will give to the children of Israel. From every tribe of their fathers you shall send a man; every one shall be a prince among them.
3. And Moses sent them out from the Wilderness of Paran according to the command of the LORD. All those men were heads among the children of Israel.
4. And these were their names: From the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur.
5. From the tribe of Simeon, Shaphat the son of Hori.
6. From the tribe of Judah, Caleb the son of Jephunneh.
7. From the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph.
8. From the tribe of Ephraim, Hosea <note>Hosea is later renamed Joshua.</note> the son of Nun.
9. From the tribe of Benjamin, Palti the son of Raphu.
10. From the tribe of Zebulun, Gaddiel the son of Sodi.
11. From the tribe of Joseph, from the tribe of Manasseh, Gaddi the son of Susi.
12. From the tribe of Dan, Ammiel the son of Gemalli.
13. From the tribe of Asher, Sethur the son of Michael.
14. From the tribe of Naphtali, Nahbi the son of Vaphsi.
15. From the tribe of Gad, Geuel the son of Machi.

One sees from Deuteronomy 1:22 that the people first came up with the idea that they wanted to send out spies, who might show them the way they could go up and describe the cities they would come to. Moses consented to this, but—as appears here—he first asked the LORD and then received permission and the command that twelve heads from the twelve tribes should be sent out.

Thus, whatever one begins out of self-will <note>German: *Eigenheit*, referring to acting on one's own initiative rather than purely through divine leading.</note>, even with good intentions, never prospers, even if God sometimes permits it and then rules over it so holily that one must finally recognize His hand in it; for His hand must execute everything and, after many trials, turn it for the best. And so they should have simply moved forward in the simple obedience of faith; then they would have entered the promised land much sooner and more easily.

<column-break/>

16. These are the names of the men whom Moses sent to scout the land. And Moses called Hosea the son of Nun, Joshua.
17. So Moses sent them to scout the land of Canaan and said to them: Go up here toward the South and go onto the mountains;
18. And see the land, what it is like, and the people who dwell therein, whether they are strong or weak, few or many;
19. And how the land is where they dwell, whether it be good or bad; and what kind of cities they are in which they dwell, whether in camps or in strongholds;
20. And how the land is, whether it be fat or lean, whether there are trees in it or not: and be of good courage, and take of the fruit of the land. Now it was the time of the first-ripe grapes.
21. And they went up and scouted the land from the Wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, as one goes toward Hamath.
22. They

---

**v. 16. Moses called Hosea — Joshua)** Or rather, *Yehoshua*, as a chief prototype <note>The author uses the German *Vorbild*, seeing Joshua as a "type" or shadow of Jesus.</note> of the Lord our Savior. This name is a most artistic composition of *Jehovah* (the LORD) and *Yeshua* (the Savior), from which the name JESUS is derived. Through the obscuring of such a glorious name, the most clear and vivid archetype of the Lord JESUS is also obscured.

Even if the original meaning is to be held as nothing other than divine, it is the inner working, virtue, and power that one must look for in this change of name. That is the divine nature present in *Yehoshua*, in which (or in whose name and power) *Yehoshua* performed all his great works. These vividly prefigured the wonderful works that the essential JESUS also worked then and before, and should work hereafter, as the divine Immanuel and the very principle <note>Original Latin: *Principium*.</note> of light, life, strength, and power, through which the people of God alone may do and perform all their works. Isaiah 26:12; John 15:5.

**v. 17-20.** These spies, who were to view the promised land from the mountain to see what it was like, represent to us in a figure those who were permitted at the dawn of the Gospel to catch a glimpse into the Land of the Living: such as Peter, James, and John, who were with Christ at the Transfiguration on the mountain; and Paul, who was caught up into Paradise and the third heaven.

**v. 21. From the Wilderness of Zin to Rehob)** That is, from the path of hedges and thorns into the open fields. See Ezra 7:7. Therefore, Rehob was the inheritance of the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:24, 28), which means "blessedness." The tribulations and sufferings of Christ precede the salvation found through Christ. 2 Corinthians 1:5, 6. Through the narrow way into the broad expanse.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XIII.

22. They went up toward the South and came to Hebron; and Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were there. Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.

23. And they came to the Valley of Eshcol, and there they cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they had it carried by two men on a pole, along with some pomegranates and figs.

24. That place was called the Valley of Eshcol <note>Eshcol means "cluster."</note> because of the cluster which the children of Israel had cut down there.

25. And they returned from scouting the land at the end of forty days.

26. And they went and came to Moses and Aaron and to the entire congregation of the children of Israel in the Wilderness of Paran at Kadesh; and they brought back word to them and to the entire congregation, and let them see the fruits of the land.

*v. 22. When one enters into the reflections of reason, one soon falls into all sorts of difficulties and scruples: these are the giants that later appear to one in the overly profound investigations of reason. There, faith dies away, just as the faithful patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—lay buried here at Hebron with their wives (Genesis 23:19, etc.), and this place was later inhabited by giants.*

*Hebron built 7 years before Zoan)* Josephus <note>original: "l. 5. de bell. Jud." — referring to Book 5 of The Jewish War</note> writes that from its founding until his time, 2,300 years had passed. From this, Pererius <note>original: "comment. in Gen. 1 3. quest. 5." — referring to his Commentary on Genesis</note> concludes that it was built 90 years before the Deluge. Ifingius, however, maintains from Berosus that it was built in the year of the world 1716, and Zoan in 1723—which would be 60 years after the Deluge.

*v. 23. Had it carried by two)* in order to bring it back undamaged and to show it alongside the other magnificent fruits, the pomegranates and figs, which ripened at the same time. *Song of Solomon 2:13.*

The Jews claim that eight men carried it, and they apply the word <term>מוט</term> <note>Hebrew: *mot*, meaning a pole or carrying-bar.</note> to the poles. Likewise, the Greek translation of the Seventy <note>The Septuagint.</note> indicates "on poles," implying many carriers, and does not mention only two bearers.

*v. 24.* One cannot know the earth except by its fruits. This exceedingly large cluster of grapes, which was brought back by those sent out to scout the promised land, is a sign of its fertility. Now, this fruit is a cluster that carries within itself the most pleasant wine of pure love: not for itself, however, but for those who will press it out. GOD receives all the glory from it, and the neighbor receives all the benefit. This cluster also indicates the community held by those who have arrived in GOD, who is the promised land: just as the grape-kernels are all united on one stem. But this unity is founded upon Jesus Christ, who is the true Cluster and the Vine.

*v. 25. 26. From scouting the land)* we must all make our profession according to this model. And just as this Holy Land is a spiritual land (*Psalm 143:10; Isaiah 8:8, 33:21*), so also must the exploration of it be spiritual. It is best explored, however, by entering into it: just as these scouts recounted here what they had recognized and seen.

</margin>

<column-break/>

27. And they told him, saying: We came into the land where you sent us. It truly flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit.

28. Except that the people who dwell in the land are strong, and the cities are very fortified and large. Moreover, we saw the children of Anak there.

29. The Amalekites dwell in the land toward the South, and the Hittites, Jebusites, and Amorites dwell in the mountains; but the Canaanites dwell by the sea and along the banks of the Jordan.

30. But Caleb stilled the people before Moses and said: Let us go up at once and take possession of it! For we shall certainly overcome it. 31. But...

After their forty-day return, they deliver their report: then the great multitude of ten witnesses breaks through. Through their fearful presentation—wherein they cannot deny the goodness of the land, but nonetheless emphasize the great strength and power of the people and their cities, and how dangerous giants dwelt therein—they seek in their unbelief and despondency to strip the people of all courage and thus turn them away.

*v. 27.* Now, if these men, who were sent out and were in the land and could speak of what they had seen, delivered such bad reports; what then should be said of the intolerable audacity of so many novices who speak much of the holy land, the heavenly fatherland, and the kingdom of God, of which they have no experience because they have never been there!

*The land flows with)* Or from the land—which is GOD Himself, our center, our origin and end—flow streams of milk and honey. The sweetness of those who have entered into it is infinite, and from them flows a great multitude of holy words, pure sweetness and pleasantness, which are like small streams of milk and honey.

*v. 28.* It is true, one encounters the children of Anak as one attains the possession, and one has to deal with the strong armed men, and with princes and powers that rule in the air, and with forces of wickedness in high places; and from the outside, their power appears very great.

*v. 29.* But he who is free and follows the Lord shall nevertheless possess the earth: He who overcomes the Canaanites within himself shall inherit the beautiful land.

Faith and hope push through all strife. There is no giant so strong that the children of faith cannot overcome him. He who believes, triumphs, and stands in the power of GOD’S promise!

*v. 30. Stilled the people)* Either by a pleasant sound, perhaps indicated by the large final letter <term>ם</term> <note>The Hebrew letter *Mem*. Some mystical interpretations of the Hebrew text suggest the size or shape of certain letters indicates specific actions or tones.</note> in the Hebrew; much as we might call out "St!" <note>Similar to "shh!" or "hush!"</note> after the Latin fashion when we want silence; or by a motioning with the hand, as in *Acts 13:17.*

*Let us go up at once)* Or, word for word: "By ascending let us ascend"; namely, from one degree to another. No one who wishes to destroy spiritual enemies according to the divine will goes otherwise than by degrees and steps; as can be seen in *Exodus 23:29-30*: leading the person in gradually, just as Jacob led his sheep. *Genesis 33:14.*

31. But the men who had gone up with him said: We are not able to go up against the people; for they are too strong for us.

32. And they brought an evil report of the land which they had scouted to the children of Israel, saying: The land through which we have gone to scout is a land that devours its inhabitants; and all the people we saw in it are men of great height. <margin>Isaiah 45:14.</margin>

33. We also saw the giants (a) there, the children of Anak of the giants: and we were in our own eyes as grasshoppers, and so we were also in their eyes. <margin>(a) Genesis 6:4.</margin>

---

v. 31. **But)** the others and the great multitude most violently resist those two faithful witnesses <note>The "two faithful witnesses" are Joshua and Caleb, who believed God would grant them victory.</note>; they claim it is simply impossible to undertake such a task against so mighty a people. In doing so, they infect the people with a very wicked opinion, so that their hearts are turned entirely away.

Some also note in the name **Setur** (v. 13) the number of the Antichrist, 666 <note>The author is using gematria, a system where letters represent numbers, to link the scout Setur to the biblical "Number of the Beast."</note>, who is certainly the head of all false witnesses in the external church. This figure seeks only an external happiness—which is what the word **Asher** (the tribe to which Setur belonged) signifies. Such people keep others from attaining the spiritual inheritance of perfection by willfully remaining stuck in the weakness of their flesh.

**We are not able --- too strong for us)** Is this not precisely the cry and shout of most "scouts" even to this day—that spiritual enemies are too strong for us, and that sin in this life cannot be entirely subdued or overcome? This is claimed even though the promises of the Gospel are expressly made upon the condition of overcoming our spiritual enemies. "To him who overcomes," etc. If we are not able to drive out or overcome the enemy, why then are we exhorted to fight and struggle? The question is whether anything is too difficult for God—not whether the enemy is strong and mighty.

If one believes that something is impossible, who will put much effort into striving for it? Who will try to win when they know that no one has the natural strength or ability to do so? In this way, all exhortations and warnings become vain if people are first persuaded that it is impossible for them to obey.

What do those others do, who elevate the size and strength of the enemy and the insurmountable high walls of Jericho above God's power? They say: "The flesh is too strong; the devil too cunning and mighty; the temptations too great. It is impossible to struggle with them, impossible to overcome them, impossible to follow Christ." These are truly nothing but repeated speeches of those ancient wicked scouts who gave the Promised Land an evil report and spoke only of impossibilities. This is why so few want to progress from the "Egypt" of the world and nature, or from the "Mount Sinai" of the law, toward true Christianity and the inner sanctuary. For in this way, all zeal in Christianity is utterly crushed; one holds back not only oneself but also others when they hear that these things are impossible. For

The common people and the great multitude naturally avoid spiritual effort and labor, being more inclined to wicked desires. Therefore, regarding the obedience required by God, they would rather listen to the false scouts who say: "We cannot."

These are the unfaithful preachers whose doctrine is: "It is impossible to live so holily and without sin; we are weak humans!" By this, they strengthen the people in their unbelief, so that they are ready with a shameful answer when reminded of their duties: "Who can live like that?" Thus, through unbelief and mistrust, everything is made impossible for poor souls, and the conquest of the Kingdom of God within them is frustrated.

v. 32. **Brought an evil report of the land)** Why might they have done this? Answer: Solely because they saw that the people were afraid and discouraged, and they did not want to displease the people.

<note>There is a slight logical gap in the original German text here, likely due to a typesetting error or a missing line transition between columns.</note>

They will be able to manage, and they also make others strive for an elevated state. And this is indeed true: man can never reach it on his own; but on God's side, all things are possible. All that is required is faith, according to the promise of Jesus Christ: (b) if you can believe; all things are possible to him who believes.

<column-break/>

**The land through which we have gone to scout is a land that devours its inhabitants; and all the people we saw in it are men of great height.**

->The<-

First, they praise the land highly and tell the people that it is a glorious land; afterward, they say the exact opposite. This follows a ruinous yet common manner of preaching: first, because the "method" requires it, the preacher exhorts to repentance, speaks of renewal, requires the necessity of a godly life, and praises its beauty so they can claim they promote holy living. Finally, however, as they approach the conclusion, everything said before is thrown into a heap through false persuasion: "But we are weak humans, we cannot keep God's commandments"—and then they cover this with "the righteousness of Christ."

But you are unfaithful scouts who make the noble land stink! Yet, it shall cost you dearly enough!

**A land that devours its inhabitants)** They lived among one another in wars and robberies, and thus consumed each other like a very barbaric people, among whom one should not dare to venture.

**v. 33. Giants --- grasshoppers)** Certainly, it is so in comparison to human and devilish nature: we are grasshoppers and they are giants. And when we leave behind our faith and allow ourselves to be hunted by fears, then they are truly giants and we are grasshoppers.

**In our own eyes)** Yes, our five external senses—and through these, the five internal senses of our souls—are the very false witnesses. Like the image of the ten opposing scouts, they make the precious promises of the Gospel, and thus also the commandments of Christ, seem so difficult to our reason that it appears impossible for them to be kept, or for the great promises of Christ to be fully attained here. But here now are the two faithful witnesses: **Joshua**, or the Spirit of Christ; and **Caleb**, our heart touched by the love of Christ, or the inner spirit. These two also agree together, and the Spirit of Christ gives witness to our spirit (Romans 8:16) that all such reasonings and high things that exalt themselves against the knowledge of God, and all the machinations of our senses, can be overcome through the power of Christ in faith (2 Corinthians 10:4-5). All those mighty enemies from without, who are true giants against whom we seem like powerless grasshoppers—like sheep among wolves, such as Satan and the world—will finally have to yield. See John 11:31, 14:30, 16:11, 33; 1 Peter 5:8-9; 1 John 2:14-15, 5:4-5; also Romans 8:5, etc.; Galatians 5:16-17.

A soul that finds itself full of trust expects everything from the strength and goodness of God. Because she herself is full of courage, she also encourages others. "Let us go," they say, "and do not fear, even if apparent obstacles should arise!" For that which we do not expect to obtain through our own strength, we can yet expect from the goodness of God. And it is easy for Him to make us masters of it, according to His promise. (a) In God we shall do great things; and He Himself will bring our enemies to nothing.

On the contrary, those souls who are entirely full of their own pieces <note>Meaning their own limited resources or self-will.</note>, and look at this only in a human way and from their own power, immediately despair so that they turn away, saying that one is too weak to strive for such an elevated state. And this is indeed true; if one takes it from the side of one's own strength, then

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Ch. XIV. 606

## Chapter XIV.

->The rebellion of the people and Moses' intercession: The punishment of the people and their disobedience.<-

Then the whole congregation lifted up their voice and cried; and the people wept that night.
2. And all the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron; and the whole congregation said to them: "Oh, that we had died in the land of Egypt! Or that we might die in this wilderness!"
3. "And why does the LORD bring us into this land, to fall by the sword? Our wives and our children will become a prey! Is it not better for us to return to Egypt?"

---

Thus they allowed themselves to be brought into unrest and unbelief by the majority of false and fainthearted witnesses. They not only resisted Moses and Aaron but even reproached the Lord, as if He had led them to such a place where He could not help them, and where they must all necessarily perish. Therefore, in total despair, they abandoned the Providence of God, which had hitherto led, protected, and preserved them so mightily and kindly. Now they think they can manage much better on their own; they wish to return to Egypt under a self-chosen leader of their own appointing. They do not consider what might happen to them in the future—whether they would be capable of helping themselves, or whether the angered God would continue to help them as He had before.

v. 1. It is a strange thing that those who are filled with self-love and confidence in their own strength have such power to weaken the faith and trust of <term>composed souls</term> <note>original: "gelassenen Seelen." In Pietist and mystical tradition, "Gelassenheit" refers to a state of total surrender and tranquil submission to God's will.</note> through their false reasonings, and to cast them down entirely. It reaches such a point that nothing remains in them but weeping and regret for having left their first captivity <note>Referring to Egypt as a symbol of the worldly, unregenerate life.</note>, in which they imagined they lived in greater safety, even if it was with much labor.

v. 2. These people generally tend to regret that they did not die in the <term>Land of Multiplicity</term> <note>original: "Lande der Vielfältigkeit." A mystical term referring to the material world of many distractions, contrasted with the "Unity" of God.</note>, where they considered themselves much more certain of their salvation. For they still believe that they have no hope of returning to Egypt since all entrances are closed to them. And therefore they wish that they might only die in this vast wilderness of faith, where a little hope might remain for them, for they would not yet find themselves completely lost.

v. 3. O you poor blind ones! You believe that such a multitude of enemies—whose strength is revealed to you little by little as you recognize your own weakness—must be destroyed by your own power! Oh, how you deceive yourselves! And for this reason, you also say that your "wives and children"—which represent your lower parts and your senses <note>The author uses an allegorical reading where "wives and children" represent the physical senses and emotions that the "higher soul" fears will be corrupted.</note>—will be brought into a new captivity forever, and you yourselves will fall under the sword of sin. No, no! You will never fall as long as you do not depart from your state of surrender! The evil you do in placing mistrust in God is much greater than all the other evils you fear! For in the souls of this stage, this is the source of all sins into which they can fall.

The reason why, among so many who have walked the path of <term>moderation</term> <note>original: "Mäßigkeit." This refers to a balanced spiritual life of self-control.</note>...

v. 4. They are so blind that they even counsel returning to their <term>former state of activity</term> <note>original: "erste Wirksamkeit." In this context, it refers to a soul's attempt to return to its own self-directed efforts and religious "works" rather than trusting God's leading.</note>. They should consider that it is impossible for them to do this; and that, by no longer having God as their leader (because He requires something else of them), they would fall into the hands of even greater enemies than those they fear in the land where God wants to lead them. The "leader" they wish to choose for themselves is a guide they are willing to accept so that he might bring them back to their first activities: namely, a leader who must flatter their senses.

v. 5. The prostration of Moses and Aaron represents the willingness of such completely spiritual people to let go of the leadership of the souls entrusted to them. Others do not do this easily, for they have a thousand attachments and therefore strive in every way to keep souls under their leadership. Truly spiritual people act this way because they have been "annihilated" <note>An "annihilated" soul is one that has died to self-will and personal ambition.</note>; since they recognize nothing good in themselves nor any power to help souls other than what God gives them, they gladly lay down such an office. But the others do exactly the opposite through a strong esteem for themselves, imagining themselves to be much more fit than others for the leadership of souls.

v. 6-7. Often, however, among the great crowd of weak souls, some strong and far-seeing people are found who support the others. Out of their own experience of the goodness of the promised land, they assure those who have completely surrendered of the benefit that can be drawn from it once one is established therein.

v. 8. "If the Lord delights in us," they say—that is, if He leads and if one is willing to be led by Him—then it will be easy to enter, and one will certainly be brought in.

...and have walked the path [of moderation], so few are found who actually reach God, and almost all die along the way, is because they fall into mistrust and thereby delay themselves, and indeed, for that very reason, they depart from the way.
