### Ch. XIV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

9. Only do not rebel against the LORD, and you should not fear the people of the land! For they shall be as bread to us. Their protection has departed from them; but the LORD is with us: Do not fear them!

10. Then the whole congregation said that they should be stoned.

<note>The following sections in smaller type are commentary on the preceding verses.</note>

When these two faithful witnesses <note>Joshua and Caleb</note> sought to encourage them, and Moses and Aaron also threw themselves down in prayer before God in their presence, seeking to move them to the fear of God and trust in His omnipotence; yet their rage and madness went so far that they undertook to stone these two witnesses. Moses and Aaron would have fared no better had they not been deterred by the sudden appearance of the LORD in a bright, fiery cloud—for they had previously experienced the divine fire with terror and harm. (Chapter 11, verse 1).

This can now represent to us how things usually go when the LORD occasionally wishes to reinforce the Gospel promises to mankind through individual witnesses. While people in the wilderness of this world long only for the lusts of the flesh, striving for the flesh-pots of Egypt <note>original: "Egypti"</note> and the pleasures therein, they do not think of the heavy servitude of the spirit under those same things, from which Christ was meant to redeem us. The greatest multitude—those who love pleasure more than God—always resists. They present the impossibility of such exact holiness and perfection, regarding others as boasters and hypocrites <note>original: "Schein-heilige"</note>. They stir up an uprising against them as if they were erring deceivers, and they cling to their earthly leaders and the man-made orders they have established, believing they will fare well by them. And so the testimony and the witnesses would soon be destroyed by the greatest multitude and its leaders, if the LORD did not also sometimes appear then, breaking in with sudden judgments and thereby striking some terror into people.

Verse 9 applies this way: Let us not be such shameful, fainthearted hares that we allow our courage to be taken by such false lying-spirits who tell us we are not fit, or cannot and lack the power to go into battle against our spiritual enemies; and who wish to persuade us that they are too strong for us.

Holy Scripture testifies that it is a rebellion and apostasy when one leaves the path of <term>surrender</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit," a central concept in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God</note> and refuses to be led by God; when one steps out of the divine order and one's dependence on Him, in order to enter into one's own guidance through one's own reflection. It assures us that one must not fear, but must give oneself over with heartiness: because through the power of God we can devour our enemies—even sin itself—like bread, without them being able to harm us. For they cannot harm us as long as we do not leave the state of surrender. For as long as we are under the hand of God, all the power and poison of sin remains far from us and remains powerless against us, just as the devils themselves do. For the help and strength of sin are its sting and its malice. Since this is now taken from them, and God no longer separates Himself from us, and our will remains united with His will; so we have no more reason to fear. But one must take heed that it is said: as long as we remain united with God and with His will, and stand in self-denial. For otherwise, everything can harm us. Nevertheless, we shall never be put to shame except through mistrust and through lack of faith and courage to leave ourselves to God through all dangers, without taking to heart our own benefit or what might happen.

Verse 10: the whole congregation) Does it not happen exactly this way to this very day? The majority of those who are scouts and seers, and wish to be held as such—who seem to have explored the holy land—assert firmly that the enemies of life, the spiritual Canaanites, are too strong for us, and that we are not able to overcome them. And these, alas, are believed by more than six hundred thousand. If one or two witnesses come and assert that it is possible to overcome the spiritual enemies through the power of the true Joshua <note>The Hebrew name for Jesus is Yeshua/Joshua; the author is making a typological connection</note>, they are blasphemed, and few believe them. Why? These are few, and those are many. What is to be concluded from this, or what follows from this?

<column-break/>

Then the glory of the LORD appeared in the Tabernacle of Meeting to all the children of Israel.

11. And the LORD said to Moses: How long will this people despise me? And how long will they not believe in me, despite all the signs I have done among them?

12. I will strike them with pestilence and destroy them, and I will make of you a greater and mightier nation than they are.

<note>Commentary continued.</note>

NB <note>Latin "Nota Bene," meaning "Note well"</note>. In divine things, in things concerning the service of God and the duty of man, it is not a good proof or conclusion to say: "The multitude, the greatest number of people, is of this or that opinion; therefore it must be <term>orthodox</term> <note>meaning "correct belief"</note> and the right faith." It is the same kind of conclusion to say: "The greatest part of the priests and prophets is of this opinion; therefore it must be the true opinion." 1 Kings 18:22.

Then appeared) Those who are shackled in their own calculations and stand in their adopted fear do not accept any instruction that one might offer them. Indeed, they even want to stone those who give them such healthy counsel. And this happens when one tries to convince oneself through motives taken from the hardness of the heart. But God, whose goodness is infinite, when He sees that they are very near to destruction, sends them a ray of His enlightenment, which is the glory of His Majesty, clearly revealing itself to them.

In the Tabernacle) Or perhaps over the Tabernacle, because otherwise it would not have been visible to the eyes of the children of Israel.

Verse 11. At that same time He rightly complains about the meager faith of this people, which always doubts, and which would plunge itself into the abyss through this doubt if God did not still hold His hand over them. For nothing offends Him more than mistrust, especially when He has already given so many proofs of His power and His protection.

How long will this people despise me? How long will they not believe? The Lord may well bring this complaint against us too. People do not believe the Lord; they do not believe the Lord's omnipotence; they do not believe His promise. They do not believe His power—that He can overcome and tread underfoot all the enemies of life in us, and that He can cleanse us from our sins. On the contrary, people believe that the enemy can make a person perfectly godless, but not that God is powerful enough to make a perfectly honest man. The Lord’s arm is not shortened; but we lack faith in His power. Matthew 13:58. One also does not believe His threats—that this or that evil will befall us—until one feels it.

Verse 12. I will make of you a greater and mightier nation) This speech also contains a mystery within it, says Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD)</note>, which was to reach its fulfillment in future times. And in this respect, it is not a pronouncement of wrath, but a prophecy. For God indeed wanted to adopt another and greater people, but not through Moses. As Moses also excused himself, knowing well that this great people which is promised should not be called through him, but through Jesus Christ, and therefore should not be called Mosaic, but Christian.

# 608 The Fourth Book of Moses. Ch. XIV

13. But Moses said to the **LORD**: Then the Egyptians will hear of it; for you brought this people up from among them by your power:
14. And they will tell it to the inhabitants of this land, who have heard that you, the **LORD**, are in the midst of this people; that you, o **LORD**, are seen face to face, and that your cloud <margin>(a) Exodus 40:38.</margin> (a) stands over them, and that you go before them in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night. <margin>Exodus 9:15.</margin>
15. If you were to kill this people as if they were a single man, then the heathens who have heard the report of you would say and speak:
16. Because the **LORD** was by no means able to bring this people into the land which he had sworn to them, he has therefore slaughtered them in the wilderness.

The content of Moses' intercession is directed toward this: that he did not seek his own offered glory, but rather the best interests of his people. In doing so, he presents the **LORD** with His own honor, which would be attacked by the Egyptians and other heathens: that although God had initially shown Himself present among the people, He had later lacked the power to lead them into the land inhabited by such a strong nation. Furthermore, he presents to God His own nature, which He had so gloriously proclaimed in <note>original: "2. Mos. 34 / 6. 7."</note> Exodus 34:6–7. Though He is indeed just, He does not punish immediately, but only in the third and fourth generation. Thus, he desires that both aspects of God be made manifest: His power over His enemies, and His patience toward His people, continuing to graciously forgive them as He has done until now.

First, he represents to God that His honor is at stake, so that He might not let this people perish in their wandering—from which wandering they would then fall into the commission of actual sin, thinking to escape a seemingly apparent misfortune, and thereby actually be sunk into a true abyss.

A rational man (like Moses) no longer looks to any self-interest. Therefore, he does not even answer the many graces which God promised to him for himself: but since he stands only for the benefit of the path for which he was chosen as leader, he reminds God of how active men—when they see that those walking in the ways of <term>yieldedness [Gelassenheit]: a central Pietist concept meaning the total surrender of one's own will to God</term>, faith, and simplicity fall into some visible errors—immediately take occasion to present two things, both of which are highly displeasing to God and to those who have abandoned themselves to Him.

The first is that they blame everything on "yieldedness" and do not see the fault in the creature, who fell precisely because it withdrew itself from that state of yieldedness. They say at once: "Look, this comes from yieldedness! This path is nothing but a delusion! For instead of leading the soul to God, it draws it out of itself (which is Egypt) only to kill it in the wilderness of faith." They argue the soul cannot be brought to God from this wilderness because it finds itself without strength, having lost its own practices which sustained it until now; even though it had hoped for such redemption in the way of yieldedness. Instead, He lets them perish as a punishment for their presumption. This is one of the most common abuses among men who value calculation and are easily led astray.

...that he should live in this way, and that he should drag his life along in the same forever.

<column-break/>

17. And now, I pray, let the power of the **LORD** be great, just as you have spoken and said:
18. The **LORD** is long-suffering and of great goodness, who forgives iniquity and transgression, and who will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. He visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation.
19. Forgive, I pray, the iniquity of this people according to your great goodness, even as you have forgiven this people from Egypt until now.
20. Then the **LORD** said: I have forgiven them, according to your word.
21. But as truly as I live, the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of the **LORD**! <margin>Psalm 72; Isaiah 6:3.</margin>

The second thing is that they always strive to persuade one that those who have unfortunately fallen in their good progress had never truly been in the holy state and in the life of God—wherein everything is in an essential unity and from which the soul cannot possibly fall, unless through a great unfaithfulness. Therefore they say that those who have so fallen were of the number of those to whom God let Himself be seen face to face, just as Moses agrees in verse 14. And this is a trick of Satan to cause souls to reject entering into yieldedness: because this sanctified yieldedness cuts off all his power over such souls.

v. 17–19. Thus Moses prays to God that He might snatch souls out of the great danger in which they are stuck, for the sake of His honor: so that others might not thereby take the opportunity to reject this guidance.
He also holds God’s mercy before His eyes, and how He can just as easily stretch out a hand through His goodness as punish with His justice.

Now, since the wrath of the **LORD** over His deviating people in the New Testament is clear enough in these last times—now that the bowls <note>Referring to the bowls of wrath in the Book of Revelation.</note> are already beginning to be poured out, and wrath consumes men and the world through heavy judgments here and there—this is the most distressing thing, over which the Spirit of God also laments in such times: that He sees that "there is no one," and wonders that "no one intercedes." <note>original: "Jes. 59. v. 16. c. 63 / 5. 64 / 7."</note> Isaiah 59:16, 63:5, 64:7. Indeed, there is no lack of schoolmasters and <term>Boanerges [Sons of Thunder]: a name given to the apostles James and John, here referring to preachers who speak only of judgment and punishment</term> who punish and point out sin and thunder out the judgments of God; but there is a lack of merciful fathers who would take this misery to heart with great compassion and make themselves into a wall, standing in the breach against the **LORD** for the land, so that He might not destroy it; but there the **LORD** finds no one, as the prophet laments. <note>original: "Ezech. 22 / 30. 13 / 5. Amos 6 / 6."</note> Ezekiel 22:30, 13:5; Amos 6:6.

v. 20. Through the humble intercession of Moses, who was quite accustomed to it, the **LORD** allowed Himself to be held back to the extent that He indeed forgave them the sin. Yet, to save His holiness, He earnestly declared that all those men of age, who could have understood the **LORD's** signs but nevertheless allowed themselves to be so quickly turned away by men to doubt the **LORD’s** power—those same men should not see the good land.
And thus, a punishment can still follow upon forgiveness. God often forgives sin in regard to eternal punishment, yet reserves for Himself a temporal one.

v. 21. God indeed forgives, but He testifies at the same time that this iniquity is forgiven solely for the sake of His honor, so that the whole world may recognize how great His power is in the leading of His souls who surrender themselves to Him. He testifies this by His life and by Himself; to indicate,

"As truly as I live, the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of the **LORD**!" Such glorious statements can be prompted even by the greatest misdeeds.

<summary>Moses intercedes for the Israelites after their rebellion, successfully pleading for God's mercy by appealing to His reputation and His character as a long-suffering God. While God grants forgiveness for the eternal soul, He declares that the rebellious generation will still face the temporal punishment of never entering the Promised Land.</summary>

# 609 The Fourth Book of Moses. Ch. XIV
Gggg 3
<meta>catchword: 29. Your</meta>

22. Because all those men who have seen my glory and my signs, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have now tempted me ten times, and have not obeyed my voice;
23. They shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers: indeed, all those who have despised me shall not see it.
24. But my servant Caleb, because another spirit is with him, and he has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land where he has gone; and his seed shall possess it as an inheritance.

---

**v. 22. 23.** All those wavering and doubting people, who depart from <term>abandonment</term> <note>The original German term is *Gelassenheit*, a central concept in mysticism referring to a state of yielding one's will entirely to God.</note> and often surrender themselves to mistrust—when they should instead follow blindly—and who hope to test God through their small faith; all these will not see the promised land. That is to say, they will nevermore in this life enter into God alone, but will die in the wilderness and upon the path. And for this single reason they do not enter: whereas, on the contrary, if they had allowed themselves to be led blindly, without thinking of themselves, they would most certainly have arrived there. But alas! they almost all die along the way: some sooner, others later. Meanwhile, everyone is deprived of the happiness of seeing it. They not only fail to enter, but they never have any true knowledge of it (which is symbolized here by "seeing"). Just as those who grumble against this path, and find faith and divine abandonment to be a burden, will never attain the light of truth to see this path and this earth—that is, what this rest of the soul in God actually is. They will never comprehend such things in this world.

This image is so perfect and so clear to express the great number of those who die through their unfaithfulness in the way of the inner wilderness, and the small number of those who are faithful enough to reach the goal, that one will hardly find another place in Holy Scripture that sets this forth more clearly.

**v. 24.** Caleb, who had a firm and strong spirit in faith, who neither wavered nor doubted, who allowed himself to be led without resistance in the way of abandonment, and who had already seen the land and had been there by decree; he had departed from the secret state to enter into the divine state, in which he was only there as a trial and not yet established forever. This so-faithful Caleb I will lead into the land which he scouted. I will give him the true, constant state in God alone, of which he already has knowledge, and into which he has already entered in passing. His descendants—which are the souls of his kind, who are likewise not mistrustful and who, without looking at themselves, accommodate themselves to perfect abandonment—shall have this state as an inheritance. This means that they shall possess it in a lasting and constant manner, and that this state will become so common and familiar to them, and they would so increase in it, that it will seem to them as if it were natural; and they shall remain in the same as if in their own property.

Caleb was of the tribe of Judah, which represents the strong souls in Jesus Christ, who is the head, the middle, and the end of this lineage. It is a "lion-heartedness"; because all their courage is to be found in Jesus Christ, and they no longer have any courage of their own. But among all the tribes, there is only this single tribe of Judah: that is, among all spiritual souls, there are no others found except these souls resembling lions in strength, who abandon themselves to the hand of God without taking themselves back, and thus enter into God alone. Yet this courage is not in themselves, but in Jesus Christ.

<column-break/>

25. (But the Amalekites and Canaanites dwell in the valley.) Therefore turn tomorrow and journey into the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea.
26. And the **LORD** spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying:
27. How long shall I have to do with this evil congregation, as they grumble against me? I have heard the grumbling of the children of Israel, with which they have grumbled against me.
28. Say to them: As truly as I live, says the **LORD**, I will do to you exactly as you have spoken in my ears!

---

**v. 25.** They were then warned about the surrounding enemies, the Amalekites and Canaanites, against whom God would not assist them now; rather, they should pull back again toward the Red Sea and there await further commands.

If one knew how great the damage is that arises from doubts and "re-possessions" <note>The author uses *Wiedernehmungen* to describe the act of a soul taking back the will it had previously surrendered to God.</note>, one would be amazed by it. These acts of faithlessness cause one to fall far back again. Therefore, those souls stand under the image of this people: those who are near to entering the promised land, and yet turn back; souls who come straight back again and turn toward the first wilderness from which they had just emerged. O, how many there are of this kind, who spend their whole time making and unmaking, and who, without the slightest progress, die after twenty years in the very same state, having done nothing in the meantime but go forward and then back again. For in the ways of the spirit, one must necessarily either go forward or go backward.

**v. 26. 27.** God calls those people an "evil people" who contradict the way of truth, through which He leads souls blindly in abandonment. And should those not be considered evil who are against God and against His friends, and who contest that which He loves most? Even if their opinion be as good as it may, their zeal is not according to knowledge nor according to true discernment.

**v. 28.** (*As truly as I live*) Thus God repeated the heavy oath, that all those over twenty years old who had been counted in the public census should die bit by bit in the wilderness, and none should come into the promised land. David expresses this thus: that God swore to them in His wrath that they should not come to His rest <note>original: "Ps. 95/11"</note> (Psalm 95:11). The Apostle also holds up this example of unbelief to the people of the New Testament, so that they may see themselves mirrored in it, and strive through faith and apply all diligence to enter into the promised rest of the glorious kingdom of Christ <note>original: "Hebr. 3/17. 18. 19. 4/11"</note> (Hebrews 3:17-19, 4:11).

This oath, which God makes by Himself, indicates the magnitude of the offense against Him. To doubt His power is the same as if one doubted His essence. And one robs God of His divine attributes when one doubts both His power and His goodness. His power: that He cannot do what He promises; and His goodness: that He does not want to do it. Therefore God adds: *I will do to you as you have spoken in my ears!* As if He were saying: Just as you have entrusted yourselves to my power and goodness, and just as you have doubted both, so will I also deal with you.

<summary>This page provides a mystical interpretation of God's judgment on the Israelites, contrasting the "wavering souls" who die in the inner wilderness with the "lion-hearted" Caleb who achieves total abandonment to God. It warns that doubt and reclaiming one's will after surrendering it causes spiritual stagnation and prevents one from entering divine rest.</summary>

<header>The Fourth Book of Moses, Chapter XIV</header>

## 29. Your carcasses shall fall in this wilderness; and all of you who were numbered, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me.

## 30. You shall not come into the land, concerning which I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell therein, save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.

v. 29. Yes, you and all those like you—unbelieving and unruly people—shall die on the way and in the wilderness, without attaining that for which I redeemed you from your manifold labors <note>original: "manchfaltigen Arbeit"; referring to the slavery in Egypt.</note>.

v. 30. This, however, is the Land of Holiness; to dwell therein means that one—as Paul wished for the Thessalonians—be sanctified through and through, in spirit, soul, and body. Even to this day, people do not want to believe in the possibility of this <note>The author is referring to the doctrine of Christian perfection or entire sanctification, which was a point of theological debate.</note>, and for that very reason, they remain excluded from the entire inheritance.

Without Caleb and Joshua) Soul and Spirit <note>The author provides a mystical allegory: Caleb represents the Soul and Joshua represents the Spirit, the only parts of the human being capable of entering the divine rest.</note>.

Out of 600,000 and more who departed from Egypt or from the dispersion, only two people were found who reached GOD Himself; meanwhile, all the others died along the way due to a lack of <term>faithfulness</term> <note>original: "Treue"; here meaning a loyal, active reliance on God.</note> and <term>abandonment</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central mystical concept meaning the total surrender of one's will to God.</note>. This indicates very clearly that although all are called to this path and goal—namely, to enter into their Origin, which is GOD—if they were faithful enough to let themselves be led therein. GOD calls them all: but very few attain it. Nevertheless, this does not come from GOD, whose goodness is infinite, and who does not fail to offer the necessary means to those who only wish to use them. He wills not only (a) that all should be saved; but, what is even more, that all should reach the purpose of their creation (b), which is GOD Himself. Or rather, no one can be blessed unless they have reached this goal before attaining the enjoyment of blessedness. And this must necessarily happen in the next life for every chosen soul, if it has not already happened in this life. For this is Christian perfection, without which (c) no one will reach the enjoyment of eternal bliss. For nothing imperfect—indeed, not even the slightest <term>self-will</term> <note>original: "Eigenheit"; referring to the ego or the quality of acting for oneself rather than for God.</note>—can enter into GOD, nor into the paradise of His glory. Thus, all those who do not enter are only excluded because they were not faithful.

Those who hear so much about "faithfulness" here might wish to understand this in an active sense. For they will believe that this faithfulness consists in being careful, taking heed, and working hard on one's own part. Ah, no! That is not the great faithfulness; which consists only in
<margin>NB</margin> believing and surrendering oneself: believing that GOD is kind and almighty; entirely kind, never to forsake those who give themselves entirely to Him. Just as He assures through Isaiah (d): Can a mother forget her child, and not have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will never forget you. Now, if GOD carries so much goodness for all those who entrust themselves to Him, then we do Him the greatest insult when we doubt it. He is also equally almighty to support us. You shall know, He adds in the same prophet (e), that I am the LORD, and that all those who trust in me shall not be put to shame. Just as it is written (f) of Daniel, that he received no harm in the lions' den because he believed in his GOD.

The second point of this faithfulness is abandonment: which does not take itself back through any human worry, and never puts itself into anxiety or unrest regarding its condition, yes, even letting its salvation and its eternity depend on GOD alone. This is properly called a blind abandonment, which seeks no self-interest, but rather lets itself be led by Him, just as a blind man does who only follows his guide.

(a) 1 Timothy 2:4. (b) Matthew 5:48. (c) Hebrews 12:14.
(d) Isaiah 49:15. (e) Isaiah 49:23. (f) Daniel 6:23.

<column-break/>

## 31. But your little ones, whom you said would be a prey, them I will bring in, and they shall know the land which you have rejected.

## 32. But as for you, your own carcasses shall fall in this wilderness. <margin>Hebrews 3:17</margin>

## 33. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years, and bear your whoredoms, until your carcasses are all consumed in the wilderness.

34. —

v. 31. Children are best suited for this. and therefore those are excepted from the Lord's threat who, as simple and young hearts, have not yet entered into mistrust with knowledge and will; those who either fell into it only out of sheer weakness and by being dragged along by others, or who remained standing in the simplicity of their hearts and, though they were still young and had not come far, nevertheless did not doubt or murmur.

These little children, though they have not come far, nevertheless reach the goal because they—without following their own resolutions—let themselves be led like little children, without worrying about where they are being taken.

These simple and innocent people, says the Lord and His Spirit, whom you supposed would be given as a prey to the enemies, shall be those whom I will draw into myself and introduce into the divine life: so that you may thereby recognize what an advantage it is to rely on me, and the infinite happiness which you despised when I called you to lead you into it.

v. 32. Man must truly have died before he shall reach the promised land; and not only died, but he must also through the experience of his decay completely rot, according to the pronouncement of Jesus Christ: This rotting is the death of the grain (a), and death causes its rotting. And here too, the people who are to rot in the wilderness are an image of that terrible death and decay through which one must enter the interior in order to find a new life in GOD.

To the unbelieving, however, GOD does not show the promised land in this life; instead, when their bodies have died, they must remain in the wilderness: which is to say, they must be purified in the other world, and serve as an example in this one, because they were taken away by death before they reached their perfection.

The true secret sense of this passage is that He only allows those who resist Him to go through a much more grim death and humiliation than those who let themselves be led without resistance. And because the former lack this faithfulness, they remain in this state of death and decay without ever coming out of it into this life; it is as if GOD said to those who resisted Him: You shall remain stretched out in the sleep of death in your own corruption, without ever arriving there; while on the contrary, the others whom I have drawn there have happily come out of the same, because they believed and entrusted themselves to me.

v. 33. The children are those who doubted, wavered, and took part in the sin of the others out of weakness. All must, without exception, remain in the light of faith and not depart from this secret wilderness-darkness until all the decay is entirely consumed. For nothing of this decay can reach into GOD. It is indeed the way through which one must go to come to Him: but no decay whatsoever can remain in Him. Thus, it must then be entirely consumed in the wilderness and turned to ashes through total annihilation <note>original: "Vernichtung"; in mystical thought, the "annihilation" of the self is necessary for union with God.</note>, which is the end of all life: then it leads to the goal.

This decay is nothing other than the corruption that comes from us, through the foul odor of bodies and vices—that is, from the flesh, which has been corrupted through the sin of Jesus <note>This likely refers to the "sin-flesh" or the fallen nature that Jesus took upon himself to redeem, or a typo in the OCR where it means "Adam's sin." Given the context of "corrupted flesh," it refers to the fallen human nature.</note>.

(a) John 12:24.

v. 34. As a memorial of this righteous wrath, as many years are appointed for the execution of this judgment as they spent days in scouting the land; namely, 40 years: which, however, are reckoned from the departure out of Egypt.

The sin of one day may bring upon us the punishment of a year—even many years, even an entire eternity—if it is not repented of and abandoned in time. And if a punishment of so many years follows the days of sin, it is to be feared that, since we sin daily and hardly a day of our lives is spent without sin, entire eternities, even eternities of eternities, would scarcely be enough for punishment; because there is an equality between God’s temporal and future eternal judgment: unless that which one may have worked of good or suffered of evil in this life is also taken into account. The forty days of sin may bring 400 years, even an eternity of eternities, upon us. And therefore, an eternal punishment awaits impenitent, disobedient people in whom all hope for improvement is lost.

v. 35. (Those who have gathered together against me) How many an evil alliance of an evil congregation, a fallen church, party, or sect, is thus made against the LORD and His Anointed, where people unite against the Spirit of the LORD, which gives and desires freedom. 2 Corinthians 3:17.

v. 36. It is testified of all these scouts that they were men; that is, men of reputation, as the Jews understand the word <term>Anaschim</term> <note>original Hebrew: "Anashim" (אנשים), meaning men, but often interpreted in this context as men of high rank or "heads" of the people.</note>. Chapter 13:3. They were great and wise and powerful and rich men, because they were heads and leaders of the people. But what is all strength and manliness, dignity and majesty, other than inability and weakness—even contemptible meanness—when they rely upon themselves?

v. 37. Therefore, all of this could not stand in the judgment, which was executed upon them by a sudden death immediately before the face of the LORD, who appeared in the cloud (v. 10), as a terror to the others. None of the rest could expect a great age, just as they all fell within the 38 years, over which Moses led a lamentation and composed the ninetieth Psalm for that reason <note>Tradition often attributes Psalm 90, which reflects on the brevity of life and God's wrath, to Moses during the wilderness wandering.</note>.

...stands, in that they had broken His covenant, and thus forfeited the promises of the covenant on their part.

Those who recognize their iniquity and take it upon themselves to turn back, commit a double sin, which is as bad as the first: namely, they want to reach God again through their own strength, and believe that they could come to their goal through themselves. Therefore, they force themselves by their own impulse to climb to the height of the mountain.

v. 38. (Joshua and Caleb) These are very often placed together, and not without good reason. Jehouschuah <note>The Hebrew name Yehoshua (Joshua).</note>, the LORD the Redeemer or Savior (according to the divinely composed word from the great name Jehovah and Jeschuah), is with Caleb, the courageous and brave man after God’s heart and will, and makes us inwardly fit to fulfill all righteousness and to work God’s work after Him. Philippians 4:13.

These provide a picture of the faithful messengers, like the holy prophets, who sought and diligently searched, and prophesied of the grace that should come into us. 1 Peter 1:10. These are the

(Men who had gone to scout out the land) But nowadays one can become a "scout" even if one has not gone there, and hardly takes a step toward it, but rather occupies oneself with maps and the reading of them; just as the learned scribes knew how to tell where Christ should be born and searched the Scriptures, yet did not wish to come to Him. John 5:39, 40.

v. 39. (Mourned) True repentance of the heart consists in a person completely renouncing his own will and submitting himself entirely to the only-good will of God.

v. 40. But when a person murmurs against the righteous judgment of God and is dissatisfied, he then wants to help himself according to his own mind, and thereby only plunges himself into a heavier judgment. First, they did not want to enter the Promised Land according to the command of the LORD; now they want to go up against the LORD’s command and take it by their own strength; though their faithful leader Moses warns them so heartily and tells them beforehand how they will not succeed, but rather be struck down by their enemies: which then also happened to them, and they thus had to actually experience that God had turned away from them, as in v. 34.

v. 41-43. The enlightened leader, however, warns them wisely when he sees their error, that they should not ascend, so that they might not fall by their enemies: since those who enter into such states of their own accord will certainly perish therein. For God is not with them then.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XIV.

**29.** Your corpses shall fall in this wilderness; and all of you who were counted according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me.
**30.** You shall not come into the land over which I have raised my hand <note>original: "meine Hand habe aufgehaben"; a biblical idiom for swearing a solemn oath.</note> to let you dwell therein: except for Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun.

---

**v. 29.** Indeed you, and all your kind—unbelieving and ill-mannered people—shall die on the way and in the wilderness, without attaining that for which I redeemed you from your manifold labor.

**v. 30.** But this is the Land of Holiness, intended as a place to dwell so that one might be—as Paul wished for the Thessalonians—sanctified through and through, in spirit, soul, and body: a possibility that people even to this day do not want to believe, and for that very reason, they remain excluded from the entire inheritance.

(Except for Caleb and Joshua) Soul and Spirit. <note>The author uses Caleb and Joshua as allegories for the higher faculties of the human soul and spirit which, unlike the rebellious "fleshly" nature, are capable of entering into God's presence.</note>

Out of 600,000 and even more who departed from Egypt or from the dispersion, only two people were found who would have attained unto GOD Himself; while in the meantime, all the others died along the way for lack of faithfulness and abandonment <term>Gelassenheit: a key mystical concept meaning the release of self-will and total surrender to God.</term>. This indicates very clearly that all are indeed called to enter this way and end—namely, into their Origin, which is GOD—if they were faithful enough to let themselves be led therein. GOD calls them all: But very few attain to it. Nevertheless, this does not come from GOD, whose goodness is infinite, and who does not fail to offer the necessary means to those who simply wish to use them. He does not only desire (a) that all should be saved; but, what is more, that all should attain the ultimate purpose of their creation (b), which is GOD Himself. Or rather, no one can be blessed unless they have first come to this ultimate purpose before they attain the enjoyment of bliss. And this will necessarily happen in the next life for every elect soul, if it has not already happened in this life. For this is that great Christian Perfection, without which (c) no one will reach the enjoyment of eternal bliss. For nothing imperfect, indeed not even the slightest self-interest <note>original: "Eigenheit"; refers to the ego or the quality of acting for oneself rather than for God.</note>, can enter into GOD, nor into the paradise of His glory. Therefore, all those who do not enter are excluded only because they were not faithful.

<margin>NB</margin> Those who hear so much about "faithfulness" here might well want to understand this in an active sense. For they will believe that this faithfulness consists in being careful, taking heed, and having to work hard on one's own part. Oh no! That is not what this great faithfulness is; it consists only in believing and surrendering oneself: Believing that GOD is kind and almighty; entirely kind, so as never to forsake those who give themselves entirely to Him. Just as He assures through Isaiah (d): Can a mother forget her child, and not have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget such a one, yet I will never forget you. Now, if GOD carries so much goodness for all those who entrust themselves to Him, we surely do Him the greatest insult when we doubt it. He is also equally almighty to support us. You shall know, He adds in the same prophet (e), that I am the LORD, and that all who trust in me shall not be put to shame. Just as (f) it is written of Daniel, that he received no harm in the lions' den because he had believed in his GOD.

The second point of this faithfulness is abandonment: which does not reclaim itself through any human anxiety, and never puts itself into worry or unrest regarding its condition, but lets even its salvation and its eternity depend on GOD alone. This is properly called a blind abandonment, which looks to no self-interest, but lets itself be led by Him just as a blind man does who simply follows his guide.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XIV

->**29. Your carcasses shall fall in this wilderness, and all of you who were numbered, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, who have murmured against me.**<-
->**30. You shall not come into the land concerning which I lifted up my hand to make you dwell therein, except for Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun.**<-

***

**v. 29.** Yes, you, and all your kind—unbelieving and unruly people—shall die on the path and in the wilderness without attaining that for which I redeemed you from your manifold labors.
**v. 30.** This, however, is the Land of Holiness, meant for dwelling in such a way that one—as Paul wishes for the Thessalonians—might be sanctified through and through, in spirit, soul, and body. Even to this day, people do not wish to believe in the possibility of this <note>The author is referring to the doctrine of Christian perfection or entire sanctification, a major theme in Pietist and mystical circles.</note>, and for that very reason, they remain excluded from the entire inheritance.
**(Except Caleb and Joshua)** Soul and Spirit. <note>In mystical interpretation, Caleb and Joshua represent the higher faculties of the human being that remain faithful to God, while the "murmuring" Israelites represent the rebellious lower nature.</note>
Out of 600,000 and even more who departed from Egypt or from the dispersion, only two men were found who had attained God Himself; meanwhile, all the others died along the way due to a lack of faithfulness and **serene surrender** <term>Gelassenheit: A central mystical concept meaning a state of letting go, internal stillness, and total submission to God's will.</term>. This indicates very clearly that while all are called to enter this way and end—namely, into their Origin, which is God—if they were faithful enough to let themselves be led therein. God calls them all, but very few attain it. Nevertheless, this does not come from God, whose goodness is infinite and who does not fail to offer the necessary means to those who merely wish to use them. He does not only will (a) that all should be saved, but, what is more, that all should attain the ultimate purpose of their creation (b), which is God Himself. Or rather, no one can be truly blessed unless they have reached this ultimate purpose before they attain the enjoyment of salvation. And this must necessarily happen in the next life for every elect soul, if it has not already happened in this life. For this is that great Christian perfection, without which (c) no one will attain the enjoyment of eternal bliss. For nothing imperfect—not even the slightest trace of self-will—can enter into God, nor into the paradise of His glory. Thus, all those who do not enter are only excluded because they were not faithful.
<margin>NB</margin> Those who hear so much about "faithfulness" here might wish to understand it in an active sense. They will believe that this faithfulness consists in being careful, taking heed, and having to work much on one's own part. Ah, no! This is not that great faithfulness; rather, it consists only in believing and surrendering: believing that God is kind and almighty; entirely kind, never to forsake those who give themselves entirely over to Him. Just as He assures through Isaiah (d): "Can a mother forget her child, and not have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget such a thing, yet I will never forget you." Now, if God carries so much goodness for all those who entrust themselves to Him, then we do Him the greatest insult when we doubt it. He is likewise almighty to support us. "You shall know," He adds in the same prophet (e), "that I am the LORD, and that all those who hope in me shall not be put to shame." Just as it is written (f) of Daniel, that he received no harm in the lions' den because he had believed in his God.
The second point of this faithfulness is **serene surrender**; which does not take itself back through any human worry, and never sets itself in anxiety or unrest concerning its state—yes, it even lets its salvation and its eternity depend on God alone. This is properly called a "blind surrender," which looks to no self-interest but lets itself be led by Him just as a blind man does who merely follows his guide.
(a) 1 Tim. 2:4. (b) Matt. 5:48. (c) Heb. 12:14.
(d) Isa. 49:15. (e) Isa. 49:23. (f) Dan. 6:23.

<column-break/>

->**31. But your children, of whom you said they would become a prey, them I will bring in, that they shall know the land which you have rejected.**<-
->**32. But as for you, your own carcasses shall fall in this wilderness.**<- <margin>Hebrew</margin>
->**33. And your children shall be shepherds in the wilderness forty years, and shall bear your whoredom, until all your carcasses are in the wilderness.**<-
**34.**

***

**v. 31.** For this purpose, children are now the best suited. And therefore, those are exempted from the Lord's threat who, as simple and young hearts, have not yet entered into mistrust with knowledge and will—whether they fell into it merely out of sheer weakness and by being dragged along by the others, or remained standing through the simplicity of their hearts; and even if they were young and had not yet come far, they nonetheless did not doubt or murmur.
These little children, though they have not yet come far, nonetheless attain the goal; because, without following their own reasonings, they let themselves be led just like little children, without worrying about where they are being taken.
These simple and innocent people, says the Spirit—and His Spirit—whom you supposed were given up to the enemies as prey, shall be the ones whom I will lead into my Light and into the divine life: so that you may thereby recognize what an advantage it is to rely on me, and the infinite happiness which you abandoned when I called you to lead you into it.
**v. 32.** A person must truly have died before he shall attain the promised land; and not only outwardly, but he must also completely rot through the experience of his corruptibility, according to the saying of Jesus Christ (a): this rotting is the death of the grain, and the death of all things is their decay. And herein also, the people who are to rot in the wilderness are an image of the terrible death and decay through which one must pass inwardly in order to find a new life in God.
To the unbelievers, however, God does not show the promised land in this life; instead, when their bodies have died, they must remain in the wilderness: which is to say, in the other world they must let themselves be purified, being brought to a burning in that world because death took them away before they attained their perfection.
The true hidden sense of this passage is that He allows those who resist Him to go through a much greater death and humiliation than those who let themselves be led without resistance. And because the former take much longer detours, they remain in this state of death and decay without ever coming out of it in this life; it is as if God said to those who resisted Him: "You shall lie stretched out in your own corruption through the sleep of death without ever escaping it; whereas, on the contrary, the others whom I have drawn in have happily come out of it because they believed and entrusted themselves to me."
**v. 33.** The "children" are those who doubted or wavered out of simplicity and did not take part in the sin of the others. All of them, without exception, must remain in the land of faith and not depart from this secret wilderness-darkness until all the decay is entirely consumed. For nothing of this decay can reach God. It is indeed the way through which one must go to come to Him, but no decay whatsoever can remain in Him. Thus, it must be entirely consumed in the wilderness and turned to ashes through total annihilation, which is the end of all [self-]life: for that is what leads to the end.
This decay is nothing other than the corruption that comes from us, through the "evil smell of the bodies of our fathers"—that is, from the flesh, which has been corrupted in us through sin.
(a) John 12:24.

# Chapter XIV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

34. According to the number of the days in which you scouted the land, the forty days / you shall bear your iniquities each day for a year, forty years / so that you may experience my turning away.
35. I the LORD have spoken / I will surely do this to all this evil congregation / who have gathered together against me. In this wilderness they shall all come to an end, and there they shall die.
36. And the men whom Moses had sent to scout the land / and who had returned and caused the whole congregation to murmur against him / because they had brought forth an evil report about the land;
37. Those men died / who had brought forth an evil report about the land / by a plague before the face of the LORD.

---

**v. 34.** As a memorial of this righteous wrath, the same number of years is appointed for the execution of this judgment as the number of days they spent in scouting the land; namely, 40 years: which, however, were counted from the time of the departure from Egypt.
The sin of a single day may bring the punishment of a year / indeed many years / yes, an entire eternity / upon us / when it is not repented of and abandoned in time. And if a punishment of so many years follows the days of sin / it is to be feared / since we sin daily / and hardly a day of our lives is spent without sin / that entire eternities / yes, eternities of eternities / would scarcely be enough for punishment; because there is an equality between God’s temporal and future eternal judgment: unless perhaps that which one may have worked of good in this life / or suffered of evil / is also considered therein. The forty days of sin may bring 400 years / yes, an eternity of eternities / upon us. And therefore, an eternal punishment awaits unrepentant, disobedient people / in whom all hope for improvement is lost.
**v. 35. (Who have gathered together against me)** How many an evil alliance of a wicked community / a fallen church / party, and sect / is thus made against the Lord and his Anointed / when people unite against the Spirit of the Lord / who gives and desires freedom. 2 Cor. 3:17.
**v. 36.** It is testified of all these scouts that they were men / that is / men of renown / as the Jews understand the word <term>Anashim: Hebrew for "men," often used to denote those of high status or rank</term>. ch. 13:3. They were great and wise and powerful and rich men / because they were heads and leaders of the people. But what is all strength and manliness / dignity and highness / other than inability and weakness / yes, contemptible baseness / when they rely only upon themselves?
**v. 37.** Therefore, all of this could not stand in the judgment / which was carried out upon them by a sudden death immediately before the face of the LORD / who appeared in the cloud / v. 10. This was done to the terror of the rest / who now could not expect a great age / just as they all fell away within the 38 years / over which Moses lamented / and for which reason he composed the ninetieth Psalm.

40. And they rose up early in the morning / and went up to the heights of the mountain / and said: See, here we are and we will go up to the place / of which the LORD has spoken! for we have sinned.

**v. 38. (Joshua and Caleb)** are often found placed together / and not without good reason. <note>original: "Jehoschuah"</note> Joshua / the Lord the Redeemer or Savior / (according to the divinely-composed word from the great name <term>Jehovah: The sacred name of God</term> and <term>Yeshuah: Hebrew for salvation or deliverance</term>) is with Caleb / the courageous and brave man according to the heart and will of God / and makes us inwardly capable of fulfilling all righteousness / and working God’s work after him. Phil. 4:13.
These provide a picture of the faithful messengers / like the holy prophets / who sought and diligently searched / and prophesied of the grace that should come to us. 1 Pet. 1:10. These are
**Men who had gone to scout the land)** but nowadays one can become a scout / even if one hasn't gone / and hardly takes a step toward it / but rather occupies oneself with land-maps and the reading of them / just as the learned scribes knew how to tell where Christ should be born / and searched in the Scripture / but did not wish to come to him. John 5:39, 40.
**v. 39. (Mourned)** True repentance of the heart consists in a person entirely renouncing their own will / and completely submitting themselves to the only-good will of God.
**v. 40.** But when a person murmurs against the righteous judgment of God and is dissatisfied / he then wants to help himself according to his own mind / and thereby only plunges himself into a heavier judgment. First, they did not want to enter the promised land according to the command of the LORD / now they want to go up against the LORD’s command / and take it by their own strength; though their faithful leader Moses warns them so heartily / and tells them beforehand / how it will not prosper for them / but they would be struck down by their enemies: which then also happened to them / and they thus truly had to experience / that God had turned away from them / as it says in v. 34 / because they had broken his covenant / and had thus forfeited the promises of the covenant on their part.
Those who recognize their iniquity / and yet take themselves back into it / commit a double sin / which is as bad as the first: namely / they want to reach God again through their own powers / and believe / that they could come to their goal through themselves. Therefore, they force themselves by their own impulse to climb to the height of the mountain.
**v. 41-43.** But the enlightened leader warns them wisely / since he sees their error / that they should not climb up / so that they do not perhaps fall before their enemies: since those / who enter into such states by themselves / will certainly perish therein. For God is then not with them.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XV.

44. **But they presumed to go up to the heights of the hill country: however, the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord and Moses did not depart from the middle of the camp.**
45. **Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites / who dwelt in those mountains / came down and struck them / and struck them down as far as Hormah.**

<margin>v. 44. But they presumed)</margin> Thus, the good counsel of the faithful witnesses of God is always despised when the multitude sets itself against it, and thereby plunges itself into its own ruin. See Proverbs 1:24, etc.; Ecclesiastes 9:15, 16.

Now they wanted to break into the land of the Canaanites headlong and take it. This was again to no avail: and such is the way of man; he either stumbles to the right or to the left, and can rarely hit the middle path. He falls either into the fire or into the water, like one who is moon-struck <note>original: "Mondstüchtigen," referring to the lunatic or epileptic boy in Matthew 17:15; here used as a metaphor for spiritual instability</note>; because he prefers to follow his unbroken natural impulse rather than the counsel of God.

<margin>To go up to the heights—)</margin> They ventured with a haughty and presumptuous heart to fight against their enemies, and thereby to undo what Moses had told them of the 40 years. And

So does the self-willed, proud, and presumptuous spirit act even among those who, in their own power and the strength of their imagination—which they call faith—want to go against spiritual enemies; just as in Acts 19:13–16, but with the same or even worse outcome.

Indeed, there are those who, through their own strength, wish to walk in such ways to which God has not called them, even though they think they can force their way in despite all warnings. But because neither God nor the leaders guide them therein, they are not only wounded in those ways by their enemies, but they must return with a thousand wounds.

From this we must now draw two great truths. First, that God alone can lead souls in His ways; second, that one must not force oneself into them; just as one must not resist or waver when God wants one to be there. In this people, both fear and audacity, mistrust and self-conceit, are punished with the same penalty. One must let oneself be led by God, and follow His holy movements and obedience step by step, without running ahead of Him or drawing back. One must surrender to God through an entire Gelassenheit <note>a technical term in German mysticism meaning "yieldedness" or "letting-go" to God's will</note> as He wills, and wait with patience for the delay caused by the fall, and drink deeply from the humiliations that it brings, being well-satisfied that God satisfies Himself and His justice in every way, without desiring to diminish any of it: then one must be satisfied to remain in a state of humiliation throughout one's whole life, without striving or working to come out of it again, unless God Himself does it; and to let oneself be led like a child wherever He wishes.

<margin>v. 45. The Amalekites and Canaanites struck them)</margin> A notable example of how it goes for all those who run ahead of God with their own spirit, and want to force by violence what the time is not yet ripe for.

<margin>Struck them down)</margin> Because they had no new command, as before, and the word of the Lord was not with them in the least; so they had to fall before their enemies and be put to shame. And what is written is written for our instruction. God, who still is what He was, will also, through His Spirit and Word in His own time, let everyone experience and find what an incomprehensible difference there is between that which comes from man's own spirit, heart, mind, and courage—and from the impulse of blind-creeping selfhood and self-conceit, even if under the guise and pretext of the written Word—and that which comes from the Word and light of the power of God.

Who teaches us where and how we should show goodness and let it flow out from our own...

### Chap. XV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

8. And when you prepare a young bull for a burnt offering or a sacrifice, to fulfill a special vow, or for a peace offering to the Lord:
9. Then he shall bring with the young bull a grain offering of three-tenths of fine flour mixed with half a hin of oil;
10. And you shall bring half a hin of wine as a drink offering. This is an offering by fire, a pleasing aroma to the Lord.
11. Thus shall it be done for each ox, or for each ram, or for a lamb from the sheep or from the goats.
12. According to the number that you prepare, so shall you do for each one according to their number.
13. Every native-born shall do these things in this way, to offer an offering by fire as a pleasing aroma to the Lord.
14. And if a stranger dwells among you, or whoever is among you throughout your generations, and wishes to prepare an offering by fire as a pleasing aroma to the Lord; he shall do just as you must do.

---

v. 8. 9. **Peace offering — Grain offering)** Here the Apostle <note>Referring to the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews</note> makes mention of only these two types of offerings: the sacrifice of praise, which is the fruit of the lips that confess His name; to which all exercises of faith and all types of prayer belong: and then he considers these grain offerings in the New Testament: *Do not forget to do good and to share; for such sacrifices please God.* Hebrews 13:15, 16. These good deeds are also what Christ intends to praise. Matthew 25:35, etc.

v. 10. **Wine for a drink offering)** could always be purchased in the Temple.
**A half Hin)** is as much as one measure, or what fits into 36 eggshells. <note>A "hin" was a Hebrew liquid measure approximately equal to 4 to 6 liters; the author’s "eggshell" calculation is a traditional rabbinic method of volume estimation.</note>

v. 11. **Thus — for)** Some suggest that no sacrifice was offered without a grain and drink offering: But the Scripture assigns it only to the peace and burnt offerings of cattle, sheep, or goats, which were offered either by individuals or the whole congregation, both on and outside of feast days. Regarding the burnt offerings of birds, as well as sin and guilt offerings, one reads nowhere that a grain offering belonged to them, except only in the cleansing of a leper. Leviticus 14.

v. 12. The grain offerings belonging to the animal sacrifices did not have a single prescribed amount. Not only was the measure of the grain offering adjusted according to whether the animals were small or large, or one, two, or three years old: but also, for however many animals there were, the grain offering was doubled that many times: namely, for every animal its certain grain offering. Every animal had its appointed flour and oil.

<column-break/>

15. The assembly shall have one ordinance for you and for the stranger who dwells among you. It shall be a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations: as you are, so shall the stranger be before the Lord.
16. There shall be one law and one rule for you and for the stranger who dwells among you.
17. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
18. Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you come into the land <gloss>v. 2.</gloss> into which I will bring you;
19. Then it shall be, when you eat of the bread of the land, you shall lift up a heave offering to the Lord.
20. You shall lift up a cake from the first of your dough as a heave offering: as the heave offering from the threshing floor, so shall you lift it up.
21. From the first of your dough you shall give to the Lord a heave offering throughout your generations. <gloss>(a)</gloss>

<margin>(a) Neh. 10:37.</margin>
22. And

---

v. 13–16. In matters of religion and in punishments, the strangers had one law with the native-born: Exodus 12:49, Leviticus 24:22. In civil matters, however, there was some difference between them. See Leviticus 25:44, etc.; Deuteronomy 23:20.

v. 17. etc. Here God ordained that from their doughs—namely, as often as they would bake—they should give the Lord a cake or loaf as a heave offering <note>A "heave offering" or *Terumah* was an offering "lifted up" or separated for the use of the priests.</note>, just as they had to bring the first sheaf of their fruits. Leviticus 23:10, 11. Thus, they were permitted to put almost no morsel into their mouths unless they had first presented a portion of it to the Lord, as if to the Master of the House.

v. 18. **When you come into the land)** Thus these were only given in the Promised Land, and were not accepted from anyone else who did not dwell therein.
**Into which I will bring you)** or "am bringing," gradually, little by little: by which model He gives or assigns the eternal inheritance—which is the true Holy Land—spiritually to the believers.

v. 19. **To the Lord)** They gave this cake to the priest or Levite who lived among them and performed some holy service in their schools and in instruction.

v. 20. 21. **From the first of your dough)** From every baking, they always had to take a portion when they kneaded their dough and bake a cake from it for the priests. If someone forgot, they gave a loaf from the finished batch.
How much of the dough should be taken for this purpose was initially left to their free will. Later, a 44th part of the whole dough was ordained (a).
Through this priest-cake lifted from it, the whole dough was sanctified; Paul refers to this in Romans 11:16. And so the Lord wishes to be honored by our income: Proverbs 3:9. There we would already experience it in the spirit, where it could happen, if only the heart were taken up with a zeal for the honor of God and not so entirely with fleshly self-interest and love of the world. See 1 Timothy 6:10.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chap. XV

22. And if you should err, so that you do not observe all these commandments which the Lord has spoken to Moses;
23. Everything that the Lord has commanded you by the hand of Moses, from the day that the Lord gave the command and forward unto your descendants:
24. Then it shall be, if anything is committed unintentionally <note>original: "aus Versehen"; referring to sins of ignorance or oversight</note> out of the sight of the congregation, that the entire congregation shall prepare one young bull for a burnt offering, for a pleasing aroma to the Lord, together with its grain offering and its drink offering, according to the ordinance, and one male goat for a sin offering.
25. Thus the priest shall make atonement for the entire congregation of the children of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them. For it is an unintentional error. And they have brought their offering as an offering by fire to the Lord and their sin offering before the face of the Lord because of their error.

---

Here again, the sins of an entire congregation, and then of a single soul, are reported, as in Leviticus 4:13 etc. and 27 etc., when they happen out of oversight or haste; at which time they were to be reconciled with their burnt and sin offerings.

<margin>v. 23.</margin> **Unto your descendants)** who were to be brought into the land of Canaan, for whose sake specifically this repeated summary of all the Lord’s commandments is made, in order to confirm the Sinai covenant with them.

<margin>v. 24.</margin> **For a pleasing aroma)** Although the burnt flesh of animals cannot exactly give off a pleasing smell, that which is understood spiritually through it—namely, the consumption and eradication of sin and animalistic lusts—cannot but give the Lord a most pleasing and delightful aroma; a scent or taste and sensation of rest, as it is properly called: since sin causes the all-holy God nothing but unrest, vexation, trouble, and labor.

->O what a divine work, to provide stillness, rest, and relief even to Him who alone can give relief, rest, and peace to your soul!<-

Therefore, offer up your daily burnt offering, and die daily to your sin: that will refresh the Lord like a good aroma, and He will give rest to your soul.

<margin>v. 25.</margin> **So it shall be forgiven them)** For the Father and Lord, Lord God, is merciful and gracious and of great goodness and faithfulness, and is quite inclined to forgive sin if we only make petition to Him for it. *If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive them,* 1 John 1:9, especially when they occur out of oversight or haste.

Furthermore, there is a strange dispute which some carry on regarding the nature of sins—which are mortal or not mortal sins, which are venial or unpardonable sins—falling short therein if they do not understand all sins through the number seven <note>likely referring to the seven deadly sins or a totality of sin</note>. For all sins are mortal and deadly insofar as one lives in them. And among those who die to sin, there are no unpardonable or mortal sins. Why then should we "strive for Baal" <note>a German idiom meaning to fight over something useless or false</note>? Blessed are those who, by laying aside their sins, die from now on! These always receive forgiveness: for they bring their sacrifice.

<column-break/>

26. And it shall be forgiven the entire congregation of the children of Israel, and the stranger who dwells in their midst. For the whole people were in error.
27. But if a single soul sins unintentionally, then he shall bring a female goat of one year old for a sin offering.
28. And the priest shall make atonement for the soul that has erred with a sin of oversight before the face of the Lord, that he may make atonement for him and it may be forgiven him.
29. As for the native-born among the children of Israel and the stranger who dwells in their midst, there shall be one law among you for him who does something out of oversight.
30.

---

<margin>v. 26--28.</margin> God shows here quite clearly what a difference exists between those inward-turned people <note>original: "eingekehrte Menschen"; those who practice an internal, mystical faith</note> who are His chosen people, and the others who do not have this advantage. The former commit no sin except through oversight and weakness: because their will remains bound with the will of God, so that they would rather die than offend Him. And for these, it is true that when they imagine that what they have done is sin, they feel the pangs of death because of it. Indeed, even if they were to sin with intent, they would thereby depart from their station, and from the holiness, unity, or union of their will with the will of God, according to their degree. For since one cannot tolerate sin, the will, if it were perhaps guilty, would necessarily be separated from God instantly. This would then plunge these souls into hell if they were convinced that they had committed willful sins. But as long as they remain in equanimity <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a key term in German mysticism for letting go of self-will</note>, in self-denial, in the unity of their will with the will of God, in a total sacrifice of themselves to God, in a magnanimous preference for His honor over all personal advantage, in a living impression and experience of His good love, and in a total abandonment to His guidance; then they certainly have not sinned with their will, even though they have fallen into the most apparent sins. This is the fruit of grace, and indeed of very high grace, that they never reconcile themselves to sin. Therefore, even if they assure you they have sinned, you will nonetheless see that when you ask them to confess whether they have a clear knowledge that they sinned intentionally, they will tell you in words—provided they are being justified—that they did not know such a thing. It is certain that grace is still found in these souls, and that because the will is held back in God, even if this happens under a secret darkness, it is entirely separated from that which goes on in the lower parts <note>referring to the physical or lower emotional self</note>.

<margin>v. 29.</margin> This law also concerns the strangers: that is, those who join themselves to the spiritual ones who have already come a long way, and enter into that same state, even if they were not raised in it; and also all people who have not yet come so far, who sin without knowing it.

The commentary provides a mystical interpretation of "aroma" as the spiritual destruction of lust and highlights the equality of strangers in these laws.</summary>

# Chapter XV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

30. **But the soul that does anything with a high hand** <margin>(a)</margin> <note>original: "mit erhabener Hand"; a Hebrew idiom for acting with defiance, pride, or "a raised fist" against God’s law.</note>**, whether he is native-born or a stranger, the same has blasphemed the Lord; and that soul shall be cut off from among his people.**
<margin>Gen. 17:14. Exod. 30:38. Lev. 17:4. (a) Exod. 17:16.</margin>

31. **Because he has despised the word of the Lord and has broken His commandment; that soul shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be upon him.**

---

<margin>v. 30.</margin> On the other hand, if someone sinned with a "high hand"—namely, quite boldly and willfully, with full knowledge and intent, so that he would not allow himself to be restrained at all—he was to be punished as a defiant despiser of God. Whether these were sins that deserved the death penalty, so that he was then killed; or if they were scandalous sins, that he was banished from the congregation and left to the judgment of God, which would avenge the iniquity lying upon him in its own time. These are then the proud and reigning sins, where one truly raises his hand against God: Job 15:26, Psalm 19:14. For such willful sins, no sacrifice remains, but a fearful expectation of judgment and fiery indignation which will devour the adversaries. Hebrews 10:26, 27.

O, if only authorities would wake up and notice how the lands are becoming full of such defiant sinners, who with their Epicurean <note>A lifestyle devoted to sensual pleasure and the denial of divine involvement in human affairs.</note>, even quite atheistic lives, provoke the righteous wrath of God upon themselves and their subjects, so that the rooting out threatened by God must soon come upon both! It is not enough to root out murderers and thieves with death sentences; rather, the vices of gluttony, fraud, pride, cursing, and the like, which have broken in far and wide, should be restrained with all seriousness, and such things rooted out from Christendom, which we nevertheless claim to be.

<margin>v. 31. That soul shall be cut off)</margin> Both those who have already come quite far, who have kept the love of God from their birth and entered this path early; as well as those who, after growing old in other ways, finally harmonized themselves with this path, yet afterward become enemies. And precisely in this, they are cut off from the people of God when they are separated from those who are truly one through the union of their will with the will of God. This, however, does not prevent them from repenting again and thus being saved. But they are no longer of the chosen people, who may still have much misery about them and commit sins of frailty; but never with any intent do they displease their Well-Beloved, nor consent to be His enemy: because they would thereby depart from the union of such a beloved people, whose true characteristic is love.

Then what Paul says becomes true <margin>(:)</margin>—that it is impossible for those who have once tasted God and afterward forsaken Him to return to Him again; or at least to the same degree in which they were before their fall. For such, it is much harder to be converted than for the greatest of sinners: because no insult is more painful to the Well-Beloved than when a soul, which He had graced with so many benefits and to whom He had let the sweetness of His love be tasted, intentionally lets this love go and withdraws itself from His arms, with which He had embraced it for so long, in order to nourish itself from the outside with pure vanities, and afterward gives itself out as His enemy. The memory of this alone is terrifying: because then the will is a thousand times more evil, and the spirit more perverse, than they ever were; since they have now separated themselves from the highest Good after having known and tasted it, which other sinners have not yet done.
<margin>(a) Heb. 6:4.</margin>

<column-break/>

32. **And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day.**

33. **And those who found him gathering wood brought him to Moses and Aaron, and to the entire congregation.**

34. **And they put him in custody; for it was not clearly expressed what should be done to him.**

35. **And the Lord said to Moses: The man shall surely be put to death; the entire congregation shall stone him outside the camp.**

36. **Then the entire congregation led him outside the camp and stoned him so that he died, as the Lord had commanded Moses.**

37. **And**

---

Thus, more malice is found in the disobedience of those who have received more knowledge of God and experienced more of His goodness. And the most certain sign of their apostasy is that they depart from His ways to serve lusts, and tread such paths with the pretense that they know them and well know they are erroneous, and then give themselves entirely over to sin. On the contrary, with others, while they are united with God and faithful in remaining in His ways, it is not to be believed that they sin visibly, even though the appearance of sin is seen in them. As long as they remain tender and obedient, and surrender and leave themselves to God, regardless of their misery—so that they find themselves humbled by it, and wish they did not offend or had not offended God, and suffer greatly because they believe they have sinned—so long is it certain that no sin is to be found there.

God had already imposed the death penalty on violators of the Sabbath in Exodus 31:14 and 35:2. But since such a case now occurred—where one, likely not out of extreme necessity but out of a liberty he claimed for himself by despising this commandment, gathered wood (for what purpose is not reported)—they wished to seek counsel from God as to what kind of death he should be sentenced to, just as happened with the blasphemer in Leviticus 24:12, etc.

It is noteworthy, however, that of these two death sentences against the third and fourth commandments, only here in the wilderness do they occur, which had to be carried out with the most painful punishment of stoning. With this, God intended to avenge the contempt for His name and the Sabbath rest commanded of them, and thereby give an example of how they should watch over the rooting out of these vices, by which God was especially angered. Nevertheless, these very vices increased greatly among them, as can be seen from the prophets' laments (Ezek. 20:13, 16; Hos. 4:2, etc.). And it is also a commandment that is more transgressed by the common crowd under the New Testament than these. And yet, little is zealously done against it, regardless of the teachers who—though they consider the fourth commandment regarding rest from physical works to be ceremonial—maintain (a) "that the transgression of rest on the Lord's Day, as well as other days ordained for public worship, through works and even more through sins, must now still be earnestly abolished and punished." But the great and prominent themselves sin the most against it, and therefore it is punished all the less in the lowly. But he who does not respect the Lord God in His command will fare no better than the aforementioned despisers, whether it comes sooner or later.
<margin>(a) Burmanni's <note>Frans Burman (1628–1679), a Dutch Reformed theologian and professor.</note> interpretation of the Books of Moses, at this place.</margin>
