# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XVI

37. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
38. Speak to the children of Israel and tell them to make tassels on the corners <note>original: "Flügeln," literally "wings," referring to the corners of the garment.</note> of their garments throughout their generations, and they shall put a sky-blue cord upon the tassel of the corner.
39. And it shall be a tassel for you to look upon, that you may remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them, and not follow after your own heart or your own eyes, after which you used to go whoring:
40. So that you may remember and do all my commandments, and be holy to your God.
41. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God: I am the Lord your God.

These tassels—which are otherwise many small strings like fringes that emerge from a knot where they are wound—can represent the many commandments, all of which flow out of the love of God and of one's neighbor.
v. 38. And that such things were fastened with a sky-blue cord shows the heavenly and spiritual sense of the commandments, and that they must also be kept from a heavenly mind through power from above, and that throughout their entire walk of life: therefore they had to be placed on the "wings" or the outermost hem of the garment. See Matthew 23:5 and Luke 8:44, from which place many conclude that Christ also wore such things.
Nowadays, they <note>Referring to the Jewish people of the author's time.</note> no longer have the sky-blue color, but the threads are of white wool, which they merely let hang out so that they can see them. This garment is called the "Four Corners" <note>Referring to the *Arba Kanfot* or the *Tallit*.</note>.
v. 39. **Not follow after your heart or your eyes)** A person should not walk according to his own opinion or the lust of his eyes, which are directed toward the love of the world, and thus let go of sincere love toward God. See Hosea 2:4 etc. and v. 21.
v. 40. **That you may do all my commandments, and be holy)** This has always been the goal of true religion, and still is. Truly, among the many false and hypocritical religions that have ever been and still are in the world today, the only true and pure religion is that which makes those who profess and practice it most like God.
But we must take good care to understand what it means to be "holy" and what the word "holy" signifies. We find in the Scriptures—which can give us the best instruction on this—that not only people but also animals, even vessels, clothes, places, and the like, are called holy. We need only see in what sense this occurs. All such things were dedicated to God; and whatever vessel was holy was never allowed to leave the Temple or be pulled into common worldly use. So the Law intends that the one it wishes to be holy should serve no one else but God alone. A person should dedicate himself to God alone and not entangle himself in worldly affairs if he wishes to please the One who has accepted him: he should be separated from the rest of humanity who live according to their fleshly mind in the world, and he should not seek what is on earth, but what is in heaven. Whoever is so constituted is holy.
v. 41. **I your God -- I your God -- I your God)** There are three that bear witness, and these three are one. 1 John 5 <note>A reference to the "Johannine Comma," a traditional Trinitarian proof-text.</note>. And if only we sought this God as much in our hearts as we seek to track Him down in the letter of the text, we would be much more at one in Him than we are in quarreling with one another about Him.

<column-break/>

# Chapter XVI.

->The Rebellion of Korah and the Whole People.<-

**A**nd Korah, son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, along with Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took action;
2. And they rose up before the face of Moses, along with two hundred and fifty men of the children of Israel, who were leaders in the congregation, called to the assembly, and famous men.

v. 1. **Korah took action)** It may well be, as some hold, that it annoyed this Korah that he was not chosen as a prince among the Kohathites, but that Elizaphan, the son of Uzziel (the younger son of Kohath), was preferred over him, though Korah was from Izhar, the older son. See Exodus 6:18, 21, 22 and Numbers 3:30.
**Along with Dathan, Abiram, and On, the sons of Reuben)** Who were annoyed that all preeminence had escaped the firstborn.
v. 2. **They rose up)** It is a strange thing that the punishment they had just received on the mountain—because they wanted to climb higher up the mountain by themselves than was permitted <note>Likely referring to the limits set at Sinai or the previous judgments for presumption.</note>—did not prevent them from following their self-conceit and infringing upon the offices of Moses and Aaron. It is common enough that people who have progressed a little further, before God calls them to this office, nevertheless dare to lead others and imagine to themselves that they could do this better than others whom God has chosen for it. It is an abuse in the spiritual life which creeps in right at the beginning: that one is so eager to work for others, and indeed at the wrong time. And it is also only a false zeal when one undertakes to help others from one's own initiative before receiving the gift and the calling to bring such a thing successfully into effect. Many imagine they are in a state where they could lead others to the way of the saints, yet they have not even stepped upon it themselves. Therefore, while they want to share the graces which were given to them alone, they not only lose the benefit of them themselves, but they also cannot help others with them. As long as one has such a craving—and even more so if one has no experience of spiritual things nor a calling for it—one must not venture to help one's neighbor. One must first be grounded and established in the inward life oneself.
Our perfect pattern, Jesus Christ, spent thirty years in a hidden, unknown life (during which long time he practiced remaining in diligent prayer and in self-abnegation <note>original: "Vernichtigung," a mystical term for the emptying of the self before God.</note> before his Father, though he could have brought much good to the world in the meantime) before he visibly concerned himself with the salvation of men. This was so that we might learn that we must first die to all desire to help our neighbor—which desire is usually quite natural <note>Meaning "of the fallen human nature" rather than divinely inspired.</note>—and remain in stillness and rest until the hour and the moment arrive in which God will give us His word and command to be able to promote the neighbor's salvation, however He wishes to use us for that purpose.

# Chapter XVI. The Fourth Book of Moses.

3. And they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said to them: You take too much upon yourselves! For the whole congregation is holy, every one of them, and the Lord is in their midst. Why then do you lift yourselves up above the congregation of the Lord?
4. When Moses heard this, he fell upon his face.
5. And he spoke to Korah and to all his company, saying: Tomorrow the Lord will make known who is his, and who is holy, that he may let him come near to him; and whomsoever he shall choose, him will he let come near to him.
6. Do this: take your censers <note>original: "Kohlpfannen," literally coal-pans used for burning incense.</note>, Korah and all his company;
7. And put fire in them, and put incense upon them before the face of the Lord tomorrow: and it shall be that the man whom the Lord shall choose, he shall be holy.

---

v. 3. Envy and pride are the sources of all rebellion, where one is unwilling to submit to the order of God, because they think they must also have a share in the priesthood and in the government. Therefore they also incited some from the tribe of Reuben—as the firstborn of Jacob—to oppose Moses and Aaron, but in truth to destroy the holy order of the Lord.
They also seek to make the whole congregation rebellious under the pretense that they are all holy and thus have the power to perform their own sacrifices, as was done in former times; and as a people of God, they could not be brought under the dominion of a single person, as such power had never before rested with just one man.
Thus, unbelief does not lack for a pretext to put its evil mind to work against those in authority, whose power they would gladly cast off.
v. 4. Since Moses was well aware of his divine calling and the gentleness <note>original: "Gelindigkeit," a term often used in Pietist literature to describe a Christ-like softness or lack of self-assertion.</note> he had practiced—just as Samuel had also done (1 Sam. 12:3)—and was therefore also aware of the malice of these men, he turns his prayer instead against them, regarding their persistent stubbornness, after he had confronted them with their great mischief.
v. 5. Moses's answer, and his manner of speaking where he lets everything depend on how God will make it known, is admirable. Therefore he says: God himself will make known those who belong to him, and those who are his saints, whom he has chosen for this office. By what sign will they be able to recognize such people?
v. 6. 7. One cannot easily distinguish these people except through the fire and through pure love; which, having nothing else but God as its object <note>original: "Furwurff," meaning the focus or object of one's attention.</note>, just as He is also its end purpose, sends forth a pleasant incense from the censer of the heart, which rises up to Him straightly and without detour. There it no longer has any "self-ness" <note>original: "Eigenheit," referring to the ego or the desire to possess things for oneself.</note> and thus keeps nothing for itself, but sends all praise and honor back to God—from whom it was received and through whom it was accomplished—directly as a sacrifice of sweet aroma. Now, since the one whom God had set apart to help others has received from Him the incense of sweet aroma, he is truly holy. For since he possesses nothing more of himself as his own, he must necessarily be of God, and thus also be holy.

You take too much upon yourselves, you sons of Levi!
8. And Moses said to Korah: Hear now, you sons of Levi!

v. 7. (You take too much upon yourselves, you sons of Levi!) Thus that which they had blamed Moses and Aaron for in verse 3 is turned back upon them.
This phrase, "O you sons of Levi!" which was pushed out with a heavy breath, indicates Moses's sorrow for these souls, which is greater for them than for other souls. For since they have progressed further, so too is their sin greater. It is as if he said to them: You who were called to do what I do; you who were soon to be introduced [to higher service]; you who were marked for such holy duties: how have you dared to do such a thing, when you should have recognized your much greater dignity than that of the others! This way of speaking sufficiently shows Moses's gentleness, love, and discernment.
v. 8. 9. First of all, he turns to Korah, as the primary author of this uprising, and through him to all others who might also stand in the same degree. Moses is also so sensitive regarding their sin because the state from which they fell was so much more elevated above the state of other souls, and for that reason, he gives them such a necessary and just rebuke.
Is it too little for you, he says, that the God of souls has thus separated you from all that is common and earthly; that he has cut off from you everything that could hinder his most intimate communication; that he thereafter called you to draw near to him to serve him in his sanctuary—that is, to sacrifice to him in the ground of your own selves—and also in this state to serve him in those inner things, whereby he prepares you to be able to help souls in the future? He has done even more: for you already had the power to serve them with your sacrifices and with your intercession, and were, so to speak, the mediators between God and the people.
v. 10. Has the Lord shown you and your sons such great graces so that you should strive to become priests? In that you would presume to reveal the divine will—which is the highest state of a shepherd—to which you are not yet called: and through a great sin have dared to appropriate to yourselves that which belongs to God alone; since you have meddled in a matter for which he had not chosen you? For whoever wishes to be the "answer of God" <note>An idiom for a spokesperson or oracle of God.</note> must be annihilated <note>original: "vernichtiget," a mystical term for the total emptying of the self/ego to allow God to act through the person.</note>: so that he mixes in nothing of his own, but speaks only that which God says.

<margin>v. 32. This is the punishment deserved by those who place themselves into roles that GOD does not require of them, and who intrude themselves—out of their own imagination and self-importance—into leading others. Namely, that the earth which seemed to be under their feet (that is, all earthly things which they seemed to have conquered and brought under their feet) and all sensuality opens up again and takes them back into its bosom. Then they are overwhelmed by those very things which they had supposedly already overcome; and this earth of sensuality swallows even their dwellings, which represent their place of rest: to show that in such a case, both the center and the will are found to be entangled.</margin>

<margin>v. 33. They went down) Into the depths of the earth. Alive) Where other men only arrive after death.</margin>

<margin>v. 34. All Israel) was struck with great terror by this event because of their own bad consciences.</margin>

<margin>v. 35. But the Fire of Love proceeding from GOD, which searches all things and works—burning that which is combustible and sparing that which is not—consumed the men who dared to do what GOD did not ask of them; because all their works deserved the fire, being merely works of self-will <note>original: *Eigenheit*, meaning selfhood or acting from one's own ego</note>. Conversely, the works of pure love, which are freed from all self-will, cannot be consumed; and their fire burns only for GOD, consuming itself for His honor. But self-will, in stealing from GOD what is His, draws the fire of His wrath, and not His love, upon itself. For the fire of His love rises quickly to Him from whom it proceeded, and with the same purity as when it went out. But the fire of His justice does not rise again until it has consumed the self-will that resisted it.</margin>

<margin>The 250 men) along with whom the chief rebel and author, Korah, also seems to have perished, as many believe.</margin>

<margin>On) who is mentioned only at the beginning of the rebellion, but not by a single word in its progress or its wretched end, may have recognized his error in time and asked GOD for grace.</margin>

<margin>This terrifying judgment is otherwise threatened against the false Christians and teachers who have crept in, and especially against the mockers among them in the last times: Jude v. 4, 11, 18. Therefore, one can take it as a symbolic image of the last great rebellion, which the Beast and the False Prophet—and with them their followers, the godless and crude masses—will stir up against the few witnesses of the truth. These witnesses constitute the royal priesthood along with the other faithful souls who sigh over all the abominations that are publicly in vogue.</margin>

<margin>So too the names in this passage are significant: Dathan (a word derived from "law") represents the Beast that has power to give laws; Abiram (meaning "exalted father") represents the False Prophet who gives himself out as such a high father; and finally Korah (meaning "ice and coldness") represents the great mass stuck in injustice, in whom the love for the truth and its witnesses has grown completely cold. Matthew 24:12.</margin>

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XVI <note>The Book of Numbers</note>

36. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
37. "Speak to Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, that he pick up the censers <note>firepans used for burning incense</note> out of the blaze, and scatter the fire far and wide; for they have become holy.
38. The censers of these sinners against their own souls—let them be fashioned into broad-beaten plates as an overlay for the altar. For they brought them before the face of the LORD; therefore they have become holy, and they shall be a sign to the children of Israel."
39. And Eleazar the priest took the bronze censers which those who were burned had brought, and hammered them broad for an overlay for the altar:
40. As a memorial-sign to the children of Israel, so that no stranger who is not of the seed of Aaron should draw near to burn incense before the face of the LORD; that he might not become like Korah and like his company, just as the LORD had spoken to him through the service of Moses.

---

<insert>By this, God intended to establish a monument to His judgments.</insert>

v. 37. Concerning this matter, Origen writes <margin>(a) Homily 9 on Numbers 16.</margin> that if such a case were judged today—as an example over those who have introduced erroneous teachings and been punished by God for it—a judgment would surely be passed by the leaders of the Church. It would likely be said that all their writings and books should be burned and rooted out along with them. But God's mind, thoughts, and judgments are entirely different from those of men. He wishes to preserve the censers, even though they were misused (just as the Holy Scriptures are sometimes misused when "strange fire" or the erroneous opinions of one's own intellect are brought into them), and not have them destroyed. This is precisely what the Spirit says: "Test all things, and hold fast that which is good" <note>1 Thessalonians 5:21</note>. However, He will not allow that same fire to come upon the altar again.

v. 38. **These sinners**) To be called a "sinner" in Scripture is the brand of openly godless people and is no small disgrace.

v. 39. **Bronze**) or copper.

v. 40. **As a memorial-sign**) Which was intended to strike terror into the children of Israel, so that no one might draw near to the service of the Levites, much less to the priestly office, to which he was not called.
Since in the New Testament the Lord also wishes to take priests and Levites from among the believers <note>Isaiah 66:21</note>, who seek to promote and maintain the service in spirit and truth among the faithful and preside over them; so too should no one take this honor for himself or intrude into the office unless he has received gifts from the Lord and is then orderly called according to the providence of God. This providence has its various wonderful ways, which will reveal themselves to those who wait for such a calling in humility. See Ephesians 4:8 etc., 2 Timothy 1:6, Hebrews 5:4, Titus 1:5.

<column-break/>

41. And the entire congregation of the children of Israel murmured the next day against Moses and against Aaron, saying: "You have killed the Lord's people!"
42. And it happened, as the congregation gathered against Moses and against Aaron, they turned toward the Tabernacle of Meeting; and behold, the cloud covered it, and the glory of the LORD appeared.
43. Then Moses and Aaron came before the Tabernacle of Meeting.
44. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
45. "Get away from the midst of this congregation, that I may consume them as in a moment!" And they fell upon their faces. <margin>Matthew 26:39.</margin>
46. And Moses said to Aaron: "Take the censer, and put fire in it from the altar <gloss>(*)</gloss>, and put incense on it, and go quickly to the congregation and make atonement for them! For a great wrath has gone out from the face of the LORD; the plague has begun." <margin>Revelation 8:5. (a) Leviticus 16:12, 13.</margin>

---

So great was the stubbornness of the people that despite yesterday’s heavy judgment—which quite clearly confirmed the divine calling of Moses and Aaron, just as they had previously experienced with Miriam—they would not become any wiser. Instead, they persisted in their obstinacy and wished to attribute all evil to these faithful servants of God.
And so great is the stubbornness in the outward form of the New Testament that people will not allow themselves to be warned by the many special judgments of God to take heed of the testimony of God's faithful servants; rather, they eternally wish to attribute all unrest and disruption in the church to them. See 1 Kings 18:17, 18.

v. 42. But this also teaches us what great grace is distributed during persecutions, how God proves Himself to be a protector, and how richly the Holy Spirit is poured out there. For we read nowhere before that the cloud covered and, as it were, took them into itself. God's grace reveals itself most abundantly when human rage is at its greatest: and then we have peace with God when men stir up war against us for the sake of righteousness. Where sin became powerful, grace shows itself even more powerful.

v. 45. Here they would have been destroyed had they not been extinguished through the intercession of Moses and the incense of Aaron at divine prompting.
**They fell upon their faces**) As disciples of the Gospel, and not merely of the Law.
At the impending destruction of Sodom and the other cities, ten righteous men could have turned away the judgment if they had been found. Here, however, there are also enough to preserve the Israelite congregation.

v. 46. **From the altar**) No common fire was allowed to be taken for the burning of incense.

### The IV. Book of Moses. Chapter XVII. <note>The Book of Numbers</note>

8. **And it happened on the next day / when Moses went into the Tabernacle of the Testimony / behold, the staff of Aaron of the house of Levi had sprouted / and had brought forth buds / and the blossoms had opened / and it bore almonds.**

9. **And Moses brought out all the staffs from before the LORD to all the children of Israel / and they saw them / and each man took his staff.**

<margin>v. 8. Sprouted --- had buds --- blossomed --- and almonds).</margin> The fulfillment is greater than the promise. God had promised in verse 5 only that a staff should sprout; and in the fulfillment, He gives four times as much. So it is with all places in Holy Scripture where a promise of the Lord is contained. God gives His promised goods more abundantly than the promise itself sounds.

<margin>It bore almonds)</margin> For it was made from an almond tree / as Josephus <note>original: "Josephus (a)" referring to Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, Chapter 4</note> says. And it is to be believed of all twelve: because it was customary among the children of Israel to make the staffs of governance from almond wood <note>original: "vid. Dieteric. antiq. bibl. ad Exod. 39. 32. Ursin. arborer. bibl. c. 31. n. 3. 4." - See Dieterich's Biblical Antiquities and Ursinus's Biblical Trees.</note>.

This prefigured the ever-green priesthood of Christ / which should never wither / as later happened to the priesthood of Aaron: (See Ezekiel 17:24. Luke 13:6. Matthew 21:19.) which at first was hidden like a bud in the shadows of the Old Testament / but in the beginning of the New Testament opened and was revealed like a beautiful blossom / and will bring forth the glorious fruits of a perfect holiness and blessedness in the glorious kingdom of Christ.

It also represents the believers / who in themselves are nothing other than dry sticks / but when they are united with Christ / they do not remain dry branches / but they sprout / leaf out, and bring forth much fruit. John 15:4, 5. See also Psalm 92:13, etc. Romans 7:4, 11:17.

God let the staff of Aaron blossom / so that it might serve as an eternal image / that one must be as he was / if one wishes to become an apostle. His staff had sprouted; that is to say / it had brought forth a living seed from its very essence. This happens / when from mysterious ashes <note>The author uses "geheime Aschen" to refer to the state of spiritual death or insignificance</note> / as if from dead wood / a new life grows forth through the inward resurrection. But it is not enough that this staff has buds; (which indicates that it has received life again / and is full of sap:) it must also blossom; (this is a state that has progressed somewhat further after the resurrection:) and also bear fruit: and all its leaves must be found spread out; which represents that the soul is set into a wide space / so that its works are no longer restricted: and finally, its fruits must also become ripe.

All this excellently indicates the inner seasons of a soul that has come as far as this one has. After the winter / which is the state of mysterious death / just as this staff was also dead / comes the spring / which awakens / causes buds to grow and blossoms to bloom. The summer shapes the fruits / and makes them grow. The autumn, however, gives them their ripeness. This is indeed visibly enough the resurrection of souls in God / their renewal in Him / their confirmation in this state / and their complete outward expansion with a full freedom / and the fruits of such a time / which must serve for the nourishment and support of others.

<margin>v. 9. They saw it)</margin> This was to be a constant reminder to the disobedient people / that they should cease from their murmuring / and resign themselves to God's holy ordinance and be satisfied with it. Therefore, this sprouted staff had to be kept before the Ark of the Covenant / as well as the little jar with the Manna / as a sign of the great wonders of the Lord in the government of His people. Exodus 16:33. Hebrews 9:4.

(a) Book 4. Antiquities. chapter 4.
(b) See Dieterich's Biblical Antiquities regarding Exodus 39:32.
Ursinus's Biblical Trees chapter 31. numbers 3. 4.

<column-break/>

10. **And the LORD said to Moses: Bring Aaron’s staff back before the Testimony / that it may be kept as a sign for the rebellious children / that you may put an end to their murmuring before me / so that they do not die.**

11. **And Moses did as the LORD had commanded him / so he did.**

12. **And the children of Israel spoke to Moses and said: Behold, we give up the ghost and perish; yes, we all perish together!**

13. **Whoever approaches even in some measure to the dwelling of the LORD / he must die! Shall we then all pass away and give up the ghost?**

<margin>v. 10. The LORD wills that this staff should be kept /</margin> (which represents the power and authority that apostolic men have over those who have submitted to them / ) as a sign of the state / in which those / who are called to lead others / must stand. They must / as already said / have flowers and fruits / as well as fully spread leaves / in order to be permitted to lead from behind.

God hereby confirms the priesthood to the tribe of Levi / that is / to those who cling to Him through faith and love / from whatever tribe they may otherwise be: and He wishes thereby to keep away all ungodly men / who seek to usurp the priestly office.

And so this matter concerns you and me as well. If you are already dry / unfruitful, and without the sap of grace / even worse than dry dead bones; yet we may sprout again and become alive. With God all things are possible.

<margin>v. 11. Moses did it)</margin> He laid this sprouted staff down before the Ark of the Covenant: and because only the two stone tablets of Moses came into the Ark itself / 1 Kings 8:9 / it is conjectured / that it was placed in the side-chest <note>An auxiliary container or compartment</note> / in which the Manna was kept / at the side of the Ark of the Covenant toward the East. Just as the same manner of speaking as here is used regarding the Manna in Exodus 16:33, 34. And these two pieces were held in such high regard by the children of Israel / that they had both of them stamped upon their coins / (a) and thus displayed them before all the world (a).

When Aaron’s staff appears / and shows us / when the law / which is prefigured thereby / appears: then he alone steps into the judgment / which rages over the world. Jeremiah.

<margin>v. 12. 13.</margin> But this seems to be a lamentation uttered out of resentment / as if it seemed / that they were all rejected like such dry sticks / and would finally all have to give up the ghost / after so many of them had now been snatched away by the judgment of God; and it seems / as if they were entirely cast out from the Tabernacle of the Congregation / the dwelling of the LORD.

Indeed, the heart of man is a defiant and despondent thing. Jeremiah 17:9. Now it opposes the Lord quite insolently / and wants everything according to its own mind; but afterward / when the Lord lets it feel His righteous hand / then it wants to despair of the Lord altogether / and not approach in humble lowliness and good confidence: whereas it should at all times in true serenity submit itself to the will of God in everything.

The believers themselves sometimes utter such vehement complaints / as if God would be angry with them forever / and let His wrath go on and on; Psalm 85:6. as if He had cast them off entirely / and would show no more grace / etc. Psalm 77:8, 9, 10. whereas one should instead consider / how much we have abused the riches of God's long-suffering / and that the right hand of the Lord can soon change everything. So Isaiah 64:8, 9.

Chapter XVIII. The IV. Book of Moses. <note>The Fourth Book of Moses is commonly known as the Book of Numbers.</note>

# The XVIII. Chapter.
-> The Provision of the Priests and Levites. <-

And the Lord spoke to Aaron: You and your sons and your father’s house with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary; and you and your sons with you shall bear the iniquity of your priesthood.

2. So bring also your brothers <gloss>(a)</gloss> the tribe of Levi, your father’s tribe, here with you, that they may be joined to you and serve you: but you and your sons with you shall be before the Tabernacle of the Testimony.
<margin>(a) 2 Chronicles 29:34.</margin>

3. And they shall keep your charge, and the charge of the whole Tabernacle. Yet they shall not come near the vessels of the sanctuary and the altar, so that neither they nor you die.
-> Exodus 29:37. <-

4. Instead, they shall be joined to you, to keep the charge of the Tabernacle of Meeting, in all the service of the Tabernacle: and no stranger shall come near you.
<margin>Chapter 3:38.</margin>

5. Therefore, keep the charge of the sanctuary and the charge of the altar, so that a great wrath may no longer come upon the children of Israel.

---

-> Now that Aaron and his descendants, and also the Levites, were confirmed anew in their calling; their respective duties are once again set before them, and their provision is assigned and repeated. <-

v. 1. They, the priests, were to be held responsible if anything in the service of the sanctuary or the offerings was neglected, or if any disorder crept in, such as allowing a stranger to draw near. See 2 Chronicles 26:16. etc.

v. 1. The Lord spoke to Aaron) Through Moses, as some maintain. See Leviticus <note>original: "3. Mos."</note> 16:1, 2.

v. 2. The Levites were assigned to the priests for the lesser duties of the offerings and were otherwise given and gifted by the Lord.

v. 3. Yet they had to refrain from priestly functions; they were not to sprinkle blood, nor offer sacrifices, nor approach the Altar of Burnt Offering: much less were they to bless, burn incense, prepare the lamps, set out the showbread, or enter into the Holy Place.

**They)** If they approach where they should not.

**And you)** If you allow it.

v. 4. Instead) that was their duty and their charge: they had to keep watch at the Tabernacle, in the morning lift the curtain at the door of the court and open the entrance, and in the evening close it again, and thereafter open and shut the gates. During the divine service, they had to attend, assist the priests, sing, look after the wine, oil, incense, and the like, and bake, roast, or boil the grain offerings, etc.

v. 5. Those who are priests, or claim to be, find their lesson here especially, and should rightly pay attention to what the divine law says to them. But the Lord, who searches hearts and minds, knows best how each person fulfills his duty and keeps his charge.

<column-break/>

6. For I, behold, I have taken your brothers, the Levites, <gloss>(a)</gloss> from among the children of Israel: they are given to you as a gift for the Lord, to attend to the service of the Tabernacle of Meeting.
<margin>(a) Chapter 8:18, 19.</margin>

7. But you and your sons with you shall attend to your priesthood in every matter of the altar, and in what is within the veil, that you may serve. I will give your priesthood as a gifted service: but the stranger who comes near shall be put to death.
<margin>Chapter 1:51, 3:38.</margin>

8. And the Lord spoke to Aaron: And I, behold, I have given you the charge of my heave offerings, of all the holy things of the children of Israel; these I have given to you because of the anointing, and to your sons, as an eternal statute.

9. This shall be yours from the most holy things, from the fire offerings: all their offerings, with all their grain offerings, and with all their sin offerings, and with all their guilt offerings, which they shall bring to me; that shall be most holy for you and for your sons.

10. In the most holy place you shall eat it. Everyone who is male shall eat of it. It shall be holy to you.

11. Also

---

v. 6. For the Lord) and in His service, but not for private or personal household business, should the priests make use of the Levites.

v. 7. The priestly office is emphatically called a gifted service, which was to be assigned to them freely as their turn came, and as it were, given as a gift: so that it would have been a most extreme injustice if anything had been demanded of a priest or Levite by those who were older or held greater prestige.

Christ therefore also says of His ministers: as they have received it freely, so they should give it freely. Matthew 10:8. And it is therefore a great sin to take or give anything for such a service. Acts 8:18. etc. <note>This refers to the sin of simony—buying or selling sacred offices.</note>

v. 9. 10. The priests received all types of offerings of which only a portion was burned, as they were to have the remainder for their food. This had to be eaten in the most holy place—which here is understood to mean the Holy Place or the court of the Tabernacle of Meeting. Leviticus <note>original: "3. Mos."</note> 6:9, 19.

<margin>Exodus 34:19, 20.</margin>
<margin>v. 11.</margin>
Furthermore, these were the firstfruits of all the produce that was in the land: rye, wheat, oats, barley, figs, pomegranates, legumes, wine, oil, honey, and everything that receives its growth from the earth or grows on trees; even the smallest herbs used for food, such as dill, pennyroyal, curly mint, rue, cumin, and the like.
This heave offering or firstfruits was given from processed produce: from threshed and winnowed grain, and from pressed, pure oil and wine.
The amount to be given was at first left to each person's discretion. Later, according to a certain regulation, a generous person was said to give one out of forty; a moderate person one out of fifty; and a stingy person one out of sixty. Generally, they would have given two out of a hundred.

<margin>v. 12.</margin>
**Best)** Meaning the fat or the choice part.
**I have given to you)** Since all firstfruits belong to the priest—

<margin>v. 13.</margin>
**Shall be yours / belong to you)** Thus we must also necessarily look for a priest to whom we may bring those firstfruits directed to us in Holy Scripture: namely, the fruits of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, patience, etc. Galatians 5:22. And who is this priest other than He who is Himself called the Firstfruit? 1 Corinthians 15:20. And what else are the firstfruits of love but that we should love the Lord our God with all our heart and all our soul, according to the first and greatest commandment; and so on with the rest.

<margin>v. 14.</margin>
**Devoted)** That which someone had so consecrated to the Lord by a vow that a curse was simultaneously placed upon it if anyone should use it for any other purpose or benefit. That which was devoted simply and without additional conditions belonged to the priests.

<margin>v. 15.</margin>
**Redeem the firstborn of men)** From this law the priests themselves and the Levites were exempt, as were the daughters of priests and Levites if they married into another tribe.

<margin>v. 16.</margin>
**From one month old)** <margin>The redemption money became due on the 31st day. If a Sabbath fell on that day, the redemption was postponed until the following day.</margin>
**5 shekels of silver)** That is, two and a half Reichsthalers. <note>The *Reichsthaler* was a standard silver coin in the Holy Roman Empire; the translator is providing a contemporary value for the reader.</note> The poor person had to give as much as the rich, and no one was permitted to haggle with the priest over the redemption money. However, if the priests wished to return the money to a poor father out of their own free will, they were free to do so.
**Gerah)** Is equal to 9 hellers. <note>A *heller* was a small German copper coin of low value.</note>

<margin>v. 17.</margin>
The Lord requires the first and best fruits of everything. To the First and Best, the first and best things are rightly due. They are not so much given to Him as they are given back. For what do you have, O man, that you have not received? Therefore, all things we are said to give to God happen more out of gratitude than out of charity. And even that gratitude is given by Him. 1 Chronicles 30:14.

<margin>v. 18.</margin>

And since the Lord Christ commanded His servants that they should give freely what they had received freely as gifts, He also said shortly thereafter that they should not worry about any physical need: for a worker is worthy of his food. Matthew 10:8, 9, 10. As if to say: those who receive the Gospel should also provide for the necessary maintenance of their teachers. Therefore, the faithful should not withdraw from dedicating the heave offerings and firstfruits of their wealth to the servants of God, being mindful of what the Apostle says: "If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?" 1 Corinthians 9:11. And if indeed the so-called "fees" for holy rites are so offensive, the faithful should not save their acts of kindness for such occasions, but should not forget to demonstrate at other times their "sweet-smelling savor," which is a testimony of their noble spirit—the acceptable sacrifice that fulfills the needs of Christ's servants and is pleasing to God. Philippians 4:16-18.

### Chapter XVIII. The Fourth Book of Moses. 625

<margin>Sirach 45:27.</margin>
**20.** Furthermore, the Lord spoke to Aaron: You shall possess nothing in their land; nor shall you have any portion among them: I am your portion and your inheritance among the children of Israel.

<margin>Deuteronomy 14:28, 29.</margin>
**21.** And behold, I have given the children of Levi all the tithes in Israel as an inheritance for their service which they perform, the service of the Tabernacle of the Congregation.

<margin>Chapter 1:51.</margin>
**22.** Henceforth, the children of Israel shall not come near the Tabernacle of the Congregation, lest they bear sin and die.

**v. 20.** Oh, what a happy portion the Apostolic souls <note>term: "Apostolic souls"; in this context, it refers to those who live in total devotion to God, following the example of the early apostles by forsaking earthly possessions.</note> possess! Others may possess an inheritance of holiness as they wish, yet it is a holiness mixed with earth and self-interest. But the inheritance of the tribe of Levi, which is the inheritance of Apostolic souls, is nothing in heaven or on earth: God alone is their inheritance; God is their portion and their possession. And God is so much everything to them that He alone rules them and works within them. They desire nothing, nor do they long for anything, whatever it may be; because they possess that very inheritance which one will possess in heaven, and which is God Himself—truly and essentially, though still under the veil of faith. Souls that do not possess God Himself in a constant state will want, wait, and sigh, more or less according to the measure of their distance from Him. But these have neither longing nor desire for it; they no longer stand in expectation, even of eternity itself: because they possess the God of eternity Himself in an excellent manner. And since they possess the highest Good, they lack nothing: therefore, they now desire nothing more.

One might perhaps say: Such people should at least wish that they might not lose God through sin. Ah, if they could still think of that, they would still be occupied with their own benefit, and thus with something less than God is. Thus, they would not be in the state of which we speak, in which one rests in God through a total surrender <note>term: "total surrender" (German: *Gelassenheit*); a key concept in German mysticism meaning a state of letting go of self-will to be filled by God.</note>, without care or anxiety about what concerns them. God must prevent them from offending Him. They could not occupy themselves with anything outside of Him, however holy it might be, without leaving the state of being lost in God. But whoever speaks of "loss" says a thousand times more than "forgetfulness." One often remembers a forgotten thing: but what is once completely lost is not found again. What is merely misplaced can be found again: but what is lost in God cannot possibly be found again without leaving God. If such a soul could think of, or fear, losing that which it possesses, it would be acting out of its own self and would lose its state for as long as that disposition lasted. God alone; and nothing of all this.

It will further be objected: that if such a soul has any concern, it is for the honor of God. To this, the answer serves: that it is impossible for such a soul to think of the honor of God outside of God. The honor of God is God; and that is enough, without the soul needing to think upon it. The whole work of such a soul is to "be" no more. God is responsible for His own honor; He must care for it. It is not the work of this creature, which has nothing more to do because it no longer exists as an independent self.

**v. 21, 22.** The Levites had much business and labor with the sacrifices for the reconciliation of the children of Israel: for such service, God wanted them to be provided for by the children of Israel with the tithes of the land, especially since they were also denied an inheritance of land.

<column-break/>

**23.** But he, the Levite, shall perform the service of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, and they shall bear their iniquity. It shall be an everlasting statute among your descendants that they shall possess no inheritance among the children of Israel.

<margin>(a) Leviticus 27:30.</margin>
**24.** For the tithes of the children of Israel, which they offer to the Lord (a) as a heave offering, I have given to the Levites as an inheritance. Therefore, I have said to them: they shall possess no inheritance among the children of Israel.

**25.** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

**26.** You shall also speak to the Levites and say to them: When you take the tithes from the children of Israel, which I have given you from them for your inheritance, then you shall offer up a heave offering of it to the Lord, a tithe of the tithe.

**27.** And...

**v. 23, 24.** Therefore, if they, along with the priests, were not allowed to possess an inheritance, but the Lord willed to be their portion and inheritance, then the priests and Levites in the New Testament should also rightly claim this for themselves. They should lead others with a good example, not striving for what is here below on earth, but longing for their inheritance, Christ, who will most gloriously reward all faithful service in grace.

**v. 25, 26.** Here it was ordained that even the Levites themselves should tithe their tithes again, and give such a tithe to the priest Aaron, and thus to his descendants, the priests. This was so that the priests should not occupy themselves in the least with earthly things, as the Levites had to do to some extent when lifting the tithes. The priests were to handle even nobler occupations: the contemplation of God’s Law, the instruction of the people from the same, and the sacrifices—and thus also the intercessions for the people. And this was again a very wise and just order. Since all the tithes were left to the Levites, the descendants of Aaron—who were, as it were, the "tenth" tribe of Levi—should also receive the tenth part due to them from this total tithe. For Levi had eight grandsons from his three sons; and the one grandson, Amram, had two sons, Moses and Aaron: so that Aaron was effectively the tenth. <note>note: This refers to a genealogical calculation from Exodus 6:16-20 used to justify the "tithe of the tithe" by showing the priestly line as a tenth part of the tribe's leadership.</note> For although the other grandsons also had children, the Lord wanted to designate the tithe from such portions so that the priests would have an abundant provision, in order to be charitable and hospitable toward others, as is also required of the overseers <note>term: "overseers" (German: *Aufsehern*); often used to translate the Greek *episkopos*, referring to church leaders or bishops.</note> in the New Testament (1 Timothy 3:2).

Furthermore, tithing is noted as a sign of submission, as even Levi, in Abraham, gave the tithe to Melchizedek. This was a prototype <note>term: "prototype" (German: *Fürbild*); a prophetic symbol or "type" in the Old Testament that foreshadows a reality in the New Testament.</note> showing that we are all indebted to sacrifice all our means to the true, eternal, and constant High Priest, Christ (Hebrews 7:5-10). From this, He gladly grants us our nourishment, but in such a way that we should also set aside something of our own for the maintenance of needy members, which the Savior will accept as if it were given to Him. See 1 Corinthians 16:1, 2, 3; Matthew 25:40; Mark 12:41, etc. Thus, the twelfth portion of the land was left to the Levites.

### Chapter XIX.
->The Ashes of the Red Heifer.<-

And the Lord spoke unto Moses and unto Aaron, saying:

**2.** This is the ordinance of the law which the Lord has commanded, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring you a reddish heifer, which is perfect, in which there is no blemish, and upon which never came yoke.

<gloss>Here now the ordinance was made regarding the holy water (Chapter 5:17) through which the unclean were to be cleansed and thus purged of sin; how it was to be prepared: for which reason it was also called a water of purification (Chapter 8:7).
v. 2. A reddish heifer) It had to be so entirely red throughout that even just two white or black hairs could make the cow unfit for this purpose. (a)
This red heifer was purchased from the common treasury and often had to be paid for very dearly, because such entirely red cows were very rare and difficult to obtain.
This perfect red heifer, along with what had to be done with it, prefigured Christ’s sacrifice and the purification from our sins brought about by it. Christ’s body was colored entirely blood-red by those bloody wounds when He presented Himself as a sacrifice. He was innocent and separated from sinners, and thus perfect. No yoke of sin came upon Him (see Lamentations 1:14), and He also showed that He was free from the yoke of men (Matthew 17:25-26).

On the Mount of Olives, directly opposite the Temple, a large pit was made in the earth in the shape of a winepress and filled with wood. Upon this the cow was laid after being bound with many ropes, but she lay with the wood facing south and turned her face toward the west, toward the Temple.

# Cap. XIX.) The Fourth Book of Moses.

<margin>v. 5. Burned</margin> Christ allowed himself to be entirely consumed in the hot love of God and for mankind.

<margin>v. 6. The Priest</margin> This was done by another priest / who stood at a distance / and watched the fire / until it was ignited; he then split open the belly of the heifer / and threw the cedar wood with the rest upon the burning heifer.

<gloss>(p)</gloss> Some believe rather that it was rosemary, for fairly credible reasons; as it is also a herb of great power and virtue.

**Scarlet Wool** Or crimson / of which more is said elsewhere.

**Cast into the fire** All of which represented Christ as both God and man / the guarantor surrounded by our sins / and his surrender unto death / to endure the fiery zeal of the wrath of God / but also by the power of his divinity to extinguish and reconcile it.

<margin>v. 7. 8.</margin> Both priests / both the one who burned the heifer and the one who threw the bundle of sprinkling herbs upon it / were made unclean by it.

<margin>v. 9. Water of separation</margin> Whereby those separated from the sanctuary due to uncleanness were cleansed again / and thus readmitted to the sanctuary / to bring their offerings / and otherwise to gather there for edification.

Through the death of Christ, who was humbled to dust and ashes, the holy water of de-sinning <note>original: "Entsündigung"; the process of removing sin or its ritual effects.</note> and separation has been prepared for us / so that we, being sprinkled therewith in faith, may be delivered from sin / and no longer separated / but may be brought back into the communion of God.

**Sin offering** it is called so because of its similarity to the sin offering of the High Priest or the whole congregation: though strictly speaking it was not otherwise a sacrifice / and the heifer was not slaughtered in the inner court / nor did any part of it come upon or near an altar.

<margin>v. 10.</margin> That all who dealt with this sacrifice were made unclean / indicated our own uncleanness of sin / which necessitated this sacrifice of Christ / which must first be recognized in true repentance / until we afterward come into the communion of this sacrifice through true faith / and thus are sprinkled with this blood of Christ for the sanctification of the spirit and for the obedience of faith. 1 Peter 1:2.

**11.** He who touches a dead body of any soul of man / shall be unclean seven days.

**13.** Whoever touches a dead body of a soul of man / who has died / and does not purify himself / defiles the dwelling of the Lord / and such a soul shall be cut off from Israel: because the water of separation was not sprinkled upon him / he shall be unclean; his uncleanness is still upon him.

<margin>v. 11. Seven days unclean</margin> The uncleanness of a human being is much more shameful and foul / and makes people more unclean / than the uncleanness of cattle. The uncleanness of an animal makes a person unclean only until evening. Lev. 11:31. But the uncleanness of a human defiles and makes unclean for 7 days. Brutish and fleshly uncleanness certainly defiles; but the uncleanness of a human / as he is a human / defiles seven times more.

<margin>v. 12. On the 3rd and on the 7th day</margin> Between the first and second sprinkling or purification, there had to be 3 full days.

If he delayed his cleansing / the day was only counted from the third / on which he was sprinkled for the first time / and the 4th after that became the 7th.

However, he was not permitted to be sprinkled before the 3rd day after the defilement occurred / nor a second time before the 7th.

Some believe / that this pointed toward the third and seventh age in the Church / when in that time the dragon had to leave his place in heaven / heathenry was publicly overthrown / and the works of the devil in public idolatry were destroyed: in this / the seventh time, however / the dragon will be bound in the abyss / and the beast and the false prophet will be cast into the lake of fire; when the great cleansing of the Church will take place / just as it was brought about on the third day of Christ's resurrection / when Christ brought about the free, open fountain for the believers against sin and uncleanness. Zech. 13:1. See also 1 Cor. 15:17. Now, among these, this blood of Christ cleanses our conscience from dead works / to serve the living God; as the Apostle compares this with the symbolic cleansing through the water and ashes of this heifer, Heb. 9:13, 14. And here we should now draw near with a true heart / in full assurance of faith / sprinkled in our hearts / and free from an evil conscience / and washed in body with pure water. Heb. 10:22, 23. David, in the spirit, already saw this purification with hyssop and the washing of the soul / when he asked to be washed and cleansed from his iniquities and blood-guilt, Ps. 51:4, 9. So it is a wonder / that people wanted to reintroduce such external consecrated water into the Church / when they should instead point souls solely and alone to the essential cleansing / through the tears of righteous heart-repentance / and the faith that seizes Christ's blood for cleansing from all our sins / and lead them away from all ceremonies and external holiness in such physical exercises / which only had a place in the Old Testament / and must now yield to the body as shadows.
<meta>v. 14. 15.</meta>

17. And for the unclean person, they shall take some of the **ashes** of the burned sin offering and put fresh water upon them in a vessel.

<margin>
v. 14. 15. **Unclean**) Since the dead body was once the dwelling place of the human soul, and is now abandoned by it and lies in a state of decay, sin is hereby indicted, as death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). Through this, it was simultaneously intended to show that transgression was not yet atoned for, and eternal righteousness not yet brought forth (Daniel 9:24). Therefore, everyone who came into any kind of fellowship with a dead person—whether by touching them to perform the final act of love at burial, or by being in the house where someone died—was declared unclean, along with everything in that house.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 16. Indeed, if someone outside had to touch a dead body to move it out of the way, or otherwise touch a human bone or a grave, all these had to be sprinkled by a clean man on the third day with this **water of separation** <note>term: "water of separation"; water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer used for ritual cleansing</note> using a bundle of hyssop dipped in the water. They only became clean on the seventh day after a second sprinkling.
</margin>

<margin>
**A grave**) Therefore, they marked the place where someone was buried with a certain upright sign, so that everyone could protect themselves; they also used to place a monument over it (a).
</margin>

<margin>
v. 17. **Ashes of the sin offering**) These actually contain within them the resurrection and the life of Christ—the **quintessence** <note>In alchemical and early scientific thought, the "quintessence" was the purest essence of a substance. Here, the author uses it to describe the spiritual power remaining in the ashes.</note> of the cow—in its exaltation and sublimation. For in the ashes are the spirit and the salt, and from these a new body emerges. In this way, the **Israel of God**, when they are humbled and brought low to dust and ashes, shall emerge from the furnace of humiliation, purified and cleansed of their dross and slag, and clothed in white fire-garments.
</margin>

</margin>

<margin>
v. 19. 21. **Wash clothes and bathe**) Both the clean person, who became unclean through performing this duty, and the unclean person had to do this.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 20. Whoever does not wish to be purified, or does not ask for cleansing, but wants to enter heaven with their **old man** <note>A Pauline theological term referring to the unregenerate, sinful nature of a person.</note>, heart, and mind, shall be cut off from the assembly. It will be said then: "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment? # Chapter XX. The Fourth Book of Moses.

**2. And the congregation had no water: then they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron.**

**3. And the people quarreled with Moses, and they spoke, saying: "Oh, that we had perished when our brothers perished before the face of the Lord!"**

<margin>Exodus 17:3</margin>
**4. "Why then have you brought the assembly of the Lord into this wilderness, that we and our livestock should die there?"**

<margin>Numbers 21:5</margin>
**5. "And why have you led us out of Egypt, to bring us to this evil place, which is no place for seed, nor for fig trees, nor for vines, nor for pomegranates; and there is no water to drink?"**

Since they were soon to enter the land of Canaan, they were once again tested with a lack of water. That water which they had miraculously received from the rock at Horeb (Exodus 17) and which had always followed them in the wilderness—as can be seen from 1 Corinthians 10:4—appears to have been withdrawn here. This can be a symbol of how the Lord is accustomed to testing His believers at the end of life with a lack of comfort; in such times, one must persist in faith and certainly not sin by grumbling against God.

Even though the children of those who had died in the wilderness because of their grumbling fell into the same sin of grumbling as their fathers—due to necessity, or rather, the lusts of this life (Exodus 16:3; Numbers 11:4-5)—and had thereby made themselves unworthy of the promise; nevertheless, the Lord wanted to demonstrate His pure goodness and mercy by fulfilling the promise He had made to them, the children. See Chapter 14:31.

This encampment of the people in the wilderness of Kadesh signifies the progress through the "wilderness of faith," which looks all the more wretched the purer it is: because it loses its supports more and more, and simultaneously loses everything that could give the soul any assurance outside of God.

The soul complains about this poverty, seeing that it is robbed of all its best things; it feels it can no longer even use the very best fruits of the Church, which are the Holy Sacraments and the Holy Exercises. "There is no place here," it says, "in which one can sow," because we cannot perform a single work through our own strength. It seems as if the Church has no more fruits for us; because we are stripped of all the Holiest things she possesses—the Holy Sacraments (from which God may well turn souls away when He wishes to lead them far into 'stripping' <note>term: "Entblößung"; a mystical state where the soul is divested of all spiritual comforts and intellectual insights to rely solely on God</note>). There are no fig trees (representing the sweetness felt in performing good works), nor vines (which give us the grapes of virtue to taste), nor pomegranates (representing love through their fruit) to be found here. We seem to be entirely divested of all such beautiful fruits. And what is more, there is no water here either. For the water of all sensible graces <note>term: "empfindliche Gnaden"; spiritual feelings, joys, or comforts that can be perceived by the emotions</note> has dried up for us.

Then the pains of death are felt: "Why," they say, "did we not die in our abundance?" And they say this as often as they enter a new wilderness and a new, more stripped state. For

<column-break/>

**6. And Moses and Aaron went from the assembly to the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, and they fell on their faces, and the glory of the Lord appeared to them.**

**7. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:**

**8. "Take the staff and assemble the congregation, you and your brother Aaron, and speak to the rock before their eyes; then it will give its water. Thus you shall bring water out of the rock for them, and give the congregation and their livestock drink."**

**9. Then**

One must note that every state has its stages: each stage has its beginning, progress, and end. Thus the land of faith is long, and one goes through it from one wilderness to another, from nakedness to nakedness; and the last wilderness is always the most dreadful. As soon as one goes from one stripping to another, this last one always seems like something new, and the previous one still seems to have great comforts compared to the poverty of the following one. And what is most strange is that those who have come this far—even though they have received so many graces and seen so many miracles performed for their sake—can never imagine that they will reach the end. And just as they imagine they have already arrived when they are in the rest of the union of their powers (even though it is only the beginning of faith) and do not think there is more to be attained; so when they stand in bare faith and in this nakedness, they do not think they will ever emerge from it, nor do they think they will reach the end. This is a characteristic of the fearful human: that he allows himself to be discouraged by the slightest obstacles and, because he does not believe he can reach the end, begins to despair of his entire undertaking.

v. 6. Moses and Aaron) humbled themselves before the Lord, and the congregation should have done so properly as well.

v. 7. 8. Thereupon came the command to take the staff that had been laid before the testimony of the Lord (Chapter 17:10) and to speak to the rock, commanding it in the name of the Lord to give its water.

The rock was struck with the staff of Moses, but the rock was only to be spoken to with the staff of Aaron: a lesson for the ministers of the Gospel that they should use the staff of the Law moderately, so that they do not forget the gentleness of the staff in the reconciliation of Christ's High Priestly office, wherein one must again deal with souls in kindness. See Zechariah 11:7 etc. In this, the behavior of the disciples toward the unfriendly Samaritans and Christ's rebuke is well worth taking to heart: *Do you not know what kind of spirit you are of?* (Luke 9:54-56).

Since God perceived that this people lacked the strength to pass through such a bare state, He commanded Moses to speak with the rock; because it was time for the rock to give water to this people. All necessarily had to drink from the living water of this rock before they should enter other states; as has already been said above (a). This living water drawn from the rock is the grace earned through Jesus Christ, which is the refreshment of those who find themselves in the wilderness through the conformity they have with His states: not in the thoughts, insights, or enlightenments of the states themselves, but through an essential similarity, albeit in an incomprehensible way: because God hides such things from souls so that they might walk with greater faith, and thus with greater purity.

---

But here one must no longer use the staff for striking. For the Word is enough to make the water come forth—namely, Jesus Christ: and since He is the WORD <note>original: "WORT"</note> of the Father Himself, nothing further was necessary but this very WORD to communicate such to souls.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XX.

**9.** Then Moses took the staff from before the face of the LORD, as He had commanded him.

**10.** And Moses and Aaron gathered the assembly before the rock, and he said to them: "Hear now, you rebels! Must we bring water out of this rock for you?"

**11.** And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock with his staff twice. Then much water came out, so that the congregation and their livestock drank.

For this reason, apostolic souls <note>The author uses "apostolic souls" to refer to spiritual leaders or teachers who carry the divine message to others.</note> also bring such things into other souls through speech, and not through the staff of leadership. For here, their own power no longer works, but rather the divine inflow, which spreads itself through their words.

Thus, the soul enters into the form of Jesus Christ through faith, without thinking of Jesus Christ as being separate from her, nor even perceiving this harmony. In the passive state of illumination <note>original: "Leidenſchafft der Erleuchtungen," a mystical term referring to the soul's experience of receiving divine light without active effort.</note>, many insights concerning Jesus Christ are given, which nourish and satisfy the soul. But here she has no light at all from Jesus Christ: and although she has never been more like Him, she has nevertheless never understood Him less. Yet she enters into His state through a true harmony, even if she does not think of it, as she possesses such a path within herself, until she reaches God Himself alone through Jesus Christ. There she (a) will remain hidden with Him, until she receives the power to bring Him forth again, and to let Him become flesh anew in other souls through her word. For the soul that has, in a certain way and through communication, become one with God, has the power of the WORD of God entrusted to her, so that she can make the WORD grow in others. The essential word produces the God-Word within itself: and the substantial word, when it has been received into the soul, also produces the WORD in others. Or even more clearly:

God generates His WORD from eternity through His word: and so also the same word which is spoken through the mouth of an annihilated soul <note>original: "vernichtigten Seelen." In mystical theology, an "annihilated" soul is one that has completely emptied itself of ego and self-will to be filled by God.</note>—although this then happens only mediately and not essentially—which performs the office of a priest for the inner communion, brings forth the WORD in the souls to whom she speaks. And this is the very reason why so many people are converted through the mere word of such souls. This is quite clear in Paul (b). "My little children," he says, "for whom I labor in birth again until Christ is formed in you." Without doubt, he bears them to the Savior through the word, just as he clearly says elsewhere (c): "I have begotten you in Jesus Christ through the Gospel." And it is through this word that Jesus Christ has also gained a form in them, as God makes it powerful and penetrating, so that it can be brought into the hearts and made conformed to Him.

v. 10. 11. It is a mistake which those who are leaders commonly commit, that they do not want to be satisfied with the mere word of God, which is given to them in the time of need for the sake of souls as soon as they ask for counsel. They always want to make use of the old manners and the common ways of leadership as they are accustomed; and the more they have experienced that such ways have succeeded for them, the more they cling to them. But it is a thing which displeases God beyond measure: both because He Himself wants to be the leader, and because He alone knows best the need of souls according to the decree by which He wishes to guide them. Therefore, the apostolic leader must in all things surrender to the movement of the Spirit of God.

This error is very visible in Moses: and although he was very perfect, God nevertheless permitted him to fall into this unfaithfulness as a warning to others.

<margin>(a) Colossians 3:3.</margin> <margin>(b) Galatians 4:19.</margin> <margin>(c) 1 Corinthians 4:15.</margin>
<meta>catchword: become</meta>

<column-break/>

**12.** But the LORD spoke to Moses and to Aaron: "Because you did not believe in Me, to hallow Me in the eyes of the children of Israel, therefore you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them."

**13.** This is the Water of Strife <note>original: "Haderwaſſer," a translation of the Hebrew name Meribah.</note>, because the children of Israel strove with the LORD, and He was hallowed among them.

Just as he was accustomed to performing great miracles by striking with his staff, and such had never failed him; so he wished to do the same here to bring water out of the rock. But God had not commanded it of him, but had only bidden him to take the staff in his hand as a sign of his power, as a leader. He, however, added the striking of the rock from his own head, whereas God had only commanded him to speak to it. Thereby he himself entered into a certain kind of mistrust; namely, that it might perhaps not be enough merely to speak to the rock, unless he also struck it with the staff to complete this great miracle: and while he thought he was doing well, he confused the work of God with his own activity.

Moses' mistake consisted in this: that when God had told him to take the staff but only to speak to the rock, he struck it instead of such speaking. Thus God was not glorified by him, which He would have been if he had used only the word alone. The reason why this displeased God was because He wanted to show the people that what was from the old time should pass away: and that He also sought thereby to take away from them every support they had placed upon such a wondrous staff. After this time, the staff of Moses indeed performed no more miracles. The second reason was that God wanted to make known that Jesus Christ would perform all His miracles with the word, just as He was the WORD of His Father Himself; and that from Him, as from the living rock, streams of grace would flow, which He was to pour out upon the people. Since miracles belonged more to the old than the new law; and moreover, Jesus Christ saw that the people, who were accustomed to miracles, founded their faith almost entirely on miracles; He came to teach us the mystery of faith, which must be fixed only upon His pure and simple word.

It is something incomprehensible that a minor mistake or a minor reliance, on whatever it may be, is so severely punished in such advanced men, and that God testifies how much He is indignant over it! Nevertheless, He does not take away their graces, nor does He let them depart from their state. He does not say: "You shall not enter into the promised land." For Moses, who had possessed the essential communication and had seen God face to face, had nothing more to hope for before him, and could not enter into any lesser state because he was at such a high level. Rather, God said: "You shall not lead this people into the land that I will give them," and thereby indicated that from now on He took away from him the old grace and the full end of his leadership; and that although he himself had passed through the states which lead to the perfection that can ever be reached in this life, he would nevertheless not have the pleasure of leading his flock to the perfection of their origin.

Thus God punishes the leaders who want to mix their own art <note>term: "Kunſt" (art/skill). Here it refers to human cleverness or artificial methods as opposed to pure divine inspiration.</note> with His word. For while such art may indeed make the water of grace flow, it does not give the living water of Jesus Christ or bring it forth in souls. For this art prevents such divine production, which the single word of God alone performs. Therefore God complains here that this unfaithfulness prevented Him from being glorified before the people, as he did not trust in His word and had struck the rock.

### Chapter XXI. The Fourth Book of Moses.

2. Then Israel vowed a vow to the LORD and said: If you will indeed deliver this people into my hand / then I will utterly banish <note>original: "verbannen," referring to the Hebrew 'herem', or devoting a city entirely to destruction as an offering to God</note> their cities.

3. And the LORD heard the voice of Israel / and delivered up the Canaanites. Then they banished them along with their cities / and called the name of the place Horma <note>Horma means "destruction" or "devoted thing."</note>.

4. And they journeyed from Mount Hor by the way of the Reed Sea <note>original: "Schilffmeer," traditionally translated as the Red Sea</note> / to go around the land of the Edomites: and the soul of the people became weary on the way.

<margin>(a) ch. 20:5. (b) Zech. 11:8.</margin>
5. And the people spoke against God and against Moses: Why have you led us up out of Egypt / to die in the wilderness? For there is no bread or water (a) here / and our soul has a loathing (b) for this so light bread! <note>The "light bread" refers to the Manna, which the Israelites began to despise as insufficient.</note>

---

v. 2. But as soon as Israel—which signifies the resigned souls <note>original: "gelaſſenen Seelen." This refers to the mystical concept of 'Gelassenheit' or yieldedness to God's will.</note>—vowed to their God through a new resignation / that / if they were only to reach their first calling again / they would keep nothing for themselves / and that they would truly repent by not appropriating anything for themselves / but on the contrary / were willing to destroy the cities in which self-love was fortified;

v. 3. So God himself sets them over their enemies: the LORD promises such victory by his hand / and thereby shows both the malice of the slander and the innocence of his people.

<term>Delivered up the Canaanites</term> This first victory over the Canaanites / whereas they had previously also achieved one over the Amalekites (Exodus 17:13) / but had also suffered a defeat from these very two at this same place because of their disobedience (Numbers 14:45) / where the name Horma was mentioned in advance / should remind us of the first victory that Christ granted to his people of the New Testament / when he bestowed upon the Emperor Constantine in his spirit a victory through which Christ began to destroy paganism and its public idolatry for his people. And oh, that he and his successors had only been faithful to him / and had truly banished all pagan customs! Just so should this also occur in every believer. When one learns to know the world in their first repentance / and achieves the first victory; how faithful should one then be / to banish everything earthly within oneself! But what sluggishness and temptations follow everywhere thereafter!

v. 4. 5. They now had to travel around the land of the Edomites / so as not to do them the slightest harm (Deuteronomy 2:1 etc.). And as the people became very resentful through this long detour / this new generation also began to murmur against God and Moses / and even to complain about the Heaven-Bread / the Manna / as a far too light food / which did not properly satisfy their appetite.

Almost the entire time in this wilderness of faith / such weaknesses occur / because of its darkness. The weak souls become resentful / grow sorrowful / and even develop a loathing for it. But God / who wishes to save this people and not destroy them / punishes them immediately for this weakness.

<column-break/>

6. Then the LORD sent fiery serpents among the people / which bit the people / so that a great many people of Israel died.

7. Then the people came to Moses / and they said: We have sinned / because we have spoken against the LORD and against you! Pray to the LORD / that he may take the serpents away from us. And Moses prayed for the people.

8. Then the LORD said to Moses: Make for yourself a bronze serpent / and set it upon a pole; so it shall happen / everyone who is bitten / when he looks upon it / he shall live.

---

v. 6. <term>fiery serpents</term> which are also called fiery flying dragons (Isaiah 14:29, 30:6) / as much because of their fiery appearance / as their effect / as their bite caused a terrible burning in the blood / as a just retribution for their burning anger and resentment / and their fleshly appetite for excess.

He sends them such serpents / whose poisoned tongues give them deadly stings. These poisoned stings of the tongue are very hard to bear; and all the harder / as those who must endure them have more guilt in certain things. They must bear all the shame of it / both internally and externally / both before God and before men.

v. 7. Then such poor, utterly shamed souls are accustomed to confess everything / with which they have sinned / and that all this has come upon them because of their guilt: indeed that / even if they are perhaps not guilty of that for which they are slandered / they are nonetheless guilty in many other things.

They then take refuge in their leader / and say to him; they well recognize / that this misery has come upon them because of their wickedness / and that they had well deserved it: but they could do nothing / by which they could deliver themselves from their misery or from the serpent bites: He, however / could accomplish with God whatever he willed. Then he prays for these anxious souls; and God shows him the way in which he can free them from the serpent bites.

v. 8. Thus God commands / that a bronze serpent should be made; because the remedy for this evil must be found within the evil itself. This serpent was of copper <note>The German "ehern" can mean bronze, brass, or copper; here it is equated with "Kupfer" or copper.</note> / so that it might shine like fire / (Revelation 1/15) / and thus resemble those serpents which bit fiery wounds into the people of Israel. Nothing makes the soul so die within itself / or draws it more out of the resentment and reluctance regarding this path / than the sight of its weaknesses / and the memory of what might be said of it. This greatly hastens its death. For when no slanders follow upon the weaknesses / it passes much more easily: but when slander makes the memory of the terrifying state / which one carries within oneself / active again / it also renews the pain / and thus makes the matter unbearable.

Just as the most noble and clear prefigurement <note>original: "Fürbild," a type or symbolic precursor</note> of Christ in the 1st Book of Moses Ch. 22 is Isaac / and in the 2nd Book of Moses Ch. 12 the Passover Lamb / and in the 3rd Book of Moses Ch. 16 the scapegoat for the sin offering on the Day of Atonement / so here in the 4th Book of Moses the bronze serpent lifted up on a pole is a glorious prefigurement of Christ / as he himself points out (John 3:14, 15) / when he was lifted up on the height of the cross / whereby he obtained victory over the ancient serpent (Genesis 3:15) / but also first had to become a curse for us (Galatians 3:13, 1 Peter 2:24). So that we now / who are not only poisoned through original sin by the hellish serpent / Satan / but also through true faith in our falls into sin may look upon him / and thus be healed through him (Hebrews 12:1, 2) / namely to stand in true repentance for the fall / and to obtain a new life in his power. See Isaiah 45:22. Since we specifically also sometimes / after obtaining the grace of God / nevertheless become easily resentful again in the struggle on the path of godliness / where there are also many detours / and complain about Christ, the bread of life: whereupon the fiery temptations of the Evil One then do not rest from inflicting many a deadly bite upon us. Regarding the misuse of this serpent, see 2 Kings 18:4.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXI.
