<margin>Deuteronomy 2:8-14.</margin>
13. From there they journeyed onward / and camped on the other side of the Arnon / which is in the wilderness / coming out from the border of the Amorites. For Arnon is the border of Moab / between Moab and the Amorites. Judges 11:18.

14. Therefore it is said in the **Book of the Wars of the Lord**: Vaheb at the Reed Sea <note>original: "Schilfmeer." While often translated as the Red Sea, the German specifically refers to the "Sea of Reeds."</note> / and the brooks of the Arnon;

---

v. 9. **Looked upon the bronze serpent**) The word used here implies an inward, focused attention. 
Gazing at the serpent, which was set up according to God's command, calms and heals: just as the soul becomes a participant in what JESUS Christ suffered when the soul makes itself a partaker of it through contemplation; which God often allows to happen by letting the soul see his crucified and despised Son through a single glance / and in the vision of faith / which appears like a fiery ray. At other times, He awakens in the depths of the soul a love for the Cross: and this restores life to it. Anyone who has experienced this must confess that it is as true as it is beautiful; and that it is experienced as vividly in the soul as it is represented under this veil of images / which, according to outward appearance, might be judged to be far removed from it.

**Remained alive**) That is / was healed.

v. 11. **The wilderness opposite Moab**) is called the "wilderness of Moab" in Deuteronomy 2:8.

v. 14. **Book of the Wars of the Lord**) some consider this a revelation given to Moses / that God wished to do the same at these brooks as He had done at the Red Sea.

Rupertus <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129), a prominent Benedictine theologian known for mystical and symbolic interpretations of scripture.</note> points, not ineptly, to the whole of Holy Scripture / which could certainly be so named / because nothing else is contained therein but a war and struggle of the Word against sin and death / for their destruction. For we should know of no other wars of the Lord than those arising from the enmity placed between the woman and the serpent / the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent / which will endure until the end of this world.

v. 19. **Bamoth**) means in English / *death comes*. <note>original: "heist auf teutsch / der Tod kommt." The author is providing an etymological interpretation of the Hebrew name Bamoth.</note>
There is no doubt that all these names of places in Israel's travels contain a spiritual meaning. When one follows the order of this path of salvation / and passes through all the names and states / one finally comes to death / and death comes to him. And this is the way to life.

The entire stretch of land from the Reed Sea to the border of Moab is briefly reported here; which they, it seems, traveled the second time / when they had to pull back again toward the Reed Sea: Chapter 14:25. They were situated at Vaheb / and from there reached the river Arnon / and further into the region of the Moabite capital city Ar / and thus to the border of Moab. This path or march-route was recorded in the *Book of the Wars of the Lord* by Moses / or someone else / yet at that time / even if it were Joshua / which was later entered into the Book of Joshua / where the wars of the Lord / which the children of Israel waged against the Canaanites / are described. For although the place Vaheb is not mentioned further / the river Arnon / and the high bank of the river at Mount Pisga are mentioned / in Joshua 12:1, 2, 3 / where these regions are also spoken of.

v. 16. On this journey, GOD now also quite freely, without their previous murmuring, gave them a well.

v. 17. 18. For which they then praised GOD / and dug it with special solemnity through the princes and nobles or volunteers among the tribes; namely those who were heads in their families / and might also have been appointed to certain duties because of their status / which one must approach willingly: thus, a sensible and willing mind is a truly noble mind / and those endowed with this are the true nobles among the people.

It all happened through the guidance of Moses / as their lawgiver ordained by God / who also directed them to this well at God’s command.

This shows how / if one were quiet / and waited for the goodness of the Lord / it would reveal itself quite freely in its own time / so that one would not need to labor with much complaining / running, and racing to obtain something; which one does not receive as uniquely as when it is freely bestowed by the goodness of the Lord: for which one also praises and honors Him so much more / as happened here at this well / and did not happen on previous occasions / when they obtained water through murmuring. See Exodus 17:6 / Numbers 20:4 / and also especially Isaiah 30:15, 16.

v. 20. Finally, the Israelites came into the plain of Moab / which was their last campsite / Chapter 33:48 / where everything occurred that is told until the end of the books of Moses.

### Chapter XXI. The Fourth Book of Moses.

21. And Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, and had it said to him:
22. Let me pass through your land: we will not turn aside into a field or a vineyard; we will not drink well water: we will travel on the King's Highway until we have passed through your border.
23. But Sihon did not allow Israel to pass through his border: and Sihon gathered all his people and went out against Israel toward the wilderness, and came to Jahaz; and he fought against Israel.
24. But Israel struck him with the edge of the sword and took possession of his land as an inheritance, from the Arnon to the Jabbok, even to the children of Ammon: for the border of the children of Ammon was strong.
25. Thus Israel took all these cities; and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon and in all its daughters <note>original: "Töchtern." In biblical terminology, the "daughters" of a city are the surrounding villages or satellite settlements.</note>.

---

Even though the land of this Amorite king had already been given to them as an inheritance (Deuteronomy 2:24), they still had to first offer him peace, to see if they could pass through his land over the Jordan to the promised land.

But since they were hostilely attacked by him, he was also overcome by them according to God's promise; just as it happened afterward to the King of Bashan.

v. 21. **Sihon**) which signifies one who "sweeps out" or "takes away" <note>original: "auskehret, wegnimmt."</note>, carries the figure and image of the Devil, who has taken the image of God away from us, and must also be swept and scrubbed out of us like a house of filth.

v. 22. This one now is the Prince of this world: and are we not, or should we at least be, those who wish to pass through this, his land, as strangers—without lingering or settling down—so that we may come into the promised land of holiness? That is where Israel's calling leads. And we have pledged ourselves to renounce the devil and all his nature and works, and also not to drink from his poisonous well-water of false and perverse fleshly teaching. For Israel itself has its own little wells of God, which have an abundance of water. They have no need to leave the living spring and drink water from foreign wells.

v. 23. **But**) this annoys the devil all the more when we only pass through his land and do not stop there, nor wish to touch anything of his. Therefore he becomes embittered and enraged, stirring up war and persecution against the peaceable people who would gladly behave as pilgrims, and he sets everything in motion against them.

v. 24. But God crushes Satan under their feet before they realize it (Romans 16:20) and also gives them power to tread on snakes and scorpions and all the power of the enemy (Luke 10:19).

v. 25. Thus, the cities of the heathens and of the heathen mind become sanctified cities of Israel. This shall also occur one day in the glorious Kingdom (Isaiah 14:4, etc.).

<column-break/>

26. For Heshbon was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites; and he had fought against the former king of the Moabites and taken all his land out of his hand as far as the Arnon.
27. Therefore those who deal in proverbs say: Come to Heshbon; let Sihon's city be built and fortified!
28. For a fire has gone out from Heshbon, a flame from the city of Sihon; it has devoured Ar of the Moabites, the lords of the heights at the Arnon.
29. Woe to you, Moab! You people of Chemosh <note>original: "Camos." The national deity of the Moabites.</note> are lost! His sons have been surrendered as fugitives, and his daughters as captives to Sihon, king of the Amorites.
30. And we have struck them down: Heshbon is lost as far as Dibon, and we have laid it waste as far as Nophah, which reaches to Medeba.
31. Thus

---

v. 26. **Heshbon**) in German means "Thoughts" <note>The author links the Hebrew *Cheshbon* to the German *Gedanken*, meaning thoughts or calculations.</note>, and so we soon recognize how and why it is the capital city of Sihon. For the greatest power of the devil's kingdom reigns in the thoughts.

v. 27. Therefore the children of wisdom say—who understand something deeper in their speech than the literal letter alone conveys—that one should indeed destroy and overturn this city of Sihon, but not let it lie destroyed; rather, it should be rebuilt and fortified again. This happens in such a way that vain, evil, and impure thoughts are indeed abolished, but in their place are exchanged for good ones; and thus the city is renewed, and from a city of the Amorites, it becomes a city of Israel.

v. 28. Then a fire of love and zeal for God's honor is ignited in the heart, also infecting and igniting others, so that whatever cannot endure in the fire of wrath may be consumed.

v. 29. But woe to you if you come into the captivity of Sihon! For then you are lost.

v. 30. Even Heshbon is lost if it remains a city of Sihon.

We have all been, and each one of us is, a city of Sihon, or we still are: where folly, pride, and arrogance, bitterness and malice, and everything that is the devil's portion reigns within us. We cannot become a city of Israel in any other way, nor come to the portion of God's inheritance, except when this devil's fortress is conquered, the strong armed man is overcome and cast out, and his power and dominion within us is struck down, while we receive the seed of God.

One sees, moreover, how in the earliest times they sought to keep their deeds of war in memory through proverbs and short narratives of deeds, which they may also have sung at their joyful feasts; since no writing was yet common among any people, but only first arose among the people of God through divine instruction and inspiration. In these proverbs or songs regarding the enemy places and idols, a triumph of Christ over the king of the spiritual Babylon is led forth.

# Chapter XXIII. The IV. Book of Moses.

7. **Then he took up his proverb and said: From Syria has Balak, the King of the Moabites, let me be brought, from the mountains toward the sunrise: Come, curse Jacob for me; yes, come, revile Israel!**

8. **How shall I curse whom God does not curse? and how shall I revile whom the Lord does not revile?**

9. **For from the top of the rocks I see him, and from the hills I behold him. Behold, the people shall dwell separately, and not be reckoned among the nations!**

10. **Who can count the dust** <margin>(a) Gen. 15:5 etc. 28:14.</margin> **of Jacob, and the number of the fourth part** <note>original: "Viereck," literally "square." This refers to the four-sided arrangement of the camp of the twelve tribes around the Tabernacle.</note>

<margin>v. 7. Curse Jacob — revile Israel!</margin> Jacob is a figure of the Church in her weakness; Israel is a figure of her power and strength. By the name Israel, a "perfect man" is understood—one who overcomes in and with God. The stronger and more powerful he becomes, the more violent the resistance he must expect. As long as a person is merely a "Jacob," used in lower duties, and as long as we are still weak with Jacob (see Amos 7:5), we must expect resistance and cursing. But when we grow in power and strength and overcome and triumph like Israel, we must expect even greater curses.

<margin>v. 8.</margin> Balaam, however, makes it known in this first blessing that his being summoned from afar to curse Israel is in vain, because he can perceive no disfavor from God toward this people.

<margin>v. 9.</margin> Indeed, he sees in advance how this people would be a very special people, who would not be governed like other nations according to their laws, but whom God would govern through His own laws, thus distinguishing them from other nations. See Psalm 147:19–20.

**I see him, I behold him.** Here we have the "fruitless knowledge" of Christ <note>A warning that one can see the truth or the "heights" of faith, like Balaam, without being transformed by it.</note>.

**The people shall dwell separately.** God’s people will always remain alone, even though they are in the midst of the whole world. Because their heart is separated from it, they are always alone with God alone. Therefore, they are not reckoned among any nation, because they are not a nation of the earth, but the chosen people of God, reserved for Him alone.

<margin>v. 10. Dust.</margin> God’s people are called "dust," partly because of their great number, and partly because of the humiliations this people must endure; thus, in appearance and esteem, they would seem to be nothing other than dust.

The **number of the fourth part <note>or "square"</note> of Israel** is very full of mystery; there is a wonderful harmony and agreement of the Apostolic tribes within it, matching the division of the symbolic family of Jacob, as discussed in Chapter 7 above.

The **Number Twelve** consists of four sets of three, and is divided into four sides, just as happens with the twelve heavenly signs <note>the Zodiac</note>.

Thus, as some hold, the twelve Apostles were divided for the preaching of the Gospel into different lands: three had to go toward the Eastern regions, three toward the South <note>original: "Mittag," literally "Mid-day"</note>, three toward the West <note>original: "Abend," literally "Evening"</note>, and three toward the North <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally "Midnight"</note>.

The New Jerusalem is also seen built in this way, according to the description of John: "On the east three gates," etc.

Now, whoever comes to see by faith the heavenly Jerusalem lying in a square (Revelation 21:16)—which will be manifested in the glorious Kingdom of Christ in the four corners of the heaven over the whole earth—receives in their heart a holy fear not to contradict such a testimony in the least. This is true even though most of the "mighty ones" are against it, always thinking their own kingdoms would be diminished by it. Consequently, they get many "Balaams" on their side who, to please them, gladly contradict this Kingdom so that, in their opinion, no unrest may arise. On the contrary, however, the hearts of the faithful witnesses are strengthened, knowing that the innumerable people will manifest themselves in their own time. They will not be governed at all according to the former ways of the corrupt worldly kingdoms and the churches within them, but directly through Christ and His Spirit, and will exercise themselves only in the praise of God and Christ. Revelation 7:9–10, etc.

<column-break/>

**of Israel? Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like his!**

11. **Then Balak said to Balaam: What are you doing to me? I had you brought to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them altogether!**

12. **Then he answered and said: Must I not take heed to speak that which the Lord puts in my mouth?**

(Israel) will indeed be an uncountable dust! And who will be able to count all their virtues and graces which God shares with them?

O how happy they will be in the hours of their death! For they will be received into grace all the more highly, the more lowly they have conducted themselves here.

**O why can I not die the death of the righteous!** This is the death that fears nothing, because they are made righteous through the righteousness of God. They can attribute nothing to themselves of all that God has placed in them, but they leave everything to Him and see everything in Him alone. All human righteousness is nothing but "filthy rags" <note>original: "Unflat," literally "filth" or "impurity"</note> before Him, as Isaiah (a) has clearly expressed. Ah, why is my end not like theirs? Why am I not also, like them, stripped of all my own righteousness, so that I might possess only the righteousness of God? Then my death would be like theirs; because through this "stripping away," a person is placed back into their true end.

Regarding the death of Balaam and the phrase "must die" in the Hebrew here, the Hebrews note from the Kabbalah that this appears in a "wishful" way twice in Scripture: here and in Judges 16:30 ("Let my soul die with the Philistines"), and Job 36:14 ("Their soul must die in youth!"). They note that what Balaam wished for did not happen, but instead, what is written in the other two places was fulfilled in him. For he died with the Philistines (or the ungodly), and indeed in his 24th year, and thus in his youth.

<margin>v. 11. what are you doing? I had you brought to curse.</margin> It often happens that even though the will of a person is ready for a shameful deed against the "inner people" <note>the spiritual believers</note>, and he is ready to carry it out himself, God nonetheless makes him do and speak the complete opposite.

<margin>v. 12.</margin> When He <note>God</note> wants a prophecy to be given, even the enemies themselves must testify to it. Balaam must speak good of Israel and proclaim the future salvation.

**Must I not.** Even if I gladly wanted it otherwise, I cannot.

Josephus (b) gives his answer more extensively as follows: "Do you then think it is in our power to say what we want when the Spirit drives us? He speaks and prophesies through us what He wants. I know well why you and the Midianites have called for me; I also made the journey for that purpose, and it was certainly my will and intention to satisfy your desire. But God is mightier than those whom I wished to please. As soon as He takes possession of us, we are no longer masters of ourselves. Therefore, although I was not willing to prophesy good to this people, God has nonetheless put it into me against my intention."

<margin>(a) Isa. 64:6. (b) Book 4, Chapter 6, Jewish Antiquities.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the account of Balaam and Balak in Numbers 23. Following the first unsuccessful attempt to curse Israel, Balak takes Balaam to a second location, the heights of Pisgah, hoping for a different result. The commentary continues to interpret the text through a mystical, Pietist lens, focusing on the internal state of the soul and the victory of God within the "ground" of the believer.</meta>

## The IV. Book of Moses. Chapter XXIII

13. And **Balak** spoke to him: Come now with me to another place, from where you may see them. You shall see only their outermost part, but you shall not see them all: and curse them for me from there.

14. And he took him to the field of the Watchers, to the height of **Pisgah**, and built seven altars, and offered a bullock and a ram on each altar.

15. And he spoke to **Balak**: Stand here by your burnt offering, while I go over there to meet the Lord.

16. And the **Lord** met **Balaam**, and put the word in his mouth and said: Return to **Balak**, and thus shall you speak.

17. And when he came to him, behold, he stood by his burnt offering, and the princes of the **Moabites** with him. And **Balak** spoke to him: What has the **Lord** spoken?

<margin>v. 13. Curse them for me from there)</margin> Why is it that so much depends on this cursing for Balak? Why do you not do as the others, O Balak! and march out in time against the army of Israel before they come closer to you?
He places his trust more in Balaam and in his words than in the weapons of his men of war, and instead of arrows, he wished to have temptations shot at Israel. 
Where has it ever been heard that a king, upon the invasion of enemies, neglects military preparations and takes refuge in the words of a soothsayer?
In this regard, he was not entirely wrong, for sometimes words can accomplish what bodies and instruments cannot. 
Who, however, says <term>Origen</term> <note>original: "Origenes," an early Christian scholar (c. 185–254 AD) who interpreted the Bible allegorically.</note>, is invited and commissioned for cursing, if not the devils and evil spirits? Thus, he [Balaam] must have been experienced in these things through a certain art that deals with specific words, and for that reason had a great name in the East. For if he had not already frequently given proof of this and cursed enemy nations, Balak might not have easily come upon the thought that he could accomplish with a few words what could hardly be done with defense and weapons.

<margin>v. 14. 15.</margin> Balaam thinks he intends to and must receive the power to curse from **God**, and wants to force it by his sacrificing.

<margin>v. 16.</margin> But the **Lord's** thoughts are quite different from the thoughts of perverse men; and it is nothing unusual for **God** to do His work when the devil would like to do his own, directing superstition elsewhere than intended.

<margin>v. 17. What has the Lord spoken?)</margin> He was so eager to know the **Lord's** mind and opinion, in the hope that it would sound better than before, that he could not even wait until Balaam began of his own accord, but anticipated him with questions: certainly to our shame, among whom such diligence and zeal and desire to search out the **Lord's** will and to bring Him to our side is not often found. Therefore, this heathen, with many others, will stand up in judgment against the present generation and make their condemnation heavier.

<column-break/>

18. And he took up his proverb and said: Rise up, **Balak**, and hear! Incline your ears to me, you son of **Zippor**!

19. **God** is not a man, that He should lie: <gloss>(a) Malachi 3:6.</gloss> nor a son of man, that He should repent of anything. Should He say something and not do it? Or speak something and not confirm it? <margin>Nehemiah 9:8. Psalm 33:4.</margin>

20. Behold, I have received the command to bless: Since He has now blessed, I will not reverse it.

21. He beholds no vanity in **Jacob**, and sees no misery in **Israel**. The **Lord** his **God** is with him, and the shout of the King is with him.

<margin>v. 18. Rise up)</margin> in the prophetic sense. For otherwise he was already standing, according to the previous verse, but in idolatry: and that is called lying down rather than standing. Ephesians 5:14.

<margin>v. 19.</margin> Human justice is changeable and variable: but that which comes from **God** is firm, and never denies itself.

<margin>v. 20.</margin> Therefore, those whom **God** has clothed in His righteousness cannot possibly be deprived of His blessing. For if that were so, His own property would be cursed. If they were to be cast off by **God**, they must first lose His righteousness and take up their own again. Without this, they remain immovable in their blessing.

<margin>v. 21.</margin> Self-hood <note>original: "Eigenheit," referring to the ego or the self-centered nature that Pietists believed must be overcome.</note> is banished from the inner people, and they are as far from hypocrisy and double-heartedness as they are from self-hood. Self-love gives birth to lies; but pure love is the mother of truth. Therefore, one finds no lies of self-hood in this innocent people. For this reason, the **Lord God** is with them: for He cannot remain separated from any soul that is no longer self-loving. For He Himself is the fulfillment of that emptiness <note>original: "Ledigkeit," a term used by mystics like Meister Eckhart to describe a soul "empty" of worldly desires and ready for God.</note> into which she has placed herself through the denial of her self-hood.
Therefore, a victory-shout also resounds in such a person. Since it is no longer the person acting, but **God** alone as a King, whom nothing resists, is found within him, this rejoicing and shout of the King's victory is heard in him.
Observe that it is the victory of the King, and not of the people; and that this King is found not outside, but in the midst of His people. Oh, what a beautiful distinction! As long as man can fight with weapons from his own strength, the victory is also attributed to him. When **God** went before him, it was said: the **Lord** fights for them, and also goes before them. But then the union is only in the faculties, and some enemies remain whom **God** Himself drives out while the soul remains passive under His action. But this is the victory-shout of the King in steadfast souls: and since **God** has taken possession of their ground <note>original: "Grund," the innermost essence of the soul where God dwells.</note>, He is the victorious King; and this ground unceasingly sings the victory of its King: it lets such a shout resound with a great cry because there is no more struggle to endure. As long as the union exists only in the faculties, even though **God**, who goes before the army of the people, retains the victory, it still costs something, and the victory is seldom attained without receiving some wounds: Here, however, it is not so. This proceeds without struggle, and is also constant and everlasting, just as the sovereignty of **God** in the soul is unchangeable.

<summary>Balaam delivers his second oracle to Balak, declaring God's unchangeable blessing over Israel. The commentary interprets "the shout of the King" as the internal spiritual victory of God within a soul that has surrendered its self-hood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Balaam’s second prophecy in Numbers 23. The previous page discussed Balak's attempt to use Balaam's curses as a weapon against Israel. This page moves into the mystical interpretation of verses 22 through 24, where the strength of Israel is compared to a unicorn and a lion, and the absence of sorcery is highlighted as a mark of God’s direct governance.</meta>

### 22. **God / who brought them up out of Egypt / is like the strength of the unicorn with him.**

### 23. **For there is no divination in Jacob / and no soothsaying in Israel. At this time it shall be said of Jacob and of Israel what God has wrought.**

Who does not see that the Holy Spirit here, through Balaam, had to vividly represent the state of the glorious Kingdom of Christ, in which everything will be fulfilled with full emphasis; namely, when the spiritual Israel now stands in readiness to inherit the glorious promises of God, of which that Canaan was a prototype. See Isaiah 58:14.

He speaks here of a people whom one should not violate, to whom God has promised a blessing and would in no way revoke it; as He who does not let Himself be guided like a man, but remains faithful to His promises. There would be no vain idolatry to be felt there, nor a violent regime that only causes misery. See Isaiah 59:4. And because they constantly praised God in their worship service established according to God's will, they could at all times take comfort in the powerful help of the Almighty God. Because they also did not deal with the superstitious ways common among the heathens—where they invented such ceremonies out of their own minds through which they might search out God's will according to their own will—so also would the great deeds of God be proclaimed far and wide among this people, because they heard what is commanded of them by the true God; whereas the heathens, through their soothsayers, have mostly been deceived for a price: and therefore the people would carry away the great victory over their enemies, which was also promised by God to Judah with these very words in Genesis 49:9. For

SO also will God never repent of His promises of grace, which He made to His dear Son, that He will give him all heathens for an inheritance and the ends of the world for a possession. In this kingdom, no more vanity and misery will prevail under the righteous and peaceful scepter of this King. There, one will shout for joy to this King with happy songs of praise. Psalm 47. There, God will give His people perfect strength and bless His people with peace. Psalm 29:10-11. There, no more ceremonies introduced by men and self-chosen worship will prevail, but one will proclaim quite purely and cleanly the glorious deeds that God has worked now and then in His church; since He governs everything for their salvation and protection and has carried it out gloriously. And then also the complete victory over all enemies of Christ will be carried out, which was spoken of in the symbol of Judah. Then it will be said with emphasis: Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed! Revelation 5:5. See also Psalm 110.

<margin>v. 22.</margin> *Like the strength of the unicorn*) Whose horn is said to be about 12 feet long, and so sharp or pointed, and also firm, that it may either toss into the air or pierce through everything it encounters. It is said to seek to wound the elephant, with which it enters into battle, in the belly and thus strike it down. Concerning this and the reasons why some deny that such a thing exists, more perhaps elsewhere.

<margin>v. 23.</margin> *There is no divination in — and no soothsaying in*) Others translate this not unfittingly as: No soothsaying prevails against Jacob, nor sorcery against Israel; or; No curse clings to Jacob, and no sorcery has power against Israel.

The diviners and soothsayers also indicate those who stand in the state of illumination, which is much lesser than the one just described: because the soul still possesses itself in this state. Oh, how far is this removed from the state of faith and total <term>Gelassenheit</term> <note>A German mystical term meaning "yieldedness" or the total surrender of one's own will to God.</note>!

When one eventually comes to know oneself, either through the day of this faith or in eternity, one will recount with wonder all the miraculous works that God has done in this people (who will have been led through the way of faith and surrender). For the expression used here indicates a great wonderment, just as it is written in the Book of Wisdom (a) that when the wicked see the good redeemed with so much glory, they will be seized with wonder and taken with cruel terror.

<column-break/>

### 24. **Behold, the people shall rise up like a fierce lion / and shall lift themselves up like a lion. It shall not lie down until it has eaten the prey and drunk the blood of the slain.** 25.

This people, who no longer possess any self-centeredness <note>original: "Eigenheit," referring to the ego or the "own-self" that must be surrendered in mystical tradition.</note>, lifts its courage just like a lion. It rises through the movement of its faith and inner state, as it penetrates into God, which is the highest elevation it can reach. It is so certain of its victory that it can fear nothing; because all its strength is in the Lion of the tribe of Judah (a) Himself: and since it has become one with Him, it rises as He does; for it is clothed with the power of God.

It will not lie down in death, nor in any weakness, until it has consumed its prey; that is, until it has cleared out of the way all bitternesses and obstacles that might encounter it. Although the soul has already come far on the secret path and is stripped of many things, as well as being free from the self-centeredness of its own faculties: it nevertheless still likes to retain a sense of self-ownership; namely, it attributes the power of God to itself; and this commonly happens. One recognizes, to be sure, that one has departed from one's own power; but one still finds oneself strong in God: and since one no longer expects anything from oneself, being assured of one's nothingness, one hopes for much more from God through a subtle desire that this emptiness should be filled by Him. But the truly annihilated person, because he is nothing, has no strength either in himself or in God; rather God alone is strong, God alone is powerful, God alone is everything. This, however, is a much more perfect stage.

This soul, thus elevated through the resurrection and clothed with the strength of God, will not lie down through sin, nor will it die, until it has eaten its prey, which is that which still remains to be suffered in sins in order to reach the power in God and the power of God. There are no more victories now, but things which must be eaten, indeed even swallowed. There is no longer anything that must be destroyed, no: it is a thing that must enter into us and which must necessarily be swallowed. One must drink blood down to the last drop without leaving anything behind. Oh, if only one could express that! But one might not even be understood. Those souls who have come this far should certainly not spare themselves, nor become sluggish, nor take themselves back. For they must fulfill all the will of God, let it seem as repulsive to them as it will—just as drinking blood is offensive to everyone—so that one may be able to say with Jesus Christ; (b) Holy Father, I have finished the work which you gave me to do! Now the more these souls have swallowed and consumed of such things, the more God will swallow and consume them into Himself.

One must eat and swallow all the will of God, and let oneself be drenched with all those bitternesses, before one can be swallowed by God and passed into Him through the state of transformation. The will of God must have passed entirely into us and become natural (just as that which one eats and drinks is transformed into our being) before God eats us. This "eating by God" is the receiving of the soul into Him, as He continues to annihilate it through its perfection into Himself, which is to be compared with the digestion of the food eaten. For then this soul, thus swallowed, digested, and thoroughly annihilated, enters into its being through the transformation into God Himself, wherein it then remains lost in Him forever.

(a) Rev. of John 5:5. (b) John 17:4.

### Chapter XXIV.
->The further blessing and prophecy of Balaam.<-

1. Now when Balaam saw that it was good in the eyes of the Lord that he should bless Israel, he did not go, as before, to seek omens <note>original: "Zeichendeutereren," referring to divination or the seeking of auguries</note>, but set his face toward the wilderness.

2. And Balaam lifted up his eyes and saw Israel as it lay according to

**v. 1.** Through the double blessing, Balaam's own eyes were opened, so that he now abandoned all efforts to obtain a prophecy against Israel that would suit Balak. He no longer seems to have observed the usual ceremonies in his sacrifices, as he was otherwise accustomed to perform in gestures, words, and deeds during such actions—which are here called omen-seeking or sorceries <note>original: "Zeichendeuterey oder Zaubereyen"</note>. This refers to when men think they can please God and steer Him according to their will through such public ceremonies and formulas. Instead, he directed himself in his spirit toward God, just as one should call upon God in spirit and in truth, and thus investigate His will in calm surrender <term>Gelaſſenheit|A key Pietist concept meaning "yieldedness" or a state of letting go of one's own will to be filled by God</term> and submit to the same:

**v. 2.** And then he immediately received an answer and an impulse from the Spirit of God, so that he had to speak of the great blessing of this people of God.

Those people who have recognized the goodness of the **path of suffering** <term>leidenden Weges|The spiritual journey of inner refinement through trials and the death of the ego</term> and have indeed entered into it, still sometimes pause to seek "enlightenments"—that is, comprehensible things in which they desire some knowledge of the future. But as soon as they recognize that the greatest blessings of God belong to the people who walk in faith, they themselves turn back to the **wilderness of faith**, without seeking any further enlightenments. One cannot reach this state, however, unless God leads one there. To turn toward the wilderness is nothing other than to surrender oneself to God, so that He may lead one in, if it be His holy will; and to let go of all our acquired and sought-after enlightenments in order to remain in this nakedness and surrender, and to await that which God might please to work.

Through this, such a soul later receives opened eyes to see this "People of Faith" in its nakedness and in the wilderness of bare faith wherein it rests. But one only rests or "lies" therein when one has already come far in this same faith, so that one remains in it without vexation and is content with it.

29. And Balaam said to Balak: Build me seven altars here, and prepare seven bulls and seven rams for me here.

30. And Balak did as Balaam said, and offered a bull and a ram on each altar.

Thus man always thinks his undertaking is entirely fair and right, and that God must grant it to him; he then wants to force the same, as it were, through a worship service arranged according to his own fashion.

3. And he began his oracle and said: Thus speaks Balaam, the son of Beor; and thus speaks the man whose eye is closed: <note>In some mystical traditions, the "closed eye" refers to being blind to the physical world while the inner eye is open to God.</note>

4. Thus speaks he who hears the words of God, who sees a vision from the Almighty; who falls down, and his eyes are opened:

This people rested in their huts according to their various tribes; that is, each according to his **degree** <term>Staffel|Refers to a spiritual rank or stage of progress in the inner life</term>. For there is no state in which some degrees are not to be found: some have come further, others not so far, according to the gift of God or according to their faithfulness. For it is certain that among many souls who walk the very same path, some are found who have progressed further than others.

As soon as this inner man—represented here under the image of Balaam—had surrendered himself in order to enter the way of faith and had left behind all his various and perceived "enlightenments," the Spirit of God immediately came over him to lead the soul. This is the soul that willingly lets go of all natural and acquired light and all supernatural inquiry and surrenders itself to Him. From that moment on, He possesses the soul and becomes its sole mover.

**v. 3. Whose eye is closed)** One can understand this as a reference to what happened to him on his journey, where he did not even see the angel whom the donkey had seen.

**v. 4.** As soon as man is stripped of his own self and clothed with the Spirit of God, he is placed into the truth. And then he is in the Spirit to hear God's words, which are words of truth because they take everything away from the creature and attribute everything to God. Then he also sees the vision of the Almighty, which God sees, and in the truth of God Himself—He who well knows His own absolute power and the infinite beauty of the creature. Finally, he knows in an indescribable way the **All of God** and the **Nothingness of the creatures**.

<meta>This page continues the commentary on Balaam’s third prophecy over Israel in Numbers 24. While the previous page focused on Balaam’s transition from sorcery to genuine spiritual vision, this page interprets the specific imagery of the blessing—the tents, the water, and the strength of the nation—both as a historical promise for the land of Canaan and as a mystical allegory for the soul's relationship with God.</meta>

# Chapter XXIV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

5. How beautiful are your tents (a) / 
O Jacob! and your dwellings / O 
Israel! <margin>(a) Malachi 2:12.</margin>
6. They have spread out like the valleys / 
like the gardens by a 
river / like the aloes which the LORD has plant-
ed / like the cedars by the waters.
7. Water shall flow out of his 
buckets / and his seed 
shall be by great waters /

He prophesies of the beautiful order of the currently unstable tents, but also of the permanent dwellings that followed in the promised land of Canaan: where they would find themselves in a blessed land, spread out like vast valleys that are as pleasant as fertile gardens by rivers; and they would also be blessed with descendants, who are like the aloe <note>Original: "Aloe." In this botanical context, it refers to the "Lign-aloes" or agarwood, prized for its fragrance and mentioned in the Bible as a tree planted by God.</note> which produces a great multitude of flowers, and the cedars which are full of sap and enduring.

**v. 5.** The Church is compared here to tents and tabernacles, not to certain permanent and fixed houses, which only follow afterward.

How beautiful are your tents / O Jacob!) According to the spirit, this means: O true resignation <term>Gelassenheit: a key term in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of self-will to be fully surrendered to God.</term>, represented by Jacob, how lovely are your tents! For this tent is nothing other than the rest found in resignation, which is total surrender. O, what a beautiful thing this surrender is to those who know it! To remain in one's resignation under the hard trials through which one must pass is indeed something: but not to lose the peace of this resignation in the midst of trials when these things occur—that gladdens the HEART of GOD. This resignation is the resignation of His servants. One can indeed be in resignation and yet not at peace: but when one is moved by sheer confusion and doubt, and pierced with deadly pains, and yet remains standing—not only in the peace of resignation, but in resignation itself—that is a very rare perfection.

But if the tent of Jacob is so beautiful, the dwellings of Israel shall not be any less lovely. Israel is, as has been said, the strength of God. O, what a beautiful thing it is when one has lost all their own strength—specifically through the experience of our weakness—and has thereby entered into the strength of God! But it is something much more beautiful to remain in the peace of this strength in the midst of our weakness. The more miserable the soul finds itself, the more it recognizes that God alone is strong. And this is a very glorious thing. But to be entirely stripped of all one's own power, and yet remain at peace, even to be covered in all weakness while being satisfied that God alone is strong—without leaving this peace by dwelling on that weakness or seeking to come to its aid—thereby glorifying God's infinite strength through one's own exceeding weakness; this cannot be admired enough.

**v. 6.** Such souls are like the valleys because of their annihilation <note>original: "Vernichtung," a mystical term for the "nothingness" of the self before God</note>; for the more empty they are of themselves, the more God fills them with His high communications. They resemble the garden of the Bridegroom, in that they are moistened by the waters of His grace. They are near the rivers because they draw close to their source, which is God, as their only origin. They are also like cedars because of the uprightness of their hearts, which have nothing but God as their aim; and because of the fragrance of their simplicity. For cedars are very straight and also have a good scent. They are also planted by the water-brooks because uprightness and simplicity always possess a sweet, cool, and pleasant air.

**v. 7.** From the bucket of these souls, which shall be filled by their source, one outpouring of His grace shall flow after another upon those who are lesser than they; who shall thereby obtain help from them and be, as it were, watered. And their seed, who are the children of grace whom God will have given them, will spread out like great waters into a thousand branches and bring much good to the earth,

**v. 7.** Higher than Agag) The kingdom of Israel should, according to this prophecy, become more powerful than the kingdom of the king of the Amalekites, who may have been the most powerful in the region at that time; Agag was the common name of their kings, just as Pharaoh was for the kings in Egypt. See 1 Samuel 15:9 etc.

**v. 8.** To lead out of Egypt is to be freed from self-centeredness <note>original: "Eigenheit," the state of being trapped in one's own ego or "selfhood"</note>, which rules so strongly in a fleshly land.

The unicorn <note>original: "Einhorn." In historical Bibles, this referred to the "Re’em" or wild ox, symbolizing indomitable strength.</note> is an image of the strength of GOD, of which it is written in a Psalm (a): Through your help we will push down our enemies; and through the power of your name we will despise those who rise up against us. <margin>(a) Psalm 44:6.</margin>

Once God has taken all self-centeredness away from the soul and is Himself within it, He will, through His power, consume everything that might be harmful or an obstacle to reaching His purpose.

To break their bones is to destroy self-love (which is the soul's worst enemy), even down to its very substance. And

To pierce his enemies with arrows is to exercise a great, willing love toward them, even when one has been treated most poorly by them. Then they become all the more ashamed the more one repays them with good for evil; which is called piercing them innocently with the brilliance of virtues, as is described elsewhere (b): The arrows of little children have become their wounds, and the malice of their tongues has turned against themselves. <margin>(b) Psalm 64:8.</margin>

**v. 9.** After the victory is gained, a great peace is promised, which no one would venture to disturb; Jacob also prophesied of such rest with these same words in Genesis 49:9. This occurred at the end of David's reign in Psalm 18, and afterward under the peaceful reign of Solomon.

However, this entire third blessing also applies with emphasis to the blessed state of the glorious kingdom of Christ. Of this, the believers will first receive internal eyes of the spirit, so that they may be instructed by the Spirit of God, and many will again be deemed worthy of such divine revelations. And how this kingdom will be exalted above all the kingdoms of the world was prophesied by Daniel in Chapter 2:44. And how all enemies will be overcome is spoken of in Psalm 110 and by the prophets in very many places.

When the soul is established in the power of God and finds itself in that same rest, never to leave it again but to remain there as a permanent being, then it sleeps and rests like a lion. For neither devils, nor men, nor sin, nor any creature dare wake it from its rest in God once it is truly established therein.

Those who bless—blessed; those who curse—cursed) With this ends the fellowship of blessing and curse that the friends and enemies of Israel would have; just as God promised to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. With this, he intended to dissuade Balak from his hostile disposition toward Israel.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXIV.

**10. Then Balak’s anger burned against Balaam, and he struck his hands together; and Balak said to Balaam: I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have altogether blessed them these three times!**
**11. And now, flee to your place! I had said I would surely honor you, but behold, the LORD has kept you back from honor.**
**12. Then Balaam said to Balak: Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me, saying:**
**13. If Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the command of the LORD, to do either good or bad out of my own heart; what the LORD speaks, that I must speak?**
**14. And now, behold, I am going to my people: Come, I will give you counsel as to what this people will do to your people in the latter days.**

<margin>But he <note>Referring to King Balak.</note> would not be warned; such is the fate of those who lie under the judgment of hardening <note>Original: "Verstockung," a theological term for a heart hardened against God's will.</note>. On the other hand, Balaam showed himself steadfast in this moment, proving he would not let himself be swayed by gifts to act against the LORD’s will. Nevertheless, it seems he still wishes to show some readiness to serve Balak by warning him not to rebel against Israel, as he would surely lose (v. 17). Therefore, Balak should have met Israel with all friendship. This "counsel," however, later turned out poorly for Israel, as they were led into lust and idolatry with the Moabites through this advice, for which Balaam is also blamed in Chapter 31:16.</margin>

<margin>v. 10. *I called you to curse, and you have blessed these three times.* The more the children of this world curse and mock the children of God, the more benediction and blessing they receive.</margin>

<margin>v. 11. Those who proclaim such truths, and gain special insights and reveal them, receive little honor from the "great ones" of this world, who still believe that such witnesses must surely be in God’s disfavor.</margin>

<margin>v. 12, 13. Here, all earthly advantages and all the honor of the world must yield to the will of God, and the "reproach of Christ" must be esteemed higher than the "treasures of Egypt." <note>A reference to Hebrews 11:26, comparing Balaam’s choice to that of Moses.</note></margin>

<margin>v. 14. In particular, witnesses must guard themselves against the false prophet of hypocritical reason and false "theological cleverness." For while they praise the glorious state of the believers to the world, they might simultaneously seek to establish a fleshly friendship between the two, trying to unite light and darkness, Christ and Belial. This "counsel of the serpent," harmful as it is, still befuddles and charms many because of its good outward appearance.</margin>

<column-break/>

**15. And he took up his oracle and said: Thus speaks Balaam, the son of Beor; and thus speaks the man whose eye is closed:**
**16. He speaks, who hears the words of God and knows the knowledge of the Most High; who sees a vision from the Almighty, who falls down and his eyes are opened.**
**17. I shall see him, but not now! I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall come out of Jacob, and a scepter shall rise out of Israel; it shall strike down the princes of the Moabites and destroy all the children of Seth.**

<margin>Balaam continues to speak through the prophetic spirit regarding the circumstances of Christ’s Kingdom—first under the physical Israel and then the future spiritual Israel of God. He repeats his previous introduction about the grace God granted him to give this prophecy more weight.</margin>

<margin>v. 16. He boasts of God's revelations, which occur when the outer eyes are closed—as is common with ecstatic persons—so that they are not disturbed by external senses and objects. Then, the inner eyes of the spirit are opened. He was deemed worthy of the inspirations and visions of God according to his measure. God did not leave Himself without a witness even among the heathens; through this Balaam, many precious truths about the Lord God were spread, even though the man tolerated the use of omens and ceremonies. Concerning this prophetic gift, see the praise of David in 2 Samuel 23:1, etc.</margin>

<margin>Therefore, not every closed eye is dark and blind, and not all open eyes are enlightened. Just as there is a difference in eyes, there is a difference in closing and opening. Adam and Eve’s eyes were unhappily opened through transgression. In sinners, the "good eye" is closed, while the "mind of the flesh"—opened by the serpent's counsel—stands wide open. It is the same with the ear.</margin>

<margin>*He who falls down, and his eyes are opened:* O blessed falling down, which brings so much good in its wake! It brings men out of their pride and opens their eyes to see their own powerlessness and God's strength.</margin>

<margin>v. 17. He prophesies of the rising star out of Jacob, who would rule as a King; the one whom Jacob, in his own prophecy, calls "Shiloh," to whom all nations shall be subject (Genesis 49:10). He beholds Him in the spirit from afar, noting the time is not yet near. This is, of course, Christ. At His birth, an extraordinary star had to rise to announce this King, whom the Wise Men from the East honored as a new King in His tender infancy (Matthew 2). And why should it be thought absurd that this prophecy of Balaam—who was also one of the "Wise Men of the East"—was preserved and passed down among his successors, so that upon the appearance of this unusual star, they were reminded of it by divine impulse?</margin>

A star, a scepter) Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretation.</note>, Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop, often called the "Father of Church History."</note>, and others understand the "star" as Christ’s divinity and the "scepter" as His humanity.
Clearly indicated here are the two glorious virtues of Christ: Light and Strength. Light in the star, Strength in the scepter (Psalm 43:3, 84:11, 132:17).
Out of Jacob, out of Israel) Note the rising, growth, and increase of the Kingdom of Christ within us: from Jacob to Israel, from the star to a scepter, from light to strength. <note>In mystical tradition, "Jacob" often represents the soul in struggle/training, while "Israel" represents the soul that has seen God.</note>

<meta>This page continues the prophecy of Balaam in Numbers 24. While the previous page focused on the "Star of Jacob" and the immediate victory of Israel, this page details the destruction of Israel's historical enemies (Edom, Amalek, and the Kenites) and extends into a broader prophetic vision of world empires and the eventual triumph of Christ's kingdom.</meta>

### Chapter XXIV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

18. **And Edom shall be a possession; Seir also, his enemies, shall be a possession; but Israel shall act valiantly.**
19. **Out of Jacob shall come he who shall have dominion, and shall destroy the remnant of the city.**
20. **And when he looked on Amalek, he took up his oracle and said: Amalek was the first of the nations; but his latter end shall be to perish.**
21. **And he looked on the Kenites, and took up his oracle and said: Strong is your dwelling place, and you put your nest in a rock.**
22. **Nevertheless, Cain shall be wasted, until Assur <note>Assyria.</note> shall carry you away captive.**

v. 18. *Edom*) signifies the hateful brothers, who, along with their leaders—Seir—will be made subject.
In a spiritual sense, Edom is understood as the flesh, which in Christ is made subject to the Spirit.
v. 19. And the hostile city of Babylon, with its inhabitants, will be destroyed. Revelation 17, 18.
v. 20. *Amalek -- shall be to perish*) This, along with what preceded it, was also fulfilled regarding the physical Israel when David overcame the Moabites and Edomites, and Saul struck the Amalekites. See 1 Samuel 15, 2 Samuel 8, Psalm 60:10, 108:10.
The Amalekites signify, according to the word, those who "lap up" or "consume and destroy" the people (see Chapter 22:4), whom the Lord also intends to destroy. Revelation 11:18.
v. 21, 22. *Regarding the Kenites*, it is difficult to reach the literal understanding, as they indeed lived among the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:6) but also sided with the Israelites and lived among them (Judges 1:16, 4:11), being descendants of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law. Therefore, they were carried into the Assyrian captivity with the Israelites, of which it is spoken here.
However, when one keeps the spiritual Israel of the New Testament in view, where all these histories will also be fulfilled in the nations—which are understood throughout the Prophetic Word as symbols of these ancient peoples—the spiritual meaning is much easier to grasp and understand. In this sense: 1. The Moabites signify all worldly people who nonetheless confess Christ, just as Moab descended from Lot, who was of Abraham's kin, though conceived through incest <note>Original: "Blut-Schande," referring to the origin of Moab from Lot and his daughter.</note>. These world-people who profess Christ are not capable of true rebirth, but are of the false birth of the flesh; therefore, they will be destroyed along with all their leaders standing in the fleshly mind at the coming of the glorious Kingdom of Christ, when the Lord sends the scepter out of Zion and makes all His enemies a footstool for His feet. Psalm 110. But there also, all the "children of Seth"—which refers to all remaining humanity, since the descendants of Cain perished in the Great Flood—will be disrupted; namely, as many as will oppose the Kingdom of Christ during the general calling of all nations through the preaching of this Gospel in the whole world. See Psalm 2:8-9, Matthew 24:14. However, since this word <note>Referring to the Hebrew root for Seth.</note> also has a significant meaning of "luring," like a hen lures her chicks; so also, in a hidden sense, it can refer to the conversion of all well-meaning souls among all nations.
Thus, Cain is also a symbol of the first Cain and all persecutors, whose head has placed his seat in a firm place, as is also spoken of figuratively in Isaiah 22:15-16, from which he will be violently cast out. See Jude v. 11. And how this will be carried out by "Assur" in the New Testament—the Turks <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, commentators often identified biblical "Assur" or "Gog" with the Ottoman Empire.</note>—is spoken of by the prophets in various places.

<column-break/>

23. **And he took up his oracle and said: Alas, who shall live when God does this!**
24. **And ships shall come from the coast of Kittim <note>Chittäer.</note>, and shall afflict Assur, and shall afflict Eber: and he also shall perish forever.**
25. **And Balaam rose up, and went and returned to his place: and Balak also went his way.**

v. 23. *Alas, who shall live etc.*) This person sighs with pain because he knows well that all these inner wonders—which are still far off for him—will necessarily cause him death when they are to be wrought in him by the power of God. O, who could see the workings of God when He brings forth His WORD in souls through the expression of His speech, as long as even a small breath of one's own life remains! This is entirely impossible.
v. 24. Because it is necessary that the Hebrews of the Lord Himself and the most holy souls must finally pass away, so that the unique Kingdom of God alone may remain.
As for the overcoming of the Assyrians and Hebrews by the people of Kittim; by these the Romans are understood (1 Maccabees 1:1), who overpowered the Assyrian Empire toward the East—which was first brought under subjection by the Persians, then the Persians by the Greeks, and then the Greeks by the Romans. These then also overcame the Hebrews (the Jews) and destroyed Jerusalem; but they themselves were also destroyed when the old Roman Empire fell and took on an entirely different form in following times.
How the European princes will also finally overcome the Turks after they have devastated far and wide is prophesied in Micah 5:5-6.
Whatever the circumstances may be with the Hebrews or Jews, and how all that is high and exalted among men will experience the mighty arm of the Lord on His great day of slaughter, and thus go to destruction according to Joel 2 and many other places; the Prophetic Word will provide more information on this.
Thus, a brief summary of the judgments over the various enemies of the Kingdom of Christ has been presented here, where the Israel of God shall prove itself valiant and finally carry away the victory. And this is also the ultimate goal of all prophets: to announce the downfall of the enemies of Christ and the glorious victory of all believers, which is also spoken of in the conclusion in Revelation 19.
v. 25. *Balaam -- returned -- to his place*) He did not, however, actually return all the way to his place in Mesopotamia. See Chapter 31:8.
Philo <margin>(a) On the Life of Moses, Book 1.</margin> reports that when the King, in his anger, told him to pack up and leave before he did something worse to him, the prophet took him by the right hand and led him aside alone, and gave him the shameful counsel mentioned above in verse 14 (and the effect of which is contained in the next chapter), so that he might finally reach his goal. Namely, he knew that the Hebrews could offend God with nothing more than idolatry. To that, however, they could be brought—this was his counsel—if the Moabite maidens showed themselves friendly toward the Israelites, and once they had drawn them in with their love, they would then entice them to the service of idols. This would succeed if they refused to sleep with them unless they had actually burned incense to their gods; by which they would know that they were truly loved by the Israelites. This was the "fine" counsel. And because it did not seem groundless to Balak, the Moabite women were recommended to carry this out.

<meta>This page transitions from the prophecies of Balaam in Numbers 24 to the tragic aftermath in Numbers 25. # The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.

### The 25th Chapter.
->Whoredom with the Moabites.<-
->1 Kings 11:1.<-

And Israel remained in Shittim <note>Shittim means "Acacia Trees"; it was the final encampment before crossing the Jordan.</note>, and the people began to commit whoredom with the daughters of the Moabites: chapter 31:16.

2. They invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down before their gods.

3. And Israel joined (a) itself to Baal Peor: Then the anger of the Lord burned against Israel; Hosea 9:10.

<margin>(a) Psalm 106:28.</margin>

***

<margin>v. 1. Shittim)</margin> This was the last campsite, not far from the Jordan, Chapter 33:49, where the people of Israel were brought to a fall through the cunning counsel of Balaam, and were seduced into both physical and spiritual whoredom <note>"Spiritual whoredom" is a common biblical metaphor for idolatry or being unfaithful to God.</note>: which evil outcome is attributed to Balaam by the Spirit of God; as also mentioned in Revelation 2:14. For this reason, he was also slain with the sword. Chapter 31:8.

From the trees growing there, the boards were cut from which—because they were very beautiful and light—the Ark of the Covenant was made, and which were otherwise used for the construction of the Tabernacle.

<margin>With the daughters of Moab)</margin> Whom Balak <note>The King of Moab.</note> sent out like an army in order to overcome Israel through them.

So the spirit of the world constantly presents such images before our eyes from within and without, which are intended to draw our love to themselves. Everything seeks to make itself common with us; everything presents itself to our senses and wants to bring us into disgrace with God, and thereby deprive us of His friendship.

<margin>v. 2. Since they had joined the sacrificial feasts of the Moabites, overindulging in food and drink, they were led to physical whoredom, 1 Corinthians 10:7, 8, which was common at such heathen idol-feasts; thus spiritual whoredom followed in the form of idolatry, just as the wise King Solomon allowed himself to be led into the service of idols through the love of foreign women. 1 Kings 11:1 etc.</margin>

It is a strange thing that even the most advanced souls, until they have reached a state of fortification in God, can still sin. Among such holy souls, enough are found who are cowardly and inclined to fall into idolatry: which is the only sin (along with the sin of lying) through which they sin. But it is remarkable that this did not happen to them except when they sinned with strangers, by attaching their hearts to diverse and evil people through natural friendship and distraction.

Thus the coarse sins of Israel represent those inner works which are more subtle and penetrate deeper: such as the whoredom of the mind, which one commits when looking at a woman and lusting after her; Matthew 5:28. Likewise when one allows a vehement desire to be awakened to make the acquaintance of this or that soul, though through association with them a snare may easily be laid for our spirit. So also is spiritual idolatry; which consists either in excessive self-love, 2 Timothy 3:2, or when a person directs the fullness of their love, with which they should cling to God, toward the creature <note>Any created thing or person, as opposed to the Creator.</note>, since God alone, and no one else, should be loved with our whole heart. Another kind of such idolatry consists in relying too much on ourselves, or some other person or creature outside of God, be it wealth or honor, power or wisdom. Jeremiah 17:5. 1 Timothy 6:17.

<margin>v. 3. Baal Peor)</margin> was a shameful idol of the Midianites and a filthy image, which Jerome, Theophylact, and many others held to be Priapus <note>A Greco-Roman god of fertility, often associated with lewdness.</note>; whose worship is said to have consisted of shameful exposure and such things. (a)

<margin>(a) See Schindler’s *Lexicon Pentaglotton* regarding the word "Baal" <note>Hebrew: בעל</note>, page 1463 and following.</margin>

<column-break/>

4. And the LORD said to Moses: Take all the heads of the people, and hang them to the LORD against the sun, that the fierce anger of the LORD may turn away from Israel.

5. And Moses said to the judges of Israel: Let everyone slay his people who have joined themselves to Baal Peor!

***

<margin>v. 4. The LORD wanted to punish this terrible idolatry—which was almost even grosser than that which their fathers had practiced with the Golden Calf—with an exemplary punishment. All the heads among the tribes, who may have been those over the thousands and were explicitly called heads (Exodus 18:25), had to be hanged in the open sun as a public spectacle for the whole people (see Joshua 10:26, 2 Samuel 21:9). This was because they did not observe their office in warning and punishing the people regarding such fellowship in the idol-feasts; indeed, they may well have been the most prominent among them, as appears from verse 14; so that through their punishment, they might in some measure still the anger of God.</margin>

Do you see now what a position the heads and rulers of the people have? They must give account not only for their own sins, but also for the sins of their people. The anger of God begins with them. Whoever considers this will not desire to be a head, nor should they think much of their status, but rather fear it. I have, says Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD).</note>, enough with my own sins and the account for them; why is it necessary for me to be hanged in the sun for the sake of others' sins!

Since the sin happened out of free will, God took their leaders to punish them: because the highest part must suffer the punishment for this. He must be hanged on the gallows: for while God wanted to love him, even though he had gone out from his own land, he must—after having done penance for his unfaithfulness—hang between heaven and earth, to find nothing more on earth upon which he can rest; just as he could also find no entrance to heaven, which was otherwise the place of his rest and peace. Through this hanging between heaven and earth, he suffers very great pains, which are the pains of fire, whereby the soul—being outside of itself and not finding God to receive it—feels a pain similar to the pain of hanging, which cruelly torments it until it must finally suffocate.

These leaders of the people are hanged against the sun; both because it will no longer be beneficial to them, and because they will see that, as its light shines powerfully into their eyes, this only increases their pains. This happens to fallen men when they are made more sorrowful by the memories of the graces received from God and by the impression of His truth.

Such is also the punishment of those souls of this rank who take themselves back <note>Reclaim their self-will from God.</note> and go out again into their own self-interest; a punishment very different from the first punishment for idolatry mentioned above (2). This punishment alone can reconcile God and place the soul in a much higher degree.

<margin>v. 5. Furthermore, the judges in Israel, who may have been the remaining supervisors over hundreds, fifties, and tens, also had to slay those who had particularly sinned in this shameful idolatry. For</margin>

Idolatry and whoredom are such sins that God [rarely] intends to overlook <note>original: "durch die Finger sehen," an idiom meaning to turn a blind eye or be lenient.</note> the one who commits them.

<margin>(2) Exodus 32:5.</margin>

<summary>This page describes Israel's fall into idolatry and sexual immorality at Shittim with the Moabites and Midianites, resulting in God's command to execute the tribal leaders and sinners. The commentary provides a spiritual interpretation of these events, emphasizing the heavy responsibility of leaders and the nature of spiritual "whoredom" and idolatry.</summary>

### Chapter XXV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

6. And behold, a man from the children of Israel came and brought a Midianite woman to his brothers, before the eyes of Moses and before the eyes of the entire congregation of the children of Israel, while they were weeping before the door of the Tabernacle of Meeting.

7. When Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, saw this, he rose up from the midst of the congregation and took a spear in his hand,

8. And went after the Israelite man into the **den of harlotry** <note>The German "Huren-Winckel" refers to a secret or shameful tent; Phinehas followed them directly into the private quarters where the sin was being committed.</note> and pierced both of them through, the Israelite man and the woman, through her belly. Then the plague was stayed among the children of Israel.

9. And those who died in the plague were twenty-four thousand.

And while a prince of the Israelites still dared, unabashed before Moses and the congregation, to bring one of the prominent daughters of the Midianites into the camp and to carry out his shameful will with her in his tent; Phinehas, the son of Eleazar—to whom the High Priestly office had come after the death of his father Aaron—went there in a holy zeal and pierced them through by a secret divine judgment in the very limbs with which they committed the shame.

<margin>v. 6.</margin> **While they were weeping)** It is not enough to weep and lament because of the sin committed or the judgments connected to it; therefore, the wrath was not stayed by that alone. Rather, we must desist from sin and strive with all earnestness for its killing and uprooting, so that both the sin may be forgiven and the torment associated with it may be removed. This was done here by

<margin>v. 7.</margin> **Phinehas, the son of Eleazar)** that is, *Confidence and trust of the countenance in or from God's help*, as the names imply in their meaning.
He was a priest. Mark this, you priests who so gladly let sin live under the name of weaknesses, frailties, and imperfections!

<margin>v. 8.</margin> **Pierced them both)** Do this yourself with the **Sword of the Spirit** <note>A reference to Ephesians 6:17, meaning the Word of God used as a spiritual weapon.</note> which is recommended to you, upon your own self, whenever the mind after God wants to mingle with the mind of the flesh; and do not spare even sinful thoughts, piercing them right at their birth and in the "harlot-corner" of the heart.

<margin>(Then the plague was) stayed)</margin> **Then the plague was)** stayed by the killing performed by the judges, which Moses may have ordered according to the Lord's command.

<margin>v. 9.</margin> **24,000)** Because the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10:8 says 23,000, it may be that the common people numbered that many, while the leaders—who alone numbered over 600 among those set over the 600,000 of the people—may have been added here. Although one should not dwell particularly on such apparent contradictions in Scripture, which are of no weight, or how they may have arisen: since Scripture is given to us primarily for our salvation, which we must observe in the core truths, and not in such circumstances that ultimately contribute nothing to the main point. It is enough that a heavy judgment was executed on the people because of this idolatry, as also happened at the first occurrence. Exodus 32:27, 28.

Phinehas, however, is rewarded because he does not presume to punish except through God's will, and because he kills self-love.

<column-break/>

10. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

11. Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, in that he was zealous with my zeal in their midst, so that I did not consume the children of Israel in my zeal.

12. Therefore say: Behold, I give to him my **Covenant of Peace**;

13. And he and his seed after him shall have the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the children of Israel.

14. Now the name of the slain Israelite man, who was slain with the Midianite woman, was Zimri, the son of Salu, a prince of a father's house among the Simeonites.

As the righteous zeal of the High Priest Phinehas is praised here, so it was also done by David when he recounts this deed and then reports: *And it was counted to him for righteousness for evermore* (Psalm 106:28-31); namely, that such a righteous deed brought him a reward of grace here in this life as well.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> Furthermore, this Phinehas is said by many to have lived to a very great age: by some 300 years; by others even much older. <note>original: "(a) vid. Druſ. comment. ad loc. diffic. Num. c. 115. Glaſſ. Gram. ſacr. p. 818."; See Drusius, *Commentary on Difficult Passages in Numbers*, ch. 115; Glassius, *Sacred Grammar*, p. 818.</note> And indeed, that he reached a very high age is to be concluded from Judges 20:28, since he was still living at the time of that conflict against Benjamin. Here it is said:

<margin>v. 12.</margin> **I give him my Covenant of Peace)** Thus he was received into the inner covenant of peace from God, which belongs only to the saints, who alongside the outward sacrifice also make the heart-covenant with God in the heart through the obedience of faith. Psalm 50:5.

<margin>v. 13.</margin> And then his descendants are also promised the High Priestly dignity; just as they are then recounted in order down to Ezra after the Babylonian captivity. Ezra 7:1-5.
How it happened, however, that Eli attained this dignity—from whom Abiathar of the lineage of Ithamar, the brother of Eleazar (from whom Phinehas was), was High Priest in David's time; (see 1 Chronicles 24:3, 6)—cannot be known. At one point Solomon gave it back to Zadok, who descended from Phinehas, and deposed Abiathar; just as it had been threatened to Eli: 1 Kings 2:27, 1 Samuel 1:9, 2:30, when they had previously both been priests. 2 Samuel 15:35. And finally, his descendants, after the long time of the Old Testament had passed, had to give way to him who is a High Priest forever according to the order of **Melchizedek** <note>A mysterious king and priest mentioned in Genesis and Psalms, seen as a precursor to Christ's eternal priesthood.</note>, who also gave his own life in zeal for the honor and righteousness of God, and thus redeemed us from the fierce wrath of the Lord against shameful idolatry and apostasy from the living God. Psalm 110:4, Hebrews 7:21, 25.

**Because he was zealous for his God)** As the first true **Zealot**; whereas afterward there were always more false zealots, who out of lack of understanding wanted to be zealous for God's honor and killed the witnesses of the truth. Romans 10:2.

God punished Korah and his company when they usurped the office of a leader; because they sought their own honor, and thereby the preservation <note>original: "(b) Oben Cap. 16 / 32."; See above, Chapter 16:32.</note> of their own self-will.

<insert>
God has always honored and made glorious the tribe of Judah—from whom Christ was to be born—for that very reason: just as he also has the greatest number of people here among all the tribes. After him, Dan was the most numerous tribe, and after that, Issachar.

Otherwise, throughout the entire census, as is easily seen, the order did not look to dignity or status—otherwise Judah would have had to stand first—nor to birth order; otherwise Judah, and not Gad, would have to follow Reuben and Simeon; likewise Dan and Naphtali would have to go before Gad, Asher, Zebulun, and Issachar. Rather, the order follows how the camps and banners followed one another, which was the most convenient order to keep here. And thus, a beginning was made with those on the South side <note>original: "Mittags-Seite," literally the side of the midday sun</note>, and so proceeded toward the North <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally the side of midnight</note>, and finally toward the West <note>original: "Niedergang," the setting of the sun</note>.
