### Chapter XXVI. The Fourth Book of Moses (Numbers)

52. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

53. To these the land shall be divided as an inheritance, according to the number of names.

54. To those who are many, you shall increase their inheritance, and to those who are few, you shall decrease their inheritance. To each, their inheritance shall be given according to the requirement of those numbered.

55. Nevertheless, the land shall be divided by lot; they shall inherit according to the names of the tribes of their fathers.

56. According to the determination of the lot, their inheritance shall be divided between the many and the few.

---

<note>Commentary on verses 52-56</note>

There are two kinds of enemies against which the Israel of God is numbered and mustered for battle: namely, the impurity of the flesh and of the spirit. The muster in chapter 1 was against the former, namely the defilements of the flesh. And the one here was against the latter, or the impurities of the spirit. When these enemies are overcome, then we take possession of the eternal inheritance. And therefore, when they were mustered here for the second time, the LORD spoke:

**v. 53. To these the land shall be divided as an inheritance)** However, the first people—those of the circumcision—were also rejected, and the Gentiles <note>The "Heathen" or non-Jewish nations.</note> were set in their place; this was done not through Moses, but by Joshua (or Jesus) <note>In many older German texts, the names Joshua and Jesus are spelled the same (Josua/Jesus), emphasizing Joshua as a "type" or precursor to Jesus Christ.</note>, according to the following chapter.

**v. 54. Many — few)** According to the thoughts of Origen <note>An influential early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for symbolic interpretations of Scripture.</note>, the "many" are on the broad path, and the "few" are on the narrow path. Therefore, the former receive more of the earth, and the latter receive less; for the more one receives their portion in God Himself, the smaller the portion of earthly things becomes.
According to the literal sense, the numerous tribes, houses, and families were to have larger pieces of land than the others. And nothing prevents—nor is it contradictory—that, according to

**v. 55. 56.** the lot should make the decision. For even among the larger portions, the more numerous could cast lots, and among the smaller portions, the fewer could do the same.

<margin>Regarding how the distribution by lot may have occurred, the Jews have various thoughts. However, one does not need to reflect or guess much on the manner of it, as God will have given them wisdom from within, so that Joshua had to arrange it according to the will of God; and then each was pleased with what Providence had already intended for them. See Joshua 18:10, etc., where the lots are recounted one after another, and how this happened at Shiloh before the LORD, who rules it according to His will: Proverbs 16:33, which also was able to maintain peace and unity among them. Proverbs 18:18.</margin>

This should also represent to us how we receive eternal life, as if by lot, ahead of others, just as David recognizes this in Psalm 16:6: *The lot has fallen for me in pleasant places; yes, I have a beautiful inheritance.* And Peter says emphatically that the believers have obtained the precious faith through the lot <note>Original: "durchs Loos überkommen haben"; Peter uses a Greek word suggesting "obtained by lot" in 2 Peter 1:1.</note>, 2 Peter 1:1, because the special and greater grace is the pure and clear pleasure of God, which some obtain over others according to the unsearchable counsel of God, as if by lot. Just as Abraham and his seed especially attained such great grace and can serve as an example of election for all other men; which also appeared again afterward in Ishmael and Isaac, in Esau and Jacob, where the former were the firstborn according to nature, but the latter became the same according to grace. Romans 9:11, 12, 13.

<column-break/>

57. And these are the numbered of the Levites according to their families: Of Gershon, the family of the Gershonites; of Kohath, the family of the Kohathites; of Merari, the family of the Merarites.

58. These are the families of Levi: The family of the Libnites, the family of the Hebronites, the family of the Mahlites, the family of the Mushites, the family of the Korahites. And Kohath fathered Amram.

<margin>Exodus 6:20.</margin>
59. And Amram's wife was named Jochebed, a daughter of Levi, who was born to Levi in Egypt; and she bore to Amram: Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister.

60. And to Aaron were born Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar.

<margin>Leviticus 10:2. 1 Chronicles 24:2.</margin>
61. But Nadab and Abihu died when they brought strange fire <note>original: "fremd Feuer"</note> before the face of the LORD.

62. And those numbered of them were twenty-three thousand, all males from a month old and upward. For they were not numbered among the children of Israel, because no inheritance was given to them among the children of Israel.

63. These are those numbered by Moses and Eleazar the priest, who numbered the children of Israel in the plains of the Moabites, by the Jordan across from Jericho.

64. And...

---

<note>Commentary on verses 57-63</note>

**v. 57. 58.** Only four or five of the grandsons of Levi are mentioned here, whereas there were otherwise eight. Exodus 6:17, etc. Why the descendants of Shimei and Uzziel were omitted, one cannot know; because the Scripture does not always deem it necessary to recount all circumstances.

**v. 62.** Otherwise, there were more of them here than at the first census, where 22,000 were reported, although there were actually 22,300: see Chapter 3:39. Thus, there were 700 more at the entry into Canaan; showing that the LORD also wished to preserve them in their number.

**v. 63.** Eleazar is now mentioned here in place of his father Aaron, as he exercised his office with Moses in carrying out the commands of the LORD just as his father did. And it is likely that this Eleazar also came into the land of Canaan, since he, with Joshua, was able to administer the office in the Church and government before the beginning, just like Moses and Aaron. See Chapter 27:18, 19.

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.

64. And among these there was not a man of those numbered by Moses and by Aaron the priest, who numbered the children of Israel in the wilderness of Sinai.

<margin>
This final census, therefore, actually concerns the second people, who came in place of the first who had fallen in the wilderness and were reborn, so to speak. This occurred as a testament to divine truth, which proved itself partly in avenging punitive justice and partly in the fulfillment of the promise to multiply the seed of Israel.
</margin>

<margin>
However, the LORD had fulfilled His sworn oath upon the unbelieving and disobedient generation (Psalm 95:9, 10, 11). The Apostle <note>Refers to St. Paul in the New Testament.</note> also presents this as a warning,

## Chapter XXVII.

->The Succession of Inheritance, and Moses' Successor, Joshua.<-

And there came forward the daughters of Zelophehad, the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, from the families of Manasseh the son of Joseph: and these were the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, and Hoglah, and Milcah, and Tirzah.

2. And they stood before Moses and before Eleazar the priest, and before the princes and the whole congregation, at the door of the Tabernacle of the Congregation, and said:

3. Our father died in the wilderness, and he was not among the company of those who gathered themselves together against the LORD in the company of Korah <note>Korah led a famous rebellion against Moses' authority earlier in the journey (Numbers 16).</note>; but he died for his own sin and had no sons.

4. Why should the name of our father be taken away from among his family because he has no son? Give us a possession among our father's brothers.

5. And Moses brought their legal case before the face of the LORD.

<margin>
v. 1-4. On the occasion of these five daughters (who also appear in Chapter 26:33, 36:11, and Joshua 17:3) who had no brothers, a difficulty arose. Because the land of Canaan was to be distributed as an inheritance only to the fathers of households, the question was whether the father's memory should not be preserved through them by granting them their father's inheritance—especially since they had not forfeited the inheritance through any specific guilt of their own, but rather their father had died for his own and the general guilt when they sinned against God through unbelief.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 5. *Moses brought — before*) Learn here, you judges, to be ready to grant access to everyone in their petition, to give them a hearing, and to provide justice: especially to widows and orphans. Ask God for counsel whenever you have a difficult matter, and present it to Him.
</margin>

<margin>
If they were still unmarried, they were to marry one from their own tribe. See Chapter 36.
</margin>

<column-break/>

65. For the LORD had said to them: they shall surely die in the wilderness. And there remained not a man of them, except only Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun.

<margin>
...just as it was for the first Christians, so also especially for the time when the entrance into the glorious kingdom of Christ shall be at the door (1 Corinthians 10:5, 6; Hebrews 4:1, etc.). Then, furthermore, the unbelieving and disobedient will be excluded, while those who stand in the spirit of faith—like the two faithful witnesses Caleb and Joshua—and who understand and accept the testimony of the "two hidden ones" <note>A reference to the "Two Witnesses" in apocalyptic theology.</note> in the days of the great Antichrist, shall enter. See Revelation 11:3, etc.
</margin>

6. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

7. The daughters of Zelophehad speak rightly. You shall surely give them an inheritance of a possession among their father's brothers, and you shall cause the inheritance of their father to pass to them.

8. And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: If a man dies and has no son, then you shall cause his inheritance to pass to his daughter.

<margin>
v. 6, 7. The friendly goodness of God deems these maidens worthy not only of an answer themselves, but He even makes their presentation—as Origen <note>An early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> notes here—into an occasion to establish eternal laws for mankind, which are to be followed in all times and among all peoples as living according to eternal decrees.
</margin>

<margin>
However, we must investigate something else even more spiritual. For it could be that I or you have neither flesh nor daughters, nor any land which they could inherit. Should such an ordinance of God then be of no concern? Here it must certainly be understood spiritually. And indeed, there is no doubt that under this image it was expressed:
</margin>

<margin>
Even pious women shall be co-heirs of grace and eternal salvation, for the Lord makes no distinction and allows neither male nor female to count for more <note>A reference to Galatians 3:28: "There is neither male nor female... for you are all one in Christ Jesus."</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Furthermore, every one of us has five daughters within ourselves, and God grant they might be five wise virgins as these were: namely, our five outward senses, which must be used for household and bodily affairs or external matters. These must also certainly find an inheritance among the people of God and not be cast out.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 8. The LORD gave here a legal statute regarding how succession was to be handled: namely, because the land of Canaan was to be regarded as a special fief <term>Lehen (fief)</term><note>A legal term for land held on condition of loyalty; the author uses this medieval concept to explain biblical land distribution.</note> that should remain more firmly with the male line, through which the families are propagated—and not through the women, who enter into another family through their marriage when they become one flesh with them. Thus, the inheritance first went to the sons regarding the "immovable" property (land). As for the rest—the "movables" or personal property—the daughters undoubtedly shared in the inheritance. Afterward, the daughters were to be admitted to the succession of the paternal estate so that the father's memory would be preserved. This was to be understood if they were not yet married; for otherwise, the inheritance would pass to another family, to whom the paternal estate could not be turned over; for they had to ensure that the estate remained hereditary within the same tribe.
</margin>

This is the Water of Strife <note>The "Water of Strife" refers to Meribah, where Moses struck the rock in anger instead of speaking to it as God commanded.</note> at Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin.

16. May the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, appoint a man over the congregation;
17. Who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may lead them in: so that the congregation of the LORD may not be like sheep that have no shepherd.

---

**v. 9.** When no daughter was present, the brothers received the inheritance, among whom their sons also seem to be included; for they were the grandsons of the grandfather to whom the paternal inheritance had belonged.
**v. 10.** When none of these were present, it went to the father’s brother, who took precedence over all other relatives because he was closest to the one from whom the paternal fief <note>A "fief" or "Lehn-Gut" refers to land held under a lord; here, the author views the Israelites as holding land granted by God.</note> had originated.
**v. 11.** After that, however, followed the one who was closest in the lineage, where they undoubtedly had to count the degrees of birth to see who was nearest to the common ancestor of those who claimed it, who once held the inheritance or fief in possession.
Thus, they were specifically the LORD’S vassals, as it were, who divided the land among the families; and He wanted it preserved in the families particularly for the sake of the line of Christ’s birth, so that they might remain with their properties and also be preserved together in friendship by living near one another and marrying among themselves according to kinship.
Since in the New Testament we look not upon a physical inheritance but only upon a spiritual one, we should strive above all else that spiritual goods might be shared with our own, and that they might not fall to worldly strangers. This requires spiritual labor and wrestling through prayer, and that one should well-commend these spiritual goods to one’s children in their final decree or testament, just as the Testament of Tobit can serve as a beautiful model in Chapter 4. <note>The Book of Tobit is part of the Apocrypha, often included in Bibles of this period for moral instruction.</note>
**v. 12. 13.** God announces to Moses his approaching end, and thereby shows him the land before his eyes, into which he should have led them if he had not sinned with disobedience, like his brother Aaron, who had already gone before and did not get to see the land: a grace which Moses still enjoyed over him, because he had otherwise shown greater faithfulness.
God also left Moses in this world for a while longer to lead His people in the wilderness: but because of his unfaithfulness, He let him view the promised land only from afar, without him being able to have the comfort of seeing his people established in complete security.
**v. 13.** He must die just like Aaron, for the spirit was taken from both of them and given to another.
In this way, God often chooses to announce the end to His faithful servants and also to a believer, just as David prays in Psalm 39:5: *LORD, make me to know mine end, and what is the measure of my days! I would know what my lifetime is.* As it says more precisely according to the original text.
**v. 14.** *Because you were disobedient to my word &c.* Here He may also represent to them in spirit wherein they might have specifically sinned against the LORD, so that they might once more heartily repent and ask God’s forgiveness. Indeed, those who have stood especially in the service of the LORD should likewise specifically ask God to show them their particular faults committed in service, in order to earnestly implore God for forgiveness.
**v. 15. 16.** Moses was first and foremost concerned about a good successor in his office, to request such a one from the LORD. For though one might think that he should have left this entirely to God, who would ordain this even without him; yet God desires to be called upon by us in those things He has commanded us, so that we may show love for those placed under our care and call upon God for a capable leader. And for this reason, he specifically calls God:
**The God of the spirits of all flesh)** who weighs the spirits and hearts of all men (Proverbs 16:2, 21:2), so that He knows their understanding and inclinations, and therefore can choose the most capable. In this regard, elective kingdoms would perhaps be the best—if indeed God were rightly called upon by those who choose—over hereditary kingdoms, in which one must accept the successors as they are: in which case parents must call upon God for wisdom and grace for their sons, and subjects for these their certain rulers.
However, Moses’ humble heart manifested itself in that he did not think of his own sons to request them from God as successors, but left this entirely to God. God also did not wish to take any of them: not so much because their mother was a Midianite <note>Moses' wife, Zipporah, was a Midianite, a group often in conflict with Israel.</note>, and their descendants later soon fell into idolatry (Judges 18:30), but because God wished to reserve the immediate government over this people for Himself: therefore, it was not entrusted to any certain family until they later requested a king, and thus the kingdom had to be handed over to a specific family. See 1 Samuel 8:7.
Thus he petitions God without thinking of his own benefit. It is all the same to him, and he is gladly satisfied that he shall die without bringing his people into the promised land. Such a soul can see nothing outside of the will of God: and since it is void of all self-interest, it thinks of nothing but what can serve the glory of God and the benefit of His children.
**v. 17.** For this reason, he asks Him rather to give a man who possesses his spirit, to be able to lead this people in everything that remains for them to travel until they have entered into it. Otherwise, he says, these souls will go astray, like sheep without a shepherd.

### Chapter XXVII.

->Inheritance Rights and Moses’ Successor, Joshua.<-

5. And Moses brought their legal case before the face of the LORD.

<margin>
v. 1-4. On the occasion of these five daughters (who also appear in Chapter 26:33, 36:11, and Joshua 17:3) who had no brothers, a difficulty arose. Since the land of Canaan was to be divided as an inheritance only among the fathers of households, the question was whether the father's memory should be preserved through them by granting them his inheritance. This was especially relevant as they had not forfeited the inheritance through any specific crime, but rather their father had died due to his own and the general guilt when the people sinned against God through unbelief.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 5. *Moses brought—before:* Learn here, you judges, to be ready to grant everyone access to bring their case, to give them a hearing, and to provide justice—especially to widows and orphans. Ask God for counsel when you have a difficult matter, and present it to Him.

6. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

7. The daughters of Zelophehad speak rightly. You shall surely give them an inheritance among their father’s brothers, and you shall cause the inheritance of their father to pass to them.

8. And you shall speak to the children of Israel, saying: If a man dies and has no son, then you shall cause his inheritance to pass to his daughter.

9. <unclear>And</unclear>

<margin>
v. 6. 7. The friendly goodness of God deigns not only to give the young women an answer Himself but even approves their presentation. Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) known for allegorical interpretations of the Bible.</note> notes here that God takes this occasion to present eternal laws and rights to mankind, which are to be observed by all people in all times.
However, we must also seek something else and something spiritual within this. For it could be that I or you, according to the flesh, have neither daughters nor any land-holding which they could inherit. Should such a wise ordinance of God therefore be of no concern to us? Here, the inheritance must be understood spiritually. Without a doubt, this image expresses how even pious women are to be co-heirs of grace and eternal salvation in Him who makes all things new, and where neither male nor female is counted above the other (Galatians 3:28).
Furthermore, each of us has five "daughters" within ourselves—and may God grant they be five wise virgins like these—namely, our five outer senses, which we use for household and physical business or external things. These must also find an inheritance among the people of God and not be cast out.
</margin>

<margin>
v. 8. The LORD gave a legal statute here by which inheritance should be governed: namely, that the land of Canaan was held as a special fief, as it were, from God. It was to remain always with the male line, through which families are propagated, and not through women, who enter another family through marriage when they become one flesh with a husband. Thus, the inheritance first went to the sons regarding landed property; as for other "movables" or personal goods, they undoubtedly inherited those together. Thereafter, daughters were to be admitted to the inheritance of the paternal estate so that the father's memory might be preserved. This is to be understood, however, as applying while they were still unmarried and would marry someone from their own tribe so that the estate remained within that tribe (See Chapter 36). For otherwise, they would already belong to another tribe to which the paternal inheritance could not be transferred.
</margin>

# 656 The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXVII.

18. And the LORD said to Mo-
ses: Take to yourself Joshua, the
son of Nun, a man in whom the
Spirit is, and you shall lay your hand 
upon him;
19. And you shall set him before the
face of Eleazar the priest and before 
the face of the entire congregation and 
shall give him a charge before their eyes:
20. And you shall lay some of your honor 
<note>original: "Herrlichkeit," meaning majesty or visible authority</note> upon him, 
so that the entire congregation of the 
children of Israel may obey him.
21. And he shall stand before the 
priest Eleazar, who shall for him 
inquire through the judgment of the Urim 
before the face of the LORD.

---

Joshua was now chosen by the Lord for such a high office. Having already experienced service under Moses, he had learned humility and gentleness—which are among the most distinguished qualities of a ruler—and how he ruled under God rather than in self-will <note>original: "Eigenheit," a term often used in Pietist literature to describe the ego or acting out of one’s own desires rather than God's will</note>, so that he might now also apply these qualities in his own government. God also gives him the testimony that His Spirit was in him, and thus a true fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom and an outflow of God’s Spirit.

**v. 18. 19.** God therefore tells Moses that he should take the one into whom He has placed the spirit of leadership, and that this person should lead the people. He was to lay his hands on him as a certain type of induction, in order to transfer into him that which God wished to communicate to him of His graces and distinctions as His vessel. By the laying on of his hands, he was also to point him out, as if by hand, before the whole congregation and present him to them as the ruler by whom they were now to be governed, in order to obey him in all things.

**v. 20.** You shall continue to interpret my will to him, and cast your power and your majesty upon him, so that he may be heard by those he is to lead, leaving it behind as an inheritance.

**v. 21.** However, before he began anything, he himself was first to have the will of God explored through the Urim by Eleazar the High Priest (see Exodus 28:30; 1 Samuel 23:9) and then take care to follow this command of God given to him through the priest.

Just as Joshua was not made subject to the High Priest through this, so too would rulers not become subject to the ministers of the Gospel if they, according to this wise order of God, also sought counsel through them from Christ; the ministers could then request such counsel from Christ in important matters and make it known to the rulers.

(Inquire through the judgment of the Urim) On this occasion, the High Priest put on all his garments and turned toward the Ark of the Covenant. The one who was inquiring stood directly behind his back.

Regarding how the answer was given, even the most learned Hebrews confess their ignorance. Those who believe they have come closest to the mark claim that when a rightful inquiry was made—whether by the King himself, his general, or another prominent royal official—the inquirer had to stand behind the High Priest in prayer and devotion and bring forth the question with humble gestures and a low voice. Then, a special glow and radiant letters were observed on the gemstones of the breastplate <note>original: "Brustschildlein," referring to the Hoshen or Breastplate of Judgment</note>, from which the answer could be read. However, since Moses was commanded during the making of the breastplate and the arranging of the gemstones to put the Urim and Thummim *into* it, it seems to have been something other than the gemstones themselves. It may have been similar to a mirror or other transparent glass, such as superstitious people are accustomed to using in so-called crystal-gazing <note>original: "Glaskall-Sehen"</note>, which Moses had to place into the lined or double breastplate. The apostate Jews may have later imitated this with their Teraphim <note>Household idols or cult objects</note> and Ephod (Judges 18:14, etc.), and the heathens with their *speculis* <note>Latin: mirrors</note>.

<column-break/>

At his word they shall go 
out, and at his word they shall 
come in, he and all the children of Israel 
with him and the entire congregation.
22. And Moses did as the 
LORD had commanded him, and took Joshua 
and set him before the face of Elea-
zar the priest and before the face 
of the entire congregation:
23. And he laid his hands upon 
him, and gave him a charge, as the LORD 
had spoken through the service of Moses.

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

---

Moses obeyed willingly and laid aside not only his power but also the majesty he had acquired. Many souls, when they have reached a very high state, may easily lay their power upon others and away from themselves; but none are found who, for the sake of others, relinquish the honor they have earned in their administration. If some good plan succeeds for those to whom leadership is entrusted, one is usually quick to credit oneself, claiming it happened because the things one well-begun were faithfully followed. But if something bad results, it is attributed to the one who followed in leadership: because, it is said, he did not faithfully follow the footsteps of the first administration. Oh, how few there are who, when they rid themselves of power, simultaneously rid themselves of the honor and the prestige! In this, Moses was very faithful and an example to all the most faithful servants; as it is written: he did as the Lord commanded him. See Hebrews 3:5. For a servant does nothing other than what he is commanded.

**v. 23. He laid his hands upon him)** From this, the laying on of hands for the ministers of the Gospel came into use (see Deuteronomy 34:9 and Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14), with which one also intended to present them to the congregations and pray to God for greater capability and wisdom for them.

But what does Moses represent here other than the first dispensation of the Father, which draws us to the Son and delivers us to him? John 6:44.

Joshua <note>original: "Ieboschua," a variant of Yehoshua/Joshua</note> prefigures Christ in us and his dispensation, which now takes up the government that previously belonged to the Father, and in cooperation with the Father, fights against sin and Satan in the soul.

Joshua was first Moses' servant, and Christ is also placed under the Law; he then grows within us under the working of Moses or the Father, and redeems us step-by-step from sin and the impulse of the Law, until he breaks through to the governing administration in us and begins to rule in his gentle love; he then carries out everything in the soul through the power and emphasis of free grace, into a living feeling and perception of the Gospel and the grace, sweetness, and loveliness connected with it.

When we arrive at this, we experience and perceive—by means of new openings of the love of God—that the Father has committed all judgment to the Son. John 5:22. And precisely through this, one also arrives into the other Covenant, which is full of power, where the soul is mightily strengthened to fight against sin and selfhood, to live through faith in the Son of God, and to reach the promised rest through his victory.

<summary>Moses formally ordains Joshua as his successor by the laying on of hands and establishes the Urim as a means of divine consultation. The commentary provides a mystical interpretation, viewing Moses as the Law and Joshua as the emerging rule of Christ within the believer's soul.</summary>

# 657 Chapter XXIX. The Fourth Book of Moses.

### Chapter XXIX.
->The Festivals of the first half of the year.<-

AND the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:

2. Command the children of Israel and say to them: <margin>(a) Leviticus 21.</margin> My offering, which is my bread (a) from my offerings made by fire for my soothing aroma, you shall be careful to offer to me at its appointed time.

3. And say to them: This is the offering made by fire which you shall offer to the LORD; two lambs of the first year without blemish, daily, as a regular burnt offering.

4. The one lamb you shall prepare in the morning, and the other lamb you shall prepare between the two evenings. <note>original: "zwischen den beyden Abenden," a Hebrew idiom referring to the period between sunset and total darkness, or late afternoon.</note>

5. Also a tenth of an ephah <term>ephah: a dry measure, roughly 22 liters</term> of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with a fourth part of a hin <term>hin: a liquid measure, roughly 4 liters</term> of beaten oil.

6. This is a regular burnt offering, which was ordained at Mount Sinai for a soothing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

7. Also its drink offering, a fourth of a hin for each lamb. In the Holy Place, the drink offering of strong drink <note>original: "starcken Geträncks," likely referring to fermented wine</note> shall be poured out to the LORD.

8. And the other lamb you shall prepare between the two evenings; like the grain offering of the morning and like its drink offering, you shall prepare it: it is an offering made by fire of a soothing aroma to the LORD.

---

God now wished to prescribe to this second generation the form of divine service which they were to perform daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly on various appointed days. This service had been mostly neglected during the forty years in the wilderness, as can be concluded from Amos 5:25.

v. 2. He calls the offerings in general "his bread," because they were mostly assigned to the priests for their sustenance. In the same way, Christ chooses to accept that which is given to the believers and his servants for their sustenance and refreshment as if he himself had enjoyed it, because they are his members in whom the Head is strengthened. Matthew 10:40, 21:25, 25:40.

But note also that you give God nothing of your own, but only what was already His. Therefore, God is not so much given something when you do such things, but rather it is only returned. For everything that the human race enjoys, it has from Him.

v. 3-8. The daily offering and its mystery were treated in Exodus 29:38 etc.

<column-break/>

9. And on the Sabbath day, two lambs of the first year without blemish, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering, mixed with oil, and its drink offering.

10. This is the burnt offering of the Sabbath for every Sabbath, in addition to the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.

11. And in the beginning of each of your months, you shall offer a burnt offering to the LORD: two young bulls and one ram, seven lambs of the first year without blemish.

12. And three tenths of fine flour for a grain offering mixed with oil for each bull, and two tenths of fine flour for a grain offering mixed with oil for the one ram.

13. and one tenth of fine flour for a grain offering mixed with oil for each lamb. This is the burnt offering of a soothing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

---

v. 9. 10. On the Sabbath day, the daily divine service had to be doubled, as it were, with a double offering besides the usual daily one; thus, three times as much was offered as on a daily basis.

v. 11. *In the beginning of each of your months*) When the Jews caught sight of the new moon, a new month began for them, and it lasted until they caught sight of the new moon again, namely 29 and a half days approximately. Because in two months, two half-days made a whole one, some months had 29 days, while others had 30. If, when the 29th day was over, the new moon was seen that evening or the following night, the following 30th day became the first of the new month, and the previous month thus had 29 days. But if the moon was first seen on the evening after the 30th day, then the 31st day was the first of the new month, and the previous month thus received 30 days. They did not look for the appearance of the moon beyond that, nor would they have added another day if it had not yet been seen.

Because a great deal depended on this, as the festivals were calculated according to the moon (Sirach 43:7), the High Court <note>likely referring to the Sanhedrin</note> had oversight in this matter and ordained the New Moons. For this reason, they met on the 30th day, which was sometimes reckoned to the old month and sometimes to the new, and was immediately sanctified.

v. 12. 13. *Three — two — one*) These measurements were observed in all burnt and thank offerings, except only when the wave-sheaf was offered on the second day of Easter <note>original: "Ostertag," referring here to Passover/Unleavened Bread</note>. Leviticus 23:12, 13.

# 658 The IV. Book of Moses. Cap. XXVIII.

14. And their drink offerings: it shall be half a hin <term>hin: a liquid measure of about 4 liters; half a hin is roughly 2 liters</term> for the bull, and a third of a hin for the ram, and a fourth of a hin for the lamb, of wine. This is the burnt offering of the new moon at every new moon of the months of the year.
15. In addition, one male goat shall be prepared for a sin offering to the LORD, besides the regular burnt offering and its drink offering.
16. And in the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, is the Passover to the LORD.

<margin>v. 14. At every new moon</margin>
The New Moon is otherwise not to be found among the feasts in Leviticus 23. For what reason, one cannot know. Otherwise, mention of it has already been made here in Chapter 10:10. And it appears from 1 Samuel 20:27 that they celebrated not only the first day of the new moon, but also the last day of the previous month, because it also held something of the new light. And just as they could remind themselves of the Creation of the world on the Sabbath, so they could remind themselves of the Preservation and Governance of the same at the New Moon. They also used to go to the prophets on both of these days to seek counsel from the LORD. 2 Kings 4:23. They also had their special meals upon it. 1 Samuel 20:5, 24.

However, "New-Light" <note>the lunar phase of the new moon</note> occurs when the moon stands closest to the sun, and thus is swallowed up by its clarity. When, therefore, the Church or the soul stands in union with Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, and is near to him, she celebrates the true feast of the New Moon. Then she can also be least recognized and perceived by natural men, just like the moon. For her life is hidden with Christ in God: and when a soul has united itself entirely with the LORD, and entered into the brilliance of His light—so that she thinks of nothing earthly anymore, seeks nothing temporal, nor desires to please men, but yields herself entirely to Wisdom, entirely to the Light, and entirely to the warmth of the Holy Spirit as a bondservant—then she becomes entirely spiritual. And how then shall she be seen by men, or recognized by the natural mind? Since indeed the natural man does not perceive what is of the Spirit of God, and cannot recognize it. <note>Refers to 1 Corinthians 2:14.</note>

Thus, the New Moon especially signified the renewal of the creature through the new light of Grace, which has dawned in Christ: just as the Apostle says, that in Christ nothing counts but a new creature; the old has passed away, and all has become new. 2 Corinthians 5:17. Therefore, the New Moons also had to give way as shadows. Colossians 2:16–17.

<margin>v. 15.</margin>
But since in Christendom, almost throughout every month—though not strictly at the time of the new light, but according to voluntary and various determinations—a day of Penance and Prayer <note>German: "Buß- und Bet-Tag"</note> is appointed to specifically take to heart the sins that are prevalent monthly in public, just as here on this day a sin offering was specifically ordained (and not daily, nor on the Sabbaths); so one can well say that this also was foreseen and prophesied for the time of the New Testament in Isaiah 66:23. And that one should not complain about "human commands" regarding such an edifying arrangement, because this is indeed most necessary for the awakening of repentance given the great imperfection of the outward Church.

<margin>v. 16.</margin>
Next, the two feasts of Easter <note>Passover</note> and Pentecost are repeated here in succession with their offerings, which had to be celebrated in the first half of the year, in the first and second months of the year.

<margin>v. 17. 18.</margin>
Among which is also to be understood the feast of the second day after the Sabbath of the first Passover day, when the holy assembly was and no servile work was allowed to occur, on which the first sheaf of their harvest had to be waved before the LORD. Leviticus 23:10–11. Where also the mystery of the death and slaughter of the Passover Lamb, and the resurrection of Christ in the waving of this first sheaf, was treated.

<margin>v. 19-23.</margin>
After the daily morning offering—which occurred daily as well as on all feast days, and must not be omitted, no matter how many offerings were to be sacrificed during the day—the regularly established festival offerings followed. These had to be sacrificed daily for as long as the feast lasted, along with the associated grain and drink offerings, as a burnt offering, together with a goat for a sin offering, which the priests afterwards consumed.

<margin>v. 24.</margin>
There, while the drink offering was poured out by the priests, trumpets were blown, and the Levites sang and made music; the whole congregation also sang along with their singer the Hallelujah <note>original: "Halleluiah"</note> or the 6 Psalms of David, from 113 to 118, just as on the New Moons as well (a).

<note>Concerning the Feast of Pentecost, as the prefiguration <note>original: "Fürbild"</note> of the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, it is also treated in the aforementioned place where the Passover was discussed.</note>
<margin>v. 27--29.</margin> This is to be noted here: that the offerings for both feasts were the same in terms of the animals and gifts brought for the grain and drink offerings. However, for the first [Passover], this had to happen daily for seven full days; for Pentecost, on the other hand, it happened only on one day.
<margin>v. 30.</margin> So too must a sin offering be brought at both feasts, because in all our faithful remembrance of all the benefits of Christ, we must still always be mindful of the dying away of lusts and the putting to death of the "old man" <note>a theological term for the sinful human nature</note>.
<margin>v. 31.</margin> Furthermore, all the offerings had to be perfect; not only the animals, so that they were without defect and healthy, but the best and freshest flour had to be brought, which was not in the least bit musty; and no sour wine or cloudy oil, but that which was fresh, pure, and clear. For God otherwise complains about the deceitful heart when they brought Him something sick from the animals, or something damaged from the other gifts. Malachi 1:8, 14. This serves as a warning to the believers of the New Testament, that they should not have a deceitful heart in the physical blessings they dedicate to the honor of God: just as things went very poorly for Ananias and his wife Sapphira, which was meant to serve as an example to all others. Acts 5:1 etc.

This feast of the Lord was celebrated at the perfection of the early fruits.
If you now also wish to celebrate such a feast to the Lord, see to it that your field is well plowed and tended, and also how and where you sow, so that you may reap such fruits from which God may draw joy for the blessing of your soul. You will not be able to put this into practice unless you give ear to the Apostle, who says: "He who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life." <note>Galatians 6:8</note>. If you sow thus and reap thus, you will also be able to celebrate the feast of the first fruits. Whoever renews his heart and himself according to the inner man from day to day approaches it rightly, and does not sow among the thorns, but on good land that will bring him 30, 60, and a hundredfold fruit. But the fruit of the Spirit is first of all joy: and that belongs primarily to the right celebration of a true feast, in which God and His angels themselves have their delight.

# The XXIX. Chapter.
->The Feasts of the other half of the year.<-

1. And in the seventh month, on the first of the month, there shall be a holy assembly for you; you shall do no servile work at all: it shall be a day of blowing [trumpets] for you.
2. And you shall prepare a burnt offering for a pleasing aroma to the Lord; one bull, namely a young ox, one ram, seven lambs that are one year old and without blemish.

4. And one tenth-part for each lamb of the seven lambs.
5. And one male goat for a sin offering, to make atonement for you.

<insert>
In this chapter, the last three feasts in the second half of the year, which were celebrated together in the seventh month, are repeated, and the offerings for them are ordained, which had not been done previously. Leviticus 23:24 etc.
</insert>

<margin>v. 1.</margin> From the Feast of Pentecost onward, there was no annual feast until the month of Tishri <note>original: "Tifri"</note>, which was the seventh month starting from Nisan, in which several feasts occurred.
The first fell on the New Moon, or on the first of the month, when the civil New Year began, according to which they counted the years of the world.
Therefore, this day was a double feast day: once because it was exactly the New Moon, and then because a special blowing [of trumpets] was held on this New Moon, and special sacrifices were offered; regarding which:
<margin>v. 2--5.</margin> This festival offering differed from the standard New Moon offering in that for the New Moon, 2 bulls were brought for the burnt offering, but for the offering of the Festival of Blowing [Trumpets], only one.
<margin>v. 6.</margin> The daily morning offering was first in order: followed by the New Moon offerings, and after those, the special festival offerings.
And thus the New Year was consecrated with its burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink and sin offerings, as a prefiguration of how the New Year of Grace in Christ has brought us all these essential goods through Christ's sacrifice, so that in Him we might again become an acceptable offering in repentance, faith, and love.
<margin>v. 7.</margin>

23. And on the fourth day, ten bulls, two rams, fourteen lambs of one year, which are without blemish.

33. Together with their grain offering and their drink offerings, for the bulls, for the rams, and for the lambs, in their number, according to the ordinance.

<insert>
On this seventh day, the altar of burnt offering was surrounded with willow branches <note>original: "Weiden-Meyen" — fresh green willow boughs used for decoration</note>, each eleven ells long, so that the tips projected about one ell above the altar and were bent slightly over the top of the altar.

Something special also occurred at this festival on all seven days, which did not happen at any other time of the year: for the drink offering, not only wine but also water was offered, which was fetched from the Pool of Siloam. <note>The "Water Libation" ceremony was a joyous highlight of the festival, associated with prayers for rain and the Holy Spirit.</note>
</insert>

36. And you shall offer as a burnt offering, a fire offering of a pleasing aroma to the Lord, one bull, one ram, seven lambs of one year, which are without blemish:
37. Their grain offering and their drink offerings, for the bull, for the ram, and for the lambs, in their number, according to the ordinance.
38. And one goat for a sin offering; besides the regular burnt offering, with its grain offering and its drink offering.

<insert>
v. 35. **On the eighth day — a holy day)** This final day signifies the Holy Spirit of God, as is sufficiently given for us to understand in John 7:2, 10, 37-39; or rather, it is the Day of the Spirit.
Therefore, just as there is a difference in days according to the literal and outward sense, so it is also in the spiritual and inward sense.
The eighth day was, as many believe from John 7, the most glorious under the Law, because of the spiritual excellence of the eighth day, which is the true Day of the Lord.
v. 36. **One bull, one ram)** Thus, the festival offerings of this day were not identical to the previous ones; the number of bulls did not merely decrease by one, and there were not as many rams and lambs as on the previous days. <note>The numbers drop significantly on the eighth day to signify a new beginning or a singular focus.</note>
v. 37. O, if only someone were skilled here to fully remove the veil from the reading of the Old Testament, so that in all this sacrificial work they might fully perceive the mind of the Lord! Such a person would certainly recognize an astonishing wisdom therein, which otherwise becomes loathsome and tedious for the unintelligent to read so often! And that is without doubt also true of
**(In their number)** which now concludes here with this great solemn ceremony, and yet remains inclusive.
v. 38. **One goat for a sin offering)** Thus, in addition to the regular burnt offering, the festival sacrifices totaled 71 young bulls, 15 rams, 121 sheep, and 8 goats; which in total made 215 animals. Furthermore, all the priests and Levites had to be fed at this feast during the eight days.
Through this, the festival represents the great blessing—both spiritual and physical—in the glorious Kingdom of Christ, of which Isaiah speaks in Chapter 66:23 and 30:26, where this feast is explicitly aimed at, which they were to celebrate with great joy.
And although the mystery of the number of sacrifices—where the number of bulls always decreased—remains very hidden (until at the conclusion of all sacrifices in the designated feasts only one bull, one ram, seven lambs, the two lambs of the regular burnt offering, and one goat were offered), it likely points to the sacrifices in the mysterious Temple of Ezekiel. There, the sacrifices are not to be offered in such great quantities, but for this feast in the seventh month, only seven bulls, seven rams, and one goat are ordained daily for seven days. Generally, the decrease of the sacrifices and their power can be understood to continue until the one sacrifice, Christ, was offered. He is prefigured in the one bull for his patience and industriousness; in the one ram for his masculine gentleness; in the seven lambs for the seven spirits that rested upon him (Isaiah 11:2, Revelation 1:4); and in the one goat for the guilt of sin that lay upon him. And just as he would bring an end to all physical sacrifices, so by his death and resurrection, he would provide a glimpse into the eighth day, the time of the glorious Kingdom of Christ—indeed, even into blessed eternity itself.
</insert>

## The XXX. Chapter.

->Concerning vows, especially those of a daughter and a wife.<-

<columns>2</columns>

AND Moses spoke to the heads of the tribes of the children of Israel and said: This is the word that the Lord has commanded.

2. When a man vows a vow to the Lord, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not profane his word; he shall do according to all that has proceeded out of his mouth.

3. And when a woman vows a vow to the Lord and binds herself with a bond in her father’s house in her youth;

4. And her father hears her vow and her bond wherewith she has bound her soul, and her father remains silent toward her: then all her vows shall stand, and every bond wherewith she has bound her soul shall stand.

<margin>Vows in general were dealt with above in Leviticus 27:1, etc.</margin>

<margin>v. 2. etc. A vow)</margin> is when one promises God something of one's own: which can happen in various ways. Hannah vowed to God the fruit of her womb; another vows animals, houses, or similar inanimate things. A Nazirite vows himself to God: and that is above all other vows. For everything else is outside of us and is "something": but this is "everything," and leaves nothing remaining. Whoever makes this vow becomes like Christ.

<margin>Not profane)</margin> For everything that is vowed to God is holy: and no one is holy who does not truly vow himself to God, with a bond upon his soul. But what is holy must not be drawn away from God's service for any other use.

<column-break/>

5. But if her father forbids her on the day that he hears it; then none of her vows or her bonds wherewith she has bound her soul shall stand; and the Lord will be gracious to her, because her father forbade her.

6. And...

<margin>God intended here to confirm the authority of parents over their children and, in what follows, of husbands over their wives, so that they should not be authorized to undertake anything without their consent. And
If those things which were vowed to God could be broken and set aside—so that God would overlook it when a father or husband thought his child or wife had done it out of lack of understanding or haste—how much more can such promises made to men be set aside.</margin>

<margin>From this one also reasonably concludes that marriage bonds which occur without the parents' consent and will are entirely invalid: since children should do nothing in these important matters without the parents' advice and consent, so that they do not cause them much annoyance and heartache, as can be seen with Esau in Genesis 26:35.</margin>

<margin>The Savior once rebuked the Pharisees because they permitted children, against the parents' will, to dedicate something as a sacrificial gift which the parents themselves still needed; and they thereby withdrew the children from the dutiful honor toward father and mother—whom God wants honored as much as Himself—and which is therefore also to be understood as included here. Matthew 15:5.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore, since children with the parents' consent are sometimes encouraged quite young to make a vow to the Lord in Holy Communion; they should consider that they are nonetheless bound to observe the bond of their souls, even if they do not yet understand the mystery of faith so well, so that they are bound to take it to heart all the more eagerly as they grow in years. Indeed, the parents who brought them to this vow in childhood at Holy Communion have anew bound their own souls to be faithful to the Lord, and to renounce the world and all earthly lusts, and thus also to encourage their children to do the same; which are the very gifts one brings to the Lord through vows, of which the Psalm says: "Vow and pay to the Lord your God, all you who are around Him; bring gifts to the Terrible One," Psalm 76:12, who is indeed terrible to all such people who take their holy vows so little to heart and break them almost daily.</margin>

Since God is a Spirit, we must also grasp such an understanding from His words that is worthy of God as a Spirit. Thus, a soul that is still young in the ways of God and in spiritual growth—one who still stands in the first beginnings and requires milk-food—is to be viewed as a child who still stands under her parents. But when she grows up and becomes "marriageable" or capable of receiving the seed of the divine Word and perceiving the secret teaching of the Spirit, she is to be regarded as a wife who stands under a husband. But whoever grows up into a "perfect man" <margin>Ephesians 4:13.</margin> is master of his own vows. However, if the soul is still of a feminine or childlike nature and quality, she requires a leader to direct her paths, so that she does not lead herself astray through her own choices and outward appearances.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXIX.

39. These things you shall prepare for the Lord at your appointed times, besides your vows and your voluntary offerings, for your burnt offerings, your grain offerings, your drink offerings, and your peace offerings.

<margin>Besides your [vows])</margin> In the final five days of the seven-day Feast of Tabernacles, before the eighth day, all sorts of offerings were sacrificed alongside the ordinary ones; for instance, if someone owed an offering to the Lord, or had promised one, or wished to present one out of their own free will.

<column-break/>

40. And Moses spoke to the children of Israel according to all that the Lord had commanded Moses.

<margin>To the children of Israel)</margin> (Ephesians 2:12, Galatians 6:16.) If you belong to Israel, then this truly must concern you. But if it is to concern you, it must truly have a meaning that is applicable to you.

<margin>See to it then, that you may be provided with offerings for this feast of great joy, according to their exceedingly large number. For</margin>
We must keep this feast in gratitude for the life and the fruit of the Tree of Life within us, and for the rich growth or blessing of the oil and wine that we draw from it. Also, in thankful remembrance of how we have been able to dwell under the shadow of the Almighty and under the green branches and boughs—or new revelations of grace, strength, and peace—through all our wearisome pilgrimage in the wilderness. Also as a testimony of grateful praise that the Word, which became flesh <note>original: "das Wort, das Fleisch worden"; a reference to John 1:14</note>, still erects His tabernacle within us, and constantly overshadows us, shielding us from the burning rays of the fire of divine justice. It also serves to remind us that our rest should not be in transitory tabernacles or outward revelations, but that we travel onward as pilgrims and strangers, keeping a steady eye on the eternal house in heaven, the Tabernacle of God, into which we shall fully enter on the eighth day of the Spirit. When the sensing of these things becomes more genuine, powerful, and enduring in our spirits through the abundant overshadowing or opening of divine goodness and light, then that is the appointed and best time to celebrate this feast.

### The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXXI.

**3.** Then Moses spoke to the people and said: Let men among you arm themselves for the host, that they may set out against the Midianites to execute the vengeance of the Lord upon the Midianites.

<margin>v. 3-5.</margin> They were to have twelve thousand—a thousand from each tribe—arm themselves, those who would offer themselves quite voluntarily for this purpose, to carry out this vengeance. This also happened in later times under Gideon against the same Midianites, where the fully willing had to fight against them: Judges 7:3. This serves as a sign of how the people of the Lord, who will carry away the great victory in the latter days against the enemies of the Lord and their own enemies, will be purely volunteers. Psalm 110:2-3.
<margin>v. 6.</margin> The zealot for the Lord’s honor, Phinehas, was sent along with the holy vessels <margin>(a)</margin>, namely the Ark of the Covenant along with that which was within and near it: the tablets of the Law, the small jar of Manna, and the budding rod of Aaron. This was so that, before these signs of God's presence, they might hold themselves all the more closely to God, in order to bring about the victory over their enemies through faith in Him. Otherwise, Joshua was undoubtedly the leader of the host, as he had already been publicly appointed to that role. Chapter 27:17-21.
<margin>v. 7.</margin> Midianite means as much as "Strife" and "Contention." Proverbs 18:18. This, however, is a fruit of the flesh, against which one must fight, and the same must be suppressed and put to death through earnest resistance. Galatians 5:20.
Those now who give room to the spirit of contention in the Church are like those Israelites who united themselves with the daughters of the Midianites and brought wrath upon the congregation; therefore, wrath is announced to such people. Romans 2:8-9.
<margin>v. 8.</margin> They struck five kings, who according to Joshua 13:21-22 were mighty ones or princes of Sihon, and thus as his vassals. Among them was Zur, the father of the Midianite woman <note>Cozbi</note>, of whom mention is made in Chapter 25:15, 18.
Those who were previously overcome by the women have now also slain kings, after repentance and reconciliation followed. So much can conversion to God and the improvement of life achieve.
<margin>(a)</margin> Others understand by this the high-priestly garment with Urim and Thummim <note>Sacred lots used by the priest for divining the will of God</note>, or the Ephod <note>A ceremonial vestment worn by high priests</note>. 1 Samuel 23:9, 30:7.

<column-break/>

and Zur, and Hur, and Reba; five kings of the Midianites. They also slew Balaam, the son of Beor, with the sword. <margin>Joshua 13:22.</margin>
**9.** And the children of Israel took captive the women of the Midianites and their children, and they plundered all their cattle, all their livestock, and all their goods.
**10.** And they burned with fire all their cities with their dwellings and all their castles.
**11.** And they took all the spoil and all that was to be taken, of both humans and cattle.
**12.** And they brought the captives, the take, and the spoil to Moses and to Eleazar the priest and to the congregation of the children of Israel into the camp, upon the plains of the Moabites, which lie by the Jordan across from Jericho.

---

Undoubtedly, their names are expressed by Holy Scripture not merely for the sake of history, but much more for the sake of the mystery. Thereby are depicted the vices that rule in man above others, and the fleshly lusts which war against the soul, all of which depend upon the five senses. These five senses, which ruled among the Midianites unto offense, must likewise be slain; the eye that offends you plucked out, the hand and the foot that offend you cut off. By this, the fleshly sense is meant, not the physical limb. <note>An allegorical reference to Matthew 5:29-30.</note>

Thus also Balaam had to feel the divine judgment, who it seems still tarried with the Midianites at their seeking, and they sought counsel from him as to how they might yet prevail over the children of Israel. His evil counsel—however he may have intended it—turned out to his own destruction and failed him, so that the flesh had to be judged and come to ruin again, so that perhaps the spirit might be preserved, which must be left to God's secret and holy decree. Meanwhile, it is an example that every undertaking that one does not begin and continue rightly with God—even if one has much and beautiful knowledge whereby others are brought to God—finally turns out to the harm of the counselor.

<margin>v. 9.</margin> They took captive the women and children; they wished, it seems, to gladly let live what yet should not live, as was soon made known to them through the command of Moses.
All their livestock and goods) A large number of gold and silver vessels.
<margin>v. 10. They burned all their cities and castles with fire)</margin> To thus avenge the blaze of lewdness with the fire of passion that had been thrown into the camp of the Israelites by them.
<margin>v. 11. All the spoil)</margin> Of other useful and precious things besides the humans and cattle.
<margin>v. 12.</margin> They brought all captives and the spoil to Moses, and to the High Priest and the congregation, in order to show that they now left this glorious victory received from the Lord and the great booty entirely to the Lord's ordinance, and did not wish to seize the least of it for their own property nor keep anything for themselves.

v. 13. **Went out to meet them**) Out of honor to congratulate them / and to rejoice with them. Genesis 14:18. Exodus 15:5. Judges 5. 1 Kings 18:6, 7.

v. 14. **Moses was angry**) in whom the Spirit of GOD / which searches all things / well recognized the intentions / why they had done it / which is why he became angry.

v. 15. **All the women**) Even those who dealt you such an evil blow / that 24,000 perished because of it. <note>This refers to the plague at Baal-Peor described in Numbers 25.</note>

v. 16. **Through the counsel of Balaam**) Here it is now clearly expressed / what the counsel of Balaam consisted of / and that he, through the Midianite women, was the author of the stumbling block for the children of Israel.

v. 17. The heavy vengeance on the Midianites has its basis partly in the absolute power of GOD / which He has over us humans because of sin even from birth: but partly also GOD wanted to establish such a sharp example because of spiritual and physical harlotry / how both are highly hateful to Him. But here also, in a hidden spiritual sense / since Midian means as much as "strife" and "quarrel," it can represent the heavy vengeance that GOD will have executed in the last times on all the quarrelsome nature in religious and other matters against the authors and all their offspring / their polemical writings <note>original: "Zanck-Schrifften"</note> / as a sample of this was demonstrated in the first church in the time of the Apostles / when they brought together a great multitude of such polemical writings from the ancient philosophers and their idol-worshippers / and burned them; Acts 19:19. Whereby an example is given to the believers in the last times / how all such quarrelsome nature / which resists the truth / and only introduces sectarianism <note>original: "Sectirerey"</note> / as a part of spiritual harlotry / will be utterly destroyed by them.

v. 18. But as for what are innocent sciences / which have not been impregnated, as it were, by reason <note>This likely refers to secular knowledge or philosophies that have not been corrupted by human pride or false doctrine.</note>; they will be maintained in their state / indeed, brought to their right perfection. See 1 Timothy 6:4, 5. 2 Timothy 3:8, 9.

v. 19. 20. **You shall purify yourselves**) Through the sprinkling-water of the red heifer. ch. 19.

v. 21. **Men of the army -- in the war**) are not all among the people of GOD / but only some: and indeed those who do not entangle themselves in the worldly affairs of this life and sustenance. 2 Timothy 2:4. These go out to war / and fight against the enemies and against spiritual wickedness on behalf of the rest of the people / who are too weak either because of age / or gender / or courage.

v. 22. **You shall certainly**) not only now / but also in the future / do likewise with all the booty / that you bring away through victory in war.

v. 26. **And the heads**) So that the people would be all the more satisfied with it / and the matter would proceed all the more easily and quickly.

<margin>v. 43-45.</margin> Sheep — Cattle and Donkeys) Because these species are specifically mentioned, it is to be believed that no others were included in the division, even though Midian also had an abundance of camels and dromedaries. <note>See Isaiah 60:6.</note>

<margin>v. 46. The Humans)</margin> Namely, none other than the young virgins: for all the others had been put to death.

<margin>v. 47. One out of fifty)</margin> For there were far more Levites than there were Priests. <note>The Priests received 1 in 500 from the soldiers' half, while the Levites received 1 in 50 from the community's half.</note> Thus, the proportion was observed in two ways: first, that the Levites were granted ten times more than the Priests, and second, that the common people gave to the Levites, while the fighting men gave to the Priests.
The Levites therefore received 6,750 sheep, 720 cattle, 610 donkeys, and 320 virgins.
Regarding the <term>numerical mystery</term> of the 50 and 500, something may be brought forward on another occasion.

<margin>v. 48. That there are various ranks, ages, and spiritual degrees among the believing people of God is shown frequently throughout the Scriptures. And so we find here</margin>
**Commanders and Officers)** Whereas others are to be regarded merely as common soldiers.

<margin>v. 49. Not one man among us is missing)</margin> This was indeed a most wonderful victory, the likes of which has perhaps never occurred as long as the world has stood: that of the 12,000 who slaughtered and struck with the sword (see v. 19), not a single one perished. This is similar to another miraculous war involving the Midianites—specifically the descendants of those who escaped, whom the children of Israel likely did not reach—where the 300 men under Gideon were all preserved while the enemies slaughtered one another. <note>Judges 7:22.</note> Likewise, the wonderful victory of Jehoshaphat occurred when the enemies destroyed each other, and the army of Israel stood by with praise and thanks, watching without having to lift a hand. <note>2 Chronicles 20.</note> All of this is a glorious symbol and prototype of the great, magnificent victory in the latter days, which will also be won without loss among the believers, as prophesied more fully in Joel Chapter 3 and Revelation Chapter 19, where the plunder shall also be consecrated to the Lord; <note>Isaiah 23:18.</note> just as here the gift from the officers was placed in the Tabernacle of the Congregation as a memorial, and the believers shall also have their portion of it for their refreshment.

50. "Therefore we have brought an offering to the Lord, what every man found of golden jewelry: anklets and bracelets, rings, earrings, and girdles, to atone for our souls before the face of the Lord."

51. And Moses and Eleazar the priest took the gold from them, all kinds of fashioned jewelry.

52. And all the gold of the offering which they lifted up for the Lord was sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels, from the captains of thousands and from the captains of hundreds.

53. (For the men of the army had taken plunder, every man for himself.)

<margin>v. 50, 51. But they bring nothing but gold:</margin> for the best belongs to the Lord—that which adorns the head, the hands, and the feet; the intellect and the will; the works and the conduct—all fulfilled in obedience. This was done partly out of gratitude that they were all preserved, and partly **to atone for their souls** because of the oversight where, contrary to God's intention, they had allowed the Midianite women to live and brought them back as captives.

<margin>v. 52. 16,750 shekels)</margin> According to some calculations, nearly 700 pounds.

<margin>v. 53.</margin> O blessed is he who holds himself brave in the spiritual struggle and does not fear the enemy there, but rather slaughters and strikes down vices, evil customs, bad habits, slander, and judgmental spirits—acting as Midianites both within himself and his neighbor. Such a man of the army, one of the 12,000 <term>sealed ones</term> <note>A reference to the 144,000 in Revelation.</note>, will carry away enough plunder—indeed, the very crown of life!
Let us, oh dear ones, let us set out and fight the wars of the Lord!

<margin>v. 54. Let this memorial of the children of Israel also serve as a memorial for us, and give us an impression, even courage, to set out into the righteous war which the Lord Himself has publicly proclaimed from heaven, read aloud, and whose decrees He has posted everywhere in the depths of our souls! Genesis 3:15.</margin> What exquisite commanders and officers we have! The Son of the King rides ahead on a white horse to conquer. Oh, in Him we shall overcome and do great deeds! The goods of our enemies shall become ours, and the signs of victory shall stand forever as memorials before the face of our God!

### Chapter XXXII. The Fourth Book of Moses.

13. And the LORD’s anger was kindled against Israel, and He made them wander to and fro in the wilderness for forty years, until all the generation that had done evil in the sight of the LORD was brought to an end.

v. 13. Those who do not stand in this quality <note>meaning: those who lack faith or a right spirit</note>, nor rely upon the help of God, not only remain excluded from the inheritance of the promise, but must also spend a long time in the wilderness of misery, and, as it were, die a slow death.

**A multitude**) Whereas there were only ten of those <note>referring to the ten unfaithful spies mentioned in Numbers 13</note>.
v. 15. Moses saves the most important reason for last and brings it forward here: that they would be the cause of the total ruin of the people if the wrath of God were stirred up anew—a wrath which had already been held back twice through his intercession.
**Them**) Namely, the people of Israel.
v. 16. etc. Since they agree to help their brothers in the struggle, Moses grants their request, allowing them to receive this conquered land on this side of the Jordan <note>the eastern side</note> as their inheritance.
v. 17. **Because of the inhabitants**) Not of the land itself, which the two and a half tribes <note>original: "dritthalb" meaning two and a half (Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh)</note> wanted to have, for those inhabitants had been slain; but rather for the sake of the neighbors—the Ammonites, Edomites, and Moabites—whose prey they could easily have become.
v. 18. **We will not — until**) They indeed fulfilled this promise, though in such a way that only 40,000 armed men crossed over, according to Joshua 4:13. The rest remained in the fortified cities to protect their wives and children, because these two and a half tribes consisted of many more armed men—110,580 men according to Chapter 26, verses 7, 17, and 34. Thus, they were able to protect themselves against their enemies: the Moabites, Midianites, Amalekites, and Edomites; a situation to which the children of Israel willingly consented.

<column-break/>

19. For we will not inherit with them on the other side of the Jordan and beyond, because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan toward the sunrise.
20. And Moses said to them: If you will do this thing, that you will arm yourselves before the face of the LORD for war;
21. And every armed man of you will pass over the Jordan before the face of the LORD, until He has driven out His enemies from His sight,
22. And the land is subdued before the face of the LORD: then afterward you may return, and you shall be guiltless before the LORD and before Israel; and you shall have this land for a possession before the face of the LORD. <margin>Joshua 12:6.</margin>
23. But if you will not do so, behold, you have sinned against the LORD, and you will experience your sin when it finds you out.
24. Build cities for your children and folds for your sheep, and do what has proceeded out of your mouth.
25. And

---

v. 19. **Not beyond — on this side**) So it goes! When we see some happiness in this world before us, we satisfy ourselves with it as if it were rest itself, and we forget that we should continue toward the land of rest <note>a spiritual metaphor for heaven or the ultimate divine promise</note>.
v. 20–22. **If — then**) This teaches us how we must not abandon our brothers when we see them in conflict against their enemies. When they are tempted or attacked by them, we should not think that we can remain quietly in what is ours. Rather, we are then bound before the Lord to join with them and help them in the struggle, according to the ability that God grants to each. And if we can do nothing else, we should help them strive through prayer and sighing before God. Then we can also enjoy our rest in blessing before the face of the Lord. Just as Moses commands them both—to arm themselves and then to possess the land—to show how the latter would not be blessed without the former. John commands us in such a precious duty: that we should also lay down our lives for the brothers (1 John 3:16) when we see them in need and danger and are able to help them.
v. 23. **You will experience your sin when it finds you out**) This might well be said to every one of us: You will experience your sin when it finds you! It is good if we find it before it finds us, and judge ourselves, so that we might not be judged.
v. 24. **Do what has proceeded out of your mouth**) Here, but not always. <margin>Matthew 15:11, 18.</margin> <note>The commentator notes that while keeping an oath is good here, Jesus later teaches that what comes out of the mouth can also be defiling.</note>

### The Fourth Book of Moses, Chapter XXXII.

25. And one spoke from among the children of Gad and the children of Reuben to Moses and said: Your servants shall do as my Lord has commanded.
26. Our children, our wives, our possessions, and all our livestock shall remain there in the cities of Gilead.
27. But your servants shall all cross over, equipped for the army before the face of the Lord into the battle, just as my Lord speaks.
28. Then Moses gave a command concerning them to Eleazar the priest, and Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers of the tribes among the children of Israel;
29. And Moses spoke to them: If the children of Gad and the children of Reuben cross over the Jordan with you, everyone equipped for battle before the face of the Lord, and the land is subdued before you; then you shall give them the land of Gilead as a possession.
30. But if they do not cross over equipped with you, then they shall receive a possession among you in the land of Canaan.

---

<margin>v. 25. One)</margin> And they also acted as one and were of one mind in this matter.

<margin>v. 26. In the cities of Gilead)</margin> Of the entire region they had already brought under their control; Gilead, Bashan, and the land of the Amorites.

<margin>v. 27. As my Lord speaks) v. 20-22.</margin>

<margin>v. 28-30. The inheritance, or the twelve tribes of Israel to whom it is intended, encompass—according to the thoughts of Origen <note>original: "Origenis"</note> <meta>homily 26 on Numbers</meta>, by virtue of some hidden and secret reasons—the figure of the entire human race, or at least all those who attain the knowledge of God. Of these, one part receives its inheritance through Moses on this side of the Jordan, and one part on the other side in the Land of Promise through Joshua. Indeed, all those to whom their inheritance is determined on this side of the Jordan at their own request are firstborn. Reuben is the firstborn of Jacob, although he did not remain blameless because he went up to his father’s bed. And although Gad was born of a maidservant, he is also a firstborn. So too is Manasseh, although he was born of an Egyptian woman, yet he is a firstborn. These firstborn represent, therefore, the first people of the Law, who receive their inheritance on this side of the Jordan, not through Jesus Christ, but through Moses.</margin>

The reason why the first people or the first man <note>referencing 1 Corinthians 15:47</note> does not receive land and inheritance on the other side of the Jordan in the Holy Land is because he has much livestock, or is "animal-minded" <note>meaning focused on worldly or physical needs rather than spiritual ones</note>. For the natural man cannot recognize the things that are of the Spirit of God. And although the others also still have livestock and an animalistic sense, they do not have so much of it that it would hold them back from desiring and taking up their inheritance across the Jordan.

<column-break/>

31. And the children of Gad and the children of Reuben answered and said: As the Lord has spoken to your servants, so we will do.
32. We will cross over equipped before the face of the Lord into the land of Canaan: so that the possession of our inheritance on this side of the Jordan remains with us.
33. Thus Moses gave to them—to the children of Gad, the children of Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, the son of Joseph—the kingdom of Sihon, king of the Amorites, and the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan, the land with its cities within its borders; namely, the cities of the land round about.
34. Then the children of Gad built Dibon, and Ataroth, and Aroer;
35. And Atroth-Shophan, and Jazer, and Jogbehah;
36. And Beth-Nimrah, and Beth-Haran: namely, fortified cities and sheepfolds.
37. And the children of Reuben built Heshbon, and Elealeh, and Kiriathaim.
