Thus, every soul that believes in God reaches an inheritance after the exodus from the "Egypt" of this world; however, this inheritance is determined in one place for those who have lived under the Law, and in another for those who have stood in the faith and grace of Jesus Christ.

<margin>v. 32. Yet those who seem to be the first, and who stood under the administration of Moses, do not reach their determined inheritance until they go across the Jordan with the others who are led by Jesus <note>Note: The name Joshua (Josua) is the Hebrew equivalent of Jesus; the commentator is making a typological connection between the leader Joshua and Christ.</note>, marching equipped before them, fighting alongside them against their enemies, and thus bringing them into the peaceful possession of their inheritance; and this is exactly what Paul says in Hebrews 11:39-40.</margin>

<margin>v. 33. The half-tribe of Manasseh)</margin> This tribe was not mentioned as being among them previously.

According to the secret meaning, however, these are they who, in joy and pleasure, forget themselves in manifest sins; they do not consider that they must also cleanse themselves from all other sins and proceed toward the land of holiness; instead, they sit down and rest on this side of the Jordan (which means the water or river of judgment); they do not want to enter into judgment and do not cross over to the people of God.

<margin>v. 34. 37. Built)</margin> Anew upon the cities previously destroyed. Death goes before life, and preparation before renewal.

<margin>v. 35. Atroth-Shophan)</margin> This is one city, though the word is composed of two words.

<margin>v. 36. Beth)</margin> This is an addition that appears with many names, and in German <note>and English</note> it means a "House."

### Chapter XXXIII.
->The Journey and Encampments of Israel in the Wilderness.<-

These are the journeys of the children of Israel, who went out of the land of Egypt according to their armies, by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

Since the Lord commanded that all the encampments be gathered together—which the people of Israel had to keep from their first departure out of Egypt until the entrance into the promised land of Canaan, also by God’s command—He intended, through this wonderful detour, to instruct them all the more clearly regarding His miraculous leadership in these barren wildernesses, dangerous because of wild beasts, and regarding His omnipotence; so that they might henceforth rely on God in all needs, seeing how He wonderfully preserved them therein and could also deliver them from the same.

**Went out of the land of Egypt)** The figure of the exodus from Egypt can be understood according to the spirit in two ways. When someone is brought from the darkness of error to the light of knowledge, and from an earthly mind and pagan life to a spiritual and heavenly walk, he then goes out of the dark Egypt into the wilderness, wherein he is instructed in the divine laws and heavenly teachings and brought so far that he hastens across the Jordan into the promised land, or through the baptism of repentance into the grace of the Gospel and to Christ.

But there is also an exodus from Egypt when a soul leaves the darkness of this world and the blindness of physical nature and is brought into another land; there, when it departs from the body, or rather is clothed again with the body, it also comes into various encampments: whether it be the bosom of Abraham, as with Lazarus; or Paradise, as with the thief on the cross; or also another place, of which there are many in the Father’s house, through which a soul that has believed in God must pass until it comes to the river which makes glad and rejoices the city and the land of God, to obtain its inheritance there.

The Lord dictated them to Moses, who was only the Lord’s scribe. They are named and specified, some of which are not found in the previous history, while others which stand there (chapter 21) are passed over here in silence, and so it was given to Moses to write them: which indeed makes this narrative most significant; also from the interpretation of the Hebrew names, the deep foundation will become so much clearer, as they visibly confirm what Paul writes of the things that befell Israel in the wilderness in 1 Corinthians 10:11: namely, that they happened to them only as prefigurations <note>original: "Fürbildern"</note>.

<column-break/>

41. And Jair, the son of Manasseh, went and took their villages; and he called them Havoth-jair.
42. And Nobah went and took Kenath with its daughters <note>meaning the surrounding villages or suburbs</note>, and called it Nobah after his own name.

**He named them—after his own name)** We, however, should not name what we obtain from the world after the manner of the world with our own names, Psalm 49:12, but as Christians possess it in self-denial, as if we did not possess it. 1 Corinthians 7:30. Therefore we have much more reason, like Eve, to call all our goods a "Habel" <note>Abel, meaning vanity or breath</note> or vanity, rather than a "Cain" <note>meaning a possession or acquisition</note>; she indeed found herself greatly deceived in the latter, just as we would do if we wanted to rely upon them. But if we rather recognize the correctness of this, we can use these things in blessing according to the Lord’s will.

---

2. And Moses wrote down their departures in their journeys according to the command of the Lord, and these are their journeys according to their departures.

3. And

**Who is so skillful,** writes Origen, **and who has looked so deeply into the secret cabinet of God, that he might describe the dwelling places of this soul-journey and explain the hardships and refreshments of each one?** How in the first, second, and third, Pharaoh and the Egyptians still pursue, even if they cannot seize them. How thereafter, following the deliverance and several completed dwelling places, the first song of triumph is sung. Certainly, it is to be doubted that if someone wished to show the nature of these dwelling places according to the meaning of the names, the mind of the explainer would be as insufficient for the weight of such mysteries as the hearing of the listener would be to grasp it. For how would he then explain the war of the Amalekites, or the various temptations, or show who those are who fell in the wilderness, or explain what it signifies that the sons of Israel—not the fathers, but the sons of the sons of Israel—were able to come into the holy land, while the old people passed away entirely, who had lived among the Egyptians and associated with them? Only the new people, who had not known the Egyptians, entered into the promised land, except for the priests and Levites. Meanwhile, these dwelling places nevertheless also have their names. For it would not be fitting that every place under heaven should bear the name of a mountain or a hill or a field, while the dwelling places on the journey of a soul toward the kingdom of God had no names.

**By the command of the Lord)** It would be authority and proof enough for these journeys or encampments if they were only described at the command of the Lord. But it adds much to the authority of this journey, which comprises 42 stages or encampments of Israel, that Moses described them from or according to the mouth of the Lord; as the words may be given even more precisely; so that the Lord let these journeys flow and divided them...

<header>The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIII.</header>

3. **And they departed from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month; on the day after the Passover the children of Israel went out with a high hand in the sight of all the Egyptians.**

4. **For the Egyptians were burying all their firstborn, whom the LORD had struck down among them; and the LORD had also executed judgments upon their gods.**

5. **So the children of Israel departed from Rameses and camped in Succoth.**

<margin>(a) Exodus 12:37. Genesis 33:17.</margin>

**v. 3. (From Rameses)** A city and region in Egypt where the children of Israel had to assemble before they could march forth as a single army. Therefore, this departure from their various dwellings, in which they were scattered, and their gathering at this assembly point, is not unfairly counted as their first journey. This is done when the journeys are counted as 42 in number, according to the wonderful mystery by which Christ also came to us in this world through 42 generations. For from Abraham to David are 14 generations, and from David until the Babylonian captivity are 14, and from then until the birth of Christ are 14. *Matthew 1:17.* Thus Christ comes down to us through 42 steps, and we must go back up to Him through just as many, until we come to the beginning of the promised inheritance: where we must then make our first resting place where He had His last, He who was born of a virgin. And this also corresponds to the 42 months of time which the Church shall dwell in the wilderness. <note>This refers to the "forty and two months" mentioned in Revelation 11:2 and 13:5, often interpreted by Pietists as a period of spiritual testing or the duration of the world-age.</note>

**On the 15th day of the first month)** Nisan or Abib; in April according to our calendars. The Hebrews used to begin their New Year according to nature, when all things begin to turn green and grow anew.

**The day after the Passover)** That is, on the Feast of Unleavened Bread, after they had slaughtered and eaten the Easter Lamb <note>original: "Oster-Lamm"; in this period, the German word for Passover was often synonymous with Easter</note> the day before.

When we become conformed to the death of Christ—the slain Lamb—and begin to sweep out the old leaven of malice and godlessness, then this journey is undertaken.

**Rameses** signifies the melting away and dissolution of sin and unrighteousness, which decays and consumes itself through conformity with the death of the Lamb.

**v. 4. (Upon their gods)** And thereby upon the devil and the unclean spirits themselves who hide behind them. We must, however, take careful heed that we do not reawaken within ourselves the firstborn of the Egyptians and their gods, which the Lord has struck down, to work that which the Lord hates.

**v. 5. (Departed from Rameses)** 2 miles.

According to the mystery hidden therein, and upon which the Holy Spirit has fixed His eye, Rameses is a very fitting word to represent the beginning of the new birth. For as soon as we begin to leave Egypt—or the earthly life with its corruption and the murky waters of Sihor <note>original: "trüben Wassern Sihors"; Sihor is a biblical name for the Nile, here representing worldly life</note>—and earnestly set ourselves toward heaven, sin immediately begins to melt away or decrease. And with the decrease of sin, conversion takes its beginning.

**(Camped in Succoth)** In huts, booths, or tents, which were first erected there; *Leviticus 23:43.* from which God the Lord took the first occasion to institute the Feast of Tabernacles.

This represents to us the state in which we now begin to conduct ourselves as people torn loose from the world and as strangers, who journey until they find a city that has foundations, whose builder and maker is GOD. *Hebrews 11:10.*

The word **Succoth** also signifies as much as "covering" or "protection," and thus the protection and watch of such holy pilgrims who enjoy the presence of God, who accompanies them on all their ways, according to the promise in *Isaiah 44:2, 3.*

<column-break/>

6. **And they departed from Succoth and camped in Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness.**

7. **And they departed from Etham and turned back toward Pi-Hahiroth, which is opposite Baal-Zephon, and they camped before Migdol.**

<margin>(a) Exodus 14:2, 9.</margin>

**v. 6. (They departed from Succoth)** 8 miles.

**(Camped in Etham)** This means (1) perfection, sincerity, integrity; (2) as much as "their plows."

When we resolve to follow GOD without any condition, which is a kind of perfection, we find ourselves in this state and camp. Thus, this camp of Israel represents those souls who have come to the state of unfeigned sincerity and strive with all their might to subject themselves to the will of GOD and work toward perfection.

The means by which the soul is brought to such earnest inwardness in the inner work and exercise is likewise contained in the spiritual interpretation of this name: for the **plowshare** represents the spiritual turning inward into oneself, whereby our souls—which according to the unregenerate part are a wilderness—shall be so cultivated that they no longer bear the thorns and thistles of earthly lusts and desires, but bring fruit to GOD, according to the Spirit’s exhortation in *Hosea 10:12.* whereby we become God's field-work <note>or "husbandry"</note>, according to Paul’s saying in *1 Corinthians 3:9.* And if we work faithfully in this labor, we shall thereby participate in the inner guidance and protection of our Immanuel, as in the Pillar of Cloud and Fire, which appeared for the first time at this camp. *Exodus 13:20.*

**(At the edge of the wilderness)** or at the entrance to the wilderness. It is sometimes called the Wilderness of Etham, and sometimes the Wilderness of Shur. *Exodus 15:22.*

**v. 7. (They departed from Etham)** over 4 miles.

**(Turned back toward Pi-Hahiroth)** The word signifies as much as "the mouth of freedoms," and thus the interpretation is made true here. For:

This place was indeed at first a place of great distress for the children of Israel, and also of great danger if they had been left to themselves; but it was also a place of deliverance and salvation from the pursuing Pharaoh, in which the mercy of the Lord revealed itself so gloriously.

By means of an earnest inwardness in the inner work of the new birth, by watching over our ways, and walking sincerely in the light we have received, we reach true freedom from the captivity and the snares of sin and Satan. At the same time, however, the false and impermissible freedom is also indicated, through which we can fall into danger of a relapse if we allow ourselves to be convinced of a false concept of grace. Oh, how many has Satan ensnared through this, leading them back to a false rest and fleshly security after they had made a good beginning! Therefore, this is a dangerous state, just like Pi-Hahiroth.

**(Opposite Baal-Zephon)** Likewise, the state of false freedom is situated in Satan's territory, who is the great Baal-Zephon, or "Lord of Hiding," and is always vigilant to do harm to the Church of God. It is said that a small town or idol-temple stood on a high mountain by the Red Sea and was called Baal-Zephon, in which there was an idol that, according to the opinion of the Hebrews, was intended to prevent the fleeing Egyptian slaves from escaping out of Egypt.

**(Camped)** Between the mountains located there and near the Red Sea, which were placed apart and split as if enclosed by one another.

**(Before Migdol)** Which signifies a "tower," and was an accessory and excellence; and according to the inward sense, it signifies the temptations one has regarding the honor and glory of this world, which Christ also had to endure. *Matthew 4.*

8. And they departed from **Pi-Hahiroth**, and passed through the midst of the sea <margin>(a) Wisdom of Solomon 19:7.</margin> into the wilderness, and went three **days’ journey** in the wilderness of **Etham**, and camped in **Marah**.
9. And they departed from **Marah**, and came unto **Elim**; and in **Elim** were twelve **fountains of water**, and seventy **palm trees**; and they camped there.
10. And they departed from **Elim**, and camped by the **Red Sea** <note>original: "Schilfmeer," literally "Sea of Reeds."</note>.

---

<margin>1 Corinthians 10:2.</margin>
v. 8. *Midst of the sea*) This signifies the **baptism of suffering**, intended to further wean us from the pomp and pleasures of the world. Just as all manner of blessings grow for the children of **GOD** out of the **wrathful attributes of GOD**, so conversely, nothing but downfall and destruction arises therefrom for His and their enemies, as happened with the Egyptians.
*Went*) about 10 miles <note>The "German mile" used here was significantly longer than a modern English mile, roughly 4.5 miles or 7.5 kilometers.</note>.
*Three days’ journey*) Not that they did not rest in any way on the entire journey from the Red Sea to **Canaan**, but that on this entire stretch no proper encampments were made. For otherwise, it is beyond doubt that during such a time they rested a little at least twice a day in this wilderness to refresh themselves with necessary food and sleep. But because this happened only under the open sky and not by pitching tents, it is not counted among the official camping stations.
*Camped in Marah*) That is, "Bitterness," named thus after its waters. Exodus 15:23. Here, the joy felt over the destruction of the Egyptians was soon turned into mourning. For in the state of the spiritual wilderness, joy seldom lasts long. All these are living representations of new and great sufferings that usually follow great joys in the inward process—joys such as **Israel** enjoyed on the shore of the sea when they saw their enemies dead.
v. 9. *Departed from Marah*) 2 miles.
*Came to Elim*) That means "Powers," "Strength," or the "mighty angels of **GOD**." It was therefore a place named after life-giving and strengthening names. It is also said to have been named thus because many stags and hinds were often seen around the 12 **fountains of water** and palms, and thus in German it could be called **Hirschfeld** <note>"Deer-field."</note>.
*12 fountains of water*) represent the spiritual refreshment that is guided by the Holy Spirit onto the whole Church, which is prefigured by the 12 tribes of **Israel**. Likewise, the 12 **Apostles** of our **Savior**, through whom, as so many instruments, the streams of heavenly light, life, and comfort were channeled elsewhere; whose pure teachings are also of no small help to Christian wanderers and holy **pilgrims** on their journey.
*70 palm trees*) By which the **Presiding Angels**, who rule the world under **GOD**, may be depicted, according to the number of the 70 elders and the 70 disciples of **Christ**. Luke 10:1. For the Jews generally hold that things below express things above, and that 70 angels, who surround the throne of glory, are appointed as overseers of the generations on earth.
v. 10. *Here they camped by the sea*) through which they had previously passed. Because we so easily forget the most remarkable judgments and **tokens of GOD's grace**, it is necessary that we be reminded of them again, so that we may be both humbled and awakened to more eagerly consider and admire the astonishing effects of both the wrathful and loving attributes of **GOD** before His face.

<column-break/>

11. And they removed from the **Red Sea**, and encamped in the wilderness of **Sin**.
12. And they took their journey out of the wilderness of **Sin**, and encamped in **Dophkah**.
13. And they departed from **Dophkah**, and encamped in **Alush**.
14. And they departed from **Alush**, and encamped in **Rephidim**, where there was no water for the people to drink. <margin>Exodus 17:1.</margin>

---

v. 11. *Departed from the Red Sea*) 3 miles.
This **Sea of Edom** (from which it is also called the Red Sea) signifies that suffering which is common to flesh and blood, or **Edom**, the earthly man; of which Paul speaks in 1 Corinthians 10:13.
*Sin*) however, signifies "thornbushes," "hatred," "envy," and "grudge." When we move on from overcoming that temptation which is common to man, we are hated by men, who are like thorns in our sides. It was here that the **Israelites** conceived a hostility against their leaders. Exodus 16:2-3. Sinful desires and fleshly hostilities are like hedges and thorns in a person's heart, which torment the one in whom they arise. This camp of **Israel** reveals how inclined man is to manifest his murmuring and discontent against the sharp chastenings that temptation imposes upon him, and through which the flesh is driven into some distress and suffering. Against this, however, we should rather apply ourselves to composure and contentment in the will of **GOD**, who seeks our best. This was the wilderness in which the Lord, to save His honor, let **Manna** rain from heaven, Exodus 16:14, Wisdom of Solomon 16:20, as an image of the inward soul-nourishment, the power of the living Word, with which the Lord feeds the spiritual **pilgrims**.
v. 12. *Dophkah*) i.e., "striking," "knocking," "beating"; when inward hatred breaks out into blows. The closer we come to the heavenly **Canaan**, the more and greater hatred we must expect from our external and internal enemies. But it also means "to knock," and points to the earnest effort of **GOD** to penetrate deeper into our hearts. Revelation 3:20. It may also signify an earnest **knocking in prayer** and intercession to remain faithful under those trials.
v. 13. *Departed from Dophkah*) 3 miles.
*Encamped in Alush*) This and the previous journey are not mentioned with distinct words in the preceding history, but it seems they are included in Exodus 17:1. **Alush** has its name from "kneading," "leavening," or mixing water and sourdough with flour, and thus represents the Kingdom of **GOD** in us, as it is compared in Matthew 13:33. After earnest prayer, the Kingdom of **GOD** begins to move within us anew and leads us into the interior, so that we take heed in the silence how the leaven of the Kingdom secretly and gradually transforms us into its nature. In this state, the soul increases gloriously when we begin to stay more at home <note>A Pietist metaphor for inward meditation and self-examination.</note>, seeking the Kingdom of **GOD** within ourselves.
v. 14. *Departed from Alush*) 2 miles.
*In Rephidim*) The "wearying" or "weakening of the hands," as well as the "healing" and "strengthening of the hands." The former occurred here due to the lack of water; the latter upon its subsequent inflow. So changeable is the state in the wilderness. When we find ourselves in the utmost soul-drought and abandonment, so that one might almost ask whether **GOD** is indeed gracious to us; then Christ, the Rock of our salvation, opens at His own hour a brook of comfort and a streamlet of divine refreshment in us, to convince us thereby that **GOD** is faithful and will not allow us to be tempted beyond our ability. 1 Corinthians 10:4, 13.

<header>The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXXIII.</header>

**15. And they departed from Rephidim,**
**and camped in the Wilderness of Sinai.**
**16. And they departed from the Wilderness**
**of Sinai, and camped at the Graves of Lust.** <note>original: "Lustgräbern," traditionally known as Kibroth-Hattaavah.</note> c. 11:34.

v. 15. *Sinai*) and *Sin* (v. 11) mean the same thing, only in *Sinai* a <insert>י</insert> <note>The Hebrew letter Yod.</note> has been added; which in numbering signifies 10, and therefore may express the 10 Commandments that were given there, as the Jews note.

When we reach this state according to our **inner process**, we will know and feel the fire in which the Law was given. It will awaken a living sensation of that attribute of **GOD** which we otherwise tend to call His **Justice**: whereby the understanding of the words, *our God is a consuming fire* (Hebrews 12:29), is unlocked for us; and from which, as an immediate effect, zeal and enmity against sin arise. In this state, however, one may also be led into all sorts of judgments and exercise too great a severity toward others in things that seem sinful to him.

One can otherwise quite fittingly divide all the camping stations of this chapter into three parts: the first journey extends to this point in the Wilderness of Sinai, where they received the Law. The second journey can be taken as far as Mount Hor, upon which Aaron had to ascend and die (v. 37, 38, 39). The third journey from there to Mount Nebo, upon which Moses had to die (Deuteronomy 34:1, etc.).

Just as this journey through the wilderness is an image of the **pilgrimage of believers**, which they accomplish through the wilderness of this world toward the heavenly Canaan under the wonderful governance of **GOD**—wherein **GOD** also seems to lead them through wondrous detours until He brings them to a blessed eternity—so one can also remarkably notice three "states" here, which can be represented by these three noteworthy camping stations, which the Apostle also describes in Romans 7. First, the state in which one lives without the Law (v. 9 and previously v. 7). Afterward, under the Law (v. 8, 10, etc.). And then under grace in Christ (v. 17, etc.).

Up to this point, in the Wilderness of Sinai at Mount Horeb from which the Law was given, there were eleven camping stations, as they are mostly named in the Second Book of Moses <note>Exodus</note>: c. 12:37 Succoth; c. 13:20 Etham; c. 14:2 Pi-hahiroth; c. 15:23 Marah; v. 27 Elim; c. 16:1 the Wilderness of Sin; c. 17:1 Rephidim; c. 19:2 the Wilderness of Sinai. Note that those at the Red Sea, Dophkah, and Alush were omitted here, perhaps because nothing noteworthy occurred there.

All the names and events at these places can also represent the various dispositions of the soul in such a state, where one lives as if without the Law in ignorance and security; yet **GOD** does not cease to knock through all kinds of temptations, thereby drawing the soul to the knowledge of Himself—which is the "drawing of the Father." There, lack, adversity, and the like must discover the evil condition of man in his murmuring and discontent, to see if he will turn to **GOD** and thus be made worthy of His gracious guidance; whereby **GOD** also tends to entice through physical blessings, as happened in Elim, to see if one would notice how **GOD** is a most benevolent Being (Acts 14:17). During this time, however, man mostly remains in ignorance (Acts 17:30).

v. 16. *They departed from the Wilderness of Sinai*) 2 miles. <note>Approximately 9 modern miles.</note>

*Camped at the Graves of Lust*) Named so by the Lord Himself.

After we have recognized and felt the purity and power of the **Love of GOD** inwardly, we must also come to the condemnation, death, and burial of all evil lusts and desires, whether they be coarse or subtle, so that we may in this manner perfect our sanctification in the fear of **GOD**. The body of sin must be weakened, and all disorderly lusts and desires killed and buried, so that we may rise again and walk in a new life (Romans 6:4). On the other hand, there is no greater judgment than when **GOD** gives us over to our own extravagant desires and lets us enjoy them according to our own will.

Hosea 14:6 <note>Likely referencing the watering of the soul.</note> Such pure inner streams of goodness have been purified through earnest supplication.

**17. And they departed from the**
**Graves of Lust, and camped in Hazeroth.**
**18. And they departed from Hazeroth,**
**and camped in Rithmah.**
**19. And they departed from Rithmah,**
**and camped in Rimmon-Parez.**

**20. And they departed from Rimmon-**
**Parez, and camped in Libnah.**
**21. And they departed from Libnah, and**
**camped in Rissah.**

<meta>catchword: 22. And</meta>

v. 17. *They departed from the Graves of Lust*) 2 miles.
*Hazeroth*) signifies a trembling and fearful division, and clearly represents what occurred here when Miriam and Aaron went against Moses (c. 12:1, 2), which we are then also to regard as a prefiguration and example of the truth.

v. 18. *They departed from Hazeroth*) 2 miles.
*Camped in Rithmah*) This place received its name from the juniper trees growing there, and in German might be called *Wacholdern* <note>Juniper</note>. It seems believable to some that Elijah rested here under a juniper tree.

The word also means as much as a "binding." The whole company was bound together here with unbelief and faint-heartedness and hindered from continuing their journey (c. 14:1-3). And when we give ear to those spirits who want to make us timid and speak unbelief into us, we have the same to fear on our journey.

v. 19. *They departed from Rithmah*) One and a half miles.
*Rimmon-Parez*) signifies a "Pomegranate-Breach," as well as a trembling because of the breaking due to exaltation.

The Israelites were so daring here—despite having been in the utmost faint-heartedness and entirely disinclined shortly before to venture into the war against the Canaanites—that they now went up the hill against Moses’ command and without the Ark of the Covenant of **GOD**, wanting to be ready and determined all at once, even if contrary to the command of the **LORD**. This turned out very poorly for them. From this misstep and the resulting defeat, the name "Breach of Exaltation" is derived.

Thus, man is easily carried away from timidity to immoderation, from Rithmah to Rimmon-Parez, through the influence of Satan and the instability of our own nature.

v. 20. *They departed from Rimmon-Parez*) One and a half miles.

Tribulation because of past exaltation tends to work a humiliation, purification, and holy prayer (Isaiah 26:16). Therefore, one comes from there
*Into Libnah*) that is, "Incense-Castle" or "White-Castle."
The word from which this name arises also means to "become white," and according to the spiritual sense, to be washed and purified from the stains of sin (Psalm 51:9; Daniel 12:10).

It also means as much as "incense," which is an image of the spirit of prayer (Psalm 141:2; Revelation 5:8).

As long as we are in the inner wilderness, the sorrow that falls upon us because of our sins (so that they may be turned away and prevented) should purify us more and more and awaken us to earnest prayer. Thus the believers wandered out of the wilderness like pillars of smoke, with the incense of myrrh, frankincense, and all sorts of powders of the merchant (Song of Solomon 3:6).

v. 21. *They departed from Libnah*) One and a half miles.
*Rissah*) signifies as much as a "sprinkling," "dew," and "moistening" or "heavenly dew," and expresses the fruit of purification and earnest prayer.

Spiritual refreshments follow the trials, like a steady growth of what the **LORD** has planted in us. These divine comforts, which are as it were spiritual waterings of the soul, are often presented under the names of dew and rain. The blessings of **GOD** generally tend to follow after sins have been purified through earnest supplication.

<summary>This page provides a spiritual and typological interpretation of the Israelite camping stations from Sinai to Rissah, equating the geographical journey to the "inner process" of a believer's soul. It emphasizes the progression from the Law to the burial of lusts, through trials of unbelief and pride, toward spiritual purification and prayer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the allegorical commentary on the stations of the Exodus. ### Chapter XXXIII. The Fourth Book of Moses (Numbers).

22. And they departed from Rissa, and camped in Kehelatha.
23. And they departed from Kehelatha, and camped in Mount Sapher.
24. And they departed from Mount Sapher, and camped in Haradah.
25. And they departed from Haradah, and camped in Makheloth.

---

v. 22. They departed from Rissa) One and a half miles.
**Kehelatha**) signifies a gathering, an assembly, particularly one established for the exercise of godliness and the service of **GOD**: Psalm 22:22 <note>Original: "Ps. 22/13." The author likely refers to the "great congregation" mentioned in Psalm 22:25 (v. 23 in German numbering).</note>, Ecclesiastes 1:1. Because the word here has an added suffix, it may signify a more frequent and earnest gathering to wait upon the Lord. 
After the soul has enjoyed all kinds of divine refreshments and sweet inward fellowship with **GOD**, the holy pilgrim is finally brought to more frequent and earnest assembly to worship **GOD** in spirit and in truth. Through this, the soul becomes a partaker of His purest and living power, thereby confirming the truth of the Scriptures.
However, in a more precise sense, the word Kehelatha may also indicate the diligence and earnest effort to gather oneself and all one's soul-powers into One, in order to more conveniently wait upon the great **GOD** and perceive the inward inspirations of His Spirit, so that the soul may be brought into a more complete and sincere obedience. Psalm 86:11.

v. 23. They departed from Kehelatha) 1 mile.
**Sapher**) could be rendered as "Beautiful Field" or "Beautiful Dwellings." For it means as much as beauty, loveliness, pleasantness, or a lovely trumpet or horn. 
Spiritual growth, which must be maintained through frequent and earnest coming together in the service of **GOD**, prepares the soul and leads it there. It carries the soul beyond outward and sensible things and the animal part of nature, raising it to the state of divine contemplation, in which it beholds the loveliness and beauty of inward, spiritual, and eternal things; either in the understanding, or by means of such a representation, sight, and enjoyment as happened to the disciples on the mountain. Matthew 17.
The end of such a sensation, however, is our spiritual growth and also to make us into a lovely trumpet that proclaims the Lord's word and will.

v. 24. They departed from Mount Sapher) One and a half miles.
**Haradah**) indicates a great fear and trembling. Genesis 27:33, Exodus 19:16, 1 Samuel 14:15.
The state in the wilderness is subject to many such alternations. 
After we have been upon the mountain of divine revelations and lovely openings, we must expect to be led again into a state of humiliation, so that we do not become conceited, but are proven in lowliness under the cross of Christ. And we may fall into such circumstances through all sorts of accidents.

v. 25. They departed from Haradah) 1 mile.
**Makheloth**) means assemblies or gatherings in the plural number, just as *Kehelath* in v. 22 was in the singular. 
The Church, as long as it is in the state of the wilderness, is divided into many churches, which differ from one another in opinions and forms. 
Some hold that this camp received its name from the rebellious company of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram. ch. 16.
Certainly, in the present state, there are no means available that one could use as legitimate to remedy the manifold opinions and forms in divine worship into which the Church has fallen; since infallible leaders and prophets are no longer present. If only **GOD** may be honored in spirit and in truth among all those various opinions and forms, it is nonetheless to be regarded as a work of God's providence: just as such forms may not be displeasing to the Lord, if only the zeal for holiness remains greater than the zeal for opinions, and thus the healing ground of love is kept alive.

<column-break/>

26. And they departed from Makheloth, and camped in Tahath.
27. And they departed from Tahath, and camped in Terah.
28. And they departed from Terah, and camped in Mithkah.
29. And 

---

v. 26. Accordingly, various kinds of assemblies may be indicated by the word Makheloth: such as (1) rebellious and seditious groupings that aim at the disruption and abolition of Christian friendship, love, and community, due to mere opinions or even worse intentions; (2) the manifold church and religious constitutions, along with their attachments to different opinions and forms of worship. 
However, this camp also signifies a confluence and connection of inward holy influences that proceed from **GOD’s** Spirit and angels, to assist us against the subtle temptations and scatterings of Satan.
They departed from Makheloth) 1 mile.
**Tahath**) means as much as "below," "lowly," "contrition," or "breaking"; and indicates that the rebellious grouping and restless church-gathering, in a natural and just consequence, brings nothing other than sharp rods and chastisements along with all sorts of spiritual breakings: and that the best means to keep the divided assemblies in peace is to camp in deep humility, self-abasement, and brokenness of spirit; and so also the best means to overcome the rebellious assemblies of the inner peoples and fallen spirits—who incite us through their suggestions to leave the light of life—is to throw oneself into the deep valley of self-denial. Matthew 11:29.

v. 27. They departed from Tahath) 1 mile.
**Terah**) means as much as rest, a taking of breath, or a refreshment, such as one perceives in hot weather when a lovely breeze blows. 
When we are smothered in humility and bow down to the cross of Christ, we are thereby made fit for divine refreshments and the pure comforts of the Holy Spirit: the eternal wind and breath of **GOD** enlivens and refreshes the inner man, as a healthy air and cool wind does the outer man. 
It also means to smell or perceive, Isaiah 11:3, and may express the opening of our inward senses and the extraordinary sensations which they enjoy; 1 John 1:1, especially the angelic scents with which the soul is most sweetly touched. For though these sensations belong among the least of the Lord's special leadings, He nonetheless sees fit to use them at times to refresh some of His pilgrims in this howling wilderness.

v. 28. They departed from Terah) 1 mile.
**Camped in Mithkah**) that is, "sweetness," which here must be understood spiritually, and is infused into the soul by means of fellowship with **GOD**.
This sweetness is of two kinds: one which touches the understanding and arises from its activity, such as hearing, reading, or meditating: Psalm 104:34. And one that flows from the sensation which opens itself in the soul through various means. 
The same comes and goes in a freer and more hidden way than the sudden blowing of the wind and the fresh breathing of the unrestricted air. Often it is awakened by the reading and hearing of the Scripture. Psalm 119:103. Luke 24:32. 
The noblest, most divine, and most sensible sweetness is expressed by Paul in Romans 5:5, which opens itself to our inward feeling through inexpressible sweetness and the deepest sensation of divine delight, whereby the innermost ground of the soul is penetrated and swallowed up in living touches of the divine nature. 
The effects that these divine sensations leave behind are indeed not a little conducive to spiritual perfection: yet there may be few who have much experience of the latter kind in the state of the wilderness. For it is the beginning of the new wine of the Kingdom, and a deep enjoyment of the powers of the Gospel.

<summary>This page provides a spiritual and etymological commentary on the stations of the Israelites' journey from Kehelatha to Mithkah, interpreting each place name as a stage of the soul's progress through humility, gathering, and divine sweetness.</summary>

### The Fourth Book of Moses, Chapter XXXIII.

**29.** And they journeyed from **Mithka**, and camped in **Hasmona**.

**30.** And they journeyed from **Hasmona**, and camped in **Moseroth**.

**31.** And they journeyed from **Moseroth**, and camped in **Bene Jaakan**.

**32.** And they journeyed from **Bene Jaakan**, and camped in **Hor Hagidgad**.

**33.** And they journeyed from **Hor Hagidgad**, and camped in **Jotbatha**.

**34.** And they journeyed from **Jotbatha**, and camped in **Abrona**.

<margin>1 Kings 9:26.</margin>
**35.** And they journeyed from **Abrona**, and camped in **Ezion-Gaber**.

---

**v. 29. They journeyed from Mithka)** 2 miles. <note>A German mile at this time was significantly longer than a modern English mile, roughly 4.6 miles or 7.5 kilometers.</note>
**Hasmona)** signifies a hasty counting, and is a place where the Church or individual souls in their "wilderness days" occasionally feel an eager desire to settle. 
It often happens that when souls have enjoyed much sensible comfort and divine sweetness in a spiritual way at **Mithka**, having substantially tasted the powers of the world to come, they imagine the time has arrived for such powers to pour out further. Are there not many who have torn themselves away from dead forms and followed the **Lord** through the more inward guidance of a self-denying life, only to be tempted by such "hasty counting"? Some are even led into a misstep because they have felt, tasted, and perceived the living works and sensible powers of the eternal world. This weakness clings to us all too much: that we gaze outward for great things and changes, instead of quietly observing the inward growth of the Kingdom of **GOD**! Acts 1:6. Entire churches, along with their leaders, have fallen into this through their scriptural research and the study of secret numbers.
However, this hasty determining of times and hours in which the glorious works of the **Lord** are to be carried out is, according to another interpretation of the word, merely a **counting of chaff**—a worthless, vain, and useless thing; a work that belongs in the fire.

**v. 30. They journeyed from Hasmona)** 8 miles.
**Moseroth)** signifies bonds, disciplines, or instructions. Psalm 94:12; Proverbs 29:17. For in this way, our missteps must be set right again.

**v. 31. They journeyed from Moseroth)** 6 miles.
**Camped in Bene Jaakan)** Among the sons of suffering and great distress. 
Regarding the remaining campsites, a prayerful and attentive reader can now easily make the application themselves, following the examples given thus far.

**v. 32. They journeyed from Bene Jaakan)** 5 miles.
**Hor Hagidgad)** is a hole or narrow passage where much must be cut away and broken (2 Kings 12:9; Isaiah 7:8; Matthew 19:24). This points to the entrance through the narrow gate on the small path, and a true growth in constant mortification, self-denial, and the renunciation of our own will.

**v. 33. They journeyed from Hor Hagidgad)** 6 miles.
**Jotbatha)** means "good" or "goodness." According to this interpretation, it represents the good, lovely, and sweet blessing of the **Holy Spirit**, which is poured out abundantly over the inner man.

**v. 34. They journeyed from Jotbatha)** 6 miles.
**Abrona)** signifies wrath, the cloud of a loud cry, or also a powerful intercession.

**v. 35. They journeyed from Abrona)** 7 miles.
**Ezion-Gaber)** signifies a mighty counsel, a counsel of power, or the counsel of a strong and mighty man, like Christ (Isaiah 9:6), who is also called a master of help in chapter 63:1.

<column-break/>

**36.** And they journeyed from **Ezion-Gaber**, and camped in the Wilderness of **Zin**, which is **Kadesh**.

**37.** And they journeyed from **Kadesh**, and camped at **Mount Hor**, at the edge of the land of **Edom**.

**38.** Then the priest **Aaron** went up to **Mount Hor** at the command of the **Lord** and died there, in the fortieth year after the children of **Israel** came out of **Egypt**, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month.

**39.** And **Aaron** was a hundred and twenty-three years old when he died on **Mount Hor**.

<margin>Numbers 21:1.</margin>
**40.** And the **Canaanite** king **Arad**, who dwelt in the south in the land of **Canaan**, heard that the children of **Israel** were coming.

**41.** And they journeyed from **Mount Hor** and camped in **Zalmona**.

---

**v. 36. They journeyed from Ezion-Gaber)** 12 miles.
**Zin)** signifies a thorn, a sharp sting, an arrow, or also coldness, cooling, or a shield. This place was also called
**Kadesh)** which signifies holiness.

**v. 37. They journeyed from Kadesh)** 12 miles.
**At Mount Hor)** which is called **Moshera** in Deuteronomy 10:6.

**v. 38. In the fifth month on the first day of the month)** Which occurred approximately in the middle of July; some believe it fell on the 19th of that month.

**v. 39. On Mount Hor)** The reigning administration of the Law dies, and another begins. 
From **Sinai** to **Mount Hor**, there are twice as many campsites—namely twenty-two—of which only a few previous ones were mentioned, such as the Graves of Lust or **Tabeerah** in the Wilderness of **Paran** (Numbers 10:12, 11:3); **Hazeroth** (v. 35); and then the Wilderness of **Paran** is mentioned (Chapter 13:2), in which all the following thirteen campsites were located. After these follows the Wilderness of **Zin**, specifically **Kadesh** (Chapter 20:1), and then **Hor** (v. 22).
This long journey can be compared to the state under the Law. When a person gains a true feeling and knowledge of **GOD**, they remain for a long time in all kinds of exercises, where they must struggle with many **affections** <note>In this context, "affections" refers to unruly passions or worldly desires.</note> which must be killed and buried through repentance, and which the **Lord** also burns away in the fire of love. Here there is sometimes a **Zarada** <note>A term used by the author to mean "terror" or "dread" before the Law.</note> or terror of the Law, and then again a **Mithka** and the sweet comfort of the Gospel. Here the sting of conscience, which is called **Zin**, also very often manifests itself, as one is constantly reminded to walk in holiness, which is called **Kadesh**. Thus one is driven by the Law until one climbs **Mount Hor**, where, in the fellowship of **Christ's** death, one attains the knowledge of the new birth. 
Thus one enters the state under Grace, whereupon **Zalmona**—the **Image of GOD**—is revealed in the soul (Colossians 3:10). There, one walks in the new being of the Spirit and not in the letter of the Law; there, life is born to the Spirit of **Christ** in the believer, in whom the deeds of the flesh are then put to death (Romans 8:13).

**v. 41. They journeyed from Mount Hor)** 7 miles.
**Zalmona)** which means an image, just as the place where the image stands takes its name from the bronze serpent which the **Lord** commanded to be made and set up at this location (Chapter 21:8, 9).

<summary>This page lists the Israelites' journey from Mithka to Zalmona, interpreting each location as a symbolic stage in the soul's transition from the "terror of the Law" to the "state of Grace" and the "Image of God." It specifically notes the death of Aaron on Mount Hor as the end of the Law's administration.</summary>

# Chapter XXXIII. The Fourth Book of Moses.
#### Qqqq
<meta>Catchword: The</meta>

**42.** And they journeyed from **Zalmona**, and camped in **Phunon**.
**43.** And they journeyed from **Phunon**, and camped in **Oboth**.
**44.** And they journeyed from **Oboth**, and camped at the **hills of Abarim**, in the border of the Moabites.
**45.** And they journeyed from the hills, and camped in **Dibon-Gad**.
**46.** And they journeyed from **Dibon-Gad**, and camped in **Almon-Diblathaim**.

**v. 42. They journeyed from Zalmona)** 5 miles. <note>As noted previously, a German mile at this time was approximately 4.6 modern English miles.</note>
**Phunon)** lay in Idumaea <note>original: "Idumäa," the Greek name for the land of Edom</note> and was very well known for its ore mines. Therefore, some hold that the metal used for the bronze serpent was taken from there.
The name signifies as much as a great doubt, terror, or a displacement of the mind; also as much as the face or the beholding of the Son. The former refers to the fiery serpents, the latter to the bronze one.
**v. 43. They journeyed from Phunon)** 6 miles.
**Oboth)** may mean as much as enchantments, sorcerers, or those who have communion with evil spirits and seek their utterances; also the spirits of divination themselves. See Deuteronomy 18:10 and 1 Samuel 28:10.
The most common sorcery which occurs in and around the Church of God is that which is mentioned in Galatians 3:1 <note>"O foolish Galatians, who hath bewitched you?"</note>, against which an honest pilgrim must guard himself all the more.
**v. 44. They journeyed from Oboth)** 4 miles.
**Hills of Abarim)** The translations and commentators are as confused regarding the naming of this place as the meaning of the name itself is confused, which signifies as much as confused heaps of the streets and travelers, or the confusions and devastations of the passages and ways.
It represents the state in which holy pilgrims are placed in doubt and confusion.
**v. 45. They journeyed from the hills)** Also 4 miles.
**Camped in Dibon-Gad)** So named by the tribe of Gad, who, after the defeat of the Amorite kings Sihon and Og, took possession of Dibon and rebuilt it. Chapter 32:34.
According to the spiritual sense, it signifies a full understanding of breaking or cutting off, the full understanding of an army, of arming, or of a hostile attack.
**v. 46. They journeyed from Dibon-Gad)** 4 miles.
**Almon-Diblathaim)** signifies as much as a hidden place of figs, a heap, lump, or cake of figs; 1 Samuel 25:18. This serves as a prototype of the good things according to the Spirit and hidden spiritual refreshments that should flow out in a rich measure.
Just as also on this way there arises in the soul the living spring of the Spirit, the "army" or "well" mentioned in Chapter 21:10 etc., where the journey from Zor to Oboth is reported, along with several other places like Mattanah, Nahaliel, and Bamoth, which are not mentioned here. Here too, the streams of God's grace or **Nahaliel** <note>original: "Nahaliel" translates to "Torrents of God"</note> are to be felt, as in Psalm 36:9. And finally, they arrive with Moses at Mount Nebo, which signifies "prophecy," and can mean the great level of the contemplation of God, of which Christ says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Matthew 5:8. There they also get to see the promised eternal inheritance in the Spirit from God, and attain a living assurance of it in the heart, so that like Simeon they can depart from here in peace, because their inward eye has seen the salvation of God: just as here the promised land was shown to Moses, Deuteronomy 34:1 etc., and he was thereafter taken up into the Heavenly through a blessed death. And so God leads His own according to His counsel, and finally receives them into glory. Psalm 73:24.

<column-break/>

**47.** And they journeyed from **Almon-Diblathaim**, and camped at the **mountains of Abarim**, before Nebo.
**48.** And they journeyed from the **mountains of Abarim**, and camped in the **plains of the Moabites**, by the Jordan across from Jericho.
<margin>(a) Joshua 2:1.</margin>
**49.** And they camped by the Jordan from **Beth-Jesimoth** as far as **Abel-Shittim** <gloss>(a)</gloss>, in the plains of the Moabites.
**50.** And the **Lord** spoke to Moses in the plains of the Moabites, by the Jordan across from Jericho, saying:
**51.** Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When you have gone over the Jordan into the land of Canaan;
**52.** Then you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land before your face, and you shall destroy all their significant images, and destroy all their molten images, and demolish all their high places.
**53.** That you may thus possess the land as an inheritance and dwell therein. For I have given you the land that you may possess it as an inheritance.

### 54. And

**v. 47. They journeyed from Almon-Diblathaim)** 4 miles.
**The mountains of Abarim)** were many connected hills in the borders of the Moabites and Amorites, which had their name from the many ways and streets that went through them, so that one could travel and drive through everywhere in between; or also, as some hold, from the crossings <note>original: "Ueberfahrten," referring to the fords of the Jordan</note> of the Jordan that were near there. For **Abarim** means "passages."
**Nebo)** was the uppermost part of these, which lay right across from Jericho.
**v. 48. They journeyed from the mountains)** downward. This indicates that the soul should further humble itself under the cross and must submit itself to discipline.
**v. 49.** Moses continues to give a more precise description of this last campsite and also notes its boundaries.
**Beth-Jesimoth)** signifies as much as a house of desolations and a house of designations or names.
**Abel-Shittim)** signifies as much as the sorrow because of the thorns and rods, and points to the fierce rod of anger and the subsequent sadness with which the Israelite people were afflicted at this place. Chapter 25:4, 9. <note>This refers to the judgment following the sin at Baal-Peor.</note>
**v. 50. etc. God** lets them be so faithfully warned here how they should utterly root out all the heathens with their idolatrous image-worship, since corrupt nature could all too easily be led into such visible idolatry <term>Götzendienst</term>: which God expressly wanted to forbid in the Second Commandment, so that man might be drawn away from the outward service—with which he so easily lets himself be satisfied—and might be brought all the more to the inward service of the fear and love of God.

### Chapter XXXIV. The Fourth Book of Moses.

10. And you shall mark out your eastern border from Hazar Enan to Shepham.
11. From Shepham the border shall go down to Riblah, on the east side of Ain. Then the border shall go further down and shall reach the shore of the Sea of Chinnereth <note>original: "Meers Cinnereth"; this is the Old Testament name for the Sea of Galilee</note> toward the east:
12. Then the border shall go down to the Jordan, and its end shall be at the Salt Sea. This shall be your land according to its borders all around.
13. And Moses commanded the children of Israel, saying: This is the land that you shall take as a hereditary possession by lot, which the LORD commanded to be given to the nine tribes and the half-tribe.
14. For the tribe of the children of Reuben according to their fathers' house, and the tribe of the children of Gad according to their fathers' house, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, have received their inheritance.
15. Two tribes and a half-tribe have received their inheritance on this side of the Jordan across from Jericho, toward the east, toward the sunrise.

---

<margin>v. 10. 11.</margin> Toward the east was the Sea of Chinnereth, which in the New Testament is called the Lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1); the Jordan River and the Salt or Dead Sea.
<margin>v. 12.</margin> (This shall be the land according to its borders all around) Since the length of the land from Dan to Beersheba—which are set as the outermost border places (Judges 20:1), as well as the Brook of Egypt and Hamath (1 Chronicles 13:5)—is said to have been up to 67 hours’ journey or 40 German miles <note>A "German mile" (teutsche Meile) in the 17th century was roughly 4.6 modern miles or 7.5 kilometers; the total length described is about 185 miles.</note>, and the width from the Jordan to the Mediterranean Sea 15 to 18 miles. Compared to today’s kingdoms, this was a small realm, yet it was very fertile and blessed in everything. With this, the people of God were meant to be content, and not strive at all for the expansion of their land and empire: just as God has set the boundaries for all nations, with which they should be content (Acts 17:26). Therefore, those who profess the Christian faith will face a very heavy accountability if they destroy or diminish such ancient borders of lands and kingdoms.
<margin>v. 13.</margin> Just as every place, every mountain, and every city in the Jewish land had its own name; so too it is not to be doubted that in the heavenly realm there is a distinction of places. Regarding their names—according to Origen’s report <note>original: "Origenis Bericht"; referring to the early Christian scholar Origen of Alexandria</note>—many secret things are said to be contained in the little books of Enoch; but because these are not accepted by everyone, he relies meanwhile on what Holy Scripture itself reports of certain places, where the people of God and the True Israel shall one day be brought, and shall take up the inheritance according to the lot of good conduct and faithfulness.
<margin>v. 14. 15.</margin> There, some may belong to the sons of Israel according to faith, yet, because they retain in their life and conduct some sluggishness and love of earthly things, they are to be counted among the tribes of Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh <note>These tribes chose to settle outside the Promised Land proper, east of the Jordan, because the land was good for livestock.</note>; others on the contrary, for reasons best known to God, may obtain their inheritance even under the tribe of Judah or Benjamin, where Jerusalem itself and the Temple of God are found.

Whether these men called to distribute the land—the High Priest, the ruler, and the twelve most distinguished heads of the tribes—performed the task only generally for the tribes according to the lot (Joshua 19:51), or also specifically assigned estates to families within the tribes; more on this will appear in the Book of Joshua. At the very least, they were the judges who were to see that everything proceeded justly and peacefully, so that no one might have cause to complain against another.
In the same way, among Christians—since the great weakness of men makes it unavoidable—holy and God-fearing men should be appointed as judges, who also possess wisdom and worthiness or capability from the Spirit of God, to judge between brother and brother in earthly matters, as they are the lesser things (1 Corinthians 6:1–9).

# The XXXV. Chapter.

## The Cities of the Levites, the Cities of Refuge for the Manslayer, and their Punishment.

1. AND the LORD spoke to Moses on the plains of the Moabites, by the Jordan, across from Jericho, saying:
2. Command the children of Israel that they give to the Levites, from the inheritance of their possession, cities to dwell in. In addition, you shall give the Levites a suburb around the cities.
3. And they shall have the cities to dwell in, and their suburbs shall be for their cattle, and for their goods, and for all their animals.
4. And the suburbs of the cities which you shall give to the Levites shall extend from the city wall outward a thousand cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> all around.
5. And you shall measure from outside the city, the corner toward the East <note>original: "Morgen"</note> two thousand cubits, and the corner toward the South <note>original: "Mittag"</note> two thousand cubits, and the corner toward the West <note>original: "Abend"</note> two thousand cubits, and the corner toward the North <note>original: "Mitternacht"</note> two thousand cubits: so that the city is in the middle. These shall be the suburbs of their cities.

---

Since the LORD had given the Levites—among whom the priests are also to be understood here—no inheritance of the land of Canaan for their possession as he did the other tribes; he nevertheless willed that they be given certain cities for their dwelling from the tribes. For their necessary maintenance, for vegetables, as well as for pasture for their livestock, and thus for gardens and meadows, he granted a space of 1000 cubits on each side, and thus 8000 cubits in total circumference, for suburbs, which they were to use as a farmstead or dairy-farm <note>original: "Vorwerk oder Meyerey"</note>, as we are accustomed to say, for their cattle.

<margin>v. 2. 3.</margin> (Cities to dwell in) They did not necessarily have to live in them permanently, but could sell their houses and move elsewhere. Many could not live in their own cities but had to live in foreign ones; namely, those who sat in the middle-courts and those who taught in all cities on the Sabbath. Therefore, it is often written in the Scripture of the Levites who are "within the gates" of other tribes; as in Deuteronomy 12:12, 18.

<margin>v. 4. 5.</margin> (One thousand -- two thousand cubits) How this is to be understood is a matter of very different opinions, as it is expressed somewhat obscurely.

Many of the Hebrews set 1000 cubits for the suburb and pasture for the cattle, and another 1000 cubits for fields and vineyards, so that from the city to the outermost corner was 2000 cubits, or a "Sabbath day's journey" (a); an opinion also held by Philo (b) and Josephus (c).

(a) Drusius, *Difficult passages in Numbers* <note>original: "loc. diffic. ad Num."</note>, ch. 137. Lightfoot, *Chorographical Century prefixed to Matthew* <note>original: "cent. chorogr. Matth. praemiss."</note>, ch. 97. & on Acts 1:7.
(b) *Book on the Honors of Priests* <note>original: "lib. de sacerd. honorib."</note>, p. 643.
(c) *Antiquities [of the Jews]* <note>original: "antiq."</note>, Book 4, ch. 4.

<column-break/>

6. But the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be six cities of refuge, which you shall appoint so that the manslayer <note>One who kills another unintentionally or without premeditation.</note> may flee there: and in addition to these, you shall give forty-two cities.
7. All the cities that you shall give to the Levites shall be forty-eight cities: these, namely, with their suburbs.
8. Namely, the cities which you give from the possession of the children of Israel: from those who have much, you shall take much, and from those who have little, you shall take little. Each shall give of his cities to the Levites according to the measure of his inheritance, which they shall possess by heritability.
9. And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:
10. Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you cross over the Jordan into the land of Canaan,
<meta>II.</meta>

<insert>They were to receive forty-eight cities from all the tribes, which the tribes had to distribute among themselves according to whether one had more or less land, as was put into effect according to Joshua 21. With this, God willed to scatter them among all the tribes, according to Genesis 49:7, but in such a way that He turned the curse back into a blessing; thus they could more conveniently serve all the tribes for instruction in the Law. Consequently, their cities were like so many schools in which they taught the Law, and from there spread and propagated knowledge and understanding through all the tribes. See Malachi 2:4, etc.</insert>

<margin>v. 7. 48 Cities)</margin> It is asked why 48 cities were assigned to the tribe of Levi, since this tribe was one of the smallest and least numerous of all the people; whereas other tribes, which were often more than twice as populous, received so few, and some only 12 cities? Some, however, hold that Scripture indeed mentions all the cities of the priests and Levites by name, but does not name the cities of the other tribes, mentioning only some of them. It may also be that the other tribes could live in the countryside, in villages and homesteads, while the Levites could not, because they had no [other] lands.

<margin>v. 8. Much -- much -- little -- little)</margin> Thus, proportion is something holy and divine.

<margin>v. 10. In Canaan)</margin> Regarding the "heavenly" Canaan, they believed that according to this image, there will also be similar cities or places of refuge for certain sins committed by men without intent; where they will have to spend and dwell for a time, provided they did not commit such sins willfully. Some, he says, hold that every star could be considered a city in heaven; though he did not dare to assert this as certain: even though he thought and concluded from Scripture that because all creation is subject [to vanity] and waits for the freedom of the children of God, it therefore also waits for something higher and more glorious.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the laws given to Moses regarding the inheritance of the Levites and the establishment of legal protections for those who commit accidental homicide, transitioning from the physical boundaries of the cities to the judicial function of the Cities of Refuge.</meta>

# Chap. XXXV. The IV. Book of Moses.

11. You shall choose for yourselves convenient cities; these shall be Cities of Refuge <note>original: "Freystädte"</note> for you, so that a manslayer who has killed a person <note>original: "Seele," literally "soul"</note> by mistake may flee there.
12. And these cities shall be a refuge for you from the blood-avenger, so that the manslayer does not have to die until he has stood before the congregation for judgment.
13. And the cities that you shall give shall be six Cities of Refuge for you.
14. Three cities you shall give on this side of the Jordan, and three cities you shall give in the land of Canaan: these shall be Cities of Refuge.
15. For the children of Israel, and for the stranger, and for the sojourner <note>original: "Beysaß," referring to a resident alien with limited rights</note> in their midst, these six cities shall be for refuge, so that everyone who has killed a person by mistake may flee there. Joshua 20:9.

---

Among the 48 cities, six were to be chosen as Cities of Refuge, into which one who had committed a manslaughter unexpectedly—and thus not out of enmity—was to flee. This was so that he might be protected in his innocence from the blood-avenger <note>The "blood-avenger" was typically the closest male relative of the deceased, tasked with upholding the family's honor and justice</note>, who was the closest kinsman of the slain and had the power—indeed, was required—to slay the manslayer out of righteous vengeance, so that the blood would not go unavenged.

**v. 11. Cities of Refuge)** or reception-cities, where certain people were received and taken into protection.

**Flee there)** When this happened, such a person remained outside at the gate of the city, where the elders of the city were always gathered for judgment, and there he presented his case. Then they took him into the city and let him dwell with them until the blood-avenger appeared. If the avenger then pursued him and demanded him as a murderer, he was brought to trial and his case was examined.

**v. 12. Until he has stood for judgment)** This trial was not held in the City of Refuge, but in the city where the deed had occurred. To that end, two or three guards were sent with the perpetrator to keep the blood-avenger from any violence with good words, so that he might not touch him until the perpetrator had answered before the court.

**v. 13. Six)** Five belonged to the Levites, and one to the priests.

**v. 14. Three on this side, and 3 in Canaan)** But why just as many for the two-and-a-half tribes as for the nine-and-a-half tribes? <note>original: "dritthalb" (2.5) and "zehendhalb" (9.5)</note> It is held that although the land on this side of the Jordan was inhabited by only two-and-a-half tribes, it was nevertheless a very vast and large territory.

**v. 15. Who has slain a soul by mistake)** But it is asked: why only those, and not also other sinners, such as thieves, adulterers, perjurers, and the like, had protection in these Cities of Refuge? Answer: Because none of those are without guilt, but they mostly happen knowingly and willfully.

<column-break/>

16. But if he has struck him with an iron tool so that he died, he is a murderer: the murderer shall certainly be put to death.
17. And if he has struck him with a stone in the hand by which one can die, so that he died, he is a murderer: the murderer shall certainly be put to death.
18. Or if he has struck him with a wooden tool in the hand by which one can die, so that he died, he is a murderer: the murderer shall certainly be put to death.
19. The avenger of blood himself shall kill the murderer: when he meets him, he shall kill him.
20. And if he has pushed him out of hatred, or has thrown something at him by lying in wait so that he died;
21. Or out of enmity has struck him with his hand so that he died: then he who struck him shall certainly be put to death; he is a murderer: the avenger of blood shall kill the murderer when he meets him.
22.

---

**v. 16–18.** Intentional, knowing, and willful murderers had no freedom therein, but had to die without any mercy or compassion. They could be redeemed by nothing in all the world to keep their lives, because they had defiled the land with the shedding of blood, and the land could not be atoned for until their own blood was shed in return.

**v. 19. when he meets him)** For a murderer, where the deed was obvious, a trial did not always have to be held; rather, the blood-avenger could slay him immediately. But if he would not or could not do it, or if no avenger was present, the court had to condemn him to death. (a)

**v. 20. if)** such an intentional, willful murderer immediately took refuge in a City of Refuge;

**v. 21. Then)** he still had no protection there, but was demanded from there by the elders of his own city and handed over to the blood-avenger, who had to put him to death.

---

**The avenger of blood)** must, however, absolutely be the closest blood-relative and heir of the deceased; otherwise, he had no right to avenge himself on the murderer of the deceased, even if he was otherwise related to him. If it therefore happened that a father wickedly slew his son, who in turn had a son; then the son of the deceased had to kill his grandfather as the murderer. But if the deceased had no son, then the brother of the deceased could not do it; because not he, but the father himself, was then the closest relative to the deceased.

Qqqq 3
<meta>catchword: v. 15, 21, 22.</meta>

(a) <note>original: "Selden. de J.N. & G. l. 4. c. 1." refers to John Selden, *On the Law of Nature and Nations according to the Teachings of the Hebrews*, Book 4, Chapter 1.</note>

<summary>This page details the establishment of six Cities of Refuge intended to protect those who commit accidental manslaughter from the immediate vengeance of the victim's family. It distinguishes between accidental death and intentional murder, for which no sanctuary or ransom is permitted.</summary>

# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter XXXV.

<columns>
22. But if he pushed him suddenly, without enmity, or threw any tool at him without lying in wait;

<margin>Deuteronomy 19:4, 5</margin>
23. Or with any stone by which one may die, having not seen him, so that he let it fall upon him and he died, yet he was not his enemy and did not seek his misfortune:

24. Then the congregation shall judge between the one who struck the blow and the avenger of blood according to these laws.

25. And the congregation shall rescue the manslayer from the hand of the avenger of blood, and the congregation shall let him return to his city of refuge where he had fled, and he shall remain there until the high priest dies, who was anointed with the holy oil.

---

v. 22. **Suddenly)** However, among the Hebrews, sudden manslaughters and manslayers are of various kinds, and according to their reports, not all enjoyed the protection of the cities of refuge—specifically those who came very close to being intentional, willful killers. For example: if someone intends to kill one person but hits another whom he did not mean to harm and kills him; although such a person was not condemned by the court, <note>the court might not execute him, but he might not find safety in the city of refuge either.</note>

v. 23. **And he died)** Namely, immediately. For if he had lived for a while longer, the perpetrator would have had no cause to flee, and the avenger of blood would not have been permitted to venture anything against such a person.

v. 24. **The congregation shall judge)** It had to be investigated by judges appointed for that purpose to see if he was entirely innocent of such manslaughter. If that was not the case, he certainly had to be put to death in the place where the killing was committed; in such a case, neither a city of refuge nor the holy place—the altar—helped, even if someone had taken refuge there (as may have happened in the wilderness; see Exodus 21:14 and 1 Kings 2:31). If he was found guilty, he would be handed over to the avenger of blood, who was required to demand blood for blood and strike him down. (a)

If the matter was doubtful, or if there was only one witness, or if the carelessness and recklessness were so great that he was more like an intentional killer than an accidental one: the court did not condemn him, yet the avenger of blood was free to strike him down, and the perpetrator had to be very careful.

If someone had hired a murderer to kill someone, the King could have him executed by the sword, even though the court likewise did not condemn him.

v. 25. **But if he were found innocent)** he still had to remain in the city of refuge until the death of the High Priest; only then could he return to his fatherland and his inheritance.

**The congregation shall let him return to his city of refuge)** The court sent him back to the city of refuge to which he had fled, and from which he had been brought for trial, with a safe conduct so that the avenger of blood could not reach him. Thus, the judgment over him was not held in the city of refuge, but rather where the deed occurred and where the matter could best be investigated.

**Until the high priest dies)** So that they would not hasten the death of the high priests through their prayers, the mothers of the high priests—as the Hebrews say—gladly gave these accidental manslayers their sustenance in their misery. <note>Jewish tradition suggests the High Priest's mother provided food and clothing to the refugees so they wouldn't pray for her son's death to secure their own freedom.</note>

<note>(a) Thomas Goodwin, *Moses and Aaron*, book 2, chapter 5. Johann Adam Osiander, *System of Hebrew Antiquities*, section 23.</note>

<column-break/>

26. But if the manslayer should indeed go out beyond the border of his city of refuge where he had fled,

27. And the avenger of blood finds him outside the border of his city of refuge, and the avenger of blood kills the manslayer: he shall not be guilty of blood.

28. For he must remain in his city of refuge until the death of the high priest; and after the death of the high priest, the manslayer shall return to the land of his possession.

29. And these things shall be a legal statute for you throughout your generations in all your dwellings.

---

v. 26. **Outside the border of his city of refuge)** He might well go out into the suburbs, within the mile, but no further; he had to keep himself within the borders of the suburbs.

v. 27. **He shall not be guilty of blood)** Because the manslayer had willfully surrendered the right granted to him.

v. 28. This should now teach us in a symbolic way that through sin and the resulting envy and hatred toward our neighbor, we could indeed be condemned before God as manslayers (1 John 3:15) and handed over to the vengeful enemy, Satan (as he is called in Psalm 8:3). Nevertheless, God willed to give His dear Son to all repentant and believing sinners as such a city of refuge, as it says in Proverbs 18:10: **The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous run to it and are safe, or protected;** so that we can be secure from the avenger of blood. See Romans 8:33–34, where the death of our true High Priest, Christ, is also cited, through which we are now entirely freed from guilt and can reach the lost inheritance in heaven again; see also Hebrews 2:14–15 regarding the power of Satan and redemption through Christ's death.

But if this "Kinsman" and "Avenger" is also a figure of Christ—just as Job, through the Spirit of God, calls Him his *Goel* <note>original: "Goel" — a Hebrew term for a kinsman-redeemer who avenges blood or buys back property.</note> or Blood-Friend, because He would take on our flesh and blood and thus be his Redeemer (Job 19:25), who would redeem him from destruction and from death through the atonement made by Him (Job 33:23)—then it is understood by this that He has thereby avenged Himself on Satan, who was the murderer from the beginning (John 8:44). He has redeemed His creatures, indeed His brothers, from Satan's power and taken revenge on their murderer by condemning him to the pit, while being able to restore life to the believers who by nature lay in the death of sin (Ephesians 2:1, 5, 6), who have thus become His brothers through faith.

However, whoever will not turn to Him through repentance and faith remains under the power of Satan, who will drag him into eternal death as a manslayer who has killed the image of God within himself through sin.

v. 29. The fact that in modern times people have wanted to turn churches and monasteries into such cities of refuge has often allowed willful murderers to escape and be withdrawn from just judgment here on earth. This happened because no one dared to avenge a blood-relative, even though all manslaughters had to be properly investigated by the judges to see if they occurred out of malice or by accident. This practice is entirely against the meaning of this law and is therefore completely unjustifiable before God. See further on this in Deuteronomy 19 and Joshua 20.

### The Marriage of Inheriting Daughters within their Tribe.

<margin>ch. 27.</margin>

It teaches us in the New Testament to look more toward the spiritual, since we have received the precious faith by lot along with the rest of the believers (2 Peter 1:1), so that we should strive through prayer, admonition, and in every other way to maintain such a glorious inheritance among our kin, so that it might not be entirely squandered through vain upbringing or other negligence; just as descendants are likewise to carefully observe the commands and ordinances of their godly ancestors,

**v. 22. Suddenly)** However, even among the Hebrews, there are different types of accidental manslaughter and manslayers, and according to their reports, not all enjoyed the protection of the cities of refuge—specifically those who came very close to being intentional, willful manslayers.
