# The Fourth Book of Moses. Chapter 36.

5. And Moses commanded the children of Israel according to the command of the **LORD**, saying: The tribe of the sons of Joseph speaks rightly.

6. This is the word that the **LORD** has commanded regarding the daughters of Zelophehad, saying: They may become wives to whomever pleases them in their eyes; only they shall become wives within the family of the tribe of their father.

7. So that the inheritance of the children of Israel shall not be shifted from one tribe to another. For every one of the children of Israel shall remain attached to the inheritance of the tribe of his fathers.

8. And every daughter who inherits an inheritance from the tribes of the children of Israel shall become a wife to one from the family of the tribe of her father: so that every one of the children of Israel may inherit the inheritance of his fathers;

Although these five daughters were bound to marry into their own family line, it was nevertheless left to them to choose whom they wished to take and to whose suit they might consent. This represents a particular divine wisdom that should be observed in marriages: that while the male sex is given the free choice of where they wish to seek marriage, the female sex also has the power to consent according to the inclination of her heart, or to refuse such a proposal. In such an important business, both have need to turn to **GOD** and to call upon Him for His holy guidance in this: a special model of this is the godly and blessed marriage of Isaac with Rebecca, Genesis 24, especially verses 14 and 58.

<column-break/>

9. And the inheritance shall not be shifted from one tribe to another tribe, but the tribes of the children of Israel shall each remain attached to his own inheritance.

10. As the **LORD** had commanded Moses, so did the daughters of Zelophehad.

11. And the daughters of Zelophehad—Machlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah <gloss>(a)</gloss>—became the wives of the sons of their uncles.

<margin>(a) chapter 26, verse 33.</margin>

12. They became wives among the families of the sons of Manasseh, the son of Joseph. Thus their inheritance remained with the tribe of the family of their father.

13. These are the commandments and the laws which the **LORD** commanded through the service of Moses to the children of Israel on the flat fields of the Moabites by the Jordan across from Jericho.

Otherwise, those who were not heiress daughters had the power to marry wherever they wished: just as Jehoshabeath <note>original: "Josabaht"</note>, the daughter of King Jehoram <note>original: "Joram"</note> from the tribe of Judah, had Jehoiada <note>original: "Jojada"</note> the priest from the tribe of Levi (2 Chronicles 22:11). However, the heiress daughters had to remain within their tribe and—as some believe—even within their own family line. See 1 Chronicles 23:22, Tobit 6:12, 14, 7:14. From this, some also wish to conclude that Mary, the mother of our **Savior**, was such an heiress daughter and had also married according to this law (Luke 1:2, 2:4, 5).

<meta>This page serves as the preface to the Fifth Book of Moses, commonly known as Deuteronomy. It follows the conclusion of the Book of Numbers, transitioning from the laws of inheritance to a broader theological reflection on the purpose of the Law and its repetition for the new generation of Israelites.</meta>

# The Fifth Book of Moses

Among the Hebrews, this book is called either *The Words* <note>Hebrew: *Devarim*</note>, from the opening words of the book, or based on its content, *The Repetition of the Law* <note>Greek: *Deuteronomion*</note> (chapter 17, verse 18), or even the *Book of Rebukes*. Indeed, *Moses* provides a repetition of the Law within it, adding a supplement and **application** in which the punishments for breaking the Law are emphasized to the people. This was done to imprint the Law more deeply upon them and to better incline the hearts of the Israelites toward obedience.

Obedience is the principal matter in every **dispensation** <note>original: *dispensation*; a theological term for the way God administers or orders human history in different eras</note> and household of God: *Moses* required it in the Law; *Christ* urged it in the **Gospel** <note>original: *Evangelio*</note>; and in the days to come, the Holy Spirit will write a new law in the heart for that same purpose, which is prefigured by this very book.

Certainly, the name given to it by the 70 Greek Translators <note>the Septuagint</note>, which the **Latins** and other languages have followed, aligns perfectly with this purpose. Among them, it bears the name "The Second Law." This is partly due to the repetition of the Law already given, which was certainly necessary because so many children had been born in the wilderness who were not present at the first **publication** of the Law, or at least could not remember it; yet, it also hints at something more excellent contained within.

*Jerome* <note>original: *Hieronymus*</note> seems to have noticed this when he asks (a): Does not the fifth book of *Moses* contain the previous matters in such a way that much of the Old is simultaneously new? Likewise, he calls it an introduction to the contemplation of the **Gospel** (b).

With *Origen*, who also observed this, his modesty was so great that he freely confessed (c): "I consider myself too unworthy to uncover the mysteries held within the fourth book of *Moses*; and I am even less fit to point out those in the fifth book of *Moses*. Therefore, I must hasten to *Joshua*—not the son of *Nun*, but to *Jesus Christ*." <note>The name Joshua and Jesus are the same in Hebrew and Greek; Origen is making a typological connection to Christ.</note> Consequently, he bypassed this fifth book of *Moses* in his commentary.

In a certain sense, then, this book may well be called another and new Law. For a new people—as this generation was—and one that prefigures a new and second generation from the second *Adam* <note>A reference to Jesus Christ, as described in 1 Corinthians 15</note> (Numbers 26:64–65), a new Law is quite fitting; just as they also received a new leader and ruler. Yet it is a "new Law" only in the sense that *John* writes of the old and new commandment of love.

Therefore, this book has a great affinity with the **Gospel**, which was also often called the "New Law" by the ancients, just as it is otherwise known by the name of the New Testament.

Thus, a new life and new obedience are the goals toward which it aims.

*Luther* also briefly and effectively summarizes the content in this sense (d), stating that nothing else is taught therein but faith in God and love for one's neighbor. Up until the 20th **chapter**, everything that hinders faith in God is cleared away and forbidden, and in the remainder, everything that hinders the love of neighbor.

This teaching originates from the one who was proclaimed as a King in the First **Book of Moses** (chapter 49), and presented as a High Priest in the figure of **Aaron** in the Second, and is now promised in this book (chapter 18) as the true **Prophet**.

Otherwise, the entire book is not improperly divided into four main parts: I. A preparation of the people for the now imminent occupation of the Promised Land, in the first four **chapters**; II. An explanation of the Law, in which the people are reminded of their duties anew: from **chapter** 5 to 26; III. The confirmation of what preceded, with signs, promises, threats, and the renewal of the covenant: from **chapter** 27 to 31; IV. A narrative of what occurred shortly before and after the death of *Moses*. Here, much from the spirit of prophecy flows in, and the entire book and Law conclude with a very mysterious prophecy in the form of a song, concerning the subsequent straying and the resulting wretched state of **Israel according to the flesh**, as well as the arrival, nature, and chief events of **Israel according to the spirit**, presented as a blessing in chapters 32 and 33.

---

The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter I.

# Chapter I.

->The account of the appointment of the leaders, the sending out of the spies, the grumbling, and the punishment because of it.<-

---

These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel on this side of the Jordan, in the wilderness on the plain opposite the Sea of Reeds, between Tophel and Laban, Hazeroth and Di-Zahab:

In conclusion, Moses wished to present to this second generation of the children of Israel both the great blessings of God that He showed to their fathers, as well as their manifold deviations and ingratitude and the resulting righteous judgments. He did this to exhort them to heartfelt repentance and careful avoidance of such wickedness and disobedience, so that they might pass this on to their children who were yet to be born, and these in turn might proclaim it to their own children; that they might set their hope in God and not forget the works of God, but keep His commandments; and that they might not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation whose heart was not steadfast and whose spirit was not faithful to God. (Psalm 78:6, 7, 8). And so it shall happen when the Law of the New Testament <note>The author is drawing a parallel between the "repetition" of the Law in Deuteronomy and the future spiritual renewal under Christ.</note> is repeated during the second full outpouring of the Spirit of God in the glorious Kingdom of Christ. Then the Spirit of God will remind the believers of all the former deeds in the Kingdom of the Cross: there they shall all unanimously and sincerely confess wherein their predecessors failed and were disobedient to the Spirit of Christ, and what judgments were consequently imposed upon the external Church, and what chastisements were also hung over the believers—just as Moses here sincerely confesses his own fault in verse 37. Then an impartial church history shall come to light, where all such accounts will stand constantly before the eyes of this blessed generation as a blessed warning. See Isaiah 66:14.

All the places named here are considered very remarkable in their circumstances regarding the speech of Moses.

But what might be the cause for why Moses shows himself so exceedingly careful in describing the place where he spoke these words to Israel? The matter he deals with is, without doubt, of great importance. Yet there are many other matters that are not noted so circumstantially with the names of places—not even the first giving of the Law in Exodus 20.

The Chaldean Interpreter <note>original: *Chaldäische Dolmetsch*; referring to the Aramaic Targum, a translation and commentary of the Hebrew Bible</note> may come quite close to the purpose here, as he summarizes the entire content of the book in these words: such that in the first verse is contained a reminder and a punishment of Israel for the sake of their sins which they committed in the mentioned places. And these were:

**The words that Moses spoke)** harsh and punishing words: because they sinned in the wilderness, and because they had tempted God on the plain, and in Paran, where they murmured against the manna, and in Hazeroth, where they provoked God for meat.

**Opposite the Sea of Reeds)** if one wishes to keep the common translation. Otherwise, the word "Sea" is not here in the Hebrew; and since the Jordan is mentioned at the same time—which was indeed far from the Red Sea and not opposite it—others understand the word *Suph* <note>original: *Suph*; often translated as reeds or weeds</note> rather to mean a reed-thicket, according to its consistent meaning, as the border of the promised land located near the Dead Sea.

**Tophel)** is said to be, according to the testimony of Jerome <note>original: *Hieronymi*; the 4th-century scholar who translated the Vulgate</note>, the place where Moses is said to have written the fifth book of his history.

**Di-Zahab)** many also take to be the name of a place that is mentioned nowhere else. Others, however, follow the opinion of the Chaldean Interpreter, who looked rather at the meaning of the word, which is the "misuse of their abundance of gold," when they made themselves a golden calf for an idol. <note>The name *Di-Zahab* can be etymologically interpreted as "enough gold."</note>

<column-break/>

2. It is eleven days' journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir to Kadesh Barnea.

3. And it happened in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month, that Moses spoke to the children of Israel according to all that the LORD had commanded him concerning them.

4. After he had struck down Sihon the king of the Amorites, who dwelt at Heshbon; and Og the king of Bashan, who dwelt at Ashtaroth and Edrei. <margin>Numbers 21:25, 26, 33. Joshua 13:12</margin>

5. On this side of the Jordan in the land of the Moabites, Moses began to explain this Law and said:

6. The LORD our GOD spoke with us at Horeb and said: You have stayed long enough at this mountain.

7. Turn and set out and come to the mountains of the Amorites and to all their neighbors on the plain, on the mountains, and in the valley, and toward the South, and by the seacoast, in the land of the Canaanites and to Lebanon, as far as the great river, the river Euphrates <note>original: *Phrat*</note>.

---

**v. 2. Eleven days' journey from Horeb to Kadesh Barnea.)** In such a short time they had accomplished so much of their journey, and only then did they refuse in unbelief and disobedience to go forward into the Holy Land; whereupon they then had to travel for a full 38 years what was still remaining of their journey. Chapter 2:14. Note the inestimable damage of unbelief!

However, there are 11 days or "legal lights" <note>An allegorical interpretation of time or distance</note> between Mount Horeb—the sword and terror and the deadly letter of the Law—and Kadesh-Barnea, or the wandering holiness of the child, in the bypassing of Mount Seir, which is the terrifying doctrine that causes a shuddering of the skin and makes the hair stand on end.

**v. 3. In the 11th month)** And thus in the last weeks of the last year.

The number eleven is of an evil omen, the connotations of which mostly forebode something bad; therefore it is called the number of transgression.

**v. 6. 7. You have stayed long enough at this mountain: Turn)** The Law cannot make one perfect: It can neither fully destroy sin nor fully restrain it. We must therefore not stand still there. The true Light will call us away to go further, as the LORD did to Israel after they had spent almost a year at Sinai.

### Chapter I. The Fifth Book of Moses.

8. **"Behold, I have set the land before your face; go in and possess the land as an inheritance, which the Lord swore to your fathers—to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob—to give it to them and to their seed after them."**

9. **"And I spoke to you at that time, saying: I am not able to bear you alone."** <margin>Exodus 18:18.</margin>

10. **"The Lord your God has multiplied you, and behold, you are this day as the stars of heaven in multitude."**

11. **"May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add to you a thousand times more than you are, and bless you as He has promised you!"**

---

*v. 8. Go in — possess)* I give you full power to do so, and at the same time, I promise you my help.

*v. 9. etc. A splendid lesson)* which Moses—the "King in Jeshurun" <note>original: "König in Jeschurun"; Jeshurun is a poetic, symbolic name for Israel meaning "the upright one."</note> according to Chapter 33:5—gives to all kings, princes, and other regents. He teaches how they must view their high office and authority not as anything other than a toil and a burden, which has been laid upon them by God’s Providence. In this, they must first look for wise and understanding men who fear God—men who possess a divine rather than a carnal wisdom. They must heartily call upon God for such wisdom, that He might make known to them those whom they can set over many or few, according to the various gifts each man possesses. And so it must also be in the Church, where bishops and teachers must have others joined to them according to the different gifts of the Spirit to help them carry this great toil. <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 12.</note>

*I am not able to bear you alone)* Here one might well ask: *Who is sufficient for these things?* <note>original: "Wer ist hiezu tüchtig?"; referencing 2 Corinthians 2:16.</note> Certainly no one, save by divine shoulders alone.

*v. 10. as the stars)* The promise made to Abraham concerned a twofold seed: one was to be *as the dust of the earth* <note>Genesis 13:16</note> and *as the sand on the seashore* <note>Chapter 22:17</note>; the other was to be *as the stars of heaven* <note>Chapter 15:5</note>. The first was fulfilled in Israel according to the flesh; the other was to be fulfilled in Israel according to the promise. The first was fulfilled in the fathers of these Israelites to whom Moses spoke here; they had multiplied greatly but were of a hard, unrepentant heart <note>Romans 2:5</note> like the sand, and earthly-minded like the dust. The other part of the promise was fulfilled in the people to whom Moses spoke here only as a type <term>type: a biblical person or event that foreshadows a future reality</term>, which was only truly to be fulfilled in the true Israel. And for this reason Moses prays:

*v. 11. May the Lord add to you)* As He does with all those whom the Father brings to the Son, whom He daily adds to His Church and community; as it is written in <note>Acts 2:47</note>. In this "adding" consists a great part of God's blessing upon His people <note>Psalm 115:13, 14</note>, and from it God’s glory follows <note>Isaiah 26:15</note>.

*As you are)* Under the figure of Israel, Moses prays for the Israel of God <note>Psalm 73:1; John 1:48</note>. For just as God added no others to Israel, so Moses could pray for no others. And such are those for whom he prays who is like unto Moses <note>John 17:6-21</note>. Those who are like the sand and the dust—though they be ever so many in number—God can neither bless nor add to the Church of Christ. Therefore, neither Moses nor any other faithful servant of God can pray for the addition of such people, according to the counsel of the wise man <note>Sirach 16:1-12; also known as the Book of Ecclesiasticus.</note>.

<column-break/>

12. **"How can I alone bear your cumbrance, and your burden, and your strife?"**

13. **"Provide from among you wise, understanding, and experienced men according to your tribes, that I may set them as your heads!"**

14. **"Then you answered me and said: The thing which you have spoken is a good thing for us to do."**

15. **"And I took the heads of your tribes, wise and experienced men, and set them as heads over you: captains over thousands, captains over hundreds, captains over fifties, and captains over tens, and officers among your tribes."**

16. **"And I commanded your judges at that time, saying: Hear the causes between your brothers, and judge righteously between every man and his brother, and the stranger that is with him."**

17. **"You shall not respect persons in judgment. You shall hear the small as well as the great. You shall not be afraid of any man's person, for the judgment is God’s. But the cause that is too hard for you, bring it to me, and I will hear it."**

18. **"Thus I commanded you at that time all the words that you should do."**

---

*v. 12. Your burden)* of governance, or of ruling you; and *Your strife)* your legal disputes, which you all brought before me wanting me to decide them.

*v. 13. wise and understanding)* The former in divine things, the latter in human things. For more qualities of a ruler, see <note>Exodus 18:21</note>.

*v. 14. That is a good thing)* We recognize it ourselves as useful.

*v. 15. etc. O, a beautiful lesson for magisterial persons, judges, and regents! Part of it commanding, part of it forbidding.*

*v. 16. Judge righteously)* Properly: "Justice"; so that it indicates the matter being judged. Just as in <note>Deuteronomy 16:20; Psalm 58:1; Zechariah 8:16</note>, where "judging rightly" properly qualifies the judge. In <note>Leviticus 19:15</note> both are united.

*v. 17. You shall not respect persons in judgment)* Or: you shall not recognize faces in judgment. For this reason, the wise heathens <note>Referring to the ancient Greeks or Romans.</note> depicted judges as being without eyes. The judge's concern should be directed at the case itself, without paying heed to the plaintiff or the defendant, and excluding all things that do not serve the case. <note>Psalm 82:2; James 2:1.</note>

*v. 18. All the words)* or commandments, which were issued to you at various times and in various places in the wilderness.

### The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter 1.

19. **Then we departed from Horeb and wandered through all this great and terrible wilderness (a) which you have seen, on the way to the mountains of the Amorites, as the Lord our God commanded us; and we came as far as Kadesh-Barnea.** <note>See Deuteronomy 8:15.</note>

20. **And I said to you: You have come to the mountains of the Amorites, which the Lord our God will give to us.**

21. **Behold, the Lord your God has set the land before your face; go up and possess it as an inheritance, as the Lord, the God of your fathers, has spoken to you: Do not fear and do not be dismayed!**

<margin>v. 19. From Horeb)</margin> Where the Law was received: (1) in the heat of lustful desire, which is stirred up by the Law; Romans 7:8. (2) in drought and thirst, without any rain or dew of grace to quench or alleviate it; (3) in the terror of the sword, of the killing letter: all of which Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> understands by the name Horeb. Then we come into the
<margin>Wilderness)</margin> of Paran, where Hagar and Ishmael dwelt, Genesis 21:20-21, which are allegorically understood as the first covenant. Galatians 4:21–25.
<margin>Wilderness, great and terrible)</margin> The descriptions of this Arabian wilderness give it this quality among others: The soil can be neither plowed nor sown; one sees there neither man, nor cattle, nor birds, nor any trees (except for the Shittim <note>original: "Schittim"; likely Acacia wood used for the Ark of the Covenant.</note> wood around Sinai) or any growth, but only mountains and cliffs; it is also very deep sandy soil, which is made very hot by the sun's heat, making travel very difficult (a): one sees no paths there at all; therefore, those who travel through it must have a compass with them by which they direct themselves, just like sailors who sail through the sea and must direct their journeys by the stars, and also have true pilots as guides, as at sea (b).
This wilderness signifies a lonely and desolate state. 
It is
<margin>Great)</margin> It is a state of long-lasting loneliness and abandonment.
<margin>Terrible)</margin> Because of the fiery serpent—the devil—who commonly visits such wildernesses often and harms us with his poisonous temptations.
This wilderness must be wandered through before we come
<margin>as far as Kadesh-Barnea)</margin> Into the unstable holiness of childhood: and even then, we have still not yet come to rest.
<margin>v. 20. To the mountains)</margin> or mountainous land. 
<margin>Will give)</margin> or "is giving": such expressions indicate those actions of God which He does continually.
<margin>v. 21. Do not fear)</margin> Fear demonstrates a poor, womanish, and despondent spirit, and not an Israelite, who must be brave and courageous. The portion and allotment of the fearful is in a land that is far too hot, dry, and parched. Revelation 21:8.

[Philo of Alexandria's "Life of Moses"]; Drusius in notes on Sulpicius Severus l. 1. c. 26; Dietericus biblical antiquities on Joshua 9:3-5.</note>

22. **Then you all came near to me and said: Let us send men before us to explore the land for us, and bring us word again by which way we should go up into it, and the cities to which we shall come.**

23. **And the matter pleased me in my eyes, and I took twelve men from you, one man from each tribe.**

24. **And they turned and went up into the mountains, and came as far as the Valley of Eshcol, and scouted it out.**

25. **And they took of the fruits of the land in their hands and brought them down to us, and brought us word again and said: The land is good, which the Lord our God has given to us.**

26. **A<unclear>nd</unclear>**

---

After contemplating the Word of God, a further occupation of our spirit may well be found in the consideration of Church History, which is commended to us here by the example of Moses in the repetition of remarkable events, so that we may recognize the wonderful ways of God and of Christ our King in His sanctuary, and note the footprints of His goodness and wisdom, justice and holiness, as well as the wonders of His power. For here too, in its measure, everything that happened before and is thus written and recorded on the foundation of truth and as a type <note>In theology, a "type" is a person or event in the Old Testament believed to foreshadow something in the New Testament.</note> is written for our teaching and edification, and may be used profitably for the strengthening of our faith and as a warning against all the sins with which our ancestors sinned.

And indeed, a great similarity and agreement of these stories with the following history could easily be established if there were space for it here: as may be clear enough to a reader from the mere mention of a few circumstances. For has not Christ also led His people out of the dark Egypt of the Gentiles and appointed good men, Apostles and the seventy disciples, who should govern the spiritual Israel? Has He not also sent out scouts who took the good land into the view of the spirit and knew how to bear good witness of the promised Kingdom of the Lord? But were all of them upright? Have not also false and deceitful workers arisen who held the people back from further breakthrough? And what has now come of it, but that the people had to go into the wilderness, and must still spend time therein?

<margin>v. 23. The matter pleased me)</margin> Because I saw that the Lord was not opposed to this request of yours but consented to it; therefore I also let it please me. God was thus not the first initiator of this mission, as it seems in Numbers 13:2-3, but it is attributed to God only by way of permission. Otherwise, the matter could please neither God nor Moses, because the source of their request was nothing other than unbelief and mistrust.
<margin>v. 24. Whoever wishes to be a spiritual scout must bring back a report of how good the holy land is; he must, following the example of these scouts, necessarily have been in it himself, so that he may speak of it from his own knowledge and experience. John 3:11. Which may be shame enough to all those who know how to speak more from hearsay and denial than from their own experience.</margin>
<margin>v. 25. They said: The land is good)</margin> This was the common answer and testimony of the twelve men.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Deuteronomy Chapter 1. The previous page ended with a description of the "great and terrible wilderness" as an allegory for the spiritual state under the Law. Here, the text addresses the Israelites' refusal to enter the Promised Land and provides a mystical interpretation of God’s guidance through the soul's "wilderness of faith."</meta>

### Ch. I. The Fifth Book of Moses.

**Column 1:**

26. But you would not go up, and were disobedient to the mouth of the Lord your God.
27. And you murmured in your tents, and said: Because the Lord hates us, he has led us out of the land of Egypt to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us.
28. Where shall we go up? Our brothers have made our hearts discouraged, saying: The people are greater and taller than we; the cities are great and fortified up to heaven (*); moreover, we have seen the children of the Anakim there. <margin>(a) Genesis 11:4.</margin>
29. But I said to you: Do not be terrified, and do not be afraid of them!
30. The Lord your God goes before you; he himself will fight for you, according to all that he did for you in Egypt before your eyes;

---

<margin>v. 26. 27.</margin> But because the people did not believe, but rather rebelled and murmured against the Lord; they <note>Referring to the faithless spies.</note> "turned the handle" <note>An idiom meaning they changed their tune or reversed their position.</note> and knew how to quickly change their speech to please the people and accommodate themselves to their mindset: as can be seen from
<margin>v. 28. where the people appeal to them.</margin>
Now, since all these things happened to that people as examples <note>original: "Vorbilder"; patterns or types.</note>, and are written for our warning, upon whom the ends of the world have come (according to the Apostle’s teaching in 1 Corinthians 10:11); then without doubt in these times of the Gospel there must also be those whom these people prefigured. And it is even worse when those who have been in the "Holy Land"—having tasted the good word of God and the powers of the world to come (Hebrews 6:5)—nevertheless, to please the people or out of self-love, seek to maintain a good reputation among the people as "orthodox," right-minded, and proven men, yet cause the hearts of people to melt and become discouraged. For unbelief and fear make the heart soft and melted, whereas it is strengthened by faith and courage.
<margin>v. 29. Do not be afraid).</margin> Do not listen to or obey the fearful, discouraged, and unbelieving scouts.
Even if we must expect many contradictors, both from without and within, who want to make us faint-hearted and hinder us from the pursuit of perfection and the total killing of sin—who say: "It is impossible to be so perfect in this life; in this world we cannot hope to see the dawning day or the morning star rise in our hearts," etc.—we must give no hearing to such spirits, even if there were ten of them against two. Instead, we must listen to Jesus Christ, the faithful witness (Matthew 5:48; Luke 12:32), who gave himself for us that he might redeem us from all unrighteousness (Titus 2:14).
<margin>v. 30.</margin> Let us only become truly at one with this precious ultimate purpose of his incarnation, and we shall have no cause to fear; rather, he himself will stand by us with a strong arm on the path of self-denial until the judgment against sin is carried out unto victory. For
God is the guide of souls as long as they find themselves on the path of suffering; he stands up for them and allows them to yield to him. In this state, he also fights for them against all their enemies to bring about a passage for them.

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

31. And in the wilderness, where you saw how the Lord your God carried you, just as a man carries his son, through all the way that you traveled, until you came to this place. <margin>(a) Luke 15:5.</margin>
32. But in this matter you did not believe the Lord your God:
33. Who went before you on the way to search out a place for you to camp, in a fire by night to show you the way you should go, and in a cloud by day.
34.

---

<margin>v. 31.</margin> In the wilderness of faith, have we not all—all of us who find ourselves in it or have already passed through it—seen that he himself has carried the soul in his arms (to hasten its course), just as a father (but a father full of compassion and love) carries his little children? This expresses very well the love with which God carries souls (as soon as they have blindly surrendered themselves into his arms) through all those dark and difficult paths that one must walk to come to him alone and be received into him.
This also excellently shows how beautifully God's protection and help correspond with the different stages of <term>yieldedness</term> <note>original: "Gelassenheit"; a central term in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of self-will and surrendering to God.</note>. When such a state is, so to speak, only newly born, God first begins by calling from afar; he lets the people be led through the instrument of guidance—men—just as happened during the departure from Egypt. When yieldedness has progressed further, God himself comes and is the guide: which happened when the people arrived in the wilderness, where God went before them in the cloud. But as soon as yieldedness is at its "blindest," and thus at its most perfect, God takes this, his beloved people, into his arms and carries them with as much speed as safety into the true Promised Land, which is the transformation <note>original: "Vergestallung"; literally 're-shaping' or 'transfiguration.'</note> into himself.
One must further note that, just as it is natural that where there is more assurance and evidence, there is less faith and yieldedness; and conversely, where more faith and yieldedness are required, there must necessarily be less evidence and less assurance. So too, as long as yieldedness is still weak and imperfect, God does not do as much for the sake of such souls, because they still have many supports outside of him. But the more they become "blind" <note>Refers to "blind faith," or trust without sensory or intellectual proof.</note> and detach themselves to trust in him alone, the more he leads them through unknown ways, so that he may all the more exercise their loyalty and thus prove it. And finally, when it seems to them as if they are entirely lost—finding themselves in a great and terrifying wilderness without a single light of hope, where one might say they lack everything and that such impenetrable paths could lead to nothing but their destruction—precisely then God holds them in his arms and carries them with even greater speed and safety into himself. For he is delighted that one hopes (*) against all hope, and that one trusts him even without the slightest hope of a good outcome. <margin>(a) Romans 4:18.</margin>
<margin>v. 32.</margin> But where faith is lacking in this matter, and one does not trust God enough out of self-love, nor wishes to risk oneself entirely in God;
<margin>v. 33.</margin> Then, although our unbelief may not cancel out God’s faithfulness and truth (for he always remains fatherly-minded), we only come more slowly to the goal and the place of rest that God has prepared for us, and we remain subject to change, to darkness and light, to night and day, in which God must also bear witness to himself in various ways.

### The Fifth Book of Moses. Ch. I.

34. But when the **Lord** heard the voice of your words, he became very angry, and swore and said:

<margin>Ps. 95:11.</margin>
35. Not one of these men of this evil generation shall see the good land that I swore to give to your fathers.

36. Except **Caleb**, the son of **Jephunneh**; he shall see it, and to him I will give the land upon which he has trodden, and to his children, because he has fully followed the **Lord**.

<margin>Num. 20:12, 27:14.</margin>
37. The **Lord** was also angry with me for your sakes, and said: You also shall not go in there.

38. **Joshua**, the son of **Nun**, who stands before your face, he shall go in there; strengthen him: for he shall distribute it to **Israel** as an inheritance.

*The repetition of what came before is very clear here, which will occur quite often in this book: therefore, in many places we may only refer back to what was previously written, while here and there catching up on a few things that found no place there.*

<margin>v. 36. To him I will give the land) But not without a struggle. The Lord’s promises do not exempt people from their duty and from the application of their utmost strength in the same.</margin>

<margin>To his children) These are either his children according to the flesh, or according to the spirit. By spiritual children and the seed of men, those are understood who are like them in their minds, wills, inclinations, senses, and opinions. Rom. 4:12, Josh. 8:39. Thus the children of Caleb are those who, like him, are servants of the Lord, who have another, a new spirit, and fulfill the will of the Lord after him.</margin>

<margin>Fully followed the Lord) This almost unanimous translation of others is kept for the sake of its good sense, although in the Hebrew no word is found that means "to follow"; just as in Num. 14:24, 32:11, Josh. 14:8, 9, 14, 1 Kings 11:6. Rather, it says: "he fulfilled after me," namely, the word and the will of God. This establishes the foundation that the Lord himself fulfilled that same will before him. But the one who speaks here is Christ. Those things he wishes others to do after him, he does first himself. Jer. 9:24. Just as the Lord presents the doing of his word and will, so he also presents himself to us as a pattern and example, so that as he has done, we should also do. What servant will complain about doing that which his lord and master does before him? Or do we think Christ fulfilled the Law before us so that we should not fulfill it after him, in him, and through him? Truly, just as the Son fulfills the will of the Father after him, John 6:38, so also the believers fulfill the will of the Father and Son after them in the Father and Son, Eph. 5:1, and it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. Matt. 3:15. This is what God the Father himself practices, and which the Son fulfills after him, and which the holy angels fulfill after the Son, Ps. 103:20, and all faithful and obedient people fulfill after God. This must be done not only because God wants it: but God wants it because it is holy, just, and good in and of himself and in his own nature, and is therefore called an eternal righteousness. It is thus not left to our free will and whim to fulfill or leave undone what God himself, the Son of God, all good angels, and all good desires fulfill—he fulfills his father the Devil and his desires.</margin> <note>The text here appears to break off or transition into a warning about following the opposite path of the devil.</note>

<margin>v. 37. Also over me) Who, along with Aaron, when they should have sanctified the Lord, displayed their weakness through unbelief. But the Lord does not overlook sin even in the best of men.</margin>

<column-break/>

39. And your children, of whom you said they would become a prey, and your sons, who this day understand neither good nor evil, they shall go in there, and to them I will give it, and they shall possess it as an inheritance.

40. But as for you, turn, and journey into the wilderness by the way of the **Red Sea** <note>original: "Schilff-Meer"; literally "Reed Sea."</note>.

41. Then you answered and said to me: We have sinned against the **Lord**; we will go up and fight, according to all that the **Lord** our **God** commanded us. And when every one of you had girded on his weapons of war, and you were willing to go up into the mountain;

42. Then the **Lord** said to me: Say to them: You shall not go up, and you shall not fight; for I am not among you; lest you be struck down before your enemies.

<margin>v. 39. Your children) The descendants of those who, in our days, have despised and rejected the testimony of the glorious kingdom of Christ in unbelief, shall get to see it.</margin>

<margin>Actually it says, "your little one," in the singular, from which it is to be concluded that the Holy Spirit does not only aim at the literal <note>original: "stäblichen"; related to the letter or the staff.</note> sense, for otherwise he would have expressed it in the plural. But there is one within us whom we do not know: John 1:26, 14. And that same one is a little one, kind, lowly, and small in his own eyes, and also a body of lowliness. Matt. 11:29, Phil. 2:8. This is the one who obtains the prize. 1 Cor. 9:24.</margin>

<margin>They shall come there) The sins of evil parents shall not harm their children regarding the entrance into the heavenly land.</margin>

<margin>Children and little ones are recognized by the Savior alone as heirs of the Kingdom of God. Luke 18:17. For if we also wish to become partakers of it, we must turn back and become like children, Matt. 18:3, who are humble, lowly, and small in his eyes, innocent, simple, without deceit. 1 Cor. 14:20. Conversely, when we outgrow this childhood, we lose our innocence, becoming crafty, haughty, malicious, proud, etc., and are thereby excluded from the holy kingdom. Let us therefore pray to the Lord that he would bless the little one in our midst, the new man, who is renewed in knowledge after the image of him who created him; Col. 3:10. so that we may receive heavenly power as the little ones, through the Little One, the heir of the kingdom, Jesus Christ our Lord.</margin>

<margin>They shall possess it as an inheritance) Here one could mention what the best inheritance is that parents can give to their children. Namely, that one makes them heirs of the kingdom in faith. James 2:5. And what a great privilege and blessing it is for children when they have good parents! Prov. 20:7.</margin>

<margin>v. 40. turn yourselves) By this the truth is also confirmed, which must precede before the entrance into the kingdom of God may happen: because it is only indicated for the children.</margin>

<margin>v. 41. We will) When the Lord willed, you did not will: now they will, but the Lord does not. Here obedience is better than a good intention.</margin>

### Column 1

43. When I spoke this to you, you did not listen, and became disobedient to the command of the **Lord**, and acted presumptuously, and went up into the mountains.
44. Then the **Amorites**, who dwelt on that same mountain, came out against you and pursued you, as bees do, and struck you down in **Seir** as far as **Hormah**.

<margin>b. 43. You acted presumptuously and went up)</margin>
It is dangerous to start a war without mature reflection, especially when one relies on one's own strength in doing so.

However, the Church in its present state is also easily overhasty in entangling itself in thoughtless disputes: whereby, because it thus sets aside the purest dictates of conscience and the soundest teachings of the Gospel, it draws upon itself similar chastisements and punishments, as Israel did here, according to

<margin>v. 44. Oh, let nothing be undertaken in spiritual matters to which the **Lord** has not given His consent, no matter how plausible it may always seem to us! Rather, await the **Lord's** counsel and will, when He commands it and precedes and leads us in His Word. Otherwise,</margin>

Where we venture into a struggle in our own strength and self-presumption against the **Amalekites** and **Amorites**—the sensual and devilish sins—by presumptuously relying on our own spiritual strength and virtue which we imagine we possess: then we shall fail, and we will realize that we are a match neither for the **Amalekites**, those hidden locusts of earthly desires and inclinations, nor for the **Amorites**, the spirit of bitterness; but rather they will triumph over us, turn us away from our **God**, and like **Canaanites** incline our heart to the world and its commerce and bow us down to the earth. And thus they will bring the curse of **God** upon us and the utter ruin of destruction. For that is what the word **Hormah** <note>The name Hormah means "destruction" or "devoted to God for destruction."</note> signifies.

<margin>v. 45. Then the Lord did not hear)</margin>
In the holiness of the un- <unclear>certainty</unclear> <note>original: "un- [illegible]"</note> as it seems, they would have liked to go up once more and persisted for victory.

<margin>v. 46. You remained in Kadesh)</margin>
In the holiness of unstable childhood. Such is the state of many thousands, because they are taught by many that we cannot go further, that we are already pious enough, and that the rest is replaced through **Christ**.

All those who seal themselves and are satisfied with a good will or an intention to do good, remain sitting in a lower grave of life and want to rest therein: yet the essence of a Christian consists in progress. This should indeed rightly shame us and remind us that we should not place our rest in the first beginning of the journey or pilgrimage, but powerfully encourage ourselves to go from one power and strength to another, until we may appear in **Zion**.

Oh, it is not good for a soul when it sits down and takes its rest on the way before it has come to **God's** rest!

# Chapter II.
## The avoidance of other borders and the overcoming of Sihon.

1. Thereafter we turned and traveled into the wilderness, by way of the **Red Sea**, just as the **Lord** had spoken to me: and we circled **Mount Seir** for many days.
2. Then the **Lord** spoke to me and said:
3. You have circled this mountain long enough; turn toward the north. <meta>4. And</meta>

---

<insert>
In the first part of this chapter, **Moses** once again earnestly enjoins upon the children of **Israel** that they should not interfere in the slightest with the land of the **Edomites**, **Moabites**, and **Ammonites**: which was to be understood even more so in the sense that they should not concern themselves with their corrupted worship, though they might think they should particularly apply themselves to converting these peoples to the true faith, since they all descended from one origin, **Abraham** and his father; rather, they should leave them peacefully in their possession, both in physical matters and otherwise in their supposed worship. Which indeed Christians should notice all the more: to leave every people undisturbed within their borders and their worship, and to be content with one's own, and to act in worship according to the impulse of one's conscience; the omission of these two parts has at all times been the cause of so many bloody wars, whose authors will have a heavy accountability. This great offense will also be completely abolished in **Christ's** glorious kingdom, where every people and family will let one another dwell quite peacefully in their possession, and all will encourage one another to simple praise in the unanimous knowledge of **God**. Then war will no longer be waged for land and people or for the sake of religion. They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the land shall be full of the knowledge of the **Lord**, as the waters cover the sea. **Isaiah 2:4, 11:9**.
</insert>

<margin>v. 1. we traveled)</margin>
The Law of the **Lord** is a way, **Ps. 119:1**, and the Gospel is also a way, **Acts 19:9**, both of which go into one another and bring us to **Canaan**, we who by virtue of our confession do not belong at home here, but are pilgrims who seek, or indeed should seek, a fatherland that is better and heavenly. **Heb. 11:16**.

This way to **Canaan** and the journey upon it is not completed all at once, but requires progress: it is interconnected, and the movement and walking therein are continuous. There are different campsites, various steps, distinct degrees on the way of life, where sometimes there is a broadening or expansion, and sometimes a narrowing or contraction in divine graces. It is an increase of faith, **Rom. 1:17**, an abundance in hope, **Rom. 15:13**, a walking and growth in grace, according to which we may precede and surpass one another.

On this way, **Mount Seir** or the land of the **Edomites**—that is, flesh and blood—must also be circled.

<margin>v. 3. You have circled this mountain long enough.)</margin>
The **Lord** knows when it is enough to turn the endured hardship and thus to deliver us from it, and thereafter to give one victory after another, as they then, after such a laborious detour, attained one victory after another over their enemies and brought away the fat, fertile **Bashan** as an inheritance. When we have also avoided contact with the sedentary and disorderly brothers who will not be obedient to the word of admonition, **2 Thess. 3:14, 15**, we must also know when it is enough to have withdrawn from them, so that they are not provoked to anger but may be won through friendliness. See **2 Cor. 2:6**.

## Chapter II. The Fifth Book of Moses [Deuteronomy].

16. And it happened, when all the men of war had come to an end, having died from among the people;
17. Then the **LORD** spoke to me, saying:
18. Today you shall pass through the border of the Moabites, through Ar;
19. And you shall come near the children of Ammon: you shall not harass them, nor engage in strife with them. For I will give you no inheritance from the land of the children of Ammon: for I have given it to the children of Lot as an inheritance.
20. It is also counted as a land of giants: giants formerly lived therein; and the Ammonites called them Samsummim <note>The author later interprets this name as representing "perverse thoughts."</note>.
21. It was a great and strong and tall people, like the Anakim; and the **LORD** destroyed them before them, and they took it as an inheritance and lived in their place:
22. Just as he did for the children of Esau, who dwell in Seir, when he destroyed the Horites before them, and they took their inheritance and lived in their place until this day.
23. And as for the Avvites, who lived in Hazarim as far as Gaza, the Caphtorim, who came out of Caphtor <note>Caphtor is traditionally identified with Crete or parts of the Nile Delta; the Caphtorim are associated with the ancestry of the Philistines.</note>, destroyed them and lived in their place.

<note>
**v. 16. All the men of war)** those who had marched out of Egypt and were included among those counted and mustered.
**v. 17.-19.)** Repeated as in verse 9 and those following.
**v. 20. Samsummim)** are the high, giant-like thoughts that contemplate perverse things.
**v. 21. The Anakim)** were the giants of Canaan who lived around Hebron, of whom more is said elsewhere.
**v. 22. Just as he did)** And thus all four related peoples descended from Isaac and Lot—the Edomites, Moabites, Ammonites, and Israelites (the latter being the last)—received a land assigned by the **LORD**, from which they first had to drive out the inhabitants.
**v. 23. The Avvites)** are those who are elsewhere called Hivites in the Scripture.
**The Caphtorim)** were a people in Palestine who belonged to the Philistines, or at least lived mingled among them. See Jeremiah 47:4.
</note>

<column-break/>

24. Arise, journey forth and cross the brook Arnon! See, I have given Sihon, the King of Heshbon, the Amorite, into your hand with his land: begin to take possession, and engage him in strife.
25. This day I will begin to put the dread and fear of you upon the peoples under the whole heaven: whoever hears the report of you shall tremble and be in anguish before your face.
26. Then...

---

-> All who intend to travel toward the spiritual Canaan find themselves encouraged here to let go of all false and imperfect rest that they might encounter on the way, and to pursue perfection. <-

**v. 24. Cross the brook Arnon)** Out of the adjacent curse that rises in full force against those who have a mere appearance of godliness but lack the life.
**Arnon** is the name of a rock, a city, and a brook.
**Rivers** were the boundaries of lands in ancient times. So too was this brook. Numbers 21:13.
According to the mystery, **Arnon** means as much as the **light of a child** <note>This likely refers to a mystical etymology connecting the Hebrew 'Or' (light) and 'Nin' (descendant/child).</note>; and therefore, to cross the brook Arnon means the progress and increase of the divine light: we should not always be children, but grow up. Ephesians 4:15.
It is a shame for a Christian to always plead and pretend childish weakness, especially when one desires to be a grown man in Christianity.
This exhortation, therefore, primarily concerns those who are engaged in a real beginning and progress of the new birth.
**See)** Take good note! The matter is presented to the eye of faith.
**I have given)** Here we have the Lord's free gift. **GOD** has a manifold right to dispose of the persons and goods of men, of kings and their land, according to His pleasure. After the Great Flood, He made a general covenant with all peoples in Noah: all who transgress this covenant have fallen under the just judgment of **GOD** and the penalty of confiscation.
**Sihon)** the destroyer, the demolisher; that is, Satan himself: whose court and residence is
**At Heshbon)** In the thoughts or rational reflections, which in 2 Corinthians 10:4-5 are called strongholds, or rather, robber-castles and nests of evil spirits.
**The Amorite)** the bitter, envious spirit which devastates and destroys all good thoughts and senses of the heart, as well as all good and wholesome words.
When, therefore, heavenly thoughts lodge within us, the Spirit of **GOD** rules us; and the essential Word of **GOD** takes up its residence in us. But when vain, sinful, impure, ungodly thoughts dwell in a person, then Sihon the Amorite rules in them. He then also ignites their tongues to vain, sinful, bitter words (James 3:6); and thus the word of Belial dwells in them.
**Engage in strife)** There must be a struggle for everything you wish to possess. The promises of **GOD** do not exempt us from the duty required of us to obtain the promises.
**With him)** Set good thoughts against his evil thoughts. If the enemy meets you with bitterness, answer him with gentleness. If the Amorite approaches you with harsh words, give him soft words in return. If the Amorite proceeds to cursing, then you must bless. Matthew 5:44.
**v. 25.** Therefore, it should be far from the Israel of **GOD** to fear their enemies and to let themselves be terrified and discouraged by them; rather, they should face their enemies boldly, and through the name of their **GOD**, which must stand and shine upon their foreheads, they shall be a terror to all their enemies.

# The Fifth Book of Moses [Deuteronomy]. Chapter II.

34. And we took all his cities at that time, and utterly destroyed <note>original: "verbanneten" — refers to the biblical 'ban' (herem), where a city was completely devoted to destruction as a religious act.</note> every city with the men and the women and the children; we left no one remaining.

35. Only the livestock we took as plunder for ourselves, and the spoil of the cities which we captured.

36. From Aroer, which lies on the bank of the Arnon valley, and the city that lies in the valley, even as far as Gilead, there was no city too high for us: the **LORD** our God gave them all before us.

37. Only to the land of the children of Ammon you did not come near, to the whole region of the Jabbok valley and the cities on the mountains, nor to anything that the **LORD** our God had forbidden.

---

<columns>2</columns>

The first enemy who must be overcome before the conquest of Canaan is Sihon, the king of Heshbon: Since then—as already partially indicated—according to the secret meaning of the Hebrew words, **Heshbon** signifies a "conclusion of reason" or a "prejudice," and **Sihon** signifies a "sweeping away." <note>The author uses Hebrew etymology to argue that Heshbon (from 'heshbon', meaning account or reasoning) and Sihon represent the mental barriers of worldly logic that must be swept away.</note>

Before obtaining the heavenly inheritance of true wisdom, first all reasonings and prejudices of fleshly wisdom must be overcome—indeed, swept away like dung. *Ecclesiastes 7:29. 2 Corinthians 10:5. Philippians 3:8.*

**v. 28.** In our pilgrimage through the world, we must desire no comforts; we should not wish to be carried by horses or in litters, nor to be treated delicately. If we have food and clothing, let us be content.

**v. 29. Until across the Jordan, into the land that God will give us)** This is the image of eternity, and of the kingdom that lies beyond and is not of this world.

**v. 30. Sihon — would not)** show friendship. The enemy must first be discovered before we can fight him. But Sihon, the "man of sin," the leader of evil thoughts, cannot be discovered unless a falling away occurs first. *2 Thessalonians 2:3.*

**v. 31. Begin)** A beginning must be made before you should imagine that you are near the end. Learn from this to test your false confidence, O vain man! Who has bewitched you, O false Christian, to build such beautiful castles of confidence in the air, when you have not yet even laid the foundation for them, nor rightly commenced the work of salvation? Surely none other than Sihon, the king of Heshbon. You are completely assured and certain of your salvation before you have denied yourself and formed a serious mind to follow your Savior on the cross. Consider how you deceive yourself!

<column-break/>

**v. 33. God delivered him so that we struck him down)** It then depends on this: even if giants of thoughts rise up against us! Could any be too powerful for God, that He should not be able to overcome them? Let us only put on the armor of God!

**v. 34. All cities)** those under the tyranny of Sihon must be captured, the strongholds and heights of reason torn down, and bitter strife and envy rooted out. We must take possession of our thoughts and reason, taking them in little by little as our own inheritance, tearing our mental powers from his dominion and from the claws of Satan, who had unlawfully subjected them to his power and influence through cunning and violence.

**v. 35. The spoil of the cities)** however, and what can still be used of the heathens' things, we may keep for ourselves.

**v. 36.** Why then do we now complain about weakness and the difficulty of the matter! Whatever one undertakes, the beginning is difficult. The progress will already be easier, and the outcome glorious and joyful. No city shall be too high for us; the **LORD** our God will give them all into our power: so that we need not blame Him that we have no grace, no strength for it. But it must be attacked.

**v. 37.** God also does not demand too much from us. He only wants the kingdom of sin destroyed, not that of nature; indeed, this is contrary to Him.

<columns>1</columns>

**His land)** is the land of Gilead. But Gilead means "a heap of witnesses" <note>The Hebrew name 'Gilead' (Gal-ed) literally means 'heap of witness'.</note> and signifies the multitude of divine promises, which are turned into mere chatter when and where Sihon is king. This Gilead is still in the hands of men. Therefore, there are indeed many **chatter-Christians** <term>Schwätz-Christen: a derogatory term for those who talk much about theology but lack spiritual practice or "deeds."</term>, but few **deed-Christians**. Everything that people read, everything they hear, everything they contemplate—everything they learn and grasp through reading, hearing, and contemplating—happens only so that they can discourse about it. *Ezekiel 33:30.*

---

Because God’s threats generally contain the condition that one should heartily repent of the sins and transgressions for which they were issued; (see Jeremiah 18:4, Jonah 3:4, where God turned away from His threat upon such repentance;) so Moses also supposed here, after the threat had been made that he should not enter the promised land (Numbers 20:12), that he might plead for its withdrawal. The Lord, however, for holy and secret reasons, did not wish to be turned from His decree, though He otherwise gladly does what those who fear God desire. This teaches us to submit ourselves humbly when God will not take a certain chastisement from us, for which He will otherwise richly refresh us in spirit, so that we can let ourselves be satisfied with that.
<margin>v. 23, 24.</margin> The Jews consider it a mystery of these prayers that a person should always first set forth the praise of the LORD and only afterward ask for their necessities.
<margin>v. 25.</margin> Consider the humble address of Moses.
<margin>Please let me go over the Jordan)</margin> Honest hearts are willing to go with Moses through the judgment of humiliation as the true means that leads them to the enjoyment of salvation. They are ready to be baptized with Him into Christ and to become like His death, so that they may also participate in His resurrection, see His glory, and enjoy His heart as the center and origin of all blessing: from whence they also expect the strong, blessed Spirit, like a stream flowing from Lebanon, from the heart of the Son. Song of Solomon 4:15.
<margin>This good mountain)</margin> upon which he looks, was Mount Zion, which was a prototype of the other covenant, or the Church under the Gospel (Galatians 4:24, 25) and of Heaven itself (Hebrews 12:22).
<margin>Lebanon)</margin> Under this, one can understand the heart of the Son or of the Eternal One, in which all treasures of wisdom and love are hidden. The desire and longing of the souls of the honest-minded are directed there most of all, even if they are still under the first guidance, and their sighing goes toward this perfection: they set their desires on the goods that are above, on the lovely, sweet-smelling holy mountain. They long for the perfect beauty of the internal inheritance, the heart of Christ, which is presented there as the pure object of sweet contemplation.
<margin>v. 26. On your account)</margin> By your occasion, since your unbelieving murmuring caused me not to rightly direct the rock in bringing forth the water. <note>original note: "Schuld" — Guilt</note> Numbers 20:24.

<note>This does not forbid the gift of prophecy / when we strive to explore the meaning of the Word / and the will of God through His Spirit: rather, it warns only that we should not present such prophecy and explanation as God's infallible Word or as an eternal truth / which we must instead leave to the judgment of the believers, according to 1 Corinthians 14:29. <note>v. 2. However, this does not exclude God’s own infallible opening and explanation of the same through the Saints themselves / or the revelation of that same Spirit / who first dictated and inspired it; as people often cite and misuse this passage and Revelation 22:18 against extraordinary revelations: as if such explanations / if they were written down / would be entirely new scriptures. And has not also the observation of the entire ceremonial law in its literal sense been done away with and abolished / which was nevertheless commanded by Moses to be kept? Accordingly, these prohibitions do not bind the Spirit of God / so that He might not give infallible explanations of those things that were written before / or give clearer openings of those mysteries / which were previously only touched upon briefly or somewhat obscurely / or rescue the written Word from the false glosses and interpretations of others / by which the sense and meaning of the Holy Spirit has been greatly obscured or even lost.</note>

<margin>v. 6. This people is a wise and understanding people*)</margin>
From this, the Jews of today wish to prove their cleverness and sharpness of mind. However, as long as the people of Israel clung to the Word of God—to which they were urged by the prophets—they were indeed the only wise and understanding people on the earth. But as soon as they exalted the traditions of their elders too highly, and searched after them more than the word of the prophets, they (along with their elders) were unable to recognize the Messiah when He appeared, and they rejected Him. Therefore, by the righteous judgment of God, they have become a blind, unwise, and senseless people. <note>original: "Esa. 42/19. Jer. 5/21."</note> This should serve as a warning to Christians, whose wisdom consists solely in the contemplation of the infallible work of God. For if one clings only to the wisdom of the schools and the world, one is unexpectedly led away from true wisdom and gradually falls into the greatest follies and lack of understanding.

<margin>v. 7. The comparison here is made between the presence and help of the gods of the heathens, which they provide to their various peoples, and the presence and help of the one true God, which He demonstrates to His people Israel. Of this, experience has hitherto become known from the histories of the Egyptians, Amalekites, and Midianites: to which the people's own experience the words refer.</margin>

<margin>So near as the LORD our God)</margin> Can He be any nearer to you than in your very midst? <margin>chapter 23:14; 30:14. Leviticus 26:11–12. Numbers 5:3. Ezekiel 37:26.</margin>

<margin>Keep your soul)</margin> For it is in danger of being lost. Gather your wandering thoughts and desires.

<margin>well) Carefully.</margin>

Thus God has entrusted to us the guardianship and oversight of ourselves and our souls.

<margin>v. 10. At Horeb) otherwise Sinai. Exodus 20:1.</margin>

<margin>v. 11. Into the midst of heaven)</margin> or, to the heart of the heaven: by which emphasis, though expressed figuratively, an immense height is indicated.

<margin>v. 12. One can indeed hear the speech of God, as it is His word and the voice of God Himself; but one can see neither image nor likeness of Him that would be similar to Him, because nothing that can be formed or imagined can be God. From this it also happens that so many errors are found in matters of "enlightenments" and visions.</margin>

This also indicates the necessity of being stripped of all forms and images—both those of the senses and those existing in the understanding—in order to arrive at pure contemplation and inner union. For nothing perceptible, nor anything that may be grasped by the human spirit with a distinction, can be sufficient to lead the soul into God; because He is infinitely far beyond all of this. <note>This commentary reflects a mystical theology often called "Apophatic," which suggests God is best known by looking past physical or mental images.</note>

<margin>v. 13. His covenant — the 10 words)</margin> The words can present the Covenant of Grace or the Covenant of Works. For what are the 10 words to a believer other than a Covenant of Grace? And what can they be to an unbeliever other than a Covenant of Works? There are three different things in the 10 words: 1) Commands, 2) Promises, 3) Threats. If one now connects the commands with the promises for the comfort of the believers, what is that but a Covenant of Grace? But when one attaches the commands to the threats, what can they look like but a Covenant of Works? <note>The "Covenant of Works" refers to the idea of earning salvation through perfect obedience, while the "Covenant of Grace" refers to God's unmerited favor.</note>

# Chapter IV. The Fifth Book of Moses

**15.** So take good heed of your souls! For you saw no form whatsoever on the day the Lord spoke to you at Horeb <note>Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai, the site where the Ten Commandments were given.</note> from the midst of the fire.
**16.** Lest you corrupt yourselves and make for yourselves a carved image, the form of any likeness, the shape of a man or a woman.
**17.** The shape of any beast that is on the earth; the shape of any winged bird that flies through the heavens.
**18.** The shape of any creeping thing on the land; the shape of any fish that is in the water under the earth.
**19.** And lest you lift up your eyes to heaven and see the sun and the moon and the stars, the whole host <gloss>(a) Jeremiah 8:2.</gloss> of heaven, and be driven to worship them and serve them, which the Lord your God has distributed to all peoples under the whole heaven.
**20.** But the Lord has taken you and led you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt, that you should be his people of inheritance <gloss>(a) 1 Peter 2:9.</gloss>, as it is this day.

---

v. 15. **No form whatsoever of any likeness**) For every true vision, one finds a great number that are false. The human spirit often imagines all sorts of things for itself, and the imagination immediately creates images based on things it might have seen. Therefore, in the path of faith, there is no more talk of such things: both because all sensory things are taken away from the soul so that it may become purer, and because such things would hinder the soul from proceeding further by always keeping it within itself—in sensation and in discernment—all of which is contrary to faith.
v. 16. **The shape of a man**) Although God appeared in the form of a man and an "Ancient of Days" <note>original: "Alten von Tagen"; a reference to the vision in Daniel 7:9.</note>, see Exodus 24:10 and Daniel 7:9, 13, the nature, size, and other properties of this human essence in which God appears remain hidden from us. Therefore, it is indeed highly sinful to depict God in such a form like our own; this is something for which Christendom will be heavily visited <note>In this context, "visited" implies being judged or punished by God.</note>, as it has partly made itself guilty of this.
v. 17. 18. **The shape**) is little recommended anywhere in divine service or in Holy Scripture. See Romans 2:20 and 2 Timothy 3:5.
v. 19. God distributed the host of heaven to the heathens, not so they would worship them, but so that through the contemplation of them, they might rise to the knowledge of the Creator. See Isaiah 40:26. To His people, however, He has communicated Himself quite clearly through His Word and the wonders shown among them, so that they should have Him—and not lifeless creatures and other mute idols—as their portion. See Chapter 29:26 and Psalm 16:5.
v. 20. **Out of the iron furnace**) of Egyptian servitude. Thus, all heavy tribulation is called a "furnace of misery" in Isaiah 48:10, because through it, people are melted down, as it were, like metals in a furnace.

<column-break/>

**21.** And the Lord was angry with me for your sakes, so that He swore I should not go over the Jordan, nor enter into the good land <gloss>(a) chapter 1:37, 3:26.</gloss> which the Lord your God will give you for an inheritance.
**22.** But I must die in this land; I shall not go over the Jordan: but you shall go over, that you may possess this good land as an inheritance.
**23.** So take heed now, lest you forget the covenant of the Lord your God, which He made with you, nor make for yourselves a carved image of any form, which the Lord your God has forbidden you.
**24.** For the Lord your God is a consuming fire <gloss>(a) Nahum 1:6.</gloss>, a jealous God. <gloss>Exodus 20:5, 34:7.</gloss> **25.**

---

v. 21. **The Lord was angry with me—that He swore I should not, etc.**) Why this happened, see Numbers 20:12 and 27:14. Note the severity of God in punishing sin, even in His most chosen ones. You will not easily find a single misdeed mentioned in Scripture upon which the proper reward does not follow, and most often it is set down immediately thereafter. First, among the saints, came the conviction and punishment of the conscience, and then the actual chastisement followed, and indeed with great earnestness and zeal from the offended God. They were also so upright that they confessed and did not deny it. Their hearts were convicted by the omniscience and holiness of the Lord. Therefore, the Lord also took away their sins; but even after the forgiveness of their sins, He nevertheless chastised them all, so that they might escape eternal punishment. For punishment is so inseparably linked with sin by virtue of divine justice that you would be the first among all men who had sinned and not been punished. And if it did not happen here, you would be all the more miserable after death. Mark this!
v. 22. **I must die in this land**) In the fields of Moab, as a prototype of the goal of the divine economy <term>Economy: Here meaning God's plan or management of the world and salvation.</term> and the stewardship of the Father.
v. 23. **Take heed, lest you forget the covenant of your God**) O soul, guard your heart against forgetfulness! Let not the commandments of wisdom depart from your heart! Guard them, indeed, eat them constantly into your spiritual mouth, and let them become the life of your heart.
v. 24. **God is a consuming fire**) Which leaves nothing of the "self" <note>original: "eigenes"; referring to the selfish nature or ego.</note> in the creature without turning it into ashes. As soon as He enters a heart, He must annihilate, consume, and destroy everything else within it. He is also
**A jealous God**) O, if one truly recognized the jealousy of God, and how He can suffer nothing alongside Himself—be it ever so great and holy—how would one not be terrified by it! there is nothing He does not employ to hold mastery and to remove and destroy all hindrances that prevent Him from being alone in the soul. He can tolerate nothing else, whatever it may be. No virtue, no holiness, can walk in His company. He is jealous: that says it all. And just as He is the most lovely and the most faithful of all beloveds, so He is also the most jealous lover. Therefore, He also calls Himself a consuming fire, so that He may turn everything into ashes that causes Him any displeasure.

---

v. 25. **Old in the land)** that is, long-time inhabitants.
v. 26. **Heaven and earth)** Angels and men, as some explain it (a). <note>original: "Hieron. ad Esa. 1, 2." refers to St. Jerome’s commentary on the prophet Isaiah.</note> But even inanimate creatures may give sufficient testimony in God's cause, often showing people they are neither mute nor blind witnesses when, by God's righteous judgment, they withhold what would otherwise be abundantly provided during a godly life according to the promise.
v. 27. **A small number)** A group so few they are easily counted. Genesis 34:30. Such is also the Church. Luke 12:32.
v. 28. Moses proclaims to this people that if they do not allow themselves to be consumed by the aforementioned fire <note>The "fire" refers to the presence of God at Sinai, interpreted here as a refining spiritual fire that purifies the believer.</note> and instead choose to live in images and outward supports, they would serve gods made by human hands: they would then be subjected to the labor of an "active life" in order to acquire good and holy things through it <note>The author contrasts the "active life" of external religious works with the "contemplative life" of inner faith.</note>.
v. 29. Nevertheless, he assures them that even in the midst of their activity, they will find God, if only they seek Him in their heart; for that is the place where He wishes to be found. But this will happen only in the midst of the cross and tribulations that accompany this state: which cross is nonetheless much sweeter than all sweetness. God must be sought with the whole heart within the heart: and by seeking God with the whole heart, one finds the God of the heart.
(a) Jerome on Isaiah 1:2.

v. 32. 33. Holy Scripture assures us that no other people but those on the "inner way" and the "surrendered heart" <note>original: "gelassene Herz." These spiritual states pass by and are worked so that the soul recognizes that God alone is Lord, and that outside of Him it is impossible to find any other life.</note>

This happens once all foreign thoughts, lusts, and the desires of the "heathen" will have been driven out. In this way, the soul preserves all of God's commandments; herein lies true happiness and the right long life, which is well-spent in attaining eternal life.</note>
