# Chapter XV.

->The Year of Release.<-

At the end of seven years you shall hold a Year of Release.
2. And this is how it shall be with the Year of Release: every creditor shall release what he has lent to his neighbor; he shall not demand it from his neighbor or from his brother: because a Year of Release for the Lord has been proclaimed.
3. From a foreigner you may demand it: but what you have with your brother, your hand shall release.

---

Concerning the Year of Release—insofar as it was a Sabbath or Rest Year, just as the 7th day was a Day of Rest, in which both the land and those who cultivated it rested—this has been discussed above. Exodus 23:10, 11; Leviticus 25:1–7.

Here it is now commanded, moreover, that in that same year all debts should be released—namely, to those who were poor and unable to pay.

From this one can observe that those who were rich and wealthy should not have undertaken anything for which they would have to borrow money from their neighbor, and thus have had to carry out such a thing with someone else's money: something to which people in these modern days are all too inclined. They do not know what a heavy responsibility before God they take upon themselves when their successors—even if they be their own children—are so negligent in paying and do not concern themselves with it in the slightest.

v. 1. This 7th year did not begin with the month of Nisan <note>The first month of the religious calendar, roughly March-April.</note>, by which all other festivals in the year were otherwise determined, but from the month of Tisri <note>The first month of the civil calendar, roughly September-October.</note>, when the civil year began, for the benefit of the land. For otherwise, in many places, the grain and the fruits of the sixth year would have remained standing in the fields.

v. 2. How this year was distinguished from other years, and why it was specifically called the "Year of Release," was that whatever one had advanced to a needy neighbor who could not pay it back, had to be released in this year, and thus love and mercy were to be shown to him.

*Should every man release what was borrowed?* If the creditor held a written bond <term>Handschrifft: a signed legal document acknowledging debt</term> from the poor debtor, he had to return it to him and say in addition: "I give this to you!"

By "neighbor," we are to understand whoever from other nations became a companion to the Jews by adopting the Jewish religion; and for that very reason, such a person was also counted among the "brothers."

v. 3. And so this did not happen toward each and every person, but only toward fellow believers, if they were poor and destitute.

From the foreigners, who had not adopted the Jewish religion, they were certainly permitted to demand their debt.

Just so does the New Testament desire that we should do good to everyone, but especially to those of the household of faith, Galatians 6:10. It makes a distinction between brotherly love and general love, 2 Peter 1:7; yet in that passage, it places the latter as the highest step of virtue at the very end. Likewise, Christ praises love toward enemies—and thus toward all people in general—as the perfection in which believers should strive to be like their heavenly Father. Matthew 5:43–48.

<column-break/>

4. Except that there shall be no poor among you. For the Lord will greatly bless you in the land which the Lord your God gives you for an inheritance to possess as a heritage.
5. If only you will diligently obey the voice of the Lord your God, that you observe to do all this commandment which I command you today.
6. For the Lord your God will bless you, just as he has spoken to you. Thus you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow: and you shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you.
7. When

---

v. 4. The purpose of this ordinance was to remedy all poverty: and at the same time, this was a magnificent promise, that the Lord—through such charity which they would show to brothers in need—would grant them such a blessing that no beggar should be found among them. In this regard, the Law actually surpassed the Gospel in its effect, practice, and execution, since there are all too many poor and miserable persons around and among us whom we nevertheless recognize as fellow believers.

Oh, how should this commandment not shame Christendom, since all lands are so filled with beggars! This is certainly a sign that the Spirit of Christ is to be found in very few: not even among the rulers, who should care for the poor as fathers, let alone that they bring them to a state of beggary through heavy taxes and the neglect of good civil order, the maintenance of good morals, and the abolition of wasteful habits.

This is truly a great shame for us, as the Gospel must far surpass the Law, not only in its foundation and content but also in the Evangelical duties that should flow from it; just as it had this effect in the first, purest Church, where they held everything in common.

Can you then not understand that, if you wish to be a people of the New Testament and claim the name of Christian, what the Law requires here applies to you even more?

*That there shall be no poor among you?* Since love must indeed be the hallmark of Christians. But the failure is not in understanding, but in the ears to hear and in the will to act.

v. 5. *If only you—do* what is pleasing to the Lord and what your duty requires.

v. 6. *Will lend to many* Yet nothing is mentioned here of usury or interest <term>Wucher und Zinsen: high interest or exploitative lending</term>, though the patrons of such things would like to apply this passage according to the Jewish sense. Rather, it simply means: you will be so blessed that you will not only have enough for yourself and your needs but will also be able to assist others from your abundance without lacking anything yourself.

In Christ's glorious kingdom, this will then truly come to pass, and there, in that rest, the forgiveness of the debt of sin will be gloriously revealed. At that time, transgression will be restrained and sin will be sealed up, Daniel 9:24: so that the great physical blessing will also be found everywhere on the earth. Psalm 72:16.

The commentary criticizes contemporary 17th-century Christian society for failing to eliminate poverty and begging, contrasting it unfavorably with the ideals set forth in the Mosaic Law and the early Church.</summary>

**The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XV.**

**7.** If there is a poor man among you from one of your brothers, in any of your gates <note>In biblical terms, "gates" refers to the towns or settlements within the land.</note> in your land which the LORD your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart nor shut your hand from your brother who is poor: <margin>1 John 3:17.</margin>

**8.** But you shall open your hand generously to him, and shall willingly lend him as much as is necessary for his need, whatever he may lack.

**9.** Beware that there be not a wicked thought <note>original: "Belials-Wort." Belial is a Hebrew term meaning "worthless" or "wicked," often used to describe lawless or base impulses.</note> in your heart, saying, "The seventh year, the year of release, is approaching," so that your eye is evil toward your brother who is poor, and you give him nothing! Then he will cry out to the LORD against you, and it will become a sin in you.

**10.** You shall give to him willingly, and your heart shall not be grieved when you give to him. For because of this thing the LORD your God will bless you in all your works and in everything to which you stretch out your hand. <margin>(a) 2 Cor. 9:7.</margin>

**11.** For the poor will never cease from the midst of the land; therefore I command you and say, you shall open your hand generously toward your brother, toward your wretched, and toward your poor in your land.

**12.** If your brother, a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman, has sold himself to you, he shall serve you six years, and in the seventh year you shall let him go free from you.

---

This matter was previously dealt with in Leviticus 25:35, etc. Here, however, the qualities of willingness, generosity, and cheerfulness are added to the beautiful virtue of charity. Because God would also allow the poor to remain among them for just and holy reasons, He willed to command this virtue so that the poor might not be left without refreshment.

<margin>Mark 14:7. Matt. 5:42. Luke 16:9.</margin>
Since Christ has now also proclaimed such a condition in His Gospel-Kingdom and commanded us to do good to them, the Apostles have also strongly recommended such voluntary, generous, and cheerful charity to the believers. <margin>2 Cor. chapters 8 and 9. Phil. 4:10, etc. Heb. 13:16.</margin>

How does it happen then, that one sees far more hungry people than hungry dogs on the streets of Christendom?

Should not the condition of Christians be more glorious and far more excellent in holiness than that of the Jews in the Old Testament? Who nevertheless—as we heard above in verse 4—received a law from the Lord that there should be no poor man among them; yet even here it was found necessary to give more exhortations on the matter, because it would not turn out so perfectly, on account of their hardness of heart, that there would not still be poor among them.

Christians are to be recognized by their love: but what is practiced less, even though much is spoken of it?

Commonly, one searches for the smallest coin among his money when something is to be given to the poor, and does not even give that with the greatest willingness.

And what coldness and deficiency there is in public institutions! No matter how one looks at the matter, no one can deny that in many places there is better supervision of cattle than of human beings.

But if the provision for the poor in a land is a most obligatory and necessary matter and duty, how much more is one then indebted to the sick poor, who are thus doubly wretched?

Yet where are those republics <note>In this context, "Republics" refers generally to any organized state or commonwealth.</note> which show true zeal in this? And yet no republic is so small that it could not easily find enough means and ways to make arrangements for the preservation of the sick as well as the rest of the poor.

Many infirmaries and hospitals are in such a state that many sick people would rather lie in a stable or on a dunghill than allow themselves to be brought into them. And yet such institutions are only found in large cities. In lesser governments, the "Fathers of the Land" <note>A term for rulers or local princes.</note> know little of the distress of their children, and let them languish carelessly and thoughtlessly in sickness, as in other misery and poverty; they use everything they have from revenues <note>original: "Intraden."</note> for their own state and pleasures, so that they can spare little for the improvement of the public administration <note>original: "Policey." In the 18th century, this referred to the general social welfare and internal order of a state.</note> in these and other matters.

<column-break/>

Such a condition is found almost throughout the Christian world.

Thus, one sees a truly ghastly spectacle, to the shame of the Christian religion—nay, of human society itself!

Certainly, you great and wealthy ones are not a little to blame that many such poor people must be unhappy in the time of eternity! Your horses are so well-fed that, out of fatness and spirit, they hardly know where to set their feet; and yet so many poor people, created in the image of God, are so gaunt from deprivation that nothing but skin and bone is to be found on them.

O, how the Christians in the first Church—when she still lived, so to speak, in her infancy in blessed simplicity and innocence—observed so precisely the commandment of love renewed by their Lord, and held all their goods in common! In this way, both excess and luxury, as well as want and need, could easily be remedied.

In short: if love were more prevalent among Christians, they would only then truly learn how to manage their households.

**v. 12. If — has sold himself)** As others give <note>As other commentators suggest.</note>, when they are sold to you. See then how the Hebrews understand this passage and Exodus 21:2, etc., as referring to such servants who have been forced to serve by the court. Namely:

The Hebrews distinguish three kinds of servants who were of Israelite descent: two types of male persons, and one of the female sex. The male persons either sold themselves as servants out of extreme poverty—of whom, however, according to the Hebrew teaching, Leviticus 25:39 etc. speaks—or here it refers to a servant who was sold by the authorities because of theft. Exodus 22:3.

**In the 7th Year)** This is indeed commonly understood as the Year of Release, but it does not seem to follow from the text; rather, it is to be understood as the 7th year after entering service, whether it subsequently falls in a Year of Release or in another year. He who was sold in the first year after the Year of Release served exactly until the next Year of Release. But for those who were sold in the 2nd, 3rd, or 4th year after the Year of Release, the Year of Release itself gave no freedom as a Year of Release; rather, they had to wait until the 7th year from the commencement of their service arrived.

# Chapter XV. The Fifth Book of Moses.

**13.** And when you let him go free from you, you shall not let him go empty-handed.
**14.** You shall furnish him liberally from your sheep, and from your threshing floor, and from your winepress: you shall give to him from that which the LORD your God has blessed you.
**15.** And you shall remember that you were a servant in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; therefore I command you this thing today.
**16.** But if it should happen that he says to you: "I will not depart from you," because he loves you and your house, and because it is well with him in your service:
**17.** Then you shall take an awl and pierce his ear and the door <margin>(a) Exodus 21:6; Psalm 40:7.</margin>, so that he may be your servant forever; and you shall also do likewise with your female servant. <note>The "forever" mentioned here typically meant until the next Jubilee Year or the death of the master.</note>
**18.** Let it not seem hard in your eyes when you let him go free from you; for he has served you for six years for double the wages of a hired hand: so the LORD your God will bless you in all that you do.

---

**v. 13.** Upon his release, the master was required to give him a gift of honor:
**v. 14.** Of sheep, grain, and wine, worth at least 30 shekels <note>A "shekel" was a standard unit of weight and currency; 30 shekels was the legal compensation for a servant in other contexts.</note>; so that he would have something in his hands when he went out on his own.
**v. 15.** Their own servitude in Egypt is brought to their minds as a lesson in humility, so that they do not exalt themselves over their poor fellow brother, but rather show themselves friendly and generous toward him. This is to be observed even more so in the New Testament. See Ephesians 6:9; Philemon v. 16.
The love and benevolence shown to us—as particularly seen in the work of Redemption, as well as in other matters—and the memory of our own formerly miserable state, should in turn inspire love and mercy in us.
**v. 16.** If the servant did not wish to leave his household, or perhaps the foreign wife his master had given him and the children fathered with her; or if he did not know how to provide for himself and fared well with his master:
**v. 17.** Then he could remain further in service, but he had to confess this publicly before a court, declaring that he did not desire his freedom. Thereupon the master of the house held his head and ear against the house door and marked him as his property; he then remained a servant until the Jubilee Year or until his master died.
Regarding the mystical significance of this commandment, see the commentary on Exodus 21:5, etc.
**Also with your female servant)** This is not to be understood as piercing the ear, for that did not happen to girls; rather, it refers to what precedes in v. 14—namely, the parting gift that the master was to provide upon release in the seventh year.
**v. 18. Let it not seem hard)** Do not let this burden or grieve you.
**For a double reward)** Hired hands were typically contracted for three years, as can be seen from Isaiah 16:14. Therefore, this means: It would have cost you twice as much if you had kept a hired hand during that time.

<column-break/>

**19.** Every firstborn male that is born of your cattle and your sheep, you shall sanctify to the LORD your God. You shall do no work with the firstling of your ox, nor shear the firstlings of your sheep.
**20.** You shall eat them year by year before the face of the LORD your God in the place which the LORD shall choose, you and your household. <margin>ch. 12:17; 14:23.</margin>
**21.** But if there be a blemish in it, as if it be lame or blind, or have any other evil blemish, you shall not sacrifice it to the LORD your God. <margin>ch. 17:1; Leviticus 22:21, 22.</margin>
**22.** You may eat it within your gates; the unclean and the clean person alike may eat it, as if it were a roebuck or a deer.
**23.** Only you shall not eat its blood; you shall pour it upon the earth like water. <margin>Leviticus 17:10.</margin>

->**The**<-

---

**v. 19.** Regarding the sanctification of the firstborn, see Exodus 13:2; Numbers 3:13; 8:17.
**v. 20. You shall eat them)** Since the priests received all the meat of the firstborn, as appears from Numbers 18:17, 18, Josephus <note>original: "l. 4. Antiq. c. 4" refers to Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, Chapter 4.</note> (a) and others (b), this is understood here to mean that you eat *with* them or from them as invited guests.
**v. 21. Not sacrifice)** The priest could sell it, alive or slaughtered, but only for use at home:
**v. 22.** Or he could eat it there himself, like any other common clean food.
Toward our neighbor, our service always remains imperfect; one must have patience with another's faults and bear them as a burden. Galatians 6:1, 2. But toward God, our service, our surrender, and our sacrifice must be <term>artia</term> <note>original: "ἀρτία," meaning complete, perfect, or sound in every part.</note>, perfect: there must be nothing "limping" there, as if we wished to love the world as well; nor should any willful blindness remain in us. 1 Thessalonians 5:23.
**v. 23. Only you shall not eat its blood)** Although using blood in food is forbidden through such frequent repetitions, in the New Testament it is in a certain way—especially in the mystery of the Holy Supper—not only permitted to drink blood, but even commanded. How can this be? Answer: The Israelites in Moses' day had not yet come to the renewal of life, but were reminded and exhorted every day to improve their lives; though they were very slow in doing so. Therefore, they were not permitted to eat blood. For the life is in the blood: ch. 12:23. They could not attain to that life because of their unbelief and disobedience. Hebrews 3:19 and 4:11. But to the disciples of Christ, who have now passed out of the flesh and come from death into life, Christ gives his flesh to eat and his blood to drink: namely, for the renewal of life.

(b) Rabbi Levi of Barcelona in Hottinger's "On Hebrew Law," number 9.</margin>

# The Fifth Book of Moses, Chapter 16.

## Chapter 16.

->Concerning the three high festivals, the judges, and the forbidden groves.<-

1. Observe the month of Abib, that you may keep the Passover to the LORD your God. For in the month of Abib, the LORD your God brought you out of Egypt by night.
2. And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the LORD your God, sheep and cattle, at the place which the LORD will choose to let his Name dwell there.
3. You shall eat no leavened bread with it. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the bread of affliction; <note>The original German "Elend" can mean misery, distress, or exile.</note> for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste: so that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of Egypt all the days of your life.

---

<margin>v. 1. In the month of Abib) The Hebrews begin their ecclesiastical year here.</margin>
<margin>v. 2. Sheep and cattle) Not that the young sacrificial lamb, which was initially ordained by the Lord, was changed into a grown sheep or a bull and ox: as some of the learned Jews have thought, wanting to know the reason, because in a large household one lamb was not sufficient. For the Passover lamb was not ordained for the filling of their bellies, but for the grateful remembrance of their redemption from Egypt, so that the heart might be strengthened by grace, and not by food. Hebrews 13:9.</margin>
However, as at all festivals, the appropriate sacrifices should occur, and these should be slaughtered alongside the Passover lamb. Thus Moses speaks here both of the Passover lamb itself and first, which was slaughtered and eaten alone on the 14th day; as well as immediately thereafter of the sacrifices which were attached to it, and occurred during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which began on the 15th day and lasted 7 days, consisting of young cattle, rams, and lambs. Numbers 28:18–24.
The practice and the example in 2 Chronicles 30:15 and chapter 35 may best explain this law and rule; whereby, however, we should not hang and stick strictly to the letter.
Truly, the Spirit of God requires of us herein that, alongside the memory and remembrance of the death of our Lord, who is the true Passover lamb, we should also offer up our spiritual sacrifices and become such ourselves. Romans 8:36. But
All our services that we offer up presuppose the sacrifice of the Lamb and have their color and power from Christ’s sacrifice.
<margin>v. 3. The Feast of Unleavened Bread was always added to the Passover; and according to the mind and will of God, sincerity and truth must always follow the slaughtered lamb; indeed, the grown sheep—which is gentle and innocent, fruitful and useful—must follow the young Passover lamb at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and we must not always remain young children in the truth. God demands from everyone, according to the power and ability they have, an increase of what he has given them: a lamb-like innocence and sincerity from the weakest: from those more grown, a fruitfulness and usefulness.</margin>
There are indeed many who can exceedingly exalt, boast, and praise the grace and mercy of God and his love toward the children of men—because he made the innocent and spotless Lamb, who was silent, a sacrifice for sin—as well as the precious merit of the life and death of Christ, and can make extensive speeches of praise about it. But they forget the Feast of Unleavened Bread: they are not sincere, nor do they sweep out the old leaven of malice and wickedness, and they do not wish to eat
(The bread of affliction) Which tastes bitter to the "Old Adam" <note>The "Old Adam" refers to the sinful, unregenerate nature of humanity in Lutheran theology.</note> and is difficult to swallow.

<column-break/>

4. And for seven days no leaven shall be seen with you in all your borders: and nothing of the meat that you slaughter on the evening of the first day shall remain overnight until the morning.
5. You shall not be able to sacrifice the Passover within any of your gates <note>Meaning within the local towns or individual tribal settlements.</note> which the LORD your God will give you.
<margin>2 Chronicles 35:1, 2.</margin>
6. But at the place which the LORD your God will choose, to let his Name dwell there, there you shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening, when the sun goes down, at the appointed time when you came out of Egypt.
7. And you shall cook and eat it at the place which the LORD your God will choose, and in the morning you shall turn and go to your tents.
8. Se <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "Se" likely begins "Sechs Tage" (Six days).</note>

<margin>v. 4. This festival, however, must be kept in total abstinence from the Old-Adamic leaven, especially of malice, lusts, hypocrisy, and error, and in the eating of the unleavened bread of purity and truth: also in the offering up of our sacrifices of prayer and praise to God, joys for the Lamb's reconciliation, through the shedding of his blood on the Cross; and further through the resolution of a firm purpose toward humble obedience all the days of our life.</margin>
<margin>v. 5. Not in one of your gates) The Feast of Unleavened Bread could be kept outside of Jerusalem, but not the Passover lamb, as some (a) indeed think.</margin>
<margin>v. 6. At the place) Yet this is to be understood as the entire location or the city where the Tabernacle or the Temple was located: considering they may also slaughter the Passover in the houses.</margin>
<margin>v. 7. Cook) Since this word must necessarily be taken in a general and broad sense, because it is expressly said in Exodus 12 that it should not be boiled but roasted.</margin>
In the morning) Some (b) understand this as the 15th of the month, or the day after the Passover lamb was slaughtered and eaten: others, however, as the morning of the 8th day, which followed the entire festival being held. Most probable, however, is what Lightfoot (c) cites from the Hebrews regarding this place, namely that after eating the Passover lamb, they may well go out into their tents—which they pitched outside the city of Jerusalem—early the next morning, but were not at all allowed to travel home: because the first day was a Sabbath, on which they were not allowed to travel more than a Sabbath-day's journey: on the other day, however, all had to appear before the LORD in the Temple.

# The 5th Book of Moses. Chap. XVI.

## The XVI. Chapter.
->Of the three high feasts, judges, and forbidden groves.<-

---

Observe the month of **Abib**, that you keep the **Passover** to the **LORD** your **God**. For in the month of **Abib** the **LORD** your **God** led you out of **Egypt** by night.
2. And you shall slaughter the **Passover** to the **LORD** your **God**, sheep and cattle, at the place which the **LORD** will choose to let his name dwell there.
3. You shall eat nothing leavened with it. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the **bread of misery**; for in haste you departed from the land of **Egypt**: so that you may remember the day of your departure from the land of **Egypt** all the days of your life.

---

v. 1. **In the month of Abib)** the Hebrews begin their ecclesiastical year. <note>Abib, later called Nisan, occurs in March/April; it marks the start of the religious calendar to commemorate the Exodus.</note>
v. 2. **Sheep and cattle)** Not that the young sacrificial lamb, which was originally ordained by the **LORD**, had been changed into a grown sheep or cattle and oxen: as some of the learned Jews have wondered, seeking the reason because a lamb was not sufficient for a large household. For the **Passover lamb** was not ordained for the filling of their bellies, but for the grateful remembrance of their redemption from **Egypt**, so that the heart might be strengthened by grace, and not by food. Hebrews 13:9.
However, as at all feasts, so also at this one, the proper sacrifices were to occur and be slaughtered alongside the **Passover lamb**. Thus Moses speaks here both of the **Passover lamb** itself first, which was slaughtered and eaten on the 14th day alone; as well as immediately thereafter of the sacrifices which were attached to it, occurring during the **Feast of Unleavened Bread**, which began on the 15th day and lasted 7 days, consisting of young cattle, rams, and lambs. Numbers 28:18-24.
The practice and example in 2 Chronicles 30:15 and chapter 35 may best explain this law and rule; however, we should not hang and stick only to the letter.
Truly, the **Spirit of God** requires of us through this that, alongside the memory and reminder of the death of our **LORD**, who is the true **Passover Lamb**, we should also offer up our spiritual sacrifices and become such ourselves. Romans 8:36. But
all our services that we offer up presuppose the sacrifice of the **Lamb**, and have their essence <note>original: "Tinctur," referring to a medicinal or spiritual infusion</note> and power from **Christ’s** sacrifice.
v. 3. The **Feast of Unleavened Bread** was always joined to the **Passover**; and following the slaughtered lamb, according to the mind and will of **God**, sincerity and truth must always follow. Indeed, after the young **Passover lamb** at the **Feast of Unleavened Bread**, the grown sheep—which is gentle and innocent, fruitful and useful—must follow, so that we do not always remain young children in the truth. **God** demands from everyone, according to the strength and ability they have, an increase of what he has given them: a lamb-like innocence and sincerity from the weakest; and from those more mature, fruitfulness and usefulness.
There are indeed many who highly exalt, boast of, and praise the grace and mercy of **God** and his love toward the children of men—since he, the silent, innocent, and spotless **Lamb**, was made a sacrifice for sin—as well as the precious merit of the l... <note>likely "life"</note> and death of **Christ**, and can make extensive speeches of praise about it. A... <note>likely "But"</note> they forget the **Feast of Unleavened Bread**: they are not sincere, nor do they put away the old leaven of mal... <note>malice</note> and wickedness, and do not wish to eat
**The bread of misery)** Which tastes bitter to the "old Adam" <note>a theological term for the sinful human nature</note> and is hard to swallow.

<margin>v. 8. On the 7th day is a holiday)</margin> or a solemn assembly, a "gathering together."
The *Passover* or *Feast of Transition* requires the sweeping out of the leaven—a casting off of sin and injustice, replaced by the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. It is also a gathering and collection of all our wandering thoughts, loose inclinations, thoughtless words, and coarse works and deeds, bringing them toward Christ.
<margin>v. 9–12. Of the Feast of Pentecost)</margin> which is still kept in Christendom seven weeks after Easter, even if one cannot yet begin with the sickle in the grain on the second day of Easter. <meta>This page continues the legal and religious statutes of Deuteronomy. Having concluded the instructions for the pilgrimage festivals, the text now transitions to the establishment of the judicial system and the specific prohibitions against idolatry and imperfect sacrifices.</meta>

<header>The 5th Book of Moses. Ch. XVI.</header>

<margin>
v. 18. *You shall appoint judges and officials in all your gates*) The Jews had three types of courts in their land: the High Court in Jerusalem, and thereafter other courts in all cities; in some, Middle Courts, and in others, Lower Courts. In cities with 120 or more inhabitants, there was a Middle Court, which was called the Lesser Council. It consisted of 23 councilors, made up of priests, Levites, and the most prominent Israelites.

These courts were held in the gates of the cities. In cities where there were not 120 citizens, there was a Lower Court of 3 persons. For in all courts, the number was odd so that the votes could not result in a tie.

In all places, there were certain officials at these courts. However, regarding who these <term>Schoterim (officials or overseers)</term> were and what their office entailed, opinions differ. By the seventy translators <note>original: "70 Dolmetschen," referring to the Septuagint</note> they are commonly called scribes or scholars. Augustine and others consider them teachers of the people. But the Hebrews unanimously testify (a) that they were court servants who walked the streets by day, inspected weights and measures, watched over people's actions and public conduct, and if they found something unjust, reported it to the court or even punished the people themselves and executed the court's judgment. As such, it was a very respectable office among them.
</margin>
<margin>Judge. Ex. 18:21; 23:6. Lev. 19:15.</margin>
**18. You shall appoint judges and officials for yourself in all your gates, which the LORD your God will give you among your tribes, so that they may judge the people with a righteous judgment.**

<margin>
v. 19. *Take no gift*) A righteous judge or official will consider it the most offensive form of bribery even if someone only offers him a gift. For he judges from this that he is perceived as so unjust and godless that he would allow his eyes to be plastered shut in such a shameful manner.

(a) <note>original: "Schickard. de jur. reg. Hebr. c. 4. theor. 14. Goodwin. Mos. & Aar. l. 7. c. 3."</note> Wilhelm Schickard, *On the Rights of the Hebrew Kings*, ch. 4, th. 14. Thomas Goodwin, *Moses and Aaron*, book 7, ch. 3.
</margin>
**19. You shall not pervert justice; you shall not show partiality, and otherwise take no gift: for a gift blinds the eyes of the wise and perverts the words of the righteous.**

<column-break/>

<margin>
v. 20. *Only justice*) Or even more precisely: "justice, justice." The twofold repetition of the word means: to love, desire, and pursue this and this alone. Now, nothing is more highly to be desired than holiness and justice, as it is in these that the image of God consists, and which in truth is essentially God Himself. If it is God Himself, then it is indeed most lovely, most to be desired, and to be pursued above all things.
</margin>
**20. You shall follow only justice, so that you may live and inherit the land that the LORD your God will give you.**

<margin>
v. 21. 22. See regarding this Ex. 34:13; Lev. 26:1; and here Ch. 12:3.
</margin>
**21. You shall not plant for yourself a grove of any kind of trees near the altar of the LORD your God, which you shall make for yourself.**

**22. And you shall not set up for yourself any pillar, which the LORD your God hates.**

<note>
The name of "groves" <note>original: "Haynen"</note>, which remains in many places in our Germany and from which many people take their names, should remind us of the great idolatry in which our ancestors were mired, from which we have been redeemed by God’s goodness through the Gospel.
</note>

# Ch. XVII.

### Ch. XVII. The 5th Book of Moses.

**5.** So you shall lead that same man or that same woman, who have done such an evil thing, out to your gates—namely, the man or the woman—and you shall stone them so that they die.

**6.** On the testimony of two witnesses or three witnesses shall he who is to die be put to death; no one shall be put to death on the testimony of a single witness.

<margin>1 Cor. 5:13</margin>
**7.** The hand of the witnesses shall be first upon him to kill him, and afterward the hand of all the people, so that you put away the evil from your midst.

**8.** If a matter for judgment is too difficult for you, between blood and blood, between legal claim and legal claim, and between injury and injury—matters of dispute within your gates—then you shall arise and go up to the place which the LORD your God will choose;

---

**v. 5.** In addition to the heavy punishment of stoning, idolaters and blasphemers were also hanged on a wooden post after their death. For this purpose, a thick piece of wood was set into the earth, from which another piece extended for both hands <note>This describes a T-shaped or cross-like structure used for post-mortem display.</note>. The hands of the deceased were tied back to the wood, and he was thus hung, specifically toward the evening of the day; when he had hung for a little while, he was taken down again. His body was buried in a special place appointed for this by the High Court. The stone that the first witness had thrown at the condemned person was also buried with him, and where he was hanged, the wood was also buried: though not in the grave itself, but within 4 cubits of it. For more on this, see Lev. 24:14.

Women, as "weaker vessels," were not spared, in order to draw the people of Israel away from the almost universal and apparently oldest idolatry: the worship of the host of heaven <note>The "host of heaven" refers to the sun, moon, and stars, which were common objects of worship in the ancient Near East.</note>. People may have come to the thought that the gods wished to present themselves for worship in such a visible form; therefore, the worship of the one true invisible God was to be confirmed all the more among the people of God.

**v. 6.** Regarding the two witnesses, see Num. 35:30. Christ also commands this to be observed in other offenses before one should be condemned for them. Matt. 18:16.

**v. 7. The hand of the witnesses first)** See Lev. 20:27.

**v. 8.** All difficult matters that could not be decided in the middle and lower courts came before the High Court, to which one could appeal from the former.

**If a matter is too difficult)** For sometimes the deed is the same, but the causes and circumstances are different: from which a manslaughter or injury or something else arose. It was then to be investigated by the judges what sort of law and judgment should be pronounced regarding it, according to the law prescribed in the Statutes. This had to happen when the parties could not reach an agreement themselves, and the matter was thus too difficult for them.

**To the place which God will choose)** Before the building of the Temple, this High Court sat at the place where the Tabernacle was. After the building of the Temple, however, they met in the Temple, in the upper court-room, and sat there daily—except on Sabbath, feast days, and their preparation days—from the morning sacrifice until the evening sacrifice, and thus almost the entire day.

<column-break/>

**9.** And you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days, and ask; and they shall show you the sentence of judgment.

<margin>Matt. 23:2, 3</margin>
**10.** And you shall do according to the content of the word that they show you from that place which the LORD will choose; and you shall be careful to do according to all that they shall teach you.

<margin>Isa. 30:21. (a) ch. 5:20</margin>
**11.** According to the content of the law (a) which they teach you, and according to the judgment they shall tell you, you shall do; you shall not deviate from the word they show you, neither to the right nor to the left.

<margin>(a) ch. 19:17</margin>
**12.** And if anyone should act presumptuously, so that he does not obey the priest who stands there to serve the LORD your God, or the judge (a); then that same man shall die, and you shall put away the evil from Israel:

<margin>(a) Rom. 13:3, 4</margin>
**13.** That all the people may hear it and fear, and no longer be presumptuous.

**14.**

---

The Hebrews consider this place to be the proper seat and description of the High Court.

**v. 9.** The judges were partly from the priests, who had to investigate the law of the LORD to see if something for such a case might be expressly provided therein (see Mal. 2:6, 7); and then also from the "eldest fathers" <note>Referring to the tribal elders or heads of families.</note> who were appointed as judges and officials; these likewise had to keep the law of the LORD before their eyes, as well as their other established laws and customs in civil matters.

When they appealed to Jerusalem from a court outside that city, they came first to the Middle Court within the city. If they could be decided there, it was well; if not, they went to the High Court.

**v. 10, 11.** Although no infallibility or "unerringness" of a spiritual judge is established here—much less can such be forced upon the times of the New Testament from this—since they were explicitly bound to the rule of the Law as a prescription; nonetheless, one absolutely had to live according to their rulings.

**v. 12.** Whoever resisted this court had to die the death. So strictly did GOD wish to enjoin obedience to the priests and judges, that disobedience was to be punished with death. Just as Christ also wishes to take the contempt of His servants as if it had happened to Him: which will already have its powerful effect in eternity. Matt. 10:14, Luke 10:16. So also 2 Cor. 10:5, 2 Thess. 3:14.

**Or)** From this little word, it does not follow—as some (a) would have it—that there were two High Courts in Jerusalem: one spiritual and one secular, which would only have come together as one when matters arose that were partly secular and partly spiritual. For <term>Or</term> can here just as well mean "and," as the Scripture itself explains in ch. 19:17.

**the judge)** By this, however, one should not understand a single person, but without doubt the assessors <note>Associate judges or council members.</note> from other tribes are meant by it.

<margin>(a) Leusden. <note>original: "philol. hebr. mixt. diss. 50. quæst. 1."</note> Hebrew Philological Miscellany, Dissertation 50, Question 1.</margin>

# The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XVII.

> 14. When you come into the land that the LORD your God will give you, and you take it as an inheritance and dwell therein, and you say: "I will set a king over me, like all the nations that are around me":
>
> 15. Then you shall surely set as king over you the one whom the LORD your God will choose. You shall set one from among your brothers as king over you; you cannot set a foreign man over you who is not your brother.
>
> <margin>ch. 28:68. (a) Gen. 24:6.</margin>
> 16. However, he shall not acquire many horses for himself, so that he does not lead the people back to Egypt by acquiring many horses, since the LORD has said to you: "You shall never again return by this way."
>
> <margin>(a) 1 Kings 11:1, 28.</margin>
> 17. He shall also not take many wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn away; he shall also not acquire for himself too much silver and gold.

---

The LORD, in His wisdom, was well able to see that the people, according to their stubborn and proud disposition, would not long be able to endure the paternal and simple government of the priests and the elders of the fathers. Therefore, although they would choose a king for themselves out of pride, they would by that very act burden themselves with a heavy yoke, through which their stiff-necked and stubborn spirit could be better bowed—as the outcome later showed more fully in 1 Samuel 8. <note>In 1 Samuel 8, the prophet Samuel warns the Israelites that a king will tax them, take their children for service, and seize their lands.</note>

**v. 15.** However, God wished to limit the desires of the people and the future king through several explicit laws. Regarding the people, they were not to choose someone from the foreign nations—who were already established in such royal dignity—out of pride, for such a man would soon have seduced and forced them into idolatry. Instead, they were to look to one from among their brothers, specifically the one whom the LORD would choose.

**v. 16.** Regarding the king, (1) a multitude of horses is forbidden to him, so that he should not strive to acquire such carnal power. Such power would prevent him from placing his trust in God and incite him to much violence. It would also lead him and his people into harmful common dealings with the pagan Egyptians, who possessed many horses. See Isaiah 31:1–3 and Ezekiel 17:15.

**v. 17.** (2) He shall refrain from polygamy and conduct his marriage in chastity with one wife according to divine institution, and thus not indulge his lusts. Such indulgence would make him guilty of adultery and fornication before God, causing him to lose all of God's grace and making him deserving of eternal judgment.

(3) He shall not devote himself to the amassing of treasures, for which the increase of revenues also served; through this, the heart is enticed to too much vanity and injustice. A ruler should, as Gregory of Nyssa explains it, not be devoted to greed, nor consider himself permitted to extort money from his subjects through all kinds of excessive taxes, the collection of tithes, and the like. <note>Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–395 AD) was a prominent Christian theologian who often wrote on social justice and the duties of leaders.</note>

<column-break/>

> 18. And it shall happen, when he sits upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write for himself a copy of this law in a book from that which is before the priests, the Levites.
>
> 19. And it shall be with him, that he may read therein all the days of his life: so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God, that he may keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do according to them: <gloss>(a) Joshua 1:8.</gloss>
>
> 20. That his heart may by no means be lifted up above his brothers, and that he may by no means turn aside from the commandment neither to the right nor to the left, so that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he and his children, in the midst of Israel.

<meta>catchword: Since</meta>

---

**v. 18. (+)** He was to copy the Law of Moses himself, specifically so that he might read it frequently with all attention, and thus concern himself with its observation. In this way, the people might also be kept by him in obedience to it. See Chapter 31:26, and how this was later neglected in 2 Kings 22:8, 11. <note>Reference to the "Lost Book of the Law" found during the reign of King Josiah.</note>

**A copy of this law)** By this, most Hebrews understand a "double law"—that he should not merely have the whole law copied twice, as Luther translated it, but should copy it with his own hand. One copy he was to have constantly with him, whether he was at home or traveling, in order to read it diligently; the other was to remain in the treasury. <margin>(a) Schickard, *On the Rights of the Hebrew King*, ch. 2, theory 5, & Carpzov.</margin> <note>Wilhelm Schickard and Johann Benedict Carpzov were 17th-century scholars who studied Hebrew law and traditions.</note>

**From that which is before the priests)** Following the exemplar that Moses gave to the priests or the tribe of Levi and wrote with his own hand. This was the most holy copy, and as many maintain, written solely in Assyrian letters—which we today call Hebrew. <note>The "Assyrian script" refers to the square Hebrew alphabet used today, which tradition says replaced the older Paleo-Hebrew script.</note> Conversely, all other copies that Moses gave to the remaining 12 tribes were written in the common script, which was later called Samaritan.

**v. 19. That he may read therein all the days)** This would indeed be an all-too-melancholy pastime for many rulers among those who nevertheless wish to confess Christ. <note>The author is making a pointed critique of contemporary 17th/18th-century monarchs who find religious study boring.</note>

**v. 20. (5)** He should apply himself to humility, and remember that he rules over brothers, and thus not abuse the dignity entrusted to him.

(6) Obedience to God's commandments is commanded of him, both in general and in particular, as the source of all blessing for himself and for his family.

These few commandments are from the Most High Lawgiver, which all rulers should take to heart—especially since they wish to know Christ and desire to be saved through Him. They must also remember that they rule over brothers, just as Christ says of all who wish to believe in Him in Matthew 23. And though He leaves them the title of kings and lords, they should nevertheless think on the fact that He is the King of kings and the Lord of lords (Revelation 19:16), under whose authority they stand. They must one day view their subjects as brothers, so that believers in the New Testament might not have a greater privilege than those in the Old Testament. Therefore, they must not hold them as servants and serfs against the will of Christ—which the Spirit of Christ forbade to kings in 1 Corinthians 7:23. Against this, no lordly right will protect them before the strict judgment seat of Christ. See Revelation 6:15, 16.

<summary>This page discusses the biblical laws for kings in Deuteronomy 17, emphasizing that a ruler must be an Israelite, avoid excessive wealth and power, and personally copy and study the Law to remain humble before his "brothers." The commentary criticizes contemporary rulers for neglecting these spiritual duties and warns that they will be judged for treating subjects as serfs.</summary>

# The XVIII. Chapter.

->Concerning the portion of the priests, evil arts, the true prophet, and the false ones.<-

The priests the Levites, and all the tribe of Levi, shall have no part nor inheritance with Israel: they shall eat the offerings of the LORD made by fire, and his inheritance.
2. Therefore they shall have no inheritance among their brothers: the LORD is their inheritance (a), just as he has said to them. <margin>(a) Psalm 16:5, 6.</margin>
3. And this shall be the priest's due from the people, from those who offer a sacrifice, whether it be ox or sheep; that they shall give to the priest the shoulder, and the two cheeks, and the maw. <note>The "maw" refers to the fourth stomach of a ruminant, considered a choice part in ancient sacrificial laws.</note>
4. The firstfruits of your grain, of your wine, and of your oil, and the first of the fleece of your sheep, shall you give him.
5. For the LORD your God has chosen him out of all your tribes, to stand to minister in the name of the LORD, him and his sons forever.

<column-break/>

6. And if a Levite comes from one of your gates out of all Israel, where he sojourns, and comes with all the desire of his mind unto the place which the LORD shall choose;
7. Then he shall minister in the name of the LORD his God, as all his brothers the Levites do, who stand there before the LORD.
8. They shall have like portions to eat, besides that which comes of the sale of his patrimony. <margin>Leviticus 25:33.</margin>
9. When you are come into the land which the LORD your God gives you, you shall not learn to do after the abominations of those nations.
10. There shall not be found among you any one that makes his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that uses divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch;
11. Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer. <margin>Leviticus 19:26, 31.</margin> 12.

---

<insert>
It is here once again impressed upon the Levites how they are to possess no earthly goods among Israel, but should let themselves be satisfied with the abundant maintenance that God has assigned to them, of which we have already treated in Numbers 18:8, 20.
</insert>

v. 1. 2. **No part with Israel**] Not that they should possess absolutely nothing of their own, but only that they were not given equal parts with the other tribes in the distribution of the land, as has been reminded elsewhere.
**The LORD's inheritance they shall eat**] While all other tribes had to seek their own bread and nourishment and till the land, God provided for and maintained the priests from His own portion: so that the priests and Levites had their maintenance and their income not from the children of Israel, but from God Himself, the supreme Lord and Owner of the earth and all its goods.
v. 3. Just as the animal is divided as if into three parts—the head, the flesh or body, and the entrails—so here something is apportioned to the priests from each. From the head: the cheeks; from the body: the breast and shoulders (Leviticus 7:31, 32); from the entrails: the maw.
v. 4. **The firstfruits of the fleece**] or wool, which had to be delivered clean and combed. (a)
v. 5. **In the name of the LORD**] As a type or foreshadowing of Christ.
<margin>(a) Buxtorf's Talmudic Lexicon under the word <term>גיזה</term> <note>original: "gizah," meaning shearings or fleece.</note></margin>

<column-break/>

v. 6. 7. The descendants of Levi were, as is known, distributed among all the tribes, among whom they received their 48 designated cities (Numbers 35:6, 7). If now a Levite perhaps had no desire to live there, but rather longed to be always present at the sanctuary, even outside of his appointed rotation, and wished to wait upon it daily;
v. 8. Then he could sell his belongings and property, and had the same right to enjoy the provisions as the others who had to appear regularly and perform their service: so that he did not find it necessary to use the money he received for his sold inheritance, but could always redeem it with the same whenever he wished (Leviticus 25:32).
**Whoever thus wished to give himself voluntarily to the LORD at all times with his belongings and property, one was not to be a hindrance to him, but rather a promoter.**
And so the Church has likewise not done wrong in this regard, that she has ordained some places for the residence of such voluntary souls, in which they might occupy themselves with heavenly things entirely undisturbed. But because the Enemy has defiled such a glorious undertaking with so many human statutes, it has unfortunately come to pass that the good use has been entirely abolished along with the well-known abuse. <note>The author is likely referring to the Reformation-era critique of monasticism, where the original intent of spiritual retreat was seen as corrupted by excessive rules or corruption.</note>
v. 9-11. **Nine types of false worldly wisdom**

---

are recounted here, which the heathens practiced in order to serve their gods, and also to show others the way thereto; which is properly the work of true wisdom: to give us to know the true God and the manner of service well-pleasing to Him. Because the heathens had let go of this knowledge, they were deceived in so many ways by the Devil and his instruments, through which they sought partly to serve God, or to search out His will, and to bring about His blessing for their undertakings, or the prevention and reconciliation of His wrath. It is not necessary, however, to know all these ways and their distinctions; rather, it is more to be wished that such things might remain forever sunk in the abyss.

### The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter 18.

12. **For everyone who does such things is an abomination to the LORD, and because of such abominations the LORD your God drives them out from before you.**
13. **You shall be perfect with the LORD your God.**
14. **For these nations, which you shall possess, listen to observers of times <note>The German "Tagwähler" refers to those who superstitiously choose "lucky" or "unlucky" days for certain actions.</note> and diviners. But as for you, the LORD your God has not allowed you to do so.**
15. **The LORD your God will raise up for you a Prophet like me from your midst, from your brothers; to him you shall listen.**
<margin>Hebrews 12:19.</margin>
16. **According to all that you desired of the LORD your God at Horeb <note>Another name for Mount Sinai.</note> on the day of the assembly, when you said: "Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God, nor let me see this great fire anymore, lest I die."**

---

v. 12—14. Because, unfortunately, many abominations may still be in vogue among ignorant people and heathens, and because the Holy Spirit warns even the believers against "philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and the basic principles of the world" (Colossians 2:8); these things are all the more to be taken to heart, so that they may not cling to any kind of such evil arts in a hidden, spiritual way, which will be revealed on that day. It is also sufficiently recognizable from the warnings of the Spirit that such dark effects can arise from the "fire of the dark world," to which the inner man is also susceptible during the process of rebirth.

Rather, believers should cling perfectly to GOD and strive for the "wisdom from above," the glorious fruits of which can be read in James 3:17. This wisdom is gladly given by GOD and will teach us how to conduct ourselves rightly toward GOD and men, to obtain blessing and prevent evil, so that no one can harm us without God's will; and even what He ordains will promote our best interest.

v. 15. 16. Set against the abominations of earthly wisdom and all its unfortunate instruments is the one true Prophet, who is heavenly wisdom itself, and thus the source of all wisdom and true prophecy, which must be enlightened and taught by him. A very clear promise of him is given here: just as in the first four books four glorious types <note>Historical figures or objects that "foreshadow" Christ in Christian theology.</note> of him were presented—Isaac, the Passover lamb, the scapegoat of the sin offering on the Day of Atonement, and the bronze serpent (as can be seen in the notes on Numbers <note>original: "4. Mos."</note> 21:8)—all of which represent Christ's high-priestly office; so he is now made known here as the Prophet whom GOD would raise up from the Jewish lineage, namely from Judah (Genesis <note>original: "1. Mos."</note> 49:8 etc.). He would also confirm his mission with many glorious miracles, just like Moses, though according to the prophecy of the prophets, these would focus more on the misery of incurable men who were to be healed through these miracles (Isaiah 35:5-6). They were otherwise alike in great meekness (Numbers <note>original: "4. Mos."</note> 12:3 and Matthew 11:29), in constant intercession (Exodus <note>original: "2. Mos."</note> 32:32 and Luke 23:34), and in other ways. Just as this Prophet spoke lovingly "mouth to mouth" with the people, as they were able to bear it. Chiefly, however, the similarity consists in this: that as Moses led a great people out of physical Egyptian bondage, so Christ has led the great people of his believers out of the spiritual bondage of sin, and still leads them out daily: wherein he, as the true essence, far surpasses those shadows.

<column-break/>

17. **And the LORD said to me: "They have spoken well in what they have said."**
18. **"I will raise up for them a Prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak to them all that I command him."**
<margin>Luke 10:16.</margin>
19. **"And it shall come to pass, that whoever will not listen to my words which he speaks in my name, I will require it of him."**
<margin>(a) 2 Peter 2:1.</margin>
20. **"But the prophet who presumes to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or who speaks in the name of other gods, that prophet shall die."**
21. **"And if you say in your heart: 'How shall we know the word which the LORD has not spoken?'"**
22. **"When a prophet speaks in the name of the LORD, and the thing does not happen or come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD has not spoken; the prophet has spoken it presumptuously: you shall not be afraid of him."**

---

v. 17. The LORD who speaks here is therefore the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But the one of whom He speaks can be no one else than the great Prophet, Jesus Christ.

It cannot be understood as referring to Moses; otherwise, he would not be spoken of in a future tense, where it says:

v. 18. **I will raise up**) and v. 19. (**which he will speak**) Therefore, it must refer to someone else.

The Jews see this well enough themselves, but they apply it to Joshua, even though he was not nearly as great as Moses, with whom the LORD God spoke "mouth to mouth" and who saw the LORD in His form. But here, one is spoken of who would be even greater than Moses.

John the Baptist, to whom they also wish to apply it when they cannot make it fit <unclear>Moses</unclear>, says of himself that he is not that Prophet (a).

Thus, no one else is meant but the one whom the voice from heaven presents, saying that one should "listen to him" (Matthew 3:17), which gloriously explains this prophecy. This prophecy was also held up to the Jews by Peter (Acts 3:22-23), placing before their eyes the sharp judgment of disobedience: which also occurred to the Jews in their destruction from the land, as the Apostle explains the "requirement" <note>Referring to God "requiring it" of those who don't listen in v. 19.</note> threatened here and <unclear>demonstrates</unclear> it to their conscience.

v. 20—22. Since a "presumptuous prophet" is also mentioned who would speak in his own name, this points in the Spirit to the Antichrist, who would come in his own name (1 John 2:18), whose flattering promises of an everlasting happiness for the outward church—which is rather contrary to the teaching of Christ—will not come to pass.

## Chapter XIX.
->Concerning Cities of Refuge, Boundaries, and Witnesses.<-

WHeN the LORD your God has cut off the nations whose land the LORD your God is giving you, so that you possess them as an inheritance and dwell in their cities and in their houses:
2. Then you shall set apart three cities for yourself in the midst of your land, which the LORD your God is giving you to possess as an inheritance.
3. You shall prepare the way for yourself and divide the territory of your land, which the LORD your God will cause you to inherit, into three parts: and it shall happen that whoever has committed a homicide <note>German: *Todtschlag*; refers to unintentional killing or manslaughter in this context.</note> may flee there.
4. And this shall be the case of the killer who flees there, so that he may remain alive: Whoever kills his neighbor unintentionally, not having hated him in the past <note>Literal: "yesterday and the day before yesterday."</note>;
5. As when he goes into the forest with his neighbor to cut wood, and his hand swings the axe to cut down the tree, and the iron head slips from the handle and strikes his neighbor so that he dies: he shall flee to one of these cities, that he may remain alive.

---

The command concerning the three cities of refuge in the land of Canaan is repeated here, which was treated in Numbers 35:9 etc., and there also three were ordained on this side of the Jordan in the conquered land, making six in all. All six were situated very conveniently and opposite each other, and equally distant from one another.
**v. 2. Three cities)** These were Kedesh in Galilee, in the mountains of Naphtali; Shechem, in the mountains of Ephraim; and Kiriath-Arba <note>Also known as Hebron.</note>, in the mountains of Judah.
**v. 3. The roads there had to be very well-paved, at least 32 cubits wide, not rocky, bumpy, pitted, or uneven.**
For this reason, people were also sent out annually on the 15th of the month of Adar <note>The twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly February/March.</note> to repair the roads damaged by the winter weather. At the crossroads leading to these cities stood high pillars inscribed with "City of Refuge," so that the killer would know which way to take at various junctions.
**v. 4. Unintentionally)** Even the greatest sin, committed unintentionally without hatred or envy, is in vain <note>In this context, it means the sin does not lead to the death penalty.</note>: just as some kill the Lord Jesus out of ignorance by suppressing and dampening the movements of His Spirit in their souls, because they do not know that such things originate from Him.
**v. 5. is spoken of as an example.**

<column-break/>

6. Lest the blood-avenger <note>German: *Blut-Rächer*; the kinsman of a deceased person who had the right/duty to seek retribution.</note> pursue the killer when his heart is heated and overtake him because the way is so far, and strike him dead: though there is no sentence of death against him, because he did not hate him in the past.
7. Therefore I command you and say, you shall set apart three cities for yourself.
8. And if the LORD your God expands your borders, as He swore to your fathers, and gives you all the land He promised to give to your fathers:
9. When...

---

**v. 6. When his heart is heated)** In the first rush of anger and desire for revenge.
God will count as blood-guilt upon the land the blood shed from a heated mind—where one thought they had a right to it, as can happen in many cases where one believes they have a sufficient reason to kill their neighbor, but where the other has not deserved that his blood should be shed, which must first be investigated according to the law—for which God's righteous wrath would come upon a land itself or all its inhabitants, just as here all of Israel is addressed as one man. Therefore, with the greatest care, such innocent blood must be avenged, and the perpetrators punished, who—like the biting blood-avenger here—have brought such blood-guilt upon themselves and the land. God will also powerfully punish this in all authors of wars conducted from a heated mind, and even more so in those harsh executions decreed from such a heated heart, even against disobedient subjects whom one is in no way authorized to kill.
**v. 7. Set apart three cities)** Which happened through Joshua.
But that the cities of refuge or places of protection are everywhere—on this side and that side of the Jordan, and also in the addition promised immediately thereafter—grouped in the number three, deserves attention. The Holy Trinity is the best place of protection: Whoever unites with it finds a secure refuge. "The name of the LORD," it says in Proverbs 18:10, "is a strong tower; the righteous runs into it and is protected."
In particular, these cities were a lovely prefiguration of Christ, in whom the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells. Oh, how excellent is the refuge which tempted sinners have in Him, so that no sin, no law, no curse, no Satan, no death, no hell, can reach them! He Himself calls and invites them all kindly to Himself in Matthew 11:28 and John 6:37, and the signposts point to Him with John the Baptist in John 1:29. But whoever wants to have protection with Him must also give up his dearest friends: father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters. Psalm 45:10; Luke 14:26.
**v. 8. If the LORD expands your borders)** Meaning that they would obtain all the lands of the ten nations, as was promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Genesis 15:18, etc.; 26:3; 28:13-14. However, this condition is based on what follows in the next verse. Because the same was not fulfilled, but rather the opposite happened through the manifold apostasy of the children of Israel, nothing came of it. And although David and Solomon expanded their power as far as the Euphrates, the lands were not settled with Israelites; rather, the people remained in the land and became tributary. 2 Samuel 8:3 etc.; 1 Kings 4:21.

<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Ch. XIX.</header>

**9.** If you shall keep all these commandments to do them, which I command you this day, that you love the **Lord** your **God** and walk in His ways all your days; then you shall add three more cities for yourself to these three.

**10.** So that innocent blood is not shed in the midst of your land, which the **Lord** your **God** gives you as an inheritance, and blood-guiltiness comes upon you.

**11.** But if anyone hates his neighbor, lies in wait for him, and rises up against him, and strikes his life so that he dies, and he flees into one of these cities:

**12.** Then the elders of his city shall send and have him fetched from there, and deliver him into the hand of the avenger of blood <note>German: *Blut-Rächer*; a relative of the deceased authorized to seek justice.</note> so that he may die.

**13.** Your eye shall not pity him, and you shall put away the innocent blood from Israel, that it may go well with you.

---

v. 9. **All these commandments)** or rather the whole commandment, which is expressed in the following words, namely the first and great commandment of the love of **God**, which is the highest service to **God**, and the perfect thing which is to come, 1 Cor. 13:10. <note>original: "das Vollkommene welches kommen soll"</note> the resurrection and eternal life, the new birth. Whoever keeps this commandment keeps them all. 1 John 5:3.

**You / you)** The **Lord** speaks to all Israel as to a single man, and therefore demands obedience from every individual: but from us all the more, the more that spirit and power have been granted for it in the days of the New Testament. Namely

**To add three more cities)** Because this, as thought, has not happened, and **God's** word speaks only of depths that point further ahead, and since nothing can have been spoken in vain; then the opinion of the Jews might not be far off, that this will be fulfilled in the days of the coming of the Messiah.

v. 10. **What kind of innocent blood is shed in the midst of our land** when we set aside **God's** commandment and the love for Him, and do not walk in His ways; anyone can easily notice that. There is one within us who is often crucified. Gal. 3:1. When you kill the life of **God** in you, quench the Spirit of **God**, suppress His good impulses and movements and do not let them emerge; if you, for example, let yourself be overcome by anger, and thereby let gentleness suffer need: then you shed the blood of the life of the innocent and spotless Lamb (1 Pet. 1:19) or of the gentle lamb-like mind <note>German: *Lammes-Sinnes*; refers to a Christ-like or peaceful disposition.</note> which should dwell in you at all times. Which can then happen in two ways, either with deliberate intent and will, or against one's will and out of ignorance.

v. 11-13. A malicious murderer now has no right to use such freedom, which is granted to him who harms the true life out of ignorance or against his will, and he must therefore be handed over again from those places of sanctuary <note>German: *Frey-Oerter*; cities of refuge.</note>. See Exodus 21:13-14. Thus, no willful sinner is authorized to claim the gracious provision that **God** shows toward those who have instigated an evil out of carelessness.

<column-break/>

**14.** You shall not move back your neighbor's boundary, which those of old have set in your inheritance, which you shall inherit in the land that the **Lord** your **God** will give you to possess as an inheritance.

**15.** A single witness shall not rise up against anyone concerning any iniquity or concerning any sin, of all kinds of sin that one may commit. At the mouth of two witnesses or at the mouth of three witnesses shall a matter be established.

**16.** If a malicious witness rises up against anyone to testify of a transgression against him:

**17.** Then both men who have a dispute with each other shall stand before the face of the **Lord**, before the face of the priests and the judges who shall be in those days.

**18.** And the judges shall investigate diligently. See, if the witness is a false witness who has testified falsely against his brother:

**19.** Then you shall do to him as he intended to do to his brother, that you put away the evil from your midst.

**20.** So that the rest may hear it and fear, and no longer continue to do such evil things among you.

**21.** And your eye shall not pity: soul for soul, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.

---

v. 14. **God** intended to forbid all civil wars among His people, so that they should never arbitrarily change the boundaries once set after the distribution made by lot, but every tribe, and likewise every man, should be maintained in them, in the inheritance that once fell to him. See Ch. 27:12, Proverbs 22:28.

v. 15-21. All kinds of disputes, where one complains about another, and thus one is in debt or sins against his neighbor, should be judged by the testimony of two or three witnesses: because one cannot give justice to anyone in his claim so readily, on account of the deeply-rooted, perverse self-love, where one only accuses the other, or also will not confess where one is guilty, [concerning] what they [the witnesses] confess and have heard to have happened among those in dispute. Should even these [witnesses] have a perverse inclination toward one or the other and give false testimony, they themselves make themselves guilty of the punishment which the perpetrator deserved, which they must suffer with him.

[The punishment] from which they intended to deliver him with their false testimony — And if here on earth such false testimonies are not discovered, such false witnesses will still not escape the judgment of **God**, who will then bring to light the hidden counsel of the heart, and punish all the more sharply the more deceitfully people acted therein, and how they went unpunished here in their sins. See also Ch. 17:6 and Numbers 35:30.

# Chapter XX.
->Laws of War.<-

When you go out to war against your enemies, and see horses and chariots, a people greater than you; do not be afraid of them: for the **Lord** your **God** is with you, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.
2. And it shall be, when you draw near to the battle, that the priest shall step forward and speak to the people,
3. And say to them: Hear, O Israel! Today you are drawing near to the battle against your enemies: let your heart not be faint, do not fear, do not tremble, and do not be terrified before their face!
4. For it is the **Lord** your **God** who goes with you, to fight for you against your enemies, to save you.

---

<margin>
In the earthly land of Canaan, the people were continually attacked by the surrounding nations because of their sins, and therefore **God** also wished to give them laws—not so that they should attack nations of their own accord (since they were only commanded at most to destroy the ten Canaanite nations, but otherwise not to expand their borders by the sword, as the false prophet Mahomet <note>original: "Mahomet"; a common early-modern German spelling for Muhammad.</note> permits his followers). Rather, after the enemies had exceeded their power and sought to avenge themselves according to their own will out of an ancient enmity to destroy them (Ezekiel 25:12, 15), **God** permitted them such <term>Nothwehr</term> <note>Self-defense out of necessity.</note>. Understand it thus:
</margin>

<margin>v. 1. A war) One which was either commanded by **God** or otherwise caused by necessity.</margin>

<margin>v. 2. The priest) Who was anointed for this purpose with the holy anointing oil, and therefore called the <term>Kriegs-Gesalbte</term> <note>The "War-Anointed" priest; a specific role in Jewish tradition for encouraging troops.</note>.</margin>
This man had to address the people going into war several times and speak courage into them, assuring them that **God** would not forsake them in such acts of necessary defense.

<margin>v. 3. Say to them) Namely, when it came to the encounter and the battle order was to be set; the War-Anointed stepped onto an elevated place and called out the words prescribed here to the people in a loud voice.</margin>
But because the entire multitude could not hear his voice, another common priest—as well as as many officers as were necessary—had to repeat all these words to the whole people, each to his own company.

<margin>v. 4. To save you) Or to rescue you: from which it is also evident that this is not to be understood as referring to wars where they intended to hostilely invade other nations' lands to make themselves masters of them; but rather to those wars necessitated by an enemy invasion. See 2 Kings 18:9, 13, etc.</margin>
Thereupon the battle order was arranged, and the captains, each for his own company, were placed at the head.

Just as the officers were to have oversight in all things, so here some were expressly released from the defense of the land and held as excused; specifically, the despondent were not forced into service.

<column-break/>

5. And the officers shall speak to the people, saying: What man is there who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the war and another man dedicate it.
6. And what man is there who has planted a vineyard and has not yet made it common? <note>original: "gemein gemacht"; referring to the biblical law where the fruit of a new vineyard was not eaten for the first three years and was consecrated in the fourth, only becoming "common" or available for general use in the fifth year.</note> Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the war and another man make it common.
7. And what man is there who has betrothed a wife and has not yet taken her home? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in the war and another man take her home.
<margin>c. 24/5.</margin>
8. And the officers shall speak further to the people and say: What man is there who is fearful and whose heart has become faint? Let him go and return to his house, so that his brothers' hearts do not melt like his heart.
9. And it shall be, when the officers have finished speaking to the people, that they shall appoint the commanders of the armies at the head of the people. 10.

---

<margin>
According to the common narrative of the Hebrews, the War-Anointed first read these words from the book publicly to all the people in the Hebrew language at the borders of the land. Whereupon anyone exempt from war might go home. Before the encounter took place, he called these out once more, which the officers then clearly repeated to the people just like the previous words.
</margin>

<margin>v. 5. Who has not dedicated a new house</margin>
<margin>v. 6. Who has not made a vineyard common</margin>
<margin>v. 7. Who has not taken home a wife</margin>
According to the report of the Hebrews, these men had to march as far as the border before they were then released.

<margin>v. 8. (Further) the War-Anointed spoke no more, but the highest-ranking officer called this out to the people: which the other officers then indicated further to each of their companies.</margin>
Whoever is afraid, let him return home) However, these fearful ones who were sent back, although they might return to their homeland, were nevertheless not allowed to live in their houses, but had to bring provisions and water to the army.

<margin>v. 9. As soon as these had stepped away from the army, the battle order was set, and the captains, each for his own company, were placed at the head.</margin>

How unjustifiable is it then to force someone into military service even outside of necessity! This, along with all unruly wars—which were not even allowed in the Old Testament—is now entirely inexcusable in the New Testament. However, because the majority otherwise overlooks everything, and **God** yet executes His judgments through enemies (though these also exceed all measure and exercise their own revenge and ancient enmity), such acts of necessary defense in such wars of protection are indeed still unavoidable. Into these, even good-hearted souls are drawn due to a lack of greater light, and therefore must still be warned by teachers and instructed according to the teaching of John the Baptist. Luke 3:14.
