<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Ch. XX.</header>

10. When you draw near to a city to fight against it, then you shall offer it terms of peace. <margin>Matthew 10:11-13.</margin>

11. If it happens that they answer you in peace and open up to you, then all the people found therein shall be tributary to you and serve you.

12. But if they will not make peace with you, but rather wage war against you, then you shall besiege them.

13. And when the **Lord** your **God** delivers it into your hand, you shall strike all its males with the edge of the sword.

14. Except for the women, the children, the livestock, and everything that is in the city. All its spoil you shall take as plunder for yourself, and you shall eat of the spoil of your enemies, which the **Lord** your **God** has given you.

15. Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not of the cities of these nations.

---

<margin>v. 10. When -- then you shall) Even among the secular nations, such a law has been observed: that they did not attack anyone as an enemy without publicly announcing the war through a herald.</margin>

Here **God** intends that His people should first present all means of peace, to see if the enemies will desist from their offense and make restitution for the damage.

<margin>v. 11. Answer in peace and open up) Oh, what else has the **Lord** done against us for so many years now, other than offering us peace through His long patience! But we are so bold and daring against Him that we want to have peace according to our own will and conditions—a relief and peace in the flesh, a peace without righteousness. But He offers only such a peace which is the effect and a fruit of righteousness. Isaiah 32:17. Oh, let us then still accept the offered peace while there is still time! Especially as we see that for the Jews themselves, because they rejected it, nothing remained but the sword.</margin>

<margin>v. 12. 13. But if -- then -- then) Mercy precedes judgment.</margin>

If, even in this day, people are first warned to desist from their offenses to see if they will settle in kindness; then—since the kingdoms otherwise still mostly stand in the "state of nature" <note>A political philosophy term referring to a condition without a common sovereign or shared Christian law.</note> and have not yet become the kingdoms of our God and His Christ (Revelation 11:15)—when all such kind proposals find no entry, and the enemies moreover continue with their offense, and especially with the oppression of consciences, one may certainly compel them to their duty with force, just as **God** permitted His people here. This is then to be regarded as a judicial vengeance upon all such injustice, which one righteous authority is authorized to exercise over another that walks in injustice, by virtue of its office, thereby protecting and rescuing the oppressed. This is especially true when they have furthermore bound themselves through special treaties, and the transgressors of the same have thereby effectively submitted themselves, so that the former are all the more authorized to judge and punish them.

The great severity, however, which **God** formerly permitted against such heathen nations, may not be practiced among those who bear the name of Christians: for they would thereby act directly against all the commandments of Christ.

<margin>v. 14. 15. Although a distinction in severity is also indicated here: in the case of distant cities that did not belong among the Canaanite nations, only the men were to be killed and the rest spared; whereas by contrast, nothing of the Canaanites was to be left remaining.</margin>

<column-break/>

16. But of the cities of these peoples, which the **Lord** your **God** gives you for an inheritance, you shall let nothing live that has breath. <margin>Joshua 11:11.</margin>

17. But you shall utterly destroy them: the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, just as the **Lord** your **God** has commanded you.

18. So that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominations which they have committed with their gods, and you sin against the **Lord** your **God**.

19. When you must besiege a city for many days to fight against it to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them; for you can eat of them; therefore you shall not cut them down (since the trees of the field are for man) so that they should be used by you for the siege-work.

20. Only the trees which you know are not trees for food, those you may destroy and cut down, so that you may build siege-works against the city that wages war against you, until it has been subdued.

---

<margin>v. 16. Let nothing live that has breath) Just as Babylon, or the kingdom of sin, seeks to kill everything in us that breathes toward **God**; so it is fair, according to the law of retribution, that it be paid back as it does to us. Thus Cain, who laid the foundation and the ground for the building of the city of the devil, killed Abel—who had a breath, or a longing and sighing, after **God**, and sighed against the vanity, which the word "Abel" <note>A reference to the Hebrew word 'Hevel', meaning breath, vapor, or vanity.</note> signifies.</margin>

<margin>v. 17. Note what is said here in a figure to you, the Seed of Israel: You shall utterly destroy them) You shall spare none of the sins within you, but exterminate them all. If you do not root out all the bitter roots, your field will not be clean: And when you sweep out the leaven from every corner, only then will you become a truly sweet dough. If only one traitor remains within us, you cannot dwell in safety. Therefore, kill what the **Lord** wants killed, so that there may be peace in your whole territory!</margin>

<margin>v. 18. Here alone is tolerance and permissiveness harmful, unholy, and not to be endured.</margin>

<margin>v. 19. 20. Since the fruitful trees were not allowed to be cut down, it is even less justifiable when the same is done to the standing crops of the field, or other such land-devastating cruelties are undertaken, which can be excused before **God** by no "custom of war," however common.</margin>

# Chapter XXI.

->Concerning a slain man, a captive woman, the firstborn, a disobedient son, and a hanged man.<-

IF a slain man is found in the land which the **LORD** your **GOD** will give you to possess as an inheritance, lying in the field, and it is not known who has slain him:

2. Then your elders and your judges shall go out and measure the distance to the cities that are round about the slain man.

3. And it shall be, whichever city is nearest to the slain man, the elders of that city shall take a heifer from the herd, one that has not been worked and has not pulled in a yoke:

4. And the elders of that city shall bring the heifer down into a rough valley, in which there is neither plowing nor sowing, and shall break the heifer's neck there in the valley.

**God** intended to show herewith what a particular abomination he has for the cruel sin of homicide, and that he wishes it to be avenged in every way.
v. 1. (It is not known) <note>original: "da es nicht ist kund worden"</note> and one could not find out at all, even after applying all possible diligence to discover the perpetrator.
v. 2. (Your elders and your judges) The High Court or Great *Sanhedrin* <note>original: "Synedrium," the supreme judicial council in ancient Jerusalem</note> in Jerusalem appointed several from their midst who had to travel to the site.
v. 3. (Whichever city is nearest) Jerusalem was exempt from this law.
(The elders of that city) Namely the twenty-three judicial lords who were in that city, as in every city, along with all other elders or aged people found there.
(One) If the slain man lay equally near to two cities, two heifers were not given, but rather one heifer was provided by both cities together.
v. 4. (In a rough valley) As the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, Josephus, Luther, and others interpret it: but the Hebrews understand it as a stream from which no channels or pipes flowed to water the nearby land, and where the land around was uncultivated,
(In which there is neither plowing nor sowing) Which also, in eternity after the decapitation of the heifer was performed, had to remain uncultivated thereafter. <note>The commentator notes that the land was essentially "retired" from use to mark the gravity of the blood shed there.</note>
(Break the neck) Its head was chopped off from behind with an axe: no differently than if the poor heifer had committed the murder.
If the murderer was caught before the cow's neck was chopped off, or if information was received as to who had done it, the cow remained alive and was driven back to the pasture; however, because it was holy and had been designated for this grave work, it could not be used for labor by anyone, nor slaughtered and eaten, nor could its hide be stripped if it died of natural causes; rather, it was buried whole. The same applied if the murderer was apprehended after the cow's head had already been chopped off.

<column-break/>

5. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall come forward; for the **LORD** your **GOD** has chosen them to serve him and to bless in the name of the **LORD**: and according to their word shall every controversy and every injury be handled.

6. And all the elders of that city, who are nearest to the slain man, shall wash their hands over the heifer whose neck was broken in the valley;

7. And they shall testify and say: Our hands have not shed this blood, and our eyes have not seen it.

8. Atone for your people Israel, whom you, **LORD**, have redeemed, and lay not innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel! So shall the blood be atoned for them.

9. Thus you shall put away the innocent blood from your midst, that you may do what is right in the eyes of the **LORD**.
10. When

v. 5. (Every controversy and every injury) Thus, the priests certainly also judged secular matters.
v. 6. (Wash their hands over) the severed head, to signify their innocence.
v. 7. (Shall testify) calling **God** as a witness that they neglected or omitted nothing in maintaining safe roads, and also diligently investigated all persons passing through, and yet could not discover the perpetrator at all.
v. 8. Whereupon the present priests, who were undoubtedly in the court of such a nearby city, publicly called upon **God** for atonement.
v. 9. (Thus you shall — do) and seek to atone for the guilt with such a sacrifice, and with an earnest prayer seek to ask forgiveness for all other blood-guilt lying on the land because of the slain man, and thus to reconcile **God**.
Which among other things also allows us to recognize that we should heartily beg **God**'s forgiveness for our unrecognized sins of spiritual murder—which we commit with hatred and ill-will against our neighbor (1 John 3:15) or which we commit against ourselves with impurity and the love of creatures (which is idolatry before **God**), whereby the true life from **God** in us is killed (Ephesians 4:17-19)—which **God** nevertheless knows and understands, just as he knows the murderer hidden from men, and places such things in the light before his countenance (Psalm 90:8). We do this for the sake of the blood of Christ, which was shed by **God** in the deep valley of humility and in the great drought of his heart's condition, so that **God** might not reckon these blood-guilts to us, but would be gracious to us and forgive our sins for the sake of the sacrifice of his dear Son.

---

Now, if **God** wanted an unknown perpetrator to be investigated so carefully, and commanded such an atonement to be arranged for that reason; how much more should a known murderer—who has either murdered his neighbor himself or had him murdered by others—be avenged? Thus should the blood-guilts be turned away from the land, which certainly rest upon it as long as such shed blood has not been avenged: as the earth, and thus also every land, is cursed when it has opened its mouth, as it were, and received blood from the murderer’s hand. See Genesis 4:10-12, 9:5-6.

# The Fifth Book of Moses [Deuteronomy]. Chapter XX.

10. When you draw near to a city to fight against it, you shall first offer it terms of peace. <margin>Matthew 10:11–13</margin>

11. And it shall be, if it gives you an answer of peace and opens its gates to you, then all the people found within it shall be tributary to you and shall serve you.

12. But if it will not make peace with you, but chooses to wage war against you, then you shall besiege it.

13. And when the **LORD** your **GOD** delivers it into your hand, you shall strike every male within it with the edge of the sword.

14. But the women, the children, the livestock, and everything that is in the city, you shall take as plunder for yourself; and you shall eat the spoil of your enemies, which the **LORD** your **GOD** has given you.

15. Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not of the cities of these nations here.

---

v. 10. (When — so you shall) Even among the pagan nations, such a law was observed, that no one was attacked as an enemy without first publicly announcing war through a herald. <note>The author refers to the ancient Roman practice of the *fetiales*, priests who acted as heralds to ensure a war was "just."</note> Here, **God** desires that His people first present all means of peace, to see if the enemies will desist from their offense and wish to make amends for the damage.

v. 11. (Answer in peace and open) Oh, what has the **LORD** done toward us for so many years now, other than offering us peace through His long-suffering patience! But we are so bold and presumptuous against Him that we wish to have peace according to our own will and conditions—a relief and peace in the flesh, a peace without righteousness. He, however, offers only such a peace which is the effect and fruit of righteousness. <margin>Isaiah 32:17</margin> Oh, let us then still accept the offered peace while there is time! For we see that even for the Jews themselves, because they rejected it, nothing remained but the sword.

v. 12. 13. (But if — then — then) Mercy goes before judgment. Even today, if men are first warned about their offenses to see if they will settle in kindness; then—since kingdoms mostly still stand in the "state of nature" <note>A philosophical term referring to a condition without established divine or civil order.</note> and have not yet become the kingdoms of our **God** and His **Christ**, <margin>Revelation 11:15</margin>—if all such kindly proposals find no entry, and the enemies moreover continue with their offense (especially with the oppression of consciences), one may indeed compel them to their duty with force, just as **God** permitted His people here. This is to be viewed as a judicial vengeance upon all such injustice, which one righteous authority is authorized to exercise over another that walks in injustice, by virtue of its office, thereby protecting and rescuing the oppressed. Especially so when they have bound themselves to it through special treaties, and the transgressors have thus subjected themselves to such action, so that the former are all the more authorized to judge and punish them.
However, the great severity that **God** formerly permitted against such heathen nations may not be practiced among those who bear the <unclear>name</unclear> of Christians: for they would thereby act directly against all the commands of **Christ**.

v. 14. 15. Although a distinction in severity is indicated here: for in those distant cities that did not belong to the Canaanite nations, only the men were to be killed, while the rest were to be <unclear>spared</unclear>; whereas from the Canaanites, nothing was to be left remaining.

<column-break/>

16. But of the cities of these nations which the **LORD** your **GOD** gives you as an inheritance, you shall let nothing live that draws breath. <margin>Joshua 11:11</margin>

17. But you shall utterly devote them to destruction: the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, just as the **LORD** your **GOD** has commanded you.

18. So that they may not teach you to do according to all their abominations which they have committed with their gods, and you sin against the **LORD** your **GOD**.

19. When you must besiege a city for many days, fighting against it to take it, you shall not destroy its trees by wielding an axe against them; for you can eat from them. Therefore, you shall not cut them down (since the trees of the field are for man) <note>original: "sintemal die Bäume des Feldes für den Menschen sind"</note> so that they should serve you in the siege-works.

20. But the trees which you know are not trees for food, those you may destroy and cut down to build siege-works against the city that makes war with you, until it is subdued.
<meta>Catchword: D [referring to the next section or chapter]</meta>

---

v. 16. (Let nothing live that draws breath) <unclear>Just as</unclear> Babylon, or the kingdom of sin, seeks <unclear>to</unclear> kill everything in us that breathes toward **God**; so it is just, according to the law of <unclear>re-</unclear>taliation, that it be repaid as it <unclear>does to</unclear> us. For every good inspiration from **God**, the longing for **God**, <margin>Galatians 5:17</margin> is destroyed by Babylon <unclear>within</unclear> us. Thus Cain—who laid the foundation and <unclear>ground</unclear> for the building of the city of the devil—killed Abel, who <unclear>had</unclear> the breath, or a longing and sighing, for **God**, and who sighed against vanity, which the word "Abel" signi<unclear>fies.</unclear> <note>The Hebrew name "Habel" (Abel) translates literally to "breath" or "vanity."</note>

v. 17. Note what is said here in a figure <note>A "figure" or "type" is a symbolic representation of a spiritual truth.</note> to you, Seed of Isr<unclear>ael!</unclear>
(You shall utterly destroy them) You shall spare no <unclear>sin</unclear> within you, but root them all out. When <unclear>you</unclear> root out all the bitter roots, your field will be clean: when you sweep out the leaven from every corner, <unclear>then you</unclear> will first become a truly sweet dough. If but one traitor <unclear>always</unclear> remains, you cannot dwell in safety. Therefore, kill wh<unclear>at the</unclear> **LORD** wants to have killed, so that peace may come to <unclear>the</unclear> whole region!

v. 18. Here alone is tolerance and treaty-making harmful, unholy, and not to be endured. <note>The author argues that while we should be tolerant of people, we must be intolerant of the "Canaanites" (sins) within our own souls.</note>

v. 19. 20. Since the fruitful trees were not allowed to be <unclear>cut</unclear> down, it is even less justifiable <unclear>that</unclear> the same should happen to the standing crops of the field, or that other such land-devastating cruelties <unclear>be</unclear> undertaken, which cannot be excused before **God** by any such common custom in war.

<header>Chapter XXI. The Fifth Book of Moses.</header>

# Chapter XXI.

->Concerning a slain person, a captive woman, the firstborn, a disobedient son, and one who is hanged.<-

WHen a slain person is found in the land that the Lord your God will give you to possess as an inheritance, lying in the open field, and it has not become known who slew him:
2. Then your elders and your judges shall go out and measure [the distance] to the cities that are around the slain person.
3. And it shall happen that whichever city is closest to the slain person, the elders of that city shall take a young cow from the herd, which has not been worked and has not pulled a yoke:
4. And the elders of that city shall lead the cow down into a rugged valley, in which there is neither plowing nor sowing, and shall break the neck of the young cow there in the valley.

---

God wanted to show by this how He holds a particular horror for the cruel sin of murder, and that He wants it avenged in every way.

**v. 1.** (Since it has not become known) and even with all possible diligence applied to discover it, it could not be found out.

**v. 2.** (Your elders and your judges) The High Court or Great Sanhedrin <note>The supreme legal council of ancient Israel</note> in Jerusalem appointed several from their midst who had to travel to the location.

**v. 3.** (Whichever city is closest) Jerusalem was exempt from this law.

(The elders of that city) Namely, the twenty-three judges who were in that city—as was the case in every city—along with all the other elders or elderly people present there.

(One) If the slain person lay equally close to two cities, two cows were not offered; instead, one cow was provided by both cities together.

**v. 4.** (In a rugged valley) This is how the Seventy Interpreters <note>original: "70 Dollmetschen," referring to the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, Josephus, Luther, and others translate it; the Hebrew scholars, however, understand this to mean a stream from which small channels or pipes departed to water the nearby land, and where the surrounding land is also uncultivated.

(in which there is neither plowing nor sowing) Which, for all eternity after the beheading of the cow, must never be sown or cultivated again.

(Break the neck) Its head was cut off from behind with an axe: just as if the poor cow itself had committed the murder.

If the murderer was caught before the cow’s neck was cut, or if news was received about who did it, the cow remained alive and was driven back to the pasture. However, because she was holy and designated for this great work, she could not be used for labor, nor slaughtered and eaten, nor—if she died on her own—could her skin be removed; rather, she was buried whole. This was also the case if the murderer was apprehended after the cow’s head had already been cut off.

<column-break/>

5. Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall step forward; for the Lord your God has chosen them to serve Him and to bless in the name of the Lord: and according to their word shall every dispute and every injury be handled.
6. And all the elders of that city, who are closest to the slain person, shall wash their hands over the young cow whose neck was broken in the valley;
7. And they shall testify and say: Our hands have not shed this blood, and our eyes have not seen it.
8. Atone for Your people Israel, whom You, O Lord, have redeemed, and lay not innocent blood in the midst of Your people Israel! Thus the blood shall be atoned for them.
9. Thus you shall put away the innocent blood from your midst, so that you may do what is right in the eyes of the Lord.
10. When

---

**v. 5.** (Every dispute and every injury) Meaning that the priests certainly also judged secular and civil matters.

**v. 6.** (Wash their hands over) the severed head, to signify their innocence.

**v. 7.** (Shall testify) They call God as a witness that they, in their efforts to maintain safe roads, neglected or omitted nothing, and also diligently investigated all travelers and passers-by, and yet could not discover the perpetrator at all.

**v. 8.** Whereupon the present priests, who were undoubtedly members of the court of that nearest city, publicly called out to God for atonement.

**v. 9.** (Thus you shall—do) and seek to atone for the guilt with such a sacrifice, and with an earnest prayer seek to beg forgiveness for all blood-guilt otherwise lying on the land because of the slain person, and thus reconcile God.

Which also allows us to recognize, among other things, that we should heartily beg God for forgiveness for our unacknowledged sins of spiritual murder—which we commit with hatred and ill-will toward our neighbor (1 John 3:15) or even those we commit against ourselves through impurity and the love of created things (which is idolatry before God)—since through this, the true life from God within us is killed (Ephesians 4:17, 18, 19). Though God knows and recognizes these sins, just as He knows the murderer hidden from men, and places them into the light before His face (Psalm 90:8), we should ask for forgiveness for the sake of the blood of Christ. His blood was shed in the "deep valley" of humility and in the "great drought" of His heart's abandonment by God, so that God will not credit these blood-debts to us but will be merciful to us for the sake of the sacrifice of His dear Son and forgive our sins.

Now, if God has so carefully sought out an unknown perpetrator and commanded such an atonement for that reason, how much more should a known murderer—who either murdered his neighbor himself or had him murdered by others—be avenged? In this way, the blood-guilt is turned away from the land, which certainly rests upon it as long as such shed blood has not been avenged; for the earth, and thus also every land, is cursed when it has opened its mouth, so to speak, and received blood from the murderer's hand. See Genesis 4:10, 11, 12 and 9:5, 6.

<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XXI.</header>

10. When you go out to war against your enemies, and the LORD your God delivers them into your hand, so that you carry away captives from them;
11. And you see among the captives a woman of beautiful form, and you have a desire for her so that you would take her as your wife:
12. Then you shall bring her into your house, and she shall shave her head and let her nails grow;
13. And she shall put off the clothes of her captivity from her, and shall sit in your house and bewail her father and her mother for a full month; and after that you may go in to her and be her husband, so that she may be your wife.
14. And it shall happen, if you have no delight in her, then you shall let her go according to her desire, and you shall by no means sell her for money: You shall not make a profit from her, because you have humbled her.

---

When one encounters a pagan- or earthly-minded soul in its reasoning and worship, and sees that there is something good in it that attracts us to its fellowship, then one must, above all things, shave away the proud reason—which must be taken captive under the obedience of Christ—and its manifold *reasonings* <note>original: "raisonnements"</note>, like the multitude of hairs. Thereupon, she shall bewail her old religion and the conclusions of her erroneous reason—signified by the renunciation of her father and her mother—through true tears of repentance, and betake herself to the house of right worship. Only then may one unite with her.

<margin>v. 11.</margin> Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin</note> understands the captive pagan woman to represent the learning of the heathens, which has an enchanting beauty and, when it is taken in, also very much takes one in and captures one in return; so that under the great power of will it exerts over the inclinations of the human mind, there is also a very great danger that men might love the slave or handmaid to their own ruin more than their lady, divine Wisdom.

<margin>v. 12.</margin> For this reason, it is highly necessary that she be humbled, that the haughty and foul baggage be brought under the obedience of Christ, and her honor be put to shame: so that she may learn to know herself, that she was born for slavish labor, and should perform the same upon the letter, as the servant-word of the Lord. Therefore, it is also significantly stated:
(She shall let her nails grow) But not cut them off, as many have translated it. For the purpose is to make the captive misshapen and ugly: so that perhaps the man's desire for her might pass away, since otherwise they were not permitted to marry foreign women. Exodus 34:16.

<margin>v. 13.</margin> If, however, he remained constant in his attachment to her, she was then permitted to him in marriage; so that they might not disgrace or kill such women in their captivity: and thus this was also permitted because of the hardness of their hearts. Matthew 19:8.

<margin>v. 14.</margin> But if he afterwards conceived a displeasure toward her, he was not allowed to <unclear>buy</unclear> <note>The context suggests "treat as a slave" or "sell," though the OCR says "kaufen" (buy)</note> her as a captive slave, but had to let her go entirely free.
Such laws, however, have no place in today's wars, because the conquered are no longer regarded as slaves—which were pagan customs that God still tolerated because the redemption of all people through the blood of His Son had not yet been revealed—but are instead regarded as subjects.

<column-break/>

15. If a man has two wives, the one loved and the other hated, and they bear him children, and the firstborn son is from the hated wife:
16. Then it shall happen on the day when he divides the inheritance among his children of what he possesses, that he may not make the son of the loved wife the firstborn ahead of the son of the hated wife, who is the actual firstborn:
17. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as the firstborn, so that he gives him two parts of everything that is found with him: for he is the first of his strength <gloss>(a)</gloss>; to him belongs the right of the firstborn. <margin>(a) Genesis 49:3.</margin>
18. If...

---

God did not hereby approve of polygamy, but rather, if they indeed fell into it according to the hardness of their hearts, the firstborn's right—consisting of dominion and a double portion of the inheritance—could not be taken from him, even if such a man loved one wife more and wished to declare the later-born son from her as the firstborn to please her. See Genesis 29:31, 1 Samuel 1:4-5, 8, 1 Chronicles 5:1.
Yet the right of the firstborn could be taken by the father due to a great offense and given to another, as happened with Reuben. Genesis 49:4.
Christ has, as it were, chosen two wives for Himself: the Jews, to whom He showed much favor; and the Gentiles, whom He set behind the former and treated as dogs.
But because the Gentiles were the first to accept the Lord in faith and were blessed by Him, they brought the firstborn into the world and were preferred over the Jews. For—
In Christ Jesus, who is impartial, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith which is active through love.
Therefore, the birthright now remains with the Gentiles, after they became fruitful from Christ, and they receive the inheritance portion in the inheritance of the saints in light: although nothing is taken away from the future fruitfulness of the Jewish Church in faith in Christ. For—
God wishes to show both things here in a mystery: and indeed also how He had accepted His people Israel—whom He had taken as His first people and thus as the firstborn because of the beloved fathers (refer to Exodus 4:22, Jeremiah 31:9)—even though their mother, the Jewish Church, afterwards became "hated" because of her idolatry, Hosea 1:9, 2:4, 20. Nevertheless, God accepted the Gentiles as His beloved people (Romans 11, from Hosea 2:23, 25; Romans 15:9–12); yet He does not cast off the former, who previously did not enjoy such love, but will in His own time receive them back into grace and make them His people on earth again, whom He will crown with His glory and joy, as the most glorious promise is especially to be seen in Jeremiah 30:17–22.

<page-num>753</page-num>
<header>Ch. XXI. The Fifth Book of Moses.</header>

18. If a man has a stubborn and rebellious son who will not obey the voice of his father or the voice of his mother, and though they discipline him, he will not listen to them:
19. Then his father and his mother shall take hold of him and bring him out to the elders of his city and to the gate of his place,
<margin>ch. 22:15, 25:7. Ruth 4:1, 2.</margin>
20. And they shall say to the elders of his city: "This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he does not obey our voice; he is a glutton and a drunkard."
21. Then all the men of his city shall stone him so that he dies; and so you shall put away the evil from your midst, that all Israel may hear and fear.

---

With this, God intended to confirm obedience and honor toward parents and to deter disobedient children from their stubbornness and godlessness through such a harsh punishment. See more on this in the notes on Exodus 21:15 and Leviticus 20:9.
<margin>v. 19. To the gate)</margin> Trials were formerly held in the gates of towns <note>The "gate" of a city served as the public square and seat of the local court, ensuring that justice was visible to all citizens.</note> so that it would be more manifest to everyone, and also so that the judges might be encouraged to diligently observe their office.
<margin>v. 20. Our son is stubborn and rebellious, a drunkard)</margin> One hears such complaints even today more than enough. But
How many parents complain about the wickedness and naughtiness of their children, who were themselves led into all evil by those very parents and their un-Christian and vice-ridden lives! They are not disciplined themselves; how then do they expect to discipline children?
If parents truly wished to have godly and well-bred children, they should first live in the fear of God themselves and thus raise their young with them for the Lord.
Now, however, since children are poorly raised and youths are left in their unrestrained freedom, one should not wonder later when they eventually become dissolute men; just as unbridled calves in time transform into butting and bellowing oxen.
And therefore, in the commonwealth, everything should be looked upon with all seriousness, and no expense spared to remedy all the mischief prevailing in this regard.
<margin>v. 21. And you shall put away the evil from your midst.)</margin> Thus, even today, the authorities should pay more attention to such stubborn and disobedient children—since such vice will greatly spread in the latter times, 2 Timothy 3:2—so that such wickedness might be checked through houses of correction <note>term: <term>Zucht-Häuser</term> (houses of correction). These were early modern institutions intended to reform the idle or deviant through labor and religious instruction.</note> and other means, and the wicked do not so easily gain the upper hand, but through such sharp discipline may either be improved or removed from human society through confinement.
How can parents, however, be zealous against the evil habits of their children—whether they be drunkards or otherwise devoted to a dissolute life—when they themselves are drowned in these and those, indeed perhaps all vices? And how should or can authorities exercise proper oversight in this when they themselves make a "gallantry" <note>original: "Galanterie". In this context, the author uses the term sarcastically to mean a fashionable social grace or a trivial matter.</note> out of those vices, and let drunkenness and other sins pass among them as something blameless?

<column-break/>

22. And if a man has committed a sin worthy of a death sentence, so that he must be put to death, and you have hanged him on a tree:
23. His corpse shall not remain overnight on the tree (a), but you shall certainly bury him on the same day; for one who is hanged is cursed by God: so that you do not defile your land which the LORD your God gives you as an inheritance. 1 Peter 1:4.
<margin>(a) Joshua 8:29. John 19:31.</margin>
<meta>catchword: The</meta>

---

<insert>
The Jews say that blasphemers and idolaters, when they had first been stoned, were subjected to this punishment of being hanged on a tree.
</insert>
In such hanged persons, God wanted to show a particular example of the curse which sin in general deserved.
<margin>v. 22. A sin worthy of a death sentence—he must be put to death)</margin> According to the spirit of the Old Testament. But according to the grace of the New Covenant, God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn and live. According to which evangelical word of grace a Christian authority must also know how to conduct its office—which is otherwise strict by nature—under Christ, whose name and teaching it confesses, in Christian moderation. This is especially so since, in the time of the New Covenant, we lack a clear divine command and will for death sentences over malefactors <note>original: "Maleficanten", meaning criminals or evil-doers.</note>; one also takes the liberty to leave other worldly or judicial laws of the Old Testament out of regard and observance.
In the Old Testament, the way of perfect holiness and knowledge of the innermost sinful corruption was not yet revealed; therefore, only the gross outward vices were declared worthy of death, and the people of Israel had to perform the execution of death determined in divine law in a physical manner. In the New Testament, however, with greater holiness revealed, not only the outward but just as much the inward sins of human wickedness—which come to no outward outbreak—are in themselves declared worthy of death before Christ. <margin>Matthew 5:20–48.</margin> But the holy people of Christendom have had to perform the execution no longer in the manner of a physical rooting out and killing, but a spiritual one: until the time of the breaking out of corruption, when death penalties were reintroduced—doubtless not without divine providence <note>original: "Providenz"</note> and the hidden hand of God, who rules the world with His wisdom and directs worldly lawmakers to order and carry out what should happen according to His secret judgments over human wickedness.
Yet the perfect economy <note>term: <term>Oeconomie</term> (economy). In theology, this refers to God's management or arrangement of human history and salvation.</note> of evangelical grace may not be overturned by this; and how far it harmonizes with it is the only question here. Otherwise, as just thought, both are God's will and order; but each in its time and in its kind. Grace does not abolish wrath in its order, and wrath does not abolish grace in its order. Yet, after such a great fullness of grace has spread over us through the shed blood of the New Covenant, mercy triumphs over judgment, and grace—where it is recognized—is to be preferred.
<margin>v. 23. Not overnight—buried on the same day)</margin> Because the curse was to be taken away through the death of Christ—who Himself wished to become a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and for that reason also let Himself be hanged on a tree—so also such hanged persons were not to be left overnight on the tree; just as Joshua also observed this with the foreign kings in Joshua 8:29 and 10:26.
Also, because around the carcass of one cursed, or by the corpse of a sinner, unclean spirits tend to gather in heaps.
**That you do not defile your land)** That would have happened if they had left the "curse" (as the hanged man was called) thus in the eyes of the world, and thereby signaled partly their irreconcilability, partly the denial of their hope: that in its time, the memory and remembrance of the curse and sins should be put away from the land and buried through the burial of Christ.

<page-num>754</page-num>
<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Ch. XXII.</header>

# Chapter XXII.
->Various laws, particularly regarding jealousy and adultery.<- <note>Although the heading mentions jealousy and adultery, these specific topics appear later in the chapter; the initial verses focus on the recovery of lost property and helpfulness toward neighbors.</note>

---

YOU shall not see your brother’s ox or his small livestock going astray and hide yourself from them; you shall certainly bring them back to your brother. <margin>Philippians 2:4.</margin>

2. And if your brother is not near you, or if you do not know him, then you shall bring it into your house, and it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it; then you shall give it back to him.

3. And so you shall do with his donkey, and so you shall do with his garment; yes, so you shall do with everything your brother has lost, which has gone missing from him and you have found: you cannot hide yourself.

4. You shall not see your brother’s donkey <gloss>(a)</gloss> or his ox fallen down on the way and hide yourself from them:
<margin>(a) Exodus 23:5.</margin>

---

Here, helpfulness is commanded as a necessary outflow of love, as we are duty-bound to ward off our neighbor’s harm and to seek and promote his benefit. This is something that the "great ones" of the world usually expect to see in the commissions of their servants; we should then remember that God our Lord imposes the same upon us in return for His great benefits—to demonstrate such love toward our neighbor, since we can neither harm nor benefit God Himself.

There is no greater motivation for love than love already received, especially when this love is practiced frequently on every occasion.

But should the Spirit of God not look further here than the literal letter? Does God care for donkeys or oxen? Or does He not speak entirely for our sake? <note>original: "1. Cor. 9/9.10"</note> Therefore, these words undoubtedly have their spiritual meaning.

If we are not to let our neighbor’s ox, donkey, horse, etc., go astray or lie fallen, how much less then should we neglect his soul or the soul of one of his kin, so that we do not lead them back to our firstborn brother, Christ, who is not ashamed to call us His brothers? <note>original: "Hebr. 2/11"</note> And must we not then first be fit for this ourselves?

v. 2. Has not this Son of Man—and for that very reason our brother—come to seek and to save that which was lost? <note>original: "Luc. 19/10"</note>

v. 3. The donkey is our natural, earthly man, who through the Fall has lost himself, straying from the right path and the order of God; whereby the garment of innocence and the image of God were also lost.

v. 4. Thus, our Lord Jesus could not bear to see humanity lying there, sticking to the earth, being earthly-minded, striving after earthly things, or "embracing dung heaps." <note>A reference to Lamentations 4:5, describing the extreme reversal of fortune and spiritual degradation.</note> He could not hide Himself from His own flesh, <note>original: "Esa. 58/7"</note> but rather bent down, or humbled Himself, to raise the fallen human out of the dust and filth of earthly striving, restoring him to a divine conduct in the heavens. <note>original: "Phil. 3/19. 20"</note> Yet He did not want the fallen human to remain like a dumb, unruly, and lazy beast; <note>original: "Ps. 32/9"</note> rather He wants you, and you shall
<meta>catchword: and you shall</meta>

<column-break/>

you shall certainly help him lift them up.

5. A woman shall not wear anything that pertains to a man, nor shall a man put on a woman’s garment; for whoever does these things is an abomination to the LORD your God.

6. If...

---

v. 4. *Help him lift them up*) Or more precisely, *lift them up with him*. Herein lies a thoughtfully important meaning, both according to the literal and the spiritual understanding. We should help others up, but they must also help themselves.

In a fallen ox or donkey, there is a principle of life and a power to be able to help lift itself up; how much more then is there in the fallen human for his own resurrection? Otherwise, all admonitions, warnings, punishments—yes, all the dealings of God with fallen man—would be in vain and useless. Our Brother would want to lift them up, but they would have no power within them to work with Him. God would also be found partial, and could thus be accused of injustice, for raising one and not the other.

Even if man is dead to the good through the Fall and dead in sins, yet the Lord of Hosts has left behind a seed. <note>original: "Esa. 1/9. Rom. 9/29"</note> This divine seed lives when everything that is temporal and earthly is dead and gone.

Therefore, the "lazy animals" who rest and lie still upon the dregs of their sins—of vanity, pride, lust, greed, etc.—must not imagine that an irresistible power of grace must seize them and force them from within to rise from their lazy sleep of sin to righteousness. On the contrary, they might sooner experience a heavy hand which they will not be able to resist.

The grace of God does not work with violence, but softly and gently, and draws people with "cords of a man." <note>A reference to Hosea 11:4, implying God leads with human kindness rather than brute force.</note> If grace is resisted, the Lord laments over it. <note>Citations for Matthew 23:37, Acts 7:51, Isaiah 5:4, 65:2-3, and John 5:40.</note> For it is contrary to the nature of obedience to be coerced.

Whoever, therefore, waits for such irresistible force displays as much understanding as an ox or a donkey, a horse or a mule. Our Brother wants to lift us up, but *with* us, not *without* us.

We are also commanded to help lift up our brother’s ox and donkey, but how much more our brother himself. <note>original: "Gal. 6/1"</note> To that end, let us stir up the gift that is in us, so that we may better offer one another a helping hand, and that each may be more united in his concern for the other’s salvation and well-being.

v. 5. Since God here on earth has distinguished the gender among us humans into male and female—which will no longer be so in eternity—external decency should also be required to be distinguished in clothing, thereby avoiding all secret shame.

It was likely not without compelling reason that a prohibition was given regarding this; for Clericus <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous theologian and critic.</note> proves from Julius Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Christian writer and former astrologer.</note> and M. Servius <note>Marius Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian.</note> that such things were customary among the heathens for the sake of unchastity <note>Referring to ritual cross-dressing in pagan festivals.</note>.

However, if an Israelite hid himself in women's clothing to escape the hands of his enemies, he would hardly have sinned against the divine commandment by doing so.

But if a man, especially a teacher, wears what is unbefitting of him, it is regarded as if he had changed his clothes; whereby not only he, but also the office he holds, is defamed, so that people can have little respect for it. In this sense, God means much the same as what is written in Titus 2:15.

Otherwise, it is also unseemly for men to imitate the ornamentation and finery to which women are devoted. See 1 Peter 3:3.

6. If you come across a bird's nest on the way, in any tree or on the ground, with young ones or with eggs, and the mother is sitting on the young or on the eggs; you shall not take the mother along with the young: <note>Leviticus 22:28.</note>
7. You shall by all means let the mother fly away, but the young you may take for yourself, that it may go well with you and that you may prolong your days.
8. When you build a new house, you shall make a railing on your roof: so that you do not bring blood-guilt upon your house if anyone were to fall from it.
9. You shall not sow your vineyard with two kinds of seed, so that you do not defile the dry fruit you have sown alongside the yield of the vineyard. <note>Exodus 22:29.</note>
10. You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together. <note>2 Corinthians 6:14.</note>

---

v. 6. 7. Since God wishes to have mercy shown even toward the lowly birds—of which two are bought for a penny, as Christ says—so that the young are not robbed of their mother who cherishes and cares for them; and just as the righteous man has mercy on his livestock (Proverbs 12:10), how much more then should one have mercy on his poor and miserable neighbor, so that he is not robbed of his necessary sustenance. And if God commends this seemingly minor commandment with such a gracious promise, what will the Lord then do in grace for him who has practiced much mercy on earth? Conversely, it will also go ill for the unmerciful who have practiced cruelty even toward animals, let alone toward human beings. <note>James 2:13.</note>

v. 8. Here, for a literal understanding, it is necessary to note that in the land of Judea and in the Orient, they made the roofs of their houses flat, so that one could walk, eat, sleep, hold secret conversations with someone, and perform other tasks upon them; as can be seen from Joshua 2:6, 2 Samuel 11:2, and Matthew 10:27. This custom is still to be found throughout the entire Orient today, according to the accounts of travel writers. Therefore, the roofs had to be provided with a railing all around to prevent any accident. By this, God intended to command us to be prudent, even in physical actions, so that we might avert all disaster while calling upon His protection; for otherwise one "tempts God" when one does not prevent all danger to the best of one's ability. For this reason, even today in houses, one should secure all dangerous places so as not to bring blood-guilt upon one's house.

v. 9. *Not with two kinds in the vineyard*) In warm, fertile lands, it is common to sow grain between the vines.

v. 10. *Not plowing with ox and donkey together*) A donkey is indeed suited for carrying loads, but not for plowing; on the other hand, the ox is suited for plowing, but not for carrying. Thus they are two incompatible colleagues who do not fit together. Whoever yokes them together does not act reasonably.
In our calling, the old and the new man also cannot be yoked together.

v. 11. And the robe of righteousness and the stained robe of the flesh also do not rhyme with each other. (Isaiah 61:10, Jude v. 23). The former is of the Spirit of Christ, as the unspotted Lamb; the latter is like the linen from the earthly-minded nature. 
*Not wool and linen together*) We should not be hypocrites, trying to make people believe we are gentle sheep when something else lies beneath; just as in such a garment, one does not see the linen that is covered with wool.

v. 12. *Tassels*) Christ also wore such fringes on His clothing. See Luke 8:44 and the notes on Numbers 15:38. 
Modern Jews wear this garment quite short under other clothes, so that they are not laughed at by Christians for such attire, since such four-cornered clothing is no longer in common use.

v. 13. 14. God specifically intended to command His people toward chastity so that pure and undefiled marriages could be established among them, which are conducive to peace and pleasure; whereas from impure souls who have made themselves common, nothing but aversion and enmity can later arise.

---

v. 18. 19. Thus the jealous husband was flogged and fined money, so that men might be deterred from such unfounded jealousy.
v. 20. But should it be found true, that her virginity and honorable conduct could not be demonstrated, but rather she could be proven to be pregnant, or that she had made herself common to others:
v. 21. then she had to be stoned: as a terror to all virgins in Israel, so that they might preserve their youth in chastity and commit no fornication; which is here branded as a particular **folly**.
**You shall put away the evil from your midst**) In this, God looks upon everything: that evil—namely, not only all coarse and manifest sins, but also the hidden ones: lust, vain honor, people-pleasing, hypocrisy, the desire to rule, cunning, evil habits, hatred, unbelief, envy, self-love, pride, and the like—be put away from our midst. Through this, **true virginity** is established again in us and among us, which consists in complete purity from all defilement of the flesh and spirit and from a divided, desecrated life.
If people now seek and love physical virginity so much, why then do they not much more love and seek the virginity that is from GOD? If you wish to be a Christian and pass as such before GOD, you have in Christ a great Bridegroom, and you must see to it that you bring Him a pure virgin. For there must also be pure virgins who wish to entrust themselves to the Lord Christ as the rightful Husband.
When the love of the world still reigns in a soul, so that it defiles itself with the same, and thus commits **spiritual fornication**, yet wishes to play the hypocrite as if it also loved the Lord Christ; such a soul will be discovered by His holy jealousy and be sentenced to eternal death. See 2 Corinthians 11:2, 3.
The souls, then, who wish to belong to the Israel of GOD under the New Testament (Galatians 6:16), must be virgins who are not defiled with women: meaning they remain outside the entanglements of the world, and serve their neighbor only in freedom, and in such a way of life follow the Lamb wherever He goes; to which testimony Christ wishes to call them, to be faithful to Him alone therein. See Revelation 14:3, 4, 5. Otherwise, they commit a **folly** among this spiritual Israel when they bind themselves to the world for its service, or even join in with it and keep friendship with it, and they will be condemned by the Lord JESUS as adulterers and adulteresses. James 4:4.

v. 23. 24. Here it is now added how a betrothed bride should be valued the same as a wife; and if she had relations with someone, both should be punished with death just like adulterers, because the **promise**, and not only the cohabitation, constitutes the marriage before GOD.
v. 25-27. Thus **rape** <note>original: "Nothzüchtigung"</note> is also reckoned here as being equal to manslaughter, because the life and happiness of such a violated bride are, as it were, taken from her, since her betrothed bridegroom might very easily despise her for it and separate from her.
Whoever wishes to force the souls who have surrendered themselves to Christ’s special guidance into something external against their conscience, commits thereby also a **spiritual rape**, and will load a heavy judgment upon himself.

# The Fifth Book of Moses, Chapter XXIII.

9. When you go out into camp against your enemies, then you shall keep yourself from every evil thing.
10. If there is any man among you who is not clean because of an occurrence at night, then he shall go outside the camp; he shall not come into the camp.
11. And it shall be that before evening approaches, he shall bathe himself with water; and when the sun has gone down, he shall come into the camp.
12. And you shall have a place outside the camp where you may go out.
13. And you shall have a little shovel <note>original: "Schäufflein"; a small trowel or digging tool</note> among your gear; and it shall be that when you sit down outside, you shall dig with it, and then cover up what has come from you.
14. For the LORD your God walks in the midst of (a) your camp to deliver you and to give over your enemies before your face; therefore shall your camp be holy, so that He sees nothing shameful among you and turns away from you.

> (a) Joshua 3:10. Psalm 46:6. Zephaniah 3:15. Matthew 18:20.
> 2 Corinthians 6:16.

**v. 9.** One must indeed always guard oneself against evil, but especially when one hovers daily in the danger of death, as a soldier does when he goes out against his enemies, for he holds his soul, as it were, in his hand. Judges 12:3. 1 Samuel 19:5.
**v. 10. 11.** Ceremonial uncleanness was treated above in Leviticus 15.
**v. 12. 13.** Here, however, the cleanliness of the camp is also specifically commanded, that they should diligently bury that which comes from them.
**v. 14.** And a very important reason is given: namely, because GOD is present among them with His presence for protection against their enemies.
In this is contained a clear and notable representation of the **Church Militant** <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians on earth struggling against sin and the devil, as opposed to the "Church Triumphant" in heaven.</note> of God.
Cleanliness and holiness are the ornaments of His house.
To this end is ordained the bath of water in the Word and the Blood of JESUS.
It is included in the third Article of Faith, that we believe in a **holy Church**; and therein the Holy One alone wishes to reveal Himself gloriously as the Head to His own glory.
And therefore let us seek the true Church where it is to be found; namely, in union with GOD: and for that reason, let us not point men toward men or toward ourselves, but toward GOD and Christ JESUS in the Spirit. For it is grounded and ends solely in Immanuel, which means **GOD with us**.

<column-break/>

15. You shall not deliver a servant to his master who has escaped from his master to you.
16. He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place he shall choose in one of your gates where it seems good to him; you shall not oppress him.
17. There shall be no harlot among the daughters of Israel, and there shall be no male prostitute <note>original: "Hurer"; often referring to male cult prostitutes or those engaging in sexual immorality</note> among the sons of Israel.
18. You shall not bring the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog <note>original: "Hunde-Gelt"</note> into the house of the LORD your God for any vow. For both of these are an abomination to the LORD your God.
19. [Text continues...]

**v. 15. 16.** Protection should be given to those who complain of the unmercifulness and injustice of others—even if they were their masters and authorities—and especially regarding the coercion of conscience; one should answer for them against that vengefulness. GOD will punish those who fail to provide such protection and do not assist their neighbor in the distress of his heart.
However, when the delivery happens as with Onesimus to Philemon by Paul, it is of no concern <note>Referencing the New Testament Book of Philemon, where Paul returns a runaway slave to his master, but as a "brother in Christ."</note>.
**v. 17.** GOD wants the estate of marriage observed among His people, so that those who have come to their years and feel this inclination—and thus long for a spouse—should procreate children with them. These they should raise in the knowledge of GOD for His honor, and thus they should carry out His command to "be fruitful and multiply" in a lawful manner. Genesis 1:28. 1 Corinthians 7:9.
Conversely, He wants the heathen, impure lust of harlotry to be completely rooted out from among His people, whereby the order of the generations is entirely confused, and children must lament their parents' shame in time and eternity. Ephesians 4:17, 19.
Among those who now confess Christ, harlotry should be even more abhorred; it is a great stain of shame where it breaks in and is overlooked through all sorts of excuses, rather than being rooted out with all severity. 1 Corinthians 6:15, 20. Ephesians 5:3.
*There shall be no harlot among Israel)* Would it not be highly proper that this law were written on the gates of all Christian cities and places?
Should it now be more foul and godless within the spiritual Israel of Christendom than in the physical Israel?
Why then are public harlots not rooted out in Christendom? Is it not misfortune enough that one must tolerate secret harlots, among high and low? What if the Devil were to fetch one away, and seize their protector along with the one who has care of her—and is thus one body with her (1 Corinthians 6:16)—all at once?
**v. 18.** He who leaves an obvious vice unpunished, or even seeks his own profit thereby, or takes his protection from the hire of a harlot; he makes himself as guilty of such sins as if he had committed them himself. Therefore, no father confessor should absolve such an authority with a good conscience.
*Dog-money)* is indeed interpreted in various ways, but with Bochart (b) <note>original: Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar known for his work on animals in the Bible.</note> one understands it most naturally as the money obtained for a sold dog. GOD did not want this because the dog was a very unclean, unchaste animal which publicly mingled with its kind on all the streets.
No one should apply anything from a "doggish" or lewd nature to holy things; that would be the same as if one were to sacrifice an unclean dog and break its neck. Isaiah 66:3. Micah 1:7.
Also, whatever is brought to the Lord resulting from "doggish" bickering and biting among one another is likewise an abomination to the Lord.

### Chapter XXIII. The Fifth Book of Moses.

<margin>Exodus 22:25. Leviticus 25:35.</margin>
19. **You shall not charge interest to your brother—interest on money, interest on food, or interest on anything that can be lent at interest.**
20. **To a foreigner you may lend at interest, but to your brother you shall not lend at interest: so that the LORD your God may bless you in all that you set your hand to, in the land which you are entering to possess as an inheritance.**

This is a primary scriptural passage against usury <note>The term "usury" here refers to any interest charged on a loan, not just excessive interest.</note>, which certainly, in its very essence, contradicts the law of nature.
It is a shame that people wish to be seen as better than the Jews, and yet in their own religion they do not employ laws as good as those the Jews have.
Does not one brother charge interest to another without shame in Christendom, attempting to justify it by saying that the neighbor makes use of the loan and benefits from it?
It is remarkable, however, that the Latin word for interest, *usura*, takes its name from "using" (*usu*), and thus the very thing people use as a cover for the practice is what is actually meant and forbidden. On the other hand, the Hebrew word <note>original: "neshek"</note> takes its name from "biting" or "gnawing"; therefore, according to the literal meaning, it could be translated: "You shall not gnaw at your brother." For through usury, the wealth of one who does not have much is secretly consumed bit by bit. For this reason, the Hebrew teachers judge that there is also a reminder contained here for those who gladly deal in loans: that they should not allow themselves or their household to be so "gnawed upon."
The distinction people make between different ranks of persons and ways of life has no basis in Scripture; not even in the Old Testament, let alone the New. A **brother** is a brother. The teaching of Scripture is: **Do not turn away from him who wants to borrow from you. Matthew 5:42.** He has entirely forgotten about interest. And lest anyone should say that He does not forbid desiring and taking such things, or seek a loophole in the distinction between an annual percent and actual usury, one should note how He explains Himself in Luke 6:34-35. It is the work of sinners to lend where they hope to receive back. Sinners do this for one another. But you, who wish to be devoted to the Christian religion and call yourselves my disciples, lend expecting nothing in return! That is the law of the New Covenant, and that is what the Christian religion brings with it. To the poor and needy, however, that same religion intends for things not to be merely lent, but rather given.
v. 20. It seems there must be no more brothers left on earth, and religion and religious kinship must be banished, because everyone treats everyone else like a foreigner.
So this is the matter: He who has his bread should not lend in order to have more and become richer; <margin>Sirach 29:32.</margin> and he who cannot easily obtain bread should be given what his necessity requires by the one who has it, without being charged interest. (a) **Shall he give interest, asks Ambrose (b), who has no bread? Is there anything more burdensome? He seeks medicine, and you give him poison: he cries for bread, and you hand him a sword!**
But the usurers—even those who deal in food—and all those who enrich themselves and carry on dishonest gain with grain, victuals, and other things belonging to human necessity, God will judge them; for they are judged very slowly by men and authorities. They, who take their reward now, will find their testing in whatever they stretch their hand toward in the dark land of spirits, where they must eventually go.

<margin>(a) Sirach 29:11-12. Thus, in the entire chapter, the rules of lending are presented so that no one may abuse the love they are owed. v. 5–10.</margin>
<margin>(b) Volume 4. Book on Tobit. Chapter 3.</margin>

<column-break/>

21. **When you make a vow to the LORD your God, you shall not delay to pay it. For the LORD your God will surely require it of you, and it would be a sin in you.**
22. **But if you refrain from vowing, it shall be no sin in you.**
23. **That which has gone out of your lips you shall keep and perform, just as you have voluntarily vowed to the LORD your God, what you have spoken with your own mouth.**
24. **When you go into your neighbor's vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes at your pleasure; but you shall not put any in your vessel.**
<margin>(a) Matthew 12:1. Mark 2:23. Luke 6:1.</margin>
25. **When you go into your neighbor's standing grain, you may pluck the ears with your hand (a); but you shall not move a sickle into your neighbor's standing grain.**

->The<-

Vows were discussed in Leviticus 27:2 and Numbers 30:2. See also Report 1:15 and Ecclesiastes 5:4.
v. 21. <gloss>not delay</gloss> By this they were not necessarily bound to bring a vowed sacrifice immediately; rather, they could—especially those living far from Jerusalem—save this until the next upcoming festival.
v. 22. A person has free will in vowing before they do it; however, a promise creates a debt even here.
v. 23. <gloss>what you have vowed</gloss> Understand, however, that it must be otherwise permitted and within your power.
For in this regard, a great abuse of vows can occur, just as the Jews eventually fell into improper vows, which they nevertheless felt compelled to keep strictly according to the Pharisaic teaching.
<gloss>You shall keep</gloss> So must one also keep what is promised to a neighbor; for such a thing is done as if before God. Therefore, one is all the more bound by justice to that which was promised to him by us or by our ancestors whose property we have inherited. Psalm 15:4.
v. 24. 25. Here, God intended to command generosity and goodwill toward one's neighbor, so that he might enjoy something of ours in moderation for his refreshment, just as the disciples plucked ears of grain when they were hungry: Matthew 12:1. But one should not be shameless and immoderate, taking something home and abusing the act of kindness.
A certain "community of goods" <term>community of goods: the idea of shared resources</term> thus still finds a place at present, but not so far that it might be called theft according to the current laws and the neighbor’s circumstances. "All things are yours," says the law of Christians. But if you claim this in an improper way and in false freedom, it does not apply to you. For the LORD also requires contentment in His own, 1 Timothy 6:8, and does not wish to raise idlers from among them.

The Fifth Book of Moses, Chapter XXIV.

# Chapter XXIV.
->Concerning Divorce and Various Laws of Love.<-

When a man has taken a wife and married her, if it should happen that she finds no favor in his eyes because he has found something shameful in her, let him write her a certificate of divorce, put it in her hand, and send her out of his house:
<margin>Sirach 25:34.</margin>

The custom and practice of the Jews regarding divorce is a misunderstanding of God’s Law, which is based on these four verses. In fact, this practice is reinforced by the common translation, according to which one can hardly understand the words of Moses in any other way than that the Jews were given the power to divorce their wives and cast them out. However, when one properly considers the lawgiver's intent, these four verses are all linked together and, in their full concept, constitute nothing more than a single, continuous principle.

**Something shameful)** This shameful act or thing, which some also translate as an "uncleanness," cannot be adultery; for that had to be punished by death: Chapter 22:22. Nor is it a mere suspicion of such, which had to be tested by the "Water of Jealousy" <note>Referring to the ritual in Numbers 5.</note>. Rather, it may have been her domineering behavior, through which great enmity might arise between them; or also, as the Jews believe, leprosy or another disease that could awaken a physical aversion in the man: a shamefulness of reason, speech, or matter, according to the broad meaning of the word.

From this, however, the Jews took the opportunity to take Moses' words in an even broader sense and to divorce their wives for all sorts of reasons—whether they had a weak intellect, difficult speech, or anything else unpleasant about them. But Moses speaks so obscurely because of the "hardness of the hearts" of the Jews; otherwise, if he had clearly and distinctly indicated the lawful, valid reasons for divorce, nothing more would have been permitted to those hard hearts than what is allowed to us in the New Testament. This would have only increased the evil, and many a wife might even have been murdered. Christ, however, brings the words of Moses back into their proper order and clarity, turns them around, and shows that <term>porneia logos</term> <note>original Greek: "πορνεια λόγος"</note>, "shamefulness of speech or matter," is nothing other than <term>logos porneias</term> <note>original Greek: "λόγος πορνειας"</note>, "a matter of fornication" and whorish shamefulness.

Meanwhile, God nevertheless willed to allow divorce under certain conditions: and indeed, as Christ also explains, for the sake of the hardness of their hearts, so that a greater evil—adultery or even murder—might be prevented; just as the great corruption of the people was also lamented by the prophets. Malachi 2:14, 20.

Christ, however, wished to bring the state of marriage back to its first institution among His believers, who must no longer have such a hard mind; so that among His own, no such divorce should be permitted, unless it be for the sake of adultery.

Whoever, therefore, wishes to take comfort in His grace must simply be obedient to His will according to the first institution, and therefore strive to prevent all ill-will through love and rational conduct, and patiently bear every "cross" of illness or otherwise, seeking to crucify all their lusts, in order to maintain the marriage state in all faithfulness and love until the end of life. See Matthew 5:31, 32; 19:3, etc.

**That he)** These words are indeed expressed by many translators in the imperative, as a commandment or order: "so let him," or "so shall he." But since in verse 3, where these same words appear, they do not translate them as such; for that very reason, the preceding words should not be translated that way either.

If they have lived together, he may take her back to himself,

<column-break/>

2. And if she has departed from his house, and has gone and become the lot of another man:

3. And the latter husband hates her, writes her a certificate of divorce, puts it in her hand, and sends her out of his house; or if the latter husband dies, who took her to be his wife.

4. Then her first husband, who let her go, may not take her again to be his wife after she has been defiled; for such is an abomination before the face of the LORD: so that you do not cause the land to sin, which the LORD your God gives you for an inheritance.

---

**v. 2. And if she has departed from his house)** The very worst kind of divorce may and must still be considered as existing when it remains "stuck inside": that is, when hearts and minds are contrary to one another, yet are obliged and bound by the marriage bond to maintain a physical presence with each other.

This is something that greedy, proud, and ambitious parents should seriously consider in the state of marriage—those who so frequently force their children and relatives into perpetual bonds of "unequal marriages" <note>Mismatched marriages, often forced for status rather than love.</note> and thereby establish a kind of hell on earth, which will never end without God’s great mercy: solely out of vain worldly intentions of wealth or honor; and without any regard for that which one should look to above all things: namely, the fear and love of God, and a Christian upbringing, which are the best dowries; as well as a hidden harmony and agreement of nature, which inclines and moves hearts and minds toward each other and makes them, in a sense, one. And where these are missing—even if there were an abundance of everything else one might wish for—nothing but fire and flames arise from such unequal marriages of those joined together without foundation. This binding together, like "Simoniac foxes," <note>An allusion to the foxes of Samson, but here referring to those who buy their way into marriage for profit (Simony).</note> turns everything into fire. Instead of the constant foundation of love, friendship, and union being laid between persons and families, the greatest breach of love is found, and nothing but discord and disunity is caused. Such marriages are truly never, ever made in heaven!

**v. 3. Certificate of divorce)** This is still in use among the Jews today and is called by them **Get** <note>original Hebrew: "גט"</note>. It must have precisely (no more and no less than) 12 lines, because the word **Get** <note>original: "גט"</note> has the numerical value of 12; however, the Rabbis have added so many ceremonies to it that divorce is very laborious and also expensive, and therefore very rare. (a) 3. E.

No certificate of divorce can be written except where there are two flowing waters with different names: as, for example, in Hamburg the Elbe and the Alster; in Mainz the Rhine and the Main; in Koblenz the Rhine and the Moselle. The reason is: because a separation of marriage is a parting and segregation of the husband from the wife, just as a separation occurs between such two waters.

**v. 4. So can &c.)** That this is the primary purpose of this law is clear from Jeremiah's reference to this text. Jeremiah 3:1.

**Not again)** But if she has not yet belonged to another, and he repents of the divorce.

<meta>catchword: When</meta>

<margin>(a) Buxtorf, *Jewish Synagogue*, ch. 4, p. 642 seq. Selden, *On Hebrew Law*, book 5, ch. 7, p. 589 seq. & *On the Hebrew Wife*, etc.</margin>
