<header>Chapter XXIV. The Fifth Book of Moses.</header>

### 5. When a man has recently taken a wife, he shall not go out with the army, and no burden of any kind shall be laid upon him: he shall be free in his house for one year, that he may gladden his wife whom he has taken.
### 6. No one shall take a mill or an upper millstone as a pledge: for that would be taking a soul as a pledge.

v. 5. That newlyweds should be exempt from all burdens, including military service, for the first year is also stated in Chapter 20:7; this was intended to make the beginning of their marriage joyful (see Proverbs 5:18), so that they might better endure such burdens in the future.

The Lord also spares new Christians from heavy trials and gives them various sweet experiences of knowledge and comfort, so that they may afterwards better bear the Cross, which is the customary burden of Christians. Matthew 11:29-30.

**He shall not go out)** This means not even going as far as the border.

The Hebrews also understand this to apply to those who have already dedicated their house or made their vineyard common <note>Meaning it has reached the year where its fruit can be harvested by the public or the owner</note>, but have not yet completed a full year since doing so; these were not permitted to set a foot outside their door. Others, however, who had not yet brought their wives home, etc., would have had to march as far as the border, according to Chapter 20:5–7.

**Into the army)** This refers to a permitted war undertaken without a special command from God. For in a war expressly commanded by God, no one was exempt—not even the bridegroom in his chamber; everyone had to go forth.

v. 6. Here God commands mercy among His people and gives the example that no one should be deprived of the means of their livelihood. This would happen if someone took a man's tools of his trade as a pledge, thereby disturbing him in obtaining his daily bread.

Hugo <note>original: "(a) ap. Osiand. in comment. ad h. l." — Referring to the scholar Hugo of St. Victor as cited in the commentary by Lucas Osiander on this passage.</note> notes that in the Promised Land, every person had a mill consisting of two millstones in their own house, like a hand-mill, because the land was not well-supplied with rivers. These then are

A beautiful image of marriage, or of husband and wife, as indispensable tools for the maintenance of the family. Job 31:10.

**the soul)** or the life; that is, the means and tool which must serve to maintain his life, and without which he cannot live.

**The upper millstone signifies fear, and the lower signifies hope:** says Gregory <note>Likely referring to Pope Gregory the Great's allegorical interpretations.</note>.

Hope lifts the soul up, yet also puts it in danger. However, so that it does not rise up into presumption, fear is necessary to press it down. But if fear gains the upper hand, it likewise puts the soul in danger. Therefore, hope is necessary so that the soul does not sink into despair. You will walk most safely on the path between hope and fear. Neither of these two can be taken as a pledge without endangering the Christian life, which is the soul of souls. Hope must not be taken away, lest the soul sink into unbelief. Fear must constantly bow hope down and keep it low, lest it rise into pride. Therefore, the Apostle wisely points to a middle way in Romans 11:20 and places the upper millstone upon the lower.

Those who make souls—who are still living in their sins—feel free and secure from all fear, take away the upper millstone, which is the Fear of God. Those who take this from man, making them presumptuous and giving them assurance through flattery for which they are not yet capable, take the soul as a pledge; that is, they rob them of their souls through pleasant and hypocritical preaching. Therefore, the wise man says: Blessed, blessed is the soul that lives always in fear! Namely, so that it may not slip and sin.

<note>(a) See Osiander in his commentary on this place.</note>

<column-break/>

### 7. If anyone is found stealing a soul from among his brothers, from the children of Israel, and treats him as merchandise or sells him: then that thief shall die, that you may put away the evil from your midst.
### 8. Take heed in the plague of leprosy, that you carefully observe and do according to all that the priests, the Levites, shall teach you: as I have commanded them, so you shall observe and do.
### 9. Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the way as you came out of Egypt.
### 10. When you lend your neighbor any kind of debt, you shall not go into his house to seize a pledge from him.
### 11. You shall stand outside, and the man to whom you have lent shall bring the pledge out to you.

v. 7. **Who steals a soul)** This can also include those who seek to rob people of their noble freedom, under whatever appearance it may be, and then sell them again to others, making a profit and a trade out of human souls. This is not much better than the slave trade of the barbarians, who first snatch people away and rob them of their freedom; God will certainly punish this with eternal death. But

Oh, what shall one say of such "soul-thieves" who conduct business, profit, and commerce with the souls of their brothers and fellow believers, and even sell them into the slavery of the Devil! All of Scripture is full of this, even unto Revelation 18:13, John 10:1, 8, 10.

May God Himself root out this unheard-of trade and check the evil on this earth through the death of the "Old Man" <note>A theological term for the sinful human nature.</note> who orchestrates all this mischief!

v. 8. **that you carefully observe)** and take exact notice of the laws which are to be read in Leviticus 13 and 14.

They were to take care that they did not give themselves over to disobedience so much that they would refuse to be quarantined or undergo the proper cleansing;

v. 9. And also that they should not sin through disobedience against those in authority, and thus easily be punished with leprosy, as happened to Miriam. Numbers 12:1, 14.

In the same way, Christians should have watched over disobedient and vice-ridden souls, being diligent to remove such people from among them, so that the whole lump of dough might not be leavened by the sour leaven—as has now, alas, happened. 1 Corinthians 5:2, 6, 13.

v. 10. 11. If the law of the Old Covenant already required gentleness and fairness toward one's neighbor—that one should not take security for a debt to the neighbor's detriment, such that his basic needs are taken away—what then shall be said of the violent "executions" <note>In this context, *Executionen* refers to the legal seizure of property to pay debts.</note> among Christians? Where people break into houses and take away necessary things as a pledge, sometimes tearing out the stoves and the like, so that the neighbor is forced by violence and plunged into misery. These are the ones who so violently leap over the thresholds and boundaries of houses and goods to fill their own and their masters' houses and barns with robbery and deceit. Zephaniah 1:9.

12. **But if he is a needy man,** you shall not lie down to sleep with his pledge. <margin>Exodus 22:26, 27.</margin>
13. **You shall certainly give him back the pledge** when the sun goes down, so that he may lie down in his own garment and bless you: and it shall be reckoned to you as righteousness before the face of the LORD your God.

<margin>v. 12. Shall [not] with his pledge)</margin> which he cannot easily do without <note>This typically refers to a cloak or garment used as collateral, which the poor man would also need as a blanket at night.</note>,
<margin>Not lie down)</margin> do not let it rest with you or keep it overnight.
<margin>v. 13. Become righteousness)</margin> it will be recognized, accepted, and rewarded by God as a righteous work of mercy.
<margin>v. 14. Not exploit)</margin> to deceive, to shorten his wages, to withhold much from his hard labor, and furthermore to make him wait a long time for payment.
<margin>v. 15. On his day)</margin> on which he earned it,
**Give)** do not postpone it, as those who are careless, frivolous, greedy, and unmerciful toward their neighbors are accustomed to do.
**Lest he cry against you to the LORD)** Who is still above you, and who may accuse you of an injustice before God.
It must truly be a great sin, indeed a genuine cruelty and horrific unmercifulness before God, when people are made to run and wait so long—those to whom one owes wages for labor—especially when one has the means, or could have enough if one managed the household properly and the income is counted in the thousands. Indeed, it is counted among the sins that cry out to heaven when one withholds, diminishes, or turns to nothing that which is legally due to workers or others who have little and must earn their bread for themselves and their families with bitter sweat—especially when those doing the withholding do not find their own livelihood difficult to obtain. Go and read how the Spirit addresses the rich and powerful in James 5:4.
**Believe certainly,** everything you do for the poor, all your alms, are not only in vain and for nothing, but truly contrary to God, if you do not even give a penny of your own before you have paid all your debts, especially what has been earned through bitter labor! Rule yourself accordingly.
Furthermore, since the customary services of subjects <note>Refers to "corvée" or feudal labor obligations (Frondienst) common in the 17th century.</note> do not receive a daily wage, but only some refreshment; such services should also be moderately arranged, so that the subjects are not forced by excessive burdens to cry out to the Lord, which might then result in a great debt of sin for the authorities: whose lands should not be houses of bondage like Egypt, but realms of Christ, in which the freedom of the children of God is proclaimed—which in the present time can still coexist with the enduring of some physical and tolerable servitude. See Matthew 17:24 etc. and Job 31:39, 40.

16. **Fathers shall not be put to death for the children,** and children shall not be put to death for the fathers <gloss>(a)</gloss>: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.
<margin>(a) 2 Chronicles 25:4.</margin>
17. **You shall not pervert the justice due to a stranger <gloss>(a)</gloss>** and an orphan, and you shall not take a widow’s garment as a pledge. <margin>(a) Exodus 22:21, etc. 23:9. Leviticus 19:33.</margin>
18. **For you shall remember that you were a servant in Egypt,** and the LORD your God redeemed you from there: Therefore I command you to do such a thing. <margin>ch. 16:12.</margin>
19. **When you reap your harvest in your field,** and have forgotten a sheaf in the field: you shall not turn back to fetch it; it shall be for the stranger, for the orphan, and for the widow: so that the LORD your God may bless you in every work of your hands.
20. **When you have shaken your olive tree, <gloss>(a)</gloss>** you shall not search through the branches after you: it shall be for the stranger, for the orphan, and for the widow. <margin>(a) Isaiah 17:6. 24:13.</margin>

<margin>v. 16. Fathers shall not be put to death for the children)</margin> when the children alone, and not also the parents, have deserved death.
See an example of this in Numbers 26:11, 2 Kings 14:6, and also its further explanation in Jeremiah 31:29, 30 and Ezekiel 18:20.
<margin>Children not for the fathers)</margin> But when God also visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, that has its holy and just reasons, as both parents and children are sinners before Him and subject to His judgment. Exodus 20:5, Joshua 7:24.
<margin>Put to death)</margin> Specifically here, by the verdict of a judge.
<margin>For his own sin)</margin> Not for the sin of another. But if you make yourself a partaker of another’s sin, then it becomes your own.
<margin>v. 17.</margin> The LORD wants the rights of a stranger to be upheld so strictly that He wants them treated the same as widows and orphans. Indeed,
<margin>v. 18.</margin> a reason and cause is given for this which has its primary and sole regard for strangers: because the Israelites were also strangers in Egypt.
<margin>v. 19.</margin> Since the LORD so often reminds us of generosity toward these people, He wants to show how we should often be mindful of our own state—we who are also only poor, miserable pilgrims before Him, who momentarily stand in need of His merciful goodness. Psalm 39:13, Hebrews 11:13.
<margin>Forgotten)</margin> The greedy have a poor memory in this regard.
<margin>v. 20. For the stranger, orphan, and widow)</margin> From the fullness of the God of Israel, in the latter days, the strangers among the Gentiles shall also eat, and the widows and orphans shall be made partakers of His eternal good. Jeremiah 49:11.

## Chapter XXV.
### Laws of outward justice, and the command for the destruction of the Amalekites.

1. **If there be a dispute** between men, they shall come before the court, and they shall judge them; and they shall justify the righteous and condemn the wicked.

2. **And it shall happen,** if the wicked man has deserved to be beaten, the judge shall command him to fall down and have him beaten before his face,

<gloss>
**v. 1. If there be a dispute, they shall [come] before the court)** This will no longer be necessary when "righteousness and peace kiss each other" <note>A reference to Psalm 85:10, often interpreted as a prophecy of a messianic age of perfect justice.</note>, when the law is written in the hearts of the nations, and every person does to another what they wish for themselves.
**Justify the righteous and condemn the wicked)** This is the duty of the judge in both spiritual and worldly matters. For the office of judge is a "character of God," who by virtue of His holiness cannot judge otherwise. However, one often hears divine justice lamenting that the righteous are condemned and the wicked absolved—indeed, that injustice is declared right. Thus, the character of God is turned into a character of the Devil.
**v. 2. Have him beaten)** According to the hard-hearted nature of these people of the Old Testament, God also imposed on them such servant-like lashings. With these, all crimes of brawling and similar vices—which were not punishable by death or another set penalty—were punished before the judges (as the Jews believe, and not publicly). The wrongdoers were to be lashed, more or less according to the measure of the crime, as if with a fatherly rod. And so that they might not be accused of cruelty or miscount the blows, they usually gave one stroke less—namely 39—as Paul testifies of himself having received such five times. <margin>2 Corinthians 11:24.</margin>
This was the heaviest punishment next to capital punishment, which proceeded briefly as follows: When a man or woman was sentenced to scourging, both hands were fastened to a low pillar, about one and a half cubits high, one hand on each side of the pillar, so that the person stood. The court attendant <term>Schul-diener: a synagogue or court official responsible for administering lashes</term> would take the person's garment and bare the chest, without much concern if the clothing tore.
Behind the person lay a stone, upon which the attendant stood, holding a scourge <term>Karbatsche: a heavy whip, often of leather</term> in his hand, which was made of ox-hide with different strands and had two knots. The handle was a palm’s width, as were the strands. When one blow landed on the chest, two landed on the shoulders. While he struck, one of the judges read aloud from Deuteronomy 28:58–59, then from chapter 29:9, and concluded with Psalm 78:38. If the scourging was not yet finished, the judge repeated the verses anew.
Another judge counted the blows, and the third constantly called out to the attendant: "Whip him!"
</gloss>

22. **And you shall remember** that you were a servant in the land of Egypt: therefore I command you to do such a thing.

<gloss>
**That you — were in the land of Egypt)** a stranger, poor and needy.
**That you do)** As you wished in the land of Egypt that others might act and be minded toward you.
This law of charity was also discussed regarding Leviticus 19:9–10.

according to what shall be sufficient for his wickedness, by number.

3. **If he has him beaten forty times,** he shall not do it further: lest, perhaps, if he were beaten further with many blows, your brother should become loathsome before your eyes.

4. **You shall not muzzle an ox** when it threshes.

5. **If**

<gloss>
**By number)** Strength was also taken into account, as to how much one could endure. They preferred the number three in their counting, so that they assigned a number that could always be multiplied or divided by 3: e.g., 18, 24, 30.
**v. 3. Forty times)** Thirteen on the chest, 26 on both shoulders, and the 40th between the shoulders, as some claim. Mostly, however, it remained at 39, because 3 stripes always occurred in one blow, so 13 times exactly made 39. If this number was assigned to someone, and it was seen that they could not endure that many without danger to their life, they were spared.
If the attendant gave a person one blow more than he should, and the person died from it, the attendant had to flee to one of the cities of refuge as an accidental manslayer.
**No further)** But certainly fewer. For:
Exactly 40 strokes are not commanded, but only that the blows should not exceed the number forty, even if one wanted to set the punishment at its highest.
The time of chastisement and humiliation shall not exceed the number forty, which is its number. Christ therefore fasted for 40 days; and the people were in the wilderness for that many years. Our body is composed of 4 elements, each of which must be humbled and kept in check through the number ten.
**v. 4. When it threshes)** The ancient Romans, and before them the Greeks and Jews, did not beat their grain out of the ears in enclosed barns with threshing flails; rather, they sought out the highest place near their fields, which they called the threshing floor <term>Tenne: an outdoor leveling for processing grain</term>. Upon this, they laid the cut fruit in a circle and turned it so that it became dry. Afterward, they had it trodden out by horses or oxen harnessed to a yoke: and it seems that they harnessed such oxen before certain threshing sledges <term>Egen: heavy frames used to break stalks</term>, and thus had the fruit threshed out by the oxen and the sledges. See 2 Samuel 24:22, Isaiah 28:27–28.
Since one should allow the oxen their fodder during their work, the Apostle <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul</note> applies this much more to teachers who "tread out the grain," bringing the spirit out from the letter and separating the pure grain from the chaff. They must also be constantly occupied with admonishing and punishing to separate the chaff of earthly-mindedness and vanity from their listeners, and to promote the production of the fruits of righteousness. 1 Corinthians 9:9, 1 Timothy 5:18. And thus the prophet Isaiah (21:10) also calls the people his "threshing floor" upon which he threshes—namely, to whom he proclaims what he has heard from the LORD.
</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral statutes of Deuteronomy, specifically addressing the Levirate marriage (the duty of a brother-in-law to his deceased brother's widow) and the symbolic rituals associated with refusing this duty. It shifts from the general justice mentioned on the previous page to specific familial obligations intended to preserve the lineages of Israel.</meta>

<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XXV.</header>

### 5. When brothers dwell together, and one of them dies and has no child, the wife of the deceased shall not marry a stranger outside the family; her brother-in-law shall go in to her and take her as his wife, and marry her as a brother-in-law. <note>This practice, known as Levirate marriage (from the Latin 'levir' meaning brother-in-law), ensured that a man’s name and property remained within his family tribe.</note>

### 6. And it shall be that the firstborn whom she bears shall stand in the name of his deceased brother, so that his name is not blotted out from Israel.

This law was already in practice among the first fathers, or the so-called Patriarchs of the Jews, as can be seen with the sons of Judah in Genesis 38:8. This surely did not happen without divine inspiration, so that the family of the children of God would not be defiled by marriage with foreigners and strangers. However, God also intended through this law to provide that the families among the Jews would not be mixed, but each preserved separately. This was so that the Messiah could be better recognized, who was to be born from the otherwise completely fallen and despised lineage of David. This lineage was maintained in public knowledge—not least (though it may have happened before) according to this law—after the heiresses were required to marry their closest kinsmen. See more on this in the notes on Numbers 36 at the end.

**v. 5. Her brother-in-law shall take her)** The High Priest was exempted from this, because he was not permitted to marry a widow (Leviticus 21:14). But when he died, his closest friend <note>original: "nächster Freund," meaning the nearest kinsman or 'goel'.</note> could marry the widow left behind.

But when no brothers were present, the nearest kinsman had to marry the widow, as is seen in the history of Ruth. There, the lineage of Nahshon and Salmon, from whom Elimelech may have descended, was preserved through Boaz, from whom Christ was to be born. See Ruth 3 and 4; Matthew 22:25–26.

**v. 6. Shall stand in the name of the deceased)** He shall be regarded as his son and enter into all his rights and inheritance.

The name of the Lord must be awakened upon His inheritance. His people must be called by His name. They are His inheritance and His bride, who is nonetheless barren and bears Him no children in the days of His flesh. But His Apostles—whom He calls His brothers in John 20:17—awaken a seed for their brother after He has died through the imperishable seed of the Word of God. Thereby they raise their brother’s name upon His inheritance, the Church or Congregation, which is called not after their names, but after the name of their brother (Acts 11:26).

From this, one can already recognize where the spirit of this law aims.

The ministers of the Word should awaken the name of Christ upon His inheritance, not exalt their own names. Otherwise, they are false brothers. <meta>catchword: And</meta>

How does it happen then, that such a large part of Christendom today names itself after human names? Why do people seek to cling to this or that church, this or that teacher, and try to bring or keep people in the society of specific churches? For one should rather strive to establish Christ's Church universally, and to be called and truly be Christians.

Even if a faithful servant of Christ works in a congregation and his testimony does not yet seem to bring forth seed, his successor in office is bound to faithfully carry that testimony of truth further. Thus, he awakens a seed for his predecessor; otherwise, he will face great accountability before the Lord and might carry away eternal shame.

<column-break/>

### 7. But if it does not please the man to take his sister-in-law, then his sister-in-law shall go up to the gate to the elders and say: My brother-in-law refuses to raise up a name for his brother in Israel; he will not marry me as a brother-in-law.

<margin>Ruth 4:5, 20.</margin>
### 8. Then the elders of his city shall call him and speak to him. If he then persists and says: It does not please me to take her:

### 9. Then his sister-in-law shall approach him before the eyes of the elders, and pull his shoe off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall testify and say: So shall it be done to the man who will not build up his brother’s house.

### 10. And his name shall be called in Israel: The house of him who had his shoe pulled off.

### 11. <meta>catchword: Whe-</meta>

**v. 7. My brother-in-law refuses)** to comply with the divine ordinance, and cares nothing for whether his brother’s memory shall vanish in Israel.

**v. 8. Speak to him)** present the matter to him and remind him of the law, and counsel him as much as they can to submit.

**v. 9. Pull his shoe off his foot)** as a sign that he has lost the right to enter into his brother’s inheritance. <note>In ancient legal symbolic language, the shoe represented the right to walk upon and claim land.</note>

**Spit in his face)** There has never been a nation provided with so many commands for polite interaction and good manners, or one that could show more examples of refined people of both sexes, than Israel—whether one means the people of the Old Covenant or the spiritual Israel. Because of this, some must doubt whether this [spitting] is to be taken literally, or whether such a display would have been unseemly for an Israelite woman, or inconsistent with other holy laws, or fitting before God, the most holy lawgiver.

Spittle is a foul discharge; and to be spat upon, especially in the face, and that with full intent, and moreover by a woman, is a great insult and disgrace (Isaiah 50:6). Indeed, it is a sign of the highest low-esteem and contempt. It is therefore not considered probable that God commanded something of this kind, whereby the man would have become contemptible in the eyes of the woman—especially since she had wished to submit to him as her lord.

Therefore, although the words may be translated literally, as they are in Numbers 12:14—where it is important to note the great difference, as that speaks of a father against his child (a superior toward a subordinate)—yet the same idiom may be given as "in his presence" or "before him." Just as in Leviticus 11:25 and 4:37 this same word is placed with "his face," one can understand it here in the same way to avoid these difficulties, just as the Jewish Bible has it. And the learned Jews understood it exactly so: she shall spit on the earth before him.

Furthermore, in the following **v. 10**, the brand of shame upon such a man and his house is placed in the naming of the "shoe-pulling" as the greatest dishonor. Yet it would certainly be more shameful to be called "The house of him who was spat in the face."

The commentary emphasizes the spiritual application for Christian ministers and argues for a more dignified interpretation of the spitting ritual.</summary>

12. Then you shall cut off her hand; your eye shall not pity her.

13. You shall not have in your bag two kinds of weights, large and small.

<margin>Leviticus 19:36</margin>
15. You shall have a full and just weight; a full and just ephah you shall have: so that your days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD your God will give you.

<column-break/>

16. For whoever does such things is an abomination to the LORD your God, everyone who acts unjustly.

17. Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you came out of Egypt!

18. How he met you on the way, and struck down all the weak ones among your rear guard who lagged behind you, when you were weary and faint; and he did not fear God.

19. And it shall come to pass, when the LORD your God has given you rest from all your enemies round about, in the land which the LORD your God will give you as an inheritance to possess as a heritage: then you shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven; you shall not forget it.

<meta>Catchword: The</meta>

---

v. 11. The Lord’s intent here is that nothing should be undertaken among His people that runs contrary to outward modesty, and that they should apply themselves to all discipline and honorability in everything. 
Since we also—according to the remarkable naming found here—have right to be ashamed of our sinful conception and birth, there is no better remedy than to turn to Christ's pure and holy conception and birth, so that through faith in Him, our own may be purified. And 
The believers of the New Testament have particular reason to consider how God has especially given them the spirit of discipline <note>original: "Geist der Zucht"</note>, 2 Timothy 1:7, according to whose impulse we should conduct ourselves chastely and modestly in all thoughts, words, and deeds. 
Since discipline and modesty are especially fitting for the female sex (Proverbs 11:22), God therefore wished to punish such immodesty—whereby a woman, out of sudden anger <note>original: "jrrzorn"</note>, could have caused a man great harm—with such a sharp penalty, in order to deter others from such a shameless act.

v. 12. **Shall cut off the hand**) that which acted offensively, and also pluck out **your eye**) that which wishes to offend you and overlook the sin: and thus 
**Not pity**) by remitting the punishment, should she or someone else plead for her, or for any other motivating reasons.

v. 13. **In your bag**) In ancient times, people kept weights in small pouches.

v. 14. **Not two kinds**) Neither should you carry "two kinds of speech" in your mouth, as the modern world is accustomed to doing—even under the name of Christianity—and is masterfully trained to perform. 
Words in conversation with one another testify of nothing but friendship and readiness to serve: but if one looks at the manner in which most people interact (especially behind one's back), one realizes that one must always understand the opposite of what the words mean in their proper sense. Alas, 
The simplicity of the first Christians is gone; love is dead; the art of disguise has taken over false hearts. Nowadays, one must guard oneself against no one so much as those who behave in the most friendly and loving manner.

v. 15. **So that your days may be lengthened**) and that you may also attain a right and full measure of them.

<column-break/>

v. 16. **Whoever does such things**) dealing with deceit, is a great abomination before God, because man thereby completely sets aside the fear of God, who desires justice to be maintained among men, without which no love can exist. See Proverbs 20:10 and the note on Leviticus 19:35. Likewise 1 Thessalonians 4:6.

v. 17. The Amalekites were descendants of Esau (Genesis 36:12) and therefore held a rightful hereditary hatred against the descendants of Jacob. They sought to exercise this during their journey to the land of Canaan in a treacherous manner—which is not mentioned in the history of this war in Exodus 17:8 etc., but is reported here: just as they were also the first among the heathens to rise up against Israel. 
However, in a prophetic sense, they also represent the enemies of the Church in the last times, and according to the spirit, the clinging evil lusts and desires in the flesh, acting as the "secret grasshoppers" <note>a wordplay on a possible etymology of the name Amalek</note> according to the meaning of the word.

v. 18. This is the spiritual Amalek, who hinders the people from entering the land of holiness to God. Namely: the earthly, fleshly spirits, desires, and temptations that cling to fleeting things and ambush us on our spiritual pilgrimage; especially those who are weakest, who fall behind in their work, and come too close to the earthly spirit. 
Therefore we must not become weary or faint, lest we remain behind and be seized and struck by our spiritual enemies along with the limping, lame, and weary Israelites who stayed behind. Hebrews 12:12–15. Everyone must seek to be the first and foremost, and like John, seek to run ahead to the grave of Christ: otherwise, one does not obtain the prize. Luke 13:24.

v. 19. **You shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven**) As a just retribution for such a malicious and false disposition toward their relatives according to the flesh: which, however, was only put into effect over 400 years later by Saul (1 Samuel 15:2–3) and continued thereafter (1 Chronicles 4:43; Esther 3:1, etc., compared with 1 Samuel 15:9, as Haman descended from the Amalekites). 
So will God root out the memory of those who lay hands upon His weak children—the Israel of God—who long for the promised Canaan of the glorious kingdom of Christ, and who seek to harm them. 
But where does that leave the Jewish slaughterers <note>original: "Megger," likely referring to ritual slaughterers</note>? Of whom it is said in the Talmud (a): The best slaughterer is the companion of Amalek. 
<note>(a) Tractate Kiddushin folio 82, column 1.</note>

<header>The Fifth Book of Moses, Ch. XXVI.</header>

# Chapter XXVI.

->Concerning the firstfruits and tithes, along with a description of the covenant.<-

And it shall come to pass, when you come into the land that the LORD your God will give you for an inheritance, and you possess it and dwell therein:
2. That you shall take of the first of all the fruits of the land, which you shall bring from your land that the LORD your God gives you, and shall put them in a basket, and go to the place which the LORD your God will choose, to make his name dwell there.

The firstfruits spoken of here—and also in Exodus 23:19, 34:26, and Ezekiel 44:30—which were ordained for the maintenance of the priests, and which were discussed in Numbers 18:11–12, must not be confused (a) with the other firstfruits that had to be offered to the LORD as described in Leviticus 23:10 etc., as they are quite distinct from them.

v. 2. **Of all the fruits of the land**) The Hebrews interpret this as seven types of fruits, and they all agree on this (b): namely wheat, barley, figs, pomegranates, olives, grapes, and dates. See Chapter 8, verse 8.

**Which you shall bring**) No one was permitted to eat of the harvest until these firstfruits had been brought and thanks had been given to God.

However, this could not happen before Pentecost, nor after the Feast of Dedication <note>The Feast of Dedication is Hanukkah, occurring in winter.</note>.

The delivery of these fruits was carried out with great solemnity and magnificence, some of which ceremonies are mentioned in the text and explicitly ordained.

When a head of a household went out into his field and saw a fig, or a cluster of grapes, or a pomegranate, or any other of the seven fruits emerging, he would tie a band around it and say: "These shall be the firstfruits." When it was time to bring these set-aside firstfruits to the house of the LORD, all the inhabitants of all the towns in each province would gather, each with his firstfruits.

**In a basket**) Wealthy, high-ranking, and noble people took beautiful, costly baskets, decorated and interwoven with gold and silver.

**Go there**) They all met in the principal city of that province. They stayed there overnight in the streets and did not enter any houses, so that they might not perhaps be made <term>unclean</term> <note>referring to ritual impurity (ritual impurity) which would prevent them from entering the Temple</note>.

As soon as day broke, the one chosen as their leader called out: "Arise! And let us travel to Zion, to the house of the LORD our God!" Whereupon they all set out on their way. Before them went a young ox whose horns were overlaid with gold and whose head was decorated with an olive wreath; this ox was intended for a <term>thank-offering</term> for the whole company. Throughout the entire journey, the <term>shawm</term> <note>a woodwind instrument, a precursor to the oboe</note> was played until they reached Jerusalem. When they were near, they sent messengers ahead to announce their arrival. Meanwhile, they adorned their baskets and put everything in order. Then the most noble of the city of Jerusalem, as well as the treasurers of the Temple, came out of the city to meet them and led them into Jerusalem. At their entry, everyone became active and called out to them: "Welcome, dear brothers and citizens of the city of [N.]!" The shawm was played continuously until they reached the Temple. As soon as they arrived there, everyone took his basket on his shoulder, even the king himself (for one sought honor in this rather than being ashamed of it), and כך went further into the Temple, toward the Court of Israel. When they entered, the Levites began to sing Psalm 30:1.

(a) as written by Varenius in *The Sacred Clover* <note>original Latin: "trifol. sacr." refers to August Varenius’s "Trifolium sacrum"</note>, chapter 3 and following.
(b) according to Lund in *Jewish Antiquities* <note>original: "Lund. Jüd. Heil." refers to Johann Lund's 'Die Alten Jüdischen Heiligthümer'</note>, Book 3, Chapter 54, number 3.

<column-break/>

3. And you shall come to the priest who shall be in those days, and say to him: I declare today to the LORD your God that I have come into the land which the LORD swore to our fathers to give us.
4. And the priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it down before the altar of the LORD your God.
5. Then you shall testify and say before the face of the LORD your God: My father was a wandering Syrian (a), and he went down into Egypt and stayed there as a stranger with few people, and there became a great, mighty, and numerous nation. (a) Genesis 28:5.

v. 3. Thereupon, one after another stepped up to the priests standing there. First, they gave the pigeons that they had hanging from the baskets for a burnt offering, and those they carried in their hands they gave to the priests as a gift, and said what God commanded to be said here: wherein they first acknowledge the fulfillment of God’s promise and thus present themselves as God's vassals and <term>tenants</term> <note>acknowledging God as the true owner of the land</note>.

v. 4. Whereupon each one took his basket down from his shoulder and held it by the rim; then the priest placed his hand under the basket, and they both <term>waved</term> the basket with fruit before the LORD. Then the priest set the basket down by the altar and asked the one who brought it why he had brought this.

v. 5. Here now, as some of the Hebrews report, the other should first have answered:

**My father was a wandering Syrian**) Or according to Luther's translation, though somewhat changed: "A Syrian was destroying my father" <note>original: "Ein Syrer war meinen Vater verlorgend"</note>. Thus, the Syrian would have to be understood as Laban. But according to the other translation, Jacob is called a Syrian because he stayed for 20 years in Syria (Mesopotamia), had a Syrian mother, fathered 11 sons in Syria, and also had his wives and most of his servants from Syria. Likewise, he was poor and miserable when he served Laban. However, one prefers to focus on the purpose, which is the same in both translations.

Moses teaches the people of Israel to lay their foundation low in deep humility, and how they should confess not only their own misery but also that of their father, just as the fathers, Abraham and Jacob, had also done. Genesis 15:27 <note>likely intended as 18:27</note>, 32:10.

The fruits that sprout from the deep root of humility are most pleasing to our God.

For us, this ordinance should teach how we ought to offer up to the LORD primarily our "firstfruits"—that is, our spirit—which is the most noble and excellent part of us, so that we begin to be a rational creature as soon as the LORD creates the spirit within our inner being even in the mother's womb. Zechariah 12:1. In doing so, we should recognize our miserable state by nature, how we were children of sin and transgression and children of wrath, finding ourselves of Gentile descent, whom God has allowed to be redeemed through Christ from the slavery of Satan and sin; therefore, we are indeed obligated to offer ourselves entirely to the LORD with spirit, soul, and body. Romans 12:1, 1 Corinthians 6:20.

v. 6. **Treated us badly and afflicted us**) Philo reports <note>Philo of Alexandria was a Jewish philosopher who often provided historical and allegorical context for the Pentateuch.</note> that the Hebrews were forced to wear different clothes than the Egyptians as a mark of shame so they could be identified, and that they were eventually tormented with beatings, labor, and hunger unto death; they were also cast out of the cities, and it was not permitted for them to bury their own, nor even to mourn or weep for them.
v. 7. **Looked upon**) Not our merit or worthiness, but [etc...]
v. 8. **With a mighty hand**) Through a visible and majestic demonstration of his power.
**With great terror**) Which also fell upon the neighboring peoples.
v. 9. **Brought us in**) This is always God's purpose: to bring us inward <note>A common mystical theme: the physical "inward" journey into the land represents the soul's "inward" journey to God.</note>, for that is where the best land is.
v. 10. **Of the land which you have given me**) Whether this be on this side or the other side of the Jordan. Some Hebrews conclude—though without sufficient reason—from the preceding words that those living on the other side of the Jordan were not obligated to bring firstfruits. (a) <note>original: "ap. Lightfoot. decad. chorogr. Marc. præm. c. 2. §. 5." This refers to John Lightfoot, a 17th-century Hebraist.</note>
v. 11. During this solemnity, they did not rush home immediately, but remained joyful and in good spirits throughout the day, consuming their thank-offering with joy, which was previously offered while the Levites sang and the priests blew trumpets; they also stayed overnight in Jerusalem.

<column-break/>

v. 12. **All the tithes**) Of which there were different kinds. (Leviticus 27:30). One belonged to the Levites as their income. (Numbers 18:21, 24, 31). The second had to be consumed in Jerusalem. (Deuteronomy 12:6–7, 11–12, 17–18; 14:22–23; 26:11, 14). The third, occurring every third year from the Year of Release, had to be distributed at home among the Levites, strangers, widows, and orphans (Chapter 14:28–29), which is primarily what is being discussed here.
**In the 3rd year**) It is said that no firstfruits were given then. Instead, it was uniquely
**A Year of Tithing**) in which the most tithes fell due, and, as some believe, not just a double but even a triple tithe had to be given, whereas in other years only two were required.
v. 13. **Shall say before the face of the LORD**) This confession had to take place on the last day of the Passover feast, when nothing more was to be found in their houses that should have been paid out, and they had to testify before God that they had correctly distributed the tithes, and had not deceitfully withheld anything, nor used it for any unauthorized purpose.
**I have... the sacred portion**) referring to the third tithe.
**Removed from my house**) and kept none of it inside.
v. 14. **In my mourning**) Meaning if I became unclean through a dead person and went into mourning.
**Removed nothing while unclean**) but rather took good care and guarded it so that it did not become unclean, if, for example, someone died in my house. (Numbers 19:14–15).
**Nothing given for a dead person**) or spent any of it on a funeral feast (Jeremiah 16:7; Tobit 4:18) <note>original: "Erbmähl"</note>; or purchased anything for a burial.

These tithes should teach us in the New Testament how we must specifically bring and sacrifice our will to the Lord. For just as the number ten is something secret—where the 1 is combined with the 0 (the significant number with that which is a naught or nothing) to signify something real or certain—so, when a person is united with God, then "nothingness" (2 Corinthians 12:11) comes to its true essence and becomes something glorious and great. Just as 10 (ten), 100 (one hundred), 1000 (one thousand), and so on, is something large; and indeed, the more zeros there are, the greater the sum: that is, the more a person annihilates themselves here, the greater they become. This union now happens through the surrender of our will to God.

<header>The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XXVI.</header>

### 15. Look down from your holy habitation, from heaven (a) / and bless your people Israel and the land that you have given us / just as you swore to our fathers / a land flowing with milk and honey. <margin>(a) Isaiah 53:16. <note>original: "Esa. 53/16"; this is likely a scribal error for Isaiah 63:15, which matches the text "Look down from heaven and see from your holy and glorious habitation."</note></margin>

### 16. This day the LORD your God commands you / to perform these statutes and judgments / that you may keep and do them with all your heart and with all your soul.

### 17. You have caused the LORD to say today / that he has become a God to you / and that you have walked in his ways / and kept his statutes and his commandments and his judgments / and have obeyed his voice.

### 18. And the LORD has today caused you to say / that you have become a people of his own possession / just as he had spoken to you / and that you have kept all his commandments:

### 19. And that he has made you the highest over all nations / which he has made / for praise and for a name and for an honor; and that you have become a holy people to the Lord your God / just as he had spoken.

Solomon speaks of these two surrenders of the spirit (or understanding) and the will: "My son, give me your heart"; those are the firstfruits of the spirit: "and let your eyes delight in my ways"; those are the tithes of the will. Proverbs 23:26.

Whoever is faithful in this will also be faithful in earthly goods, according to the opening of his soul, with his physical wealth—partly for the support of the poor, and partly for those things that serve the expansion of the Kingdom of Christ, to be excluded: see Proverbs 3:9-10, where the blessing of God will flow back to him as it is promised there.

---

<column-break/>

v. 15. **Look down**) through a constant influence of your grace / from the loftiness of your glory / into the deep lowliness of the poverty of your creature and your people: upon whom God's special oversight / in gracious government / arrangement / provision and preservation / is directed. But it would be a childish lack of understanding and coarse blindness / if we wanted to make for ourselves a coarse physical concept / as of God / who is a pure spirit / and of the "looking down" / so also of his holy and glorious habitation and

**From heaven**) Where God is / there is his heaven: and since God is a spirit and is everywhere / so must his heaven also be spiritual and everywhere. But where he is / there is "above." On the one hand, God dwells within himself / and is thus to that extent his own uncreated heaven. But if we also wish to understand something created by this / then this is the mystery. God as the Center is the innermost part / and also the highest over all. His heaven or habitation is nothing other than a pure, lovely, and refreshing outflow from himself. But the circumference or the circle of visible matter must necessarily be the outermost / and thus also the lowest / because it is the furthest from the spiritual essence of God / the <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centro"</note> / while the nearest is the aforementioned pure outflow: which highest or uppermost heaven can then be nothing other than a pure, simple, and fiery clarity / which according to its nature and essence is always quiet and unmoved / transparent and bright / an immovable source of all temporal things / and the physical kingdom of God and all the saints / the palace and throne of the divine majesty / in which God lives and reigns with all his friendship and household: but he himself is above all heavens and over everything that is: nevertheless / he is also in all heavens / yes, in the whole world and in all creatures / which he governs and orders according to his will; but especially in this highest heaven / which he fills with his glory.

v. 16. On the occasion of paying their due physical duties, every master of the house had to, as it were, renew the covenant with God for himself and his family: wherein they should first represent to themselves the ground upon which this covenant stands; namely, in obedience to all the commandments of God / which partly concerned their sanctification / and partly the prefiguration of the goods of grace in Christ / which were contained in so many kinds of external ordinances / like the kernel within its shell.

v. 17. Thereafter the Lord announces his confirmation / which he hereby confirmed to them upon their witnessed obedience: that they have caused him to say / that he will be their God; wherein everything / that a human may wish for according to body and soul in time and eternity / is also contained, alongside God's requirement / that they must henceforth persevere in such obedience toward all his commandments.

<column-break/>

v. 18. Against which, then, the people's mutual pledge and promise is announced / how it was so effected in their souls by the grace of God / and not by their natural powers / that the Lord let them say / and thereto pledge and promise / that they would conduct themselves as his own special people in obedience to all his commandments:

v. 19. And that they, in turn, should receive power and <term>boldness</term> <note>original: "Freymüthigkeit"; refers to the spiritual liberty and confidence of a believer before God.</note> / to consider themselves children of God / John 1:12. who would be the highest people before all and to the glory of God; whom God would then also protect and crown with all grace as his holy people. Wherein the nature of the Covenant of Grace is presented very mysteriously. Man must confirm God’s promise through his consent and acceptance of God and his will: and so he, as it were, makes God say and promise his grace to him anew. But God himself originally worked this very consent in the will / and allowed the human to say such a thing. Thus all good gifts are from God / and yet also primarily require our acceptance / since God offers the same to all without distinction; see Psalm 81:11.

Now, at the 7th Trumpet, this covenant will especially go into its full power / and the Israel of God / both the whole host of the firstborn of the Lamb in the upper church / as well as the host of believers in the lower church / will truly be the highest people / because all nations must come under the scepter of Jerusalem.

Today he elevates his people / that is / into his eternal day / so that they can be a special people to him alone. Therefore he makes them much more glorious than any other / and than all other nations / which he has made for the sake of his honor and the greatness of his name. All other good and holy ways are made for the sake of God’s honor / and one also works in the same for his honor / and to praise his holy name. But his honor / his name / and his glory / are still much more glorious than he himself is <note>This suggests the outward manifestations of God are more "glorious" to the human eye than his hidden essence.</note> / and they are not he himself either / in that they are outside of him.

But the **annihilated souls** <note>original: "vernichtigte Seelen"; a mystical term for souls that have completely surrendered their own will and ego to God.</note> are the holy people to the Lord / without thinking of either his praise or his honor: because they have lost everything / so that they can bring him a perfect reverence / of his holiness / through their lowliness and misery / of his strength through their weakness / of his righteousness through the loss of all their own righteousness. The others indeed praise God / in that they praise him with all their powers: but these are the saints of the Lord through their annihilation; because all their own power is lost in them / so that the righteousness of God alone remains firm. They are not holy for the sake of men / so that they are not known: nor for their own sake; for they believe of themselves / that they are full of sin. Nor do they act for the sake of any honor / praise, and glory / nor for the sake of any thing which has a great appearance / but because they, on the contrary, have contempt / mockery, and scorn / as their portion.

<header>Chapter XXVII. The Fifth Book of Moses.</header>

# THE XXVII. Chapter.
->The Two Mountains of Blessing and Curse.<-

And Moses, with the elders of Israel, commanded the people, saying: Keep the whole commandment which I command you today.

**2.** And it shall be, on the day when you pass over the Jordan into the land which the LORD your God gives you, that you shall set up large stones for yourself and coat them with lime;

**3.** And you shall write upon them all the words of this law when you have crossed over, so that you may come into the land which the LORD your God gives you, a land flowing with milk and honey, just as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.

**4.** And it shall be, when you have crossed the Jordan, that you shall set up these stones, of which I command you today, on Mount Ebal, and you shall coat them with lime.

**5.** And there you shall build an altar to the LORD your God, an altar of stones; you shall not use any iron tool upon them.

---

After the mention of the Covenant at the end of the previous chapter, the public renewal of the same by the entire people is commanded here upon their entry into the land of Canaan.

**v. 2. Large stones)** Twelve, as some suspect, according to the number of the tribes.

**Set up)** As a landmark on the borders, to show that this land is dedicated to the service of the true God and Creator of heaven and earth by the people He has chosen above all other nations; and that they should therefore behave as holy and obedient inhabitants in this land.

**v. 3. All the words of the law)** Namely—as is also suspected—the Ten Commandments, and then the blessing and curse contained in this and the following chapters, and perhaps also some other laws fitting for edification.

**v. 4. On Mount Ebal)** These stones were to be set up on the mountain where the curse was to be pronounced, to show how the Law and the administration of the Old Testament would primarily rebuke the curse lying upon the entire human race because of sin, in order to awaken their longing for the Messiah, who should take away the curse and bring about the true blessing.

<margin>(a) Josephus agrees in Antiquities of the Jews, Book 4, final chapter. <note>original: "l. 4. antiq. c. ult."</note></margin>
<margin>(b) Osiander on this passage; Drusius on Joshua 8:32; Masius on Joshua 8:30, 31. <note>original: "Osiand. ad h. l. Drus. ad Jos. 8, 32. Mas. ad Jos. 8, 30. 31."</note></margin>
And indeed, they were to be set up as an altar, as those (a) hold who believe that no other stones were set up than those from which the altar was made. Nevertheless, the plastered stones and **v. 5. the altar** are mentioned separately here; from which some (b) conclude that, besides the altar, other large stones were set up as pillars and plastered over, and the Law was written upon them, not upon the altar itself: yet in Joshua 8:31-32, only the altar is mentioned.

<column-break/>

**6.** You shall build the altar of the LORD your God of whole stones, and offer burnt offerings thereon to the LORD your God.

**7.** And you shall sacrifice thank-offerings <term>Danckopffer: offerings of peace or thanksgiving shared as a meal</term> and eat there, and rejoice before the face of the LORD your God.

**8.** And you shall write all the words of this law upon the stones very clearly.

**9.** And Moses and the priests, the Levites, spoke to all Israel, saying: Take heed and listen, O Israel! This day you have become a people to the LORD your God.

**10.** And you shall obey the voice of the LORD your God, and do His commandments and His statutes which I command you today.

---

**v. 6. Of whole)** Unhewn and untouched stones.

**v. 7.** Thereupon they were to bring the first general thank-offering in the name of the entire people, because God had brought them into the promised land, and hereby took them anew as His people in this land, wherein He would henceforth protect and bless them, provided they would also remember His holy commandments from then on and prove themselves obedient.

**v. 8. Write upon the stones)** For this very purpose the altar was coated with lime, so that it would be entirely white and smooth on all sides, and one could write upon it all the better, which could not easily have been done upon the uneven, unhewn stones themselves.

**v. 9. This day you have become a people to the LORD your God)** One truly becomes a people of the Lord only in the moment (in the "Today") of departing from oneself, even if one was already dedicated to Him before through the life of His grace. For on this day, in which the soul loses all self-centeredness <note>German: "Eigenheit," referring here to the mystical surrender of the will</note>, it finds itself in a state to be received into God. It becomes His people specifically to the extent that it has gone out of itself and no longer opposes Him. For every soul opposes God insofar as it keeps itself within itself; and becomes all the more pliable before Him, the more it goes out of itself. And on that day when the Spirit of God shall be poured out over the whole house of Israel, and they shall no longer have stony hearts, but such in which God writes His law by the finger of His Spirit so that they serve Him willingly; when the kingdoms of the world shall have become our God’s and His Christ’s; when the Lord shall be but one, and His name also but one; when God shall gather all His children after the destruction of their enemies and bring them to rest, where they had been scattered here and there until such time: from that day forward, the Lord's own people will be made truly manifest in that gathering, and within it constitute a holy and universal Church.

**v. 10.** Then one will also keep His commandments and act accordingly, and no longer depart from Him. Jeremiah 3:19.

# The Fifth Book of Moses. Chapter XXVII.

**11.** And Moses commanded the people on 그 same day, saying:
**12.** These shall stand upon Mount Gerizim to bless the people <margin>(a) Joshua 8:33.</margin> (a) when you have crossed over the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
**13.** And these shall stand for the curse upon Mount Ebal: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.

Regarding these two mountains, various things have already been noted above in Chapter 11:29, etc. For their location, see Ruth 9:7. <note>The original text cites Ruth 9:7, but as the Book of Ruth has only four chapters, this is likely a printer's error intended to reference Judges 9:7, where Jotham speaks from Mount Gerizim.</note>
**v. 12.** Here the tribes are divided so that six sons of Leah and Rachel—among whom the tribe of Levi had to take a place, and the two tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh were counted as one under their father Joseph—were to stand on the Mountain of Blessing and speak or receive the blessing. Although the blessing is not explicitly recorded here, it can be recognized by its opposite in the curses: "Blessed is the man who makes no idol or molten image!"
Gerizim lay toward the **South** <note>original: "Mittag," literally "midday," the traditional German term for the South</note> and was a very pleasant mountain that had various springs.
**v. 13.** Ebal, on the other hand, lay toward the **North** <note>original: "Mitternacht," literally "midnight," the traditional German term for the North</note>; it was rugged and infertile, had many cliffs and stones, as well as many caves and depths, and is said to be frequently troubled by earthquakes.
The remaining six sons included the oldest and the youngest of Leah; the first <note>Reuben</note> had earned the curse with his vile deed, which is also explicitly cursed here again in verse 20, and the four sons of the two handmaids.
What is remarkable here is that the blessing is mostly pronounced toward the children of Leah and Rachel, while the curse is toward the children of the handmaids. This was surely intended to depict how the children of the free woman—of the Jerusalem which is above, which would be revealed in the New Testament—would only proclaim and inherit the blessing. Therefore, Christ on the mountain spoke of nothing but blessing and beatitude. Conversely, the children of the handmaid—who would be subservient under the Old Testament—would primarily have to hear the curse, as it was not yet done away with in 그 state; even the Jews, as the firstborn, would have to bear this in their hardening for a time. See Galatians 4:21, etc., Romans 11:1, etc., and verse 25. One can also notice how our Savior, at another time, announced the curse alongside the blessing when He spoke "Woe" over the rich, the full, the joyful in this world, and those who seek honor and praise in this world—those who despise His narrow way of repentance and denial of this world, and thus would not be obedient to Him nor truly believe in Him. Luke 6:24–26.
These 12 tribes, in their ultimate and deepest sense, contain a great deal within themselves, and therefore receive in this image the entire influence of heaven according to its two qualities. The 12 Apostles also correspond to these 12 tribes, who shall judge the 12 tribes of Israel and will thus necessarily curse those who have been ungodly, but bless the godly. All of this further corresponds, by virtue of a great mystery, to the 12 angels whose names John saw over the 12 gates of the city that is above.
Do we not also have here an image of what is read in the Gospel, where the sheep are placed on the right hand or toward the South, but the goats on the left or toward the North? For
Gerizim actually takes its name from "parting" or "division," while Ebal comes from a "deep hole." And just as the curse was received here on this mountain, so it is said there to those on the left: *Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire!*

<column-break/>

**14.** And the Levites shall testify and say to every man of Israel with a loud voice:
**15.** Cursed be the man who makes a carved or molten image, an abomination to the LORD, a work of the hands of the craftsman, and sets it up in secret! And all the people shall answer and say: Amen!
**16.** Cursed be he who dishonors his father or his mother! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**17.** Cursed be he who moves his neighbor's boundary stone! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**18.** Cursed be he who makes a blind man wander out of the way! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**19.** Cursed be he who perverts the justice due to a stranger, an orphan, or a widow! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**20.** Cursed be he who lies with his father's wife, because he has uncovered his father's skirt! <note>A biblical idiom for violating the father's marriage bed.</note> And all the people shall say: Amen!
**21.** Cursed be he who lies with any kind of beast! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**22.** Cursed be he who lies with his sister, whether she is the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**23.** Cursed be he who lies with his mother-in-law! And all the people shall say: Amen!
**24.** Cursed be he who strikes his neighbor in secret! And all the people shall say: Amen!

**v. 14. The Levites to Israel)** For when they were divided from one another, one half stood in 6 tribes on Mount Gerizim, and the other half was to stand on Mount Ebal.
Since the tribe of Levi is explicitly added to the tribes in verse 12 and placed on Mount Gerizim, those standing in the middle may not have been the common Levites, but rather the Priests, Joshua 8:33, who stood down in the valley and pronounced the blessing and curse to the 12 tribes on the two mountains.
**v. 15. etc. Amen)** That is: "Yes, I agree to it, and I am satisfied with it."

# Chapter XXVII. The Fifth Book of Moses.

**25.** Cursed be he who takes bribes to strike down the soul of innocent blood! And all the people shall say: Amen!

**26.** Cursed be he who does not uphold the words of this law to act according to them! And all the people shall say: Amen! <margin>Num. 5:22; Jer. 11:5.</margin>

<note>The following note block extends across both columns in the original layout.</note>

There are 12 curses, matching the number of the tribes of Israel. Indeed, it is thought that the last one, being the general curse, was spoken first, followed by the specific ones. 
In the same way, and also first, 12 blessings were spoken; the general one first: *Blessed be he who upholds the words of this law, to act according to them!* This served both as a testimony and an assurance of how they would all share in the blessing and also in the curse, depending on whether they showed themselves to be obedient or disobedient.

# Chapter XXVIII.
-> The Blessing and the Curse. <-

AND it shall come to pass, if you diligently obey the voice of the LORD your God, that you observe and do all His commandments which I command you today; then the LORD your God will make you the highest above all nations of the earth.

**2.** And all these blessings shall come upon you and reach you: because you have obeyed the voice of the LORD your God.

---

<note>Detailed commentary section following the biblical text, arranged in two columns.</note>

<margin>In the renewal of the Covenant, God wanted once again to present the blessing and the curse as the inevitable effects of obedience and disobedience toward what this Covenant required of them. And indeed, the blessing is placed first here, because this is, as it were, a natural work of God, flowing from His nature of love, since He would rather bless than punish with a curse.</margin>
<margin>v. 1. *if — that*) Even through Moses, God conditioned His promises so precisely upon these words: "if" and "that."</margin>
<margin>These testimonies of God should powerfully bind our consciences and lead us to the faithfulness of God's love. For that is what He seeks.</margin>
<margin>His conditions focus on nothing other than obedience and the keeping of His commandments.</margin>
<margin>v. 2. Concerning the blessing and its various parts, as well as their spiritual significance, more has already been discussed in the commentary on Leviticus 26:1–13.</margin>
<margin>Blessing is good in its essence and pleasing to God; otherwise, it would not be a blessing. Therefore, it must work nothing but good in us, according to God's intent. It rests upon a faithful and obedient heart, where it is meant to benefit someone. No unbelieving, false person enjoys its salvation.</margin>
<margin>We must, therefore, once and for all, commit ourselves to obedience and a holy life if we wish to become the Blessed of the LORD.</margin>
<margin>God gladly desires to set us all for a blessing; and we are called by our Creator through His Spirit with all earnestness out of the curse and into the blessing. Let everyone see to it how they follow.</margin>
<margin>v. 3. You must seek a dwelling in the City of God if you wish to be blessed: For in and with Babylon there are only plagues; and he who is in the field, let him not turn back. <note>Babylon is often used in Pietist literature as a symbol for the corrupt world or a false church, contrasted with the "City of God" or the New Jerusalem.</note> Matt. 24:18.</margin>
<margin>Just as all believers have their citizenship in the Jerusalem that is above—their metropolis or mother city—so they also strive for the heavenly blessing. Phil. 3:20; Gal. 4:26; Eph. 1:3.</margin>

<column-break/>

<margin>v. 4. External happiness, however, cannot truly be the right blessing: for God often gives it to the most wicked rascals, Ps. 73:12, whose bellies He fills and to whom He gives plenty of children; Ps. 17:14; whose sheep bring forth thousands and ten thousands in their villages. Ps. 144:13. Thus, a better blessing must necessarily be intended for the godly, and God must have something more certain for them, even if He also helps them physically, since godliness is profitable for all things and has the promise of this life and the life to come.</margin>
<margin>v. 5. *Kneading trough*) or also "your remainder," as Luther gave it: both all your remaining supply, and what you leave over after being satisfied, such as leftover crumbs.</margin>
<margin>v. 7. The enemies must fall when God is with us. But God is with us when we are with Him.</margin>
<margin>v. 8. For those of us in the New Testament, such promises of blessed nourishment etc. should remind us of the greatest and most precious promises, which are far to be preferred over those physical ones: that we shall become partakers of the divine nature, and all things shall be given to us that pertain to life and godliness. 2 Pet. 1:3, 4. Which is precisely the spiritual blessing in heavenly goods through Christ. Eph. 1:3.</margin>

# The Fifth Book of Moses [Deuteronomy]. Chapter XXVIII.

### Column 1

9. The Lord will establish you as a holy people for himself, just as he has sworn to you, if you will keep the commandments of the Lord your God and walk in his ways.
10. And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the Lord is called over you, and they shall be afraid of you.
11. And the Lord will let you have an abundance (a) of goods, in the fruit of your body, and in the fruit of your livestock, and in the fruit of your land, in the land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give you.
<margin>(a) John 10:10.</margin>
12. The Lord will open to you his good treasure, the heavens, to give rain to your land in its season, and to bless every work of your hand; and you will lend to many nations, but you shall not need to borrow.
13. And the Lord will make you the head and not the tail <note>The "tail" refers to a state of being last or subservient.</note> (*), and you will only be the uppermost, and not the lowest: if you will obey the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you today to keep and to do;
<margin>(*) Isaiah 9:14.</margin>

---

<margin>v. 9. Therefore we should strive all the more for holiness, 2 Cor. 7:1, so that we might be found as the glorious congregation that has no spot or wrinkle, but is holy and blameless. Eph. 5:27.</margin>
But when this is not to be found, it is also no wonder that neither physical nor spiritual blessing is willing to show itself thoroughly; instead, much physical misfortune, poverty, and want is felt in almost all places. God will, however, shortly prepare such a people for himself, and—

(Establish him as a holy people) It will not only be a people for the Lord through a passing decree, but it will be established in this state, and God will so fasten it in his holiness for himself that it will do all his will and be faithful in walking in his ways.

<margin>v. 10. All peoples of the earth) all around will see) with eyes at the last time,</margin>
That the name of the Lord over) the Israel of God is named) that Christ rules over them;

And shall fear) before the camp of the saints, the Church of God, which shall then be as terrible or formidable as armies or troops of soldiers. Song of Solomon 6:9. <note>Often cited as Song of Solomon 6:10 in English bibles: "terrible as an army with banners."</note>

<margin>v. 12. The heavens) that is, everything that is found in heaven, both from him himself, to possess him, as well as those insights which are only communicated in heaven, or to such souls who have reached this point.</margin>

### Column 2

14. And you shall not deviate from all the words which I command you today, to the right or to the left (*), to go after other gods to serve them.
<margin>(*) Isaiah 30:21.</margin>
15. But it shall come to pass, if you will not obey the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and his statutes which I command you today, then all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you.
16. Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field.
<margin>Isaiah 24:6. etc.</margin>
17. Cursed shall be your basket and your kneading trough.
18. Cursed shall be the fruit of your body and the fruit of your land, the increase of your cattle and the flocks of your sheep.
19. Cursed shall you be when you come in, and cursed shall you be when you go out.
20. <unclear>D</unclear>

---

<margin>With the perverse, all things are perverse.</margin>
Regarding the curses and their spiritual meaning, however, these were also dealt with more extensively in Leviticus 26:14-39, where many more of them are recounted than the blessings, in order to deter them all the more from disobedience. These curses then manifested themselves sufficiently in the two great destructions of Jerusalem and in the now long-lasting captivity, where one can very clearly behold the severity of God upon those who fell. Romans 11:22.

Under the New Testament, Christ also spoke with few words the "Woe" upon the people of the world who wish to remain sunk in the love of the world, and who are hostile toward his narrow way of self-denial and closed off from the world. Luke 6:24, 25, 26. And the Apostle expresses the curse explicitly for a second time over those who would preach a Gospel other than what he and his fellow Apostles had preached and the first believers had received: Galatians 1:8, 9. And whoever would not love the Lord JESUS should be an <term>Anathema, Maranatha</term> <note>original: "Anathema / Maranatha"; Greek and Aramaic terms meaning "Accursed, our Lord comes."</note>, at the great curse on the great Day of Judgment, when he will hear from the Lord's own mouth at his coming: "Depart from me, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels," because they did not practice the works of love and mercy toward the least of his believers, or even toward the poor and needy among their neighbors. Matthew 25:41-45.

The one who leaves the beautiful path of the blessing of peace, and who goes out from his God through a terrifying unfaithfulness, shall instantly feel the curse as he thus returns into his own self-centeredness; and also at his going out, in that he departs from God through such a misfortune, as that of <term>Lucifer</term> <note>The Latin name for the "Morning Star," referring here to the fallen angel.</note> was in a certain way.

It is better, then, to bear the mockery and curse of the world and its servants and worshipers while entering through the narrow gate (Matthew 7:13) and while going out from Babylon <note>Meaning the corrupt or worldly system.</note> and all deceit and seduction (2 Cor. 6:17), than to pull down the wrath and curse of God upon one's neck by the opposite path of disobedience and joining in with the world.

### Chapter XXVIII. The Fifth Book of Moses [Deuteronomy].

20. The LORD will send upon you curses, confusion, and rebuke in everything you set your hand to do, until you are destroyed and perish quickly because of your evil deeds, for having forsaken me.
21. The LORD will cause the pestilence <term>plague or infectious disease</term> to cling to you, until he has consumed you from the land you are entering to possess.
22. The LORD will strike you with consumption <term>a wasting disease</term>, with burning fever, with inflammation and extreme heat, with the sword, and with blight and mildew; and these shall pursue you until you perish.
23. And your heaven that is over your head shall be bronze, and the earth that is under you iron. <note>This describes a catastrophic drought where the sky yields no rain and the ground becomes too hard to farm.</note>
24. The LORD will give to your land thin and thick dust instead of rain; it shall come down from heaven upon you until you are destroyed.
25. The LORD will deliver you to be defeated before your enemies. You shall go out against them one way and flee before them seven ways, and you will be scattered into all the kingdoms of the earth.
26. And your carcass shall be food for all the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth, and there will be no one to frighten them away.

---

v. 20. O souls, do not forsake GOD so light-mindedly, lest he forsake you in turn! Think of the woe prophesied by him: *Woe to them when I have departed from them!* Hosea 9:12. You will then feel every conceivable plague and be, as it were, in hell, where sin and the devil will take their revenge on you.
v. 21. 22. Sin will cling to you like the plague, and all other misfortunes will follow it.
v. 23. The heaven will be bronze for you, in that it will no longer hear your prayers: so that you will be able to neither improve yourselves nor be converted.
v. 24. Misfortune upon all misfortune! Instead of the dew of grace, there is now nothing but dust.
v. 25. 26. One will be beaten before all one's enemies, who kill such souls through deadly sins. Everything comes bit by bit, and from bad to worse.

<column-break/>

27. The LORD will strike you with the boils of Egypt, and with tumors, and with scabs and the itch, so that you cannot be healed.
28. The LORD will strike you with madness and with blindness, and with astonishment <term>a numbing or hardening</term> of the heart.
29. And you shall grope at noonday, just as the blind man gropes <margin>(a)</margin> in the dark, and you shall have no success in your ways: and you shall be only oppressed and robbed all the days, and there will be no one to save you. <margin>(a) Isaiah 59:10. 2 Peter 1:9.</margin>
30. You shall betroth a wife, but another man shall lie with her. You shall build a house, but you shall not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, but you shall not make use of it <term>literally: "make it common," meaning to harvest its first fruits</term>. <margin>Isaiah 65:22.</margin>
31. Your ox shall be slaughtered before your eyes, but you shall not eat of it. Your donkey shall be snatched away before your face and not returned to you. Your sheep shall be given to your enemies, and you shall have no one to save them. <margin>2 Timothy 4:18.</margin>
32. Your sons and your daughters shall be given to another people, while your eyes look on and pine for them all day long; but it shall not be in the power of your hand to help.
<meta>catchword: 33. The</meta>

---

v. 27--29. What were otherwise only wounds will become pure death. For afterward comes blindness and the judgment of total hardening in this state: and finally the numbing of the heart, which is despair.
v. 31. This is how it goes for all those—and how it ends for them—who are worse than oxen and donkeys! Isaiah 1:3. Those who, as sheep of a friendly shepherd, could have had a table prepared for them against their enemies (Psalm 23:5) if they had wanted to follow his voice, must now watch as a table is prepared for their enemies before their very eyes from their own goods, and recognize that *with the perverse, God shows himself perverse*. <note>A reference to Psalm 18:26, suggesting God responds to people according to their own conduct.</note>
v. 32. **Pine for them**) To look for them with eyes cried out, wondering if they might return; or to constantly repeat the sorrowful memory that one cannot help them.
Ah, if only our eye would instead pine for the Lord our GOD until he was gracious to us; we might then accomplish more toward the help of ourselves and others.
